details.common_mistake: Candidates often blame eventual consistency in backend databases or try to synchronize session state across regions, ignoring that the client sends full context and the root cause is a model version mismatch during routing.
details.napkin_math: With a 10% canary and random routing, the probability of a 5-turn conversation staying on the same model version is (0.9^5) + (0.1^5) = 0.59049 + 0.00001 = ~59%. Thus, ~41% of multi-turn sessions will experience a version mismatch and fail.
details.realistic_solution: The ingress load balancer is likely using random or round-robin routing. Implement sticky routing (session affinity) using consistent hashing on the `session_id` or `user_id` at the API Gateway to guarantee that all requests within a conversation are routed to the exact same model version.

scenario: Your team is rolling out a new conversational LLM (70B parameters) across 3 regions using a 10% canary deployment. Shortly after starting the rollout, users report 'context amnesia' where the model suddenly misinterprets multi-turn conversations midway through a session. The telemetry shows a spike in tokenization errors caused by prompt template mismatches between the v1 and v2 models. You verify that the client sends the full conversation history with every request. Analyze the root cause of this failure and propose a networking-level fix.
title: Diagnosing Context Amnesia in Canary Rollouts

details.common_mistake: Focusing on local storage I/O bottlenecks or assuming the 6-hour window provides enough throughput to upload the daily 50GB payload without calculating the absolute data transfer capacity of the link.
details.napkin_math: Link speed: 5 Mbps = 0.625 MB/s. Active window: 6 hours = 21,600 seconds. Daily capacity: 0.625 MB/s * 21,600 s = 13,500 MB = 13.5 GB/day. Deficit: 50 GB - 13.5 GB = +36.5 GB/day added to local storage. Time to fill 2TB drive: 2000 GB / 36.5 GB/day ≈ 54 days.
details.realistic_solution: The daily data generated (50GB) far exceeds the daily transfer capacity of the satellite link during its active window (13.5GB). The system must employ local ML inference to filter out uninformative images or apply heavy compression before the store-and-forward step, reducing the daily payload to under 13GB.

scenario: A remote agricultural monitoring system collects 50GB of high-resolution crop images daily. The local edge server (2TB NVMe) connects to the cloud via a satellite link providing 5Mbps bandwidth for exactly 6 hours a day during off-peak times. The system uses a store-and-forward architecture to batch images and upload them for central ML analysis. Operations reports that the local storage is gradually filling up, leading to dropped frames by the end of the month despite the daily syncs.
title: Diagnosing Edge-to-Cloud Satellite Storage Saturation

details.common_mistake: Assuming the degradation is an infrastructure bottleneck, memory leak, or application-layer software bug, instead of recognizing the breakdown of the stationarity assumption caused by the newly introduced geographic data distribution.
details.napkin_math: If the training dataset contained 1% international transactions, but the new live traffic mix is 35% international, the input distribution P(X) has severely shifted. A Population Stability Index (PSI) calculation: PSI = sum((Actual_% - Expected_%) * ln(Actual_% / Expected_%)) would yield PSI = (0.35 - 0.01) * ln(0.35 / 0.01) ≈ 1.2. Any PSI > 0.2 indicates a critical distribution shift requiring immediate retraining.
details.realistic_solution: Implement statistical distance monitoring (e.g., Kullback-Leibler divergence or Population Stability Index) on the live feature distributions compared to the training baseline. The international launch introduced user behavioral patterns absent from the training set, violating the stationarity assumption. You must deploy a data validation pipeline and trigger retraining on the new distribution.

scenario: You are serving a cloud-based transaction fraud detection model handling 25,000 TPS on AWS g5.4xlarge instances. Hardware utilization is stable (GPU compute at 65%, P99 latency at 45ms). However, the business team reports a 30% spike in false positives over the last 48 hours following a new international product launch. System metrics and infrastructure health checks are completely green. How do you analyze the root cause of this degradation?
title: Diagnosing Silent Failures in Cloud Fraud Detection

details.common_mistake: Failing to convert between megabits (Mbps) and megabytes (MB/s) when calculating transfer windows, leading to an 8x overestimation of transfer capacity.
details.napkin_math: Daily data generated: 15 GB/hr * 12 hrs = 180 GB/day. Uplink speed: 120 Mbps / 8 = 15 MB/s. Nightly transfer capacity: 15 MB/s * 3600 sec/hr * 5 hrs = 270,000 MB = 270 GB. Since 270 GB > 180 GB, the daily transfer clears the queue. Blackout buffer sizing: 4 days * 180 GB/day = 720 GB minimum local storage required.
details.realistic_solution: Convert 120 Mbps to 15 MB/s to calculate the 5-hour window capacity of 270 GB. Confirm this exceeds the 180 GB daily generation, then multiply the daily generation by the 4-day blackout period to size the minimum local buffer at 720 GB.

scenario: You are designing a data ingestion pipeline for remote agricultural ML sensors that connect to a central cloud. Each edge site generates 15 GB of sensor telemetry and imagery per hour during a 12-hour active daily window. Connectivity is limited to a 5-hour nightly satellite pass offering a consistent 120 Mbps uplink. Calculate the daily data transfer capacity, determine if the nightly window is sufficient to offload the daily data, and size the local SSD buffer required to safely store-and-forward data if the site experiences up to 4 consecutive days of satellite weather blackouts.
title: Sizing Edge Buffers for Satellite ML Pipelines

details.common_mistake: Prioritizing daytime synchronous streaming over the unreliable 256 kbps link, leading to TCP timeout cascades, high power consumption, and incomplete telemetry ingestion.
details.napkin_math: Daytime streaming limit: 256 kbps * 12 hrs = 3,072 kbits/s * 3600s = 11,059 Mb = 1.38 GB (< 2 GB payload). Nightly store-and-forward limit: 50 Mbps * 2 hrs * 3600s = 360,000 Mb = 45 GB. The 2-hour satellite window easily clears the 2 GB daily queue with a >20x safety margin, avoiding cellular bottlenecks.
details.realistic_solution: Deploy a store-and-forward architecture where telemetry is batched locally to Flash storage. The edge device flushes the 2GB payload sequentially during the 2-hour, 50 Mbps satellite connectivity window.

scenario: Your fleet of 5,000 edge ML devices in remote agricultural sites generates 2GB of inference telemetry daily. During the day, they have an unreliable 256 kbps cellular link, but at night they connect to a stable 50 Mbps satellite uplink for 2 hours. You must evaluate the architecture for ingesting this data into your cloud data lake. Compare a synchronous daytime streaming approach with aggressive retries against a store-and-forward architecture utilizing local flash storage.
title: Edge-to-Cloud Telemetry Ingestion Architecture

details.common_mistake: Selecting exactly 1,000 clients and waiting for 100% completion, which allows the slowest 20% of network connections to bottleneck the entire global training round.
details.napkin_math: Model size = 50MB = 400Mb. Fast upload = 400Mb / 50Mbps = 8s. Slow upload = 400Mb / 5Mbps = 80s. Fast round time = 8s + 2s compute = 10s. Slow round time = 80s + 2s = 82s. To guarantee 1000 fast clients from an 80% fast population, select 1000 / 0.8 = 1250 clients. Round time is reduced from 82s to 10s.
details.realistic_solution: Implement an over-selection strategy by sampling 1,250 clients per round and aggregating only the first 1,000 responses, effectively pruning the slow-network tail.

scenario: A cloud parameter server orchestrates a synchronous federated learning round for a 50MB model, requiring 1,000 successful updates per round. Client compute time is 2 seconds. 80% of the fleet has 50 Mbps upload speeds, while 20% are stragglers with 5 Mbps upload speeds. Calculate the required client selection size (N) to avoid waiting for stragglers and the resulting latency reduction per round.
title: Federated Learning Over-selection for Stragglers

details.common_mistake: Switching to fully asynchronous SGD (which destabilizes convergence due to extreme gradient staleness) or aggressively dropping slow clients (which introduces geographic bias).
details.napkin_math: Synchronous step time = max(t_1...t_N) = 6000ms. With a concurrency buffer of K=50 out of N nodes, the effective step time becomes the 50th fastest response (~300ms). Training 10,000 rounds drops from 16.6 hours to 50 minutes (a 20x speedup) while safely handling up to 100+ epochs of staleness.
details.realistic_solution: Implement Buffered Asynchronous Aggregation (FedBuff). The cloud aggregator updates the global model whenever a concurrency buffer of K updates fills, allowing slow clients to contribute stale updates that are incorporated with staleness-aware learning rate dampening.

scenario: Your cross-silo federated learning pipeline coordinates 2,000 T4 GPUs across 15 global cloud regions. Using synchronous FedAvg, the median local update takes 250ms, but the global aggregation step consistently blocks for over 6 seconds. Logs show that 2-3% of nodes experience transient network partitions or instance migrations. How do you mitigate this straggler effect while preserving the statistical contribution of nodes in high-latency regions?
title: Diagnosing Cross-Silo Straggler Bottlenecks

details.common_mistake: Assuming asynchronous aggregation is strictly superior for round times without accounting for the severe convergence penalty introduced by gradient staleness, which often requires more total time to reach target accuracy.
details.napkin_math: If median completion is 15s and P99 is 300s, a strict sync barrier takes 300s per round. With 1.5x over-selection (ask 1,500, wait for 1,000), the aggregator only waits for the ~66th percentile (e.g., 20s), yielding a 15x speedup per round without the convergence degradation of staleness.
details.realistic_solution: Over-selection is typically the most robust practical approach. By querying 30% to 50% more clients than needed and dropping the stragglers, you maintain the convergence stability of synchronous updates while drastically clipping the long tail of latency.

scenario: A distributed federated learning system is training a recommendation model across 10,000 heterogeneous mobile devices. The central aggregator waits for 1,000 updates before performing a global model step (synchronous aggregation). However, due to stragglers (devices taking up to 5 minutes to complete local training and upload vs. the median 15 seconds), the global round time is heavily bottlenecked. Evaluate the trade-offs of switching from synchronous FedAvg with a strict barrier to an asynchronous protocol (like FedAsync) versus an over-selection strategy (e.g., selecting 1,500 clients but only waiting for the fastest 1,000).
title: Evaluating Straggler Mitigation Strategies in Federated Learning

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose micro-batching with Redis for operational simplicity, failing to evaluate the P99 network latency overhead of 500k RPS remote point lookups which easily violates the 30ms SLA.
details.napkin_math: Remote Redis lookup: ~2ms P99 network round-trip. Micro-batch scheduling overhead: ~15ms. 15ms (batch) + 2ms (fetch) + 10ms (model) = 27ms, leaving only a 3ms buffer for network jitter before missing the 30ms SLA. Local NVMe RocksDB read: ~100µs. 0ms (no batch) + 0.1ms (fetch) + 10ms (model) = 10.1ms, leaving an ample 20ms buffer.
details.realistic_solution: Adopt a pure streaming architecture utilizing an embedded state backend (like RocksDB) on local NVMe SSDs. This eliminates remote network hops for data enrichment, guaranteeing the 30ms P99 SLA at the cost of more complex state rebalancing during node failures.

scenario: You are designing the ingestion tier for a global ad-bidding platform that receives 500,000 bid requests per second. The system must enrich each event with a 2KB user profile and evaluate a model within a strict 30ms P99 end-to-end latency budget. Evaluate whether to use a pure streaming engine (e.g., Apache Flink) with local state versus a micro-batching engine (e.g., Spark Streaming) with a remote in-memory KV store (e.g., Redis). Justify your design decision focusing on backpressure handling, state management, and the latency breakdown.
title: Streaming Architecture for Strict Ad-Bidding SLAs

details.common_mistake: Calculating broker count based solely on the incoming data rate (1000 MB/s) while ignoring the write amplification caused by the replication factor, which leads to a severely undersized estimate of 2 brokers.
details.napkin_math:
Base ingestion rate = 2,000,000 events/sec * 500 bytes/event = 1,000,000,000 bytes/sec = 1000 MB/s.
Total disk write throughput = 1000 MB/s * 3 (replication factor) = 3000 MB/s.
Minimum brokers = 3000 MB/s / 800 MB/s per broker = 3.75 -> ceil to 4 brokers.
details.realistic_solution: Account for replication overhead on disk writes. The total cluster write throughput is 3000 MB/s. Dividing by the 800 MB/s per-node limit gives a strict minimum of 4 brokers, though 5-6 would be typical for operational headroom.

scenario: A global ML telemetry pipeline ingests 2 million events per second continuously. Each event payload is 500 bytes. The data is ingested into an Apache Kafka cluster configured with a replication factor of 3 to ensure fault tolerance. Each Kafka broker node is equipped with an NVMe drive capable of 800 MB/s sustained sequential write throughput. Assuming network bandwidth is not a bottleneck, calculate the absolute minimum number of broker nodes required to handle this peak ingestion rate without triggering backpressure due to disk I/O saturation.
title: Sizing Kafka Brokers for Peak Ingestion

details.common_mistake: Assuming network bandwidth is saturated by the event volume, or blindly scaling horizontally by adding more instances instead of fixing the application's concurrency model.
details.napkin_math: Network: 100,000 msgs/s * 1 KB = 100 MB/s (easily handled by 12.5 Gbps instance limits). CPU cost: Deserializing a 1KB JSON payload typically takes ~10µs. 100,000 msgs * 10µs = 1,000,000µs = 1.0 CPU seconds. A single thread reaches exactly 100% utilization just parsing the data, causing immediate backpressure.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a single-threaded consumer loop bottlenecked by CPU-intensive JSON deserialization. The solution is to decouple the Kafka network polling thread from the processing logic using a worker thread pool, distributing the deserialization across all 16 vCPUs, and ideally migrating from JSON to a faster binary format like Protobuf.

scenario: A real-time fraud detection pipeline ingests 100,000 events/sec from Kafka. Events are JSON-encoded, averaging 1KB each. The ingestion service runs on `c6i.4xlarge` (16 vCPU, 32GB RAM) instances. During peak bursts, consumer lag spikes drastically, and p99 ingestion latency jumps from 50ms to over 2 seconds, triggering backpressure. System metrics show one CPU core pegged at 100% while the remaining 15 are nearly idle. Network I/O is steady at ~100 MB/s. Diagnose the root cause of this ingestion bottleneck.
title: Diagnosing Single-Threaded Consumer Lag in Kafka

details.common_mistake: Using the hardware maximum batch size of 16 to optimize throughput, forgetting that accumulating 16 sequential chunks takes 320ms, which instantly violates the 200ms SLA before computation even begins.
details.napkin_math: Total Latency = Network + Buffering Wait + Compute. 200ms = 30ms + (N-1) * 20ms + 15ms. 155ms = (N-1) * 20ms. N-1 = 7.75. Max N = 8 chunks. The first chunk waits 7 * 20ms = 140ms for the batch to fill.
details.realistic_solution: Limit single-stream batch size to 8 (140ms buffering wait time) or multiplex multiple independent audio streams so the dynamic batcher can build a full batch of 16 from different concurrent users without waiting for future sequential chunks.

scenario: You are designing a streaming pipeline for a live audio transcription model on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Audio arrives in 20ms chunks. The service-level agreement (SLA) requires end-to-end latency to be under 200ms. Network I/O overhead is 30ms. Model compute time is fixed at 15ms per batch (for any batch size up to 16). If you buffer chunks from a *single* audio stream to increase throughput, what is the maximum batch size you can accumulate without violating the SLA for the first chunk in the batch?
title: Streaming Inference Batch Size Limits

details.common_mistake: Assuming 2:4 sparsity perfectly halves the memory footprint (50% reduction) by forgetting the 2-bit metadata index required for each preserved non-zero element.
details.napkin_math: Dense matrix: 8192 × 8192 = 67,108,864 elements (~67M). Dense size: 67M * 2B (FP16) = 134 MB. 2:4 Sparsity keeps 50%: ~33.5M elements = 67 MB. Metadata required: 2 bits per non-zero element = 33.5M * 2 bits = 67M bits ≈ 8 MB. Total compressed memory: 67 MB + 8 MB = 75 MB. True memory savings: 134 MB - 75 MB = 59 MB (a ~44% reduction, not 50%).
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the memory of the 50% non-zero FP16 elements, then add the 2-bit index metadata required per non-zero element to find the true compressed hardware size.

scenario: You are optimizing a Transformer model's linear layers for inference on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. A specific FP16 weight matrix has dimensions 8192 x 8192. To double the theoretical compute throughput using Ampere's Sparse Tensor Cores, you apply 2:4 structured sparsity. Calculate the total memory footprint of the compressed weight matrix, accounting for the required metadata, and determine the exact memory savings compared to the dense FP16 baseline.
title: A100 2:4 Structured Sparsity Memory Overhead

details.common_mistake: Assuming 70% unstructured sparsity will automatically yield better latency and throughput than 50% structured sparsity by purely looking at the reduction in theoretical FLOPs, ignoring the constraints of the accelerator's microarchitecture.
details.napkin_math: Dense FP16 throughput on A100: 312 TFLOPS. 2:4 Sparse FP16 throughput: 624 TFLOPS (2x speedup). Unstructured 70% sparsity mapped to dense Tensor Cores yields 1x speedup, because the dense matrix multiply hardware pipeline cannot dynamically skip unstructured zeros and requires loading the full dense weight matrices.
details.realistic_solution: The 2:4 structured sparsity is the optimal choice. A100 Sparse Tensor Cores natively support the 2:4 pattern, allowing them to compress weights in memory by 2x and double the matrix math throughput. Unstructured sparsity cannot be easily accelerated on dense Tensor Cores, often resulting in fallback to slower vector ALUs (CUDA cores) or inefficient, irregular memory access patterns that degrade actual inference performance.

scenario: You are evaluating pruning strategies for deploying a 7B parameter language model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU cluster. The model must meet a strict P99 latency SLA. The research team proposes an unstructured pruning method that achieves 70% sparsity with a 1% accuracy drop. The systems team argues for 2:4 structured sparsity (50% sparse) which has a 0.5% accuracy drop. Evaluate the architectural trade-offs between these approaches for this specific hardware and justify the optimal deployment strategy.
title: Evaluating 2:4 Structured Sparsity on A100

details.common_mistake: Assuming that any zero values automatically skip compute and save time, ignoring the fact that irregular sparsity patterns cause poor memory coalescing, cache misses, and branch divergence on GPUs without specialized hardware support.
details.napkin_math: Unstructured (75% sparse): Load 100% of dense weight matrix -> perform sparse irregular reads -> branching overhead > compute savings = Slowdown. Structured 2:4 (50% sparse): Load 50% compressed weights -> Tensor Cores process at 2x rate = ~2x speedup.
details.realistic_solution: The A100 Tensor Cores require '2:4 structured sparsity' to accelerate operations. In this format, exactly 2 out of every 4 elements in a contiguous block must be zero. The model must be pruned to fit this 2:4 pattern and represented in a compressed format, allowing the A100 to skip the zeros predictably and achieve up to a 2x throughput increase for math operations.

scenario: Your team compresses a large language model using unstructured magnitude pruning to 75% sparsity, expecting roughly a 4x speedup on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. However, after deploying the pruned model using standard PyTorch, profiling reveals a 15% slowdown in inference latency compared to the original dense model. Analyze the root cause of this performance degradation and identify the hardware-specific mechanism required to actually achieve acceleration.
title: Unstructured vs Structured Sparsity Slowdown on A100

details.common_mistake: Assuming the GPU lacks compute (FLOPs) to handle the batch size of 40, or trying to tune the dynamic batching timeout, completely missing the memory capacity wall and PCIe swapping.
details.napkin_math: Model weights = 16 GB FP16. KV cache per token = 32 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 dim * 2 (K,V) * 2 bytes = 131 KB. Max sequence (2048 tokens) = 268 MB per stream. 40 streams * 268 MB = 10.7 GB. Total Memory = 16 GB (weights) + 10.7 GB (cache) = 26.7 GB. This exceeds the A10G's 24 GB VRAM, causing OOM at 40 streams.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is VRAM exhaustion causing requests to queue or swap to host RAM. Switch to PagedAttention to dynamically allocate memory in small blocks (pages) only as tokens are generated.

scenario: You are deploying a real-time voice assistant backend using Llama-3-8B (FP16, ~16GB weights) on a single A10G GPU (24GB VRAM) for streaming token generation. The SLA requires Time-Between-Tokens (TBT) < 50ms. At 20 concurrent streams, TBT is 30ms. However, at 40 concurrent streams, P99 TBT suddenly spikes to over 200ms, and GPU compute utilization drops below 30%. The server uses static, contiguous memory allocation for the KV cache per request, assuming a maximum sequence length of 2048 tokens.
title: Streaming LLM TBT Spikes

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose the stateless Transformer to easily leverage existing dynamic batching infrastructure and stateless load balancing, failing to realize that accumulating the minimum 1.5s audio chunk duration natively violates the 300ms TTFW SLA before any compute even begins.
details.napkin_math: Stateless Latency = 1500ms (audio buffer) + 50ms (compute) = 1550ms TTFW (Fails 300ms SLA). Stateful Latency = 100ms (buffer) + 15ms (compute) = 115ms TTFW (Passes SLA). Memory requirement: 5,000 streams * 20MB state/stream = 100GB total state. Minimum GPUs = ceil(100GB / 24GB A10G capacity) = 5 GPUs.
details.realistic_solution: Adopt the stateful streaming RNN-T to easily meet the 300ms SLA, and implement session-aware routing (sticky sessions). Since 5,000 sessions requiring 20MB of hidden state each results in 100GB of persistent memory demand, shard the traffic across at least 5 A10G GPUs using consistent hashing, and perform continuous batching across concurrent incoming 100ms frames on each node.

scenario: You are designing the backend for a real-time voice agent handling 5,000 concurrent active sessions. You must choose between two ASR architectures: a stateless Transformer that requires 1.5-second audio chunks to decode accurately (utilizing dynamic batching), and a stateful streaming RNN-T that incrementally processes 100ms frames. The strict SLA dictates a Time-To-First-Word (TTFW) of <300ms. The deployment targets an autoscaling cluster of NVIDIA A10G (24GB VRAM) GPUs. Evaluate the latency, memory, and throughput trade-offs to justify your final architectural design and cluster sizing.
title: Stateful Streaming vs Stateless Batching ASR

details.common_mistake: Attributing the control group's decline to an external macro-trend or seasonality, rather than recognizing that the treatment and control groups are not independent.
details.napkin_math: Assuming a user's attention is zero-sum (total 60 mins/day). If Treatment (T) users create 5% more content, they capture more of the feed. Control (C) users see more T content, reducing their own engagement/creation by 2%. True global lift = 0.5 * 5% (T) + 0.5 * -2% (C) = 1.5%.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose a Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) violation where treatment users outcompete control users for attention. Switch from user-level randomization to network-cluster randomization (graph partitioning) to isolate treatment effects.

scenario: You are running a 50/50 A/B test on a new dual-encoder recommendation model serving a social network with 100M DAU. The treatment group shows a +5.0% increase in content creation, while the control group shows an unexpected -2.0% decrease in content creation compared to pre-experiment baselines. Total platform content creation only increased by +1.5%. You must root-cause the discrepancy between the treatment lift and the global platform metrics.
title: Diagnosing A/B Test Interference in Social Networks

details.common_mistake: Relying on the measured 0.5 minute difference between treatment and control as the true effect, leading to a 50% underestimation of the model's ROI and potentially rejecting a profitable rollout.
details.napkin_math:
Historical Baseline = 5.0 min.
Treatment Avg = 4.0 min.
Control Avg (during test) = 4.5 min (spillover benefit).
Measured A/B Delta = 4.5 min - 4.0 min = 0.5 min improvement.
True Global Delta = 5.0 min - 4.0 min = 1.0 min improvement.
Error = (1.0 - 0.5) / 1.0 = 50% underestimation of the true model impact.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the true global impact as the full 1.0-minute reduction from the historical baseline. To prevent this resource spillover (SUTVA violation) in future tests, implement switchback testing (time-based randomization) or geo-spatial cluster randomization to isolate the shared driver pool.

scenario: You are testing a new ML dispatch model for a ride-sharing cloud service processing 10,000 requests/hour. A naive 50/50 user-level A/B test is deployed. The new model reduces treatment rider wait times from a historical 5.0 minutes down to 4.0 minutes. However, because treatment riders occupy drivers for less time, overall driver availability increases across the shared pool, causing the control group's wait times to also drop to 4.5 minutes. Calculate the measured A/B test delta versus the true global rollout impact, and identify the required testing methodology to resolve this SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption) violation.
title: SUTVA Violations in Dispatch A/B Testing

details.common_mistake: Failing to identify the SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption) violation. Candidates often incorrectly attribute the discrepancy to data drift, novelty effects, or Simpson's paradox, rather than recognizing that treatment units simply cannibalized finite demand from the control units.
details.napkin_math: Assume fixed demand of 100 riders, 10 T-drivers, 10 C-drivers. Baseline: T gets 50, C gets 50. Test: T-model is more aggressive, capturing 60 riders. C drops to 40. Measured A/B Delta = (60-40)/40 = +50% lift. True Global Lift upon 100% rollout = (100-100)/100 = 0%. The measured +50% lift was 100% cannibalization.
details.realistic_solution: Identify the bipartite interference causing a SUTVA violation. The treatment drivers efficiently captured more of the fixed rider demand pool, starving the control drivers and artificially inflating the relative delta. Justify transitioning from user-level randomization to Switchback Testing (time-based randomization) or spatial clustering (geohashing) to properly isolate treatment and control states in constrained marketplaces.

scenario: You are evaluating the rollout of a new ML model for dispatching drivers in a two-sided marketplace network. A standard A/B test (50/50 driver-level randomization) shows the treatment model increases driver earnings by +18% compared to the control group. Based on this, the team decides to roll out the model to 100% of drivers globally. However, after global rollout, the actual overall driver earnings only increase by +2%. Evaluate the experimental setup, identify the critical statistical assumption that was violated, and justify a more robust testing architecture for this deployment environment.
title: Bipartite Network Interference in A/B Testing

details.common_mistake: Assuming the bottleneck is the cross-node network bandwidth limits or the NCCL barrier synchronization overhead required to coordinate the 1024 GPUs.
details.napkin_math: Total checkpoint size = 2.8 TB. Total cluster network capacity = 128 nodes * 12.5 GB/s = 1.6 TB/s. Theoretical time to transfer over network = 2.8 TB / 1.6 TB/s = 1.75 seconds. Actual observed time = 300 seconds. Effective storage bandwidth = 2.8 TB / 300s = ~9.3 GB/s. The storage backend is the clear bottleneck.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck is the centralized storage system's write throughput (e.g., a shared NFS drive). To resolve this, implement two-stage checkpointing: workers synchronously write shards to their local NVMe SSDs, and a background thread asynchronously uploads the files to persistent object storage.

scenario: You are training a 175B parameter LLM on 128 nodes (1024 A100 80GB GPUs). The training framework uses synchronous checkpointing to save the global model and optimizer state (totaling 2.8 TB) every hour. Each node is equipped with a 100 Gbps network interface. However, checkpointing pauses training for a full 5 minutes each time, reducing your effective training throughput by over 8%. Network monitoring reveals that peak interconnect utilization is under 1% during the checkpoint phase. Diagnose the primary bottleneck causing this delay.
title: Diagnosing Synchronous Checkpoint Bottlenecks

details.common_mistake: Candidates often only calculate the theoretical transfer time and ignore the massive opportunity cost of idling 4096 GPUs, or they prematurely suggest fully asynchronous checkpointing without considering the complexities of state consistency.
details.napkin_math: Direct to PFS via IB NDR (50 GB/s link, bottlenecked by storage): 4,800 GB / 40 GB/s = 120s pause. Over 3h, 120/10800 = 1.1% idle. Two-tier sync: local NVMe write = 4,800 GB / (512 nodes * 3 GB/s) = 3.1s pause. Async drain to PFS in background reduces synchronous GPU stall by ~97%.
details.realistic_solution: Adopt a two-tier checkpointing architecture. First, synchronously write the checkpoint shards to the node-local NVMe drives, which unblocks the GPUs almost immediately. Then, use a background process to asynchronously drain the local NVMes to the centralized parallel file system before the next checkpoint interval.

scenario: You are orchestrating the training of a 300B parameter model on a 4096-GPU cluster (A100 80GB). The total optimizer and model state size per checkpoint is 4.8 TB. The cluster experiences a hardware failure on average every 3 hours. Your team currently uses synchronous checkpointing every 1 hour to a centralized parallel file system with a peak ingest bandwidth of 40 GB/s. During checkpointing, all GPUs are blocked. Evaluate the training time overhead of this synchronous approach and justify whether adopting a two-tier strategy (synchronous to local NVMe, then asynchronous to the file system) is required.
title: Evaluating Synchronous Checkpointing Overheads

details.common_mistake: Calculating the checkpoint size based solely on the FP16 model weights (600 GB) instead of the full training state, which drastically underestimates the pause time and operational overhead.
details.napkin_math:
State per parameter: 2B (FP16 weights) + 4B (FP32 master weights) + 8B (FP32 Adam moments) = 14 Bytes.
Total state size: 300,000,000,000 * 14 = 4.2 TB (4200 GB).
Pause duration: 4200 GB / 600 GB/s = 7 seconds.
Total cycle time: 1200s (compute) + 7s (pause) = 1207 seconds.
Overhead: 7 / 1207 ≈ 0.58%.
details.realistic_solution: Determine the full state size per parameter (14 bytes), calculate the total checkpoint footprint (4.2 TB), divide by the storage bandwidth to find the pause duration (7 seconds), and calculate overhead as pause time over total cycle time (0.58%).

scenario: You are training a 300B parameter language model using mixed-precision Adam. The training state checkpoint must include FP16 parameters, FP32 master weights, and FP32 Adam moments (momentum and variance). The cluster uses synchronous checkpointing, pausing all workers to write to a parallel file system with an effective aggregate write bandwidth of 600 GB/s. If you trigger a checkpoint every 20 minutes of active compute time, calculate the exact duration of the training pause per checkpoint and the resulting checkpointing overhead as a percentage of total runtime.
title: Synchronous Checkpoint Overhead Calculation

details.common_mistake: Assuming the model can achieve the 312 TFLOPS peak by ignoring memory bandwidth constraints, or incorrectly calculating AI by only accounting for read traffic instead of total memory (read + write) traffic.
details.napkin_math:
AI = 500 * 10^9 FLOPs / 10 * 10^9 Bytes = 50 FLOPs/Byte.
Ridge Point = 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOPs/Byte.
Max Throughput = min(Peak_FLOPs, AI * Mem_BW)
Max Throughput = min(312 TFLOPS, 50 FLOPs/Byte * 2.0 TB/s)
Max Throughput = 100 TFLOPS (Memory-Bound)
details.realistic_solution: First, calculate the Arithmetic Intensity (AI) of the layer: AI = Total FLOPs / Total Bytes = 500 GFLOPs / 10 GB = 50 FLOPs/Byte. Next, determine the hardware's ridge point, which dictates the transition from memory-bound to compute-bound: Ridge Point = Peak FLOPs / Memory Bandwidth = 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOPs/Byte. Since the workload's AI (50) is significantly lower than the Ridge Point (156), the layer is strictly memory-bound. The maximum achievable throughput is dictated by the memory wall: AI * Memory Bandwidth = 50 FLOPs/Byte * 2.0 TB/s = 100 TFLOPS. You will never see 312 TFLOPS on this workload without architectural changes to improve data reuse.

scenario: You are benchmarking a custom dense retrieval model on an NVIDIA A100-80GB GPU. The vendor spec sheet advertises a peak FP16 throughput of 312 TFLOPS and an HBM bandwidth of 2.0 TB/s. During profiling, you isolate a critical custom layer that executes 500 GFLOPs of computation while reading and writing a total of 10 GB of data to HBM per forward pass. Calculate the workload's Arithmetic Intensity (AI), determine its theoretical maximum throughput using the Roofline model, and state whether the system is compute-bound or memory-bound.
title: Roofline Benchmarking of Custom Layers

details.common_mistake: Calculating the time to breach the SLA (20 days) but failing to account for the 24-hour training lead time, resulting in a delayed deployment and an SLA violation.
details.napkin_math:
Allowable drop = 88.0% - 85.0% = 3.0%
Days to breach = 3.0% / 0.15%/day = 20 days
Trigger retrain = 20 - 1 (training time) = Day 19
Cost per retrain = 24h * $32/h = $768
Annual cost = (365 / 19) * $768 ≈ 19.21 * $768 = $14,753
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the total allowable degradation (88.0% - 85.0% = 3.0%). Divide by the daily decay rate (3.0% / 0.15%) to find the absolute breach point at 20 days. Subtract the 1 day of training time to find the trigger point (Day 19). Calculate the per-cycle cost and extrapolate to an annual figure.

scenario: A large-scale CTR prediction system deployed across 50 T4 GPUs is subject to System Entropy due to continuous data drift. At deployment, the model accuracy is 88.0%. Historical metrics indicate an absolute accuracy degradation of 0.15% per day. The business SLA mandates an accuracy strictly above 85.0%. Retraining the model from scratch requires exactly 24 hours on an 8x A100 cluster (costing $32/hour total). Calculate the maximum number of days the model can serve before retraining must be initiated to prevent an SLA breach, and the expected annualized compute cost for this retraining cadence.
title: Predicting Model Degradation Thresholds

details.common_mistake: Focusing on infrastructure metrics like GPU utilization or latency profiling, or immediately deciding to retrain the model without quantifying which input feature distributions have shifted.
details.napkin_math: If base CTR is 2.0% and degrades by 12%, new CTR is 1.76%. If 'sale-seeking' features comprised 30% of traffic during training but only 5% post-sale, the absolute drift is 25%. A PSI calculation > 0.2 on core embedding features confirms significant population shift requiring a targeted retrain.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose the system entropy (data drift) by computing statistical metrics like the Population Stability Index (PSI) or Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the static training dataset and the live inference queries. The post-event user behavior shifted, invalidating learned priors.

scenario: Your team deployed a deep learning recommendation model (DLRM) for an e-commerce platform on a fleet of 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Over the last 3 weeks since the Black Friday sale ended, the model's p99 latency remains stable at 45ms, and throughput is steady at 15,000 QPS. However, the overall Click-Through Rate (CTR) has gradually degraded by 12% relative to the baseline. Engineering confirms no code changes, hardware failures, or latency regressions have occurred. How do you diagnose the root cause of this silent failure?
title: Diagnosing CTR Degradation Post-Peak Event

details.common_mistake: Accepting the vendor's peak TFLOPS benchmark as the primary metric for low-batch inference, failing to realize the workload operates entirely in the memory-bound regime of the Roofline model.
details.napkin_math: For a 70B model in FP16 (140GB weights), generating 1 token at batch size 1 requires loading the entire 140GB of weights from HBM to SRAM. A100 max tokens/sec = 2000 GB/s / 140 GB = ~14.2 tokens/sec. H100 max tokens/sec = 3350 GB/s / 140 GB = ~23.9 tokens/sec. Expected speedup is 3350 / 2000 = 1.675x, significantly lower than the 3x compute improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Reject the 3x latency reduction claim. Low-batch LLM inference is heavily memory-bandwidth bound, not compute-bound. The benchmarking strategy must focus on achievable memory bandwidth and interconnect latency. The H100 provides 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the A100's 2.0 TB/s, yielding a realistic theoretical speedup closer to 1.6x for token generation.

scenario: A team evaluates replacing a cluster of 8x A100 (80GB, SXM4) servers with 4x H100 (80GB, SXM5) servers for serving a 70B parameter LLM. The workload consists of latency-sensitive chat applications with very low concurrent requests (batch size = 1). The vendor benchmark highlights a 3x increase in peak FP16 TFLOPS on the H100, claiming a proportional 3x reduction in generation latency. Evaluate this vendor claim and design a benchmarking strategy that correctly measures the expected performance improvement for this specific workload.
title: Evaluating LLM Inference Benchmarks

details.common_mistake: Blaming CPU-to-GPU PCIe transfer latency, unoptimized CUDA kernels, or Python framework overhead without analyzing the workload's inherent arithmetic intensity.
details.napkin_math:
A100 Ridge Point = 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOPs/Byte.
Batch 1 Linear Layer (Matrix-Vector) AI = (2 * N * M FLOPs) / (N * M * 2 Bytes for FP16 weights) ≈ 1 FLOP/Byte.
Theoretical Max Performance = AI * Bandwidth = 1 FLOP/Byte * 2.0 TB/s = 2.0 TFLOPS.
The observed 2-4 TFLOPS perfectly matches the memory-bound limit.
details.realistic_solution: The system is functioning perfectly but is severely memory-bandwidth bound. Single-batch autoregressive generation relies on matrix-vector multiplications, which have an extremely low arithmetic intensity (approx 1-2 FLOPs/Byte). According to the Roofline model, performance is hard-capped by the memory bandwidth, making the 312 TFLOPS compute peak mathematically unreachable for this workload.

scenario: You are benchmarking a 1.5B parameter language model on an NVIDIA A100-80GB SXM4 (312 TFLOPS FP16 peak, 2.0 TB/s HBM bandwidth). During single-batch autoregressive inference (sequence length 1024), profiling shows the GPU is achieving only about 2 to 4 TFLOPS per GPU (less than 2% of advertised peak). The infrastructure team suspects defective hardware or severe PCIe transfer bottlenecks. Diagnose the root cause of this massive gap between promised and observed performance.
title: Diagnosing Low TFLOPS in Single-Batch Inference

details.common_mistake: Assuming continuous learning is always superior due to faster reaction to new trends, ignoring the massive operational complexity of state management, risk of catastrophic forgetting, and lack of rollback infrastructure compared to a stateless daily batch retrain.
details.napkin_math: Daily Retrain Compute: 64 GPUs * 12 hours = 768 GPU-hours/day. Continuous Training Compute: 8 GPUs * 24 hours = 192 GPU-hours/day. While continuous training saves ~576 GPU-hours/day (approx. $1,150/day at $2/GPU-h), the engineering overhead of building robust continuous evaluation, state snapshots, and rollback mechanisms for a 100GB model far exceeds the compute savings unless sub-hour reactivity is a hard business requirement.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a daily batch retrain as the primary baseline to ensure stability and stateless reproducibility. If intraday reactivity is strictly required, adopt a hybrid approach: stateless daily retrains combined with lightweight online fine-tuning, enabling easy rollbacks to the stable daily checkpoint.

scenario: A large-scale e-commerce recommendation system (using a 100GB DLRM model deployed on a fleet of A100 GPUs) is experiencing continuous accuracy degradation (System Entropy) at a rate of -0.5% CTR per week due to shifting user behavior. The team is evaluating two mitigation strategies: 1) A daily full retrain using a 30-day sliding window of data (requires 64 A100s for 12 hours), or 2) Continuous incremental training (online learning) where models are updated every 15 minutes using micro-batches from a Kafka stream (requires 8 A100s continuously, plus complex state management and rollback mechanisms). As a Staff Engineer, evaluate the trade-offs between these two approaches regarding compute cost, operational complexity, and effectively mitigating statistical drift, and justify which architecture to implement.
title: Evaluating Mitigation Strategies for Recommendation System Drift

details.common_mistake: Failing to account for the batch size and sequence length dimensions when sizing the activation payload, or attempting to stream gigabytes of raw tensor data synchronously over the serving network.
details.napkin_math: State size per layer = 16 (batch) * 1024 (seq) * 8192 (hidden) * 2 bytes (FP16) = 256 MiB. Total for 5 layers = 256 * 5 = 1280 MiB (1.25 GiB). Synchronously streaming this over a dedicated 10 Gbps link (1.25 GB/s) adds ~1.07s of latency per inference step.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the exact activation footprint (1.25 GiB per step) and configure the control plane to asynchronously write this state to host RAM via PCIe before background-uploading to the observability datastore.

scenario: Your cloud serving control plane must expose internal model states to operators debugging hallucinations in a 70B LLM (hidden size 8192). Operators request full FP16 activations from 5 specific layers to be routed to an observability backend. For a single inference step with batch size 16 and sequence length 1024, calculate the data payload size that the control plane must offload.
title: LLM Activation Observability Offload Overhead

details.common_mistake: Assuming the control plane CPU is the bottleneck processing the 2GB of data, and recommending upgrading the host CPU or heavily downsampling the explainability state to reduce payload size.
details.napkin_math: Extracting 2GB over PCIe Gen5 x16 (~50 GB/s effective) takes 2GB / 50 GB/s = 40ms. If done synchronously layer-by-layer, stream synchronization overheads starve the GPU. Asynchronous transfers hide this 40ms transfer latency behind the 55ms token generation compute time.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose that synchronous PCIe transfers are blocking the main CUDA compute stream. The solution is to allocate pinned host memory and use `cudaMemcpyAsync` on a secondary CUDA stream to extract the state asynchronously without blocking the forward pass.

scenario: A trust-and-safety API serves a 70B parameter LLM on an 8x H100 (80GB) node. The control plane captures per-layer attention entropy and MoE routing probabilities for real-time explainability dashboards. At peak load (batch size 128, sequence length 1024), P99 latency spikes from 55ms/token to over 400ms/token. Profiling shows GPU utilization drops from 85% to 30%, while CPU utilization on the control plane node remains under 40%. The system extracts 2GB of internal state tensors per forward pass via standard Device-to-Host PCIe transfers.
title: Diagnosing Explainability Control Plane Latency

details.common_mistake: Candidates often forget that a single Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operation counts as two floating-point operations (one multiply, one add), or they fail to correctly correlate the 2D array dimensions with parallel operations per clock cycle.
details.napkin_math: MACs/cycle = 256 × 256 = 65,536. FLOPs/cycle = 65,536 × 2 = 131,072. Peak Throughput = 131,072 FLOPs/cycle * 1.2 * 10^9 cycles/sec = 157.28 * 10^12 FLOPS ≈ 157.3 TFLOPS.
details.realistic_solution: First, calculate the number of MACs performed per clock cycle by squaring the grid dimension (256 * 256). Multiply by 2 to convert MACs to FLOPs per cycle, then multiply by the clock frequency to find the final peak throughput in TFLOPS.

scenario: You are evaluating the theoretical peak throughput of a new cloud AI accelerator featuring a single 256x256 systolic array operating at a 1.2 GHz clock speed for BF16 matrix multiplication. To size the workload for a large Transformer feed-forward layer, you need to calculate the theoretical peak TFLOPS (Tera Floating-Point Operations Per Second) of this hardware.
title: Systolic Array Peak Throughput Estimation

details.common_mistake: Assuming the 256x256 systolic array will inherently provide higher throughput due to a higher peak TFLOPS rating, while ignoring the severe padding penalties incurred when workload dimensions do not align with the array grid.
details.napkin_math: On the 256x256 array, the 64x1024 input matrix must be padded to 256x1024. Utilization = (64 * 1024) / (256 * 1024) = 0.25. Therefore, 75% of the systolic array's compute cycles and SRAM reads are wasted on zero-padded tiles.
details.realistic_solution: The 256x256 systolic array requires padding the sequence length from 64 to 256, destroying utilization. The distributed 16x16 units perfectly tile the 64x1024 operation, yielding significantly higher effective utilization and minimizing wasted memory bandwidth.

scenario: You are evaluating hardware for serving a dense LLM. The workload consists of requests with short sequence lengths (sequence length 64, embedding dimension 1024). You must compare a custom AI accelerator featuring a monolithic 256x256 systolic array against a GPU with distributed smaller 16x16 matrix multiply units. Evaluate the compute utilization and efficiency trade-offs when executing the attention QKV projections (64x1024 multiplied by 1024x1024) on these two architectures without cross-request batching.
title: Systolic Array Sizing and Padding Overhead

details.common_mistake: Candidates often incorrectly diagnose this as an SRAM bandwidth limitation, CPU-to-accelerator transfer bottleneck, or framework overhead, failing to analyze how physical fixed-grid MAC arrays handle misaligned tensor dimensions.
details.napkin_math: Theoretical Useful MACs = 64 (Batch) × 100 (Features) × 64 (Output) = 409,600. Padded Hardware MACs executed = 128 × 128 × 128 = 2,097,152. Hardware Compute Utilization = 409,600 / 2,097,152 ≈ 19.5%. Over 80% of the systolic array's cycles are wasted multiplying zeros.
details.realistic_solution: Because the TPU's systolic array is a physical 128x128 grid, any matrix dimension that isn't a multiple of 128 is hardware-padded with zeros. The system evaluates a `[128, 128] x [128, 128]` matrix multiply under the hood. The solution is to redesign the network dimensions (Batch, Features, Output) to be multiples of 128, which will dramatically increase useful throughput without taking any additional execution time.

scenario: A team is running a custom deep learning model on Cloud TPU v4, which features 128x128 Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs). Profiling reveals that a specific dense layer with input shape `[Batch=64, Features=100]` and weight matrix `[100, 64]` is achieving less than 20% compute utilization. The layer is fully resident in on-chip SRAM, so memory bandwidth is not the bottleneck. Diagnose the root cause of this severe underperformance in the systolic array.
title: Systolic Array Padding Underutilization: Transformer Systems Cost

details.common_mistake: Assuming overall system latency remains close to the median, or linearly scaling the 1% probability (0.01 * 50 = 50%) instead of correctly calculating the joint probability of independent events.
details.napkin_math:
P(1 node < 200ms) = 0.99
P(all 50 nodes < 200ms) = 0.99^50 ≈ 0.605
P(system >= 200ms) = 1 - 0.605 = 0.395 (39.5% of user requests hit the tail)
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the probability that at least one of the 50 services hits the p99 latency. The correct approach yields ~39.5%. Mitigate this by implementing hedged requests (sending a duplicate request if the first takes too long) or enforcing a strict 50ms timeout and returning partial results.

scenario: Your e-commerce recommendation system fans out each user request to 50 independent ML ranking microservices running on NVIDIA T4 GPUs. Each service evaluates a subset of the catalog. The median latency of a single service is 20ms, but the 99th percentile (p99) latency is 200ms due to occasional garbage collection and varying batch sizes. Calculate the percentage of overall user requests that will experience a latency of 200ms or higher, assuming the system must wait for all 50 responses (scatter-gather).
title: Fan-out Tail Latency Probability

details.common_mistake: Believing the system-level P99 equals the individual node P99. Candidates often incorrectly choose over-provisioning to eliminate queueing delays without realizing it fails to mitigate non-deterministic OS/network jitter and has a terrible cost-to-benefit ratio.
details.napkin_math: Without hedging: Probability all 50 shards respond in < 200ms = (0.99)^50 ≈ 60.5%. This means 39.5% of overall user requests take > 200ms (the system P60 is 200ms!). With hedging at 25ms: Probability that BOTH the original and hedged request hit the 1% tail = 0.01 * 0.01 = 0.0001. Probability all 50 finish fast = (1 - 0.0001)^50 ≈ 99.5%. System P99.5 is now well under the SLA, and because we wait 25ms to hedge, >90% of requests finish before triggering it, adding < 10% compute overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Choose Strategy A (Hedged Requests). In a high fan-out architecture, the probability of at least one server hitting the P99 is extremely high, dictating the median user experience. Hedging after the 90th percentile latency suppresses the tail mathematically with minimal extra compute load, whereas over-provisioning doubles hardware costs while still leaving the system vulnerable to background noise.

scenario: A cloud recommendation system fans out incoming queries to 50 separate embedding shards hosted on NVIDIA T4s via Triton Inference Server. The individual server median latency is 20ms, but the P99 is 200ms due to dynamic batching queues and network jitter. A user request is blocking and requires responses from all 50 shards. You must evaluate two architectural options to guarantee a strict 50ms overall system P99 SLA: (A) Issue hedged requests to a secondary replica if no response is received within 25ms, or (B) Over-provision GPU capacity by 2x to reduce individual server utilization from 80% down to 40%.
title: Evaluating Hedged Requests for Fan-Out Inference

details.common_mistake: Failing to calculate the massive network bandwidth required for logging full high-dimensional activations at scale, or proposing computationally heavy attribution methods like Integrated Gradients in the synchronous serving path.
details.napkin_math: Full activations per token (FP16): 80 layers * 8192 dim * 2 bytes = ~1.3 MB/token. Total bandwidth = 5,000 QPS * 100 tokens * 1.3 MB = 650 GB/s (prohibitive for a logging plane). Probe scores per token: 80 layers * 1 float * 4 bytes = 320 bytes/token. Total bandwidth = 5,000 * 100 * 320 bytes = 160 MB/s (easily handled by standard telemetry queues).
details.realistic_solution: Reject full activation logging due to its extreme network bottleneck. Implement intermediate linear probes that compress the massive internal state into low-dimensional semantic scores (e.g., hallucination risk) on the fly, reducing the telemetry payload by over 2000x while still giving human operators actionable, layer-wise debugging signals.

scenario: You are architecting the observability control plane for a 70B parameter LLM (80 layers, 8192 hidden dimension) serving 5,000 QPS with an average of 100 generated tokens per request. The trust and safety team requires system explainability to debug model hallucinations in real-time. They propose logging the full layer activations for every token to fully reconstruct the model's internal state offline. You must evaluate this proposal against an alternative approach: deploying lightweight linear probes at intermediate layers to predict hallucination risk and logging only these scalar scores. Justify your design decision quantitatively based on network bandwidth, compute overhead, and diagnostic utility.
title: LLM Control Plane Explainability Trade-offs

details.common_mistake: Assuming that combining multiple services with a 10ms median will result in a 10ms overall system median, ignoring that a parallel scatter-gather request must wait for the absolute slowest response.
details.napkin_math: A single service hits the p99 latency 1% of the time. The probability a single service is FAST (<150ms) is 0.99. The probability that ALL 50 services are fast is (0.99)^50 ≈ 0.605. Therefore, there is a ~39.5% chance the user request is delayed by at least one 150ms response. If fanned out to 100 services, the probability of hitting the tail is 1 - (0.99)^100 ≈ 63.4%, meaning the 150ms tail actually becomes the median overall system latency.
details.realistic_solution: Identify that the overall system latency is bounded by the max of 50 independent probability distributions. To mitigate this without fixing the underlying 150ms spikes, implement 'hedged requests' (sending a duplicate secondary request to a different replica if the primary hasn't responded within the expected p90 time) or allow returning partial results to truncate the tail.

scenario: A distributed recommender system processes a user request by fanning out queries to 50 independent inference microservices in parallel (e.g., candidate generators, embedding lookups). Monitoring metrics show that the median (p50) response time of an individual service is a fast 10ms, but the 99th percentile (p99) latency spikes to 150ms due to garbage collection and network jitter. The overall user request is only complete when all 50 parallel responses are received. Despite the 10ms component median, dashboards show the overall system median latency is severely degraded and unpredictable. Diagnose why the median user experience is bottlenecked and calculate the probability of an overall request experiencing the tail latency.
title: Diagnosing Parallel Fan-out Tail Latency

details.common_mistake: Candidates often suggest blindly scaling up the Kafka ingestion cluster or using aggressive random sampling, failing to realize that random sampling destroys the statistical validity of P99 tail latency monitoring and drops rare out-of-memory (OOM) traces.
details.napkin_math: Raw throughput: 50,000 req/s * 4KB = 200 MB/s (~17 TB/day). With sidecar aggregation: 500 nodes * (100 histogram buckets * 8 bytes) / 10s = 40 KB/s for metrics. Tail-based sampling (1% of traffic as errors/tails): 500 req/s * 4KB = 2 MB/s. Total reduction: 200 MB/s to 2.04 MB/s (99% reduction) while preserving 100% of critical diagnostic data.
details.realistic_solution: Deploy an OpenTelemetry Collector sidecar on each node to pre-aggregate latencies into exponential histograms (forwarded every 10s) and implement tail-based trace sampling. This forwards 100% of errors and P99 traces, but only 0.1% of baseline traffic.

scenario: You operate a global fleet of 500 inference nodes (8xH100 each) serving an LLM at an aggregate 50,000 requests per second. Each request generates 4KB of telemetry (token-by-token latencies, generation stats, GPU metrics). The centralized ingestion pipeline is dropping logs, and cross-AZ egress costs exceed $50,000/month. Evaluate the trade-offs between implementing 1% head-based random sampling at the API gateway versus deploying node-level telemetry sidecars to compute HDR histograms and pre-aggregate metrics.
title: Evaluating Telemetry Aggregation for LLM Inference Fleets

details.common_mistake: Scaling up the centralized collector or upgrading the network link without addressing the unbounded telemetry generation at the source, or using simple random sampling which drops the rare tail-latency events needed for debugging.
details.napkin_math: Raw telemetry generation: 500 nodes * 2,000 req/sec * 10 KB = 10,000,000 KB/sec = 10 GB/sec = 80 Gbps. This consumes 80% of the 100 Gbps link. With 1% sampling for normal traffic and assuming 5% tail/errors, volume drops by ~94%, reducing bandwidth to ~4.8 Gbps.
details.realistic_solution: Implement local aggregation and tail-based sampling on each node. Calculate metrics (e.g., latency histograms) locally instead of sending raw traces. Sample 100% of traces exceeding the P95 latency threshold and only 1% of normal requests. Batch and compress (e.g., zstd) the sampled traces every 5 seconds before transmission.

scenario: A distributed LLM inference cluster with 500 nodes processes 2,000 requests per second per node. To debug P99 latencies, the team enables high-resolution tracing, generating a 10KB JSON trace payload per request. All nodes send these traces directly to a centralized observability cluster over a shared 100 Gbps inter-cluster uplink. Shortly after deployment, the uplink saturates, dropping critical control-plane traffic and causing cascading timeouts. Diagnose the bottleneck and propose a node-level aggregation strategy.
title: LLM Inference Trace Saturation

details.common_mistake: Attempting to stream 100% of raw request logs to a central server, which saturates network egress and spikes ingestion costs, or applying uniform random sampling which drops rare but critical failure traces.
details.napkin_math: Raw bandwidth = 100,000 req/s * 2KB = 200 MB/s. Errors (kept 100%) = 500 req/s * 2KB = 1 MB/s. Successes (sampled 1%) = 99,500 req/s * 0.01 * 2KB = 1.99 MB/s. Metrics = 0.1 MB/s. Total egress = 1 + 1.99 + 0.1 = 3.09 MB/s (a 98.4% reduction in bandwidth).
details.realistic_solution: Deploy a local telemetry agent (like OpenTelemetry Collector) on each edge node to calculate aggregated metrics (histograms) locally. Use tail-based sampling to retain 100% of error traces and 1% of successful traces, dropping the rest of the raw payloads.

scenario: You manage an ML inference cluster processing 100,000 requests per second. Each request generates 2KB of raw telemetry data (features, predictions, latencies). Sending all raw telemetry to your central observability platform requires 200 MB/s of network egress, which is bottlenecking your network and driving up costs. Calculate the resulting bandwidth if you implement edge telemetry aggregation that retains 100% of logs for errors (assuming a 0.5% error rate), samples 1% of successful request logs, and sends lightweight aggregated metrics (e.g., counters, histograms) that consume roughly 100 KB/s in total.
title: Edge Telemetry Aggregation for High-Throughput Inference

details.common_mistake: Calculating arithmetic intensity without accounting for the output matrix write, assuming 1 byte per element instead of 2 for FP16, or mixing up MACs (1 MAC = 2 FLOPs) with FLOPs.
details.napkin_math:
FLOPs = 2 * M * N * K = 2 * (8192^3) = 1.1e12.
Bytes = 3 * (8192^2) * 2 = 402e6.
Intensity = 1.1e12 / 402e6 = 2736 FLOPs/B.
Ridge Point = 312e12 / 2.0e12 = 156 FLOPs/B.
Min Time = 1.1 TFLOPs / 312 TFLOPS = 3.52 ms.
details.realistic_solution: The operation requires 2 * 8192^3 = 1.1 TFLOPs. Total memory traffic involves reading two inputs and writing one output: 3 * (8192^2) * 2 bytes = 402 MB. The arithmetic intensity is 1.1 TFLOPs / 402 MB = 2736 FLOPs/byte. The A100's ridge point is 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOPs/byte. Since 2736 >> 156, the operation is heavily compute-bound by the Tensor Cores. The minimum execution time is the theoretical compute time: 1.1 TFLOPs / 312 TFLOPS = 3.52 milliseconds.

scenario: You are optimizing a custom dense layer on an NVIDIA A100 GPU (312 TFLOPS peak FP16 Tensor Core, 2.0 TB/s memory bandwidth). The layer performs an FP16 matrix multiplication (GEMM) with dimensions M=8192, K=8192, N=8192. Calculate the arithmetic intensity, determine if the operation is compute-bound or memory-bound, and estimate the absolute minimum execution time.
title: Tensor Core Bottlenecks in GEMM

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the memory bandwidth cost of implicit `.contiguous()` calls when passing tensors to the legacy NCHW custom kernels, or assuming NCHW is globally optimal.
details.napkin_math: Tensor size: 256 * 1024 * 14 * 14 * 2 bytes (FP16) = 102,760,448 bytes (approx 102.7 MB). A transposition requires a full read and write (205.4 MB total). At 2 TB/s bandwidth, the copy takes 205.4 MB / 2,000,000 MB/s = 102.7 microseconds. If the NHWC Conv2D saves more than 102.7 microseconds per layer compared to NCHW, the global layout change is a net positive.
details.realistic_solution: Adopt the NHWC layout to unlock 2-3x Tensor Core speedups for convolutions. The overhead of dynamically converting to NCHW for the custom kernels is bandwidth-bound but justified if the convolution time savings exceed the memory copy penalty.

scenario: You are optimizing a ResNet-based vision pipeline on an NVIDIA A100 GPU (80GB, 2TB/s bandwidth) using FP16. Tensors currently use the legacy NCHW memory layout. A proposal suggests migrating the tensor abstraction to the NHWC ('channels_last') layout to maximize Tensor Core utilization for Conv2D operations. However, three custom CUDA kernels in the pipeline strictly require contiguous NCHW tensors. Evaluate the trade-offs of switching the global tensor layout, given a critical bottleneck tensor of shape [N=256, C=1024, H=14, W=14].
title: Evaluating Tensor Memory Layouts for Tensor Cores

details.common_mistake: Assuming that simply enabling FP16 guarantees Tensor Core usage, or incorrectly blaming the data loader since overall GPU utilization is high.
details.napkin_math: A100 Tensor Cores require matrix dimensions (M, N, K) to be multiples of 8 for FP16. If N=105, the operation falls back to standard CUDA cores. Padding N to 128 allows Tensor Core execution, bypassing the 19.5 TFLOPS (FP32) limit and utilizing the 312 TFLOPS (FP16 TC) peak.
details.realistic_solution: Identify that the final layer dimension (105) is not a multiple of 8, which is required for Tensor Core alignment in FP16 on A100. Pad the classification layer output to 112 or 128 and ignore the dummy classes in the loss calculation to fully engage Tensor Cores.

scenario: A team reports that their mixed-precision ResNet-50 training on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is unexpectedly slow. Despite setting `fp16=True` in PyTorch, `nvidia-smi` shows GPU utilization at 98%, but profiling with Nsight Compute reveals that Tensor Core utilization is below 15%. The batch size is 256, and the hidden layer dimensions are mostly powers of 2, except for the final classification layer which was modified to predict 105 classes instead of 1000. How do you analyze and resolve the bottleneck preventing high Tensor Core utilization?
title: Diagnosing Tensor Core Underutilization

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume the new attention math is computationally heavier or blame Python interpreter overhead, completely missing how logical tensor metadata (strides) impacts physical memory layouts.
details.napkin_math: For a tensor of shape [B=32, H=16, S=4096, D=128] in FP16, the physical size is 512 MB. An implicit clone forces a 512 MB read + 512 MB write = 1 GB of memory traffic. On an H100 (3 TB/s HBM3), each implicit clone adds ~0.33 ms of pure memory overhead. With 10 non-contiguous operations per layer across 32 layers, this adds ~106 ms of pure memory transfer delay per forward pass, completely starving the compute units.
details.realistic_solution: The `transpose()` and slicing operations only alter the tensor's metadata (shape and strides), creating a non-contiguous memory view. Subsequent operations (like cuBLAS GEMMs or layer norms) require contiguous memory, forcing PyTorch to implicitly trigger synchronous `aten::clone` operations. The fix is to explicitly call `.contiguous()` immediately after the reshape to amortize the cost, or utilize `einops` / custom Triton kernels to fuse the operations and avoid materializing the intermediate non-contiguous tensor.

scenario: You are profiling a PyTorch transformer training loop on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. After introducing a novel multi-head attention mechanism that heavily relies on tensor reshaping, slicing, and `.transpose()`, the GPU SM (compute) utilization drops from 75% to 20%, while memory bandwidth utilization spikes to 95%. Profiling shows that time spent in `aten::clone` and uncoalesced element-wise kernels has increased by 10x, severely bottlenecking the iteration. What is the root cause of this degradation at the tensor abstraction level, and how do you resolve it?
title: Diagnosing Non-Contiguous Tensor Memory Bottlenecks

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume `.contiguous()` only updates tensor metadata (strides) like `.view()` resulting in 0 bytes of traffic, or they calculate only the read operation (256 MiB) and neglect the memory write.
details.napkin_math:
Elements = 64 * 1024 * 16 × 128 = 134,217,728 elements.
Size in bytes = 134,217,728 * 2 bytes (FP16) = 268,435,456 bytes.
Size in MiB = 268,435,456 / (1024^2) = 256 MiB.
Total memory traffic = Read (256 MiB) + Write (256 MiB) = 512 MiB.
details.realistic_solution: The `.transpose()` operation merely creates a non-contiguous view by modifying tensor strides in O(1) time. However, calling `.contiguous()` on this strided view forces a physical deep copy in GPU HBM to enforce a sequential memory layout. This operation requires reading the entire fragmented tensor and writing it to a newly allocated buffer. The total traffic is 1x Read + 1x Write of the tensor's size. Modern kernels (like FlashAttention) support strided memory layouts natively, avoiding this massive overhead.

scenario: You are profiling a custom Transformer attention mechanism running on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using PyTorch. The code prepares a query tensor of shape `[batch=64, seq_len=1024, num_heads=16, head_dim=128]` via a `.transpose(1, 2)` operation, followed immediately by a `.contiguous()` call to feed it into a legacy CUDA kernel. Assuming FP16 precision, calculate the exact High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) traffic (in MiB) generated strictly by this `.contiguous()` operation.
title: Tensor Contiguity Memory Overhead

details.common_mistake: Assuming that a smaller matrix dimension (3000 vs 3072) guarantees lower latency and memory bandwidth usage by saving FLOPs, while ignoring the strict tile size alignment requirements necessary to instantiate optimized Tensor Core MMA (Matrix Multiply-Accumulate) instructions.
details.napkin_math: Unpadded FLOPs per token: 2 * 768 × 3,000 = 4,608,000. At 25% of A100 FP16 peak (312 TFLOPS * 0.25 = 78 TFLOPS), time = ~59 ns. Padded FLOPs per token: 2 * 768 × 3,072 = 4,718,592 (+2.4%). With 3072 aligned to multiples of 64/128, efficiency can easily reach 70% (218 TFLOPS), resulting in a compute time of ~21.6 ns. Adding 2.4% more math yields a ~2.7x practical speedup.
details.realistic_solution: Pad the intermediate dimension to 3072. Tensor Cores execute operations in fixed-size blocks (e.g., 16x16x16 for FP16). A dimension of 3000 is not cleanly divisible by optimal tile sizes (e.g., 64, 128, or 256 for optimal wave quantization), leading to highly inefficient tile processing, thread divergence, and underutilized SMs. Padding increases theoretical FLOPs by 2.4% but allows the scheduler to dispatch dense, fully-utilized Tensor Core instructions.

scenario: Your team is pre-training a custom Transformer on a cluster of NVIDIA A100 GPUs using FP16 mixed precision. To strictly limit the parameter count, the model architecture specifies a hidden size of 768 and an intermediate Feed-Forward Network (FFN) size of 3000 (instead of the standard 3072). Profiling reveals that the FFN linear layers achieve only 25% of peak Tensor Core TFLOPS. You are tasked with evaluating the trade-off of padding the FFN dimension to 3072 versus maintaining the 3000 dimension, justifying the architectural change using hardware-specific quantitative reasoning.
title: Optimizing Tensor Core Utilization via Dimension Padding

details.common_mistake: Recommending that clients send uncompressed NCHW tensors to bypass server-side processing entirely, failing to evaluate the massive network bandwidth explosion and the resulting client-side transmission latency penalty.
details.napkin_math: A typical 224x224 RGB JPEG is ~20KB. An uncompressed FP16 tensor (224 x 224 x 3 channels x 2 bytes) is ~301KB. Requiring pre-formatted NCHW tensors increases payload size by 15x. At 500 QPS, inbound bandwidth jumps from 10 MB/s to ~150 MB/s per server. Over a public internet connection, the TCP transmission time for 301KB will severely degrade end-to-end latency, making the GPU-accelerated format transformation mathematically superior.
details.realistic_solution: Maintain small network payloads by accepting compressed JPEGs over gRPC to minimize transmission latency, and offload the JPEG decoding, NHWC-to-NCHW memory layout transformation, and FP16 casting to the GPU using a Triton DALI backend ensemble.

scenario: Your team is deploying a vision model on NVIDIA A100 GPUs via Triton Inference Server. The TensorRT engine requires an NCHW memory layout in FP16. Currently, clients send base64-encoded JPEGs via REST. The server's CPU decodes the JPEG (yielding an NHWC array), transposes the layout to NCHW, casts the payload to FP16, and copies it to the GPU. At 500 QPS, the CPU is at 100% utilization, GPU utilization is bottlenecked at 30%, and p99 latency exceeds 250ms. Evaluate the architectural trade-offs between requiring clients to send pre-formatted, uncompressed FP16 NCHW binary tensors over gRPC versus moving the decoding and NHWC-to-NCHW format transformation directly onto the GPU using NVIDIA DALI.
title: Evaluating Payload-to-Tensor Transformation Architectures

details.common_mistake: Candidates often suggest optimizing the ViT model with quantization, TensorRT, or kernel fusion, entirely missing that the CPU string-to-float parsing and layout transposition is the dominant latency bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Elements per batch: 32 imgs * 3 * 224 × 224 = 4,816,896 floats. JSON payload size: 4.81M * 10 bytes ≈ 48.1 MB. JSON parsing time at 250 MB/s = 48.1 MB / 250 MB/s = 0.192 seconds (192 ms). The CPU string-to-float transformation alone (192ms) takes 24x longer than the actual GPU inference (8ms).
details.realistic_solution: Switch the transport layer from REST/JSON to gRPC with binary Protobufs (or Triton's binary data extension) to eliminate character parsing. Additionally, send raw NHWC byte arrays and offload the NHWC->NCHW transposition and float conversion to a fused GPU kernel.

scenario: You are optimizing a cloud inference service for a Vision Transformer (ViT) on an NVIDIA A10G. Clients submit inference requests via a REST API, sending batches of 32 images (3x224x224) as flat JSON arrays of floats. The Python backend parses this JSON, transposes it from NHWC to NCHW layout, and copies it to the GPU. The model's GPU execution time is only 8ms per batch, but end-to-end latency exceeds 200ms. Assuming a CPU JSON parsing speed of 250 MB/s and an average of 10 bytes per float string in the JSON payload, calculate the network payload transformation overhead and propose an architectural fix.
title: JSON to Tensor Parsing Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Candidates often suggest scaling up the number of CPU nodes, adding more GPU workers, or switching web frameworks, failing to realize that JSON string parsing and cache-unfriendly memory transpositions on the CPU are the mathematical root cause of the latency.
details.napkin_math: 1 image (224x224x3) = ~150K integers. In JSON (e.g., '255, '), this is ~750KB. Batch 16 = 12MB text payload. Python `json.loads` on 12MB takes ~15-20ms. `np.transpose` on NHWC creates a strided, non-contiguous memory view. The subsequent `.astype(np.float16)` forces a cache-unfriendly copy across 12MB of non-contiguous RAM, adding another ~15ms. Total CPU tax is >30ms, completely dwarfing the 1.5ms GPU inference.
details.realistic_solution: Switch the payload transport from JSON to a binary format like gRPC/Protobuf. More importantly, offload the format transformation (NHWC to NCHW transpose and uint8 to FP16 cast) to the GPU by either exporting the model to accept NHWC directly or using NVIDIA DALI for GPU-accelerated tensor layout transformation.

scenario: You are serving a TensorRT-optimized Vision Transformer on an NVIDIA A10G using a Python FastAPI inference server. The GPU compute takes only 1.5ms per image. However, under peak load (batch size 16), end-to-end latency spikes to 45ms. Profiling reveals the GPU utilization is at 15%, while the single CPU core handling the Python worker is pegged at 100%. Clients are sending image pixels as JSON arrays in NHWC (Height-Width-Channel) format. The server uses `numpy.array(json_data).transpose(0, 3, 1, 2).astype(np.float16)` to convert the incoming data to the contiguous NCHW FP16 memory layout expected by the TensorRT engine.
title: CPU Bottleneck in Tensor Format Transformation

details.common_mistake: Candidates often suggest optimizing the NCCL algorithms, increasing batch size, or tweaking network routing, missing that TP's extreme communication frequency fundamentally violates cross-node bandwidth constraints.
details.napkin_math: Within a node, A100 NVLink provides ~600 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth. Between nodes, InfiniBand HDR provides 200 Gbps (~25 GB/s). Moving an All-Reduce operation across the node boundary drops available bandwidth by a factor of 24x (600 / 25), causing synchronous blocking at every single Transformer layer.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose the issue as an interconnect bandwidth cliff. Restrict Tensor Parallelism strictly to the intra-node boundary (TP <= 8) to leverage NVLink. Use Pipeline Parallelism (PP) or Data Parallelism (DP/FSDP) for cross-node scaling.

scenario: You are training a 70B parameter LLM on a cluster of 8-GPU A100 (80GB) nodes. To increase memory headroom, the infrastructure team expands the Tensor Parallelism (TP) degree from TP=8 (single node) to TP=16 (across two nodes). Immediately, Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) plummets from 48% to 11%. Nsight Systems profiling reveals GPUs are entirely stalled on NCCL `AllReduce` kernels. Analyze why this specific parallelism topology failed and identify the architectural mismatch causing the bottleneck.
title: Diagnosing MFU Collapse in Cross-Node Tensor Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Assuming .transpose() physically moves data in memory, or believing the hardware cache hierarchy will automatically absorb non-sequential memory access patterns without penalty.
details.napkin_math: Original strides for [B, H, S, D] are (8388608, 524288, 128, 1). Transposed shape [B, S, H, D] has strides (8388608, 128, 524288, 1). A warp (32 threads) reading along the 'Heads' dimension (stride=524288 elements = 1MB for FP16) requests 32 distinct addresses separated by 1MB. Each request pulls a 128-byte cache line to use only 2 bytes, resulting in 1.56% (2/128) transaction efficiency and massive L2 thrashing.
details.realistic_solution: Identify that .transpose() only modifies the tensor metadata (shape and strides), creating a non-contiguous view. The linear memory layout remains [B, H, S, D]. Reading along the transposed 'Heads' dimension causes massive stride jumps, destroying spatial locality and resulting in completely uncoalesced global memory reads. The solution is to call .contiguous() before the kernel to physically repack the data in memory, trading a one-time memory copy cost for fully coalesced accesses during the compute-intensive kernel.

scenario: Your team deployed a custom CUDA kernel for a novel attention mechanism on an H100 GPU cluster. When the FP16 input tensor of shape [Batch=32, Heads=16, Seq=4096, Dim=128] is passed directly from a linear projection, the kernel achieves 85% memory bandwidth utilization. However, when the tensor is first transposed to [Batch=32, Seq=4096, Heads=16, Dim=128] for a routing operation and then passed to the exact same kernel, memory bandwidth utilization plummets to 12%, and overall latency spikes by 6x. Profiling indicates massive L2 cache thrashing. Diagnose the root cause of this performance collapse.
title: Transposed Tensor Bandwidth Collapse

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose TP=16 to maximize aggregate memory bandwidth and minimize per-device compute, failing to evaluate the severe latency penalty of executing high-frequency All-Reduce operations over the slow 25 GB/s inter-node network.
details.napkin_math: For a hidden size of 12288 and batch size of 64, an activation tensor is 64 * 12288 * 2 bytes ≈ 1.5 MB. TP requires 2 All-Reduces per layer. Across 96 layers, TP=16 requires 192 All-Reduces. Using the Ring All-Reduce formula `2*(N-1)/N * data`, this transfers `192 * 1.5 MB * 1.875 ≈ 540 MB` per step over the network. At 25 GB/s inter-node bandwidth, network wait time is `540 MB / 25 GB/s ≈ 21.6ms` per token. PP=2 only transfers the 1.5 MB activation once between nodes per step, taking < 0.1ms.
details.realistic_solution: Choose TP=8 and PP=2. Tensor Parallelism must be confined within a single node to leverage the 600 GB/s NVLink, as it requires blocking All-Reduce operations inside every transformer layer. Pipeline Parallelism is ideal across nodes because it only requires point-to-point communication of activation tensors at layer boundaries, perfectly matching the lower-bandwidth InfiniBand link.
