details.common_mistake: "Actors are always faster because they avoid the synchronization barriers of BSP." This ignores that BSP's synchronization barriers enable global optimizations (sort-merge joins, optimal shuffle planning) that actors cannot do without explicit coordination.
details.napkin_math: Uniform pipeline (tokenize + filter): BSP overhead per stage = ~2s barrier sync × 4 stages = 8s overhead per batch. Actor overhead per task = ~0.5ms scheduling × 2B tasks = ~280 hours cumulative — but amortized across 100 nodes = 2.8 hours wall time. BSP wins on uniform work. Heterogeneous pipeline (some docs need 10ms, others 10s): BSP straggler in a 100-task stage (1 task per node) = max(100 draws from [10ms, 10s]) ≈ 10s. 99 nodes idle for 9.99s. Actor model: no idle time, each actor pulls next task immediately.
details.realistic_solution: BSP (Spark) excels at homogeneous, shuffle-heavy workloads: joins, aggregations, sort-based deduplication. The barrier synchronization enables the query optimizer to plan globally optimal data movement. The actor model (Ray) excels at heterogeneous, stateful, and irregular workloads: when different documents need different processing (e.g., some need OCR, some need language detection, some need decompression), when processing time varies 100× across documents, or when the pipeline has complex branching logic. BSP handles stragglers poorly — every stage waits for the slowest task. Actor model handles stragglers naturally — fast actors pull more work from a shared queue. For the described pipeline (read → tokenize → filter → write), BSP is superior: the operations are uniform, embarrassingly parallel, and benefit from Spark's optimized I/O and shuffle. Switch to actors only when processing is heterogeneous or stateful.

scenario: Your team preprocesses training data using a Spark (BSP) pipeline: read raw text, tokenize, filter by quality score, write shards. The pipeline processes 2 TB/hour on a 100-node cluster. A colleague proposes rewriting it in Ray (actor model) because 'actors are more flexible.' Under what conditions would the actor-model approach outperform BSP for data processing, and when would it be strictly worse?
title: Actor Model vs BSP for Data Processing Pipelines

details.common_mistake: "The shuffle is necessary because we need all tokens for the same domain on the same reducer." This is true for non-associative operations, but counting is associative and commutative — it can be partially aggregated before the shuffle.
details.napkin_math: Without combiner: 20 TB corpus × ~0.9 overhead ratio = 18 TB shuffle. At 25 Gbps bisection bandwidth per node: 18 TB / (500 × 3.125 GB/s) ≈ 12 seconds — but the shuffle is not perfectly parallel due to hotspots, so 3 hours is realistic. With combiner: 500 nodes × 10M domains × 20 bytes/record = 100 GB shuffle. Same bandwidth: 100 GB / (500 × 3.125 GB/s) = 0.064 seconds. Even with overhead: ~1 minute total.
details.realistic_solution: Add a combiner (local pre-aggregation) phase. Before shuffling, each of the 500 nodes locally aggregates its (domain, 1) pairs into (domain, local_count). If the corpus has ~10M unique domains, each node emits at most 10M records instead of billions. The shuffle volume drops from 18 TB (billions of (domain, 1) pairs) to 500 nodes × 10M domains × 20 bytes = 100 GB — a 180× reduction. The mathematical requirement: the aggregation function must be associative and commutative (counts, sums, min, max). Non-decomposable aggregations (median, percentiles, count-distinct) cannot use simple combiners and require approximate algorithms (HyperLogLog for count-distinct, t-digest for percentiles).

scenario: You are computing per-domain token counts across a 20 TB web corpus distributed over 500 nodes. Each node holds a 40 GB shard. The naive MapReduce approach emits (domain, 1) for every token and shuffles all pairs to reducers. The shuffle phase transfers 18 TB across the network and takes 3 hours. Your colleague points out that the final output — domain counts — is only 2 GB. Why is 18 TB moving across the network to produce a 2 GB result, and how do you fix it?
title: The Missing Combiner in Distributed Aggregation

details.common_mistake: "Wikipedia is high quality, so using it as the positive class is correct." This confuses domain with quality. Wikipedia has a specific style (encyclopedic, formal, citation-heavy) that is not representative of all high-quality text. The classifier learns 'Wikipedia-like' rather than 'high-quality.'
details.napkin_math: 15T tokens at 4 bytes/token = 60 TB raw. FastText inference: ~1M documents/sec on a 32-core machine. At 500 tokens/document: 30B documents. Time: 30B / 1M = 30,000 seconds = 8.3 hours on 1 machine, or ~5 minutes on a 100-node cluster. The classifier itself is cheap — the bias it introduces costs months of wasted pre-training compute. A 3T token pre-training run on 2,000 H100s at $3/GPU-hour costs ~$2M. If biased filtering degrades the model by even 2% on downstream tasks, the data pipeline cost savings are irrelevant.
details.realistic_solution: The bias is domain-quality conflation. The classifier will assign high scores to encyclopedic text and low scores to high-quality but non-encyclopedic text (e.g., technical forums, literary fiction, scientific papers, code documentation). This systematically removes diverse high-quality content, reducing the corpus's domain coverage. A robust pipeline: (1) Multi-signal quality scoring: combine a classifier score with heuristic signals — perplexity from a small language model, text statistics (sentence length, vocabulary richness, repetition ratio, symbol-to-word ratio), and URL reputation scores. (2) Stratified sampling for human annotation: sample 10K documents from each quality quartile × domain cluster, have 3 annotators label quality, measure inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha > 0.7). (3) Iterative refinement: train a better classifier on the human labels, re-score, re-sample for annotation. (4) Diversity constraint: after quality filtering, ensure domain distribution entropy remains above a threshold — if filtering removes >80% of any domain, investigate.

scenario: You are building the data pipeline for a 3 trillion token LLM pre-training corpus. The raw crawl is 15 trillion tokens. You need to filter to high-quality text, but you have no labeled quality dataset. Your plan: train a fastText classifier on 'Wikipedia + curated books = positive, random web = negative' and score every document. A senior researcher warns this approach has a critical systematic bias. What is the bias, and how do you build a more robust quality scoring pipeline at this scale?
title: Bootstrapping a Quality Classifier for Trillion-Token Corpora

details.common_mistake: "Just upsample the rare domains to equal proportions." Equal mixing wastes capacity on domains with diminishing returns (web text has 8T tokens — you only need a fraction) and risks overfitting on small domains (math has only 50B tokens — sampling 200B means 4 epochs, introducing memorization).
details.napkin_math: Proxy model search: 20 mixture configs × 1B params × 50B tokens × 6 FLOPs/token = 3 × 10²⁰ FLOPs (300e18) per config. On 64 H100s at 50% MFU: 3e20 / (64 × 989e12 × 0.5) = ~9,500 seconds (~2.6 hours) per config. Total proxy search sequentially: 20 × 2.6h = ~52 hours. Compare to full-scale run: 1T tokens × 70B params × 6 FLOPs/token = 4.2 × 10²³ FLOPs on 2,000 H100s = ~4.9 days. The 52-hour proxy search saves potentially weeks of wasted full-scale training with a bad mixture.
details.realistic_solution: The optimal mixture requires empirical search because there is no closed-form solution for how domain proportions affect downstream performance. The standard approach: (1) Train small proxy models (1B params, 50B tokens) with different mixtures using a grid or Bayesian optimization over the mixing proportions. (2) Evaluate on a diverse benchmark suite (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, etc.) to find Pareto-optimal mixtures. (3) Apply the winning mixture to the full-scale run. The systems constraint: each domain has a maximum epoch count before overfitting. Math at 50B tokens can be repeated ~4× (200B tokens max) before quality degrades. This creates hard constraints: the mixture must satisfy both the target proportions AND the per-domain epoch limits. This means you need an online curriculum scheduler that tracks per-domain token counts during training and adjusts sampling weights dynamically as small domains hit their repetition limits.

scenario: You are designing the data mixing strategy for a 1 trillion token LLM pre-training run. Your corpus consists of 5 domains: web text (8T tokens available), code (2T tokens), scientific papers (500B tokens), books (200B tokens), and math (50B tokens). You need exactly 1T tokens total. A naive approach samples proportionally to availability (73% web, 18% code, 5% science, 2% books, 0.5% math). However, Llama and Chinchilla papers show that proportional sampling produces weak math and reasoning. How do you determine the optimal mixture, and what systems constraint makes this problem harder than it appears?
title: The Curriculum Data Mixing Problem

details.common_mistake: "Increase the checkpoint interval to 30 minutes." This extends the window of data loss on failure and doesn't solve the fundamental problem of unbounded state growth.
details.napkin_math: Bloom filter sizing: n=100B elements, p=0.01 FPR → m = -n × ln(p) / (ln 2)² ≈ 10 × 100B = 1 trillion bits = 125 GB. After 2 weeks at 500 GB/hr: ~400B additional docs → Bloom grows to 500 GB. Flink checkpoint of 500 GB state to S3 at 2 GB/s = 250 seconds = 4.2 minutes — but RocksDB compaction + serialization overhead 5× → 25 minutes. Hot-only Bloom (7 days, 170B entries): 200 GB checkpoint in ~100 seconds — feasible with 5-minute intervals.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is unbounded state growth in both the Bloom filter and the RocksDB LSH index. The Bloom filter for 50 TB of documents (at ~500 bytes/doc average, that's ~100B documents) requires ~120 GB at 1% false positive rate (10 bits per element). After 2 weeks of ingesting 500 GB/hour = 168 TB new data, the filter has grown to hold ~400B+ entries (500+ GB), exceeding memory. The RocksDB state similarly grows linearly. The fix: externalize the dedup index. Use a tiered architecture: (1) Hot tier: in-memory Bloom filter covering only the last 7 days of ingested documents (~84 TB, ~170B entries, manageable at ~200 GB). (2) Warm tier: an external service (Redis cluster or dedicated dedup microservice) holding the full corpus hash index, queried asynchronously. (3) The Flink job checks the hot Bloom filter synchronously (sub-millisecond) and queries the external index asynchronously with batched lookups. Checkpoint only contains the hot tier. (4) Periodically compact the hot tier into the external index and reset.

scenario: Your data pipeline ingests a continuous web crawl at 500 GB/hour and must deduplicate documents against the existing 50 TB corpus in near-real-time (within 10 minutes of ingestion). A colleague proposes a Flink streaming job that maintains a Bloom filter of all document hashes in memory for exact dedup, plus a MinHash LSH index in RocksDB state for fuzzy dedup. After 2 weeks, the job's checkpoint time has grown from 30 seconds to 25 minutes, exceeding the 10-minute checkpoint interval, and the job starts failing. Diagnose the root cause and propose an architecture that handles unbounded state growth.
title: The Streaming Deduplication State Explosion

details.common_mistake: "Use sort-merge join for everything because the tables are large." This ignores that broadcast join is dramatically more efficient when one side fits in executor memory, and that join strategy choice depends on the size ratio between the two tables.
details.napkin_math: Broadcast breakeven point: broadcast costs R × N (where R = small table size, N = number of nodes). Shuffle costs L + R (both tables shuffled). Broadcast wins when R × N < L + R, i.e., R < L / (N - 1). For N=500, L=50 TB: R < 50 TB / 499 ≈ 100 GB. So tables under 100 GB should be broadcast. 5 GB: broadcast. 200 GB: shuffle (200 > 100). 2 TB: shuffle.
details.realistic_solution: Join 1 (50 TB × 5 GB on language key): Broadcast the 5 GB table. Each of the 500 executors receives a copy: 5 GB × 500 = 2.5 TB network I/O, but the 50 TB table stays put (zero shuffle). Total: 2.5 TB. Join 2 (50 TB × 200 GB on domain key): 200 GB fits in executor memory (64 GB with some overhead — marginal). If it fits, broadcast: 200 GB × 500 = 100 TB — this is MORE than shuffling both sides (50.2 TB). So use shuffle hash join: shuffle both sides by domain key. Network I/O: 50 TB + 200 GB ≈ 50.2 TB. Join 3 (50 TB × 2 TB on URL key): Both tables are large. Sort-merge join: shuffle both sides by URL. Network I/O: 50 TB + 2 TB = 52 TB. Total across all 3 joins: 2.5 + 50.2 + 52 = 104.7 TB. Optimization: if you order the joins so that Join 1 (broadcast) happens first, the output is still ~50 TB. Then chain Join 2 and Join 3 — but with careful co-partitioning, you can make Join 2's output already partitioned by URL for Join 3, saving one shuffle.

scenario: You need to enrich a 50 TB training dataset with metadata from three lookup tables: a 5 GB language-detection table, a 200 GB domain-quality table, and a 2 TB URL-to-category mapping. Each join is on a different key. You have a 500-node Spark cluster with 64 GB RAM per executor. For each of the three joins, determine the optimal join strategy (broadcast, shuffle hash, or sort-merge) and calculate the total network I/O across all three joins.
title: The Distributed Join Strategy Selection

details.common_mistake: "Compute everything in a single monolithic Spark job that reads the raw data, runs all scorers, and writes the output." This fails the ablation requirement — changing one weight forces re-running every signal computation, including the expensive LM perplexity inference.
details.napkin_math: Phase 1 total compute cost: Heuristics (500 CPU nodes × 2 hours × $0.10/hr) = $100. Classifier (500 CPU nodes × 2 hours × $0.10/hr) = $100. Perplexity (64 A100s × 86 hours × $3/hr) = $16,500. Dedup (500 nodes × 4 hours × $0.10/hr) = $200. Total: ~$17K per crawl. Phase 2 per ablation: read 20 GB score table, apply weights, write 5 GB output. Cost: $0.50 on a single node. 100 ablation experiments: $50 vs re-running Phase 1 each time: $1.7M. The decomposed architecture saves 34,000× in ablation cost.
details.realistic_solution: Use a columnar, append-only architecture with signal decomposition. Phase 1 — Signal Computation (run once per crawl): (a) Heuristic signals: embarrassingly parallel Spark job, ~100 TB/hour on 500 nodes. Write 15 score columns to a Parquet table keyed by doc_id. (b) Quality classifier: batch inference on CPU cluster, ~50 TB/hour. Write classifier_score column. (c) Perplexity scoring: batch inference on GPU cluster (1B model, ~10K tokens/sec per GPU). 100 TB ≈ 200B tokens. On 64 A100s: ~200B / (64 × 10K) = 312,500 seconds ≈ 3.6 days. Write perplexity column. (d) Deduplication: MinHash LSH pipeline. Write dedup_flag and cluster_id columns. Phase 2 — Score Composition (run per experiment): Read only the pre-computed score columns (not the raw text). Apply weighted combination: final_score = w1 × classifier + w2 × (1/perplexity) + w3 × heuristic_composite + w4 × dedup_penalty. This reads ~20 GB of score columns instead of 100 TB of raw text. Ablation runs complete in minutes. All columns are versioned with the pipeline git hash for reproducibility. The architecture is essentially a feature store for data quality signals.

scenario: You are the tech lead for the data team at an LLM lab. Your task: build a reusable data quality scoring pipeline that processes 100 TB of raw web crawl per week and assigns a composite quality score to each document. The score must combine: (1) a learned quality classifier, (2) a perplexity score from a 1B parameter reference LM, (3) 15 heuristic signals (repetition ratio, boilerplate fraction, toxic content score, etc.), and (4) a deduplication flag. The pipeline must be deterministic (same input always produces same output) and fully reproducible. The research team wants to ablate each quality signal by rerunning the pipeline with different scoring weights. Design the distributed systems architecture.
title: Designing a Multi-Signal Data Quality Pipeline at Petabyte Scale

details.common_mistake: "Curriculum learning is strictly better — it's been proven to help in supervised learning." The evidence for curriculum learning in large-scale LLM pre-training is mixed, and the systems costs are significant. Also, 'i.i.d. is required for SGD convergence' is an oversimplification — large enough batches approximate i.i.d. even with ordered data.
details.napkin_math: Random shuffling throughput: 500 nodes reading random 1 GB shards from a 10 PB corpus — each node issues 1 random read/second from any of 10M shards. Parallel filesystem handles this easily at 500 GB/s aggregate. Strict curriculum throughput: 500 nodes must read from the same 'easy' tier (1 PB, 1M shards) simultaneously. Storage hotspot: 500 GB/s concentrated on 10% of the filesystem. If the PFS has non-uniform shard placement, throughput drops to ~200 GB/s (60% degradation). Soft curriculum (tier-shuffled): 500 nodes read randomly within the current tier. As long as the tier has >5,000 shards (each node reads different shards), throughput remains near 500 GB/s.
details.realistic_solution: The tension is between statistical efficiency (curriculum ordering may improve learning per token) and systems efficiency (random shuffling enables optimal data pipeline throughput). The key insight: at the scale of LLM pre-training (trillions of tokens, thousands of GPUs), the systems costs dominate unless the curriculum provides substantial per-token learning improvement. Systems costs of curriculum ordering: (1) Sequential shard access eliminates random prefetching — throughput drops because the data pipeline cannot read-ahead from arbitrary shards. (2) All GPUs in a data-parallel group must read from the 'current difficulty level' simultaneously, creating storage hotspots on a subset of shards. (3) If using global ordering, the data pipeline becomes a centralized bottleneck (a coordinator must track global position). Resolution: use a soft curriculum — within each difficulty tier (e.g., 10 tiers by perplexity), randomly shuffle shards. This preserves i.i.d. within each tier while gradually increasing difficulty across tiers. Systems cost is minimal: the pipeline pre-computes tier assignments, and each epoch reads tiers sequentially but shuffles within tiers.

scenario: Your research team proposes curriculum learning for a 70B LLM pre-training run: start with 'easy' documents (short, simple vocabulary, low perplexity) and gradually increase difficulty. The hypothesis is that this will improve convergence speed. However, your infrastructure team pushes back: the standard pipeline randomly shuffles shards to ensure each training batch is i.i.d., which is critical for SGD convergence guarantees. The curriculum approach requires reading shards in a specific order, which breaks i.i.d. sampling AND forces sequential reads from the storage system (eliminating the ability to prefetch random shards). Evaluate both positions. Under what conditions does curriculum ordering beat random shuffling, and what are the systems costs?
title: The Curriculum Ordering vs Random Shuffling Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: "Just run the pairwise dedup iteratively until no more duplicates are found." This is O(k) iterations where k is the maximum cluster size, and each iteration requires re-running the full 800M-edge dedup — totaling 80 × 800M = 64B pair comparisons.
details.napkin_math: Graph: 5B nodes, 800M edges. Average component size after convergence: ~15 documents (yielding ~53M components with duplicates + 4.2B singleton components). 53M components × 15 docs/cluster × 14 removals/cluster = 742M documents removed (vs 200M with pairwise). Hash-to-Min iterations: ~8. Per iteration: emit (neighbor_id, min_label) for each directed edge: 1.6B edges × 16 bytes = 25.6 GB/iteration. 8 iterations = 205 GB total shuffle. On 500 nodes at 3 GB/s each: 205 GB / 1,500 GB/s = 0.14 seconds per iteration. Total: ~1 second of shuffle time + overhead ≈ 10 minutes wall time.
details.realistic_solution: This is a connected components problem on a graph with 5B nodes and 800M edges. Build the similarity graph (document = node, near-duplicate pair = edge), find connected components, and within each component keep only the highest-quality representative. Distributed connected components at this scale: use the Hash-to-Min algorithm (or the more efficient Alternating algorithm): (1) Initialize each node's component label as its own ID. (2) Each node sends its current minimum label to all neighbors. (3) Each node updates its label to the minimum received. (4) Repeat until convergence (~log(diameter) iterations). For the news-syndication clusters with diameter ~2-3, this converges in 5-10 iterations. In MapReduce: each iteration is a single shuffle. Total: 10 iterations × 1.6B directed edges × 16 bytes/edge = 25.6 GB shuffle per iteration = 256 GB total network I/O. Within each component: rank documents by a quality score and keep the top-1.

scenario: After running MinHash LSH deduplication on your 5 billion document corpus, you have 800 million candidate pairs of near-duplicate documents. Now you must decide which documents to keep and which to remove. A colleague proposes: for each pair, keep the longer document and remove the shorter one. After running this, you discover you only removed 200 million documents, but manual inspection shows there are clusters of 50-100 near-identical documents (e.g., the same news article syndicated across 80 sites). The pairwise approach only removed one document per pair, leaving 49 duplicates in each cluster. How do you efficiently resolve this at the scale of 800M edges over 5B nodes?
title: The Connected Components Problem in Fuzzy Deduplication

details.common_mistake: "Build a single Airflow DAG that chains Spark jobs." This fails on several fronts: monolithic stages cannot be independently re-run for ablation, the dedup step requires state across monthly crawls (not just within one), PII removal may need GPU inference (different compute shape than CPU-heavy heuristics), and reproducibility requires deterministic execution (random shuffles, hash seeds, floating-point ordering must all be pinned).
details.napkin_math: Stage 1: 500 TB input, spot instances at $0.03/vCPU-hr. At 100 MB/s/core throughput: 500 TB / (0.1 GB/s × 3600) = 1,389 core-hours. With overhead (HTML parsing, language detection): ~10,000 core-hours × $0.03 = $300. Stage 2: MinHash (128 hashes × 500B documents = 64 trillion hash computations). At 10M hashes/s/core: 6.4M core-seconds = 1,778 core-hours × $0.03 = $53. LSH index queries: 500B docs × 20 bands = 10T lookups against RocksDB. 100K lookups/s/core: 100M core-seconds on-demand (need durability) at $0.05/hr = $1,389. Stage 3: Perplexity scoring on GPUs: 500 TB ≈ 1T tokens at 10K tokens/s/GPU: 100M GPU-seconds = 27,778 GPU-hours × $1.50 (spot A100) = $41,667. Heuristics (CPU): ~5,000 core-hours × $0.03 = $150. Stage 4: Tokenization + packing: ~2,000 core-hours × $0.03 = $60. Total: $300 + $53 + $1,389 + $41,667 + $150 + $60 ≈ $43,600/month. Within the $50K budget, with ~$6K margin for re-runs and debugging.
details.realistic_solution: Use a staged, columnar architecture with heterogeneous compute. Stage 1 — Ingestion & Extraction (CPU, 2 days): Download raw WARC files, extract text with trafilatura, detect language (fastText), write Parquet with columns [doc_id, url, text, language, source]. Technology: Spark on spot instances (cheap, embarrassingly parallel, tolerant of spot interruptions with lineage-based recovery). Stage 2 — Deduplication (CPU, 1 day): Exact dedup via SHA-256 hash (trivial). Fuzzy dedup via MinHash LSH against an external persistent index (not Spark state). The index is a sharded RocksDB cluster that persists across monthly runs. New documents query the index; matches are flagged; new hashes are inserted. Technology: Ray actors for the LSH index service + Spark for the batch MinHash computation. Stage 3 — Quality & Safety Scoring (GPU + CPU, 1 day): GPU workload: perplexity from 1B reference LM, toxicity classifier. CPU workload: heuristic scores. Write score columns to the same Parquet table. Technology: Ray for heterogeneous GPU/CPU scheduling. Stage 4 — Composition & Packaging (CPU, 0.5 days): Apply domain mixing weights, sample documents, tokenize (SentencePiece), pack into 1 GB shards with curriculum-aware ordering (tier by quality score, shuffle within tier). Write final training shards. Technology: Spark. Reproducibility: every stage logs a manifest (input files, code version, config hash, random seeds). The pipeline's output is uniquely determined by its manifest. Budget check below.

scenario: You are hired as the founding data infrastructure engineer at a new LLM lab. Your mandate: design the complete data pipeline from raw web crawl to training-ready token shards for a 2 trillion token pre-training corpus. The pipeline must handle: (1) ingestion of 500 TB/month of Common Crawl + proprietary data sources, (2) language detection and filtering, (3) PII removal, (4) exact and fuzzy deduplication against the full historical corpus, (5) quality scoring with multiple signals, (6) domain classification and mixing, (7) tokenization and shard packaging, and (8) curriculum-aware shard ordering. The pipeline must be fully reproducible (given the same raw inputs and config, produce bit-identical outputs) and complete processing of each monthly crawl within 5 days using a budget of $50K/month in cloud compute. Design the architecture, justify your technology choices, and calculate whether the budget is feasible.
title: Designing the End-to-End Pre-Training Data Pipeline

details.common_mistake: "Each GPU independently shuffles its assigned shards using the same random seed." This only shuffles within each GPU's partition — it doesn't create a global shuffle. Documents assigned to GPU 0 in epoch 1 stay on GPU 0 in epoch 2, creating data ordering correlations across epochs that can harm convergence.
details.napkin_math: Naive coordinator approach: 2M shard indices × 8 bytes = 16 MB permutation. Broadcasting 16 MB to 2,048 GPUs via AllBroadcast: 16 MB × log₂(2048) = 176 MB total network traffic per epoch. Not terrible, but adds a synchronization barrier. PRP approach: each GPU computes 2M/2048 = 977 Feistel cipher evaluations per epoch. At ~100ns per evaluation: 97.7 μs per GPU — negligible. Zero network traffic for shuffle coordination. For mid-training GPU count change (2,048 → 1,536 due to node failure): consumed shards = global_step × 2,048 × shards_per_step. Remaining shards: 2M - consumed. Redistribute remaining over 1,536 GPUs. Each GPU recomputes its new assignment in <1ms.
details.realistic_solution: Use a pseudorandom permutation function (PRP) that maps (epoch, global_index) → shard_index without materializing the full permutation. Implementation: a Feistel cipher with the epoch as the key. Each GPU computes its own shard assignments locally: for GPU rank r in epoch e, it reads shards at indices PRP(e, r × shards_per_gpu + 0), PRP(e, r × shards_per_gpu + 1), ..., PRP(e, r × shards_per_gpu + k-1). This is coordinator-free (every GPU computes independently), deterministic (same seed + epoch → same permutation), and produces a true global shuffle (the Feistel PRP is a bijection over the shard index space). For elastic scaling (GPU count changes from N₁ to N₂ at step S): record the consumed_shard_set up to step S (which is deterministically computable from the PRP). Recompute assignments for N₂ GPUs over the remaining shards. The key invariant: no shard is seen twice within an epoch, and every shard is seen exactly once. This requires maintaining a global 'cursor' that tracks how far through the permutation training has progressed, but the cursor is a single integer (the global step count), not a 2M-element list.

scenario: Your LLM pre-training uses 2,048 GPUs with data parallelism. Each GPU must see a unique, non-overlapping subset of the 2 trillion token corpus per epoch, and the global ordering must be deterministically shuffled (so that if training resumes from a checkpoint at step 50,000, every GPU sees exactly the same data it would have seen without the interruption). The corpus is stored as 2 million 1 GB shards on a parallel filesystem. A naive approach: generate a global permutation of all 2M shard indices, split into 2,048 contiguous chunks. But this requires a coordinator to hold and distribute a 2M-element permutation, and the shuffle must change every epoch. How do you implement a deterministic, coordinator-free global shuffle that scales to millions of shards and thousands of GPUs, and what happens when the GPU count changes mid-training due to elastic scaling?
title: The Deterministic Global Shuffle at Trillion-Token Scale

details.common_mistake: "SSA is just an internal detail — any graph representation works equally well for optimization." Without SSA, reaching-definition analysis becomes expensive and error-prone, making many optimizations impractical.
details.napkin_math: For a graph with 1,000 operations, reaching-definition analysis without SSA requires O(1,000²) = 1M iterations per pass. With SSA, dependency lookup is O(1) per variable. For a compilation pipeline with 20 optimization passes, this saves ~20M iterations — the difference between milliseconds and seconds of compile time.
details.realistic_solution: SSA ensures every variable is defined exactly once, which makes def-use chains explicit and trivial to traverse. This is critical because most compiler optimizations — dead code elimination, constant propagation, common subexpression elimination — require knowing which definition reaches which use. Without SSA, the compiler must run iterative dataflow analysis to compute reaching definitions, which is O(n²) in the number of statements per pass. With SSA, the answer is immediate: there is exactly one definition per variable, and phi nodes at control-flow merge points make the choice explicit. For ML compilers specifically, SSA enables efficient operator fusion decisions: the compiler can trivially trace data dependencies to determine which operators can be fused without violating correctness.

scenario: A colleague asks why ML compilers convert computation graphs into Static Single Assignment (SSA) form before running optimization passes. What property of SSA makes it essential for compiler optimization, and what would go wrong without it?
title: The SSA Form Purpose

details.common_mistake: "Multiple levels add unnecessary complexity — a single-pass compiler would be simpler and faster." This ignores that different optimizations are only valid and efficient at specific abstraction levels.
details.napkin_math: A typical MLIR pipeline for a transformer block: `torch` dialect (semantic ops) → `linalg` dialect (tensor algebra, ~5 fusion passes) → `affine` dialect (loop nests, ~8 tiling/vectorization passes) → `gpu` dialect (thread mapping, ~3 passes) → `nvvm` or `llvm` (codegen). That is ~4 dialect levels and ~20 passes — each pass operating on the representation where its optimization is most natural.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-level IRs enable optimizations at the right abstraction level. At the highest level (e.g., MLIR's `linalg` dialect), the compiler reasons about entire tensor operations — fusing a matmul with its subsequent bias add and ReLU. At the mid level (e.g., `affine` or `scf` dialects), the compiler reasons about loop structures — tiling, unrolling, vectorization. At the lowest level (e.g., `llvm` or `gpu` dialects), the compiler reasons about register allocation and instruction scheduling. A direct single-pass compilation would either lose the high-level semantic information needed for operator fusion (if it lowers too early) or fail to exploit hardware-specific features like Tensor Cores (if it stays too abstract). The progressive lowering also enables retargetability: the same high-level optimizations apply whether the target is an NVIDIA GPU, AMD GPU, or TPU — only the final lowering pass changes.

scenario: MLIR uses a hierarchy of 'dialects' — from high-level ML operations down to hardware-specific instructions. Why does an ML compiler need multiple IR levels instead of compiling directly from the computation graph to machine code?
title: The Dialect Hierarchy Lowering

details.common_mistake: "The search space is 4 × 8 = 32 configurations." This confuses additive and multiplicative combinatorics. Each parameter is independent, so the configurations multiply.
details.napkin_math: $8^4 = 4{,}096$ configs/kernel × 80 unique kernels = 327,680 total. At 5ms/trial: exhaustive = $327{,}680 \times 0.005 = 1{,}638\text{s} \approx 27\text{ min}$. With guided search (100 trials/kernel): $100 \times 80 \times 0.005 = 40\text{s}$. Speedup = $41\times$, with typically <5% performance gap vs exhaustive optimum.
details.realistic_solution: The search space is $8^4 = 4{,}096$ configurations per kernel. But a transformer model typically has 50-100 distinct kernel shapes (different attention heads, FFN layers, varying sequence lengths). The total search space for the full model is $4{,}096 \times 80 \approx 327{,}680$ kernel configurations. Each configuration requires a benchmark run (~5ms for a single kernel trial), making exhaustive search for one kernel feasible ($4{,}096 \times 5\text{ms} \approx 20\text{s}$) but exhaustive search for the whole model expensive ($327{,}680 \times 5\text{ms} \approx 27\text{ minutes}$). This is why ML compilers use cost models and guided search (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, or learned cost models) to prune the space to ~100 trials per kernel, cutting total tuning from 27 minutes to ~40 seconds.

scenario: You are auto-tuning a matrix multiply kernel for an H100 GPU. The kernel has 4 tunable tiling parameters (M_tile, N_tile, K_tile, and number of pipeline stages), each with 8 possible values. How large is the search space, and why does this make exhaustive search impractical for a full model compilation?
title: The Tiling Factor Search Space

details.common_mistake: "Triton is just a wrapper around CUDA, so it should achieve the same performance." Triton operates at a higher abstraction level, which means certain hardware-specific optimizations are harder to express.
details.napkin_math: H100 FP16 peak: 989 TFLOPS. CUDA hand-tuned: $989 \times 0.85 = 841$ TFLOPS (3 weeks effort). Triton: $989 \times 0.75 = 742$ TFLOPS (2-3 days effort). Performance gap: $841 - 742 = 99$ TFLOPS (12% relative). Engineering efficiency: CUDA = $841/15\text{ eng-days} = 56$ TFLOPS/eng-day. Triton = $742/2.5\text{ eng-days} = 297$ TFLOPS/eng-day. Triton is $5.3\times$ more engineer-efficient.
details.realistic_solution: A well-written Triton kernel typically achieves 70-80% of peak FLOPS — about 5-15% behind hand-tuned CUDA. The performance gap comes from the abstraction level: Triton programs operate on tiles of data (block-level programming) while CUDA operates on individual threads. This means Triton's compiler must infer the optimal shared memory usage, pipeline scheduling, and register allocation from the tile-level description. For standard patterns (GEMM, reduction, elementwise fusion), the Triton compiler's heuristics are excellent and close the gap to <5%. The gap widens for irregular patterns (sparse attention, variable-length sequences) where CUDA's explicit thread-level control enables hand-tuned memory access patterns that Triton's block-level abstraction cannot express. The engineering tradeoff is stark: the Triton version takes 2-3 days instead of 3 weeks, enabling faster iteration on algorithmic ideas. For most teams, 75% of peak in 2 days beats 85% of peak in 3 weeks.

scenario: Your team needs to write a custom fused attention kernel. The senior GPU engineer proposes writing it in CUDA; a newer team member suggests Triton. The CUDA version will take 3 weeks of engineering time and achieve 85% of peak H100 FLOPS. Estimate what fraction of peak FLOPS a Triton implementation would likely achieve, and explain why the abstraction gap creates this performance difference.
title: The Triton vs CUDA Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: "The compiler is buggy — file an issue and wait for a fix." While compiler bugs exist, most fusion failures are caused by pattern-matching limitations at specific IR levels, not bugs.
details.napkin_math: Unfused SwiGLU with hidden_dim=8192: Two matmul writes to HBM ($2 \times 8192 \times B \times 2\text{B} = 32\text{KB} \times B$) + elementwise reads of those outputs ($32\text{KB} \times B$) + final write. Fused version eliminates both the intermediate HBM writes and subsequent reads, saving $64\text{KB} \times B$ of bandwidth per token. At B=2048 tokens: $64\text{KB} \times 2048 = 128\text{MB}$ saved per layer, $\times 80$ layers = 10.24 GB of memory traffic saved per forward pass. At 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, that is ~3.0ms saved — significant for inference.
details.realistic_solution: The fusion failure occurs at the graph-level IR (e.g., MLIR's `linalg` dialect or XLA's HLO). Standard fusions like matmul+bias+ReLU are implemented as pattern-matching rewrite rules: the compiler recognizes the specific subgraph and replaces it with a fused kernel. SwiGLU has the form $\text{SwiGLU}(x) = (xW_1) \otimes \sigma(xW_2)$, which requires two parallel linear projections followed by an elementwise multiply — a non-trivial data dependency pattern. The fusion pass sees two matmuls feeding into a multiply, which doesn't match its matmul+activation fusion template. The fix is either (1) register a custom fusion pattern for the SwiGLU subgraph in the compiler's pattern database, (2) implement SwiGLU as a single custom Triton kernel that handles both projections and the gating internally, or (3) lower the SwiGLU components manually and hint the compiler to fuse them. Option 2 is most common in practice.

scenario: After adding a custom activation function (SwiGLU) to your model, you profile the compiled kernel and find that the compiler failed to fuse it with the preceding linear layer. The standard ReLU version of the same architecture fuses perfectly. Why would SwiGLU break the fusion pass, and at which IR level does the failure occur?
title: The Lowering Pass Fusion Loss

details.common_mistake: "The compiler is just slow — buy more CPU cores for compilation." Compilation speed is a symptom; the root cause is excessive graph fragmentation from unsupported operations.
details.napkin_math: 1,000 graph breaks × ~2s compilation each = 2,000s = 33 minutes of compilation overhead. After fixing: 8 large graphs × ~15s each = 120s = 2 minutes. The compiled kernels are also faster because larger fused graphs enable more cross-operator optimizations. Net first-epoch improvement: $45\text{min} \to 7\text{min}$.
details.realistic_solution: Graph breaks occur when TorchDynamo encounters Python operations it cannot trace into the computation graph — data-dependent control flow (if tensor.item() > threshold), in-place operations on tensors with aliasing, calls to non-compilable external libraries, or dynamic shapes that change every iteration. Each graph break creates a separate subgraph that must be independently compiled by the backend (TorchInductor). With thousands of graph breaks, you get thousands of tiny compiled kernels instead of a few large fused kernels. Diagnosis: set `torch._dynamo.config.verbose = True` and `torch._dynamo.config.log_level = logging.DEBUG` to see exactly which Python line triggers each break. Common fixes: replace `tensor.item()` with `torch.where()`, replace data-dependent branches with masking operations, use `torch.compiler.allow_in_graph` for safe custom ops, and set `dynamic=True` for varying shapes. After fixing graph breaks, you should see 5-10 compiled graphs instead of thousands.

scenario: After enabling `torch.compile()` on your training loop, you observe that the first epoch takes 45 minutes instead of the expected 5 minutes. Subsequent epochs run at the expected speed. The profiler shows thousands of compilation events in the first epoch. What is causing the recompilation storm, and how do you diagnose which operations are triggering graph breaks?
title: The Graph Break Recompilation Storm

details.common_mistake: "Just retrain the cost model on H100 data." This fixes the immediate problem but creates a maintenance burden for every new GPU generation.
details.napkin_math: Analytical model tuning on H100: 0 calibration cost, 30% suboptimal → wastes $0.30 per $1.00 of GPU compute. Random search: $4{,}096 \times 5\text{ms} = 20\text{s}$ per kernel, finds optimum, but $20\text{s} \times 80$ kernels = 27 min per model compilation. Learned cost model: 1,000 calibration samples × 5ms = 5s one-time cost, then <5% suboptimal per kernel, 100 guided trials × 80 kernels × 5ms = 40s per model compilation. The learned model saves 26.3 min of compilation time while staying within 5% of optimal.
details.realistic_solution: The cost model broke because the H100 changed several microarchitectural parameters that the analytical model didn't account for: (1) The TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) unit changes the cost of shared memory loads — the A100 cost model assumes explicit `cp.async` loads while H100's TMA can load entire tiles asynchronously. (2) The H100's L2 cache is 50MB vs A100's 40MB, changing the effective working set boundary. (3) The H100's Transformer Engine with FP8 changes the compute-to-memory ratio, shifting optimal tile sizes. The scalable fix is a hybrid approach: use a learned cost model (small neural network trained on profiling data) instead of a purely analytical one, with a hardware feature vector as input. The feature vector encodes cache sizes, memory bandwidth, compute units, and special hardware features. When new hardware arrives, run a small calibration set (~1,000 profiling samples) to fine-tune the model. This amortizes the cost model across GPU generations. XLA, TVM, and Triton all use variants of this approach.

scenario: Your ML compiler's auto-tuner uses an analytical cost model to predict kernel performance and select tiling configurations. After upgrading from A100 to H100 GPUs, you find that the cost model consistently selects suboptimal tile sizes — the auto-tuned kernels run 30% slower than the best configuration found by random search. Analyze why the cost model broke across GPU generations and propose a fix that scales to future hardware.
title: The Cost Model vs Profiling Dilemma

details.common_mistake: "XLA is for TPUs and TorchInductor is for GPUs — just pick based on hardware." Both support multiple hardware targets; the real difference is in compilation strategy, not hardware support.
details.napkin_math: For a standard 70B transformer with fixed shapes: XLA achieves 55-60% MFU (global fusion, buffer planning). TorchInductor achieves 50-55% MFU (fragment-level fusion, less cross-layer optimization). Gap: ~10% relative. For a MoE model with dynamic routing: XLA requires padding all experts to max capacity (wasting 20-40% compute on padding). TorchInductor compiles the dynamic dispatch natively, executing only active expert paths. Net: TorchInductor wins by 15-25% on dynamic MoE workloads.
details.realistic_solution: The fundamental architectural difference is whole-program vs per-operator compilation scope. XLA performs whole-program compilation: it captures the entire computation graph ahead of time, runs global optimization passes (cross-layer fusion, memory planning across the full model, buffer donation), and produces a single optimized executable. This gives XLA a structural advantage for static, regular workloads (standard transformer training with fixed shapes) because it can make globally optimal decisions — e.g., fusing the layer-norm at the end of one layer with the linear projection at the start of the next. TorchInductor uses graph-fragment compilation: TorchDynamo traces subgraphs between graph breaks and compiles them independently. This gives TorchInductor a structural advantage for dynamic workloads (variable sequence lengths, data-dependent control flow, custom Python logic) because it preserves Python's flexibility while compiling the hot paths. The tradeoff is compilation scope vs dynamism: XLA's global view enables better optimization but requires static shapes; TorchInductor's local view misses cross-fragment optimizations but handles dynamism gracefully.

scenario: Your infrastructure team must choose a compiler backend for a large-scale transformer training job. XLA (used via JAX) and TorchInductor (used via torch.compile) are the two candidates. Both produce fused kernels from high-level operations. Analyze the architectural differences between these two compilation strategies and explain when each has a structural advantage.
title: The XLA vs TorchInductor Decision

details.common_mistake: "Add `--use-tensor-cores` to the compiler flags." There is no such flag. Tensor Core usage depends on specific preconditions being met during code generation.
details.napkin_math: HMMA throughput on H100: 989 TFLOPS (FP16). FFMA throughput: 67 TFLOPS (FP32). Ratio: $989/67 \approx 14.8\times$. At 35% Tensor Core utilization, effective throughput = $0.35 \times 989 + 0.65 \times 67 = 346 + 44 = 390$ TFLOPS. After fixing alignment to achieve 90% Tensor Core utilization: $0.90 \times 989 + 0.10 \times 67 = 890 + 7 = 897$ TFLOPS. Speedup: $897/390 = 2.3\times$ — purely from fixing the code generation pipeline.
details.realistic_solution: Tensor Cores have strict shape and alignment requirements: matrix dimensions must be multiples of 16 (for FP16 HMMA) or 8 (for FP8), input tensors must be in specific memory layouts (row-major A, column-major B for `mma.sync`), and data must be aligned to 128-byte boundaries in shared memory. The compiler's code generation is falling back to FFMA because one or more of these preconditions fails. Common causes: (1) The tiling pass chose tile sizes that are not multiples of 16 — this is a mid-level IR problem (affine/SCF dialect). (2) The memory layout pass did not insert the required transpose to get operand B into column-major — this is a lowering pass problem. (3) Padding was not inserted for non-aligned dimensions (e.g., hidden_dim=768 is fine, but sequence_length=513 is not a multiple of 16). The fix must be applied at the tiling and layout passes in the mid-level IR, not at the final code generation. By the time the compiler reaches NVVM/PTX emission, the tile shapes and layouts are already locked in.

scenario: You profile a compiled transformer training job on H100 GPUs and find that Tensor Core utilization is only 35% despite the workload being compute-bound. The compiler's generated SASS shows that many matrix multiplies are using FFMA (FP32 fused multiply-add) instructions instead of HMMA (half-precision matrix multiply-accumulate on Tensor Cores). Diagnose why the compiler's target-specific code generation is failing to use the Tensor Cores and identify at which compilation stage the fix must be applied.
title: The Tensor Core Codegen Gap

details.common_mistake: "Just tune for the most common shape — it will work well enough for others." Optimal tile sizes depend critically on the ratio of compute to memory traffic, which shifts with every shape change.
details.napkin_math: Shape space: 6 batch sizes × 8 seq lengths = 48 shape combinations. Exhaustive tuning: 48 × 4,096 configs × 5ms = 983s ≈ 16 min. Bucketed approach: 10 buckets × 4,096 configs × 5ms = 205s ≈ 3.4 min (with guided search: 10 × 100 × 5ms = 5s). Performance: exhaustive achieves optimal per-shape; bucketed achieves <3% gap for 97% of shapes, with outliers at bucket boundaries.
details.realistic_solution: The auto-tuned configuration fails to generalize because the optimal tiling parameters are a function of the problem shape. For batch_size=32, seq_len=2048, the matmuls are large and compute-bound — the auto-tuner picks large tiles (128×128) to maximize Tensor Core utilization. For batch_size=1, seq_len=128, the same matmul is small and memory-bound — large tiles waste shared memory and leave most Tensor Cores idle, while small tiles (32×32) better match the problem size. The solution is a multi-configuration dispatch table: (1) Partition the shape space into ~8-12 buckets based on arithmetic intensity boundaries (memory-bound, transitional, compute-bound). (2) Auto-tune one representative shape per bucket. (3) At runtime, compute the arithmetic intensity of the incoming shape and dispatch to the nearest tuned configuration. (4) For Triton kernels, use `torch.compile`'s `dynamic=True` mode with specialized re-compilation for frequently-seen shapes (the JIT will cache compiled versions). This gives near-optimal performance across the full shape range with 8-12× less tuning effort than per-shape tuning.

scenario: Your team auto-tuned a set of transformer kernels for batch_size=32, seq_len=2048 on H100. When serving traffic arrives with variable sequence lengths (128-8192) and batch sizes (1-64), the auto-tuned kernels perform 40% worse than the default configurations for many input shapes. Analyze why tuning for one shape fails to generalize, and design a strategy that covers the dynamic shape space without requiring exhaustive per-shape tuning.
title: The Auto-Tuning Transfer Problem

details.common_mistake: "The operator is just inherently slower — recurrence is fundamentally sequential." While recurrence introduces serial dependencies, parallel scan algorithms can parallelize it, and the real bottleneck is often the compiler's inability to map the scan to hardware primitives.
details.napkin_math: FlashAttention-2 on H100 at seq_len=4096, d=128, 32 heads: ~0.8ms (Tensor Core-bound, 85% utilization). Naive GLA scan: 4096 sequential steps. Instead of summing across heads (which run in parallel on the SMs), the true bottleneck is the loop-carried dependency forcing 4096 irreducible serial HBM reads per head. At ~200ns latency per read, 4096 × 200ns = ~0.8ms of purely sequential memory stall time. With scalar FFMA and uncoalesced read/write overheads, the naive kernel takes ~1.6ms (2× FA2). Chunked scan (chunk=64): 64 inter-chunk serial steps × ~200ns = ~12.8μs stall + 64-way parallel intra-chunk computation. With Triton fusion to eliminate intermediate HBM writes, it achieves ~1.0-1.1ms. Gap: 1.1/0.8 = 1.4× — close to the theoretical minimum imposed by the residual serial dependency.
details.realistic_solution: The performance gap has three sources rooted in compiler-hardware mismatch: (1) **No hardware primitive**: FlashAttention maps to HMMA Tensor Core instructions because it is fundamentally a sequence of GEMMs. GLA's recurrent scan maps to no hardware primitive — the compiler generates scalar FFMA loops, underutilizing the Tensor Cores by ~15×. (2) **Suboptimal memory access pattern**: The scan's recurrent state (a d×d matrix per head, updated at each position) creates a loop-carried dependency. The compiler cannot tile across the sequence dimension because each position depends on the previous one. This forces sequential shared memory reads with no opportunity for the TMA to prefetch. (3) **Missing fusion opportunity**: The compiler cannot fuse the scan with the preceding linear projection because the scan has a data-dependent loop structure that breaks standard fusion patterns. Strategy to close the gap: (a) Implement a chunkwise parallel scan — process the sequence in chunks of 64 positions, compute intra-chunk with a parallel scan (maps to warp-level reductions), then propagate inter-chunk state serially. This converts O(L) serial steps to O(L/64) serial steps with O(64) parallel work per step. (b) Write a custom Triton kernel that fuses the linear projection with the chunked scan, manually managing the recurrent state in shared memory. (c) Register the fused operator with the compiler so it appears as a single opaque node that is not lowered through standard passes. Expected result: 1.3-1.5× slower than FlashAttention instead of 2× — the residual gap is the irreducible cost of the serial dependency.

scenario: Your research team invents a novel 'Gated Linear Attention' (GLA) operator that replaces softmax attention. It achieves great accuracy but runs 2× slower than FlashAttention-2 on H100 despite having lower theoretical FLOP count. The operator involves a recurrent scan over sequence positions that cannot be expressed as a single GEMM call. Evaluate the compiler-hardware co-design challenge: why is the compiler failing to generate efficient code for this operator, and design a strategy to close the performance gap.
title: The Custom Op Compiler Co-Design

details.common_mistake: "MLIR's whole point is retargetability — just swap the backend and it should work." MLIR provides retargetability at the IR level, but performance portability requires hardware-specific optimization at multiple levels, not just the final lowering.
details.napkin_math: H100 training throughput (baseline): 100% (MFU ~55%). Naive MLIR retarget to MI300X: 60% of H100 throughput. Breakdown of the 40% gap: tiling mismatch = ~15% (wrong working set sizes), missing TMA codegen = ~10% (extra synchronization overhead), library coverage gap = ~15% (fallback to unoptimized kernels). After dedicated optimization work (~2 engineer-weeks): 88% of H100 throughput. Net cost savings: MI300X at 88% throughput × 70% cost = effective $0.80 per $1.00 H100-equivalent → 20% real savings.
details.realistic_solution: The retargetability promise breaks down at three levels: (1) **Tiling and memory hierarchy mismatch**: Tile sizes auto-tuned for H100 (80GB HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s, 50MB L2, 228KB shared memory per SM) are suboptimal for MI300X (192GB HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s, 256MB Infinity Cache, 64KB LDS per CU). MI300X's much larger cache favors different working-set sizes. The tiling passes in the mid-level dialects must be re-tuned. (2) **Missing hardware primitives**: NVIDIA's TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) for async tile loads has no direct MI300X equivalent — the compiler must generate explicit DMA commands, requiring different shared memory orchestration at the GPU dialect level. (3) **Library fallback gap**: cuBLAS/cuDNN provide hand-tuned kernels for common shapes on NVIDIA. rocBLAS/MIOpen on AMD have less coverage for exotic shapes (grouped GEMM for MoE, variable-length attention). The compiler must generate these kernels from scratch rather than dispatching to libraries. The fix requires: re-running auto-tuning on MI300X (~30 min), adding MI300X-specific tiling heuristics to the affine dialect passes, and writing custom Triton kernels for the 5-10 operator shapes where rocBLAS falls short. After this work, expect 85-90% of equivalent H100 throughput, making the 30% cost savings real.

scenario: Your company trained a 70B transformer on NVIDIA H100s using PyTorch. A cloud cost analysis shows that AMD MI300X GPUs offer 30% lower $/TFLOP. The plan is to retarget the compiled model using MLIR's multi-target lowering — keep the high-level dialects identical and swap only the final backend from NVVM to AMDGPU. After migration, actual training throughput is only 60% of the H100's, despite MI300X having comparable peak TFLOPS. Evaluate where the retargetability promise of MLIR breaks down and what additional work is required.
title: The MLIR Retargetability Boundary

details.common_mistake: "Just increase the cold-start SLA to 60 seconds." This is a product cop-out; the technical solutions have real tradeoffs worth analyzing.
details.napkin_math: Model with 80 unique kernel shapes. JIT compilation: 80 × 0.5s = 40s cold start (violates 5s SLA). Option A (cache load from S3): 80 × 25ms = 2s (meets SLA). Option B (AOT, load .so from disk): 80 × 12ms = 1s (meets SLA). Option C (eager fallback): 0s cold start, but eager throughput = 60% of compiled → at 1000 QPS, need 67% more GPUs for the first 40s = 0.75 extra GPU-minutes per deployment × 100 deployments/day = 75 GPU-minutes/day ≈ $2.50/day.
details.realistic_solution: **Option A (Kernel caching)**: Works because compiled kernels depend on the computation graph structure and input shapes, NOT on weight values. If the architecture is unchanged, all cached kernels are valid. Tradeoff: requires a cache invalidation strategy (architecture changes must bust the cache), and the cache must be distributed across the serving fleet (shared filesystem or object store). Cold start: ~2s (cache load from S3) — meets SLA. Risk: stale cache after architecture change causes silent correctness bugs. **Option B (AOT compilation in CI/CD)**: The most robust approach. Compile the model with representative input shapes during the build pipeline, serialize the compiled artifacts (TorchInductor's `.so` files), and deploy them alongside the weights. Cold start: ~1s (load pre-compiled .so + weights). Tradeoff: the CI/CD pipeline must know all input shapes in advance — unexpected shapes at serving time trigger fallback to eager mode or JIT compilation. For LLM serving with variable sequence lengths, this requires compiling for multiple shape buckets. Risk: CI/CD build time increases by 5-10 minutes. **Option C (Background compilation)**: Serve the first requests in eager mode (no compilation) while compiling in a background thread. Once compilation finishes, hot-swap to compiled kernels. Cold start: ~0.5s (eager mode is fast to start). Tradeoff: the first 10-45 seconds of traffic runs at 40-60% lower throughput (un-compiled), which may cause cascading latency if the load balancer sends too many requests. Risk: thread-safety issues during the hot-swap if not carefully implemented. **Recommendation**: Option B for production (most predictable), with Option C as a fallback for unexpected shapes.

scenario: Your serving fleet uses `torch.compile` to optimize inference kernels. When deploying a model update (same architecture, new weights), the first request after deployment takes 45 seconds because the compiler recompiles all kernels from scratch. This violates your 5-second cold-start SLA. The engineering team proposes three solutions: (A) cache compiled kernels and reuse across weight updates, (B) AOT-compile during CI/CD and ship pre-compiled artifacts, (C) serve un-compiled for the first 10 seconds while compilation happens in the background. Evaluate all three approaches and their tradeoffs.
title: The Compilation Latency Wall in Serving

details.common_mistake: "Fork the NVIDIA GPU backend and modify it for our hardware." GPU compilers assume SIMT execution (thousands of threads, shared memory, warp-level synchronization) — none of which applies to a message-passing dataflow architecture.
details.napkin_math: For a 70B model matmul (M=4096, N=8192, K=4096) on a 16×16 PE array (256 PEs): Each PE computes a $(256 \times 512)$ output tile. Per-PE SRAM needed: A tile (256×4096×2B = 2MB — too large!) → must K-tile: K_tile=128, A tile = 256×128×2B = 64KB, B tile = 128×512×2B = 128KB, output = 256×512×2B = 256KB. Total = 448KB > 256KB budget. Must further tile: reduce output to 128×256 → 64KB, A tile (128x128x2B) = 32KB, B tile (128x256x2B) = 64KB. Now total = 32+64+64 = 160KB ≤ 256KB. This requires 4× more communication rounds but fits in SRAM. Search space: 5 M_tile × 5 N_tile × 5 K_tile × 3 comm schedules = 375 configs × 100ms/eval = 37.5s auto-tuning time per kernel.
details.realistic_solution: The compiler stack requires 4 dialect levels with custom lowering passes: **Level 1 — Reuse `torch`/`linalg` dialects**: The top of the stack is hardware-independent. TorchDynamo captures the graph, and standard passes (operator fusion, constant folding, shape inference) apply unchanged. **Level 2 — Create a `dataflow` dialect**: This is the key innovation layer. Unlike GPU's `affine` loops, this dialect represents computation as a DAG of tiles mapped to PEs, with explicit communication edges. Operations: `dataflow.map_to_pe(tile, pe_id)`, `dataflow.send(tensor, src_pe, dst_pe)`, `dataflow.barrier(pe_group)`. The critical lowering pass here partitions the computation graph into subgraphs that fit within each PE's 256KB SRAM, minimizing inter-PE communication. This is a graph partitioning problem (NP-hard in general, but greedy heuristics with SRAM budget constraints work well). **Level 3 — Create a `pe_isa` dialect**: Lower the dataflow operations to per-PE instruction streams. Each PE gets a linear sequence of compute + send/receive instructions. The key optimization pass is communication-computation overlap: schedule `send` instructions early so the on-chip network transfers happen while the next computation executes. **Level 4 — Target codegen**: Emit the binary instruction stream for each PE plus the network routing configuration. Auto-tuning integrates at Level 2: the tile sizes, PE mapping strategy, and communication schedule form the search space. Because each configuration requires simulating the dataflow (not just timing one kernel), use a cycle-accurate simulator as the cost function, with Bayesian optimization to handle the expensive evaluation (~100ms per trial instead of 5ms for GPU kernels).

scenario: Your company is designing a custom AI accelerator with a novel dataflow architecture: a 2D array of processing elements (PEs), each with 256KB of local SRAM, connected by a configurable on-chip network. Unlike GPUs (SIMT) or TPUs (systolic arrays), your PEs execute independent instruction streams and communicate via explicit message passing. Design the compiler stack — from PyTorch model to executable — specifying which MLIR dialects you would create or reuse, where the key lowering passes occur, and how auto-tuning integrates with the novel hardware.
title: The New Accelerator Compiler Stack

details.common_mistake: Thinking cuDNN always uses the fastest algorithm regardless of context. In reality, algorithm selection depends on input/filter dimensions, available workspace memory, and whether deterministic mode is required.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-50 has ~53 conv layers. With `cudnn.benchmark=True`, first iteration benchmarks ~5-8 algorithms per layer = ~300-400 timed trials. Adds ~30-60 seconds to first iteration. Subsequent iterations see 10-20% throughput improvement from optimal algorithm selection — pays back within the first epoch on ImageNet.
details.realistic_solution: cuDNN selects convolution algorithms based on a combination of input tensor shape, filter size, stride, padding, available GPU workspace memory, and whether deterministic reproducibility is required. Implicit GEMM works well for standard 3×3 convolutions. FFT-based convolution wins for large spatial filters. Direct convolution is used for very small or 1×1 filters where the GEMM reshape overhead exceeds compute. Setting `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True` forces cuDNN to auto-tune by timing each algorithm on the first batch, then caching winners — essential for fixed-shape workloads.

scenario: You profile a ResNet-50 training job and notice that different convolutional layers use different cuDNN algorithms — some use implicit GEMM, others use FFT-based convolution, and one small layer uses direct convolution. You expected cuDNN to use the same algorithm everywhere. Why does cuDNN select different algorithms for different layers, and what is the primary factor driving this selection?
title: The cuDNN Convolution Dispatch

details.common_mistake: Blaming 'Python overhead' generically. The real issue is the framework dispatch stack: Python → PyTorch dispatcher → ATen operator selection → cuBLAS/cuDNN call → CUDA driver → kernel launch. Each hop adds latency, and with small/fast kernels, this overhead dominates.
details.napkin_math: 100 operators × 20μs GPU each = 2ms of GPU compute. 100 operators × 40μs CPU dispatch = 4ms overhead. Total = 6ms, GPU utilization = 2/6 = 33%. With torch.compile: CPU overhead drops to ~0.5ms (graph dispatch once). Total = 2.5ms, GPU utilization = 80%. With CUDA Graphs: CPU overhead ≈ 0. Total ≈ 2.1ms, GPU utilization ≈ 95%.
details.realistic_solution: The 65% idle time is the PyTorch dispatch overhead: (1) Python interpreter overhead per operator call (~10-20μs), (2) PyTorch's dispatcher traverses multiple dispatch keys (autograd, autocast, batched, vmap) even in inference mode (~5-15μs), (3) operator selection and argument marshaling (~5μs), (4) CUDA kernel launch latency (~5-10μs). For a 125M model with ~100 operators per forward pass, each taking ~20μs of GPU compute, the CPU overhead of ~40μs per operator dominates. Fixes: (1) `torch.compile()` to trace and fuse the graph, eliminating per-operator dispatch, (2) CUDA graphs to replay a captured kernel sequence with zero dispatch overhead, (3) TorchScript or export to remove Python entirely, (4) `torch.inference_mode()` to skip autograd dispatch keys.

scenario: You profile a small transformer model (125M parameters) doing inference with batch size 1 in PyTorch eager mode. The nsys trace shows that GPU kernels occupy only 35% of the wall-clock time — the rest is CPU-side overhead between kernel launches. Your colleague says 'the model is too small to saturate the GPU.' Is that the whole story? What specifically is happening in the 65% of time the GPU is idle, and what are your options to fix it?
title: The Framework Dispatch Overhead

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to 'always use vendor libraries' or 'always write custom kernels.' The correct answer depends on the operation's position on the library-coverage spectrum and the business cost of waiting.
details.napkin_math: Current: 23ms per token, routing = 5ms. Custom kernel (fused): routing drops to ~1.5ms. New total: 19.5ms (15% end-to-end speedup). Savings: 3.5ms per token. At 10,000 QPS serving fleet: saves 3.5ms × 10K = 35 GPU-seconds/second, meaning exactly 35 fewer GPUs needed. At $2/hr per GPU: ~$613K/year savings. Triton kernel development cost: ~2 engineer-weeks. ROI: <1 week.
details.realistic_solution: Evaluate across four axes: (1) Performance gap: 22% of latency in routing means a custom kernel could save 3.5ms per token on a 23ms budget — significant for SLA and fleet cost (saving 35 GPUs). (2) Maintenance cost: Triton kernels are ~10× easier to maintain than raw CUDA, but still require updates per GPU generation. (3) Correctness risk: MoE routing has complex data-dependent control flow; bugs cause silent accuracy loss. (4) Time value: 6 months of serving at 22% overhead costs real money. Decision framework: if the operation is on the critical path AND vendor coverage is >3 months away AND the operation's data access pattern is non-standard (irregular scatter/gather, not dense GEMM), write the custom kernel. Dense matmul → always use cuBLAS. Custom attention variants → use FlashAttention or Triton. Non-standard data movement patterns (MoE routing, speculative decoding verification) → custom kernel territory.

scenario: Your inference serving team runs a 70B MoE model. Profiling shows that the top-K expert routing + scatter/gather operations account for 22% of per-token latency. These operations use PyTorch's native indexing and scatter_ operators, which dispatch to generic cuBLAS/cuDNN routines. A kernel engineer proposes writing a custom Triton kernel that fuses the routing decision, expert dispatch, and result gathering into a single kernel. The library vendor (NVIDIA) says their next cuDNN release will include optimized MoE primitives in 6 months. How do you make this build-vs-wait decision?
title: The Library vs Custom Kernel Decision

details.common_mistake: Confusing nvidia-smi's 'used memory' with PyTorch's allocated memory. The 15GB gap (45GB - 30GB) is not 'free' — it's held by PyTorch's caching allocator as a pool of freed-but-not-returned CUDA blocks.
details.napkin_math: 45GB reported by nvidia-smi = 30GB actively allocated + 15GB in caching allocator free list. The 15GB free list might contain 3,000 blocks averaging 5MB each. Largest contiguous free block: ~50MB. Needed: 20GB contiguous. Gap: 400×. Even `empty_cache()` may not help if CUDA driver memory is itself fragmented from repeated alloc/free cycles.
details.realistic_solution: PyTorch's caching allocator (CUDACachingAllocator) never returns memory to the CUDA driver by default. When tensors are freed, their CUDA blocks go into a free list, fragmented by size. The 15GB in the cache is split across many small blocks (e.g., thousands of 2MB and 8MB fragments from previous forward passes). The 20GB KV-cache needs a single contiguous allocation that no combination of cached fragments can satisfy. Diagnosis: `torch.cuda.memory_stats()` shows `allocated_bytes`, `reserved_bytes`, and `num_alloc_retries`. Fix: (1) `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` returns all cached blocks to the CUDA driver (but causes re-allocation overhead), (2) Pre-allocate the KV-cache at startup before fragmentation occurs, (3) Use `max_split_size_mb` environment variable to limit block splitting, (4) Use memory-pool-aware allocation like vLLM's PagedAttention which manages KV-cache in fixed-size blocks.

scenario: Your serving system runs a 13B model on an A100-80GB GPU. `nvidia-smi` reports 45GB used, and `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()` shows 30GB. Yet when you try to allocate a 20GB KV-cache buffer, PyTorch throws an OOM error despite 50GB appearing 'free' on the device. The ops team says 'the GPU has plenty of memory.' Why does the allocation fail, and what is the role of PyTorch's caching allocator in this failure?
title: The Caching Allocator Fragmentation Trap

details.common_mistake: Treating graph breaks as harmless warnings. Each graph break forces torch.compile to exit the compiled region, fall back to Python eager execution, then re-enter compilation — destroying the fusion and memory planning benefits across break boundaries.
details.napkin_math: Expected: 1 compiled graph, full operator fusion, ~2× speedup. Actual: 48 subgraphs. Average subgraph: ~3 operators (150 total / 48). Per-subgraph fusion benefit: minimal (need 5+ operators to amortize compile overhead). Cross-subgraph dispatch overhead: 48 × ~30μs = 1.4ms added. If baseline inference is 15ms, the overhead alone eats 10% of runtime — turning a 2× speedup into 1.1×.
details.realistic_solution: A graph break is where TorchDynamo (the Python bytecode tracer) encounters an operation it cannot represent in the FX graph, forcing a fallback to eager mode. Your 47 breaks come from three sources: (1) Data-dependent control flow (`if token_count > max_len`) — the tracer cannot statically resolve the branch. Fix: use `torch.cond()` or guard with `torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic()`. (2) Python side effects (logging inside forward) — I/O operations cannot be captured in a computational graph. Fix: move logging outside the compiled region or use `torch._dynamo.allow_in_graph()`. (3) Third-party library calls (tokenizer) — opaque Python functions break tracing. Fix: move tokenizer outside the compiled function boundary. Priority: eliminate breaks in the hot path first. The 47 breaks likely fragment the model into ~48 tiny subgraphs, each compiled independently — no cross-subgraph fusion is possible. Reducing to 0 breaks allows the entire model to be one fused graph.

scenario: You apply `torch.compile()` to your custom 7B transformer and expect a 2× inference speedup based on published benchmarks. Instead, you see only a 1.1× improvement. The compilation log shows 47 graph breaks. The model uses dynamic control flow (`if token_count > max_len: truncate()`), custom Python logging inside the forward pass, and calls a third-party tokenizer library within the model. What is a graph break, why did you get 47 of them, and how do you systematically eliminate them to recover the expected speedup?
title: The torch.compile Graph Break Cascade

details.common_mistake: Assuming PyTorch automatically skips gradient tracking during inference. Without explicit `torch.no_grad()` or `torch.inference_mode()`, PyTorch's autograd engine records the computational graph for every forward pass, storing intermediate activations for potential backward passes that will never happen.
details.napkin_math: 7B model in FP16 = 14GB weights. Without inference_mode: autograd stores ~1 activation tensor per layer. 32 transformer layers × ~430MB activations per layer ≈ 13.8GB. Total: 14 + 13.8 ≈ 28GB. With inference_mode: 14GB weights only. Memory savings: 50%. Latency improvement: ~5-15% from eliminated autograd bookkeeping CPU overhead.
details.realistic_solution: The extra 14GB is autograd's activation stash. By default, PyTorch's autograd system records intermediate tensors (activations at each layer boundary) during the forward pass so gradients can be computed during backward. For a 7B transformer at batch=1 with sequence length 2048, activations consume roughly 1× the model size. Fix: wrap inference in `torch.inference_mode()` (preferred over `torch.no_grad()` because it also disables version counting and view tracking, saving additional memory and CPU overhead). This eliminates the activation stash entirely. Additional optimization: set `model.eval()` to switch BatchNorm/Dropout to inference behavior, and ensure `requires_grad=False` on all parameters.

scenario: A production inference service running a 7B model in PyTorch shows that `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()` reports 28GB, but the model weights are only 14GB in FP16. The serving code uses a simple `model(input)` call. No optimizer or gradient accumulation is present. Where is the extra 14GB coming from, and how do you reclaim it?
title: The Autograd Overhead in Serving

details.common_mistake: Standardizing on TensorRT or ONNX Runtime for everything. Each runtime makes architectural assumptions (static shapes, dense compute, single-model-per-GPU) that break down for at least one of these workloads.
details.napkin_math: BERT on TensorRT vs PyTorch eager: 1.2ms vs 5ms (4× faster). 70B LLM on vLLM vs naive PyTorch: 40 tokens/s vs 8 tokens/s per GPU (5× throughput from PagedAttention + continuous batching). Object detection: TensorRT + CUDA Graphs gives P99 < 15ms; PyTorch eager P99 = 45ms with jitter spikes to 100ms. RecSys: embedding lookup is 80% of latency — no amount of compute optimization helps if embeddings don't fit in VRAM. Diffusion: 50 denoising steps × 20ms per step = 1s; CUDA Graphs eliminate 50 × 15μs = 0.75ms dispatch overhead — small but compounds with batching.
details.realistic_solution: Each model has a different bottleneck that favors a different runtime: (1) BERT classifier → TensorRT: static shapes, INT8 quantizable, layer fusion gives 3-5× over eager PyTorch. Rebuilt weekly via TensorRT build cache. (2) 70B LLM → vLLM/TensorRT-LLM: needs PagedAttention for KV-cache, continuous batching for throughput, tensor parallelism across GPUs. Generic runtimes lack these LLM-specific memory management features. (3) Object detection at 30 FPS → TensorRT with CUDA Graphs: hard real-time latency constraint means you cannot tolerate jitter from dynamic batching or Python dispatch. Pre-built engine with captured CUDA graph gives deterministic <33ms. (4) Recommendation model → custom serving (HugeCTR/TorchRec): 500M embedding rows cannot fit in GPU memory; needs CPU-GPU hybrid serving with embedding-specific sharding. Standard runtimes assume dense models that fit in VRAM. (5) Diffusion model → PyTorch with torch.compile or ONNX Runtime: iterative denoising loop (20-50 steps) means the runtime must efficiently handle repeated kernel launches of the same graph. CUDA Graphs work well here. The principle: runtime selection is determined by the model's dominant resource bottleneck (compute-bound → TensorRT, memory-bound → vLLM, latency-bound → CUDA Graphs, capacity-bound → hybrid serving).

scenario: Your ML platform team must serve five models in production: (1) a BERT classifier updated weekly, (2) a 70B LLM with continuous batching, (3) a real-time object detection model at 30 FPS, (4) a recommendation model with a 500M-row embedding table, and (5) a diffusion model for image generation. The team wants to standardize on a single inference runtime. You argue this is a mistake. Design a runtime selection strategy, explaining which runtime or serving framework best fits each model and why a single runtime cannot serve all five optimally.
title: The Runtime Selection for Multi-Model Serving

details.common_mistake: Abandoning CUDA Graphs entirely and reverting to eager mode. Or trying to pad everything to max dimensions, which wastes compute proportional to the padding ratio.
details.napkin_math: Eager mode decode step: 1.5ms (0.5ms compute + 1.0ms dispatch overhead). CUDA Graph decode step: 0.6ms (0.5ms compute + 0.1ms graph replay). With padding overhead (average 20% wasted compute): 0.7ms. Net speedup over eager: 1.5/0.7 = 2.1× per decode step. For a 500-token generation: eager = 750ms, CUDA Graph bucketed = 350ms. Memory cost: 192 graphs × 80MB = ~15GB. On 80GB GPU with 14GB model (FP16 7B): leaves 51GB for KV-cache — acceptable.
details.realistic_solution: Use a bucketed CUDA Graph strategy combined with padding. (1) Bucket batch sizes into powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) and sequence lengths into fixed strides (e.g., multiples of 128). This yields ~6 × ~32 = ~192 graph variants instead of thousands. (2) Pad inputs to the next bucket boundary. Wasted compute from padding is bounded: worst case is 2× for batch and ~128 tokens for sequence — in practice ~15-25% overhead. (3) Pre-capture all graph variants at startup during warmup. Each graph consumes ~50-100MB (kernel parameters, not model weights), so 192 graphs ≈ 10-20GB — manageable on 80GB GPUs. (4) For continuous batching: capture graphs per decode step, not per entire generation. Each step has a fixed graph selected by current (padded_batch, padded_seq) bucket. This is exactly what TensorRT-LLM and vLLM implement internally. The tradeoff: you accept ~15-25% padding waste to eliminate ~30% dispatch overhead. Net improvement: ~10-20% over eager mode with full dynamic shape support.

scenario: Your team captures the entire LLM decode loop as a CUDA Graph to eliminate kernel launch overhead, achieving a 30% latency reduction for fixed-length generation. But when you deploy to production, you discover that real user requests have highly variable output lengths (10 to 4,000 tokens) and variable batch sizes (continuous batching adds/removes requests mid-generation). The CUDA Graph breaks because it was captured with a fixed batch size and fixed sequence length. The naive fix — capturing a separate CUDA Graph for every possible (batch_size, seq_len) combination — would require thousands of graphs consuming hundreds of GB of GPU memory. Design a practical solution that preserves most of the CUDA Graph benefits while handling dynamic shapes.
title: The CUDA Graphs vs Dynamic Shapes Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Assuming that any sparsity ratio can be accelerated, and that higher sparsity always means more speedup. The hardware supports exactly one sparsity pattern.
details.napkin_math: Dense 4 elements: 4 multiplies, 4 values stored. 2:4 sparse: 2 multiplies + 2-bit index, 2 values + metadata stored. Memory reduction: ~50%. Compute reduction: exactly 2x on the supported datapath. 1:4 would save 75% compute but requires custom hardware that doesn't exist in current Tensor Cores.
