The cloud, having abundant compute, receives the INT16 updates, casts them to FP32, performs the global aggregation (FedAvg), updates the global FP32 model, applies Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) to convert it back to INT8, and pushes the INT8 model back to the edge.

scenario: A cloud system aggregates weights for Federated Learning on Cortex-M0+ devices (no FPU). The edge model must be INT8 for inference speed and memory. However, computing gradients and updating weights strictly in INT8 leads to catastrophic catastrophic quantization error and training divergence. The cloud must orchestrate updates without requiring FP32 on the edge.
title: Mixed-Precision Federated Aggregation

details.common_mistake: Assuming pausing jobs completely during high-carbon periods will strictly reduce total carbon footprint without factoring in idle power draw.
details.napkin_math: Active node: 8 GPUs * 400W + 1000W host = 4.2kW. Idle node: 8 GPUs * 75W + 500W host = 1.1kW. Pause strategy for 6h: burns 1.1kW * 6h = 6.6 kWh of dirty energy (600g/kWh) for 0 tokens. Total CO2 = 3.96 kg CO2 per node just idling! DVFS cap at 250W/GPU: Node draws 8*250 + 1000 = 3.0kW. You burn 3.0kW * 6h = 18 kWh, but retain ~80% throughput, radically improving the carbon-per-token compared to idling.
details.realistic_solution: Pausing jobs is often suboptimal because a suspended GPU node still draws significant idle power (often 20-30% of peak) while accomplishing zero useful work, degrading the overall energy-efficiency metrics. Furthermore, prolonging the training time reduces the amortization of the embedded carbon (manufacturing footprint) of the GPUs over useful jobs. Instead of a full pause, a better tradeoff is implementing DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) during peak carbon hours. Capping power to 60% of peak TDP might retain 80% of throughput due to non-linear power-to-frequency scaling (CMOS power equation $P \propto fV^2$). This reduces the immediate power draw when grid carbon is dirty, keeps the GPUs in a high-efficiency regime (perf/watt), and avoids wasting baseline idle power.

scenario: Your 2,000-GPU cluster in Texas runs flexible offline RLHF training. The grid's carbon intensity fluctuates daily from 200g CO2/kWh (high wind/solar) to 600g CO2/kWh (gas/coal peaks). The sustainability team proposes pausing all training for 6 hours daily during peak carbon hours to meet ESG goals. A hardware engineer objects, citing idle power and TCO. Evaluate the tradeoffs of this pause strategy.
title: Carbon-Aware Scheduling Tradeoffs

details.common_mistake: Optimizing solely for SLA by forcing batch size 1, ignoring that memory bandwidth dominates power draw at low batch sizes and destroys perf/watt.
details.napkin_math: BS=1: 3.5 kW. Throughput = 50 tokens/sec. Energy/token = 3500 W / 50 tps = 70 Joules/token. BS=64: 6.5 kW. Throughput = 2000 tokens/sec. Energy/token = 6500 W / 2000 tps = 3.25 Joules/token. Operating at BS=64 is ~21.5x more energy efficient per token. If you charge per token, BS=1 ruins unit economics.
details.realistic_solution: Enforcing a strict 50ms TTFT by keeping batch sizes near 1 leads to severe underutilization of the GPU's compute capacity while still incurring massive static and memory-transfer power costs. At BS=1, the operation is heavily memory-bandwidth bound; you are paying to power the entire HBM stack and interconnect just to process a single sequence. This results in an extremely high energy cost per token and poor TCO. To balance the tradeoff, you should implement continuous batching and decouple the prefill phase from the decode phase (chunked prefill). By processing prefill chunks in parallel with decodes, you can maintain high compute density (pushing power draw up, but drastically increasing tokens/second) while keeping TTFT within SLA. The goal is to maximize the ratio of active compute power to fixed background power, minimizing the Joules per token.

scenario: You are serving Llama-3-70B on 8xH100 instances. At batch size 1, Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) is 20ms, and the node draws 3.5 kW. At batch size 64, TTFT rises to 400ms, and the node draws 6.5 kW. The product team demands a strict 50ms TTFT SLA. Analyze the tradeoff between meeting this SLA and the serving cost per token, and propose a solution.
title: LLM Serving Batch Size Energy

details.common_mistake: Assuming throughput scales linearly with power, leading to the false conclusion that 10,000 GPUs at 1000W yield the same throughput as 14,000 GPUs at 700W.
details.napkin_math: Option A: 10,000 GPUs * 1000W = 10 MW. Perf = 10,000 units. Option B: 14,000 GPUs * 700W = 9.8 MW. At 700W (70% TDP), GPUs retain ~85% performance. Perf = 14,000 * 0.85 = 11,900 units. Option B yields 19% more total throughput for the same 10 MW power envelope, but increases CapEx by 40%.
details.realistic_solution: Power and clock frequency scale non-linearly. Because dynamic power scales with the cube of frequency/voltage ($P \propto fV^2$), reducing the power cap by 30% (from 1000W to 700W) typically only reduces the GPU clock frequency and overall throughput by about 10-15%. Therefore, overprovisioning the data center with 14,000 GPUs running at 700W will yield significantly higher total cluster throughput than 10,000 GPUs at 1000W. The tradeoff, however, is Capital Expenditure (CapEx) and networking. You must purchase 4,000 additional GPUs, switches, and host nodes. You must calculate if the ~19% gain in total throughput generates enough revenue to offset the massive CapEx increase of buying 40% more hardware. In cloud environments where power is the absolute bottleneck (power wall), hardware overprovisioning with aggressive power capping is the optimal path for maximizing perf/watt.

scenario: You are designing a new cluster with a hard 10 MW facility limit. You can either deploy 10,000 GPUs running at their full 1000W TDP, or overprovision by buying 14,000 GPUs and aggressively power-capping them to 700W each. Both scenarios max out the 10 MW limit. Evaluate the tradeoff between cluster throughput and TCO.
title: Overprovisioning Under Power Caps

details.common_mistake: Calculating savings based on the IT load (5 MW) rather than the overhead power saved via the PUE delta, or ignoring the payback period entirely.
details.napkin_math: Current Total Power = 5 MW * 1.5 PUE = 7.5 MW. New Total Power = 5 MW * 1.15 PUE = 5.75 MW. Power Savings = 1.75 MW. Annual Energy Savings = 1,750 kW * 8760 hours/yr = 15,330,000 kWh/yr. Financial Savings = 15,330,000 * $0.12 = $1,839,600 / year. Payback Period = $8,000,000 / $1,839,600 ≈ 4.35 years.
details.realistic_solution: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of total facility power to IT equipment power. A PUE of 1.5 means for every 1 Watt of IT load, 0.5 Watts is spent on cooling and overhead. Retrofitting to liquid cooling drops the overhead from 50% to 15%. However, evaluating this tradeoff requires calculating the payback period against the CapEx. While liquid cooling vastly improves energy-efficiency metrics and allows for denser racks (reducing network cable lengths and latency), an $8M retrofit for a legacy facility might have a payback period that exceeds the remaining lifespan of the current hardware generation. The tradeoff is between long-term TCO/sustainability vs upfront CapEx and downtime during the retrofit. If the facility is slated for high-TDP next-gen GPUs (like B200s), the retrofit becomes mandatory due to thermal limits, overriding pure ROI calculations.

scenario: Your 5 MW (IT load) datacenter currently relies on air cooling, operating at a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.5. A proposal suggests retrofitting to Direct-to-Chip (D2C) liquid cooling, which would lower the PUE to 1.15 but costs $8,000,000 in CapEx. Electricity costs $0.12 per kWh. Evaluate the financial and operational tradeoffs of this retrofit.
title: Liquid Cooling Retrofit ROI

details.common_mistake: Assuming quantization always yields an immediate carbon benefit without quantifying the massive upfront emission cost of the retraining and distillation process.
details.napkin_math: Retraining: 512 GPUs * 400W * 1.5 PUE = ~307 kW. For 14 days (336h): 307 * 336 = 103,152 kWh. Inference savings: INT8 saves ~200W per 8-GPU node. Processing 5M requests takes ~10,000 node-hours/day. Savings = 10,000 * 200W = 2,000 kWh/day. Break-even = 103,152 kWh / 2,000 kWh/day = ~51.5 days. If the model lifespan > 2 months, it is carbon-positive.
details.realistic_solution: Evaluating the carbon ROI requires comparing the one-time carbon cost of retraining against the recurring carbon savings during inference. Distillation and Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) are highly compute-intensive. While INT8 reduces memory bandwidth requirements and utilizes efficient tensor cores, lowering the per-token inference energy, the upfront training emissions are massive. If the model is updated frequently (e.g., retrained monthly) or has low inference traffic, the project will be carbon-negative overall. The tradeoff balances model accuracy, upfront compute cost (CapEx/Carbon), and long-term serving efficiency (OpEx/Carbon). A proper decision requires calculating the break-even point in days to see if it fits within the model's deployment lifespan.

scenario: Your team serves a 175B parameter FP16 model, processing 5 million requests daily. An engineer proposes distilling and quantizing the model to INT8 to save inference power. The retraining/distillation process will require 512 A100 GPUs running continuously for 14 days. Evaluate the carbon footprint tradeoff: when do we break even on the carbon emitted during retraining?
title: Model Compression Carbon ROI

details.common_mistake: Believing FL is greener because edge devices don't have cooling overhead (PUE=1.0), ignoring the severe compute inefficiency of mobile SoCs compared to datacenter GPUs.
details.napkin_math: Cloud: 500 hours * 700W (GPU) * 1.3 PUE = ~455 kWh. FL Edge Compute: 500,000 phones * 2 hours/round * 10 rounds * 4W (SoC active power) = 40,000,000 Wh = 40,000 kWh. FL Network transfer: 500,000 phones * 100MB/round * 10 rounds = 500 TB transferred. At ~0.1 kWh/GB for mobile networks = 50,000 kWh. Total FL Energy = 90,000 kWh. FL consumes ~200x more energy than the cloud.
details.realistic_solution: While Federated Learning avoids the energy cost of transferring massive datasets to the cloud and benefits from an effective PUE of 1.0 (smartphones passively cool into the air), edge processors are orders of magnitude less energy-efficient per FLOP than datacenter accelerators like the H100. Furthermore, FL introduces significant communication overhead; transmitting weight updates across cellular/WiFi networks consumes massive amounts of energy. The tradeoff heavily favors the centralized cloud for total energy efficiency. Shifting to FL is an active choice to prioritize data privacy and data locality at the direct expense of a drastically increased global carbon footprint and total energy consumption.

scenario: To improve data privacy, your team proposes moving a personalization model's training from a centralized cloud cluster to Federated Learning (FL) across 500,000 user smartphones. Cloud training takes 500 GPU-hours on H100s. FL requires 10 rounds of training, with each smartphone computing for 2 hours per round. Analyze the energy and carbon tradeoffs of this architectural shift.
title: Cloud vs Edge FL Energy Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Provisioning racks homogeneously based on the worst-case TDP (650W), resulting in only 1 node per rack and severely underutilizing the facility footprint.
details.napkin_math: Compute node (8 × 650 W + 2 kW host) = 7.2 kW. Inference node (8 × 350 W + 2 kW host) = 4.8 kW. Homogeneous compute: 2 nodes = 14.4 kW, 16 GPUs. Homogeneous inference: 3 nodes = 14.4 kW, 24 GPUs. Mixed rack: 1 compute node (7.2 kW) + 1 inference node (4.8 kW) = 12.0 kW, 16 GPUs with 3 kW headroom. This serves both workload types from one rack. Better: dynamic power-aware scheduling. When compute jobs finish, those GPUs shift to inference workload (350 W), dropping the node from 7.2 kW to 4.8 kW. This frees power budget for bursting other nodes. Peak: 2 × 7.2 = 14.4 kW (16 compute GPUs). Off-peak: 2 × 4.8 = 9.6 kW (16 inference GPUs) with 5.4 kW headroom for a 3rd partial node. Time-multiplexing power budgets across workload phases is more effective than static mixed allocation.
details.realistic_solution: If you deploy homogeneous compute-bound nodes, a single node draws (8 * 650W) + 2000W = 7.2 kW. You can only fit two nodes (14.4 kW) per 15 kW rack. If you deploy inference nodes, a node draws (8 * 350W) + 2000W = 4.8 kW. You could fit three nodes (14.4 kW). To maximize data center throughput and rack density, you should implement spatial workload colocation: scheduling a mix of memory-bound and compute-bound workloads on the *same* node or within the *same* rack. By pairing workloads that stress different hardware components (HBM vs. SMs), you smooth out the power draw. The optimal tradeoff involves accepting higher scheduling complexity (orchestrating Kubernetes to bin-pack pods based on real-time power profiles rather than just CPU/RAM) to achieve higher hardware density and lower TCO.

scenario: Your infrastructure has 15 kW power limits per rack. You run two workloads: LLM inference (memory-bandwidth bound, low Tensor Core utilization, draws 350W/GPU) and offline batched MatMuls (compute-bound, heavily utilizes Tensor Cores, draws 650W/GPU). A standard node has 8 GPUs and uses ~2 kW of host overhead. Propose a scheduling strategy to maximize rack utilization without tripping the 15 kW breakers.
title: Rack-Level Thermal Colocation

details.common_mistake: Confusing TSVs with interposers. TSVs go through the die; the interposer is the silicon substrate that connects stacks to the GPU laterally.
details.napkin_math: HBM3: 1024-bit bus × 6.4 Gbps per pin = 819 GB/s per stack. 4 stacks on H100 = 3.35 TB/s. DDR5: 64-bit bus × 6.4 Gbps = 51 GB/s per channel. Would need 64 DDR5 channels to match.
details.realistic_solution: TSVs are microscopic copper pillars etched directly through silicon dies, providing thousands of parallel vertical connections in the area where wire bonds would only fit dozens. Each TSV is ~5-10 micrometers in diameter vs. ~25 micrometers for wire bonds, enabling 1024+ simultaneous data paths per stack. This massive parallelism is how HBM achieves 1024-bit bus width vs. DDR5's 64-bit bus, yielding ~16x more bandwidth per pin.

scenario: A hardware architect explains that HBM3 achieves 3.35 TB/s bandwidth by stacking DRAM dies vertically. Your interviewer asks why traditional wire-bonding between dies cannot achieve the same bandwidth density.
title: Cloud Through Silicon Vias L2 0

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply by 4 stacks for total HBM bandwidth, or confusing Gbps (bits) with GB/s (bytes).
details.napkin_math: HBM3: 4 stacks × 1024-bit × 6.4 Gbps ÷ 8 = 3,276 GB/s. DDR5: 64-bit × 6.4 Gbps ÷ 8 = 51.2 GB/s. Need 3,276 / 51.2 ≈ 64 channels.
details.realistic_solution: HBM3 total bandwidth: 1024 bits × 6.4 Gbps / 8 = 819.2 GB/s per stack × 4 stacks = 3276.8 GB/s ≈ 3.35 TB/s. DDR5 per channel: 64 bits × 6.4 Gbps / 8 = 51.2 GB/s. Channels needed: 3276.8 / 51.2 = 64 DDR5 channels. This is physically impractical — each channel needs its own traces, pins, and DIMM slots, illustrating why TSVs are essential for AI accelerators.

scenario: You are comparing an HBM3-based accelerator (1024-bit bus, 4 stacks, 6.4 Gbps/pin) against a hypothetical design using DDR5 (64-bit bus, 6.4 Gbps/pin). How many DDR5 channels would match the HBM3 bandwidth?
title: Cloud Through Silicon Vias L3 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming compute (FLOPS) is the bottleneck for LLM decode. At batch=1, decode is purely memory-bandwidth-bound since each weight is used only once per token.
details.napkin_math: 70B × 2B/param = 140 GB. 4-stack: 140/3.35 = 41.8 ms/tok → 24 tok/s. 6-stack: 140/5.0 = 28 ms/tok → 36 tok/s. 50% throughput gain for ~40% cost increase.
details.realistic_solution: 70B model in FP16 = 140 GB. At batch=1 autoregressive decode, each token reads all weights once. With 3.35 TB/s: 140 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 41.8 ms/token ≈ 24 tok/s. With 5.0 TB/s: 140 GB / 5.0 TB/s = 28 ms/token ≈ 36 tok/s. The 6-stack design gives 50% more tokens/s. If SLA requires >30 tok/s, the cheaper option fails. Cost per token: if 6-stack costs 40% more but serves 50% more tokens, it is more cost-efficient at high utilization.

scenario: Your team is choosing between an accelerator with 6 HBM3 stacks (expensive, 5 TB/s) and one with 4 HBM3 stacks (cheaper, 3.35 TB/s) for serving a memory-bandwidth-bound 70B LLM. How do you evaluate the trade-off?
title: Cloud Through Silicon Vias L5 0

details.common_mistake: Treating network failures as independent per-server events. In reality, a single ToR switch failure is correlated — it takes out all servers in that rack simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: Typical rack: 8 GPU servers × 8 GPUs = 64 GPUs per rack. A 256-GPU cluster = 4 racks, 4 ToR switches. Single ToR failure = 25% of compute lost. MTBF of a switch ≈ 100K hours.
details.realistic_solution: A ToR switch is the first aggregation point connecting all servers in a single rack (typically 32-48 ports). It exists because cabling every server directly to a spine switch is physically impractical — cable lengths, port counts, and cost all explode. The key implication: a ToR switch failure takes down an entire rack (8-16 servers). This defines the minimum failure domain for distributed training — checkpoint strategies and job placement must account for rack-level failures.

scenario: During a datacenter design review, someone proposes connecting all 256 GPUs in a training cluster directly to a single large switch. Explain why top-of-rack switches exist and what failure domain implications they create.
title: Cloud Top Of Rack Switch L2 0

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that all GPUs in the rack share the same ToR uplink bandwidth. The per-GPU cross-rack bandwidth is the uplink divided by the number of GPUs, not the raw link speed.
details.napkin_math: ToR uplink: 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s. 64 GPUs per rack sharing uplink. Per-GPU cross-rack BW: 50/64 = 0.78 GB/s. NVLink intra-node: 600 GB/s (A100). Ratio: 600/0.78 ≈ 769x slower cross-rack.
details.realistic_solution: Each rack has 64 GPUs. ToR uplink to spine: 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s. During ring AllReduce across racks, data must traverse the ToR uplink. With 64 GPUs in a rack all needing cross-rack bandwidth: 50 GB/s / 64 GPUs = 0.78 GB/s per GPU cross-rack. Compare to intra-rack NVLink at 600 GB/s per GPU (for A100) — cross-rack is ~769x slower. This is why AllReduce topology must minimize cross-rack traffic.

scenario: You have a 512-GPU training cluster spread across 8 racks with 400 Gbps ToR uplinks. Each rack has 64 GPUs performing AllReduce. Estimate the maximum cross-rack AllReduce bandwidth per GPU.
title: Cloud Top Of Rack Switch L3 0

details.common_mistake: Always waiting for full repair. For long training runs, the opportunity cost of idle time far exceeds the small throughput penalty of running on fewer GPUs.
details.napkin_math: Option A: 5 min restore + 93.75 samples/s ongoing. Option B: 30 min idle + 100 samples/s. Equation for breakeven time T: (T - 5) × 93.75 = (T - 30) × 100. -> 93.75T - 468.75 = 100T - 3000 -> 6.25T = 2531.25 -> T = 405 minutes.
details.realistic_solution: Option A: 960 GPUs at ~93.75% original throughput = 93.75 samples/s. Checkpoint restore takes ~5 min. Net: training resumes in 5 min but 6.25% slower. Option B: wait 30 min idle, then resume at full 100 samples/s. Break-even calculation: (T - 5) × 93.75 = (T - 30) × 100. T = 405 minutes (6.75 hours). If the remaining training time is longer than 405 minutes, option A (restarting immediately) will process more total samples. For most large training runs (days/weeks), restart immediately on 960 GPUs.

scenario: Your 1024-GPU training job experiences a ToR switch failure in one of 16 racks, killing 64 GPUs. You can either (A) restart from checkpoint on remaining 960 GPUs or (B) wait ~30 min for rack repair. Training processes 100 samples/s across 1024 GPUs. Evaluate the trade-off.
title: Cloud Top Of Rack Switch L5 0

details.common_mistake: Believing TorchDynamo eliminates all graph breaks. It handles them gracefully (compile what it can, fall back for the rest), but graph breaks still reduce optimization opportunities.
details.napkin_math: Typical model: 90% of compute is in linear attention/FFN blocks (compilable). 10% is dynamic routing/control flow. TorchDynamo compiles the 90%, eager-executes 10%. Net speedup: if compiled code is 2x faster, overall = 1 / (0.1 + 0.9/2) = 1.82x.
details.realistic_solution: Traditional tracing (like torch.jit.trace) records operator calls for one execution path and misses branches. TorchDynamo intercepts Python bytecode instructions, so it sees if-statements, loops, and data-dependent branches before they execute. When it encounters untraceable code (graph breaks), it compiles the captured subgraph, falls back to eager Python for the break, then resumes capturing. This gives the best of both worlds: compiled fast paths for linear code and correctness for dynamic Python.

scenario: A colleague says 'TorchDynamo captures the computation graph by tracing at the Python bytecode level instead of the operator level.' Explain why bytecode-level capture matters and how it handles dynamic control flow.
title: Cloud Torchdynamo L2 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming graph breaks have zero overhead. Each break incurs Python interpreter re-entry, guard checks, and prevents cross-region fusion optimizations.
details.napkin_math: With breaks: 12 + 8 = 20 ms, 1.75x speedup. Compiled speedup ratio: (35-8)/(12) ≈ 2.25x on compiled portion. If 8 ms also compiled at 2.25x: 8/2.25 = 3.6 ms. Best case: 12 + 3.6 = 15.6 ms → 2.24x.
details.realistic_solution: Current total: 12 ms (compiled) + 8 ms (eager) = 20 ms. Speedup vs. baseline: 35 / 20 = 1.75x. The uncompiled time of the compiled regions was 35 - 8 = 27 ms. Thus, the compiled speedup is 27 / 12 = 2.25x. Applying similar optimization to the 8 ms eager portion: 8 / 2.25 ≈ 3.56 ms. Potential total: 12 + 3.56 = 15.56 ms → 35 / 15.56 = 2.25x. Eliminating graph breaks could yield an additional 28% speedup (from 20ms to 15.56ms).

scenario: You profile a Transformer model with torch.compile(). TorchDynamo reports 3 graph breaks. The compiled regions take 12 ms total, and the eager fallback regions take 8 ms. Without compilation, the full model takes 35 ms. Calculate the speedup and estimate the potential if graph breaks were eliminated.
title: Cloud Torchdynamo L3 0

details.common_mistake: Only considering the current training run. Compilation speedups persist for all future runs, making the refactoring investment amortize over time, while extra GPU costs recur.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 64 × 14 × 24h × $2 = $43,008. Refactor: 14 days / 1.4x = 10 days. Cost: 64 × 10 × 24 × $2 = $30,720. More GPUs (Linear scaling): 83 GPUs × 10.8 days × 24h × $2 = $43,027. Savings for refactoring: ~$12.3K per run + future runs. Adding GPUs doesn't cost more overall compute money than baseline, but requires procuring 30% more hardware.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (refactor): 2 weeks dev time. If torch.compile gives 1.5-2x speedup on compiled regions and the model is ~60% compilable currently, eliminating breaks could yield 1.4x overall speedup. Training: 14 / 1.4 = 10 days. Option B (more GPUs): 30% more = 83 A100s. Linear scaling: 14 / 1.3 = 10.8 days. Cost: 83 A100s × 10.8 days × 24h × $2/hr = $43,027. Option A is ~$12.3K cheaper per run and reduces absolute cluster size requirements. Option B avoids engineering time but permanently blocks larger hardware allocations.

scenario: Your team debates whether to invest 2 weeks refactoring a custom model with many graph breaks to be fully torch.compile-compatible, or to keep eager mode and buy 30% more GPUs. Current training takes 14 days on 64 A100s. Evaluate both options.
title: Cloud Torchdynamo L5 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming the train-serve split means the edge device never needs updates. In practice, you need a model update pipeline to push retrained/fine-tuned models to edge devices periodically.
details.napkin_math: 7B model: training needs ~112 GB optimizer state (AdamW), impossible on edge. Inference: 7B × 0.5B/param (INT4) = 3.5 GB, fits on a phone with 6 GB RAM. Training: 1000s of GPU-hours. Inference: single device, milliseconds per token.
details.realistic_solution: Train-serve split separates the compute-intensive training phase (requiring many GPUs, large datasets, high bandwidth) from the inference phase (requiring low latency, lower compute). Training stays in the cloud because it needs massive parallelism (hundreds of GPUs), huge datasets, and runs for days/weeks. Inference runs locally because it needs low latency, works offline, and the model (after quantization) fits on edge hardware. The bridge is model export: train in FP16/BF16, quantize to INT8/INT4, and deploy the compressed model.

scenario: Your company trains a 7B parameter language model in the cloud but wants to deploy inference on edge devices. Explain the train-serve split architecture and what makes it work for ML systems.
title: Cloud Train Serve Split L2 0

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that training memory (optimizer states, gradients, activations) is 10-20x larger than inference memory. A model that needs 8 A100s to train can often serve on a single edge device.
details.napkin_math: FP16: 3B × 2B = 6 GB. Orin BW: 204.8 GB/s. Decode: 6/204.8 = 29 ms → 34 tok/s. INT8: 3 GB. Decode: 3/204.8 = 14.6 ms → 68 tok/s. 2x speedup from quantization.
details.realistic_solution: FP16 deployment: 3B × 2 bytes = 6 GB model weights + KV cache. Fits on Orin's 32 GB. Throughput limited by memory bandwidth (Orin: 204.8 GB/s). Decode: 6 GB / 204.8 GB/s = 29.3 ms/token ≈ 34 tok/s. INT8 deployment: 3B × 1 byte = 3 GB weights. Decode: 3 GB / 204.8 GB/s = 14.6 ms/token ≈ 68 tok/s. INT8 halves memory and doubles decode throughput. Both fit comfortably; INT8 is preferred for edge latency targets.

scenario: You train a 3B model in the cloud on 8 A100s, then deploy on a Jetson Orin (32 GB, 275 TOPS INT8). Estimate the memory footprint and throughput at inference for both FP16 and INT8 deployments.
title: Cloud Train Serve Split L3 0

details.common_mistake: Ignoring network latency and availability. Cloud inference adds 50-200 ms round-trip, which is unacceptable for real-time applications like speech recognition or autonomous driving.
details.napkin_math: Cloud: 10M queries/day × $0.003/query = $30K/day = $900K/month. Edge: one-time quantization + OTA infra ≈ $50K/year. Edge is astronomically cheaper at scale.
details.realistic_solution: Cloud inference: simpler deployment, full-precision model, but adds 50-200 ms network latency per request, requires persistent connectivity, and costs ~$0.001-0.01 per query. For 10M daily queries: $10K-$100K/day ($300K-$3M/month). Edge inference: no network latency (local), works offline, privacy-preserving (data stays on device), but requires quantization pipeline and OTA updates. Cost: zero per-query marginal cost after device purchase. Choose edge when: latency-sensitive (<50 ms), offline required, privacy-critical, or high query volume makes cloud cost prohibitive.

scenario: A product manager asks why you don't just run inference in the cloud too, since you already have the GPU cluster. The edge deployment adds complexity (model export, quantization, OTA updates). Evaluate cloud-only vs. train-cloud/serve-edge.
title: Cloud Train Serve Split L5 0

details.common_mistake: Only tracking code versions (git) but not the parameters, configs, or data versions. A pipeline can produce different outputs with the same code but different config values.
details.napkin_math: Typical ML pipeline: 5-15 transformation steps. Without lineage, debugging a regression: ~2-5 engineer-days of manual investigation. With lineage: diff two DAG versions in minutes, pinpoint the change in <1 hour.
details.realistic_solution: Transformation lineage tracks every operation applied to data: what code ran, what parameters were used, what version of the code, input/output checksums, and timestamps. It creates an immutable audit trail from raw data to training-ready dataset. When a regression occurs, you can diff the lineage of the current pipeline against the last known-good version, immediately identifying which transformation changed. Without lineage, you must manually bisect weeks of pipeline changes — a slow, error-prone process.

scenario: After a model regression in production, the team discovers the training data pipeline was modified two weeks ago but nobody documented the change. Explain how transformation lineage prevents this class of failures.
title: Cloud Transformation Lineage L2 0

details.common_mistake: Storing full copies of intermediate datasets for lineage instead of just hashes. This explodes storage costs — a hash is 32 bytes vs. gigabytes for the actual data.
details.napkin_math: Metadata: 600 bytes × 8 steps = 4.8 KB/run. 1000 runs/day = 4.8 MB/day. Hashing: 10 GB dataset at 1 GB/s = 10s. 8 steps × 2 hashes × 10s = 160s overhead per run.
details.realistic_solution: Per-step lineage metadata: SHA-256 hash of input (32 bytes) + output hash (32 bytes) + timestamp (8 bytes) + code git SHA (20 bytes) + params JSON (~500 bytes) ≈ 600 bytes per step. 8 steps = 4.8 KB per pipeline run. If you run 1000 pipeline runs/day: 4.8 MB/day = ~1.75 GB/year. Latency: computing SHA-256 on a 10 GB dataset at ~1 GB/s = 10s per hash, 2 hashes per step = 20s, 8 steps = 160s total. This is the main cost — hashing large intermediate datasets.

scenario: Your data pipeline has 8 transformation steps. Each step reads its input, processes it, and writes output. You want to add lineage metadata (hash, timestamp, code version, params) to each step. Estimate the storage and latency overhead.
title: Cloud Transformation Lineage L3 0

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to record-level lineage without considering the cost. Most ML debugging needs only dataset-level lineage to identify which pipeline step caused a regression.
details.napkin_math: Dataset-level: 8 × 600B = 4.8 KB. Record-level: 100M × 8 × 100B = 80 GB. Storage ratio: 80 GB / 4.8 KB ≈ 17 million × more. Query: dataset-level is O(1); record-level needs indexed DB.
details.realistic_solution: Dataset-level (A): 8 hashes per run, ~5 KB metadata, 160s hashing overhead. Simple, low cost. Can tell you which step changed but not which records were affected. Record-level (B): 100M records × 8 steps × ~100 bytes lineage = 80 GB metadata per run. Can trace any output record to its exact inputs. Useful for debugging individual predictions but 10,000x more storage. Choose A for most training pipelines (sufficient for regression debugging). Choose B only for regulated domains (healthcare, finance) where per-prediction audit trails are legally required.

scenario: You can implement lineage at two granularities: (A) dataset-level (hash entire output of each step) or (B) record-level (track provenance of each individual record). Your pipeline processes 100M records across 8 steps. Evaluate both approaches.
title: Cloud Transformation Lineage L5 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming ECC protects against all transient errors. ECC covers memory (DRAM) but not compute units (ALUs, tensor cores). A bit flip during matrix multiplication produces a silently wrong result.
details.napkin_math: Single GPU transient rate: ~1 error per 1e21 FLOPs. H100 at 989 TFLOPS (9.89e14 FLOPs/sec): 1e21 / 9.89e14 ≈ 1e6 seconds ≈ 11.5 days. With 512 GPUs: 1 error per 11.5/512 days ≈ 32 minutes. At scale, transient errors are routine, not rare.
details.realistic_solution: Transient failures are temporary hardware errors — cosmic rays flipping bits (single-event upsets), voltage fluctuations, or thermal noise causing incorrect computation without permanent damage. They differ from hard failures (dead GPU) because the hardware still works. At scale they matter due to probability: if one GPU has a transient error rate of 1 per 1e21 FLOPs, across 512 GPUs running at peak, you expect an error every ~32 minutes. ECC memory catches most, but compute errors in tensor cores are often unprotected, silently corrupting gradients.

scenario: During a large-scale training run on 512 GPUs, one GPU produces an NaN gradient in iteration 4,721 but works fine on retry. Your interviewer asks you to explain transient failures and why they matter more at scale.
title: Cloud Transient Failures L2 0

details.common_mistake: Treating transient failures like hard failures and restarting the entire job. Transient failures should be handled with lightweight mitigations like gradient clipping or step rollback, not full restarts.
details.napkin_math: GPU-hours: 1024 × 30 × 24 = 737,280. Rate: 1 per 500 GPU-hours. Expected events: 737,280/500 ≈ 1,475. P(zero failures) = e^(-1475) ≈ 0. Average: ~2 failures per hour.
details.realistic_solution: Total GPU-hours: 1024 GPUs × 30 days × 24 hours = 737,280 GPU-hours. Expected failures: 737,280 / 500 = 1,474.6 transient events. Probability of zero failures: P(0) = e^(-λ) where λ = 1474.6 → P(0) = e^(-1474.6) ≈ 0 (effectively impossible). This means transient failures are guaranteed at scale. You must design for them: gradient clipping to bound NaN propagation, periodic validation checks, and checkpoint-and-rollback when anomalies are detected.

scenario: Your 1024-GPU cluster has a per-GPU transient failure rate of 1 event per 500 GPU-hours. Training takes 30 days. Calculate the expected number of transient failures and the probability of completing training without any.
title: Cloud Transient Failures L3 0

details.common_mistake: Relying solely on gradient norm monitoring. Subtle transient errors that produce slightly-off but plausible gradients will pass norm checks but still degrade model quality over thousands of steps.
details.napkin_math: A: 2x GPU cost ($2M → $4M for large run). B: <1% overhead, catches ~95% of errors. C: 100-step validation = ~2 min overhead per check. Max rollback: 100 steps × 30s/step = 50 min wasted. B+C combined: <2% overhead, >99% detection.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy A (redundancy): catches 100% of transient errors, but doubles GPU cost — 2x compute overhead is prohibitive for large training. Strategy B (gradient monitoring): near-zero overhead (<1%), catches most corruption (NaN/Inf and outlier norms), but misses subtle bit flips that produce plausible-looking gradients. Strategy C (validation checks): catches corruption that affects model quality, but detection is delayed up to 100 steps, requiring rollback and wasted compute. Best practice: combine B + C. Gradient monitoring catches acute corruption instantly; validation loss catches subtle drift with bounded rollback cost.

scenario: To handle transient failures, your team proposes three strategies: (A) redundant computation (run every step on 2 GPUs, compare results), (B) gradient norm monitoring with rollback, (C) periodic validation loss checks every 100 steps. Evaluate the trade-offs.
title: Cloud Transient Failures L5 0

details.common_mistake: Thinking power management is only about total energy consumption. The rate of change (dP/dt) of power draw is often more dangerous to infrastructure than the absolute magnitude.
details.napkin_math: H100 TDP: 700W. 10,000 GPUs idle-to-compute swing: ~300W each. Synchronized spike: 10,000 × 300W = 3 MW transient. Grid expects steady 5 MW average but sees 3-8 MW oscillation. Capacitor banks needed: 3 MW × 0.5s = 1.5 MJ of buffering.
details.realistic_solution: Transient loads are sudden, short-duration power demand spikes caused by synchronized operations across many accelerators. During AllReduce, all GPUs transition from compute (high power) to network I/O (lower power) and back simultaneously. The synchronized return to compute creates a coordinated power spike. This matters because: (1) grid infrastructure is provisioned for average power, not peak spikes, (2) voltage regulators and UPS systems have finite response times, and (3) repeated transients can trigger breaker trips or damage power distribution equipment.

scenario: A datacenter operator reports that when a 10,000-GPU training cluster starts an AllReduce synchronization, the facility's power draw spikes by 2 MW for 500 ms. Explain transient loads and why they are a problem.
title: Cloud Transient Loads L2 0

details.common_mistake: Provisioning power infrastructure for average utilization instead of peak. The transient spike, not the average, determines the required capacity of power distribution units and UPS systems.
details.realistic_solution: Full power at 95% utilization: 4096 × 700W × 0.95 = 2,723,840W ≈ 2.72 MW. During AllReduce at 40%: 4096 × 700W × 0.40 = 1,146,880W ≈ 1.15 MW. Power swing: 2.72 - 1.15 = 1.57 MW in <1 ms transition. To smooth this with a capacitor bank: Energy = Power × Time = 1.57 MW × 0.2s = 314 kJ. Using supercapacitors at ~5 Wh/kg, need 314 kJ / 3600 × 1000 ≈ 87 Wh ≈ 17.4 kg of supercapacitors. Alternatively, stagger AllReduce across groups to spread the transient.

scenario: A training cluster has 4,096 H100 GPUs (700W TDP each). During synchronized AllReduce, GPUs drop to 40% utilization for 200 ms, then spike back to 95%. Calculate the transient power swing and the energy buffer needed to smooth it.
title: Cloud Transient Loads L3 0

details.common_mistake: Choosing power capping because it is the simplest to implement. The 20% throughput loss compounds over weeks of training and costs far more than hardware buffering solutions.
details.napkin_math: A: $300K capex, 0% perf loss. B: +100-200 ms per AllReduce, ~2% slower. C: 20% throughput loss, 30 days → 37.5 days. Extra GPU cost of C: 7.5 days × 4096 GPUs × $2/GPU-hr × 24h = $1.47M — far more than option A's cost.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (energy buffering): eliminates transient impact on grid, zero training performance loss, but costs $200-500K for MW-scale buffering and requires floor space. Option B (staggered AllReduce): reduces peak power by spreading transitions over time, but adds 50 ms × N_groups latency to each AllReduce, increasing communication overhead by 5-15%. For a 1-second training step, this is a 1-3% throughput hit. Option C (power capping at 80%): reduces both steady-state and transient power, but caps compute throughput at ~80%, directly losing 20% training speed — 30-day job becomes 37.5 days. Best choice: A if capital budget allows, B as a software-only alternative with small perf hit, C only as last resort.

scenario: To mitigate transient power loads, your team proposes: (A) install battery/supercapacitor banks to buffer spikes, (B) stagger AllReduce operations across rack groups with 50 ms offsets, (C) power-cap GPUs to 80% TDP. Evaluate each approach's impact on training performance and cost.

details.common_mistake: Assuming Ultra Ethernet is just faster Ethernet. The key innovation is not speed (both can run at 400/800 Gbps) but traffic distribution — packet spraying vs. flow-level ECMP hashing.
details.napkin_math: Standard RoCE with ECMP: 4 equal-cost paths but elephant flows pin to 1 path → 25% utilization. Ultra Ethernet packet spraying: all 4 paths used evenly → ~95% utilization. For 400 Gbps links: effective BW goes from 100 Gbps to 380 Gbps per flow.
details.realistic_solution: Ultra Ethernet is designed specifically for AI collective communication patterns. Key innovations: (1) native packet spraying — distributes packets across all available paths simultaneously (standard Ethernet uses ECMP which pins flows to single paths), (2) in-order delivery guarantees at the receiver despite multi-path spraying, (3) optimized for AllReduce and collective patterns rather than traditional request-response. Standard RoCE struggles with AI workloads because ECMP creates hotspots when many GPU-to-GPU flows hash to the same path. Ultra Ethernet eliminates this by spraying at packet granularity.

scenario: Your team is evaluating Ultra Ethernet as an alternative to InfiniBand for a new AI training cluster. Explain what makes Ultra Ethernet different from standard RoCE and why it matters for AI workloads.
title: Cloud Ultra Ethernet L2 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming ECMP distributes flows perfectly evenly. Hash collisions cause load imbalance, and with large AllReduce transfers, a single overloaded path becomes the bottleneck for the entire collective.
details.napkin_math: ECMP: 32 flows, 4 paths. Worst path: ~10 flows × 400 Gbps / 10 = 40 Gbps/flow. Packet spray: 32/4 = 8 per path → 400/8 = 50 Gbps/flow. Gain: 50/40 = 1.25x. At 256 flows: ECMP worst path ~80 flows, spray = 64 → 1.25x.
details.realistic_solution: With ECMP: 32 flows hash to 4 paths. By birthday paradox, distribution is uneven. Expected max-loaded path: ~32/4 + sqrt(32×3/16) ≈ 8 + 2.4 ≈ 10.4 flows. Bottleneck path has 10.4 flows sharing 400 Gbps = 38.5 Gbps per flow. With packet spraying: all 32 flows spread evenly across all 4 paths. Each path carries 32/4 = 8 flow-equivalents. Per-flow bandwidth: 400/8 = 50 Gbps. Improvement: 50/38.5 = 1.3x better bandwidth utilization. At scale with more flows, the ECMP imbalance worsens further.

scenario: A 256-GPU cluster uses a fat-tree topology with 400 Gbps links and 4 equal-cost paths between any two racks. With standard ECMP, a ring AllReduce creates 32 large flows that hash to paths. Estimate effective bandwidth under ECMP vs. packet spraying.
title: Cloud Ultra Ethernet L3 0

details.common_mistake: Choosing purely on per-port cost without considering ecosystem maturity. A 5% reduction in effective AllReduce bandwidth due to immature NCCL support could add 3+ days to a 60-day training run.
details.napkin_math: 2048 ports. IB: 2048 × $15K = $30.7M. UE: 2048 × $9K = $18.4M. Savings: $12.3M. But 1 day of 2048-GPU downtime = 2048 × 24h × $2/hr = $98K. If UE issues cause 5 days of debugging: $490K. Still saves $11.8M — if it works.
details.realistic_solution: InfiniBand NDR: mature ecosystem, NCCL optimized for IB, SHARP in-network reduction reduces AllReduce latency by 2x, proven at scale (10K+ GPUs). Cost: ~$15K per port. Ultra Ethernet: 30-40% cheaper per port (~$9K), uses commodity switches, packet spraying gives good bandwidth utilization, but ecosystem is newer — driver maturity, NCCL backend optimization, and operational tooling are less proven. For a 60-day critical training run, the risk of UE debugging delays could cost more than IB's price premium. For inference or less time-critical workloads, UE's cost advantage is compelling.

scenario: For a new 2048-GPU training cluster, you must choose between InfiniBand NDR (400 Gbps, proven, $$$) and Ultra Ethernet (400 Gbps, newer, $$). The job is a 175B GPT model trained over 60 days. Evaluate the trade-offs.
title: Cloud Ultra Ethernet L5 0

details.common_mistake: Confusing clock speed with throughput. A 1.8 GHz GPU vastly outperforms a 5 GHz CPU for ML because throughput = operations per cycle × cores × clock speed, and GPUs have thousands more parallel units.
details.napkin_math: CPU (AVX-512): 512-bit SIMD = 16 FP32 ops per cycle × 3 GHz = 48 GFLOPS. H100 GPU: 16896 CUDA cores × 2 ops × 1.83 GHz = 61.8 TFLOPS. GPU is ~1300x more throughput through massive vector parallelism.
details.realistic_solution: Vector operations apply a single instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously (SIMD — Single Instruction, Multiple Data). A CPU processes one addition at a time (scalar), while a GPU tensor core processes a 4×4 matrix multiply (256 multiply-adds) in one cycle. Neural networks are dominated by matrix multiplications and element-wise operations on large tensors — perfectly suited for SIMD. A GPU has thousands of simple cores, each executing vector operations in lockstep, achieving massive data parallelism. The lower clock speed is compensated by orders of magnitude more parallel operations per cycle.

scenario: A junior engineer asks why GPUs are so much faster than CPUs for neural network inference despite having lower clock speeds. Explain the role of vector (SIMD) operations in ML workloads.
title: Cloud Vector Operations L2 0

details.common_mistake: Trying to optimize element-wise operations by using faster compute (tensor cores). They are memory-bound — the only way to speed them up is higher memory bandwidth or kernel fusion to reduce memory traffic.
details.napkin_math: Arithmetic intensity: 1 FLOP / 8 bytes = 0.125 FLOP/byte. H100 roofline: compute-bound above 989e12 / 3.35e12 = 295 FLOP/byte. ReLU at 0.125 is 2360x below the ridge → purely memory-bound.
details.realistic_solution: ReLU is max(0, x) — 1 FLOP per element, but reads and writes 4 bytes per element. Compute: 10M FLOPs. Memory: 10M × 4B read + 10M × 4B write = 80 MB. CPU: 10M / (16 elements × 3 GHz) = 0.208 ms compute. Memory: 80 MB / 50 GB/s ≈ 1.6 ms. Memory-bound on CPU. GPU: 10M / 989 TFLOPS = 0.01 μs compute. Memory: 80 MB / 3.35 TB/s = 0.024 ms. Memory-bound on GPU too. Element-wise operations like ReLU are always memory-bound because arithmetic intensity is O(1) — one FLOP per element loaded.

scenario: You need to apply ReLU activation to a 10M-element tensor. Estimate the time on a CPU (AVX-512, 3 GHz, 16-wide FP32 SIMD) vs. an H100 GPU (3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth). Is this compute-bound or memory-bound?
title: Cloud Vector Operations L3 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming GPU branching works like CPU branching with branch prediction. GPUs have no branch predictor — all threads in a warp must execute both paths if any thread diverges.
details.napkin_math: 32 threads per warp. If 50% take branch A, 50% take branch B: both branches execute sequentially → 2x slowdown per warp. With additional register pressure and instruction cache misses from two code paths: ~3-5x total slowdown. Branchless: 1x (all threads execute same instruction).
details.realistic_solution: The branching activation causes warp divergence — threads in a 32-thread warp take different paths through the if-else, serializing execution. ReLU uses a branchless max() intrinsic. Solutions: (A) Rewrite as branchless using select/ternary: if(x>0, f(x), g(x)) → blend both results with a mask. This eliminates divergence. (B) Use torch.where() which compiles to a predicated select. (C) Approximate with a smooth function (e.g., SiLU) that has no branches. Option A is best — maintains exact semantics with no divergence. The 5x slowdown is consistent with ~50% of warps having divergent threads, each taking 2x cycles.

scenario: Your model has a custom activation function with an if-else branch per element. Profiling shows this kernel is 5x slower than standard ReLU on GPU despite similar FLOP count. Diagnose the issue and evaluate solutions.
title: Cloud Vector Operations L5 0

details.common_mistake: Thinking wafer-scale is just 'a bigger GPU.' The fundamental difference is on-chip SRAM (no HBM bottleneck) and on-chip interconnect (no NVLink/PCIe bottleneck), changing which operations are feasible.
details.napkin_math: WSE-2: 850,000 cores, 40 GB SRAM, 220 Pb/s on-chip BW ≈ 27.5 PB/s. 8×H100 NVLink: 450 GB/s per GPU = 3.6 TB/s total. WSE advantage: ~7,600x more communication bandwidth. Latency: on-chip ~1 ns vs. NVLink ~1 μs = 1000x lower.
details.realistic_solution: A wafer-scale engine uses an entire silicon wafer (~46,000 mm²) as a single chip instead of dicing it into hundreds of small dies. This provides: (1) hundreds of thousands of cores on one die with on-chip interconnect at ~100 TB/s aggregate bandwidth, (2) elimination of PCIe/NVLink/network bottlenecks since all communication is on-die at silicon speeds, (3) massive on-chip SRAM (40 GB on CS-2) avoiding off-chip memory bandwidth limits. A traditional 8-GPU node has inter-GPU bandwidth of ~450 GB/s (NVLink) — the WSE's on-chip fabric is 200x faster, making communication essentially free relative to compute.

scenario: Cerebras claims their Wafer-Scale Engine eliminates the need for multi-GPU parallelism for large models. Explain how a wafer-scale chip differs from a traditional multi-GPU setup and what communication advantage it provides.
title: Cloud Wafer Scale Engine L2 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming the WSE advantage applies to all workloads. For compute-bound operations (large batch matmuls), traditional GPUs with tensor cores can match or exceed WSE because raw FLOPS, not memory bandwidth, is the bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Model: 13B × 2B = 26 GB, fits in 40 GB SRAM. WSE decode: 26 GB / 27.5 PB/s ≈ 0.95 μs. H100 decode: 26 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 7.76 ms. Ratio: ~8,000x. Caveat: WSE's 850K cores have lower per-core FLOPS than GPU tensor cores.
details.realistic_solution: 13B parameters in FP16: 13B × 2 bytes = 26 GB. WSE-2 has 40 GB SRAM → model fits with 14 GB remaining for activations. SRAM bandwidth: ~27.5 PB/s across all cores (each core has local SRAM at register-file speeds). Effective per-weight access: ~1 ns. Compare H100 HBM: 3.35 TB/s, access latency ~100 ns. For decode (memory-bound): WSE reads 26 GB from SRAM at ~27.5 PB/s → 0.95 μs per token. H100 reads 26 GB from HBM at 3.35 TB/s → 7.76 ms per token. WSE is ~8000x faster for pure memory-bound decode.

scenario: A WSE-2 has 40 GB of on-chip SRAM and 850K cores. You want to run a 13B parameter model in FP16. Calculate whether the model fits on-chip and estimate the compute advantage of SRAM-speed access vs. HBM.
title: Cloud Wafer Scale Engine L3 0

details.common_mistake: Choosing the WSE for throughput workloads where batching on GPUs is sufficient. WSE excels at latency-sensitive, small-batch inference, not bulk throughput where GPU batching amortizes memory access cost.
details.napkin_math: Load: 2B tok/day = 23K tok/s. H100 ×16 capacity at batch=32: ~1M tok/s. Utilization: 2.3%. Cost/tok: $400K / (2B × 365) = $0.0000005. CS-2 cost/tok: $2M / (2B × 365) = $0.0000027 — 5x more expensive for this workload.
details.realistic_solution: H100 cluster: 13B FP16 = 26 GB, fits on 1 GPU. Decode at batch=1: 26 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 7.76 ms/tok. At batch=32: amortized ~0.5 ms/tok. 16 GPUs, batch=32 each: 16 × 32 / 0.5ms = 1.024M tok/s. 10M requests × 200 tok = 2B tok/day ÷ 86400s = 23,148 tok/s — easily handled. CS-2: 26 GB in SRAM, decode effectively instant at μs-level latency. Throughput exceeds H100s for small batches. But: $2M vs $400K, 5x cost. H100 cluster handles the load with room to spare. CS-2 wins only if ultra-low latency (<1 ms per token) is the SLA, not throughput.

scenario: Your startup must choose between 16 H100 GPUs ($400K, 16×80 GB HBM) and 1 Cerebras CS-2 ($2M, 40 GB SRAM, 850K cores) for serving a 13B model. Daily traffic is 10M requests at 200 tokens each. Evaluate both options.
title: Cloud Wafer Scale Engine L5 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming warm restart means no checkpoint is needed. You still checkpoint periodically for catastrophic failures (power loss, multi-node failure). Warm restart handles single-node failures between checkpoints.
details.napkin_math: Cold restart: load 70B model checkpoint from NFS at 5 GB/s = 28s + 256 workers re-init = ~5 min total. Warm restart: 1 node receives state from peer over NVLink/network at 50 GB/s = 2.8s + rejoin = ~30s. Savings per failure: 4.5 min × $8.53/min (256 GPUs at $2/hr each) = ~$38.40.
details.realistic_solution: A warm restart preserves the in-memory state (model weights, optimizer state, data loader position) on all 255 surviving workers and only replaces the failed node. The replacement node receives the latest state from a surviving peer. This avoids: (1) reloading the full checkpoint from storage (minutes), (2) reinitializing all 256 data loaders and shuffling states, (3) re-warming learning rate schedules or batch norm statistics. Cold restart: all 256 workers reload from disk → 5-15 min downtime. Warm restart: 1 replacement node syncs from peer → 30-60 seconds. At scale, failures happen hourly, so warm restart saves hours of wasted compute daily.

scenario: During a 256-GPU training run, GPU #47 fails with a hardware error. Your colleague suggests cold-restarting the entire job from the latest checkpoint. Explain why warm restart is preferable and how it works.
title: Cloud Warm Restart L2 0

details.common_mistake: Only counting wall-clock downtime. During cold restart, all 1024 GPUs are idle, so 8 min downtime = 8 × 1024 = 8,192 GPU-minutes wasted. With warm restart, only 1 GPU is being replaced — the other 1023 can potentially do useful work.
details.napkin_math: Failures: 344,064 / 2000 = 172. Cold downtime: 172 × 8 min = 1,376 min = 23 hrs. Warm downtime: 172 × 0.75 min = 129 min = 2.15 hrs. Savings: 20.85 hrs × 1024 GPUs × $2/hr = $42.7K.
details.realistic_solution: Total GPU-hours: 1024 × 14 × 24 = 344,064. Expected failures: 344,064 / 2000 = 172 failures. Cold restart: 172 × 8 min = 1,376 min = 22.9 hours. Warm restart: 172 × 0.75 min = 129 min = 2.15 hours. Savings: 20.75 hours of training time. In GPU-hours: 20.75 × 1024 = 21,248 GPU-hours saved. At $2/GPU-hr: $42,496 saved. Additionally, warm restart loses only the current mini-batch on the failed GPU; cold restart may lose up to the checkpoint interval of work across all GPUs.

scenario: Your 1024-GPU training job has a per-GPU failure rate of 1 per 2000 GPU-hours. Each cold restart takes 8 minutes; each warm restart takes 45 seconds. Training runs for 14 days. Calculate total downtime under each strategy.
title: Cloud Warm Restart L3 0

details.common_mistake: Viewing spare GPUs as pure waste. At high failure rates, the cost of cluster-wide idle time during cold restarts dwarfs the cost of maintaining a small spare pool.
details.napkin_math: Failures/hr: 2048/1000 = 2.05. Cold downtime cost: 2.05 × 8 min × 2048 GPUs × $2/hr / 60 = $1,117/hr. Spare cost: 16 × $2 = $32/hr. ROI: $1,117/$32 = 35x. Break-even spares: $1,117/hr downtime cost / $2/hr per spare = ~559 spares needed to equal downtime cost; 16 spares far exceed ROI threshold.
details.realistic_solution: Expected failures per hour: 2048 / 1000 = 2.05 per hour. Cold restart: 2.05 × 8 min = 16.4 min/hr downtime → 27.3% of training time lost. Warm restart with hot spares: 2.05 × 0.75 min = 1.54 min/hr → 2.6% lost. Cost of 16 spares: 16 × $2/hr = $32/hr. Cost of cold restart downtime: 16.4 min/hr × 2048 GPUs / 60 × $2 = $1,117/hr. Net savings: $1,085/hr. The 16 spare GPUs pay for themselves 35x over. Even accounting for spare GPUs being idle, the ROI is overwhelming at this failure rate.

scenario: Warm restart requires keeping a pool of spare standby GPUs (hot spares). For a 2048-GPU cluster with 1 failure per 1000 GPU-hours, evaluate whether maintaining 16 hot spares (0.8% overhead) is worth the cost vs. cold restarts.
title: Cloud Warm Restart L5 0

details.common_mistake: Thinking the GPU skips the branch not taken. Both (or all) branches execute — threads on the 'wrong' branch are masked but still consume a cycle. The warp completes in time proportional to the sum of all branch execution times.
details.napkin_math: 32 threads per warp. If 3 branches taken: each branch runs sequentially. Worst case: 32 unique branches → 32x slowdown (all serial). MoE with 3 experts per warp: 3x slowdown. Effective occupancy: 32 threads but only ~11 active at any time.
details.realistic_solution: In NVIDIA's SIMT model, 32 threads execute in lockstep as a warp. When an if-else branch occurs, all threads that take the 'if' path execute first while the 'else' threads are masked (idle), then the 'else' threads execute while the 'if' threads are masked. If a warp has threads routed to 3 different experts, all 3 code paths execute sequentially — the warp takes 3x as long as a non-divergent warp. Effective utilization drops to 1/3. This is warp divergence: serial execution of divergent paths within a SIMD group.

scenario: A GPU kernel for a mixture-of-experts model routes different tokens to different expert networks within the same warp. Performance is 3x worse than expected. Explain warp divergence and why it causes this slowdown.
title: Cloud Warp Divergence L2 0

details.common_mistake: Computing average per-thread time (32.5 cycles) as the warp time. In SIMT, the warp time is the sum of all distinct branch durations (50 cycles), not the average, because both paths execute sequentially.
details.napkin_math: P(divergent warp) ≈ 99.99%. Divergent time: 10 + 40 = 50 cycles. Ideal average: 0.25×10 + 0.75×40 = 32.5 cycles. Overhead: 50/32.5 = 1.54x → 35% efficiency loss.
details.realistic_solution: A warp diverges if any thread takes a different path. Probability all 32 threads take the same path: P(all short) = 0.25^32 ≈ 0 or P(all long) = 0.75^32 ≈ 0.0001. So nearly every warp diverges. Divergent warp time: short path + long path = 10 + 40 = 50 cycles. Non-divergent average: 0.25×10 + 0.75×40 = 32.5 cycles. Efficiency: ideal throughput per cycle = 32 threads / 32.5 cycles = 0.985 threads/cycle. Actual: 32 threads / 50 cycles = 0.64 threads/cycle. Efficiency loss: 1 - 0.64/0.985 = 35%.

scenario: You have a custom CUDA kernel where each thread processes one token. 25% of tokens take a 'short path' (10 cycles) and 75% take a 'long path' (40 cycles). Threads are randomly assigned to warps of 32. Calculate the expected warp execution time and efficiency loss.
title: Cloud Warp Divergence L3 0

details.common_mistake: Choosing padding (C) because it is simplest to implement. Padding converts a divergence problem into a pure compute waste problem, which is worse when the short and long paths differ significantly in cost.
details.napkin_math: A: sort 4096 tokens = ~0.1 ms overhead. Saves 35% divergence penalty on 10 ms attention kernel = 3.5 ms. Net gain: 3.4 ms. B: zero sort overhead but potential 20% load imbalance. C: all warps run longest path → 40 cycle × all warps, wastes 25% compute on padding.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (pre-sort): groups tokens with same attention pattern into contiguous warps, eliminating divergence. Overhead: O(n log n) sort on CPU/GPU. For large batch sizes, sort cost is amortized and this is the best approach. Used by MegaBlocks for MoE. Option B (block-level branching): each thread block handles one pattern type. Eliminates warp divergence but may cause load imbalance between blocks (some patterns have more tokens). Need dynamic scheduling. Option C (padding): executes all code paths even when unnecessary — no divergence but wastes compute on padding. Worst option for sparse patterns where most paths are short. Best: A for batch inference (sort is cheap relative to compute), B for real-time (avoids sort latency).

scenario: To fix warp divergence in a sparse attention kernel, your team proposes: (A) sort tokens by attention pattern before the kernel, (B) use thread-block-level branching instead of thread-level, (C) pad all paths to equal length. Evaluate each approach.
title: Cloud Warp Divergence L5 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming weight-stationary is always best. For small models with large batch sizes, input traffic dominates and output-stationary can be more efficient because it minimizes partial sum accumulation traffic.
details.napkin_math: Weight-stationary: for a 1024×1024 weight matrix with batch=64, weights loaded once (2 MB FP16). Inputs stream: 64 × 1024 × 2B = 128 KB per batch. Weight reuse: 64x. Output-stationary: outputs fixed (64×1024×2B = 128 KB), weights stream once per input = same total, but different PE utilization pattern.
details.realistic_solution: In weight-stationary dataflow, model weights are loaded once into local registers/scratchpad and remain fixed while input activations stream through. Each processing element (PE) holds one weight and accumulates partial sums as inputs flow past. This minimizes weight memory traffic — critical when the model is large relative to on-chip memory. In output-stationary dataflow, partial output sums stay fixed in PEs while both weights and inputs are streamed in. Weight-stationary excels for inference (weights reused across many inputs in a batch); output-stationary excels for training (accumulating gradients across a sequence).

scenario: An accelerator designer describes their chip as using a 'weight-stationary dataflow.' Explain what this means, when it is advantageous, and how it differs from output-stationary dataflow.
title: Cloud Weight Stationary L2 0

details.common_mistake: Thinking weight-stationary means weights are never reloaded. When the weight matrix exceeds on-chip capacity, it must be tiled — but each weight is still loaded minimally (once per forward pass), unlike inputs which may be re-streamed per tile.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 2048² × 2B = 8 MB. On-chip: 256 × 2 KB = 512 KB. Tiles: 8 MB / 512 KB = 16. Weight traffic: 8 MB total (weight-stationary loads each weight once). Input traffic per batch element: 2048 × 2B × 16 tiles = 64 KB (inputs re-streamed per tile).
details.realistic_solution: Total weight size: 2048 × 2048 × 2 bytes = 8 MB. Per-PE SRAM: 2 KB. Total on-chip weight capacity: 256 PEs × 2 KB = 512 KB. Tiles needed: 8 MB / 512 KB = 16 tiles. Each tile loads 512 KB of weights, processes all inputs against that tile, then loads the next. Total weight traffic: 16 tiles × 512 KB = 8 MB (each weight loaded exactly once across all tiles). If batch size is B, inputs stream B times per tile: total input traffic = 16 × B × 2048 × 2B / 16 = B × 8 KB per tile × 16... Simplifying: weights loaded once (8 MB), inputs loaded once per tile pass.

scenario: A weight-stationary accelerator has 256 PEs, each with 2 KB local SRAM. You want to run a 2048×2048 FP16 weight matrix through it. Calculate how many times weights must be tiled (reloaded) and the total weight traffic.
title: Cloud Weight Stationary L3 0

details.common_mistake: Selecting one dataflow for all workloads. LLM decode (weight-dominated, batch=1) and vision inference (activation-dominated, large batch) have opposite memory traffic patterns and need different dataflow strategies.
details.napkin_math: 70B decode: 140 GB weights, ~4 KB activations per token. Weight:activation ratio = 35,000,000:1. Weight-stationary wins. ResNet batch=256: 50 MB weights × 1 load vs. 256 × 25 MB activations. Activation traffic dominates. Output-stationary saves 256 partial sum writes.
details.realistic_solution: Workload A (70B decode, batch=1): Weights dominate traffic — 140 GB read per token, activations are tiny (single token). Weight-stationary is ideal: load weights once, stream the single input. Reuse factor for weights = 1 (no batch reuse), but weights are the bottleneck so minimizing their movement is critical. Workload B (ResNet-50, batch=256): weights are small (~50 MB) and reused 256× across the batch. Output-stationary is better: keep partial sums local, stream weights and inputs. Weight reuse from batching already amortizes weight traffic. Verdict: no single dataflow is optimal for all workloads. A reconfigurable dataflow or separate accelerators per workload class is ideal.

scenario: You are choosing a dataflow for a custom inference accelerator targeting two workloads: (A) 70B LLM decode at batch=1, (B) vision model (ResNet-50) at batch=256. Evaluate weight-stationary vs. output-stationary for each.
title: Cloud Weight Stationary L5 0

details.common_mistake: Checkpointing as frequently as possible 'to be safe.' Very frequent checkpoints can waste more compute on I/O than they save in rework prevention — the Young-Daly formula shows the optimum is a balance.
details.napkin_math: δ = 2 min save time, M = 240 min MTBF. τ_opt = √(2 × 2 × 240) - 2 = √960 - 2 = 31 - 2 = 29 min. Overhead: δ/τ = 2/29 = 6.9%. Expected rework: τ/2 = 14.5 min per failure. Total waste: 6.9% + 14.5/240 = 6.9% + 6.0% = 12.9%.
details.realistic_solution: The Young-Daly formula calculates the optimal checkpoint interval: τ_opt = √(2 × δ × M) - δ, where δ is the checkpoint save time and M is the mean time between failures (MTBF). It balances two costs: (1) checkpoint overhead — saving too frequently wastes compute on I/O, and (2) rework after failure — saving too infrequently means more lost work when a failure occurs. The formula minimizes total wasted time (checkpoint overhead + expected rework). Checkpointing every 5 min with a 2-min save time wastes 40% on I/O; every 30 min with MTBF of 4 hours wastes only ~11% and limits max rework to 30 min.

scenario: Your manager asks why you checkpoint every 30 minutes instead of every 5 minutes during a large training run. Explain the Young-Daly formula and the trade-off it optimizes.
title: Cloud Young Daly Formula L2 0

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to subtract δ from the square root term. The formula is τ = √(2δM) - δ, not just √(2δM). Also, M is the system MTBF (whole cluster), not per-GPU MTBF.
details.realistic_solution: Young-Daly: τ_opt = √(2 × δ × M) - δ. δ = 3 min, M = 480 min (8 hours). τ_opt = √(2 × 3 × 480) - 3 = √2880 - 3 = 53.67 - 3 = 50.67 min ≈ 51 min. Checkpoint overhead fraction: δ / (τ + δ) = 3 / 54 = 5.6%. Expected rework per failure: τ/2 = 25.5 min. Rework fraction: (τ/2) / M = 25.5 / 480 = 5.3%. Total efficiency: 1 - 5.6% - 5.3% = 89.1%. So ~89% of wall-clock time is useful training.

scenario: A 512-GPU training cluster has MTBF of 8 hours per failure. Checkpoint save takes 3 minutes. Using the Young-Daly formula, calculate the optimal checkpoint interval and the expected training efficiency (fraction of time doing useful work).
title: Cloud Young Daly Formula L3 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming better hardware reliability always helps more than faster checkpointing. The Young-Daly formula shows that reducing δ has a superlinear effect because it both reduces overhead and enables more frequent checkpoints with less rework.
details.napkin_math: Baseline efficiency: 80.6%. Option A (fast ckpt): 91.0% (+10.4%). Option B (reliable HW): 86.1% (+5.5%). GPU cost: $368K. A saves $38K/run, costs $50K — ROI in 1.3 runs. B saves $20K/run, costs $100K — ROI in 5 runs.
details.realistic_solution: Baseline: δ=5 min, M=240 min. τ_opt = √(2×5×240) - 5 = √2400 - 5 = 49 - 5 = 44 min. Efficiency: 1 - 5/49 - 22/240 = 1 - 10.2% - 9.2% = 80.6%. Option A (faster storage): δ=1 min, M=240 min. τ_opt = √(480) - 1 = 21.9 - 1 = 20.9 min. Efficiency: 1 - 1/21.9 - 10.5/240 = 1 - 4.6% - 4.4% = 91.0%. Gain: 10.4%. Option B (better reliability): δ=5 min, M=480 min. τ_opt = √(4800) - 5 = 69.3 - 5 = 64.3 min. Efficiency: 1 - 5/69.3 - 32.2/480 = 1 - 7.2% - 6.7% = 86.1%. Gain: 5.5%. Option A gives 10.4% vs 5.5% efficiency gain. GPU cost: 256 × 30 × 24 × $2 = $368K. 10.4% savings = $38K. 5.5% = $20K. Option A ($50K) nearly pays for itself in one run; Option B ($100K) does not.

details.common_mistake: Thinking zero-copy just means 'fast serialization library.' The key insight is that deserialization cost is literally zero — you read directly from the network buffer. This requires the format to match the CPU's memory layout (endianness, alignment).
details.napkin_math: JSON ser/deser: parse 1 MB of text ≈ 4-8 ms (string processing + allocations). FlatBuffers: 0 ms deserialization (pointer cast), ~0.05 ms serialization (memcpy). Speedup: 8 ms → 0.1 ms = 80x on serialization alone. P99: 15 - 8 + 0.1 = 7.1 ms.
details.realistic_solution: Zero-copy serialization uses binary formats (FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto) where the serialized bytes are the same as the in-memory representation. The receiver can read fields directly from the byte buffer without parsing or copying — just a pointer cast. JSON requires: parse string → allocate objects → populate fields → type-convert values. This involves memory allocation, string parsing, and data copying. Zero-copy eliminates all three: the wire format IS the memory format. For your pipeline: 8 ms of JSON ser/deser could drop to <0.1 ms with FlatBuffers, reducing P99 from 15 ms to ~7.1 ms.

scenario: Your ML serving pipeline uses JSON to serialize model inputs between microservices. P99 latency is 15 ms, with 8 ms spent on serialization/deserialization. Explain how zero-copy serialization would help.
title: Cloud Zero Copy Serialization L2 0

details.common_mistake: Only comparing serialization speed and ignoring bandwidth. Zero-copy binary formats are typically 2-4x smaller than JSON, reducing both network transfer time and serialization cost simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: JSON: 8 KB × 10K req/s = 80 MB/s parse throughput, ~0.4 CPU cores. FlatBuffers: 0 parse CPU, 2 KB × 10K = 20 MB/s wire. Bandwidth savings: 75%. CPU savings: 0.4 cores. At 100K req/s: JSON needs 4 cores just for parsing; FlatBuffers needs ~0.
details.realistic_solution: Payload: 512 × 4 bytes = 2 KB per request (binary). JSON: 512 floats as strings ≈ 5-6 KB text + field names ≈ 8 KB total. JSON parsing at ~200 MB/s throughput: 8 KB × 10,000 = 80 MB/s → 0.4 CPU cores. Plus allocation of 512 float objects per request = 5.12M allocations/s → GC pressure. FlatBuffers: 2 KB binary, zero parse cost, just pointer arithmetic. CPU cost: essentially zero (pointer offset computation). Bandwidth: 2 KB × 10,000 = 20 MB/s wire traffic vs. 80 MB/s for JSON. Total savings: 0.4 CPU cores + 75% bandwidth reduction + eliminated GC pauses.

scenario: Your inference server receives 10,000 requests/second. Each request carries a 512-dim FP32 embedding vector. Compare the CPU cost of JSON deserialization vs. FlatBuffers zero-copy access for this traffic.
title: Cloud Zero Copy Serialization L3 0

details.common_mistake: Using JSON everywhere for simplicity. In a 10-hop microservice chain, JSON serialization overhead compounds: 10 × 0.5 ms = 5 ms added latency, which can exceed the actual inference time for small models.
details.napkin_math: Latency per request (1 KB payload): JSON parse ~0.5 ms, Protobuf deser ~0.05 ms, FlatBuffers ~0.001 ms. At 50K req/s: JSON = 25 CPU cores parsing. Protobuf = 2.5 cores. FlatBuffers ≈ 0.05 cores.
details.realistic_solution: FlatBuffers: zero deserialization cost, smallest wire size, but schemas are rigid — adding/removing fields requires schema evolution planning. Best for internal service-to-service calls where latency matters and schemas are stable. Protobuf: ~10x faster than JSON, compact binary format, excellent schema evolution (field numbers), but still requires deserialization into objects. Good balance for APIs that evolve frequently. JSON: human-readable, universal tooling, but 10-100x slower to parse and 3-4x larger on wire. Only suitable for external APIs or debug endpoints. For latency-sensitive inference: FlatBuffers internally (model server ↔ preprocessing), Protobuf at API boundary (client ↔ gateway), JSON only for monitoring/debugging endpoints.

scenario: Your team debates using FlatBuffers (zero-copy, but rigid schema) vs. Protobuf (fast binary, but requires deserialization) vs. JSON (flexible, human-readable, slow) for your ML serving API. Evaluate for a latency-sensitive inference service.
title: Cloud Zero Copy Serialization L5 0

details.common_mistake: Thinking ZeRO is free — it trades memory for communication. ZeRO-3 requires an all-gather of the full parameters before each forward/backward layer computation, adding communication volume proportional to model size.
details.napkin_math: 7B model, 8 GPUs. Baseline per GPU: 14+14+84 = 112 GB (doesn't fit A100 80 GB). ZeRO-1: 14+14+10.5 = 38.5 GB. ZeRO-2: 14+12.25 = 26.25 GB. ZeRO-3: 112/8 = 14 GB. ZeRO-3 enables 8x larger models in same memory.
details.realistic_solution: In standard data parallelism, every GPU holds a full copy of: model parameters (P), gradients (G), and optimizer states (OS). For AdamW, OS = 12 bytes/param (FP32 param copy + momentum + variance). For a 7B model: P=14 GB, G=14 GB, OS=84 GB → 112 GB per GPU — all replicated. ZeRO partitions these across N GPUs: Stage 1 partitions OS only → each GPU holds P+G+(OS/N) = 14+14+84/8 = 38.5 GB on 8 GPUs. Stage 2 partitions OS+G → P+(G+OS)/N = 14+98/8 = 26.25 GB. Stage 3 partitions P+G+OS → 112/8 = 14 GB per GPU. Each stage trades communication for memory savings.

scenario: A colleague says 'standard data parallelism replicates the entire model on every GPU, which wastes memory.' Explain how ZeRO optimizations solve this and describe the three stages.
title: Cloud Zero Optimizations L2 0

details.common_mistake: Forgetting optimizer states dominate memory. For AdamW, optimizer states are 12B/param vs. 2B/param for weights — 6x more. ZeRO-1 (partitioning only OS) often provides the biggest single-stage memory reduction.
details.napkin_math: 30B × 16 bytes = 480 GB total. 8 GPUs × 80 GB = 640 GB cluster memory. ZeRO-1: 165 GB/GPU — no. ZeRO-2: 112.5 GB/GPU — no. ZeRO-3: 60 GB/GPU — fits with 20 GB headroom for activations.
details.realistic_solution: 30B params. Per-param memory: FP16 params = 2B, FP16 gradients = 2B, AdamW optimizer states (FP32 copy + momentum + variance) = 12B. Total = 16 bytes/param × 30B = 480 GB. No ZeRO: 480 GB per GPU — impossible. ZeRO-1 (partition OS): params 60 GB + grads 60 GB + OS 360/8 = 45 GB → 165 GB per GPU. Still too large. ZeRO-2 (partition OS+G): params 60 GB + (grads+OS)/8 = 420/8 = 52.5 GB → 112.5 GB. Still too large. ZeRO-3 (partition all): 480/8 = 60 GB per GPU. Fits in 80 GB with 20 GB for activations. Need ZeRO-3 minimum.

scenario: You want to train a 30B parameter model using AdamW on 8 A100 80GB GPUs. Calculate the per-GPU memory for ZeRO Stage 1, 2, and 3 and determine which stage is the minimum needed to fit.
title: Cloud Zero Optimizations L3 0

details.common_mistake: Assuming ZeRO-3 is always better because it uses less memory. The extra all-gather communication before every layer can significantly slow down training when the network is already a bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: ZeRO-2: 1.0s step. ZeRO-3: comm +50% → 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2s. With 2x batch: compute doubles → 1.2 + 0.6 = 1.8s, but half the steps. Throughput: 2 / 1.8 = 1.11x improvement. Marginal gain for 50% more communication.
details.realistic_solution: Current (ZeRO-2): step time = 1.0 (normalized). 60% compute + 40% communication. ZeRO-3: communication increases 50% → new communication = 40% × 1.5 = 60%. If compute stays same: new step = 60% + 60% = 120% → 1.2x slower per step. But ZeRO-3 frees memory for 2x larger micro-batch → 2x fewer gradient accumulation steps → effective throughput: 2x / 1.2x = 1.67x faster. If compute scales linearly with batch (often true for matmuls), compute portion also doubles: 120% + 60% = 180% per step, but 2x fewer steps → net 2/1.8 = 1.11x faster. ZeRO-3 is modestly beneficial if the freed memory enables meaningfully larger batches.

scenario: For training a 13B model on 32 A100 GPUs, ZeRO-2 suffices for memory but ZeRO-3 would free more memory for larger batch sizes. However, ZeRO-3 adds 50% more communication volume. Your training step is currently 60% compute, 40% communication. Evaluate whether ZeRO-3 is worth it.
title: Cloud Zero Optimizations L5 0

details.common_mistake: Confusing FSDP with model parallelism. FSDP is still data parallelism — every GPU processes different data batches. The sharding is of redundant state (parameters are needed by all GPUs but stored on only one at rest), not partitioning the model graph.
details.napkin_math: 13B model with AdamW: 16 bytes/param = 208 GB total. DP/DDP on 8 GPUs: 208 GB each — doesn't fit 80 GB. FSDP on 8 GPUs: 208/8 = 26 GB each — fits easily with room for activations. Memory savings: 8x.
details.realistic_solution: Standard DataParallel (DP) replicates the full model on every GPU — each GPU holds all parameters, gradients, and optimizer states. DDP improves communication with bucketed AllReduce but still replicates everything. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs (like ZeRO-3). Before each layer's forward pass, FSDP performs an all-gather to reconstruct that layer's parameters. After backward, it reduces and reshards gradients. At rest, each GPU holds only 1/N of the model. This trades communication (all-gather per layer) for memory, enabling models N× larger than single-GPU memory allows.

scenario: You are explaining FSDP to a team that has only used PyTorch's DataParallel. Describe how FSDP differs from standard DP and DDP, and why it enables training larger models.
title: Cloud Fully Sharded Data Parallel L2 0

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that FSDP requires communication for BOTH forward and backward passes. Unlike DDP which only communicates gradients in backward, FSDP must all-gather parameters before each layer in both forward and backward.
details.napkin_math: Params: 40 GB. All-gather × 2 + reduce-scatter × 1 = 3 × 40 GB = 120 GB comm. NVLink: 450 GB/s. Time: 120/450 = 0.27s. Compute: ~2s. Overhead: 0.27/2.27 = 11.9%. With overlap: ~4%.
details.realistic_solution: Model size in FP16: 20B × 2 bytes = 40 GB. FSDP all-gather: each GPU sends its 40/16 = 2.5 GB shard to all others. Total data moved per all-gather = 40 × (N-1)/N ≈ 40 GB. Two all-gathers per step (forward + backward) + one reduce-scatter for gradients (40 GB). Total communication: ~120 GB. NVLink bisection bandwidth: 450 GB/s. Time: 120 GB / 450 GB/s = 0.27 seconds. If compute per step (matmuls) takes ~2 seconds, communication overhead is 0.27 / (2 + 0.27) = 11.9%. With overlap (prefetching next layer's all-gather during compute), effective overhead drops to ~3-5%.

scenario: You are training a 20B parameter model using FSDP on 16 A100 80 GB GPUs with NVLink (450 GB/s bisection). Each training step requires an all-gather of full parameters for forward+backward. Estimate the communication overhead per step.
title: Cloud Fully Sharded Data Parallel L3 0

details.common_mistake: Using FSDP uniformly across all GPUs regardless of network topology. The key insight is to match communication-heavy operations (all-gather, TP) to fast links (NVLink) and minimize traffic on slow inter-node links.
details.napkin_math: Cross-node BW: 100 Gbps = 12.5 GB/s. A (full FSDP 64 GPUs): 3 × 60 GB × (63/64) ≈ 177 GB cross-node → 14.2s. B (FSDP within 8-GPU node + DDP across 8 nodes): gradient AllReduce cross-node: 2×(8-1)/8 × 60 GB = 105 GB → 8.4s. C (TP within node + FSDP across 8 nodes): intra-node TP uses NVLink; FSDP cross-node shard size = 60GB/8 = 7.5GB per node; 3 × 7.5GB = 22.5 GB cross-node → 1.8s. C minimizes cross-node traffic by keeping heavy tensor-parallel communication on fast NVLink.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (full FSDP): all-gathers across all 64 GPUs. Inter-node communication for every layer. Very high communication overhead (~40%). Option B (hybrid FSDP+DDP): FSDP within 8-GPU node (fast NVLink), DDP gradient sync across 8 nodes. Intra-node all-gather is fast. Cross-node gradient AllReduce: 2*(8-1)/8 * 60 GB = 105 GB at 12.5 GB/s = 8.4s — still slow. Option C (TP+FSDP): tensor parallel within node (small activation all-reduces on NVLink), FSDP across nodes. Cross-node traffic: FSDP transfers 3x the per-node shard size (all-gather + reduce-scatter) = 3 * 7.5 GB = 22.5 GB. Time = 1.8s. Best: C minimizes cross-node traffic by keeping heavy communication on fast NVLink.

scenario: For a 30B model on 64 GPUs, you can use: (A) FSDP across all 64 GPUs, (B) FSDP within each 8-GPU node + DDP across 8 nodes, or (C) tensor parallelism within nodes + FSDP across nodes. Evaluate communication efficiency for each.
title: Cloud Fully Sharded Data Parallel L5 0

details.common_mistake: Using a high constant LR and relying on gradient clipping to prevent divergence. Clipping prevents NaN but doesn't solve the fundamental problem — the optimizer needs smaller steps to navigate the loss landscape as training progresses.
