details.realistic_solution: Option A 2-year cost: $500K + 24 × $50K = $1.7M. Revenue: 24 × $200K = $4.8M. Profit: $3.1M. Option B 2-year cost: $100K + 24 × $20K = $580K. Revenue with 3% accuracy drop: assume 3% accuracy → ~5% revenue impact = $190K/month. Revenue: 24 × $190K = $4.56M. Profit: $3.98M. Option B yields $880K more profit despite lower accuracy, because the compliance infrastructure savings ($1.12M) far outweigh the revenue loss ($240K). However, this analysis is sensitive to the accuracy-revenue relationship — if the 3% accuracy drop maps to patient safety outcomes rather than just revenue, the calculation changes fundamentally.

scenario: A healthcare company must comply with HIPAA. Option A: build a centralized data lake with full compliance infrastructure ($500K setup + $50K/month). Option B: federated learning ($100K setup + $20K/month) but model accuracy drops 3% due to non-IID data. The model generates $200K/month revenue. Which has better 2-year ROI?
title: Federated Learning ROI Under Regulatory Constraints

details.common_mistake: Believing 'no raw data leaves the device' equals privacy. Gradients are sufficient for reconstruction attacks, especially with small batches.
details.napkin_math: Gradient inversion success rate: ~95% for batch=1, ~60% for batch=8, <10% for batch≥64. Adding DP noise (ε=1) drops accuracy by 2-5%.
details.realistic_solution: While raw data stays on-device, shared gradients leak information. Gradient inversion attacks (e.g., Zhu et al., 2019) can reconstruct training images from their gradients with pixel-level accuracy for small batch sizes. The attack works by initializing random dummy data, computing its gradients, and iteratively optimizing the dummy data until its gradients match the shared gradients. For batch size 1, reconstruction is nearly perfect. Defenses include: (1) differential privacy — adding calibrated noise to gradients (ε-DP guarantees), (2) secure aggregation — cryptographic protocols ensuring the server only sees the sum of gradients, not individual contributions, and (3) increasing local batch sizes to make inversion harder.

scenario: A colleague claims that federated learning is fully private because raw data never leaves the device. Explain why this is insufficient and what attack vector remains.
title: Gradient Inversion Attacks in Federated Learning

details.common_mistake: Optimizing purely for ε without considering the practical attack surface. ε=8 with secure aggregation across millions of users provides strong practical privacy.
details.napkin_math: 10M users typing ~50 words/day. At 25% accuracy: 12.5 correct predictions. At 22%: 11. At 18%: 9. Users notice the 25→18% drop but not 25→22%.
details.realistic_solution: Option B (ε=8) is likely the pragmatic choice. Option A exposes users to gradient inversion attacks — for a keyboard model, this could reconstruct typed passwords, medical queries, or private messages. The reputational and legal risk far outweighs the 3% accuracy gain. Option C (ε=1) provides strong mathematical privacy guarantees but the 7% accuracy drop significantly degrades user experience — keyboard prediction at 18% feels noticeably worse, risking user churn. Option B (ε=8) provides meaningful privacy protection (gradient inversion becomes impractical with this noise level at the per-user contribution level) while maintaining competitive accuracy. Apple's deployment of federated learning for keyboard uses ε ≈ 2-8 per user per day.

scenario: A mobile keyboard prediction model trains federally on 10M devices. Option A: no differential privacy, best accuracy (25% next-word accuracy). Option B: DP with ε=8, accuracy drops to 22%. Option C: DP with ε=1 (strong privacy), accuracy drops to 18%. Which configuration should ship?
title: Privacy-Accuracy Trade-off in Federated Deployment

details.common_mistake: Forgetting optimizer states. Adam alone requires 12 extra bytes/param (FP32 master weights + momentum + variance) beyond the FP16 working copies.
details.napkin_math: 1B param model: Inference = 2GB (FP16 weights). Training = 16GB (weights+grads+optimizer) + activations. That's 8x+ more memory.
details.realistic_solution: During inference, you store only weights + activations for the current layer. During training, memory is consumed by: (1) Model weights — same as inference (2 bytes/param FP16). (2) Gradients — same size as weights (2 bytes/param). (3) Optimizer states — Adam stores momentum + variance in FP32 = 8 bytes/param. (4) Activations — saved for backward pass across ALL layers simultaneously, often the largest consumer for large batch sizes. For mixed-precision training with Adam: 2 (FP16 weights) + 2 (FP16 gradients) + 4 (FP32 master weights) + 4 (momentum) + 4 (variance) = 16 bytes/param, which is 8x the 2 bytes/param for FP16 inference weights alone.

scenario: Explain why training a model requires 4-8x more memory than inference, breaking down the major memory consumers during a training step.
title: Training Memory Footprint Breakdown

details.common_mistake: Only counting FP16 weights (13B × 2 = 26GB) and concluding it fits on one GPU. The optimizer states alone are 12 bytes/param = 156 GB.
details.napkin_math: 13B × 16 bytes/param = 208 GB. A100 = 80GB. 208/80 = 2.6 → 3 GPUs minimum. With activations: 4 GPUs realistic.
details.realistic_solution: Per-parameter memory in mixed-precision Adam: FP16 weights = 2B, FP16 gradients = 2B, FP32 master weights = 4B, FP32 momentum = 4B, FP32 variance = 4B. Total = 16 bytes/param. 13B × 16 = 208 GB for parameters alone. Each A100 has 80 GB. Minimum GPUs = ⌈208/80⌉ = 3 GPUs. But in practice, activations for a 13B model with reasonable batch size add 20-40 GB, and framework overhead takes 2-5 GB. So realistically you need 4 GPUs minimum with model parallelism (ZeRO Stage 3 or tensor parallelism) to shard optimizer states across devices.

scenario: You need to fine-tune a 13B parameter model with Adam optimizer in mixed precision on A100-80GB GPUs. Weights in FP16, optimizer in FP32. Calculate total parameter-related memory and determine the minimum number of GPUs needed (ignoring activations).
title: Will This Model Fit in GPU Memory?

details.common_mistake: Assuming gradient checkpointing alone solves OOM. It only reduces activation memory, not optimizer states, which are often the dominant consumer.
details.napkin_math: A: 129GB > 80GB (fails). B: ~56GB < 80GB (fits). C: ~77GB/GPU (works but 2x cost). LoRA wins for single-GPU.
details.realistic_solution: The 154GB breaks down as: ~14GB weights + ~14GB gradients + ~84GB optimizer + ~42GB activations. Option A: Gradient checkpointing reduces activations from ~42GB to ~17GB. New total: 14+14+84+17 = 129GB. Still exceeds 80GB. Option C: 2 GPUs with ZeRO-3 splits optimizer+gradients+weights, giving ~(14+14+84)/2 + 42 = 98GB/GPU — still OOM on 80GB without CPU offloading! Option B: LoRA with r=16 trains ~7M params. Optimizer states: 7M × 12 = 84MB. Gradients: 7M × 2 = 14MB. Total: 14GB weights + 0.1GB LoRA overhead + ~42GB activations = ~56GB. Fits on one GPU. Best choice if 1-2% accuracy trade-off is acceptable.

scenario: A 7B model needs fine-tuning on a single A100-80GB. Full fine-tuning needs ~154GB. Option A: Gradient checkpointing (saves 60% activation memory, 30% slower). Option B: LoRA (r=16, trains only 0.1% of params, may lose 1-2% accuracy). Option C: Use 2 GPUs with ZeRO Stage 3. Which approach and why?
title: Memory Reduction Strategy Selection

details.common_mistake: Using peak GEMM TFLOPS to estimate training time. Real workloads are a mix of compute-bound and memory-bound kernels.
details.napkin_math: Typical training step: 60% matmul (high FLOPS), 20% memory-bound ops, 10% communication, 10% overhead. Blended: 0.6×98% + 0.4×~5% ≈ 60% → ~45% after framework overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Micro-benchmarks isolate a single operation under ideal conditions: data pre-loaded in cache, no kernel launch overhead, steady-state execution. Real training involves: (1) Kernel launch latency — thousands of small kernels with GPU idle time between them. (2) Memory-bound operations — LayerNorm, softmax, and element-wise ops are bandwidth-limited, not compute-limited. (3) Data loading — CPU-to-GPU transfer pipeline stalls. (4) Communication — gradient synchronization across GPUs (AllReduce). (5) Python/framework overhead — graph tracing, memory allocation. The 280 TFLOPS GEMM only applies during large matmuls; the rest of the model execution hits different bottlenecks. MFU measures actual useful FLOPs across the entire step including all overheads.

scenario: A team measures GEMM throughput at 280 TFLOPS on H100 (98% of peak) but end-to-end training throughput is only 45% MFU. Explain the gap between micro-benchmark and system-level performance.
title: Why Micro-Benchmarks Mislead at System Level

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to count both reads AND writes in bandwidth calculation. Vector addition moves 3× the array size, not 1×.
details.napkin_math: Vector add: read A + read B + write C = 3 × array_size. For 95% peak: 3 × size / time = 0.95 × 2.0 TB/s. At 80GB total transfer: 80/0.042 = 1.9 TB/s (95%).
details.realistic_solution: Vector addition reads two arrays and writes one: 3 × 80GB = 240 GB total data movement. Achieved bandwidth = 240 GB / 0.042s = 5,714 GB/s = 5.71 TB/s. Wait — this exceeds peak bandwidth (2.0 TB/s). The calculation must be wrong. Correcting: 80GB is likely the total memory, not the array size. If the array is 80GB, we read 80GB + 80GB and write 80GB = 240GB. At 42ms: 240/0.042 = 5,714 GB/s which is impossible. The array must be smaller. If we get 42ms for an 80GB total transfer: 80GB / 0.042s = 1,905 GB/s = 1.9 TB/s ≈ 95% of peak 2.0 TB/s. This is a well-optimized micro-benchmark achieving near-peak memory bandwidth.

scenario: You run a vector addition micro-benchmark on an A100: 80GB array copied and added element-wise in 42ms. Calculate achieved memory bandwidth and compare to A100's peak 2.0 TB/s.
title: Isolating Memory Bandwidth via Micro-Benchmark

details.common_mistake: Blaming hardware when micro-benchmarks pass. The gap between micro and macro performance is almost always a software integration, configuration, or workload composition issue.
details.napkin_math: Vendor tests large GEMMs (4096×4096). Real model has 50% small ops. If small ops run at 10% peak: 0.5×95% + 0.5×10% = 52% → 35% after communication = plausible.
details.realistic_solution: The vendor micro-benchmarks show hardware is healthy — 35% MFU is a software/integration problem. Diagnostic micro-benchmarks to run: (1) NCCL AllReduce bandwidth test at your actual message sizes (small messages have high latency overhead vs vendor's large-message test). (2) Kernel launch latency measurement — if framework launches thousands of tiny kernels, GPU sits idle between them. (3) DataLoader throughput — measure if CPU preprocessing keeps up with GPU consumption. (4) Memory allocation profiling — frequent cudaMalloc/cudaFree causes fragmentation stalls. (5) Mixed workload benchmark — interleave matmul with LayerNorm to measure real kernel scheduling. The gap likely comes from small-kernel launch overhead, data pipeline stalls, or suboptimal NCCL topology configuration, not raw hardware capability.

scenario: Your team sees 35% MFU on a new H100 cluster. The hardware vendor's micro-benchmarks show 95% peak GEMM, 92% peak bandwidth, and 90% peak NVLink. Should you blame the hardware or the software stack? What micro-benchmarks would you run to diagnose?
title: Diagnosing Performance with Micro vs Macro Benchmarks

details.common_mistake: Equating higher throughput (samples/sec) with faster training. Larger batch sizes increase throughput but often require more total steps to converge.
details.napkin_math: System A: 100 steps/sec, needs 10K steps = 100s. System B: 80 steps/sec, needs 7K steps = 87.5s. B is slower per-step but 12.5% faster to target.
details.realistic_solution: Time-per-epoch measures raw throughput but ignores statistical efficiency — a system that processes data faster but converges slower could win on throughput yet lose on time-to-solution. Target accuracy captures the full optimization: hardware throughput, software efficiency, numerical stability, and hyperparameter tuning all contribute. A team might use larger batch sizes (higher throughput per step but worse convergence), or mixed precision (faster compute but potentially more steps needed). Time-to-target-accuracy is the only metric that captures these trade-offs holistically. It also prevents gaming — you cannot claim a fast system if it never reaches the quality threshold. The target is statistically verified across multiple runs to account for training variance.

scenario: Explain why MLPerf Training uses 'time to reach target accuracy' rather than 'time per epoch' or 'time for N steps' as its primary benchmark metric.
title: Why Time-to-Train Uses Target Accuracy Not Epochs

details.common_mistake: Using peak TFLOPS instead of effective TFLOPS (peak × MFU). Real MFU is 30-55%, making actual training 2-3x slower than peak calculations suggest.
details.napkin_math: 64 × 312 TFLOPS × 0.45 ≈ 9 PFLOPS. 3.2e18 / 9e15 ≈ 356 seconds ≈ 6 minutes.
details.realistic_solution: Effective throughput = 64 GPUs × 312 TFLOPS × 0.45 MFU = 8,985.6 TFLOPS = 8.99e15 FLOPS. Time = 3.2e18 / 8.99e15 = 356 seconds ≈ 5.9 minutes. This seems fast because 3.2e18 FLOPs is relatively modest (roughly a small ImageNet training run). For context, GPT-3 required ~3.14e23 FLOPs, which on the same 64-GPU cluster would take: 3.14e23 / 8.99e15 = 3.49e7 seconds ≈ 404 days. This illustrates why large model training requires thousands of GPUs. Doubling to 128 GPUs with linear scaling halves time to ~202 days, but communication overhead typically reduces scaling efficiency to 85-95%.

scenario: Training a model requires 3.2e18 total FLOPs to reach target accuracy. You have 64 A100 GPUs (312 TFLOPS each) at 45% MFU. Estimate wall-clock time to train.
title: Estimating Time-to-Train from Hardware Specs

details.common_mistake: Comparing only step throughput without accounting for the total number of steps needed. Larger batches process more data per step but often need more total computation to converge.
details.napkin_math: A: total FLOPs = 8K×2048×F, throughput 39.9 PFLOPS → T_A = 4.10e-10 × F. B: 12K×4096×F, throughput 202.5 PFLOPS → T_B = 2.43e-10 × F. B wins by 1.7x.
details.realistic_solution: Cluster A throughput: 256 × 312 TFLOPS × 0.50 = 39,936 TFLOPS. Per-step FLOPs (batch 2048): let F be FLOPs per sample. Step time = 2048F / 39.936e15. Total time = 8000 × 2048F / 39.936e15 = 16.384e6 × F / 39.936e15 = 4.10e-10 × F. Cluster B throughput: 512 × 989 TFLOPS × 0.40 = 202,547.2 TFLOPS. Per-step FLOPs (batch 4096): Step time = 4096F / 202.5e15. Total time = 12000 × 4096F / 202.5472e15 = 49.152e6 × F / 202.5472e15 = 2.43e-10 × F. Cluster B is 1.7x faster despite lower MFU and more steps, because 512 H100s at 989 TFLOPS each provide 5x more raw throughput. However, Cluster B's 40% MFU suggests communication or software issues — improving MFU to 50% would make it 2.1x faster.

scenario: For an MLPerf submission: Cluster A has 256 A100s at 50% MFU, known to converge in 8,000 steps at batch size 2048. Cluster B has 512 H100s at 40% MFU, but larger batches (4096) may need 12,000 steps. Which wins on time-to-train?
title: Evaluating Two Clusters for Training Competition

details.common_mistake: Reporting raw agreement without chance correction. With imbalanced classes, even random labelers achieve high raw agreement.
details.napkin_math: 90% observed, 90.5% chance → κ = (0.90 - 0.905)/(1 - 0.905) ≈ -0.053. Negative Kappa indicates agreement is slightly worse than random chance despite 90% raw match.
details.realistic_solution: Raw agreement percentage ignores chance agreement. If 95% of samples are class A, two labelers randomly guessing with that distribution would agree 90.5% of the time (0.95² + 0.05²). Cohen's Kappa (κ) corrects for this: κ = (observed_agreement - chance_agreement) / (1 - chance_agreement). With 90% observed and 90.5% expected by chance: κ = (0.90 - 0.905) / (1 - 0.905) = -0.053 — essentially zero real agreement beyond chance. Kappa values: >0.8 = strong, 0.6-0.8 = moderate, <0.4 = poor. For multi-class tasks with >2 labelers, Fleiss' Kappa or Krippendorff's Alpha generalize this correction. Always report κ alongside raw agreement.

scenario: Two labelers agree on 90% of 1,000 binary classification labels. A manager claims this is 'excellent agreement.' Explain why raw percentage agreement is insufficient and what metric should be used instead.
title: Why Raw Agreement Percentage Misleads

details.common_mistake: Using the overall class distribution instead of each annotator's marginal distribution to compute expected agreement.
details.realistic_solution: Observed agreement P_o = 400/500 = 0.80. Expected agreement P_e: P(both say Pos) = (360/500) × (340/500) = 0.72 × 0.68 = 0.4896. P(both say Neg) = (140/500) × (160/500) = 0.28 × 0.32 = 0.0896. P_e = 0.4896 + 0.0896 = 0.5792. κ = (P_o - P_e) / (1 - P_e) = (0.80 - 0.5792) / (1 - 0.5792) = 0.2208 / 0.4208 = 0.525. κ = 0.525 indicates moderate agreement. This is significantly worse than the 80% raw agreement suggests. The team should investigate disagreement patterns — are they systematic (one annotator consistently stricter) or random (ambiguous edge cases)?

scenario: Three annotators label 500 samples as Positive/Negative. Annotator pair (A,B) agrees on 400/500. Class distribution: 350 Positive, 150 Negative. A labels 360 Pos, B labels 340 Pos. Compute Cohen's Kappa for pair (A,B).
title: Computing Cohen's Kappa

details.common_mistake: Throwing more money at labeling when the root cause is an ambiguous taxonomy. If humans cannot agree on the label, the label categories need redesigning.
details.napkin_math: 10 classes at κ=0.45 → ~55% reliable labels. 6 classes at κ=0.75 → ~80% reliable labels. Model accuracy roughly tracks label quality.
details.realistic_solution: Option C is likely optimal. κ=0.45 on 10 classes means annotators fundamentally cannot distinguish certain intents — no amount of relabeling fixes an ambiguous taxonomy. Option A ($80K for adjudication) fixes surface disagreements but if the label schema itself is ambiguous, experts will also disagree. You spend $80K and may only reach κ=0.55. Option B (noisy labels + label smoothing) is cheap but trains the model on confused signal — the model inherits the annotators' confusion, and label smoothing just prevents overconfidence without fixing the underlying issue. Option C addresses the root cause: merge intents that humans cannot distinguish (e.g., 'complaint' vs 'negative feedback'). κ=0.75 means cleaner training signal, likely yielding better real-world accuracy with 6 reliable classes than 10 noisy ones.

scenario: Your team measures κ=0.45 (moderate) for a 10-class intent classification task. Labeling 50K samples costs $200K. Option A: relabel disagreements with expert adjudicators (+$80K). Option B: accept noisy labels and train with label smoothing. Option C: reduce to 6 classes (merge confusable intents) expecting κ=0.75. Which strategy?
title: Handling Low Agreement in Production Labeling

details.common_mistake: Storing learnable weights as plain tensors instead of nn.Parameter. They won't appear in model.parameters() and won't be updated by the optimizer — a silent bug.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-50: 25.6M parameters, but also ~100 buffer tensors (BN stats). Without explicit registration, optimizer would incorrectly update buffers.
details.realistic_solution: Explicit parameter registration separates learnable state from non-learnable state within a module. A layer may contain: (1) learnable parameters (weights, biases) that need gradients and optimizer updates, (2) buffers (running mean/variance in BatchNorm) that are part of model state but should NOT receive gradients, and (3) temporary tensors (intermediate computations) that are neither saved nor updated. nn.Parameter signals 'this tensor needs grad=True and should appear in model.parameters()'. Without this distinction, model.parameters() would return everything, the optimizer would try to update BatchNorm statistics via gradient descent (wrong), and serialization would save temporary tensors. The registration pattern also enables automatic recursive parameter discovery — model.parameters() traverses all submodules, collecting only registered Parameters.

scenario: Explain why PyTorch's nn.Module requires explicit parameter registration (nn.Parameter) rather than automatically treating all tensors as learnable parameters.
title: Why nn.Module Uses Parameter Registration

details.common_mistake: Forgetting bias terms in Linear layers or the two learnable parameters (scale, shift) in each LayerNorm. These add up in deep models.
details.napkin_math: Embedding: 25.6M. 6 blocks: ~2.1M × 6 = 12.6M. Final linear: 25.65M. Total ≈ 64M params = 128MB in FP16.

scenario: A model has: Embedding(50000, 512), 6× TransformerBlock each containing [Linear(512,2048), Linear(2048,512), LayerNorm(512), LayerNorm(512)], and a final Linear(512,50000). Count total parameters (include biases).
title: Counting Parameters in a Module Hierarchy

details.common_mistake: Using torch.save(model) for production checkpoints. Pickle serializes the class reference, creating a fragile coupling between code structure and saved weights.
details.napkin_math: Team B: 1 pickle file, breaks on any refactor. Team A: state_dict + versioned code, survives arbitrary refactoring.
details.realistic_solution: Team B's approach breaks because torch.save(model) uses Python's pickle, which stores a reference to the class's module path. When they refactor (rename class, move file, change __init__ signature), unpickling fails with ImportError or AttributeError because pickle tries to import the original class at its original path. Team A's state_dict approach is robust: the state_dict is a plain {name: tensor} dictionary that is architecture-agnostic. Loading requires reconstructing the model in code first (model = MyModel()), then loading weights (model.load_state_dict(dict)). This decouples architecture evolution from weight storage. The trade-off: Team A must maintain code to reconstruct every historical architecture version, but this is version-controllable. Team A's pattern is the industry standard for production deployment.

scenario: Team A stores model architecture in code and only serializes state_dict. Team B uses torch.save(model) to serialize the entire module including class definition. Six months later, Team B refactors their module class. Diagnose what breaks and recommend the better pattern.
title: Module Design for Serialization Robustness

details.common_mistake: Forgetting model.eval() before inference. This causes non-deterministic predictions from Dropout and batch-dependent predictions from BatchNorm.
details.napkin_math: Dropout(p=0.5) in train mode: 50% of features randomly zeroed. In eval mode: all features active, outputs scaled. Difference can be >10% per prediction.
details.realistic_solution: Two layer types behave differently in training vs eval mode: (1) Dropout: In training mode, randomly zeroes activations with probability p and scales remaining by 1/(1-p). In eval mode, dropout is disabled — all activations pass through unchanged. Without eval(), identical inputs produce different outputs each forward pass due to random dropout masks. (2) BatchNorm: In training mode, normalizes using the current batch's mean and variance (noisy, batch-dependent). In eval mode, uses the stored running mean and running variance accumulated during training (deterministic). Without eval(), predictions depend on the batch composition. The fix is calling model.eval() before inference, which sets self.training=False for all submodules, changing these layers' behavior to their deterministic inference variants.

scenario: A developer deploys a model without calling model.eval() and notices prediction quality varies between identical inputs. Explain which layers cause this and why.
title: Why model.eval() Matters for Inference

details.common_mistake: Thinking momentum=0.1 means 10% of the running average is kept. PyTorch convention: new = (1-momentum)×old + momentum×batch. So 0.1 means 10% NEW, 90% old.
details.napkin_math: Eval: uses 2.0 (stored). Train: uses 5.0 (batch), updates running to 0.9×2.0 + 0.1×5.0 = 2.3. A 2.5x difference in normalization!
details.realistic_solution: In eval mode: Uses running_mean = 2.0. The batch mean (5.0) is irrelevant — eval mode always uses the stored running statistics for deterministic behavior. In train mode: Uses the current batch mean = 5.0 for normalization. Additionally, it updates the running statistics: new_running_mean = (1 - momentum) × running_mean + momentum × batch_mean = 0.9 × 2.0 + 0.1 × 5.0 = 1.8 + 0.5 = 2.3. So training mode both uses batch statistics (noisy) AND updates the running statistics as a side effect. This is why running BatchNorm in training mode during inference is doubly wrong: predictions are batch-dependent, AND it corrupts the stored statistics that were carefully accumulated during training.

scenario: A BatchNorm layer has running_mean=2.0 (accumulated over 100K training steps, momentum=0.1). A single eval batch has batch mean=5.0. What value does BatchNorm use for normalization in train mode vs eval mode?
title: BatchNorm Statistics Divergence

details.common_mistake: Blaming Dropout for train-eval gaps. Dropout typically improves eval accuracy (it's a regularizer). The culprit is usually BatchNorm running statistics not matching the test distribution.
details.napkin_math: Training with batch=4: batch stats variance is high. Running stats = smooth average of 100K batches. If model memorized batch-specific noise, eval drops 10-15%.
details.realistic_solution: A 14-point train→eval drop with correct eval() usage points to BatchNorm running statistics divergence, not Dropout (which should improve or maintain accuracy in eval). Common cause: the training data distribution shifted during training (e.g., curriculum learning, data augmentation changes), so the running_mean and running_variance accumulated early in training don't match the data distribution the model converged on. Fix: after training completes, run a calibration pass over a representative dataset with model.train() but torch.no_grad() to recompute fresh running statistics that match the final data distribution. Alternatively, switch to GroupNorm or LayerNorm which have no running statistics. Another possibility: very small training batches (e.g., 4-8) cause high-variance batch statistics during training, but running stats are smooth averages — the model learned to exploit batch-specific statistics it won't have at eval time.

scenario: A model achieves 92% accuracy during training but drops to 78% when deployed (with model.eval() correctly called). The model uses BatchNorm and Dropout(0.3). Diagnose the most likely cause and the fix.
title: Diagnosing Train-Eval Performance Gap

details.common_mistake: Thinking pure functions are just a coding style preference. The purity constraint is what makes mathematical transform composition (grad of vmap of jit) provably correct.
details.napkin_math: JAX: jit(grad(vmap(f))) — 3 transforms compose cleanly. PyTorch equivalent requires torch.compile + torch.func.grad + torch.vmap with careful state management.
details.realistic_solution: Pure functions guarantee that output depends only on input — no hidden state, no randomness, no mutation. This mathematical property enables: (1) jit — the compiler can safely cache and reuse compiled kernels because the function always produces the same output for the same input. (2) grad — automatic differentiation can trace through the function knowing there are no side effects that could invalidate the gradient tape. (3) vmap — the compiler can automatically vectorize a function over a batch dimension because each element is independent (no cross-element mutation). In PyTorch, nn.Module maintains mutable state (parameters, buffers, training flag), making these transforms harder — you cannot naively JIT compile a stateful module without handling its state carefully. JAX trades ergonomic mutability for composable, mathematically sound transformations.

scenario: Explain why JAX requires pure functions (no side effects, no in-place mutation) and how this constraint enables powerful transformations like vmap, jit, and grad that are difficult in PyTorch.
title: Pure Functions Enable Composable Transforms

details.common_mistake: Expecting exactly 256x speedup. Memory constraints and GPU occupancy limits typically cap practical vmap speedups at 50-150x for realistic model sizes.
details.napkin_math: Loop: 256 × 12.5ms = 3.2s. vmap: ~32ms (100x speedup). Bottleneck was kernel launch overhead, not compute.
details.realistic_solution: A Python loop over 256 samples incurs: 256 individual kernel launches, 256 separate backward passes, and Python interpreter overhead between each. vmap transforms this into a single batched kernel call. Theoretical speedup: 256x (perfect vectorization). Practical speedup: typically 50-150x due to memory overhead (storing all 256 computation graphs simultaneously) and diminishing GPU parallelism at high batch sizes. At 100x speedup: 3.2s / 100 = 32ms. The key bottleneck in the loop version is not compute but kernel launch overhead (~10μs per launch × 256 × multiple kernels per backward pass). vmap eliminates this by fusing everything into one launch. Memory cost: vmap materializes all per-sample gradients simultaneously, requiring 256x more memory than a single gradient.

scenario: Computing per-sample gradients for 256 samples using a loop takes 3.2 seconds. Using vmap(grad(loss_fn)) vectorizes this into a single batched operation. If the GPU has sufficient parallelism, estimate the speedup and wall-clock time.
title: Vectorization Speedup via vmap

details.common_mistake: Choosing a framework based on popularity rather than the specific workload requirements. JAX excels at mathematical transforms; PyTorch excels at ecosystem and deployment.
details.napkin_math: Per-sample grads: JAX = 1 line (vmap(grad(f))). PyTorch = 10-20 lines with torch.func or manual loop. Higher-order: JAX = grad(grad(f)). PyTorch = create_graph=True + manual management.
details.realistic_solution: JAX is likely the better fit for this specific project. Per-sample gradients (vmap(grad(f))) and higher-order derivatives (grad(grad(f))) compose naturally in JAX's functional paradigm — they are first-class operations, not bolted-on features. In PyTorch, per-sample gradients require torch.func.vmap (still maturing) or manual tricks, and higher-order derivatives need create_graph=True with careful memory management. Trade-offs favoring JAX: mathematical composability, XLA compilation for custom ops, reproducibility (pure functions = deterministic). Trade-offs favoring PyTorch: larger ecosystem (HuggingFace, torchvision), easier debugging (eager mode by default), more hiring availability, mutable state is natural for standard training loops. The team should consider: if the project is research-focused with novel math, JAX wins. If it needs production deployment with existing infrastructure, PyTorch's ecosystem advantage matters more.

scenario: A research team is starting a new project involving novel architectures with heavy use of per-sample gradients, custom higher-order derivatives, and auto-vectorization. They currently use PyTorch. Should they switch to JAX? What are the trade-offs?
title: Choosing Between Stateful and Functional Paradigms

details.common_mistake: Assuming a kernel that is compute-bound on A100 is also compute-bound on H100. The higher ridge point means workloads shift toward memory-bound on newer hardware.
details.napkin_math: A100 ridge: 312T/2.0T = 156 FLOPs/byte. H100 ridge: 989T/3.35T = 295 FLOPs/byte. Ridge nearly doubled → more ops are memory-bound on H100.
details.realistic_solution: Hardware balance = peak FLOPS / peak bandwidth. A100: 312e12 / 2.0e12 = 156 FLOPs/byte. H100: 989e12 / 3.35e12 = 295 FLOPs/byte. The H100's ridge point is nearly 2x higher than the A100's. This means workloads need ~2x higher arithmetic intensity on H100 to be compute-bound. Operations that were compute-bound on A100 (e.g., large matmuls at AI=200) may become memory-bound on H100 (since 200 < 295). This is the 'compute-bandwidth gap' widening each GPU generation. It means: (1) kernel fusion and data reuse become more critical on newer GPUs, (2) memory-bound operations (attention, LayerNorm) become relatively more expensive, and (3) batch sizes may need to increase to push arithmetic intensity above the new ridge.

scenario: The A100 has 312 TFLOPS (FP16) and 2.0 TB/s memory bandwidth. The H100 has 989 TFLOPS and 3.35 TB/s. Compare their hardware balance points and explain what this means for workload optimization.
title: The Ridge Point and Hardware Balance

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that Q×K^T is compute-bound but the softmax that follows is memory-bound. The overall attention block is a mix of both regimes.
details.napkin_math: AI = 537M FLOPs / 0.5MB = 1,024 FLOPs/byte >> 156 ridge point. Compute-bound. Time ≈ 537M/312T = 1.7μs per head.
details.realistic_solution: FLOPs = 2 × 2048 × 2048 × 64 = 536,870,912 ≈ 537M FLOPs. Data loaded: input matrices Q and K, each 2048×64 in FP16 = 2048×64×2 = 262,144 bytes each. Total = 524,288 bytes. Arithmetic intensity = 537M / 524,288 = 1,024 FLOPs/byte. A100 ridge point = 156 FLOPs/byte. Since 1,024 >> 156, this matmul is compute-bound on A100. Expected throughput is limited by peak FLOPS (312 TFLOPS), not bandwidth. Time estimate: 537M FLOPs / 312e12 FLOPS = 1.72 μs. However, this is a single attention head; with 16 heads the total is 16× larger. The attention softmax and value multiplication that follow have much lower arithmetic intensity and may be memory-bound.

scenario: A self-attention layer with sequence length 2048 and head dimension 64 computes Q×K^T: a (2048×64) × (64×2048) matmul. It performs 2×2048×2048×64 FLOPs and loads 2×2048×64×2=524,288 bytes. Is this compute-bound or memory-bound on A100?
title: Determining Bottleneck from Hardware Balance

details.common_mistake: Confusing ML Test Score with model evaluation metrics. It does not measure accuracy — it measures the system's ability to maintain accuracy over time in production.
details.napkin_math: 28 tests, each scored 0-1. Max score = 28. Typical org first assessment: 5-8 out of 28. Google's recommendation: score >20 before production deployment.
details.realistic_solution: The ML Test Score (proposed by Google, Breck et al. 2017) is a rubric of 28 tests across four categories: (1) Data tests — feature schema validation, data freshness, distribution monitoring. (2) Model tests — training reproducibility, fairness checks, performance on slices. (3) Infrastructure tests — training pipeline reliability, serving latency, resource utilization. (4) Monitoring tests — prediction drift detection, feature attribution tracking, alerting coverage. It deliberately ignores model accuracy because high accuracy with poor infrastructure is fragile — a model with 95% accuracy but no data validation, no drift detection, and no rollback capability will silently degrade in production. The score quantifies operational readiness: 'Can this system detect, diagnose, and recover from failures?' A team can have a state-of-the-art model (high accuracy) but score 0 on the ML Test Score if they have no testing infrastructure.

scenario: Explain what the ML Test Score measures and why it was designed to assess technical debt rather than model accuracy.
title: The ML Test Score Framework

details.common_mistake: Treating all 28 tests as equally important. Data tests and monitoring should be prioritized first because they catch the most common production failures (silent data degradation).
details.napkin_math: Gap: 12 tests × ~2 weeks avg = 24 engineer-weeks. At 1 engineer: 6 months. At 2 engineers: 3 months. Infrastructure debt compounds if deferred.
details.realistic_solution: Current ML Test Score: 8/28 = 0.286 (29%). Production-ready target: 20/28 = 0.714 (71%). Gap: 12 tests to implement. Category breakdown of the gap: Data monitoring (drift detection, feature monitoring, data freshness) = 3 tests, ~2 weeks each. Model quality (fairness tests, slice evaluation, regression tests) = 3 tests, ~2 weeks each. Infrastructure (canary deploy, rollback, A/B testing) = 3 tests, ~3 weeks each. Monitoring (alerting, dashboards, prediction logging) = 3 tests, ~1 week each. Total estimated time: 3×2 + 3×2 + 3×3 + 3×1 = 6 + 6 + 9 + 3 = 24 engineer-weeks ≈ 6 months with one dedicated ML platform engineer. This illustrates why ML infrastructure is the hidden cost of production ML.

scenario: A team has: automated training pipeline (1 pt), model unit tests (1 pt), data schema validation (1 pt), but no feature monitoring (0 pt), no fairness tests (0 pt), no data drift detection (0 pt), no canary deployment (0 pt), no slice-level evaluation (0 pt). They pass 8 of 28 total tests. Calculate the score and estimate time to reach production-ready (score 20).
title: Scoring a Production ML System

details.common_mistake: Investing in deployment automation (canary, rollback) before data monitoring. You cannot roll back from a problem you cannot detect.
details.napkin_math: B: 5 tests, covers 60% of production failures (data issues). A: 3 tests, covers ~15% (fairness). C: 2 tests, covers ~20% (deployment failures). B has best coverage/week ratio.
details.realistic_solution: Option B is the best investment. It addresses 5 tests in 8 weeks (from 10 to 15) compared to A's 3 tests and C's 2 tests. More importantly, data drift and feature validation catch the #1 cause of production ML failure: silent data quality degradation. Studies show ~60% of ML production incidents stem from data issues, not model issues. Option A (fairness testing) is critical for responsible AI but doesn't prevent the most common production failures — it catches bias issues that are relatively stable over time. Option C (canary + rollback) provides a safety net but only after damage is detected — it's reactive. Option B is proactive: drift detection catches problems before they affect users, feature validation prevents bad data from entering the pipeline, and alerting notifies the team immediately. The ideal sequence: B first (detect problems) → C second (respond to problems) → A third (ensure equity).

scenario: You have 8 engineering weeks to improve an ML system scoring 10/28 on the ML Test Score. You can invest in: (A) comprehensive model fairness testing (+3 tests, 8 weeks), (B) data drift monitoring + feature validation (+4 tests, 6 weeks) + basic alerting (+1 test, 2 weeks), or (C) canary deployment + automated rollback (+2 tests, 8 weeks). Which investment maximizes operational reliability?
title: Prioritizing ML Test Score Improvements

details.common_mistake: Confusing Level 1 and Level 2. Level 1 automates the ML training pipeline. Level 2 automates the deployment and testing of the pipeline itself — it's meta-automation.
details.napkin_math: Level 0: weeks to retrain. Level 1: hours (automated pipeline). Level 2: minutes (CI/CD triggers on code or data change). Each level: ~10x faster iteration.
details.realistic_solution: Level 0 (Manual): Data scientists work in notebooks, manually train models, and hand off artifacts to engineers for deployment. No pipeline automation, no CI/CD, no monitoring. Retraining requires a human to re-run the entire process. Key limitation: no reproducibility. Level 1 (ML Pipeline Automation): Training is automated as a pipeline — data ingestion, preprocessing, training, validation, and deployment run as an orchestrated workflow (e.g., Kubeflow, Airflow). Feature stores provide consistent features. Continuous training triggers automatically on new data or schedule. Key milestone: automated retraining. Level 2 (CI/CD Pipeline Automation): The pipeline code itself is tested and deployed automatically. Changes to data processing, model architecture, or hyperparameters go through CI (unit tests, integration tests) and CD (staged rollout). Both the model AND the pipeline are versioned, tested, and continuously deployed. Key milestone: automated pipeline deployment, not just automated model training.

scenario: Describe the three MLOps maturity levels (0, 1, 2) and identify the key automation milestone that distinguishes each level.
title: MLOps Maturity Levels Explained

details.common_mistake: Only counting direct retraining time. The hidden costs of Level 0 are incidents from stale models, reproducibility failures, and engineer context-switching overhead.
details.napkin_math: Level 0: $154K/yr. Level 1: $84K Year 1, $74K Year 2+. Savings of $80K/yr after payback period of 11 months.
details.realistic_solution: Retraining cost: 5 models × 3 days × 12 months × $800/day = $144,000/year. Incident cost: 2 incidents × 4 hours × 12 months × ($800/8 hours) = 2 × 4 × 12 × $100/hr = $9,600/year. Total Level 0 cost: $153,600/year. Now compare to Level 1 automation costing $60K to build + $2K/month infrastructure: Year 1: $60K + $24K = $84K. Year 2+: $24K/year. Engineer time drops to 1 day/model/month for monitoring: 5 × 1 × 12 × $800 = $48K. Incidents drop by 80%: $1,920/year. Level 1 total Year 2: $24K + $48K + $1.9K = $73.9K. Savings: $79.7K/year from Year 2. ROI payback: ~11 months.

scenario: A Level 0 team manually retrains 5 models monthly. Each retrain takes 3 engineer-days (data prep, training, validation, deployment). Engineers cost $800/day. The team also experiences 2 incidents/month from stale models, each costing 4 hours of firefighting. Calculate annual cost of manual MLOps.
title: Cost of Manual MLOps (Level 0)

details.common_mistake: Over-engineering MLOps infrastructure for a small team. The Google ML maturity model was designed for Google-scale (thousands of models). Startups should optimize for iteration speed, not automation maturity.
details.napkin_math: 2 engineers × 6 months = 12 engineer-months (240 working days) on infra vs shipping. At 3 models, Level 2 saves ~2 days/month. Payback: 240 days / 2 days/month = 120 months (10 years). Not worth it.
details.realistic_solution: No — jumping to Level 2 is premature. With 2 engineers and 3 models, the bottleneck is feature development, not pipeline automation. Six months building CI/CD for ML pipelines means 6 months NOT shipping models, while the competitor ships 10. Level 2 pays off when you have: (1) enough models that manual management doesn't scale (>10-15), (2) enough engineers to staff both platform and product ML (>5), (3) frequent retraining where automation saves significant time. The startup should implement Level 1 first — a simple orchestrated pipeline (even cron + scripts) that automates retraining. This takes 2-4 weeks, not 6 months, and eliminates 80% of manual toil. Level 2 should be a goal for Year 2 when model count and team size justify the investment. Premature infrastructure is a form of technical debt — it adds complexity before it adds value.

scenario: A startup with 2 ML engineers and 3 models in production wants to jump straight to Level 2 MLOps (full CI/CD for ML pipelines). Their competitor ships 10 models at Level 0. Should the startup invest 6 months building Level 2 infrastructure?
title: When Level 2 MLOps Is Premature

details.common_mistake: Treating pipeline complexity as a code problem solvable by refactoring. The real issue is the lack of explicit data contracts and lineage tracking between pipeline stages.
details.napkin_math: Typical pipeline jungle: 20+ scripts, 50+ intermediate files, ~5 undocumented dependencies per script. Change impact analysis: intractable without data lineage tooling.
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline jungles grow incrementally: (1) v1 has a simple ETL script. (2) A new data source requires a join, added as a separate script with an intermediate file. (3) A feature engineering step is inserted, reading from both scripts' outputs. (4) A data quality fix adds a cleaning step that only some downstream scripts use. (5) A model needs historical features, adding a backfill script. After 12-18 months, you have 20+ scripts with implicit dependencies through intermediate files, no centralized schema, and no documentation of data lineage. This is worse than code complexity because: (1) failures are silent — a corrupted intermediate file produces wrong features, not an error. (2) Testing is nearly impossible — you cannot unit test a pipeline that depends on production data state. (3) Changes are terrifying — modifying one script may break unknown downstream consumers. The fundamental issue is that pipelines encode implicit contracts through file formats rather than explicit interfaces.

scenario: Explain how a well-intentioned ML data pipeline evolves into a 'pipeline jungle' and why these are particularly dangerous compared to regular code complexity.
title: How Pipeline Jungles Form

details.common_mistake: Only counting the direct time savings. Pipeline jungles also cause incidents (2-3/month), context-switching overhead, and onboarding delays for new engineers — the true cost is 2-3x the direct time estimate.
details.napkin_math: Current: 42 hrs/month. Post-rewrite: 4.5 hrs/month. Savings: 37.5 hrs/month. Rewrite: 66 days = 528 hrs. Payback: 528/37.5 = 14.08 months. Total ROI timeline: 3 months build + 14 months payback = 17 months.
details.realistic_solution: Current cost per feature: 4 scripts × 2 hrs + 6 hrs validation = 14 hours. Monthly: 3 × 14 = 42 hours. Annual: 504 hours. Post-rewrite cost per feature: 1 script × 0.5 hrs + 1 hr validation = 1.5 hours. Monthly: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 hours. Annual: 54 hours. Monthly savings: 42 - 4.5 = 37.5 hours. Rewrite cost: 3 months × 22 days/month × 8 hours/day = 528 hours. Payback: 528 / 37.5 = 14.08 months after completion. Total ROI timeline: 3 months build + ~14.1 months payback = ~17.1 months to break even. This means the investment takes over a year to pay off in direct time savings, highlighting why pipeline refactors must often be justified by qualitative improvements (fewer incidents, onboarding speed) alongside raw time savings.

scenario: A team's pipeline jungle has 25 interconnected scripts. Adding a new feature requires modifying 4 scripts, testing each against production data (2 hours/script), and a full pipeline validation run (6 hours). The team adds 3 features/month. A pipeline rewrite to a managed DAG (Airflow) takes 3 months (1 engineer) but reduces feature addition to 1 script change + 30 min test + 1 hour validation. Calculate when the rewrite pays for itself.
title: Pipeline Jungle Impact on Iteration Speed

details.common_mistake: Choosing the full rewrite because it feels cleaner. Pipeline rewrites fail at high rates because they underestimate the implicit business logic embedded in years of accumulated scripts.
details.napkin_math: A: 4 months, high risk (all-or-nothing cutover). B: 8 months, low risk (incremental). C: 1 month, no fix (just visibility). B = safest path to clean architecture.
details.realistic_solution: Option B (strangler fig) is typically safest. Option A (full rewrite) is the 'second system effect' trap: a 4-month rewrite of 30 scripts with 12 model dependencies will inevitably miss edge cases, require simultaneous revalidation of all 12 models, and risk production outages during cutover. History shows full pipeline rewrites take 2-3x longer than estimated. Option C (add monitoring) is a band-aid — it helps detect failures but doesn't fix the root cause of untestable, rigid dependencies. You still can't safely change anything. Option B wraps each existing script as a task node in the DAG, preserving current behavior while adding: explicit dependency tracking, retry logic, monitoring, and testability. Then you migrate one pipeline path at a time, validating each migration against the old path. This is slower but has near-zero risk of production disruption and can be paused if priorities shift.

scenario: Your ML system has a pipeline jungle: 30 scripts, 80 intermediate files, 12 models depending on various stages. Option A: full rewrite to a modern orchestration framework (4 months, 2 engineers, all models retrained). Option B: strangler fig pattern — wrap existing scripts in a DAG, migrate one pipeline at a time (8 months, 1 engineer, models migrate incrementally). Option C: add data contracts and monitoring around the existing jungle (1 month, 1 engineer). Which approach?
title: Pipeline Jungle Remediation Strategy

details.common_mistake: Thinking the solution is writing less glue code. The issue is that glue code grows organically without the testing discipline applied to production software. It needs proper engineering, not elimination.
details.napkin_math: Typical ML service: ~200 lines model code, ~4,000 lines infrastructure/glue code. 200/4200 = 4.8% model code, 95.2% glue.
details.realistic_solution: ML models are typically implemented using off-the-shelf packages (sklearn, PyTorch, TensorFlow) that handle training and inference in few lines. The remaining 95% consists of: (1) Data collection and validation — ingestion pipelines, schema enforcement, missing value handling. (2) Feature extraction — transforming raw data into model-ready features with business logic. (3) Configuration management — hyperparameter configs, feature flags, model version routing. (4) Serving infrastructure — API endpoints, batching, caching, load balancing. (5) Monitoring — prediction logging, drift detection, alerting. (6) Integration adapters — converting between the ML library's data format and the company's internal systems. The ratio is extreme because ML libraries provide a powerful but generic abstraction; adapting that abstraction to a specific business domain requires extensive custom code. This glue code is the source of most bugs and maintenance burden because it has no standardized testing framework.

scenario: Google's technical debt paper found that in many ML systems, only 5% of the code is actual ML model code while 95% is 'glue code.' Explain why this ratio is so extreme and what the glue code consists of.
title: Why Glue Code Dominates ML Systems

details.common_mistake: Focusing optimization efforts on the 500 lines of model code (hyperparameter tuning, architecture changes) while ignoring the 8,000 lines of glue that generate 99.5% of maintenance costs.
details.napkin_math: Model: 0.25 bugs × 2h = 0.5h/mo. Glue: 24 bugs × 4h = 96h/mo. Glue code = 99.5% of maintenance burden despite being 94% of codebase.
details.realistic_solution: Model bugs: 0.5 bugs/1000 lines × 0.5K lines = 0.25 bugs/month × 2 hours = 0.5 hours/month. Glue bugs: 3.0 bugs/1000 lines × 8K lines = 24 bugs/month × 4 hours = 96 hours/month. Total: 96.5 hours/month, of which 99.5% comes from glue code. This illustrates why glue code is the primary maintenance burden: it has 6x higher bug density (3.0 vs 0.5 per 1000 lines) because it lacks the testing rigor of the ML library, AND each bug takes 2x longer to fix because glue code bugs often involve complex interactions between systems (data format mismatches, API version incompatibilities, timing issues). At $100/hour engineer cost: glue code costs $9,600/month = $115,200/year in maintenance alone.

scenario: An ML service has 500 lines of model code and 8,000 lines of glue code. Bug fix rate: 0.5 bugs/month per 1,000 lines of model code, 3.0 bugs/month per 1,000 lines of glue code. Each model bug takes 2 hours; each glue bug takes 4 hours. Calculate monthly maintenance hours.
title: Quantifying Glue Code Maintenance Cost

details.common_mistake: Keeping the off-the-shelf package because 'it works.' The true cost is the 6,000 lines of glue code that grow with every new requirement, eventually exceeding the cost of a custom solution.
details.napkin_math: Current: 6K glue + 500 model = 6.5K lines, ~20 bugs/mo. Proposed: 1.5K glue + 2K model = 3.5K lines, ~8 bugs/mo. 60% fewer bugs if implemented well.
details.realistic_solution: This is a classic glue code trade-off. Current state: 6,000 lines glue + generic AutoML = high maintenance, rigid coupling, compliance risk (glue may not properly transform all edge cases). Proposed state: 2,000 lines custom model + 1,500 lines minimal glue = 3,500 total lines, 46% reduction. Benefits: (1) 46% less code to maintain, (2) data contracts are explicit in the model, not implicit in glue, (3) compliance logging can be built into the training pipeline, (4) team gains deep understanding of the model for regulatory audits. Risks: (1) custom model needs expertise to build and maintain, (2) AutoML may yield better accuracy through automated HPO, (3) regulatory changes may require model changes (harder with custom). The proposal is sound IF the team has the expertise. In fintech, regulatory explainability often requires custom models anyway — AutoML's black-box nature makes compliance harder despite reducing model development effort.

scenario: A fintech company uses an off-the-shelf AutoML package for credit scoring, wrapped in 6,000 lines of glue code for data formatting, feature engineering, and compliance logging. A senior engineer proposes replacing AutoML with a custom model (2,000 lines) that natively handles the company's data schema, reducing glue to 1,500 lines. Should they do it?
title: Build Custom vs Use Off-the-Shelf ML Package

details.common_mistake: Assuming data pipeline changes are safe if the schema (column names, types) doesn't change. Silent changes to computation logic or data semantics are the real danger.
details.napkin_math: 30-day avg engagement: mean=0.65, std=0.1. 7-day avg: mean=0.58, std=0.25. Distribution shift causes ~5-15% accuracy degradation, undetected for weeks.
details.realistic_solution: The model was trained on features computed with a 30-day window. The new 7-day window produces systematically different values: higher variance, more recency bias, different scale. The model doesn't error out — it receives validly formatted floating point numbers — but its predictions degrade because the input distribution has shifted. This is a silent failure because: (1) no schema violation occurs (the column name and type are unchanged), (2) no error is thrown (values are within plausible ranges), (3) standard monitoring (latency, error rate) shows nothing wrong, (4) only prediction quality metrics degrade, often slowly enough to miss without statistical testing. The root cause is an undeclared dependency: the ML model implicitly depends on the upstream feature's computation method, but this dependency exists nowhere in code, contracts, or documentation. The upstream team had no way to know their change would affect the ML model.

scenario: A recommendation model uses a 'user_engagement_score' feature. Unknown to the ML team, the upstream data engineering team changes the engagement score calculation from 30-day rolling average to 7-day rolling average. Explain why this causes a silent failure.
title: How Undeclared Data Dependencies Cause Silent Failures

details.common_mistake: Setting alert thresholds without accounting for multiple comparisons. Monitoring 50 features at 2-sigma generates ~1 false alarm per day, causing alert fatigue.
details.napkin_math: Z = (0.42-0.38)/0.015 = 2.67. Raw threshold 2σ: triggers. Bonferroni-corrected for 50 tests (3.29σ): does not trigger. Practical: alert but lower priority.
details.realistic_solution: Z-score = |observed_mean - expected_mean| / historical_std = |0.38 - 0.42| / 0.015 = 0.04 / 0.015 = 2.67. Alert threshold is 2-sigma (z > 2.0). Since 2.67 > 2.0, YES, this triggers an alert. But with 50 features monitored daily, you expect false alarms: at 2-sigma threshold (2-tailed), ~4.55% of checks are false positives = 50 × 0.0455 = 2.27 false alarms/day. To reduce alert fatigue, use Bonferroni correction: adjusted threshold = 2-sigma for 50 tests ≈ 3.29-sigma. At this corrected threshold: 2.67 < 3.29, so this would NOT trigger with correction. The tension: Bonferroni reduces false alarms but may miss real distribution shifts. A practical compromise: use 2.5-sigma threshold and investigate any feature with persistent multi-day shifts.

scenario: You monitor 50 features with daily distribution checks (mean, std, min, max). A feature's mean shifts from 0.42 to 0.38 (a 9.5% change) overnight. Your alert threshold is a 2-sigma deviation. Historical daily mean variation has std=0.015. Does this trigger an alert?
title: Detecting Undeclared Dependencies via Feature Statistics

details.common_mistake: Choosing monitoring (Option B) over prevention (Option A). Detecting a broken feature after predictions degrade is far more expensive than preventing the breakage via versioned schemas.
details.napkin_math: 50 models × 4 features avg = 200 dependencies. At 5% silent breakage rate/year: 10 incidents × $200K avg impact = $2M/year. Feature store ($500K) = 3-month payback.
details.realistic_solution: The correct answer is A + C, with B as a safety net — but if forced to choose one, Option A (feature store) is most impactful. Option C (shared catalog) is cheapest but relies on human compliance — upstream teams must remember to register changes, which fails under time pressure. It catches ~60% of issues. Option B (statistical monitoring) detects problems after they occur but doesn't prevent them. It's reactive: by the time you detect a shift, predictions have already degraded. Detection-to-fix latency is typically days. Option A (feature store) is the only preventive solution. Versioned feature schemas mean the ML model pins to a specific feature version. When upstream changes the computation, it creates a new version — the ML model continues using the old version until explicitly migrated. This decouples upstream changes from downstream consumption. The $500K cost pays for itself after preventing 2-3 silent failures (each costing $100K-$500K in degraded recommendations or incorrect decisions).

scenario: Your organization has 50 ML models consuming features from 200+ upstream data sources. Option A: build a centralized feature store with versioned feature schemas ($500K, 6 months). Option B: add statistical monitoring on all model inputs ($100K, 2 months). Option C: require upstream teams to register all schema/logic changes in a shared catalog ($50K, 1 month). Which strategy best prevents silent failures?
title: Preventing Undeclared Dependencies at Scale

details.common_mistake: Jumping straight to A/B testing without shadow validation. If the new model has a catastrophic failure mode, A/B testing exposes 50% of users to it.
details.napkin_math: Shadow: 0% user risk, days to validate. Canary: 1-5% risk exposure, hours to validate system health. A/B: 50% exposure, weeks for statistical significance.
details.realistic_solution: Shadow deployment: The new model runs in parallel with production, processing real traffic, but its predictions are logged — never served to users. Purpose: validate that the model produces reasonable outputs on real data without any user impact. Use when: first deploying a new model type or making large architecture changes. Risk mitigated: catastrophic prediction errors on real-world data not captured in offline eval. Canary release: Route a small fraction (1-5%) of real traffic to the new model and serve its predictions. Monitor key metrics (latency, error rate, business KPIs). Use when: the model has passed shadow testing and you need to validate end-to-end system performance including latency. Risk mitigated: system-level issues (serving latency, memory leaks) under real load. A/B testing: Randomly split users 50/50 between old and new model for a statistically significant period. Measure business impact. Use when: model changes are incremental and you need to quantify revenue/engagement impact. Risk mitigated: deploying a model that is technically correct but hurts business metrics.

scenario: Explain the three main online evaluation strategies, when each is appropriate, and what risk each mitigates.
title: Shadow Mode vs A/B Testing vs Canary Releases

details.common_mistake: Running the A/B test for a fixed time rather than a fixed sample size. Peeking at results before reaching statistical significance inflates false positive rates.
details.napkin_math: Detecting 5% relative improvement in 3.2% CTR needs ~200K samples per group. At 100K/day: ~4 days minimum, 7-14 days recommended.
details.realistic_solution: Minimum sample size per group for a proportion test: n = (Z_α/2 + Z_β)² × (p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)) / (p2-p1)². Where p1=0.032, p2=0.0336, Z_0.025=1.96, Z_0.20=0.84. n = (1.96+0.84)² × (0.032×0.968 + 0.0336×0.9664) / (0.0336-0.032)². n = 7.84 × (0.03098 + 0.03247) / (0.0016)² = 7.84 × 0.06345 / 0.00000256. n = 0.4974 / 0.00000256 = 194,297 per group. Total needed: 2 × 194,297 = 388,594 impressions. At 100K/day: 388,594 / 100,000 = 3.89 days ≈ 4 days minimum. In practice, run for 1-2 full weeks to account for day-of-week effects and reduce novelty bias.

scenario: Your current model has a 3.2% click-through rate (CTR). The new model is expected to improve CTR by 5% relative (to 3.36%). Your site gets 100K daily impressions. At 95% confidence and 80% power, estimate the minimum A/B test duration.
title: A/B Test Duration Calculation

details.common_mistake: Using A/B testing for safety-critical models. The potential loss from exposing 50% of traffic to a flawed model far outweighs the statistical power gained vs a canary approach.
details.napkin_math: A/B at 50%: if new model FNR is 2% worse on a fraud pattern, 50% × 1000 daily frauds × 2% × $10K = $100K/day exposure. Canary at 1%: same scenario = $2K/day exposure.
details.realistic_solution: Use shadow deployment first, then a careful canary release — NOT direct A/B testing. Reasoning: (1) The cost asymmetry is extreme: false negatives cost 200x more than false positives ($10K vs $50). A/B testing at 50% traffic means 50% of transactions use the unvalidated model — if the new model has an unexpected failure mode (e.g., misses a new fraud pattern), thousands of fraudulent transactions go undetected at $10K each. (2) Shadow deployment: run the new model on all traffic, compare predictions to the production model without serving them. This reveals disagreements — cases where the new model would miss fraud the old model catches. Analyze these cases manually. (3) After shadow validation, canary at 1% traffic. Monitor false negative rate in real-time with an automatic rollback if fraud losses exceed threshold. (4) Only after 2-4 weeks of stable canary metrics, gradually ramp to 100%. Never A/B test at 50% for safety-critical models.

scenario: You are deploying an updated fraud detection model. The current model catches 92% of fraud (recall) with 1.5% false positive rate. The new model shows 94% recall and 1.2% FPR in offline evaluation. Given that false negatives cost $10K average (missed fraud) and false positives cost $50 average (customer friction), which online evaluation strategy should you use and why?
title: Choosing Evaluation Strategy for a Safety-Critical Model

details.common_mistake: Believing pipelining reduces latency for individual requests. It only increases throughput by overlapping stages across requests. Per-request latency stays the same or slightly increases.
details.napkin_math: Sequential: 55.6 req/s, 55.6% GPU util. Pipelined: 100 req/s, ~100% GPU util. 1.8x throughput gain. Latency unchanged at 18ms/request.
details.realistic_solution: Without pipelining: each request completes all three stages sequentially before the next begins. Latency per request = 5 + 10 + 3 = 18ms. Throughput = 1/18ms = 55.6 requests/second. GPU utilization: 10/18 = 55.6%. With 3-stage pipelining: while request N is on the GPU, request N+1 is being preprocessed on CPU, and request N-1 is being postprocessed. The throughput bottleneck is the slowest stage (GPU at 10ms). Throughput = 1/10ms = 100 requests/second (1.8x improvement). GPU utilization rises to ~100%. Latency for a single request remains 18ms (pipeline doesn't reduce individual request latency), but throughput nearly doubles because stages execute concurrently across different requests. This is the same principle as CPU instruction pipelining — overlap different stages of different requests to maximize hardware utilization.

scenario: An inference server processes requests in three stages: CPU preprocessing (5ms), GPU inference (10ms), and postprocessing (3ms). Without pipelining, explain the throughput vs with 3-stage pipelining.
title: How Request Pipelining Hides Latency

details.common_mistake: Calculating throughput as 1/(sum of all stages). In a pipeline, throughput is determined by the SLOWEST stage, not the total latency.
details.napkin_math: Bottleneck: 15ms transformer. Throughput: 1/15ms = 66.7 req/s. Pipeline efficiency: 21ms total / 60ms pipeline slots = 35%. Splitting GPU stage 3-way → 200 req/s.
details.realistic_solution: In a pipelined system, steady-state throughput = 1 / max_stage_latency. Bottleneck stage: transformer inference at 15ms. Throughput = 1/15ms = 66.7 requests/second. Stage utilizations: tokenization = 2/15 = 13.3%, embedding = 3/15 = 20%, transformer = 15/15 = 100%, detokenization = 1/15 = 6.7%. The transformer stage is fully utilized while all other stages are idle most of the time. Pipeline efficiency = sum_of_stages / (num_stages × max_stage) = 21 / (4 × 15) = 35%. To improve: split the transformer into 3 micro-stages of 5ms each (tensor parallelism across 3 GPUs), making the new bottleneck the embedding lookup at 3ms. New throughput: 1/5ms = 200 req/s if transformer splits perfectly, or 1/3ms = 333 req/s if transformer stages are < 3ms each.

scenario: A 4-stage inference pipeline: tokenization (2ms), embedding lookup (3ms), transformer inference (15ms), detokenization (1ms). With 100 concurrent requests arriving, calculate the steady-state throughput and identify the bottleneck.
title: Pipeline Throughput with Unbalanced Stages

details.common_mistake: Treating pipelining and batching as mutually exclusive. They are complementary — pipelining overlaps stages while batching amortizes per-request GPU overhead within a stage.
details.napkin_math: A: 250 req/s, p99 ~30ms (safe SLA). B: 400 req/s, p99 ~45ms (risky SLA). Combined A+B: ~350 req/s, p99 ~40ms (best balance).
details.realistic_solution: The decision depends on the traffic pattern and SLA strictness. Option A (pipelining): 250 req/s with 18ms p50 latency. Pipelining has predictable latency — p99 is typically 1.5-2x p50 = 27-36ms, well within SLA. But at 200 req/s load, utilization is 80% — close to the throughput ceiling with little headroom for traffic spikes. Option B (batching): 400 req/s with 35ms p50. Batching latency is more variable — p99 depends on batch filling time. With dynamic batching, worst case is waiting for the batch timeout. If timeout=10ms: p99 ≈ 35ms + 10ms = 45ms, barely under SLA. But throughput headroom is 2x (400 vs 200 req/s). Best approach: combine both — pipeline the CPU/GPU overlap AND batch requests at the GPU stage. This achieves ~350 req/s at ~25ms p50 and ~40ms p99. Both SLA and throughput requirements are met with headroom.

scenario: An inference server handles 200 req/s. Option A: request pipelining (overlap CPU/GPU stages) achieving 250 req/s max at 18ms p50 latency. Option B: dynamic batching (batch requests for GPU, batch size up to 32) achieving 400 req/s max at 35ms p50 latency. Your SLA is p99 < 50ms. Which approach?
title: Pipelining vs Batching Trade-off

details.common_mistake: Monitoring only p50 or p99 of individual services. With fan-out, the user experience is determined by extreme tail percentiles (p99.9, p99.99) of individual components.
details.napkin_math: 100-way fanout: user p99 requires per-shard p99.99. 0.99^100 = 0.366, so 63.4% of users see at least one slow shard. Tail latency is amplified by fanout.
details.realistic_solution: When a request fans out to N services in parallel, the response time is the MAX of all N response times. The probability that all N services respond within time T is P(max < T) = P(single < T)^N. For p99=50ms: P(single < 50ms) = 0.99. P(all 100 < 50ms) = 0.99^100 = 0.366. So only 36.6% of user requests complete within 50ms — meaning p99 at the user level is much worse than 50ms. To find user-facing p99: we need P(max < T) = 0.99, so P(single < T) = 0.99^(1/100) = 0.9999. This means the per-shard latency at the 99.99th percentile becomes the user's p99 latency. Tail latency that is negligible for a single service becomes dominant when you fan out to many services. This is 'tail at scale' — Dean & Barroso's key insight motivating tail-tolerant design.

scenario: A service has p50=5ms and p99=50ms latency. A user request fans out to 100 backend shards in parallel, waiting for ALL to respond. What is the effective p99 latency the user experiences?
title: Why Tail Latency Matters at Scale

details.common_mistake: Setting the hedge threshold too low (e.g., at p50). This doubles backend load while providing minimal latency improvement. Hedge at p90-p95 for best cost/benefit ratio.
details.napkin_math: Hedging at 15ms fires ~8% of the time (1.08x backend load). New p99 ≈ max(15ms + p50, typical) = ~20ms. 4x improvement from 80ms to 20ms.
details.realistic_solution: Without hedging: p99 = 80ms. With hedging at 15ms threshold: a request is slow (>15ms) with probability ~8% (between p90 and p95). When hedged, the user gets min(original_latency, hedge_latency + 15ms). For a request that would have been slow (say 80ms for p99): the hedge fires at 15ms and independently has a p50 of 5ms completion time. So hedge completes at 15 + 5 = 20ms. P(both exceed 80ms) = P(original > 80ms) × P(hedge > 65ms). P(original > 80ms) = 0.01. P(hedge > 65ms) ≈ 0.02 (well past p95=20ms for the hedge). New p99: P(slow) = 0.01 × 0.02 = 0.0002 = p99.98 equivalent. Effective new p99 ≈ 20-25ms (the hedge's p95 + 15ms offset). Hedging cut p99 from 80ms to ~25ms at the cost of ~8% extra backend load.

scenario: A service has p50=5ms, p95=20ms, p99=80ms. You implement hedged requests: after 15ms with no response, send a duplicate request to a different server. Assuming independent latency distributions, calculate the new p99.
title: Hedged Request Latency Improvement

details.common_mistake: Over-engineering the solution. Hedged requests are the industry-standard solution for tail latency at scale (used by Google, Amazon). Complex migration schemes rarely justify their engineering cost.
details.napkin_math: A: 3-5% extra load, p99 drops to ~90ms. B: 5-50ms migration overhead, complex. C: 2x GPU cost ($$$). A wins on cost-effectiveness.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (hedged requests) is the most practical. Option B (request migration) sounds elegant but transferring KV cache between GPUs during inference introduces its own latency (NVLink/PCIe transfer of potentially GBs of KV cache state takes 5-50ms), and the coordination logic adds complexity. By the time you detect, migrate, and restart, you may have already exceeded the SLA. Option C (2x over-provisioning) is wasteful — doubling GPU count for tail latency is economically unjustifiable ($$$). With 100 shards returning 50 responses, you ignore the 50 slowest, but this still requires all 100 shards to be loaded with the model. Option A fires backup requests to already-warm shards. At 80ms threshold (between p95 and p99), only ~3-5% of requests trigger hedges — adding just 3-5% extra load. If the backup shard is not experiencing fragmentation, it responds in ~10ms, meeting the 90ms effective latency target. Simple, proven, minimal overhead.

scenario: Your ML serving system has p99=200ms (SLA: 100ms) with 50-way fan-out across GPU inference shards. Root cause: occasional GPU memory fragmentation causes 1-2 shards to spike to 500ms. Option A: hedged requests (re-send to backup shard after 80ms). Option B: request migration (detect slow shard at 50ms, migrate request's KV cache to a fast shard). Option C: over-provision by 2x (run 100 shards, only need 50 responses). Which approach?
title: Tail Latency Mitigation Strategy Selection

details.common_mistake: Using simple LRU eviction without considering model size. Evicting one 70B model frees space for multiple small models, but LRU doesn't account for size-to-frequency ratios.
details.napkin_math: 200 models, 20 fit in VRAM. If traffic is Zipfian (top 20 models = 80% traffic), cache hit rate ≈ 80%. Miss penalty: 2-30s vs hit: 20ms. Effective mean latency ≈ 0.8×20ms + 0.2×5s = 1.02s. Note: p50 (median) latency is 20ms since >50% of requests are cache hits; 1.02s is the mean, not p50.
details.realistic_solution: Model caching addresses the mismatch between the number of deployed models and available GPU memory. Unlike web caching where cache misses cost ~100ms (fetch from origin server), model cache misses cost 2-30 seconds (load model weights from CPU RAM or SSD to GPU VRAM). This 100-1000x penalty makes cache policy critical. Key differences from web caching: (1) Load cost asymmetry — loading a 7B model (14GB) at PCIe 4.0 (32 GB/s) takes ~0.4s, but larger models or SSD loading takes 2-30s. (2) Cache entry size varies enormously — models range from 50MB to 140GB, unlike uniform web objects. (3) Eviction impact is severe — evicting a model means ALL subsequent requests for that model incur the load penalty until reloaded. (4) Warmup matters — the first inference after loading may be slower (JIT compilation, CUDA kernel caching). LRU eviction is common but frequency-based (LFU) or priority-weighted policies often perform better for serving.

scenario: A serving platform hosts 200 models but GPU VRAM can hold only 20. Explain why a model caching strategy is needed and how it differs from traditional web caching.
title: Model Caching in Multi-Model Serving

details.common_mistake: Celebrating a 89% hit rate. With high miss penalties (seconds), even 11% misses make average latency unacceptable. Model serving needs 99%+ hit rates.
details.napkin_math: 50 small (25GB) + 8 medium (32GB) + 1 large (20GB) = 77GB of 80GB. Hit rate: 89%. Avg latency: 0.89×20ms + 0.11×5s ≈ 568ms. Misses dominate.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy 1 (proportional to traffic): Allocate 60% VRAM to small, 30% to medium, 10% to large. Small: 48GB / 500MB = 96, but only 50 exist → 50 models, 25GB used. Medium: 24GB / 4GB = 6 of 10 models. Large: 8GB for 20GB models → 0 fit. Remaining: 80 - 25 - 24 = 31GB. Use remaining for 1 large (20GB) + 2 more medium (8GB) + 6 more small (3GB but all already loaded). Final: 50 small (all), 8 medium, 1 large. Hit rate: 60% × 100% + 30% × 80% + 10% × 50% = 60% + 24% + 5% = 89% hit rate. Miss rate 11%. If miss penalty = 5s and hit latency = 20ms: avg latency = 0.89 × 20ms + 0.11 × 5000ms = 17.8ms + 550ms = 567.8ms. The 11% miss rate dominates average latency despite 89% hit rate.

scenario: A serving platform has 80GB GPU VRAM. Model sizes: 50 small models (500MB each), 10 medium models (4GB each), 2 large models (20GB each). Traffic: 60% to small, 30% to medium, 10% to large. With LRU caching, how many models of each size fit, and what is the approximate cache hit rate?
title: Model Cache Hit Rate and Latency Impact

details.common_mistake: Optimizing for cache hit rate alone. The combination of hit rate, miss penalty, and inference latency determines whether the SLA is met. A high hit rate with an occasional 5s miss still violates a 200ms p99 SLA.
details.napkin_math: A: $30K, p99~50ms. B: $18K, p99~1s (SLA fail for misses). C: $16K, p99~150ms (within SLA). C is cheapest viable option.
details.realistic_solution: Option A: 160GB VRAM, top 20 models fit. Traffic to top 15 = 95%, models 16-20 ≈ 3%. Hit rate: ~98%. p99 depends on the 2% miss rate — cold loading from CPU RAM takes 2-5s, violating SLA. Need pre-warming. With pre-warming: p99 ≈ 50ms (GPU inference). Cost: $30K/month. Option B: 80GB VRAM (top 15) + SSD warm tier (next 30 models). VRAM hit rate: 95%. SSD hit rate for remaining: 30/85 ≈ 35% of misses. SSD loads in 1s. p99 for SSD-cached: ~1.05s — violates SLA. Need SSD for pre-warming only, not serving. Option C: 96GB total but split across 4 GPUs — each holds ~24GB of models. With model replication overhead, ~20 models fit. Hit rate similar to A (~98%), but A10 inference is 3x slower than A100. p99 ≈ 150ms — within SLA. Cost: $16K/month. Option C wins on cost while meeting SLA, if slower inference is acceptable.

scenario: Your platform serves 100 models with 95% traffic going to the top 15. Option A: 2× A100-80GB ($30K/month) keeping top 20 models hot. Option B: 1× A100-80GB + 1TB NVMe SSD ($18K/month), using the SSD as a warm cache tier (1s load time). Option C: 4× A10-24GB ($16K/month, 96GB total VRAM) for more models but slower per-model inference. Which minimizes cost while maintaining p99 < 200ms?
title: Model Caching Strategy Under Cost Constraints

details.common_mistake: Believing the embedding layer provides position information. Token embeddings encode what a word means, not where it appears. Position encoding is a separate, explicit mechanism.
details.napkin_math: Attention: O(n²d) computation over n tokens. Without PE: f(permute(x)) = permute(f(x)) — output is order-independent. PE breaks this symmetry.
details.realistic_solution: Self-attention computes pairwise similarity scores between ALL token pairs simultaneously via Q×K^T. This operation is permutation-equivariant: swapping the order of input tokens simply permutes the rows and columns of the attention matrix, producing the same set of attention-weighted values (just reordered). Without positional information, the attention mechanism has no way to distinguish 'cat' in position 2 from 'cat' in position 5. The architecture processes tokens as an unordered SET, not a SEQUENCE. Positional encoding fixes this by adding position-dependent signals to each token's embedding before attention computation. Sinusoidal encodings use fixed frequency patterns: PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/d)). This gives each position a unique signature that attention can learn to interpret. The key insight: attention provides content-based addressing; positional encoding provides position-based addressing. Both are needed for sequence understanding.

scenario: Explain why a Transformer without positional encoding treats 'the cat sat on the mat' identically to 'mat the on sat cat the' — and why this is architecturally inevitable.
title: Why Transformers Need Positional Encoding

details.common_mistake: Worrying about positional encoding memory cost. At 0.5% of model size, it's irrelevant. The real concern is whether the encoding generalizes to unseen sequence lengths.
details.napkin_math: Learned PE: 8K × 4K × 2B = 64MB (0.46% of 7B model). RoPE/Sinusoidal: 0 extra parameters. PE memory cost is negligible; the real cost is length generalization.
details.realistic_solution: Learned positional embedding table: 8192 positions × 4096 dimensions × 2 bytes (FP16) = 67,108,864 bytes = 64 MB. 7B parameter model weight size: 7B × 2 bytes = 14 GB. Positional embeddings as fraction: 64 MB / 14 GB = 0.46% — negligible. However, the hidden cost is that extending context length requires retraining or interpolation. If you want 32K context: 32,768 × 4096 × 2 = 256 MB (still small in memory but requires training on long sequences). With sinusoidal (fixed) encodings: zero parameters — positions are computed analytically.
