On A100, however, EfficientNet's compound of SE blocks and MBConv can suffer from kernel launch overhead and low occupancy on small spatial resolutions. Profile with Nsight to verify whether EfficientNet-B4 actually achieves higher images/sec than ResNet-50 despite fewer FLOPs.

scenario: Your team needs a cloud image classifier at 84% ImageNet top-1 accuracy. You have three candidates: EfficientNet-B4 (19M params, 4.2 GFLOPs), a naively widened ResNet-50 (35M params, 8.2 GFLOPs), and a naively deepened ResNet-101 (44M params, 7.8 GFLOPs). All run on A100 SXM4 80GB. Analyze which achieves best accuracy-per-FLOP and best throughput at batch=64.
title: Analyze EfficientNet compound scaling vs. naive width/depth scaling on throughput

details.common_mistake: Assuming the depthwise conv is always the bottleneck because it has the most spatial work; ignoring that the 1×1 expand conv generates large intermediate tensors that stress L2/HBM bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: A100 arithmetic intensity roofline: peak 312 TFLOPS / 2 TB/s = 156 FLOP/byte. Depthwise: 43M FLOPs, reads ~4.8MB → 9 FLOP/byte — severely memory-bound. Expand: 154M FLOPs, reads 32·112·112·2B = 0.8MB → 193 FLOP/byte — compute-bound. Project: 154M FLOPs, reads 4.8MB → 32 FLOP/byte — memory-bound. Performance engineer is partially wrong: depthwise and project are bandwidth-limited.
details.realistic_solution: Expand (1×1): input 32ch → 192ch at 112×112. FLOPs = 2·32·192·112² = 154M. Output tensor = 192·112·112·2B = 4.8MB. Depthwise (3×3): 192ch, 112×112. FLOPs = 2·192·9·112² = 43M (memory-bound). Project (1×1): 192→32. FLOPs = 2·192·32·112² = 154M. The expand layer produces the largest intermediate activation; at t=6 the expand ratio balloons memory, not compute. On A100 HBM2e (2TB/s), depthwise is most bandwidth-bound (43M FLOPs / 4.8MB read ≈ 9 FLOP/byte → below roofline). Expand is compute-dominant but its large output strains L2.

scenario: You are analyzing MobileNetV2's inverted residual block (expand→depthwise→project, expansion ratio t=6) running on A100. The block takes 112×112×32 feature maps. A performance engineer claims the expand layer is the bottleneck. Analyze the memory traffic and compute intensity for each sub-layer to validate or refute this claim.
title: Analyze inverted residual bottleneck memory access patterns on A100

details.common_mistake: Loading each model into separate GPU memory partitions with MIG, which fragments the 80GB HBM3 and prevents cross-tenant batching; alternatively, hot-swapping models which incurs PCIe transfer latency.
details.napkin_math: All 10 models: ~120M params × 2B = 240MB — fits easily in 80GB HBM3. EfficientNet-B0: 0.39G FLOPs/image. At batch=32: 12.5 GFLOPs. H100 BF16 peak 989 TFLOPS at 50% util: 494 TFLOPS. Latency: 12.5G/494T = 0.025 ms compute. Add 5ms batching window + 2ms kernel launch = 7ms total — well under 50ms p99. B7 at batch=8: 8×37G = 296 GFLOPs → 0.6ms compute + 10ms queue = 10.6ms.
details.realistic_solution: Keep all 10 EfficientNet variants resident in HBM3 simultaneously (B0=5.3M, B7=66M params — total ~120M params × 2B BF16 = 240MB, trivial vs 80GB). Use a dynamic batching queue per model with 5–10ms wait windows to coalesce requests. Use CUDA streams for concurrent kernel execution across models. For B0–B3 (small), batch aggressively up to 64; for B6–B7 reduce to 8–16. Compile with torch.compile and cudnn benchmark mode.

scenario: You need to serve 10 different EfficientNet variants (B0–B7) simultaneously on a single H100 SXM5 for a multi-tenant vision API. Each tenant sends sporadic bursts of 1–32 images. Design a batching and memory management strategy that maximizes H100 utilization while keeping p99 latency under 50 ms.
title: Design an efficient CNN serving pipeline for H100 multi-tenant inference

details.common_mistake: Testing models only at their default input resolution and batch size, missing that throughput scales non-linearly with input resolution and that A100 utilization varies significantly across model sizes.
details.napkin_math: 200K QPS across 32 A100s = 6,250 images/GPU/sec. MobileNetV3-Large: ~0.22 GFLOPs/image. At batch=128, A100 achieves ~3,500 img/sec → insufficient. EfficientNet-B0: ~0.39 GFLOPs, ~2,800 img/sec per A100 → also insufficient. Need INT8 quantization: 2–3× throughput boost → 7,000–8,000 img/sec per A100 → sufficient. Cost at $3/GPU-hr: 32 × $3 = $96/hr for 200K QPS = $0.48 per million queries.
details.realistic_solution: Test grid: MobileNetV3-Small/Large, EfficientNet-B0/B2/B4, RegNetX-400MF/800MF/1.6GF. For each: (1) measure ImageNet top-5 accuracy, (2) measure throughput at batch={16,32,64,128} on single A100, (3) compute cost = 1/throughput × GPU-hour rate. Plot accuracy vs. images/(GPU·sec). Add TensorRT INT8 variants for each model. Pareto frontier is set of models where no other model achieves both higher accuracy and lower cost.

scenario: Your ML platform team needs to select a CNN backbone for a cloud-based product classification service targeting 200K QPS at 80% top-5 accuracy on a 1000-class taxonomy. Budget is 4 A100 nodes (32 GPUs total). Design an experiment to find the Pareto-optimal model on the FLOP-accuracy frontier, including which architectures to test and how to measure serving cost.
title: Design a FLOP-accuracy Pareto frontier experiment for MobileNet family selection

details.common_mistake: Using DDP without gradient checkpointing on EfficientNetV2-XL, which requires ~6.4GB activation memory per image at full resolution (480×480), causing OOM at any practical batch size on 80GB H100s.
details.napkin_math: EfficientNetV2-XL: 208M params × 4B (FP32 optimizer states Adam: ×4) = 3.3GB params + 3.3GB grad + 13.3GB optimizer = 20GB. Activations at 380×380 batch=64: ~18GB with checkpointing. Total: 38GB < 80GB HBM3. Training throughput at 224×224 batch=256: EfficientNetV2-XL ~8.5 GFLOPs/image × 256 = 2.2 TFLOPs/step. H100 BF16 at 60% util = 593 TFLOPS → 3.7ms/step. 50M images / (256×8) = 24,414 steps/epoch. At 48hr: 172,800 sec / 3.7ms = 46.7M steps total → ~1,900 epochs. With progressive schedule, ~60 epochs sufficient.
details.realistic_solution: Use DDP across 8 H100s with gradient checkpointing on the MBConv/Fused-MBConv blocks (reduces activation memory by ~60% at 30% compute overhead). Progressive training: epoch 1–20 at 128×128 (batch=512/GPU), epoch 21–40 at 224×224 (batch=256/GPU), epoch 41–60 at 380×380 (batch=64/GPU). Use BF16 mixed precision. Gradient accumulation of 4 steps at high resolution to maintain effective batch of 2048. Total effective batch = 8 GPUs × 64 × 4 accum = 2048.

scenario: You need to fine-tune EfficientNetV2-XL (208M params) on a proprietary 50M-image dataset using 8× H100 SXM5 GPUs. The model uses Fused-MBConv blocks with progressive learning (small images early, larger later). Design the distributed training strategy, gradient accumulation schedule, and memory optimization plan to complete training in under 48 hours.
title: Design EfficientNetV2 training pipeline for large-scale cloud fine-tuning

details.common_mistake: Assuming the fix is simply increasing batch size without diagnosing whether the bottleneck is CPU preprocessing, Python overhead, or memory copy latency — scaling batch size on a CPU-bound pipeline doesn't help.
details.napkin_math: MobileNetV3-Large: 0.22 GFLOPs at batch=1. H100 peak 989 TFLOPS BF16 at 12% util = 119 TFLOPS. Actual compute time: 0.22G/119T = 1.8 μs — nearly zero! H100 is idle 99.9% of the time. With dynamic batching at batch=50: 50×0.22G = 11 GFLOPs, 10ms batching window. Compute: 11G/594T (60% util) = 0.019ms << 10ms window. GPU util jumps to ~50% with 5K QPS and batch=50.
details.realistic_solution: At 5K QPS with batch=1, each forward pass takes ~0.8ms at 12% SM util. Root causes: (1) batch size=1 means each 0.22-GFLOP inference is dominated by kernel launch overhead (~50 μs per kernel × many kernels); (2) CPU preprocessing (decode + resize) taking 3–5ms per image; (3) H2D PCIe transfers serializing GPU work. Fix: implement server-side dynamic batching (10ms window → batch=50), move preprocessing to GPU with DALI, use CUDA graphs to fuse kernel launches.

scenario: A production MobileNetV3-Large serving endpoint on H100 shows only 12% GPU-SM utilization in nvidia-smi despite receiving 5,000 QPS. The model processes 224×224 images in BF16. Each request is a single image. Diagnose the root causes and propose fixes.
title: Diagnose low GPU utilization when serving MobileNetV3 on H100

details.common_mistake: Blaming the depthwise separable operation itself and reverting all changes, rather than diagnosing that the representational capacity drop comes from channel mixing being decoupled and that expansion ratios need to increase.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-34 standard: 3×3 conv C→C. Cross-channel connections per spatial location: C². Depthwise sep: depthwise (C groups, no cross-channel) + pointwise (C×C). Effective rank of channel mixing: pointwise has rank C. Standard conv: rank C². With C=256: standard has 65,536 cross-channel paths per position; depthwise+pointwise has 256. To restore capacity with expansion t=4: pointwise becomes C→4C (1024 channels), depthwise at 4C, project 4C→C. Parameters: 256×1024 + 1024×9 + 1024×256 = 271K vs 256×256×9 = 589K — still 2.2× fewer params but better capacity.
details.realistic_solution: Depthwise separable convolutions separate channel mixing (pointwise) from spatial filtering (depthwise), reducing cross-channel interaction. With identical channel counts, the pointwise 1×1 layers are the only cross-channel communication. Diagnosis steps: (1) check if batch norm statistics diverged (depthwise layers have C groups, not C² interactions); (2) add width multiplier α=1.4 to compensate; (3) use inverted residuals with expansion t=4–6 to restore representational capacity. The MobileNetV2 design explicitly addresses this with expansion before depthwise.

scenario: After replacing all 3×3 convolutions in a custom ResNet-34 with depthwise separable convolutions (maintaining same channel counts), top-1 accuracy drops from 73.8% to 68.2% on ImageNet after full retraining on 8× A100s. The training loss curves look normal. Diagnose why accuracy degraded and what architectural changes could recover it.
title: Diagnose accuracy degradation after replacing standard convs with depthwise separable

details.common_mistake: Immediately switching to FP32 training, which quadruples memory and halves throughput, rather than diagnosing the specific numerical instability point which is usually the sigmoid in SE blocks with BF16.
details.napkin_math: BF16 range: ±3.4×10³⁸ (same as FP32) but mantissa precision: 7 bits → relative error ~0.8%. SE squeeze: GAP over 14×14 spatial dims (EfficientNet-B5 last stage). Excitation: two FC layers with sigmoid. If FC pre-activation reaches ~500 (feasible with Mixup), sigmoid(500)=1.0 exactly in BF16, gradient=0. Gradient clipping at 1.0 norm: typical SE gradient ~0.01 → no issue. The problem is vanishing gradients from saturated sigmoid, not exploding. FP32 SE: +200MB memory for 30M-param model = negligible. Overhead: SE blocks are ~2% of total FLOPs.
details.realistic_solution: SE blocks apply sigmoid to a global average pool output. With aggressive Mixup (α=0.4) and CutMix, input activations can be very small or large, causing sigmoid(x) to saturate. In BF16, the reduced mantissa bits (7 vs 23 for FP32) can cause overflow in the large pre-sigmoid values. Fix: (1) clamp SE pre-activation to [-20, 20] before sigmoid; (2) keep SE blocks in FP32 with autocast(enabled=False) context; (3) reduce RandAugment magnitude to 15; (4) add gradient clipping at 1.0. These targeted fixes preserve BF16 throughput for 95% of the model.

scenario: You are training EfficientNet-B5 (30M params) on A100 with BF16 mixed precision, RandAugment magnitude=20, Mixup α=0.4, and CutMix. After 8,000 steps training diverges with NaN losses. The SE (squeeze-excitation) blocks are suspected. Diagnose the failure chain and implement fixes.
title: Diagnose NaN losses during EfficientNet training with aggressive augmentation

details.common_mistake: Choosing based on raw FLOP count without TensorRT INT8 profiling, since both models have different layer compositions (H-swish activations in MobileNetV3, Swish/SiLU in EfficientNet-B0) that affect TRT kernel fusion differently.
details.napkin_math: INT8 A100: 624 TOPS. MobileNetV3-Large batch=64: 64×0.22G = 14.1 GOPS → 14.1G/624T = 0.023ms compute (plus overhead). EfficientNet-B0 batch=64: 64×0.39G = 25G GOPS → 0.04ms compute. Both are heavily compute-bound but kernel launch overhead dominates. At $3/A100-hr: MobileNetV3 throughput ~28,000 img/sec → $0.030/million queries. EfficientNet-B0 ~17,000 img/sec → $0.049/million queries. For 1.9pp accuracy, EfficientNet-B0 costs 1.63× more.
details.realistic_solution: Profile both with trtexec at INT8, batch=64. MobileNetV3-Large with H-swish (piecewise linear approximation) fuses well in TRT. EfficientNet-B0 Swish (sigmoid × x) is slower in TRT INT8 unless approximated. Expected: MobileNetV3 ~1.8ms/batch, EfficientNet-B0 ~2.9ms/batch at batch=64 INT8. Accuracy: EfficientNet-B0 is 1.9pp better. Decision: if accuracy delta matters, EfficientNet-B0 still meets 30ms SLA with headroom. Cost: MobileNetV3 allows ~1.6× more throughput per GPU → lower cost per query.

scenario: Your team must choose between MobileNetV3-Large (75.2% top-1, 0.22 GFLOPs) and EfficientNet-B0 (77.1% top-1, 0.39 GFLOPs) for a cloud inference API. Both will run on A100 SXM4 with TensorRT INT8 optimization. Requests come in batches of 64. Evaluate which model gives better cost per unit accuracy at your target SLA of 30 ms p99.
title: Evaluate MobileNetV3 vs EfficientNet-B0 accuracy-latency tradeoff for A100 batch serving

details.common_mistake: Assuming accuracy scales linearly with φ and that H100 HBM3 bandwidth eliminates memory bottlenecks for all EfficientNet variants; ignoring that resolution scaling (γ^φ) quadratically increases activation memory.
details.napkin_math: B4 input: 380×380. Stage 7 feature map: 12×12×320. Depthwise 3×3: reads 12×12×320×2B = 92KB, computes 2×320×9×144 = 829K FLOPs → intensity = 829K/92K = 9 FLOP/byte. H100 roofline: 3.35TB/s × 9 = 30 TFLOPS — far below 989 TFLOPS peak. All depthwise layers are memory-bound regardless of HBM3 bandwidth. B4 total memory bandwidth per image: ~800MB/s needed. At batch=32: 32×800M = 25.6 GB/s — trivial for 3.35TB/s HBM3. Bandwidth not the bottleneck; it is kernel launch and low arithmetic intensity.
details.realistic_solution: B1→B4 accuracy gains: B1 79.1%, B2 80.1%, B3 81.6%, B4 82.9% — diminishing returns. Resolution scaling dominates memory: B1 240×240, B4 380×380. Feature map sizes scale as (380/240)² = 2.5× larger. At batch=32: B4 activation memory ~3.2GB vs B1 ~1.3GB. H100 HBM3 bandwidth: depthwise layers at B4 (380×380) become increasingly memory-bound. Saturation around B5/B6 where accuracy gain per FLOP drops below 0.1pp.

scenario: EfficientNet compound scaling uses φ to jointly scale width (α^φ), depth (β^φ), and resolution (γ^φ) with constraint α·β²·γ²≈2. You are evaluating whether increasing φ from 1 (B1) to 4 (B4) provides proportional accuracy gains on H100 with HBM3 bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s. Evaluate the memory bandwidth utilization at each scaling level and identify the saturation point.
title: Evaluate EfficientNet compound scaling coefficient impact on H100 memory bandwidth

details.common_mistake: Forgetting the factor-of-2 for multiply-accumulate (each MAC = 1 multiply + 1 add = 2 FLOPs), or computing the pointwise FLOP with spatial kernel size k²=1 correctly but applying k²=9 to the pointwise layer.
details.realistic_solution: Standard 3×3 conv: 2 × Cin × Cout × k² × H × W = 2 × 128 × 128 × 9 × 28 × 28 = 1,031M FLOPs. Depthwise sep: depthwise (2 × Cin × k² × H × W) + pointwise (2 × Cin × Cout × H × W). Depthwise: 2 × 128 × 9 × 28 × 28 = 18.1M FLOPs. Pointwise: 2 × 128 × 128 × 28 × 28 = 51.4M FLOPs. Total: 69.5M FLOPs. Reduction: 1031/69.5 = 14.8×. General formula: reduction = 1/(1/k² + 1/Cout) ≈ 1/(1/9 + 1/128) ≈ 8.1× (exact ratio varies with specific k and C).

scenario: A new ML engineer on your team asks you to explain the FLOP calculation for a standard 3×3 convolution vs a depthwise separable convolution for a layer with Cin=128 input channels, Cout=128 output channels, and 28×28 spatial resolution. Walk through the exact formulas and compute the reduction ratio.
title: Recall depthwise separable convolution FLOP formula

details.common_mistake: Saying that inverted residuals simply 'flip' the bottleneck without explaining why: ResNet bottleneck compresses then expands (wide→narrow→wide) to reduce compute in the 3×3 layer; MobileNetV2 does narrow→wide→narrow because the 3×3 depthwise layer is cheap regardless of channel count.
details.napkin_math: ResNet bottleneck C=256: 3×3 at C/4=64: 2×64×64×9×HW = 73.7K×HW FLOPs. MobileNetV2 C=32, t=6: 3×3 depthwise at 192ch: 2×192×9×HW = 3.5K×HW FLOPs. Pointwise project 192→32: 2×192×32×HW = 12.3K×HW. Total: 15.8K×HW. Even at narrow channels, inverted residual uses 5× fewer FLOPs than ResNet bottleneck of similar capacity.
details.realistic_solution: ResNet bottleneck: wide(C) → narrow(C/4) → 3×3 conv at narrow → wide(C). The 3×3 standard conv is expensive, so you compress first. MobileNetV2 inverted residual: narrow(C) → wide(t·C, t=6) → 3×3 depthwise at wide → narrow(C). The 3×3 depthwise is cheap (O(C·k²·HW) not O(C²·k²·HW)), so you can afford to run it at expanded channel count for richer spatial features. The ReLU6 is only applied before the final pointwise projection; the projection itself has no activation to preserve information in the low-dimensional residual stream (linear bottleneck hypothesis).

scenario: During a system design interview, you are asked to explain the key architectural difference between a standard ResNet bottleneck block and MobileNetV2's inverted residual block. Explain the channel count pattern, why it is called 'inverted,' and the rationale behind removing the non-linearity before the residual addition.
title: Recall MobileNetV2 inverted residual structure and why it inverts the bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Misidentifying which coefficient controls which dimension, or stating the constraint as α·β·γ=2 (linear) instead of α·β²·γ²≈2 (accounting for the quadratic scaling of FLOPs with resolution and width²).
details.realistic_solution: 1.75² = 3.0625 (not 2.07 which is 1.44²). Corrected compound scaling: 1.46² × 3.06 × 1.2⁴ ≈ 13.5×.

scenario: Your team is onboarding a new research engineer. They ask what distinguishes EfficientNet's scaling strategy from simply making a model wider or deeper. Explain the compound scaling constraint α·β²·γ²≈2 and what each coefficient controls, referencing EfficientNet-B0 as the baseline (5.3M params, 0.39 GFLOPs, 224×224 input).
title: Recall EfficientNet compound scaling constraints and baseline architecture

details.common_mistake: Using the default entropy calibration (IInt8EntropyCalibrator2) without considering that H-swish's piecewise linear nature can cause calibration to underfit the activation range, leading to clipping and accuracy degradation beyond 1%.
details.napkin_math: MobileNetV3-Large: 5.4M params. FP32: 21.6MB. INT8: 5.4MB (4× compression). A100 INT8 tensor core peak: 624 TOPS. BF16: 312 TFLOPS. Speedup: ~2× for compute-bound layers. MobileNetV3 is memory-bound (0.22 GFLOPs, 5.4M params × 4B = 21.6MB read per inference). Memory bandwidth bound: 21.6MB / 2TB/s = 10.8 μs minimum. INT8: 5.4MB / 2TB/s = 2.7 μs minimum. Real throughput improvement: ~1.5–1.8× (not full 2× due to activation quantization overhead).
details.realistic_solution: Use IInt8MinMaxCalibrator for H-swish layers to capture the full activation range. Steps: (1) export model to ONNX with opset 17; (2) build TRT engine with INT8 flag + calibrator; (3) provide 5K calibration images through custom IInt8Calibrator; (4) for H-swish layers specifically, register per-tensor scale factors from MinMax calibrator. Verify with trtexec --iterations=100. If accuracy drop >1%, try layer-by-layer mixed precision keeping H-swish in FP16.

scenario: You need to deploy MobileNetV3-Large in production on A100 using TensorRT INT8 quantization. The model has H-swish activations (piecewise linear approximation of Swish). Your calibration dataset has 5,000 representative images. Implement the calibration and conversion pipeline and verify accuracy drops below 1% vs FP32 baseline.
title: Implement INT8 quantization for MobileNetV3 on TensorRT with calibration

details.common_mistake: Trying to use tensor cores for depthwise convolutions — tensor cores require matmul patterns (MMA instructions) and cannot be used for depthwise ops where each output channel depends only on one input channel.
details.napkin_math: Input: 32×512×14×14 = 3.2M elements × 2B = 6.4MB. Output: same = 6.4MB. Total HBM traffic: 12.8MB. At 3.35TB/s (H100): 3.8 μs minimum. FLOPs: 2×32×512×9×196 = 57.5M FLOPs. At 18% of 989 TFLOPS = 178 TFLOPS: 57.5M/178T = 0.32 μs compute. Ratio: memory is 12× slower → severely memory-bound. Shared memory tiling reduces HBM traffic by 3×3=9× for spatial halo. Target: <0.5 μs per invocation at 70% HBM bandwidth utilization.
details.realistic_solution: H100 SM has 228KB shared memory per SM. Key optimizations: (1) load input halo into shared memory, coalesced global → shared memory load; (2) use warp-level parallelism across the spatial dimension; (3) fuse BN + ReLU6 into the depthwise kernel; (4) use __half2 or __nv_bfloat162 vectorized loads for 2× memory bandwidth; (5) tile along channel dimension so each thread block handles 32 channels. Alternatively, use torch.compile with triton which auto-generates fused depthwise+BN+activation kernels. PyTorch 2.x with inductor backend achieves ~2× over cuDNN for these small depthwise shapes.

scenario: The standard cuDNN depthwise conv achieves only 18% SM utilization on H100 for a 3×3 depthwise layer with C=512 channels, 14×14 spatial resolution, batch=32. You need to write or configure a higher-performance implementation. Describe the key optimizations for a CUDA kernel targeting H100's architecture.
title: Implement custom depthwise conv CUDA kernel with shared memory optimization

details.common_mistake: Applying uniform pruning ratios across all layers, which over-prunes the first layers (critical for feature extraction) and under-prunes the last expansion stages (which dominate FLOPs).
details.napkin_math: EfficientNet-B3: 1.8 GFLOPs baseline. 40% reduction target: 1.08 GFLOPs. Channel pruning at 40% of channels: FLOPs scale as (C_out × C_in), so pruning 37% of channels → 0.63² = 40% FLOP reduction. Need ~37% average channel sparsity. Memory: 12M params × 0.63² ≈ 4.8M params (for conv layers, roughly). Model size: 4.8M × 4B = 19.2MB (FP32) or 4.8MB (INT8). A100 serving: 1.08G FLOPs at batch=64 = 69 GFLOPs, at 50% INT8 utilization (312 TOPS) → 0.22ms/batch, ~290K img/sec/GPU.
details.realistic_solution: Use layer-sensitivity analysis: prune each layer independently to 50% and measure accuracy drop. First and last layers are typically sensitive; middle MBConv blocks are robust. Apply higher pruning ratios (50–60%) to middle stages and lower (20–30%) to first/last stages. Implementation: (1) forward hook to collect L1-norm of each filter; (2) rank filters globally by importance; (3) zero out bottom-p% filters; (4) fine-tune 30 epochs with cosine LR schedule; (5) export to ONNX, convert with TRT INT8. Target: 40% FLOP reduction → ~1.08 GFLOPs.

scenario: You need to reduce EfficientNet-B3 (12M params, 1.8 GFLOPs) serving costs on A100 by 40% while retaining 81% top-1 accuracy on your product dataset (originally 81.6%). Implement a structured channel pruning pipeline using L1-norm filter importance scoring, fine-tuning schedule, and verify the result with TensorRT profiling.
title: Implement channel pruning for EfficientNet-B3 to reduce serving costs

details.common_mistake: Accepting the FLOP-only explanation without analyzing that the depthwise layer in inverted residuals has much lower arithmetic intensity than standard convolutions, and that this matters only when the bandwidth ceiling is the constraint.
details.napkin_math: Standard 3×3 conv weight bandwidth: filter_size × in_channels × out_channels × bytes. For typical conv layer: 3×3×64×128×4B = 294,912B = 288KB. Plus input activations: H×W×C×4B. For 28×28×64 input: 28×28×64×4B = 200,704B = 196KB. Total bandwidth: 288KB + 196KB ≈ 484KB... for specific layer with 3×3×64×64: 3×3×64×64×4B = 147,456B = 144KB weights. Input: 56×56×64×4B = 802,816B = 784KB. Total: ~928KB. Corrected: weights alone ≈ 1.18MB for the specific layer described (not 0.8MB which underestimates by ~48%).
details.realistic_solution: Standard conv weight bandwidth depends on kernel size × in_channels × out_channels. For the specific layer, weight BW ≈ 1.18MB + input BW ≈ 1.2MB total (not 0.8MB).

scenario: A senior engineer claims that inverted residuals in MobileNetV2 are faster than ResNet bottlenecks on A100 purely because of fewer FLOPs. You disagree and believe the memory access pattern is equally important. Construct a roofline model argument using the A100's arithmetic intensity threshold to explain the performance difference.
title: Mastery: explain why inverted residuals outperform standard bottlenecks on memory-bandwidth-limited hardware

details.common_mistake: Computing SE FLOPs only for the FC layers without including the global average pooling, or failing to account for the fact that SE blocks have near-zero arithmetic intensity (tiny FC on scalars) and incur disproportionate kernel launch overhead.
details.napkin_math: FLOPs fraction: 311K FLOPs / 390M total model FLOPs = 311,000 / 390,000,000 = 0.000797 = 0.08% (not 30% — 30% would require 117M FLOPs for this component, not 311K). The 311K already accounts for all blocks in this layer.
details.realistic_solution: 311K FLOPs / 390M total = 0.08% of model FLOPs (not 30%). 30% would require ~117M FLOPs for this component.

scenario: EfficientNet uses Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks with reduction ratio r=4, adding a global average pool + two FC layers per MBConv block. For EfficientNet-B0 (16 MBConv blocks with SE), quantify the total FLOP overhead from SE modules and determine whether removing SE while compensating with width scaling achieves equivalent accuracy at lower cost on H100.
title: Mastery: trade-off analysis of SE block overhead vs accuracy gain in EfficientNet

details.common_mistake: Using only KL divergence on soft logits (Hinton-style distillation) which provides signal only at the final layer; with an 8-GFLOP capacity gap, the student cannot learn the rich intermediate representations needed without intermediate supervision.
details.napkin_math: 4 A100 nodes = 32 GPUs. MobileNetV3-Large training: 0.22 GFLOPs/image, batch=256/GPU, total batch=8192. EfficientNet-B7 teacher inference: 37 GFLOPs/image at batch=256 = 9.5 TFLOPs/step → 9.5T/156T (A100 50% util) = 61ms/step. Student forward: 0.22G×256 = 56G FLOPs → 0.36ms. Teacher dominates. Solution: precompute teacher soft labels and feature maps, store on NVMe (256 images × 37G FLOPs → pre-generate 50M×10K-dim = 500GB for logits + ~2TB for features). Online teacher forward is 170× more expensive than student.
details.realistic_solution: Three-component loss: (1) CE with soft targets (T=4 temperature), weight 0.5; (2) intermediate feature matching on 3 stages using adapters (linear projectors B7_channels → MV3_channels), weight 0.3; (3) attention transfer from SE excitation maps, weight 0.2. Adapter design: since B7 has 2× more channels, use 1×1 conv adapters trained jointly. Training: first 30 epochs with adapters only (frozen student backbone), then 90 epochs end-to-end with cosine LR 0.1→0.001. Expected gain over soft-label only: +1.5–2pp accuracy.

scenario: You are leading a project to distill EfficientNet-B7 teacher (84.3% top-1, 37 GFLOPs) into a MobileNetV3-Large student (target 78%+ top-1, 0.22 GFLOPs) using 4× A100 nodes. Design the distillation loss, intermediate feature alignment strategy, and training schedule. Justify why feature-based distillation is needed beyond soft-label distillation alone.
title: Mastery: knowledge distillation from EfficientNet-B7 to MobileNetV3 at scale

details.common_mistake: Attempting to fuse all three operations into a single kernel, which is impractical because the expand and project 1×1 operations are suited for tensor-core matmul while depthwise requires custom spatial indexing — different compute patterns cannot share tensor core instructions.
details.napkin_math: Original: 47 kernel launches × 5μs overhead = 235μs overhead. Fused: 4 kernels × 5μs = 20μs. Overhead reduction: 215μs saved per block. MobileNetV2 has 17 MBConv blocks: 17×215μs = 3.7ms saved per inference. At batch=1, MobileNetV2 total inference ~8ms → 46% speedup from kernel fusion alone. Memory traffic: original reads/writes activations between each kernel (HBM). Fused: intermediate tensors stay in L2/SRAM. For expand output (4.8MB): fused keeps it in L2 for depthwise, saving 2× HBM round-trip.
details.realistic_solution: Optimal fusion strategy: (1) Fuse expand 1×1 + BN + ReLU6 into one kernel (tensor core matmul + elementwise epilogue using cuBLAS/cuDNN epilogue fusion); (2) Fuse depthwise 3×3 + BN + ReLU6 into one kernel (custom CUDA or Triton with shared memory tiling); (3) Fuse project 1×1 + BN (no activation for linear bottleneck) into one kernel; (4) Fuse residual addition with project output. Result: 47 kernels → 3–4 kernels per MBConv block. torch.compile with Inductor backend performs this automatically.

scenario: A profiling session with Nsight Compute shows that a MobileNetV2 block (expand 1×1 → depthwise 3×3 → project 1×1) on H100 has 47 kernel launches and 62% of time in memory transactions rather than SM compute. Describe the kernel fusion strategy to reduce memory transactions and kernel launch overhead.
title: Optimize depthwise separable convolution throughput via kernel fusion on H100

details.common_mistake: Applying gradient checkpointing to all layers, which recomputes activations for every forward pass in the backward pass, reducing memory but also reducing throughput by ~30-40% — too expensive if memory is not the binding constraint.
details.napkin_math: Speedup from architectural improvement: (256/128) × (2/1.15) = 2 × 1.739 = 3.478 ≈ 3.48× (not 4.35× — 4.35 would require 2 × 2.174 = 2 × (2/0.92) which uses 0.92 not 1.15 in denominator).

scenario: EfficientNet-B6 training on H100 at batch=128 achieves 420 images/sec/GPU but hits OOM at batch=256 due to activation memory. The target is 1,200 images/sec/GPU to meet a 24-hour training deadline. Optimize the pipeline using gradient checkpointing, BF16, and CUDA graphs.
title: Optimize EfficientNet training throughput with gradient checkpointing and mixed precision

details.common_mistake: Assuming FLOPs scale linearly with the width multiplier α, when they actually scale as α² (both input and output channels scale by α), so a width multiplier of 1.4× costs 1.96× more FLOPs.
details.napkin_math: MobileNetV3-Large α=1.0: 0.22G FLOPs, 1.4ms at batch=128 on A100. FLOPs ∝ α². Budget: 2ms → 2.0/1.4 × 0.22G = 0.314G FLOPs max. α = sqrt(0.314/0.22) = sqrt(1.43) = 1.20. MobileNetV3-Large 1.25×: reported 0.356 GFLOPs, ~77.0% top-1 (timm library). Expected latency: 1.4 × (0.356/0.22) = 2.27ms — slightly over! Use α=1.1: 0.22 × 1.21 = 0.266 GFLOPs, estimated ~76.0% top-1, latency ~1.4 × 1.21 = 1.69ms — fits budget.
details.realistic_solution: Width multiplier α scales FLOPs as α² and params as α². Current: 0.22G FLOPs at α=1.0. Target latency headroom: 2.0 - 1.4 = 0.6ms → can afford 0.6/1.4 = 43% more FLOPs → α² ≤ 1.43 → α ≤ 1.2. MobileNetV3-Large at α=1.2 (sometimes denoted 1.25): ~0.22 × 1.44 = 0.32 GFLOPs, ~76.6% top-1 (published results). Check 1.4ms × 1.43 = 2.0ms — just fits. For α=1.4: 0.22 × 1.96 = 0.43 GFLOPs, ~1.4×1.96ms = 2.74ms — exceeds budget.

scenario: You have a 2ms latency budget per batch of 128 images on A100 for a product search feature. MobileNetV3-Large (0.22 GFLOPs, 75.2% top-1) meets the budget at 1.4ms but you want to close an accuracy gap to EfficientNet-B0 (77.1%) without exceeding 2ms. Optimize by finding the best width multiplier for MobileNetV3 that fits the budget.
title: Optimize MobileNetV3 width multiplier selection for a fixed A100 latency budget

details.common_mistake: Using DALI without pinned memory buffers, causing D2H/H2D copies to block the preprocessing stream; or using a single CUDA stream for both preprocessing and inference, preventing overlap.
details.napkin_math: Target: 2,000 QPS. CPU preprocessing: 12ms/image → max 83 QPS on 1 CPU core, need 24 cores for 2K QPS. With DALI GPU: 1920×1080 JPEG decode via nvjpeg: ~2ms for batch=64 (32 img/ms). Resize 1920×1080→380×380: GPU bilinear ~0.3ms batch=64. Normalize: 0.1ms. Total DALI: ~2.4ms/64 images = 37μs/image. EfficientNet-B4 TRT FP16 at batch=64: ~2ms. Pipeline latency: max(2.4, 2) = 2.4ms/batch = 26,667 QPS >> 2,000 target. Use 1/13 of H100 capacity, leave rest for burst.
details.realistic_solution: DALI pipeline: GPU JPEG decode (nvjpeg) + resize (480→380 with bilinear) + normalize. Run on CUDA stream 1. TensorRT engine on CUDA stream 2. Double-buffer: while batch N is on GPU for inference, batch N+1 is being preprocessed. DALI GPU pipeline: ~0.5ms per image on H100 vs 12ms CPU. At batch=64: 32ms CPU preprocessing eliminated, ~1ms DALI. Pipeline: DALI batch fills 64 images in ~1ms, TRT inference in ~2ms (4.2G×64=269G FLOPs, at 494 TFLOPS 50% util = 0.54ms + overhead). Total: ~3ms/batch = 64/3ms = 21K QPS — exceeds 2K QPS requirement.

scenario: You need to deploy EfficientNet-B4 (19M params, 4.2 GFLOPs, 380×380 input) for a medical imaging API that must process 2,000 QPS of 1920×1080 JPEG images on a single H100 node. The current CPU preprocessing pipeline (JPEG decode + resize + normalize) takes 12ms per image. Realize the full inference pipeline with GPU-accelerated preprocessing.
title: Realize end-to-end EfficientNet-B4 serving with DALI preprocessing on H100

details.common_mistake: Exporting with torch.onnx.export without disabling torch.compile tracing first, which can produce a graph with compiled IR artifacts that ONNX cannot parse; or using a fixed batch size in ONNX export and then trying to change it in TensorRT (requires dynamic axes).
details.napkin_math: MobileNetV2: 3.4M params. FP32 model: 13.6MB. FP16 TRT engine: ~7MB + TRT overhead ~50MB. ONNX export time: ~2s. TRT build time: ~3 min (polygraphy caches engine). Inference FP16 vs FP32 accuracy: typical max abs diff < 0.005 for ImageNet models. TRT FP16 speedup over PyTorch FP32: ~3–4× for small CNNs like MobileNetV2 (kernel fusion + FP16 compute + reduced memory). At batch=64: PyTorch ~8ms → TRT FP16 ~2.5ms. Throughput: 64/2.5ms = 25,600 img/sec per A100.
details.realistic_solution: Step 1: model.eval() + disable torch.compile. Step 2: ONNX export with dynamic_axes={'input': {0: 'batch'}, 'output': {0: 'batch'}} and opset=17. Failure point: custom H-swish (relu6(x+3)/6 × x) — register as onnx custom op or decompose to standard ops. Step 3: onnxsim to simplify graph. Step 4: trtexec --fp16 --minShapes=input:1x3x224x224 --optShapes=input:64x3x224x224 --maxShapes=input:128x3x224x224. Step 5: validate accuracy with 1K images, check max abs diff FP16 vs FP32 < 0.01.

scenario: You need to export a fine-tuned MobileNetV2 (3.4M params) from PyTorch to TensorRT FP16 for deployment on A100. The model was trained with torch.compile and has custom H-swish activations. Describe the complete export chain with known failure points at each step.
title: Realize MobileNetV2 export pipeline from PyTorch to ONNX to TensorRT

details.common_mistake: Running full NAS with differentiable architecture search (DARTS) on the full dataset, which takes weeks; or using random search without a supernet, which requires training each candidate from scratch.
details.napkin_math: Training schedule: total_time = 22,500 seconds for 300 epochs. Per epoch = 22,500 / 300 = 75 seconds = 1.25 minutes (not 22,500 seconds per epoch which would be 6.25 hours per epoch).
details.realistic_solution: 22,500 total seconds / 300 epochs = 75 seconds/epoch = 1.25 minutes/epoch (not 22,500s/epoch).

scenario: Your team needs a custom EfficientNet-style backbone for a proprietary dataset (3M images, 500 classes) with hard constraints: <1 GFLOPs, >82% top-1, deployable on A100 within 1ms at batch=64. Using 8× H100s and a 5-day search budget, realize a once-for-all NAS pipeline to find the optimal architecture.
title: Realize automated NAS-style width and depth search for EfficientNet-style backbone

details.common_mistake: Specifying only average latency targets without defining what constitutes an accuracy failure (e.g., model drift, input distribution shift) or specifying hardware without accounting for head-of-line blocking at high QPS.
details.napkin_math: 50K QPS across 32 H100 GPUs = 1,563 QPS/GPU. Dynamic batching: 5ms window × 1,563 = 7.8 images/window → batch=8. EfficientNet-B2 at batch=8, TRT FP16: 8 × 1.0G = 8G FLOPs. H100 FP16 at 50% util: 494 TFLOPS. Compute: 8G/494T = 0.016ms. Overhead + memory: ~2ms total. Well under 10ms p50. At batch=128: 128 × 1.0G = 128 GFLOPs → 0.26ms compute → 2.3ms total. GPU utilization: 1,563 QPS × 1.0G FLOPs = 1.563 TFLOPS needed. H100 effective: 494 TFLOPS → 0.3% utilization. Massively over-provisioned; reduce to 2 H100 nodes.
details.realistic_solution: Hardware: 4× H100 SXM5 nodes (32 GPUs). Model: EfficientNet-B2 (9.1M params, 1.0 GFLOPs, 80.1% top-1) or MobileNetV3-Large with TRT INT8. Batching: dynamic batching with 5ms window, max batch=128. SLA spec: (1) p50 < 10ms = batching_wait(5ms) + inference(3ms) + overhead(2ms); (2) p99 < 50ms = max batching_wait(20ms) + inference(3ms) + 2× overhead; (3) accuracy: shadow eval on 1K held-out images hourly, alert if top-1 < 79%; (4) failure modes: model OOM → fallback to smaller model, preprocessing timeout → return error 504.

scenario: You are writing the technical specification for a cloud vision API that must serve 50K QPS using efficient CNN models on H100 infrastructure. The SLA requires p50 < 10ms, p99 < 50ms, accuracy > 80% top-1 on ImageNet. Specify the hardware configuration, model choice, batching strategy, and failure mode definitions.
title: Specification: define latency-accuracy SLA for efficient CNN cloud API

details.common_mistake: Explaining depthwise separable convolutions as 'just a factorization trick' without explaining that the separation of spatial filtering from channel mixing is a semantic change that reduces the model's ability to jointly reason across channels and space in a single operation.
details.napkin_math: Standard conv C=128, k=3: 128×128×9 = 147,456 params per layer. Depthwise sep: depthwise 128×9 = 1,152 + pointwise 128×128 = 16,384 → 17,536 params. 8.4× fewer params. FLOPs: same ratio. At H100 batch=256: standard conv 14×14 spatial: 256×2×128²×9×196 = 14.9B FLOPs. Depthwise sep: 256×(2×128×9×196 + 2×128²×196) = 256×(451K+6.4M) = 1.76B FLOPs. 8.5× fewer FLOPs. Latency improvement in practice: 2–4× (not 8.5×) because depthwise is memory-bound on H100.
details.realistic_solution: Standard convolution: every output feature at a spatial location combines information from ALL input channels AND all spatial neighbors simultaneously, using Cin×Cout×k² parameters. Depthwise separable: first, a depthwise conv applies one filter per input channel independently (spatial filtering only, k² params per channel). Then, a pointwise 1×1 conv mixes across channels (no spatial, Cin×Cout params). Together they approximate the standard conv but with 8–9× fewer operations. Functional difference: the joint cross-channel-spatial reasoning is decoupled, which is why MobileNets trade a small accuracy reduction for large efficiency gain.

scenario: A backend engineer on your team is reviewing a PR that replaces standard convolutions with depthwise separable convolutions in a MobileNet-based service. They ask why this changes the latency and whether it affects the model's behavior. Explain depthwise separable convolutions in terms of what computation is happening, why it's faster, and any functional differences.
title: Fluency: explain depthwise separable convolution to a non-ML systems engineer

details.common_mistake: Assuming the LLM generation step is always the bottleneck and spending effort on speculative decoding or quantization before profiling the other stages.
details.napkin_math: Reranker scales linearly with candidate count: 120ms * (20/50) = 48ms. LLM generation: 3072 tokens / 40 tok/s = 76.8s... wait, 40 tok/s means 3072/40 = 76.8s for generation — that cannot be right for 210ms. Re-read: 210ms total generation at batch decode. At H100 throughput: 3072 context tokens prefill at ~10ms, decode 200 tokens at ~200ms = 210ms total. Reducing context to 2048: prefill ~7ms + decode ~140ms = 147ms. Pipeline total: 50+48+147 = 245ms.
details.realistic_solution: Profile each stage independently. Reranking 50 docs with a cross-encoder at 120ms is disproportionate — it dominates relative to retrieval. Reduce reranker candidates from 50 to 20 (cuts to ~48ms). Parallelize retrieval across shards. With reranker at 48ms: 50+48+210=308ms, still over SLA. Also reduce context to 2048 tokens: 210*(2048/3072)=140ms. Total: 50+48+140=238ms, comfortably under 300ms.

scenario: A RAG pipeline on H100 (80GB HBM3) runs: FAISS retrieval (50ms), cross-encoder reranking of top-50 docs (120ms), and LLM generation with a 3072-token context (210ms at 40 tok/s). End-to-end P95 latency is 420ms but the SLA is 300ms. The team proposes adding a query cache. Analyze where the latency budget is being spent and identify which stage is the primary bottleneck.
title: RAG Pipeline Latency Budget on H100

details.common_mistake: Optimizing for router accuracy in isolation without computing the expected latency cost of misroutes. A 9% error rate sounds small but the latency penalty on the fallback path can dominate P95.
details.napkin_math: Expected cost: 0.91*$0.002 + 0.09*($0.002+$0.03) = $0.00182 + $0.00288 = $0.0047/query vs $0.03 always-large. Cost savings: 84%. P95 with 9% error: with Poisson approximation, P(at least 1 fallback in 1 query) = 9%, so P95 latency = 2188ms (fallback path). Need error rate < 5% to keep P95 < 300ms threshold.
details.realistic_solution: Compute expected latency per query: 0.91*(8+180) + 0.09*(8+180+2000) = 0.91*188 + 0.09*2188 = 171 + 197 = 368ms expected. Compare to always-large: 2008ms. Always-small: 188ms (but quality failure). The 9% misroute inflates P95 significantly — at P95 you hit the fallback path. To hit a 300ms P95: need fallback rate < 5% or a confidence-threshold abort (send to large immediately if router confidence < 0.85).

scenario: A cloud pipeline routes queries between GPT-4-class (2000ms, $0.03/query) and a fine-tuned 7B model on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 180ms, $0.002/query). The router itself is a 350M classifier running at 8ms. Current routing accuracy is 91% — 9% of complex queries incorrectly go to the cheap model and require a fallback retry, adding 180ms+2000ms=2180ms latency. Analyze whether the routing accuracy is sufficient given the cost-latency tradeoffs.
title: Router Model Accuracy vs Latency Tradeoff in Multi-Model Pipeline

details.common_mistake: Explaining each stage's metrics independently without explaining how errors compose across stages. Stakeholders conclude 'everything is green so the system should work,' missing the multiplicative error compounding phenomenon.
details.napkin_math: Stage accuracies: retrieval=0.85, reranker=0.90, LLM grounding=0.95. Compound: 0.85*0.90*0.95=0.727. To reach 90% end-to-end: need geometric mean per stage of 0.9^(1/3)=0.965. Improving retrieval from 0.85 to 0.97 alone: 0.97*0.90*0.95=0.829. Need all three stages above 0.965 to hit 90% system accuracy.
details.realistic_solution: Use a concrete analogy: each stage has an accuracy rate. If retrieval recall is 85% (misses 15% of relevant docs), reranker precision is 90%, and LLM grounding is 95%, the end-to-end accuracy is 0.85*0.90*0.95 = 72.7%. Even with each stage appearing healthy, the system fails on nearly 1 in 4 queries. The fix requires either improving the weakest stage (retrieval at 85%) or adding a verification stage.

scenario: Your H100 cluster runs a 5-stage compound AI pipeline: query rewrite → embedding → FAISS retrieval → reranker → LLM generation. A product manager asks why the system sometimes gives wrong answers even though each individual stage looks fine in isolation. The reranker scores show high-confidence results and the LLM produces fluent text, but factual errors slip through. Explain the compound failure mode clearly.
title: Explaining Compound AI Pipeline Behavior to Non-Technical Stakeholders

details.common_mistake: Treating KV cache as per-request rather than per-prefix. Teams rebuild the system prompt KV cache on every request even when the prefix is identical, wasting both compute and memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: True savings from optimization. Before: 100% baseline cost. After optimization: 42% of baseline. True savings: (100-42)/100 = 58% cost reduction (not 37% — 37% would imply after-cost is 63% of baseline, not 42%).
details.realistic_solution: If optimized cost is 42% of original, savings = 58% (not 37%). 37% is the reduction from a different baseline calculation.

scenario: An orchestration system on H100 (80GB HBM3) runs 8 parallel agents, each with a 4096-token system prompt and 2048-token working context. Each agent independently prefills its system prompt on every request. The system prompt is shared across all agents. At bf16, each token's KV cache consumes 2 * 2 * num_layers * head_dim bytes. For a 70B model with 80 layers and head_dim=128, calculate the waste from redundant system prompt prefill and design a prefix caching strategy.
title: Mastering KV Cache Sharing Across Agents in Multi-Model Orchestration

details.common_mistake: Assuming all hops are strictly serial because they involve LLM calls. In practice, hop3 validation can often run concurrently with hop4 generation using speculative execution, and hop1 tool calls can overlap with prior LLM decoding.
details.napkin_math: Serial: 30+150+60+200+100+300=840ms. Parallel retrieval+tool: max(30,60)=60ms. Parallel LLM decisions: max(150,200)=200ms. Parallel validation+generation (speculative): max(100,300)=300ms. Total: 60+200+300=560ms. Additional 15% overlap from streaming: 560*0.85=476ms. P95 with 10% jitter: 476*1.05=500ms — exactly at SLA boundary.
details.realistic_solution: Analyze dependencies: hop1 tool call (30ms) can start while hop2 retrieval (60ms) runs in parallel if the tool call is independent. Hop3 validation can speculatively start with a draft from hop2 while hop4 begins optimistically. Restructured: parallel(hop1_tool+hop2_retrieval)=60ms, then parallel(hop1_LLM+hop2_LLM)=200ms, then parallel(hop3+hop4_speculative)=300ms. Total: 60+200+300=560ms. Further: overlap hop1 LLM decode with hop2 retrieval: 60+200+300=560ms. With streaming and pipeline parallelism: 480ms achievable.

scenario: A 4-hop agent chain on A100 (80GB HBM2e) executes: hop1=tool call (30ms) + LLM decision (150ms), hop2=retrieval (60ms) + LLM synthesis (200ms), hop3=validation LLM (100ms), hop4=final generation (300ms). Serial execution takes 840ms. You must meet a 500ms P95 SLA. Identify which hops can be parallelized and calculate the achievable latency after restructuring.
title: End-to-End Latency SLA for Multi-Hop Agent Chains on A100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to account for KV cache memory when planning model parallelism. Teams allocate GPU memory for model weights and activation memory but neglect that 16 concurrent sessions each holding 8192-token KV caches can consume more memory than the model weights themselves.
details.napkin_math: 13B model bf16: 13B*2 bytes=26GB, tensor parallel across 4 GPUs: 6.5GB/GPU. KV per session: 2(K+V)*40 layers*128 head_dim*2 bytes*8192 tokens = 2*40*128*2*8192 = 167,772,160 bytes ≈ 160MB. 16 sessions: 2.56GB KV total, distributed across 4 GPUs = 640MB/GPU. Activation memory ~2GB/GPU. Total per GPU: 6.5+0.64+2=9.14GB. Remaining: 70.86GB for batching headroom. Reranker: 14GB/2=7GB/GPU + KV.
details.realistic_solution: Per 13B model shard across 4 GPUs: 26GB/4=6.5GB weights per GPU. Per 7B reranker shard across 2 GPUs: 14GB/2=7GB per GPU. KV cache per session for 13B (40 layers, 128 head_dim, bf16): 2*40*128*2*8192=167MB per session. 16 sessions: 16*167MB=2.67GB. Total per GPU on 13B shards: 6.5+0.67+activation=~9GB. Feasible on 80GB. Reranker GPUs: 7GB weights + batch KV for concurrent reranks. NVLink enables all-reduce across shards at 600GB/s.

scenario: You are deploying a compound AI system on a single H100 node (8x H100 80GB, NVLink) where 16 concurrent agent sessions each run a 13B LLM plus a shared 7B reranker. Each agent session holds 8192-token KV cache. The 13B model in bf16 requires 26GB weights, the 7B reranker requires 14GB weights. Calculate whether all components fit and design a memory allocation strategy with tensor parallelism.
title: Memory Capacity Planning for Concurrent RAG Agents on H100

details.common_mistake: Either keeping the full A100 instance always warm (expensive: $3.50/hr * 24 = $84/day for zero traffic periods) or accepting cold starts for all requests (18s unacceptable for interactive use).
details.napkin_math: NVMe load: 13GB / 1.2GB/s = 10.8s. PCIe CPU→GPU: 13GB / 64GB/s = 0.2s (52x faster). Always-on CPU cost: $0.05/hr * 720hr/month = $36/month vs A100 always-on: $3.50 * 720 = $2,520/month. Savings: $2,484/month (98.6%). With predictive pre-warm (2min lead time, 90% accuracy): effective cold start rate = 10% * 4.1s + 90% * 0s = 0.41s average cold start added latency.
details.realistic_solution: Tiered warm strategy: (1) Keep a CPU-only instance always warm with model weights in RAM (64GB CPU RAM, ~$0.05/hr). On demand signal, begin GPU transfer at PCIe bandwidth (64GB/s, 7B model=13GB/64GB/s=0.2s vs NVMe's 10.8s). (2) Pre-load FAISS index into CPU RAM (4GB). (3) Use predictive scaling: analyze traffic patterns, pre-warm GPU 2 minutes before predicted burst. (4) Keep one GPU warm during business hours. Effective cold start: 0.2s (CPU→GPU) + 3.9s warm-up = 4.1s.

scenario: A serverless compound AI deployment on A100 (80GB HBM2e) has cold start latency of 18 seconds: model weight loading from NVMe (13GB 7B model at ~1.2GB/s) takes 10.8s, FAISS index loading (4GB) takes 3.3s, and warm-up inference takes 3.9s. Traffic is bursty — 80% of hours have zero requests. Implement a keep-warm strategy that reduces cold start impact without paying for always-on A100 time.
title: Cold Start Latency for Serverless Compound AI on A100

details.common_mistake: Using exact-match string caching instead of semantic caching, catching only 2-3% of duplicate queries instead of 35%. Also failing to invalidate cached responses when the underlying knowledge base updates, serving stale answers.
details.napkin_math: Daily queries: 50,000. Semantic hit rate: 35% = 17,500 queries served from cache. LLM savings: 17,500 * $0.03 = $525/day = $15,750/month. Cache infrastructure cost: Redis cluster with 100GB RAM (for 1M cached embeddings * 1.5KB + responses * 5KB avg) = ~$200/month. Net savings: $15,550/month. Cache lookup adds 5ms (embedding) + 2ms (HNSW search) = 7ms vs 300ms LLM call. Latency improvement for cache hits: 97.7%.
details.realistic_solution: Deploy a Redis vector store with HNSW index for sub-millisecond similarity search. Cache key: query embedding (384-dim float32 = 1.5KB). Cache value: full response + retrieval metadata + timestamp + knowledge_base_version. Invalidation: tag each cached response with KB version hash; on 6-hour KB update, batch-invalidate all responses tagged with prior version. Warm the cache by pre-embedding the top-1000 most frequent query clusters. Hit rate target: 35% semantic hits → $0.03 * 50,000 * 0.35 = $525/day savings.

scenario: A RAG system on H100 processes 50,000 queries/day. LLM generation costs $0.03/query = $1,500/day. Query analysis shows 35% of queries are semantically near-duplicate (cosine similarity > 0.95 with a prior query within 24 hours). Implement a semantic cache layer using a 384-dim embedding model (5ms lookup) to intercept these duplicate queries before LLM invocation. Design the cache invalidation strategy for a dynamic knowledge base updated every 6 hours.
title: Implementing Semantic Caching for RAG on H100 to Reduce LLM Calls

details.common_mistake: Assuming the device plugin exposes GPUs as a divisible resource like CPU millicores; believing `nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5` is valid syntax in a standard NVIDIA plugin deployment.
details.napkin_math: H100 80 GB divided into 7 MIG 1g.10gb instances = 7 independent 10 GB / ~155 TFLOPS BF16 slices per card. A cluster with 8 H100s can expose 56 MIG slices, up from 8 allocatable GPU units, increasing pod density 7×.
details.realistic_solution: The NVIDIA device plugin registers each physical GPU as a single discrete resource via the Kubernetes Device Plugin API (ListAndWatch). Kubelet tracks integer counts; fractional GPU sharing requires separate mechanisms like MIG partitioning on H100 or time-slicing via the NVIDIA GPU Operator's `deviceConfig`. Without those, every pod claiming `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` monopolizes one full device.

scenario: A junior engineer asks why a pod spec requesting `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` always gets an entire physical GPU even when the workload only uses 4 GB of the H100's 80 GB HBM3. They want to know how the NVIDIA device plugin communicates available GPUs to the kubelet and why fractional allocation isn't the default behavior.
title: K8s GPU Device Plugin: Why Pod Requests Whole GPUs

details.common_mistake: Specifying only temperature-based economizer switching without incorporating carbon intensity; a cold night with high wind-power availability favors free cooling both thermally and from a carbon perspective, but a warm afternoon with high solar availability may have lower carbon intensity than a cold night with fossil-heavy baseload — temperature alone misses this.
details.napkin_math: Free cooling mode: overhead = 23 kW (fans + pumps), PUE = (358.4 + 23) / 358.4 = 1.064. Mechanical cooling mode: overhead = 125 kW (chillers + CRAC), PUE = (358.4 + 125) / 358.4 = 1.35. Annual hours in each mode (Austin climate): free cooling ~7,500 hr, mechanical ~1,260 hr. Blended annual PUE = (7,500 × 1.064 + 1,260 × 1.35) / 8,760 = (7,980 + 1,701) / 8,760 = 1.105. Carbon savings from carbon-aware mode selection (defer high-intensity hours by 2 hr avg): reduces mechanical cooling overlap with high-carbon periods by ~30% = further 0.015 PUE improvement annually.
details.realistic_solution: Define a two-axis control matrix: X-axis = ambient wet-bulb temperature (cold <15°C, moderate 15–25°C, warm >25°C), Y-axis = grid marginal carbon intensity (low <150 gCO₂/kWh, medium 150–300, high >300). Policy: cold+low → full free cooling + maximize IT utilization (good carbon time); warm+high → engage full mechanical cooling + defer flexible batch jobs; moderate+any → mixed mode with economizer assist. Implement as a SCADA control loop reading WattTime `/v3/index` (5-min updates) and weather station wet-bulb data. Hysteresis window: ±2°C, ±30 gCO₂/kWh to prevent mode oscillation. Log all mode transitions to a time-series DB for PUE attribution analysis.

scenario: A hyperscaler runs a 512-GPU H100 cluster (358.4 kW IT load) at a facility with both mechanical chilled-water cooling (PUE contribution 0.35) and free-air economizers (PUE contribution 0.08). The facility is grid-connected with real-time carbon intensity data from WattTime. Specify a cooling control policy that dynamically switches between cooling modes based on both ambient temperature and grid carbon intensity to minimize operational carbon footprint.
title: Specifying a Carbon-Aware Cooling Control Policy for H100 Clusters

details.common_mistake: Using standard Kubernetes `Job` + pod anti-affinity: pods schedule one-by-one, and when the cluster is 90% full, half the training pods land while the other half pend indefinitely, holding reserved GPU resources and starving inference.
details.napkin_math: 64 H100s × 700 W = 44.8 kW power draw during training. At 8 GPUs/node that's 8 nodes. Gang scheduling window: with Volcano, allocation completes in one scheduling cycle (~200–500 ms) vs. default scheduler's O(n) sequential binding which can take 30–60 s for 64 pods, during which partial GPU hold wastes up to 44.8 kW.
details.realistic_solution: Use Volcano `Job` with `minAvailable: 64` under a `gang` scheduling plugin. Volcano holds all 64 pods in a `Pending` state until the full gang can be co-scheduled atomically. Set `policies.action: RestartJob` on `PodEvicted` events. Combine with a `PriorityClass` hierarchy (training=1000, inference=900) so the scheduler preempts lower-priority inference pods when burst training capacity is needed.

scenario: You are architecting a Kubernetes-native distributed training platform for 64-GPU runs on H100 nodes (8 GPUs per node, NVLink intra-node, InfiniBand inter-node). PyTorch DDP requires all-or-nothing scheduling: if even one pod fails to schedule, the entire job must not start. Design the scheduling configuration that prevents partial-allocation deadlock in a cluster shared with inference workloads.
title: Designing a Volcano Job for Multi-Pod Distributed Training

details.common_mistake: Setting `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` as both request and limit is correct for device allocation, but teams often forget to tune the container's CPU memory limit. The vLLM process pins large CPU RAM buffers for KV cache paging; if the RAM limit is hit, the Linux OOM killer terminates the process, not just the GPU allocation.
details.napkin_math: 7B params × 2 bytes/param (BF16) = 14 GB model weights. KV cache for batch=32, seq=2048, 32 layers, 32 heads, 128-dim: 32 × 2048 × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 dim × 2 (K+V) × 2 bytes ≈ 34 GB. (Alternatively with 16 heads: ≈17 GB.) Total GPU: 14 + 34 = 48 GB < 80 GB HBM2e (with 32 KV heads); still fits within A100 capacity. CPU RAM: page table + activation buffers ≈ 8–12 GB; limit at 24 Gi avoids OOM with headroom.
details.realistic_solution: Set `resources.requests.memory` and `resources.limits.memory` to at least 2× the model's CPU-resident data: for a 7B parameter model in BF16 (14 GB) with a ~34 GB KV cache (32 layers, 32 heads, 128 dim), set RAM limit to 64 Gi. Set `resources.requests.nvidia.com/gpu: 1` and `limits.nvidia.com/gpu: 1`. Use `LimitRange` at the namespace level to enforce a floor. Add a readiness probe on the vLLM health endpoint so Kubernetes withholds traffic during KV cache warmup.

scenario: An inference service runs vLLM on A100 80 GB HBM2e nodes inside Kubernetes. Ops notices pods are occasionally OOMKilled and restarted, causing 30-second cold-start latency spikes. The pod spec currently sets CPU/RAM limits but no GPU memory limits. Specify a resource configuration that reduces evictions without over-provisioning.
title: Specifying Resource Limits to Prevent GPU Memory OOM Eviction

details.common_mistake: Implementing a full custom scheduler from scratch; most teams don't realize Kubernetes exposes a `scheduler extender` HTTP webhook interface that receives filter/prioritize calls with node lists, allowing topology scoring without forking the main scheduler binary.
details.napkin_math: NVSwitch 3.0 all-to-all: 900 GB/s aggregate. InfiniBand HDR inter-node: 200 Gb/s = 25 GB/s per link. Ratio: 36×. An AllReduce on 1 GB gradient tensor over NVLink takes ~1.1 ms intra-node vs. ~40 ms over IB — 36× latency difference. Topology-aware scheduling eliminates this for single-node fits.
details.realistic_solution: Deploy a scheduler extender sidecar that reads GPU topology from `nvidia-smi topo -m` output cached as a ConfigMap per node. Register it in `KubeSchedulerConfiguration.extenders` with `prioritize: true`. The extender scores each node 0–100 based on the number of NVLink P2P paths available between requested GPUs. For 8-GPU H100 nodes with full NVSwitch mesh, all intra-node pairs score 100; cross-socket PCIe paths score 40. The scheduler selects the top-scored node set. Refresh the ConfigMap via a DaemonSet that runs `nvidia-smi topo` every 5 minutes.

scenario: Your data center has 16-GPU H100 nodes interconnected via NVLink Switch (NVSwitch 3.0, 900 GB/s all-to-all). A multi-node training job spans 4 nodes and must maximize NVLink bandwidth within each node while minimizing cross-node RDMA traffic. The default Kubernetes scheduler is topology-unaware. Implement a scheduler extension that scores nodes based on GPU-to-GPU bandwidth topology.
title: Implementing a Custom Kubernetes Scheduler Extender for GPU Topology

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to gang scheduling because it is simpler to configure; failing to account for the compounding effect of node failures on gang jobs — a single node failure in a 16-node gang causes full job restart, wasting all accumulated gradient steps.
details.napkin_math: Gang restart cost: checkpoint save at 70 GB/s NVMe × 140 GB model = 2 s write + 10 s barrier + relaunch = ~60 s overhead per restart. With 56% restart probability over 7 days, expected wasted time = 0.56 × 60 s = 33.6 s — negligible. But if a restart causes 30 min of re-computation before next checkpoint, expected waste = 0.56 × 30 min = 16.8 min/week, vs. elastic's 0-restart, 12.5% throughput loss = 12.5% × 7 days = 21 hr of equivalent lost compute. Gang wins on short jobs; elastic wins on long ones.
details.realistic_solution: With 5% weekly failure rate across 16 nodes, the probability of at least one failure during a 7-day run is 1 − (0.95)^16 ≈ 56%. Gang scheduling means a coin-flip chance of full restart. Elastic training with `--nnodes=4:8` lets the job continue on 7 nodes after a failure, accepting a ~12.5% throughput drop. For long runs, elastic training amortizes checkpoint overhead and maintains forward progress. Prefer elastic for week-long jobs; reserve gang scheduling for short (<4 hr) jobs where setup overhead dominates.

scenario: Your team must choose between strict gang scheduling (Volcano) and elastic distributed training (PyTorch Elastic / torchrun with `--nnodes=4:8`) for a shared H100 cluster running week-long LLM fine-tunes. The cluster has 128 H100 GPUs across 16 nodes and experiences 5% node failure rate per week. Evaluate which approach yields higher cluster utilization and training throughput under these conditions.
title: Evaluating Gang Scheduling vs. Elastic Training Tradeoffs

details.common_mistake: Using GPU utilization as the HPA metric: GPU utilization is a lagging indicator. A100 at 95% utilization means the queue is already full and latency is degrading; by the time HPA fires, scales up, the new pod cold-starts (30–90 s for large models), and warms up, the traffic spike is over.
details.napkin_math: A100 inference throughput for 7B model: ~2000 tokens/s at batch=16. At 10× traffic spike = 20,000 tokens/s needed = 10 pods. HPA scale-up latency: 15 s metric lag + 30 s pod schedule + 60 s model load = 105 s. Traffic spike duration: 120–180 s. HPA barely responds before the spike ends. KEDA queue-based scaling with warm pods: 15 s metric lag + ~5 s pod ready = 20 s response — capturing 85%+ of the spike duration.
details.realistic_solution: Use queue depth or pending request count as the HPA metric via a custom metrics adapter (e.g., Prometheus Adapter + KEDA). Set scale-up trigger at queue_depth > 10 with a 15-second polling interval. Pre-provision warm standby pods using KEDA's `ScaledObject` with `minReplicaCount: 1` to eliminate cold-start latency. GPU utilization works as a scale-down signal (utilization < 20% for 5 min → scale down), but not scale-up. For 2–3 minute spikes, proactive scaling based on request rate is more effective.

scenario: An ML platform team is debating whether to use Kubernetes HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) based on GPU utilization metrics from DCGM Exporter to auto-scale a vLLM inference deployment on A100 nodes. The service receives bursty traffic with 10× spikes lasting 2–3 minutes. Evaluate whether HPA with GPU utilization is the right scaling signal for this workload.
title: Evaluating Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for GPU Inference Scaling

details.common_mistake: Manually constructing a `StatefulSet` with custom init containers to handle rendezvous; not knowing the Training Operator CRD exists or how its `masterPort` and `replicaSpecs` fields map to `torchrun` arguments.
details.napkin_math: 4 nodes × 8 H100 GPUs = 32 GPUs total. NVLink intra-node bandwidth: 900 GB/s (NVSwitch). Inter-node IB: 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s. For a 70B model with 140 GB BF16 gradients, AllReduce over 4 nodes via IB takes 140 GB / 50 GB/s × 2 = 5.6 s per step at theoretical peak.
details.realistic_solution: Use `kind: PyTorchJob` with `replicaSpecs.Worker.replicas: 4`, `replicaSpecs.Worker.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits['nvidia.com/gpu']: 8`, and `pytorchReplicaSpecs.Worker.restartPolicy: OnFailure`. Set `rdzvBackend: c10d` in the container env. Add `nodeAffinity` under `template.spec.affinity` with `matchExpressions: [{key: accelerator, operator: In, values: [h100]}]`. The operator automatically sets `MASTER_ADDR`, `MASTER_PORT`, `RANK`, and `WORLD_SIZE` env vars.

scenario: A researcher hands you a `torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 --nnodes=4 --rdzv_backend=c10d train.py` launch command. They need it translated into a production Kubernetes manifest using the Training Operator's `PyTorchJob` CRD on an H100 cluster. They have a prebuilt image and need the job to use node affinity for H100 nodes and request 8 GPUs per worker pod.
title: Fluency: Translating a PyTorch DDP Job into a Kubernetes Manifest

details.common_mistake: Conflating Cluster Autoscaler's decision time (~30 s) with EC2 instance launch time; assuming 'autoscaler triggered' equals 'node ready.'
details.napkin_math: p4d.24xlarge: 8 × A100 × 400 W = 3.2 kW per idle standby node. Monthly standby cost: 3.2 kW × 720 hr × $0.12/kWh ≈ $276 electricity + ~$9.83/hr instance = $7,080/month per warm standby node. Trade-off: pay $7,080/month to eliminate 8-min cold-start latency for bursty training jobs.
details.realistic_solution: The 8–12 min breakdown: CA scan loop (10–30 s) + EC2 instance launch API call (30–60 s) + instance boot (2–3 min) + kubelet registration + CNI plugin initialization (1–2 min) + NVIDIA device plugin pod startup and GPU enumeration (1–2 min) + container image pull for training workload (1–3 min for large images). Total: 6–11 min is expected for p4d.24xlarge. Mitigate with pre-warmed node pools (keep 1 node in standby) and pre-pulled images via DaemonSet. Use Karpenter instead of CA for faster launch loops (~1 min improvement via direct EC2 Fleet API calls).

scenario: A cloud ML team enables Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler on an AWS EKS cluster with a GPU node group (p4d.24xlarge, 8× A100 80 GB, 400 W each). They expect the autoscaler to provision a new node within 2 minutes when a GPU pod is pending. After deploying, they observe nodes taking 8–12 minutes to join. Trace what actually happens during node provisioning and explain the delay.
title: Realizing Cluster Autoscaler Behavior with GPU Node Groups

details.common_mistake: Assuming pod status `Running` means the training process is making progress; not setting `NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1` or a watchdog timeout in the training loop.
details.napkin_math: 8 nodes × 8 H100 GPUs = 64 GPUs × 700 W = 44.8 kW idle burn. 45 min hang = 0.75 hr × 44.8 kW = 33.6 kWh wasted. At $0.12/kWh = $4 in electricity + 64 × $0.75/GPU-hr (cloud pricing) × 0.75 hr = $36 in compute credits lost from a single undetected hang.
details.realistic_solution: PyTorch DDP/NCCL collective operations (AllReduce) block until all ranks respond. When rank N is evicted, the remaining ranks block inside the NCCL barrier indefinitely — no timeout by default. The pods appear Running because the process is alive but blocked in a CUDA kernel call. Detection: emit a `step_timestamp` metric from each rank every N seconds; alert if any rank's timestamp is stale for >5 min. Fix: set `NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1` (raises exception after timeout) and implement a heartbeat watchdog thread that calls `dist.monitored_barrier(timeout=300s)` to surface the failure.

scenario: A distributed training job running 8× H100 nodes hangs indefinitely after one node is preempted by a higher-priority workload. The surviving 7 nodes' pods are still Running, GPU utilization drops to 0%, and no error appears in pod logs. The job has been hung for 45 minutes. Explain what is happening and how to detect this class of failure proactively.
title: Realizing Why GPU Jobs Hang After Node Preemption

details.common_mistake: Immediately blaming quota limits; not checking whether the issue is in the scheduler decision loop, the pod binding step, or resource fragmentation at the node level.
details.napkin_math: 200 H100 GPUs across 25 nodes (8 GPU/node). Team B deploys 24 inference pods of 1 GPU each = 3 nodes fully consumed, 22 nodes with 7/8 GPUs used. Team A's 8-GPU job needs a fully free node. With 22 nodes each missing 1 GPU, zero valid nodes exist for Team A — despite 22 'available' GPUs. Fragmentation blocks Team A even with 22 GPU quota remaining.
details.realistic_solution: Systematic analysis: (1) Check `kube-scheduler` latency metrics — `scheduler_scheduling_duration_seconds` histogram. (2) Inspect `kubectl describe pod` for the pending pod's events; 'Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu' means fragmentation, not quota. (3) Compare Team A's pod spec: if requesting 8 GPUs and only 7-GPU gaps exist across nodes due to Team B's 1-GPU inference pods, scheduling fails despite quota headroom. (4) Solution: implement bin-packing policy (`MostAllocated`) in scheduler config so small pods fill nodes completely, leaving full-node gaps for training jobs. Add a `preferredDuringScheduling` anti-affinity to Team B inference pods to discourage fragmenting H100 nodes.

scenario: A 200-GPU H100 cluster serves 5 teams via Kubernetes ResourceQuotas. The ML Ops team reports that GPU pods from Team A are taking 15–20 minutes to schedule during peak hours, while Team B's pods schedule in under 30 seconds. Both teams are within their quota limits. Analyze the scheduling bottleneck and identify the root cause.
title: Analyzing Pod Scheduling Latency Under Quota Pressure

details.common_mistake: Trying to namespace-scope a DaemonSet (not possible — DaemonSets are node-scoped); attempting to solve metric isolation via NetworkPolicy alone, which doesn't restrict API server RBAC access to metric endpoints.
details.napkin_math: H100 supports 7× MIG 1g.10gb instances per GPU. 25-node cluster × 8 GPUs × 7 MIG slices = 1,400 isolatable GPU slices. Per-slice HBM3 bandwidth: 3.35 TB/s ÷ 7 ≈ 479 GB/s per MIG instance. Metric cardinality per node: DCGM exports ~150 metrics × 56 MIG instances = 8,400 time series per node × 25 nodes = 210,000 series cluster-wide — requires careful Prometheus retention tuning.
details.realistic_solution: DCGM Exporter exposes metrics at node level without namespace awareness. Isolation requires: (1) Deploy per-namespace metric proxies (e.g., `prometheus-operator` per namespace with `namespaceSelector`) that only scrape pods within their namespace. (2) Use RBAC to restrict `metrics.k8s.io` endpoint access: bind `ClusterRole` with `get` on `/metrics` only to the owning service account per namespace. (3) For GPU-level isolation, use MIG on H100 — each team gets a named MIG instance (`nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb`), and DCGM can be configured to report per-MIG metrics. (4) PodSecurityAdmission to block `privileged: true` which could allow `/proc` enumeration of sibling containers.

scenario: A regulated enterprise runs ML workloads on a shared H100 Kubernetes cluster. A security audit finds that researchers in Namespace A can inadvertently see GPU metrics from Namespace B via the cluster-wide DCGM Exporter DaemonSet, which scrapes all GPUs on every node. Analyze the blast radius and design a RBAC + metric isolation strategy.
title: Analyzing RBAC and Security Context for Multi-Tenant GPU Namespaces

details.common_mistake: Cordoning all nodes at once for the upgrade; not accounting for the fact that GPU driver upgrades require a node reboot (kernel module), meaning the upgrade is not a hot-swap and all pods on the node must be evicted.
details.napkin_math: 64 nodes, 10 min per node upgrade (drain 3 min + reboot 5 min + validate 2 min) × 1 node at a time = 640 min = 10.7 hr total upgrade window. Inference capacity during upgrade: 63/64 = 98.4%. Training: each job loses at most 1 node = at worst 12.5% throughput reduction for 8-node jobs during that node's 10-min window. Total training disruption per job: 10 min at reduced throughput = acceptable for week-long runs.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy: (1) Cordon and drain one node at a time using `kubectl drain --grace-period=300 --ignore-daemonsets`. (2) Inference pods: use PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 90%` to ensure 90% of inference capacity remains during drain. With 64 nodes, draining 1 node at a time leaves 63/64 = 98% capacity. (3) Training pods: configure elastic training (`torchrun` with fault tolerance) or checkpoint-and-preempt: save checkpoint, evict, relaunch on upgraded node. (4) Upgrade driver via GPU Operator's `ClusterPolicy` with rolling update strategy — set `maxUnavailable: 1` on the driver DaemonSet. (5) Validate each node: run `nvidia-smi` + NCCL bandwidth test before uncordoning. (6) Rollback: maintain previous driver image tag in GPU Operator config; redeploy DaemonSet with old tag if error rate increases.

scenario: You must upgrade the NVIDIA GPU driver from 525 to 550 on a production 512-GPU H100 cluster (64 nodes, 8 GPUs each) running 24/7 ML inference and batch training workloads. The cluster cannot tolerate more than 5 minutes of total inference downtime and cannot lose training job progress. Design a complete rolling upgrade strategy with rollback capability.
title: Mastery: Designing a Zero-Downtime GPU Cluster Upgrade Strategy

details.common_mistake: Believing PUE = 1.0 is achievable (it would mean zero overhead power for cooling, lighting, networking, and UPS); confusing PUE with energy efficiency of the compute hardware itself.
details.napkin_math: 64 H100 nodes × 8 GPUs × 700 W = 358.4 kW IT load. At PUE 1.3: total facility = 358.4 × 1.3 = 465.9 kW. At PUE 1.1: 358.4 × 1.1 = 394.2 kW. Savings: 71.7 kW × 8,760 hr/yr × $0.08/kWh = $50,200/yr by moving from 1.3 to 1.1 PUE on this single cluster.
details.realistic_solution: PUE = Total Facility Power / IT Equipment Power. IT equipment is the denominator, so PUE ≥ 1.0 always, with 1.0 meaning zero overhead — physically impossible. A PUE of 1.3 means for every 1 W of GPU compute, 0.3 W goes to cooling, PDUs, lighting, and UPS. Hyperscaler PUEs of 1.1–1.2 require direct liquid cooling (cold plates on H100s), free-air economizers in cold climates, and fully optimized power distribution. On-premise air-cooled deployments typically achieve 1.4–1.6. Each 0.1 improvement in PUE on a 1 MW GPU cluster saves 100 kW of overhead power — significant at scale.

scenario: A new ML infrastructure engineer asks why the team targets a PUE of 1.3 rather than 1.0 for the H100 cluster datacenter, and whether lower is always better. They have seen hyperscaler marketing claiming PUE of 1.1 and wonder if that is achievable for on-premise GPU deployments.
title: Recall: What PUE Measures and Why 1.0 Is Physically Impossible

details.common_mistake: Looking only at steady-state TDP and ignoring peak power draw; not accounting for PDU overhead, cooling capacity per rack, and breaker sizing for high-density racks.
details.napkin_math: 1 DGX H100: 8 GPUs × 700 W = 5,600 W GPU TDP + 4,600 W system (CPUs, NVSwitches, memory, storage) = 10,200 W. Peak burst can reach 120% of TDP = 12,240 W. Standard datacenter 15 kW budget: fits 1 DGX H100 with 2.76 kW headroom. To double density, upgrade to 30 kW/rack circuit — requires 3-phase 208V/80A dedicated circuit per rack.
details.realistic_solution: Two DGX H100 nodes: 2 × 10.2 kW = 20.4 kW — exceeds the 15 kW rack budget. Even one DGX H100 at 10.2 kW + networking (300 W) + server chassis overhead (500 W) = 11 kW, leaving only 4 kW headroom. High-density H100 deployments require 30–40 kW per rack power circuits (3-phase 60A or higher), specialized in-rack liquid cooling manifolds or rear-door heat exchangers, and floor load ratings >1,000 kg. Hyperscalers deploy H100 in custom-built pods with 30–50 kW/rack capacity, not standard 15 kW datacenter allocations.

scenario: An ML platform engineer proposes filling a standard 42U server rack with H100 SXM5 servers (DGX H100, 10.2 kW per 8-GPU node) to maximize GPU density. The datacenter's standard rack power budget is 15 kW. The engineer argues they can fit 2 DGX nodes per rack. Evaluate whether this is feasible and what datacenter constraints apply.
title: Recall: Rack Power Budget Limits for H100 Dense Deployments

details.common_mistake: Assuming liquid cooling only reduces GPU temperature without understanding the system-level cooling chain; not realizing that CRAC/CRAH units (chillers, fans, compressors) account for the majority of the 0.55 PUE overhead in air-cooled facilities.
details.napkin_math: 512 H100 × 700 W = 358.4 kW IT load. Air cooling at PUE 1.55: total facility = 555.5 kW, overhead = 197.1 kW. DLC at PUE 1.15: total = 412.2 kW, overhead = 53.8 kW. Savings: 143.3 kW. Annual: 143.3 kW × 8,760 hr × $0.10/kWh = $125,530/yr electricity savings. DLC infrastructure cost: ~$500–800K for a 500 kW deployment. Payback: 4–6 years on electricity alone, faster with carbon credits.
details.realistic_solution: In air cooling, CRAC units and associated compressors consume 30–50% of IT load. With DLC: cold plates on H100 SXM5 capture 70–80% of GPU heat directly into water loop (inlet temp 35–45°C), bypassing room-level air handling. Remaining heat (CPUs, memory, storage) still uses air cooling or rear-door heat exchangers. The warm water loop uses dry coolers or cooling towers — no compressor-based refrigeration needed if ambient temp allows free cooling. Infrastructure changes: chilled water CDU (Coolant Distribution Unit) per row, manifolds to each server, leak detection, secondary loop isolation valves, and deionized water treatment systems.

scenario: A datacenter team air-cools a 512-GPU H100 cluster and measures PUE = 1.55. They are evaluating direct liquid cooling (DLC) with cold plates on H100 SXM5 modules to reduce PUE. A vendor claims DLC will bring PUE to 1.15. Walk through where the power savings come from and what infrastructure changes are required.
title: Realizing How Liquid Cooling Changes PUE for H100 Deployments

details.common_mistake: Treating carbon-aware scheduling as a purely time-shifting problem (run at night when grid is greener) without considering cross-region workload migration; also ignoring the data gravity problem — moving a large dataset to a lower-carbon region has its own carbon cost.
details.napkin_math: 512 H100 × 700 W = 358.4 kW. 7 days = 168 hr. Total energy = 358.4 × 168 = 60,211 kWh. At US-East 350 gCO₂/kWh: 60,211 × 350 g = 21,074 kg CO₂ ≈ 21 tonnes. At US-West solar peak 80 gCO₂/kWh: 60,211 × 80 g = 4,817 kg ≈ 4.8 tonnes. Carbon savings from spatial shift: 16.2 tonnes CO₂ — equivalent to ~35,000 miles of driving.
