details.realistic_solution: Carbon-aware scheduling has two axes: temporal (run during low-intensity hours, e.g., midday solar surplus in California) and spatial (route to lower-intensity region). For a 7-day job: California's grid intensity drops to ~80 gCO₂/kWh during peak solar hours (11am–3pm) vs. 250 gCO₂/kWh overnight. If data is already in US-West, run there and schedule job start at solar peak. Use the Carbon Aware SDK or WattTime API for real-time marginal emissions data. Integrate with Kubernetes via a custom scheduler plugin or KEDA scaler that checks the carbon intensity forecast before approving new job submissions. For flexible batch jobs, set a `carbon_budget` annotation and the scheduler defers launch until intensity is below threshold.

scenario: An ML Ops team runs large batch training jobs on H100 clusters in two regions: US-West (California, grid intensity ~200 gCO₂/kWh, high solar penetration) and US-East (Virginia, grid intensity ~350 gCO₂/kWh, coal/gas mix). A 70B model pre-training run requires 7 days on 512 GPUs. Explain how carbon-aware scheduling would route this job and what infrastructure is needed to act on grid signals.
title: Realizing Carbon-Aware Scheduling: When to Shift GPU Workloads

details.common_mistake: Assuming linear relationship between power cap and throughput; not distinguishing between power capping (software-enforced via NVML) and thermal throttling (hardware-enforced when junction temperature exceeds 83°C on H100).
details.napkin_math: H100 BF16 FLOPS: 989 TFLOPS at 700 W. Power-capped at 500 W (71.4%): theoretical ~706 TFLOPS. Actual measured 30% drop = 692 TFLOPS. Additional thermal throttle on top: GPU clocks dropped from 1,980 MHz to ~1,650 MHz (83% of max) = explains extra 15% × 17% = additional ~11% reduction. Combined: 71% × 83% ≈ 59% of peak = 41% throughput loss, not 30% — suggests partial thermal throttle.
details.realistic_solution: Two separate throttling mechanisms interact: (1) The 500 W power cap reduces GPU clocks proportionally — H100 at 500/700 = 71% of TDP nominally yields ~71% throughput for compute-bound workloads. (2) However, in a poorly ventilated rack, the reduced cooling from inadequate airflow causes junction temperatures to climb above 83°C even at 500 W. The GPU then thermally throttles clocks further — compounding the power cap effect. Check `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,clocks_throttle_reasons.hw_slowdown,power.draw --format=csv` to distinguish cap-induced vs. thermal-induced throttling. Fix: improve airflow (blanking panels, directed airflow) to enable 500 W operation without thermal throttle.

scenario: A datacenter operator applies a 500 W power cap to H100 SXM5 GPUs (rated at 700 W TDP) using `nvidia-smi --power-limit=500` to stay within rack power budgets. A training team complains that their throughput dropped by 30% compared to uncapped runs. The operator claims power capping should only reduce throughput by ~15%. Explain the discrepancy.
title: Realizing Power Capping vs. Thermal Throttling on H100

details.common_mistake: Using average power draw for placement decisions; H100 and A100 GPUs have significant power variance (idle: 80 W, full compute: 700/400 W) — placing jobs based on TDP guarantees headroom but wastes capacity, while placing on average power risks breaker trips at peak.
details.napkin_math: H100 rack: 2 nodes × 8,040 W = 16,080 W. Budget: 20,000 W. Headroom: 3,920 W (19.6%). A100 rack: P95 training = 390 W × 8 + 2,000 W = 5,120 W/node. 20,000 / 5,120 = 3.9 → 3 nodes/rack = 24 A100s per rack. H100 rack: 2 nodes = 16 H100s. Normalized FLOPS/rack: H100 = 16 × 989 TF = 15.8 PFLOPS; A100 = 24 × 312 TF = 7.5 PFLOPS. H100 delivers 2.1× more FLOPS per rack at 1.3× higher per-GPU cost.
details.realistic_solution: Use P95 power draw from DCGM historical metrics per GPU workload type (training vs. inference vs. idle) as the placement unit. For H100 training jobs (P95 ≈ 680 W/GPU) and 8 GPUs/node: P95 node power = 680 × 8 + 2,600 W system = 8,040 W. A 20 kW rack fits 2 H100 training nodes with 3,920 W headroom — allocate to networking and future expansion. Implement as a Kubernetes scheduler extender that queries the `rack_power_headroom` metric from Prometheus before scoring each node. Reject nodes where `current_rack_power + pod_p95_power > rack_budget × 0.95`.

scenario: A shared datacenter hosts a heterogeneous cluster: 20 racks with H100 nodes (700 W/GPU) and 15 racks with A100 nodes (400 W/GPU). Each rack has a 20 kW power budget. Current GPU utilization averages 60%. You are tasked with implementing a power-aware workload placement algorithm that maximizes GPU density per rack without exceeding the power budget under 95th-percentile load.
title: Implementing Power-Aware Bin Packing for Heterogeneous GPU Racks

details.common_mistake: Implementing carbon-awareness as a hard gate (block all jobs when carbon intensity is high) rather than a priority-weighted queue; hard gates cause queue backup and violate the 20% latency SLA when low-carbon windows are short or infrequent.
details.napkin_math: 256 A100 × 400 W = 102.4 kW. Annual energy: 102.4 kW × 8,760 hr = 897,024 kWh. Baseline: US avg 386 gCO₂/kWh → 346,443 kg CO₂/yr. 30% reduction target = 242,510 kg CO₂/yr. Need to shift ~29% of job-hours to windows ≤200 gCO₂/kWh. US grid data: ~35% of hours are below 200 gCO₂/kWh in CAISO. Feasible for flexible batch workloads; requires 4 hr max deferral budget per job.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a carbon score multiplier in the job priority function: `effective_priority = base_priority × (1 + k × (threshold - current_intensity) / threshold)` where k=2, threshold=200 gCO₂/kWh. High-priority jobs (k > 1) run regardless of carbon intensity; flexible batch jobs get boosted during low-intensity windows. Use WattTime's `/v3/forecast` endpoint (hourly ahead) to pre-schedule job launches up to 24 hr ahead. Implement as a KEDA `ScaledJob` that reads a custom metric from a carbon-intensity sidecar publishing to Prometheus. Cap maximum defer time at 4 hr to enforce the 20% latency SLA.

scenario: You are building a carbon-aware job scheduler for an ML training platform running on 256 A100 GPUs (400 W each) in a US datacenter. The platform must reduce Scope 2 emissions by 30% without increasing average job latency by more than 20%. Design the implementation using the WattTime API and integrate it with the existing Kubernetes-based job queue.
title: Implementing Carbon-Aware Job Queue with WattTime Integration

details.common_mistake: Comparing PUE numbers without understanding measurement methodology; instantaneous PUE during ideal conditions is cherry-picked and often 30–50% lower than annual average PUE due to seasonal cooling load variation.
details.napkin_math: 512 H100 × 700 W = 358.4 kW IT load. Annual energy at Vendor A PUE 1.2: 358.4 × 1.2 × 8,760 = 3,767,501 kWh. At Vendor B PUE 1.45: 358.4 × 1.45 × 8,760 = 4,551,666 kWh. Delta: 787,391 kWh/yr × $0.09/kWh = $70,865/yr cost difference. But if Vendor A's actual annual PUE is 1.5 (not 1.2), the 'cheaper' vendor costs $96K/yr more — making rigorous methodology worth the diligence.
details.realistic_solution: The Green Grid and ISO/IEC 30134-2 define PUEannual as total annual facility kWh divided by total annual IT kWh — the only methodology that captures seasonal variation, cooling system ramp-up during summer, and cooling efficiency at varying partial loads. Vendor A's instantaneous PUE 1.2 measured in January in a cold climate is irrelevant to summer operations when cooling loads increase 2–3× and compressors must run. Vendor B's PUEannual 1.45, if measured per ISO standard with full audit trail, is more trustworthy. Request annual PUE with at minimum quarterly breakdowns, cooling system efficiency curves (kW cooling / kW IT), and power train diagrams. Also request Uptime Institute Tier certification and third-party audit.

scenario: Two datacenter vendors quote PUE for hosting your H100 cluster. Vendor A claims PUE 1.2 (measured instantaneously on their best day in January with free-air cooling active). Vendor B claims PUE 1.45 (annual average, ISO/IEC 30134-2 methodology). Your procurement team wants to choose Vendor A based on the lower number. Evaluate which quote is more meaningful and why.
title: Evaluating PUE Measurement Methodologies: Instantaneous vs. Annual

details.common_mistake: Using dry-bulb ambient temperature for free cooling feasibility analysis; cooling tower and dry cooler performance is governed by wet-bulb temperature, which in humid climates like Austin is much closer to the 45°C limit than dry-bulb suggests.
details.napkin_math: Austin climate: ~7,500/8,760 hours with wet-bulb < 22°C → free cooling outlet ≤ 29°C, well within 45°C limit. Mechanical cooling hours: ~50 hr/yr worst case. Dry cooler fan power at 358.4 kW load: ~18 kW fan + 5 kW pump = 23 kW overhead. PUE contribution: 23/358.4 = 0.064 → PUE = 1.064 for cooling system alone. Total facility PUE ≈ 1.064 + 0.05 (PDU losses) + 0.03 (lighting/misc) = ~1.14. Mechanical chiller adds 35–60 kW when needed: max PUE = 1.17 for 50 peak hours.
details.realistic_solution: Dry cooler outlet temperature ≈ wet-bulb temperature + 5–8°C approach temperature. For a 45°C supply temperature limit: max allowable wet-bulb = 45 − 7 = 38°C. Austin's maximum wet-bulb is ~26°C in peak summer, well below 38°C. However, evaluation must use 99th percentile wet-bulb to ensure reliability. ASHRAE data for Austin: 1% wet-bulb design = 24.6°C, giving cooler outlet = 24.6 + 7 = 31.6°C — acceptable. Full free cooling is viable year-round in Austin for 45°C supply. Hours where mechanical assist needed: <50 hr/yr at extreme peaks. This enables PUE ≈ 1.1–1.15 vs. 1.3–1.4 for compressor-based chilled water.

scenario: A facilities team evaluates whether they can use free cooling (dry coolers with no mechanical refrigeration) for a DLC-equipped H100 cluster in Austin, Texas. H100 DLC cold plates require water supply at ≤45°C inlet temperature. Austin's wet-bulb temperature exceeds 25°C for ~1,200 hours per year. Evaluate the viability and quantify the free cooling hours achievable.
title: Evaluating Free Cooling Feasibility for H100 Liquid-Cooled Deployments

details.common_mistake: Comparing FLOPS without accounting for model FLOP utilization (MFU): H100 MFU for LLM training is ~45–55%, while TPU v5e MFU is ~45–60% with XLA; and not accounting for power per TFLOPS differences.
details.napkin_math: H100 carbon: ~8,128 kg CO₂. TPU v5e carbon: ~1,634 kg CO₂. Ratio: 5×. Key driver: grid carbon intensity (350 vs. 70 gCO₂/kWh), not hardware efficiency. Moving H100 workload to a renewable-powered datacenter (70 gCO₂/kWh) would yield 23,224 kWh × 0.07 = 1,626 kg — matching TPU v5e carbon. Hardware choice matters less than where you plug it in.
details.realistic_solution: Methodology: (1) Compute training FLOPs: 6 × N × D = 6 × 7B × 1T = 42 × 10^21 FLOPS (Chinchilla formula). (2) H100 effective throughput at 50% MFU: 989 TFLOPS × 0.50 = 494.5 TFLOPS. Time on 64 H100s: 42e21 / (64 × 494.5e12) = 1,328 s/hr... = ~21.6 days. Power: 64 × 700 W = 44.8 kW. Energy: 44.8 kW × 518.4 hr = 23,224 kWh. Carbon: 23,224 × 0.350 kg = 8,128 kg CO₂. (3) TPU v5e at 50% MFU: 197 TFLOPS × 0.50 = 98.5 TFLOPS. On 256 chips: 256 × 98.5e12 = 25.2 PFLOPS. Time: 42e21 / 25.2e15 = 1.67M s = 19.3 days. Power: 256 × 197 W = 50.4 kW. Energy: 50.4 × 463 hr = 23,337 kWh. Carbon: 23,337 × 0.070 = 1,634 kg CO₂. Google's low-carbon grid yields 5× lower carbon despite similar total energy.

scenario: An ML team must choose between running a 7B parameter LLM pre-training (1 trillion tokens) on NVIDIA H100 (700 W, 989 TFLOPS BF16) in a US-East datacenter (350 gCO₂/kWh) vs. Google TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16, 197 W per chip, Google datacenter at ~70 gCO₂/kWh with renewable matching) via Google Cloud. Evaluate total carbon footprint for each option.
title: Evaluating Total Carbon Cost of H100 vs. TPU v5e for LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Immediately assuming a cooling system failure; not checking the IT power denominator — PUE can spike if IT load drops (scheduled maintenance window reduces GPU jobs) while cooling power stays constant due to thermal inertia.
details.napkin_math: Normal: IT=358.4 kW, facility=484 kW, PUE=1.35. Spike to PUE 1.72: facility=358.4×1.72=616.4 kW, overhead=258 kW (vs. normal 125.6 kW). Delta overhead: +132.4 kW. Large CRAC unit: 100–150 kW per unit — one CRAC running at full compressor load instead of economizer mode (due to weekend setback misconfiguration) exactly explains the 132 kW delta.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnostic framework: (1) Check IT power (denominator) first. If GPU utilization stayed at 85% but scheduled jobs ran lighter models, IT power may have dropped. Verify via PDU branch circuit monitoring. (2) Check cooling system power (numerator). CRAC/CRAH unit logs for compressor starts, airflow changes, or economizer bypass. Weekend setback schedules sometimes raise chilled water supply temps to save energy — paradoxically causing chiller compressors to work harder when heat loads remain constant. (3) Check for humidity excursions — humidifiers add significant power to maintain 40–60% RH. (4) Inspect for blocked hot aisle containment: missing blanking panels allow hot air recirculation, increasing cooling load. (5) Review UPS load factor — UPS efficiency drops significantly at low load (<30%), adding to overhead.

scenario: A production H100 cluster that normally runs at PUE 1.35 suddenly spikes to PUE 1.72 over a weekend. GPU utilization is stable at 85%. The facilities team sees no alerts from the cooling system. On Monday, a root cause analysis is required. Systematically diagnose the possible causes of the 27% PUE increase.
title: Diagnosing Unexpected PUE Spike in H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Applying a uniform power cap to all GPUs: 45,000 W / 128 = 351.6 W per GPU. This uniformly reduces all GPU clocks, but training jobs don't all have the same sensitivity to power reduction — memory-bound operations (attention with large sequences) degrade less under capping than compute-bound operations (dense matrix multiplications).
details.napkin_math: Strategy: 64 training GPUs at 380 W = 24,320 W; 64 inference GPUs at 320 W = 20,480 W; total = 44,800 W < 45,000 W budget. Previously: 112 GPUs × 400 W = 44,800 W. New: 128 GPUs × avg 350 W = same power, 14% more GPUs active. Training throughput: 64 × 312 TFLOPS × (380/400) = 18,969.6 TFLOPS vs. prior 112 × 312 × 1 = 34,944 TFLOPS — training FLOPS actually decreased but more jobs can co-run. Optimize cap split based on job mix to maximize total system throughput.
details.realistic_solution: Implement heterogeneous power caps using GPU workload classification: (1) Profile each running job's compute vs. memory boundedness using `nvml.nvmlDeviceGetUtilizationRates()` — jobs with memory utilization > compute utilization are memory-bound and tolerate deeper power caps. (2) Assign deeper caps (300 W) to memory-bound inference pods and lighter caps (380 W) to compute-bound training pods. (3) Implement a power budget controller (runs every 10 s) that reads current power draw from NVML and adjusts per-GPU caps to maintain total ≤ 45 kW. (4) Use NVML `nvmlDeviceSetPowerManagementLimit()` per device. This enables all 128 GPUs while respecting budget.

scenario: A 128-GPU A100 cluster (400 W TDP each) is constrained to 45 kW total IT power by the datacenter PDU. At full load (128 × 400 W = 51.2 kW), it exceeds budget. Currently, only 112 GPUs are powered on, leaving 16 GPUs stranded. Design a dynamic power capping strategy that enables all 128 GPUs to be powered and maximizes aggregate training throughput within the 45 kW budget.
title: Optimization: Reducing Stranded Power Through Dynamic GPU Power Capping

details.common_mistake: Sizing PDUs to exactly 40 kW without accounting for power factor (PF < 1.0 for switching power supplies), N+1 redundancy requirements, and NEC 80% continuous load rule for branch circuits.
details.napkin_math: 64 MI300X nodes × 9 kW = 576 kW IT load. 16 racks × 37.2 kW/rack = 595.2 kW (includes networking). At PUE 1.25 (DLC): total facility = 595.2 × 1.25 = 744 kW. Transformer sizing: 744 kW / 0.95 PF = 783.2 kVA → specify 1 MVA transformer with 25% headroom for future expansion. MI300X aggregate: 64 nodes × 8 GPUs × 192 GB HBM3 = 98,304 GB total HBM capacity; 64 × 8 × 5.3 TB/s = 2.7 PB/s aggregate memory bandwidth.
details.realistic_solution: Specification: (1) Nodes per rack: 40 kW / 9 kW = 4.4 → 4 nodes/rack = 36 kW load, leaving 4 kW for networking (2 × 100GbE switches = 600 W each) and rack PDU losses (2%). (2) Power circuits: 4 nodes × 9 kW = 36 kW + 1.2 kW networking = 37.2 kW. NEC 80% rule: circuit capacity = 37.2 / 0.80 = 46.5 kW minimum. Use 3-phase 208V, 130A per PDU (3ph × 208V × 130A × 1.732 = 46.9 kVA). (3) Redundant PDUs: 2× PDU per rack (A+B feed), each sized to carry full 37.2 kW load (N+1 active-standby). (4) Upstream breaker: 150A 3-phase per PDU feed. (5) For 64 nodes: 16 racks × 2 feeds = 32 × 150A 3-phase circuits from primary switchgear.

scenario: You are specifying the rack power distribution architecture for a new 64-node MI300X cluster. Each MI300X node has 8 GPUs at peak 750 W/GPU (6 kW GPU TDP) plus 3 kW system overhead = 9 kW/node. The facility supports 40 kW per rack. Specify the rack layout, PDU configuration, power circuit requirements, and breaker sizing with N+1 redundancy.
title: Specification: Designing Rack Power Distribution for MI300X Dense Cluster

details.common_mistake: Assuming more data always improves calibration; ignoring that duplicates create implicit up-weighting of certain probability distributions.
details.napkin_math: 10TB at avg 4 bytes/token = 2.5T tokens. If 20% duplicates exist (500B tokens), those phrases appear 2x more often, shifting log-prob by ln(2) ≈ 0.69 nats, directly inflating confidence on memorized sequences.
details.realistic_solution: Run MinHash deduplication at 5-gram shingles; measure token frequency distribution before/after. Near-duplicates inflate P(token|context) for repeated phrases, causing overconfident predictions.

scenario: You are training a 70B LLM on an H100 cluster (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s). After three epochs the model achieves high accuracy but poor calibration (ECE > 0.15). Your data pipeline ingests 10TB of web-scraped text with no deduplication. Explain why near-duplicate data causes calibration failure and what the data statistics reveal.
title: Dataset Curation: Why Data Quality Degrades Model Calibration on H100

details.common_mistake: Running all filters sequentially in a single Python process; not parallelizing across the cluster.
details.napkin_math: 50TB / 4 bytes/token = 12.5T tokens. Language filter removes ~60% → 5T tokens. Heuristics remove ~30% → 3.5T tokens. Dedup removes ~25% → 2.6T tokens. Quality classifier keeps ~80% → 2.1T tokens ≈ ~8TB raw bytes before tokenization, yielding ~5TB tokenized.
details.realistic_solution: Stage 1: language ID (fastText, discard non-English) → Stage 2: heuristic filters (length, perplexity via small KenLM) → Stage 3: MinHash dedup → Stage 4: quality classifier (small BERT). Run stages 1-2 on CPUs in parallel, stages 3-4 on GPU workers.

scenario: You are building a data curation pipeline for a 13B LLM pre-training run on 128 H100s (80GB HBM3). You have 50TB of raw Common Crawl data. Design a multi-stage quality filtering system that outputs ~5TB of high-quality tokens within 48 hours of wall-clock time.
title: Dataset Curation: Design a Multi-Stage Quality Pipeline for LLM Pre-Training

details.common_mistake: Sending all 100M samples to human annotators, which is infeasible. Or fully automated labeling without human quality checks.
details.napkin_math: 10 annotators × 8 hr/day × 30 days = 2,400 person-hours. At 2 min/label = 72,000 labels from humans. So: GPT-4V labels 100M at $0.001/call = $100K total for 100M samples. Humans validate 72K samples as gold set. Train classifier on 1M GPT4V + 72K human labels, apply to 99M remaining.
details.realistic_solution: Use active learning: 1) GPT-4V labels 100% at ~$0.01/sample = $1M (too expensive). Better: label 1M with GPT-4V ($10K), train a small CLIP-based classifier on those, use it to label remaining 99M, humans review the 5% lowest confidence samples (5M × 10 min/sample / 10 annotators = 83K hours — too slow). Revise: humans review 0.5% = 500K samples.

scenario: Your team needs to label 100M image-text pairs for vision-language model training on an H100 cluster. You have a budget for 10 human annotators and access to GPT-4V for automated labeling. Design a labeling pipeline that achieves > 95% label accuracy within 30 days.
title: Dataset Curation: Design a Labeling Pipeline for Multi-Modal Training Data

details.common_mistake: Choosing A purely for speed without quantifying the quality difference in downstream benchmarks.
details.napkin_math: 20TB dataset, training run = 2 weeks = 336 hours. Dedup overhead: 18h vs 2h = 16h difference = 4.8% of total run time. Expected quality gain from near-dedup: 1-2% on benchmarks per published studies (LLM360, Dolma). Cost: 128 H100s × $3/hr × 16h = $6,144 one-time cost for potentially 2% better model.
details.realistic_solution: Exact URL dedup misses content-level duplicates (same article, different URLs). MinHash catches semantic near-duplicates. Train two small 1B proxy models, evaluate on MMLU and HellaSwag. The quality difference typically justifies the 16-hour overhead on a multi-week training run.

scenario: You compare two deduplication strategies for a 20TB pre-training dataset on an H100 cluster: (A) exact URL dedup only, (B) MinHash near-dedup at 0.8 Jaccard similarity threshold. Strategy A takes 2 hours, B takes 18 hours. Evaluate which is better for downstream model quality.
title: Dataset Curation: Evaluate Deduplication Strategies for Pre-Training Data Quality

details.common_mistake: Always using proportional mixing; not considering that rare high-value domains (math) get under-represented.
details.napkin_math: Total = 750K samples. Proportional: code=66.7%, general=26.7%, math=6.6%. T=2 scaling: sqrt(500K)=707, sqrt(200K)=447, sqrt(50K)=224, total=1378. Code=51.3%, general=32.4%, math=16.3%. Math training proportion increases 2.5x, improving GSM8K without major MMLU regression.
details.realistic_solution: Temperature-scaled sampling upsamples small high-quality domains. At T=2, effective weights = count^(1/2): code=707, general=447, math=224. Math goes from 6.6% to 18.3% of batches. Evaluate on HumanEval (coding) and GSM8K (math) plus MMLU (forgetting). Strategy B typically wins on specialized tasks.

scenario: You are fine-tuning a 7B model on H100s (80GB HBM3) for a coding assistant. You have 500K code examples, 200K general instruction examples, and 50K math examples. Compare two mixing strategies: (A) proportional mixing by count, (B) temperature-scaled sampling with T=2. Evaluate which yields better coding performance without catastrophic forgetting.
title: Dataset Curation: Evaluate Domain Mixing Ratios for Instruction Tuning

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that a mismatched tokenizer increases sequence length, inflating memory and compute costs.
details.napkin_math: English-only: 512 tokens/seq at fertility 1.3 = 394 words. With 20% non-English at fertility 4.0: effective fertility = 0.8×1.3 + 0.2×4.0 = 1.04 + 0.8 = 1.84. Same 512-token context now fits only 512/1.84 = 278 words. Sequence length budget effectively cuts 29%. Attention memory scales O(n²): (278/394)² = 0.498, so attention memory roughly halves — but you process fewer words per batch.
details.realistic_solution: English fertility ≈ 1.3 tokens/word. Non-English with English-only tokenizer ≈ 3-5 tokens/word (byte fallback). Measure actual fertility per language, then compute effective sequence length inflation.

scenario: You are preparing a multilingual dataset for a 30B model on H100 (80GB HBM3). Your 32K-vocab tokenizer was trained on English-only data. You add 20% non-English content (10 languages). Estimate tokenizer fertility (tokens per word) for the new data and its effect on effective sequence length and memory.
title: Dataset Curation: Napkin Math for Tokenizer Coverage on Multilingual Data

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to apply quality multipliers before normalizing; treating all domains as equal quality.
details.napkin_math: Effective weights: web=5000B, books=400B, code=100B, papers=30B. Total=5530B. Fractions: web=90.4%, books=7.2%, code=1.8%, papers=0.54%. Allocations out of 1.3T: web=1175B, books=94B, code=24B, papers=7B tokens. Books contributes 47B unique tokens sampled 2× each.
details.realistic_solution: Apply quality multiplier to books: effective weight = 200B × 2 = 400B. Total effective pool = 5T + 400B + 100B + 30B = 5.53T. Normalize to 1.3T target.

scenario: You are curating training data for a 65B model to be trained on 256 H100s. Chinchilla-optimal compute says train on ~1.3T tokens. You have web data (5T tokens), books (200B tokens), code (100B tokens), and papers (30B tokens). Compute the token budget for each domain assuming proportional mixing with a quality multiplier of 2× for books.
title: Dataset Curation: Napkin Math for Data Mixing Budget

details.common_mistake: Using a GPU-based neural LM scorer for all 1B documents — too slow. KenLM on CPU is 100× faster for this use case.
details.napkin_math: 1B documents / 6 hours = 166.7M docs/hour = 46,300 docs/second needed. 512 cores × 10K docs/core/sec = 5.12M docs/second. Way more than enough — could process in 1B / 5.12M = 195 seconds ≈ 3.3 minutes. Real bottleneck is I/O: 1B docs × 2KB avg = 2TB data. At 10GB/s network = 200 seconds read time. Total wall time dominated by I/O ≈ 10-20 minutes.
details.realistic_solution: KenLM 5-gram model at 125M parameters. Each CPU can score ~10K documents/second. Distribute across 16 nodes × 32 cores = 512 cores. Set quality threshold at perplexity < 200 (tuned on held-out human ratings). Flag and discard documents scoring > 500 perplexity.

scenario: You need to score 1B text documents for quality before LLM pre-training on H100s. Design and quantify a perplexity-based quality scorer using a small 125M KenLM model. The scorer must process the full 1B documents within 6 hours on a 16-node CPU cluster.
title: Dataset Curation: Implement a Data Quality Scoring Function

details.common_mistake: Under-investing in data quality vs model architecture; not versioning datasets; not monitoring data pipeline throughput vs training throughput.
details.napkin_math: 512 H100s at 35% MFU: 512 × 989 TFLOPS × 0.35 = 177,228.8 TFLOPS. 100B model, 6 FLOPs/token: tokens/sec = 177,228.8T / (6 × 100B) = 177,228.8T / 600B = 295,595 tokens/sec. Over 3 months = 90 days × 86,400s = 7.78M seconds × 295,595 tokens/s = 2.3T tokens. Data pipeline must sustain 295K tokens/sec = 1.18MB/s (at 4 bytes/token) — trivially achievable with NFS. Budget: 512 × $3/hr × 2,160hr = $3.32M compute.
details.realistic_solution: Source: 10T raw tokens (web 70%, code 15%, math 5%, books 7%, instructions 3%). Filter: language ID (keep 6 languages) → heuristic (65% pass) → KenLM perplexity < 300 (70% pass) → MinHash dedup (75% pass). Final: ~3.4T unique tokens. Chinchilla for 100B model: 2T tokens optimal. Mix with quality weighting: code/math 3×. Pipeline must sustain 512 H100s training at 35% MFU.

scenario: You are the ML lead responsible for data strategy for a 100B parameter LLM to be trained on 512 H100s (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) for 3 months. The model must excel at code, math, and instruction following. Design the complete data curation strategy: sourcing, quality filtering, deduplication, mixing, and versioning. Quantify every decision.
title: Dataset Curation: Mastery — End-to-End Pre-Training Data Strategy for 100B Model

details.common_mistake: Retraining from scratch without first auditing and correcting the dataset; assuming model architecture is the problem.
details.napkin_math: 500K pairs. Audit: 10 CPU hours for name classification. Found 60K pairs (12%) with non-Western names. Refusal rate in labels: 35% vs 8% for Western names → 4.4× disparity. Rebalancing: upsample non-Western pairs 3× to 180K, downsample Western from 440K to 320K. New total: 500K pairs, 36% non-Western. Expected bias reduction: from 40%/12% gap to ~18%/12% gap (3× reduction). Validate on 10K held-out pairs per demographic group.
details.realistic_solution: 1) Audit: name-based demographic proxy labeling on 500K pairs. 2) Measure refusal rate correlation with demographics in training labels. 3) Rebalance: oversample underrepresented preference pairs. 4) Retrain reward model. 5) Re-run RLHF. 6) Evaluate on held-out demographic-stratified test set.

scenario: Your 7B instruction-tuned model on H100 shows demographic bias: it declines 40% of requests from users with non-Western names versus 12% for Western names. You suspect labeling bias in 500K RLHF preference pairs. Walk through the full diagnosis, measurement, and correction pipeline with concrete numbers.
title: Dataset Curation: Mastery — Detect and Fix Systematic Labeling Bias

details.common_mistake: Collecting all user data without consent or privacy filtering; not having a quality gate; not measuring data freshness vs model staleness.
details.napkin_math: 50M queries/day × 20% opted-in = 10M/day. Quality filter keeps 60% = 6M/day. Dedup removes 30% = 4.2M/day. Human review: 1% = 42K/day × $0.10/review = $4,200/day = $29,400/week. Weekly dataset: 4.2M × 7 = 29.4M new examples. Fine-tuning: 7B model, 29.4M examples × 512 tokens = 15B tokens. At 512 H100s, 295K tokens/sec → 51,000 seconds ≈ 14 hours/week. Fits comfortably in weekend maintenance window.
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline: 1) Anonymize (k-anonymity, differential privacy ε=1.0) 2) Consent filter (keep opted-in users only, ~20%) 3) Quality gate: perplexity + length filters 4) Dedup vs existing corpus 5) Human review sample (1%) 6) Weekly fine-tuning run 7) A/B test before full rollout.

scenario: You are designing a data flywheel for a production LLM serving 10M users/day on H100 clusters. User interactions generate 50M queries/day. Design the pipeline that converts user signals into training data, ensuring quality, privacy, and freshness. The model should be updated weekly.
title: Dataset Curation: Mastery — Data Flywheel Architecture for Production LLM

details.common_mistake: Adding more DataLoader workers without diagnosing whether the bottleneck is CPU, I/O, or decompression.
details.napkin_math: Current: 180ms/batch → GPU utilization = 45ms/(45+180) = 20%. Wait: 45ms compute vs 180ms I/O. Fix local NVMe: 6.4 GB/s per node × 16 nodes = 102 GB/s. 4MB batch in 0.04ms. New batch time: 45ms compute + 0.04ms I/O ≈ 45ms. MFU recovers to ~44%. Speedup: (180+45)/45 = 5× faster wall time. Monthly savings: 256 H100s × $3/hr × 720hr × (1 - 28/44) = $314K.
details.realistic_solution: Bottleneck is NFS I/O: 256 GPUs × 1 batch/45ms = 5,689 batches/second. Each batch = 512 sequences × 2048 tokens × 4 bytes = 4MB. Bandwidth needed: 5,689 × 4MB = 22.7 GB/s. NFS likely capped at 10 GB/s. Fix: pre-tokenize and shard data to local NVMe SSDs per node, use memory-mapped files, prefetch 3 batches ahead.

scenario: Your 256 H100 training job is GPU-starved: GPUs run at 28% MFU instead of expected 45%. Profiling shows DataLoader workers are the bottleneck — each H100 waits 180ms per batch vs 45ms compute. Your dataset is 2TB stored on distributed NFS. Diagnose and fix.
title: Dataset Curation: Optimize Streaming Data Pipeline Throughput for H100 Training

details.common_mistake: Simply adding more nodes without understanding whether the bottleneck is compute, memory, or all-to-all communication in the Jaccard similarity computation.
details.napkin_math: 5TB / 4 bytes/token = 1.25T tokens. At 100 tokens/document avg = 12.5B documents. MinHash generation: 32 nodes × 32 cores × 100K docs/sec = 102.4M docs/sec. Time = 12.5B / 102.4M = 122 seconds. Bottleneck is LSH candidate pairs: with 20 bands, ~0.1% false positive rate → 12.5B × 0.001 = 12.5M pairs to compare. At 1M pairs/sec per node × 32 nodes = 32M pairs/sec → 0.4 seconds. Real bottleneck is shuffle/sort across nodes: 12.5B × 200 bytes/sig = 2.5TB shuffle. At 100Gbps network = 200 seconds. Optimize: pre-filter by domain (10 domains) → 10× less cross-domain shuffle → 20 seconds. Total < 24 hours achievable.
details.realistic_solution: Profile: MinHash signature generation is CPU-bound (parallelizable). LSH bucketing is memory-bound. Candidate pair comparison is the bottleneck: O(n²) worst case. Fix: use banding with b=20 bands, r=5 rows. Reduce false negative rate analysis. Shard by domain to avoid cross-shard comparison. Use Spark with hash partitioning.

scenario: Your MinHash deduplication pipeline takes 72 hours for 5T tokens on a 32-node CPU cluster. Training starts in 48 hours. Identify the bottleneck and propose an optimized pipeline that completes in under 24 hours without sacrificing dedup quality.
title: Dataset Curation: Optimize Deduplication Pipeline Scalability

details.common_mistake: Computing token count without accounting for filtering drop rates, or not verifying DataLoader can sustain GPU throughput.
details.napkin_math: 64 H100s at 40% MFU: 64 × 989T × 0.4 = 25,318 TFLOPS. 30B model: 6 FLOPs/token. Token throughput = 25,318T / (6 × 30B) = 25,318T / 180B = 140,656 tokens/sec. Data rate = 140,656 × 4 bytes = 563KB/s. Trivially achievable even from NFS. But if using 2048 context, batches = 140,656 / 2048 = 68.7 sequences/sec. Each batch (BS=64): 64 × 2048 × 4 = 524KB → needed every 64/68.7 = 0.93 seconds. DataLoader needs to deliver one 524KB batch per second — easily done with 4 prefetch workers.
details.realistic_solution: Chinchilla: 20 tokens/param for optimal compute. 30B × 20 = 600B tokens needed. Apply filtering: typically 60% of raw data passes. Need 1T raw tokens = ~4TB raw text. Storage: 600B tokens × 4 bytes = 2.4TB tokenized. DataLoader must sustain GPU training throughput.

scenario: You are planning data curation for a Chinchilla-optimal 30B parameter model to be trained on 64 H100s (80GB HBM3). Realize the complete data requirements: token count, raw data volume, filtering pipeline output, storage I/O specs, and DataLoader throughput needed to keep GPUs fed.
title: Dataset Curation: Realize Token Budget for Chinchilla-Optimal 30B Training

details.common_mistake: Storing raw JPEGs and decoding on-the-fly without pre-resizing; not accounting for decoder CPU overhead eating into DataLoader capacity.
details.napkin_math: 1B images × 200KB = 200TB raw. Pre-process to 224×224×3 uint8 = 150KB/image. 1B × 150KB = 150TB processed. WebDataset: 10K samples/shard = 1.5GB/shard → 100K shards. Training throughput: 128 H100s, batch=512, time/batch=0.5sec → 1024 samples/sec. Data rate: 1024 × (150KB + 500B) = 153MB/sec. Need distributed storage delivering 153MB/s read. S3/GCS can do this easily. DataLoader: 16 workers × 8 node = 128 workers decoding 1024 samples/sec = 8 samples/worker/sec. CPU decode at 50 img/sec/core → 0.16 cores/worker needed. Very manageable.
details.realistic_solution: Pre-process: resize images to 224×224, store as uint8 tensors in WebDataset tar shards. Each shard = 10K samples. Pre-compute image features if using frozen vision encoder. Use DALI for GPU-accelerated decoding if needed.

scenario: You are building the data infrastructure for training a 20B vision-language model on 128 H100s. The dataset contains 1B image-text pairs: images average 200KB (JPEG), text average 500 bytes. Realize the storage architecture, indexing strategy, and DataLoader design to sustain training throughput.
title: Dataset Curation: Realize Multi-Modal Dataset Storage and Access Architecture

details.common_mistake: Confusing model perplexity (eval metric) with document perplexity used for quality filtering; not knowing that a small reference LM is used, not the model being trained.
details.napkin_math: KenLM scoring: ~10K docs/sec/CPU core. For 1B documents on 512 cores: 1B / (512 × 10K) = 195 seconds ≈ 3.3 minutes total scoring time. Common CCNet setup uses perplexity buckets: head (< 100), middle (100-1000), tail (> 1000) — only head + middle buckets used for training.
details.realistic_solution: A small N-gram LM (e.g., KenLM 5-gram) or small neural LM scores each document. Low perplexity = document resembles training distribution of the reference LM. Thresholds: perplexity < 100-300 = high quality; > 1000 = noise/gibberish.

scenario: In the context of LLM pre-training data curation on H100 clusters, what is perplexity-based filtering, and what threshold range is commonly used to classify low-quality versus high-quality documents?
title: Dataset Curation: Recall — What is Perplexity-Based Data Filtering?

details.common_mistake: Writing qualitative SLAs ('data must be high quality') without measurable thresholds and automated enforcement.
details.napkin_math: 100M docs/week = 14.3M docs/day = 165 docs/sec. Pipeline must sustain: language detection 165 docs/sec (trivial), perplexity scoring 165 docs/sec (need 0.017 CPU cores at 10K docs/sec/core), dedup requires accumulating 100M/week batch → weekly dedup run in < 4 hours: 100M / (512 cores × 10K/sec) = 19.5 seconds compute time, I/O dominated. Storage: 100M × 2KB = 200GB/week = 10.4TB/year. Weekly dedup batch processing budget: 4 hours compute.
details.realistic_solution: Define: (1) Perplexity SLA: P95 doc perplexity < 500 using 125M KenLM reference. (2) Dedup SLA: < 2% near-duplicate rate (MinHash 0.8 Jaccard). (3) Freshness SLA: data ingested within 24h of production. (4) Throughput SLA: pipeline must sustain 16.7M docs/day. (5) PII SLA: < 0.01% docs contain email/SSN patterns.

scenario: You are writing the data quality specification for a continuous pre-training system on 256 H100s that ingests 100M new documents per week from production traffic. Define quantitative SLAs for data quality, freshness, deduplication, and pipeline throughput that must be enforced before any data reaches the training job.
title: Dataset Curation: Specification — Design a Data Quality SLA for Continuous Pre-Training

details.common_mistake: Checkpointing too frequently (wasting GPU time) or too infrequently (losing hours of work on failure). Not accounting for the 512-node MTBF vs single-node MTBF.
details.napkin_math: MTBF_single = 200 days = 288,000 minutes. MTBF_cluster = 288,000 / 512 = 562.5 minutes = 9.375 hours. Checkpoint write time t_ckpt = 8 minutes. C_opt = sqrt(2 × 8 × 562.5) = sqrt(9,000) = 94.9 minutes ≈ 95 minutes. So checkpoint every ~95 minutes. Expected wasted time per failure: C_opt/2 + t_ckpt = 47.5 + 8 = 55.5 minutes. Failure rate: 1/562.5 = 0.00178/minute. Expected wasted time/minute = 55.5/562.5 = 9.9% overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Optimal checkpoint interval minimizes E[wasted time] = C/2 + C²/(2×MTBF_cluster), where C = checkpoint interval, MTBF_cluster = MTBF_single / num_GPUs. Solve for C_opt = sqrt(2 × t_ckpt × MTBF_cluster) where t_ckpt = checkpoint write time.

scenario: You are training a 70B model on 512 H100s (80GB HBM3, 700W). The mean time between failures (MTBF) for a single H100 is 200 days. A checkpoint takes 8 minutes (writing 280GB model state to shared storage). Analyze the optimal checkpoint interval to minimize expected training time lost to failures.
title: Fault Tolerance: Analyze Checkpoint Frequency vs Recovery Cost on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Blocking all GPUs during checkpoint write — 700GB / 200 GB/s = 3.5 seconds minimum write, but in practice 30-60 seconds with Lustre contention from 1024 nodes writing simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: 700GB checkpoint. Naive: 700GB / 200 GB/s = 3.5 seconds write, but 1024 nodes × metadata ops creates contention → actual 45-90 seconds. Sharded async: each node snapshots 683MB to CPU RAM in 683MB / (NVLink 900 GB/s) ≈ 0.76ms (GPU→CPU PCIe 32 GB/s) = 21ms. Training continues. Each node writes 683MB to Lustre: 683MB / (200GB/1024 nodes = 195MB/s) = 3.5 seconds per node. Total pause: 21ms for snapshot. Background write: 3.5 seconds (overlapped with training). Effective overhead: 21ms checkpoint pause every 95 minutes = 0.037% time overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Use asynchronous sharded checkpointing: each node writes its own shard in parallel. 1024 nodes write 700GB / 1024 = 683MB each. Pipeline: snapshot model state to CPU memory (fast), continue training, async write to Lustre in background.

scenario: You are designing checkpointing for a 175B model training on 1,024 H100s (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s). The full checkpoint is 700GB. Your shared Lustre filesystem peaks at 200 GB/s write throughput. Design a checkpoint strategy that minimizes training interruption while maintaining full recovery capability.
title: Fault Tolerance: Design Checkpointing Architecture for 1024-GPU Training

details.common_mistake: Choosing incremental without considering that a broken delta chain requires full recovery from last full checkpoint — losing potentially hours of work.
details.napkin_math: (A) Full only: 2 weeks = 20,160 minutes. Checkpoints: 20,160/30 = 672 full checkpoints × 120GB = 80.6TB storage at $0.023/GB-month = $1,854/month. Overhead: 60s/30min = 3.3% training time. (B) Incremental only: 20,160/10 = 2,016 checkpoints × 2GB = 4TB storage = $92/month. Overhead: 4s/10min = 0.67% training time. Recovery risk: delta chain failure (realistic 2% chain corruption rate) → full retrain from last good point. (C) Hybrid: 1 full/day × 14 = 14 full × 120GB = 1.68TB + 2,016 deltas × 2GB = 4TB. Total: 5.68TB = $131/month. Recovery: max 144 deltas to replay. Overhead: 0.67% + 60s/24h = 0.67% + 0.069% = 0.74%. Winner: Hybrid (C).
details.realistic_solution: Hybrid: full checkpoint daily + incremental every 10 minutes. Recovery: latest full + replay incremental deltas. Delta chain length: 24h / 10min = 144 deltas max. If any delta is corrupted, roll back to last full checkpoint.

scenario: For a 30B model training on 256 H100s, compare (A) full checkpoint every 30 minutes (120GB per checkpoint, 60 second write) vs (B) incremental checkpoint every 10 minutes using optimizer state delta (2GB per checkpoint, 4 second write). The training run lasts 2 weeks. Evaluate storage cost, recovery completeness, and overhead.
title: Fault Tolerance: Evaluate Full vs Incremental Checkpointing for LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Using strategy (B) — gather to rank 0 — which serializes 280GB through rank 0's 80GB HBM, requiring offloading and creating a massive bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, ZeRO-3 across 256 GPUs. Per-rank shard: 280GB / 256 = 1.094GB. Strategy A: each rank writes 1.094GB in parallel. At 2 GB/s NVMe per node: 0.55 seconds. All 256 nodes write simultaneously → total 0.55 seconds. Strategy B: rank 0 collects 280GB. Across NVLink (900 GB/s): 280GB / 900 GB/s = 0.31 seconds collection. Rank 0 then writes 280GB: at 2 GB/s = 140 seconds. All other 255 ranks idle. Lost time: 255 × 140 seconds = 35,700 GPU-seconds. At $3/GPU-hr = $3/3600 × 35,700 = $29.75 per checkpoint. 672 checkpoints in 2-week run = $20K waste. Strategy A wins decisively.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy (A) distributed checkpoint is always correct for ZeRO-3. Each rank saves its shard. Recovery: all ranks restore their own shards. Partial failure: if 1 node fails and its shard is lost, must restore from previous checkpoint.

scenario: Your 70B model training uses ZeRO-3 across 256 H100s, sharding optimizer state, gradients, and parameters. Compare checkpointing strategies: (A) each node saves its ZeRO shard (distributed checkpoint), vs (B) rank 0 gathers full model and saves. Evaluate time, storage, and recovery complexity.
title: Fault Tolerance: Evaluate ZeRO vs Full Replica Checkpointing

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that ZeRO-2 shards optimizer state but NOT model parameters — all ranks store full bf16 parameters. Not accounting for fp32 master weights in the checkpoint.
details.napkin_math: Parameters (bf16, full replica): 13B × 2B = 26GB per rank. Optimizer state (fp32, ZeRO-2 sharded across 64 ranks): fp32 weights 13B×4B/64 = 813MB. fp32 momentum: 813MB. fp32 variance: 813MB. Total optimizer/rank: 2.44GB. Gradient buffer (bf16, sharded): 13B×2B/64 = 406MB. Misc (scheduler, step, RNG state): ~10MB. Total per rank: 26 + 2.44 + 0.406 + 0.01 = 28.86GB. Within 100GB NVMe budget. Total checkpoint: 64 ranks × (2.44 + 0.406) = 182GB optimizer/grad + 26GB params (de-dup) = 208GB total. Alternative: store params once from rank 0 + per-rank optimizer = 26 + 182 = 208GB. Lustre write at 200 GB/s: 208GB / 200 = 1.04 seconds (parallel write).
details.realistic_solution: ZeRO-2: parameters bf16 = 13B × 2B = 26GB (replicated on all ranks). Optimizer state (sharded): fp32 params + fp32 momentum + fp32 variance = 3 × 13B × 4B / 64 ranks = 2.44GB/rank. Full checkpoint/rank = 26GB + 2.44GB + gradient buffer (bf16, sharded) = 29.06GB.

scenario: You are implementing checkpointing for a 13B parameter model trained with ZeRO-2 on 64 H100s (80GB HBM3). The model uses bf16 parameters and fp32 master weights, AdamW optimizer. Calculate the exact checkpoint size per rank and total, and verify it fits within your 100GB per-node NVMe budget.
title: Fault Tolerance: Implement Checkpoint Size Calculation for Mixed-Precision Training

details.common_mistake: Treating fault tolerance as only a checkpointing problem; not designing automatic recovery and spare GPU provisioning.
details.napkin_math: 2,048 GPUs. MTBF per GPU: 150 days. Expected failures in 90 days: 2,048 × (90/150) = 1,229 GPU failures. With proactive replacement catching 70%: 369 surprise failures. Without spares: each failure halts training for recovery. Recovery time: checkpoint restore (checkpoint size: 500B × 4B/4 [ZeRO-3 shard] = 500GB total, each of 2048 nodes writes 244MB → 0.12 seconds), rejoin collective ops: 5 minutes. 369 × 5min = 1,845 minutes = 1.28 days lost. With 64 hot spares: failed node → hot spare preloaded with model shard → 2 minutes. 369 × 2min = 738 minutes = 0.51 days. Uptime: (90 days - 0.51 days) / 90 = 99.4% > 95% target. Spare cost: 64 × $3/hr × 2,160hr = $414,720 for 3 months.
details.realistic_solution: Full FT architecture: (1) Async sharded checkpoint every 60 min. (2) Health monitoring: heartbeat every 30s, GPU telemetry (temp, ECC errors as precursor). (3) Hot standby: 64 spare GPUs (3% reserve). (4) Automatic replacement: failed node → spare → rejoin from checkpoint in < 15 min. (5) Proactive replacement: ECC error rate > threshold → swap before failure.

scenario: You are responsible for reliability engineering for a 3-month training run of a 500B parameter model on 2,048 H100s (80GB HBM3, 700W). Expected GPU failure rate: 1 per 150 days. Design the complete fault tolerance architecture: checkpointing, failure detection, recovery automation, and spare capacity management. The run must complete with > 95% uptime.
title: Fault Tolerance: Mastery — Design Full Fault Tolerance Architecture for 1000-GPU Training

details.common_mistake: Blaming network bandwidth without profiling whether the bottleneck is metadata ops, stripe misconfiguration, or node-level I/O serialization.
details.napkin_math: Observed: 15 GB/s out of 200 GB/s = 7.5% efficiency. 256 nodes writing 140GB/256 = 547MB each. If stripe count = 1: all 256 nodes write to same OSS. One OSS: 200GB/256 nodes = 781MB/s → 547MB / 781MB/s = 0.70 seconds/checkpoint — but actual 9.3 seconds due to serialization. Fix: stripe count = 32 OSSs (lfs setstripe -c 32). Each OSS serves 256/32 = 8 nodes. 8 × 781MB/s = 6.25 GB/s per OSS × 32 = 200 GB/s aggregate. Expected: 140GB / 200GB/s = 0.7 seconds. With 64MB stripe size: 547MB / 64MB = 8.5 large I/O ops per node → minimal lock contention. Realistic: 120 GB/s = 1.17 seconds. Speedup: 9.3/1.17 = 7.9×.
details.realistic_solution: Common Lustre bottlenecks: (1) Default stripe count = 1 (single OSS) → fix: stripe across all OSSs. (2) All ranks writing at the same time with lock contention on MDT. (3) Small I/O requests (4KB vs optimal 64MB). Profile with lfs and iostat.

scenario: Your 256 H100 training job writes checkpoints to a Lustre filesystem at only 15 GB/s (measured) vs the theoretic 200 GB/s peak. Each checkpoint is 140GB and takes 9.3 seconds. Diagnose the Lustre bottleneck and optimize to achieve at least 60% of peak throughput (120 GB/s).
title: Fault Tolerance: Optimize Checkpoint Write Throughput on Lustre Filesystem

details.common_mistake: Setting RTO and RPO without accounting for the cost of lost compute time; not quantifying the acceptable loss in training tokens.
details.napkin_math: Training throughput: 512 H100s × 40% MFU × 989 TFLOPS / (6 × 100B FLOPs/token) = 337K tokens/sec. 1 hour = 3600 × 337K = 1.21B tokens. 1.21B tokens = 0.06% of 2T total training — acceptable RPO. Checkpoint size: 100B model ZeRO-3/512: 400GB total / 512 = 781MB/rank. Write time: 781MB at 2 GB/s NVMe = 0.39 seconds/rank (parallel). Total checkpoint overhead: 0.39s / 45min = 0.014% — negligible. Storage: checkpoints retained 3 generations × 400GB = 1.2TB + daily full = 14 × 400GB = 5.6TB. Total: 6.8TB × $0.023/GB-month × 3 months = $470. RTO: restore 781MB from NVMe (0.39s) + rejoin collective (5min) + warmup (5min) = 11 minutes << 30 minute SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Cost model: 512 × $3 × 90 × 24 = $3.32M compute. RTO target: < 30 minutes recovery after failure (< 1% of daily compute time). RPO target: < 1 hour of work lost (< 1% of daily training). Checkpoint: every 45 minutes.

scenario: Write the fault tolerance specification for a $5M, 90-day training run of a 100B model on 512 H100s. Define RTO (Recovery Time Objective), RPO (Recovery Point Objective), checkpoint frequency, storage requirements, and automated recovery SLAs. The run costs $3/GPU-hr.
title: Fault Tolerance: Specification — Define Recovery Time Objective for LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Using a feature store that adds 20-50ms retrieval latency (e.g., DynamoDB without caching) for a system requiring < 5ms. Not co-locating feature store with serving infrastructure.
details.napkin_math: H100 SXM5: 700W TDP. At $0.10/kWh: $0.10 × 0.7kW = $0.07/hr electricity per GPU. For 256 H100s: $0.07 × 256 = $17.92/hr electricity. Cloud instance cost (H100 × 8 per node): ~$32/hr per 8-GPU node × 32 nodes = $1,024/hr. Power cost as fraction: $17.92/$1,024 = 1.75% of compute cost. Single H100 power: 700W at $0.10/kWh = $0.07/hr = $0.396/hr at PUE 1.3 × 4.37 factor... correction: $0.10/kWh × 0.7kW × 1.3 PUE = $0.091/hr ≈ $0.09/hr per GPU (not $396/hr).
details.realistic_solution: GPU power costs are a small fraction of cloud compute costs. At $0.10/kWh and 700W per H100, electricity is ~$0.07/hr per GPU, far below the $2–4/hr cloud rental price.

scenario: You are designing a feature store for a recommendation LLM serving 100K requests/second on H100s (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s). Each request requires 500 pre-computed user features (retrieval latency SLA: < 5ms p99). Design the feature store architecture: storage tier, caching, serialization format, and compute placement.
title: Feature Store: Design a Low-Latency Feature Store for Real-Time LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Blaming the model or retraining before diagnosing the data pipeline; not checking feature distributions before vs after migration.
details.napkin_math: CTR drop: 8.2% → 6.1% = 25.6% relative degradation. Feature importance: if user_30day_purchase_history explains 25% of CTR lift (common for collaborative features), nulling it explains the drop. Diagnosis: compute feature_i variance across 1K requests. Expected variance for purchase_history: σ² ≈ 0.15 (30-day window). Observed: σ² = 0. Root cause: feature computation job failed silently, serving all-zero vectors. Fix: add feature validation in pipeline: assert variance > 0.01 for each non-sparse feature. Alert if variance drops > 90% from baseline. Recovery: restore old feature computation job → features normalize in < 1 hour → CTR recovers within 2 hours (as real-time features update). Cost of outage: 1 week × 100K RPS × (8.2%-6.1%)/100% × $0.01/click = 7 × 86400 × 100K × 0.021 × $0.01 = $12.7M estimated revenue impact.
details.realistic_solution: Zero variance on a feature = all values are the same (likely default/null). This means the feature pipeline broke during migration and is serving stale or null values. The model learned to rely on this feature; with it nulled out, predictions default to global average, causing accuracy drop.

scenario: Your recommendation model on H100s starts degrading (CTR drops from 8.2% to 6.1%) one week after a feature store migration. The model and weights are unchanged. Diagnose the root cause. You observe that 'user_30day_purchase_history' features show 0 variance in the new store.
title: Feature Store: Diagnose Feature Staleness Causing Model Accuracy Degradation

details.common_mistake: Building separate stores without a synchronization mechanism → training-serving skew where the feature computation logic differs between systems.
details.napkin_math: Revenue at $0.001/1K tokens, 1M token/s throughput: $0.001/1K × 1M tokens/s × 3600s/hr = $3,600/hr = $86,400/day. Infrastructure: 256 H100s × $3/hr = $768/hr = $18,432/day. Gross profit: $86,400 - $18,432 = $67,968/day ≈ $1.728M/day. Annual: $630.7M. (Not $20K/day which would imply $8.3/hr revenue vs $768/hr cost — below breakeven.)
details.realistic_solution: At $0.001/1K tokens with 1M tokens/s throughput, hourly revenue is $3,600. Infrastructure cost for 256 H100s at $3/hr is $768/hr. This yields strong positive margins at scale.

scenario: You are choosing between (A) unified online/offline feature store (Feast with Redis + Parquet) vs (B) separate online store (Redis) and offline store (Hive). Your H100 training jobs run batch feature computation nightly, and inference on H100s requires real-time features. Evaluate consistency, latency, and operational complexity.
title: Feature Store: Evaluate Online vs Offline Feature Store Architectures

details.common_mistake: Using latest-value joins and being surprised when model performs well in training but poorly in production — classic data leakage from future feature values.
details.napkin_math: Training dataset: 10M labeled fraud events over 2 years. Without PIT: join current user_credit_score (computed today) to events from 2 years ago. Users who committed fraud may have different credit scores today vs at fraud time. Leakage magnitude: credit score at fraud time vs today can differ by 50-100 points. Expected AUC inflation: 5-15% (from PIT-naive to PIT-correct). Production AUC drop: model achieves 0.94 AUC in training (leaky), 0.79 AUC in production. Cost: 10M events × 500 features × 4B = 20GB feature history. PIT join: for each event, binary search in feature history by timestamp → O(n log m) where m = history entries. At 10 events/user, 10M users: 100M binary searches in 20GB = ~10 seconds on Spark. Worth it: eliminates 15% AUC inflation.
details.realistic_solution: Without PIT-correctness: model sees features computed after the label timestamp (e.g., account balance after fraud occurred). Model learns from future information → inflated training AUC → production degradation. PIT-join: for each label timestamp T, use feature values as of T-ε (just before event).

scenario: Your training dataset for an H100-based fraud detection model uses user features from a feature store. Without point-in-time correctness, you join the latest feature values to historical labels. Compare: (A) latest-value join vs (B) point-in-time correct join. Evaluate data leakage risk and implementation complexity.
title: Feature Store: Evaluate Point-in-Time Correct Feature Joins for Training Data

details.common_mistake: Forgetting Redis overhead (hash maps have ~100% overhead vs raw bytes); not accounting for key string overhead.
details.napkin_math: User features: 10M users × 200 × 4B = 8GB raw. With 3× Redis overhead: 24GB. Item features: 5M items × 100 × 4B = 2GB raw × 3 = 6GB. Total Redis: 30GB. At 50K RPS, each request fetches: 1 user + 1 item = 2 Redis GET ops. 50K × 2 = 100K ops/sec. Redis can handle 1M ops/sec → fine. Network: 50K × (200+100) × 4B = 60MB/sec from Redis to H100 servers. At 100Gbps NIC = 12.5 GB/s >> 60 MB/s. Trivial. Redis nodes: 30GB / 32GB Redis node = 1 node (plus replica). Redis GET latency: 0.1ms within datacenter. Feature retrieval: 2 GETs × 0.1ms = 0.2ms. Well within 5ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Redis hash storage overhead: raw data plus key, hash table overhead, allocator fragmentation ≈ 2-4× raw byte size for small hashes. Plan for 3× overhead.

scenario: Your recommendation system on H100 serves 50K requests/second. Each request needs user features (200 float32 features) and item features (100 float32 features). Features are stored in Redis. Estimate Redis memory requirement for 10M active users and 5M catalog items, and verify the network bandwidth needed.
title: Feature Store: Fluency — Feature Vector Size and Retrieval Latency Estimation

details.common_mistake: Storing all feature types in one store without considering their different staleness requirements; not using different serialization formats for different feature sizes.
details.napkin_math: 200K RPS. Per request: 6KB + 0.2KB + 4KB = 10.2KB. Total feature bandwidth: 200K × 10.2KB = 2.04 GB/s from feature store. Session context (200B, real-time): compute inline per server, zero retrieval cost. Text embeddings (6KB, 100M users × daily): 100M × 6KB = 600GB. Too large for Redis. Use L2 SSD-backed store (Aerospike): 600GB at SSD throughput. L1 in-process cache (hot 1M users): 1M × 6KB = 6GB per H100 server. 200K RPS × 80% L1 hit = 160K/sec from L1 (0.01ms), 40K/sec from Aerospike SSD (1ms). P99: 1ms. Image embeddings (4KB, 50M items): 50M × 4KB = 200GB. L2 SSD. P99 retrieval: 1ms SSD. Total P99: max(session 0ms, text 1ms, image 1ms) = 1ms << 3ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Layered by staleness and size: text embeddings (updated daily, large, L2 cache) → session context (real-time, small, L1 per-server) → image embeddings (updated weekly, large, L2/L3). Different retrieval paths for different feature types.

scenario: You are designing a feature store for a multi-modal LLM serving system on 256 H100s handling 200K requests/second. Features include: user text embeddings (1536-dim float32 = 6KB), real-time session context (50 float32 = 200B), and image embeddings (2048-dim float16 = 4KB). P99 feature retrieval must be < 3ms. Design the complete feature store architecture.
title: Feature Store: Mastery — Design Feature Store for Multi-Modal Real-Time LLM

details.common_mistake: Parallelizing all features equally; not identifying that the 5 expensive features are the bottleneck and targeting those specifically.
details.napkin_math: Current: 6 hours for 500 features × 100M users. 70% on 5 features = 4.2 hours. Remaining 495 features = 1.8 hours. Strategy: (1) 5 expensive features: incremental delta (only compute for users with events today = 20M users = 20%). Time: 4.2h × 20% = 0.84 hours. (2) 495 simple features: unchanged = 1.8 hours. Total: max(0.84, 1.8) if parallelized = 1.8 hours < 2-hour deadline. Savings: 6h → 1.8h = 3.3× speedup. GPU utilization: 32 H100s. Simple features: data-parallel across users. Each H100 handles 100M/32 = 3.125M users. Feature computation: SQL-style aggregations on GPU using cuDF. H100 at 3.35 TB/s: scan 10TB raw data in 10TB/3.35TB/s = 2.99 seconds per H100 over network. I/O bound, not compute bound. Optimize: partition raw logs by user_id, each H100 reads its partition from object storage in parallel.
details.realistic_solution: Incremental computation: the 5 expensive features (e.g., 90-day rolling aggregations) change slowly. Compute full refresh weekly, daily delta updates only. Simple features (last 24h) remain daily full computation.

scenario: Your nightly batch feature computation on 32 H100s takes 6 hours but must complete in 2 hours to feed the morning training job. The pipeline computes 500 features for 100M users from raw event logs (10TB/day). Profiling shows 70% of time is spent on 5 expensive aggregation features. Optimize to meet the 2-hour deadline.
title: Feature Store: Optimize Feature Computation Pipeline for H100 Training Throughput

details.common_mistake: Building one monolithic feature store for all use cases; not accounting for different latency, freshness, and access pattern requirements across model families.
details.napkin_math: Common features (50 universal, 500M users): 500M × 50 × 4B = 100GB. Redis cluster: 300GB (3× overhead). Per-model features (150 features each, 10 models): 500M × 150 × 4B × 10 models = 300GB raw each model = 3TB total raw. Optimize: only store features for active users (last 30 days = 100M active): 100M × 150 × 4B × 10 = 600GB. With 3× Redis = 1.8TB. Redis cluster: 50 × 64GB nodes = 3.2TB capacity. Catalog items: 1M × (2000/10 per model avg features × 4B) = 800MB per model = 8GB total. Redis: 24GB for catalog. Total Redis: 3.2TB for users + 24GB catalog. At $3/hr per 64GB node: 50 nodes × $3 = $150/hr = $108K/month. Feature read bandwidth: 500K RPS × (50 common + 150 model) × 4B = 500K × 800B = 400 MB/s. 100Gbps NIC handles 12.5 GB/s >> 400 MB/s.
details.realistic_solution: Federated feature store per model family with shared infrastructure for common features. Common user features (demographics, device type) in shared Redis. Model-specific features in per-model stores.

scenario: Realize the complete feature store infrastructure for a production ML platform serving 10 model families (recommendation, fraud, ranking, NLP, etc.) on H100s. Combined: 500M users, 200 features per user per model family (2,000 total features), 1M catalog items. Serve 500K requests/second total. Specify every infrastructure component.
title: Feature Store: Realize Feature Store Sizing for Production ML Platform

details.common_mistake: Setting the same freshness SLA for all features regardless of how quickly they change; not accounting for pipeline latency adding to staleness.
details.napkin_math: Tier 1 (real-time, last 5 min): features like 'transactions_last_5_min', 'amount_last_5_min'. Max staleness: 30 seconds. Implementation: stream processing (Flink/Kafka) → Redis with 30s TTL. Computation latency: < 10 seconds. Features: 20 features. Tier 2 (near-real-time, 1 hour): 'ip_velocity_1h', 'merchant_fraud_rate_1h'. Max staleness: 5 minutes. Implementation: micro-batch (5-minute Spark) → Redis. Features: 50 features. Tier 3 (batch, 24h): 'user_30day_avg_spend', 'device_risk_score'. Max staleness: 2 hours. Implementation: nightly Spark → Redis (refreshed in 2h after midnight run). Features: 130 features. Monitoring SLAs: alert if Tier 1 staleness > 60s (2× SLA), Tier 2 > 10min, Tier 3 > 4h. Check: compute feature_max_age = max(now - feature_computed_at) across 1K sampled requests per minute. Total features: 200. Cost: Flink for Tier 1 (real-time) adds $50K/month infra cost vs all-batch = budget for high-impact features only.
details.realistic_solution: Freshness SLA = max allowed age of feature value at serving time. This includes computation lag + storage propagation + cache TTL. Each tier has different requirements and costs.

scenario: Write the feature freshness specification for a fraud detection system on H100s serving 50K transactions/second. Different features have different freshness requirements: real-time (last 5 min), near-real-time (last 1 hour), and batch (last 24 hours). Define quantitative SLAs for each tier, pipeline latency budgets, and monitoring requirements.
title: Feature Store: Specification — Define Feature Freshness SLA for Real-Time Fraud Detection

details.common_mistake: Describing fusion as purely a compute optimization; missing that the primary benefit for elementwise ops is reducing HBM round trips, not FLOPs.
details.napkin_math: Unfused: N elementwise ops on tensor T (size S bytes). Each op: read S + write S = 2S bytes. Total: N × 2S bytes HBM. Fused: read S + write S = 2S bytes total regardless of N. Savings: (N-1) × 2S bytes. For N=5 ops (LayerNorm+bias+GELU+dropout+residual), S=1GB: unfused = 10GB HBM traffic. Fused = 2GB. 5× reduction. At H100 3.35 TB/s: unfused = 10GB/3.35TB/s = 3ms. Fused = 0.6ms. 2.4ms saved per layer. 32-layer LLM: 32 × 2.4ms = 76.8ms latency reduction per forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Operator fusion: combine multiple kernels (e.g., LayerNorm + GELU + dropout) into one kernel. Each kernel normally reads tensor from HBM, computes, writes back. Fused kernel: reads once, applies all ops in registers/L2, writes once. Primary benefit: reduce HBM bandwidth, not compute.

scenario: In the context of H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) LLM inference, what is operator (kernel) fusion, what is the key memory bottleneck it addresses, and what is the memory bandwidth savings formula for a fused vs unfused elementwise sequence?
title: Kernel Fusion: Recall — What is Operator Fusion and Why Does It Matter?

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the O(n²) attention matrix memory: for seq_len=4096, the full attention matrix is 4096² × 64 heads × 2B = 2GB — doesn't fit in 512KB SRAM. Tiling is mandatory.
details.napkin_math: Attention Q,K,V projections for GPT-4 class (seq=1K, hidden=12288, heads=96, head_dim=128): Q matrix: seq × hidden = 1024 × 12288 × 2B = 25.2MB. K,V per layer: same. GQA with 8 KV heads: K,V = 1024 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 2MB each. Full Q: 1024 × 96 × 128 × 2B = 25.2MB. Standard MHA Q,K,V at seq=1K: 1024 × 12288 × 2B = 25.2MB each (using full hidden dim projection). For head_dim=128 × 32 heads: Q,K,V = 1024 × 32 × 128 × 2B = 8MB each (not 128MB — 128MB would require head_dim×heads = 64K which is unrealistic).
details.realistic_solution: Q,K,V tensor sizes depend on sequence length, number of heads, and head dimension. For typical LLM configurations, Q,K,V are in the MB range per layer per batch element.

scenario: You are designing a custom fused attention kernel for H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS BF16). The attention layer for a 70B model processes sequences of length 4096 with 64 heads and head dimension 128. Design the FlashAttention-style tiled computation to fit in SRAM and quantify the memory bandwidth savings.
title: Kernel Fusion: Design a Fused Attention Kernel for H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming FlashAttention is faster at all sequence lengths — at very short sequences (< 512), the tiling overhead may reduce gains. Flash attention primarily helps at longer sequences.
details.napkin_math: Q,K,V at Seq=1K: 1024 × 32 heads × 128 head_dim × 2B = 1024 × 4096 × 2B = 8MB each (not 48MB). Attention scores: 1024 × 32 × 1024 × 2B = 67MB. Context expansion 8K: Q,K,V = 8192 × 4096 × 2B = 67MB each. Attention scores: 8192² × 32 × 2B = 4.3GB — the memory wall.
details.realistic_solution: Q,K,V activation memory at seq=1K is 8MB each for standard 32-head, 128-dim configurations. The real memory problem is the O(seq²) attention score matrix at long contexts.

scenario: Compare FlashAttention-2 vs standard unfused attention on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS BF16) for a 7B LLM with 32 heads, head dim 128, sequence lengths 1K, 4K, and 16K. Evaluate memory usage, throughput, and latency for each configuration.
title: Kernel Fusion: Evaluate Flash Attention vs Standard Attention on H100

details.common_mistake: Not checking if the operation is compute-bound or memory-bound before claiming fusion helps — if compute-bound, fusion has minimal benefit.
details.napkin_math: Batch=64, seq=2048, hidden=5120, intermediate=20480. Sequence len × batch = 64 × 2048 = 131,072 tokens. Linear 1 (5120→20480): FLOPs = 2 × 131K × 5120 × 20480 = 2.75T FLOPs. Bytes: weights 5120×20480×2B = 209MB, input 131K×5120×2B = 1.34GB. AI = 2.75T / (209MB + 1.34GB) = 1,797 FLOPs/B >> 295 ridge. Compute-bound. GELU: FLOPs ≈ 6 × 131K × 20480 = 16B. Bytes: 131K×20480×2B = 5.37GB in + out. AI = 16B / 5.37GB = 3 FLOPs/B << 295. Memory-bound. Fusion impact: Linear1 is compute-bound — fusion doesn't help. GELU is memory-bound — fusing GELU with Linear2 saves 5.37GB HBM traffic. Latency savings: 5.37GB / 3.35TB/s = 1.6ms. At batch=1 (decode), Linear becomes memory-bound too → fusion helps much more.
details.realistic_solution: Check arithmetic intensity: compute FLOPs / bytes accessed. If AI > ridge point (H100 ridge ≈ 295 FLOPS/B for bf16), it's compute-bound. For large matrix multiplications, AI is high → compute-bound, fusion has less impact. Elementwise ops (GELU, bias) are memory-bound → benefit from fusion.

scenario: For a 13B LLM on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS BF16), compare fused vs unfused MLP block (Linear → GELU → Linear). Batch size 64, sequence length 2048, hidden size 5120, intermediate size 20480. Evaluate roofline position, memory bandwidth savings, and latency.
title: Kernel Fusion: Evaluate Fused vs Unfused MLP Blocks on H100

details.common_mistake: Implementing fusion for batch=1 decode without noting that GEMM (Linear) at batch=1 is already memory-bound — fusion helps even more here than in training.
details.napkin_math: Batch=1, seq=1, hidden=4096. Input tensor: 1 × 4096 × 2B = 8KB. LayerNorm output: 8KB (if written to HBM). Linear weight: 4096 × 4096 × 2B = 32MB. Unfused: read input (8KB) + write LayerNorm output (8KB) + read LayerNorm output (8KB) + read weights (32MB) + write output (8KB) = 32MB + 32KB ≈ 32.03MB HBM. Fused: read input (8KB) + read weights (32MB) + write output (8KB) = 32.02MB HBM. Savings: only 16KB saved (the LayerNorm intermediate is tiny vs 32MB weights). Insight: at batch=1, weights dominate. Fusion savings are minimal for Linear (compute/weights dominate). Savings = 16KB / 32MB = 0.05%. But: eliminating kernel launch overhead (2-3 µs saved) matters more at this size. Useful fusion targets: fusing multiple small elementwise ops, not LayerNorm+Linear.
details.realistic_solution: Fused kernel: load weight matrix once, compute LayerNorm statistics on-the-fly from input, apply normalization, multiply by weight matrix — all without writing intermediate LayerNorm output to HBM.

scenario: Implement a fused LayerNorm + Linear kernel for H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) processing a 7B model with hidden size 4096. Batch size 1 (decode mode), sequence length 1. Quantify the memory bandwidth reduction vs unfused implementation and expected latency improvement.
title: Kernel Fusion: Implement Fused LayerNorm + Linear on H100

details.common_mistake: Applying fusion uniformly without first profiling which kernels are memory-bound vs compute-bound; applying fusion to compute-bound matmuls where it adds overhead without benefit.
details.napkin_math: GPT-3 (175B params) training: 300B tokens × 6 × 175B = 315 PFLOPs. H100 cluster 1024 GPUs at 989 TFLOPS × 0.45 MFU = 445 TFLOPS each. Total cluster: 1024 × 445T = 455.7 PFLOPs/s. Training time: 315P / 455.7P = 0.69 seconds? No — 315 PFLOPs = 3.15×10^17 FLOPs. 455.7 × 10^15 FLOPS. Time = 3.15×10^17 / 4.557×10^17 = 0.69s per step. Over 1M steps: 8 days. 420 PFLOPs total estimate for 175B × 300B × 8 (forward+backward+optimizer) / some_factor — the key fix: 420 PFLOPs is the correct order of magnitude for GPT-3 (not 6 PetaFLOPs which is too low by 70×).
details.realistic_solution: GPT-3 training required ~3×10^23 FLOPs total. 420 PFLOPs/day × several days gives correct order of magnitude. 6 PetaFLOPs total is too low by ~50000×.

scenario: You are optimizing throughput for 70B LLM prefill on 8 H100s (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS BF16) processing batches of 512 sequences × 2048 tokens. Current MFU is 38%. Identify the top fusion opportunities, implement a fusion roadmap, and quantify the expected MFU improvement.
title: Kernel Fusion: Mastery — Design Fusion Strategy for High-Throughput LLM Prefill

details.common_mistake: Applying prefill-optimized fusion strategies to decode — different bottleneck structure. Decode is dominated by weight loading (memory-bound), not compute.
details.napkin_math: 7B model decode, batch=1. Weight memory: 14GB loaded per token. At 3.35 TB/s: 4.2ms/token → 238 tokens/sec theoretical. Current: 4.2ms / 0.38 MFU interpretation for decode: actually 4.2ms is already the memory bandwidth limit. Elementwise ops on 1 × 4096 activations: 4096 × 2B = 8KB. 60% time in elementwise: 0.6 × 4.2ms = 2.5ms (as claimed — but this can't be right if weights are 14GB). Re-check: 60% of time in elementwise on batch=1 likely means 60% of kernel launch count, not time. Actual elementwise HBM traffic: 32 layers × 6 elementwise ops × 8KB = 1.5MB → 1.5MB / 3.35TB/s = 0.45µs. Fusion benefit: eliminate 32×6 = 192 kernel launches × 3µs = 576µs = 0.58ms. New decode: 4.2ms - 0.58ms = 3.62ms → 276 tokens/sec. 16% throughput improvement purely from reduced kernel launch overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Decode bottleneck: loading 7B × 2B = 14GB model weights per forward pass. At H100 3.35 TB/s: 14GB / 3.35TB/s = 4.2ms minimum. Elementwise ops run on the tiny (1 × hidden_dim) activation tensors — their memory bandwidth is negligible vs weight loading. Fusion helps by eliminating kernel launch overhead, not bandwidth.

scenario: You are analyzing kernel fusion impact for 7B LLM autoregressive decode on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s). Decode is batch=1, seq=1 (single token generation). Profile shows 60% of decode time is in elementwise ops (LayerNorm, GELU, residuals, rotary embeddings). Design and quantify a fusion strategy for decode mode.
title: Kernel Fusion: Mastery — Fusion Impact Analysis for Autoregressive Decode

details.common_mistake: Not knowing that LayerNorm is multi-pass in naive implementations; claiming fusion reduces FLOPs (it doesn't materially change FLOPs, only HBM accesses).
details.napkin_math: 30B model, training batch = 256 × 2048 tokens. Hidden = 6144. LayerNorm input tensor per call: 256 × 2048 × 6144 × 2B = 6.44GB. Naive: 3 reads + 1 write = 4 × 6.44GB = 25.8GB HBM per LayerNorm call. There are 96 layers × 2 LayerNorms = 192 LayerNorm calls per forward pass. Total: 192 × 25.8GB = 4,954GB = 4.95TB HBM per forward pass just for LayerNorm. Fused: 1 read + 1 write = 2 × 6.44GB = 12.88GB per call. Total: 192 × 12.88GB = 2.47TB. Savings: 2.48TB per forward pass. At H100 3.35 TB/s: unfused 4.95TB = 1.48s, fused 2.47TB = 0.74s. 740ms saved per forward pass. Training step time: if LayerNorm was 8% → total step time = 1.48s / 0.08 = 18.5s. After fusion: 18.5s - 0.74s = 17.76s. New LayerNorm fraction: 0.74/17.76 = 4.2%.
details.realistic_solution: Naive LayerNorm: Pass 1: read X, compute mean → write mean. Pass 2: read X + mean, compute variance → write variance. Pass 3: read X + mean + variance, compute normalized output → write output. 3 reads of X. Welford's single pass: compute mean AND variance simultaneously → 1 read of X.

scenario: Your profiler shows LayerNorm is taking 8% of total H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) training time for a 30B model. The unfused LayerNorm requires 3 passes over the data (compute mean, compute variance, normalize). A fused single-pass LayerNorm is possible using Welford's online algorithm. Quantify the memory bandwidth improvement.
title: Kernel Fusion: Optimize CUDA Kernel Fusion for Transformer LayerNorm

details.common_mistake: Applying the same analysis as full multi-head attention without accounting for the very different KV cache access pattern in MQA — 32× smaller KV reads changes the memory profile dramatically.
details.napkin_math: Decode mode, batch=1, 1 new token. MHA: 32 Q heads × 128 dim + 32 K heads × seq_len × 128 + 32 V heads × seq_len × 128. For seq_len=2048: KV = 2 × 32 × 2048 × 128 × 2B = 33.6MB. MQA: 32 Q + 1 K + 1 V: KV = 2 × 1 × 2048 × 128 × 2B = 1.05MB. KV read reduction: 33.6MB → 1.05MB = 32× less KV cache bandwidth. Fusion in MQA: fused Q projection + attention scores: read Q_weight (32 × 128 × 4096 × 2B = 33.6MB) + input (1 × 4096 × 2B = 8KB) + K (1.05MB/2) → write attention scores (32 × 2048 × 2B = 131KB). Unfused: writes intermediate Q (32 × 128 × 2B = 8KB) before attention. Fusion saves: 8KB HBM write + 8KB read = 16KB — negligible. Main benefit of MQA: KV bandwidth reduction (31.55MB saved), not fusion.
details.realistic_solution: In decode mode, MQA loads 1 K head and 1 V head (vs 32 in MHA). This dramatically reduces KV cache reads. The fusion opportunity is different: fuse the query projection + attention score computation to avoid intermediate storage.

scenario: You are optimizing Multi-Query Attention (MQA) on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) for a 13B LLM. MQA uses 1 KV head shared across 32 query heads, reducing KV cache by 32×. Compare fused vs unfused MQA kernel designs and quantify the bandwidth difference in decode mode.
title: Kernel Fusion: Optimize Fusion Strategy for Multi-Query Attention

details.common_mistake: Not distinguishing that with 32 concurrent users, the workload is batch=32 decode — significantly different from batch=1 in terms of arithmetic intensity.
details.napkin_math: Single Transformer layer attention FLOPs (seq=8192, hidden=8192, batch=1): QKV projection: 3 × 2 × 1 × 8192 × 8192² = 3 × 2 × 8192³ ≈ too large. Fix: QKV = 3 × 2 × batch × seq × hidden² = 3 × 2 × 1 × 8192 × 8192 × 8192 is wrong — hidden is the projection dim, not seq. Correct: QKV = 3 × 2 × seq × hidden × hidden = 3 × 2 × 8192 × 8192 × 8192 for full self-attention with hidden=8192. But per standard formula: QKV proj = 3 × 2 × B × S × d² = 3×2×1×8192×8192² is the matmul. Actually: 2×32×8192×8192 = 4.29 GFLOPs for a single layer's QKV attention scores (not 8.59 TFLOPs which is 1000× too high).
details.realistic_solution: Attention FLOPs for a single layer at seq=8192: QK^T scores = 2 × heads × seq² × head_dim = 2 × 64 × 8192² × 128 = 140 GFLOPs. Full attention including projections: ~560 GFLOPs per layer. 8.59 TFLOPs per layer is too high by ~15×.

scenario: Realize the complete kernel fusion impact for 70B LLM inference on 8 H100s (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) in decode mode serving 32 concurrent users. The model has 80 layers, hidden size 8192, 64 heads, GQA with 8 KV heads. Quantify fusion gains for each kernel category.
title: Kernel Fusion: Realize Kernel Fusion Gains for 70B LLM Inference

details.common_mistake: Not quantifying the monetary value of throughput improvement; computing ROI in terms of speed without translating to infrastructure savings.
details.napkin_math: Current: 32 H100s × 5K tokens/sec = 160K tokens/sec capacity. After 15% improvement: 160K × 1.15 = 184K tokens/sec with same 32 H100s. 10K req/sec × 100 tokens/req avg = 1M tokens/sec needed? Wait, re-read: 10K requests/second at 100 tokens/response = 1M tokens/sec — need 1M/5K = 200 H100s. After fusion: 1M / (5K×1.15) = 174 H100s. Savings: 26 H100s × $3/hr = $78/hr = $683K/year. Engineering cost: 6 person-months × $25K/month = $150K. Break-even: $150K / $78/hr = 1,923 hours = 80 days. Annual ROI: ($683K - $150K) / $150K = 355% first year. Subsequent years: $683K/year savings. 10-year NPV: $150K investment → $5M return. Clear winner.
details.realistic_solution: Throughput improvement → can serve same load with fewer GPUs, or serve more requests with same GPUs. Compute savings or revenue gain.

scenario: Realize the ROI analysis for implementing kernel fusion in a production LLM serving system on 32 H100s (700W each). The system serves 10K requests/second. Current throughput: 5K tokens/sec/H100. After fusion, expected 15% throughput improvement. Engineering cost: 6 person-months. Compute the break-even time.
title: Kernel Fusion: Realize Fusion ROI Analysis for Production LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Not specifying numerical tolerance bounds; not requiring backward pass fusion for training use; not defining test coverage requirements.
