details.napkin_math: Unfused: 3.2ms for 70B layer × 80 layers. RMSNorm (3 passes → 1 pass): saves 2/3 of RMSNorm HBM. QKV projection: already a single GEMM (no fusion benefit for compute-bound matmul). Main fusion: eliminate RMSNorm output tensor write + QKV input tensor read = 2 × (seq × hidden × 2B). Batch=512, seq=2048, hidden=8192: 2 × (512 × 2048 × 8192 × 2B) = 34.4GB saved per layer. At 3.35 TB/s: 10.3ms per forward pass (80 layers × 0.13ms each). Performance target: unfused 3.2ms → fused 1.4ms → 2.3× speedup. Validation: test on 1K random inputs, compare vs float32 reference. Max error threshold: bf16 precision limit ≈ 1e-2 relative, 1e-3 absolute. Regression test: run daily on CI with performance threshold ±5%.
details.realistic_solution: Correctness: max absolute error < 1e-3 vs float32 reference (for bf16). Performance: >= 1.8ms (>= 1.78× speedup vs unfused). Memory: must not allocate any intermediate HBM buffers. Backward: must support gradient computation.

scenario: You are specifying requirements for a custom CUDA kernel to fuse RMSNorm + QKV Projection for a 70B model on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS BF16). The unfused version takes 3.2ms. Define correctness requirements, performance targets, precision requirements, and validation methodology.
title: Kernel Fusion: Specification — Define Fusion Requirements for Custom CUDA Kernel

details.common_mistake: Pre-allocating max sequence length KV cache for every request — wastes memory for short sequences. Not accounting for the KV cache's share of HBM vs model weights.
details.napkin_math: 70B model: 70B × 2B bf16 = 140GB model weights across 8 H100s = 17.5GB/GPU. Remaining: 80 - 17.5 = 62.5GB/GPU for KV cache. KV cache per token per layer: 2 × num_kv_heads × head_dim × 2B bf16. For GQA 8 KV heads, head_dim=128: 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 4KB/token/layer. 70B model has 80 layers: 4KB × 80 = 320KB per token total KV. 62.5GB / 320KB per token = 195,312 tokens capacity per GPU. 8 GPUs: tensor-parallel, each stores full KV for its token range... wait: with tensor parallelism, KV is partitioned: 195K tokens total (single-GPU metric). 100 concurrent requests × avg 2048 tokens = 204,800 tokens < 195K... tight. Avg 1024 tokens = 102K tokens → fits. Page size 16 tokens: page = 16 × 320KB = 5.12MB. Pages per GPU: 62.5GB / 5.12MB = 12,207 pages.
details.realistic_solution: PagedAttention: allocate KV in pages of fixed size (e.g., 16 tokens per page). Assign pages dynamically. Only allocate as many pages as needed. Share KV pages across beam search branches (copy-on-write).

scenario: You are designing a KV cache for a multi-tenant 70B LLM serving system on 8 H100s (80GB HBM3 each = 640GB total). You expect 100 concurrent requests with varying sequence lengths (128 to 4096 tokens). Design a PagedAttention-based KV cache that maximizes GPU utilization and supports up to 100 concurrent requests.
title: KV-Cache: Design PagedAttention KV Cache for Multi-Tenant LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Not accounting that prefix caching only helps TTFT (prefill), not decode latency. Also forgetting that cached prefixes must be invalidated when the model is updated.
details.napkin_math: 7B model, 32 layers, GQA 8 KV heads, head_dim=128. KV per token: 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131KB per token. 1024-token system prompt KV: 1024 × 131KB = 134MB. At 80 GB H100: 134MB/80GB = 0.17% of HBM for one cached prefix. TTFT without prefix caching: prefill 1024 system + 256 user suffix = 1280 tokens. Prefill throughput at 40% MFU: 7B × 6 FLOPs × 1280 / (989T × 0.4) = 53.76T / 395.6T = 0.136 seconds. With prefix caching: only prefill 256 tokens: 53.76T × 256/1280 = 10.75T / 395.6T = 0.027 seconds. TTFT reduction: 0.136s → 0.027s = 5× faster. For 80% of requests. Compute savings: 80% × (1024/1280) = 64% compute reduction for prefill. At 10K req/sec: saves 0.64 × (0.109s prefill) × 10K = 697 H100-seconds/second = significant.
details.realistic_solution: Store the KV cache for the 1024-token system prompt in HBM. All requests sharing this prefix skip prefill for the first 1024 tokens. Only compute KV for the user-specific suffix.

scenario: You serve a 7B LLM on H100s (80GB HBM3) where 80% of requests share the same 1024-token system prompt. Currently you recompute the KV cache for the system prompt on every request. Design a prefix KV cache that shares this computation, and quantify the TTFT reduction and compute savings.
title: KV-Cache: Design Prefix Sharing KV Cache for System Prompt Optimization

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT4 KV cache has 4× less memory than FP16 without accounting for quantization overhead (scale factors). Not measuring the actual quality impact of quantized KV.
details.napkin_math: 13B model: 40 layers, GQA 8 KV heads, head_dim=128. KV per token per layer: 2 × 8 × 128 × {2B, 1B, 0.5B} = {4096B, 2048B, 1024B}. 40 layers: {160KB, 80KB, 40KB} per token. 50 users × 4096 tokens = 204,800 token slots. (A) FP16: 204,800 × 160KB = 32.77GB. 13B weights: 26GB. Total: 58.77GB > 80GB? Wait: 26GB weights + 32.77GB KV = 58.77GB < 80GB. Fits! But barely. (B) INT8: 16.38GB KV + 26GB = 42.38GB. Saves 16.4GB → allows 16.4GB/80KB per token = 205K more tokens = 50 more users. (C) INT4: 8.19GB KV + 26GB = 34.19GB. Decode bandwidth: KV read per step = 50 users × attended_tokens × 160/80/40KB per token. At seq=2048 avg: 50 × 2048 × {160KB, 80KB, 40KB}/40layers × 40/3.35TB/s = {0.98, 0.49, 0.245ms}. INT4 decode 4× faster than FP16. Throughput: 50 users × 1/(0.98ms) → vs 1/(0.245ms). Quality: INT8 acceptable (< 0.5% perplexity), INT4 needs evaluation.
details.realistic_solution: KV quantization reduces memory and bandwidth, enabling more concurrent requests. Quality impact: INT8 typically < 0.5% perplexity increase, INT4 < 2%. Scale factors add overhead: 1 scale per group of 128 values.

scenario: For a 13B LLM on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s) serving 50 concurrent users with max 4096-token sequences, compare three KV cache strategies: (A) FP16, (B) INT8, (C) INT4. Evaluate HBM usage, decode throughput, and quality impact.
title: KV-Cache: Evaluate KV Cache Quantization Tradeoffs on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming static batching is simpler and therefore faster — it's actually much less efficient for variable-length workloads due to padding waste and KV memory fragmentation.
details.napkin_math: 7B model: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128. KV per token: 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131KB. Model weights: 14GB. Available HBM: 80 - 14 = 66GB. Static batching (max 2048 tokens per request): KV per request = 2048 × 131KB = 268MB. Max concurrent: 66GB / 268MB = 246 requests. But 50% are short (256 tokens actual): wasted KV = 246 × 50% × (2048-256) × 131KB = 123 × 1792 × 131KB = 28.8GB wasted. Effective concurrent (if we count actual tokens): 66GB / (0.5 × 2048×131KB + 0.5 × 256×131KB) = 66GB / (134MB + 16.8MB) = 66GB / 150.8MB = 437 effective request slots. But static allocates for 2048 all: only 246. Efficiency: 246/437 = 56%. PagedAttention: allocates exactly needed. 437 concurrent requests. Throughput: PagedAttention 437/246 = 1.78× more concurrent requests → ~1.78× higher throughput.
details.realistic_solution: Static batching: allocate 2048-token KV for every request. Short requests waste 2048-256 = 1792 tokens (87.5%) of their KV allocation. GPU utilization tanks on mixed workloads. PagedAttention: allocate only needed pages, pad-free, much higher throughput.

scenario: Compare two KV cache management strategies for 7B LLM on H100 (80GB HBM3): (A) static batching with pre-allocated KV cache (max seq 2048), vs (B) PagedAttention with continuous batching. Evaluate GPU utilization, memory waste, and throughput for a workload with 50% short requests (< 256 tokens) and 50% long requests (1024-2048 tokens).
title: KV-Cache: Evaluate PagedAttention vs Continuous Batching Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for tensor parallelism splitting KV heads across GPUs; forgetting that with TP=8 and 8 KV heads, each GPU gets 1 KV head.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, TP=8. Per-GPU model weights: 70B × 2B bf16 / 8 = 17.5GB. KV per token per layer per GPU: 2 × (8 KV heads / 8 GPUs) × 128 × 2B = 2 × 1 × 128 × 2B = 512B per token per layer. 80 layers: 80 × 512B = 40KB per token total (across all layers) on one GPU. Available HBM per GPU: 80GB - 17.5GB model - 1GB activations = 61.5GB. Tokens cached per GPU: 61.5GB / 40KB = 1,537,500 tokens. 8 GPUs all cache same tokens (each stores its KV head's data): total concurrent token capacity = 1.54M tokens. At avg 2048 tokens/request: 1.54M / 2048 = 750 concurrent requests max. Impressive capacity due to GQA reducing KV heads 8×.
details.realistic_solution: With tensor parallelism TP=8: each GPU holds 1/8 of model weights. KV heads: 8 KV heads / 8 GPUs = 1 KV head per GPU. Each GPU caches KV for its KV head only.

scenario: Implement the KV cache sizing calculation for a 70B LLM (GQA: 64 Q heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128, 80 layers, bf16) deployed on 8 H100s with tensor parallelism. Compute the per-GPU HBM allocation for: model weights, KV cache, and activations. How many tokens can be cached simultaneously?
title: KV-Cache: Implement KV Cache Size Calculation for LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Not calculating the aggregate KV cache requirements across the fleet; treating KV cache as a single-server problem rather than a distributed fleet problem.
details.napkin_math: Solve: 14GB + 123GB/N ≤ 80GB. 123GB/N ≤ 66GB. N ≥ 123/66 = 1.86 → minimum 2 H100s for KV alone. But for 100K RPS throughput: decode rate = 100K × 128 tokens/100ms = 128M tokens/sec needed. Per H100 decode: 7B at batch=? tokens/sec. At H100 bandwidth: weight load 14GB per pass. KV per step: 10K×12.3MB... this is the full KV, per step you read current position only: 10K × 384 tokens × 32KB = wait: per step KV read = 10K requests × (avg attended tokens) × KV_per_token. At step 64 (mid-decode), attend to 320 tokens: 10K × 320 × 32B (per-layer per-token KV = 2×8×128×2B=4KB wait no per-token-per-all-layers=32KB) = 10K × 320 × 32KB = 102GB per decode step. At 3.35 TB/s: 102GB / 3.35TB/s = 30.4ms per step → 100K × 128 steps / (1000ms / 30.4ms) = 100K × 128 / 32.9 = 389K active tokens per step / 100K RPS = need ~4-5 H100s for decode bandwidth.
details.realistic_solution: Per-request KV: (256+128) × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 384 tokens × 32KB per token = 12.3MB per request. Fleet sizing: target 100ms latency → at 100K RPS, concurrent requests = 100K × 0.1s = 10K requests simultaneously. Total KV: 10K × 12.3MB = 123GB. Number of H100s: 7B weights = 14GB per server, KV = 123GB/N_servers per server + 14GB ≤ 80GB.

scenario: You are designing KV cache infrastructure for a 7B LLM serving platform targeting 100K requests/second on a fleet of H100 servers. Average request: 256 input tokens, 128 output tokens. Design the complete KV cache strategy: per-request sizing, caching policy, eviction, prefix sharing, and hardware allocation.
title: KV-Cache: Mastery — Design KV Cache Infrastructure for 100K RPS LLM Platform

details.common_mistake: Allocating 10 × 5.24GB = 52.4GB + 26GB model = 78.4GB and declaring it fits in 80GB without accounting for activation memory, CUDA overhead, and fragmentation.
details.napkin_math: 13B model bf16: 26GB. 10 × 32K KV at FP16: 10 × 5.24GB = 52.4GB. Sum: 78.4GB. CUDA overhead (context, streams, PyTorch): 1.5GB. Fragmentation: 0.3GB. Total: 80.2GB > 80GB HBM. Doesn't fit by 200MB. Fix 1: INT8 KV cache: 52.4GB / 2 = 26.2GB KV. Total: 26 + 26.2 + 1.8 = 54GB. Fits! Now capacity: (80 - 26 - 1.8) / (5.24GB/2) = 52.2GB / 2.62GB = 19.9 → 19 concurrent 32K-context requests. Fix 2: INT4 KV: 13.1GB KV for 10 requests. Capacity: 52.2GB / 1.31GB = 39.8 → 39 concurrent. Quality: INT8 KV perplexity < 0.3% increase, INT4 < 1.5%. For code generation: INT8 recommended (accuracy matters). Throughput: decode at 10 requests × 32K tokens (avg 16K attended): KV read per step = 10 × 16K × 40KB/token (INT8) = 6.4GB. At 3.35 TB/s: 1.9ms per decode step.
details.realistic_solution: Tight budget: 26GB model + 52.4GB KV = 78.4GB. Add: 1GB CUDA overhead + 0.5GB fragmentation buffer. Total: 79.9GB — barely fits. Need optimization: use INT8 KV to halve KV cache.

scenario: Your 13B LLM serving on H100 (80GB HBM3) needs to support 32K-token context windows for code generation. A single 32K-token KV cache requires: 40 layers × 2 × 8 KV heads × 128 head_dim × 32K tokens × 2B = 5.24GB. Design a memory budget that allows at least 10 concurrent 32K-context requests.
title: KV-Cache: Mastery — KV Cache Memory Budget Optimization for Long-Context Serving

details.common_mistake: Using LRU eviction — this evicts in-progress long requests (being actively generated) to make room for new short requests, causing expensive recomputation.
details.napkin_math: KV cache per token: num_layers × 2(K+V) × num_kv_heads × head_dim × bytes. For 32 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head_dim=128, fp16: 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131,072 bytes ≈ 131KB per token (not 32KB — 32KB would require head_dim=32 or 4× fewer layers).
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token = 2 × num_layers × num_kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element. For Llama-class models with GQA-8: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131KB per token.

scenario: Your H100 (80GB HBM3) LLM serving system (7B model) serves requests with bimodal length distribution: 20% of requests are 4096 tokens (long), 80% are 256 tokens (short). KV cache fills up within 100ms under peak load. Design an eviction policy that maximizes throughput while minimizing recomputation.
title: KV-Cache: Optimize KV Cache Eviction Policy for LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Replicating the full KV cache on every GPU (8×) instead of partitioning. With TP=8 and 8 KV heads, each GPU handles exactly 1 KV head.
details.napkin_math: GQA: 8 KV heads, TP=8. Per GPU: 1 KV head. Per-GPU KV per token per layer: 2 × 1 × 128 × 2B = 512B. 80 layers: 80 × 512B = 40KB per token per GPU. 200 requests × 2048 tokens = 409,600 token slots. Per-GPU KV total: 409,600 × 40KB = 16.4GB. Per-GPU model weights: 70B × 2B / 8 = 17.5GB. Activations: 1GB. Total per GPU: 16.4 + 17.5 + 1 = 34.9GB << 80GB. Well within budget! 50.6% HBM headroom. Can scale to: (80 - 17.5 - 1) / 40KB per token = 61.5GB / 40KB = 1.54M token slots = 1.54M / 2048 = 750 concurrent requests. 3.75× more than required. Memory layout: PyTorch tensor [80, 2, 409600, 128] bf16 per GPU = 80 × 2 × 409600 × 128 × 2 = 16.7GB. Addressing: request_id → token_offset (via PagedAttention table, 16-token pages = 1,600 pages × 80 layers per request).
details.realistic_solution: With GQA and TP=8, each GPU naturally holds 1 KV head. KV layout: [num_layers, 2 (K+V), num_tokens, head_dim] per GPU. Total KV is partitioned, not replicated.

scenario: Realize the KV cache memory layout for a 70B LLM served with tensor parallelism TP=8 across 8 H100s (80GB each). The model uses GQA with 64 Q heads and 8 KV heads. Maximum 200 concurrent requests, 2048 token sequences. Specify per-GPU layout, addressing scheme, and total capacity.
title: KV-Cache: Realize KV Cache Memory Layout for Tensor-Parallel 70B Serving

details.common_mistake: Not accounting that shared KV cache pages must be read-only (copy-on-write) to prevent one request modifying another's cache; forgetting that attention is autoregressive and document KV depends on position in the prompt.
details.napkin_math: KV per token: 32 layers × 2 (K and V) × 8 KV heads × 128 head_dim × 2B = 131KB (not 32KB).
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token for GQA-8 model with 32 layers: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131KB per token.

scenario: Realize a KV cache sharing architecture for a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) application on H100s (80GB HBM3) where 1000 documents (avg 512 tokens each) are frequently retrieved and included in prompts. 60% of requests use one of the top-50 most popular documents. Design the shared document KV cache.
title: KV-Cache: Realize Cross-Request KV Cache Sharing for RAG Applications

details.common_mistake: Not connecting KV cache spec to latency SLAs; specifying KV cache size without a model of how cache size affects throughput and latency.
details.napkin_math: KV per token: 131KB (corrected from 32KB). For 4K context window: 131KB × 4096 = 537MB KV cache per request. At 80GB H100: (80GB - model_size) / 537MB = max concurrent requests.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token for 32-layer GQA-8 model = 131KB. At 4K context, each request occupies 537MB of KV cache.

scenario: Write the KV cache specification for a production LLM API serving 7B model on H100s. The API must provide: P50 TTFT < 500ms, P99 TTFT < 2s, P50 TBT (time between tokens) < 50ms, P99 TBT < 100ms, concurrent users: 500. Define KV cache size requirements, eviction policy, prefix cache policy, and monitoring SLAs.
title: KV-Cache: Specification — Define KV Cache SLAs for Production LLM API

details.common_mistake: Not accounting that two models must share HBM; not specifying what happens when one model's requests surge.
details.napkin_math: GQA-8 model: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128, fp16. KV per token: 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131,072B = 128KB (using powers-of-2: 32×2×8×128×2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB ≈ 128KB).
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token = 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131,072 bytes ≈ 128KB (not 40KB).

scenario: Write the KV cache specification for a multi-model serving setup on a single H100 (80GB HBM3): Model A (7B, 30 concurrent) and Model B (3B, 70 concurrent). Both use bf16. Define memory partitioning, priority policy, and overflow handling.
title: KV-Cache: Specification — KV Cache Budget for Multi-Model Serving

details.common_mistake: Not accounting that speculative decoding generates K candidate tokens whose KV must be stored but may be rolled back; not budgeting for both models' KV simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: 80-layer model (GPT-4 class), GQA-8, head_dim=128, fp16: KV per token: 80 layers × 2 × 8 heads × 128 × 2B = 327,680B = 320KB (not 40KB — 40KB would require only 10 layers or 2 KV heads).
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token for 80-layer GQA-8 model: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 320KB per token.

scenario: Write the KV cache specification for a speculative decoding setup on H100 (80GB HBM3): target model 70B, draft model 7B, speculative lookahead K=4 tokens. Specify KV cache for both models, how speculative KV tokens are managed, and rollback mechanism.
title: KV-Cache: Specification — KV Cache Sizing for Speculative Decoding

details.common_mistake: Using only surface-level metrics (format compliance) without assessing whether responses are diverse and high-quality; not measuring the actual downstream task (customer satisfaction, resolution rate).
details.napkin_math: 200K examples. Metric A (format compliance): run regex check across all examples: 200K × 0.1ms = 20 seconds. Found 8% non-compliant = 16K examples. Filtering them improves BLEU-4 by 0.3 points. Metric B (semantic diversity): embed all 200K with a 768-dim sentence encoder. At H100 throughput (batch=512): 200K / 512 × 5ms/batch = 1,953 seconds ≈ 32 minutes. Compute pairwise distances on 200K samples: O(n²) = 40B comparisons → too slow. Sample 10K subset: 100M comparisons = 1 second on GPU. Found avg cosine distance = 0.42. After filtering near-duplicates (distance < 0.1): removes 12K examples. Improves BLEU-4 by 1.2 points. Metric B is 4× more predictive. Combined: A+B filtering removes 28K examples (14%), improves BLEU-4 by 1.5 points — better than either alone.
details.realistic_solution: Instruction-following rate catches formatting issues but misses quality. Semantic diversity catches repetitive data that causes mode collapse. Best: combine both + a held-out task metric (customer resolution proxy). Evaluate correlation of each metric with held-out task performance.

scenario: You are fine-tuning a 13B LLM on H100s (80GB HBM3) for a customer service bot using 200K conversation examples. Before training, evaluate two proposed dataset quality metrics: (A) instruction-following rate (% of responses that follow the format template), (B) semantic diversity score (average pairwise cosine distance of response embeddings). Which better predicts downstream task performance?
title: Dataset Curation: Evaluate Training Data Quality Metrics for LLM Fine-Tuning

details.common_mistake: Using git for large binary dataset files (impractical for TB-scale data); not tracking data provenance for individual examples; not designing for compute-efficient rollback.
details.napkin_math: Weekly ingestion: 100M tokens × 4B = 400MB/week. After 1 year: 52 × 400MB = 20.8GB new data/year. Total dataset: ~10TB. Content-addressed chunks: split data into 64MB chunks. SHA256 per chunk: 64MB × 10TB/64MB = 156,250 chunks. Manifest: 156,250 × 32B SHA256 = 5MB manifest file. Version manifest in git: trivial. Rollback: switch manifest pointer, re-mount data via content-addressed storage = instantaneous (< 1 second). A/B dataset testing: create two manifest files with different mixing ratios. Training job reads manifest at start. No data copying needed. Audit trail: manifest includes: dataset_version, creation_date, filtering_params, dedup_params, mixing_weights, annotated by (human/automated). Storage: git history of 52 weekly manifests × 5MB = 260MB git history/year = trivial. Actual data: 10TB in S3 (immutable, content-addressed). Cost: 10TB × $0.023/GB = $235/month.
details.realistic_solution: Use DVC (Data Version Control) or a custom manifest system. Store data in immutable content-addressed chunks (SHA256). Manifests are small (version-controlled), actual data in object storage. Rollback = switch manifest.

scenario: Realize the data versioning infrastructure for a continuous LLM training system on 256 H100s (80GB HBM3). New data arrives weekly (100M tokens per week). The system must support: reproducible training runs, rollback to previous data versions, A/B testing of dataset compositions, and audit trails for all data decisions.
title: Dataset Curation: Realize Data Versioning Infrastructure for Continuous LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Candidates assume batching always reduces latency; they ignore that decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and batching increases decode time per request.
details.napkin_math: Model weight read per decode step: 13B × 2 bytes = 26GB. H100 BW = 3.35TB/s. Single-request: 26GB/3.35TB/s ≈ 7.8ms/token. Batch-32: same 26GB read, amortized over 32 requests → 7.8ms/token still (memory-bound), but 32 tokens generated per step → effective throughput 32× higher. TTFT (prefill) at batch=32: compute-bound at H100 989 TFLOPS BF16.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy A: prefill time ≈ (32×512×2×13B params×2 bytes)/3.35TB/s ≈ compute-bound. Decode: 256 steps × (13B×2 bytes per token)/3.35TB/s × 1/32 batch ≈ 2.3ms/token for batch. Strategy B: per-request decode ≈ 7.8ms/token (bandwidth-bound). Batching lowers per-token memory bandwidth pressure; Strategy A gives lower throughput latency but higher per-request tail latency.

scenario: You are comparing two serving strategies for a 13B-parameter LLaMA model on a single H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s bandwidth). Strategy A batches 32 requests and processes them together; Strategy B streams each request individually with continuous batching. Prefill is 512 tokens, decode is 256 tokens per request. Evaluate the end-to-end latency profile of each strategy.
title: Latency Decomposition: Compare Batched vs. Streaming Inference on H100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that without KV-cache, attention cost scales quadratically with sequence length, making recomputation increasingly expensive at long contexts.
details.napkin_math: KV per layer per token: 2 × 4096 × 2 bytes = 16KB. 32 layers × 1024 tokens = 512K entries × 16KB = ~524MB KV. Weights: 7B × 2 = 14GB. Total read: ~14.5GB. 14.5GB / 3.35TB/s ≈ 4.3ms/token.
details.realistic_solution: With KV-cache: each decode step reads 14GB weights + 2×(1024 tokens)×(4096 dim)×2 bytes×32 layers ≈ 14GB + 0.54GB = 14.54GB → 14.54GB/3.35TB/s ≈ 4.3ms/token. Without cache: full attention over 1024 tokens adds O(n²) ops. At 1024 tokens, attention FLOPs ≈ 2×1024²×4096×32 ≈ 275B FLOPs → 0.28ms on H100 at 989 TFLOPS, but memory for Q/K/V reads grows. KV-cache wins on latency at long sequences.

scenario: A serving team debates whether to enable KV-cache for a 7B-parameter model on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s). With KV-cache, each decode step reads model weights (14GB at FP16) plus KV entries for past tokens. Without KV-cache, the full attention recomputes over the sequence. Compare the per-token decode latency for both approaches at sequence length 1024.
title: Latency Decomposition: Compare KV-Cache vs. No-Cache Decode Latency on H100

details.common_mistake: Candidates account only for model compute and ignore network RTT (50–100ms for cross-AZ), queue wait under load, and tokenization overhead.
details.napkin_math: 70B model decode: 140GB weights / 3.35TB/s ≈ 41.8ms/token × 128 = 5.3s. 13B model: 26GB / 3.35TB/s ≈ 7.8ms/token × 128 = 998ms. With speculative decoding (3× speedup): ~333ms decode. Prefill 13B at 512T: 512×2×13B×2 FLOPs = 26.6T FLOPs / 989TFLOPS ≈ 27ms. Total ≈ 416ms << 2s SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Budget: network ingress 5ms, tokenization 1ms, queue wait P99 50ms, prefill (512 tokens, 70B model) ≈ 512×2×70B×2/989TFLOPS ≈ 144ms, decode (128 tokens × 20ms/token) ≈ 2560ms — this alone blows the SLA. Fix: reduce model size to 13B (decode ≈ 4ms/token → 512ms total), or enable speculative decoding to cut decode latency 2–3×.

scenario: You own latency SLA for a production LLM API backed by H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, 700W) nodes. The SLA is P99 < 2 seconds for a 512-token prompt generating 128 tokens. Break down all latency components — network, queue, prefill, decode, detokenization — assign budgets, identify the dominant term, and propose a concrete optimization if the SLA is being missed.
title: Latency Decomposition: Full-Stack E2E Latency Budget for LLM API on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Assuming the latency increase is purely proportional to weight size; missing that higher memory pressure reduces effective KV-cache capacity, causing cache evictions and re-prefills.
details.napkin_math: 20B model FP16: 40GB. KV at 4096 tokens, 40 layers, batch=1: 4096×2×5120×2×40 = 3.4GB. Total: 43.4GB of 80GB = 54%. But at batch=4: 40 + 4×3.4 = 53.6GB (67%). KV INT8 halves KV to 1.7GB/request → at batch=4: 40 + 4×1.7 = 46.8GB (58%), restoring headroom.
details.realistic_solution: At 89% memory utilization, KV-cache for long sequences gets evicted. Each eviction triggers a re-prefill that adds 50–200ms. Fix: quantize KV-cache to INT8 (halves KV memory), freeing ~8GB for more concurrent sequences. Or reduce max sequence length from 4096 to 2048, halving KV footprint.

scenario: After deploying a new model checkpoint (13B → 20B parameters, same architecture) on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s), decode latency increases from 7.8ms/token to 12ms/token — a 54% increase, but model size increased 54% so this seems proportional. However, a team member notices GPU memory utilization jumped from 58% to 89%. Diagnose what is happening and quantify the fix.
title: Latency Decomposition: Diagnose and Fix Decode Latency Regression on H100

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for NVLink all-reduce overhead in tensor parallelism, and treating 4-GPU as if it's a single GPU with 4× compute.
details.napkin_math: 8-GPU H100 node NVLink: NVLink 4.0 = 900 GB/s total bidirectional (not 600 GB/s which is A100 NVLink 3.0). AllReduce for 10GB gradients: 2 × (8-1)/8 × 10GB / 900 GB/s = 2 × 0.875 × 10 / 900 = 0.0194s ≈ 19.4ms. At 50% bandwidth utilization: ~39ms. Sub-ms for small tensors.
details.realistic_solution: H100 NVLink 4.0 provides 900 GB/s total bidirectional bandwidth (not 600 GB/s — that is A100 NVLink 3.0). AllReduce time scales as 2×(N-1)/N×data/bandwidth.

scenario: Concretely size the per-component latency breakdown for serving a single request to a 70B LLaMA model on one H100 node (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, 989 TFLOPS BF16). The request is 256 tokens prompt, 64 tokens output. Assume no batching, no speculative decoding, and that weights fit in HBM after tensor-parallel split across 4 GPUs with NVLink (600GB/s bidirectional).
title: Latency Decomposition: Size the Per-Component Latency for a 70B Model Serving Request

details.common_mistake: Solving for TTFT and TPOT independently without considering that larger batches improve TTFT amortization but can degrade TPOT for individual requests.
details.napkin_math: TPOT: 26GB/3.35TB/s = 7.8ms/token. TTFT for 512 tokens: 26.6T FLOPs / 989TFLOPS = 27ms. Budget remaining for queue+network: 200 - 27 = 173ms. Spec: max_prompt=2048, max_decode=512, batch_size≤64 (memory fits: 26GB + 64×2048×4096×2×40layers = 26+43GB = 69GB < 80GB).
details.realistic_solution: TPOT constraint: 13B model = 26GB FP16. Single H100: 26GB/3.35TB/s ≈ 7.8ms/token < 30ms. ✓ Max batch for TPOT < 30ms: memory-bound, batching doesn't increase per-token time (same weights read). TTFT constraint: at batch=1, prefill for N tokens at 13B: 2×N×13B×2/989TFLOPS = N×52.5M FLOPs/989TFLOPS. For N=512: 26.6T/989T ≈ 27ms << 200ms. Max prompt: 200ms budget → N = 200ms × 989TFLOPS / (2×13B×2) ≈ 3785 tokens. So max prompt ~3K tokens with margin.

scenario: Design a latency budget specification for a chat application using a 13B model on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s). The SLA requires TTFT < 200ms and time-per-output-token (TPOT) < 30ms at P95. Specify: maximum prompt length, maximum decode length, minimum hardware requirements (number of H100s), and batch size constraints that satisfy both SLA components simultaneously.
title: Latency Decomposition: Specify Prefill/Decode Split Requirements for SLA on H100

details.common_mistake: Designing a generic software CI/CD pipeline without accounting for ML-specific concerns: checkpoint storage size (7B FP16 = 14GB per checkpoint), GPU reservation overhead, and non-deterministic eval scores.
details.napkin_math: 7B FP16: 14GB. LoRA adapters: rank 64 × 2 matrices × 80 layers × 4096 × 64 × 2 bytes = 80×2×4096×64×2 = 84MB (tiny). Checkpoint: base 14GB + adapter 84MB = ~14GB. Training 100K examples, batch 16, 8 GPUs: 100K/(16×8)×1 epoch = 781 steps. At 3s/step: 2344s ≈ 39min. Eval: 5 suites × 1000 examples each = 5000, at 7.8ms/token × 100 tokens = 780ms/example → 65min on 1 H100. 2×H100 parallel: 32.5min.
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline stages: (1) Data validation (5min, CPU), (2) Fine-tuning (LoRA rank 64, 1 epoch, 100K examples, 8×H100, ~2hrs), (3) Checkpoint to S3 (14GB × 3 checkpoints = 42GB, at 10GB/s = 4.2s), (4) Benchmark eval (5 suites, parallel on 2×H100, 30min), (5) Canary deploy via shadow traffic (automated), (6) Promote or rollback. Total pipeline: ~3.5hrs. Storage: 14GB × 30 daily checkpoints = 420GB/month. Rollback: swap model pointer in registry < 1min.

scenario: Design a CI/CD pipeline for continuous fine-tuning of a 7B LLaMA model on an H100 cluster (8× H100, 80GB HBM3, NVLink). The pipeline must support: nightly fine-tuning runs on new data, automated evaluation against 5 benchmark suites, canary deployment (5% traffic), and rollback in < 5 minutes. Quantify storage requirements and pipeline execution time.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Design a CI/CD Pipeline for LLM Fine-Tuning on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Evaluating only feature parity without quantifying the operational cost of self-hosting MLflow at scale (DB maintenance, artifact storage, concurrent user load).
details.napkin_math: Artifact storage: 50 runs/day × 50GB = 2.5TB/day. S3 at $0.023/GB/month: 50TB × $0.023 = $1,150/month. W&B storage: $2,940/month overage. MLflow wins by $1,790/month. MLflow ops: 0.1 FTE × $150K/year = $15K/year = $1,250/month. Break-even: $1,790 - $1,250 = $540/month savings. Self-hosted still wins at this scale.
details.realistic_solution: Self-hosted MLflow: 1000 experiments × 10MB metrics = 10GB in Postgres. Query performance: indexes on run_id/metrics, P99 query ~500ms. Artifact storage: 1000 × 50GB = 50TB in S3 ($1150/month). Ops overhead: 0.1 FTE for DB maintenance. W&B SaaS: $50/seat/month for 10 engineers = $500/month, hosted storage at 1TB included, overage $0.06/GB → 49TB × $0.06 = $2940/month overage. Self-hosted wins on storage cost at scale; W&B wins on zero ops overhead.

scenario: A team running 50 concurrent LLM fine-tuning experiments on H100s (each producing 50GB of checkpoints, 10MB of metrics per run) evaluates MLflow (self-hosted) vs. Weights & Biases (SaaS) for experiment tracking. Compare operational overhead, storage costs, and query latency for retrieving best runs across 1000 experiments.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Compare MLflow vs. Weights & Biases for LLM Experiment Tracking at Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming blue-green is always safer without calculating the cost: maintaining 32 H100s during deployment transition (H100 at $3/hr spot = $96/hr for 32 nodes) vs. rolling risk of partial failure.
details.napkin_math: Spot interruption recovery: 16 nodes need replacement. At $3/hr spot price for 8×H100 node. Replacement time: 30 min = 0.5 hr. Cost: 16 nodes × $3/hr × 0.5hr = $24 extra (not $96). If on-demand premium is $3/hr extra over spot and full 1 hr: 16 × $3 × 1hr = $48 extra for on-demand fallback (not $96 which would require 2hr at $3 or $6/hr premium).
details.realistic_solution: Spot interruption recovery cost depends on replacement duration and price differential. 16 nodes × $3/hr premium × 1hr = $48 extra cost (not $96).

scenario: A team deploys a new 13B model checkpoint on 16 H100 nodes. They compare blue-green deployment (full parallel fleet) vs. rolling deployment (replace nodes 2 at a time). The model requires 4 H100s (tensor parallel), so 16 nodes serve 4 model replicas. Evaluate deployment risk, cost, and downtime for each strategy.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Compare Blue-Green vs. Rolling Deployment for LLM API on H100

details.common_mistake: Storing full 14GB model checkpoints per region without deduplication, paying 3× storage costs when regions can share the same artifact via CDN or shared S3.
details.napkin_math: 14GB model × 3 regions: 42GB storage at $0.023/GB = $0.97/month. With central + replication: 14GB × 1 = $0.32/month storage + replication cost $0.56 one-time. Monthly savings: $0.65. At 30 deploys/month: $0.56×30 = $16.80 transfer vs. $0.32 storage. Transfer dominates. Better: regional S3 replicas, no transfer per-deploy. Cost: $0.97/month storage. Rollback: serving pods watch registry, pull new pointer → model reload 3-5min.
details.realistic_solution: Registry: central S3 bucket (us-east-1) with model artifacts. Artifact hash-addressed (SHA256 of weights file). Regions pull on deploy → pre-warm regional caches. 14GB model at S3: $0.023/GB = $0.32/month per copy. Cross-region replication: 14GB × 2 replicas × $0.02/GB transfer = $0.56 per deploy. Total: $0.32 + $0.56 = $0.88/deploy vs. $0.96 for 3 copies. Rollback: update 'current' pointer in registry → serving pods reload → <5min with pre-warm. Schema: {model_id, version, sha256, s3_uri, deploy_time, region_status}.

scenario: Design and quantify the model registry architecture for a production LLM API serving 3 regions (US, EU, APAC) from H100 clusters. Each region runs 8 H100 nodes with a 13B model (14GB FP16). Requirements: artifact deduplication across regions, version rollback < 5 minutes, and storage cost minimization. Specify the registry schema and replication strategy.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Implement Model Registry Versioning Strategy for Multi-Region LLM

details.common_mistake: Designing each component independently without specifying the integration contracts (schema for model cards, evaluation thresholds for promotion, alert thresholds tied to SLA).
details.napkin_math: Erlang-C at ρ=0.95, target P(wait) < 5%. Server count needed. At 1000 req/s, 57.9ms mean service time: λ=1000, μ=1/0.0579=17.27. ρ_per_server=1000/(s×17.27). For ρ=0.95: s = 1000/(0.95×17.27) = 61 servers. λ/μ = 57.9 represents average concurrent requests in system (Little's Law: L = λW = 1000×0.0579 = 57.9 concurrent requests in service), not requests per second arriving.
details.realistic_solution: 57.9 represents average concurrent requests in service (Little's Law: L = λ × W = 1000 req/s × 57.9ms = 57.9 in service), not the arrival rate.

scenario: Design the complete MLOps system for a production LLM API (13B model, H100 cluster, 10M requests/day). Include: training pipeline, experiment tracking, model registry, A/B testing framework, monitoring, alerting, and auto-rollback. Quantify throughput, storage, and cost at each layer. Identify the top 3 failure modes and their mitigations.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: End-to-End MLOps System Design for Production LLM on H100

details.common_mistake: Calculating total storage without applying lifecycle policies; storing all 200 experiments × 52 weeks indefinitely when most are superseded within months.
details.napkin_math: 26GB × 5 checkpoints × 200 exp × 52 weeks = 1.352PB. At $0.023/GB: $31,096/month. With lifecycle (keep 1 best, archive after 30 days): active = 200 exp × 26GB = 5.2TB = $120/month. Archive (1 year - 1 month): 1.352PB × 11/12 = 1.239PB × $0.004 = $4,956/month. Total: $5,076/month vs $31K. 6× savings.
details.realistic_solution: Average model: 13B (mid-size). 13B FP16 = 26GB. Best-5 checkpoints per experiment: 5 × 26GB = 130GB. 200 experiments/week × 130GB = 26TB/week. 52 weeks = 1.352PB — far too expensive. Apply lifecycle: keep best-1 per experiment after 30 days (90% reduction), S3 Glacier for experiments older than 90 days ($0.004/GB vs $0.023/GB). Active storage: 200 × 26GB = 5.2TB × $0.023 = $119/month. Archive: 1.352PB × $0.004 = $5,408/month.

scenario: A ML platform team at a large company runs 200 experiments/week across model sizes ranging from 1B to 70B parameters on H100 clusters. Size the total model registry storage requirements for 1 year, including: full checkpoints every 10 epochs, best-5 checkpoints per experiment, and evaluation artifacts. Propose a cost-effective tiering strategy.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Concretely Size Model Registry Storage for a Large ML Organization

details.common_mistake: Setting thresholds arbitrarily (e.g., 'must be within 2%') without statistical grounding; failing to account for evaluation set size needed for significance.
details.napkin_math: KV cache at batch 32, 4096 ctx, 40 layers, hidden 5120: 32×4096×2×5120×2×40 = 107GB. Too large for single H100. Reduce to batch 16: 32×4096×2×5120×2×40/2 = 53.7GB. Model 14GB + KV 53.7GB = 67.7GB < 80GB. ✓ Statistical power: 5000 examples, metric std ~7% → SEM = 7%/√5000 = 0.1%. 0.5% threshold = 5σ — very strict. Loosen to 1.5% (15σ too strict). Realistic: 2% threshold at 5000 examples.
details.realistic_solution: Benchmark regression: no more than 0.5% relative drop on any of 5 suites (statistical power: 5000 eval examples per suite gives σ ≈ 0.7% → 0.5% threshold is within 1σ, low false positive rate). Latency: P99 TTFT < 200ms, TPOT < 30ms measured over 10K shadow requests. Memory: model must fit in 80GB HBM with batch 32 (14GB model + 32×4096×4096×2×40layers KV ≈ 68GB < 80GB). Win rate: > 45% on GPT-4 judge eval (200 head-to-head comparisons, binomial test α=0.05). Error rate: < 0.01% over 100K shadow requests.

scenario: Specify quantitative promotion criteria for automatically promoting a new 13B LLM checkpoint to production on H100 infrastructure. The system serves 10M requests/day. Define thresholds for: benchmark score regressions, latency SLA compliance, memory footprint, output quality (ROUGE, win rate), and shadow traffic error rate. Make each threshold a concrete number with a statistical justification.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Specify a Model Evaluation Gate for Production Promotion on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming the model can simply be split evenly across GPUs without understanding that tensor parallelism requires all-reduce communication overhead, and pipeline parallelism introduces micro-batch latency.
details.napkin_math: H100 NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s bidirectional total across all NVLink connections (not 600 GB/s which is A100 NVLink 3.0). 8-way tensor parallel AllReduce: 2 × (8-1)/8 × data / 900 GB/s. For 1GB activation: 1.75 × 1GB / 900 GB/s = 1.94ms.
details.realistic_solution: H100 uses NVLink 4.0 at 900 GB/s total bidirectional. A100 uses NVLink 3.0 at 600 GB/s. Always use 900 GB/s for H100 NVLink calculations.

scenario: A new engineer asks why a 70B parameter model requires 140GB of GPU memory in FP16 but a single H100 has only 80GB HBM3. Explain the relationship between parameter count, precision, and memory, and explain what strategies enable inference of 70B models on hardware with less VRAM than the model size.
title: Model Size Estimation: Analyze Why 70B Model Needs 140GB but Only 80GB Fits in H100

details.common_mistake: Choosing maximum parallelism (e.g., TP-64) without considering that all-reduce communication across 64 GPUs over InfiniBand becomes the dominant latency term, worse than pipeline bubbles.
details.napkin_math: H100 NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s (not 600 GB/s). Tensor parallel communication for 70B model, 8-way TP: activation shard per layer ≈ seq × hidden/8 × 2B. AllReduce: 2×7/8 × shard_size / 900 GB/s.
details.realistic_solution: H100 NVLink bandwidth is 900 GB/s total bidirectional. Using 600 GB/s underestimates H100 by 33% (that is A100 spec).

scenario: Design the GPU sharding strategy for serving a 405B-parameter LLaMA model (FP8 precision) on H100 nodes (80GB HBM3 per GPU, NVLink 600GB/s intra-node, InfiniBand 200Gb/s inter-node). Minimize end-to-end latency for interactive generation while maximizing throughput. Specify tensor parallelism degree, pipeline parallelism degree, and number of nodes.
title: Model Size Estimation: Design Sharding Strategy for 405B Model on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Applying uniform INT4 quantization to all layers including embedding and LM head, which causes catastrophic accuracy degradation vs. keeping embeddings in FP16.
details.napkin_math: W4A16: 70B × 4 bits / 8 = 35GB. Embeddings FP16: 32K×8192×2B = 512MB. LM head: 512MB. KV: 4096×2×8192×2×80=8.59GB. Total: 35+0.5+0.5+8.59=44.59GB < 80GB ✓. Decode: read 35GB per step at 3.35TB/s = 10.4ms/token. FP16 baseline: 140GB/3.35TB/s = 41.8ms/token. Speedup: 4×. Accuracy: GPTQ INT4 perplexity delta on Wikitext-2: ~0.3 points.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy: INT4 weights + FP16 activations (W4A16). Memory: 70B × 0.5B = 35GB weights. Embeddings (vocab 32K × 8192 hidden × FP16): 32K×8192×2=512MB. LM head: same 512MB. KV cache (batch=1, seq=4096, 80 layers, 8192 hidden): 1×4096×2×8192×2×80=8.6GB. Total: 35+0.5+0.5+8.6=44.6GB ✓ (fits with 35GB headroom). Inference: weight dequantize INT4→FP16 on-the-fly: 35GB reads at 3.35TB/s = 10.4ms/token. 6× faster than FP16 (62.5ms). Accuracy: GPTQ INT4 on LLaMA-70B: <1% perplexity increase.

scenario: Design a quantization strategy to fit a 70B LLaMA model on a single H100 (80GB HBM3) for low-latency single-request inference (no batching). Consider: weight-only quantization (INT4, INT8), activation quantization (FP8), mixed precision (INT4 weights + FP16 activations), and their accuracy/latency tradeoffs. Specify exact memory layout.
title: Model Size Estimation: Design Quantization Strategy for Fitting 70B on Single H100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that LLaMA-2 uses Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with 8 KV heads instead of 64, dramatically reducing KV-cache size — this is the primary memory efficiency advantage.
details.napkin_math: LLaMA-2 70B GQA KV cache: KV heads=8, head_dim=128. Per token per layer: 2×8×128×2B = 4096B. 80 layers × 2048 tokens × 16 batch = 80×2048×16×4096B = 10.7GB. GPT-3 KV: KV heads=96, head_dim=128. Per token: 2×96×128×2=49,152B. 96×2048×16×49152=156GB. GQA advantage: 156/10.7 = 14.6× less KV memory.
details.realistic_solution: GPT-3 175B FP16: weights 350GB (needs 5 H100s). KV-cache: 16×2048×2×12288×2B×96 layers = 16×2048×2×12288×2×96 = 155GB. Total: 505GB — needs 7 H100s. LLaMA-2 70B FP16: weights 140GB (needs 2 H100s). KV-cache GQA: 16×2048×2×4096×2B×80 layers × (8 KV heads/64 query heads) = 16×2048×2×512×2×80 = 4.3GB. Total: 144.3GB — 2 H100s. GQA reduces KV-cache 8×.

scenario: Compare the memory footprints of GPT-3 (175B params, dense attention) vs. LLaMA-2-70B (70B params, GQA with 8 KV heads vs. 64 query heads) at inference time on H100 (80GB HBM3). For a batch of 16 requests with sequence length 2048, compute weights memory, KV-cache memory, and activations memory for both models.
title: Model Size Estimation: Compare GPT-3 vs. LLaMA-2 Memory Footprint on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming MoE memory = active params × dtype_bytes; the full weight tensor for all experts must reside in HBM even though only 2 of 8 experts activate per token.
details.napkin_math: Mixtral-8×7B: 46.7B × 2B = 93.4GB. Single H100: 80GB. Need TP-2. KV-cache Mixtral (32×1024 seq, 32 KV heads, 128 dim, 32 layers): 32×1024×2×32×128×2×32 = 8.6GB. Per H100 (TP-2): 93.4/2+8.6/2=51.0GB ✓. Decode: each step reads active experts (2/8 × 46.7B=11.7B × 2B=23.4GB) + 93.4 total loaded in HBM. BW: 23.4/3.35T=7ms/token (active params only, 2 experts per GPU in TP-2). LLaMA-13B: 26/3.35T=7.76ms/token. Similar!
details.realistic_solution: Mixtral-8×7B FP16: all 46.7B params must be in HBM = 93.4GB. Exceeds single H100! Need 2 H100s. Active compute: 12.9B params per token = 25.8GB accessed per decode step. LLaMA-2-13B FP16: 26GB. Fits in single H100 with KV cache. KV-cache LLaMA-2-13B at batch=32, seq=1024: 32×1024×2×5120×2B×40 layers = 26.8GB. Total LLaMA-2-13B: 26+26.8=52.8GB < 80GB ✓. Mixtral: 93.4GB + KV-cache → 2×H100.

scenario: Compare the inference memory footprint of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model (Mixtral-8×7B: 46.7B total params, 12.9B active per token) vs. a dense 13B model (LLaMA-2-13B) on H100 (80GB HBM3). Both serve at batch size 32, sequence length 1024.
title: Model Size Estimation: Compare MoE vs. Dense Memory Footprint on H100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that inference requires memory for weights, KV-cache, AND activations; candidates often compute only weights × dtype.
details.realistic_solution: Weights: 7B × 2B (FP16) = 14GB. KV-cache: 8 requests × 512 tokens × 2 (K+V) × hidden_dim × 2B × n_layers. For 7B LLaMA (hidden=4096, 32 layers): 8×512×2×4096×2×32 = 4.3GB. Activations (peak, 1 layer): 8×512×4096×2B = 32MB (negligible). Total: ~18.3GB. Fits in single H100 (80GB) or A100 (40/80GB). Answer in 30 seconds with rounding.

scenario: In a live interview, you're asked without any reference material: 'How much GPU memory does a 7B parameter model need at FP16 for inference with a batch of 8, generating up to 512 tokens?' Walk through the napkin math in under 60 seconds.
title: Model Size Estimation: Fluency — Estimate 7B Model Memory From Scratch

details.common_mistake: Forgetting optimizer states in the memory budget: AdamW stores momentum (m) and variance (v) in FP32, each the same size as the model parameters, creating a 3× memory multiplier on top of weights.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 26GB. Grads: 26GB. Adam m: 13B×4B=52GB. Adam v: 52GB. Total: 156GB. Single H100: impossible. ZeRO-3 on 4×H100: 156/4=39GB. Activations (4 checkpoints, seq=2048, hidden=5120): 4×2048×5120×2B=84MB per layer × 4 = 336MB. Total per GPU: 39.3GB. At batch=4: activation memory × 4 = 336MB×4 = 1.3GB. Total: 40.3GB < 80GB ✓ with ZeRO-3 on 4 H100s.
details.realistic_solution: Weights BF16: 13B × 2B = 26GB. Gradients BF16: 13B × 2B = 26GB. Optimizer states FP32 (m + v): 13B × 4B × 2 = 104GB. Total for training: 26+26+104 = 156GB >> 80GB. Fix: use ZeRO-3 (sharded across 4 GPUs): 156/4 = 39GB per GPU. Plus activations with checkpointing: 1 checkpoint per 4 layers → only 4 layers of activations in memory: 4×4×2048×5120×2B = 0.84GB. Total per GPU: 39+0.84 = 39.84GB < 80GB ✓.

scenario: Compute the full GPU memory budget for training a 13B parameter model on H100 (80GB HBM3) with batch size 4, sequence length 2048, using AdamW optimizer in BF16 with FP32 optimizer states (mixed precision). Include: model weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations with gradient checkpointing, and KV-cache for attention. Determine if it fits in a single H100.
title: Model Size Estimation: Master Full Memory Budget for LLM Training on H100

details.common_mistake: Using hidden_dim instead of KV head count × head_dim for KV-cache calculation; in multi-head attention, only the KV projections contribute to cache, not the full hidden dimension.
details.napkin_math: KV per token per layer: 2×n_kv×head_dim×2B. MHA (n_kv=40): 2×40×128×2=20,480B=20KB. 40 layers: 800KB/token. GQA (n_kv=8): 2×8×128×2=4096B=4KB. 40 layers: 160KB/token. Available HBM: 54GB. MHA max tokens: 54×10^9/800×10^3=67,500. GQA max: 54×10^9/160×10^3=337,500. GQA: 5× more context capacity.
details.realistic_solution: KV per token per layer: 2 (K+V) × n_KV_heads × head_dim × 2B = 2×40×128×2 = 20,480 bytes = 20KB per layer. Per request, per token (all layers): 40×20KB = 800KB/token. Available: 54GB. Max tokens (batch × seq): 54GB/800KB = 67,500 tokens (e.g., batch=16 × seq=4096 = 65,536 tokens ✓). With GQA (8 KV heads): 2×8×128×2B = 4,096 bytes per layer. Per token all layers: 40×4KB = 160KB. Max tokens: 54GB/160KB = 337,500 tokens (batch=32 × seq=10K or batch=64 × seq=5K). GQA gives 5× more capacity.

scenario: Derive and apply the KV-cache scaling law for LLM inference on H100 (80GB HBM3). For a 13B LLaMA model (40 layers, hidden_dim=5120, 40 KV heads, head_dim=128), compute: (1) KV-cache memory per token per request, (2) maximum batch size × context length product at FP16 given 80GB - 26GB weights = 54GB available, (3) how GQA (8 KV heads) changes this.
title: Model Size Estimation: Master Attention KV-Cache Scaling Laws on H100

details.common_mistake: Immediately switching to ZeRO-3 (complex, adds communication overhead) when simpler fixes (8-bit Adam, gradient checkpointing) may suffice within a single GPU.
details.napkin_math: Full FP16 Adam: weights 26GB + grads 26GB + m (FP16) 26GB + v (FP16) 26GB = 104GB. 8-bit Adam: m (INT8) 13GB + v (INT8) 13GB. Total: 26+26+13+13=78GB < 80GB. With 2GB activations at batch=8: 80GB exactly. Very tight. LoRA rank 64: trainable params = 2×64×5120×80 layers/2 (half layers) = 52M. Grads: 0.1GB. Adam: 0.2GB. Total: 26+0.1+0.2=26.3GB. 53.7GB headroom.
details.realistic_solution: Full FP16 training (wrong for stability): weights 26GB + grads 26GB + Adam FP32 states 104GB? No: full FP16 Adam has FP16 m+v = 13B×2B×2=52GB. Total: 104GB > 80GB. Fix options: (1) 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes): optimizer states 13B×1B×2=26GB. New total: 26+26+26=78GB < 80GB ✓ (barely). (2) LoRA: only train 2% of params. LoRA grads: 0.26B×2B=520MB. LoRA optimizer: 1.04GB. Total: 26+0.52+1.04=27.56GB ✓ massively. Recommend LoRA for minimal overhead.

scenario: A team hits OOM (out of memory) on H100 (80GB HBM3) while fine-tuning a 13B model with batch size 8, sequence length 2048, using full FP16 training (no mixed precision). Memory profiler shows: weights 26GB, gradients 26GB, optimizer states 52GB — total 104GB. Diagnose and quantify the minimum changes to fit in 80GB.
title: Model Size Estimation: Diagnose OOM Error During Fine-Tuning on H100

details.common_mistake: Blaming model weight memory (constant at 26GB) when the growth is entirely from KV-cache not being freed after request completion.
details.napkin_math: KV per token (13B, MHA): 800KB. Per request (640 tokens): 640×800KB=512MB. At 100 req/min steady state (avg 5s service time): concurrent requests = 100/60×5=8.3. KV in use: 8.3×512MB=4.3GB. Leak rate: 43GB/4hr=10.75GB/hr. Per request: 10.75GB/3600s/(100/60)=1.8MB/req. Fix: find requests leaking 1.8MB = 2.25 tokens worth of KV never freed. Likely 1 padding block per request not freed.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: KV-cache memory leak. At 100 req/min × 60 min/hr × (512+128) = 38,400 tokens/hr context accumulation? No — if freed properly, memory stays constant. Growth: 78-35=43GB over 4 hours = 10.75GB/hr leak. Per request: 640 tokens × 800KB/token = 512MB. 100 req/min: 51.2GB/min released correctly → 10.75GB/hr growth = 10.75/(100×60) = 1.79MB per request leaked. Fix: audit KV-cache eviction logic — likely a reference counting bug where some requests' KV blocks aren't returned to pool.

scenario: A production LLM serving system (13B model, H100 80GB) shows memory usage growing from 35GB to 78GB over 4 hours under constant load (100 req/min, avg 512 token context, 128 token output). No OOM yet but the team expects failure. Diagnose the root cause and quantify how long until OOM.
title: Model Size Estimation: Diagnose KV-Cache Memory Leak on H100 Serving System

details.common_mistake: Not pre-allocating the KV-cache pool at startup (vLLM's approach), leading to fragmentation and inability to serve long requests under high concurrency.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 26GB. Framework: 2GB. KV pool: 52GB. KV/token: 2×40×128×2B×40 layers = 819KB ≈ 800KB. Pool tokens: 52×10^9/800×10^3 = 65,000 tokens. At seq=1024: 63 concurrent. At seq=512: 126 concurrent. At seq=2048: 31 concurrent. Throughput: 63 requests × 128 decode tokens × (1/7.8ms per token) = 63×128/7.8ms × 1000 ≈ 1034 tokens/s.
details.realistic_solution: Weights: 13B × 2B = 26GB. Framework overhead (PyTorch CUDA context, vLLM allocator): ~2GB. Activation buffer (1 forward pass, 1 layer at a time): 1×2048×5120×2B = 20MB (negligible). KV-cache pool: 80GB - 26GB - 2GB = 52GB available. KV per token (MHA, 40 heads, 128 dim, 40 layers): 40×2×40×128×2B = 819,200B ≈ 800KB/token. Pool capacity: 52GB / 800KB = 65,000 tokens. At avg seq length 1024 tokens: 65,000/1024 = 63 concurrent requests.

scenario: Concretely size every memory component for serving a 13B LLaMA-2 model on a single H100 (80GB HBM3) in FP16 inference mode. Include: model weights, KV-cache pool (allocated at startup for max concurrency), activation buffers (forward pass), framework overhead (PyTorch/vLLM). Compute maximum sustainable concurrent requests.
title: Model Size Estimation: Realize Full Memory Layout for 13B Model Serving on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming FP8 activation quantization is as simple as FP16 without noting that FP8 requires scaling factors per tensor (adding ~1-2% memory overhead) and that KV-cache is typically kept in FP16 for stability.
details.napkin_math: FP16 70B: 140GB. 2 H100s: 70GB/GPU ✓. KV budget: (80-70)×2=20GB. 20GB/800KB=25,000 tokens. 4 H100s: 35GB/GPU. KV: 45GB/GPU, total 180GB → 225K tokens. FP8 70B: 70GB. Single H100: 10GB KV = 12,500 tokens (batch=12 seq=1024). 2 H100s: 35GB/GPU, 45GB KV each = 90GB → 112K tokens.
details.realistic_solution: FP16: 70B × 2B = 140GB. Single H100: NO. 2 H100s (160GB): fits with 20GB for KV. 4 H100s: 35GB per GPU, 45GB KV budget per GPU = 180GB total KV. FP8: 70B × 1B = 70GB + 1% scaling overhead = 70.7GB. Single H100: BARELY (70.7GB < 80GB). KV budget: 9.3GB (KV in FP16). At 800KB/token: 11,625 tokens (e.g., batch=11, seq=1024). 2 H100s FP8: 35.35GB per GPU, 44.65GB KV per GPU = 89.3GB total → 111K tokens.

scenario: Concretely compute and compare the H100 memory layout for a 70B LLaMA model in FP16 vs. FP8 (E4M3) format. Determine for each: whether it fits on a single H100 (80GB HBM3), on 2 H100s with NVLink, on 4 H100s, and the KV-cache budget remaining in each configuration.
title: Model Size Estimation: Realize FP8 vs. FP16 Memory Comparison for 70B on H100

details.common_mistake: Sizing only the language model and ignoring the vision encoder, which adds 614MB (307M × 2B) — significant but not the binding constraint here.
details.napkin_math: Vision: 614MB. LM: 26GB. KV at batch=8, seq=4096: 8×4096 tokens × 800KB/token = 26.2GB. Total: 52.8GB < 80GB. Max batch for full 4096 ctx: (80-27.2)GB / (4096 tokens × 800KB/token per request) = 52.8GB / 3.2GB = 16.5 → batch=16. Total: 27.2+16×3.2=78.4GB ✓.
details.realistic_solution: Vision encoder: 307M × 2B = 614MB ≈ 0.6GB. MLP projection: 20M × 2B = 40MB. LLaMA-2-13B: 13B × 2B = 26GB. KV-cache (batch=8, seq=4096, 40 layers, MHA 40 heads): 8×4096×2×40×128×2B×40 = 8×4096×800KB = 26.2GB. Total: 0.6+0.04+26+26.2 = 52.84GB < 80GB ✓. Maximum batch: (80-26.6)/800KB/4096 = 53.4GB/3.2GB per request = 16.7 → batch=16. Check: 16×4096×800KB=52.4GB. Total: 26.6+52.4=79GB ✓.

scenario: Concretely size the memory requirements for a multi-modal LLM (LLaVA-13B architecture) on H100 (80GB HBM3). Components: (1) CLIP ViT-L/14 vision encoder (307M params FP16), (2) MLP projection layer (20M params FP16), (3) LLaMA-2-13B language model (13B params FP16), (4) KV-cache for 4096-token context at batch 8. Verify fit and compute maximum batch size.
title: Model Size Estimation: Realize Memory Budget for Multi-Modal LLM on H100

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for TP-2 all-reduce overhead in the TPOT calculation, and not reserving memory for the PagedAttention block allocator metadata.
details.napkin_math: 70B model prefill, seq=512 tokens, H100: FLOPs = 2 × 512 × 70B = 71.68 TFLOPs. H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 × 0.4 MFU = 395.6 TFLOPS effective. Time = 71.68T / 395.6T = 0.181s = 181ms? No — using 2×S×N formula: 2 × 512 × 70×10^9 = 71.68×10^12 FLOPs. At 989 TFLOPS × 0.5 MFU: 71.68T/(989T×0.5) = 0.145s = 145ms. At 989 TFLOPS effective (no MFU factor in calculation since 2× already accounts for fwd+bwd): 71.68T / (2 × 989T) = 36ms... Standard prefill formula: 2 × seq × N / FLOPS = 2 × 512 × 70B / 989T = 72ms. Corrected estimate: ~72.4ms (not 37ms which would require higher TFLOPS or lower param count).
details.realistic_solution: 70B model prefill at seq=512: 2×512×70B FLOPs / 989 TFLOPS ≈ 72ms. 37ms would require either 2× higher TFLOPS or half the parameters.

scenario: Specify the memory layout and serving configuration for running a 70B LLaMA model on exactly 2 H100 nodes (160GB total HBM3) to maximize throughput while keeping P99 TTFT < 200ms and P99 TPOT < 50ms. Define: precision, tensor parallelism, batch size, max sequence length, KV-cache size, and expected tokens-per-second.
title: Model Size Estimation: Specify Memory-Efficient Serving for 70B on 2-H100 Budget

details.common_mistake: Assuming all GPU-GPU communication uses NVLink; in practice, gradient AllReduce in data-parallel training may cross PCIe to CPU/InfiniBand when GPUs are in different NVLink domains.
details.napkin_math: TP-2 all-reduce: per layer, 2 all-reduces of hidden_dim=5120 activations × seq_len × batch × 2B. Batch=4, seq=2048: 4×2048×5120×2=84MB per all-reduce? Too large. Actually: only the output of each linear layer is all-reduced. For one matmul with TP-2: output size = batch×seq×hidden/2? No: output is full hidden_dim after all-reduce: 4×2048×5120×2=84MB per all-reduce × 2 per layer × 40 layers = 6720MB. NVLink at 900GB/s: 6720/900000=7.5ms per step for TP all-reduces. DP grad sync: 13GB/900GB/s=14.4ms. Total comm: ~22ms.
details.realistic_solution: 8×H100 on DGX: NVLink 900GB/s (DGX H100 spec). Within TP-2 pair: use NVLink for activation all-reduce (inter-GPU): ~4MB/layer × 2 all-reduces × 40 layers = 320MB. NVLink BW: 320MB/900GB/s = 0.36ms per step. DP-4 gradient AllReduce (after backward): 13B/2 params (per TP shard) × 2B = 13GB gradient. Ring-AllReduce across 4 DP groups: 2×(4-1)/4 × 13GB = 19.5GB per GPU. Over NVLink 900GB/s: 21.7ms per step. PCIe: only for CPU-GPU data loading (not in critical path if NVMe prefetching). NVLink dominates performance.

scenario: Design the interconnect topology for an 8×H100 DGX node (NVLink 600GB/s bidirectional, PCIe 5.0 ×16 at 64GB/s per GPU to CPU) for training a 13B model with data-parallel + tensor-parallel (TP-2, DP-4). Specify which communication operations use NVLink vs. PCIe, and quantify bandwidth utilization for each.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Design NVLink vs. PCIe Topology for 8×H100 Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming data loading is always CPU-bound and not limited by PCIe bandwidth; at high batch sizes with high-resolution images, PCIe can become the bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: ImageNet training batch memory: batch=256, images 224×224×3, float32. Activations: 256 × 224 × 224 × 3 × 4B = 256 × 150,528 × 4B = 154,140,672 bytes ≈ 154MB (not 3.3GB — that would require batch=5488 or float64).
details.realistic_solution: Input activation memory for batch=256 ImageNet images: 256 × 224² × 3 × 4B = 154MB. 3.3GB would require batch ~5500.

scenario: A training cluster uses H100 GPUs with either PCIe 4.0 ×16 (32GB/s) or PCIe 5.0 ×16 (64GB/s) for CPU-GPU data transfer. Training a vision model with 256×256 images, batch size 256, 4 workers per GPU. Compare data loading bottleneck risk for each PCIe generation.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Compare PCIe 4.0 vs. 5.0 Impact on H100 Data Loading

details.common_mistake: Computing AllReduce bandwidth as total gradient size / link bandwidth without applying the ring-AllReduce formula (2(n-1)/n × data per participant).
details.napkin_math: NVLink AllReduce: 2×7/8×26GB/8 per GPU = 5.69GB/GPU. 5.69/600=9.5ms. IB 200Gb/s=25GB/s. Ring across 8 via IB: same 5.69GB but bottleneck is slowest link: 25GB/s. 5.69/25=227ms? Ring across 8 fully: each step passes 3.25GB across IB. 4 IB links: concurrent. 3.25GB/25GB/s=130ms. Efficiency: NVLink 200/(200+9.5)=95.5%. IB: 200/(200+130)=60.6%. NVLink: 13.7× faster comm.
details.realistic_solution: Ring-AllReduce data per GPU: 2×(8-1)/8 × 26GB/8 = 2×7/8 × 3.25GB = 5.69GB per GPU. NVLink 600GB/s: 5.69/600=9.5ms. InfiniBand 200Gb/s = 25GB/s per link. But 8 GPUs across 4 servers: 2 GPUs per server, intra-server NVLink (600GB/s), inter-server InfiniBand (25GB/s × 1 rail). Inter-server traffic: 26GB/8=3.25GB per GPU crosses IB. 3.25/25=130ms. Ratio: 130ms/9.5ms = 13.7× slower for inter-server. Training throughput: if step=200ms, AllReduce=9.5ms intra-node: 200/(200+9.5)=95.5% efficiency. Inter-node: 200/(200+130)=60.6% efficiency.

scenario: A distributed training job runs data-parallel with 8 H100 GPUs across two scenarios: (A) single DGX node (NVLink 600GB/s all-to-all) vs. (B) 8 GPUs across 4 servers connected by 200Gb/s InfiniBand HDR. For a 13B model (26GB FP16 gradients), compute AllReduce time for both and determine the effective training throughput ratio.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Compare AllReduce over NVLink vs. InfiniBand

details.common_mistake: Quoting NVLink bandwidth as unidirectional when the spec is bidirectional; H100 NVLink 4.0 is 900GB/s total bidirectional = 450GB/s per direction.
details.napkin_math: PCIe 5.0: 64GB/s bidir. NVLink: 900GB/s bidir per GPU. NVSwitch: 3.6TB/s. Ratio NVLink/PCIe: 900/64=14×. For 26GB checkpoint save via PCIe to CPU: 26/32=812ms (PCIe bottleneck). Via NVLink to another GPU: 26/450=57.8ms. Checkpoint saves should use NVLink paths when possible.
details.realistic_solution: PCIe 5.0 ×16: 64GB/s bidirectional (32GB/s per direction). NVLink 4.0 per GPU: 900GB/s bidirectional total (18 links × 50GB/s each = 900GB/s). NVSwitch (DGX H100): 3.6TB/s non-blocking all-to-all across 8 GPUs. When each limits: PCIe limits during data loading for very large batch sizes or model checkpoint saves/loads. NVLink limits during tensor-parallel all-reduces with large hidden dims. NVSwitch enables full NVLink bandwidth between all 8 GPUs simultaneously.

scenario: A systems engineer asks: 'What are the key bandwidth specifications for H100 GPU interconnects: PCIe 5.0, NVLink 4.0, and NVSwitch, and when does each limit ML training performance?' Provide exact numbers.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Recall PCIe and NVLink Bandwidth Specs for H100

details.common_mistake: Using total bandwidth (N × 900GB/s) in the formula instead of per-GPU bandwidth; in ring-AllReduce, each GPU communicates only with 2 neighbors at a time.
details.napkin_math: Pipeline parallel scheduling: 1.277 PFLOPs forward / 7.912 PFLOPs total budget → fraction = 16.1%. At 989 TFLOPS × 256 GPUs × MFU: 989T × 256 × 0.45 = 113.8 PFLOPs/s. Time = 7.912P / 113.8P = 69.5ms ≈ 161ms at 43% effective MFU. Bubble overhead for pp=8, pp-stages: bubble fraction = (p-1)/(m+p-1) where m=microbatches. With m=8, p=8: 7/15 = 46.7% bubble. Effective step time: 161ms (not ~100ms which underestimates bubble overhead).
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline parallel bubble overhead with pp=8 stages and m=8 microbatches: bubble fraction = 7/15 = 46.7%. Effective step time increases to ~161ms including bubble.

scenario: Derive and apply the ring-AllReduce time formula for a 13B model (26GB FP16 gradients) distributed across N=8 H100 GPUs on NVLink (900GB/s per GPU). Compute exact AllReduce time and compare against the compute step time to determine if training is compute-bound or communication-bound.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Implement Ring-AllReduce Time Formula for H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Analyzing each parallelism dimension independently without noting that TP and PP run synchronously within a micro-batch while DP is overlapped with backward computation.
details.napkin_math: TP all-reduce: 2×80layers×(1×2048×8192×2B)/225GB/s = 2×80×33.6MB/225GB/s=2×80×0.15ms=23.9ms/fwd, ×2 for bwd=47.8ms. PP bubble (1F1B, M=8): (4-1)/(4×8)=3/32=9.4%×200ms step=18.8ms. DP AllReduce: 70B×2B/(4TP×4PP)=70B/(16)=4.375B per shard×2B=8.75GB gradient per shard. Ring-AllReduce over 8 DP: 2×7/8×(8.75/8)=7×8.75/8/8=0.956GB per GPU. 0.956/25GB/s(IB)=38.3ms × ... wait: data per GPU = 8.75GB/8=1.09GB moved per ring step. 2×7/8×1.09=1.91GB over IB 25GB/s=76.5ms. DP is dominant.
details.realistic_solution: TP-4 (within node, NVLink): per layer, 2 all-reduces of shape [batch/4, seq, hidden] = 2×[1, 2048, 8192]×2B = 67MB per step × 80 layers = 5.4GB total. NVLink 900GB/s/4: each TP all-reduce: 67MB/225GB/s × 2 steps = 0.6ms/layer × 80 = 48ms. PP bubble: 4 pipeline stages, 1 micro-batch (Gpipe). Bubble fraction: (PP-1)/PP=75%. Fix: interleaved 1F1B with 8 micro-batches: bubble = (PP-1)/(PP×M) = 3/32 = 9.4%. DP AllReduce: 70B/32 params × 2B × 2×7/8 / (200Gb/s/8=25GB/s per node's IB) = 9.63GB/25=385ms. PP bubble: 200ms×9.4%=18.8ms. Dominant: DP AllReduce (385ms) >> PP bubble (18ms) >> TP comm (48ms).

scenario: Analyze all communication bottlenecks in a 3D-parallel training setup (TP-4, PP-4, DP-8) for a 70B model on 128 H100 GPUs (8-GPU DGX nodes, NVLink 900GB/s intra-node, 200Gb/s InfiniBand inter-node). Quantify: TP all-reduce time, PP bubble overhead, DP gradient AllReduce time, and identify the dominant bottleneck.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Master Full Communication Analysis for 3D-Parallel LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming NVLink is the bottleneck because it's labeled a 'limit'; in multi-node training, InfiniBand inter-node bandwidth is almost always the binding constraint.
details.napkin_math: 7B gradient: 14GB. Per GPU: 437.5MB. Ring: 843MB per GPU exchanged. IB: 200Gb/s=25GB/s. Time: 843/25=33.7ms. Step: 100ms. Overhead: 33.7/(100+33.7)=25.2%. With overlap (DDP): start AllReduce during backward. Backward: 100ms. AllReduce: 33.7ms. If overlapped 100%: total step≈100ms. GPU util: 100%. In practice, 50% overlap: step=100+16.85=116.85ms. GPU util: 100/116.85=85.6% ✓.
details.realistic_solution: AllReduce bottleneck: 7B model, 32 GPUs (4 nodes × 8 GPUs). Gradient size: 7B × 2B = 14GB. Per GPU: 14/32=437.5MB. Ring AllReduce data per GPU: 2×31/32×437.5MB=843MB. Intra-node: NVLink 900GB/s → negligible. Inter-node: all 4 nodes exchange via IB 25GB/s per node (200Gb/s). AllReduce over IB: 843MB/25GB/s=33.7ms per step. Compute: 7B fwd+bwd on H100: ~100ms. AllReduce fraction: 33.7/133.7=25.2% (close to observed 35% with overhead). Fix: overlap AllReduce with backward pass (DDP overlap) → AllReduce runs during backward. Gradient bucketing: 25MB buckets. Effective overhead: ~5ms sequential at end.

scenario: A 32-GPU training job (4 DGX nodes, H100) shows 65% GPU utilization (target: >85%) during data-parallel training of a 7B model. Profiling shows 35% of step time is in AllReduce. Diagnose the bottleneck: is it NVLink (900GB/s) or InfiniBand (200Gb/s = 25GB/s) between nodes, and quantify a fix.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Diagnose Bandwidth Bottleneck in Multi-Node Training

details.common_mistake: AllReducing the full 70B gradient when each DP rank holds only its TP shard (70B/8 = 8.75B params per GPU in this TP-8 setup).
details.napkin_math: Per GPU gradient (TP-8): 17.5GB. Ring-AllReduce: 2×7/8×17.5=30.6GB moved. IB 25GB/s: 30.6/25=1.22s. Compute step: ~500ms for 70B. AllReduce is 2.4× step time → 71% overhead. Fix: 800Gb/s IB (InfiniBand NDR, 100GB/s per port): 30.6/100=306ms. Still longer than compute. ZeRO-3: same 30.6GB moved but overlapped with forward. Effective overhead: ~150ms (50% overlap). ✓
details.realistic_solution: TP-8: each GPU holds 70B/8=8.75B params × 2B = 17.5GB model. Gradient per GPU: 17.5GB. DP-8 AllReduce: ring-AllReduce data per GPU = 2×(8-1)/8 × 17.5GB = 30.6GB moved per GPU. Time over IB 25GB/s: 30.6/25=1.224s per step. That's extremely slow! Fix: use ZeRO stage 3 to shard gradients: instead of AllReduce, use ReduceScatter+AllGather = same data but pipelined. ReduceScatter: (8-1)/8 × 17.5 = 15.3GB. Time: 15.3/25=0.61s. Still slow. Increase IB to 400Gb/s (50GB/s) or reduce DP degree.

scenario: Concretely size the AllReduce data volume for training a 70B model (FP16 gradients) across 64 H100 GPUs (8 DGX nodes) with data parallelism degree=8 (8-way DP, each DP group uses 8 GPUs for TP). Compute: total gradient bytes per DP group, bytes moved per GPU in ring-AllReduce, and time over 200Gb/s InfiniBand.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Realize AllReduce Data Volume for 70B Model Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming checkpointing is embarrassingly parallel (8 GPUs × 64GB/s = 512GB/s); in practice, CPU memory is the bottleneck (DDR5 at 100GB/s), not PCIe.
details.napkin_math: 140GB model. CPU DDR5: 100GB/s. GPU→CPU: 140/100=1.4s. CPU→NVMe (3.5GB/s): 140/3.5=40s. Training 1000 steps: 1000×100ms=100s. Checkpoint overhead: 40/100=40%. Async write: 140GB to /dev/shm (requires 140GB+ CPU RAM). 32GB CPU RAM: overflow. Solution: write 8 shards in parallel to 8 NVMe SSDs: 8×3.5=28GB/s. 140/28=5s total checkpoint. 5/100=5% overhead. Acceptable.
details.realistic_solution: 70B FP16: 140GB total across 8 GPUs (17.5GB each). PCIe 5.0 per GPU: 32GB/s (one direction). Time for 17.5GB: 0.55s per GPU. With 8 GPUs parallel: CPU must absorb 8×32=256GB/s → CPU DDR5 BW: 100GB/s (bottleneck). Time: 140GB/100GB/s=1.4s to CPU. Then to NVMe (3.5 GB/s): 140/3.5=40s. Checkpoint every 1000 steps (100ms each): 100s of training. Checkpoint overhead: 40s/100s=40%. Solution: async checkpoint — write to /dev/shm first, then background NVMe write overlapped with next training steps.

scenario: Concretely size the PCIe bandwidth impact on checkpointing a 70B FP16 model from 8×H100 GPUs to NVMe SSDs via CPU. Each H100 connects to CPU via PCIe 5.0 ×16 (64GB/s). Compute checkpoint time and determine if it can be hidden within training.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Realize PCIe Bandwidth Impact on Model Checkpointing

details.common_mistake: Specifying a single-tier fat-tree when 256 ports per switch isn't enough; 256 GPUs with 32 NICs per node = 32 uplinks, requiring a 2-tier or 3-tier fat-tree for non-blocking.
details.napkin_math: Per GPU IB: 400Gb/s=50GB/s. 32 DP nodes: AllReduce data per GPU (70B FP16, DP-32, TP-8): per GPU gradient = 17.5GB. Ring: 2×31/32×17.5=33.9GB moved. IB 50GB/s: 33.9/50=678ms. Still slow! With ZeRO-3 and 50% overlap: ~340ms overhead on 500ms step. GPU util: 500/(500+340)=59.5%. Needs 200Gb/s × 4 rails or 800Gb/s IB to achieve >85% util.
details.realistic_solution: 256 GPUs across 32 nodes. Each node: 8 H100 × 400Gb/s (ConnectX-7) = 3.2Tb/s intra-node NVLink + 8 × 400Gb/s IB per node = 3.2Tb/s IB uplinks per node. 32 nodes × 8 IB ports = 256 ports. Non-blocking fat-tree: 2-tier with 512-port Quantum-2 switches or HDR 36-port leafs. Recommended: 2-tier fat-tree with 256-port leaf switches (1:1 oversubscription). Bandwidth per GPU: 400Gb/s = 50GB/s. AllReduce 70B across 32 DP ranks: 2×31/32×140B/32 = 8.45GB per GPU. 8.45/50=169ms. Bisection BW: 256×400Gb/s/2=51.2Tb/s.

scenario: Specify the InfiniBand fabric topology for a 256-GPU H100 training cluster (32 DGX nodes × 8 H100s) optimized for training 70B+ models with 3D parallelism. Specify: IB switch tier, rail count, bandwidth per GPU, target AllReduce time for 70B model, and maximum cluster bisection bandwidth.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Specify InfiniBand Fabric for 256-GPU LLM Training Cluster

details.common_mistake: Dividing 14GB by 900GB/s directly; the ring-AllReduce moves 2×(N-1)/N × data_per_GPU, not the full tensor size.
details.napkin_math: 7B FP16 grads: 14GB. Per GPU: 1.75GB. Ring data per GPU: 2×7/8×1.75=3.0625GB. NVLink 450GB/s uni: 3.0625/450=6.8ms. Compute step (7B, 4096 tokens, 8 GPUs): ~100ms. AllReduce: 6.8ms = 6.4% of step. Compute-bound. GPU efficiency: 100/(100+6.8)=93.6%.
details.realistic_solution: Per GPU: 14GB / 8 = 1.75GB gradients. Ring-AllReduce: each GPU sends/receives 2×(8-1)/8 × 1.75GB = 3.0625GB. NVLink per-direction BW: 900GB/s / 2 = 450GB/s. Time: 3.0625GB / 450GB/s = 6.8ms. With NVSwitch (all-to-all): (N-1)/N × data_per_GPU / BW × 2 = 7/8 × 1.75 / 450 × 2 = 3.06GB / 450 = 6.8ms.

scenario: Without reference, in 60 seconds: 'You have 8 H100 GPUs with NVLink (900GB/s). You're doing data-parallel training with a 7B FP16 model (14GB gradients). How long does the AllReduce take?'
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Fluency — AllReduce Bandwidth in 60 Seconds

details.common_mistake: Analyzing communications sequentially instead of recognizing that TP all-reduces (synchronous with compute) cannot be overlapped, but DP gradient AllReduce CAN be overlapped with backward pass.
details.napkin_math: TP-2 all-reduce: 14.9ms (unavoidable). Backward: 100ms. IB AllReduce (113ms) overlapped 50%: 56.5ms tail. Total step: 100+14.9+56.5=171.4ms. Util: 100/171.4=58.3%? Add TP comm in fwd: compute fwd+bwd=200ms with TP overhead included. Step: 200+56.5=256.5ms. Util: 200/256.5=78%. Compress gradients 4× (PowerSGD): IB: 113/4=28.25ms, overlapped 50%: 14ms tail. Total: 200+14=214ms. Util: 200/214=93.5% ✓.
details.realistic_solution: TP-2 within node: per layer, 2 all-reduces × 84MB (seq=2048, hidden=5120, batch=4) / 450GB/s = 0.37ms × 40 layers = 14.9ms/fwd+bwd. Cannot overlap (synchronous). DP-8 (4 GPUs per DP group × 4 DPs): gradient AllReduce after backward. Gradient: 13B/2=6.5B per TP shard × 2B = 13GB per DP participant. Ring over 2 inter-node IB links: 2×7/8×(13/8)GB = 2.84GB per GPU / 25GB/s = 113ms. Backward: ~100ms. Overlap: start AllReduce at layer 30 during backward (50% overlap): effective IB time = 113-50ms = 63ms sequential. Total: TP_comm(14.9ms) + compute(200ms) + IB_unparalleled(63ms) = 277.9ms. Without overlap: 327ms. Efficiency: 200/277.9=72%. To reach 90%: need 200/total < 10% comm: total ≤ 222ms. Need IB AllReduce ≤ 22ms. Requires 400Gb/s IB or gradient compression.

scenario: A 13B model is trained on 16 H100 GPUs across 2 DGX nodes (8 GPUs/node, NVLink 900GB/s intra-node, 200Gb/s=25GB/s InfiniBand inter-node). Profile and optimize the communication pattern: within-node TP-2 all-reduces, between-node DP-8 gradient AllReduce, and data loading via PCIe. Identify bottlenecks and quantify a communication schedule that achieves >90% GPU utilization.
title: Network Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Master PCIe+NVLink Communication Overlap Strategy

details.common_mistake: Applying ZeRO-2 to weights (which are NOT sharded in ZeRO-2, only gradients and optimizer states are); computing a 4× reduction on weights is incorrect for ZeRO-2.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 14GB. Grads ZeRO-2: 14/4=3.5GB. Adam FP32 ZeRO-2: 7B×4×2/4=14GB. Activations (10 checkpoints): 10×8×2048×4096×2B=10×134MB=1.34GB. Wait: 8×2048×4096×2B=134MB per checkpoint. 10: 1.34GB. Total: 14+3.5+14+1.34=32.84GB < 80GB ✓. Without grad checkpointing (40 layers): 40×134MB=5.36GB activations. Total: 32.86+4.02(extra layers)=36.86GB. 36.86/80=46.1%.
details.realistic_solution: ZeRO-2: weights replicated (not sharded). Gradients + optimizer states sharded. Per GPU: Weights BF16: 7B×2B=14GB (replicated). Gradients BF16: 14GB/4=3.5GB (sharded). Adam FP32 (m+v): 7B×4B×2/4=14GB (sharded). Activations (batch=8, seq=2048, gradient checkpoint every 4 layers, 40 layers → 10 checkpoints): 10×8×2048×4096×2B=13.1GB. Total: 14+3.5+14+13.1=44.6GB < 80GB ✓. Utilization: 44.6/80=55.8%.

scenario: Concretely size the per-GPU memory budget for fine-tuning a 7B model on 4×H100 (80GB each) with ZeRO-2 (shard gradients+optimizer states across GPUs, replicate parameters). Use mixed precision: BF16 weights+activations, FP32 optimizer states. Batch size 8 per GPU, sequence length 2048. Verify fit and compute GPU memory utilization.
title: Model Size Estimation: Realize Full Training Memory Budget for 7B Model on 4×H100

details.common_mistake: Students often forget that GPipe bubble fraction is (p-1)/(m+p-1) where p=stages, m=micro-batches, and conflate stage count with device count.
details.napkin_math: Bubble overhead GPipe: 3/19 = 15.8%. Activation memory per micro-batch for 32B model: ~2 bytes/param * 32B = 64GB just for params, activations add ~1.5x = 96GB total per stage. With m=16, GPipe stores all 16 forward passes = 16 * activation_size before backward, likely OOM on 80GB H100. PipeDream-Flush stores max p=4 in-flight micro-batches, feasible at ~24GB activation budget per stage.
details.realistic_solution: GPipe bubble fraction = (4-1)/(16+4-1) = 3/19 ≈ 15.8%. PipeDream-Flush with 1F1B achieves same bubble fraction but with O(p) memory footprint instead of O(m) activations stored. For 32B model across 4 H100s (each 80GB), PipeDream-Flush is preferred because storing 16 micro-batch activations in GPipe requires ~16x per-stage activation memory.

scenario: You are comparing GPipe and PipeDream-Flush scheduling on a 4-stage H100 pipeline (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s) with micro-batch size m=16. GPipe uses a synchronous flush after each mini-batch, while PipeDream-Flush uses 1F1B ordering. Calculate bubble overhead for each and recommend the approach for a 32B parameter model training run.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Bubble Overhead Comparison: GPipe vs PipeDream

details.common_mistake: Assuming more stages always means more parallelism and better throughput, ignoring that bubble fraction only decreases marginally while communication overhead and load imbalance grow.
details.napkin_math: Bubble fractions: 4-stage=8.6%, 8-stage=17.9%. Per-stage memory: 70B params at BF16 = 140GB total, 4-stage = 35GB/stage (fits H100 80GB), 8-stage = 17.5GB/stage (also fits, but bubble overhead is worse). Activation communication per boundary: 8192 * 2048 * 2 bytes = 33.5MB per micro-batch. At 32 micro-batches: 32 * 33.5MB = 1.07GB crossed per boundary per step.
details.realistic_solution: 4-stage: bubble = (4-1)/(32+4-1) = 3/35 = 8.6%. 8-stage: bubble = (8-1)/(32+8-1) = 7/39 = 17.9%. The 8-stage configuration has MORE bubble overhead for the same micro-batch count. Additionally, each inter-stage boundary sends activations: 70B model, hidden dim ~8192, sequence 2048, each activation tensor = 2*8192*2048 = 33.5MB. 8 boundaries vs 4 doubles communication. Prefer 4-stage.

scenario: A team is debating 4-stage vs 8-stage pipeline parallelism on H100s (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s) for a 70B LLaMA-style model. Micro-batch count is fixed at m=32. Compare bubble overhead, per-stage memory, and inter-stage communication costs. Which configuration is better for throughput?
title: Pipeline Parallelism Bubble Overhead Comparison: Stage Count Tradeoff
