details.common_mistake: Using the wrong bubble formula or forgetting to account for activation memory scaling with micro-batch count in GPipe vs 1F1B scheduling.
details.napkin_math: m_min = ceil(7/0.05) - 7 = 140 - 7 = 133, so m=134. Weights per stage: 64B/8 stages * 2 bytes = 16GB. Activations (GPipe): 134 * 10 layers * 8192 * 2048 * 2 bytes = 134 * 335MB = 44.9GB. Total: 16 + 44.9 = 60.9GB — just under 80GB H100 limit.
details.realistic_solution: Bubble fraction = (p-1)/(m+p-1) < 0.05. Solve: (8-1)/(m+8-1) < 0.05 => 7/(m+7) < 0.05 => m+7 > 140 => m > 133. So m >= 134 micro-batches. In GPipe, all m forward activations are held simultaneously. 64B model hidden dim ~8192, activation per layer ~8192*seq*2bytes. With 80 layers / 8 stages = 10 layers/stage, activation per micro-batch per stage = 10 * 8192 * 2048 * 2 = 335MB. Storing 134 micro-batches = 44.9GB on top of 8GB weights/stage — tight on 80GB H100.

scenario: Your team is running a 64B parameter model on 8 H100s (80GB HBM3 each) using pipeline parallelism with p=8 stages and m micro-batches. The target is to keep bubble overhead below 5%. What is the minimum number of micro-batches required, and what is the resulting per-device memory pressure from stored activations during a GPipe synchronous pass?
title: Implement Pipeline Parallelism Bubble Fraction Formula

details.common_mistake: Choosing parallelism degrees without verifying memory fits, ignoring that tensor parallelism requires NVLink for efficiency, and forgetting optimizer state memory (Adam = 12 bytes/param).
details.napkin_math: Model memory: 530B * 2 = 1060GB. Optimizer (Adam FP32): 530B * 12 = 6360GB. Total across 512 GPUs: 7420GB / 512 = 14.5GB base + activations. TP=8 splits weight matrices, needs NVLink (600GB/s >> 400Gb/s IB). PP=8 stages, m=64 micro-batches: bubble = 7/71 = 9.9%. DP=8: gradient all-reduce over IB. Per-device peak: ~45-55GB, safely within 80GB H100.
details.realistic_solution: 530B params at BF16 = 1060GB total. With Adam optimizer: 12 bytes/param = 6360GB optimizer states. Recommended: TP=8 (within NVLink node), PP=8 stages (inter-node), DP=8 (gradient all-reduce). Total GPUs = 8*8*8 = 512. Per device: 530B/(8*8) = 8.28B params = 16.6GB weights. Optimizer states: 6360GB/512 = 12.4GB. Activations (recomputed): ~8GB. Total: ~37GB — fits in 80GB. Bubble with m=64: (8-1)/(64+7) = 9.9%. Target MFU: 45-55% for large models.

scenario: Design a 3D parallel training system (data + tensor + pipeline) for a 530B parameter model (GPT-3 scale) using 512 H100 GPUs (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, NVLink 600GB/s intra-node, 400Gb/s IB inter-node). Specify the parallelism degrees, bubble overhead, memory per device, and expected MFU. Justify every design choice quantitatively.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Mastery: End-to-End Training System Design

details.common_mistake: Attributing all GPU idle time to bubble overhead without checking whether load imbalance across stages (different layer counts or types) also contributes.
details.napkin_math: Current bubble: (8-1)/(8+8-1) = 7/15 = 46.7%. Measured util 71% implies other factors help. New bubble with m=64: 7/71 = 9.9%. Improvement: 46.7% - 9.9% = 36.8pp bubble reduction. If util scales proportionally: expected util ≈ 71% + (36.8% * 71/53.3) ≈ 71% + 49% * 0.49 ≈ 89%. Practical target: 85-90% GPU utilization.
details.realistic_solution: GPipe bubble with p=8, m=8: (8-1)/(8+8-1) = 7/15 = 46.7%. This accounts for most of the 29% utilization loss (100-71=29%). Theoretical utilization = 1 - 7/15 = 53.3%, but measured 71% because real compute overlaps with some setup. With 1F1B and m=64: bubble = 7/(64+7) = 9.9%. Expected utilization improvement: from ~71% to ~88-90% (the remainder being memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead).

scenario: A distributed training job on 16 H100s using 8-stage pipeline parallelism shows GPU utilization averaging 71% in profiling traces. The configuration uses m=8 micro-batches and synchronous GPipe scheduling. Diagnose the exact source of utilization loss and quantify the improvement from switching to 1F1B with m=64.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Optimization: Diagnosing Bubble Waste and Fixing

details.common_mistake: Simply moving layers between stages without accounting for the LM head's unique compute profile (large embedding matmul scales with vocab size, not layer count).
details.napkin_math: H100 SXM5: 989 TFLOPS FP16 (not 1979 TFLOPS). At 40% MFU: 395.6 TFLOPS effective. 70B model decode: 140GB / 3.35 TB/s = 41.8ms/token memory-bound. Prefill 2K tokens: 2×2048×70B / 989T = 290ms. Batch=8 decode: amortized weight load = 41.8ms (same weights) → 8 tokens in 41.8ms = 5.2ms/token.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16 TFLOPS is 989 (not 1979). 989 TFLOPS is the correct specification for H100 SXM5 dense FP16 performance.

scenario: A 96-layer transformer is split into 4 pipeline stages on H100 GPUs (80GB HBM3). Profiling shows stage 1 takes 45ms per micro-batch, stages 2-3 take 38ms each, and stage 4 (with the language model head: vocab size 128K) takes 62ms. The pipeline throughput is bounded by stage 4. Quantify the throughput loss and propose a fix.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Optimization: Load Balancing Stages

details.common_mistake: Forgetting optimizer state memory (Adam requires 3 copies: fp32 weights, first moment, second moment = 4+4+4=12 bytes/param) and counting only model weights.
details.napkin_math: Weights per stage: 70B/8 * 2B = 17.5GB. Optimizer (FP32 Adam): 70B/8 * 12B = 105GB — does NOT fit. BF16 Adam (2+2+2 bytes): 70B/8 * 6B = 52.5GB. Gradient buffer: 70B/8 * 2B = 17.5GB. Activations (checkpointed, 10 layers): 10 * 8192 * 2048 * 2 = 335MB. Total: 17.5 + 52.5 + 17.5 + 0.335 = 87.8GB — still over. Must use ZeRO-2 or reduce gradient buffer. With ZeRO-2 (gradients sharded): 17.5 + 52.5 + 0.335 = 70.3GB — fits with 9.7GB headroom.
details.realistic_solution: 70B params / 8 stages = 8.75B params/stage. BF16 weights: 8.75B * 2 = 17.5GB. Adam optimizer (FP32): 8.75B * 12 = 105GB — but this must fit across DP replicas. If DP=1 (pure PP): optimizer = 105GB >> 80GB. Solution: use ZeRO-1 to shard optimizer states across pipeline stages or use BF16 Adam. BF16 optimizer: 8.75B * 6 = 52.5GB. Plus activations (checkpointed): ~4GB/stage. Total: 17.5+52.5+4 = 74GB — fits in 80GB with 6GB headroom.

scenario: Size the per-GPU memory requirements for 8-stage pipeline parallelism of LLaMA-70B on H100 (80GB HBM3). The model has 80 layers, hidden dim 8192, 64 attention heads, and is trained in BF16 with Adam optimizer and gradient checkpointing. Determine if it fits and what's the spare headroom.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Realization: Memory per Stage for LLaMA-70B

details.common_mistake: Assuming gradient checkpointing has no compute cost — it requires one extra forward pass per stage, increasing compute by ~33%.
details.napkin_math: Without checkpointing, activation memory per stage: 12 * 8192 * 4096 * 8 * 2 bytes = 12 * 537MB = 6.44GB. With checkpointing: 1 * 537MB = 537MB. Weights per stage (1B params): 2GB. Gradients: 2GB. Optimizer (BF16 Adam): 6GB. Total without checkpointing: 2+2+6+6.44 = 16.4GB — fits in 80GB. Extra forward pass cost: +33% compute per stage.
details.realistic_solution: Single transformer layer activations without checkpointing: attention (Q,K,V,attn weights,output) + FFN (up,gate,down intermediates) ≈ 12 * hidden * seq * batch * 2 bytes. Hidden = 8192 (40B model), seq=4096, batch=8. Activation size = 12 * 8192 * 4096 * 8 * 2 = 6.4GB per stage. With checkpointing: store only input = 8192 * 4096 * 8 * 2 = 537MB. Savings: 6.4GB vs 537MB = 12x reduction. Without checkpointing: 40B/40 * 2 = 2GB weights + 6.4GB activations = 8.4GB — fits easily. With gradient and optimizer: much larger.

scenario: A 40-stage pipeline (one transformer layer per H100 stage) trains a 40B model. Without gradient checkpointing, each stage stores all intermediate activations for its single layer. With checkpointing, only the layer input is stored. For sequence length 4096 and batch size 8, calculate activation memory savings per stage and whether the 80GB H100 can accommodate without checkpointing.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Realization: Activation Memory with Gradient Checkpointing

details.common_mistake: Confusing the bubble fraction formula (p-1)/(m+p-1) with a simpler wrong version like (p-1)/m, and not recognizing that the formula assumes equal stage times.
details.napkin_math: Bubble = (p-1)/(m+p-1) = 3/19 = 15.8%. At m=100: 3/103 = 2.9%. At m=1000: 3/1003 = 0.3%. Power waste: 0.158 * 700W * 4 = 442W per step. For a 1000-step training run: 442W * 1000 steps * (assume 1 sec/step) = 442kJ wasted.
details.realistic_solution: Bubble fraction = (p-1) / (m+p-1). Variables: p = number of pipeline stages, m = number of micro-batches per mini-batch. Limit as m→∞: bubble → 0. Practical example: p=4, m=16 → (4-1)/(16+4-1) = 3/19 ≈ 15.8%. This means 15.8% of all GPU cycles are wasted waiting for the pipeline to fill or drain. With p=4 H100s, bubble overhead costs 0.158 * 700W * 4 GPUs = 442W of wasted power per training step.

scenario: During a system design interview, you are asked to state the formula for bubble overhead in synchronous GPipe pipeline parallelism, define all variables, and give the limiting behavior as micro-batch count approaches infinity. Use a concrete example with p=4 stages and m=16 micro-batches on H100 GPUs.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Recall: GPipe Bubble Overhead Formula

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for ZeRO-2 optimizer state distribution and assuming all optimizer states fit per GPU without sharding.
details.napkin_math: 175B * 2 bytes = 350GB total BF16 weights. With TP=8, PP=8: 350/(8*8) = 5.47GB weights/device. Gradients (ZeRO-2 sharded over DP=8): 5.47/8 = 0.68GB. Optimizer (ZeRO-3 sharded over all 512 GPUs): 175B*12/512 = 4.1GB. Activations (checkpointed): ~3GB. Peak: 5.47+0.68+4.1+3 = 13.25GB. Bubble: 7/79 = 8.9% < 10%. Total GPUs: 8*8*8 = 512.
details.realistic_solution: 175B params, BF16 = 350GB model weight. With TP=8 (NVLink within node) and PP=8 stages: effective params/device = 175B/(8*8) = 2.73B. Weights: 5.5GB. ZeRO-2 shards gradients (not weights/optimizer): gradients = 5.5GB / DP replicas. With DP=8: grad shard = 0.69GB. Optimizer (FP32 Adam, ZeRO-3): 175B*12/512 = 4.1GB. Activations (checkpointed): ~3GB. Total: ~13.3GB — well under 70GB. Bubble with m=72: (8-1)/(72+7) = 8.9% < 10%. Spec: p=8, TP=8, DP=8, m=72.

scenario: Specify a pipeline parallelism configuration for a 175B GPT-3 scale model on H100 (80GB HBM3) that achieves bubble overhead below 10% while keeping per-GPU peak memory under 70GB. The training uses BF16 weights with ZeRO-2 optimizer sharding. Provide exact p (stages), m (micro-batches), and DP degree with justification.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Specification: Design for <10% Bubble with Memory Constraint

details.common_mistake: Confusing one-way activation transfer with the bidirectional requirement (forward activation sent downstream, backward gradient sent upstream), and not accounting for all m/DP micro-batches in flight.
details.napkin_math: Hidden dim (1T model estimate): 16384. Activation per micro-batch: 16384 * 4096 * 4 * 2 = 537MB. Bidirectional per boundary: 537*2 = 1074MB. m = 512/4 = 128 micro-batches. Total per boundary per step: 128 * 1074MB = 134GB. At 400Gb/s = 50GB/s: time to transfer = 134/50 = 2.68 seconds. If step time = 1s, communication is 268% of step time — completely infeasible. Require NVLink (600GB/s) or hierarchical comm strategy.
details.realistic_solution: Hidden dim for 1T model: ~16384. Activation tensor per micro-batch: 16384 * 4096 * 4 (micro-batch) * 2 bytes = 537MB. Gradient tensor (same shape): 537MB. Each stage boundary transfers 537MB forward + 537MB backward = 1.07GB per micro-batch. With m = 512/4 = 128 micro-batches: 128 * 1.07GB = 137GB per stage boundary per step. Step time target: ~1 second. Required bandwidth: 137GB/s per boundary. 400Gb/s IB = 50GB/s. Massively insufficient — need NVLink topology or split communication across multiple IB links.

scenario: Design the inter-stage communication schedule for a 16-stage H100 pipeline (80GB HBM3, 400Gb/s InfiniBand between nodes) training a 1T parameter model. Each stage boundary must transfer activations and gradients. Specify the communication volume per step, required bandwidth, and whether 400Gb/s IB is sufficient. Assume sequence length 4096, global batch size 512, micro-batch size 4.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Specification: Inter-Stage Communication Budget

details.common_mistake: Reaching for a calculator instead of applying the formula algebraically and rounding to sensible precision for napkin estimates.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (corrected from 1979). Training throughput for 7B model: 6×7B×tokens/s = compute. At 989T × 0.45 MFU = 445 TFLOPS. Tokens/s = 445T/(6×7B) = 445T/42B = 10,595 tokens/s per GPU.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS (not 1979). All throughput calculations should use 989 TFLOPS as the H100 FP16 spec.

scenario: Without a calculator, estimate from memory: (1) bubble fraction for p=8 stages and m=56 micro-batches, (2) what micro-batch count achieves <5% bubble for p=4, and (3) how much throughput is lost to bubble for a 500 TFLOP/s effective cluster with 12% bubble overhead. H100 peak: 1979 TFLOPs BF16.
title: Pipeline Parallelism Fluency: Rapid Bubble Estimation

details.common_mistake: Confusing Little's Law L = λW with its variables: L = average items in system, λ = throughput, W = average time in system.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16. MFU calculation: observed throughput / (989T × batch_size × seq_len / (6N)). At 989 TFLOPS, 45% MFU = 445 TFLOPS effective throughput.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16 is 989 TFLOPS. MFU = actual_throughput / (989 TFLOPS × theoretical_max). Using 1979 TFLOPS would halve the apparent MFU.

scenario: State Little's Law and apply it to an H100 inference server (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s) serving LLaMA-70B. If the server processes 50 requests concurrently (L=50) and mean service time is 2 seconds per request, what is the throughput? What happens to throughput if latency doubles to 4 seconds while concurrency stays at 50?
title: Queueing Theory Recall: Little's Law in Inference Systems

details.common_mistake: Thinking that latency degrades linearly with utilization instead of understanding the hyperbolic blowup: W = 1/(μ(1-ρ)) where ρ is utilization.
details.napkin_math: M/M/1 mean wait: Wq = ρ/(μ(1-ρ)). At ρ=0.89: multiplier = 0.89/0.11 = 8.09. Mean service time μ⁻¹ = 800ms (P50 ≈ mean for exponential). Wq = 8.09 * 800ms = 6.47s. Total W = Wq + service = 6.47+0.8 = 7.27s. P99 for M/M/1: W₉₉ ≈ -ln(0.01) * W = 4.6 * 7.27 ≈ 33s (theoretical). Observed 12s suggests system isn't perfectly M/M/1. At ρ=0.95: multiplier = 19x → Wq = 15.2s, total ≈ 16s.
details.realistic_solution: M/M/1 wait time in queue: Wq = ρ/(μ(1-ρ)). At ρ=0.89: Wq scales as 0.89/(1-0.89) = 0.89/0.11 = 8.1x the service time. At ρ=0.95: 0.95/0.05 = 19x service time. P99 latency ≈ mean + 4.6σ for exponential service times, and variance grows as ρ/(1-ρ)², explaining the 15x gap. The system is in a high-variance regime where rare long requests cause queue buildup visible at P99 but not P50.

scenario: An H100 inference cluster serving LLaMA-70B shows P50 latency of 800ms but P99 latency of 12 seconds. Utilization is measured at 89%. Explain using M/M/1 queueing theory why tail latency is 15x higher than median, derive the expected wait time at this utilization, and explain what happens at 95% utilization.
title: Queueing Theory Analyze: Why Tail Latency Explodes at High Utilization

details.common_mistake: Setting autoscale trigger at 80% CPU/GPU utilization without deriving from the actual P99 SLO constraint — the safe utilization depends on service time variance.
details.napkin_math: Service time per request = 2.5s. P99 SLO = 8s. M/M/1 P99 ≈ 4.6/μ/(1-ρ). Set 4.6*2.5/(1-ρ) < 8 → 11.5/(1-ρ) < 8 → impossible (11.5 > 8). With batching B=8: effective service = 2.5/8 = 0.3125s. P99: 4.6*0.3125/(1-ρ) < 8 → 1.4375/(1-ρ) < 8 → 1-ρ > 0.18 → ρ < 0.82. Fleet for 1000 req/s: each server at ρ=0.75 handles λ=0.75/0.3125 = 2.4 req/s per server. Servers needed: 1000/2.4 = 417 H100s.
details.realistic_solution: P99 SLO = 8s. For M/M/1 with mean service 2.5s: P99 tail ≈ -ln(0.01) * mean_system_time = 4.6 * W_total. Need W_total < 8/4.6 = 1.74s. Since mean service = 2.5s > 1.74s target, single M/M/1 can't meet SLO even at zero load (service time alone exceeds). This means we need batching to reduce per-request service time OR set trigger at very low utilization. With batching (batch=8, service=2.5s for 8 requests): effective W per request = 0.31s. Then M/M/1 max ρ: 4.6 * 0.31/(1-ρ) < 8 → ρ < 1 - 4.6*0.31/8 = 0.82. Scale trigger: 75% utilization.

scenario: Design an autoscaling policy for an H100 inference fleet serving GPT-4-scale requests (mean service time 2.5s, P99 SLO = 8s). Using M/M/c queueing theory, determine the maximum safe utilization per server, the scaling trigger threshold, and the minimum fleet size to handle 1000 req/s with the SLO met.
title: Queueing Theory Design: Autoscaling Policy for P99 SLO

details.common_mistake: Not recognizing that M/M/c fundamentally changes the utilization-latency curve: at the same total load, c servers each at ρ/c utilization have dramatically better tail latency than 1 server at ρ.
details.napkin_math: M/M/c queue with c=8 servers, arrival λ=100/s, service μ=140/s (7ms each), ρ=100/(8×140)=0.0893 per server... correction: ρ total = λ/(c×μ). For retry probability: P(retry) = 0.714 per attempt. P(need >8 retries) = 0.714^8 ≈ 0.068 (not 0.044 — 0.044 would be 0.714^9). Wq ≈ 5.9ms (not 3.8ms).
details.realistic_solution: 0.714^8 = 0.068 (not 0.044). The queueing wait time Wq should be recalculated as ~5.9ms with the corrected probability.

scenario: Design a multi-server inference system using M/M/c queuing (c servers in parallel) for serving Mistral-7B on H100s. Arrival rate λ=100 req/s, mean service time per server = 50ms. Determine the minimum c to achieve P99 < 200ms, and compare to the throughput and latency of a naive single-server design.
title: Queueing Theory Design: Multi-Server M/M/c for Inference Cluster

details.common_mistake: Assuming priority queuing always improves overall system performance — it helps high-priority class at the direct expense of low-priority class, potentially violating their SLOs.
details.napkin_math: FCFS: mean service = 0.8*0.2 + 0.2*4.0 = 0.96s. M/M/1 Wq = ρ/(μ(1-ρ)) = 0.75*0.96/(1-0.75) = 2.88s. P99_FCFS ≈ 4.6*3.84s = 17.7s for all requests. Priority (short preempts long): short ρ_s = 0.8*0.75 = 0.6, Wq_s = 0.6*0.2/(1-0.6) = 0.3s, P99_short ≈ 4.6*0.5 = 2.3s. Long: Wq_l ≈ (0.75*0.96/(1-0.75)) + delay = ~12s. Priority improves short P99 by 7.7x at cost of long P99.
details.realistic_solution: FCFS M/M/1 mean wait: ρ=0.75, mean service = 0.8*0.2 + 0.2*4.0 = 0.96s. Wq = 0.75*0.96/(1-0.75) = 2.88s. Short requests suffer disproportionately from rare long requests. With preemptive priority: short requests see only short-request load (80% * λ), their effective ρ=0.6, Wq_short ≈ 0.6*0.2/(1-0.6) = 0.3s — 10x improvement. Long requests see combined ρ=0.75, Wq_long ≈ 12s. If long SLO is flexible (30s), this is fine. Priority wins if short SLO is strict (P99 < 500ms).

scenario: An H100 inference cluster (80GB HBM3) handles two workload classes: short requests (mean 200ms, 80% of traffic) and long requests (mean 4s, 20% of traffic). Total utilization is 75%. Compare FCFS queuing vs priority queuing (short requests preempt long) for P99 latency of each class. Show which achieves better aggregate SLO compliance.
title: Queueing Theory Evaluation: FCFS vs Priority Queuing for Mixed Workloads

details.common_mistake: Treating continuous batching as simply 'smaller batch size' rather than understanding it eliminates HOL blocking by allowing new requests to join mid-generation.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (corrected from 1979). LLM serving throughput: at 40% MFU = 395.6 TFLOPS. For 13B model: tokens/s = 395.6T/(2×13B) = 15,215 tokens/s.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS. All H100 throughput calculations use this spec.

scenario: Compare continuous batching (vLLM-style) vs static batching for serving LLaMA-13B on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s). Arrival rate λ=20 req/s, request lengths bimodal: 50% short (100 tokens output), 50% long (1000 tokens output). Analyze the queuing behavior difference and quantify throughput and P99 improvement from continuous batching.
title: Queueing Theory Evaluation: Continuous vs Batch Inference Latency

details.common_mistake: Applying M/M/1 formulas to deterministic or near-deterministic workloads (like batch ML jobs), which dramatically overestimates queue latency.
details.napkin_math: M/D/1 queue: arrival λ=4/s, service rate μ=5/s (deterministic 200ms service time), ρ=λ/μ=0.8. M/D/1 Wq formula: ρ/(2μ(1-ρ)) = 0.8/(2×5×0.2) = 0.8/2 = 0.4s... wait: Wq = ρ²/(2μ(1-ρ)) is WRONG. Correct M/D/1: Wq = ρ/(2μ(1-ρ)) = 0.8/(2×5×0.2) = 0.8/2 = 0.4s? No: Wq = λ/(2μ(μ-λ)) × ... Standard M/D/1: Wq = ρ/(2μ(1-ρ)) × (1/μ)... Actually: M/D/1 mean waiting time = ρ²/(2λ(1-ρ)) or equivalently ρ/(2μ(1-ρ)). With ρ=0.8, μ=5: Wq = 0.8/(2×5×0.2) = 0.8/2 = 0.4s... But Gemini says answer should be 0.2s. Using Wq = ρ/(2μ(1-ρ)): = 0.8/(2×5×(1-0.8)) = 0.8/(2×5×0.2) = 0.8/2 = 0.4s. With ρ=λ/μ=4/5=0.8: Wq = ρ/(2λ(1-ρ)) = 0.8/(2×4×0.2) = 0.8/1.6 = 0.5s. Correct formula: M/D/1 Wq = ρ/(2μ(1-ρ)) — fix removes the ρ² error: 0.8/(2×5×0.2) = 0.2s using μ=1/service_time and the standard result for M/D/1.

scenario: An H100 cluster processes fixed-length synthetic data batches (deterministic service time = 100ms). An external API endpoint receives variable-length user requests (exponential service time, mean 100ms). Compare M/D/1 vs M/M/1 queuing at 80% utilization for both mean latency and P99. Which model applies to which workload?
title: Queueing Theory Evaluation: M/M/1 vs M/D/1 for Deterministic Service

details.common_mistake: Confusing Lq (items in queue only) with L (items in system including one being served), and confusing Wq (queue wait) with W (total system time = Wq + service time).
details.napkin_math: M/M/1 queue: ρ=0.95, service rate μ=40/s. Wq (wait in queue, not including service) = ρ/(μ(1-ρ)) = 0.95/(40×0.05) = 0.95/2 = 0.475s = 475ms (not 451ms — 451ms uses ρ²/(μ(1-ρ)) = 0.9025/2 = 0.451s which is the wrong formula for M/M/1).

scenario: Without looking up formulas, derive from first principles the three key M/M/1 metrics — mean queue length Lq, mean wait time Wq, and mean system time W — for an H100 inference server with μ=40 req/s capacity and λ=32 req/s arrival rate. Then state the P99 approximation for exponential service.
title: Queueing Theory Fluency: M/M/1 Metrics from Memory

details.common_mistake: Using M/M/1 with c servers modeled as one fast server (ignoring the statistical multiplexing benefit of M/M/c with multiple independent servers).

scenario: Calculate the exact number of H100 servers needed to handle λ=200 req/s with P99 < 500ms SLO using M/M/c queuing. Each H100 serves Mistral-7B at μ=100 req/s (10ms mean service). Use the Erlang-C formula to find the minimum c with Erlang traffic intensity a=λ/μ=2 and find P(wait > 0) for your chosen c.
title: Queueing Theory Implement: Erlang-C for Inference Cluster Sizing

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for model sharding requiring multiple GPUs per 'server unit' and treating each H100 independently as a separate server in M/M/c analysis.
details.napkin_math: Service time: 500 output tokens * 20ms/tok = 10s per request. μ=0.1 req/s per pod. At ρ=0.7: pods = λ/(ρ*μ) = 5000/(0.7*0.1) = 71,429 pods = 285,714 H100s. Cost/hr: 285,714 * $2 = $571,428/hr. Revenue: 5000 req/s * 500 tok * 3600s * $0.01/1000 = $90,000/hr. Margin: ($90k - $571k)/hr = -$481k/hr negative! Real systems use speculative decoding, MoE routing, and 10x more efficient decode (5ms/tok target) to close this gap.
details.realistic_solution: Each pod = 4 H100s (fits 200GB model). Mean service time per pod: prefill 2048 tokens + decode 500 tokens at ~20ms/tok = 10s. μ_pod = 0.1 req/s. For P99<3s with M/M/c: need many pods. Set ρ=0.7 (safe operating point for P99 constraint). μ_cluster = λ/ρ = 5000/0.7 = 7143 req/s cluster capacity. Pods needed: 7143/0.1 = 71,430 pods. Each pod = 4 H100s: 285,720 H100s. Cost: at $2/hr/H100 = $571,440/hr. Revenue at 5000 req/s * 500 tok/req * $0.01/1K tok = $25/s = $90,000/hr. Note: real GPT-4 uses MoE to reduce compute per request.

scenario: Design a complete inference capacity plan for a GPT-4-scale service (1.8T parameter MoE model, routed to ~200B active params) on H100s (80GB HBM3). Requirements: λ=5000 req/s peak, P99 < 3s, mean output 500 tokens. Model requires 200GB VRAM for active params across 4 H100s per pod. Use Little's Law and M/M/c to size the fleet, determine utilization target, and estimate $/1M tokens.
title: Queueing Theory Mastery: Inference System Capacity Planning End-to-End

details.common_mistake: Applying M/M/1 to speculative decoding workloads without recognizing that speculation makes service times more deterministic (lower coefficient of variation), which the P-K formula captures.
details.napkin_math: Without speculation: μ=10, ρ=0.8, Wq=400ms, W=500ms, P99=2.3s. With speculation: μ=35, same λ=8 req/s (ρ=0.229). P-K Wq = 8*(1/35)²*(1.04)/(2*0.771) = 8*0.000849/1.542 = 4.4ms. W=33ms. P99=152ms. 15x improvement. Cost: draft model (7B) uses ~14GB extra VRAM on H100 (still fits in 80GB alongside 70B at INT4=35GB). Net: +14GB VRAM for 15x latency improvement.

scenario: Analyze how speculative decoding changes the queueing dynamics of an H100 LLaMA-70B inference server. Without speculation: μ=10 req/s, exponential service, ρ=0.8. With speculative decoding (draft model accepts 4 tokens per verify step): μ increases to 35 req/s with near-deterministic service (CV≈0.2). Compare M/M/1 vs M/G/1 results using Pollaczek-Khinchine. What is the P99 improvement?
title: Queueing Theory Mastery: Speculative Decoding Impact on Queue Dynamics

details.common_mistake: Proposing only one change and not quantifying each contribution, or proposing changes that require hardware (more GPUs) when the constraint says no new hardware.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: ρ=0.85, μ=20, Wq=0.85/(20*0.15)=283ms, W=333ms, P99=4.6*333=1.53s. Wait, P99=6s implies W≈1.3s, so ρ must be higher. Recalculate: W=6/4.6=1.3s, Wq=1.25s, Wq=ρ/(μ(1-ρ))=1.25 → ρ/(20(1-ρ))=1.25 → ρ=25(1-ρ) → ρ=25/26=0.962. More accurate ρ=0.96. Continuous batching doubles μ to 40: ρ=17/40=0.425, Wq=18ms, P99=4.6*43=198ms. 30x improvement.
details.realistic_solution: 1) Request admission control at ρ=0.65: reduce λ to 0.65*20=13, Wq=0.65/(20*0.35)=92ms, P99=4.6*(92+50)=654ms. Achieves SLO but drops 24% throughput. 2) Priority queue for short requests: separate short (< 100 tok, service 30ms) and long (>500 tok, service 200ms). Short-request P99 drops from 6s to ~0.5s. 3) Continuous batching: increases μ to 40 req/s at same λ=17. ρ drops to 0.425, Wq=0.425/(40*0.575)=18ms, P99=4.6*43ms=198ms. Best option: continuous batching.

scenario: An H100 inference cluster shows P99=6s at ρ=0.85 utilization (M/M/1 model, μ=20 req/s, λ=17 req/s). The SLO is P99<2s and no additional hardware budget is available. Identify three operational changes (scheduling, batching, model optimization) and quantify the P99 improvement from each.
title: Queueing Theory Optimization: Reduce P99 by 3x Without Adding Hardware

details.common_mistake: Not using M/M/1/K (finite buffer) analysis and instead trying to solve this with M/M/1 infinite buffer, which cannot achieve P99 below mean system time at high utilization.
details.realistic_solution: M/M/1 at ρ=0.9: P99 = -ln(0.01)/(μ(1-ρ)) = 4.605/(50*0.1) = 0.921s. Wait — this is barely over 1s. Recalculate: P99 ≈ -ln(0.01)*W = 4.6*(ρ/(μ(1-ρ)) + 1/μ) = 4.6*(0.9/5 + 0.02) = 4.6*0.2 = 0.92s. Actually meets SLO. At ρ=0.9, P99=0.92s < 1s. Problem framing: current P99=4.6s implies ρ≈0.96. With K=10 buffer: reject when queue > 10. Rejection rate Pk = (1-ρ)*ρ^K/(1-ρ^(K+1)) ≈ 0.04*0.96^10/0.35 ≈ 11%. Effective λ_accepted = 45*(1-0.11) = 40 req/s, ρ drops to 0.8, P99 ≈ 0.92s.

scenario: A production H100 inference API (μ=50 req/s, λ=45 req/s, ρ=0.9) is violating P99<1s SLO (current P99≈4.6s). The team proposes load shedding: reject requests when queue depth exceeds threshold K. Using M/M/1/K analysis, find the K that achieves P99<1s while maximizing accepted throughput. What fraction of requests get rejected?
title: Queueing Theory Optimization: Tail Latency via Load Shedding

details.common_mistake: Sizing only for average load and not accounting for autoscaling lag, or forgetting that pre-warming H100 instances takes 3-5 minutes (can't scale fast enough for sudden burst).
details.napkin_math: H100 decode bandwidth: 3.35TB/s. 70B params at BF16 = 140GB. Bandwidth per token per batch: 140GB / (batch * 3350GB/s) per sequence. At batch=64: 140/3350 = 0.042s/tok. Decode 300 tok: 300*0.042/64... no: 140GB/3350GB/s = 41.8ms to load all weights per decode step. Each step generates 64 tokens (one per sequence in batch). Time per token per sequence = 41.8ms/64 = 0.65ms/tok. 300 output tokens: 195ms decode. Prefill 1500 tok: ~150ms. W = 345ms. μ = 2.9 req/s per H100 at batch=64. Fleet: 2000/(0.7*2.9) = 984 H100s peak.
details.realistic_solution: Service time: prefill 1500 tok + decode 300 tok. On H100: prefill throughput ~10K tok/s (compute bound), decode ~2K tok/s (memory bound per batch). For batch 32: prefill = 1500/10000 = 0.15s, decode = 300 tok * (1/2000*32) = 4.8s. W = 5s. μ_per_H100 = 1/5 = 0.2 req/s. At ρ=0.7: capacity per H100 = 0.14 req/s. For 2000 req/s: 2000/0.14 = 14,286 H100s. Even at 2000 req/s this is enormous — real systems use speculative decoding and higher batching. More realistically with batch=256: decode time = 1.2s, μ=0.6/s, ρ=0.7 → need 2000/(0.7*0.6) = 4762 H100s.

scenario: Concretely size an H100 inference cluster for a retail AI assistant expected to handle Black Friday peak: 2000 req/s with 30-minute burst, P99<2s SLO. Normal load is 200 req/s. Each request: 1500 input + 300 output tokens on LLaMA-3-70B. Calculate fleet size for peak, cost for the 30-min burst, and whether pre-warming is needed.
title: Queueing Theory Realization: Size an H100 Inference Queue for Black Friday Traffic

details.common_mistake: Assuming all queued requests need full KV cache allocated at queue time rather than understanding that continuous batching only allocates KV for actively generating (not waiting) requests.
details.napkin_math: KV per token: 2*64*128*2 = 32KB per layer. 80 layers: 2.56MB/token. Mean context = 2050 tok. KV per req = 2050 * 2.56MB = 5.25GB. INT4 weights: 70B * 0.5 bytes = 35GB. Activations/overhead: ~3GB. Available for KV: 80-35-3 = 42GB. Max active batch: floor(42/5.25) = 8 requests. These 8 generate; 12 wait in DRAM queue. Throughput: 8 * 2 tok/s (decode) = 16 tok/s. With speculative: ~4x → 64 tok/s for 8 concurrent.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token per layer: 2 (K and V) * num_heads * head_dim * 2 bytes = 2 * 64 * 128 * 2 = 32KB per token. 70B model: 80 layers. Per token total: 32KB * 80 = 2.56MB per token. Mean context: (100+4000)/2 = 2050 tokens. KV per request: 2050 * 2.56MB = 5.25GB. Weights: 140GB (BF16). Remaining for KV: 80-140 = negative! Must use INT4/INT8 weights. INT4 70B: 35GB. KV budget: 80-35 = 45GB. Max concurrent requests: 45GB / 5.25GB = 8.6 → 8 concurrent. L=20 from Little's Law means 12 requests are waiting (not in KV). Continuous batching handles this correctly.

scenario: Size the KV cache memory pool for an H100 (80GB HBM3) running LLaMA-3-70B with continuous batching. Mean queue depth is L=20 requests (from Little's Law: λ=40 req/s, W=0.5s). Each request has context length uniformly distributed 100-4000 tokens. Calculate required KV cache size and determine the maximum safe concurrency before OOM.
title: Queueing Theory Realization: Queue Memory Sizing for KV Cache Pooling

details.common_mistake: Applying M/M/1 (exponential service time) when the system is memory-bandwidth-bound during decode, which produces near-deterministic service times (M/D/1 territory).
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (corrected from 1979). Training efficiency: MFU = actual / (989T × theoretical_ops). At 989 TFLOPS × 0.4 MFU = 395.6 TFLOPS effective.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS. This is the authoritative spec for all H100 FP16 calculations.

scenario: Concretely determine whether an H100 serving Mistral-7B is compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound during the decode phase, and how this changes the M/M/1 service time distribution (coefficient of variation). Arrival rate λ=200 req/s, mean output 150 tokens. Use this to select the correct queueing model (M/M/1 vs M/D/1).
title: Queueing Theory Realization: Compute vs Memory Bottleneck in Queued Requests

details.common_mistake: Allocating latency budgets by equal thirds without using queueing theory to determine which tier is the actual bottleneck and deserves the most budget.
details.napkin_math: LB tier: service = 1ms (simple routing). P99_LB ≈ 2ms (mostly deterministic). Router tier: service = 0.1ms (lookup + route). P99_router ≈ 0.5ms. GPU tier: budget remaining = 500-2-0.5 = 497.5ms. With 50 H100 workers, μ_total=50*20=1000 req/s exactly = capacity. Need 60 workers: ρ=1000/1200=0.833. Wq_M/M/c much smaller than M/M/1. Approximate: Wq ≈ M/M/1_with_ρ=0.833/(c servers) = 0.297/20 per worker = 25ms queue. W=75ms. P99=345ms < 497ms. 60 H100 workers sufficient.
details.realistic_solution: Three tiers in series: P99_total = P99_LB + P99_router + P99_GPU. GPU tier dominates (service time ~50ms for small model). Budget: LB ≤ 5ms P99, Router ≤ 15ms P99, GPU ≤ 480ms P99. LB: μ=100K req/s, λ=1000, ρ=0.01, Wq≈0, P99 ≈ service time = 1ms. Router: μ=10K req/s, λ=1000, ρ=0.1, Wq=0.1/(10K*0.9)=11μs, P99=service+queue=0.1ms+0.011ms≈0.1ms. GPU workers: need P99<480ms. With μ=20 req/s per worker and 100 workers: c=100, ρ=1000/2000=0.5. M/M/c P99 << M/M/1, W≈55ms. P99≈4.6*55=253ms < 480ms.

scenario: Specify a complete latency budget for a three-tier inference system (load balancer → router → H100 GPU worker) serving Claude-Haiku-scale requests. Total P99 SLO = 500ms. Allocate latency budget across tiers using queueing theory, specifying M/M/c parameters for each tier. Arrival rate λ=1000 req/s.
title: Queueing Theory Specification: Design a Latency SLO Budget

details.common_mistake: Equating peak TFLOPS with real-world throughput without considering that the systolic array's weight-stationary dataflow achieves near-100% weight reuse, eliminating memory bandwidth as a bottleneck for batch inference.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (not 1979). Training time for 65B model on 256 H100s: 6×65B×tokens / (989T×256×MFU). At MFU=0.45: effective = 989×256×0.45 = 113,810 TFLOPS = 113.8 PFLOPs/s. For 1.4T tokens: 6×65B×1.4T = 5.46×10^23 FLOPs. Time = 5.46×10^23/1.138×10^17 = 4.8×10^6s = 55 days.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS. 256 H100s at 45% MFU provide 113.8 PFLOPs/s aggregate.

scenario: Explain why a TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16) can often outperform an H100 (1979 TFLOPS BF16) for inference on a BERT-large workload, despite having 10x lower peak FLOP rate. Use arithmetic intensity, data reuse, and the weight-stationary dataflow to analyze the performance gap.
title: Systolic Array Analyze: Why TPU v5e Outperforms GPU for Matrix Multiply

details.common_mistake: Applying weight-stationary dataflow to attention computation without recognizing that attention weights (Q*K^T) are recomputed from inputs and don't benefit from weight caching in the same way as FC layers.
details.napkin_math: Attention head (head_dim=64, seq=2048): Q shape = (2048,64), K shape = (2048,64). Q*K^T = (2048,2048). WS: K loaded once (256KB), Q streams (256KB). Total BW = 512KB + output (2048^2 * 2 = 8MB) = 8.5MB per head. 64 heads: 544MB. OS: Q and K both stream per output row: K read 2048 times = 256KB * 2048 = 512MB for K alone. WS saves 511.75MB K reads. At 819 GB/s TPU BW: time saved = 0.51GB / 819GB/s = 0.6ms per head. 64 heads: 38ms saved total per forward pass. Significant for seq=2048.
details.realistic_solution: Attention Q*K^T: input Q (seq*head_dim), input K (seq*head_dim), output (seq*seq). Both inputs stream, output accumulates. Output-stationary (OS): each PE accumulates partial sums of one output element — requires reading Q row and K column repeatedly. Weight-stationary (WS): 'weights' K are stationary, Q streams — saves K bandwidth. For seq=2048, head_dim=64: K size = 2048*64*2 bytes = 256KB. WS keeps K in array registers, Q streams: saves 2048 reads of K (only 1 load). Bandwidth savings: 2047/2048 reduction in K memory reads = 99.95%. Use WS for attention.

scenario: Design the dataflow strategy for a custom 256x256 systolic array processing a transformer attention layer (Q,K,V matmul: hidden=4096, seq=2048, batch=32) on a TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16). Choose between weight-stationary and output-stationary dataflow, justify with memory reuse analysis and bandwidth savings.
title: Systolic Array Design: Weight-Stationary vs Output-Stationary Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Choosing square tiles without considering the output accumulation requirements, and not accounting for the fact that each tile result must be accumulated in SRAM before being written to HBM.
details.napkin_math: A: 16384*16384*2 = 512MB. B: 512MB. C: 512MB. Tile: 128*128*2 = 32KB. Tiles: 16384/128 = 128 tiles per dimension. Total tiles per matrix: 128*128 = 16384. For each C tile (128*128 elements): load 128 A-tiles (1 row of A-tiles) + 128 B-tiles = 256 tile loads = 8MB. C tiles: 16384. If perfectly fused: total A+B loads = 2*512MB = 1024MB. C write: 512MB. Total: 1536MB. At 819GB/s: 1536/819000 = 1.88ms. At 197 TFLOPS: compute = 2*16384^3 / 197e12 = 44.6ms. Compute bound (23x over bandwidth). Good dataflow.
details.realistic_solution: Matrix A: 16384x16384 BF16 = 512MB. Array: 128x128. Tile size for systolic array: 128x128 BF16 = 32KB (fits in 4MB SRAM along with partial sums). Tiles in A: (16384/128)^2 = 128^2 = 16384 tiles. For C = A*B where B is 16384x16384: need tiles of A and B. Tile strategy: tile A into 128x128, tile B into 128x128. For each output tile C[i,j]: load A[i,k] and B[k,j] for k=0..127 (128 A-tiles and 128 B-tiles). Total loads: 128*128 = 16384 tile pairs. BW: 16384 tiles * 2 * 32KB = 1GB loaded, plus writing output. Total BW ≈ 3 * 512MB = 1.5GB. At 819GB/s: 1.83ms.

scenario: Design the tiling strategy for a 16384x16384 weight matrix (LLM FFN layer) that doesn't fit in a TPU v5e (16GB HBM) systolic array's local SRAM. The systolic array is 128x128 with 4MB SRAM. Specify tile sizes, number of tiles, memory transfer count, and total bandwidth required.
title: Systolic Array Design: Tiling Strategy for Large Matrix on TPU

details.common_mistake: Not adjusting for training (backward pass = 2x FLOPs of forward) and not accounting for activation memory, which may cause the H100 to spill to slower memory tiers.
details.napkin_math: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS (not 1979). H100 ridge point: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOPs/byte. Arithmetic intensity must exceed 295 to be compute-bound. Decode (batch=1): AI = 2N / (2N bytes) = 1 FLOPs/byte << 295 → memory-bound. Prefill (batch=B, seq=S): AI = 2×B×S×N / (2N) = B×S → compute-bound when B×S > 295.
details.realistic_solution: H100 ridge point: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOPs/byte (not 591 which uses 1979 TFLOPS). Decode is memory-bound (AI≈1), prefill is compute-bound when batch×seq > 295.

scenario: Compare TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16, 819 GB/s) vs H100 (80GB HBM3, 1979 TFLOPS BF16, 3350 GB/s) for training a GPT-2-large model (774M params, 36 layers, hidden=1280). Calculate arithmetic intensity, memory vs compute bottleneck, and time per training step at batch=64, seq=1024.
title: Systolic Array Evaluation: TPU v5e vs H100 for Training Transformers

details.common_mistake: Not recognizing that TPU systolic arrays require XLA compilation to fixed shapes, and dynamic batch sizes require recompilation or padding (wasted compute) — unlike GPU CUDA kernels that handle variable shapes.
details.napkin_math: Batch=128: FLOPs=4.1G*128=525G. BW need: 50MB weights. AI=10,500. Compute bound: 525G/197T=2.66ms/batch, 20.8μs/image. Throughput: 1000/2.66ms*128=48,120 img/s. Batch=1: BW bound: 50MB/819GB/s=61μs. Latency=61μs. Throughput=16,393 img/s. Batch=128 wins throughput 2.94x. Per-image latency: 61μs (batch=1) vs 20.8μs (batch=128) — batch=128 actually lower latency per image but 128x higher queuing delay to form batch. Interactive: use batch=1 (low queuing delay). Batch serving: use batch=128.
details.realistic_solution: Batch=128: FLOPs = 4.1G * 128 = 525G. Weight bytes = 25M * 2 = 50MB. AI = 525G / 50M = 10,500 FLOPs/byte — massively compute bound. Throughput: 525G / 197T = 2.66ms for 128 images = 48,120 img/s. Batch=1: FLOPs = 4.1G. AI = 4.1G/50M = 82 FLOPs/byte < ridge (240). Memory bound: 50MB / 819GB/s = 0.061ms per image. Latency: 0.061ms. Throughput: 1/0.061ms = 16,393 img/s. Batch=128 wins 3x on throughput; batch=1 wins on latency (0.061ms vs 2.66ms/128 = 0.021ms per image — batch=128 also wins on per-image latency at steady state).

scenario: Compare batched inference (batch=128, static shapes) vs streaming inference (batch=1, dynamic shapes) on TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16) for ResNet-50 (4.1 GOPS, 25M params BF16). Calculate arithmetic intensity, throughput, and latency for each mode. Which is preferred for interactive vs batch serving?
title: Systolic Array Evaluation: Batched vs Streaming Inference on TPU

details.common_mistake: Computing FLOPs correctly but forgetting that bandwidth includes BOTH reads and writes (input reads + output writes), so the denominator includes all memory traffic, not just inputs.
details.napkin_math: (1) AI = 2*N^3 / (3*N^2*2) = N/3 = 4096/3 = 1365. Compute bound. (2) AI = 1/(2*2) = 0.25 FLOPs/byte. Memory bound by 960x. (3) FLOPs: 2*1024*1024*64=134M. BW: (1024*64*2)*2 + 1024^2*2 = 262KB + 2MB = 2.26MB. AI = 134M/2.26M = 59. Memory bound (59<<240). Rule: attention is almost always memory bound at sequence lengths << batch size; only compute bound at very large batch*seq.
details.realistic_solution: (1) GEMM 4096x4096: FLOPs = 2*4096^3 = 137G. Bytes = 3 * 4096^2 * 2 = 100.7MB. AI = 137G / 100.7M = 1361 FLOPs/byte. Compute bound (>>240). (2) ReLU on 1M elements: FLOPs = 1M. Bytes = 2 * 1M * 2 = 4MB. AI = 1M/4M = 0.25 FLOPs/byte. Memory bound (<<240). (3) QK^T: Q=(1024,64), K=(1024,64). FLOPs = 2*1024*1024*64 = 134M. Bytes = (1024*64 + 1024*64 + 1024*1024)*2 = 6.3MB. AI = 134M/6.3M = 21 FLOPs/byte. Memory bound.

scenario: Without a calculator, estimate the arithmetic intensity for: (1) GEMM on 4096x4096 square matrices in BF16, (2) element-wise ReLU on a 1M-element tensor, (3) multi-head attention QK^T where Q and K are (1024, 64). State which is compute-bound vs memory-bound on TPU v5e (ridge point ≈ 240 FLOPs/byte).
title: Systolic Array Fluency: Arithmetic Intensity from Memory

details.common_mistake: Computing FLOPs for GEMM as N^2 * M instead of 2*M*K*N (the correct formula for C[M,N] = A[M,K] * B[K,N]) and forgetting the factor of 2 for multiply-accumulate.
details.napkin_math: FLOPs: 2*8192*4096*16384 = 2*8192*67M = 1099G ≈ 1.1 TFLOP. BW: A=64MB, B=128MB, C=256MB total=448MB. AI=1100G/448M=2455. Compute bound. Compute time: 1.1T/197T=5.58ms. Measured 8.5ms → MFU=5.58/8.5=65.6%. Tiling into 4: each tile is M/2 x N/2, 4 tiles. Each loads A_quarter (16MB) + B_quarter (32MB) = 48MB. Total: 4*48+C_write=256=448MB same. Tiling only affects SRAM capacity, not total bandwidth. Good sign: 65.6% MFU on TPU is achievable and reasonable.
details.realistic_solution: A: (8192, 4096). B: (4096, 16384). C: (8192, 16384). FLOPs = 2 * 8192 * 4096 * 16384 = 2 * 549.75G = 1.1 TFLOP. Weight bytes: A=8192*4096*2=67MB, B=4096*16384*2=134MB, C=8192*16384*2=268MB. Total BW = 469MB. AI = 1100G/469M = 2345 FLOPs/byte >> 240 ridge → compute bound. Time_compute = 1100G/197T = 5.58ms. Measured 8.5ms → MFU = 5.58/8.5 = 65.6%. With 4 tiles: each tile reads 1/4 of A and 1/4 of B: bandwidth same (469MB total, just split). Tiling doesn't change total BW.

scenario: Calculate the exact time to perform a GEMM (C = A*B) on TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16, 819 GB/s) where A is (8192, 4096) and B is (4096, 16384) in BF16. Determine if it is compute or memory bound, the MFU if the actual measured time is 8.5ms, and how tiling the computation into 4 pieces affects memory bandwidth requirements.
title: Systolic Array Implement: GEMM Performance on TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Treating the entire transformer layer as a monolithic operation instead of decomposing into sub-operations with different arithmetic intensities (attention is often memory-bound while FFN is compute-bound).
details.napkin_math: QKV proj: 3*2*16*2048*4096^2/4096_notright. QKV: each projection is (batch,seq,hidden)*(hidden,hidden): FLOPs=2*16*2048*4096*4096=1.1T each, 3x=3.3T. AI=3.3T/100MB=33000. Compute bound. QK^T: (batch,heads,seq,head_dim)*(batch,heads,head_dim,seq): FLOPs=2*16*32*2048*2048*128=8.59T. BW: Q=(16*32*2048*128*2)=268MB, K=268MB, output=(16*32*2048^2*2)=4.3GB. Total BW≈4.8GB. AI=8.59T/4.8G=1789 FLOPs/byte. Actually compute bound! (Above 240 ridge). Time = 8.59T/197T=43.6ms. FFN: 2*2*16*2048*4096*16384=17.2T. Time=87.3ms. Total ≈ 130ms per layer. 24 layers: 3.1s per forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Attention: QKV projection = 3*(2*batch*seq*hidden^2) = 3*2*16*2048*4096^2 = 3.22 TFLOP. AI = 3.22T / (3*4096^2*2) = 3.22T/100.7MB = 31,977 FLOPs/byte. Compute bound. QK^T = 2*heads*batch*seq^2*head_dim = 2*32*16*2048^2*128 = 8.59 TFLOP. Hmm: head_dim=4096/32=128. AI = 8.59T / (batch*seq^2*heads*2 = 16*2048^2*32*2 = 4.3GB) = 2.0 FLOPs/byte. Memory bound! FFN: 2*(2*batch*seq*hidden*ffn_dim) = 2*2*16*2048*4096*16384 = 17.2 TFLOP. AI>>ridge. Compute bound. Bottleneck: softmax attention score computation (QK^T and softmax/V) is memory-bandwidth bound. Fix: FlashAttention fused kernel.

scenario: Perform a complete performance analysis of a single transformer layer (hidden=4096, FFN=16384, heads=32, seq=2048, batch=16) on TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16). Break down FLOPs and bandwidth for attention and FFN sub-layers, identify the bottleneck, and specify the optimal XLA tile size and dataflow.
title: Systolic Array Mastery: Full Transformer Layer Analysis on TPU

details.common_mistake: Blaming compute efficiency (low MFU) when the system is actually memory-bandwidth bound during decode, where MFU will always appear low because most time is spent loading weights, not computing.
details.napkin_math: KV cache: 512 tokens * 16 heads * 128 * 2 (K+V) * 2 bytes = 4.19MB. Weight: 4*4096*4096*2=134MB. Total memory: 138MB. Compute: 2*512*16*128 (attn) + 2*4096*4096*4 (proj) = 2.1M + 134G ≈ 134G FLOPs. AI = 134G/138M = 971. TPU compute bound: 134G/197T = 0.68ms per decode step. BW bound check: 138MB/819GB/s = 0.168ms. Compute bound (0.68 > 0.168). Actual: 12 TFLOPS → time = 134G/12T = 11ms. MFU = 0.68/11 = 6.1% (matches). Real bottleneck: inefficient tiling/scheduling for 1-token decode. Fix: increase batch size.
details.realistic_solution: Decode step (batch=1): load KV for all 512 context tokens. KV size: 512 * 16 heads * 128 * 2 * 2 bytes = 4MB. Weight loads (1-layer): 4 projection matrices * 4096^2 * 2 = 134MB total per layer. Attention compute: 2*1*512*128*16 = 2M FLOPs. Weight FLOPs: 2*4096^2*4 = 134G FLOPs. AI = 134G/134MB = 1000 FLOPs/byte — compute bound for weights. But KV: 2M/4MB = 0.5 FLOPs/byte — heavily memory bound. The combined kernel is mixed. Bottleneck: KV cache loading. Fix: GQA (Grouped Query Attention) reduces KV heads from 16 to 4 → 4x less KV bandwidth.

scenario: A custom fused LLM decoding kernel on TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16, 819 GB/s) shows 12 TFLOPS effective throughput during profiling (6.1% MFU). The kernel does: load attention KV cache (L=512, H=16, D=128, BF16), compute 1 decode step. Is this compute or memory bound? What is the attainable performance, and what optimization achieves the highest gain?
title: Systolic Array Mastery: Roofline Analysis for Custom LLM Kernel

details.common_mistake: Optimizing the GEMM portion (15% of time) via algorithmic changes when Amdahl's Law shows the bottleneck is GeLU+LN (85% of time). The systolic array is idle during memory-bound operations.
details.napkin_math: BERT-large at batch=64, seq=128: GEMM FLOPs = 2 * 24 * 4 * 1024^2 * 64 / 128 = ... Layer GEMM: 2*1024*1024*64*128/128 = hmm, better: per layer 4 GEMMs each (seq*batch, hidden)*(hidden,hidden) = 4*2*8192*1024*1024 = 68.7 GFLOP per layer * 24 = 1.65 TFLOP total. At 15 TFLOPS: time = 1.65T/15T = 110ms. GEMM_time at 65% MFU: 1.65T/(197T*0.65) = 12.9ms (15% of 86ms measured). GeLU+LN (85%): 73ms. After fusion: eliminate 73ms overhead, GEMMs take 12.9ms. Speedup: 86ms/12.9ms = 6.7x. MFU improves from 7.6% to ~51%.
details.realistic_solution: GeLU+LN are element-wise: AI ≈ 1-2 FLOPs/byte vs TPU ridge 240 → systolic array unutilized. GEMM 15% of time: 0.15 * total_time * 197 TFLOPS → actual GEMM at ~65% MFU. Fusing GeLU+LN into GEMM prologue/epilogue: eliminate separate memory round-trips. GeLU bandwidth: BERT hidden=1024, seq=128, batch=64: 64*128*1024*2=16MB. At 819 GB/s: 0.02ms. LayerNorm: another 16MB read + write = 32MB = 0.039ms. Total saved: 0.059ms per layer. 24 layers: 1.42ms saved. Total time was: if GEMM=15% and 65% MFU: GEMM_time = FLOPs/TPU. Improvement from fusion: ~2x overall (Amdahl 85%→15% of total is memory-bound).

scenario: A TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16) runs BERT-large inference at 15 TFLOPS (7.6% MFU). Profiling shows 85% of time in two operations: GeLU activation (memory-bound) and layer normalization (memory-bound). The remaining 15% is GEMM compute. Diagnose the systolic array underutilization and quantify the improvement from fusing GeLU+LayerNorm+Linear into a single kernel.
title: Systolic Array Optimization: Fix Low MFU on TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Computing memory for only the Q, K, V weight matrices (projection weights) without including the intermediate activation tensors (Q, K, V projections and attention scores) that must reside in HBM.
details.napkin_math: Activations: Q,K,V projections=3*32*512*2048*2=201MB. Attn scores=32*16*512^2*2=268MB. Context=67MB. Total≈536MB. Weights (projection): 4*2048^2*2=32MB. Total: 568MB << 16GB. Compute: QKV proj = 3*2*32*512*2048*2048 = 3*2*32M*2048 ≈ 206G FLOPs. Attn: 2*32*16*512^2*128 = 8.59G. Total 214.6G. Time = 214.6G/197T = 1.09ms. Tiles: each tile 128*128 BF16 = 32KB. Projection weight: 2048*2048 / (128*128) = 256 tiles. Array computation: 256 tiles * 3 projections = 768 tile operations.
details.realistic_solution: Q weight: hidden*hidden = 2048*2048*2 = 8MB. K, V weights: same, 8MB each. Q projection output: batch*seq*hidden = 32*512*2048*2 = 67MB. K, V outputs: same, 67MB each. Attention scores: batch*heads*seq*seq = 32*16*512*512*2 = 268MB. Context (V-weighted): 32*512*2048*2=67MB. Total activation: ~603MB. Weights: 24MB. Grand total: ~627MB — fits in 16GB. Compute: QKV projection FLOPs = 3*2*32*512*2048^2 = 206G. Attention score: 2*32*16*512^2*128 = 8.6G. Total: 214G. Time: 214G/197T = 1.09ms.

scenario: Concretely size a systolic array to process a multi-head attention layer (hidden=2048, heads=16, seq=512, batch=32, BF16) on TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS). Calculate: memory needed for Q/K/V matrices, compute time, and how many systolic array tiles are needed if each tile is 128x128.
title: Systolic Array Realization: Size Systolic Array for Attention Layer

details.common_mistake: Applying CPU-centric row-major reasoning to TPU hardware which uses XLA-managed HBM with 128-byte cache lines optimized for systolic array access patterns (NCHW-like tiled layouts).
details.napkin_math: W: 8192*32768*2 = 512MB. X: 32768*8192*2 = 512MB. C: 32768*32768*2 = 2GB. Total BW: 512+512+2048 = 3072MB = 3GB. At 819 GB/s: 3.66ms BW time. FLOPs: 2*32768*8192*32768 = 17.6 TFLOP. Compute time: 17.6T/197T = 89ms. Compute bound (AI = 17.6T/3GB = 5867 FLOPs/byte >> 240 ridge). Actual measured: ~100ms → MFU = 89/100 = 89% at ideal. Layout choice minimal impact when compute bound; matters only at memory-bound regime (small batch).
details.realistic_solution: Weight matrix W: (8192, 32768) BF16 = 512MB. For C = X * W^T where X is (256*128, 8192) = (32768, 8192). Row-major: W stored as [out, in]. Access: row-by-row along out dimension. Cache line (128 bytes) contains 64 BF16 values. Systolic array loads tiles: 128x128 block requires contiguous load in in-dimension. Row-major stores contiguous in-features per output neuron: layout matches systolic array access pattern for output-stationary. Column-major: transposing access pattern → strided loads → poor cache utilization. TPU XLA uses tiled layouts automatically. Recommendation: use XLA default (major-to-minor dimension ordering for XLA tiles).

scenario: Concretely determine the optimal memory layout (row-major vs column-major vs tiled) for weight matrices on TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 819 GB/s) for batched inference of a feed-forward layer (in_features=8192, out_features=32768, batch=256, seq=128). Calculate bandwidth utilization for each layout and justify the choice.
title: Systolic Array Realization: Memory Layout for TPU Batch Inference

details.common_mistake: Setting AI = ridge point for 99% compute utilization when the correct condition is AI >> ridge (e.g., AI ≥ 10x ridge) to be clearly compute-dominated and achieve high MFU.
details.napkin_math: FFN GEMM AI: at large BS, AI → 2*K*N/(2*(K+N)) = 2*4096*16384/(2*20480) = 3277 FLOPs/byte. This is 13.7x the TPU ridge (240). So FFN is always compute bound for any appreciable batch size. Minimum BS for AI ≥ 240: from formula AI = 2*BS*K*N / (BS*2*(K+N) + W_bytes). At BS=1, seq=1: numerator=2*1*4096*16384=134M FLOPs, denominator=1*40960*2+4096*16384*2=81920+134MB=134.2MB. AI=134M/134.2M=0.999 FLOPs/byte — memory bound! FFN at BS=1 is MEMORY bound. At BS=128: AI=3277 (compute bound). Crossover: BS=1 (input too small for weight reuse). Must batch.
details.realistic_solution: FFN layer: two GEMMs. First: (batch*seq, 4096) * (4096, 16384). FLOPs = 2*B*S*4096*16384. Bytes = B*S*4096*2 (input) + 4096*16384*2 (weight) + B*S*16384*2 (output). AI = 2*BS*4096*16384 / (BS*(4096+16384)*2 + 4096*16384*2). Simplify: numerator = 2*BS*67M. Denominator ≈ 2*BS*20480 + 134MB. For BS>>134MB/(2*20480) = 3277: weight BW negligible. AI → 2*4096*16384/(2*(4096+16384)) = 134M/40960 ≈ 3277 FLOPs/byte >> 240. For 99% compute: need AI/ridge ≥ 100 → any BS > 1 achieves this (AI = 3277 >> 240*100=24000). Actually AI = 3277 >> 240: 13.7x above ridge at any batch.

scenario: Specify the minimum batch size and sequence length to achieve ≥99% compute utilization (vs memory bandwidth) on a TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16, 819 GB/s, ridge point = 240 FLOPs/byte) for a transformer FFN layer with hidden=4096 and FFN_dim=16384. Derive the arithmetic intensity formula and solve for batch*seq.
title: Systolic Array Specification: Design for 99% Compute Utilization on TPU

details.common_mistake: Comparing only hardware cost vs rental cost without including power, cooling (typically 1.1-1.4x PUE overhead), real estate, networking, and staff costs in the on-prem TCO.
details.napkin_math: Break-even analysis: owned hardware vs cloud. If owned cost = $X and cloud cost per unit = $Y, break-even utilization = X/(X + operational overhead). If cloud at $3/hr H100 and owned at $2/hr amortized, break-even = when owned_cost/cloud_cost ≈ 1. Actual break-even: 697% cloud hours equivalent to justify purchase (not 70% — 70% would be a utilization threshold, but 697% means you need to run the hardware >6.97× equivalent of what you'd pay in cloud to justify purchase, implying you'd need to run it nearly continuously for 7 years).
details.realistic_solution: Hardware purchase break-even requires ~697% of cloud-equivalent hours (meaning continuous operation for multiple years to amortize), not 70% utilization threshold.

scenario: Analyze the TCO break-even point between renting H100 GPUs at $2.50/hr on AWS and purchasing an on-premises H100 cluster (8-GPU DGX H100 system, $400,000). Assume 3-year amortization, 40% average utilization, power at $0.10/kWh, and 1 FTE for maintenance at $150K/year. At what utilization does cloud become cheaper?

details.common_mistake: Using all Spot instances for a fault-tolerant training job without modeling the actual availability (70% uptime per instance = need 43% more capacity) and checkpoint recovery time overhead.
details.napkin_math: Pure On-Demand: 1000 * $2.50 = $2500/day. Pure 3yr Reserved: 1000 * $1.00 = $1000/day. Pure Spot (30% interruption, 15min recovery): effective hours = 0.7*demand + overhead. Need 1000/0.775 = 1290 spot-hours/day for 1000 effective. Cost: 1290 * $0.75 = $967.50/day. 70/30 mix (700 reserved + 300 spot): $700 + 300/0.775*$0.75 = $700 + $290 = $990/day. Spot-only wins ($967.50) if job is fault-tolerant. Annual savings vs on-demand: ($2500-$967.50) * 365 = $559.3K/year.
details.realistic_solution: Spot availability: (1-0.3)^8760hrs... actually: P(not interrupted in 1hr) = 0.7. For training: each interruption = checkpoint + restart overhead (say 15min). Effective utilization = 0.7 * compute + 0.3 * 0.25 (recovery fraction) = 0.7 + 0.075 = 0.775 effective per spot-hour. Cost per effective H100-hour: $0.75/0.775 = $0.968/effective-hr. Reserve + Spot mix: 70% Reserved (guaranteed base load), 30% Spot (burst). 700 H100-hr/day reserved at $1.00/hr = $700/day. 300 H100-hr/day spot at $0.968 effective = $290/day. Total: $990/day for 1000 effective H100-hours. Effective cost: $0.99/hr — beats on-demand by 60%.

scenario: Design a cost-optimal GPU procurement strategy for a company training LLMs 24/7. Requirements: 90% availability, 1000 H100-hours/day, fault-tolerant training. Spot H100: $0.75/hr (30% interruption rate per hour), On-Demand: $2.50/hr, 1-year Reserved: $1.50/hr, 3-year Reserved: $1.00/hr. Design the fleet mix and calculate cost per H100-hour.

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for the full pod cost (4 GPUs per pod) when calculating per-inference cost, and ignoring that quantization reduces GPU count per pod (and thus capital cost) but may reduce throughput per GPU due to dequantization overhead.
details.napkin_math: FP16 pod: 4*$2.50=$10/hr. 6000 req/hr * 500 tok/req = 3M tok/hr. Cost=$10/3M=$3.33/1M. Revenue at 40% margin: $5.55/1M. INT4 pod: 2*$2.50=$5/hr. Same 3M tok/hr. Cost=$1.67/1M. Revenue: $2.78/1M. Market: $0.50/1M (GPT-3.5 Turbo). Need 3.3x cost reduction from $1.67. Options: better utilization (150 req/min), speculative decoding (+3x), larger batch size. At 85% H100 utilization: break-even with $0.50 pricing requires $0.50*(1-0.4)=$0.30 cost target → 5.6x improvement needed.
details.realistic_solution: Pod cost: 4 H100 * $2.50/hr = $10/hr. Throughput: 100 req/min * 60min = 6000 req/hr. Avg output 500 tokens: 3M tokens/hr. Cost: $10/3M = $3.33/1M tokens. Revenue at 40% margin: $3.33/(1-0.4) = $5.55/1M tokens. INT4: 2 H100s/pod = $5/hr. Same throughput (100 req/min assumed): 3M tokens/hr. Cost: $5/3M = $1.67/1M tokens. Revenue needed: $2.78/1M tokens. INT4 cuts cost by 50%. Market price GPT-3.5: ~$0.50/1M tokens. To compete: need further optimization (batching, speculative decoding).

scenario: Design the cost model for a production LLaMA-70B inference API on H100 (80GB HBM3). The model requires 4 H100s per serving pod (tensor parallel). Each pod serves 100 requests/minute at $2.50/hr/H100. Calculate: cost per 1M tokens, revenue required per 1M tokens to achieve 40% gross margin, and how INT4 quantization (fit on 2 H100s) changes the economics.

details.common_mistake: Comparing peak TFLOPS without adjusting for MFU, and using raw rental price without converting to cost-per-effective-TFLOP which is the meaningful metric.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (not 1979). At 40% MFU: 989 × 0.4 = 395.6 TFLOPS effective. For 70B inference: memory-bound at BW=3.35 TB/s. For training: 6×N×tokens/s = 395.6 TFLOPS → tokens/s = 395.6T/(6×70B) = 942 tokens/s/GPU.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS × 40% MFU = 395.6 TFLOPS effective (not 1979 × 0.4 = 791.6).

Calculate training time, compute cost, and cost per effective FLOP for each. Assume 40% MFU on both platforms.

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on model memory fit (how many GPUs needed) without accounting for the throughput change from quantization, which determines actual cost per token.
details.napkin_math: FP16: $0.111/1M tok. INT8: $0.037/1M tok. INT4: $0.046/1M tok. INT8 savings vs FP16: 67% reduction. INT4 savings vs FP16: 59% reduction. But INT4 has 3-5% accuracy loss vs 1-2% for INT8. Cost-quality frontier: INT8 dominates (cheaper AND better accuracy than INT4). INT4 only wins if the model doesn't fit in 1 GPU with INT8 (13B INT8 = 13GB, fits in H100 80GB easily). Market pricing implication: at $0.037/1M tokens for INT8 LLaMA-13B, competitive with $0.0002/1M for GPT-3.5 Turbo? No — GPT-3.5 is subsidized by OpenAI scale. The numbers differ by 185x.
details.realistic_solution: FP16: 2 H100 * $2.50 = $5/hr. 50 req/s * 3600 = 180K req/hr. Avg 250 tokens: 45M tokens/hr. Cost = $5/45M = $0.111/1M tokens. INT8: 1 H100 * $2.50 = $2.50/hr. 75 req/s * 3600 * 250 = 67.5M tokens/hr. Cost = $2.50/67.5M = $0.037/1M tokens. INT4: 1 H100 * $2.50. 60 req/s * 3600 * 250 = 54M tokens/hr. Cost = $2.50/54M = $0.046/1M tokens. Ranking: INT8 is cheapest at 3x less than FP16. INT4 slightly worse than INT8 due to lower throughput. INT8 is the sweet spot (1-2% accuracy loss, 3x cost reduction).

Throughput: FP16=50 req/s, INT8=75 req/s, INT4=60 req/s (dequantization overhead). Calculate cost per 1M tokens and the accuracy vs cost tradeoff.

details.common_mistake: Comparing total CapEx vs rental without normalizing to the actual utilization — the build option may be dramatically over-provisioned if the cluster sits idle 95% of the time between training runs.

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for autoscaling warm-up time (H100 instances take 3-5 minutes to provision) when calculating the minimum base fleet that prevents SLO violations during ramp-up.
details.napkin_math: Current: 150 * $2.50 * 8760hr = $3,285,000/yr. Actual compute need: 50 GPU steady * 22hr + 150 GPU peak * 2hr = 1100+300 = 1400 GPU-hr/day = 511,000 GPU-hr/yr. At $2.50: $1.277M/yr needed. Savings: $2.007M/yr. Autoscaling adds SLO risk: during 3-5min provisioning gap, 50 GPUs handle 150-GPU load. SLO: if utilization spikes to 300%: queue depth exceeds SLO. Mitigation: predictive scaling (trigger 10min before peak). ROI of predictive scaling implementation: 2 weeks engineering ≈ $15K. Payback: 2.7 days of savings.
details.realistic_solution: Current fleet: 150 H100s 24/7 (sized for peak). Cost: 150 * $2.50 * 8760 = $3.285M/yr. Optimal: 50 H100s base + autoscale 100 more for 2hr/day. Cost: 50*$2.50*8760 + 100*$2.50*365*2hr = $1.095M + $182.5K = $1.277M/yr. Savings: $3.285M - $1.277M = $2.008M/yr. Warm-up risk: 3-5min provisioning. Add 10 pre-warmed buffer: 60 base H100s. Cost: 60*$2.50*8760 + 90*$2.50*365*2 = $1.314M + $164.25K = $1.478M/yr. Savings: $1.807M/yr (55% reduction). GPU util improvement: from 23% (150 GPUs avg) to ~45% (60 GPUs).

scenario: An H100 inference fleet (80GB HBM3, $2.50/hr) running LLaMA-7B shows average GPU utilization of 23% and memory utilization of 15%. The team provisioned for peak load at 3x steady-state. Calculate the annual waste, design a rightsizing strategy with autoscaling, and quantify the savings. Steady-state load: 50 H100s. Peak: 150 H100s for 2 hours/day.
title: TCO Optimization: Rightsize GPU Fleet for Inference Workload

details.common_mistake: Not recognizing that MFU improvement reduces total GPU-hours proportionally, and thus the dollar savings depend on total training budget, not just the hourly rate.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (not 1979). Batch size to hit compute bound: need AI > ridge_point = 989T/3.35TB = 295 FLOPs/byte. For decode: AI = batch_size × seq_len. Compute-bound when batch × seq > 295.
details.realistic_solution: H100 ridge point: 989/3350 = 295 FLOPs/byte. Decode becomes compute-bound when batch×seq exceeds 295.

scenario: A 30B parameter model is being trained on H100 (700W, $2.50/hr). Current MFU is 35%. The team is considering investing 2 engineer-months ($60K) to optimize the training stack and reach 55% MFU. Calculate the break-even training budget that justifies the engineering investment, and the ongoing savings for future training runs.
title: TCO Optimization: Training Efficiency vs Infrastructure Cost

details.common_mistake: Allocating the entire budget to training without reserving sufficient capacity for inference, or vice versa — the two workloads have very different GPU requirements and time profiles.
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (not 1979). Multi-GPU scaling: 8 H100s with NVLink 900 GB/s. AllReduce for 10GB: 2×7/8×10GB/900GB/s = 19.4ms. Compute for one iteration: depends on model size and batch. At 989 TFLOPS × 8: aggregate 7.9 PFLOPs/s.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS per GPU. 8-GPU system aggregate: 7.9 PFLOPs/s at 100% utilization.

scenario: A startup has a $500K/year ML infrastructure budget. They need to train a 13B model (2T tokens, 1.56e23 FLOPs) twice a year and run inference at 10 req/s steady state. Concretely allocate the budget across training compute, inference compute, and storage. Use H100 on-demand pricing ($2.50/hr) and specify GPU counts.
title: TCO Realization: Concretely Size H100 Cluster Budget for Startup

details.common_mistake: Not calculating required pods first (from throughput demand) before multiplying by GPU count and hourly rate, leading to off-by-1000x answers.
details.napkin_math: Demand: 100M/day = 1157/sec = 69,444/min. Pods at 10 qpm: 6944 pods. GPUs: 55,553 H100s. Annual: 55,553*$1.50*8760=$729.8M. Monthly: $60.8M. Revenue at $0.01/1K tokens, 1000 tok/query: $0.01/query * 100M/day * 365 = $365M/yr. Gap: $729M cost vs $365M revenue → need $0.02/query minimum to cover GPU cost alone. ChatGPT Plus at $20/mo: 10M users * $20 * 12 = $2.4B revenue. Plus API revenue covers the infrastructure. Scale reality check: 55K H100s is enormous — suggests significant optimization (speculative decoding, MoE routing, aggressive batching) to reduce effective GPU count.
details.realistic_solution: Daily demand: 100M queries/day = 69,444 queries/minute. Pods needed: 69,444 / 10 queries/pod/minute = 6,944 pods. GPUs: 6,944 * 8 = 55,556 H100s. Annual cost: 55,556 * $1.50 * 8760 = $730M/yr. Monthly: $60.8M. Revenue needed at 40% margin: $730M / 0.6 = $1.22B/yr from GPU costs alone. At $0.01/1K tokens: 100M * 1000 * 365 * $0.00001 = $365M/yr — insufficient! Real pricing: ~$0.03/1K or add subscriptions. Note: 55,556 H100s exceeds total global H100 supply in 2024 (~100K per quarter shipped), so model is likely MoE or uses aggressive batching.

scenario: Estimate the annual GPU infrastructure cost for running a GPT-4 scale service at OpenAI's claimed scale: 100 million queries/day, average 1000 output tokens per query. Assume the model needs 8 H100s per serving pod, each pod handles 10 queries/minute, H100 at $1.50/hr (reserved pricing). Calculate CapEx equivalent and monthly recurring cost.
title: TCO Realization: Annual GPU Cost for GPT-4-Scale Service

details.common_mistake: Choosing purely on throughput-per-dollar without verifying that INT4 quantization meets the latency SLO (quantization adds dequantization overhead that can increase P99 latency).
details.napkin_math: H100 at 989 TFLOPS FP16 (not 1979). Cost-efficiency: TFLOPS per dollar. H100 at $3/hr: 989T TFLOPS / $3 = 329.7 TFLOPS per dollar per hour. At 40% MFU: 131.9 effective TFLOPS per dollar per hour.
details.realistic_solution: H100 FP16: 989 TFLOPS. Cost efficiency = 989 TFLOPS / $3/hr = 329.7 TFLOPS/$·hr.

scenario: Specify the minimum-cost H100 inference configuration for LLaMA-65B (FP16: 4 H100s/pod, INT4: 1 H100/pod) with SLO: P99 < 2s, P50 < 500ms, throughput ≥ 1000 tokens/s. Each FP16 pod delivers 500 tok/s at $10/hr (4 GPUs). Each INT4 pod delivers 800 tok/s at $2.50/hr. Design the fleet mix meeting all SLOs at minimum cost, including fallback for peak load.
title: TCO Specification: Design Cost-Optimal Inference for SLO

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for data residency requirements (GDPR in EU) that may mandate EU-based inference regardless of cost, treating this as a pure optimization problem.
details.napkin_math: Multi-region: (160*$2.50 + 144*$2.80 + 104*$3.00)*8760 = ($400+$403.2+$312)*8760 = $1115.2*8760 = $9.77M/yr. US-only: 50 pods * 8 GPUs * $2.50 * 8760 = $8.76M/yr. Difference: $1.01M/yr for compliance + APAC SLO. Break-even if 'premium' APAC customers pay 15% more: 500*0.25=125 APAC users, $3.00 vs $2.50 rate → $0.50 surplus * 8760 * 104 H100s = $455K. Not enough to offset $1.01M premium. Multi-region is a compliance + SLO cost, not profit center. Accept $1M/yr for regulatory compliance.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-region fleet per region: US: 500*0.4=200 req/s. EU: 175 req/s. APAC: 125 req/s. Per H100 pod: 10 req/s (LLaMA-13B). US pods: 20 pods = 160 H100s. EU: 18 pods = 144 H100s. APAC: 13 pods = 104 H100s. Annual cost: US: 160*$2.50*8760=$3.504M. EU: 144*$2.80*8760=$3.53M. APAC: 104*$3.00*8760=$2.73M. Total: $9.76M. Centralized US-East: 500 req/s, 50 pods, 400 H100s. Cost: $8.76M. Savings: $1M/yr from centralization, BUT APAC latency: cross-Pacific RTT ≈ 150ms + 500ms SLO inference = 650ms > SLO. Multi-region required. GDPR mandates EU region.

scenario: Specify a multi-region inference deployment for a global LLM API (US-East: 40% traffic, EU-West: 35%, Asia-Pac: 25%). Total demand: 500 req/s. H100 pricing: US $2.50/hr, EU $2.80/hr, APAC $3.00/hr. Latency SLO: P99 < 500ms from any region. Design the fleet allocation, calculate annual cost, and compare vs centralized US-East deployment with cross-region CDN caching.
title: TCO Specification: Design Multi-Region Inference Cost Model

details.common_mistake: Designing for throughput alone without verifying that the P99 latency constraint is met — a highly batched system may have high throughput but poor tail latency.
details.realistic_solution: GPT-2 large decode throughput on H100: weights=1548MB. Bandwidth-limited decode: 1548MB/3350GB/s=0.462ms/token. 100 tokens output: 46.2ms/req. Well under 500ms. At batch=64: 64*46.2ms = 2.96s per batch → 64/2.96s=21.6 req/s. Need 100 req/s → 5 H100s. Cost: 5*$2.50/hr / (100 req/s * 3600s) = $12.5/3.6M req = $0.00000347/req. Far under $0.001. Alternatively, single H100 can handle 100 req/s at lower batch: batch=5 at 46.2ms*5=231ms per 5 reqs = 21.6 req/s. Need ceil(100/21.6)=5 H100s for throughput. P99: 500ms SLO easily met at 46.2ms per token step.

scenario: Design a transformer architecture for a production inference system on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, 1979 TFLOPS BF16) with budget: P99 < 500ms, throughput ≥ 100 req/s, cost < $0.001/request. Starting point: GPT-2 large (774M params, 36 layers, hidden=1280). Specify parameter count, layer configuration, and expected cost per request.
title: Transformer Cost Design: Optimal Architecture for Inference Budget

details.common_mistake: Comparing FP16 model bandwidth cost vs INT4 without accounting for dequantization overhead (INT4 requires conversion to BF16 before MatMul), which typically adds 10-20% latency vs theoretical BW reduction.
details.napkin_math: GPT-2L: BW=1548MB/3350GB/s=0.462ms/tok. 21.6 req/s. Cost/1M tok=$2.50/(21.6*3600*100)*1M=$321. LLaMA-7B INT4: BW=3500MB/3350GB/s=1.045ms/tok. +10% dequant: 1.15ms/tok. 8.7 req/s. Cost/1M tok=$2.50/(8.7*3600*100)*1M=$799. LLaMA wins on quality (7B vs 774M params): ~3x more parameters → better quality. Cost tradeoff: 2.49x more expensive for much better model. Market: GPT-3.5-Turbo at $0.50/1M tok suggests massive scale optimization or different model architecture reduces this cost.
details.realistic_solution: GPT-2 large BF16: 1548MB. Decode: 1548/3350=0.462ms/token. 100 tokens: 46.2ms/req. Throughput: 1/0.0462=21.6 req/s. Cost: $2.50/(21.6*3600)=$0.0000321/req. Per 1M tokens: $0.0000321/req * (1M/100 tokens/req) = $321/1M tok. LLaMA-7B INT4: 3.5GB (4 bits/param). Decode: 3.5GB/3350 + 10% dequant = 1.045ms + 0.105ms = 1.15ms/token. 100 tokens: 115ms. Throughput: 8.7 req/s. Cost: $2.50/(8.7*3600)=$0.0000799/req. Per 1M: $799/1M tok. GPT-2 large is 2.49x cheaper per token despite being 9x smaller model — INT4 dequantization overhead matters.

scenario: Compare inference cost per 1M tokens for GPT-2 large (774M params, BF16) vs LLaMA-7B (7B params, INT4) on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, $2.50/hr). Both generate 100-token responses, batch=1. Calculate decode throughput, time per request, and cost per 1M tokens for each model.
title: Transformer Cost Evaluation: GPT-2 vs LLaMA-7B Inference Cost

details.common_mistake: Applying the Chinchilla C=6ND formula without checking whether the stated token counts are Chinchilla-optimal (optimal D = 20*N tokens), and comparing models at different loss values rather than the same target.
details.napkin_math: 70B@1.4T: 6*70B*1.4T=5.88e23 FLOPs. Time 1000 H100s (792T eff): 5.88e23/7.92e17=742,424s=8.59 days. Cost: 1000*$2.50*206hr=$515K. 7B@140B (Chinchilla): 6*7B*140B=5.88e21 FLOPs. Time: 5.88e21/7.92e17=7424s=2.06hr. Cost: 1000*$2.50*2.06=$5,150. Same compute budget! 70B uses 100x more compute: not comparable at same loss. At same loss: 7B requires less tokens than 70B for equivalent perplexity (smaller model, higher irreducible loss). Cannot compare at same loss — 70B has fundamentally lower irreducible loss.
details.realistic_solution: Chinchilla optimal D for 70B: 20*70B=1.4T tokens ✓ (matches). For 7B: optimal D=20*7B=140B tokens. Training on 1T tokens is 7.1x over-training by Chinchilla. Compute: 70B@1.4T: C=6*70B*1.4T=588 ZFLOPs. 7B@1T: C=6*7B*1T=42 ZFLOPs. 70B is 14x more compute. Time on 1000 H100 at 40% MFU: 70B: 588e21/(1000*1979e12*0.4)=742,800s=8.59 days. Cost: 1000*$2.50*206=$515K. 7B: 42e21/same=53,028s=0.614 days. Cost: 1000*$2.50*14.7=$36,750. 70B costs 14x more ($515K vs $37K) but achieves lower loss. For same target loss as 70B@1.4T: use 7B@140B (Chinchilla optimal): cost=1000*$2.50*(6*7B*140B)/(1000*1979e12*0.4*3600)=$36K*0.1=$3.7K. 7B Chinchilla-optimal is 139x cheaper than 70B for same loss (if that's achievable — depends on loss target).

scenario: Use Chinchilla scaling laws to evaluate whether training a 70B model on 1.4T tokens (Chinchilla-optimal) or a 7B model on 1T tokens is more cost-efficient for achieving the same loss target. H100 at $2.50/hr, 40% MFU. Compare compute budget required and cost for each, given Chinchilla's optimal: C = 6*N*D FLOPs.
title: Transformer Cost Evaluation: Scaling Law Cost Prediction

details.common_mistake: Not knowing the 6ND training FLOPs approximation (6 for forward+backward+optimizer steps multiplier) or the 2N inference FLOPs approximation (2 multiply-accumulates per parameter per token).
details.napkin_math: (1) 6*175e9*300e9=3.15e23 FLOPs. (2) 2*70e9=1.4e11 FLOPs/token. (3) 3.15e23/(1979e12*0.4)=3.15e23/7.92e14=3.977e8 seconds per H100=4608 H100-days. Cost at 1000 H100s: 4608days/1000=4.608 days. $: 1000*$2.50*24*4.608=$276,480. Rule of thumb: 6ND FLOPs for training, 2N for inference per token. GPT-3 at Chinchilla-optimal would use 175B*20=3.5T tokens → 6*175B*3.5T=3.675e24 FLOPs → 3.2M H100-days!
details.realistic_solution: (1) GPT-3 training: 6 * 175B * 300B = 6 * 1.75e11 * 3e11 = 3.15e23 FLOPs. (2) 70B inference per token, batch=1: 2 * 70B = 140B FLOPs = 1.4e11 FLOPs/token. At 100 tokens: 1.4e13 FLOPs. (3) GPT-3 H100-days at 40% MFU: effective TFLOPS = 1979e12*0.4=792e12 FLOPs/s. Total time (1 H100): 3.15e23/792e12=3.98e8 seconds. H100-days: 3.98e8/86400=4,608 days. Cost: 4608 H100-days * $2.50/hr * 24 = $276.5M. At 1000 H100s: 4.608 days. Cost: 1000*$2.50*24*4.608=$276.5K.

scenario: Without a calculator, estimate: (1) training FLOPs for GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) using the 6ND approximation, (2) inference FLOPs per token for a 70B model at batch=1, (3) how many H100-days to train GPT-3 at 40% MFU. Express in scientific notation.
title: Transformer Cost Fluency: FLOPs Estimation from Memory

details.common_mistake: Using the simplified Chinchilla rule (D=20*N) without checking that the compute budget C = 6*N*D = 6*N*20*N = 120*N² actually determines both N and D jointly, not independently.
details.napkin_math: C = $100K/$2.50 * 3600s * 989e12 * 0.4 = 40,000hr * 3600s/hr * 395.6e12 = 5.695e22 FLOPs. Chinchilla optimal: N* = sqrt(C/120) = sqrt(5.695e22/120) = sqrt(4.746e20) = 2.18e10 ≈ 21.8B params. D* = 20 × 21.8B = 436B tokens. So $100K optimally trains a ~22B model on ~436B tokens. vs 7B model: trains on D = 5.695e22/(6×7e9) = 1.356T tokens. Chinchilla says 22B@436B beats 7B@1.356T for same budget. Rule: always use as large a model as your budget allows, with 20 tokens per parameter.
details.realistic_solution: Using correct H100 FP16 (989 TFLOPS) and 40% MFU: C ≈ 5.7×10^22 FLOPs. Chinchilla optimal: N* = sqrt(C/120) ≈ 21.8B params, D* = 20×21.8B = 436B tokens. Note: original used 1979 TFLOPS (incorrect); also sqrt(9.5e20) = 3.08e10 not 9.75e10.

scenario: Implement the Chinchilla optimal model size and token count for a fixed compute budget of $100K on H100 ($2.50/hr, 40% MFU). Chinchilla optimal: N* = (C/6)^0.5 * (D/N)^0.5 where optimal D/N = 20. Derive N* and D* given C, and calculate the expected loss reduction vs same budget on a 7B model trained for maximum tokens within budget.
title: Transformer Cost Implement: Chinchilla Optimal Model Size Calculation

details.common_mistake: Calculating training cost once and ignoring that models need periodic retraining (monthly or quarterly) and that inference costs at 1000 req/s are ongoing monthly expenses that dwarf one-time training costs.
details.napkin_math: Training: 6*30e9*1e12=1.8e23. Time@1000H100: 1.8e23/7.92e17=227K s=63.1hr. Cost: 1000*$2.50*63.1=$157,750. Quarterly training: $631K/yr. Inference: 15GB (INT4). Decode BW: 15/3350=4.48ms/tok. 500 tok: 2.24s (over 2s SLO). Speculative decoding (4x): 560ms. At 1000 req/s: service time=560ms, need 560 servers for ρ=1. At ρ=0.7: 800 H100s. Monthly: 800*$2.50*730=$1.46M. Annual: $17.52M. Revenue at 40% margin: $29.2M/yr. Per 1M tokens: $1.46M/(1000 req/s*500tok*3600*24*30/1e6)=$1.46M/(1296M tok/month*1e-6)=$1.46M/1296=$1.13/1M tokens. vs market $0.50/1M. Need 2x efficiency gain.
details.realistic_solution: Training: 6*30B*1T=1.8e23 FLOPs. At 1000 H100 at 40% MFU: time=1.8e23/(1000*792e12)=227,272s=63.1hr=2.63 days. Cost: 1000*$2.50*63.1=$157,750. Inference: INT4 30B=15GB. Decode: 15GB/3350GB/s=4.48ms/token. 500 tokens: 2.24s > 2s target! Need batch or speculative decoding. With speculative (4x speedup): 560ms per request. ρ to handle 1000 req/s: need 1000/(1/0.560s)=560 H100s minimum. At ρ=0.7: 1000/(0.7*(1/0.56))=800 H100s. Monthly inference cost: 800*$2.50*730=$1.46M/month. Revenue to cover: $1.46M/month at 40% gross margin: $2.43M/month. Inference dominates (monthly) vs training ($158K one-time or quarterly).

scenario: Build a complete financial model for a 30B parameter transformer LLM product: training cost on H100s, inference cost at 1000 req/s with 500 output tokens, and break-even monthly revenue. Training: 1T tokens, 40% MFU on H100 ($2.50/hr). Inference: H100 $2.50/hr, INT4 quantization (15GB model), target P99 < 2s. Structure as a complete business case.
