title: Transformer Cost Mastery: Full Training and Inference Cost Analysis for LLM Product

details.common_mistake: Calculating speedup incorrectly by dividing tokens_per_step by acceptance_rate without accounting for the verification step that runs the full 70B model to check all 4 draft tokens simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 6ms/tok. 7B draft: 3.5GB/3350=1.045ms/tok. Verify (70B): 35GB/3350=10.45ms per verify step + draft 4*1.045=4.18ms = 14.63ms total per speculation round. Accepted: ~3.2 tokens (α=0.8, k=4). Effective ms/token: 14.63/3.2=4.57ms. Speedup: 6.0/4.57=1.31x. Cost reduction: 1.31x fewer GPU seconds. Revenue/cost: if current $0.001/req at 600ms, new: $0.001/1.31=$0.00076/req. Disappointing 1.31x — draft model overhead limits gains. Better: α=0.9 with specialized draft. At α=0.9, k=4: accepted=4*0.9/(1-0.9^5)=3.6/0.41=3.6/0.41=3.6*... actual: sum=3.6+0.36*0.1=~3.6. Speedup: (4.18+10.45)/3.6=4.06ms/tok. Speedup=6/4.06=1.48x.
details.realistic_solution: Baseline: 100 tokens at 6ms/token = 600ms/request. Speculative: draft 7B INT4 generates 4 tokens at cost = 7GB/3350GB/s=2.09ms per draft token. 4 draft tokens: 8.36ms. Verify with 70B: parallel verification = 1 full 70B step = 35GB/3350GB/s=10.45ms + 4*compute≈10.5ms. Expected accepted tokens per verify step: 4*0.8 = 3.2 tokens. Time per token: (8.36+10.5)/3.2 = 5.9ms/token (barely better). Actually speedup = (draft+verify)/(tokens_per_step) vs (verify_only): speedup = (1+k*α)/(1+k/μ_ratio). More accurately: at α=0.8, k=4 draft: avg accepted = k*α/(1-α^(k+1)) ≈ 3.2 tokens per verify step. Speedup ≈ 3.2x vs 1 token baseline. Cost: 3.2x fewer 70B invocations. But 7B adds overhead: memory for 7B INT4 = 3.5GB. 70B INT4 = 35GB. Both fit in 80GB H100.

scenario: A 70B LLM serving on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s) in INT4 (35GB) generates 100 tokens/request at 6ms/token (memory-bound). Deploy speculative decoding with a 7B draft model. Draft generates 4 tokens speculatively (acceptance rate α=0.8). Quantify the speedup, cost reduction, and memory overhead of adding the 7B draft model.
title: Transformer Cost Optimization: Reduce Inference Cost 5x via Speculative Decoding

details.common_mistake: Applying 6ND where D is total tokens = steps * batch * seq, not total samples, and confusing gradient accumulation steps with actual training steps.

scenario: Concretely calculate the total training FLOPs for BERT-base (110M params, 12 layers, hidden=768, seq=512, 1M training steps, batch=256). Use the 6ND approximation and verify by counting FLOPs layer by layer for one forward pass. Compare the two estimates.
title: Transformer Cost Realization: Concrete FLOP Count for BERT Training

details.common_mistake: Calculating activation memory per layer only for attention without including FFN intermediates, and not multiplying by number of layers for the total stack.
details.napkin_math: Activation per layer (BF16, no checkpointing): attention intermediates=150.99+805.3=956MB. FFN intermediates=784MB. Total≈1841MB. 96 layers=172GB. OOM. With checkpointing: input only=1*2048*12288*2=48MB/layer. 96*48=4.61GB. Fits memory. But weights: 175B*2=350GB >> 80GB. Even with checkpointing: need 4-8 H100s for weights. TP=8: 350/8=43.75GB weights per device. Plus activations: 4.61/8=576MB (if split by batch). Total per H100: 43.75+0.576+optimizer_shard≈50+GB. With ZeRO-3 optimizer sharding: fits in 80GB.
details.realistic_solution: Per-layer activation (without checkpointing): QKV: batch*seq*hidden*3*2 = 1*2048*12288*3*2=150.99MB. Attention scores: heads*seq^2*2=96*2048^2*2=805.3MB. FFN up+gate: batch*seq*FFN_dim*2*2=1*2048*49152*2*2=784.4MB. LN inputs: 2*batch*seq*hidden*2=100.66MB. Total per layer: ~1841MB. 96 layers: 96*1841MB=172.2GB >> 80GB H100. With checkpointing: store layer input only. Per layer: batch*seq*hidden*2=2048*12288*2=48MB. 96 layers: 4.6GB. Fits! But: model weights at BF16: 175B*2=350GB. Single H100 (80GB) can't hold weights. Need TP=8+ to shard model.

scenario: Concretely calculate peak activation memory for training GPT-3 (175B params, 96 layers, hidden=12288, FFN=49152, heads=96, seq=2048, batch=1) on H100 (80GB). Without gradient checkpointing: all layer activations stored. With checkpointing: only layer inputs. Determine if either fits and whether model parallelism is required.
title: Transformer Cost Realization: Size Activation Memory for LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Confusing bubble ratio with throughput degradation; the bubble ratio measures idle fraction, not absolute throughput, and memory savings from fewer micro-batches may force smaller batch sizes.
details.napkin_math: Bubble ratio = (p-1)/(m+p-1). m=16: 7/23=30.4%. m=8: 7/15=46.7%. Throughput ratio: (1-0.467)/(1-0.304)=0.766. 23% throughput loss. Useful throughput at 312 TFLOP/s H100: 0.766×0.696×312=167 TFLOP/s effective vs 217 TFLOP/s at m=16.
details.realistic_solution: Bubble ratio with m=16: (8-1)/(16+8-1) = 7/23 = 30.4%. With m=8: (8-1)/(8+8-1) = 7/15 = 46.7%. Throughput decreases by (1-0.467)/(1-0.304) = 0.533/0.696 = 76.6% — a 23% throughput loss. Memory per GPU: activation memory ∝ m. At m=8, peak activation memory per micro-batch doubles (recomputation cost per micro-batch increases). The trade-off only makes sense if memory was the critical bottleneck.

scenario: A GPipe pipeline splits a 96-layer transformer across 8 H100 GPUs (12 layers/stage) with micro-batch count m=16. Training a 70B parameter model with global batch 1024, the pipeline bubble ratio is (p-1)/(m+p-1). A colleague proposes reducing to m=8 micro-batches to cut memory, arguing it won't affect throughput. Analyze the throughput impact and calculate the bubble ratio change.
title: Analyze GPipe Bubble Overhead in Pipeline Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Applying GPipe bubble formula to 1F1B; 1F1B has the same bubble ratio formula but limits in-flight micro-batches to p (not m), reducing peak activation memory from O(mp) to O(p).
details.napkin_math: Bubble ratio: (16-1)/(16+16-1) = 15/31 = 48.4%. Steady-state efficiency: 51.6%. Cycle time: 16ms (backward). Total pipeline time: 31×16ms=496ms per global batch. Throughput: 2048 samples × 2048 tokens / 496ms = 8.46M tokens/s across 16 GPUs = 528K tokens/s/GPU.
details.realistic_solution: 1F1B bubble ratio: same (p-1)/(m+p-1) = 15/31 = 48.4% as GPipe with same m and p. But memory advantage: GPipe holds all m micro-batch activations simultaneously → 16×activation. 1F1B holds only p=16 at peak but in steady state only 1 per stage → p activations max. Memory reduction: 16× vs GPipe if m>p. Throughput: steady-state = m/(m+p-1) per pipeline cycle. With m=16, p=16: 16/31 = 51.6% efficiency. Each pipeline cycle = max(F,B) = 16ms. Tokens/s: 2048×(seq_len)/0.016 = 2048×2048/0.016... need seq_len. With seq=2048: 2048×2048 / (16ms × 31 cycles) = 4M / 496ms = 8.06M tokens/s.

scenario: You are designing a 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) pipeline schedule for training a 175B GPT model across 16 H100 GPUs with pipeline parallelism degree p=16. Each forward pass per micro-batch takes 8ms per stage; backward takes 16ms. Global batch = 2048, micro-batch size = 128, giving m=16 micro-batches. Design the schedule and compute steady-state throughput and bubble ratio vs GPipe.
title: Design 1F1B Pipeline Schedule for LLM Training on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Assuming interleaved scheduling reduces bubble to zero; it reduces bubble ratio by factor v but doubles pipeline communication volume at stage boundaries.
details.napkin_math: Interleaved bubble: (p-1)/(mv+p-1) = 7/23 = 30.4%. Standard: 7/15 = 46.7%. Reduction: 16.3pp. Communication overhead: 14 extra transfers × 4.4μs = 62μs / 16,000μs stage = 0.4% overhead. Net gain: +16.3% efficiency - 0.4% comm = +15.9% throughput improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Standard 1F1B bubble: (8-1)/(8+8-1) = 7/15 = 46.7%. Interleaved with v=2: (8-1)/(8×2+8-1) = 7/23 = 30.4% — same as GPipe with m=16. Efficiency: 69.6% vs 53.3%. Improvement: 16.3pp. Communication cost: standard 1F1B has 2×(p-1)=14 activation transfers per pipeline pass. Interleaved v=2: 2×(p-1)×v=28 transfers. With NVLink 900 GB/s between H100s and 1M token activations at BF16 (4MB): each transfer = 4MB/900GB/s = 4.4μs. Extra latency: 14×4.4μs=62μs per step — negligible vs 16ms stage time (0.4% overhead).

scenario: A 48-layer transformer trains on 8 H100 GPUs with standard 1F1B achieving 46.7% bubble ratio (m=8, p=8). You propose interleaved pipeline parallelism with v=2 virtual stages per GPU (each GPU handles 2 non-contiguous layer chunks of 3 layers each). The interleaved bubble ratio formula is (p-1)/(m×v+p-1). Calculate the new bubble ratio and steady-state efficiency, and identify the additional communication cost from doubled pipeline boundaries.
title: Design Interleaved Pipeline Schedule for Reduced Bubble

details.common_mistake: Rebalancing layers by count alone (8 layers each); the embedding lookup and LM head are O(vocab×dim) operations that dominate when vocabulary is large (e.g., 128K tokens).
details.napkin_math: Current bottleneck: 14ms (Stage 3). Bubble ratio: (4-1)/(8+4-1) = 3/11 = 27.3% at 8ms stages, but actual bottleneck is 14ms → effective efficiency = 8/14×(1-3/11) = 57%×72.7% = 41.5%. Rebalanced to 10ms: efficiency = 1 - 3/15 = 80%. Throughput gain: 80/41.5 = 1.93× — nearly 2× improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Stage 0 slow: embedding lookup (128K×8192 table, FP16) = 2GB; load time = 2GB/2000GB/s (H100 HBM) = 1ms + compute = 2ms. Main issue: first 8 layers include self-attention with KV cache allocation overhead. Stage 3 slow: LM head projection (8192→128K) = 8192×128K×2B = 2GB → 4ms + layer 32. Fix: (1) Move embedding to Stage 0 but parallelize vocab dimension. (2) Move LM head to Stage 1 and pipeline embedding lookup. (3) Rebalance: Stage 0: emb + layers 1-6; Stage 1: layers 7-16; Stage 2: layers 17-26; Stage 3: layers 27-32 + LM head. Test new latencies targeting ≤10ms per stage.

scenario: A 4-stage pipeline of a 32-layer transformer on H100 GPUs shows stage latencies: Stage 0: 12ms (embedding + layers 1-8), Stage 1: 8ms (layers 9-16), Stage 2: 8ms (layers 17-24), Stage 3: 14ms (layers 25-32 + LM head). Pipeline throughput is limited to 14ms per stage cycle. The theoretical bubble-free throughput at 8ms uniform stages would be 43% higher. Diagnose and fix the stage imbalance.
title: Diagnose Load Imbalance Across Pipeline Stages on H100

details.common_mistake: Adding more GPU capacity to reduce utilization; at 60% utilization the P99 blowup is caused by high service time variance (HoL blocking), not insufficient capacity.
details.napkin_math: CV² ≈ 0.94 (bimodal 50ms vs 3200ms). M/G/1 mean wait = λE[S²]/(2(1-ρ)) = 0.6×5.12M/(2×0.4×1625) = 3072K/1300 = 2363ms. P99 ≈ mean + 4.6σ for exponential tail ≈ 4.2s observed. SJF reduces P99 for short jobs to < 300ms.
details.realistic_solution: CV of service time: mean = 0.5×50 + 0.5×3200 = 1625ms; mean² = 1625² = 2.64M; E[S²] = 0.5×50² + 0.5×3200² = 0.5×(2500+10.24M) = 5.12M. Variance = 5.12M - 2.64M = 2.48M. CV = sqrt(2.48M)/1625 = 1575/1625 = 0.97. M/G/1 wait: ρCV²/(2(1-ρ)) × mean = 0.6×0.94/(2×0.4) × 1625 = 0.564/0.8 × 1625 = 1144ms waiting. P99 ≈ 5× mean wait = 5.7s ≈ observed 4.2s. Fix: shortest-job-first (SJF) or length-based priority queues. Short prompts (<512 tokens) get priority lane. P99 for short drops to ~200ms.

scenario: An LLM serving system on H100 clusters processes requests with median latency 180ms and P99 latency 4.2 seconds at 60% utilization. The service time distribution has high variance: short prompts (128 tokens) take 50ms; long prompts (8192 tokens) take 3.2 seconds. The system uses FCFS scheduling. Queueing theory analysis shows M/G/1 P99 = median × (1 + CV²×ρ/(1-ρ)) where CV is coefficient of variation. Diagnose the root cause and prescribe the fix.
title: Diagnose Head-of-Line Blocking in LLM Serving Queue

details.common_mistake: Confusing weight-stationary with output-stationary; in weight-stationary, weights are loaded once and held in register files while inputs flow through, but outputs accumulate across multiple input vectors.
details.napkin_math: H100 NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s. Activation tensor: 4M params × 2B = 8MB. Transfer time: 8MB / 900 GB/s = 8×10^-3 / 900 = 8.89×10^-6 s ≈ 8.9μs ≈ 9.3μs with protocol overhead (not 18.5μs which would use 450 GB/s).
details.realistic_solution: NVLink transfer: 4M×2B = 8MB. At 900 GB/s: 8MB/900GB/s = 8.9μs ≈ 9.3μs with overhead (not 18.5μs which halves the bandwidth).

scenario: An interviewer asks: in a weight-stationary systolic array like the original TPU v1 (256×256 MAC array), what data moves during matrix multiply and what stays stationary? Specifically: for a 256×256 weight matrix W and a batch of 64 input vectors x, how many times is each weight element read from memory, and what is the total data movement compared to a naive implementation?
title: Recall Systolic Array Weight-Stationary Dataflow

details.common_mistake: Attributing low utilization to memory bandwidth bottleneck; at batch=1, the systolic array has a geometric mismatch — the input vector has only 1 row, filling only 1/256 of the array's row capacity.
details.napkin_math: Array size: 256×256. Batch=1: 1/256 = 0.39% row utilization ≈ observed 0.4%. Batch=128: 128/256 = 50%. Batch=256: 100%. At 50% util: 0.5×197 TOPS = 98.5 TOPS effective. With batch=256: 197 TOPS = 197×10¹² / (2×8192×4096×256) ops per step = 197T/17.2G = 11,456 steps/s.
details.realistic_solution: Systolic 256×256 array operates on 256 rows simultaneously. Input [1×8192] feeds only 1 row → 255/256 = 99.6% of PEs idle. For 50% utilization: need at least 128 rows = batch size 128. At batch 128: X=[128×8192], W=[8192×4096]. The array can process 256 rows; 128/256=50% row utilization. Column dimension: 4096/256=16 tiles, each 100% utilized. Effective utilization: 50%×100%=50%. Minimum batch for 50%: 128. Practical recommendation: batch=256 for full utilization. For latency-constrained decode: use continuous batching to aggregate requests.

scenario: A TPU v5e (256×256 systolic array, 197 TOPS BF16) is running a transformer's feedforward layer with matrix dimensions W: [8192×4096] multiplied by batch X: [1×8192] (decode mode, batch size 1). Profiling shows only 0.4% hardware utilization. Diagnose why utilization collapses at batch size 1 and propose minimum batch size for >50% utilization.
title: Diagnose Systolic Array Underutilization for Non-Square Matrices

details.common_mistake: Computing only hardware cost without including power, cooling (PUE), and utilization discount; also forgetting to amortize over utilization hours not calendar hours.
details.napkin_math: CapEx: $30K / (3×8760h) = $1.14/GPU/h. With 1.5× infra multiplier: $1.71/h. Power: 0.98kW × $0.12 = $0.12/h. Total: $1.83/GPU/h. Cloud H100 at $2.20/h: on-prem saves $0.37/h × 8 GPUs × 8760h × 0.7 util = $18,240/year per 8-GPU node.
details.realistic_solution: CapEx per GPU: $30,000. Amortization: 3 years × 8760 h/year = 26,280 h total. At 70% utilization: 18,396 productive hours. CapEx rate: $30,000/26,280h = $1.14/h/GPU (calendar). Including networking, racks, etc. (1.5× multiplier): $1.71/h. Power: 700W × 1.4 PUE = 980W per GPU. Power cost: 980W × $0.12/kWh / 1000 = $0.118/h. Total fully-loaded: $1.71 + $0.12 = $1.83/h per GPU. Cloud H100 spot: ~$2.00-2.50/h. On-prem saves ~$0.20-0.67/h per GPU if fully utilized.

scenario: During a cloud ML infrastructure interview, you are asked: for an on-premises H100 cluster with 8 GPUs at $30,000/GPU, 3-year depreciation, 70% average utilization, $0.12/kWh electricity, 700W TDP per GPU, and 1.4 PUE data center overhead — what is the fully-loaded hourly cost per GPU including CapEx amortization and OpEx?
title: Recall TCO CapEx vs OpEx Split for GPU Cloud Training

details.common_mistake: Charging only for GPU-hours without including shared infrastructure costs; storage (checkpoint I/O), networking (AllReduce), and cooling overhead are real costs that must be allocated.
details.napkin_math: 175B job: 32×336h×$1.80 = $19,354. Storage overhead: 32GPUs×$0.10×336h = $1,075. Total: $20,429. Per GPU-hour effective rate: $20,429/(32×336)=$1.90/GPU/h (5.6% overhead). 7B: $1,094 total. Cluster idle (24 GPUs): $14,515/14days = $1,037/day cluster ops cost.
details.realistic_solution: (1) 175B job: 32 GPUs × 14×24h × $1.80 = 32×336×1.80 = $19,353.60. (2) 7B job: 8 GPUs × 3×24h × $1.80 = 8×72×1.80 = $1,036.80. (3) Shared infra overhead: storage ($0.10/GPU/h for checkpoint writes): 175B job adds $0.10×32×336=$1,075; 7B adds $0.10×8×72=$57.60. Networking overhead: AllReduce at 900 GB/s NVLink — cost included in GPU rate. Idle attribution: if 24 GPUs idle for 14 days: cost = 24×336×1.80=$14,515 — charged to cluster ops budget (not jobs), unless idle is due to job scheduling gap (then charged to team that held reservation). Final: 175B=$20,429; 7B=$1,094.

scenario: You must implement a cost accounting system for a shared 64-GPU H100 cluster ($1.80/GPU/h fully-loaded). Multiple teams run concurrent training jobs. A 175B GPT training run uses 32 GPUs for 14 days. A 7B fine-tuning run uses 8 GPUs for 3 days and overlaps. Implement: (1) per-job cost calculation, (2) shared infrastructure overhead allocation (networking, storage), (3) idle time attribution policy.
title: Implement Cost Allocation Per Training Run on Shared H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Optimizing checkpoint frequency alone; S3 storage cost accumulates from retained checkpoints, not just the write rate. 3 months of checkpoints compound.
details.napkin_math: Checkpoint size: 70B×16B=1.12TB. Frequency: 10min → 144/day. 30-day retention: 4,320 stored × 1,120GB × $0.023 = $111K storage + $0.09/GB egress × evaluation reads ≈ $180K total. 7-day retention: 1,008 × 1,120 × $0.023 = $26K + egress ≈ $40K. BF16: halve to $20K.
details.realistic_solution: Steps per 3 months: 3×30×24×6 steps/hr... at 10 min/step: 3×30×24×6=12,960 checkpoints. Each 1.12TB. Storage cost: 12,960 × 1.12TB × $0.023/GB/month × 3 months = 12,960 × 1,120 × $0.023 × 3 = $1.0B — obviously wrong, retention matters. With 7-day retention: 1,008 checkpoints stored simultaneously. Cost: 1,008 × 1,120 GB × $0.023/month × 3 months = $78,145. Egress: downloading checkpoints for evaluation: 100 checkpoints × 1.12TB × $0.09/GB = $10,080. Total: ~$88K. Actual $180K suggests no retention policy (30-day). Fix: 7-day rolling retention + bf16 checkpoints (560GB) → 50% cost reduction to ~$44K.

scenario: A 70B model training run on 128 H100 GPUs (3 months, $0.50M GPU cost) shows an unexpected $180K in cloud storage and egress charges. Checkpoints are saved every 500 steps (10 min intervals) to S3. Model checkpoint size: 70B params × 4B (FP32) + optimizer states × 2 (Adam) + gradient buffer = 70B×16B = 1.12TB per checkpoint. Storage cost: $0.023/GB/month. Diagnose whether checkpoint frequency or storage retention is the primary cost driver.
title: Diagnose TCO Anomaly from Checkpoint I/O Costs on Cloud

details.common_mistake: Using peak TFLOP/s without applying MFU; at 30% MFU the effective throughput is 594 TFLOP/s per H100, which combined with model FLOP count gives tokens/second.
details.napkin_math: Effective TFLOP/s: 4×1979×0.30 = 2,375 TFLOP/s. Tokens/s: 2375T/350B = 6,786 tok/s. Cost/s: 4×$2.50/3600 = $0.00278/s. Cost/token: $0.00278/6786 = $0.41/1M tokens. Cloud markup: GPT-4 at $10/1M = 24× multiplier covering latency SLA, overhead, profit.
details.realistic_solution: Effective throughput per H100: 1,979 × 0.30 = 594 TFLOP/s. For 4 H100s: 4 × 594 = 2,376 TFLOP/s. FLOPs per token: 350 B = 350 × 10⁹. Tokens per second: 2,376 × 10¹² / (350 × 10⁹) = 6,789 tokens/s. Cost per second: 4 GPUs × $2.50/3600s = $0.00278/s. Cost per token: $0.00278 / 6,789 = $0.000000409 = $0.409 per 1M tokens. Current GPT-4 pricing: $10/1M → 24× markup for profit/overhead/latency SLA.

scenario: At a job interview, you are asked to estimate the cost per token to serve GPT-3 (175B parameters) on H100 GPUs at $2.50/GPU/h. The model requires 4 H100s for FP16 inference (fits in 320GB VRAM combined). The H100 achieves 30% MFU for decode at batch=32, theoretical peak: 1,979 TFLOP/s. Each token requires approximately 2×175B = 350B FLOPs for one forward pass. Compute cost per 1M output tokens.
title: TCO Fluency: Compute Cost per Token at Scale

details.common_mistake: Using 6ND for inference (training formula) or forgetting that attention FLOPs scale as O(S²) which becomes significant at long context even if attention parameters are small.
details.napkin_math: Transformer attention FLOPs for GPT-4 class: 4 batches, 96 heads, seq=8192, head_dim=96. Attention score matmul: 2 × batch × heads × seq² × head_dim = 2 × 4 × 96 × 8192² × 96 = 2×4×96×67,108,864×96 = 2×4×96×6,442,450,944 = 4,937,053,724,672 ≈ 4.94 TFLOPs (not 2464 TFLOPs which would require seq=8,192,000 or similar). For just the score matmul per layer: 2×4×96×8192²×96... let me recalculate: 2×4=8; 8×96=768; 768×8192²=768×67,108,864=51,539,607,552; ×96=4,947,802,324,992 ≈ 4.95 TFLOPs per layer. With QKV proj: ~10 TFLOPs total per layer. So 2.47 TFLOPs for attention scores alone is correct at half the above: 2×4×96×8192²×96/2 ≈ 2.47 TFLOPs (not 2464 TFLOPs which is 1000× too large).
details.realistic_solution: Attention FLOPs: 2×4×96×8192²×96 ≈ 4.94 TFLOPs for score matmul, or 2.47 TFLOPs for the K^T V product only. 2464 TFLOPs is 1000× too large — a TFLOPS vs GFLOPS unit error.

scenario: An interviewer asks you to state from memory: what is the standard approximation formula for total FLOPs in a single forward pass of a transformer with N parameters and sequence length S? And separately, what is the training FLOPs formula? How does inference FLOPs scale with sequence length vs model size?
title: Recall Transformer Inference FLOPs Formula

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to convert dollar budget to FLOP budget before applying Chinchilla; also using peak TFLOP/s instead of MFU-adjusted effective throughput.
details.napkin_math: C = 2M GPU-h × 3600s × 445 TFLOP/s = 3.2×10²⁴ FLOPs. N* = √(C/6) = √(5.33×10²³) = 7.3×10¹¹ ≈ 730B. D* = 6N* = 4.38T tokens. Chinchilla ratio: D*/N* = 6. GPT-3 actual: 300B/175B = 1.7 tokens/param (7× undertrained vs Chinchilla). $5M budget → Chinchilla-optimal 730B model.
details.realistic_solution: Effective throughput per H100: 989 × 0.45 = 445 TFLOP/s. Budget = $5M. GPU-hours: $5M / $2.50 = 2M GPU-hours. Total FLOP: 2M × 3600s × 445 × 10¹² = 3.2 × 10²⁴ FLOPs. Chinchilla: N* = sqrt(C/6) = sqrt(3.2×10²⁴/6) = sqrt(5.33×10²³) = 7.3×10¹¹ = 730B parameters. D* = 6 × 730B = 4.38T tokens. Comparison: GPT-3 used 300B tokens to train 175B params (under-trained by Chinchilla). GPT-4 estimated ~13T tokens for ~1.8T params.

scenario: Your team has a compute budget of $5M and access to H100 GPUs at $2.50/GPU/h. H100 achieves 45% MFU on transformer training (peak 989 TFLOP/s FP16). Chinchilla scaling law: compute-optimal training requires N* ≈ sqrt(C/6) parameters and D* = 6N* tokens (where C is total training FLOPs). Analyze: what is the compute-optimal model size and token count for your budget, and how do they compare to GPT-3's training?
title: Analyze Chinchilla Compute-Optimal Training Budget on H100

details.common_mistake: Computing only compute-bound throughput; autoregressive decode at batch=1 is always memory-bandwidth-bound because each token requires loading all model weights (one pass through 70B parameters) while performing minimal compute.
details.napkin_math: Memory bound: 3.35 TB/s / 70 GB weights = 47.9 tokens/s ≈ measured 52. Compute bound: 1979 TFLOP/s / 0.14 TFLOP/token = 14,136 tokens/s. Ratio: 295×. Batch=64: weight reads shared → 64×47.9 = 3,066 tokens/s total throughput while memory bound remains. Effective: 47.9 tokens/s per request latency unchanged, 64× throughput improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Compute-bound throughput: 1,979 TFLOP/s / 140 GFLOP/token = 14,136 tokens/s. Memory-bound throughput: 3.35 TB/s / 70 GB = 47.9 loads/s = 47.9 tokens/s. Measured 52 tokens/s ≈ memory-bound prediction (slight overestimate suggests INT8 reduces weight size to 70GB but attention KV adds overhead). Diagnosis: memory-bandwidth-bound by 14,136/47.9 = 295× margin. Fix: increase batch size. At batch=64: KV cache adds 64×context×layers×dims×1B overhead but compute scales 64× while weight loads are shared → 52×64 = 3,328 tokens/s total, 52 tokens/s/request (same latency, 64× throughput).

scenario: An H100-based LLM serving system for a 70B parameter model (INT8, 70GB) achieves only 52 tokens/s per GPU during autoregressive decode at batch size 1. The theoretical peak from compute: H100 has 1,979 TFLOP/s FP16, 70B × 2 FLOPs/token = 140 GFLOP/token. The theoretical peak from memory bandwidth: H100 HBM3 = 3.35 TB/s, 70GB model weights. Diagnose whether the system is compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound, and explain the measured 52 tokens/s.
title: Diagnose Memory-Bandwidth-Bound Decode on H100 Serving Cluster

details.common_mistake: Computing KV cache assuming full-precision weights and forgetting that Llama 3 70B uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads (not 64 full heads), significantly reducing KV cache size.
details.napkin_math: KV/request: 2×80×8×128×128K×2B = 2×80×8×128×131072×2 = 42.9GB. 32 requests: 1,372 GB. Model: 140GB. Total: 1,512 GB / 80 GB/H100 = 18.9 → 19 H100s. At $2.50/h × 19 = $47.50/h for 32 concurrent users = $1.48/user/h for 128K context.
details.realistic_solution: (1) KV per request: 2 (K+V) × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 128K tokens × 2B (FP16) = 2×80×8×128×131072×2 = 42,949,672,960B ≈ 42.9 GB per request. (2) 32 requests: 32 × 42.9 GB = 1,372.8 GB. (3) Model weights: 70B × 2B (FP16) = 140 GB. (4) Total VRAM: 1,372.8 + 140 = 1,512.8 GB. H100 80GB each: 1,512.8 / 80 = 18.9 → 19 GPUs minimum. Practical: round to 20 GPUs (4 nodes × 5, or 2 8-GPU nodes + 4 extra = use 3 8-GPU nodes = 24 GPUs for overhead). Note: this is why 128K context serving is prohibitively expensive without KV quantization.

scenario: You must specify the KV cache memory requirements for serving Llama 3 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dimension) at FP16 precision on H100 GPUs with 80GB VRAM each. Target: support 128K token context length with 32 concurrent requests. Specify: (1) KV cache size per request, (2) total KV cache for 32 requests, (3) remaining VRAM for model weights, and (4) minimum GPU count.
title: Specify KV Cache Memory Requirements for Long-Context LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that you need to store Q tile, K tile, V tile, output accumulator, and softmax statistics simultaneously — not just one tile at a time.
details.napkin_math: Q tile: 128 x 128 x 2B = 32KB. K tile: 32KB. V tile: 32KB. O tile: 32KB. Softmax stats: 128 x 8B = 1KB. Total: ~129KB out of 256KB SRAM. Leaves headroom for compiler scratch.
details.realistic_solution: Each tile of Q is B_r x 128 x 2B, K is B_c x 128 x 2B, V is B_c x 128 x 2B, output O is B_r x 128 x 2B, plus softmax row-max and row-sum vectors (B_r x 4B each). Total SRAM = 256 * (B_r + 2*B_c) + 256*B_r + 8*B_r bytes. With 256KB = 262,144 bytes, typical tile sizes are B_r = B_c = 128, consuming ~128KB for Q+O tiles and ~128KB for K+V tiles, fitting snugly. Exceeding this forces HBM round-trips for partial results, destroying the IO advantage.

scenario: An H100 GPU has 256KB of shared memory (SRAM) per SM. FlashAttention must tile Q, K, V blocks to fit within this budget. For a model with head_dim=128 in FP16, what is the maximum tile size (B_r x B_c) that fits in SRAM, and why does exceeding it force spills to HBM?
title: FlashAttention Tile Size vs SRAM Capacity

details.common_mistake: Only counting the attention matrix write and forgetting the reads of Q, K, V and the read-back of the attention matrix for the V multiplication — standard attention has 2 full round-trips of the N x N matrix.
details.napkin_math: Standard IO: 4 x (8192^2 x 2B x 32) = 16GB. FlashAttention IO: 3 x (8192 x 128 x 2B x 32) = 192MB. Ratio: ~83x. At 2TB/s: 8ms vs 0.1ms.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention materializes S = Q @ K^T (8192 x 8192 x 2B = 128MB per head, x32 heads = 4GB), writes it, reads it back for softmax, writes softmax output, reads it for V multiply. Total IO ~ 4 x 4GB = 16GB per layer. FlashAttention never materializes S; it streams Q, K, V tiles through SRAM. IO = O(N * d) per head = 8192 x 128 x 2B x 3 (Q+K+V) x 32 heads = 192MB. Speedup from IO alone: 16GB / 192MB ~ 83x. At 2TB/s, standard = 8ms, FlashAttention = 0.1ms per layer.

scenario: Standard attention on an A100 (2 TB/s HBM bandwidth) materializes the full N x N attention matrix to HBM. For a sequence length N=8192 and head_dim=128 with 32 heads in FP16, compare the HBM IO bytes of standard attention vs FlashAttention and estimate the wall-clock difference.
title: FlashAttention IO Complexity vs Standard Attention

details.common_mistake: Assuming pre-allocation waste is modest. In practice, allocating for max length when average is 8x shorter wastes 87.5% of KV cache memory.
details.napkin_math: Pre-alloc per request: 80 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 4096 x 2B / 8 GPUs = 1.28GB. At avg 512 tokens: 160MB actual. Waste: 87.5%. PagedAttention: 160MB x 256 = 40GB, fits easily.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per request at max length: 80 layers x 2 (K+V) x 8 heads/GPU x 128 dim x 4096 tokens x 2B = 1.28GB per request per GPU. For 256 requests: 328GB — exceeds 8x80GB = 640GB, so you cap at ~50 concurrent requests. At avg length 512, actual usage is 1/8th = 160MB/request. Wasted: 1.12GB/request x 50 = 56GB across the system. PagedAttention uses 16-token blocks allocated on demand via a block table (like OS virtual memory pages), achieving ~96% utilization. This allows 400+ concurrent requests.

scenario: You serve a 70B model on 8x A100-80GB with tensor parallelism. Without PagedAttention, KV cache is pre-allocated for max_seq_len=4096, but average actual length is 512. With 256 concurrent requests, calculate the wasted VRAM from internal fragmentation and explain how PagedAttention's block table eliminates it.
title: PagedAttention Memory Fragmentation

details.common_mistake: Thinking online softmax adds significant compute overhead. The rescaling is O(d) per row per tile update, which is negligible compared to the O(N*d) matmul work.
details.napkin_math: Rescaling FLOPs per tile: 2 x 128 x 128 = 32K. Matmul FLOPs per tile: 2 x 128 x 128 x 128 = 4.2M. Overhead: 0.76%.
details.realistic_solution: When processing tile j, compute local max m_j over S_ij = Q_i @ K_j^T. If m_j > m_{j-1} (running max), rescale: O_i *= exp(m_{j-1} - m_j), l_i *= exp(m_{j-1} - m_j), then accumulate O_i += exp(S_ij - m_j) @ V_j and l_i += rowsum(exp(S_ij - m_j)). The rescaling costs 2*B_r*d = 2*128*128 = 32K FLOPs per tile update. Total matmul FLOPs per tile: 2*B_r*B_c*d = 2*128*128*128 = 4M FLOPs. Overhead: 32K/4M = 0.8%. Negligible.

scenario: You are implementing FlashAttention's online softmax for head_dim=128 on an H100. The key challenge: softmax requires the global row maximum, but you process K in tiles of B_c=128 tokens. Describe the rescaling update rule when a new tile produces a larger row maximum, and compute the extra FLOPs overhead vs standard softmax.
title: Implementing FlashAttention's Online Softmax

details.common_mistake: Assuming FlashAttention is universally faster. For short sequences, the N x N matrix is small enough to fit in L2 cache, so the IO savings disappear while the tiling/rescaling overhead remains.
details.napkin_math: N=64: attn matrix = 64^2 x 2B x 32 heads = 256KB << 50MB L2. N=2048: 2048^2 x 2B x 32 = 256MB >> 50MB L2. FlashAttention kernel overhead ~5-10us, which matters when total compute is ~15us.
details.realistic_solution: At N=64, the attention matrix is 64x64x2B = 8KB per head — fits entirely in L2 cache (50MB on H100). Standard attention's 'materialization to HBM' never actually hits HBM; the hardware cache captures it. FlashAttention's overhead — kernel launch, tile loop control, online softmax rescaling, reduced parallelism from sequential tile processing — now exceeds the IO savings. At N=2048, the matrix is 2048x2048x2B = 8MB per head x 32 heads = 256MB, blowing past L2 cache, making HBM IO the bottleneck that FlashAttention eliminates.

scenario: After enabling FlashAttention-2 on an H100 serving a 7B model, you observe that latency for sequence length 64 is 5% slower than standard attention, while seq_len=2048 is 2.3x faster. Both use FP16. Diagnose why FlashAttention can regress on very short sequences.
title: Diagnosing FlashAttention Regression on Short Sequences

details.common_mistake: Using the full 64 attention heads instead of the 8 GQA KV heads per GPU. GQA dramatically reduces KV cache size — missing this leads to 8x overestimation.
details.napkin_math: KV/token/GPU: 80 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 2B = 320KB. Block(16 tokens) = 5.12MB. Budget: (80GB - 35GB weights) / 5.12MB = 8,789 blocks = 8,789 x 16 = 140K token-slots.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token per GPU: 80 layers x 2 (K+V) x 8 KV_heads x 128 dim x 2B = 320KB/token. With block_size=16: each block = 16 x 320KB = 5.12MB. Max blocks per request = 8192/16 = 512. Total for 512 requests at avg 2048 tokens: 512 x 128 blocks = 65,536 blocks x 5.12MB = 327GB across 4 GPUs = 82GB/GPU. Model weights in FP16: 70B x 2B / 4 = 35GB/GPU. Total: 35 + 82 = 117GB > 80GB. Solution: reduce to 300 concurrent requests or use FP8 weights (17.5GB), leaving 62.5GB for KV cache = ~12,200 blocks = 300 requests at avg 2048.

scenario: You are writing the deployment spec for a Llama-3 70B model on 4x H100-80GB with tensor parallelism. The model has 80 layers, 64 KV heads (GQA with 8 KV heads per GPU), head_dim=128. Target: 512 concurrent requests, max_seq_len=8192. Specify the PagedAttention block size, total block budget, and memory reservation.
title: Specifying KV Cache Budget for PagedAttention

details.common_mistake: Computing arithmetic intensity of the full fused kernel rather than the per-tile intensity, which is what actually determines whether each SM is compute-bound or memory-bound.
details.napkin_math: S matrix (attention scores) size: batch × heads × seq × seq × bytes. For 4096 seq, 32 heads, BF16 (2B): 2 × 4096² × 2B × 32 heads = 2 × 16,777,216 × 2 × 32 = 2,147,483,648 bytes = 2.15 GB (not 4 GB — 4 GB would require FP32 or double the heads). Arithmetic intensity: FLOPs / bytes accessed.
details.realistic_solution: S matrix = 2 × heads × seq² × bytes = 2 × 32 × 4096² × 2B = 2.15 GB in BF16 (not 4 GB which uses FP32).

scenario: On an H100 (989 TFLOPS FP16, 3.35 TB/s HBM3), compute the arithmetic intensity of the attention operation for seq_len=4096, head_dim=128, batch=1, 32 heads, and determine whether FlashAttention shifts it from memory-bound to compute-bound on the roofline.
title: FlashAttention Arithmetic Intensity Calculation

details.common_mistake: Thinking Ring Attention eliminates all communication. It shifts communication to overlap with compute, but total bytes transferred are the same — the advantage is hiding latency, not reducing volume.
details.napkin_math: KV per ring step: 512MB. NVLink transfer: 0.57ms. Compute per step: ~0.8ms. Comm/compute ratio: 0.71 — communication fully hidden. Total ring overhead: ~0ms effective latency addition.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache for 128K context per head: 128K x 128 x 2B = 32MB. With 64 KV heads, full KV = 2 x 32MB x 64 = 4GB per layer. Ring Attention: each GPU holds 128K/8 = 16K tokens. In each ring step, a GPU sends its K,V block to the neighbor: 4GB/8 = 512MB per step x 7 steps = 3.5GB per layer communicated. With NVLink at 900 GB/s, ring step transfer: 512MB / 900 = 0.57ms. Compute per step (FlashAttention on 16K x 16K): ~0.8ms. Communication is overlapped with compute. Ulysses (all-to-all): same 3.5GB volume but requires all-to-all, harder to overlap. Ring Attention wins for long context due to natural overlap.

scenario: Your team is deploying a 70B model with 128K context on 8x H100 (NVLink 900 GB/s bisection). Option A: FlashAttention-2 on each GPU with sequence parallelism (Ulysses). Option B: Ring Attention across 8 GPUs. Compare communication volume, peak per-GPU memory, and latency.
title: Evaluating Ring Attention vs FlashAttention for 128K Context

details.common_mistake: Caching only the token embeddings instead of the full KV cache. The expensive part is the forward pass through all layers to generate KV pairs, not the embedding lookup.
details.napkin_math: KV per prefix: 40 x 2 x 40 x 128 x 2048 x 2B = 1.6GB. 50 prefixes / 4 GPUs = 20GB/GPU. Prefill saved: 53 TFLOP / 312 TFLOPS = 170ms. Avg saving: 136ms.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per prefix (2048 tokens, 40 layers, 40 heads, head_dim=128, FP16): 40 x 2 x 40 x 128 x 2048 x 2B = 1.6GB per prefix. 50 prefixes = 80GB total — exactly one A100. With tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs: 20GB/GPU for prefix cache. Model weights: 13B x 2B / 4 = 6.5GB/GPU. Remaining for active KV: 80 - 6.5 - 20 = 53.5GB/GPU. Prefill compute saved: 2048 tokens x 13B params x 2 FLOPs = 53 TFLOP. At 312 TFLOPS: 170ms saved per cache hit. With 80% hit rate: avg TTFT improvement = 0.8 x 170ms = 136ms.

scenario: You run a RAG system on 4x A100-80GB serving a 13B model. 80% of requests share one of 50 system prompts (avg 2048 tokens each). Without prefix caching, every request recomputes the system prompt's KV cache. Design the prefix caching system: estimate memory cost, hit rate, and TTFT improvement.
title: Designing a Prefix Caching Strategy for RAG

details.common_mistake: Assuming the same tile sizes that work on NVIDIA will work on AMD. The 4x smaller SRAM per CU fundamentally changes the tile geometry and loop structure.
details.napkin_math: MI300X tile: 64x64 = 4K elements per tile. H100 tile: 128x128 = 16K. MI300X needs 4x more tiles. GEMM efficiency at 64x64x128: ~70% vs ~85% at 128x128x128. MI300X peak: 1307 TFLOPS FP16 x 0.70 = 915 effective. H100: 989 x 0.85 = 841 effective.
details.realistic_solution: With 64KB LDS, budget: Q tile + K tile + V tile + O tile + stats. Using B_r=B_c=64: Q = 64x128x2B = 16KB, K = 16KB, V = 16KB, O = 16KB = 64KB total — exactly at limit. Compared to H100's B_r=B_c=128, this means 4x more tiles per attention computation. More tiles = more loop iterations = more overhead. However, MI300X has 5.3 TB/s bandwidth vs H100's 3.35 TB/s (1.58x more). For memory-bound operations, MI300X can compensate. But for FlashAttention (compute-bound after tiling), smaller tiles mean lower matmul efficiency: 64x64x128 GEMMs achieve ~70% of peak vs 128x128x128 at ~85%. Net: MI300X FlashAttention throughput ~85% of H100 despite higher bandwidth.

scenario: AMD MI300X has 192GB HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s but smaller SRAM per CU (64KB LDS) compared to H100's 256KB SMEM. You are porting FlashAttention-2 to ROCm for a 70B model with head_dim=128, FP16. Analyze how the smaller SRAM changes optimal tile size and what throughput impact this has.
title: Optimizing FlashAttention Tile Size for MI300X

details.common_mistake: Treating these as independent choices. The attention kernel, KV cache manager, parallelism strategy, and caching layer interact: PagedAttention's non-contiguous blocks require FlashAttention to support block-sparse reads; Ring Attention's overlap budget depends on per-tile compute time.
details.napkin_math: 405B model FLOPs per token: 2 × 405B = 810 GFLOPs/token (not 810 TFLOPs — 810 TFLOPs would mean 405T params, not 405B). 810 GFLOP/token. H100 at 989 TFLOPS: 810G/989T = 0.819ms per token at 100% utilization.
details.realistic_solution: 405B model: 2 × 405B = 810 GFLOPs/token (not 810 TFLOPs — TFLOPS would imply 405T parameters). 810 GFLOPs/token at 989 TFLOPS = ~0.82ms/token.

scenario: You are the Staff ML engineer deciding the attention implementation for a new 405B model served on 64x H100 (8 nodes, NVLink + InfiniBand 400 Gb/s). Context window: 32K. Requirements: P99 TTFT < 2s, 1000 req/s throughput. Propose the complete attention stack: FlashAttention variant, KV cache management, sequence parallelism, and prefix caching strategy. Justify each choice with napkin math.
title: Full-Stack FlashAttention Deployment Decision

details.common_mistake: Assuming sliding window attention computes over the full context and just masks — the real benefit is that you only store the last W tokens in the KV cache for sliding layers, physically freeing memory.
details.napkin_math: Full: 32 x 128MB = 4GB. Sliding: 16 x 128MB + 16 x 16MB = 2.26GB. Savings: 43.6%. Concurrent requests: 29 vs 16, a 1.75x improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Full attention KV per layer: 32K x 2 x 8 x 128 x 2B = 128MB. Full model (32 layers): 32 x 128MB = 4GB. With sliding window: 16 full layers x 128MB = 2GB. 16 sliding layers x (4096/32768) x 128MB = 16 x 16MB = 256MB. Total: 2.256GB. Savings: 4GB - 2.256GB = 1.744GB per request = 43.6% reduction. This allows ~1.77x more concurrent requests: (80GB - 14GB weights) / 2.256GB = 29 vs (80GB - 14GB) / 4GB = 16.5.

scenario: Mistral 7B uses sliding window attention with window_size=4096 on some layers while keeping full attention on others. On an A100-80GB, for a 32K context request with 32 layers (16 sliding, 16 full), head_dim=128, 8 KV heads, compare the KV cache memory vs a model using full attention on all 32 layers.
title: Sliding Window Attention Memory Savings

details.common_mistake: Thinking the loop reordering is a minor optimization. FA-1 with batch=1 has only 32 thread blocks (one per head) for 132 SMs, wasting 100 SMs. FA-2 parallelizes over Q tiles too.
details.napkin_math: FA-1 blocks: 32. FA-2 blocks: 4,096. Occupancy: 24% vs 100%. Expected speedup: ~1.7-2x from occupancy alone. FA-2 measured: 230 TFLOPS vs FA-1: 140 TFLOPS on H100.
details.realistic_solution: FA-1: parallelism = batch x heads = 1 x 32 = 32 thread blocks. H100 has 132 SMs, so SM occupancy = 32/132 = 24.2%. 100 SMs idle. FA-2: parallelism = batch x heads x ceil(N/B_r) = 1 x 32 x ceil(16384/128) = 1 x 32 x 128 = 4,096 thread blocks. SM occupancy: 4,096/132 = 31 blocks per SM in waves — 100% occupancy. Each thread block processes one Q tile against all K/V tiles sequentially. FA-2 also reduces non-matmul FLOPs by keeping Q in registers and iterating K/V through shared memory. Combined: ~1.7-2x speedup over FA-1 on this workload.

scenario: FlashAttention-1 parallelizes over batch and heads (outer loop over K/V tiles). FlashAttention-2 reverses this: outer loop over Q tiles, inner loop over K/V tiles. On an H100 with 132 SMs, for a batch=1, 32 heads, seq_len=16384, head_dim=128 workload, explain why FA-2's approach achieves higher occupancy and estimate the speedup.
title: FlashAttention-2 vs FlashAttention-1 Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Setting chunk size too large (e.g., 4096) which still causes 100ms stalls, or too small (e.g., 128) which adds excessive kernel launch overhead and reduces FlashAttention's tiling efficiency.
details.napkin_math: Tokens in 30ms budget: budget × compute / FLOPs_per_token. 8 H100s × 989 TFLOPS × 0.03s / 140 GFLOPs_per_token = 8 × 989T × 0.03 / 140G = 8 × 29.67T / 140G = 237.3T / 140G = 1,695 tokens (not 212 which is ~8× too low — likely used single-GPU compute instead of 8 GPUs).
details.realistic_solution: 8 H100s × 989 TFLOPS × 0.03s / 140 GFLOPs_per_token = 1,695 tokens in 30ms window (not 212 which uses single GPU).

scenario: You run vLLM on 8x H100 serving a 70B model. A 16K-token prefill request takes 400ms, during which all decode requests stall (head-of-line blocking). Design a chunked prefill strategy that interleaves prefill and decode, and determine the optimal chunk size given a decode latency SLO of 50ms per token.
title: Chunked Prefill Scheduling with FlashAttention

details.common_mistake: Blaming the block table lookup overhead. The real issue is that block_size=1 creates thousands of tiny non-contiguous memory segments, destroying GPU memory access coalescing and L2 cache locality.
details.napkin_math: Block_size=1: 4096 random accesses per head. Block_size=16: 256 sequential reads. L2 hit rate: 15% vs 70%. Effective bandwidth at 15% hit: 2TB/s x 0.15 + (random penalty) ~ 0.8 TB/s vs 1.7 TB/s. Decode regression: 1.7/0.8 = 2.1x, but partially masked by compute = net 35%.
details.realistic_solution: With block_size=1, each token's KV is a separate allocation. For a 4096-context request with 40 layers x 2 x 40 heads x 128 dim x 2B = 800KB per token, the block table has 4096 entries pointing to scattered 800KB blocks. During attention, the GPU must gather K/V values from 4096 random memory locations per head per layer. This creates non-coalesced memory accesses: instead of sequential 128B cache-line reads, each access fetches from a different page. L2 cache hit rate drops from ~70% (contiguous) to ~15% (scattered). At block_size=16, there are only 256 blocks with 12.8MB each — large enough for coalesced access patterns. Optimal block sizes balance fragmentation (smaller = less waste) against access locality (larger = better coalescing): block_size=16-64 is the sweet spot.

scenario: After switching from block_size=16 to block_size=1 in vLLM's PagedAttention on A100, you observe that memory utilization improves from 92% to 99% but decode latency increases by 35%. Diagnose the root cause of this latency regression.
title: PagedAttention Block Size Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Not exploiting the fact that 8 query heads share the same KV head. Loading the same KV tile 8 times wastes 87.5% of KV bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Naive KV IO: 64 x 2MB = 128MB/layer. GQA-aware: 8 x 2MB = 16MB/layer. 8x reduction. Total savings: 112MB x 80 layers = 8.96GB at 3.35TB/s = 2.67ms.
details.realistic_solution: Naive approach: KV loaded 64 times total. IO = 64 x 2 x 4096 x 128 x 2B = 128MB per layer. GQA-aware: load each KV head once, process all 8 sharing query heads against it before moving to the next KV tile. IO = 8 x 2 x 4096 x 128 x 2B = 16MB. Savings: 112MB per layer x 80 layers = 8.96GB total. At 3.35 TB/s: 2.67ms saved. Implementation: for each KV tile in SRAM, iterate over the 8 query groups that share it. Each Q group has its own accumulator O_i and softmax stats (l_i, m_i). SRAM usage: K+V tiles = 2 x B_c x 128 x 2B, plus 8 sets of Q tiles and accumulators. This fits because Q tiles rotate while K/V stay pinned.

scenario: Llama-3 70B uses GQA with 64 query heads and 8 KV heads (ratio 8:1). A naive FlashAttention implementation loads K/V tiles 64 times (once per query head). On H100, for seq_len=4096, head_dim=128, FP16, calculate the wasted bandwidth and design an efficient GQA-aware tiling scheme.
title: GQA-Aware FlashAttention Kernel Design

details.common_mistake: Thinking FlashAttention's recomputation slows training significantly. The recomputation cost is small because attention is compute-bound with FlashAttention, and the memory savings often allow larger batch sizes that improve GPU utilization.
details.napkin_math: Standard: 8192^2 x 2B x 80 per layer = 10GB. 40 layers = 400GB. Flash: 643MB x 40 = 25GB. Savings: 375GB. Enables 2x batch size at 5-7% compute overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention stores S = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d)) per layer: 8192^2 x 2B x 40 heads x 2 micro_batch = 40 x 2 x 8192^2 x 2 = 80 x 128MB = 10GB per layer. Across 40 layers: 400GB — impossible on 8 GPUs (max 640GB, but model + optimizer already use ~400GB). FlashAttention stores only Q, K, V, O and softmax log-sum-exp (8192 x 4B per head): per layer = 4 x 8192 x 128 x 2B x 40 x 2 + 8192 x 4B x 40 x 2 = 640MB + 2.5MB ≈ 643MB per layer. Total: 40 x 643MB = 25.1GB. Savings: 400GB - 25.1GB = 374.9GB. This easily allows batch_size=4 instead of 2. Recomputation cost: ~33% more attention FLOPs in backward, but attention is typically 15-20% of total training FLOPs, so net overhead is ~5-7%.

scenario: You are training a 13B model on 8x A100-80GB with seq_len=8192, micro_batch=2, 40 layers, 40 heads, head_dim=128. Standard attention stores the full N x N attention matrix for the backward pass. Compute the activation memory saved by FlashAttention's recomputation strategy and determine if this enables a larger batch size.
title: FlashAttention Backward Pass Memory Savings for Training

details.common_mistake: Thinking MQA is strictly better because it minimizes KV cache. MQA with a single KV head can create a bandwidth bottleneck where all 48 query heads compete for the same KV data, and it reduces model quality more than GQA.
details.napkin_math: MQA KV: 120MB/req. GQA-8: 960MB/req. Batch 64 total: 7.5GB vs 60GB. Decode IO: 2.3ms vs 18.3ms. Quality: MQA loses 2-3 PPL. GQA-4 sweet spot: 480MB, 9.2ms decode, <0.5 PPL loss.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache at seq_len=4096 per request: MQA (1 KV head): 60 layers x 2 x 1 x 128 x 4096 x 2B = 120MB. GQA-8: 60 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 4096 x 2B = 960MB. 8x difference. For 64 concurrent: MQA = 7.5GB/GPU, GQA-8 = 60GB/GPU. GQA-8 barely fits (80-15GB model = 65GB). Decode bandwidth: MQA loads KV once = 120MB x 64 batch / 3.35 TB/s = 2.3ms. GQA-8: 960MB x 64 / 3.35 = 18.3ms. MQA is 8x faster decode. But quality: MQA-30B shows 2-3 perplexity points worse than GQA-8-30B on long-context benchmarks. Recommendation: GQA-4 as compromise — 4 KV heads, 480MB/request, 4x faster than full MHA, minimal quality loss.

scenario: You are choosing between MQA (1 KV head) and GQA-8 (8 KV heads) for a new 30B model deployed on 4x H100. Both use FlashAttention. For inference at batch=64, seq_len=4096, 48 query heads, head_dim=128, compare decode throughput, KV cache size, and quality implications.
title: Multi-Query Attention vs GQA with FlashAttention

details.common_mistake: Assuming FP8 attention gives a clean 2x speedup. The attention score computation (QK^T) is highly sensitive to precision because softmax amplifies small numerical errors exponentially.
details.napkin_math: FP16 achieved: 600 TFLOPS. FP8 achieved: 989 TFLOPS. Speedup: 1.67x. FP8 E4M3 resolution at scale 10: 10/128 = 0.08. Quality: OK for short context, degrades at 32K+.
details.realistic_solution: FP16 FlashAttention prefill at seq_len=8192: already compute-bound on H100, achieving ~600 TFLOPS (60% of 989 peak). FP8: theoretical peak 1979 TFLOPS, but FlashAttention-3 FP8 achieves ~989 TFLOPS (50% of peak) due to dequantization overhead within tiles. Speedup: 1000/600 = 1.67x, not 2x. Quality: FP8 E4M3 has 3-bit mantissa (8 significand values). For attention scores in range [-10, 10], resolution is ~0.08 — fine for sharp attention patterns but problematic for broad distributions. Empirically: FP8 attention shows <0.3% quality loss on short contexts but up to 2% on 32K+ context where many tokens have similar attention scores and quantization noise causes rank-order changes in softmax.

scenario: H100 supports FP8 with 1,979 TFLOPS (2x FP16). FlashAttention-3 adds FP8 support using the Transformer Engine's per-tensor scaling. For a 70B model prefill at seq_len=8192, compare FP16 vs FP8 FlashAttention throughput and analyze when FP8 attention degrades quality.
title: FlashAttention FP8 on H100 Transformer Engine

details.common_mistake: Thinking beam search only creates copies at the final step. Each decode step can cause beams to diverge, and without CoW, the system eagerly copies all shared KV blocks, consuming 4x memory for mostly identical data.
details.napkin_math: Naive 4 beams: 4 x 640MB = 2.56GB. CoW: 640MB shared + 4 x 5MB diverged = 660MB. Savings: 74%. Analogy: Unix fork() CoW pages.
details.realistic_solution: KV per beam at 2048 tokens per GPU: 80 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 2048 x 2B = 640MB. 4 beams naive: 4 x 640MB = 2.56GB/GPU. But beams share ~95% of tokens (diverging only at recent positions). CoW: all 4 beams reference the same physical blocks via block table. When beam i generates a new token into block j, only block j is copied (16 tokens x 80 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 2B = 5.12MB). Physical memory: 640MB (shared) + 4 x 5.12MB (diverged) = 660MB vs 2.56GB. Savings: 74%. This is exactly like Unix fork() with CoW pages. At block_size=16, reference counts track sharing. When ref_count drops to 1, the block becomes exclusively owned and in-place writable.

scenario: You run beam search with beam_width=4 on a 70B model (H100, 8 KV heads/GPU, 80 layers, head_dim=128). Without copy-on-write, each beam duplicates the entire KV cache at every branch point. At context 2048 tokens, calculate the memory waste and explain how PagedAttention's CoW mechanism avoids it.
title: PagedAttention Copy-on-Write for Beam Search

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that the causal mask is triangular, so exactly half the tiles can be skipped, but partial tiles at the diagonal boundary must still be computed (with masking).
details.napkin_math: 32x32 tile grid. Upper triangle skipped: 32x31/2 = 496 tiles. Computed: 528/1024 = 51.6% of work. Prefill speedup: 1.94x. Decode: no benefit (1 query row, all K columns needed).
details.realistic_solution: With tile size B_r=B_c=128, the attention grid is 4096/128 = 32 x 32 = 1024 tiles. Causal mask: tile (i,j) is fully zero when j > i (Q row block i cannot attend to K column block j if j > i). Fully zero tiles: upper triangle = 32x31/2 = 496. Fully computed tiles: lower triangle = 496. Diagonal tiles: 32 (partially masked). Total work: 496 + 32 = 528 out of 1024 tiles. Fraction skipped: 496/1024 = 48.4%. Effective speedup for prefill: ~1.93x vs non-causal. For decode: only 1 query token, so the causal mask doesn't help — all prior tokens are attended to.

scenario: For causal (autoregressive) attention with seq_len=4096 on H100, FlashAttention skips tiles where the causal mask is entirely zero. Calculate what fraction of tiles are skipped and the resulting speedup for both prefill and decode.
title: FlashAttention Causal Masking Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Using a naive ring order (GPU 0,1,2,...,15) which crosses the InfiniBand boundary 2 times per ring revolution. Topology-aware ordering minimizes cross-node transfers.
details.napkin_math: NVLink step: 64MB / 900 GB/s = 0.07ms. InfiniBand step: 64MB / 50 GB/s = 1.28ms. Compute: ~2ms. Overlap ratio: NVLink 0.04x, IB 0.64x — both overlap. Bottleneck threshold: when compute < 1.28ms (smaller model or shorter chunks).
details.realistic_solution: KV block per GPU: 16K tokens x 8 KV_heads x 128 dim x 2B x 2(K+V) = 64MB per layer. Per ring step, send 64MB. NVLink intra-node: 900 GB/s, transfer: 64MB / 900 = 0.07ms. InfiniBand inter-node: 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s, transfer: 64MB / 50 = 1.28ms. Compute per ring step (FlashAttention on 16Kx16K): ~2ms on H100. Naive ring: 2 cross-node transfers per revolution of 15 steps. Those 2 steps have 1.28ms transfer vs 2ms compute — still overlapped (comm < compute). But at shorter sequences or smaller models, compute drops below 1.28ms and InfiniBand becomes the bottleneck. Topology-aware ring: order GPUs 0-7 (node1), then 8-15 (node2), so only step 7->8 and 15->0 are cross-node (2 transfers unavoidable in a ring of 16 spanning 2 nodes). This is already optimal. Alternative: use 2 intra-node rings with a single cross-node all-reduce to reduce cross-node transfers to 1.

scenario: You are designing Ring Attention for a 70B model across 16 GPUs (2 nodes, 8 NVLink GPUs/node, 400 Gb/s InfiniBand between nodes). Sequence length: 256K tokens split evenly (16K/GPU). Head_dim=128, 8 GQA KV heads. Analyze whether the inter-node InfiniBand link is the bottleneck and propose a topology-aware ring ordering.
title: Ring Attention Communication-Computation Overlap Budget

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to LRU. With power-law distributions, LRU evicts infrequent but recently-used prompts over frequent ones that haven't been seen in the last few seconds, causing unnecessary cache thrashing.
details.napkin_math: Compute-equivalent analysis: actual workload FLOPs / H100 FLOPs. Workload: 6.8 PFLOPs. H100 at 989 TFLOPS: 6.8P / 989T = 6.875 ≈ 6.9 H100s worth of compute (not 1 H100 which would imply only 989 TFLOPS workload).
details.realistic_solution: 6.8 PFLOPs workload / 989 TFLOPS per H100 = 6.9 H100-equivalents (not 1 H100).

scenario: Your vLLM deployment serves 200 distinct system prompts but only has budget for 50 cached prefixes in KV cache on H100. The prompt distribution follows a power law: top 10 prompts account for 60% of traffic. Compare LRU, LFU, and ARC eviction policies and determine which maximizes cache hit rate given this distribution.
title: Prefix Caching Eviction Policy Design

details.common_mistake: Assuming perfect 3-stage overlap. In practice, the softmax stage (non-matmul) is the bottleneck because it runs on different functional units than the tensor cores, and register pressure from maintaining 3 tiles limits occupancy.
details.napkin_math: Per-tile: load 0.003ms, softmax 0.003ms, matmul 0.004ms. Pipelined: 0.004ms/tile. Sequential: 0.01ms/tile. Theoretical: 2.5x. Measured FA-3 vs FA-2: ~1.5x due to register pressure.
details.realistic_solution: Three stages: (1) TMA load: 128x128x2B = 32KB per K and V tile = 64KB total. SRAM bandwidth ~19TB/s on H100. Load time: 64KB / 19TB = 0.003ms. (2) Softmax: per-row max, subtract, exp, sum, divide. B_r x B_c = 128x128 = 16K elements, ~10 FLOPs/element = 160K FLOPs on CUDA cores at ~60 TFLOPS = 0.003ms. (3) WGMMA matmul: 2 x 128 x 128 x 128 = 4.2M FLOPs at 989 TFLOPS = 0.004ms. Pipeline depth: 3 stages at 0.004ms (matmul dominates) = 0.004ms per tile steady-state. Number of tiles: 8192/128 = 64 per head. Total per head: 64 x 0.004ms + 2 x 0.004ms (pipeline fill/drain) = 0.264ms. Without pipelining: 64 x (0.003+0.003+0.004) = 0.64ms. Speedup: 2.4x. FA-3 measured: ~1.5x over FA-2 due to register pressure limiting full overlap.

scenario: FlashAttention-3 exploits H100's asynchronous TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) and WGMMA (Warpgroup Matrix Multiply-Accumulate) to overlap data loading with computation. With 3 pipeline stages (load K/V tile N+1, compute softmax for tile N, matmul for tile N-1), estimate the pipeline efficiency for seq_len=8192, head_dim=128, tile_size=128.
title: FlashAttention-3 Asynchronous Softmax Pipelining

details.common_mistake: Thinking FP16 is fine for everything because the final output is FP16 anyway. The issue is accumulated numerical error in the online softmax rescaling across many tiles.
details.napkin_math: FP16 min subnormal: 6e-8. exp(-17) = 4.1e-8 — underflows. At 256 tiles, max can shift by >17. FP32 min: 1.2e-38. exp(-87) still representable. FP32 softmax stats: 8 bytes per row x 128 rows = 1KB per tile — negligible overhead.
details.realistic_solution: FP16 has 10-bit mantissa = 3.3 decimal digits of precision. The online softmax maintains a running log-sum-exp value l_i that accumulates across N/B_c tiles. For seq_len=32K with B_c=128: 256 accumulations. Each accumulation involves exp(m_old - m_new) which can produce very small values (e.g., exp(-10) = 4.5e-5). In FP16, values below 6e-8 underflow to zero. After 256 tiles, if the max shifts significantly, earlier contributions are zeroed out, causing attention to only attend to recent tiles — a catastrophic failure for long-context tasks. FP32 maintains these statistics with 23-bit mantissa (7 decimal digits), handling exp values down to 1.2e-38. The matmuls (Q@K, attn@V) can safely use FP16 because they're computed per-tile and immediately consumed.

scenario: FlashAttention computes attention in FP16/BF16 but maintains softmax statistics (row max and log-sum-exp) in FP32. On H100, explain why this mixed-precision approach is necessary and what numerical failure mode occurs if softmax statistics are kept in FP16.
title: FlashAttention Numerical Stability in Mixed Precision Training

details.common_mistake: Computing expected accepted tokens as K x alpha = 4. This ignores that rejection at position i means positions i+1 through K are also rejected — it's a geometric distribution, not independent.
details.napkin_math: E[accepted] = (1 - 0.8^6) / 0.2 - 1 = 2.69. E[tokens/round] = 3.69. Draft overhead: 5 x 10% = 50%. Net speedup: 3.69 / 1.5 = 2.46x.
details.realistic_solution: Tokens are accepted sequentially: token 1 accepted with probability alpha, token 2 accepted with probability alpha (conditional on 1 accepted), etc. Expected accepted tokens E[n] = alpha + alpha^2 + ... + alpha^K + correction = (1 - alpha^(K+1))/(1-alpha) - 1 = (1-0.8^6)/(1-0.8) - 1 = (1-0.262)/0.2 - 1 = 3.69 - 1 = 2.69. Plus 1 token always generated (the first correct token after rejection or end of sequence): E[tokens] = 2.69 + 1 = 3.69 tokens per round. Autoregressive: 1 token per forward pass. Speedup depends on draft model cost. If draft is free: 3.69x. If draft costs 0.1x of target: effective speedup = 3.69 / (1 + 5 x 0.1) = 3.69/1.5 = 2.46x.

scenario: A draft model proposes K=5 tokens speculatively, and the target 70B model on H100 verifies them in one forward pass. If the acceptance rate is alpha=0.8 per token, what is the expected number of accepted tokens per speculation round, and what is the effective speedup over autoregressive decoding?
title: Speculative Decoding Acceptance Rate Fundamentals

details.common_mistake: Thinking speculative decoding is always beneficial. At high batch sizes, decode becomes compute-bound, eliminating the memory-bandwidth headroom that speculation exploits.
details.napkin_math: Batch=200 no-spec: 200 tok / 9.6ms = 20.8K tok/s. With spec: 740 tok / 45.9ms = 16.1K tok/s. 22% throughput loss. Speculation only helps when decode is deeply memory-bound (low batch).
details.realistic_solution: Without speculation, batch=200 decode: KV read per step = 200 x 640MB = 128GB at 4x3.35=13.4 TB/s = 9.6ms. Compute: 200 x 140 GFLOP = 28 TFLOP at 4x989=3.96 PFLOPS = 7.1ms. Compute/IO ratio: 0.74 — approaching compute-bound. With speculation: each request generates K=5 draft tokens, then verifies K+1=6 tokens in one pass. Verification batch: 200 x 6 = 1,200 effective tokens. Compute: 1,200 x 140G = 168 TFLOP at 3.96 PFLOPS = 42.4ms. Plus draft cost: 200 x 5 x 14 GFLOP = 14 TFLOP = 3.5ms. Total: 45.9ms for ~740 tokens (200 x 3.7 avg). Without speculation: 9.6ms for 200 tokens. Throughput: speculation = 740/45.9 = 16.1K tok/s, no-spec = 200/9.6 = 20.8K tok/s. Speculation is 22% worse on throughput.

scenario: Your 70B model serves 200 concurrent requests on 4x H100. Without speculation, decode is memory-bound at 100 tok/s per request. With K=5 speculation using a 7B draft model on the same GPUs, single-request latency improves 2.5x but total throughput drops 15%. Analyze why speculation hurts throughput at high batch sizes.
title: Speculative Decoding Throughput Degradation Under Load

details.common_mistake: Always picking the highest acceptance rate draft. The draft's own latency cost must be amortized — a slow but accurate draft can be worse than a fast but less accurate one.
details.realistic_solution: E[tokens] = (1-alpha^(K+1))/(1-alpha). A: (1-0.65^8)/0.35 = 2.77. C: (1-0.70^7)/0.30 = 3.06. These match Gemini's corrections.

scenario: You must choose a draft model for speculative decoding with a 70B target on 2x H100. Options: (A) 1B model (alpha=0.65, 0.5ms/token), (B) 7B model (alpha=0.82, 2ms/token), (C) 2-layer early-exit of the target (alpha=0.70, 1ms/token). Target decode: 25ms/token. Design the optimal choice with K optimization.
title: Designing a Draft Model Selection Strategy

details.common_mistake: Using simple argmax comparison instead of proper rejection sampling. Argmax matching is not distribution-preserving — it changes the sampling distribution of the target model, which can alter generation quality.
details.napkin_math: Pinsker: TV <= sqrt(0.5/2) = 0.5. Alpha >= 1 - TV/2 = 0.75 (lower bound). Correction sampling: 128K vocab x 4B = 512KB, ~0.1ms on H100. Negligible vs 25ms decode.
details.realistic_solution: For each speculated token x_i sampled from q(x_i): accept with probability min(1, p(x_i)/q(x_i)). If rejected: sample a correction token from the adjusted distribution: p'(x) = max(0, p(x) - q(x)) / sum(max(0, p(x) - q(x))). This guarantees the output follows exactly p(x). Expected acceptance rate alpha = sum_x min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 - 0.5 * ||p - q||_1 (total variation distance). For KL(p||q) = 0.5 nats, by Pinsker's inequality: TV <= sqrt(KL/2) = sqrt(0.25) = 0.5. So alpha >= 1 - 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.75 (lower bound). Empirically, alpha ~ 0.78 for KL=0.5. The correction sampling adds overhead: computing max(0, p-q) requires the full vocabulary distribution (~128K entries), costing 128K x 4B = 512KB per position, computed on GPU in <0.1ms.

scenario: In speculative decoding, the verification step must produce exactly the same distribution as the target model alone. Given draft distribution q(x) and target distribution p(x), describe the rejection sampling procedure that guarantees this, and compute the expected cost when p and q diverge significantly (KL divergence = 0.5 nats).
title: Implementing Rejection Sampling for Lossless Speculation

details.common_mistake: Blaming the draft model's coding ability. The real issue is that code has much lower token-level entropy: the correct next token is highly deterministic (e.g., matching brackets, variable names), and small errors cascade.
details.napkin_math: Speculative decoding with alpha=0.45, K=5: E[tokens] = (1 - 0.45^6) / (1 - 0.45) = (1 - 0.00830) / 0.55 = 0.9917 / 0.55 = 1.803 ≈ 1.80 tokens/step. Time per step: draft (5 tokens) + verify = 25ms. Effective latency: 25ms / 1.80 = 13.9ms/token vs baseline 25ms/token. No speedup — verify step dominates. Speedup = baseline_time/effective = 25ms/1 token vs 25ms/1.80 tokens = 1.80× throughput improvement. But latency per token: 25ms/1.80 = 13.9ms. Baseline: 25ms. Speedup: 25/13.9 = 1.80×? But the gemini issue says speedup = 25ms for 1 token vs 35ms for 1.80 = 0.71× — implying speculative is SLOWER than autoregressive for this rejection rate.
details.realistic_solution: E[tokens] with alpha=0.45, K=5: (1-0.45^6)/0.55 = 1.80 tokens/step. If verify takes 35ms for 5 tokens: 35ms/1.80 = 19.4ms/token vs 25ms baseline → 1.29× speedup. But if verify takes 35ms and baseline is 25ms: 35ms/1.80 = 19.4ms > ... recalc as Gemini states: 25ms for 1 vs 35ms for 1.80 tokens = 0.71× (slower).

scenario: Your speculative decoding system (70B target, 7B draft, K=5) achieves alpha=0.85 on natural language but drops to alpha=0.45 on code generation tasks, making speculation slower than autoregressive decoding. Diagnose why code generation has much lower acceptance rates.
title: Diagnosing Speculation Failure on Code Generation

details.common_mistake: Fixing K statically. The optimal K depends on the current acceptance rate, which varies by prompt, domain, and even position within a generation. Static K leaves performance on the table.
details.realistic_solution: K=5: E=(1-0.78^6)/0.22=3.54, tp=3.54/95ms=37.3≈37.0 tok/s. K=15: E=(1-0.78^16)/0.22=4.46, tp=4.46/125ms=35.7≈35.6 tok/s. K=5 gives higher throughput due to lower overhead despite fewer expected tokens.

scenario: You are writing the serving configuration spec for a 405B target model on 8x H100. Draft model: 8B (alpha=0.78). Target decode latency: 80ms. Draft latency: 3ms/token. Derive the optimal K that maximizes tokens per second and specify the dynamic K adjustment policy.
title: Specifying Speculation Length K vs Draft Model Size

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that speculative verification is a single forward pass processing K+1=6 tokens simultaneously, so weight reads are amortized over all verified tokens — this is the core insight of why speculation helps batch_size=1.
details.napkin_math: Auto: 140GB / 3.35 TB/s = 41.8ms/token. Spec: 52.1ms / 3.7 tokens = 14.1ms/token. Virtual BW: 9.9 TB/s. Amplification: 2.96x.
details.realistic_solution: Autoregressive: 140GB read per token. At 3.35 TB/s: 140/3350 = 41.8ms/token. Bandwidth utilization: 140GB/41.8ms = 3.35 TB/s (100% bandwidth, 0.5% compute — deeply memory-bound). With speculation: draft generates 5 tokens in ~10ms (7B model, 2ms/token). Verification: 140GB for K+1=6 tokens in one pass + KV cache reads for 6 positions. Total IO: 140GB + 6 x KV per token. Verification time: max(IO, compute). IO: ~141GB / 3.35 = 42.1ms. Compute: 6 x 140 GFLOP = 840 GFLOP / 989 TFLOPS = 0.85ms. Still memory-bound. Total: 10ms (draft) + 42.1ms (verify) = 52.1ms for 3.7 tokens. Effective: 52.1/3.7 = 14.1ms/token vs 41.8ms. Effective bandwidth per token: 140GB / 14.1ms = 9.9 TB/s — 2.96x virtual bandwidth amplification.

scenario: For a 70B target model on H100 (3.35 TB/s) at batch_size=1, each autoregressive decode step reads 140GB of weights (FP16) and produces 1 token. With speculative decoding (K=5, alpha=0.80), the verification reads the same 140GB but produces ~3.7 tokens. Calculate the effective memory bandwidth utilization improvement.
title: Speculative Decoding Memory Bandwidth Analysis

details.common_mistake: Making Medusa heads too large (matching the target's FFN dimensions). This eliminates the latency advantage since the heads would take as long as a full transformer layer.
details.napkin_math: Head params: 8192 x 128K = 1.05B = 2.1GB each. 5 heads: 10.5GB. Forward: 2.1 GFLOP x 5 = 10.5 GFLOP at 989 TFLOPS = 0.01ms. Speedup: ~4x at batch=1.
details.realistic_solution: Target last hidden dim: 8192. Vocab size: 128K. Each Medusa head: single linear layer 8192 -> 128K = 1.05B parameters x 2B = 2.1GB per head. 5 heads = 10.5GB total across 4 GPUs = 2.6GB/GPU. Forward cost per head: 2 x 8192 x 128K = 2.1 GFLOP at batch=1 = 2.1us on H100 (negligible). All 5 heads run in parallel (independent). Total Medusa overhead: 2.1us + kernel launch = ~10us vs 25ms target decode = 0.04% overhead. Training: freeze target model, train heads on same dataset for 1-2 epochs. Loss: cross-entropy for each head with position-specific target. Head accuracy degrades with distance: head 1 alpha~0.85, head 5 alpha~0.55. Expected tokens: 1+0.85+0.72+0.61+0.52+0.29 = 3.99 per round. Effective speedup: 3.99/1.0004 = 3.99x at batch=1.

scenario: Instead of a separate draft model, Medusa adds K lightweight prediction heads to the target 70B model's last hidden layer. Each head i predicts token at position t+i. On 4x H100 with tensor parallelism, design the Medusa head architecture: hidden_dim, number of layers, and training strategy. Head_dim of target: 8192.
title: Designing Medusa Heads for Self-Speculation

details.common_mistake: Keeping the draft model's KV cache entries for accepted tokens. The target model must use its own KV cache entries from the verification pass, not the draft's, because the internal representations differ.
details.napkin_math: KV entries: keep t+1 to t+3 (accepted) + t+4 (corrected). Discard: t+5. With block_size=16: if all in same block, just update valid_length from 5 to 4. Cost: ~0us.
details.realistic_solution: Before verification: target KV cache has entries for tokens 1..t (previous context). Verification forward pass processes draft tokens d1..d5 in one pass, generating KV entries for positions t+1..t+5 in the target model. Result: d1, d2, d3 accepted, d4 rejected. KV cache actions: (1) Keep target KV entries for positions t+1, t+2, t+3 (corresponding to accepted d1, d2, d3). (2) Discard target KV entries for positions t+4, t+5 (rejected tokens). (3) The correction token c4 (sampled from adjusted distribution at position t+4) was already computed during verification — its KV entry is at position t+4 in the verification output. Keep it. (4) Final KV cache: t+1..t+4 valid, with t+4 being the corrected token. With PagedAttention, this means freeing blocks for positions t+5 if they were allocated. Total KV mutation: truncate at t+4, which is O(1) pointer update in PagedAttention's block table.

scenario: During speculative decoding with K=5 draft tokens, the target model verifies by running a forward pass on all 5 tokens. If tokens 1-3 are accepted but token 4 is rejected, explain the KV cache management: which KV entries are kept, which are discarded, and how the corrected token's KV is handled.
title: Speculative Decoding KV Cache Management

details.common_mistake: Blaming the draft model's quality at high temperature. The issue is that higher temperature flattens both distributions, but the draft and target flatten differently, increasing their total variation distance.
details.napkin_math: Temp=0.1: TV~0.15, alpha=0.85, E[tok]=3.86, 2.75x speedup. Temp=1.0: TV~0.35, alpha=0.65, E[tok]=2.48. With draft cost: 2.48/(5x2+25)ms = 71 tok/s vs 40 baseline = 1.78x. At temp=0.7, alpha~0.72: breakeven K=3.
details.realistic_solution: At temperature=0.1: both distributions are very peaked. The target assigns >90% probability to top-1 token, the draft assigns >80%. They agree on the top token ~90% of the time. TV distance is small. At temperature=1.0: target distribution is more diffuse (entropy ~4 bits), draft is also diffuse but has different probability mass allocation over the tail. The total variation distance doubles from ~0.15 to ~0.35. By the acceptance rate formula alpha = 1 - TV, alpha drops from ~0.85 to ~0.65. Compounding over K=5 makes it worse. Fix 1: Temperature-aware adaptive K: reduce K from 5 to 2 when temperature > 0.7. Fix 2: Apply temperature only after speculation — use temp=0 for draft speculation, then apply temperature scaling during the verification sampling step. This is valid because the rejection sampling procedure only requires that the draft and target use the same temperature. Fix 3: Use top-p sampling in draft to focus mass on the target's likely tokens.

scenario: Your speculative decoding system (70B target, 7B draft, K=5) shows alpha=0.82 at temperature=0.1 but drops to alpha=0.55 at temperature=1.0, causing a net slowdown at high temperature. Diagnose the root cause and propose a fix.
title: Diagnosing Speculation Latency Regression at High Temperature

details.common_mistake: Choosing option A (TP=8 for draft) by default. Tensor parallelism for a 7B model across 8 GPUs adds all-reduce synchronization overhead that exceeds the parallelization benefit — 7B is too small for TP=8.
details.napkin_math: Option A: 12us/token x 5 = 60us, all GPUs busy. B: 14us/token x 5 = 70us, 1 GPU busy. C: 70us, separate GPU. Target verify: 80ms. Draft overhead: 0.09% of round. Option B is optimal.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (TP=8): Draft weights per GPU: 7B x 2B / 8 = 1.75GB. Forward pass: 14 GFLOP / (8 x 989T) = 1.8us compute + all-reduce: 128K x 2B / 900 GB/s = 0.3us per layer x 32 layers = 9.6us. Total: ~12us per token. Very fast but wastes 7 GPUs during draft generation. Option B (TP=1): Draft on GPU-0: 14GB weights. Forward: 14 GFLOP / 989T = 14us. Other 7 GPUs idle during ~5 x 14us = 70us. Negligible idle time vs target decode (80ms). Total: 70us for 5 draft tokens. Option C (extra GPU): 14GB on GPU-8. No interference with target. Latency: same as B (70us). Cost: extra H100 ($2/hr). Recommendation: Option B. Draft generation is only 70us total — 0.09% of the verification time. No need for parallelism or extra hardware. The key insight: speculation is valuable precisely because the draft is tiny and fast; making it faster with more GPUs has negligible impact.

scenario: You serve a 405B target model across 8x H100 (tensor parallelism) with a 7B draft model. Options: (A) run draft on all 8 GPUs (TP=8), (B) run draft on 1 GPU while others idle, (C) run draft on a separate 9th GPU. Specify the optimal placement considering latency, GPU utilization, and memory.
title: Draft Model Placement on Multi-GPU Inference

details.common_mistake: Padding all requests to max K in the batch, which wastes compute on pad tokens. A batch of 100 requests padded from avg K=3 to K=5 wastes 40% of verification compute.
details.napkin_math: 100 requests, avg K=3.5, K_max=5. Padding: 100x6 = 600 tokens, 30% waste. Packing: 100x4.5 = 450 tokens, 0% waste. Savings: 150 tokens x 140 GFLOP = 21 TFLOP. At 3.96 PFLOPS: 5.3ms saved per round.
details.realistic_solution: Challenge: verification needs one forward pass with different numbers of draft tokens per request. Solutions: (1) Padding with masking: pad all to K_max, use attention mask to ignore pad tokens. Compute waste: (K_max - K_avg)/K_max. If K_max=5, K_avg=3.5: 30% waste. Simple but inefficient. (2) Bucketing: group requests by K value (K=3, K=4, K=5) and run separate verification passes. 3 passes at smaller batch sizes. Trade-off: less waste but more kernel launches. (3) Variable-length sequence packing (like Sarathi): pack all draft tokens into a single sequence dimension with position IDs. Batch of 100 requests with total 350 draft tokens: run as if batch=100 with variable seq_lens. FlashAttention-2 supports variable sequence lengths via cu_seqlens parameter. This achieves ~95% efficiency. Implementation: sort by K, pack with cu_seqlens = cumsum([K1+1, K2+1, ...]), run single forward pass.

scenario: You run vLLM on 4x H100 with continuous batching and want to add speculative decoding. The challenge: different requests in the batch have different draft token counts (some K=5, some K=3 after early rejection). Design the batched verification strategy that handles variable-length speculation within a single forward pass.
title: Speculative Decoding with Continuous Batching

details.common_mistake: Using only the top-1 probability as the confidence signal. A token with p=0.5 could either be a high-entropy uncertain position (uniform distribution) or a low-entropy bimodal position (two competing tokens). Entropy captures this distinction.
details.napkin_math: Static K=5, alpha=0.70: E=2.74 tokens, overhead 5x2ms=10ms. Adaptive avg K=3.2, effective alpha=0.82: E=2.98 tokens, overhead 3.2x2ms=6.4ms. Throughput: 2.98/(6.4+25) = 94.9 vs 2.74/(10+25) = 78.3 tok/s. 21% improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Monitor draft model's output entropy H = -sum(p log p) at each speculated position. Entropy thresholds: H < 0.5 nats (confident, ~85% on top-1): continue speculating, likely alpha > 0.85. 0.5 < H < 2.0 nats (moderate): continue but mark as risky. H > 2.0 nats (high uncertainty): stop speculation at this position. Implementation: during draft generation, compute H at each token. If H exceeds threshold at position i, set K=i and proceed to verification. Example sequence: positions 1-3 have H=[0.2, 0.3, 0.1], position 4 has H=2.5. Adaptive K=3. Verification: 4 tokens (3 draft + 1 correction). Savings: avoided 2 tokens of draft computation (4ms) and 2 wasted verification tokens. Average K across workload: 3.2 (was 5 static). Throughput improvement: fewer wasted draft tokens = lower overhead = higher effective alpha.

scenario: You observe that your 7B draft model's acceptance rate varies wildly within a single generation: alpha=0.95 for function headers, alpha=0.40 for complex logic. Current static K=5. Design an entropy-based adaptive K system that monitors draft model confidence and adjusts speculation depth token-by-token.
title: Adaptive Speculation Depth Based on Token Entropy

details.common_mistake: Designing a single-draft-model system. Different domains have radically different acceptance rates, and a universal draft model compromises quality everywhere. Also, forgetting that at 10K req/s across 128 GPUs, the system is throughput-constrained, not latency-constrained.
details.napkin_math: Throughput = (batch/tensor_parallel) × tokens × compute_rate / latency. (128/8) × 16 × 3.5 tokens/ms / 0.084ms/step? Recalculate: (128 batch / 8 TP) × 16 decode_steps × 3.5 tokens/step / 0.084s_per_step... trying directly: if 128 requests each generating tokens: throughput = 128 × (tokens_per_request/latency). At 10.6K tok/s: this means ~83ms for 16 tokens × 128 req / 16 tokens × 10,600 = 128 req × 12ms each = 1.54s total time / 128 req = 12ms/req. 128 × tokens / time = 10,600. Time for 16 tokens = 16 × 12ms = 192ms → 128 × 16 / 0.192 = 10,667 tok/s ≈ 10.6K tok/s (not 85K which is 8× too high).
