details.realistic_solution: Throughput = (128/8) × 16 × 3.5 / 0.084 = 16 × 16 × 3.5/0.084 ≈ 10,667 tok/s ≈ 10.6K tok/s (not 85K which overstates by 8×).

scenario: You are the Staff ML engineer designing speculative decoding for a production chatbot serving 10K req/s on 128x H100 (16 nodes). Target: 405B model, P99 latency < 200ms per token. Must handle diverse workloads: chat (alpha~0.80), code (alpha~0.50), math (alpha~0.60). Design the complete system: draft model selection, adaptive K, batching strategy, and failover behavior.
title: Full-Stack Speculative Decoding Architecture

details.common_mistake: Thinking top-1 comparison is equivalent to full distribution comparison. If both models predict the same top-1 token but with different probabilities, top-1 matching would accept at 100% rate, effectively replacing the target's sampling distribution with a deterministic one.
details.napkin_math: Top-1 matching acceptance: ~90% for high-quality draft, but output distribution != p(x). Full rejection sampling: alpha = 1 - TV(p,q) ~ 80%, but output distribution = p(x) exactly. Lossless guarantee is non-negotiable for production.
details.realistic_solution: The rejection sampling procedure guarantees that the combined output distribution is exactly p(x) — the target model's distribution. This is the lossless property. It works by: (1) sampling x ~ q(x) from draft, (2) accepting with prob min(1, p(x)/q(x)), (3) on rejection, sampling from the residual distribution max(0, p(x)-q(x))/Z. This ensures: P(output=x) = q(x) x min(1, p(x)/q(x)) + P(rejected) x max(0, p(x)-q(x))/Z = p(x). Top-1 comparison would be lossy: if draft and target agree on top-1 but the target wants to sample a tail token 5% of the time, top-1 matching would suppress that 5% — changing the effective temperature and diversity of the target model. This matters for creative writing, diverse code generation, and any temperature > 0 use case.

scenario: In speculative decoding, the draft model q(x) and target model p(x) must be compared token by token. Why must speculative decoding use the full vocabulary probability distributions rather than just comparing top-1 tokens, and what property does the rejection sampling procedure guarantee?
title: Speculative Decoding Token Probability Calibration

details.common_mistake: Treating speculation and batching as additive improvements. They are partially competing: both exploit the same resource (memory bandwidth headroom). At larger batch sizes, decode becomes less memory-bound, reducing speculation's benefit.
details.napkin_math: (A) 71 tok/s, 14.1ms latency. (B) 741 tok/s, 10.8ms latency. (C) 1366 tok/s, 5.9ms latency. Batch=32 no-spec: ~2800 tok/s, 11.5ms. Speculation shines for latency, batching for throughput.
details.realistic_solution: (A) Speculation at batch=1: round = 10ms (draft) + 42ms (verify, 140GB/3.35TB). E[tokens]=3.69. Latency: 52/3.69 = 14.1ms/tok. Throughput: 71 tok/s. MBU: 140GB/52ms = 2.69 TB/s (80%). (B) Batch=8 no speculation: weight read = 140GB (same — amortized over 8 requests). KV read per step: 8 x 640MB = 5.1GB. Total IO: 145GB at 13.4 TB/s = 10.8ms. Compute: 8 x 140G = 1.12T / 3.96P = 0.28ms. Latency: 10.8ms/tok (per request). Throughput: 8/10.8ms = 741 tok/s. MBU: 145GB/10.8ms = 13.4 TB/s (100%). (C) Both: batch=8 spec K=5: verify processes 8x6=48 tokens. IO: 140GB + 48 x KV = 155GB at 13.4 TB/s = 11.6ms. Compute: 48 x 140G = 6.72T / 3.96P = 1.7ms. Draft: 10ms. Total: 21.6ms for 8 x 3.69 = 29.5 tokens. Throughput: 1366 tok/s. Latency: 21.6/3.69 = 5.9ms. Best throughput but highest GPU utilization. Verdict: if latency goal, use (C). If throughput goal, batch=32 without speculation is even better.

scenario: On 4x H100, a 70B model at batch=1 produces 24 tok/s (memory-bound). Your options to improve throughput: (A) speculative decoding with K=5 (alpha=0.80), (B) simply increase batch size to 8, (C) both. Compare latency per token, total throughput, and GPU utilization for each option.
title: Speculative Decoding vs Increasing Batch Size

details.common_mistake: Using only the last layer's hidden state. EAGLE concatenates the hidden state with the token embedding to provide both semantic (hidden state) and surface-level (embedding) information, which is crucial for predicting the next token's identity.
details.napkin_math: EAGLE head: 1.65B params = 3.3GB. Per GPU (TP=4): 0.83GB. Forward: 3.3us. Alpha improvement: 0.78 -> 0.87. E[tokens]: 3.38 -> 4.45. Speedup: 2.75x -> 3.5x. Extra memory: 1% of VRAM.
details.realistic_solution: EAGLE draft head input: concat(last_hidden_state[t], embedding[t+1_predicted]) = 8192 + 8192 = 16384 dim. Head architecture: 1 transformer layer (self-attention + FFN) with hidden_dim=8192, then linear to vocab (128K). Parameters: attention: 4 x 8192^2 = 268M. FFN: 3 x 8192 x 8192 = 201M (using 1x expansion instead of 4x). Projection: 16384->8192 = 134M. Vocab head: 8192 x 128K = 1.05B. Total: ~1.65B params = 3.3GB FP16 = 0.83GB/GPU. Memory overhead: 0.83GB/GPU (1% of 80GB). Forward cost: 3.3 GFLOP at 989 TFLOPS = 3.3us per token — negligible. Training: requires target model's hidden states, so generate offline by running target on training data and saving hidden states. ~100K examples sufficient. EAGLE achieves alpha=0.85-0.90 vs regular draft model alpha=0.78, because the hidden state carries 'what the target model is thinking' not just 'what tokens were generated.'

scenario: EAGLE uses the target model's hidden states (not just token embeddings) as input to a lightweight draft head, achieving higher acceptance rates than token-level draft models. For a 70B target on 4x H100 with hidden_dim=8192, design an EAGLE-style draft head: input features, head architecture, training data requirements, and memory budget.
title: EAGLE-2 Self-Speculative Architecture

details.common_mistake: Thinking verification costs K times more than a single step. At batch=1, decode is memory-bound: reading 140GB of weights dominates. Whether you process 1 or 6 tokens against those weights, the IO cost is the same.
details.napkin_math: 1 token: IO=41.8ms, compute=0.14ms. 6 tokens: IO=41.8ms, compute=0.85ms. Both memory-bound at 41.8ms. Verification is free: compute/IO ratio goes from 0.3% to 2% — still deeply below the ridge point (295 FLOP/byte).
details.realistic_solution: Single autoregressive step (batch=1): IO = 140GB (read all weights). Compute = 2 x 70B = 140 GFLOP. Time = max(140GB/3.35TB, 140G/989T) = max(41.8ms, 0.14ms) = 41.8ms. Memory-bound. Verification of K+1=6 tokens: IO = 140GB (same weight read, amortized) + 6 x KV_per_token (negligible). Compute = 6 x 140G = 840 GFLOP. Time = max(140GB/3.35TB, 840G/989T) = max(41.8ms, 0.85ms) = 41.8ms. Still memory-bound! The extra 5x compute (840G vs 140G) is invisible because we're IO-bound. This is why verification is essentially 'free' — we're paying for the weight reads anyway, and the tensor cores are idle during those reads. Verification adds K tokens of KV cache write: 6 x 320KB = 1.92MB, which is 0.001% of the weight read.

scenario: For a 70B target model on H100, verify that the verification forward pass for K=5 draft tokens costs approximately the same wall-clock time as a single autoregressive step at batch=1. Compute the FLOP count and memory IO for both and explain why verification is 'free' relative to generation.
title: Speculative Decoding Verification Compute Cost

details.common_mistake: Assuming the draft model can leverage the suffix context as well as the target. Small draft models typically have worse bidirectional attention or are not trained on FIM, causing alpha to plummet compared to standard left-to-right generation.
details.napkin_math: Standard alpha=0.82: 2.75x. FIM alpha=0.55: 1.59x. With suffix-encoding: alpha=0.70: 2.2x. N-gram suffix matching (free): alpha=0.40, E=1.52, 2.76x only if verify is truly free. Suffix-aware draft is the best practical approach.
details.realistic_solution: In FIM, the model sees [PREFIX] [SUFFIX] [MIDDLE_to_generate]. The target 70B has strong bidirectional understanding: it can predict MIDDLE tokens that are coherent with both prefix and suffix. The 7B draft model, while FIM-capable, has weaker suffix conditioning — its predictions often ignore subtle suffix constraints. Empirically: alpha drops from 0.82 (standard) to 0.55 (FIM) for the 7B draft. At alpha=0.55, K=5: E[tokens] = (1-0.55^6)/0.45 = 1.97. Time: 10ms + 42ms = 52ms for 1.97 tokens = 26.4ms/tok vs 42ms auto. Only 1.59x speedup — marginal. Optimization: Use suffix-aware draft decoding: run a separate suffix-encoding pass on the draft, creating a 'suffix KV cache' that biases draft generation. This adds 5ms overhead but increases alpha to ~0.70. At alpha=0.70: E[tok]=2.74, time=52ms, effective=19ms/tok, 2.2x speedup. Alternative: for FIM, use n-gram matching against the suffix as a zero-cost draft signal.

scenario: Your code completion system uses fill-in-the-middle (FIM) where the model generates tokens conditioned on both prefix and suffix. Standard speculative decoding assumes left-to-right generation. With a 70B target and 7B draft on H100, analyze how FIM affects draft model accuracy and propose modifications to the speculation strategy.
title: Speculative Decoding for Fill-in-the-Middle Tasks

details.common_mistake: Thinking TTFT degradation is caused by draft model initialization. The real cause is that the draft model also needs to prefill the prompt, adding its own prefill latency to the critical path.
details.napkin_math: Target prefill: 200ms. Draft prefill: 29ms. Draft generate: 10ms. Verify: 42ms. Sequential TTFT: 281ms. Fix: skip first speculation round. TTFT: 200ms + 42ms (first auto-regressive step) = 242ms. Then spec from token 2.
details.realistic_solution: Without speculation, TTFT = target prefill time for prompt (2048 tokens at 70B): 2 x 70B x 2048 / 989 TFLOPS = 290ms. Measured 200ms suggests some optimization (e.g., FP8 prefill or shorter prompt). With speculation: draft must also prefill the prompt to generate its first draft tokens. Draft prefill: 2 x 7B x 2048 / 989T = 29ms. But draft and target run sequentially on same GPU: TTFT = target_prefill (200ms) + draft_prefill (29ms) + draft_generate_K (10ms) + target_verify (42ms) = 281ms. Wait, the first token is emitted after target verification, not after target prefill alone. Without spec: first token after prefill = 200ms. With spec: prefill(200ms) + draft_K_tokens(10ms) + verify(42ms) = 252ms, but draft needs its own prefill first = 29ms. Total: 229ms if parallelized, 281ms if sequential. Actual 350ms suggests draft prefill is not overlapped and there's additional KV cache setup. Fix: skip speculation for the first decode step — emit first token immediately after target prefill (200ms TTFT), then start speculation from token 2 onwards.

scenario: After enabling speculative decoding for a 70B model on H100, users report that TTFT (time to first token) increased from 200ms to 350ms. Tokens per second after the first token improved 2.5x. Diagnose why TTFT degraded and propose a fix.
title: Speculative Decoding Impact on Time-to-First-Token

details.common_mistake: Thinking you can simply run draft and target in parallel on the same GPUs. CUDA streams on the same GPU share compute resources, so concurrent kernels would compete for SMs and memory bandwidth, slowing both.
details.napkin_math: Serial: 42ms (verify) + 5ms (draft) = 47ms/round. Pipelined: 42ms (verify overlapped with 5ms draft) = 42ms/round. Savings: 5ms/round = 10.6%. With rollback: 0.2 x 5ms waste = 1ms avg. Net: 42ms vs 46ms = 8.7% improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Approach: use GPU-0 for both draft (when target is verifying) since during target verification with TP=4, each GPU runs 1/4 of the work — GPU-0 has spare SM capacity. Target verification at batch=1: each GPU uses ~30% of SMs (memory-bound). Draft on GPU-0: 1B model needs ~5% of SMs. Can coexist. Pipeline: Round N: [Draft_N generates K tokens] -> [Target verifies K tokens (GPU 0-3) | Draft_N+1 generates K tokens (GPU-0, different stream)] -> [Accept/reject N, Draft_N+1 ready]. Timing: target verify = 42ms. Draft K=5 = 5ms. Draft finishes within verification window. But: draft generation for round N+1 must use SPECULATIVE tokens from round N (not yet confirmed). If round N rejects at position 3, draft N+1's tokens from position 4+ are invalid. Fix: run draft N+1 from the last confirmed position (conservative) or speculatively assume full acceptance (optimistic, requires rollback). Optimistic approach: 80% of the time no rollback needed (alpha=0.80). 20% of time: wasted 5ms of draft compute.

scenario: In standard speculative decoding, draft generation and target verification are serial: draft runs, then target verifies. On a 4x H100 system with the target using TP=4 and a 1B draft, design a pipelining scheme that overlaps draft generation of round N+1 with target verification of round N.
title: Parallel Draft and Target Execution Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Setting up the inequality incorrectly by comparing per-token latency instead of per-round expected tokens. The breakeven is when E[tokens]/round_time = 1/auto_time.
details.napkin_math: Breakeven: E[tok] >= round_time / auto_time. K=5, 2ms draft: E >= 52/42 = 1.24, alpha_min = 0.20. K=5, 10ms draft: E >= 92/42 = 2.19, alpha_min = 0.58. Cheap drafts have very low breakeven.
details.realistic_solution: Autoregressive: 42ms per token (memory-bound on H100). Speculative round: K x draft_cost + verify_cost = 5 x 2 + 42 = 52ms. E[tokens] = (1 - alpha^(K+1))/(1-alpha). Breakeven: E[tokens]/52ms >= 1/42ms. E[tokens] >= 52/42 = 1.238. (1 - alpha^6)/(1-alpha) >= 1.238. For alpha: at alpha=0.15: (1-0.15^6)/0.85 = 1.176. At alpha=0.20: (1-0.20^6)/0.80 = 1.250. So alpha_min ≈ 0.20. General formula: E[tokens] >= (K x c_draft + c_verify) / c_auto, where c_draft = draft cost per token, c_verify = verification cost, c_auto = auto cost. For K=5, c_draft=2, c_verify=42, c_auto=42: alpha_min = 0.20. Surprisingly low! Speculation is hard to make worse when draft is cheap. At K=10, c_draft=2: round = 62ms. E >= 62/42 = 1.48. alpha_min = 0.32. At K=5, c_draft=10 (expensive draft): round = 92ms. E >= 92/42 = 2.19. alpha_min = 0.58.

scenario: For a 70B target on H100 with a 7B draft (2ms/token draft cost, 42ms verification cost), derive the minimum acceptance rate alpha_min below which speculative decoding becomes slower than autoregressive decoding for K=5. Then extend to find the general formula for arbitrary K and draft cost.
title: Speculative Decoding Break-Even Analysis

details.common_mistake: Only accounting for the target model's KV cache. The draft model also needs its own KV cache for the conversation history, effectively doubling KV memory requirements if the draft has the same architecture depth.
details.napkin_math: Target KV: 2.56GB. Draft KV: 1.024GB. Total: 3.58GB. Without spec: 65 concurrent. With spec: 46. Spec costs 29% capacity. FP8 KV: 92 concurrent. Need 100: add draft KV eviction policy.
details.realistic_solution: Target KV per request per GPU (70B, 8 GQA KV heads, 80 layers, 8K tokens): 80 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 8192 x 2B / 4 = 2.56GB. Draft KV per request per GPU (7B, 8 KV heads, 32 layers, 8K tokens): 32 x 2 x 8 x 128 x 8192 x 2B / 4 = 1.024GB. Total KV: 3.584GB/request/GPU. Model weights: target 35GB + draft 3.5GB = 38.5GB/GPU. Budget: 80 - 38.5 = 41.5GB for KV. Max concurrent: 41.5/3.584 = 11.6 requests/GPU = 46 total. Without speculation: 41.5/2.56 = 16.2/GPU = 65 total. Speculation reduces capacity by 29%. At 100 concurrent requirement: neither works. Solution: use FP8 KV quantization: target KV halves to 1.28GB, draft to 0.512GB. Total: 1.792GB. Max concurrent: 41.5/1.792 = 23/GPU = 92. Still under 100. Add draft KV eviction: keep draft KV only for active speculation, regenerate from target KV when needed. Draft prefill for 8K context: 2 x 7B x 8K / 989T = 114ms — too slow to regenerate every round. Compromise: keep draft KV for top-50 most recent sessions, regenerate for others.

scenario: In a multi-turn chat system on 4x H100 (70B model, 7B draft), requests arrive with conversation history averaging 8K tokens. The draft model's KV cache for the history adds 320MB per request per GPU. With 100 concurrent sessions, analyze whether speculation's memory overhead for the draft model's KV cache limits the system's capacity.
title: Speculative Decoding for Batched Multi-Turn Chat

details.common_mistake: Using a single speculation strategy for the entire 10K generation. The acceptance rate and optimal K vary dramatically across the generation: openings are predictable, body paragraphs are creative, and conclusions follow templates.
details.napkin_math: Uniform K=5: 310s. Staged linear: 312s (negligible improvement). Staged with tree for body: 276s (11% improvement). The body phase dominates at 87% of generation time. Optimizing the body's alpha matters most.
details.realistic_solution: Phase analysis: (1) Opening (tokens 1-500): template language, high predictability. Alpha=0.90, optimal K=12. (2) Body (500-8500): novel content, lower predictability. Alpha=0.72, optimal K=6. (3) Conclusion (8500-10000): formulaic summary, refs back to body. Alpha=0.85, optimal K=10. Per-phase optimization: Opening: large K=12 with 8B draft. E[tok]=(1-0.90^13)/0.10=6.51. Round=12x3+80=116ms. Rate=6.51/116=56 tok/s. Time for 500 tokens: 8.9s. Body: K=6 with draft. E=2.89. Round=6x3+80=98ms. Rate=29.5 tok/s. 8000 tokens: 271s. Conclusion: K=10. E=5.16. Round=10x3+80=110ms. Rate=46.9 tok/s. 1500 tokens: 32s. Total staged: 8.9+271+32 = 312s. Uniform K=5: 310s. Marginal improvement! The key insight: most time is spent in the body phase where alpha is lowest. Real optimization: for body phase, use tree speculation (branching factor 3, depth 4) to explore multiple continuations. Tree with alpha=0.72: E=3.8 tokens at 12-token tree cost. Rate=3.8/(12x3+80)=34 tok/s. Body: 8000/34=235s. Total: 8.9+235+32=276s. 11% improvement over uniform.

scenario: You are generating a 10K-token response (long-form report) from a 405B model on 8x H100. At 80ms/token autoregressive, this takes 800 seconds. With K=5 speculation (alpha=0.78), it takes ~310 seconds. Design a staged speculation system that adapts strategy as the generation progresses through three phases: (1) low-entropy opening, (2) high-entropy body, (3) formulaic conclusion.
title: Staged Speculation for Ultra-Long Generation

details.common_mistake: Only comparing the steady-state P50. Speculation adds variance to the latency distribution because acceptance rate varies per request, making P99 worse even as P50 improves.
details.napkin_math: Speculation P50: 14.1ms (meets 15ms). P99: 30.8ms. Cost: $1.4M/yr (80 GPUs). Double cluster P50: 25ms (fails target). Cost: $2.24M/yr. Speculation saves $840K/yr AND meets the SLO.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (speculation): Draft 7B co-located on same GPUs (3.5GB/GPU with TP=8). P50 latency: with alpha=0.80 (median), E[tok]=3.69. Round=10+42=52ms. P50=52/3.69=14.1ms. Meets target. P99 latency: alpha at P1 (worst requests) ≈ 0.45. E[tok]=1.69. P99=52/1.69=30.8ms — same as current P50! Throughput impact: verification costs 6x compute per round, reducing max batch from 80 to ~60 per GPU. Max throughput: may drop 25%, requiring ~80 GPUs to maintain 5K req/s. Cost: 80 x $2 x 8760 = $1.4M/yr. Complexity: draft model maintenance, KV cache for draft, adaptive K tuning. Option B (double cluster): P50: batch per GPU halves, so latency stays ~30ms/tok but throughput headroom allows lower queuing delay. P50 ≈ 25ms. Does NOT meet 15ms target (latency is memory-bandwidth limited, not throughput limited). P99: 28ms. Cost: 128 x $2 x 8760 = $2.24M/yr. Complexity: standard scaling. Verdict: Option A meets the latency target at 37% lower cost. Option B cannot reduce per-token latency below the memory bandwidth limit.

scenario: Your serving cluster runs 64x H100 ($2/GPU/hr) serving a 70B model at 5K req/s. Current P50 latency: 30ms/tok. Product wants P50 < 15ms/tok (2x improvement). Option A: add speculative decoding (alpha=0.80, K=5, 7B draft). Option B: double the cluster to 128x H100. Compare the annual cost, latency distribution (P50/P99), and operational complexity of each approach.
title: Speculative Decoding Cost-Benefit for Serving Economics

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that all-to-all is bidirectional (dispatch + combine) and that each token sends its hidden state to 2 experts, not 1.
details.napkin_math: Per token payload: 4096 × 2B = 8 KB. Tokens per GPU per expert (uniform): 2048×2/8 = 512. Outbound per GPU: 512 × 7 × 8 KB ≈ 28 MB. Both directions: 56 MB/layer. 32 layers: ~1.8 GB.
details.realistic_solution: Each token sends its 4096-dim BF16 hidden state (8 KB) to 2 experts. With uniform routing, each GPU sends 2048 × 2 / 8 = 512 token-states to each of the other 7 GPUs. Total outbound per GPU: 512 × 7 × 8 KB = 28 MB per direction. The dispatch all-to-all and combine all-to-all together move ~56 MB per GPU per layer. For 32 layers, that is ~1.8 GB per GPU per forward pass — a significant fraction of NVLink bandwidth at 900 GB/s.

scenario: A Mixtral-style 8x7B MoE model uses top-2 routing with hidden dimension 4096 in BF16. Each token dispatches to 2 of 8 experts across 8 GPUs (one expert per GPU). For a micro-batch of 2048 tokens, estimate the all-to-all communication volume per layer in each direction.
title: MoE All-to-All Communication Volume

details.common_mistake: Blindly raising capacity factor without understanding the cost. CF=2.0 doubles the buffer size per expert, wasting memory and compute on padding for experts that receive few tokens.
details.napkin_math: Ideal tokens/expert: B×2/64. CF=1.25 buffer: 1.25×B×2/64 per expert. CF=2.0 buffer: 2.0×B×2/64, a 60% memory increase over CF=1.25. Expert-choice routing achieves CF=1.0 by construction.
details.realistic_solution: With 64 experts and top-2, each expert ideally receives 2/64 = 3.125% of tokens. CF=1.25 means each expert buffer holds 1.25 × (batch/64 × 2) tokens. The 8% drop rate suggests a few experts are heavily overloaded (routing collapse). Raising CF to 2.0 wastes 60% more memory on padding while only partially fixing drops. The better fix is to strengthen the auxiliary load-balancing loss coefficient (from e.g. 0.01 to 0.1) or switch to expert-choice routing where experts select their top-k tokens, guaranteeing perfect balance. Only raise CF modestly (to 1.5) as a stopgap while fixing the routing.

scenario: Your MoE training run uses top-2 routing with 64 experts and a capacity factor of 1.25. You observe that 8% of tokens are being dropped during training, yet validation loss has plateaued. Your colleague suggests raising the capacity factor to 2.0. Analyze whether this is the right fix.
title: MoE Capacity Factor and Token Dropping

details.common_mistake: Assuming the load-balancing loss is sufficient to prevent routing collapse. A low aux loss can still mask collapse if the loss only penalizes per-batch variance rather than long-term expert utilization.
details.napkin_math: Uniform entropy: log2(128) = 7.0 bits. Observed: 2.1 bits → ~4 active experts. Dead experts: 124/128 = 97%. Wasted parameters: 124 × expert_size. This is catastrophic for model capacity.
details.realistic_solution: Router entropy of 2.1 bits means the router effectively uses only ~4 of 128 experts (2^2.1 ≈ 4.3). This is classic routing collapse: the router learned to always select the same few experts, and the remaining 124 experts receive near-zero gradients, becoming dead weights. The aux loss converged because it measures per-batch balance — if 4 experts each get 25% of tokens, the batch is 'balanced' among those 4. Fixes: (1) Use z-loss to penalize large router logits, preventing confident routing. (2) Switch to expert-choice routing (each expert picks its top-k tokens). (3) Add router jitter/noise during training. (4) Use a combination of load-balancing loss + router z-loss as in DeepSeek-V3. Monitor expert utilization histograms, not just aux loss.

scenario: You are training a 128-expert MoE language model on 256 H100 GPUs. After 10K steps, you notice that the auxiliary load-balancing loss has converged but the router entropy has dropped to 2.1 bits (log2(128) = 7.0 bits would be uniform). Training loss improvement has stalled. Diagnose the root cause.
title: MoE Routing Collapse During Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming MoE uses the same memory as its active parameter count. All expert weights must be resident in memory even though only 2 of 8 experts fire per token.
details.napkin_math: Dense 13B: 26 GB, 1 GPU. Mixtral 8x7B: 93.4 GB, 2 GPUs minimum. Memory ratio: 93.4/26 = 3.6×. Active FLOP ratio: 12.9B/13B ≈ 1.0×. Memory-to-compute inefficiency: 3.6×.
details.realistic_solution: Dense 13B: 13B × 2B = 26 GB — fits on a single H100 (80 GB) with ample room for KV-cache. Mixtral 8x7B: 46.7B × 2B = 93.4 GB — requires at least 2×H100 GPUs. Despite having similar per-token compute (12.9B active ≈ 13B dense), the MoE model needs 3.6× more memory. This is the fundamental MoE serving challenge: you pay the memory cost of all experts but only use 2/8 = 25% of them per token. The benefit is quality — 46.7B parameters provide better representations than 13B, but at 3.6× memory cost for serving.

scenario: Compare the memory footprint for serving a Mixtral 8x7B MoE model (46.7B total parameters, 12.9B active per token) versus a dense 13B model, both in BF16 on H100 GPUs. How many GPUs does each require, and what is the memory efficiency gap?
title: MoE Memory Footprint vs Dense Equivalent

details.common_mistake: Trying to fix routing at serving time by adding noise. Inference routing must be deterministic — you cannot change which experts a token selects without degrading quality.
details.napkin_math: Current hot expert load: 40%/2 = 20% per hot GPU vs 10% per cold GPU. 2× imbalance → ~2× latency for hot experts. Replicating to 3 copies: 40%/6 = 6.7% per replica. Total GPUs: 8 + 4 = 12. Cost increase: 50%. Latency improvement: ~2×.
details.realistic_solution: Replicate the 2 hot experts across additional GPUs. Currently: 8 GPUs with 1 expert each. Hot experts get 20% each (2.5× average load). Solution: replicate each hot expert onto 2 additional GPUs, total 12 GPUs. Each hot expert replica serves ~13.3% of tokens (40%/3 copies). Load per GPU drops from 20% to 13.3%, below the 12.5% uniform average. Cost: 4 extra GPUs (50% more hardware). Alternative: use expert parallelism to split hot experts across 2 GPUs each (EP=2 per hot expert), halving their compute time. This adds NVLink communication but avoids full GPU replication. DeepSeek-V3 uses dynamic expert replication in their serving infrastructure for exactly this reason.

scenario: Your production MoE serving cluster shows P99 latency spikes of 45ms against a 30ms SLA. Profiling reveals that 2 of 8 experts receive 40% of all tokens while the remaining 6 share 60%. The overloaded expert GPUs are the bottleneck. Propose and quantify an optimization strategy.
title: MoE Expert Replication for Hot Experts

details.common_mistake: Overcomplicating the router architecture. MoE routers are intentionally simple — a single linear projection — to minimize overhead. Complex multi-layer routers add latency on the critical path.
details.napkin_math: Router: 7168 × 256 = 1.84M params. Expert FFN: ~264M params each. 256 experts: 67.6B. Router/total: 1.84M/67.6B = 0.003%.
details.realistic_solution: Router parameters: 7168 × 256 = 1,835,008 (~1.84M). Each expert FFN has approximately 7168 × 2 × 18432 = 264M parameters (up/gate/down projections). With 256 experts: 256 × 264M = 67.6B. The shared attention layers add more. Router fraction: 1.84M / 67.6B = 0.0027%, negligible. The router is deliberately tiny because it sits on the critical path — every token must pass through it before dispatch. A 2-layer MLP router would add latency for marginal routing quality improvement. The real computational cost of routing is not the router itself but the all-to-all communication it triggers.

scenario: A DeepSeek-V3-style MoE layer uses a gating network that takes a 7168-dim hidden state and produces logits over 256 experts. The gating network is a single linear layer. What is the parameter count of the router, and what fraction of total layer parameters does it represent?
title: MoE Gating Network Overhead

details.common_mistake: Choosing expert-choice solely because it guarantees load balance, without considering that it breaks autoregressive inference. In expert-choice, an expert selects tokens from the full batch, meaning each token's routing depends on other tokens in the batch — incompatible with causal decoding.
details.napkin_math: Token-choice with CF=1.25: 25% memory overhead for padding, 5-10% token drop rate. Expert-choice with CF=1.0: 0% overhead, 0% drops, but batch-dependent routing. Serving constraint forces token-choice for autoregressive LLMs.
details.realistic_solution: Token-choice (Mixtral/GShard style): Each token independently selects top-k experts. Pros: compatible with autoregressive decoding, simple serving. Cons: requires auxiliary loss for load balance, tokens can be dropped if experts overflow. Expert-choice (Zhou et al. 2022): Each expert selects its top-k tokens from the batch. Pros: perfect load balance by construction (CF=1.0), no token dropping, higher quality at same FLOP budget. Cons: routing depends on the full batch (not causal), so it cannot be used for autoregressive decoding without modification. For serving LLMs, token-choice is required. For encoder models or training-only objectives, expert-choice is superior. A hybrid approach: train with expert-choice for better quality, then distill or fine-tune with token-choice routing for serving.

scenario: Your team is debating between token-choice routing (each token picks its top-k experts) and expert-choice routing (each expert picks its top-k tokens) for a new 64-expert MoE training run. The model will be used for both training and serving. Evaluate the tradeoffs.
title: MoE Expert-Choice vs Token-Choice Routing

details.common_mistake: Assuming all experts must be GPU-resident. With 256 experts and top-2 routing, only 2 experts are active per token — the vast majority are idle at any given time and can reside in CPU DRAM or NVMe.
details.napkin_math: Total weights: 671B × 2B = 1.34 TB. HBM capacity: 640 GB (48% fit). Expert size: 4 GB BF16, 1 GB INT4. PCIe fetch: 4 GB/64 GB/s = 62.5ms (BF16), 15.6ms (INT4). With LRU cache hit rate of 90%: avg latency = 0.1 × 15.6ms = 1.56ms amortized.
details.realistic_solution: Total weight memory: 671B × 2B (BF16) = 1.34 TB, far exceeding 640 GB HBM. Strategy: keep the shared attention layers + top-16 most frequently accessed experts in GPU HBM (~96 GB), offload the remaining 240 experts to CPU DRAM (host has 2TB). On each token, if a routed expert is not GPU-resident, fetch it via PCIe Gen5 (64 GB/s per GPU, ~128 GB/s aggregate with 2 root complexes). Each expert: 2B × 2B = 4 GB. Fetch time: 4 GB / 64 GB/s = 62.5ms — far too slow for real-time. Mitigation: (1) Predict expert routing for the next batch and prefetch experts asynchronously. (2) Use expert caching with LRU eviction — popular experts stay resident. (3) Quantize offloaded experts to INT4 (1 GB each, fetch in 15.6ms). (4) For batch serving, accumulate tokens for the same expert and amortize fetch cost. This is viable for offline batch inference but challenging for real-time serving under 100ms SLA.

scenario: You need to serve a 256-expert MoE model (each expert 2B params, 671B total) on a single 8×H100 node with 640 GB total HBM. The model does not fit entirely in GPU memory. Design an expert offloading strategy and calculate the latency impact.
title: MoE Serving with Offloaded Experts

details.common_mistake: Treating the aux loss coefficient as a simple hyperparameter to grid-search. The fundamental tension is that a strong balance loss fights against the language model's natural preference for specialization.
details.napkin_math: Ideal expert entropy: ~3.0 bits (8 effective experts of 16, allowing some specialization). Dead expert threshold: <0.5% of average tokens. α=0.01 → 3 dead. α=0.1 → 0 dead but 5% quality loss. α=0.03 + z-loss → 0 dead, <1% quality loss.
details.realistic_solution: The optimal approach combines multiple techniques rather than relying solely on α. (1) Use a moderate α=0.03-0.05 to provide gentle balance pressure. (2) Add a router z-loss (DeepSeek-V3 uses this) with coefficient 0.001 to prevent router logit explosion without directly forcing uniform routing. (3) Apply per-expert learning rate scaling — dead experts get higher learning rates to 'catch up.' (4) Use Sinkhorn-based routing (soft assignment) during early training, then anneal to hard top-k routing. The DeepSeek-V3 recipe: α=0.003 for balance loss + z-loss, achieving both balance and specialization. Monitor expert utilization entropy — target entropy of log2(16)−1 = 3.0 bits (not maximum entropy, which prevents specialization).

scenario: You are training a 16-expert MoE language model. With auxiliary load-balancing loss coefficient α=0.01 (Switch Transformer default), you see good language modeling loss but 3 dead experts. With α=0.1, all experts are utilized but perplexity degrades by 5%. Specify the right approach.
title: MoE Auxiliary Loss Coefficient Tuning

details.common_mistake: Viewing shared experts as purely a model quality decision. The systems implications are significant: the shared expert becomes a serialization bottleneck since every token must pass through it.
details.napkin_math: MoE routing: 8 experts, top-2 routing. Expert parallelism: each GPU handles some experts. All-to-all communication volume = tokens × top-k × hidden_dim × 2 (send + receive). For batch=1024 tokens, hidden=4096, top-2: 1024 × 2 × 4096 × 2B = 16MB per all-to-all. Both standard EP=8 and EP=16 configurations route same tokens to 2 experts each — total communication reduction claim is incorrect when expert count changes don't affect top-k.
details.realistic_solution: Both routing configurations send 8 experts' worth of all-to-all communication. The communication reduction claim is incorrect — routing 8 experts via all-to-all in both configs produces similar communication volume.

scenario: DeepSeek-V3 uses a 'shared expert' design where 1 expert is always activated for every token alongside 8 routed experts selected from 256. Your team is designing a new MoE architecture and debates whether to include shared experts. What are the system-level implications?
title: MoE Shared Expert Architecture

details.common_mistake: Attributing the gap entirely to all-to-all communication overhead. While communication is a factor, the memory bandwidth cost of loading all expert weights is often the dominant bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Dense 13B weight loads per step: 13B × 2B = 26 GB. MoE 47B weight loads: 47B × 2B = 94 GB. Weight load ratio: 94/26 = 3.6×. At 3.35 TB/s HBM3 BW, dense: 26 GB/3.35 TB/s = 7.8ms. MoE: ~30ms for full expert weight loading (with routing overhead).
details.realistic_solution: The 34% throughput gap has three main sources: (1) All-to-all communication: dispatch + combine operations per MoE layer add ~10-15% overhead even with NVLink, especially with non-uniform routing. (2) Memory bandwidth: The MoE model has 47B params vs 13B — 3.6× more weights to load from HBM per forward pass. Even though only 13B are 'active,' the expert weights still consume HBM bandwidth for loading the selected experts' weights. At batch sizes where the model is memory-bandwidth-bound (common during training with gradient checkpointing), this is the dominant factor. (3) Load imbalance: The slowest expert determines layer latency. Even with aux loss, a 10-15% imbalance means 10-15% idle time on the fastest GPUs. (4) Router overhead: computing gating probabilities and top-k selection adds serial latency. Combined: ~15% memory BW + ~12% communication + ~7% load imbalance ≈ 34% total.

scenario: A team trains both a dense 13B model and a Mixtral-style 8x7B MoE (47B total, 13B active) on 64 H100 GPUs. The dense model achieves 3200 tokens/sec/GPU. The MoE model only achieves 2100 tokens/sec/GPU despite having the same active FLOPs. Analyze where the 34% throughput gap comes from.
title: MoE Training Throughput vs Dense Model

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on model quality (fine-grained is usually better). The systems implications of expert granularity are profound and often determine whether the model is practically trainable and servable.
details.napkin_math: Option A: 8 experts × 125B × 2B = 2 TB weights. TP=4 per expert → 32 GPUs minimum. Option B: 256 experts × 4B × 2B = 2 TB weights. 1 expert/GPU → 256 GPUs minimum. All-to-all fanout: A=2/8, B=8/256. Message size per dispatch: A=large (125B expert inputs), B=small (4B expert inputs).
details.realistic_solution: Option A (8×125B): Each expert requires ~250 GB in BF16 — needs TP=4 within each expert. All-to-all dispatches to only 2 of 8 destinations (low communication fanout). Load imbalance impact is severe: one slow expert means 7 GPUs idle. Serving: 8 experts is easier to replicate and balance. Option B (256×4B): Each expert is 8 GB in BF16 — fits on one GPU. All-to-all dispatches to 8 of 256 destinations (high fanout but small messages). Load balance is naturally better with more experts and top-8 selection. Routing collapse risk is higher with 256 experts. Serving: need all 256 experts resident — requires many GPUs or expert offloading. Communication: 256-expert all-to-all across many nodes is bandwidth-intensive. DeepSeek-V3 chose fine-grained (256 experts) because: better routing flexibility, natural load balance with top-8, each expert fits one GPU (no within-expert parallelism needed), and fine-grained specialization improves quality.

scenario: You are designing a 1T-parameter MoE model. Option A: 8 experts of 125B parameters each (Mixtral-style coarse-grained). Option B: 256 experts of ~4B parameters each (DeepSeek-V3-style fine-grained), selecting top-8. Both have ~1T total and similar active FLOPs. Evaluate the systems tradeoffs.
title: MoE Granularity: Few Large vs Many Small Experts

details.common_mistake: Assuming smaller batches should always be faster. In MoE, small batches create sparse expert activation patterns that reduce GPU utilization and amplify load imbalance.
details.napkin_math: Expected distinct experts activated from N=8 total when each of M tokens picks top-2 independently: E[distinct] = 8 × (1 - (1 - 2/8)^M) = 8 × (1 - 0.75^M). For large M (batch), all 8 are activated. For M=4 tokens: 8×(1-0.75^4) = 8×(1-0.3164) = 8×0.6836 = 5.47. For 8 tokens: 8×(1-0.75^8) = 8×(1-0.1) = 8×0.9 = 7.2. For specific case giving 5.25: 8×(1-(7/8)^M). With M=8: 8×(1-(7/8)^8) = 8×(1-0.343) = 8×0.657 = 5.26 ≈ 5.25 (not 5.7).

scenario: Your MoE inference service runs well at batch size 64 (all experts utilized, P50 latency 18ms). When traffic drops and batch size falls to 4, you observe that only 3 of 8 experts receive any tokens, and latency paradoxically increases to 25ms. Diagnose why smaller batches hurt MoE serving.
title: MoE Batch Size Impact on Expert Utilization

details.common_mistake: Quantizing everything uniformly to INT4. The shared attention layers (which process every token) are more sensitive to quantization than expert FFN layers (which each see only a fraction of tokens).
details.napkin_math: Mixtral 8×7B: total params ≈ 46.7B (shared 7B + 8 experts each adding incremental FFN). But described as 141B: shared params = ~7B, expert FFN = 8 × (141-7)/8 = 8 × 16.75B = 134B expert FFN. Memory: shared (active) BF16 = 7B × 2B = 14GB. Expert FFN INT4: 134B × 0.5B = 67GB. Total: 81GB. Alternatively using stated 21B shared + 176B expert = 197B total: shared INT8 21B×1B = 21GB + expert INT4 176B×0.5B = 88GB. Total = 109GB. The issue is 42+88=130 doesn't equal 141B params. Fix using consistent params: 7B shared × 2B + 8×16.75B × 0.5B = 14 + 67 = 81GB.
details.realistic_solution: Mixtral 8×7B has ~46.7B active params (not 141B). Using consistent 7B shared: BF16 = 14GB. 8 expert FFNs (134B) at INT4 = 67GB. Total ≈ 81GB. The 42+88=130GB figure uses inconsistent param counts.

scenario: You want to serve Mixtral 8x22B (141B total params) on a single 8×H100 node. In BF16 the weights need 282 GB, barely fitting in 640 GB HBM but leaving insufficient room for KV-cache at high batch sizes. Design a mixed-precision quantization strategy for the experts vs shared layers.
title: MoE Quantization Strategy for Serving

details.common_mistake: Treating all-to-all as if all links have uniform bandwidth. The 18× bandwidth gap between intra-node NVLink and inter-node InfiniBand fundamentally changes how you must place experts.
details.napkin_math: Hidden state: 7168 × 2B = 14.3 KB. NVLink: 14.3 KB / 900 GB/s = 16 ns. IB: 14.3 KB / 50 GB/s + 1μs = ~1.3 μs. Ratio: 81×. Batch all-to-all (worst case): 469 MB / 50 GB/s = 9.4 ms. Target: <2ms by keeping 80% routing intra-node.
details.realistic_solution: With 1 expert per GPU across 32 nodes, a token routed to a remote expert must traverse InfiniBand at 50 GB/s vs NVLink at 900 GB/s (18× slower). For a 7168-dim BF16 hidden state (14.3 KB per token), intra-node transfer: 14.3 KB / 900 GB/s = 16 ns. Inter-node transfer: 14.3 KB / 50 GB/s = 286 ns + ~1μs network latency = ~1.3 μs per token. For a batch of 4096 tokens with top-8 routing, each token sends to 8 experts. In the worst case, all 8 are remote: 4096 × 8 × 14.3 KB = 469 MB per direction, taking 469 MB / 50 GB/s = 9.4ms per direction over IB. Specification: (1) Place co-activated experts (identified by routing correlation analysis) on the same node. (2) Implement hierarchical all-to-all: resolve intra-node routing first (NVLink), then inter-node (IB). (3) Overlap inter-node all-to-all with local expert computation. (4) Target <20% of routing being cross-node.

scenario: You are scaling a 256-expert MoE model across 32 nodes (256 H100 GPUs total, 1 expert per GPU). Within a node, GPUs communicate via NVLink (900 GB/s). Between nodes, InfiniBand NDR (400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s). Specify the communication constraints for the all-to-all expert dispatch.
title: MoE Fine-Grained Expert Parallelism Communication

details.common_mistake: Using the same expert parallelism layout for both prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound with uniform expert utilization; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound with skewed expert utilization.
details.napkin_math: Prefill: 512 tokens / 8 experts × 2 (top-2) = 128 tokens/expert. Matmul size: [128, 4096] × [4096, 14336] — compute-bound. Decode: 128 tokens / 8 experts × 2 = 32 tokens/expert, but skewed: 4 hot experts get ~48 each, 4 cold get ~8. Matmul [8, 4096] × [4096, 14336] at batch=8: deeply memory-bound.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill pool: Use EP=8 (1 expert per GPU). With 512 tokens and uniform routing, each expert processes ~128 tokens — large enough for efficient matmuls. All-to-all communication is amortized over the large batch. Compute-bound: H100 Tensor Core utilization >70%. Decode pool: EP=8 wastes 4 GPUs that receive near-zero traffic. Instead, use EP=4 (2 experts per GPU), consolidating the 4 hot experts across 4 GPUs. This halves the GPU count while maintaining throughput for decode (which is memory-BW-bound anyway — fewer GPUs means less aggregate BW, but each GPU has enough BW for 1-token matmuls). Alternatively, replicate hot experts and use EP=4 with selective expert placement. The key insight: MoE decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (loading expert weights for single-token matmuls), so consolidating experts on fewer GPUs with higher utilization is better than spreading across many underutilized GPUs.

scenario: Your MoE serving system disaggregates prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools. During prefill, batches of 512 tokens hit all experts evenly. During decode, batches of 128 requests generate 1 token each, and only 4 of 8 experts see significant traffic. Design different parallelism strategies for each phase.
title: MoE Prefill vs Decode Phase Routing Differences

details.common_mistake: Confusing total parameters with training FLOPs. MoE's advantage is that it has more total parameters (better representation capacity) while using the same per-token FLOPs as a much smaller dense model.
details.napkin_math: Dense 70B FLOPs/token: 6 × 70B = 420 GFLOPs. MoE 8×70B FLOPs/token: 6 × 70B = 420 GFLOPs (same). Parameter ratio: 560B/70B = 8×. FLOP ratio: 1.0×. Training speedup at iso-quality: ~2-3× (empirically, MoE reaches same loss in fewer tokens due to higher capacity).
details.realistic_solution: Dense 70B: Per-token FLOPs ≈ 6 × 70B = 420 GFLOPs (forward + backward). Total params: 70B. MoE 8×70B: Per-token FLOPs ≈ 6 × 70B = 420 GFLOPs (same — only active expert params contribute to FLOPs). Total params: ~560B. The MoE model has 8× more parameters but identical per-token compute cost. More parameters means more capacity to memorize and represent patterns in the training data. Chinchilla scaling laws show that model quality scales with both data and parameters. MoE decouples parameter count from compute cost, allowing you to scale parameters 'for free' (in FLOPs) at the cost of memory. This is why Mixtral 8x7B (47B params) matches Llama 2 70B quality while using only 13B active FLOPs — it has 3.6× less compute cost per token but comparable quality through parameter scaling.

scenario: You are comparing scaling strategies: training a dense 70B model vs an MoE with 70B active parameters and 8× expert multiplier (560B total). Both train on the same data and compute budget. Calculate the per-token FLOP cost and total parameter count for each, and explain why MoE can match quality at lower training cost.
title: MoE Parameter Count vs Active FLOPs Scaling

details.common_mistake: Computing checkpoint size from only model weights. Optimizer state (Adam) adds 12 bytes per parameter (FP32 master weights + momentum + variance), dwarfing the BF16 weight storage.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 671B × 2B = 1.34 TB. Optimizer: 671B × 12B = 8.05 TB. Total: 9.4 TB. Per-GPU shard: 9.4 TB / 2048 = 4.6 GB. GPU→CPU copy: 72ms. CPU→NVMe: 4.6 GB / 6.4 GB/s = 0.72s. NVMe→PFS: background. Training stall: <100ms with async.
details.realistic_solution: Checkpoint size: 671B params × (2B weights + 12B optimizer) = 671B × 14B = 9.4 TB total, distributed across 2048 GPUs (~4.6 GB per GPU shard). Writing to parallel filesystem: At 100 GB/s aggregate write BW (typical GPFS/Lustre), full checkpoint: 9.4 TB / 100 GB/s = 94 seconds — far too long for a 15-minute interval (10.4% overhead). Strategy: (1) Asynchronous checkpointing: copy GPU memory to pinned CPU memory (PCIe Gen5: 4.6 GB / 64 GB/s = 72ms per GPU, negligible). Then write from CPU to storage in the background while training continues. (2) Only checkpoint changed experts: with routing, many experts may not have been updated recently — use dirty-bit tracking. (3) Use NCCL-based collective checkpoint: each node writes its local shards to NVMe first (6.4 GB/s per NVMe × 8 = 51.2 GB/s per node), then async upload to parallel FS. Local NVMe write: 4.6 GB × 256 GPUs/node_count / 51.2 GB/s ≈ 23 seconds per node.

scenario: Your 671B-parameter MoE model trains on 2048 H100 GPUs with expert parallelism. You need to checkpoint every 15 minutes for fault tolerance (Young-Daly optimal). Calculate the checkpoint size, write time, and design a checkpointing strategy that does not stall training.
title: MoE Checkpointing Overhead at Scale

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the router computation and dispatch/combine as negligible. At small batch sizes during decode, these fixed overheads dominate over the actual expert computation.
details.napkin_math: Router: 5 μs. Dispatch: 10 μs. Expert FFN (8 tokens, memory-bound): 105 μs. Combine: 10 μs. Total: 130 μs/layer. Dense equivalent: 105 μs/layer. MoE routing overhead: 25 μs/layer = 24%.
details.realistic_solution: Step-by-step latency for decode batch=32, hidden_dim=4096, FFN_dim=14336, BF16: (1) Router forward: [32, 4096] × [4096, 8] linear + softmax + top-2 selection = ~5 μs (tiny matmul, memory-bound). (2) Dispatch all-to-all: Each token sends 8 KB (4096 × 2B) to 2 expert GPUs. Total payload: 32 × 2 × 8 KB = 512 KB across NVLink. Latency: ~10 μs (dominated by NVLink launch overhead, not bandwidth). (3) Expert FFN computation: Each expert processes ~8 tokens (32×2/8). Matmul [8, 4096] × [4096, 14336]: load 4096×14336×2B = 117 MB weights, producing 8×14336×2B = 229 KB output. Memory-bound: 117 MB / 3.35 TB/s = 35 μs per expert (up + gate + down projections ≈ 3× = 105 μs). (4) Combine all-to-all: ~10 μs. Total: 5 + 10 + 105 + 10 = ~130 μs per MoE layer. For 32 layers: ~4.2 ms. Dense equivalent: skip router + dispatch + combine, same FFN compute ≈ 105 μs per layer. MoE overhead: ~24% from routing machinery.

scenario: For a single MoE layer with 8 experts across 8 GPUs using NVLink, break down the end-to-end latency for processing a batch of 32 tokens during decode (1 new token per request). Include router computation, dispatch, expert computation, and combine.
title: MoE Inference Token Routing Latency Breakdown

details.common_mistake: Assuming MoE is always better because it has more parameters. Below a certain scale, the communication overhead of MoE training outweighs the parameter scaling benefit.
details.napkin_math: GPT-4 scale compute: ~1.8×10^25 FLOPs (not 1.8×10^22 which is GPT-3 scale — off by 1000×). Loss reduction: scaling by 8× compute: loss ∝ C^(-0.076). 8^(-0.076) = e^(-0.076×ln8) = e^(-0.076×2.079) = e^(-0.158) = 0.854. Reduction = 1 - 0.854 = 14.6% (not 17%).
details.realistic_solution: GPT-4 compute ≈ 1.8×10^25 FLOPs (not 10^22). Loss reduction from 8× compute: 8^(-0.076) = 0.854 → 14.6% reduction (not 17%).

scenario: Your organization has a fixed $10M training budget (H100 at $2/GPU-hr). You must choose between training a dense model and an MoE model to minimize loss on a 2T-token dataset. The MoE model has 2× training throughput overhead (all-to-all, load imbalance) compared to a dense model with the same active parameters. At what model size does MoE become the better investment?
title: MoE vs Dense Scaling Law Crossover

details.common_mistake: Assuming gradient accumulation is transparent to MoE routing. The auxiliary load-balancing loss is computed per micro-batch, but with 8 accumulation steps, each micro-batch is 8× smaller, dramatically changing routing statistics.
details.napkin_math: Before: batch=512, top-2, 64 experts. Tokens/expert = 512×2/64 = 16. Poisson variance: √16/16 = 25% CV. After: micro-batch=64, tokens/expert = 64×2/64 = 2. Poisson variance: √2/2 = 70% CV. 2.8× noisier balance signal.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is that the load-balancing loss operates on micro-batch statistics, not accumulated-batch statistics. With accumulation=8, each micro-batch is 8× smaller. A micro-batch of e.g. 64 tokens with top-2 routing across 64 experts means each expert ideally gets 2 tokens — the variance of per-expert load is extremely high at this granularity (Poisson-like with λ=2). The aux loss gradient becomes very noisy, providing poor balancing signal. Fixes: (1) Compute load-balance statistics across accumulation steps by maintaining a running expert-count buffer, updating the aux loss only after all micro-batches. (2) Use exponential moving average of expert loads rather than per-batch counts for the balancing loss. (3) Increase micro-batch size by reducing accumulation steps and using more GPUs for data parallelism. DeepSeek-V3 addresses this by computing the balance loss over a window of recent batches rather than per-micro-batch.

scenario: You switch your MoE training from gradient accumulation steps=1 to steps=8 (to simulate larger effective batch). After the change, expert utilization becomes severely imbalanced despite the same auxiliary loss coefficient. Training loss degrades. Diagnose the interaction between gradient accumulation and MoE routing.
title: MoE Auxiliary Loss Interaction with Gradient Accumulation

details.common_mistake: Treating any non-uniform routing as a problem. Domain specialization is a feature, not a bug — it means experts have learned distinct competencies. The problem arises only when specialization creates load imbalance at serving time.
details.napkin_math: Code traffic at 50% of requests: expert 3 gets 50% × 90% + 50% × 5% = 47.5% of its capacity from code alone. If code traffic spikes to 80%: expert 3 load = 80% × 90% + 20% × 5% = 73% — needs replication. Expert 7 load: 80% × 5% + 20% × 90% = 22% — underutilized.
details.realistic_solution: Expert specialization is desirable for model quality — it means each expert develops distinct capabilities rather than being redundant copies. Expert 3 becoming a 'code expert' and expert 7 a 'language expert' is the intended behavior of MoE. However, this creates serving challenges: (1) Traffic composition determines load balance. A code-heavy workload will overload expert 3 and underutilize expert 7. (2) Request routing must be traffic-aware: if your service handles mixed code+language, balance is natural. If you serve separate code and language endpoints, each will have different expert utilization patterns. (3) Consider workload-aware expert placement: replicate expert 3 on the code-serving cluster and expert 7 on the language cluster. (4) Monitor expert hit rates per traffic type and auto-scale expert replicas based on demand. The routing is healthy — the serving infrastructure must adapt to it.

scenario: After training a 16-expert MoE language model, you analyze routing patterns and discover that expert 3 processes 90% of code tokens but only 5% of natural language tokens, while expert 7 is the opposite. Is this specialization desirable or a sign of poor routing? How does this affect serving?
title: MoE Expert Specialization Analysis

details.common_mistake: Assuming you can perfectly overlap communication and computation. The dispatch all-to-all must complete before expert computation can begin (data dependency). Only partial overlap is possible through pipelining.
details.napkin_math: Communication: 40% of step. Compute: 60%. K=4 pipeline stages. Per-stage: comm = 10%, compute = 15%. Pipeline time: 10% + 4×15% + 10% = 80%. Speedup: 100/80 = 1.25×. Practical (with efficiency loss): ~1.20× or 20% improvement.
details.realistic_solution: The key insight: you can split the token batch into K sub-batches and pipeline them. Sub-batch 1: dispatch → expert compute → combine. While sub-batch 1's expert compute runs, sub-batch 2's dispatch can overlap. With K=4 sub-batches: Time without overlap: dispatch(D) + compute(C) + combine(D) per sub-batch, total = K × (D + C + D). Time with pipelining: D + K × max(C, D) + D (pipeline startup + steady state + drain). If D = 0.4T and C = 0.6T (where T is total step time): Without: 4 × (0.4T/4 + 0.6T/4 + 0.4T/4) = T (no change per total). With pipeline: 0.1T + 4 × max(0.15T, 0.1T) + 0.1T = 0.1T + 0.6T + 0.1T = 0.8T. Speedup: 1.0/0.8 = 1.25× (25% improvement). In practice, sub-batching reduces per-expert batch sizes, hurting compute efficiency. The sweet spot is K=2-4. DeepSeek-V3 uses this technique and reports ~20% training speedup from communication-computation overlap.

scenario: Your MoE training pipeline spends 40% of each step on all-to-all communication (dispatch + combine). Your colleague proposes overlapping all-to-all with expert computation by splitting the batch into sub-batches. Evaluate the feasibility and calculate the potential speedup.
title: MoE All-to-All Overlap with Expert Computation

details.common_mistake: Assuming dropless means each expert has an unlimited buffer. dMoE uses sparse matrix operations to process variable numbers of tokens per expert without padding or dropping.
details.napkin_math: Traditional MoE with CF=1.25: buffer per expert = 1.25 × B/E tokens. If E=8, B=1024: buffer = 160 tokens per expert, total = 1280 token-slots for 1024 tokens (25% waste). dMoE: exactly 1024 token-slots, 0% waste. Memory savings: 20% of expert activation memory.
details.realistic_solution: Traditional MoE pads expert inputs to a fixed capacity (CF × tokens/num_experts), wasting memory on padding and dropping overflow tokens. dMoE (Megablocks) reformulates expert computation as block-sparse matrix multiplications. Instead of dispatching tokens to fixed-size expert buffers, it creates a single sparse matrix where each block corresponds to an expert's assigned tokens. The sparse matmul processes all tokens without padding or dropping. Memory implications: (1) No padding waste — saves CF overhead (typically 25-50% of expert buffer). (2) Variable-length expert inputs use exactly the memory needed. (3) Requires block-sparse matmul kernels (Triton-based) that achieve ~90% of dense matmul throughput on H100 Tensor Cores. (4) Peak memory depends on actual routing distribution, not worst-case capacity factor. On H100 with Hopper architecture, the block-sparse matmuls leverage the TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) for efficient irregular memory access patterns.

scenario: Standard MoE architectures drop tokens that exceed an expert's capacity buffer. The 'dropless MoE' (dMoE) approach from Megablocks eliminates token dropping entirely. Explain the mechanism and its memory implications on H100 GPUs.
title: MoE Dropless (dMoE) Token Processing Guarantee

details.common_mistake: Placing experts randomly or round-robin across nodes. This ignores co-activation patterns and results in unnecessary cross-node all-to-all traffic over slower InfiniBand links.
details.napkin_math: Random placement: 8 experts activated, 8/32 GPUs on average node → probability expert is local = 8/32 = 25%. Expected local: 8 × 0.25 = 2 of 8. Optimized: 5-6 of 8 local. Cross-node reduction: from 6 remote to 2-3 remote = 50-60% less IB traffic. Latency saving: ~5ms per layer for batch of 256 tokens.
details.realistic_solution: Approach: formulate expert placement as a graph partitioning problem. Build a co-activation graph where edge weight between experts i and j represents the probability they are activated by the same token. Partition this graph into 4 groups of 8 experts (one per node, 8 experts per GPU) that maximizes intra-partition edge weight (co-activated experts on the same node). Algorithm: (1) Compute co-activation matrix from routing logs: C[i,j] = P(token activates both expert i and j). (2) Run METIS graph partitioning to get 4 balanced partitions minimizing edge cut. (3) Assign each partition to a node. With top-8 routing and co-activation rate of 70% for common pairs, optimal placement can keep 5-6 of 8 expert activations intra-node (via NVLink at 900 GB/s) and only 2-3 cross-node (InfiniBand at 50 GB/s). Expected communication reduction: 60-70% reduction in cross-node traffic vs random placement. Re-compute placement weekly as routing patterns evolve with traffic changes.

scenario: You are designing the serving infrastructure for a 256-expert MoE model across 4 nodes of 8×H100 GPUs each (32 GPUs total). The model uses top-8 routing. You have measured that certain expert pairs are co-activated 70% of the time. Design the expert-to-GPU placement strategy that minimizes cross-node communication.
title: MoE Multi-Node Placement Strategy

details.common_mistake: Treating expert loading as a simple LRU cache without considering that NVMe-to-GPU transfer goes through CPU memory and PCIe, adding latency and requiring careful prefetching.
details.napkin_math: Tier 1: 64 experts × 2 GB = 128 GB in HBM. Tier 2: 256 experts × 2 GB = 512 GB in CPU DRAM. Tier 3: 704 experts × 2 GB = 1.41 TB on NVMe. Hit rates (Zipf-distributed): Tier 1 ~90%, Tier 2 ~9%, Tier 3 ~1%. Average latency: 5.7ms/layer.
details.realistic_solution: Three-tier caching: Tier 1 (GPU HBM): Keep the top-64 hottest experts in HBM (64 × 2 GB = 128 GB, leaving 512 GB for shared layers + KV-cache). Tier 2 (CPU DRAM): Keep the next 256 experts in pinned CPU memory (512 GB). Transfer to GPU via PCIe Gen5 at 64 GB/s: 2 GB / 64 GB/s = 31ms. Tier 3 (NVMe SSD): Remaining 704 experts on SSD. Transfer: 2 GB / 7 GB/s = 286ms per expert (too slow for real-time). Pipeline: (1) Router predicts top-8 experts. (2) If expert is in Tier 1: immediate compute (~0ms load). (3) If in Tier 2: PCIe transfer (31ms) — overlap with computation of Tier 1 experts. (4) If in Tier 3: initiate async NVMe→CPU→GPU transfer and queue the request. Prefetching: use the router output from layer L to prefetch experts for layer L+1 (speculative). With 90% Tier 1 hit rate and 9% Tier 2: average load latency = 0.9×0 + 0.09×31 + 0.01×286 = 5.7ms per layer.

scenario: You want to serve a 1024-expert MoE model where each expert is 1B parameters (2 GB BF16). Total model: 2 TB. Your single server has 8×H100 (640 GB HBM) and 8×NVMe SSDs (7 GB/s each, 56 GB/s aggregate). Design a tiered expert caching system.
title: MoE Dynamic Expert Loading from SSD

details.common_mistake: Comparing only per-token FLOPs without considering that the MoE model requires the same number of GPUs despite 5× fewer active FLOPs, because all expert weights must be memory-resident.
details.napkin_math: Mixtral 8×7B active parameters: 13B active (7B shared + 2 experts × 3B FFN). Memory at FP16: 13B × 2B = 26GB (not 28GB which would require 14B params). Full model at FP16: 46.7B × 2B ≈ 93.4GB.
details.realistic_solution: 13B active params at FP16 = 13B × 2B = 26GB (not 28GB which requires 14B params).

scenario: Compare the serving cost-per-token for a dense 70B model on 2×H100 versus an MoE 8x7B (47B total, 13B active) on 2×H100. Both serve at 1000 requests/second with 512-token outputs. Factor in GPU utilization, memory efficiency, and throughput.
title: MoE Serving Cost-per-Token Economics

details.common_mistake: Assuming upcycling gives you 'free' MoE quality. The duplicated experts start identical and must differentiate, which requires significant continued training. Also, the memory cost jumps 4× immediately.
details.napkin_math: Dense 7B weights: 14 GB. Upcycled 8x7B weights: 94 GB (6.7× increase). Upcycling training: 400B tokens × 78 GFLOPs/token = 3.12×10^22 FLOPs. From-scratch: 2T × 78 GFLOPs = 1.56×10^23 FLOPs. Cost ratio: 20%. Quality: ~95% of from-scratch.
details.realistic_solution: Sparse upcycling (Komatsuzaki et al. 2023): Take a dense 7B model, duplicate each FFN into 8 copies (creating 8x7B = ~47B MoE), initialize a random router, and continue training. Systems costs: (1) Memory jumps from 14 GB to 94 GB weights (6.7× increase) — immediately requires multi-GPU serving. (2) Training: need expert parallelism setup (8 GPUs minimum vs 1 GPU for dense). (3) Continued training needed: typically 10-20% of original training tokens for experts to differentiate. At 2T original tokens: 200-400B additional tokens. (4) Training cost: 400B tokens × 6 × 13B active FLOPs = 3.12 × 10^22 FLOPs, vs from-scratch MoE at 2T tokens × 6 × 13B = 1.56 × 10^23 FLOPs. Upcycling cost is ~20% of from-scratch. Quality: upcycling reaches ~95% of from-scratch MoE quality. The 5% gap comes from experts starting identical — some redundancy persists. For many applications, this tradeoff (80% cost savings for 5% quality gap) is compelling.

scenario: Your team has a well-trained dense 7B model. Rather than training an MoE from scratch, you propose 'sparse upcycling' — duplicating the FFN layers into 8 expert copies and training the router from scratch while fine-tuning. Evaluate the systems costs and expected quality gains versus training MoE from scratch.
title: MoE Sparse Upcycling from Dense Model

details.common_mistake: Applying standard 3D parallelism without accounting for MoE's unique communication pattern (all-to-all instead of all-reduce for expert layers). The parallelism strategy must be different for attention layers vs MoE layers.
details.napkin_math: 2048 GPUs = TP(8) × PP(8) × DP(32). Per-GPU memory: ~59 GB / 80 GB HBM. EP within DP group: 32 GPUs across 4 nodes. Intra-node EP: NVLink 900 GB/s. Inter-node EP: IB 400 Gb/s. Pipeline bubble: 1/PP = 12.5% with interleaved schedule ~6%.
details.realistic_solution: Architecture: 61 layers, each with shared attention + MoE FFN. Shared attention: ~37B params. Expert FFNs: 256 × ~2.5B each = 634B params. Strategy per layer type: (1) Attention layers: TP=8 within a node (NVLink, each GPU holds 1/8 of attention weights). (2) MoE layers: EP=32 (32 GPUs, 8 experts per GPU). Place EP groups across 4 nodes to utilize NVLink within nodes. (3) Pipeline parallelism: PP=8 (8 pipeline stages, ~8 layers each). (4) Data parallelism: DP = 2048 / (TP×PP) = 2048 / (8×8) = 32 data-parallel replicas. Each DP replica: 64 GPUs across 8 nodes. EP group: within each DP replica, 32 GPUs handle expert dispatch (4 nodes). Memory per GPU: attention shard (~37B/8/8 stages = 578M → 1.2 GB) + 8 experts (8 × 2.5B × 2B = 40 GB) + optimizer state (8 × 2.5B × 12B = 240 GB → need ZeRO-1 across DP=32 → 7.5 GB) + activations (~10 GB with checkpointing). Total: ~59 GB, fits in 80 GB. Communication: EP all-to-all within 4 nodes uses mix of NVLink + IB. PP uses IB between stages. DP gradient sync uses IB ring all-reduce.

scenario: Design the full parallelism strategy for training a DeepSeek-V3-scale model (671B total, 256 experts, top-8 routing, 37B active) on 2048 H100 GPUs across 256 nodes. Specify EP, TP, PP, and DP dimensions, and justify each choice with bandwidth and memory constraints.
title: MoE Model Parallelism Topology for Training

details.common_mistake: Using the full 64 attention heads to compute KV-cache size. GQA reduces KV heads — only 8 KV heads need caching, not 64. This is the entire point of GQA.
details.napkin_math: KV per token per layer: 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 4 KB. Per token (80 layers): 320 KB. Batch 32 × 4K context: 32 × 4096 × 320 KB = 40 GB. MHA equivalent: 8× larger = 320 GB.
details.realistic_solution: KV-cache per token per layer: 2 (K+V) × 8 (KV heads) × 128 (head dim) × 2B (BF16) = 4,096 bytes = 4 KB. Per token across all 80 layers: 4 KB × 80 = 320 KB. For comparison, with full MHA (64 KV heads): 2 × 64 × 128 × 2B × 80 = 2.56 MB per token — GQA provides 8× reduction. For batch of 32 at 4096 context: 32 × 4096 × 320 KB = 40 GB. This is significant — on a single H100 (80 GB), with ~140 GB weights (2 GPUs), the KV-cache of 40 GB limits batch size. Without GQA: 32 × 4096 × 2.56 MB = 320 GB — would require 4× more GPUs just for KV-cache. GQA is essential for making large model serving economically viable.

scenario: Llama 3 70B uses grouped-query attention with 64 attention heads and 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, across 80 layers. Calculate the KV-cache size per token and for a batch of 32 requests at 4096 context length in BF16.
title: KV-Cache Size Calculation for GQA Models

details.common_mistake: Choosing the largest block size (32) to minimize page table overhead. Large blocks waste memory when sequences don't fill the last block (internal fragmentation), especially harmful for short sequences.
details.napkin_math: Fragmentation waste per request: block/2 × 320 KB. Block=16: 2.56 MB/req × 100 req = 256 MB. Block=32: 5.12 MB/req × 100 req = 512 MB. Page table: 8K tokens / 16 = 512 entries × 8B = 4 KB/req. Kernel efficiency: block=16 achieves ~90% of block=32 throughput.
details.realistic_solution: Block size 16 is the optimal choice for this workload. Analysis: (1) Internal fragmentation: average wasted tokens per sequence = block_size/2. At block=8: 4 tokens wasted × 320 KB/token = 1.28 MB/request. At block=16: 8 × 320 KB = 2.56 MB/request. At block=32: 16 × 320 KB = 5.12 MB/request. For 100 concurrent requests: 128 MB vs 256 MB vs 512 MB waste. (2) Page table overhead: each block needs a pointer entry. At block=8, a 8192-token sequence needs 1024 entries. At block=16: 512 entries. At block=32: 256 entries. Page table memory is negligible (<1 MB even at block=8). (3) Kernel efficiency: CUDA attention kernels operate on blocks — larger blocks have better compute utilization due to coalesced memory access. Block=8 leaves Tensor Cores underutilized. Block=16 achieves ~90% of block=32 efficiency while halving fragmentation. (4) Allocation flexibility: block=16 allows finer-grained memory reclamation when sequences finish. Block=16 balances fragmentation waste vs kernel efficiency.

scenario: You are configuring vLLM's PagedAttention for serving Llama 3 70B on 2×H100 GPUs. The system offers block sizes of 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Your workload has highly variable sequence lengths (50th percentile: 256 tokens, 99th percentile: 8192 tokens). Select the optimal block size and justify.
title: PagedAttention Block Size Selection

details.common_mistake: Assuming KV-cache quantization is lossless. INT8 quantization of KV values introduces quantization noise that accumulates over long sequences, potentially degrading output quality for long-context tasks.
details.napkin_math: BF16 KV per request (4K ctx): 1.31 GB. INT8 KV: 655 MB (2× smaller). 64 requests BF16: 83.9 GB. 128 requests INT8: 83.9 GB. Concurrency doubled at same memory cost. Perplexity impact: <0.3% at 4K context.
details.realistic_solution: Memory analysis: BF16 KV-cache per request at 4K context = 4096 × 320 KB = 1.31 GB. For 64 requests: 83.9 GB. With INT8: 4096 × 160 KB = 655 MB per request, 64 requests = 41.9 GB. Savings: 42 GB — enough to serve 128 requests (128 × 655 MB = 83.9 GB, same as the original BF16 budget). Quality impact: (1) Attention scores are computed as Q×K^T. INT8 keys introduce ±0.5 LSB error per element. For head_dim=128, the attention logit error is √128 × 0.5 = 5.66 LSB in expectation. Relative to typical attention logit range of ~10-50, this is 11-57% noise — significant. (2) Mitigation: use per-head dynamic quantization (compute scale/zero-point per head per layer) rather than per-tensor. This reduces relative error to <1% for most heads. (3) Empirical results: INT8 KV-cache with per-head quantization shows <0.3% perplexity degradation on short contexts (<4K) but 1-2% on long contexts (>16K) where errors accumulate through many attention steps. For 4K context: acceptable. For 128K: consider FP8 (E4M3) instead.

scenario: Your Llama 3 70B serving deployment on 2×H100 GPUs can handle 64 concurrent requests at 4K context with BF16 KV-cache. Your PM wants to double concurrency to 128 without adding GPUs. You propose quantizing the KV-cache from BF16 to INT8. Analyze the memory savings and quality impact.
title: KV-Cache Quantization to INT8

details.common_mistake: Only counting per-request memory savings without considering the TTFT (time-to-first-token) improvement. Prefix caching eliminates redundant prefill computation for the shared prefix, dramatically reducing latency.
details.napkin_math: Shared prefix: 2048 × 320 KB = 655 MB (stored once). Per-request unique: 256 × 320 KB = 82 MB. 100 requests: 655 MB + 100 × 82 MB = 8.85 GB vs 100 × 737 MB = 73.7 GB. Savings: 88%. TTFT: 25ms vs 200ms (8× faster prefill).
details.realistic_solution: Without prefix caching: Each request computes KV-cache for 2048 + 256 = 2304 tokens from scratch. KV per request: 2304 × 320 KB = 737 MB. For 100 concurrent requests: 73.7 GB. With prefix caching: Compute and store the 2048-token system prompt KV-cache once: 2048 × 320 KB = 655 MB (shared, read-only). Each request only computes KV for its 256 unique tokens: 256 × 320 KB = 82 MB, plus a reference to the shared prefix. For 100 concurrent: 655 MB (shared) + 100 × 82 MB = 8.85 GB. Memory savings: 73.7 - 8.85 = 64.85 GB (88% reduction). Latency improvement: Prefill of 2048 tokens on H100 for 70B model takes ~200ms. With prefix caching: prefill only 256 tokens = ~25ms. TTFT reduction: 175ms (8× faster for the prefill-dominated portion). Implementation: store shared prefix KV blocks in a content-addressed cache keyed by hash of the prefix token IDs. Reference-counted so blocks are freed when no active request uses them.

scenario: Your LLM serving platform handles 10,000 requests/min. 80% of requests share the same 2048-token system prompt. Each request's unique user prompt is 256 tokens. You are using Llama 3 70B with GQA (8 KV heads, 80 layers). Calculate the memory savings from prefix caching the shared system prompt.
title: Prefix Caching for Shared System Prompts

details.common_mistake: Using simple LRU eviction on individual KV blocks, which can preempt a nearly-complete long request to admit a new short request — wasting all the compute already invested in the preempted request.
details.napkin_math: Budget: 35 GB. Max KV per request: 8K × 320 KB = 2.56 GB. Conservative: 35/2.56 = 13 concurrent. With swap overcommit at avg 2K context: 35 GB / 640 MB = 54 concurrent (4× more). Swap penalty: 2.56 GB / 64 GB/s = 40ms (once per preemption).
details.realistic_solution: Design a multi-level policy: (1) Admission control: limit concurrent requests to what fits in memory. At 35 GB / 2.56 GB max = 13 full-length requests. Accept up to 13 requests; queue the rest. (2) Preemption policy (when memory is exhausted mid-generation): Use 'swap' — move preempted request's KV blocks to CPU memory (host has >>35 GB). When GPU memory frees up, swap back without recomputing. Swap bandwidth: PCIe Gen5 at 64 GB/s, a 2.56 GB cache swaps in 40ms. (3) Preemption priority: preempt the request with the most remaining tokens to generate (longest remaining latency), preserving requests close to completion. This minimizes wasted compute. (4) For prefix-shared requests: never evict shared prefix blocks — they serve multiple requests. (5) Overcommit strategy: admit up to 40 requests assuming average context is 2K (not 8K max). Average KV = 640 MB × 40 = 25.6 GB (fits). Handle the 5% of requests that reach 8K by swapping. This achieves 3× higher throughput than conservative admission control.

scenario: Your vLLM serving instance on a single H100 has 35 GB available for KV-cache after loading model weights. At peak traffic, 80 concurrent requests each need up to 8K context (2.56 GB KV-cache each). Total demand: 204 GB, far exceeding the 35 GB budget. Design an eviction and admission policy.
title: KV-Cache Eviction Under Memory Pressure

details.common_mistake: Assuming low GPU utilization means a compute scheduling problem. When memory is 99% full, the system cannot admit more requests to increase batch size, even though the GPU has spare FLOPs.
details.napkin_math: Model weights: 16 GB (BF16). KV per request (2K ctx): 2K × 65.5 KB = 131 MB. Available: 64 GB → max ~488 requests. Current memory: 79/80 GB → ~480 active requests using all KV space. GPU utilization low because decode batch=480 with 8B model has arithmetic intensity < ridge point.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck is KV-cache memory, not compute. With 64 GB free and Llama 3 8B using 4 KV heads × 128 dim × 32 layers: KV per token = 2 × 4 × 128 × 2B × 32 = 65.5 KB. At average 2K context: 131 MB per request. Maximum batch: 64 GB / 131 MB ≈ 488 requests. But the system is already at 79/80 GB — only ~1 GB free for new KV-cache, so batch size is capped at current level. Despite 200+ queued requests, the system cannot increase batch size because every additional request needs KV-cache memory. At the current small batch size, the GPU's Tensor Cores are underutilized (small matmuls during decode are memory-bandwidth-bound). Fixes: (1) Quantize KV-cache to INT8 (2× more concurrent requests). (2) Use PagedAttention to eliminate internal fragmentation. (3) Enable KV-cache swap to CPU memory for preempted requests. (4) Shorter max context length. The fundamental constraint: LLM decode throughput is limited by KV-cache memory capacity, not compute.

scenario: Your Llama 3 8B serving instance on a single H100 shows only 40% GPU compute utilization despite a queue of 200+ pending requests. The GPU has 64 GB free after loading weights (16 GB). Nvidia-smi shows 79 GB/80 GB memory used. Diagnose why throughput is limited despite available compute.
title: KV-Cache Memory as Throughput Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Thinking continuous batching is purely a scheduling optimization. It fundamentally changes KV-cache memory management — caches must be dynamically allocated and freed as individual requests enter and leave the batch.
details.napkin_math: Static batch=32, avg output 200 tokens, max 2000: GPU waste = (2000-200)/2000 × 90% (padding fraction for most requests) = ~81% waste. Continuous: each request occupies GPU only for its actual length. Throughput gain: ~2.5× for high-variance workloads.
details.realistic_solution: Static batching: all 32 requests start together, run until the longest finishes. Short requests (50 tokens) pad for the remaining 1950 tokens — wasting compute and holding KV-cache memory for completed requests. Continuous batching: when a request finishes, its KV-cache is immediately freed and a new request is admitted. Requirements: (1) Dynamic KV-cache allocation: PagedAttention is essential — allocate KV blocks on demand, free blocks when a request finishes. Cannot use contiguous pre-allocated buffers. (2) Memory fragmentation management: with requests entering/leaving asynchronously, the KV-cache memory pool fragments. Block-based allocation (like OS virtual memory) prevents fragmentation. (3) Iteration-level scheduling: each decode step must check which requests are active, which finished, and which new ones to admit. The attention kernel must handle variable-length sequences within the same batch. (4) Preemption protocol: if a high-priority request arrives but memory is full, the system must decide which existing request to preempt (swap its KV to CPU). Continuous batching typically achieves 2-3× throughput improvement over static batching for workloads with variable output lengths.

scenario: Your serving system uses static batching (batch=32, all requests start and end together). Average request length varies from 50 to 2000 output tokens. You observe 60% of GPU time is wasted on padding. Specify how continuous batching changes KV-cache management requirements.
title: Continuous Batching Interaction with KV-Cache

details.common_mistake: Assuming KV-cache transfer is negligible. For long contexts on large models, the KV-cache can be gigabytes per request — the transfer time can exceed the prefill computation time itself.
details.napkin_math: KV-cache: 8K × 320 KB = 2.62 GB. NVLink: 2.9 ms. IB NDR: 52 ms. With streaming (50% overlap): ~26 ms effective. With INT8 compression: 1.31 GB / 50 GB/s = 26 ms → 13 ms with compression. Prefill time: ~200 ms. Handoff adds ~13 ms (6.5% overhead).
details.realistic_solution: KV-cache for 8K context, Llama 3 70B (8 KV heads, 128 dim, 80 layers, BF16): 8192 × 320 KB = 2.62 GB per request. Transfer options: (1) NVLink within node (if prefill and decode GPUs are co-located): 2.62 GB / 900 GB/s = 2.9 ms — fast, viable. (2) InfiniBand between nodes: 2.62 GB / 50 GB/s = 52 ms — significant latency. (3) RDMA direct GPU-to-GPU: 2.62 GB / 25 GB/s (practical RDMA throughput) = 105 ms — too slow for real-time. Protocol design: (1) Streaming handoff: prefill GPU starts sending KV blocks for completed layers while still computing later layers. Layer L's KV-cache is ready as soon as layer L finishes prefill. This overlaps transfer with compute. (2) Pipeline: prefill sends layer 0-39 KV while computing layers 40-79. Transfer time for half: 1.31 GB / 50 GB/s = 26 ms. Prefill time for 80 layers at 8K context ≈ 200 ms. Overlap: 26 ms transfer hidden behind 200 ms compute → effective handoff overhead: max(200, 200+26-200) = ~26 ms. (3) Compression: quantize KV to INT8 for transfer (2× smaller), dequantize on decode GPU. Reduces transfer to 13 ms over IB.
