The tail is caused by ~1% of requests hitting overloaded replicas. You're considering hedged requests — sending duplicate requests to a second replica after a timeout.
title: Hedged Requests for LLM Inference on A100 Fleet

details.common_mistake: Using least-connections load balancing without accounting for request cost heterogeneity. A single long-sequence request consumes 10x the TPU cycles of a short one, so least-connections still routes long requests to 'least busy' replicas arbitrarily.
details.napkin_math: BERT-large attention is O(n^2). A 512-token request takes (512/128)^2 = 16x the compute of a 128-token request. At 50K RPS, 0.1% = 50 long requests/sec. TPU v5e at 197 TFLOPS BF16: BERT-large (340M params) needs ~680 GFLOPS/forward. 50 * 680G / 197T = 17% TPU utilization just for 0.1% of traffic.
details.realistic_solution: Implement cost-aware routing: classify requests into short (<=128 tokens), medium (129-256), long (257-512) at the load balancer using a lightweight tokenizer. Route to separate replica pools sized to their frequency (95% short, 4% medium, 1% long). Long-request pool has headroom for P999.

scenario: You're designing a load balancer for a TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16) inference service running BERT-large at 50K RPS. Round-robin distribution gives P999=800ms. Analysis shows 0.1% of requests contain sequences >400 tokens (BERT max 512), causing disproportionate compute time.
title: Load Balancing Strategy to Minimize P999 on TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Reducing batch timeout to 5ms improves P999 but reduces GPU utilization from 80% to 45%, increasing cost by ~78% with only marginal P50 improvement.
details.napkin_math: MI300X 5.3TB/s bandwidth: loading a 7B model (14GB BF16) takes 14GB/5.3TB/s = 2.6ms. Batching 8 vs 64 requests: compute scales linearly, bandwidth cost is amortized. Batch-8 at 5ms timeout: total latency = 5ms wait + 2.6ms load + compute. Batch-64: 20ms wait + same load + 8x compute. For latency-sensitive workloads, batch-8 wins.
details.realistic_solution: Implement adaptive batching: use a short timeout (5ms) for small batches (<=8 requests) but allow larger batches to form when queue depth exceeds 32. Add a per-request max-wait SLA of 15ms. Monitor queue depth as a leading indicator. MI300X's 5.3TB/s bandwidth means small batches are not significantly penalized.

scenario: An ML serving system on MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3TB/s) uses dynamic batching with a 20ms timeout and max batch size 64. P50 latency is 35ms, P99 is 95ms. A product team requests P999 < 200ms. The current P999 is 450ms, caused by requests that wait the full 20ms timeout but end up in a large batch.
title: P99 vs P999 Tradeoffs in Batching Strategy

details.common_mistake: Assuming end-to-end P99 = sum of individual P99s. This is incorrect — percentiles don't add linearly. The actual end-to-end P99 is worse because multiple independent tail events can compound.
details.napkin_math: 5 independent stages each at P99: probability all within budget = 0.99^5 = 0.951 → end-to-end is only P95.1, not P99. To achieve true P99 with 5 stages: each needs P(1 - 0.01/5) ≈ P99.8. Reranking: reduce P99.8 from ~30ms to 20ms. Generation: reduce P99.8 from ~80ms to 55ms on H100 — achievable with speculative decoding.
details.realistic_solution: Model each stage as independent with its own latency distribution. For 5 independent stages, P(end-to-end > T) = 1 - Product(P(stage_i <= T_i)). Use correlated sampling to find the true end-to-end percentile. To hit P99 end-to-end, each stage must achieve approximately P99.8 (since 0.998^5 ≈ 0.99). Tighten reranking and generation SLOs to P99.8.

scenario: A multi-stage ML pipeline on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s) has 5 sequential microservices: preprocessing (P99=5ms), embedding (P99=12ms), retrieval (P99=8ms), reranking (P99=15ms), generation (P99=40ms). End-to-end P99 SLA is 100ms. The current end-to-end P99 is 160ms.
title: Tail Latency SLO Decomposition Across Microservices

details.common_mistake: Setting a single P999 SLA without conditioning on output length. A 2000-token generation is physically 10x slower than 200 tokens and cannot meet the same SLA. Conflating TTFT (time to first token) with total generation time in the SLA.
details.napkin_math: A100 80GB, 2TB/s. 70B model at FP16 = 140GB — needs 2 A100s. Memory bandwidth bound decode: 140GB / 2TB/s = 70ms to load model weights per token. At batch=1: 1000/70ms = ~14 tok/s. At batch=8: ~14 tok/s (still BW bound). To reach 40 tok/s: need tensor parallelism across 4 A100s → 560GB/s effective per device → 140GB/560GB/s = 250ms/token → 4 tok/s per device, 4*4=16 tok/s. Still need 8-way TP for 40 tok/s.
details.realistic_solution: Define two separate SLOs: TTFT P99 < 500ms (prefill-dominated, hardware-bounded) and Token Generation Rate P50 > 40 tok/s (decode-dominated). This decouples the user experience metric (TTFT) from the compute metric. For P999 of full generation: cap at 2000 tokens, at 40 tok/s = 50s max → negotiate SLA to TTFT + streaming, not total time.

scenario: A product team wants P999 < 5s for a GPT-4-class model (70B parameters) running on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s, 400W) nodes. Requests generate 200-2000 output tokens. You must set a technically defensible SLA and architect the system to meet it.
title: Measuring and Setting Realistic P999 SLOs for Autoregressive Generation

details.common_mistake: Setting tile size to maximize SRAM occupancy without accounting for the register file pressure from multiple warps. Oversubscribing registers causes register spilling to local memory, which is as slow as global memory.
details.napkin_math: Standard attention: Q@K^T for seq=4096, d=128, BF16: 4096*4096*2 = 32MB per layer per head. With 32 heads: 1GB just for attention maps. With Flash Attention tiling (64×64 blocks): working set per tile = 64*128*2*3 = 48KB (Q,K,V tiles) + 64*64*2 = 8KB (scores) = 56KB per tile. Reads total: 2 * seq^2 * d * 2 bytes = 8GB reads vs standard 32MB mat — Flash Attention reduces HBM reads by ~8x.
details.realistic_solution: H100 SM has 256KB shared memory per SM. For Flash Attention, tile size B_r × B_c × d_head in BF16: B_r=64, B_c=64, d=128 → (64*128 + 64*128 + 64*128) * 2 bytes = 48KB per tile set. Fits in 256KB with headroom for multiple tiles. Use block size 64×64 for the attention scores tile. Profile with Nsight to verify shared memory bank conflicts.

scenario: You're implementing Flash Attention v2 for a 4096-token context Llama-2 model on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, 232KB L2 cache per SM). The attention matrix (Q, K, V in BF16) for a single head at seq_len=4096 would be 512MB in standard attention. You need to select optimal tile sizes to maximize SRAM utilization.
title: Flash Attention Tiling Strategy for H100 SRAM Constraints

details.common_mistake: Claiming Flash Attention is faster because it does fewer FLOPs. Flash Attention performs the same number of FLOPs as standard attention. The speedup is entirely from reduced HBM memory reads/writes (IO complexity), not from reduced arithmetic.
details.napkin_math: Standard attention, seq=8192, d=128, BF16: QK^T write = 8192^2 * 2 = 128MB; softmax in-place; PV read = 128MB + 8192*128*2 = 130MB. Total HBM: ~256MB per layer per head. Flash Attention: Q/K/V each = 8192*128*2 = 2MB; O = 2MB. Total HBM: ~8MB per layer per head. 32x reduction in HBM traffic. At A100 2TB/s: 256MB/2TB/s = 128μs vs 8MB/2TB/s = 4μs per head.
details.realistic_solution: Flash Attention IO complexity is O(N^2 d / M) where M is SRAM size, vs O(N^2) for standard attention. For N=8192, d=128, and M=200KB: Flash Attention HBM reads = O(N^2 * d / M) = O(8192^2 * 128 / 200K) ≈ 43M elements vs standard O(N^2) = 67M for just the attention map. Measure with nvprof memory throughput metric.

scenario: A team is deciding whether to adopt Flash Attention for training a 7B model on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s) with sequence length 8192. They want to understand the theoretical IO reduction before implementation. Standard attention stores the full N×N attention matrix.
title: Flash Attention IO Complexity vs Standard Attention

details.common_mistake: Comparing only FLOPs without accounting for memory capacity constraints. At seq_len=16384, standard attention's N×N matrix is 16384^2 * 4 bytes = 1GB per head per layer. For a 13B model with 40 layers and 40 heads, this is 1.6TB — physically impossible on any GPU.
details.napkin_math: H100 80GB HBM3. Standard attention backward: stores softmax(QK^T) for backward = 16384^2 * 2 bytes = 512MB per head. 13B model: 40 layers * 40 heads = 1600 heads. Peak memory for attention maps = 1600 × 512MB = 800 GB (0.8 TB). Impossible. Flash Attention: stores only Q, K, V, O (each 16384*128*2 = 4MB per head) = 1600 * 16MB = 25.6GB. Fits in 80GB. Recomputation cost: 2x attention FLOPs in backward = acceptable.
details.realistic_solution: Flash Attention backward recomputes the attention matrix (2x FLOPs for backward vs forward), but this is the only way to train with long sequences. The FLOP overhead is ~1.1-1.3x vs standard attention backward, but the memory saving enables training at all. Use gradient checkpointing at layer boundaries to further reduce peak memory.

scenario: During training a 13B model on H100 (80GB HBM3) with seq_len=16384, you notice that Flash Attention uses more FLOPs than standard attention during the backward pass. A colleague suggests reverting to standard attention for training to reduce compute. Evaluate this tradeoff.
title: Flash Attention Backward Pass Memory Recomputation

details.common_mistake: Applying Flash Attention to decode (autoregressive generation) and expecting a speedup. Flash Attention's tiling benefit is for prefill (full sequence attention). During decode, the KV cache for each new token is fetched from HBM — this is a different access pattern not benefited by Flash Attention's tiling.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, 80 layers, 64 heads, d=128, FP16. MHA KV cache per token: 80 * 2 * 64 * 128 * 2 = 2.62MB/token. At 2048 context: 5.37GB KV cache. Decode: load full KV cache per step. MHA: 5.37GB / 5.3TB/s = 1ms/token = 1000 tok/s. GQA-8 (8 KV heads): 5.37GB/8 = 671MB → 671MB/5.3TB/s = 0.13ms/token = 7700 tok/s. MI300X's 5.3TB/s makes GQA especially impactful.
details.realistic_solution: For decode latency at batch=1, the bottleneck is KV cache bandwidth, not attention computation. MQA reduces KV cache size by num_heads factor (e.g. 8x for 64 heads → 8 KV heads). GQA (4 groups) gives 16x reduction. On MI300X with 5.3TB/s, KV cache bandwidth becomes the limiting factor — reduce KV heads to maximize token throughput.

scenario: A team is choosing between standard MHA with Flash Attention, Multi-Query Attention (MQA), and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) for a 70B inference model on MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3TB/s). Decode latency is the primary concern at batch=1.
title: Multi-Query Attention Memory Savings vs Flash Attention

details.common_mistake: Not using the 'varlen' (variable-length) Flash Attention API. With standard padding to max length, Flash Attention still processes all padded tokens, wasting compute on padding. The theoretical speedup assumes dense sequences.
details.napkin_math: Batch of 32 sequences, max_len=2048, avg_len=1200 (60% of max). Standard Flash Attention: processes 32*2048 = 65536 tokens. Attention is O(n^2): wasted compute per sequence = (2048^2 - 1200^2) / 2048^2 = 65.6% waste. Varlen Flash Attention: processes 32*1200 = 38400 tokens. Speedup from varlen = (65536/38400)^? — attention is quadratic: speedup ≈ (2048/1200)^2 = 2.92x vs 1.8x baseline. Matches the expected 4x theoretical.
details.realistic_solution: Use flash_attn_varlen_qkvpacked_func with cu_seqlens (cumulative sequence lengths) to process only valid tokens. Pack all sequences into a single flattened tensor without padding. This eliminates compute on padding tokens entirely. On typical NLP datasets where average length is 60% of max, this recovers ~40% of wasted compute.

scenario: You're using Flash Attention (via xformers or flash-attn library) in a training pipeline on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s) with variable-length text sequences. Batches are padded to the maximum sequence length in the batch. You observe that actual speedup from Flash Attention is only 1.8x vs the theoretical 4x at seq_len=2048.
title: Flash Attention with Variable-Length Sequences and Padding Masks

details.common_mistake: Benchmarking peak FLOP/s (compute-bound regime) without testing the memory-bound regime that occurs during decode. FA3's improvements are primarily for prefill (compute-bound); decode is still memory-bandwidth-bound and sees minimal improvement from FA3.
details.napkin_math: H100 theoretical: 989 TFLOPS BF16. FA2 at 52% MFU = 514 TFLOPS effective. FA3 at 75% MFU = 742 TFLOPS effective. For prefill seq=8192, 70B model (40 layers, 40 heads, d=128): attention FLOPs = 40 × 2 × 8192² × 128 ≈ 687 GFLOP. At 742 TFLOPS: 687G/742T = 0.93ms prefill. At 514 TFLOPS: 687G/514T = 1.34ms. Decode: KV cache load = 40 * 2 * 8192 * 128 * 2 = 167MB/step. At 3.35TB/s: 50μs/step — bandwidth bound, same for FA2/FA3.
details.realistic_solution: Benchmark separately for prefill and decode. FA3 uses H100's wgmma instruction (Tensor Core v4) and pipelining to achieve higher MFU for prefill. For decode (batch=1, seq_len growing), both FA2 and FA3 are equally bandwidth-bound. Deploy FA3 for prefill-heavy workloads (batch processing, RAG) and evaluate risk vs 5-10% throughput gain for production serving.

scenario: Benchmarking Flash Attention v2 vs v3 on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s) for a 70B model with seq_len=8192 and d_head=128. FA2 achieves 180 TFLOPS (52% MFU), FA3 claims up to 75% MFU on H100. You need to decide whether to adopt FA3 in production given it's newer and less battle-tested.
title: Flash Attention v2 vs v3 Block Size Selection on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming Flash Attention is numerically equivalent to standard attention in all cases. Flash Attention uses the online softmax algorithm with per-block running max for numerical stability, but BF16's limited dynamic range (exp range ~1e-38 to 3.4e38) can cause issues when attention logits span a large range.
details.napkin_math: BF16 range: exponent 8 bits, significant 7 bits. Max representable: ~3.4e38. For seq=32768 tokens, attention logit range can reach ±100 after QK^T/sqrt(d). exp(100) = 2.7e43 — overflows BF16. Flash Attention's block-wise running max mitigates this but requires fp32 intermediate accumulation. TPU v5e runs BF16 natively; force fp32 matmul accumulation in JAX with jax.default_matmul_precision='float32'.
details.realistic_solution: Enable Flash Attention's softmax scaling (divide QK by sqrt(d_head) before the attention kernel, which Flash Attention should handle internally). Check if the model uses ALiBi or RoPE positional encodings — very long sequences with ALiBi can produce large negative logits that cause exp(-large) = 0, leading to zero-division in softmax. Use FP32 accumulation in the attention kernel even with BF16 inputs.

scenario: A model trained with standard attention is being converted to use Flash Attention for inference on TPU v5e (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16). At seq_len=32768, you observe NaN values in attention outputs that don't appear with standard attention. The model was trained in BF16.
title: Flash Attention Numerical Stability with Long Sequences

details.common_mistake: Assuming the library regression is a bug and rolling back immediately. The real issue is often a default behavior change: flash-attn 2.5+ enables attention dropout by default when a dropout_p argument is passed as 0.0, which now takes a separate code path with mask materialization.
details.napkin_math: 95 TFLOPS vs 71 TFLOPS = 25% regression. A100 peak 312 TFLOPS BF16. At seq=4096, d=128: attention FLOPs per layer = 2 * 4096^2 * 128 = 4.3 GFLOP. At 95T: 0.045ms/layer. At 71T: 0.06ms/layer. For a 40-layer model: regression = 40 * (0.06-0.045) = 0.6ms per forward pass. At batch=32: adds 19ms per step. Mask materialization for dropout at seq=4096: 4096^2 * 1 byte = 16MB per head — explains the memory bandwidth saturation causing FLOP regression.
details.realistic_solution: Profile with Nsight to compare kernel execution between versions. Check if dropout_p=0.0 is being passed to the attention function — in newer versions, explicitly passing dropout_p=0.0 may trigger a different kernel path than not passing it. Set dropout_p=0.0 and deterministic=False to use the fastest kernel path. Verify with flash_attn.utils.benchmark.

scenario: After upgrading flash-attn from 2.3 to 2.6 on an A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s) training cluster, training throughput drops from 95 TFLOPS to 71 TFLOPS for a seq_len=4096 model. No code changes were made. The upgrade notes mention improved support for dropout in attention.
title: Diagnosing Flash Attention Regression After Library Upgrade

details.common_mistake: Assuming Kubernetes' default GPU plugin can schedule MIG instances. The standard nvidia.com/gpu resource does not understand MIG profiles. Without the MIG-aware device plugin (nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb), Kubernetes sees only full GPUs, not MIG instances, causing scheduling failure despite available capacity.
details.napkin_math: 8 nodes * 8 GPUs * 2 MIG instances = 128 MIG instances total. At 60% utilization: 77 in use, 51 available. Request of 14 can be satisfied by 7 nodes (2 instances/GPU * 1 GPU each) or consolidated on fewer nodes. Scheduling failure is not capacity — it's resource type mismatch. After MIG plugin: scheduling succeeds, 14 MIG instances used, remaining 37 available. Each 3g.40gb MIG slice gets 40GB HBM + ~420GB/s bandwidth (3/7 of full H100).
details.realistic_solution: Deploy the NVIDIA MIG Kubernetes device plugin which exposes resources as nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb. Update pod spec to request nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb: 14. Ensure node labels reflect MIG configuration and that the GPU Operator is installed to manage MIG mode dynamically. Use node affinity to route MIG workloads to MIG-configured nodes.

scenario: Your Kubernetes cluster has 8 H100 (80GB HBM3) nodes, each with 8 GPUs configured with MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) in 3g.40gb profile (2 instances per GPU, 40GB each). A deployment requests 14 GPUs. The pod fails to schedule even though 16 MIG instances are available. GPU utilization across the cluster is 60%.
title: Kubernetes GPU Scheduling Fragmentation with H100 MIG

details.common_mistake: Tuning HPA scaleUp stabilization window to 0s (immediate scaling). This causes thrashing on transient spikes and increases cost by 30-40% without improving steady-state latency.
details.napkin_math: Traffic spike 3x in 2 minutes. At baseline, 4 pods serve 1000 RPS each. 3x spike = 3000 RPS total. 4 pods saturate at 4*1000 = 4000 RPS → 75% utilization, within SLA. But spike reaches 12000 RPS: need 12 pods. HPA provisions 8 more in 4 minutes. During 4-minute window at 12K RPS with 4-pod capacity (4K RPS): queue builds at 8K RPS. Pre-warming 4 pods (1/3 of typical peak) absorbs spike immediately. A100 idle power: 50W vs active 400W. 4 pre-warm pods: 4*50=200W overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Implement predictive scaling using KEDA with Prometheus metrics and a custom scaler that triggers scale-up when queue depth exceeds threshold (not GPU utilization, which lags). Pre-warm a pool of 2 idle pods (scaled to 0 GPU allocation but with model loaded) that can accept traffic immediately. Use pod disruption budgets to prevent scale-down during ramp-up.

scenario: A Kubernetes HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) scales A100 (80GB HBM2e, 400W) inference pods based on GPU utilization metric (target: 70%). Traffic spikes 3x over 2 minutes. HPA takes 4 minutes to provision new pods: 30s metrics delay + 90s scale decision + 60s pod scheduling + 60s model loading. During this window, P99 latency violates SLA.
title: HPA Scaling Latency for GPU Inference Pods

details.common_mistake: Using standard resource requests (nvidia.com/gpu: 8) per pod and expecting Kubernetes to keep multi-GPU jobs on the same node. Kubernetes doesn't understand GPU topology by default — it may split an 8-GPU request across 2 nodes if each node has 4 GPUs free.
details.napkin_math: All-reduce bandwidth for 70B model (140GB BF16 gradients): intra-node NVLink ring: 900GB/s / 8 GPUs = 112GB/s per GPU. All-reduce time = 2*(N-1)/N * data_size / bandwidth = 2*7/8 * 140GB / 900GB/s = 0.27s. Cross-node InfiniBand 400Gbps = 50GB/s: all-reduce = 2*7/8 * 140GB / 50GB/s = 4.9s. 18x slower matches 900/50 = 18x bandwidth ratio. One mis-scheduled job wastes 18x communication time, reducing GPU utilization from 70% to ~30%.
details.realistic_solution: Use NVIDIA's GPU Topology Manager with topology policy 'best-effort' or 'required'. Set pod nodeSelector to require 8 GPUs on one node. Use gang scheduling (Volcano or Koordinator) to ensure all pods in a job start simultaneously on co-located nodes. Add node affinity rules requiring nvidia.com/gpu.count: '8' on a single node.

scenario: You're deploying a 70B model training job on a Kubernetes cluster with H100 (80GB HBM3) nodes (8 GPUs/node, NVLink 900GB/s intra-node). Some pods get scheduled across 2 nodes (cross-node via InfiniBand at 400Gbps = 50GB/s). All-reduce throughput drops 18x when split across nodes. Design a scheduling solution.
title: Multi-GPU Pod Affinity for NVLink-Dependent Workloads

details.common_mistake: Baking model weights into the container image. This creates a 45GB image that must be pulled from registry on every new node, consuming network bandwidth and delaying cold start. Registry pull speeds are typically 100-500Mbps in most cloud environments.
details.napkin_math: Container image pull at 200Mbps (25MB/s): 45GB / 25MB/s = 1800s = 30 minutes (not 5 — implies dedicated pull at ~150MB/s). Model weight load from NVMe SSD (3.5GB/s): 26GB / 3.5GB/s = 7.4s. Model transfer to GPU HBM at PCIe 4.0 (64GB/s): 26GB / 64GB/s = 0.4s. Total optimized: 2GB image pull at 150MB/s = 13s + 7.4s SSD load + 0.4s GPU transfer = 21s. Under 2-minute target by 5.7x.
details.realistic_solution: Separate model weights from container image. Use a 2GB base image (runtime + dependencies only) and mount model weights from a shared NFS/EFS volume or object storage (S3/GCS) at pod startup. With a 10Gbps NFS mount, 26GB loads in 26GB/1.25GB/s = 21 seconds. Use init containers to pre-fetch weights to node-local NVMe SSD, reducing repeated loads.

scenario: A Kubernetes deployment for a 13B model (26GB FP16 checkpoint) on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s) takes 8 minutes to start a new pod: 5 minutes to pull the container image (45GB image with model weights baked in) and 3 minutes to load weights. Target is <2 minute cold start.
title: Container Image Size and Model Loading Latency on GPU Pods

details.common_mistake: Trusting GPU memory limits in Kubernetes resource requests. Standard Kubernetes GPU resource accounting tracks GPU device count, not GPU memory. Two pods can both be assigned the same GPU (if memory-based scheduling isn't used), leading to OOM conflicts.
details.napkin_math: MI300X 192GB HBM3. 70B model at FP16 = 140GB — uses 73% of one GPU. 7B model = 14GB = 7.3%. Two 70B models: 280GB > 192GB → OOM inevitable. Correct tenant isolation: tier-1 (>100GB) → dedicated GPU. tier-2 (10-100GB) → MIG 3g.64gb (64GB slice). tier-3 (<10GB) → MIG 1g.24gb. MI300X MIG support: 8 slices of 1g.24gb or 3 slices of 3g.64gb per GPU. Reduces OOM conflicts to zero with proper tiering.
details.realistic_solution: Use NVIDIA's GPU Memory Manager or MPS (Multi-Process Service) with memory limits. For MI300X with 192GB, use MIG where supported, or implement memory-aware scheduling via extended resources (nvidia.com/gpu.memory). Create separate node pools per model size tier and use namespace resource quotas with node affinity to isolate tenants by GPU memory requirement.

scenario: A multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster with MI300X (192GB HBM3) GPUs has 5 teams sharing 10 GPUs. Each team requests limits.nvidia.com/gpu: 1 but actual models range from 7B (14GB) to 70B (140GB). Teams with 70B models frequently OOM-kill other tenants' pods sharing the same GPU device.
title: Resource Quota and GPU Memory Oversubscription in Kubernetes

details.common_mistake: Using CheckpointSave callbacks that write to NFS every epoch. NFS write throughput for 140GB (70B FP16 checkpoint) is 1GB/s = 140 seconds. At 100B tokens with 2-minute epochs: checkpointing takes 12% of training time and creates a serialization bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: 64-GPU job, 3-hour failure = 64 * 400W * 3h = 76.8 kWh wasted. At $0.12/kWh = $9.22 wasted energy + $3-8/GPU-hour cloud cost = ~$600 wasted per failure. Checkpoint to S3 via multipart: 140GB at 10GB/s = 14 seconds. Every 15 minutes: 14s/900s = 1.6% overhead. Elastic training with 7/8 nodes: throughput drops 12.5%, adds 12.5% to training time — vastly better than full restart. Breakeven: if failure probability >1% per hour, elastic training pays off.
details.realistic_solution: Use Elastic Training (torch.distributed.elastic) with min_nodes=7, max_nodes=8 to continue training with 7 nodes after preemption. Write checkpoints asynchronously to S3 (5-10GB/s multipart) every 15 minutes. Use pod priority classes to prevent training pods from being preempted; reserve spot-instance nodes for training with on-demand for masters. Implement checkpoint sharding across ranks to parallelize writes.

scenario: Your team runs distributed PyTorch training jobs on H100 (80GB HBM3) using kubeflow/training-operator (PyTorchJob). A 64-GPU training run (8 nodes * 8 GPUs) fails when 1 node is preempted. The job restarts from scratch, wasting 3 hours of compute. Design a fault-tolerant orchestration strategy.
title: Kubernetes Operator Design for Distributed Training Jobs

details.common_mistake: Building a full custom scheduler from scratch. Kubernetes has a well-defined Scheduler Framework with extension points (Filter, Score, Reserve, Bind) that allow plugins without replacing the default scheduler. Writing a standalone scheduler loses all built-in features (pod affinity, taints, topology spread).
details.napkin_math: Node with 8x A100 80GB = 640GB total GPU memory. Models running: 2x70B (280GB) + 3x13B (78GB) = 358GB used, 282GB free across 6 GPUs. New 70B request (140GB): needs 1 GPU with 140GB free. A100 max is 80GB → cannot fit. Scheduler must reject node. With Extended Resources: expose nvidia.com/gpu.memory.free per GPU. Scheduler sees 6 GPUs with 33-80GB free, 2 with 0GB. 70B model: no single GPU has 140GB → correctly rejected, job queued. This prevents 100% of OOM cases.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a Kubernetes scheduler plugin using the Scheduler Framework. In the Filter plugin: query DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) for per-GPU free memory via Prometheus metrics, filter nodes where any GPU has insufficient free memory for the requested model size. In the Score plugin: prefer nodes where model fits with least fragmentation. Expose gpu.memory.free as a custom resource via Extended Resources.

scenario: A cloud ML platform team needs a custom Kubernetes scheduler that places inference pods on A100 (80GB HBM2e) nodes based on free GPU memory, not just GPU count. The default scheduler causes OOM errors when multiple models of varying sizes (7B=14GB, 13B=26GB, 70B=140GB) share nodes.
title: Custom Kubernetes Scheduler for GPU Memory-Aware Placement

details.common_mistake: Relying on namespace isolation alone for security. Kubernetes namespaces are a logical boundary but do not restrict network traffic by default. Any pod can reach any other pod by IP address regardless of namespace.
details.napkin_math: H100 cluster, 10 customers, 20 pods each = 200 pods total. Without NetworkPolicy: 200*199 = 39,800 possible pod-to-pod connections. With NetworkPolicy default-deny: each namespace allows only 20 intra-namespace connections + 1 to gateway = 21 allowed. Security surface reduced by 39,800/210 = 190x. Cilium eBPF enforcement overhead: <1μs per connection decision, negligible for inference workloads (>10ms latency per request).
details.realistic_solution: Implement Kubernetes NetworkPolicy to deny all ingress/egress between namespaces by default. Apply a default-deny policy per namespace, then allow only necessary egress to the load balancer and ingress from the API gateway. Use a CNI plugin that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium) — not all CNIs enforce NetworkPolicy. Add PodSecurityPolicy to prevent privilege escalation.

scenario: A multi-tenant inference platform on H100 (80GB HBM3) Kubernetes clusters serves multiple enterprise customers. Each customer's inference pods share the same node. A security audit finds that pods can communicate with each other across namespaces, violating customer isolation requirements.
title: Kubernetes Network Policy for Secure Multi-Tenant GPU Inference

details.common_mistake: Choosing TP=8 to maximize memory distribution without considering that each all-reduce in TP must complete before the next layer can begin. At batch=1, the model is memory-bandwidth-bound, and TP communication overhead dominates.
details.napkin_math: 70B model = 140GB FP16. TP=2: 70GB/GPU — fits in H100 80GB with 10GB headroom. TP=4: 35GB/GPU — comfortable. TP=8: 17.5GB/GPU — wastes 62.5GB/GPU. All-reduce per layer at TP=N: 2*(N-1)/N * tensor_size / BW. Tensor size = hidden_dim * 2 bytes = 8192 * 2 = 16KB per all-reduce for residual stream. At NVLink 900GB/s: 16KB/900GB/s = 0.018μs per all-reduce. But for weight shards in MLP: 8192*32768*2 = 512MB per layer → 512MB/900GB/s = 0.57ms per all-reduce. TP=8 adds 80 layers * 2 all-reduces * 0.57ms = 91ms communication overhead per token.
details.realistic_solution: TP=2 or TP=4 is optimal for latency at batch=1. TP=8 introduces 7 all-reduce operations per layer (one per attention + one per MLP), each requiring synchronization across 8 GPUs. With NVLink, all-reduce of 128MB takes ~0.14ms per operation * 80 layers * 2 = 22ms just in communication. TP=2 reduces communication to ~5ms. Use TP=4 for memory fit with minimal communication overhead.

scenario: You're serving a 70B Llama-2 model (140GB FP16) on H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35TB/s, NVLink 900GB/s) nodes with 8 GPUs each. You must choose tensor parallelism degree: TP=2, TP=4, or TP=8. Each degree has different communication overhead. Batch size is 1 for latency-sensitive serving.
title: Tensor Parallelism Degree Selection for 70B Model on H100

details.common_mistake: Applying column parallelism to both W1 and W2. This requires an all-gather before W2 to reconstruct the full intermediate activations, adding a second communication operation per MLP block and increasing communication by 2x vs the optimal scheme.
details.napkin_math: 13B model, hidden=5120, FFN=4*5120=20480. TP=4: each GPU holds W1=[5120, 5120], W2=[5120, 5120]. Column-parallel W1: input [B, 5120] is broadcast to all 4 GPUs (no comm if input already replicated). Output [B, 5120] per GPU — no all-reduce needed. Row-parallel W2: each GPU partial output [B, 5120] → all-reduce sums to [B, 5120]. All-reduce size: B * 5120 * 2 bytes. At B=1: 10KB, trivial on NVLink. At B=1024: 10MB, 10MB/900GB/s = 11μs — still fast.
details.realistic_solution: Apply column parallelism to W1 (split output/4H dimension across GPUs: each GPU holds [H, H]) — no communication needed before W1. Apply row parallelism to W2 (split input/4H dimension: each GPU holds [H, H]) — requires an all-reduce after W2 to sum partial results. This pattern requires exactly one all-reduce per MLP block. For attention: column-parallel for QKV projection, row-parallel for output projection.

scenario: A team is implementing Megatron-style tensor parallelism for a 13B model on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s) with TP=4. They're confused about whether to use column parallelism or row parallelism for the two linear layers in the MLP block (FFN: W1 of shape [H, 4H] and W2 of shape [4H, H]).
title: Megatron-LM Column vs Row Parallelism for MLP Layers

details.common_mistake: Increasing batch size to 'amortize' communication overhead. All-reduce latency in tensor parallelism is on the critical path and does not scale with batch size — it occurs once per layer per forward/backward pass regardless of batch dimension.
details.napkin_math: TP=16 cross-node all-reduce: each transformer layer has 2 all-reduces (attention + MLP). Gradient size per all-reduce: hidden=12288 for GPT-3, BF16: 12288*12288*2 = 288MB. 2*(16-1)/16 * 288MB at 25GB/s = 2*15/16 * 288/25 = 21.6s per all-reduce. 96 layers * 2 all-reduces * 21.6s = 4147s per forward pass — clearly not this; must be smaller tensors. Actual: activation tensor [B, seq, hidden] BF16: B=1, seq=2048, hidden=12288 = 48MB. 2*15/16 * 48MB/25GB/s = 2.25ms * 96 * 2 = 432ms communication vs ~200ms compute. 68% comm overhead — matches observed.
details.realistic_solution: Reduce TP degree to 8 (within a single node, NVLink only) and compensate with pipeline parallelism (PP) across nodes. TP=8 within node uses NVLink 900GB/s; PP across nodes uses InfiniBand but only sends activations (not weight gradients), reducing inter-node communication. Reconfigure as TP=8, PP=2 (2 pipeline stages, 1 node each). Expected MFU improvement: 22% → ~40%.

scenario: A 175B model (GPT-3 scale) is trained with TP=16 on MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3TB/s) nodes (8 GPUs/node). With TP=16, tensor parallelism spans 2 nodes connected by InfiniBand HDR (200Gbps = 25GB/s). Training MFU is 22% vs expected 45%. Profiling shows 60% of step time is in all-reduce operations.
title: Tensor Parallelism Communication Bottleneck on Multi-Node Cluster

details.common_mistake: Assuming Q and KV head splits must be equal. With GQA (8 KV heads, 32 Q heads), splitting evenly gives 2 KV heads per GPU for TP=4. This works, but requires all 4 KV heads (2 per GPU * 2) to be distributed before cross-GPU Q/K attention computation — the grouped structure must be respected.
details.napkin_math: 7B model, GQA: 32 Q heads, 8 KV heads, d_head=128. TP=4: 8 Q heads/GPU, 2 KV heads/GPU. Per-GPU memory for attention: Q proj [H, 8*128] = [4096, 1024] in BF16 = 8MB. KV proj [H, 2*128*2] = [4096, 512] = 4MB. Total QKV: 12MB per GPU vs 48MB for full MHA. Activation memory per layer: seq=4096 tokens, 8 Q heads * 4096 * 4096 * 2 = 256MB attention scores — still large. Flash Attention required even with TP=4.
details.realistic_solution: For GQA with TP=4: assign 8 Q heads and 2 KV heads per GPU. Each GPU computes attention for its 8 Q heads against its 2 KV heads independently — no cross-GPU communication needed for attention. The constraint is num_kv_heads must be divisible by TP degree. With 8 KV heads and TP=4: 8/4=2 per GPU. TP=8 would require 1 KV head per GPU — valid. TP=16 would fail (8/16 is not integer).

scenario: You're implementing tensor parallelism for attention in a 7B model (32 heads, d_head=128) on 4x H100 (80GB HBM3). A junior engineer proposes splitting heads as 32/4=8 heads per GPU. A second engineer says this works for MHA but breaks Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) where the model has 8 KV heads and 32 Q heads.
title: Tensor Parallelism for Attention Heads: Optimal Head Distribution

details.common_mistake: Using a shared random seed across all TP ranks without understanding which operations need identical vs independent random states. Dropout applied to tensor-parallel shards must generate consistent masks — or be intentionally independent — depending on the parallelism scheme.
details.napkin_math: 13B model, TP=4, dropout p=0.1 in MLP. Without synchronized RNG: each GPU applies independent dropout to its shard. After all-reduce, the effective dropout rate per element is: P(dropped by at least one GPU) = 1 - (1-0.1)^1 = 0.1 (each element is only on one GPU — column-parallel). Actually each element belongs to exactly one GPU, so dropout rate is correct per-GPU. The bug is subtler: if dropout is applied before the all-reduce in row-parallel, the effective rate after summation differs from applying after. Profile forward pass outputs at each layer.
details.realistic_solution: In Megatron-LM, model-parallel regions use a separate RNG state (model_parallel_rng) that is synchronized across TP ranks, ensuring identical dropout masks within a tensor-parallel region. Use torch.cuda.manual_seed_all() to seed all GPUs identically for dropout. Verify by logging the dropout mask checksum across ranks. Alternatively, move dropout to post-all-reduce positions where the full tensor is available.

scenario: A 13B model trained with TP=4 on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2TB/s) produces different loss values than the baseline single-GPU training run, even with the same random seed. The model uses dropout in the MLP layers. The differences are small (0.01%) but accumulate over training, causing divergence after 10K steps.
title: Tensor Parallelism Correctness: Dropout and Random State Synchronization

details.common_mistake: Maximizing TP degree across all GPUs (TP=256) to minimize memory per GPU. This creates an all-reduce graph that spans the entire cluster over InfiniBand, and TP communication becomes 100% of training time since all-reduces are on the critical path.
details.napkin_math: 540B model at BF16 = 1.08TB. Per GPU: 1.08TB / 256 = 4.2GB — way under 80GB. TP=8, PP=4, DP=8: per GPU = 1.08TB / (8*4) = 33.75GB. Fits. Pipeline bubble: PP=4, micro_batches=16: bubble fraction = (PP-1)/(micro_batches+PP-1) = 3/19 = 15.8%. TP communication per layer: activation [B, seq, hidden/8] all-reduce = B*seq*2304*2 bytes. At batch=2048, seq=2048: 2048*2048*2304*2 = 19GB → 19GB/900GB/s = 21ms per all-reduce, 118 layers * 2 = 4.9s comm. Compute: 540B * 6 FLOPs * 2048 tokens = 6.6 PFLOP. At 40% MFU (989 TFLOPS * 256 * 0.4 = 101 PFLOPS): 6.6P/101P = 65ms per step. Communication (21ms) / step (65ms) = 32% — acceptable if overlapped.
details.realistic_solution: Use 3D parallelism: TP=8 within a node (NVLink), PP=4 across nodes (pipeline stages of ~30 layers each), DP=8 (data parallelism across 8 DP replicas). Total: 8*4*8=256 GPUs. TP=8 uses NVLink at 900GB/s (fast). PP uses InfiniBand but only for activations (forward) and gradients (backward) between pipeline stages — not weight all-reduces. DP all-reduce for gradients overlaps with pipeline bubbles.

scenario: Design a parallelism strategy for training a 540B PaLM-scale model on a 256-GPU cluster of H100s (80GB HBM3, NVLink 900GB/s intra-node, InfiniBand 400Gbps inter-node). The model has 118 transformer layers, hidden_size=18432, 48 heads. Target: MFU > 40%.
title: TP+PP Combined Parallelism Strategy for 540B Model

details.common_mistake: Increasing TP degree to TP=8 to reduce per-GPU weight memory further. Activations are the bottleneck (45GB), not weights (7.5GB). TP does not reduce activation memory proportionally — sequence-parallel is needed for that.
details.napkin_math: 30B model, TP=4: weights = 60GB/4 = 15GB per GPU (FP32 optimizer states excluded). Activations for batch=8, seq=2048: per layer = batch * seq * hidden * bytes * num_tensors. Hidden=7168 (30B model). Per layer: 8 * 2048 * 7168 * 2 * 8 (QKV, attention, MLP activations) = 1.87GB. 48 layers: 90GB total activations. TP without SP: only weight compute is sharded, activations remain full = 90GB. SP shards activations: 90/4 = 22.5GB. Activation checkpointing (every 4 layers): keeps only 1/4 of layers' activations = 5.6GB. Total: 15GB + 5.6GB = 20.6GB per GPU for batch=8. Scale to batch=32: 20.6 * 4 = 82GB — nearly fits; use activation checkpointing for remaining layers.
details.realistic_solution: Enable Sequence Parallelism (SP) alongside TP (Megatron-LM --sequence-parallel flag). SP splits activations along the sequence dimension across TP ranks, reducing activation memory by TP factor. At TP=SP=4: activation memory drops from 45GB to 45/4 = 11.25GB. Add activation checkpointing for the most memory-intensive layers. Total: 7.5GB weights + 11.25GB activations = 18.75GB → batch_size=32 uses 4*18.75 = 75GB — fits.

scenario: Training a 30B model with TP=4 on H100 (80GB HBM3) runs OOM at batch_size=8 with seq_len=2048. Memory profiling shows 52GB used: 30GB for model weights (TP=4 → 7.5GB/GPU) + 45GB for activations — exceeding 80GB. Without TP, memory is even worse. You need to reach batch_size=32.
title: Tensor Parallelism Activation Memory and Recomputation

details.common_mistake: Splitting the vocabulary embedding along the embedding dimension (4096/4 = 1024 per GPU). This doesn't save memory in the vocabulary dimension and requires gathering partial embeddings before all downstream computations.
details.napkin_math: 128K vocab, TP=4: 32K tokens/GPU * 4096 * 2 bytes = 256MB/GPU (vs 1GB for full embedding). Memory savings: 750MB/GPU. All-reduce for embedding: batch * seq * hidden_dim * 2 bytes = 8 * 2048 * 4096 * 2 = 128MB. At MI300X NVLink bandwidth (not specified, assume similar to HBM: effectively 5.3TB/s intra-device or ~600GB/s NVLink): 128MB/600GB/s = 0.21ms per step. 50K training steps: 0.21ms * 2 (fwd+bwd) * 50K = 21 seconds of communication for embeddings — entirely negligible.
details.realistic_solution: Split vocabulary dimension: each GPU holds [32K, 4096] of the embedding matrix (128K/4 = 32K per GPU). During forward: each GPU gathers embeddings only for tokens in its vocabulary shard, then all-reduce across TP ranks to get the full embedding vector. This requires one all-reduce per embedding lookup. For the LM head: each GPU computes logits for its vocabulary shard, then all-gather for top-k sampling.

scenario: A 7B model with 128K vocabulary size is being trained with TP=4 on MI300X (192GB HBM3). The embedding layer (128K * 4096 * 2 bytes = 1GB) and the output LM head (same 1GB) together consume 2GB. A team member suggests these can also be tensor-parallelized. Analyze the approach and communication pattern.
title: Tensor Parallelism Embedding Layer Split and Vocabulary Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Calculating scaling efficiency as (new throughput / old throughput) = 2100/1800 = 116% — this is absolute throughput growth, not efficiency. Scaling efficiency measures how well additional GPUs are utilized relative to perfect linear scaling.
details.napkin_math: TP=4: 450 tok/s/GPU, 4 GPUs. Perfect TP=8 would give 450*8=3600 tok/s. Actual: 2100. Efficiency = 2100/3600 = 58.3%. Lost throughput = 1500 tok/s = 42% wasted on communication. All-reduce at TP=8: 2*(8-1)/8 = 87.5% of bandwidth used for communication vs 2*(4-1)/4 = 75% at TP=4. Communication fraction increase: (87.5-75)/75 = 16.7% more comm overhead. Actual efficiency loss is 41.7% — higher than predicted, suggesting other bottlenecks (NCCL latency, synchronization barriers).
details.realistic_solution: Scaling efficiency = (throughput_TP8 / throughput_TP4) / (GPUs_TP8 / GPUs_TP4) = (2100/1800) / (8/4) = 1.167 / 2 = 58.3%. Each additional GPU contributes only 58.3% of the value of the original 4 GPUs. The bottleneck is all-reduce communication overhead: at TP=8, 7 synchronization points vs 3 at TP=4, and the all-reduce ring involves more participants.

scenario: You're evaluating whether to scale from TP=4 to TP=8 for a 13B model on H100 (80GB HBM3, NVLink 900GB/s). At TP=4, throughput is 450 tokens/sec/GPU (4 GPUs = 1800 total). At TP=8 (8 GPUs), total throughput is 2100 tokens/sec. Calculate scaling efficiency and explain the bottleneck.
title: Tensor Parallelism Scaling Efficiency Measurement

details.common_mistake: Setting PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable=1, which allows Kubernetes to terminate up to 11 of 12 replicas simultaneously during a cluster operation. This is a floor, not a maximum disruption rate — it only guarantees at least 1 replica is running.
details.napkin_math: 12 replicas at 670 RPS each. If 2 terminate: 10 replicas at 800 RPS = 119% of normal load → overloaded. If 1 terminates: 11 replicas at 727 RPS = 109% — marginally over, P99 stress. minAvailable=10 + maxSurge=1: during rollout, 10 old + 1 new (warming) = 10 active. 8000/10 = 800 RPS = 119% of 670. Reduce to minAvailable=11: 11 active during transition = 727 RPS = 108%. A100 at 80% → 88% utilization during rollout — acceptable. Model load time: 14GB / PCIe4 64GB/s = 0.22s + container init ~25s. ReadinessProbe delay = 30s covers this.
details.realistic_solution: Set PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable=10 (maintain at least 10 of 12 replicas). This limits simultaneous disruptions to 2. Combined with maxSurge=1 in the RollingUpdate strategy, at most 1 old pod is terminated while 1 new pod starts. With 10 replicas at 8000 RPS: 800 RPS each = 95% utilization — acceptable during rollout. Set readinessProbe with a warmup period of 30s for new pods to load models before receiving traffic.

scenario: You are rolling out a new version of a 7B inference model (14GB FP16) on A100 (80GB HBM2e, 400W) pods in a Kubernetes cluster. The deployment has 12 replicas serving 8000 RPS. Each replica handles ~670 RPS at 80% GPU utilization. During a rolling update, pods are terminated before new pods are ready. Two simultaneous terminations cause P99 latency to spike above SLA.
title: Pod Disruption Budget Design for Zero-Downtime Model Rollouts

details.common_mistake: Teams profile the expert FFNs and ignore the gating softmax, assuming it is free. At scale, a full 64-way softmax over a 4096-token batch is 4096×64 = 262,144 floating-point operations per gating step, repeated every layer.
details.napkin_math: Naive router: 4096 tokens × 64 experts × 2 (linear + softmax) ≈ 0.5 MFLOPs/layer. With top-2 hard routing: 4096 × 64 (linear) + 4096 × 2 (softmax over 2) ≈ 0.27 MFLOPs/layer. Router overhead drops from 12% to ~6% without accuracy loss in most MoE literature.
details.realistic_solution: Switch to token-choice routing with a hard top-k argmax after a single linear projection, fusing the router into a single kernel. Replace full softmax with a top-k-only implementation (compute partial softmax over only k=2 candidates after cheap linear scoring). This cuts router FLOPs by ~32x.

scenario: You are running a 64-expert Mixtral-style MoE model on 8x H100 (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s). Each token activates top-2 experts. Your gating network adds a softmax over 64 logits per token, and you observe that the router overhead is eating 12% of your step time on a 4096-token batch. You need to reduce this without changing the number of experts.
title: MoE Expert Routing Overhead on H100

details.common_mistake: Practitioners assume that adding an auxiliary load-balancing loss term during training is sufficient. In production, distribution shift causes collapse to a dominant expert, and the training loss weight was too small (α=0.001) to prevent it under domain shift.
details.napkin_math: With 4096 tokens and 16 experts, balanced load = 256 tokens/expert. Expert #3 gets 68% = 2785 tokens. All-reduce sync must wait for the slowest GPU: A100 processes ~1.5× more tokens than expected, adding ~(2785/256 − 1) × step_latency ≈ 9.9× expert latency on that GPU vs. balanced.
details.realistic_solution: Add expert capacity limits at inference: cap each expert buffer at capacity_factor × (batch_size / num_experts). Tokens exceeding the cap are dropped or redirected via a secondary 'overflow' expert. Combine with online load statistics and periodically re-initialize the least-used experts with weights from overloaded ones.

scenario: A 16-expert MoE model deployed across 4x A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2 TB/s) processes a production text batch. You notice GPU utilization drops to 40% on 3 of the 4 GPUs while one GPU is pegged at 100%. NVML shows expert #3 receives 68% of all tokens in a typical step. Describe what is causing this and how to fix it.
title: Expert Load Imbalance Killing Throughput in MoE

details.common_mistake: Placing one expert per chip wastes capacity: 128 experts / 64 chips = 2 experts/chip minimum, but naively mapping all experts to all chips defeats the purpose of sparsity and blows the all-to-all volume.
details.napkin_math: Each chip holds 2 experts × 2 GB = 4 GB, well within 16 GB. All-to-all volume per step: batch_tokens × hidden_dim × 2 (BF16) = 4096 × 4096 × 2 = 32 MB per layer. TPU v5e ICI bandwidth ~900 GB/s; all-to-all: 32 MB / 900 GB/s ≈ 35 µs per layer. Acceptable for ~100ms step time.
details.realistic_solution: Use expert parallelism: partition 128 experts across 64 chips (2 experts/chip). Each chip holds 2 × 2 GB = 4 GB of expert params, leaving 12 GB for activations. Use XLA's all-to-all over the 4096-chip interconnect to route tokens to the correct expert chip. Combine with data parallelism for the dense attention layers.

scenario: You are designing a 128-expert MoE model to run on a pod of 64x TPU v5e chips (16GB HBM, 197 TFLOPS BF16 each). Each expert has 1B parameters in BF16 (2 GB). You need to fit all experts in memory while maintaining high utilization. Design the expert sharding strategy and explain the all-to-all communication cost.
title: Designing MoE Expert Sharding for TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Setting α too high early in training causes all experts to receive uniform load, preventing specialization. Setting α too low allows collapse. Teams often use a fixed α without a warmup schedule, missing the window when expert assignment is most plastic.
details.napkin_math: Target: each of 32 experts handles ~1/32 = 3.1% of tokens. Current: 3 experts handle 80% → 26.7%/each, others share 20%/29 ≈ 0.69%/each. Imbalance ratio = 26.7/0.69 ≈ 38.7×. Auxiliary loss α=0.01 contributes 0.01 × load_balance_loss ≈ 0.01 × 0.35 ≈ 0.0035 to total loss — too small relative to CE loss of ~2.5 at step 5k.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a staged α schedule: start at α=0.001 for first 1k steps (allow initial specialization), ramp to α=0.01 from 1k-5k (enforce balance), then settle at α=0.005. Add an entropy regularization term on the router distribution to prevent collapse. Log per-expert token counts every 100 steps as a training health metric.

scenario: You are training a 32-expert MoE model on 16x H100 (80GB HBM3). Your auxiliary load-balancing loss uses coefficient α=0.01. After 5k steps, expert collapse occurs: 3 experts receive >80% of tokens. The training loss is good but perplexity on the validation set deteriorates. Diagnose the problem and implement a fix.
title: MoE Auxiliary Loss Tuning for Stable Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming that larger batches always improve utilization in MoE models. With top-2 routing and batch size 4, only 8 expert slots are activated — most of the 64 experts are idle. Padding adds latency without proportionally improving utilization if the routed tokens still cluster to a few experts.
details.napkin_math: MI300X peak: 5.3 TB/s memory bandwidth. Expert FFN weight load per token: 1B params × 2 bytes (BF16) = 2 GB. At batch=1: 2 GB / 5.3 TB/s ≈ 0.38 ms just to load weights. At batch=64: same 2 GB load amortized over 64 tokens — 0.38 ms / 64 = 5.9 µs/token effective memory cost. 10× improvement in memory efficiency.
details.realistic_solution: Use continuous batching to aggregate requests from multiple users into a single large batch rather than padding a single request. At batch size 64, each expert receives ~2 tokens on average (top-2 routing), spreading load across all 64 experts. This improves MFU from ~8% to ~40% on MI300X without artificial latency padding.

scenario: You are operating an online inference service using a 64-expert MoE on 4x MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s). At low request rates (batch size 1-4), GPU utilization is 8%. A colleague suggests padding every batch to 64 tokens to improve expert routing efficiency. Explain the tradeoff and whether this is a good idea.
title: MoE Inference Batching Strategy for Throughput

details.common_mistake: Assuming MoE and the equivalent dense model have the same memory footprint because active params are equal. MoE requires all 140B parameters to be loaded into memory even though only 70B are active per token. This doubles the GPU memory requirement.
details.napkin_math: 70B dense model: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB; needs 2× A100 80GB. 140B MoE model: 140B × 2 bytes = 280 GB; needs 4× A100 80GB. Per-token active compute: both ~70B params. Memory bandwidth cost: MoE loads 4× more weights from HBM per token if experts are not batched, causing 4× lower throughput at batch size 1.
details.realistic_solution: Use MoE when you have memory capacity to spare but want to increase model capacity without increasing per-token compute. The 140B MoE needs 280 GB BF16 (140B × 2) vs 140 GB for the 70B dense model — you need 4 A100 80GB for MoE vs 2 for dense. The payoff is higher quality at the same per-token FLOPs.

scenario: A team is deciding between a 70B dense model and a 140B MoE model with top-2 routing (70B active parameters per token) for serving on A100 80GB clusters. Both models have the same active parameter count per token. Explain the memory and compute implications of the MoE approach and when it is preferable.
title: MoE vs Dense Model Memory Tradeoff at Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming ECMP distributes large elephant flows evenly. ECMP uses a hash of (src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port) — all-reduce flows from fixed GPU pairs hash to the same spine switch, creating persistent hotspots regardless of other paths being free.
details.napkin_math: 256 GPUs × 400 Gbps = 102.4 Tbps aggregate. Ring all-reduce produces N/2 concurrent flows (128 flows). With 16 spine switches, ideal: 8 flows/spine. With ECMP hash collision (birthday problem at 128 flows, 16 bins): expected max load ≈ 128/16 × (1 + sqrt(ln(16)/2)) ≈ 17.4 flows/spine vs. expected 8 = 118% overload.
details.realistic_solution: Switch to packet-spraying (per-packet ECMP or RoCEv2 with flow-level ECMP) combined with DCQCN for congestion control. Alternatively, use RDMA with explicit path selection (adaptive routing) available on modern Spectrum-3/Quantum-2 InfiniBand switches. Add flowlet switching with a 500µs idle timeout to break large flows into independently-routed sub-flows.

scenario: You have a 256-GPU H100 cluster running ring all-reduce over 400 GbE. During training, you observe 3× variance in step times across runs. Network telemetry shows some spine switches at 92% utilization while others sit at 15%. Your flows use ECMP load balancing. What is the root cause and how do you fix it?
title: ECMP Hashing Imbalance in All-Reduce Traffic

details.common_mistake: Enabling PFC globally on all priorities without isolating RDMA traffic to a dedicated priority class. When PFC pause propagates upstream it can head-of-line block non-RDMA control traffic, preventing heartbeat messages and causing timeouts that appear as training failures.
details.napkin_math: RTT in fat-tree: ~4 µs (2 µs propagation + 2 µs queuing). PFC headroom per port = RTT × 400 Gbps / 8 = 4e-6 × 50e9 = 200 KB. With 32 ports/switch: total PFC headroom = 6.4 MB. Arista 7800R3 has 48 MB shared buffer — adequate. DCQCN reaction time: ~1 ms; reduces PFC trigger rate by 10-100× in practice.
details.realistic_solution: Isolate RDMA traffic to a single PFC-enabled priority (e.g., priority 3) using DSCP marking. Enable DCQCN on all RDMA flows to react to ECN marks before PFC is needed. Set PFC headroom buffers correctly: PFC_threshold = RTT × link_rate / 8 = 4µs × 400 Gbps / 8 = 200 KB per port. Use watchdog timers to detect PFC deadlock and force-flush stuck ports.

scenario: Your 128-GPU H100 training cluster uses RoCEv2 over a 3-tier fat-tree. Priority Flow Control (PFC) is enabled to prevent packet drops. After a topology change (one spine switch failure), you observe a training stall lasting 45 seconds before recovery. Analysis shows PFC pause frames propagated back 6 hops, freezing unrelated flows. Design a solution.
title: PFC Deadlock Prevention in RoCE Cluster

details.common_mistake: Treating buffer bloat as purely a throughput problem. Teams increase buffer sizes to prevent packet drops, not realizing this increases queuing delay from <1 ms to 50-200 ms, which directly causes gradient staleness in async training.
details.napkin_math: 100 GbE switch buffer at 80% of 32 MB = 25.6 MB. Drain time: 25.6 MB / (100 Gbps / 8) = 25.6 MB / 12.5 GB/s = 2.05 ms baseline. But with 64 workers bursting simultaneously: effective contention adds 64 × burst_size / bandwidth ≈ 50-200 ms. 200 ms / 500 ms step time = 0.4 steps of induced staleness, compounding with network variance.
details.realistic_solution: Enable Active Queue Management (AQM) with CoDel or FQ-CoDel on the switch ports. Set the target queue delay to 5 ms (well under one gradient step of 500 ms). This keeps buffers shallow while avoiding drops. Also implement gradient compression (PowerSGD or TopK sparsification) to reduce the volume of traffic that triggers congestion.

scenario: You are running asynchronous SGD with 64 parameter server workers on A100 80GB nodes connected via 100 GbE. Workers are updating gradients every 500ms. You notice gradient staleness exceeding 5 steps for 20% of updates. Network monitoring shows switch buffers frequently reaching 80% capacity. Explain the connection between buffer bloat and gradient staleness.
title: Buffer Bloat Causing Gradient Staleness

details.common_mistake: Confusing incast collapse with link saturation. Incast occurs when many small flows arrive at nearly the same time and overwhelm shallow switch buffers, causing synchronized drops and TCP retransmissions — even when average utilization is low. Teams see 'normal' utilization (40-60%) but fail to capture microsecond-level bursts.
details.napkin_math: 512 workers each send 1 MB gradient shard simultaneously. 512 MB arrives at 16 PS nodes in ~1 ms (400 GbE: 1 MB / 50 GB/s = 20 µs per worker). Switch buffer per port: 2 MB (typical shallow buffer). 32 incast flows × 1 MB = 32 MB needed vs. 2 MB available: 16× buffer overflow → packet drops → TCP back-off → 4× slowdown matches observed degradation.
details.realistic_solution: Use RDMA (RoCEv2) with DCQCN instead of TCP for gradient transfers — RDMA's lossless transport avoids TCP incast collapse. If TCP must be used, implement scatter-gather: stagger worker sends with a random jitter of 0-10 ms and reduce the TCP initial congestion window. Also increase switch buffer allocation for PS-facing ports.

scenario: A 512-GPU training job on MI300X clusters uses parameter servers. All 512 workers send their gradient shards to 16 PS nodes simultaneously (fan-in ratio 32:1). Step times are 4× slower than expected. Wireshark shows massive packet loss at the PS-facing switch ports despite link utilization appearing normal. Identify the failure mode and fix it.
title: Incast Collapse During Gradient Aggregation

details.common_mistake: Using default DCQCN parameters (Rai=40 Mbps, Rcd=50%, timer=55 µs) designed for 10 GbE on a 400 GbE fabric. At 40× higher link speed, the rate increase step is proportionally tiny and the decrease is too aggressive, causing saw-tooth oscillation at larger amplitude.
details.napkin_math: BDP at 400 GbE with 4 µs RTT = 400 Gbps × 4 µs / 8 = 200 KB. Default Byte_Reset = 10 KB is 20× too small, triggering rate reductions every 10 KB instead of every RTT. Fix: Byte_Reset = 400 KB. Rate increase Rai: default 40 Mbps gives 400 Gbps / 40 Mbps = 10,000 steps to recover — too slow. At 1.6 Gbps: 400 Gbps / 1.6 Gbps = 250 steps — reasonable.
details.realistic_solution: Scale DCQCN parameters proportionally to link speed: Rai = 40 Mbps × (400/10) = 1.6 Gbps. Reduce timer to 15 µs to match lower RTT of high-bandwidth fabric. Set target_rate = 95% of link capacity. Increase byte counter threshold (Byte_Reset) from 10 KB to 400 KB to match larger BDP (Bandwidth-Delay Product) at 400 GbE.

scenario: You are configuring DCQCN (Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification) for a 1024-GPU H100 cluster running NCCL all-reduce over RoCEv2. The cluster uses 400 GbE with Quantum-2 InfiniBand switches acting as Ethernet. Default DCQCN parameters cause oscillation: throughput swings between 90% and 40% of link capacity every 50 ms. Fix the configuration.
title: DCQCN Tuning for Large-Scale All-Reduce

details.common_mistake: Using a single QoS class for all ML traffic. Large gradient transfers and small control-plane messages compete for the same buffers and scheduler slots. Large flows cause head-of-line blocking of small flows, increasing FCT for critical heartbeats and barrier synchronization.
details.napkin_math: Control message FCT (no queueing): 32 KB / (100 Gbps / 8) = 2.56 µs. With head-of-line behind a 1 GB gradient transfer: 1 GB / (100 Gbps / 8) = 80 ms delay — 31,000× worse. With strict priority for small flows: FCT ≈ 2.56 µs + serialization = ~5 µs. Acceptable for heartbeat intervals of 1-10 ms.
details.realistic_solution: Implement two traffic classes: (1) a high-priority low-latency queue for control messages (<32 KB) with strict priority scheduling, and (2) a best-effort weighted fair queue for gradient transfers (>1 MB). Use DSCP marking at the sender to classify traffic. This ensures FCT for small flows stays under 100 µs while large flows share bandwidth fairly.

scenario: Two ML engineers debate congestion control strategies for a 64-GPU A100 (80GB HBM2e, 2 TB/s) training cluster. Engineer A wants to maximize aggregate bandwidth for large gradient all-reduce. Engineer B wants to minimize flow completion time (FCT) for the parameter server's many small control messages. Explain why these goals conflict and how to address both.
title: Flow Completion Time vs Bandwidth Tradeoff in Gradient Sync

details.common_mistake: Using time-sliced GPU sharing for both tenants. GPU time-slicing adds context switch overhead (1-3 ms per switch on H100) and does not provide memory isolation. Tenant B's large training batches consume HBM3, causing Tenant A's inference kernels to stall on memory pressure.
details.napkin_math: Tenant A SLO: p99 < 50 ms. Inference latency on H100 MIG 3g.40gb (40 GB HBM3, ~1.6 TB/s bandwidth): ~5-15 ms for 7B model at batch=1. Headroom = 50 - 15 = 35 ms. Context switch overhead with time-slice: 2 ms per 10 ms quantum = 20% overhead → effective latency budget consumed before inference begins. MIG eliminates this overhead entirely.
details.realistic_solution: Use MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) to carve 30% of GPUs into 3g.40gb MIG slices for Tenant A — guaranteed memory isolation and predictable latency. Reserve 140 GPUs for Tenant B training. Use a priority preemption policy: if Tenant A demand spikes, preempt Tenant B jobs with checkpoint-resume. Monitor p99 latency with 5s rolling window and trigger scaling at p95>40ms.

scenario: You operate a shared H100 (80GB HBM3, 700W) cluster with 200 GPUs. You have two tenant classes: Tenant A (latency-sensitive inference, SLO: p99 < 50ms, 30% of cluster) and Tenant B (batch training, best-effort, 70% of cluster). Design a scheduling system that guarantees Tenant A's SLO while maximizing Tenant B's GPU utilization.
title: Multi-Tenant GPU Scheduling with SLO Guarantees

details.common_mistake: Accepting user-declared GPU counts at face value and not enforcing actual utilization requirements. Jobs pad their GPU requests to ensure they don't get preempted, creating systematic over-allocation without a utilization feedback loop.
details.napkin_math: 92 wasted GPUs × $2.50/GPU-hour (A100 spot) = $230/hour = $5,520/day. At 18% fragmentation on 512 GPUs: effective cluster size = 512 × 0.82 = 420 GPUs. Wasted capacity: 92 GPUs × 8,760 h/year = 805,920 GPU-hours/year ≈ $2M/year. BFD reduces fragmentation to ~5% in theory (from O(n) to O(1) amortized waste), recovering ~67 GPUs.
details.realistic_solution: Implement utilization-aware gang scheduling: if a job's 6-hour average GPU utilization < 20%, the scheduler renegotiates the allocation down. Use Best-Fit Decreasing (BFD) bin-packing instead of First-Fit to reduce fragmentation. Add a 'rightsizing' daemon that monitors NVML util every 60s and flags over-provisioned jobs for the scheduler.

scenario: Your 512-GPU A100 cluster scheduler uses First-Fit bin-packing to assign jobs. A workload audit shows 18% GPU fragmentation: 92 GPUs are allocated but underutilized (< 5% GPU util) because jobs request 8 GPUs but only use 6. Compute the cost of this fragmentation and propose a better allocation strategy.
title: Bin-Packing GPU Jobs to Minimize Fragmentation

details.common_mistake: Saving the full model checkpoint (all optimizer states, gradients, activations) to a shared NFS mount. NFS bandwidth (typically 10-20 GB/s) serializes checkpoint writes from 128 GPUs, creating a 1.2 TB / 10 GB/s = 120 second bottleneck that doesn't parallelize.
details.napkin_math: Preemption frequency: 72h / 4h = 18 preemptions. Overhead per preemption: 18 min = 0.3h. Total preemption overhead: 18 × 0.3h = 5.4h. Training time without preemption: 72h. Effective training time: 72 + 5.4 = 77.4h → 7.5% slower. But observed: 30% slower → additional overhead from restart warmup (optimizer momentum, data loader state) adding ~1.5h per restart.
details.realistic_solution: Switch to async distributed checkpointing: each GPU saves its shard to local NVMe in parallel (128 × ~9.4 GB = 1.2 TB / 128 nodes), then background-copy to object storage. Checkpoint time: 9.4 GB / 6.5 GB/s NVMe ≈ 1.4 seconds (vs 18 minutes). Also negotiate preemption delay with the scheduler to avoid mid-step preemptions.

scenario: A 3-day LLM pre-training job on 128 H100s (80GB HBM3) is being preempted every 4 hours by higher-priority jobs. Each preemption triggers a checkpoint save and reload that takes 18 minutes (checkpoint is 1.2 TB across 128 GPUs, written to NFS). The job is completing 30% slower than scheduled. Quantify the overhead and propose solutions.
title: Preemption Overhead in Long-Running Training Jobs

details.common_mistake: Using a Kubernetes default scheduler that treats GPUs as independent resources and allocates them greedily as they become free. Distributed training requires all N GPUs to be available simultaneously (gang) — partial allocations starve the job while holding resources.
details.napkin_math: Without gang scheduling: 20 jobs × 8 GPUs = 160 GPUs needed. 10 jobs are in partial state holding 50 GPUs (5 avg each) while waiting for 3 more. Those 50 GPUs are 'allocated' but 0% utilized. 50/200 = 25% of cluster idle due to partial allocations. Observed 35% util = 30% genuine work + 5% from jobs that did complete gang. Gang scheduling recovers the 25% → 60% utilization.
details.realistic_solution: Implement gang scheduling with all-or-nothing allocation: a job requesting 8 GPUs either receives all 8 simultaneously or waits in a queue. Use a backfill scheduler that allows smaller jobs to run during wait periods. Tools: Volcano scheduler for Kubernetes, Slurm with --ntasks-per-node and --exclusive, or YARN capacity scheduler with GPU gang support.

scenario: Your team is running 20 concurrent 8-GPU training jobs on a 200-GPU MI300X cluster. The Kubernetes scheduler is launching jobs as GPUs become available, but jobs start with 4-6 GPUs and block waiting for the remaining GPUs. GPU utilization sits at 35% even though 190 of 200 GPUs are 'allocated.' Explain why gang scheduling is necessary here.
title: Gang Scheduling for Distributed Training Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Triggering scale-out only after p95 latency breaches the SLO threshold. By the time latency degrades, the 4-minute cold start means 6+ minutes of SLO violation. Reactive scaling is too slow for sub-5-minute spikes.
details.napkin_math: 70B model BF16: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB. Loading from S3 at 10 GB/s: 14 seconds. Model loading to GPU HBM: 140 GB / 3.35 TB/s (H100) = 42 ms. Total cold start: 14s (S3) + ~4min (framework init, CUDA context) = 4.2 min. With NVMe pre-staging: 140 GB / 6.5 GB/s NVMe = 21.5s + 42ms GPU load = ~22s. 11× faster cold start.
details.realistic_solution: Implement predictive scaling based on historical traffic patterns (daily spikes at 9am, 12pm, 5pm). Pre-warm instances 5 minutes before predicted spikes. Use spot instance pools with pre-loaded model weights on NVMe to cut cold start to 45 seconds. Maintain a 'warm spare pool' of 2-3 idle instances at all times as a buffer. Use KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) with custom metrics from queue depth.

scenario: You serve a 70B LLaMA model on H100 80GB instances. SLO: p99 TTFT (time to first token) < 200ms. You experience 3× traffic spikes lasting 2-5 minutes every day. Cold start for a new H100 instance (model load from S3 + warmup) takes 4 minutes. Design an autoscaling strategy that maintains the SLO through spikes without excessive idle capacity.
title: SLO-Aware Autoscaling for Inference Under Bursty Load

details.common_mistake: Using a 'save checkpoint every N steps' policy with a fixed interval of 60 steps (15 min). When a 2-minute preemption notice arrives, the job cannot complete a full checkpoint before termination, losing up to 15 minutes of work — exceeding the 10-minute tolerance.
details.napkin_math: Full checkpoint: 32 GPUs × 5 GB model shard = 160 GB. At S3 write speed 2 GB/s per instance × 32 = 64 GB/s aggregate: 160 GB / 64 GB/s = 2.5 seconds. Wait — actual NFS or EFS bottleneck often limits to 10-20 GB/s total: 160 GB / 10 GB/s = 16 seconds. Emergency lightweight checkpoint (weights only, no optimizer): 160 GB / 2 = 80 GB → 8 seconds. Fits in 2-minute window.
details.realistic_solution: Implement incremental/delta checkpointing: save only changed optimizer state tensors (typically 20-30% of full state per step). Use PyTorch's FSDP with save_on_each_rank=True and write to local NVMe first, then async-copy to S3. On receiving SIGTERM (2-min warning), trigger an emergency lightweight checkpoint: save only model weights (not optimizer state), accepting a slight training regression. Full checkpoint every 30 steps (7.5 min).

scenario: You run a 32-GPU A100 training job on AWS spot instances to save 70% on costs. Spot interruption notices arrive with a 2-minute warning. Your training step takes 15 seconds and checkpoints take 8 minutes (full model save). You need to handle preemptions without losing more than 10 minutes of training. Implement a fault-tolerant checkpointing strategy.
title: Spot Instance Preemption Handling in Training Clusters

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the pipeline bubble entirely when calculating training throughput. The bubble fraction is (p-1)/(m+p-1) where p=pipeline stages, m=micro-batches. Many teams use m=4 micro-batches, which creates a 7/10 = 70% bubble — wasting most of the pipeline.
details.napkin_math: Bubble fraction formula: (p-1)/(m+p-1). With p=8, m=4: (7)/(11) = 63.6% bubble. With p=8, m=64: (7)/(71) = 9.9% bubble. Effective GPU utilization: m=4 → 36.4%, m=64 → 90.1%. For a 10-day training job: m=4 wastes 6.4 days of GPU-compute; m=64 wastes 1 day. Memory per GPU: m=4 micro-batches × 10 layers × activation_size must fit in 80 GB HBM3.
details.realistic_solution: Increase the number of micro-batches m to reduce bubble: with m=64, bubble = (8-1)/(64+8-1) = 7/71 = 9.9%. This requires splitting the 256 global batch into 64 micro-batches of 4 samples each. The tradeoff is increased activation memory. Use gradient checkpointing on intermediate stages to manage memory.

scenario: You are implementing GPipe pipeline parallelism across 8 H100 GPUs (80GB HBM3). The model has 80 transformer layers split evenly (10 per GPU). You use micro-batch size 4 and global batch size 256 (64 micro-batches). Calculate the pipeline bubble fraction and explain how it affects effective GPU utilization.
title: GPipe Bubble Overhead Calculation for 8-Stage Pipeline

details.common_mistake: Assuming the interleaved schedule always wins. The interleaved schedule requires more stages per device (v chunks × p stages = v × 8 stages), increasing the number of in-flight micro-batches and peak activation memory by a factor of v. With limited HBM, this forces smaller batch sizes that reduce throughput gains.
details.napkin_math: Standard GPipe bubble: (p-1)/(m+p-1) = 7/(16+7) = 30.4%. Interleaved 1F1B with v=2: bubble ≈ (p-1)/(m×v+p-1) = 7/(32+7) = 17.9%. Reduction: 30.4% → 17.9% = 41% less bubble. Memory: standard stores m=16 micro-batch activations per stage; interleaved stores 2v × micro-batch activations = 4× more peak activations. MI300X 192 GB provides enough headroom for 70B model with v=2.
details.realistic_solution: Use interleaved 1F1B with v=2 virtual stages: each GPU holds 2 non-contiguous model chunks (layers 1-8 and layers 33-40, etc.). Bubble fraction reduces to (p-1)/(m×v+p-1) = 7/(32+7) = 17.9% vs 30% with standard GPipe. Memory overhead: 2× activation recomputation checkpoints per GPU. Combine with selective activation checkpointing for the v=2 chunks to stay within 192 GB MI300X HBM3.

scenario: You have a 64-layer GPT model split across 8 MI300X GPUs. Using the standard GPipe schedule with m=16 micro-batches gives a 30% bubble. A colleague suggests switching to an interleaved (1F1B) schedule. Design the interleaved schedule, explain the memory tradeoff, and calculate the new bubble fraction.
title: Interleaved Pipeline Schedule to Reduce Bubble

details.common_mistake: Assuming equal layer counts mean equal stage time. The LM head often has more parameters than a transformer layer (50K vocab × 4096 > typical FFN size) and a large softmax over 50K logits that is memory-bandwidth-bound. Teams split layers evenly and ignore the head.
details.napkin_math: Stage time ratio: Stage4/Stage1-3 = 1.35. Pipeline throughput is determined by the slowest stage. Current throughput = 1 / t_stage4. Ideal throughput = 1 / t_stage (balanced). Throughput loss = (t_stage4 - t_stage_balanced) / t_stage4 = (1.35 - 1.0) / 1.35 = 25.9% throughput loss. With 4 A100s at $10/hr each: 0.26 × 4 × $10 = $10.4/hr wasted due to imbalance.
details.realistic_solution: Move 2 transformer layers from Stage 4 to Stage 3 to compensate for the LM head overhead. New split: Stage 1: 13 layers, Stage 2: 13 layers, Stage 3: 14 layers, Stage 4: 8 layers + LM head. Profile Stage 4 time before and after to confirm balance. Alternatively, use pipeline schedule load balancing tools (e.g., Megatron-LM's automatic stage profiler).

scenario: You deploy a 48-layer transformer in a 4-stage pipeline on 4x A100 (80GB HBM2e). Stages 1-3 hold 12 layers each but Stage 4 holds the 12 final transformer layers PLUS the language model head (unembedding, 50K vocab × 4096 = 800M parameters in BF16 = 1.6 GB extra). Stage 4 takes 35% longer than Stages 1-3. Quantify the throughput loss and fix the imbalance.
title: Stage Imbalance in Heterogeneous Pipeline

details.common_mistake: Calculating activation memory for a single micro-batch and multiplying by global batch size rather than by the number of micro-batches in the pipeline at one time. In GPipe-style pipeline parallelism, all m micro-batches accumulate activations simultaneously in the forward pass before backprop begins.
details.napkin_math: Activation per token per layer: seq=2048, hidden=4096, BF16: 2048 × 4096 × 2 = 16 MB/layer. 40B model: ~80 layers / 4 stages = 20 layers/GPU. Activation per micro-batch: 20 layers × 16 MB × micro_batch_size = 320 MB × micro_batch_size. With 8 micro-batches: 2.56 GB × micro_batch_size ≤ 50 GB. Max micro_batch_size = 50 / 2.56 ≈ 19. Practical max: 16 (power of 2). With checkpointing: 50 GB / (2.56/3) ≈ 58 → micro_batch_size = 32.
details.realistic_solution: Activation memory per layer = seq_len × batch_size × hidden_dim × bytes. With 8 micro-batches in flight, total activation memory = 8 × (activation per micro-batch). Solve for max batch size given 50 GB free. Apply gradient checkpointing to reduce activation memory by ~3× at the cost of one extra forward pass.

scenario: You are setting up pipeline parallelism on 4 H100 (80GB HBM3) for a 40B parameter model in BF16. Model parameters alone consume 80 GB across 4 GPUs (20 GB/GPU). The optimizer states (Adam) add 2× parameters × 2 bytes = another 40 GB across 4 GPUs (10 GB/GPU). You have 50 GB free per GPU for activations. What is the maximum micro-batch size you can use with 8 micro-batches in flight?
title: Micro-batch Size Selection Under Memory Constraints

details.common_mistake: Using only pipeline parallelism for 1T parameter models. Pipeline parallelism alone on 1024 GPUs with 1T model: each GPU holds 1T / 1024 ≈ 1B params × 18 bytes (model + Adam) ≈ 18 GB. This seems fine, but ignores that activation memory scales with model width and the pipeline bubble would be enormous without tensor parallelism to split within-layer computation.
details.napkin_math: 1T params × 2 bytes BF16 = 2 TB total model. Per GPU (TP=8, PP=16): 2 TB / 128 = 15.6 GB. Adam optimizer (m,v in FP32): 1T × 8 bytes = 8 TB total → ZeRO-1 shards across DP=8: 1 TB/GPU → too large. Use ZeRO-3: shard across all 1024 GPUs: 8 TB / 1024 = 8 GB/GPU optimizer state. Total: 15.6 + 8 + ~15 GB activations = 38.6 GB. Well under 70 GB. Pipeline bubble with m=32, p=16: (15)/(47) = 31.9%.
details.realistic_solution: Use 3D parallelism: Tensor Parallelism (TP=8) within a node (NVLink bandwidth 900 GB/s), Pipeline Parallelism (PP=16) across nodes (IB bandwidth), Data Parallelism (DP=8) for global batch scaling. 8×16×8 = 1024 GPUs. Model sharding: 1T / (TP × PP) = 1T / 128 ≈ 7.8B params/GPU × 2 bytes = 15.6 GB. Optimizer states: 7.8B × 12 bytes = 93.6 GB — use ZeRO-1 to shard across DP=8 → 93.6/8 = 11.7 GB/GPU. Total: 15.6 + 11.7 + activations < 70 GB.

scenario: You need to train a 1 trillion parameter model on 1024 H100 GPUs (80GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 700W). Design the 3D parallelism strategy (data × tensor × pipeline) that maximizes training throughput while keeping each GPU's HBM usage under 70 GB. Justify every dimension of the parallelism factoring.
title: Combining Pipeline and Tensor Parallelism for 1T Parameter Model

details.common_mistake: Assuming the nightly batch pipeline reliably completes and writes to the online store before serving traffic resumes. Pipeline delays (compute cluster overload, schema changes) cause the online store to serve stale features without any freshness check or fallback.
details.napkin_math: 50K RPS × 0.8% stale = 400 stale feature requests/second. At 20ms SLO: each stale response risks model quality degradation (CTR drop estimated 2-5% from literature for stale recommendations). Revenue impact: 400 RPS × 2% CTR drop × $0.002/click × 86,400s/day = $1,382/day. Redis read latency: 0.1ms for a 200-feature hash get. At 50K RPS: 50K × 0.1ms = 5 Redis operations/ms → Redis at ~5,000 ops/ms needs 3-node cluster.
details.realistic_solution: Add feature freshness metadata: each feature row includes a `written_at` timestamp. The serving layer checks staleness on read; if stale > threshold, use feature defaults or a lightweight real-time fallback (e.g., category-level average from a fast lookup table). Add SLA alerts: page on-call if batch pipeline doesn't complete within 2h of its scheduled time. Implement materialization health checks before promoting new feature values.

scenario: Your recommendation model uses 200 features: 50 real-time user interaction features (updated every 5 seconds) and 150 batch-computed item features (updated nightly). You serve 50K requests/second with a 20ms SLO. The online store (Redis) holds real-time features. The offline store (Hive) computes batch features. You observe 0.8% of requests return stale batch features >24h old. Diagnose and fix.
title: Online vs Offline Feature Store Consistency Tradeoffs

details.common_mistake: Fetching all features in a sequential waterfall: user features from Redis, then item features from DynamoDB, then context features from a third store. Each round-trip adds 2-5ms latency. Three sequential fetches = 6-15ms baseline plus queuing.
