details.napkin_math: Sequential fetches: user (2ms) + item (3ms) + context (2ms) = 7ms base + 3× RTT overhead (1ms each) = 10ms p50. P99 with tail latency (3× p50 rule of thumb) = 30ms — way over budget. Parallel fan-out: max(2, 3, 2) = 3ms base + 1 RTT = 4ms p50, p99 ≈ 10ms. In-process cache hit for top-10K items: 0.05ms (L3 cache hit). Hit rate for top-10K items in a power-law distribution: ~80% of requests. Blended p99 = 0.8 × 0.05ms + 0.2 × 10ms = 2ms.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a feature fan-out architecture: issue all feature store reads in parallel using async I/O (e.g., asyncio in Python, or gRPC streaming). Colocate the most-accessed item features in the same Redis cluster as user features to avoid cross-store fetches. Cache the top-10K item features in process memory (LRU cache, ~100 MB for 10K items × 10KB each). This drops p99 from 18ms to under 4ms.

scenario: You serve a two-tower retrieval model on H100 with an end-to-end SLO of 50ms p99. The latency budget breaks down as: feature retrieval from store (target: 5ms p99), embedding lookup (target: 10ms), ANN search over 100M items (target: 25ms), ranking (target: 5ms), and response serialization (target: 5ms). Your feature store is currently at p99=18ms. Redesign the feature retrieval layer.
title: Feature Serving Latency Budget for Two-Tower Models

details.common_mistake: Assuming that 'same feature logic' means 'same feature values.' Batch pipelines and streaming pipelines handle late-arriving events, watermarks, and session boundaries differently. A 1-hour window ending at 12:00 in batch might include events up to 12:05 (due to 5-minute late-data buffer), while the streaming window strictly cuts at 12:00.
details.napkin_math: 8% AUC drop: significant for ad ranking. If baseline AUC=0.78, new AUC=0.718. Typical business impact: 1% AUC drop ≈ 1-2% revenue impact (from industry benchmarks). 8% AUC drop ≈ 8-16% revenue impact. Shadow logging overhead: if 1% of traffic is sampled, 50K RPS × 0.01 × 200 features × 4 bytes = 400 MB/s to a logging Kafka topic — manageable. Analysis: compare P(feature_train) vs P(feature_serve) using KS-test, flag features with KS statistic > 0.05.
details.realistic_solution: Log both training-time feature values and serving-time feature values for the same user-item pairs over a 48-hour shadow period. Compute feature distribution statistics (mean, p50, p99, Jensen-Shannon divergence) between training and serving distributions. Key fixes: (1) align watermark settings between Spark and Flink, (2) use point-in-time joins in training to match exactly the features available at serving time, (3) validate with a feature monitoring dashboard.

scenario: Your ad ranking model was trained on features computed from a Spark batch pipeline using a 1-hour aggregation window for user activity counts. In serving, the feature store computes the same aggregation over a rolling 1-hour window using a streaming Flink pipeline. Model performance in production is 8% lower AUC than offline evaluation. You suspect training-serving skew. How do you confirm and fix it?
title: Feature Skew Between Training and Serving

details.common_mistake: Applying a uniform freshness requirement to all features. Using a 1-hour refresh for real-time transaction features defeats the purpose (fraud can happen in seconds); refreshing monthly risk scores every 5 seconds wastes compute and adds no value.
details.napkin_math: Real-time feature write throughput: 50K transactions/second × 5 features × 100 bytes = 25 MB/s to Redis. Redis write throughput: ~1M ops/sec per node at 100 bytes each = 100 MB/s. Need 1 Redis node for writes. Hourly feature recompute: 100M users × 20 features × 4 bytes = 8 GB materialization. Spark at 10 GB/s: 0.8 seconds to compute + 8 GB / 1 GB/s Redis write = 8 seconds per micro-batch. Achievable in 15-minute window.
details.realistic_solution: Freshness tiers: (1) Real-time features: freshness SLA < 5 seconds, use event-driven streaming writes to Redis (Kafka → Flink → Redis). (2) Hourly features: freshness SLA < 15 minutes, compute with micro-batch Spark every 15 min, write to Redis. (3) Monthly features: freshness SLA < 2 hours, nightly batch with alerting if pipeline misses. Enforce via freshness metadata and serving-layer staleness checks that degrade gracefully.

scenario: You are designing feature freshness SLAs for a fraud detection model on H100-backed serving infrastructure. The model uses three feature types: (1) real-time transaction features (last 5 transactions, updated per event), (2) hourly aggregated spending patterns, (3) monthly user risk scores. Describe the appropriate freshness requirement for each and how to enforce it in the feature store.
title: Feature Store Freshness SLAs for Time-Sensitive Models

details.common_mistake: Adding new features directly to the existing feature namespace, causing the old model to receive unexpected feature keys and potentially crashing. Or maintaining two completely separate Redis clusters for old and new features, doubling operational overhead.
details.napkin_math: Dual feature storage overhead: 3 new features × 100M users × 8 bytes/feature = 2.4 GB additional Redis memory. Total feature store with versioning: existing ~50 GB + 2.4 GB = 52.4 GB. Redis instance size: r6g.4xlarge (128 GB RAM) has headroom. Serving overhead: feature server must check model version per request (1 µs lookup from in-process hash map). At 50K RPS: 50 ms/request of version routing = 50K × 0.001ms = 50ms total, negligible.
details.realistic_solution: Use namespaced feature keys: prefix new features with model version (e.g., `v2:user_embedding_dim512` vs `v1:user_embedding_dim256`). Store both in the same Redis cluster, served by the feature server which routes based on the model version tag in the request context. After 100% rollout, run a TTL-based cleanup job to expire v1 features. Maintain a feature registry (e.g., Feast or Tecton) as the source of truth for feature-model compatibility.

scenario: You are rolling out a new version of your recommendation model that requires 3 new features not present in the current online feature store. The rollout will be gradual (1% → 10% → 100% over 3 days). Old model must keep running for the 99% not yet migrated. Design a feature versioning strategy that supports concurrent model versions without breaking either.
title: Feature Store Versioning for Safe Model Rollouts

details.common_mistake: Assuming speculative decoding always speeds up generation. If the draft model's acceptance rate α is too low, each speculative step generates k=5 draft tokens that are mostly rejected, requiring the target model to run k+1 times instead of 1 time — making latency worse than greedy decoding.
details.napkin_math: Expected tokens accepted per speculative step: E[accepted] = (1 - α^(k+1)) / (1 - α) for geometric rejection. With α=0.8, k=4: E[accepted] = (1 - 0.8^5) / (1 - 0.8) = (1 - 0.328) / 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per target model call. Speedup = E[accepted] / 1 = 3.36×. Latency: target model call = 45ms. Speedup: 45ms / 3.36 = 13.4ms per token (effective). Draft model (7B on H100): ~4ms for 4 draft tokens. Net latency = 4ms + 45ms = 49ms per step, producing 3.36 tokens → 14.6ms/token vs 45ms/token = 3.1× speedup.
details.realistic_solution: Choose the draft model to maximize acceptance rate: the 7B model should be fine-tuned on the same data distribution as queries. Target α ≥ 0.8 for k=4 draft tokens to achieve 2-3× speedup. If α < 0.6, reduce k to 2. Profile acceptance rate per query type: factual queries tend to have α > 0.85, creative writing α < 0.6. Use adaptive k: dynamically adjust based on recent rolling acceptance rate.

scenario: You serve a 70B LLaMA-2 model (target model) on 4x H100 80GB (tensor parallel, 3.35 TB/s HBM3). Single-token decode latency is 45ms. You want to use speculative decoding with a 7B draft model to reduce TTFT and per-token latency. The 7B draft fits on 1 H100. Analyze the expected speedup, acceptance rate requirements, and memory tradeoffs.
title: Speculative Decoding Draft Model Selection for 70B LLM

details.common_mistake: Using static partitioning: reserve 64 GPUs permanently for inference, 192 for training. Overnight, inference uses 13 of 64 reserved GPUs (20% of 64) while 51 sit idle; training cannot use them. This wastes 51 × 192 GB × 12h/night = massive idle HBM3 capacity.
details.napkin_math: Daytime: inference uses 60% × 256 = 154 GPUs. Training gets 102 GPUs. Overnight: inference uses 20% × 256 = 52 GPUs. Training gets 204 GPUs — 2× more throughput overnight. Annual GPU utilization improvement: (daytime_waste_static + overnight_waste_static) vs elastic: static inference reserve = 64 GPUs always reserved; overnight waste = 51 GPUs × 12h × 365 = 223,380 GPU-hours/year. At $3/GPU-hour: $670K/year recovered by elastic scheduling.
details.realistic_solution: Implement elastic resource partitioning with a priority preemption ladder. Inference has preemptive priority over training. Training jobs are classified as elastic: they register with a minimum (8 GPU) and maximum (256 GPU) allocation. The scheduler expands training during low-inference periods and preempts training GPUs within 30 seconds (one checkpoint interval) when inference load rises. Use DCGM metrics to predict inference demand 5 minutes ahead and begin graceful training preemption early.

scenario: Your organization runs both latency-sensitive inference (SLO: p99 < 100ms) and throughput-optimized training on a shared 256-GPU MI300X (192GB HBM3) cluster. Inference load follows a bimodal pattern: 60% daytime utilization, 20% overnight. Training jobs have elastic GPU requirements (can run on 8-256 GPUs). Design a unified scheduling policy that maximizes training throughput during low-inference periods without violating inference SLOs during peaks.
title: Priority-Based GPU Scheduling for Mixed Training and Inference

details.common_mistake: Assuming large GEMMs are always compute-bound without checking arithmetic intensity against the ridge point.
details.napkin_math: Ridge point: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOPs/byte. This GEMM AI ≈ 1,820 FLOPs/byte > 295, so compute-bound. Theoretical max = 989 TFLOPS, achieved = 412 TFLOPS → 41.7% efficiency.
details.realistic_solution: Arithmetic intensity = 2*M*K*N FLOPs / bytes = 2*4096*4096*16384 / ((4096*4096 + 4096*16384 + 4096*16384)*2) ≈ 2*274B / (134M + 537M + 537M)*2 ≈ 550B / 302MB ≈ 1,820 FLOPs/byte. Ridge point = 989e12/3.35e12 ≈ 295 FLOPs/byte. This GEMM is compute-bound. Gap = 989-412 = 577 TFLOPS, 58% efficiency loss — investigate tensor core utilization and tile sizing.

scenario: You're profiling a GPT-4 style MLP block on an H100 SXM5. The GEMM has M=4096, K=4096, N=16384 (FFN expansion). H100 peaks at 989 TFLOPS BF16 and 3.35 TB/s HBM3 bandwidth. You observe 412 TFLOPS measured throughput. Determine whether you're compute- or memory-bound and quantify the gap.
title: Roofline Ceiling Identification on H100 for Transformer MLP Blocks

details.common_mistake: Treating the full attention operation as one GEMM without accounting for the softmax and bandwidth cost of materializing the attention matrix.
details.napkin_math: Ridge point = 312/2 = 156 FLOPs/byte. QK^T AI ≈ 119 FLOPs/byte < 156 → memory-bound. FlashAttention fuses ops, boosts AI by ~4x, moves to compute-bound regime.
details.realistic_solution: For QK^T: ops = 2*32*2048*2048*128 = 34.4B FLOPs. Memory = 32*(2048*128 + 2048*128 + 2048*2048)*2 bytes ≈ 32*(0.5MB + 0.5MB + 8MB) = 288MB. AI = 34.4B/288MB ≈ 119 FLOPs/byte. Ridge point = 312e12/2e12 = 156 FLOPs/byte. AI < ridge point → memory-bound. Use FlashAttention to avoid materializing the attention matrix and improve AI to ~500 FLOPs/byte.

scenario: A team runs multi-head attention with sequence length 2048, 32 heads, head_dim=128 on A100 80GB. The QK^T matmul produces a 2048×2048 attention matrix per head. A100 has 312 TFLOPS BF16 and 2 TB/s HBM2e bandwidth. The observed throughput is 45 TFLOPS. Classify the bottleneck.
title: Memory-Bound vs Compute-Bound Classification for Attention on A100

details.common_mistake: Assuming FlashAttention eliminates all HBM reads/writes; it eliminates the attention matrix materialization but still reads Q, K, V once each.
details.napkin_math: Standard: 12.8GB attn matrix × 2 (write+read) + 1.2GB QKV = ~26.8GB. FlashAttention: ~804MB. Speedup from bandwidth reduction alone: 26.8/0.804 = 33×. At 3.35 TB/s: 8ms → 0.24ms.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention HBM reads: Q+K+V = 3×96×8192×128×2 = 603MB. HBM writes: attention matrix = 96×8192×8192×2 = 12.8GB. Total standard = 603MB read + 12.8GB write + 12.8GB read (for softmax) + 603MB write (output) ≈ 26.8GB. FlashAttention: Q+K+V reads = 603MB, O write = 201MB. Total ≈ 804MB — 33× less HBM traffic. At 3.35 TB/s, standard attention memory time = 26.8GB/3.35TB/s = 8ms; FlashAttention = 804MB/3.35TB/s = 0.24ms.

scenario: You're implementing FlashAttention-2 for a 70B LLM with 96 heads, head_dim=128, seq_len=8192. H100 has 80MB L2 cache and 50MB SRAM across all SMs. Standard attention would materialize a 96×8192×8192 float16 attention matrix (12.8GB). Calculate the memory savings and bandwidth improvement from FlashAttention tiling.
title: Flash Attention Arithmetic Intensity Analysis on H100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that reducing KV heads also reduces the bandwidth needed to load the KV cache per token, directly improving decode throughput.
details.napkin_math: MHA KV cache: 2×64 heads×4096×128×2B×80 layers = 10.7GB/seq × 32 = 341GB — doesn't fit. GQA-8: divide by 8 = 1.34GB/seq × 32 = 42.9GB — fits H100. Decode BW savings: 8× fewer KV bytes loaded per token.
details.realistic_solution: MHA KV per layer = 2×64×4096×128×2 = 134MB. Total 80 layers = 10.7GB per sequence. Batch 32 = 341GB — far exceeds 80GB. MQA (1 KV head) = 2×1×4096×128×2×80 = 167MB per sequence, 5.3GB for batch 32. GQA-8 = 2×8×4096×128×2×80 = 1.3GB per sequence, 42GB for batch 32 — fits in 80GB. Decode bandwidth: MHA = 134MB/layer load; GQA-8 = 16.8MB/layer. GQA-8 achieves ~8× better decode bandwidth utilization vs MHA.

scenario: A production LLM service runs a 70B model with 64 attention heads (head_dim=128) serving batch_size=32 at 4096 context. Standard MHA KV cache consumes 64×2×4096×128×2 bytes per layer × 80 layers. Compare memory footprint vs throughput for MHA, MQA, and GQA with 8 groups on H100 80GB.
title: Multi-Query vs Multi-Head Attention KV Cache Trade-off

details.common_mistake: Applying per-channel quantization to activations as well as weights; activation per-channel scaling is not hardware-friendly because scale factors must be applied dynamically.
details.napkin_math: Per-tensor quantization overhead: 1 scale/tensor ≈ negligible. Per-channel weight: 32K scales × 4B = 128KB overhead on 13B model (26GB FP16) = 0.0005% overhead. PPL gain: typically 1-2 points improvement. SmoothQuant: maintains INT8 hardware path while absorbing activation outliers.
details.realistic_solution: Per-tensor INT8: single scale per tensor, fully hardware-efficient, but suffers from outlier channels in LLM activations. Per-channel weights: one scale per output channel (13B model has ~32K channels across all layers), adds 32K×4B = 128KB overhead — negligible. Expected perplexity improvement: per-channel weight quantization typically reduces error by 1-2 PPL points. For activations, use SmoothQuant to migrate quantization difficulty from activations to weights via per-channel scaling of the weight matrix, maintaining hardware INT8 throughput.

scenario: You're quantizing a 13B parameter LLaMA model to INT8 for deployment on H100. Using post-training quantization (PTQ) with per-tensor scaling, you observe 3.2% perplexity degradation on WikiText-2. The team proposes per-channel weight quantization. Analyze the trade-off between calibration granularity and hardware efficiency.
title: INT8 Quantization Calibration Strategy for LLM Inference on H100

details.common_mistake: Using E4M3 for gradient accumulation; E4M3 has only 3 mantissa bits and limited exponent range (±448) which causes gradient underflow during backward pass.
details.napkin_math: E4M3 max value: 448. E5M2 max value: 57344. Gradient dynamic range 1e-7 to 1e3: E4M3 saturates at 448 (ok for weights), E5M2 handles range up to 57344 (ok for gradients). Memory: FP8 training ≈ 56GB for 7B vs 112GB for BF16.
details.realistic_solution: E4M3 (4-bit exp, 3-bit mantissa): range ±448, useful for weights and activations in forward pass. E5M2 (5-bit exp, 2-bit mantissa): range ±57344, better for gradients. Recommended: forward pass uses E4M3 for QKV and FFN weights, E5M2 for activations. Backward pass uses E5M2 for gradients. Master weights kept in FP32. The dynamic loss scaling used in FP16 training is still needed for FP8 gradient accumulation. With proper format selection: ~2× memory vs FP16 training = same as INT8 but with gradient stability.

scenario: H100 supports FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) at 3,958 TFLOPS and INT8 at 3,958 TOPS for matrix operations. A team is training a 7B transformer and wants to use FP8 mixed precision. The model has weight gradients with dynamic range spanning 1e-7 to 1e3. Compare FP8 E4M3 vs E5M2 for forward vs backward passes.
title: FP8 vs INT8 Quantization Throughput on H100 for Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming weights stay in L2 cache between tokens during decode; the 402MB weight matrix is 5× larger than 80MB L2, so it must be streamed from HBM every token.
details.napkin_math: QKV weight: 402MB. MLP weights: 1.07GB. Per layer: 1.47GB. 80 layers = 118GB. At 3.35 TB/s: 35ms/token, 28 tok/s. Batch=8: same weight load, 8 tokens output → 228 tok/s effective throughput.
details.realistic_solution: QKV weight matrix: 3×8192×8192×2B = 402MB >> 80MB L2. Cache miss rate near 100% for weight access. Each token decode must stream 402MB from HBM. At 3.35 TB/s: 402MB/3.35TB/s = 0.12ms for QKV alone. Full layer (add MLP 2×8192×32768×2B = 1.07GB): total ≈ 1.47GB per layer. For 80-layer model: 80 × 1.47GB = 118GB per token decode. At 3.35 TB/s: 35ms/token ≈ 28 tok/s — memory bound. Key insight: model weights must be kept in HBM for large models; increasing batch size amortizes weight loading cost.

scenario: An H100 has 80MB L2 cache and 3.35 TB/s HBM3. During LLM inference at batch_size=1, the attention QKV projection for a layer with d_model=8192 requires loading weights of shape [8192, 3×8192] = 3×8192²×2 bytes = 402MB. Determine the caching behavior and per-token latency.
title: HBM3 vs L2 Cache Access Patterns for Transformer Weights on H100

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that 2×H100 tensor parallelism introduces NVLink communication overhead that may reduce throughput below the single MI300X despite having the same total memory.
details.napkin_math: MI300X: 140GB/5.3TB/s = 26.4ms = 37.9 tok/s. 2×H100: 140GB/6.7TB/s = 20.9ms = 47.8 tok/s. NVLink overhead per token: 32KB/900GB/s × 80 layers = 2.8μs — negligible. 2×H100 wins on throughput.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X single: 140GB model fits in 192GB (52GB remaining for KV cache). Decode throughput: 140GB / 5.3 TB/s = 26.4ms/token = 37.9 tok/s. No communication overhead. 2×H100 tensor parallel: each holds 70GB. Compute: 2×989 TFLOPS = 1978 TFLOPS. NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s. Per-layer all-reduce: 2×d_model×2B = 2×8192×2B = 32KB. At 900 GB/s: 35ns overhead per layer — negligible. Memory BW: 2×3.35 TB/s = 6.7 TB/s. 2×H100 decode: 140GB/6.7TB/s = 20.9ms = 47.8 tok/s. Winner: 2×H100 at 47.8 tok/s vs MI300X at 37.9 tok/s, despite single-device simplicity of MI300X.

scenario: AMD MI300X offers 192GB HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s — the largest GPU memory available. A team wants to run a 70B parameter model (140GB at FP16) on a single MI300X without tensor parallelism. Analyze whether this is viable and calculate expected decode throughput vs 2×H100s with tensor parallelism.
title: MI300X Unified Memory Architecture for Large Model Inference

details.common_mistake: Assuming continuous batching always improves throughput; with highly variable sequence lengths it does, but with uniform lengths it adds scheduling overhead without benefit.
details.napkin_math: Static efficiency: avg 500 tokens / 2048 max = 24% slot utilization. Continuous batching: ~90% utilization. Throughput gain: 0.90/0.24 × (1 - 0.03 overhead) = 3.6× potential, but GPU utilization was only 40% → realistic gain: 2× throughput improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Static batching: worst case is 2048 tokens for a batch where 7/8 requests finish at 500 tokens but wait for the longest. Wasted compute: 7 × (2048-500) × per_token_cost = 7 × 1548 × cost. Efficiency = 500/2048 = 24% for short requests. Continuous batching: as each request completes, a new request fills that slot immediately. Expected batch occupancy improves from 40% to ~85-95%. Throughput improvement: 2.1-2.4×. Additional benefit: P50 latency drops significantly (short requests no longer wait for long ones). Implementation cost: more complex scheduler, ~2-5% overhead.

scenario: An H100 serves Llama-2-70B with static batching (batch_size=8, max_tokens=2048). GPU utilization averages 40% because shorter requests (avg 500 tokens) leave slots idle waiting for the batch to complete. Continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling) is proposed. Estimate throughput improvement.
title: Continuous Batching vs Static Batching Throughput on H100 for LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Treating prefill as linearly scaling with batch size; prefill is compute-bound (unlike decode which is memory-bound), so it scales efficiently up to the compute limit.
details.napkin_math: Prefill FLOPs: 2×1024×1024×8192×80 layers ≈ 1.37T FLOPs. A100: 312 TFLOPS. Saturate at: 312T / 1.37T ≈ 228 seq in parallel (i.e., very high batch before compute saturation). But KV memory limits: 1024×8192×2×2B×80 = 2.1GB per seq → 80GB/2.1GB = 38 sequences max. Compute-bound at batch ≥ 28.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill at batch=1: 50ms for 1024 tokens. Prefill is compute-bound (high arithmetic intensity from QK^T over full sequence). Batch scaling: compute increases linearly but GPU utilization also increases → roughly constant 50ms until compute-saturated. A100 at batch=1: likely underutilized. Saturation batch size: A100 compute budget / prefill FLOPs per sequence (1.37 TFLOPs at seq=1024). At batch=4-6, A100 likely saturates. Above saturation, TTFT = N×50ms/batch = queue wait time increases. SLA 300ms: TTFT = queue_wait + prefill_time. Max queue: 300ms - 50ms = 250ms. If prefill saturates at batch=6: throughput = 6/50ms = 120 prefills/sec. Queue wait at 100 req/s: 100/120 = 83% utilization → avg wait = 50ms/(1-0.83) ≈ 294ms. Close to limit.

scenario: An A100 80GB serves a chatbot with SLA of 300ms TTFT (time to first token). Prefill of a 1024-token prompt takes 50ms at batch_size=1. The team wants to batch prefill operations to improve GPU utilization. At what batch size does TTFT SLA become violated?
title: Prefill Batch Sizing for TTFT Optimization on A100

details.common_mistake: Summing only GPU power without including NVLink switches, CPU/DRAM, networking, and storage power consumption in the rack total.
details.napkin_math: 8 H100s: 5.44kW. Supporting HW: ~1.83kW. Total: 7.27kW / 40kW = 18% rack utilization. Adding 9th GPU (1.7kW server): 8.97kW / 40kW = 22.4%. Plenty of headroom — cooling not the constraint.
details.realistic_solution: 8 H100s: 8 × 680W = 5,440W. NVSwitch: ~300W for 4-switch config. 2× CPU servers: ~600W each = 1,200W. DRAM: 12 DIMMs × 15W = 180W. NIC (400GbE): ~100W. Storage NVMe: ~50W. Total rack: 5,440 + 300 + 1,200 + 180 + 100 + 50 = 7,270W. Rack budget: 40,000W. Current: 7,270W. Available: 32,730W. Can add 9th GPU (700W). Actually, standard DGX H100 is 1 server with 8 GPUs at ~10.2kW — entire server fits easily. But: additional GPU in separate 1U server adds ~1kW overhead → 8,270W total. Well within 40kW rack budget.

scenario: An H100 SXM5 has 700W TDP. During distributed training of a 70B model, GPU power monitors show sustained 680W draw. The data center cooling system is rated for 40kW per rack (8 GPUs). Calculate the rack-level thermal headroom and determine if you can add a 9th GPU.
title: H100 TDP Management Under Sustained Training Load

details.common_mistake: Applying the cubic power-frequency relationship directly without accounting for static power (leakage), which doesn't scale with frequency and represents ~15-20% of total GPU power.
details.napkin_math: Static power: 80W. Dynamic: 320W → target 220W. Frequency ratio: (220/320)^(1/3) = 0.883. Throughput: 312 × 0.883 = 275 TFLOPS. Trade-off: -25% power, -11.7% throughput, +17.5% perf/watt.
details.realistic_solution: Dynamic power ≈ 80% of total = 320W. Static power = 80W. Target: 300W total. Remaining dynamic: 300-80 = 220W. Dynamic power reduction: 220/320 = 0.688. P_dyn ∝ f³ → f_new/f_old = (0.688)^(1/3) = 0.883. New frequency: 1.41 × 0.883 = 1.245 GHz. Throughput reduction: ~11.7% (approximately linear with frequency for compute-bound tasks). H100 equivalent: 312 TFLOPS × 0.883 = 275 TFLOPS. Power: 300W vs 400W = 25% power reduction for 11.7% throughput loss. Performance-per-watt improves: (275/300) / (312/400) = 0.917 / 0.78 = 17.5% better.

scenario: An A100 runs at 1.41GHz base clock consuming 400W. A cloud operator proposes power-capping at 300W (75%) to fit denser server configurations. Using the cubic relationship between frequency and power (P ∝ f³), estimate the frequency reduction and throughput impact.
title: Power vs Performance Trade-off with GPU Frequency Scaling on A100

details.common_mistake: Using total NVLink bandwidth (450 GB/s) instead of per-link bandwidth in ring topology; in a ring, each step uses only the link to one neighbor.
details.napkin_math: Ring all-reduce: 2×(7/8)×52GB / 225 GB/s = 404ms. Backward pass: ~200ms. Ratio: 404/200 = 2× — communication dominates. With gradient compression (FP16 gradients, 26GB): 202ms — matches backward. Overlap requires careful bucketing.
details.realistic_solution: Ring all-reduce formula: time = 2 × (N-1)/N × data_size / bandwidth_per_link. N=8 GPUs, data=52GB, NVLink per-link: 450 GB/s / 2 (full duplex) = 225 GB/s per direction. Time = 2 × 7/8 × 52GB / 225 GB/s = 2 × 0.875 × 52/225 = 0.404s = 404ms. Typical backward pass: 13B model, batch=8, seq=2048 at BF16: ~200ms. All-reduce takes 2× longer than backward — communication is the bottleneck. Solution: gradient bucketing + overlap, or use tensor parallelism to reduce gradient volume.

scenario: 8 H100 GPUs are connected via NVLink 4.0 (450 GB/s bidirectional per GPU) in a DGX H100. During data-parallel training of a 13B model, gradients (13B parameters × 4 bytes = 52GB in FP32) must be all-reduced after each backward pass. Calculate the ring all-reduce time and determine if communication overlaps with computation.
title: AllReduce Bandwidth Requirement for Ring All-Reduce on 8×H100

details.common_mistake: Applying ZeRO sharding across all 16 GPUs when pipeline parallelism requires adjacent pipeline stages to share full parameter copies; ZeRO should shard only within the DP dimension.
details.napkin_math: ZeRO-1 DP all-reduce: 8.75B×4B/2 = 17.5GB at 450 GB/s = 39ms × 2 GPUs = 78ms/step. ZeRO-3 AllGather+RS per micro-batch per stage: 64 × 8.75GB/450 GB/s = 1.24s. ZeRO-1 much better for pipeline parallelism.
details.realistic_solution: Hybrid setup: 8-stage PP × 2-way DP = 16 GPUs. Each PP stage holds ~70B/8 = 8.75B params. ZeRO-1 within DP groups (2 GPUs): optimizer state sharded 2×. FP32 optimizer: 8.75B × 12B = 105GB per stage → sharded = 52.5GB per GPU. AllGather at update: 52.5GB at 450 GB/s = 116ms. ZeRO-3 within DP groups: params also sharded. Each PP stage needs AllGather before forward, ReduceScatter after backward = 2 collectives per stage per micro-batch. With 8 pipeline stages and 4 micro-batches: 8×4×2 = 64 collectives. Each: 8.75B×2B/2 = 8.75GB at 450 GB/s = 19.4ms. Total: 64 × 19.4ms = 1.24s additional communication per batch vs ZeRO-1 adding ~232ms.

scenario: A 16-GPU H100 cluster uses pipeline parallelism (8 pipeline stages) plus data parallelism (2-way DP). Micro-batch size is 4. Compare the communication pattern for ZeRO-1 (shard optimizer states) vs ZeRO-3 (shard all: optimizer, gradients, parameters) for a 70B model in this hybrid parallelism setup.
title: ReduceScatter vs AllReduce for Pipeline Parallelism on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Calculating AllToAll as if all tokens go to all chips; in expert parallelism, each chip sends/receives only its portion of tokens to/from chips hosting the routed experts.
details.napkin_math: Tokens: 512×2048 = 1M. Top-2 routing: 2M dispatches. Per chip: 31,250 tokens × 2KB = 62.5MB. ICI per chip: 62.5 GB/s. Latency: 62.5MB / 62.5 GB/s = 1ms AllToAll. Expert compute: 31,250 tokens × FFN FLOPs / 197 TOPS ≈ comparable → pipeline AllToAll with compute.
details.realistic_solution: Tokens per batch: 512 × 2048 = 1M tokens. Top-2 routing: each token goes to 2 experts. Token size: 1024 dims × 2B = 2KB. AllToAll: each of 64 chips sends/receives 1M/64 = 15,625 tokens per expert chip. But with top-2 routing: 2M token-dispatches total / 64 chips = 31,250 per chip. AllToAll volume per chip: 31,250 × 2KB = 62.5MB sent + 62.5MB received = 125MB per chip. Total network: 64 × 62.5MB = 4GB. At 4 TB/s aggregate ICI: 4GB / 4TB/s = 1ms. Per-chip bandwidth: 4TB/s/64 = 62.5 GB/s per chip. 62.5MB / 62.5 GB/s = 1ms — bandwidth bound.

scenario: TPU v5e pods have 256 chips connected via ICI at ~4 TB/s aggregate. A Mixture-of-Experts model routes tokens to 8 active experts out of 64 total across 64 TPU chips. Each token dispatch requires an AllToAll collective. For batch=512 with seq_len=2048, token_dim=1024 (BF16), calculate AllToAll volume and latency.
title: AllToAll Communication for Expert Parallelism in MoE on TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Assuming speculative decoding improves throughput by k× (5× in this case); the actual improvement depends on acceptance rate and the relative cost of the draft model.
details.napkin_math: E[tokens/cycle] = (1-α^(k+1))/(1-α) = (1-0.8^6)/0.2 = (1-0.262)/0.2 = 3.69 tokens accepted + 1 = 4.69. Draft cost: ~30% of target. Effective speedup: 4.69 / (1 + 0.3×5) = 4.69/2.5 = 1.88×. Target alone: 30 tok/s → spec decode: ~56 tok/s.
details.realistic_solution: Expected tokens per speculative step: E[accepted] = k×α + 1 = 5×0.8 + 1 = 5 tokens per draft-verify cycle (on average, before the first rejection, E[consecutive accepts] = (1-α^k)/(1-α) = (1-0.32)/(0.2) = 3.4, plus 1 final = 4.4 tokens but simplified formula gives ~5). Time per cycle: draft 5 tokens + 1 target verification. Draft (7B, 5 tokens): 5 × (7B×2B/3.35TB/s) = 5 × 4.2ms = 21ms. Target verify (70B, 1 forward): 21ms. Total: 42ms for ~4.4 tokens. Speedup: 4.4 tokens / 1 token per target step × target_step_time / cycle_time = 4.4 × (30 tok/s × 42ms) / 1 = 4.4 × 1.26 ≈ 5.5× — but draft overhead reduces to ~2.5× in practice.

scenario: You implement speculative decoding on H100 with a 70B target model and a 7B draft model. The draft model generates k=5 candidate tokens. Target model verifies in one forward pass. Draft acceptance rate α=0.8. Target model alone generates 30 tok/s. Calculate the expected throughput improvement.
title: Speculative Decoding Acceptance Rate Impact on H100 Inference Throughput

details.common_mistake: Calculating KV cache per sequence using only the model's context length without accounting for the number of layers and head dimensions.
details.napkin_math: KV per token: 2×40 layers×40 heads×128 dim×2B = 819KB. Contiguous (35% frag): 54GB×0.65/819KB/token = 42.8K tokens in flight. Paged (4% frag): 54GB×0.96/819KB = 63.3K tokens. Gain: 63.3/42.8 = 1.48×. Batch size increases proportionally.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token: 2 (K+V) × 40 layers × 20 heads × 128 head_dim × 2B = 2×40×20×128×2 = 409.6KB wait — recalculate: per token per layer = 2×n_heads×head_dim×2B = 2×40×128×2 = 20.5KB. Per token all layers = 20.5KB × 40 = ... let me use: 13B has 40 layers, 40 heads, head_dim=128. Per token: 2×40×40×128×2B = 819.2KB/40 = 20.48KB × 40 layers total = 819KB/token across all layers. Wait: per token = 2 (KV) × n_layers × n_heads × head_dim × dtype = 2×40×40×128×2 = 819,200 bytes ≈ 819KB. Available for KV: 54GB. Contiguous (35% frag): usable = 54×0.65 = 35.1GB. Sequences: 35.1GB / (819KB × avg_len). At avg 1000 tokens: 35.1GB/819MB = 42 sequences. PagedAttention (4% frag): 54×0.96 = 51.8GB → 63 sequences. Throughput: 63/42 = 1.5× improvement.

scenario: A vLLM deployment on H100 80GB serves a 13B model (26GB) leaving 54GB for KV cache. With standard contiguous KV allocation, average memory fragmentation is 35% (sequences reserved max_length but use avg 40% of tokens). With PagedAttention (16-token pages), fragmentation drops to <4%. Calculate the throughput improvement from increased effective batch size.
title: PagedAttention Memory Fragmentation Reduction for H100 LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Expecting throughput to scale linearly with parameter reduction; for decode-phase inference (memory-bandwidth bound), throughput scales with memory reduction, not compute reduction.
details.napkin_math: Original: 140GB. Pruned MLP 30%: 37.5B×0.3×2B = 22.5GB saved → 117.5GB. Decode: 117.5GB/5.3TB/s = 22.2ms = 45 tok/s. Speedup: 45/37.9 = 1.19×. Memory bandwidth bound — speedup proportional to model size reduction.
details.realistic_solution: Original MLP per layer: 2 × d_model × intermediate = 2 × 8192 × 28672 = 469M params. 80 layers: 80 × 469M = 37.5B MLP params. Non-MLP (attention QKV, O): remaining ~32.5B. Total: 70B. After 30% MLP pruning: MLP = 37.5B × 0.7 = 26.3B. Total model: 26.3B + 32.5B = 58.8B params. Memory: 58.8B × 2B (BF16) = 117.6GB (vs 140GB). At 5.3 TB/s: decode latency = 117.6GB/5.3TB/s = 22.2ms/token = 45 tok/s vs original 37.9 tok/s. Improvement: 18.7%. Note: accuracy impact requires 2-5 PPL points recovery via fine-tuning.

scenario: A team applies structured pruning to a 70B LLM (80 layers, MLP intermediate_size=28,672 per layer) targeting 30% weight reduction. They prune 30% of neurons from each MLP layer on MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s). Calculate the parameter reduction, memory savings, and expected throughput improvement for decode-phase inference.
title: Structured Pruning 50% of MLP Layers in 70B LLM — MI300X Impact

details.common_mistake: Assuming thermal throttling is binary (full speed or shutdown); modern GPUs gradually reduce clock speed in proportion to temperature excess, and frequency-throughput relationship is approximately linear for memory-bandwidth-bound workloads.
details.napkin_math: Clock: 1.41→1.19 GHz = -15.6%. Compute BW also scales. Throughput: -15.6% for 2 hours. Additional time: 2h × 0.156 = 0.31h. Recovery: 3 minutes. Net impact: ~20 minutes lost training time. For 72h job, 0.5% impact — monitor but not critical.
details.realistic_solution: Frequency drop: 1.41GHz → 1.19GHz = 15.6% reduction. For compute-bound training (large GEMM): throughput ≈ proportional to frequency. Throughput loss: 15.6%. Training slows by 15.6% for the remaining 24 hours. Additional cost: 24h × 15.6% = 3.74 extra hours to complete same work. Recovery: HVAC repair estimated 2 hours. After repair, GPU cools at ~2°C/minute → 5°C drop takes ~2.5 minutes for junction. Full clock restored after ~3 minutes. Training hour 49+2.1 hours: back to normal. Net delay: 2.1h at 15.6% slowdown + thermal recovery ramp = ~2.1h × 15.6% = 0.33h extra total job time.

scenario: During a 72-hour training run on H100 SXM5 (700W TDP, junction temperature limit 83°C), GPU temperature stabilizes at 78°C for the first 48 hours. On hour 49, ambient temperature in the datacenter rises 5°C due to HVAC partial failure. The GPU begins thermal throttling, dropping from 1.41GHz to 1.19GHz. Quantify the throughput impact and estimate recovery time.
title: Thermal Throttling During Long-Context Training on H100

details.common_mistake: Conflating the compute-optimal training job (minimize loss for a fixed compute budget) with the inference-optimal model (minimize inference cost for a target accuracy).
details.napkin_math: FLOPs: 6×50B×1T = 300 ZFLOPs = 3×10^23. Cluster: 1024×312e12×0.5 = 1.6×10^17 FLOPS. Time: 3×10^23 / 1.6×10^17 = 1.875×10^6s = 21.7 days. Model memory (FP16 weights alone): 50B × 2B = 100GB; full training state (16B/param): 800GB. With ZeRO-3 across 1024 GPUs: 800GB/1024 = 0.78GB per GPU for optimizer/grad shards, but model weights themselves require tensor parallelism (each GPU holds 50B/1024 ≈ 0.097GB weights shard). Memory is not the bottleneck here. Compute-bound at 50% MFU.
details.realistic_solution: 50B model training: FLOPs = 6 × N × D = 6 × 50B × 1T = 300 ZFLOPs. A100 cluster: 1024 × 312 TFLOPS = 319 PFLOPS peak. At 50% MFU: 160 PFLOPS effective. Training time: 300e21 / 160e15 = 1.875e6 seconds ≈ 21.7 days. Memory: 50B params × 16 bytes (mixed precision: 4B weights + 4B gradients + 8B optimizer) = 800GB. Across 1024 GPUs: 800GB/1024 = 0.78GB per GPU — well within 80GB. Model parallelism not needed for memory. KV cache negligible in training. For this job: GEMM arithmetic intensity >> ridge point → compute-bound training. The bottleneck is compute budget, not memory.

scenario: Chinchilla scaling laws suggest that for 1 trillion training tokens, the compute-optimal model is ~50B parameters (roughly 1:20 param:token ratio). Verify this using a roofline analysis on an A100 cluster of 1024 GPUs. Calculate the compute time, memory footprint, and whether the job is compute or memory bound.
title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws Verification with Roofline on A100

details.common_mistake: Selecting the method with best PPL without evaluating calibration dataset sensitivity; AWQ uses a small 128-sample calibration set while GPTQ uses 128 sequences of 2048 tokens — different OOD robustness profiles.
details.napkin_math: AWQ PPL: 3.9 vs FP16 3.8 = +0.1 degradation. GPTQ: +0.4 degradation. AWQ wins accuracy. Throughput: both W4A16 → same decode speed. Quantization time: GPTQ 3h vs AWQ 30min for 70B. Production: AWQ.
details.realistic_solution: AWQ advantage: 3.9 vs 4.2 PPL = 0.3 PPL better. Calibration: AWQ uses per-channel activation scales from 128 samples (faster, less sensitive). GPTQ: reconstructs weights via Hessian inverse (slower, depends on calibration distribution). AWQ tends to be more robust to distribution shift. GPTQ requires 2-4 hours quantization time for 70B; AWQ ~30 minutes. Deployment: both produce static INT4 weights — identical inference speed on H100 with AutoAWQ/ExLlamaV2. Key decision factors: (1) if production data matches calibration → GPTQ sometimes better; (2) AWQ more robust OOD; (3) AWQ faster to requantize for model updates. Recommendation: AWQ for production due to robustness + speed.

scenario: A production team quantizes Llama-3-70B to 4-bit using both GPTQ (block-wise OBQ) and AWQ (activation-aware) on H100 80GB. GPTQ achieves 4.2 perplexity (PPL) vs FP16 baseline 3.8. AWQ achieves 3.9 PPL. Both run at approximately the same inference speed. The team must choose one for production. Analyze the trade-offs beyond accuracy.
title: GPTQ vs AWQ Quantization Quality on H100 for 70B LLM

details.common_mistake: Counting only the AllReduce after the row-parallel projection and forgetting the AllGather needed before column-parallel if activations were previously scattered.
details.napkin_math: Per-layer comms: AllGather 16.4KB + AllReduce 16.4KB = 32.8KB. At NVLink 450 GB/s: 0.073μs per layer. 80 layers: 5.8μs total communication overhead. Forward compute: ~160ms total. Communication overhead: 5.8μs/160ms = 0.004% — negligible. TP efficiency: ~99.9%.
details.realistic_solution: Column-parallel QKV: each GPU holds [8192, 1024] slice of Q,K,V. Input X is broadcast (via AllGather if previously sharded): 8192×2B = 16.4KB. AllGather across 8: 16.4KB at 450 GB/s = 0.036ms. Row-parallel output projection: each GPU holds [1024, 8192] slice. After matmul, AllReduce output [8192×2B] across 8 GPUs: 16.4KB at 450 GB/s NVLink: 0.036μs. Two communications per attention layer. 80 layers × 2 × 0.036μs = 5.76μs per forward pass. Forward compute per layer: ~2ms. Communication overhead: 5.76μs / 160ms ≈ 0.004%. Efficiency: ~99.9% of perfect linear scaling.

scenario: A 70B LLM is tensor-parallel across 8 H100s. Each attention layer has weight matrices of shape [8192, 8192] for Q, K, V projections. With 8-way tensor parallelism (column-parallel for QKV, row-parallel for output), calculate the communication cost per layer and the efficiency vs perfect linear scaling.
title: Tensor Parallelism GEMM Partitioning on H100 for LLM Layer

details.common_mistake: Assuming low bandwidth utilization means compute is the bottleneck; it may indicate inefficient memory access patterns, kernel launch overhead, or CPU-GPU synchronization gaps.
details.napkin_math: Theoretical: 140GB/5.3TB/s = 26.4ms to read all weights for one batch step (regardless of batch size). Throughput = 4 tokens / 26.4ms = 151.5 tok/s at perfect 100% BW utilization. Achieved 95 tok/s = 62.7% of 151.5 tok/s ceiling. Gap: 56.9 tok/s lost. Overhead budget: kernel launches 80×50μs=4ms + synchronization gaps. Profile with rocprof --stats.
details.realistic_solution: Expected throughput: 140GB / 5.3TB/s = 26.4ms per batch step; 4 tokens / 26.4ms = 151.5 tok/s theoretical at 100% HBM utilization. Achieved 95 tok/s = 62.5% efficiency, matching 63% HBM utilization. Causes: (1) Kernel launch overhead between layers — 80 layers × 2 kernel launches = 160 launches, each ~10-50μs → 1.6-8ms per 80-layer forward = significant for 3.5ms ideal forward. (2) CPU-GPU synchronization for dynamic shapes (variable seq lengths in continuous batching). (3) Attention computation at batch=4, seq=growing: attention not purely memory-bound at this batch size. (4) HBM bank conflicts or non-coalesced accesses in custom kernels. Investigation: ROCm rocprof, measure per-kernel bandwidth.

scenario: An MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s) serving Llama-3-70B at batch_size=4 shows 95 tok/s throughput but profiling shows only 63% HBM bandwidth utilization. Diagnose possible causes of the underutilization and propose investigation steps.
title: Memory Bandwidth Bottleneck Diagnosis for LLM Decode on MI300X

details.common_mistake: Blaming network latency or model complexity for P99 spikes; the gap between P50=180ms and P99=2100ms indicates a queuing problem, not an inference performance problem.
details.napkin_math: P50=180ms = ~5.6 req/s capacity per chip. 16 chips: 89.6 req/s. Business hours load: if 100+ req/s → utilization > 100% → queue grows. Little's Law: E[wait] = (arrival_rate × service_time) / (1 - utilization). At 110% load, queue → infinite. Fix: scale to 18+ chips or rate-limit at 90 req/s.
details.realistic_solution: P50=180ms, P99=2100ms: 11.7× P99/P50 ratio is diagnostic of queue buildup, not inference speed variance. Inference itself has low variance (P99/P50 typically <2×). Cause: request arrival bursts during business hours exceed service capacity. With 16 chips at ~100 req/s capacity: if 120 req/s arrive, queue builds → P99 grows by Little's Law (L = λ×W). Fix options: (1) Autoscale: add TPU pod instances during business hours (dynamic provisioning). (2) Admission control: reject/redirect requests when queue depth > threshold. (3) Prefill-decode disaggregation: separate TPUs for prefill (high compute) vs decode (memory bandwidth), increasing throughput. (4) Request prioritization: apply strict deadline scheduling. Profile: check TPU utilization (if >95%, need more chips; if 70%, problem is batching or pipeline bubbles).

scenario: A TPU v5e deployment (197 TFLOPS BF16 per chip, 16 chips in a pod) serves Gemma-7B with P99 TTFT SLA of 500ms. During business hours, P99 TTFT spikes to 2.1 seconds while P50 remains at 180ms. Diagnose the likely cause and propose a fix.
title: SLO Violation Root Cause Analysis for LLM Service on TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Ignoring latency (α) in the α-β model for small messages; for large messages like 26GB gradients, bandwidth (β) dominates and latency becomes negligible.
details.napkin_math: Ring: 2×(63/64)×26/12.5 = 4.09s. Halving-doubling: for large bandwidth-bound messages, bandwidth-optimal AllReduce algorithms (including ring and RHD) achieve the same asymptotic bandwidth: 2×(N-1)/N×M/B ≈ 4.09s. RHD reduces latency-bound overhead (fewer steps: 2×log2(N)), but for 26GB both are bandwidth-bound ≈ 4.09s. Tree: bottlenecked at root, ~6.24s. Ring and RHD tie for bandwidth-limited 26GB sync.
details.realistic_solution: Ring all-reduce: time = 2×(N-1)/N × M/B = 2×63/64 × 26GB/12.5GB/s = 2×0.984×2.08s = 4.09s. Recursive halving-doubling: for large bandwidth-bound messages, transfers the same total data as ring: 2×(N-1)/N×M = 51.4GB per GPU, at 12.5GB/s ≈ 4.1s. RHD's formula 2×log2(N)×M/(N×B) gives the per-step bandwidth allocation, not the total time for large messages. Binary tree: log2(64)=6 steps, bottleneck at root = M/B = 26/12.5 = 2.08s per step but only reduces 1 link. Tree time: 6×2.08/2 = ~6.24s worst case. Ring and RHD tie at ~4.09s for this 26GB bandwidth-bound case; tree is slowest at ~6.24s. For large messages (>1GB), ring and RHD achieve similar bandwidth-bound performance; RHD has lower overhead for small messages due to fewer steps.

scenario: A 64-GPU H100 cluster uses InfiniBand HDR100 (100 Gbps = 12.5 GB/s per link). Gradient all-reduce with 26GB (13B model, FP16) per step. Compare ring all-reduce, recursive halving-doubling (Rabenseifner), and a binary tree reduction. Which minimizes wall-clock time?
title: AllReduce Topology Comparison: Ring vs Tree on H100 IB Cluster

details.common_mistake: Equating MFU with GPU utilization and not accounting for gradient synchronization overhead, memory pressure from large batch activations, and kernel occupancy changes.
details.napkin_math: A100 peak: 312 TFLOPS BF16. Effective: 32→45% (140T), 128→58% (181T), 512→51% (159T). Optimal: 128. Activation memory at 128: 128×2048×8192×2×5 = 21GB — uses gradient checkpointing, incurs ~30% FLOPs overhead for recomputation but still best total throughput.
details.realistic_solution: Batch=32: small batch → GEMMs are small, tensor core utilization low (tiles don't fill SM perfectly). MFU 45%. Batch=128: GEMMs larger → tile filling improves, pipeline depth increases → MFU peaks at 58%. Memory still manageable: 128×2048×8192×2B×5 (activations) ≈ 26GB per layer (too large; uses gradient checkpointing). Batch=512: activation memory pressure causes more gradient checkpointing recomputation → extra FLOPs counted; additionally, gradient sync overhead proportionally increases with larger gradients-per-step in gradient accumulation context. Or: at batch=512, optimizer state update and weight update overhead becomes significant. Optimal: batch=128 at 58% MFU = 181 TFLOPS effective.

scenario: Training a 13B LLM on A100 80GB. At batch_size=32 (seq_len=2048), MFU is 45% (140 TFLOPS). At batch_size=128, MFU is 58% (181 TFLOPS). At batch_size=512, MFU drops to 51% (159 TFLOPS). Explain the MFU curve and identify the optimal batch size.
title: Batch Size Selection for Maximum MFU on A100 During Pre-Training

details.common_mistake: Multiplying only GPU power by runtime without applying PUE, which accounts for cooling, lighting, UPS, and networking overhead in the datacenter.
details.napkin_math: IT load: 1024×680W×1.15 = 800kW. Total: 800×1.3 = 1040kW. Energy: 1040kW×520.8h = 541MWh. Cost: $65K. Carbon: 541,000×0.42 = 227 tonnes CO2e. Renewables offset: if 100% renewable, ~0 tonnes net.
details.realistic_solution: GPU power: 1024 × 680W = 696.3 kW. Supporting hardware (CPU, DRAM, networking): ~15% overhead = 804.7 kW total IT load. With PUE 1.3: total facility power = 804.7 × 1.3 = 1046 kW. Runtime: 21.7 days = 520.8 hours. Total energy: 1046 kW × 520.8 hours = 544.8 MWh. Cost: 544,800 kWh × $0.12 = $65,376. Carbon: 544,800 × 0.42 = 228,816 kg CO2e = 229 tonnes CO2e. For comparison: average US car emits ~4.6 tonnes/year → equivalent to ~50 cars for one year. Note: many hyperscalers use renewable energy credits, reducing effective carbon intensity significantly.

scenario: Training a 70B LLM requires 21.7 days on 1024 H100s at 680W each. The datacenter uses PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) of 1.3 and is located in a region with carbon intensity of 0.42 kg CO2e/kWh (US average). Calculate total energy consumption, cost at $0.12/kWh, and carbon footprint.
title: Carbon Footprint Estimation for LLM Training Run on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming attention always achieves similar MFU to MLP GEMMs because both involve matrix operations; attention is limited by its smaller effective GEMM sizes and the softmax operation.
details.napkin_math: MLP 67% × 50% weight = 33.5%. Attn 31% × 40% weight = 12.4%. Others 5% × 10% = 0.5%. Total: 46.4% ≈ 48% observed. To improve: get attention to 50%+ MFU → FlashAttention-2 + larger batch = overall MFU ≈ 55-60%.
details.realistic_solution: MLP GEMMs at seq=2048, batch=8: M=16384 (batch×seq), K=12288, N=49152 (4×d_model). These are large square-ish GEMMs → high tensor core utilization, 67% MFU reasonable. Attention QK^T: M=2048, K=128 (head_dim), N=2048 per head. These are small GEMMs (especially K=128) → tensor cores less efficient, lower MFU. Plus: softmax is element-wise, no tensor cores → near 0% MFU contribution. Weighted average: MLP ~50% of FLOPs at 67%, attention ~40% at 31%, others at 5%: 0.5×67 + 0.4×31 + 0.1×5 = 33.5+12.4+0.5 = 46.4% ≈ 48% observed. Fix: FlashAttention-2 + increase seq_len per device (longer seqs improve QK^T GEMM shape).

scenario: Profile a GPT-3 style model (175B) on H100 during training at batch=8, seq=2048. Separate profiling shows: MLP GEMMs at 67% MFU, attention at 31% MFU, layer norm/dropout at 5% MFU. The overall MFU is 48%. Explain why attention underperforms MLP and propose improvements.
title: Benchmark MFU vs Achieved FLOPS for Attention vs MLP on H100

details.common_mistake: Using the same GPU ratio as the compute ratio without accounting for the different memory bandwidth requirements of decode vs the compute requirements of prefill.
details.napkin_math: Prefill GPUs: 1000 req/s × 50ms = 50 GPUs. Decode: 1000 req/s × 256 tokens avg = 256K tok/s needed. At 480 tok/s/GPU: 533 GPU equivalents but steady-state = 256K/480 = 534/16 batched = 33 GPUs. Fleet: 50 prefill + 35 decode = 85 H100s. KV transfer: 536MB @ 100 GB/s = 5.4ms.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill GPU requirement: avg prompt 512 tokens, 70B model, 50ms prefill per request at 1 GPU. Need 1000 req/s × 0.05s = 50 concurrent prefills → 50 H100s for prefill. Decode GPU requirement: avg 256 output tokens per response, 30 tok/s per GPU at batch=16. Throughput: 16 × 30 = 480 tok/s per GPU. Need 1000 × 256 / 480 = 533 decode GPU-seconds → ~18 decode GPUs at any instant but with queuing, need 30-40 GPUs. Ratio: ~50 prefill : 35 decode = 1.4:1. KV transfer: after prefill, transfer KV cache (2×32×32×64×512×2B = 536MB) from prefill GPU to decode GPU via RDMA over InfiniBand at 100 GB/s: 5.4ms. Load balancer: route new requests to least-loaded prefill GPU; after prefill, schedule decode on GPU with most spare capacity.

scenario: Design a prefill-decode disaggregation system for serving Llama-3-70B at 1000 req/s with P50 TTFT < 200ms and P50 TPOT < 50ms/token on an H100 fleet. Specify the number of prefill GPUs vs decode GPUs, KV cache transfer mechanism, and load balancing strategy.
title: Prefill-Decode Disaggregation Architecture Specification for H100 Fleet

details.common_mistake: Trying to fit the full model in GPU HBM without considering tiered inference where inactive layers reside in CPU DRAM and are streamed to GPU on demand.
details.napkin_math: Model FP8: 405GB. 8×H100 = 640GB — fits model + some KV. Per-token KV (FP8, all layers): 2 (K+V) × 128 layers × 64 heads × 128 dim × 1B = 2MB/token. 500 users × 8192 tokens = 500×8192×2MB = 8,192GB KV. Total: 405+8,192 = 8,597GB — far beyond 8×H100 (640GB). Must limit concurrency: 100 users × 8192 tokens × 2MB = 1,638GB; use FP4 KV (0.5x): 819GB → needs 10 H100s. Alternatively: 50 users, 4096 ctx, FP8: 205GB + 405GB = 610GB → 8 H100s.
details.realistic_solution: Model: 405GB FP8. Single H100: 80GB — only 20% of model fits. Strategy: tensor parallelism across 8 H100s = 640GB HBM total > 405GB. Full model in HBM. KV cache: 500 users × 8192 tokens × 2 × 128 layers × 64 heads × 128 dim × 1B (FP8 KV) = 500×8192×2×128×64×128 = 500×8192×2097152B = ... recalculate: per token per layer KV = 2×64×128×1B = 16KB. 128 layers: 2MB/token. 500 users × 8192 = 4096MB × 2MB = no: 500×8192×2MB = 8192GB — impossible. Fix: KV cache at INT4 = 1MB/token/500 = 500×8192×1MB = 4TB — still too large. Must limit to 64 context or batch differently. Realistic: 50 concurrent, 4096 context, INT8 KV. KV: 50×4096×128 layers×64H×128D×2×1B = 50×4096×2MB = 410GB — need 460GB total. Use 6×H100 for model (360GB) + 2×H100 for KV cache.

scenario: Specify a memory hierarchy system for serving Llama-3-405B (FP8 = 405GB) on a production cluster. The model must serve 500 concurrent users with 8192 context. Available: H100 80GB (3.35 TB/s HBM3), NVMe SSD (7 GB/s), DRAM (300 GB/s). Design the tiered memory strategy.
title: Multi-Level Memory Hierarchy Specification for 405B LLM Inference

details.common_mistake: Treating encoder and decoder as having similar arithmetic intensity; decoder single-token generation is highly memory-bandwidth-bound while encoder batch processing is compute-bound.
details.napkin_math: Ridge: 197T/819G = 240 FLOPs/B. Encoder AI: 76.8T/940MB = 81.7 FLOPs/B → memory-bound, ceiling = 819G×81.7 = 66.9 TFLOPS. Decoder AI: 2.3G/1.548G = 1.49 FLOPs/B → memory-bound, ceiling = 1.22 TFLOPS. Encoder 34% of peak; decoder 0.6% of peak.
details.realistic_solution: BERT encoder (batch=64, seq=512): total FLOPs = 64×1.2T = 76.8T. Memory: 336M×2B = 672MB weights + 64×512×1024×2B×4 = 268MB activations = ~940MB. AI = 76.8T/940MB = 81.7 FLOPs/byte. TPU v5e ridge: 197T/819G = 240 FLOPs/byte. Encoder AI (82) < ridge (240) → memory-bound but approaching compute region. GPT-2-large decoder (batch=1, 1 token): FLOPs = 2.3G. Memory: 774M×2B = 1.548GB loaded per token. AI = 2.3G/1.548G = 1.49 FLOPs/byte — deeply memory-bound. Encoder throughput ceiling: 819 GB/s × 81.7 = 66.9 TFLOPS. Decoder ceiling: 819 GB/s × 1.49 = 1.22 TFLOPS effective. Ridge-to-ridge comparison: encoder 34% efficiency, decoder 0.6% efficiency.

scenario: TPU v5e runs BERT-large encoder (336M params, 1.2 TFLOP/seq at seq=512) and GPT-2-large decoder (774M params, decode step = 2.3 GFLOP at seq=1). TPU v5e: 197 TFLOPS BF16, 819 GB/s HBM. Calculate the arithmetic intensity and roofline position for each use case.
title: Roofline Model for Transformer Encoder vs Decoder on TPU v5e

details.common_mistake: Applying Top-K sparsification per-step without gradient accumulation; gradients from the non-selected 99.9% are lost permanently, causing training divergence unless error feedback is used.
details.napkin_math: Dense AllReduce: 832ms (per scenario). Sparse (0.1% = 26MB + 26MB indices = 52MB): 3.1ms. Raw speedup: 500×. Top-K selection cost: ~200ms. Net communication+selection: 203ms vs 832ms = 4.1× improvement. With error feedback: no accuracy loss.
details.realistic_solution: Without compression: AllReduce takes 832ms per scenario (2×(31/32)×26GB/50GB/s ≈ 1.55s theoretical, but scenario specifies 832ms measured). With 99.9% sparsity: compressed payload = 26MB (values) + 26MB (indices at INT32) = 52MB. AllReduce: 2×(31/32)×52MB/50GB/s = 3.1ms. Speedup: 1550ms/3.1ms = 500×. Accuracy risk: without error feedback (EF), dropped gradients cause ~5-10% accuracy loss at convergence. With EF (accumulate dropped gradients locally, add to next step): convergence matches dense gradients within 1-2%. Implementation: PowerSGD or Top-K with error feedback. Additional cost: Top-K selection on 26GB: O(n log k) → ~200ms on GPU. Net speedup: 832/(200+3.1) = 4.1×.

scenario: A 32-GPU H100 training cluster uses 400GbE (50 GB/s per link). AllReduce of 26GB gradients takes 832ms without compression. Top-K gradient sparsification at 99.9% sparsity (keep top 0.1%) reduces gradient to 26MB. Evaluate the throughput improvement and accuracy risk.
title: Gradient Compression Impact on AllReduce Bandwidth on H100 Cluster

details.common_mistake: Treating the 64-GPU AllReduce as operating on a single flat topology; the hierarchical nature (NVLink within nodes, IB across nodes) requires a two-level AllReduce strategy.
details.napkin_math: NCCL: intra-node ring 0.203s + inter-node IB ring 3.64s = 3.84s. MPI tree: 52GB/25GB/s × 6 hops = 12.5s. NCCL wins 3.3×. Bottleneck is always inter-node IB bandwidth. Adding more nodes: scale IB allocation or use rail-optimized topology.
details.realistic_solution: Two-level hierarchical AllReduce (NCCL strategy): Level 1 (intra-node, NVLink): 8-GPU ring within each node. Ring AllReduce 52GB on NVLink: 2×(7/8)×52GB/450GB/s = 0.203s. After: each of 8 nodes has locally reduced 52GB. Level 2 (inter-node, IB): ReduceScatter across 8 nodes (52GB/8 = 6.5GB each). IB AllReduce: 2×(7/8)×52GB/25GB/s = 3.64s. Total NCCL: 0.203 + 3.64 = 3.84s. MPI tree reduction (8-level binary tree, bottleneck = root node 25 GB/s link): 52GB/25GB/s × log2(64) = 2.08 × 6 = 12.5s. NCCL 3.5× faster than naive MPI tree due to parallel ring algorithms.

scenario: A team trains a 13B model on 64 H100s (8 nodes × 8 GPUs) and chooses between NCCL-based AllReduce (intra-node via NVLink 450 GB/s, inter-node via InfiniBand HDR200 at 200 Gbps=25 GB/s) vs tree-based MPI reduction. Gradient size: 52GB (FP16). Calculate times for each strategy.
title: NCCL vs MPI AllReduce Performance for Mixed-Precision Training on H100

details.common_mistake: Treating Ring Attention communication as equivalent to standard attention memory cost; Ring Attention replaces attention matrix materialization with point-to-point ring KV passing.
details.napkin_math: Per ring step KV: 8MB. 63 steps: 504MB total. Intra-node (7 steps): 56MB/450 GB/s = 0.12ms. Inter-node (56 steps): 448MB/25 GB/s = 17.9ms. Compute: 4 TFLOP/GPU / 66 TFLOPS = 60ms. Comm (18ms) << compute (60ms) → pipeline overlap hides all communication.
details.realistic_solution: Ring Attention: each GPU holds Q_chunk (15,625×128 BF16 = 4MB) and receives K,V chunks from neighbors. Per ring step: send K_chunk (15,625×128×2B = 4MB) + V_chunk (4MB) = 8MB per step. 64 GPUs: 63 ring steps. Intra-node NVLink: first 7 steps × 8MB = 56MB at 450 GB/s = 0.12ms. Inter-node IB: 56 steps × 8MB = 448MB at 25 GB/s = 17.9ms. Total ring: ~18ms for all ring steps. Parallel: compute and communicate overlap (Ring Attention is designed for overlap). Attention FLOPs per GPU: 2×15625×1M×128 = 4T FLOPs / GPU. H100 at 66 TFLOPS effective = 60ms compute. Overlap: 18ms comm << 60ms compute → communication hidden.

scenario: You're implementing Ring Attention to support 1M token context across 8 H100 nodes (8 GPUs each = 64 GPUs). Each GPU holds seq_chunk = 1M/64 = 15,625 tokens. For one attention head (head_dim=128, BF16), calculate the communication volume per ring step and total AllReduce time.
title: Long-Context Attention with Ring Attention on H100 Multi-Node

details.common_mistake: Running embedding and generation on the same GPU instance simultaneously; they have completely different compute patterns (embedding: high-throughput batch, generation: low-latency streaming).
details.napkin_math: Embedding: 10K × 2.1G = 21T FLOPs / 312T = 0.067s GPU time = $0.00006. Generation: 1000 × 500 tok / 30 tok/s = 16,667s = 4.63 h × $3/h = $13.9/day. Generation is 99.99% of cost. Embed offline in micro-batches; invest in generation optimization (speculative decode, better batching).
details.realistic_solution: Embedding phase: 10K docs × 2.1 GFLOP = 21 TFLOP/day. H100 at 312 TFLOPS sustained: 21T/312T = 0.067 seconds. Batch all embeddings: at batch=512, fully saturates H100 tensor cores. Total embedding time: 21T at 312 TFLOPS = 0.067s GPU-hours. Cost: 0.067s × ($3/hr) = $0.00006. Generation: 1000 queries × avg 500 tokens output / 30 tok/s = 1000×500/30 = 16,667 seconds = 4.6 GPU-hours. Cost: 4.6 × $3 = $13.8. Optimization: batch embeddings offline in 5-minute windows on a spot instance. Use continuous batching for generation. Total: $0.001 embedding + $13.8 generation per day. Generation dominates 99.99% of cost — optimize it, not embedding.

scenario: A RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) pipeline on H100 embeds documents using BGE-M3 (570M params, 2.1 GFLOP per 512-token doc) and then generates answers with Llama-3-8B. The embedding phase processes 10,000 docs/day, answer generation handles 1,000 queries/day. The team wants to minimize H100 hour cost. Design the batching strategy.
title: Inference Serving Cost Optimization: Batching Strategy on H100 for RAG

details.common_mistake: Measuring speedup only in FLOPS rather than in actual latency; for memory-bandwidth-limited kernels like LayerNorm and GELU, the speedup comes from reducing HBM traffic, not FLOPs.
details.napkin_math: Activation: 2GB. Unfused HBM: 4 passes × 2GB = 8GB at 3.35 TB/s = 2.39ms. Fused HBM: 2 passes × 2GB = 4GB at 3.35 TB/s = 1.19ms. Speedup: 2×. FLOPs negligible for these element-wise ops.
details.realistic_solution: Activation size: 64×2048×8192×2B = 2GB. Unfused: LayerNorm reads 2GB + writes 2GB = 4GB; GELU reads 2GB + writes 2GB = 4GB. Total HBM: 8GB. At H100 3.35 TB/s: time = 8GB/3.35TB/s = 2.39ms. Fused: single pass reads 2GB + writes 2GB = 4GB total. Time = 4GB/3.35TB/s = 1.19ms. Speedup: 2.39/1.19 = 2×. FLOPs: LayerNorm ≈ 8×activation elements = 8×64×2048×8192 = 8.6B. GELU: ~2×activation = 2.1B. Total ≈ 10.7B FLOPs. At 650 GFLOPS: 16.5ms. Wait — discrepancy: these kernels are so memory-bound that FLOPs don't matter; the 650 GFLOPS is the effective 'throughput' in GFLOPS given memory bound, not compute bound. Fused kernel achieves 1.19ms = 2× speedup, matches 2× HBM reduction.

scenario: An H100 runs LayerNorm (read+write 2×activation) followed immediately by GELU (read+write 2×activation) as separate kernels. For activation shape [batch=64, seq=2048, d=8192] (BF16 = 2GB), unfused throughput is 650 GFLOPS. Fusing both kernels into one pass reduces HBM traffic from 4× to 2×. Calculate the speedup.
title: Kernel Fusion Impact on Memory Bandwidth for Layer Norm + GELU on H100

details.common_mistake: Chunking prefill into equal-size chunks without considering that very small chunks (< 64 tokens) have high per-chunk overhead from kernel launches and scheduling, reducing effective prefill throughput.
details.napkin_math: Prefill 2048: 400ms. Chunked (128 token chunks): 16 chunks × 25ms each = 400ms total, but interleaved with decode. Decode max wait per token: 25ms (1 chunk). Original decode P99: 400ms (blocked by full prefill). After: 25ms decode P99. TTFT: 400ms → 560ms (16 interleaved decode steps at 10ms). Trade-off justified for decode-heavy workloads.
details.realistic_solution: Problem: 400ms prefill preempts 40 decode steps at 10ms each → P99 decode spikes. Chunked prefill: split 2048 tokens into C chunks, interleave one chunk with each decode step. Chunk size selection: minimum chunk for A100 efficiency ≈ 128 tokens (below this, tensor core utilization drops). With 128-token chunks: 2048/128 = 16 chunks, each taking ~25ms (attention is O(n×chunk_size)), interleaved with 16 decode steps at 10ms each. Total time: 16×(25+10) = 560ms vs original 400ms+10ms×old_decode. Decode P99: max wait = 25ms (one chunk) vs 400ms. TTFT increases (2048 tokens now take 560ms vs 400ms), but P99 decode latency drops 16× from 400ms to 25ms. Trade-off: TTFT +40%, decode interference -94%.

scenario: A LLM serving system on A100 80GB alternates between large prefill requests (2048 tokens, ~400ms) and decode requests (single tokens, ~10ms each). Full prefill preempts all decode requests, causing P99 decode latency spikes to 2 seconds. Implement chunked prefill to bound decode interference.
title: Disaggregated Serving with Chunked Prefill on A100 80GB

details.common_mistake: Calculating bubble fraction for the naive GPipe schedule instead of the 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) schedule, which significantly reduces bubble time.
details.napkin_math: Bubble fraction = (p-1)/(m+p-1). m=4, p=4: 3/7 = 42.9%. For 10% bubble: m = 9p-9 = 27. For 5%: m = 19p-19 = 57. Memory: each in-flight micro-batch stores activations for stages not yet completed. 27 micro-batches × 20 layers × activation per layer — high memory overhead.
details.realistic_solution: GPipe schedule: pipeline fill time = (p-1) = 3 stages × 100ms/stage = 300ms bubble. Total time for m=4 micro-batches: (m+p-1)×stage_time = 7×100ms = 700ms. Bubble fraction: 300ms/700ms = 42.9%. 1F1B schedule: bubble = (p-1)×2×stage_time / (m×2×stage_time + (p-1)×2×stage_time) = (3×2×100) / (4×2×100 + 3×2×100) = 600 / (800+600) = 600/1400 = 42.9%. Same formula! Bubble fraction = (p-1)/(m+p-1) regardless of schedule. With m=4, p=4: (4-1)/(4+4-1) = 3/7 = 42.9%. To get <10% bubble: m = 9×(p-1) = 9×3 = 27 micro-batches. With m=27: bubble = 3/29 = 10.3%. More micro-batches reduces bubble but increases memory for in-flight activations.

scenario: A 70B model is split across 4 pipeline stages (20 layers each) on 4 H100 nodes. Each stage processes one micro-batch in 50ms (forward) + 50ms (backward). With 4 micro-batches (1F1B schedule), calculate pipeline bubble fraction and effective GPU utilization.
title: Pipeline Bubble Analysis for 4-Stage Pipeline Parallelism on H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming that reducing attention FLOPs proportionally reduces wall-clock time; sparse attention requires irregular memory access patterns that are cache-unfriendly and hard to vectorize on GPUs.
details.napkin_math: FlashAttention 8K: QKV = 201MB at 3.35 TB/s = 60μs. Sparse (288/8K = 3.5% density): indirect gather at ~200 GB/s effective = 154MB / 200 GB/s = 770μs. Sparse 12.8× slower. Crossover point: dense = BW × n²; sparse = BW_gather × n×k. Equal at n = BW/BW_gather × k × (3.35T/200G) = 16.75 × k. With k=288: n = 4,824 — below 8K. Dense wins below n~5K.
details.realistic_solution: Full attention at 8K: FLOPs = 2×8192²×128×32 heads = 551B. FlashAttention time: 551B/TFLOPS_effective + BW_bound. At H100, FlashAttention is BW-limited: 3×8192×128×32×2B (QKV) = 201MB at 3.35 TB/s = 60μs. Sparse attention (288 active positions per token): FLOPs = 2×8192×288×128×32 = 19.3B FLOPs = 96.5% reduction. But: sparse gather requires indirect memory access. GPU sparse attention kernels (BigBird, LongFormer style): effective bandwidth = ~200 GB/s (vs 3.35 TB/s for dense due to gather inefficiency). Sparse attention time: 8192×288×2B×32 (load K,V per token) = 154MB at 200 GB/s = 770μs. FlashAttention at 8K: 60μs. Sparse is 12.8× SLOWER than FlashAttention due to gather overhead. Conclusion: sparse attention is only faster for context > 32K+ where O(n²) FlashAttention memory becomes prohibitive.

scenario: A code generation LLM (Deepseek-Coder-33B) uses dynamic sparse attention: each token attends to its 256 nearest tokens + 32 global tokens (code symbols). At 8K context, this reduces attention FLOPs from O(n²) to O(n×k). On H100, evaluate whether sparse attention provides wall-clock speedup over FlashAttention for this sparsity pattern.
title: Dynamic Sparse Attention Pattern Implementation on H100 for Code LLM

details.common_mistake: Counting one AllGather per layer without accounting for the fact that ZeRO-3 AllGathers and immediately discards parameters after each layer to free memory for the next layer.
details.napkin_math: Per-layer AllGather: (255/256)×3.64GB/25GB/s = 143ms. 96 layers FWD: 13.7s. Compute: 96×24ms = 2.3s. Ratio: 5.96× comm-dominated. With NVLink 450 GB/s (intra-node): 8-GPU subgroup gathers in 3.64GB/450GB/s=8.1ms, then IB for cross-node. Effective: ~50ms/layer with hierarchical comm = 4.8s FWD. Still 2× compute.
details.realistic_solution: Params per layer: 175B / 96 layers = 1.82B params × 2B (BF16) = 3.64GB per layer. AllGather per layer: broadcast 3.64GB from 256 GPUs. Using ring AllReduce for AllGather: time = (N-1)/N × M / BW_per_link. Assume 200 Gbps = 25 GB/s IB per GPU. Ring AllGather: (255/256) × 3.64GB / 25 GB/s = 0.143s per layer. 96 layers forward: 96 × 0.143s = 13.7s. Backward needs another 96 AllGathers + 96 ReduceScatters = 27.4s. Compute per layer: 175B/96 × 2 FLOPs × batch_tokens. At batch=2048 tokens: 2 × 1.82B × 2048 = 7.5T FLOPs. A100 at 312 TFLOPS: 7.5T/312T = 24ms per layer. Total compute: 96 × 24ms = 2.3s. ZeRO-3 comm/compute ratio: 13.7s/2.3s = 5.96× — communication completely dominates. ZeRO-3 requires much faster interconnect or gradient checkpointing reduction to be viable.

scenario: Training GPT-3 175B on 256 A100 80GB GPUs using ZeRO-3. Each GPU holds 175B/256 = 684M params (BF16 = 1.37GB) out of 80GB. For each forward pass, each layer's parameters must be AllGathered. With 96 transformer layers, calculate total AllGather communication per forward pass and the efficiency vs compute ratio.
title: ZeRO-3 Communication Volume Analysis for 175B Model on 256 A100s

details.common_mistake: Measuring occupancy as active_warps/max_warps per SM without considering whether all 132 SMs are even being used; a small kernel may not have enough thread blocks to fill all SMs.
details.napkin_math: Thread blocks: N/128 = 32. H100 SMs: 132. Active SMs: 32 (24.2%). Warps per active SM: 4/64 = 6.25% occupancy. Global: 32×4/(132×64) = 128/8448 = 1.5%. At batch=4: 32×4=128 blocks → 97% SMs used, 4/64 = 6.25% per-SM occupancy. Still low — need larger N or tile sizes.
details.realistic_solution: Thread blocks launched: 32 (one per 128 columns of N). H100 SMs: 132. Thread blocks per SM: 32/132 < 1. Only 32 of 132 SMs are active = 24.2% SM utilization. Per active SM: 1 thread block = 4 warps. Max warps per SM: 64 (H100). Occupancy per active SM: 4/64 = 6.25%. Overall occupancy: 32 blocks × 4 warps / (132 SMs × 64 warps/SM) = 128 warps / 8448 warps = 1.5% occupancy. At batch=1, this GEMM cannot fill H100. Solutions: (1) Increase N through tensor parallelism or batching. (2) Use persistent kernels that handle multiple GEMM tiles per SM launch. (3) Increase batch size to fill SMs (batch=4 → 4× SMs used). (4) Use CUTLASS grouped GEMM to process multiple small GEMMs in one kernel launch.

scenario: An H100 has 132 SMs with 2048 threads/SM. A GEMM kernel for inference at batch=1, M=1, K=4096, N=4096 uses thread blocks of [128 threads, 4 warps]. The kernel launches 32 thread blocks (N/128=32). Analyze SM occupancy and identify the underutilization issue.
title: H100 SM Occupancy Analysis for Small-Batch Inference Kernel

details.common_mistake: Applying uniform full checkpointing without recognizing that MLP activations are cheaper to recompute (simple matrix multiplications) while attention activations are expensive to recompute (O(n²) softmax).
details.napkin_math: Full checkpoint: 33% FLOPs overhead, saves 100% intermediate activations. Selective (attention only): 15% FLOPs overhead, saves ~60% of activation memory. Efficiency ratio: selective = 60%/15% = 4.0 memory/compute; full = 100%/33% = 3.0. Selective is 33% more efficient. Use selective checkpointing.
details.realistic_solution: Full checkpointing: save only layer inputs, recompute all activations in backward. Saves: all intermediate activations per layer (~4GB × 128 layers / 512 GPUs = 1GB). Cost: 33% more FLOPs. Selective checkpointing (checkpoint only attention): attention activations are large (seq²×heads) and expensive to recompute. MLP activations are small and cheap. Strategy: checkpoint attention (save softmax output), don't checkpoint MLP. Memory savings: attention activations: 32 heads × 8192² × 2B = 4GB per layer → with checkpointing saves 4GB per layer. MLP activations: 8192×32768×2B = 536MB per layer — recompute. Per GPU: 128 layers / 512 GPUs = 0.25 layers, but activation memory scales with batch. Selective saves attention activation (60% of savings) at 15% recomputation cost vs full checkpointing 100% savings at 33% cost. Efficiency: 0.6/0.15 vs 1.0/0.33 = 4 vs 3. Selective is 33% more compute-efficient per memory saved.

scenario: Training Llama-3-405B on 512 H100s. Without activation checkpointing, peak activation memory per GPU exceeds 80GB. With full checkpointing (checkpoint every layer), recomputation overhead is 33%. With selective checkpointing (checkpoint only attention, not MLP), recomputation is 15%. Analyze the memory-compute trade-off.
title: Activation Checkpointing Granularity Trade-off for 405B Model Training on H100

details.common_mistake: Confusing PUE as a multiplier on overhead only. PUE = Total Facility Power / IT Equipment Power, so PUE 1.3 means 30% overhead, not 130%.
details.napkin_math: PUE 1.3 × 10 MW IT = 13 MW total. Overhead = 3 MW = 30% of IT load. Annual overhead cost at $0.06/kWh = 3000 kW × 8760 h × $0.06 = ~$1.58M/year.
details.realistic_solution: PUE = Total Power / IT Power. So Total Power = 10 MW × 1.3 = 13 MW. Overhead = 13 MW − 10 MW = 3 MW. That 3 MW goes to cooling (CRAC units, chillers, cooling towers), power distribution losses (UPS, PDU conversion), and lighting/security. At ~$0.06/kWh, the 3 MW overhead costs $0.06 × 3000 kW × 8760 h = ~$1.58M/year. Google's best facilities achieve PUE 1.10, which would reduce overhead to 1 MW and save over $1M/year. This is why liquid cooling (which can push PUE below 1.1) is a strategic investment for GPU-dense clusters.

scenario: Your company operates a 10 MW IT-load datacenter training large language models on H100 GPUs. The facility reports a PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) of 1.3. Your CFO asks: how much total power does the facility draw, and how many megawatts are consumed purely by cooling, lighting, and power distribution overhead? Show your napkin math.
title: PUE Reality Check: Cooling Overhead in a Hyperscale Cluster

details.common_mistake: Ignoring networking switches, power distribution, and cable management overhead per rack. A DGX H100 also requires high-speed NVLink switches and InfiniBand HCAs that add to the total power envelope.
details.napkin_math: DGX H100: ~10.2 kW. At 40 kW/rack: 3 nodes + networking = ~35 kW. At 80 kW/rack with DLC: 7 nodes + networking = ~75 kW. 1000-GPU cluster = 125 DGX nodes = 18 racks at 80 kW vs 42 racks at 40 kW.
details.realistic_solution: At 40 kW per rack and ~10.2 kW per DGX node, you can fit 3 nodes per rack (30.6 kW), leaving headroom for networking (2-4 kW for leaf switches) and PDU losses. To reach 80 kW/rack — needed for 8 DGX nodes — you need direct liquid cooling (DLC) with cold plates on GPUs and CPUs. Air cooling cannot dissipate 80 kW in a standard 42U rack. DLC delivers coolant directly to heat sources, achieving >95% heat capture. This also requires upgraded PDUs (busbar distribution), higher-amperage circuits, and structural reinforcement for heavier coolant-filled racks.

scenario: You are designing a new GPU training cluster using DGX H100 nodes (8× H100 GPUs, ~10.2 kW per node). Traditional datacenter racks support 10-15 kW per rack. Your facilities team says they can deliver 40 kW per rack with rear-door heat exchangers. How many DGX nodes can you fit per rack, and what infrastructure changes are needed to reach 80 kW/rack density?
title: Rack Power Density Limits with GPU-Dense Nodes

details.common_mistake: Assuming you can simply pause training during high-carbon hours. Checkpointing, restarting, and GPU idle power all eat into savings. Also, shifting large contiguous jobs is harder than shifting elastic batch workloads.
details.napkin_math: Carbon savings from demand shifting: 30% workload × (300g - 100g CO₂/kWh) carbon intensity difference × 500 MWh usage = 0.30 × 200g × 500,000 kWh = 30,000,000g = 30 tonnes CO₂ saved (not 45 tonnes — 45 would require 50% shift or 300g differential).
details.realistic_solution: Carbon savings = shift_fraction × carbon_intensity_delta × energy = 0.30 × 200g/kWh × 500,000 kWh = 30 tonnes (not 45 tonnes which uses 300g/kWh delta instead of 200g/kWh).

scenario: Your organization trains large models on an MI300X cluster in a region where the grid carbon intensity varies from 100 gCO2/kWh (midday solar peak) to 500 gCO2/kWh (evening natural gas). A 70B model training run consumes 500 MWh over 14 days. Your sustainability team wants you to implement carbon-aware scheduling. How much CO2 can you realistically save, and what are the engineering tradeoffs?
title: Carbon-Aware Scheduling: Shifting Training to Low-Carbon Hours

details.common_mistake: Thinking you can just add more CRAH units. Air has inherently low heat capacity (~1 kJ/kg·K vs water at 4.18 kJ/kg·K), so beyond ~25 kW/rack, air cooling requires impractical airflow volumes that create noise and turbulence issues.
details.napkin_math: 8× MI300X at 750W = 6 kW GPU + 2 kW ancillary = 8 kW/server. 4 servers/rack = 32 kW. Air cooling limit ~15 kW. DLC can handle >100 kW/rack. PUE improvement: air at 1.3-1.4 vs DLC at 1.03-1.10.
details.realistic_solution: 4 servers × 8 kW = 32 kW per rack, more than double the 15 kW CRAH rating. Air cooling physically cannot remove 32 kW from a standard rack — you would need ~2700 CFM of airflow, creating deafening noise and hot-spot recirculation. Solutions: (1) Direct liquid cooling (DLC) with cold plates on each MI300X, handling ~90% of heat via liquid loop at 40-45°C supply temperature. Remaining 10% (DIMMs, SSDs) handled by reduced-capacity air. (2) Rear-door heat exchangers as an intermediate step (handles ~30 kW but adds complexity). (3) Immersion cooling (single-phase or two-phase) eliminates air entirely. DLC is the industry consensus for >700W GPUs.

scenario: An MI300X GPU has a TDP of 750W. A server with 8× MI300X draws ~6 kW for GPUs alone, plus ~2 kW for CPUs, networking, and fans, totaling ~8 kW. Your datacenter uses traditional CRAH (Computer Room Air Handler) cooling rated for 15 kW per rack. You need 4 of these servers (32 GPUs) per rack for cluster density. What is the thermal challenge, and how do you solve it?
title: The Cooling Cliff: Air vs Liquid at GPU Density

details.common_mistake: Reporting PUE at peak load only. PUE degrades at lower utilization because cooling overhead is semi-fixed (fans, pumps, chillers run even when GPUs are partially idle). GPU idle power is ~100W vs ~700W under load.
details.napkin_math: Full load: IT=1.22 MW, total=1.4 MW, PUE=1.15. At 35% util: IT≈0.8 MW, cooling overhead≈0.2 MW, total≈1.0 MW, effective PUE≈1.25. Wasted GPU idle power: 2000 × 100W idle × 65% idle fraction = 130 kW wasted on idle GPUs.
details.realistic_solution: At 35% utilization, GPU power drops from ~700W to ~300W per GPU. IT load = 2000 × 300W + ancillary = ~800 kW. But cooling is sized for 1.2 MW IT and runs at ~60% capacity = ~200 kW overhead (pumps/fans have minimum operating points). Effective PUE = 1000 kW / 800 kW = 1.25, worse than the rated 1.15. Solutions: (1) Improve GPU utilization via better data pipelines, prefetching, and overlap of compute/communication — this is the highest-ROI fix. (2) Implement power capping to lower GPU TDP and match cooling to actual load. (3) Use variable-speed drives on cooling pumps/fans. (4) Consolidate workloads to fewer fully-utilized nodes and power-gate idle nodes. Energy proportional computing — where power scales linearly with utilization — remains the holy grail.

scenario: Your 2000-GPU H100 cluster draws 1.4 MW at full load (PUE 1.15). Profiling shows average GPU utilization is only 35% because training jobs have I/O stalls, checkpoint writes, and data pipeline bottlenecks. Cooling infrastructure is sized for peak load. What is the effective PUE when utilization is factored in, and how do you improve energy proportionality?
title: Stranded Power: When GPU Utilization Tanks PUE
