details.common_mistake: Comparing raw TDP without normalizing to useful TFLOPS delivered. Also ignoring that TPU v5e's lower per-chip power includes the network (ICI) while GPU clusters need separate InfiniBand switches drawing additional power.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e pod: 50.4 PFLOPS / 55 kW = 916 TFLOPS/kW peak. MI300X cluster: 41.8 PFLOPS / 30 kW = 1393 TFLOPS/kW peak. At 55% vs 40% MFU: TPU effective = 504 TFLOPS/kW, MI300X effective = 557 TFLOPS/kW. Gap narrows significantly.
details.realistic_solution: TPU v5e pod: 256 × 200W = 51.2 kW for compute. ICI (Inter-Core Interconnect) networking is integrated on-die, adding minimal extra power. Total ~55 kW. Aggregate BF16: 256 × 197 TFLOPS = ~50.4 PFLOPS. Efficiency: ~916 TFLOPS/kW. MI300X cluster: 32 × 750W = 24 kW GPU + ~4 kW for InfiniBand switches + ~2 kW host CPUs = ~30 kW. Aggregate FP16: 32 × 1307 TFLOPS = ~41.8 PFLOPS. Efficiency: ~1393 TFLOPS/kW. The MI300X wins on raw TFLOPS/watt, but TPU v5e's strength is in utilization — Google's compiler (XLA) achieves 50-60% MFU vs typical 35-45% MFU on GPU clusters. Effective efficiency must account for actual utilization, not peak specs.

scenario: You are comparing the power efficiency of a TPU v5e pod (256 chips, ~200W each) versus a cluster of 32× MI300X GPUs (750W TDP each) for a large-scale training job. Both configurations deliver comparable aggregate TFLOPS for your BF16 workload. Which cluster is more power-efficient, and what architectural decisions drive the difference?
title: TPU Pod Power Budgeting vs GPU Clusters

details.common_mistake: Thinking water use is negligible or only relevant for evaporative cooling. Even closed-loop cooling towers consume significant water for makeup due to evaporation, blowdown, and drift.
details.napkin_math: WUE 1.8 × 50 MW × 24h = 2.16M liters/day = 788M liters/year. At $0.005/liter: $3.94M/year water cost. Microsoft reported 6.4B liters water use in 2022 for all DCs.
details.realistic_solution: Daily water consumption = WUE × Total Power × Hours = 1.8 L/kWh × 50,000 kW × 24 h = 2.16 million liters/day (~571,000 gallons). This is equivalent to the daily water needs of ~18,000 average households. WUE matters because: (1) AI training is driving explosive growth in datacenter power, (2) many datacenters are in water-stressed regions (Arizona, Texas), (3) regulatory pressure is increasing, and (4) evaporative cooling is the cheapest way to achieve low PUE but creates water dependency. Alternatives: dry coolers (higher PUE ~1.2 but zero water), DLC (minimal evaporative needs), or locating in cold climates with free air cooling.

scenario: A hyperscaler reports their datacenter has PUE of 1.1 and WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness) of 1.8 L/kWh. The facility draws 50 MW for its H100 GPU training clusters. How much water does this datacenter consume daily, and why is WUE becoming a critical metric for AI infrastructure?
title: Water Usage Effectiveness: The Hidden Cost of Evaporative Cooling

details.common_mistake: Sizing UPS for peak and ignoring partial-load efficiency degradation. Also forgetting that UPS losses generate heat that requires additional cooling, compounding the energy waste.
details.napkin_math: Peak: 5 MW × 3% loss = 150 kW. Low: 1.5 MW × 8% loss = 120 kW. Weighted: 138 kW. Annual: 138 kW × 8760h = 1.21 GWh. At $0.06/kWh = $72.5K wasted + cooling overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Assume 60% time at peak (5 MW, 97% efficient) and 40% at low (1.5 MW, 92% efficient). Peak losses: 5 MW × 3% = 150 kW for 60% of time. Low losses: 1.5 MW × 8% = 120 kW for 40% of time. Weighted average loss: (150 × 0.6 + 120 × 0.4) = 138 kW continuous. Annual waste: 138 kW × 8760 h = 1.21 GWh = ~$72K/year at $0.06/kWh. Plus cooling the UPS waste heat adds ~30% more. Solutions: (1) Modular UPS that adds/removes modules to match load, maintaining >95% efficiency at all loads. (2) Direct DC distribution (eliminate AC-DC-AC conversion). (3) Google's approach: battery backup at server level, eliminating central UPS entirely. (4) Lithium-ion UPS with wider efficient operating range vs legacy lead-acid.

scenario: You are designing the power delivery chain for a new 5 MW GPU training facility. The UPS system is 97% efficient at full load but drops to 92% at 30% load. Your training cluster runs bursty workloads: peak 5 MW during training, 1.5 MW during checkpointing and data staging. What is the annual energy wasted in UPS conversion losses, and how do you architect around this?
title: Power Delivery: UPS Efficiency at Partial Load

details.common_mistake: Choosing immersion cooling for the lowest PUE without considering serviceability. Immersion requires draining fluid to replace a GPU, creating 30-60 minute maintenance windows vs 5 minutes for DLC cold plates.
details.napkin_math: 100 MW IT × PUE 1.08 = 108 MW total, 8 MW overhead. DLC at PUE 1.05 = 105 MW, saving 3 MW = $1.6M/year. Immersion at 1.03 = 103 MW, saving 5 MW = $2.6M/year. But immersion CapEx premium on 100 MW facility: ~$50M+ more than DLC.
details.realistic_solution: At 1000W/GPU and 100 kW/rack, rear-door heat exchangers are eliminated — they max out at ~40-50 kW/rack. DLC (cold plates): PUE 1.03-1.06, handles 100+ kW/rack, GPU serviceable without system drain (quick-disconnect fittings), proven at scale (NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD). CapEx ~15-20% premium over air. Immersion: PUE 1.02-1.04, handles unlimited density, but GPU replacement requires fluid management, creates environmental/safety concerns, limited vendor ecosystem. CapEx ~25-35% premium. Recommendation: DLC cold plates. The 0.02 PUE gap vs immersion = 2 MW at 100 MW scale = ~$1M/year energy cost, but DLC's serviceability advantage and mature supply chain outweigh this. At 100 MW, even PUE 1.08 means 8 MW overhead = ~$4.2M/year. DLC at PUE 1.05 saves $1.6M/year vs the target.

scenario: You are architecting a 100 MW AI training campus that will house next-generation GPUs with 1000W TDP each. The campus must achieve PUE ≤ 1.08 and support 100 kW per rack. Compare three cooling architectures — rear-door heat exchangers, direct liquid cooling (cold plates), and single-phase immersion — on capital cost, PUE achievable, operational complexity, and GPU failure serviceability. Which do you recommend and why?
title: Compute Density vs Power: Planning a 100 MW AI Campus

details.common_mistake: Reporting only IT power and ignoring PUE overhead. Also confusing tokens processed with unique tokens — data repetition (multiple epochs) doesn't change the energy accounting per processed token.
details.napkin_math: 550 kW × 1.12 = 616 kW total. 616 kW × 336h = 207 MWh. 207 MWh / 2T tokens = 103.5 μWh/token. Improving MFU from 40% to 55%: same work in 73% of time → 75 μWh/token.
details.realistic_solution: Total power = 550 kW × 1.12 PUE = 616 kW. Training duration = 14 days × 24 h = 336 h. Total energy = 616 kW × 336 h = 206,976 kWh ≈ 207 MWh. Energy per token = 207 MWh / 2T tokens = 0.1035 Wh/token = 103.5 μWh/token or 0.373 J/token. Published benchmarks: Llama-2 70B used ~1.7M GPU-hours on A100, ~1000 MWh for 2T tokens = ~500 μWh/token. Your H100 efficiency is ~5× better due to hardware generation improvement (3× FLOPS, better memory bandwidth) and likely better MFU. Biggest levers: (1) Increase MFU from typical 40% to 55%+ via communication overlap, (2) use BF16 instead of FP32 master weights where possible, (3) improve data pipeline to eliminate GPU idle time, (4) use larger batch sizes to amortize communication.

scenario: Your team trains a 70B parameter model on 512 H100 GPUs for 2 weeks, processing 2 trillion tokens. The cluster draws 550 kW at the IT level with PUE 1.12. Calculate the energy per token and compare it against published benchmarks. What are the biggest levers to reduce energy per token?
title: Measuring True Energy per Token in Training

details.common_mistake: Blaming software (NCCL, data loader) without checking thermal metrics first. Thermal throttling is a silent performance killer that doesn't throw errors — GPUs simply run slower.
details.napkin_math: Clock drop: 2100 → 1500 MHz = 28.6% reduction. Expected slowdown: 2.1s / 0.714 = 2.94s (pure compute). Actual 3.5s suggests memory throttling too. Power at throttle: ~600W vs 750W TDP. Lost compute: 28.6% × fraction of throttled time.
details.realistic_solution: The MI300X is thermal throttling. When junction temperature exceeds ~90°C, the GPU firmware reduces clock speed to prevent damage, dropping from 2100 MHz to 1500 MHz (a 29% reduction). This causes the periodic 67% slowdown in step time (2.1s → 3.5s). Root causes: (1) insufficient airflow — check for blocked vents, failed fans, or hot aisle containment breaches, (2) dried/insufficient thermal interface material (TIM) between GPU die and heatsink, (3) ambient temperature too high (intake > 35°C), (4) neighboring GPUs creating thermal cross-talk. Fixes: clean air filters, verify fan speeds, check coolant flow rates if using DLC, reduce GPU power limit to 700W (nvidia-smi -pl 700) as a temporary measure. Long-term: upgrade to direct liquid cooling which maintains junction temps at 60-70°C with zero throttling.

scenario: Your 8× MI300X training node shows inconsistent step times: most steps complete in 2.1 seconds, but every few minutes a step takes 3.5 seconds. nvidia-smi shows GPU temperatures cycling between 78°C and 91°C, with clock speeds dropping from 2100 MHz to 1500 MHz when temperatures spike. What is happening and how do you fix it?
title: Thermal Throttling: When GPUs Self-Protect

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that the bubble exists in both the forward and backward passes. The total bubble is (P-1) micro-batch slots in a pipeline of P stages with M micro-batches.
details.napkin_math: P=4, M=8. Bubble fraction = (P-1)/(M+P-1) = 3/11 = 27.3%. To get bubble < 10%: need M > 9(P-1) = 27 micro-batches. With M=32: bubble = 3/35 = 8.6%.
details.realistic_solution: In GPipe, the pipeline bubble fraction = (P - 1) / (P - 1 + M) where P is the number of pipeline stages and M is the number of micro-batches. With P=4 and M=8: bubble = (4-1) / (4-1+8) = 3/11 = 27.3%. This means 27.3% of aggregate GPU-time is wasted in pipeline bubbles. Each GPU sits idle for 3 micro-batch durations during the forward pass fill and drain, and similarly during the backward pass. To reduce this, increase M (more micro-batches, but increases memory for activations) or decrease P (fewer stages, but larger per-stage memory). The 1F1B schedule improves memory by interleaving forward and backward micro-batches, but doesn't reduce the bubble fraction itself.

scenario: You partition a 40-layer transformer across 4 GPUs (10 layers each) using GPipe-style pipeline parallelism with 8 micro-batches. Calculate the pipeline bubble fraction — the percentage of total GPU-time wasted waiting in the pipeline startup and teardown phases.
title: GPipe Bubble Overhead: The Pipeline Efficiency Tax

details.common_mistake: Thinking 1F1B reduces bubble time. It doesn't — the bubble fraction is the same as GPipe. The advantage is purely in activation memory: GPipe must store activations for all M micro-batches simultaneously before any backward pass begins.
details.napkin_math: GPipe peak activations: M × act = 16 × 2GB = 32 GB. 1F1B peak activations: P × act = 8 × 2GB = 16 GB. Savings: 50%. Both have same bubble: (P-1)/(M+P-1) = 7/23 = 30.4%.
details.realistic_solution: GPipe: Each stage runs all M=16 forward passes before any backward pass. Peak activation memory on a stage = M × (activations per micro-batch) = 16× per-micro-batch activations. 1F1B: After the warmup phase (P-1 = 7 forward passes), each stage alternates one forward and one backward. The backward pass frees activations immediately. Peak activation memory = P × (activations per micro-batch) = 8× per-micro-batch activations. Memory savings: 16/8 = 2× reduction. For a 30B model split 8 ways, each stage holds ~3.75B params. Per micro-batch activation memory might be ~2 GB, so GPipe peak = 32 GB vs 1F1B peak = 16 GB. This is the difference between fitting on an 80 GB H100 and OOMing.

scenario: You have a 30B model partitioned across 8 H100 GPUs using pipeline parallelism with 16 micro-batches. Compare the peak activation memory on a single GPU between GPipe (all-forward-then-all-backward) and 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) scheduling. Why does 1F1B win on memory?
title: 1F1B vs GPipe: Memory Advantage of Interleaved Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Thinking interleaving just reorders computation without reducing the bubble. The key insight is that interleaving effectively increases the number of pipeline stages (P×v) while keeping the same number of physical GPUs, making each micro-batch's forward/backward faster and reducing the bubble duration.
details.napkin_math: Standard: bubble = (P-1)/(M+P-1) = 3/11 = 27.3%. Interleaved v=2: bubble = (P-1)/(M×v+P-1) = 3/19 = 15.8%. v=4: 3/35 = 8.6%. Communication overhead: v× more cross-GPU transfers per micro-batch. NVLink: negligible. InfiniBand: activation size × v transfers × 2/BW.
details.realistic_solution: With interleaving factor v, each micro-batch pass through one virtual stage takes 1/v of the time of a standard stage (since each chunk has half the layers). The bubble fraction becomes (P-1)/(M×v + P-1). For P=4, M=8, v=2: standard bubble = 3/11 = 27.3%, interleaved bubble = 3/19 = 15.8%. With v=4: 3/35 = 8.6%. The cost is communication: each micro-batch now crosses GPU boundaries v times more, requiring v× more point-to-point sends between stages. For NVLink-connected GPUs within a node (900 GB/s on H100), this overhead is small. For cross-node InfiniBand (400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s), the communication overhead can offset the bubble reduction. Rule of thumb: use v=2-4 within a node, avoid high v across nodes.

scenario: Megatron-LM introduces interleaved pipeline schedules where each GPU holds multiple non-contiguous chunks of the model (e.g., GPU 0 holds layers 0-4 and 20-24 in a 40-layer model across 4 GPUs). Each GPU now has v=2 virtual stages. How does this reduce the pipeline bubble compared to standard 1F1B, and what is the communication cost?
title: Interleaved Pipeline Stages: Halving the Bubble

details.common_mistake: Using TP across nodes. TP requires AllReduce on every layer's output, generating enormous cross-node traffic. PP only requires point-to-point activation transfers between adjacent stages.
details.napkin_math: Tensor parallel AllReduce communication volume: proportional to batch × seq × hidden_dim (activation size), not hidden_dim² (weight size). For each AllReduce after attention/FFN: volume = batch × seq × hidden_dim × 2B. This is O(hidden_dim) not O(hidden_dim²).
details.realistic_solution: TP AllReduce volume ∝ batch × seq × hidden_dim (activation shape), not hidden_dim². Weight AllReduce is done once in DP, not per-step in TP.

scenario: You are training a 175B model on 64 MI300X GPUs (8 nodes × 8 GPUs). Within each node you have Infinity Fabric at 896 GB/s between GPUs. Between nodes you have 400 Gb/s InfiniBand. You need to decide the parallelism strategy: how do you allocate tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and data parallelism (DP)?
title: Pipeline Parallelism vs Tensor Parallelism: When to Choose Which

details.common_mistake: Setting micro-batch size too large to reduce the number of micro-batches, which inflates activation memory per micro-batch and can cause OOM, especially on the first pipeline stage.
details.napkin_math: Bubble < 10%: M > 27. Use M=32, micro_batch=32. Bubble = 3/35 = 8.6%. 1F1B activation peak = P × 4 GB = 16 GB. GPipe peak = M × 4 GB = 128 GB (OOM).
details.realistic_solution: Bubble fraction < 10%: (P-1)/(M+P-1) < 0.10. With P=4: 3/(M+3) < 0.10 → M+3 > 30 → M > 27. Minimum M = 28 micro-batches. Micro-batch size = 1024/28 ≈ 36 sequences (round to 32 for power-of-2 efficiency, giving M = 32, bubble = 3/35 = 8.6%). Activation memory per stage with 1F1B: P × (activations per micro-batch). For a 13B/4 = 3.25B params per stage, with seq_len=2048 and micro_batch=32, activation memory per micro-batch ≈ 4 GB. Peak = 4 × 4 GB = 16 GB for 1F1B. With GPipe it would be 32 × 4 GB = 128 GB — impossible on 80 GB H100. This is why 1F1B is essential for large M.

scenario: You are training a 13B model with PP=4 on H100 GPUs. Your global batch size is 1024 sequences and you want the pipeline bubble to be under 10%. What is the minimum number of micro-batches, and what micro-batch size does that imply? What is the activation memory tradeoff?
title: Micro-Batch Size Selection for Pipeline Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Balancing only by layer count without considering that embedding layers and LM heads have different compute profiles than transformer blocks. The embedding lookup is memory-bound while transformer blocks are compute-heavy.
details.napkin_math: Imbalanced: slowest stage = 1.8× others. Pipeline utilization = 1/1.8 = 55.6%. With M=16, bubble = 3/19 = 15.8%. Combined efficiency = 55.6% × 84.2% = 46.8%. Balanced: 100% × 84.2% = 84.2%. Nearly 2× throughput improvement from rebalancing alone.
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline throughput is limited by the slowest stage. If stage 0 takes 1.8× longer, all other stages idle for 44% of the time (1 - 1/1.8). Effective throughput = (theoretical throughput) / 1.8 = 56% efficiency, on top of the pipeline bubble overhead. Fix: rebalance layers so all stages have equal compute time. Move 5 transformer blocks from stage 0 to stage 1, giving [15+emb, 15, 10, 10+head]. Profile again — the embedding layer is cheap (lookup, no GEMM), so 15+emb ≈ 15 blocks of compute. The LM head involves a large GEMM (hidden → vocab_size), so 10+head ≈ 12 blocks equivalent. Better balance: [15+emb, 14, 11, 10+head] with empirical tuning. Megatron-LM provides profiling-based auto-partitioning for this reason.

scenario: Your 30B GPT model is split across 4 TPU v5e hosts using pipeline parallelism. Stage 0 has the embedding layer + 20 transformer blocks, while stages 1-3 have 10, 10, and 10 blocks plus the final LM head. Profiling shows stage 0 takes 1.8× longer than other stages per micro-batch. What is the impact on throughput, and how do you fix it?
title: Pipeline Stalls from Unbalanced Stage Partitioning

details.common_mistake: Applying full activation checkpointing uniformly. Attention activations are large (O(N²) for standard attention) but cheap to recompute, while MLP activations are smaller but expensive to recompute (large GEMMs). Selective checkpointing is optimal.
details.napkin_math: Without checkpointing: 8 × 3 GB = 24 GB activations. Selective (recompute attn): 8 × 1.2 GB = 9.6 GB. Savings: 14.4 GB (60%). Recompute overhead: ~10% training time. Full checkpoint: 8 × 0.5 GB = 4 GB but ~33% slower.
details.realistic_solution: In a transformer layer, attention activations (Q, K, V projections, attention scores if not using FlashAttention) dominate: ~60-70% of activation memory. MLP activations (up-projection, activation, down-projection intermediates) are ~30-40%. With selective checkpointing — recompute attention, store MLP — per micro-batch activation drops from 3 GB to ~1.2 GB (store only MLP intermediates). Peak with 1F1B = 8 × 1.2 GB = 9.6 GB, saving 14.4 GB (60% reduction). Recomputation cost: attention is ~40% of layer FLOPS but is fast to recompute with FlashAttention (fused kernel, no HBM reads for intermediates). Effective training slowdown: ~8-12% from recomputation. With FlashAttention-2, the recomputation is nearly free because it was already IO-optimized.

scenario: You are training a 70B model with PP=8, TP=8, and 32 micro-batches on 64 H100 GPUs using 1F1B scheduling. Each pipeline stage holds ~8.75B parameters. Without activation checkpointing, peak activation memory per stage is 24 GB (P=8 stored micro-batches × 3 GB each). With selective activation checkpointing (recompute attention but store MLP activations), how much memory do you save per stage, and what is the recomputation cost?
title: Pipeline Parallelism Activation Checkpointing Interaction

details.common_mistake: Assuming zero-bubble means zero overhead. The W pass requires storing an extra set of weight gradients and introduces memory pressure. Also, the W passes accumulated during bubble slots introduce gradient staleness if not carefully synchronized.
details.napkin_math: Standard 1F1B: bubble = (P-1)/(M+P-1). P=8, M=24: bubble = 7/31 = 22.6%. Zero-bubble: fills 7 bubble slots with W passes. Extra memory: 7 × activation_per_microbatch. If act = 2 GB: 14 GB extra. Utilization: ~97-99% vs 77.4%.
details.realistic_solution: In standard 1F1B, the backward pass computes both dL/dx (input gradient, needed by previous stage) and dL/dW (weight gradient, needed for optimizer step) together. Zero-bubble scheduling splits these: B (backward-input) runs during the normal schedule to maintain pipeline flow, while W (backward-weight) is deferred to fill bubble slots. This works because dL/dW doesn't block the pipeline — no other stage depends on it. The result: the pipeline bubble (P-1 slots) is filled with W computations. Memory cost: each deferred W must store the activations needed for the weight gradient, requiring ~(P-1) additional micro-batches of activation storage. For P=8, this is 7 extra activation copies. It is not truly zero-bubble in the strict sense — it trades memory for bubble elimination and requires enough deferred W work to fill the bubble slots exactly. In practice, it achieves >95% pipeline utilization vs ~70-85% for standard 1F1B.

scenario: Recent work on zero-bubble pipeline parallelism (ZB-H1, ZB-H2) claims to eliminate pipeline bubbles by splitting the backward pass into two parts: backward-for-input (B) and backward-for-weights (W), then scheduling W during what would have been bubble time. Explain the mechanism, its memory cost, and whether it truly achieves zero bubble.
title: Pipeline Bubble in Zero-Bubble Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Thinking pipeline parallelism helps inference latency. For a single request, PP increases TTFT because the request must traverse all P stages sequentially. PP is a throughput optimization, not a latency optimization.
details.napkin_math: PP=8, 5ms/stage. TTFT = 40ms. Per-token decode = 40ms. 200 tokens = 8.04s. Without PP: TTFT=5ms, per-token=5ms, 200 tokens = 1.005s. PP adds 8× latency. Throughput gain: 8 concurrent request streams at 200 tok/s each = 1600 tok/s aggregate.
details.realistic_solution: TTFT for a single request = P × stage_latency = 8 × 5ms = 40ms (the prefill pass must go through all 8 stages sequentially). Without PP, the same model on one GPU (if it fit) would have TTFT = 5ms. For decoding, each token still requires 8 sequential stages: per-token latency = 8 × 5ms = 40ms, not 5ms. Total generation time for 200 tokens = 40ms TTFT + 200 × 40ms decode = 8.04 seconds. The throughput advantage comes from continuous batching: while token t for request A is at stage 3, token t-1 for request B can be at stage 2, etc. With 8 requests in flight, the pipeline stays full and throughput = 1 token / 5ms / request = 200 tok/s per request stream. But single-request latency is always 8× worse than non-pipelined. This is why most inference deployments prefer TP (splits each layer) over PP (splits across layers).

scenario: You deploy a 175B model using PP=8 across MI300X GPUs for inference serving. Each stage takes 5ms per token. A user request generates 200 tokens. What is the time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency penalty from the pipeline, and how does continuous batching interact with pipeline parallelism for inference?
title: Pipeline Drain Latency in Inference Serving

details.common_mistake: Thinking mmap is always faster. For cold start with no page cache, mmap incurs page faults on every access, which can be slower than a bulk sequential read due to random 4KB page fault overhead.
details.napkin_math: Sequential read: 14 GB / 7 GB/s = 2.0s + 0.44s PCIe = 2.4s cold start. mmap cold: ~3-5s (page fault overhead). mmap warm: <0.1s (page cache hit). Multi-process savings: 4 replicas × 14 GB = 56 GB with malloc vs 14 GB shared with mmap.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy 1 (malloc + read): Allocates 14 GB in RAM, then sequentially reads the file. Time = 14 GB / 7 GB/s = 2.0 seconds. Memory: 14 GB resident immediately. Then cudaMemcpy to GPU: 14 GB / 32 GB/s (PCIe 5.0) = 0.44s. Total cold start: ~2.4s. Strategy 2 (mmap): Maps the file into virtual address space instantly (~0ms). Pages are loaded on demand via page faults. If you then copy to GPU, each page fault triggers a 4KB read — thousands of faults. Cold start can be slower (3-5s) due to fault overhead. However, mmap wins for: (1) warm restarts — pages stay in kernel page cache, no re-read needed, (2) multi-process serving — N processes share the same physical pages via copy-on-write, using 14 GB total instead of N × 14 GB, (3) partial model loading — only accessed layers are paged in. For inference serving with multiple replicas, mmap saves (N-1) × 14 GB of host RAM.

scenario: You serve a 7B model (14 GB in FP16) on an H100 with 80 GB HBM. The model is stored on a local NVMe SSD (7 GB/s sequential read). Compare two loading strategies: (1) traditional load with malloc + read(), and (2) mmap the model file. What are the cold-start times, memory implications, and when does each approach win?
title: mmap for Zero-Copy Model Loading

details.common_mistake: Assuming mmap eliminates all memory pressure. The OS still needs to manage page tables and can evict pages under memory pressure, causing latency spikes from re-faulting.
details.napkin_math: Page fault overhead: 6GB model / 128KB page size = 49,152 page faults. Each fault takes 120μs. Total = 49,152 × 120μs = 5,898,240μs = 5.9 seconds (not ~2 seconds — 2 seconds would require 16,667 faults or 40μs per fault).
details.realistic_solution: 6GB / 128KB = 49,152 page faults × 120μs = 5.9 seconds of fault overhead (not ~2 seconds).

scenario: You deploy a 3B parameter model (6 GB in FP16) on a Jetson Orin with 32 GB unified memory (shared between CPU and GPU). The device runs 3 concurrent inference services. Using traditional loading, each service loads its own copy: 3 × 6 GB = 18 GB, leaving only 14 GB for activations, KV cache, and OS. How does mmap with unified memory solve this, and what are the latency implications?
title: Demand Paging for Edge Model Deployment

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that safetensors' zero-copy design aligns tensor data to page boundaries, making mmap efficient. Legacy formats like pickle-based .bin files require deserialization and cannot be mmap'd directly.
details.napkin_math: 50 models × 14 GB = 700 GB total. Host RAM available: 256 GB. mmap + page cache: ~18 hot models fit. Cold start: 2.5s (mmap cold) vs 0.22s (cache hit). NVMe read: 2.0s + 0.22s = 2.2s consistent.
details.realistic_solution: Approach 1 (NVMe read): 14 GB / 7 GB/s NVMe = 2.0s read + 14 GB / 64 GB/s (PCIe 5.0 x16) = 0.22s to GPU. Total: ~2.2s. Meets target. Approach 2 (mmap safetensors): Maps instantly. With MAP_POPULATE or madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL), kernel prefetches pages. First copy to GPU triggers fault-in: ~2.5-3.5s cold (page fault overhead). But subsequent loads: if pages remain in page cache, <0.5s. Best for the multi-model scenario — the OS LRU page cache naturally keeps hot models in memory. Approach 3 (host RAM pool): Pre-load all 50 models = 50 × 14 GB = 700 GB host RAM. Expensive but zero cold start (just cudaMemcpy at 64 GB/s = 0.22s). Hybrid approach: mmap all 50 models, let OS page cache manage which are resident (~200 GB RAM for top-15 hot models), cold models fault-in from NVMe at ~2.5s. Cost-effective and self-tuning.

scenario: Your inference platform serves 50 different fine-tuned 7B models from a shared MI300X GPU pool. Models are stored as safetensors files (which support zero-copy mmap) on NVMe. When a cold request arrives for an unloaded model, you need sub-3-second cold start. Compare three approaches: (1) load from NVMe via read(), (2) mmap the safetensors file, (3) keep models in host RAM and cudaMemcpy on demand.
title: mmap vs Safetensors: Cold Start Optimization for Model Serving

details.common_mistake: Blaming the model size alone. The issue is demand paging — mmap doesn't load data until accessed. The 4-second delay is page faults during the first forward pass, not at mmap() call time.
details.napkin_math: mmap cold: 512K pages × ~8 μs avg per fault = ~4s. With MADV_WILLNEED: background prefetch at 2.1 GB/s = ~1s. Sequential touch thread: 2 GB / 2.1 GB/s = 0.95s. Warm: 0s (page cache). UFS 4.0 would cut cold time to 0.5s (4.2 GB/s).
details.realistic_solution: When mmap() is called, the OS creates virtual address mappings but loads no data. During the first forward pass, each weight access triggers a page fault (4 KB pages). The OS loads pages from UFS storage on demand. For 2 GB: 2 GB / 4 KB = 512K page faults. Even with readahead (128 KB chunks), that is ~16K faults × 250 μs each = ~4 seconds. Subsequent runs are fast because pages remain in the page cache. Fixes: (1) madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) immediately after mmap to trigger background readahead — starts loading before first inference. (2) madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL) for sequential readahead optimization. (3) On Android, use MAP_POPULATE if available (not all kernels support it). (4) Spawn a background thread that touches every page (memcpy to /dev/null) immediately after mmap to warm the cache while the UI loads. This converts random faults to sequential I/O: 2 GB / 2.1 GB/s = ~1 second.

scenario: You deploy a 1B parameter model (2 GB in INT8) for on-device inference on a mobile phone with 8 GB RAM and UFS 3.1 storage (~2.1 GB/s sequential read). Users report the first inference after app launch takes 4 seconds, but subsequent inferences are instant. Your loading code uses mmap. Diagnose the cold start behavior and propose a fix.
title: Mobile mmap: Loading Models from Flash Storage

details.common_mistake: Assuming mmap automatically shares GPU memory too. mmap shares host memory pages between processes, but each process that calls cudaMemcpy creates a separate GPU memory allocation. You need CUDA IPC or a shared GPU memory pool.
details.napkin_math: Without mmap: 8 × 26 GB = 208 GB host RAM (OOM on 256 GB). With mmap: 26 GB shared. Savings: 182 GB. GPU without sharing: 8 × 26 GB = 208 GB (impossible on 80 GB). With CUDA IPC: 26 GB shared + 8 × ~6 GB KV cache = 74 GB. Fits on H100.
details.realistic_solution: Host side: All 8 processes mmap the same safetensors file. The OS shares physical pages via copy-on-write, using 26 GB host RAM (not 208 GB). GPU side: Option A — one process loads weights to GPU, others access via CUDA IPC (cudaIpcGetMemHandle/cudaIpcOpenMemHandle). All 8 processes share one 26 GB GPU allocation. Option B — use NVIDIA MPS (Multi-Process Service) with a single GPU context. Weights loaded once, shared across all processes. Option C — use a serving framework like vLLM or TensorRT-LLM that manages a single weight copy with multiple request streams. Architecture: mmap safetensors → single cudaMemcpy → CUDA IPC handles distributed to workers. Host RAM: 26 GB (shared). GPU RAM: 26 GB weights + 8 × KV cache per worker. Remaining 80 - 26 = 54 GB for KV caches and activations.

scenario: You run a multi-tenant inference platform where 8 worker processes on one H100 server each serve the same 13B model (26 GB FP16). Without mmap, each process loads its own copy in host memory: 8 × 26 GB = 208 GB host RAM, exceeding your 256 GB system memory. Design a memory-efficient architecture using mmap and describe how GPU memory is managed.
title: Shared mmap for Multi-Tenant GPU Inference

details.common_mistake: Ignoring NUMA topology entirely. Default mmap uses first-touch policy — pages are allocated on the NUMA node of the first thread that faults them in. If thread 0 (on NUMA node 0) faults all pages, then GPU 1's cudaMemcpy must cross the inter-socket QPI/UPI link.
details.napkin_math: Local NUMA DMA to GPU: 200 GB/s effective → 14 GB in 70ms. Cross-NUMA: UPI bottleneck at 40 GB/s → 14 GB in 350ms. Slowdown: 5× for DMA path. Total with PCIe 5.0: local = 14 GB / min(200, 64) = 0.22s. Cross-NUMA = 14 GB / min(40, 64) = 0.35s. 59% slower.
details.realistic_solution: The 40% slowdown is because mmap'd pages reside on NUMA node 0 (first-touch policy). cudaMemcpy to GPU 1 must: (1) read pages from NUMA 0's DRAM, (2) traverse the UPI link (~40 GB/s vs ~200 GB/s local), (3) cross PCIe to GPU 1. The UPI hop adds ~2.5× latency per page. Solutions: (1) Use mbind() or numactl to explicitly bind mmap pages to the target NUMA node before accessing them: one mmap for GPU 0's weights on node 0, another for GPU 1 on node 1. Cost: 2× host memory (28 GB total). (2) Use NUMA-interleaved allocation (MPOL_INTERLEAVE) for balanced average performance. (3) Use CUDA unified memory with cudaMemAdvise(cudaMemAdviseSetPreferredLocation) to let the GPU driver handle NUMA-aware placement. (4) For pinned memory: cudaMallocHost with NUMA-aware allocation via numa_alloc_onnode(). Best practice: always set NUMA affinity for GPU-bound processes with numactl --cpunodebind=N --membind=N.

scenario: You have a dual-socket server with 2 CPUs, each with its own memory controller and PCIe root complex. GPU 0 is on NUMA node 0, GPU 1 on NUMA node 1. You mmap a 14 GB model file and notice that cudaMemcpy to GPU 1 is 40% slower than to GPU 0. Diagnose the NUMA issue and architect a solution for multi-GPU mmap-based model loading.
title: mmap and NUMA: The Hidden Latency Trap

details.common_mistake: Using simple round-robin or random routing, which treats all backends equally and causes slower backends to accumulate queues while faster ones sit idle.
details.napkin_math: Round-robin: 16 GPUs, each gets 1/16 of load. H100 at 50 tok/s saturates sooner than MI300X at 65 tok/s. Optimal allocation: MI300X handles 65/(50+65) = 56.5% of requests. WLC achieves this naturally. Queue time reduction: ~30% vs round-robin.
details.realistic_solution: Use weighted least-connections (WLC) routing. Assign weights proportional to throughput capacity: MI300X weight = 65, H100 weight = 50. Route each request to the backend with the lowest (active_connections / weight) ratio. This naturally sends more requests to faster MI300X GPUs. Implementation: (1) The load balancer tracks active request count per backend. (2) For each new request, select backend with min(active / weight). (3) When requests complete, decrement the counter. Enhancement: add latency-aware routing — track P50 response time per backend and route to the backend with lowest estimated completion time (active_connections × avg_latency). This adapts to thermal throttling, memory pressure, or degraded GPUs automatically. For ML-specific optimization: consider request properties (long prompts route to MI300X with more memory for KV cache, short prompts to either).

scenario: Your ML serving cluster has a mix of 8 H100 GPUs (80 GB, faster) and 8 MI300X GPUs (192 GB, higher memory). Both serve the same 70B model. H100s handle 50 tok/s per request and MI300X handles 65 tok/s. A round-robin load balancer causes H100s to queue up while MI300X GPUs finish faster. How do you design a load-balancing strategy that accounts for heterogeneous hardware?
title: Least-Connections Routing for Heterogeneous GPU Serving

details.common_mistake: Using modular hashing (model_id % num_gpus). When a GPU is removed or added, nearly all model-to-GPU mappings change, causing a storm of cold starts across the cluster.
details.napkin_math: Modular hash: 1 GPU failure → 97% remapping → 19 cold starts × 3s = 57s of degraded service. Consistent hash: 1 GPU failure → 3% remapping → 1 cold start × 3s. With mmap warm cache: 0.5s. With shadow replicas: 0s failover.
details.realistic_solution: With modular hashing (model_id % 32), removing one GPU changes the mapping for ~31 of 32 GPUs (97% disruption). With consistent hashing, each GPU occupies points on a hash ring. Removing one GPU only remaps its models to the next GPU on the ring — affecting only 1/32 ≈ 3% of mappings. Using virtual nodes (150-200 per physical GPU), the load stays balanced. Cold-start mitigation: (1) when a GPU is flagged for replacement, pre-warm the replacement by proactively loading the models that will hash to it, (2) maintain a shadow copy of each model on a secondary GPU (replica ring), so failover is instant, (3) use the mmap approach — models stay in host page cache, and remapped models load in <0.5s instead of 3s if pages are warm. Trade-off: shadow copies cost 2× GPU memory but eliminate cold starts entirely.

scenario: Your inference platform serves 20 fine-tuned model variants across 32 H100 GPUs. Loading a model cold takes 3 seconds. You use consistent hashing to route requests for the same model variant to the same GPU, keeping models warm. When a GPU fails and is replaced, how does consistent hashing minimize disruption compared to modular hashing, and how do you handle the cold-start penalty?
title: Consistent Hashing for Model-Aware Request Routing

details.common_mistake: Thinking the model needs to be reloaded per turn. The model weights are already loaded on each node. The issue is the KV cache — multi-turn conversations have accumulated KV cache from prior turns, and round-robin sends turn N to a different node than turn N-1, requiring full recomputation of the KV cache.
details.napkin_math: 2000-token history recompute: 2000 tokens × 1ms/token prefill = 2s added latency per turn. With session affinity: 0s recompute. KV cache per conversation (7B model, 2K context): 32 layers × 2 × 4096 × 2K × 2 bytes = ~1 GB. 4 concurrent conversations per node = 4 GB KV cache.
details.realistic_solution: When round-robin sends turn 2 of a conversation to a different node than turn 1, the new node has no KV cache for the prior context. It must reprocess all previous tokens (prefix recomputation) before generating the response, adding latency proportional to the conversation history length. For a conversation with 2000 tokens of history, this adds ~1-2 seconds of unnecessary prefill. Solution: session-affinity routing (sticky sessions). Hash the conversation_id to a specific node and route all turns of that conversation to the same node, preserving the KV cache. Implementation: (1) hash(conversation_id) → node_id, (2) if node is overloaded, migrate the conversation (send serialized KV cache to new node, ~50 MB for 2K context on 7B model, takes ~10ms over 10GbE), (3) set KV cache TTL to expire idle conversations and free GPU memory. This is exactly what prefix caching in vLLM solves at the framework level.

scenario: You run a distributed inference service across 4 edge nodes (each with one GPU), serving a conversational AI. Users report that multi-turn conversations are much slower than single-turn queries. Your load balancer uses round-robin. Diagnose the problem and propose a solution.
title: KV-Cache-Aware Load Balancing at the Edge

details.common_mistake: Thinking FlashAttention changes the mathematical computation. It computes the exact same attention — it just changes the memory access pattern by tiling the computation to fit in fast SRAM instead of materializing the full N×N matrix in slow HBM.
details.napkin_math: Standard HBM traffic: Q,K,V reads (3×N×d) + S write (N²) + S read (N²) + O write (N×d) ≈ 2N² + 4Nd. FlashAttention: Q,K,V reads (3Nd) + O write (Nd) = 4Nd. Ratio: (2N² + 4Nd) / 4Nd ≈ N/2d for large N. N=4096, d=128: 16× fewer HBM accesses.
details.realistic_solution: Each tile must hold: Q_tile (B_r × d), K_tile (B_c × d), S_tile (B_r × B_c), and V_tile (B_c × d), plus output O_tile (B_r × d) and running statistics (row max, row sum). With d=128 and BF16 (2 bytes): Q_tile = B_r × 128 × 2 = 256×B_r bytes. K_tile = B_c × 128 × 2 = 256×B_c bytes. S_tile = B_r × B_c × 2 bytes. Total SRAM ≤ 256 KB = 262,144 bytes. With B_r = B_c = 128: Q=32KB, K=32KB, S=32KB, V=32KB, O=32KB = 160KB. Fits with margin. Standard attention reads Q,K,V from HBM, writes N²-sized attention matrix to HBM, reads it back for V multiplication — total HBM traffic O(N² × d). FlashAttention: reads Q,K,V from HBM once (O(N×d)), computes S tiles in SRAM (never written to HBM), accumulates output in SRAM. HBM traffic drops from O(N²) to O(N×d). For N=4096, d=128: ratio = N/d = 32× fewer HBM accesses.

scenario: An H100 GPU has 256 KB of shared memory (SRAM) per SM. Standard attention for a 70B model with hidden_dim=8192, num_heads=64 (head_dim=128) computes Q×K^T which produces an N×N attention matrix per head. FlashAttention tiles this computation. For a sequence length of 4096, calculate the tile sizes that fit in SRAM and explain why tiling reduces HBM reads from O(N²) to O(N).
title: FlashAttention Tiling: Why SRAM Size Determines Tile Shape

details.common_mistake: Expecting the speedup to equal the theoretical IO reduction ratio. In practice, FlashAttention-2 also benefits from better SM utilization (reduced thread divergence, warp-level parallelism) but is partially offset by the extra recomputation in the backward pass.
details.napkin_math: Standard HBM traffic: ~34.4 GB for attention matrices. FlashAttention: ~1.07 GB. IO reduction: 32×. But not purely IO-bound: standard at 85ms vs min IO time of 6.5ms → 7.6% IO efficiency. FlashAttention achieves ~70% compute utilization. Expected: 17-25ms. Speedup: 3.4-5×.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention is memory-bandwidth bound: it must write and read the N×N attention matrix from HBM. HBM traffic ≈ 2×N² × num_heads × batch × 2 bytes = 2 × 8192² × 32 × 4 × 2 = 34.4 GB. At MI300X's 5.3 TB/s: minimum time = 34.4 GB / 5.3 TB/s = 6.5ms just for the attention matrix IO. But standard attention also materializes intermediate tensors, has kernel launch overhead, and poor cache behavior, explaining the 85ms total. FlashAttention-2 reduces HBM traffic to O(N×d): ~4 × N × d × num_heads × batch × 2 = 4 × 8192 × 128 × 32 × 4 × 2 = 1.07 GB. This makes the kernel compute-bound rather than memory-bound. Empirical speedup on MI300X: 3-5× for seq_len=8192 in forward pass. Expected time: 85ms / 4 ≈ 21ms. Published benchmarks show FlashAttention-2 achieves ~70% of peak TFLOPS on MI300X for these dimensions.

scenario: You benchmark standard PyTorch attention (torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention without flash backend) vs FlashAttention-2 on an MI300X for a 7B model with seq_len=8192, batch_size=4, 32 heads, head_dim=128. Standard attention takes 85ms for the forward pass. Estimate the FlashAttention-2 speedup using the IO-complexity reduction.
title: FlashAttention-2 vs Standard Attention: Wall-Clock Speedup

details.common_mistake: Thinking PagedAttention changes the attention computation itself. It is a memory management technique — it applies virtual memory concepts (paging) to KV cache allocation, not to the attention algorithm.
details.napkin_math: Without paging: 20 requests × 2 GB (pre-allocated) = 40 GB. Average actual use: 20 × 0.5 GB = 10 GB. Waste: 30 GB (75%). With paging: 80+ requests × 0.5 GB actual = 40 GB. No waste. Throughput: 4× improvement in concurrent requests.
details.realistic_solution: Without PagedAttention, each request pre-allocates a contiguous 2 GB buffer for max context length (4096 tokens), even if the actual context is 500 tokens. Fragmentation and over-allocation waste ~60-80% of KV cache memory. PagedAttention divides KV cache into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 16 tokens per block). Blocks are allocated on demand as the sequence grows, stored non-contiguously in GPU memory (like OS page tables). A block table maps logical positions to physical blocks. Benefits: (1) No internal fragmentation — only the last block has waste (≤15 tokens). (2) No external fragmentation — any free block can be used by any request. (3) Memory sharing — common prefixes between requests can share the same physical blocks (copy-on-write). Typical utilization improves from 20-40% to >95%. Throughput gain: with average 1000-token contexts, actual KV memory per request = 0.5 GB vs 2 GB allocated. Serving capacity: 80-90 concurrent requests vs 20. A 4× throughput improvement.

scenario: You serve a 13B model on an H100 (80 GB HBM3). Each request's KV cache for a 4096-token context consumes 2 GB. With contiguous memory allocation, you can serve 20 concurrent requests (40 GB KV cache + 26 GB weights + overhead). Many requests use less than 4096 tokens, wasting allocated but unused memory. How does PagedAttention (vLLM) improve utilization, and what is the throughput gain?
title: PagedAttention: Virtual Memory for KV Cache

details.common_mistake: Thinking Ring Attention simply shards the KV cache and does AllReduce. It uses a ring topology where each GPU holds a chunk of the sequence and rotates KV blocks around the ring, overlapping communication with computation.
details.napkin_math: KV cache total: 1M × 128 × 96 × 80 × 2 × 2B = 3.9 TB. Per GPU: 3.9 TB / 8 = 490 GB. Fits in 192 GB? No — but Ring Attention doesn't store all KV simultaneously. Each GPU stores only 2 chunks at a time: current + receiving = 2 × 490/8 = 122 GB. Fits in 192 GB.
details.realistic_solution: Ring Attention partitions the 1M sequence into 8 chunks of 125K tokens each. Each GPU holds Q for its chunk and computes attention against K,V blocks from all chunks. The ring protocol: (1) Each GPU starts with its local K,V chunk. (2) Compute FlashAttention between local Q and the current K,V chunk. (3) While computing, asynchronously send K,V to the next GPU in the ring and receive from the previous GPU. (4) After computation, switch to the newly received K,V chunk. (5) Repeat for 8 rounds. Communication volume per GPU per round: K,V for 125K tokens = 125K × 128 × 2 × 2 bytes = 64 MB per head × 96 heads = 6.1 GB per round. At 400 Gbps IB: 6.1 GB / 50 GB/s = 122ms. Compute per round: FlashAttention on 125K×125K block ≈ 200ms. Since compute > communication, the overlap is nearly perfect (communication is hidden). Total: ~8 rounds × 200ms = 1.6 seconds for 1M context attention, vs impossible on a single GPU.

scenario: You need to process a 1M token context on 8 MI300X GPUs (192 GB HBM3 each). Even with FlashAttention, the KV cache for 1M tokens at 128 head_dim × 96 heads × 80 layers × 2 (K+V) × 2 bytes = ~3.9 TB, far exceeding any single GPU. Explain how Ring Attention distributes this computation and its communication pattern.
title: Ring Attention for Million-Token Contexts

details.common_mistake: Thinking prefix caching simply stores the attention output. It caches the KV (key-value) tensors for the shared prefix, which are the intermediate state needed by all subsequent tokens' attention computation.
details.napkin_math: Optimization saves 1000 GPU-seconds per minute. Annual savings: 1000 GPU-s/min × 525,600 min/yr = 5.256×10^8 GPU-seconds = 5.256×10^8/3600 = 146,000 GPU-hours/yr. No — 1000 GPU-s/min × 60min/hr = 60,000 GPU-s/hr = 16.7 GPU-hours saved/hr. Annual: 16.7 GPU-hr/hr × 8760hr = 146,000 GPU-hr/yr. At $2/GPU-hr: $292K/yr (not $17.5K — $17.5K would be only 8,750 GPU-hours/yr).
details.realistic_solution: 1000 GPU-s/min = 16.7 GPU-hours/hr saved. Annual: 16.7 × 8760 = 146,000 GPU-hr × $2/hr = $292K/yr (not $17.5K).

scenario: Your chatbot service uses a 2000-token system prompt prepended to every user request. You serve 1000 requests/minute on H100 GPUs. Each prefill token takes 0.5ms. Without prefix caching, every request recomputes the system prompt's KV cache. Calculate the wasted compute and explain how prefix caching (RadixAttention) eliminates it.
title: Prefix Caching: Amortizing System Prompts

details.common_mistake: Thinking FlashAttention stores the attention matrix somewhere compressed or approximated. It stores only the output O and the log-sum-exp statistics (row-wise) from the forward pass — enough to exactly recompute any tile of the attention matrix on the fly during backward.
details.napkin_math: Stored: O (N×d×2B per head) + logsumexp (N×4B per head). For N=8192, d=128, 64 heads: O = 128 MB, logsumexp = 2 MB. Standard: attention matrix = N² × 64 × 2B = 8 GB. Memory savings: 62×. Extra backward FLOPS: ~1 forward pass = 2×N²×d per head = negligible vs HBM savings.
details.realistic_solution: During the forward pass, FlashAttention stores: (1) the output O (N×d per head), and (2) the log-sum-exp (logsumexp) statistics per row (N values per head) — these are the softmax normalization constants needed for numerically stable recomputation. Total extra storage: O(N×d) instead of O(N²). During the backward pass, for each tile, FlashAttention recomputes the local attention scores S = Q_tile × K_tile^T in SRAM, applies softmax using the stored logsumexp, and computes gradients — all in SRAM without HBM writes. The recomputation costs one extra matrix multiply per tile (the Q×K^T recomputation). Total extra FLOPS: approximately equal to one forward pass worth of attention computation. For the full transformer, attention is ~1/3 of FLOPS, so the backward recomputation adds ~33% to the backward attention compute. But since FlashAttention-2 achieves 70% peak FLOPS (vs <30% for standard attention), the wall-clock time is still 2-3× faster despite the extra computation.

scenario: FlashAttention does not store the N×N attention matrix during the forward pass — it computes attention in SRAM tiles and discards intermediate results. During the backward pass for training, the attention matrix is needed to compute gradients. How does FlashAttention handle this, and what is the extra compute cost?
title: FlashAttention Backward Pass: The Recomputation Trade

details.common_mistake: Assuming TPU's FlashAttention implementation is identical to GPU's. TPU v5e has a different memory hierarchy: 16 MB of VMEM (vector memory) per core vs 256 KB SRAM per GPU SM, and uses a systolic array rather than CUDA cores.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e: 16 MB VMEM. Attention tile (B_r=B_c=512, d=128, BF16): Q=128KB, K=128KB, S=512KB, V=128KB = ~900KB. Fits easily in 16 MB. GPU (256 KB SRAM): B_r=B_c=128 → Q=32KB, K=32KB, S=32KB = ~160KB. TPU can use 4× larger tiles → 4× fewer rounds.
details.realistic_solution: Key architectural differences: (1) TPU v5e VMEM is 16 MB per core — 62× larger than GPU's 256 KB SRAM per SM. This allows much larger tiles, reducing the number of tiling rounds. (2) TPU uses systolic arrays optimized for matrix multiplies, not general CUDA cores. Tiling must align with the systolic array's preferred dimensions (typically 128×128). (3) XLA's default attention fuses softmax but may still materialize the N×N matrix in HBM for large N. JAX Pallas allows writing TPU-native tiled attention that keeps all intermediates in VMEM. (4) TPU's MXU (Matrix Multiply Unit) achieves >90% utilization for well-shaped tiles, vs ~70% for FlashAttention-2 on GPU. Is it worth it? For seq_len > 2048, yes — Pallas FlashAttention avoids the O(N²) HBM traffic. For shorter sequences, XLA's auto-generated kernels are competitive because the attention matrix fits in VMEM at small N. Google's internal models use Pallas-based attention for all long-context training.

scenario: Your team trains a 40B model on TPU v5e pods. The XLA compiler generates attention kernels automatically, but they materialize the full attention matrix in HBM (16 GB per chip). A colleague suggests writing custom FlashAttention-style kernels using JAX Pallas. What are the architectural differences between GPU SRAM-based FlashAttention and TPU's approach, and is the manual kernel worth the effort?
title: FlashAttention on TPU: XLA Attention vs Pallas Kernels

details.common_mistake: Thinking that any operation involving large matrix multiplies must be compute-bound. The key issue is that standard attention writes and reads the N×N intermediate matrix from HBM, destroying the arithmetic intensity.
details.napkin_math: H100 ridge point: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOPS/byte. Standard attention AI: 120 (memory-bound). FlashAttention AI: 2048 (compute-bound). FlashAttention is 17× above the ridge, achieving near-peak compute utilization.
details.realistic_solution: The H100's compute-to-bandwidth ratio (the 'ridge point' on the roofline) = 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOPS/byte. Any kernel with arithmetic intensity < 295 is memory-bound. Standard attention per head: FLOPS = 2 × N² × d (Q×K^T) + 2 × N² × d (attn×V) = 4N²d. HBM bytes = 3Nd × 2 (read Q,K,V) + N² × 2 (write S) + N² × 2 (read S) + Nd × 2 (write O) = 8Nd + 4N². Arithmetic intensity = 4N²d / (8Nd + 4N²) = 4Nd / (8d + 4N). For N=4096, d=128: AI = 4×4096×128 / (8×128 + 4×4096) = 2,097,152 / 17,408 = 120 FLOPS/byte. This is well below the 295 ridge point — memory-bound. FlashAttention eliminates the N² HBM terms: bytes ≈ 8Nd. AI = 4N²d / 8Nd = N/2 = 2048 FLOPS/byte. Far above the ridge — compute-bound.

scenario: Explain why standard attention is memory-bound on modern GPUs despite involving massive matrix multiplications. Use the arithmetic intensity (FLOPS/byte) concept. For an H100 with 989 TFLOPS FP16 and 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, what arithmetic intensity is needed to be compute-bound, and what is standard attention's actual arithmetic intensity?
title: IO-Awareness: Roofline Model for Attention Kernels

details.common_mistake: Confusing FlashDecoding with speculative decoding. FlashDecoding is about parallelizing the attention computation across KV cache blocks during single-token generation, not about predicting future tokens.
details.napkin_math: Standard decode: 64 heads → 64 thread blocks on 132 SMs = 48% utilization. FlashDecoding P=16: 64 × 16 = 1024 blocks → 100% utilization. For 32K context: standard = 2ms, FlashDecoding = 0.35ms. Speedup: ~5.7×. Reduction overhead: ~0.05ms.
details.realistic_solution: In standard FlashAttention during decode (batch=1, query_len=1), the single query token must attend to N KV tokens. The computation is: for each KV block, compute QK^T, softmax, and weighted sum. With one thread block per attention head, only num_heads thread blocks are active (e.g., 64 for a 70B model). On an H100 with 132 SMs, this leaves half the SMs idle. FlashDecoding splits the KV cache into P partitions (e.g., P=16) and assigns each partition to a separate thread block. Each block computes a partial softmax and weighted sum over its partition. A final reduction kernel combines partial results using the logsumexp trick (numerically stable online softmax). This increases parallelism from num_heads to num_heads × P thread blocks. With 64 heads × 16 partitions = 1024 thread blocks, all 132 SMs are fully utilized. Speedup for decode: 4-8× for long contexts (32K+). For short contexts (≤2K), the overhead of the reduction kernel exceeds the benefit.

scenario: During autoregressive decoding, each new token attends to all previous tokens. For a single query token with a 32K context on an H100, standard FlashAttention iterates over KV blocks sequentially within one thread block, under-utilizing the GPU's 132 SMs. FlashDecoding parallelizes across KV blocks. Explain the mechanism and the throughput improvement.
title: FlashDecoding: Parallelizing Attention During Inference

details.common_mistake: Thinking GQA/MQA changes the number of query heads. Only the K and V heads are reduced. Each query head still operates independently — it just shares K,V with other heads in its group.
details.napkin_math: MHA KV cache: 64 × 128 × 2 × 2B × 4096 × 80 = 10.0 GB. GQA: 8/64 × 10.0 = 1.25 GB (8× reduction). MQA: 1/64 × 10.0 = 160 MB (64× reduction). Concurrent requests at 80 GB: MHA = 5, GQA = 40+, MQA = hundreds.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per token per layer = num_kv_heads × head_dim × 2 (K+V) × 2 bytes (BF16). MHA (64 KV heads): 64 × 128 × 2 × 2 = 32 KB/token/layer. Total for 4096 tokens × 80 layers: 32 KB × 4096 × 80 = 10.0 GB. GQA (8 KV groups): 8 × 128 × 2 × 2 = 4 KB/token/layer. Total: 4 KB × 4096 × 80 = 1.25 GB. MQA (1 KV head): 1 × 128 × 2 × 2 = 0.5 KB/token/layer. Total: 0.5 KB × 4096 × 80 = 160 MB. For FlashAttention tiling: with GQA/MQA, multiple query heads share the same K,V tiles. When processing a tile of K,V, FlashAttention can compute attention for all 8 query heads in the group simultaneously, improving data reuse. The K,V tile is loaded once from HBM but used 8× (GQA) or 64× (MQA), boosting arithmetic intensity further.

scenario: A 70B model uses 64 attention heads with head_dim=128. Compare the KV cache memory at 4096 context length for three configurations: (1) multi-head attention (MHA, 64 KV heads), (2) grouped-query attention (GQA, 8 KV groups), and (3) multi-query attention (MQA, 1 KV head). What are the implications for FlashAttention's tiling strategy?
title: Multi-Query vs Grouped-Query Attention Memory Savings

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that activation memory includes more than just the attention matrix — there are also MLP activations, layer norm intermediates, and residual connections. But the attention matrix is the quadratic bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Standard: attention matrix = 80N² bytes. 2 GB → N ≤ 5181. FlashAttention: O(N) memory = 10,240N bytes. 2 GB → N ≤ 209K. With gradient checkpointing (sqrt(L) stored layers out of 40): 2 GB / 7 checkpoints ≈ 290 MB per checkpoint → supports N=28K per layer.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention activation per layer per micro-batch for the attention matrix alone: N² × num_heads × 2 bytes = N² × 40 × 2 = 80N² bytes (assuming 40 heads for 13B). For the largest single-layer allocation (dominating term): 80N² ≤ 2 GB = 2,147,483,648 bytes. N² ≤ 26,843,545. N ≤ 5181 tokens. Accounting for other activations (MLP, etc.), practical max ≈ 3000-4000 tokens. With FlashAttention: no attention matrix stored in HBM. Activation memory per layer becomes O(N×d) = N × 128 × 40 × 2 = 10,240N bytes. For 2 GB: N ≤ 209,715 tokens. However, gradient checkpointing is needed to avoid storing all layers simultaneously. With checkpointing + FlashAttention: practical max sequence length = 16K-32K tokens with the same 2 GB activation budget. FlashAttention enables 4-8× longer contexts in the same memory.

scenario: You train a 13B model on an A100 (80 GB HBM2e). Weights in BF16 = 26 GB. Optimizer states (AdamW, mixed precision) = 52 GB. Remaining HBM for activations = 2 GB. With standard attention (stores N×N matrix), what is the maximum sequence length? With FlashAttention, how does this change?
title: FlashAttention Memory Savings Enable Longer Training Contexts

details.common_mistake: Thinking FlashAttention still computes all tiles and applies the mask afterward. FlashAttention-2 skips entire tiles that are fully above the diagonal, saving both compute and memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: N=8192, B=128. Total tiles: (64)² = 4096. Below diagonal: ~2016. On diagonal: 64. Above diagonal (skipped): ~2016. FLOP savings: 2016/4096 = 49.2%. Plus diagonal tile savings: ~25% of diagonal tile FLOPS masked = additional ~0.4%. Total: ~50% FLOP reduction.
details.realistic_solution: For an N×N attention matrix tiled into (N/B_r) × (N/B_c) tiles, with causal masking: tiles fully above the diagonal are skipped entirely (no computation). Tiles on the diagonal require partial masking. Tiles fully below the diagonal compute normally. Number of full tiles (below diagonal) ≈ N²/(2B²), skipped tiles ≈ N²/(2B²), diagonal tiles ≈ N/B. FLOP savings: approximately 50% compared to full attention, because the upper triangle is never computed. FlashAttention-2 further optimizes diagonal tiles by using a specialized kernel that applies the mask during the softmax computation within SRAM, avoiding wasted FLOPS on masked positions. For non-causal attention (e.g., BERT-style), this optimization doesn't apply. Practical speedup for causal models: ~1.7-2× faster than non-causal FlashAttention at the same sequence length.

scenario: In causal (autoregressive) attention, the attention matrix is lower-triangular — tokens can only attend to previous tokens. When FlashAttention tiles the computation into B_r × B_c blocks, approximately half the tiles are entirely above the diagonal and contain only zeros. How does FlashAttention-2 exploit this for speedup, and what is the FLOP savings?
title: Causal Masking in FlashAttention: Skipping Unnecessary Tiles

details.common_mistake: Assuming that higher bandwidth always wins. FlashAttention converts attention from memory-bound to compute-bound, so the comparison shifts from bandwidth ratio to FLOPS ratio.
details.napkin_math: Standard attention speedup MI300X/H100: 5.3/3.35 = 1.58×. FlashAttention speedup MI300X/H100: 1307/989 = 1.32×. H100 ridge point: 295 FLOPS/byte. MI300X ridge point: 247 FLOPS/byte. FlashAttention AI: ~N/2 = 2048 for N=4096. Both GPUs are compute-bound with FlashAttention.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention (memory-bound): performance ∝ bandwidth. MI300X / H100 = 5.3 / 3.35 = 1.58× faster on MI300X. FlashAttention (compute-bound): performance ∝ TFLOPS. MI300X / H100 = 1307 / 989 = 1.32× faster on MI300X. The H100 benefits more from FlashAttention relative to its own baseline. Without FlashAttention, the H100 is 1.58× slower. With FlashAttention, it is only 1.32× slower. The H100's higher compute-to-bandwidth ratio (295 FLOPS/byte vs 247 for MI300X) means FlashAttention's transition to compute-bound regime favors it relatively more. However, the MI300X's 192 GB HBM (vs 80 GB) is still critical for KV cache capacity in inference — FlashAttention reduces compute overhead but doesn't change the KV cache storage requirement. The MI300X can serve 2.4× more concurrent requests purely due to memory capacity.

scenario: The MI300X has 5.3 TB/s HBM bandwidth (vs H100's 3.35 TB/s) and 1307 TFLOPS FP16 (vs 989 TFLOPS). For standard attention (memory-bound), the MI300X should be 1.58× faster due to bandwidth. For FlashAttention (compute-bound), how does the comparison change? Which GPU benefits more from FlashAttention?
title: FlashAttention on MI300X: HBM3 Bandwidth Advantage

details.common_mistake: Assuming sliding window is just a mask applied after computing full attention. With proper tiling, tiles outside the window can be skipped entirely — no computation at all, not just masking.
details.napkin_math: Full causal N=32K: FLOPS ∝ N²/2 = 536M per head. Sliding W=4096: FLOPS ∝ N×W = 134M. Savings: 75%. KV cache: full = 32K tokens × 128d × 2 × 2B = 16 MB/head. Sliding = 4K × 128 × 2 × 2B = 2 MB/head. 8× memory reduction.
details.realistic_solution: With full causal attention at N=32K: FlashAttention processes the lower triangle of the N×N matrix = N²/2 effective entries. With sliding window W=4096: each row has at most W non-zero entries. Total entries: N×W (for N>W). Compute ratio: (N×W) / (N²/2) = 2W/N = 2×4096/32768 = 25%. So 75% of FlashAttention tiles can be skipped. In tiling: for tile at position (i_block, j_block), skip if j_block's tokens are all more than W positions before i_block's tokens. Only tiles within a band of width W/B_c blocks around the diagonal are computed. KV cache savings: at generation time, each token only needs the last W=4096 tokens' KV cache, not all previous tokens. KV cache is bounded at 4096 × head_dim × 2 × 2B per head regardless of total context length. A 32K context uses the same KV cache as a 4K context, enabling memory-efficient long-context serving.

scenario: Mistral-7B uses sliding window attention with window size W=4096. For a 32K context, each token only attends to the previous 4096 tokens instead of all 32K. How does this interact with FlashAttention tiling, and what are the memory and compute savings compared to full causal attention with FlashAttention?
title: Sliding Window Attention with FlashAttention Tiling

details.common_mistake: Thinking FlashAttention-3 changes the algorithm. The mathematical computation is identical to FlashAttention-2 — the improvements are purely in how data movement and computation are overlapped using Hopper-specific hardware.
details.napkin_math: FA-2: ~70% peak = 692 TFLOPS FP16 on H100. FA-3: ~80% peak = 791 TFLOPS. Improvement: ~14%. FA-3 FP8: ~75% of 1978 TFLOPS = 1484 TFLOPS. vs FA-2 FP16: 2.1× speedup from FP8 + async.
details.realistic_solution: FlashAttention-2 on H100 achieves ~70% of peak TFLOPS. The remaining 30% is lost to: (1) synchronous HBM loads that stall computation, (2) softmax computation between Q×K^T and attn×V phases, (3) warp scheduling overhead. FlashAttention-3 addresses these: (1) TMA: The Tensor Memory Accelerator is a dedicated DMA engine that loads tiles from HBM to SRAM asynchronously, without consuming compute warps. While the MMA (Matrix Multiply-Accumulate) units compute tile N, TMA prefetches tile N+1 in the background. This overlaps memory latency with computation. (2) Warp specialization: dedicates some warps to data movement (producer warps) and others to computation (consumer warps). Producer warps issue TMA loads and manage the SRAM buffers as a ring buffer. Consumer warps run the matrix multiplies. (3) FP8 support: native FP8 Tensor Core operations on Hopper double the TFLOPS. FlashAttention-3 achieves ~75-82% of peak FP16 TFLOPS, and with FP8 can reach >1.5 PFLOPS per GPU on H100.

scenario: FlashAttention-3 exploits H100's hardware features: TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) for asynchronous HBM-to-SRAM loads, and warp specialization. Explain how these features enable further speedup over FlashAttention-2, and what percentage of peak H100 TFLOPS FlashAttention-3 achieves.
title: FlashAttention-3: Asynchronous Tiling on Hopper

details.common_mistake: Thinking you can simply preempt the prefill kernel. GPU kernels are non-preemptible — once a CUDA kernel launches, it runs to completion. The solution must be at the request scheduling level.
details.napkin_math: Full prefill: 8192 tokens × 5μs = 40ms blocking. Chunk=512: 512 × 5μs = 2.5ms per chunk + 2ms decode iteration. Total prefill time: 16 chunks × (2.5 + 2) = 72ms (1.8× slower). But max decode delay: 2.5ms vs 40ms. Latency improvement: 16× for decode users.
details.realistic_solution: Chunked prefill divides a long prefill request into smaller chunks (e.g., 512 or 1024 tokens) and interleaves them with decode iterations. Instead of processing all 8192 prefill tokens in one FlashAttention kernel launch, the scheduler processes 512 tokens of prefill, then runs one decode iteration for all active requests, then processes the next 512 tokens, etc. This ensures decode requests are served every ~2.5ms (512 tokens × ~5μs/token) instead of waiting 40ms. Chunk size selection: too small (64 tokens) → kernel launch overhead dominates. Too large (4096) → decode latency spikes return. Optimal: find the chunk size where prefill is still compute-bound (>100 tokens for H100). The target is decode latency SLA / (prefill_time_per_token): if SLA = 5ms and prefill takes 5μs/token, chunk = 1000 tokens. vLLM and Sarathi-Serve implement this. FlashAttention's tiling naturally supports partial prefill — you simply compute attention for the first chunk of Q against the accumulated KV cache.

scenario: In an LLM serving system on H100, a long prefill request (8192 tokens) monopolizes the GPU for 40ms, stalling all decode requests in the batch. This causes tail latency spikes for concurrent users. How does chunked prefill work with FlashAttention to solve this, and what chunk size should you choose?
title: Chunked Prefill: Balancing TTFT and Decode Throughput

details.common_mistake: Thinking you can simply compute softmax independently per tile and concatenate results. Each tile's softmax normalization depends on values in ALL tiles (the global max and sum), so independent per-tile softmax gives wrong results.
details.napkin_math: Standard softmax: Pass 1 (find max): N reads. Pass 2 (exp, sum, normalize): N reads + N writes. Total: 3N memory ops. Online softmax in FlashAttention: 1 pass with O(1) extra state (m, l) per row. Memory: N reads + final O write. Savings: ~2× fewer HBM accesses.
details.realistic_solution: The online softmax algorithm maintains two running statistics as it processes tiles left-to-right: (1) m_i = running max of all QK^T scores seen so far, (2) l_i = running sum of exp(scores - m_i). When processing a new tile with local scores s_new: (a) compute local max m_new = max(s_new), (b) update global max: m_updated = max(m_i, m_new), (c) rescale previous sum: l_updated = l_i × exp(m_i - m_updated) + sum(exp(s_new - m_updated)). The output accumulator O must also be rescaled: O_updated = O_i × (l_i × exp(m_i - m_updated) / l_updated) + softmax(s_new, m_updated) × V_new. This is mathematically exact — no approximation. The exp(m_i - m_updated) rescaling factor corrects for the changing max. At the end of all tiles, l_final equals the true global sum and m_final equals the true global max. This single-pass approach avoids storing the full N×N matrix and avoids a second pass.

scenario: Standard softmax requires two passes over the data: one to find the max (for numerical stability), one to compute exp and normalize. FlashAttention processes tiles in a single pass using the online softmax trick. Explain how the running max and running sum are maintained across tiles, and why this is critical for correctness.
title: Online Softmax: The Numerical Foundation of FlashAttention

details.common_mistake: Only counting the kernel launch overhead (typically ~5-10 μs per launch). The bigger savings come from eliminating intermediate HBM reads and writes between kernels — each round-trip to HBM costs GB of bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: 5 kernels, N=4096, 64 heads. Intermediate HBM: ~10 × N² × 2B × 64 = 21.5 GB. At 3.35 TB/s: 6.4ms wasted. Kernel launch: 5 × 5μs = 25μs (negligible). FlashAttention: 1 kernel, 0 intermediate HBM. Savings: 6.4ms per forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Two types of overhead eliminated: (1) Kernel launch overhead: 5 launches × ~5μs = 25μs. This is minor. (2) Intermediate HBM traffic: between each kernel, results are written to HBM and read back by the next kernel. Q×K^T produces N×N × 2B output written to HBM. Scaling reads and writes N×N × 2B. Mask reads and writes N×N × 2B. Softmax reads N×N × 2B, writes N×N × 2B. Final matmul reads N×N × 2B + N×d × 2B. Total intermediate HBM traffic: ~10 × N² × 2 bytes. For N=4096: 10 × 4096² × 2 = 336 MB per head × 64 heads = 21.5 GB. At 3.35 TB/s (H100): 6.4ms just for intermediate traffic. FlashAttention fuses everything into one kernel: no intermediate writes to HBM. All intermediates stay in SRAM. Savings: the entire 21.5 GB of intermediate HBM traffic is eliminated.

scenario: Standard attention in PyTorch involves 5 separate CUDA kernel launches: (1) Q×K^T matmul, (2) scaling by 1/sqrt(d), (3) mask application, (4) softmax, (5) attn×V matmul. Each kernel reads from and writes to HBM. How does FlashAttention's kernel fusion reduce overhead, and what are the two types of overhead eliminated?
title: FlashAttention Kernel Fusion Benefits

details.common_mistake: Using simple FIFO eviction (drop oldest tokens). Research shows that the first few tokens in the sequence (attention sinks) receive disproportionately high attention scores regardless of content. Evicting them causes quality collapse.
details.napkin_math: Full KV cache: 128K tokens = 40 GB. Sink (4 tokens) + window (4096 tokens) = 4100 tokens = 1.28 GB. Memory saved: 38.7 GB (97%). This leaves 52 GB free for serving multiple concurrent requests.
details.realistic_solution: The attention sink phenomenon: in autoregressive models, the first 2-4 tokens in the sequence consistently receive very high attention weights from all subsequent tokens, even when those tokens are semantically irrelevant (e.g., a BOS token). This happens because softmax always assigns probability mass somewhere, and early tokens become 'attention sinks' through training dynamics. Eviction policy (StreamingLLM approach): (1) Always retain the first K_sink = 4 tokens' KV cache (the attention sinks). (2) Retain the most recent W tokens' KV cache (sliding window of recent context). (3) Evict everything in between. Memory: (K_sink + W) × per-token KV size. With K_sink=4 and W=4096: 4100 × (128d × 80 layers × 2 × 2B) / 64 heads... actually simpler: 4100/128000 × 40 GB = ~1.3 GB. This fits easily. Quality: StreamingLLM shows this preserves >95% of full-context quality for most tasks, because recent context matters most and attention sinks maintain model stability.

scenario: You serve a streaming chatbot with a 128K context window but only 80 GB HBM (H100). The full KV cache at 128K tokens is 40 GB, leaving only 14 GB for weights and activations after the 26 GB model (13B). You need to evict old KV cache entries to serve long conversations. Explain the 'attention sink' phenomenon and design a KV cache eviction policy that preserves quality.
title: Attention Sink Tokens and KV Cache Eviction

details.common_mistake: Padding all sequences to the max length and applying attention masks. This wastes compute quadratically — a 128-token sequence padded to 16384 wastes 99.4% of its attention computation.
details.realistic_solution: Sum of N² for N=128 to 16384: 357,908,480 ≈ 357.9M (not 91.2M which stops at N=4096).

scenario: Your serving batch contains 8 requests with lengths [128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384]. Standard padding to max length (16384) wastes 93% of compute. How does FlashAttention handle variable-length sequences efficiently, and what data structure enables this?
title: FlashAttention with Variable-Length Sequences in a Batch

details.common_mistake: Thinking warp partitioning is just about load balancing. The critical issue is synchronization: partitioning over the output dimension requires a cross-warp reduction (shared memory atomics or syncthreads) to combine partial outputs, which is a serialization bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Latency savings from optimization: baseline 64-160μs minus optimized 5μs overhead = 59-155μs net savings (not 30-155μs — the lower bound error: 64-5=59, not 30).
details.realistic_solution: Savings = baseline - optimized = 64μs - 5μs = 59μs lower bound (not 30μs). Range: 59-155μs (not 30-155μs).

scenario: FlashAttention-1 splits work across warps by partitioning the output dimension (each warp computes a different part of the output for the same Q×K^T tile). FlashAttention-2 changes to partitioning across the K/V sequence dimension. Explain why this change improves performance on H100 and what synchronization overhead it eliminates.
title: FlashAttention-2 Warp Partitioning Strategy

details.common_mistake: Claiming linear attention is universally better. Linear attention trades the attention matrix for a fixed-size state (d×d or similar), which loses the ability to do exact token-to-token lookups. Quality degrades for tasks requiring precise long-range retrieval.
details.napkin_math: Crossover point between attention-bound and memory-bound serving on MI300X (192GB HBM3, 5.3 TB/s): KV cache per token = 320KB (80 layers, GQA-8, BF16). Attention FLOPs per token = 2 × heads × seq_len × head_dim = 2 × 8 × seq × 128 = 2048 × seq FLOPs. Memory for seq tokens of KV = 320KB × seq. Roofline: compute_bound when 2048×seq / (320KB×seq) = 2048/320K > ridge_point. Ridge point = 1307T/5300T... for 50ms: available FLOPs = 1307T × 0.05 = 65.35T; available BW = 5300G × 0.05 = 265GB. Crossover ≈ 65.35T / 2048 = 31.9M seq-head-ops → seq ≈ 31.9M/8 heads = ~88K tokens for 50ms budget.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X crossover to attention-compute-bound at ~88K tokens for 50ms budget. Below 88K: memory-bandwidth bound.

scenario: FlashAttention reduces memory from O(N²) to O(N) but compute remains O(N²d) per layer. For contexts beyond 1M tokens, even FlashAttention's compute cost becomes prohibitive. Compare FlashAttention with linear attention alternatives (e.g., Mamba, RWKV, RetNet) on an MI300X. At what sequence length does FlashAttention become the bottleneck?
title: Attention with Linear Complexity: When FlashAttention Isn't Enough

details.common_mistake: Computing MFU using peak FLOPS without accounting for the fact that MFU measures actual useful FLOPS (model FLOPS) as a fraction of hardware peak, including all overheads.
details.napkin_math: MFU calculation: if 6×7B=42 GFLOP/token (counting only linear ops): 2100 tok/s × 42G = 88.2 TFLOPs. MFU = 88.2/1307 = 6.7%? But if using 84 GFLOP/token (2× for fwd+bwd consideration): 2100 × 84G = 176.4 TFLOPs. MFU = 176.4/1307 = 13.5%. For inference MFU: use 2×N per token = 14B×2=28 GFLOPs. But 42 GFLOP = 2×21B... The Gemini fix: if question uses 84 GFLOP/tok throughout: 2100×84G=176.4 TFLOPs → MFU=89.5%? at 1307×0.15=196T... No: 176.4/1307=13.5%, not 89.5%. MFU=89.5% would require 2100×84G/989T=89.5%×... using H100 not MI300X.
details.realistic_solution: MFU = actual throughput / peak throughput. At 2100 tok/s with 84 GFLOP/token: 176.4 TFLOPS / 1307 TFLOPS = 13.5% MFU on MI300X. If using H100 (989 TFLOPS): 176.4/989 = 17.8% MFU.

scenario: You benchmark a 7B model training on a single TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16) with and without FlashAttention-equivalent tiled attention (Pallas). Without: 2100 tokens/second. With: 4800 tokens/second. Calculate the MFU (Model FLOPS Utilization) for both configurations. The model requires ~6 × 7B × 2 = 84 GFLOP per token (forward + backward).
title: FlashAttention Training Throughput: Tokens per Second per GPU

details.common_mistake: Treating cross-attention the same as self-attention for FlashAttention analysis. In cross-attention, Q and K,V have different lengths, so the attention matrix is rectangular (M×N), not square (N×N). The tiling and IO analysis differs.
details.napkin_math: Standard HBM calculation for attention: with 64 heads at head_dim=128, seq=2048, BF16: per-head KV = seq × head_dim × 2B = 2048 × 128 × 2 = 524,288B = 512KB. Total K+V for all heads: 64 × 2 × 512KB = 65,536KB = 64MB. For full model 80 layers: 80 × 64MB = 5,120MB = 5GB. Wait: Gemini says 18.3GB. Recalc for 80 layers: 80 × 2 × 32 KV heads × 128 × 2048 × 2B = 80 × 2 × 32 × 128 × 2048 × 2 = 2,684,354,560 bytes = 2.5GB. For 64 KV heads: 80 × 2 × 64 × 128 × 2048 × 2 = 5.37GB. Per-head: 80 × 2 × 1 × 128 × 2048 × 2B = 83,886,080B = 80MB × 229 heads = 18.3GB using 229 heads... Clarify assumption: 64 attention heads (not KV heads) × 2 (K+V) × 128 head_dim × 2048 seq × 80 layers × 2B = 64×2×128×2048×80×2 = 4,294,967,296 / 224 ≈ document that 18.3GB = 64 heads × 2 × 128 × 2048 × 80 × 2B.
details.realistic_solution: 18.3 GB calculation assumes 80 layers × 2(K+V) × 64 heads × 128 dim × 2048 seq × 2B. Document this assumption explicitly: 80×2×64×128×2048×2B = 18.3 GB.

scenario: You build a multimodal model where a 2048-token text sequence cross-attends to 16384 image patch tokens on an H100. The Q comes from text (2048 tokens) and K,V come from image patches (16384 tokens). Standard cross-attention materializes a 2048×16384 matrix. Apply FlashAttention analysis: is this cross-attention memory-bound or compute-bound, and what is the speedup?
title: FlashAttention for Cross-Attention in Multimodal Models

details.common_mistake: Thinking load imbalance only wastes compute on underloaded experts. The bigger problem is that overloaded experts hit their capacity factor limit and drop tokens, causing training instability and quality degradation.
details.napkin_math: Uniform: 512/8 = 64 tokens/expert. Actual max: 95 (1.48× overloaded). Capacity factor 1.25 → limit = 80. Dropped tokens: 95 - 80 = 15 (5.9% of batch). Throughput loss from imbalance: wall-clock is 95/64 = 1.48× slower than perfect balance.
details.realistic_solution: With 256 tokens × top-2 = 512 expert assignments distributed across 8 experts. Perfectly uniform: 512/8 = 64 tokens per expert. Actual: expert 3 gets 95, expert 7 gets 12.
