Total Time: ~60.4 days. (Note: Training on the full 15T would take ~275 days, proving the 5.5-day pruning overhead provides a massive ICR boost).
details.realistic_solution: The optimal design recognizes that perplexity scoring is heavily compute-bound. Because it is a single forward pass over full sequences, the arithmetic intensity vastly exceeds the H100's ridge point of ~295 FLOPs/Byte. The architecture should use an embarrassingly parallel worker pool, streaming the 15T tokens (~30TB) directly from object storage to GPU memory in large batches. No inter-GPU communication is needed for scoring, unlike the 30B training phase which requires 3D parallelism.

scenario: Your team is pre-training a 30B parameter LLM. You have a raw corpus of 15 Trillion tokens, but a compute budget strictly limited to 3 Trillion tokens. To maximize the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR), you plan to score the perplexity of the entire 15T corpus using a 2B parameter reference model to select the best 3T tokens (coreset selection). You have an allocation of 256 H100 GPUs (80 GB HBM3, 3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS FP16). Diagnose the computational bottlenecks of this pipeline, design a distributed data streaming and scoring architecture, and calculate the total time required for both scoring the raw data and training the final model.
title: Coreset Selection Pipeline for LLM Pre-training at Scale

details.common_mistake: Candidates often forget to divide the total facility budget by the PUE to find the IT power budget. They may also miss that a 15 kW air-cooled rack can only host a single 8.0 kW node, leading to extreme stranding of physical space and exploding the radix requirements for the backend network.
details.napkin_math: Total Budget: 25,000 kW. Air-cooled IT Power: 25,000 / 1.3 = 19,230 kW. Max air nodes: 19,230 / 8 = 2,403 nodes. Air nodes per rack: floor(15 / 8) = 1 node. Total air racks: 2,403 racks. Liquid-cooled IT Power: 25,000 / 1.15 = 21,739 kW. Max liquid nodes: 21,739 / 8 = 2,717 nodes. Liquid nodes per rack: floor(60 / 8) = 7 nodes. Total liquid racks: ceil(2,717 / 7) = 389 racks. Liquid cooling yields 314 more nodes (+13% compute) and reduces the physical footprint by 84%.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to calculate the IT power budget for both scenarios and translate that into node counts and rack footprints. The liquid-cooled architecture is heavily favored: the lower PUE frees up ~2.5 MW for IT load, yielding over 300 additional nodes. Furthermore, the 60 kW rack density condenses the cluster from over 2,400 racks down to under 400 racks, drastically reducing optical transceiver count, cabling length, and switch tiers.

scenario: You are designing a new large-scale training cluster using 8x H100 nodes within a strict total facility power budget of 25 MW. Each H100 GPU has a 700W TDP, and the host system plus networking adds 2.4 kW, totaling 8.0 kW per node. Your standard air-cooled racks support 15 kW maximum, yielding a facility PUE of 1.3. Alternatively, you can deploy direct-to-chip (D2C) liquid-cooled racks supporting 60 kW each, which lowers the facility PUE to 1.15. Design the optimal datacenter architecture to maximize total compute throughput, size the maximum cluster for both cooling strategies, and evaluate the trade-offs regarding physical footprint and networking.
title: H100 Cluster Power and Cooling Architecture

details.common_mistake: Candidates often misidentify the bottleneck as object storage I/O or memory bandwidth without calculating the arithmetic intensity of a large-batch inference workload. They also frequently fail to apply a realistic hardware utilization factor (MFU), erroneously assuming the theoretical peak of 312 TFLOPS can be achieved.
details.napkin_math: 1. Total Compute: 100B samples × 6 TFLOPs/sample = 600 ZFLOPs. 2. Effective Throughput: A100 peak is 312 TFLOPS FP16; assuming a realistic 40% MFU, we get ~125 TFLOPS per GPU. 3. Processing Rate: 125 TFLOPS / 6 TFLOPs = ~20.8 samples/sec per GPU. 4. Time Constraint: 14 days = 1,209,600 seconds. 5. Samples per GPU: 20.8 × 1,209,600 = ~25.1 million samples. 6. Total GPUs: 100B / 25.1M = 3,984 A100 GPUs (provision 4,000 GPUs or 500 8-GPU nodes). 7. Network I/O Check: 20.8 samples/s × 200KB = ~4.1 MB/s per GPU (~33 MB/s per node), verifying network is not the bottleneck.
details.realistic_solution: For a 10B VLM in FP16, the weights require ~20GB. The 80GB HBM2e on the A100 permits very large batch sizes, pushing the arithmetic intensity well past the A100's ridge point of 156 FLOPs/Byte, making the workload strictly compute-bound. The architecture should utilize a decoupled pattern: a distributed queue streams metadata/URLs to stateless GPU worker nodes, which asynchronously pull raw bytes from S3, run inference batches, and sink the quality scores to a fast key-value store or analytical database.

scenario: You are tasked with designing an automated data curation pipeline for a new multimodal foundation model. You have a raw data lake of 100 billion image-text pairs (average 200KB per pair) in object storage. You need to use a 10B parameter Vision-Language Model (VLM) running in FP16 to score and filter this dataset down to the highest quality 5%. The VLM requires approximately 6 TFLOPs per sample for the forward pass. Design the end-to-end distributed curation architecture, identify the primary system bottleneck, and calculate the exact number of A100 (80GB) GPUs required to complete this job in exactly 14 days.
title: VLM-Based Automated Curation at 100B Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming hipify-perl produces drop-in HIP code with zero manual intervention. In practice, about 5-15% of CUDA API calls (especially texture memory, cooperative groups, and warp-level intrinsics) require manual porting.
details.napkin_math: 15K lines x 5-15% manual = 750-2250 lines needing manual porting. At ~50 lines/hour for tricky intrinsics = 15-45 engineer-hours minimum.
details.realistic_solution: Run hipify-perl for the mechanical 85-95% translation (cuda* -> hip* renames), then audit the remaining calls. Texture references must become HIP texture objects, cooperative_groups need hipCG equivalents, and any __shfl_sync intrinsics need careful lane-mask verification on CDNA's 64-wide wavefronts vs CUDA's 32-wide warps. Budget 2-4 engineer-weeks for a 15K-line codebase, not 2 days.

scenario: Your team has 15,000 lines of custom CUDA kernels for a recommendation model. Management wants to also deploy on MI300X clusters. You propose using hipify-perl for automated translation. A colleague warns that translation is not 1:1.
title: CUDA-to-HIP Translation Overhead for a Custom GEMM Kernel

details.common_mistake: Using a single ONNX graph export and expecting identical performance across all three providers. Graph optimizations (operator fusion, layout selection) differ per EP, and some ops may fall back to CPU silently.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-50 inference batch=32: model FLOPs = 4.1 GFLOPs/image × 32 images = 131.2 GFLOPs = 0.131 TFLOPs (not 2.1 TFLOPs which is 16× too high). ResNet-50 is 4.1 GFLOPs per image at standard 224×224.
details.realistic_solution: ResNet-50 at 4.1 GFLOPs/image × 32 batch = 131.2 GFLOPs = 0.131 TFLOPs ≈ 0.256 TFLOPs accounting for the backward overhead in training context. Not 2.1 TFLOPs.

scenario: You serve a vision model via ONNX Runtime in a heterogeneous cluster with H100s, MI300Xs, and TPU v5e pods. Each node type has a different ONNX RT execution provider (CUDA EP, MIGraphX EP, and a custom XLA bridge). Latency SLA is p99 < 25ms for a ResNet-50 batch of 32.
title: ONNX Runtime Execution Provider Selection for Multi-Accelerator Inference

details.common_mistake: Blaming Triton's AMD backend as fundamentally broken. The real issue is that Triton's auto-tuning heuristics (tile sizes, num_warps, num_stages) were tuned on NVIDIA and the CDNA3 architecture has different optimal parameters.
details.napkin_math: MI300X FP16: 1,307 TFLOPS dense (not 653 TFLOPS). At 55% MFU: 1,307 × 0.55 = 718.85 ≈ 719 TFLOPS effective (not 653 × 0.55 = 359 TFLOPS). 653 TFLOPS would be the MI300X at 50% of its peak, not the correct 1307 TFLOPS spec.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X FP16: 1,307 TFLOPS (authoritative spec). At 55% MFU: 1,307 × 0.55 = 719 TFLOPS (not 653 which is incorrect base value).

scenario: You wrote a fused attention kernel in Triton that achieves 85% of peak FP16 throughput on H100. You recompile the same Triton code targeting MI300X via the AMD ROCm backend. Performance drops to 55% of MI300X peak. Diagnose the gap.
title: Triton Kernel Portability from NVIDIA to AMD GPUs

details.common_mistake: Only comparing $/TFLOP and ignoring the ongoing maintenance cost of a multi-backend stack: CI/CD for two targets, dual kernel libraries, and the risk of performance regressions on one backend when optimizing the other.
details.napkin_math: Savings per year at 50/50 split: $2M - $1.65M = $350K. Ongoing multi-backend cost: ~$100K/yr. Net annual savings: $250K. Break-even on $400K investment: 1.6 years.
details.realistic_solution: Model the TCO. Current: $2M/yr. With 50% workload on MI300X at 35% savings: $1M NVIDIA + $0.65M AMD = $1.65M, saving $350K/yr. Porting cost: $400K one-time + ~$100K/yr ongoing dual-CI maintenance. Break-even: $400K / ($350K - $100K) = 1.6 years. If AMD share grows to 70%, savings increase to $490K/yr, break-even drops to 10 months. Decision: invest, but only if the 2-year commitment is realistic.

scenario: Your ML platform team has $2M/year in GPU cloud spend, 100% on NVIDIA A100s. MI300X instances are 35% cheaper per TFLOP-hour. The CFO asks: should we invest $400K in porting our stack to be multi-vendor, or accept the CUDA lock-in? Quantify the break-even.
title: Vendor Lock-in TCO Analysis: CUDA Moat vs Multi-Backend Investment

details.common_mistake: Assuming SYCL's abstraction layer adds negligible overhead on all targets. On NVIDIA hardware, the SYCL-to-CUDA translation adds a compilation indirection that can miss NVIDIA-specific optimizations like warp shuffle and shared memory bank-conflict avoidance.
details.napkin_math: Fraction: 69 / 910 = 0.07582... = 7.58% ≈ 7.6% (not 7.5% — 7.5% = 68.25/910 which rounds 69 down). 69/910 = 0.07582, rounds to 7.6% at one decimal place.
details.realistic_solution: 69/910 = 7.58% ≈ 7.6% (not 7.5%). The difference is in rounding: 7.582... rounds to 7.6, not 7.5.

scenario: Intel offers oneAPI/SYCL as a portable programming model across Intel Max GPUs, NVIDIA GPUs (via CUDA backend), and CPUs. Your team considers SYCL to avoid writing separate CUDA and HIP kernels. How would you evaluate the performance tax of the SYCL abstraction?
title: SYCL Portability Layer Performance on Intel Max Series vs H100

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the cost of EP boundary transitions. Each transition involves a D2D memcpy plus synchronization. With 50 fallback ops scattered across the graph, you can have 20+ EP boundaries.
details.napkin_math: Each EP boundary: ~0.1-0.3ms (D2D copy + sync). 20 boundaries x 0.2ms = 4ms overhead. Total inference 14ms -> 10ms target. Reducing to 4 boundaries: 0.8ms overhead, recovering 3.2ms.
details.realistic_solution: Use ORT's graph partitioning visualization to identify the 50 fallback ops. Common culprits: custom ops, unsupported dynamic shapes, or rare activations (like GELU exact mode). Options: (1) replace unsupported ops with TensorRT-compatible equivalents at export time, (2) write TensorRT plugins for the custom ops, (3) use ORT's CUDA EP for the entire graph with operator-level TRT acceleration. Reducing EP boundaries from 20+ to 3-4 typically recovers 25-30% of the latency gap.

scenario: Your ONNX model has 340 operators. When running on the TensorRT EP, 290 operators are assigned to TensorRT and 50 fall back to the CUDA EP. Each EP boundary incurs a device-to-device memory copy. You observe that inference latency is 40% higher than expected from pure GPU execution.
title: ONNX Graph Partitioning Across Mixed Execution Providers

details.common_mistake: Using a 32-bit mask (0xFFFFFFFF) that only covers the first 32 lanes of a 64-wide wavefront. The upper 32 lanes are excluded from the shuffle, requiring an extra reduction step that the developer didn't add.
details.napkin_math: Original CUDA: 5 shuffle steps for 32-lane reduction. MI300X needs 6 steps for 64 lanes. But each step processes 2x more data. Net: same work per wavefront, but the buggy kernel was only reducing 32 of 64 lanes, wasting 50% of lanes -> 50% efficiency loss.
details.realistic_solution: On CDNA3, wavefronts are 64 lanes wide. The mask must be 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (64-bit). Additionally, the reduction tree depth changes: log2(64)=6 steps instead of log2(32)=5 steps. Update the kernel to use a 64-bit mask and add the 6th reduction step. Alternatively, use HIP's __reduce_add_sync() which handles wavefront width automatically. The fixed kernel should recover to within 5% of proportional peak.

scenario: After porting a reduction kernel from CUDA to HIP for MI300X, correctness tests pass but performance is 40% worse than expected. The kernel uses __shfl_down_sync with a mask of 0xFFFFFFFF for warp-level reductions. The MI300X uses 64-wide wavefronts.
title: Warp Size Divergence When Porting CUDA Kernels to AMD CDNA

details.common_mistake: Trying to force dynamic control flow through XLA by adding torch.jit.script wrappers. XLA fundamentally requires static computation graphs; dynamic control flow must be restructured, not wrapped.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e BF16: 197 TFLOPS. With XLA compilation overhead on first run: 30-90 seconds. Amortized over serving: negligible if batch size >= 64 and shapes are static. Dynamic shapes cause recompilation: 197 TFLOPS -> effective 40-80 TFLOPS due to recompile stalls.
details.realistic_solution: Replace dynamic control flow with torch.where() for conditional operations and torch.cond() for graph-compatible branching. Replace in-place mutations (tensor.add_()) with out-of-place equivalents (tensor = tensor + x). Use mark_step() to break long computations into XLA-compilable segments. Profile with XLA_METRICS=1 to identify remaining recompilation triggers. Expect 10-20% code refactoring effort, but the result runs on both GPU (via inductor) and TPU (via XLA).

scenario: Your PyTorch model runs on GPU via torch.compile with the inductor backend. You want to also run it on TPU v5e via PyTorch/XLA. The model uses dynamic control flow (if-statements based on tensor values) and in-place tensor mutations. Both features cause XLA compilation failures.
title: TPU v5e XLA Compilation Constraints for Portable Model Code

details.common_mistake: Building a single abstraction layer that maps to the lowest common denominator of all three backends, sacrificing hardware-specific optimizations like NVIDIA's TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) or AMD's MFMA instructions.
details.napkin_math: Dispatch overhead per operator: ~1-5 microseconds (function pointer + shape lookup). For a model with 500 operators: 0.5-2.5ms total dispatch overhead. At 50ms total inference time, that is 1-5% overhead — well within the 10% budget.
details.realistic_solution: Use a three-tier architecture: (1) Frontend: hardware-agnostic operator graph (like ONNX or MLIR). (2) Middle-tier: per-backend kernel libraries with auto-tuned implementations (cuBLAS/CUTLASS for CUDA, rocBLAS/composable_kernel for ROCm, XLA HLO for TPU). (3) Dispatch layer: runtime selects the best kernel variant per-op based on shape, dtype, and backend. Key insight: the abstraction lives at the operator boundary, not inside the kernel. Each backend gets native kernels; only the dispatch logic is shared.

scenario: You are architecting an ML inference framework that must run the same model on H100 (CUDA), MI300X (ROCm), and TPU v5e (XLA) with <10% performance penalty vs native on each target. Design the kernel dispatch architecture.
title: Designing a Hardware-Agnostic Kernel Dispatch Layer

details.common_mistake: Blaming the MPS backend entirely. While the MPS backend is less mature than CUDA, the M2 Ultra's GPU also has fundamentally lower FP16 compute (27.2 TFLOPS vs A100's 312 TFLOPS) and lower memory bandwidth (800 GB/s vs 2 TB/s).
details.napkin_math: A100: 312 TFLOPS FP16, 2 TB/s BW. M2 Ultra: 27 TFLOPS FP16, 800 GB/s BW. Arithmetic intensity crossover: A100 at 156 FLOP/byte, M2 Ultra at 34 FLOP/byte. For memory-bound 7B fine-tuning (low arithmetic intensity), bandwidth matters more -> M2 Ultra is competitive.
details.realistic_solution: The hardware ceiling explains most of the gap: M2 Ultra has ~8.7% of A100's FP16 TFLOPS, so at 60% of A100 throughput, the MPS backend is actually performing 6.9x better than raw FLOPS would predict. This is because the 7B model is memory-bandwidth-bound during fine-tuning, and M2 Ultra's 800 GB/s unified memory avoids the PCIe bottleneck entirely. The MPS backend's real weakness is in custom kernel support and operator coverage — about 15% of PyTorch ops fall back to CPU.

scenario: A researcher fine-tunes a 7B parameter model on an M2 Ultra (192GB unified memory) using PyTorch with the MPS backend. Training throughput is 60% of what an A100 80GB achieves. They ask whether the gap is the MPS backend or the hardware.
title: Metal Performance Shaders vs CUDA for On-Device Training on Apple Silicon

details.common_mistake: Expecting ONNX Runtime to gracefully degrade or emulate the unsupported op. Instead, it raises an immediate error: 'No Op registered for GroupNormalization with domain_version of 18'.
details.napkin_math: Decomposed GroupNorm (opset 17) vs native (opset 18): ~5-10% slower due to extra reshape and InstanceNorm overhead. For a model where GroupNorm is 2% of total compute, net impact: <0.2% latency increase.
details.realistic_solution: Three options: (1) Re-export with opset 17 using torch.onnx.export(opset_version=17), which will decompose GroupNorm into supported primitives (InstanceNorm + reshape). (2) Upgrade ONNX Runtime to 1.16+ which supports opset 18. (3) Register a custom op implementation. Option 1 is safest for production — always export with the opset version matching your target runtime. Maintain a compatibility matrix: ORT 1.14 -> opset 17, ORT 1.16 -> opset 18, ORT 1.17 -> opset 20.

scenario: You export a model as ONNX opset 18 from PyTorch 2.1. A production system runs ONNX Runtime 1.14, which supports up to opset 17. The model uses the new GroupNormalization op introduced in opset 18. What happens at load time?
title: ONNX Model Compatibility Matrix Across Runtime Versions

details.common_mistake: Thinking Triton directly generates PTX or AMDGPU assembly from Python. It actually goes through Triton IR -> TTIR -> TTGIR -> LLVM IR -> backend-specific assembly, with the split happening at the LLVM IR level.
details.napkin_math: Compilation time: ~0.5-2s per kernel on NVIDIA (PTX), ~1-4s per kernel on AMD (AMDGPU) due to less mature backend. Cache across runs eliminates recompilation. Typical model: 50-200 kernels -> 25-400s cold start if uncached.
details.realistic_solution: Triton's pipeline: (1) Python AST -> Triton IR (high-level, hardware-agnostic). (2) Triton IR -> TTGIR (Triton GPU IR, adds GPU concepts like shared memory, barriers). (3) TTGIR -> LLVM IR (lowering to LLVM's machine-independent representation). (4) LLVM IR -> PTX (NVIDIA) or AMDGPU ISA (AMD) via LLVM's target-specific backends. Backend-specific decisions (register allocation, instruction selection, memory coalescing patterns) happen at step 4. Auto-tuning parameters (tile sizes, num_warps) affect step 2. This is why the same Triton source can target both backends but may need different tuning configs.

scenario: Triton compiles a Python-like DSL to GPU machine code via multiple IR stages. Explain how Triton's compilation pipeline enables portability across NVIDIA PTX and AMD AMDGPU targets, and where backend-specific decisions are made.
title: Triton's IR Compilation Pipeline for Multi-Backend Targeting

details.common_mistake: Assuming ROCm has full parity with CUDA's ecosystem. While rocBLAS matches cuBLAS for standard GEMMs, specialized libraries like FlashAttention and fused RNN kernels have varying levels of AMD support.
details.napkin_math: MI300X 192GB HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s vs H100 80GB HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s. For memory-bound LLM decode: MI300X has 58% more bandwidth AND 140% more VRAM. Even at 85% software efficiency: 5.3 x 0.85 = 4.5 TB/s effective, still 34% more than H100.
details.realistic_solution: Assessment: (1) FlashAttention-2: AMD has flash-attention for ROCm (composable_kernel backend), achieving ~85-90% of the NVIDIA version's performance. (2) cuDNN fused LSTM: MIOpen's LSTM is ~80% of cuDNN's fused performance; the fusion is less aggressive. (3) NCCL: RCCL (ROCm's NCCL equivalent) achieves near-parity on AllReduce for large messages (>1MB) but is 15-20% slower for small messages due to less optimized tree reduction. Overall readiness: LLM serving is viable; LSTM-heavy workloads need benchmarking.

scenario: You are evaluating MI300X for a production LLM serving stack that currently uses FlashAttention-2, cuDNN fused LSTM, and NCCL for multi-GPU communication on H100s. Which components have ROCm equivalents at performance parity, and which do not?
title: ROCm Library Parity Gap for Production ML Workloads

details.common_mistake: Declaring any numerical difference as a bug. FP16 has a machine epsilon of ~4.88e-4, so differences of 0.003 are ~6 epsilon — in the gray zone between acceptable rounding and a real issue.
details.napkin_math: FP16 epsilon: 2^(-10) = 9.77e-4 (relative). Max diff 0.003 on logit values ~1.0 = 0.3% relative error = ~3 epsilon. This is within normal floating-point non-determinism for different hardware.
details.realistic_solution: Systematic debugging: (1) Run in FP32 on both platforms — if differences vanish, it is FP16 reduction-order sensitivity, not a bug. (2) Check if the difference is in specific layers (often softmax or LayerNorm, which are numerically sensitive). (3) MI300X's MFMA instructions use different accumulation orders than NVIDIA's Tensor Cores, causing legally different FP16 rounding. (4) The 0.2% quality drop may be within noise — run statistical significance tests over 1000+ samples. Typically, differences <10 epsilon with no statistically significant quality impact are acceptable numerical noise.

scenario: Your model produces identical outputs on A100 and H100 but gives slightly different logits on MI300X (max absolute difference of 0.003 in FP16). Quality metrics drop by 0.2% on MI300X. Determine whether this is a portability bug or acceptable numerical noise.
title: Cross-Platform Model Numerics Divergence Debugging

details.common_mistake: Assuming W4A16 means the same thing on both platforms. H100 Hopper supports native FP4/FP8 via Tensor Cores, while MI300X CDNA3 supports INT4/INT8 via MFMA. The weight packing format differs.
details.napkin_math: H100 INT4 Tensor Core throughput: ~1978 TOPS. MI300X MFMA INT4: ~3200 TOPS theoretical. But effective throughput depends on dequant overhead: typically 60-70% of peak for W4A16 GEMM on both platforms.
details.realistic_solution: GPTQ produces INT4 quantized weights with FP16 scales per group. On H100: the dequantize-then-GEMM approach uses INT4 weights unpacked to FP16, then cuBLAS FP16 GEMM — not using H100's native FP4. For native FP4 on H100, you need NVIDIA's FP4 quantization (different format). On MI300X: GPTQ INT4 maps well to MFMA INT4 instructions via AutoGPTQ's ROCm backend. For true portability, use a format like GGUF (llama.cpp) which handles platform-specific dequantization internally.

scenario: You want to deploy a W4A16 quantized LLM (4-bit weights, 16-bit activations) on both H100 and MI300X. NVIDIA uses FP4 (via Hopper's new format), while AMD supports INT4 via MFMA. Your quantization toolkit produces GPTQ format. Explain the compatibility landscape.
title: Portable Quantization Formats Across Accelerator Backends

details.common_mistake: Trying to run full hardware-in-the-loop CI on all three backends for every PR. GPU CI runners are expensive ($3-8/hour per GPU instance), and TPU access is limited.
details.napkin_math: 80 kernels x 3 backends x 5 performance runs = 1200 kernel runs per week. At ~30 seconds per kernel test: 10 hours total GPU time. At $3/hour average: $30/week = $120/month for performance CI alone.
details.realistic_solution: Three-tier CI: (1) Every PR: CPU-emulated correctness tests using reference implementations (PyTorch CPU) — catches logic bugs in seconds. (2) Nightly: GPU correctness on NVIDIA (cheapest, most available). AMD ROCm correctness via cloud MI300X instances (spot pricing). TPU correctness via GCP TPU VMs. (3) Weekly: Full performance regression suite on all three backends with statistical comparison (>5 runs per kernel per backend). Use artifact caching to diff performance against the previous week. Budget: ~$500/month for nightly + weekly GPU CI.

scenario: Your team maintains 80 custom GPU kernels that must work on H100, MI300X, and TPU v5e. Design a CI/CD pipeline that tests correctness and performance across all three backends without requiring dedicated hardware in CI.
title: CI/CD Pipeline Design for Multi-Accelerator Kernel Testing

details.common_mistake: Directly translating block(256) to HIP without checking that the LDS allocation (48KB) doesn't limit occupancy on CDNA3 CUs differently than on NVIDIA SMs. CDNA3 has 64KB LDS per CU vs H100's 228KB shared memory per SM.
details.napkin_math: MI300X: 304 CUs x 1 workgroup = 304 concurrent workgroups. H100: 132 SMs x 4 blocks = 528 concurrent blocks. Reducing LDS to 32KB: 304 CUs x 2 = 608 concurrent workgroups, better than H100.
details.realistic_solution: The kernel launch translates to hipLaunchKernelGGL(kernel, dim3(256), dim3(256), 48*1024, stream). __syncthreads() -> __syncthreads() (same name in HIP). threadIdx -> threadIdx (same). However, with 48KB LDS out of 64KB total per CU, only 1 workgroup can be resident per CU (64KB/48KB = 1.33, floor to 1). On H100, 228KB/48KB = 4 blocks per SM. This means MI300X will have much lower occupancy — consider reducing shared memory to 32KB to allow 2 workgroups per CU.

scenario: You are porting a CUDA kernel that launches with <<<grid(256), block(256), shared_mem(48KB)>>>. The kernel uses __syncthreads() and threadIdx. On MI300X with HIP, the maximum workgroup size is 1024 (same as CUDA) but the LDS (shared memory) limit per CU is 64KB. Translate the launch configuration.
title: HIP Kernel Launch Parameter Translation from CUDA

details.common_mistake: Treating MLIR as a portable binary format like JVM bytecode. MLIR is a compiler infrastructure, not a portable runtime. Code still needs to be compiled to target-specific machine code.
details.napkin_math: Engineering staffing: 2 shared infrastructure engineers + 3 target-specific engineers (one each for three deployment targets) = 5 total engineers (not 3 — 3 only counts target-specific and misses shared infra).
details.realistic_solution: Total engineers = 2 shared + 3 target-specific = 5 (not 3 which omits shared infrastructure roles).

scenario: Google's MLIR framework is used by both XLA (for TPU) and IREE (for GPU/CPU). Your colleague claims MLIR will solve the portability problem because it is vendor-neutral. Evaluate this claim critically.
title: MLIR as a Universal Compiler IR for ML Portability

details.common_mistake: Trying to express thread-level parallelism on TPU. TPUs don't have threads — they have a 2D systolic array that processes matrix tiles. Thinking in terms of thread blocks and warps leads to fundamentally wrong kernel designs.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e MXU: 128x128 systolic array at ~197 TFLOPS BF16. For sparse attention with 50% sparsity: you still process full 128x128 tiles but mask 50%, so effective throughput is ~98.5 TFLOPS. CUDA can skip sparse blocks entirely, potentially 2x more efficient for unstructured sparsity.
details.realistic_solution: Three key shifts: (1) From thread-level to tile-level: instead of each thread computing one output element, each MXU operation processes a 128x128 tile. Express computation as matrix multiplications, not per-element ops. (2) From shared memory to VMEM: TPU's vector memory (VMEM, 16MB per core on v5e) replaces CUDA's shared memory, but it is managed by the compiler, not the programmer. (3) From warp divergence to masking: sparse attention on TPU requires padding sparse patterns to dense tiles and using mask matrices, not conditional execution. Performance depends on sparsity pattern regularity.

scenario: A team accustomed to CUDA's SIMT (Single Instruction Multiple Threads) model is porting a custom sparse attention kernel to TPU v5e. They struggle because TPUs use SPMD (Single Program Multiple Data) with systolic arrays. What are the key conceptual shifts?
title: TPU v5e SPMD Programming Model vs CUDA's SIMT

details.common_mistake: Assuming torch.compile makes any PyTorch code automatically portable. In practice, each backend has different graph break triggers, and inductor's CUDA codegen is far more mature than the AMD or XLA backends.
details.napkin_math: Typical torch.compile speedup on CUDA inductor: 1.3-2x over eager mode. On AMD via inductor: 1.1-1.5x (less tuned). On TPU via openxla: 1.5-3x (XLA benefits most from whole-graph compilation). The variance is the portability tax.
details.realistic_solution: For maximum portability: (1) Avoid torch.autograd.Function custom ops (cause graph breaks on all backends). (2) Use only standard torch ops from the core aten operator set. (3) Avoid data-dependent control flow (breaks XLA backend). (4) Avoid in-place ops on views (breaks inductor fusion). (5) Test with TORCH_COMPILE_DEBUG=1 on each backend to identify backend-specific graph breaks. The inductor backend for CUDA generates Triton kernels; the AMD path generates similar Triton but with ROCm-specific tuning; the XLA path generates HLO graphs.

scenario: PyTorch 2.x's torch.compile offers multiple backends: 'inductor' (default, CUDA/CPU), 'openxla' (TPU), and experimental AMD support. You want to write model code that torch.compile can optimize for any backend. What are the portability constraints?
title: Evaluating torch.compile Backend Portability Across Accelerators

details.common_mistake: Trying to use NCCL for both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. NCCL only works with CUDA devices; RCCL only works with ROCm devices. A single process group cannot span both.
details.napkin_math: 14GB model transfer at 900 Gbps NVLink: 14GB × 8 bits/byte / 900 Gbps = 112 Gbits / 900 Gbps = 0.1244s = 124ms (not 15ms — 15ms would require 7.5 Gbps or 14 × 8/15ms = 7.47 Gbps, far below NVLink speed). At 900 Gbps: 112/900 = 0.124s = 124ms.
details.realistic_solution: 14GB at 900 Gbps: 14GB × 8 bits/byte / 900 Gbps = 112 Gb / 900 Gbps = 0.124s = 124ms (not 15ms which would require only 7.5 Gbps bandwidth).

scenario: Your distributed training job spans 32 H100 nodes (NCCL) and 16 MI300X nodes (RCCL). PyTorch's distributed backend only supports one communication library per process group. How do you architect heterogeneous multi-vendor distributed training?
title: Multi-Backend Distributed Training: NCCL vs RCCL vs Gloo Interop

details.common_mistake: Expecting all PyTorch operations to have direct ONNX equivalents on all execution providers. ONNX standard defines ops, but EPs may not implement them all — DirectML is notably behind CUDA EP in op coverage.
details.napkin_math: GPT-2 124M has ~150 unique operator instances. If 3 fail on DirectML: 2% failure rate. But those 3 ops (attention, GELU, einsum) account for ~60% of compute time — so 2% op failure blocks 60% of computation.
details.realistic_solution: Fix each failure: (1) ScaledDotProductAttention: not a standard ONNX op — decompose into MatMul + Softmax + MatMul manually in the export using a custom symbolic function. (2) Custom GELU: replace with torch.nn.functional.gelu(x, approximate='tanh') which maps to the standard ONNX Tanh-based GELU approximation. (3) Multi-input einsum: decompose into sequential 2-input einsums. Then validate with ORT's model checker per EP. Lesson: always test with your target EP before declaring an ONNX model portable.

scenario: You export a GPT-2 model (124M parameters) to ONNX opset 17. The export succeeds, but at runtime on the DirectML execution provider (Windows GPU inference), three operations fail: ScaledDotProductAttention, a custom GELU variant, and einsum with >2 inputs.
title: ONNX Operator Coverage Gap Analysis for Transformer Models

details.common_mistake: Ignoring memory layout as a performance-critical portability concern. NVIDIA GPUs historically optimized for NCHW (cuDNN's default), while TPU, AMD, and mobile accelerators prefer NHWC.
details.napkin_math: For a ResNet-50 feature map at batch 32, 64 channels, 56x56: NCHW->NHWC transpose = 32x64x56x56x2 bytes = 12.8MB memcpy. If 50 conv layers each trigger a transpose: 640MB of unnecessary data movement per forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: The 20-30% drop comes from implicit layout transpositions inserted by the framework. On TPU, XLA auto-converts NCHW to NHWC but each conversion costs a full tensor copy. On MI300X, MIOpen prefers NHWC for convolutions and inserts transposes at conv boundaries. Fix: use torch.channels_last memory format throughout the model (model.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)). This avoids transposes on TPU and AMD, and is also faster on NVIDIA with cuDNN's NHWC kernels (which are now as fast or faster than NCHW on Ampere+).

scenario: Your CNN model uses NCHW layout (PyTorch default). When deployed on TPU v5e (which prefers NHWC) and MI300X (which also prefers NHWC for convolutions), performance drops 20-30% compared to H100. Why?
title: Memory Layout Portability: NCHW vs NHWC Across Accelerators

details.common_mistake: Taking vendor benchmarks at face value. Common tricks: cherry-picked batch sizes, different precision modes (e.g., INT8 on their chip vs FP16 on H100), different sequence lengths, or measuring throughput without latency constraints.
details.napkin_math: Vendor claim: 2.3x at batch=512, seq=128 (throughput-optimal). Your workload: batch=8, seq=2048 (latency-sensitive). The 2.3x advantage at batch=512 can become 0.9x at batch=8 if the chip has high launch overhead. Always benchmark YOUR operating point.
details.realistic_solution: Apply the MLPerf methodology: (1) Fix the model architecture and weights identically. (2) Match precision: both FP16 or both INT8. (3) Report both throughput (tokens/sec) AND latency (p50, p99 at your target batch size). (4) Use the same SLA constraint (e.g., first-token latency < 200ms). (5) Include the full software stack version. (6) Run multiple iterations (>100) and report confidence intervals. (7) Test at YOUR batch size and sequence length, not the vendor's optimal point. Often the 2.3x shrinks to 1.1-1.4x under realistic conditions.

scenario: A vendor publishes a benchmark showing their accelerator is 2.3x faster than H100 for LLM inference. You need to evaluate whether this claim is valid for your workload. What methodology do you apply?
title: Benchmarking Methodology for Cross-Platform Performance Claims

details.common_mistake: Accepting the 15% regression as inevitable on MI300X. While MIOpen may not have the exact three-way fusion, other optimization strategies can recover most of the gap.
details.napkin_math: 32MB model load from MI300X HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s: 32MB / 5.3TB/s = 32×10^-3 GB / 5,300 GB/s = 0.032/5300 = 6.04×10^-6 s = 6 microseconds (not 6ms — 6ms would require 5.3 GB/s, not TB/s).

scenario: Your training pipeline relies on cuDNN's fused BatchNorm+ReLU+Conv kernel, which gives a 15% speedup over unfused execution on H100. When porting to MI300X, MIOpen does not offer an equivalent three-way fusion. How do you recover the performance?
title: Migrating cuDNN-Fused Operators to Portable Alternatives

details.common_mistake: Hardcoding FP16 as the mixed-precision dtype. Different accelerators have different optimal precision: H100 excels at FP8 (via Transformer Engine), MI300X supports both FP16 and BF16 via MFMA, and TPUs only efficiently support BF16.
details.napkin_math: FP16 range: +-65504, overflow likely for large gradients. BF16 range: +-3.4e38 (same as FP32). Switching MI300X from FP16 to BF16: zero loss scaling overhead, and MFMA BF16 throughput equals FP16 throughput on CDNA3.
details.realistic_solution: Make precision a runtime configuration: (1) Use torch.amp.autocast(device_type=device, dtype=precision) with device and precision as config params. (2) For MI300X overflow: switch to BF16 (range of FP32, less precision than FP16 but no overflow issues) — eliminates the need for GradScaler entirely. (3) For TPU: BF16 is the only option; GradScaler is not needed since BF16 has FP32's exponent range. (4) For H100: consider FP8 via NVIDIA's Transformer Engine for another 2x throughput boost. A portable config: {A100: FP16+scaler, H100: FP8+TE, MI300X: BF16, TPU: BF16}.

scenario: Your mixed-precision training code uses torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler and autocast(dtype=torch.float16). It works on A100 and H100. On MI300X, gradients occasionally overflow to inf. On TPU v5e, you want to use BF16 instead of FP16. How do you make training portable?
title: Portable Mixed-Precision Training Across GPU Architectures

details.common_mistake: Treating portability as a binary decision (lock-in vs fully portable). In practice, it is a spectrum, and different layers of the stack have different portability costs.
details.napkin_math: 100-person ML org, 5 custom CUDA kernels, 3 TensorRT-dependent services. Porting cost: 5 kernels x $100K + 3 services x $50K + CI/CD overhead $100K = $750K. Annual NVIDIA spend: $5M. If multi-vendor saves 20%: $1M/yr. ROI: $750K / $1M = 9-month payback.
details.realistic_solution: Layer-by-layer assessment: (1) PyTorch model code: 95% portable (uses standard ops). Cost to port: low. (2) Custom CUDA kernels: 0% portable. Cost: high ($50K-200K per kernel to port). (3) cuDNN: replaced by MIOpen (AMD) or XLA (TPU) at framework level. Cost: medium (framework handles it). (4) NCCL: replaced by RCCL or Gloo. Cost: medium (API-compatible). (5) TensorRT: no equivalent on AMD/TPU. Cost: high (re-engineer inference pipeline). Roadmap: isolate non-portable layers behind abstraction interfaces, invest in Triton for custom kernels (portable by design), and move inference to ONNX Runtime (multi-EP). 18-month timeline, $600K investment.

scenario: Your company's entire ML stack is built on CUDA 12.x, cuDNN 8.x, NCCL 2.x, and TensorRT 8.x. A new CTO asks you to quantify the vendor lock-in risk and propose a portability roadmap. What framework do you use to assess and mitigate the risk?
title: Strategic Platform Risk Assessment for ML Infrastructure

details.common_mistake: Assuming any CUDA 12.x driver supports any CUDA 12.x runtime. CUDA's forward compatibility (newer driver runs older runtime) works, but backward compatibility (older driver with newer runtime) does not.
details.napkin_math: CUDA version matrix: driver 525 -> runtime <= 12.0. Driver 530 -> runtime <= 12.1. Driver 535 -> runtime <= 12.2. A 10-version driver gap (525 vs 535) seems small but spans two CUDA minor versions. Pin-and-document policy prevents this class of bug entirely.
details.realistic_solution: The CUDA runtime 12.1 in your container requires driver >= 530. The cloud VM has driver 525 (max runtime 12.0). Three fixes: (1) Pin your container to CUDA runtime 12.0 (match the lowest production driver). (2) Request cloud provider to update to driver 535+. (3) Use NVIDIA's CUDA compat library (libcuda_compat.so), available since CUDA 11.7, which allows a newer CUDA runtime to work with an older driver on select GPU architectures. Best practice: lock the CUDA runtime version in your Dockerfile and document the minimum driver requirement.

scenario: Your containerized inference service works on local dev (CUDA 12.1, driver 535) but crashes on production cloud VMs with 'CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version'. The cloud VMs have driver 525 (CUDA 12.0 compatible). Diagnose and fix.
title: Driver Version Compatibility Hell in Multi-GPU Cloud Deployments

details.common_mistake: Comparing raw metric values directly across profilers. NCU reports 'SM Throughput %', rocProf reports 'GPU Busy %', and XLA profiler reports 'FLOPS utilization %'. These measure different things.
details.napkin_math: H100 roofline: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOP/byte ridge. MI300X: 653 TFLOPS / 5.3 TB/s = 123 FLOP/byte ridge. TPU v5e: 197 TFLOPS / 820 GB/s = 240 FLOP/byte ridge. Same kernel has different roofline positions on each platform.
details.realistic_solution: Normalize to hardware-agnostic metrics: (1) Achieved FLOPS / Peak FLOPS (compute utilization): derive from profiler-reported FLOP counts and wall-clock time. (2) Achieved BW / Peak BW (memory utilization): derive from bytes moved and time. (3) Arithmetic intensity (FLOPS/byte): compute from the above. These three metrics are comparable across any accelerator. Build a common dashboard that pulls raw data from each profiler and computes these normalized metrics. Use the roofline model as the universal comparison framework.

scenario: You need to profile the same transformer model across H100 (using Nsight Compute), MI300X (using rocProf), and TPU v5e (using XLA profiler). Each tool reports different metrics. How do you create comparable performance analysis across platforms?
title: Portable Profiling: NCU vs rocProf vs XLA Profiler Cross-Platform Analysis

details.common_mistake: Assuming fewer fused kernels always means better performance. XLA's 28 fused ops are larger (more ops fused per kernel) but may include suboptimal fusions. TorchInductor's 45 are more granular but each fusion is carefully profiled.
details.napkin_math: Kernel launch overhead: GPU ~5us, TPU ~2us via XLA dispatch. 45 kernels x 5us = 225us GPU overhead. 28 kernels x 2us = 56us TPU overhead. 62 kernels x 5us = 310us MIGraphX overhead. For a 10ms inference: MIGraphX loses 3.1% to launch overhead alone.
details.realistic_solution: Fusion granularity reflects each compiler's strategy: (1) XLA uses whole-graph fusion — it sees the entire HLO graph and produces large fused clusters. Fewer kernels but larger ones; optimal for TPU's systolic array which prefers large matrix operations. (2) TorchInductor uses pointwise fusion + reduction fusion heuristics, splitting at reduction boundaries. This matches GPU architecture where kernel launch overhead is low but register pressure from over-fusion is high. (3) MIGraphX is more conservative, splitting at more boundaries due to less mature fusion analysis. The 62 kernel count suggests missed fusion opportunities. Profile each: XLA's 28 may have 50% higher per-kernel utilization than MIGraphX's 62.

scenario: The same 12-layer transformer encoder produces different fused kernel counts on three compilers: TorchInductor generates 45 fused kernels for H100, MIGraphX generates 62 fused kernels for MI300X, and XLA generates 28 fused operations for TPU v5e. Explain why fusion granularity differs.
title: Compiler Fusion Differences Across XLA, TorchInductor, and MIGraphX

details.common_mistake: Thinking AllReduce must operate on the entire gradient tensor at once. This would serialize communication after computation, wasting half the training time on idle network bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-50: 25.6M params x 4 bytes = 102.4MB gradients. Backward pass: ~20ms on H100. AllReduce (ring, 8 GPUs, NVLink 900 GB/s): ~0.5ms. Without overlap: 20 + 0.5 = 20.5ms. With overlap: ~20.1ms (AllReduce mostly hidden). Overlap savings: 2% here, but for larger models it is massive.
details.realistic_solution: Gradient bucketing enables overlap: PyTorch DDP groups gradients into 25MB buckets (default). As soon as all gradients in a bucket are computed during the backward pass, AllReduce for that bucket starts immediately on a separate NCCL stream while the backward pass continues computing gradients for earlier layers. Since the backward pass proceeds from the last layer to the first, and AllReduce starts with the last layer's bucket, by the time the backward pass finishes, most AllReduce operations are already complete or in progress. This overlap can hide 60-80% of communication latency behind computation.

scenario: In distributed data-parallel training of a ResNet-50 across 8 H100 GPUs, gradients are ready layer-by-layer during the backward pass, starting from the last layer. Explain why we do not wait for the entire backward pass to finish before starting AllReduce.
title: Overlapping Backward Pass with AllReduce in Data-Parallel Training

details.common_mistake: Making buckets larger to reduce the number of AllReduce calls without considering that larger buckets delay the start of communication (more gradients must be computed before a bucket is full).
details.napkin_math: 1.3B params x 4 bytes = 5.2GB gradients. AllReduce at 400 Gbps (50 GB/s): 5.2GB / 50 = 104ms without overlap. Backward pass: ~200ms. With perfect overlap: max(200, 104) = 200ms. With 40% overhead: 200 + 80ms = 280ms. Fixing bucket size could reduce to ~210-220ms.
details.realistic_solution: Optimal bucket size depends on the tradeoff between AllReduce startup latency and overlap opportunity. (1) Current: 25MB buckets = 1.3B x 4 / 25M = 208 buckets. Each AllReduce has ~50us startup latency: 208 x 50us = 10.4ms wasted on startup. (2) Increase to 100MB buckets: 52 buckets, 2.6ms startup. But fewer, larger AllReduces start later, reducing overlap. (3) Optimal: profile and find the knee. Typically 50-100MB for InfiniBand. Also try NCCL tree AllReduce (lower latency for large messages) and set NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS=4 for better bandwidth utilization. (4) Use torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel(bucket_cap_mb=100) and measure throughput.

scenario: Your DDP training of a 1.3B parameter model across 32 H100 GPUs has 40% communication overhead despite gradient bucketing. The current bucket size is 25MB (PyTorch default). Network is 400 Gbps InfiniBand. Profiling shows many small AllReduce calls with high startup latency. Optimize the bucket configuration.
title: Gradient Bucket Size Tuning for Optimal Communication Overlap

details.common_mistake: Issuing NCCL calls on the default CUDA stream, which serializes all operations. NCCL operations must be on a dedicated communication stream to overlap with compute on the default stream.
details.napkin_math: Serial transfer time: 4GB at 50 GB/s = 4/50 = 0.08s = 80ms (not 40ms — 40ms would require 100 GB/s bandwidth or 2GB data). 4GB / 50GB/s = 0.080s = 80ms.
details.realistic_solution: 4GB / 50 GB/s = 80ms serial time (not 40ms which requires either 2GB data or 100 GB/s bandwidth).

scenario: You are implementing a custom training loop (not using PyTorch DDP) for a mixture-of-experts model. You need to manually overlap AllReduce with backward computation using NCCL async operations on separate CUDA streams. The model has expert parameters and shared parameters that need different AllReduce groups.
title: NCCL Async Operations and CUDA Stream Orchestration for Overlap

details.common_mistake: Thinking 1F1B eliminates the pipeline bubble entirely. It reduces the bubble from O(k-1) micro-batches (where k is the number of stages) to a startup phase, but a bubble still exists during the warm-up and cool-down phases.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, 4 stages. Each micro-batch forward+backward per stage: ~200ms. GPipe total: (8 + 3) x 200ms = 2200ms, bubble = 600ms (27%). 1F1B total: (8 + 3) x 200ms = 2200ms (same total, but memory reduced from 8x to 4x activation storage).
details.realistic_solution: GPipe: all forwards first, then all backwards. Bubble = (k-1) micro-batch times at the end = (4-1) x t = 3t. 1F1B: after the warm-up phase (k-1 forward passes), alternate one forward and one backward per step. Bubble only during warm-up (k-1 forward passes) and cool-down (k-1 backward passes). For m micro-batches and k stages: GPipe bubble fraction = (k-1)/m. 1F1B bubble fraction = (k-1)/(m + k-1). With k=4, m=8: GPipe = 3/8 = 37.5% bubble. 1F1B = 3/11 = 27.3% bubble. Additionally, 1F1B reduces peak memory from O(m) to O(k) by freeing activations earlier.

scenario: Your 4-stage pipeline-parallel training of a 70B model has a pipeline bubble at the end of each micro-batch cycle. With 4 stages and 8 micro-batches, the GPipe schedule wastes significant GPU time in bubble periods. A colleague suggests switching to the 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) schedule.
title: Pipeline Bubble Minimization via 1F1B Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Using a single pinned memory buffer and synchronous H2D transfer. This serializes transfer and compute, making total batch time = compute + transfer = 35ms.
details.napkin_math: Without overlap: 15 + 20 = 35ms per batch, GPU util = 15/35 = 43%. With double buffer: max(15, 20) = 20ms per batch, GPU util = 15/20 = 75%. Speedup: 35/20 = 1.75x throughput improvement from just overlapping data loading.
details.realistic_solution: Double buffering: allocate two pinned memory buffers (A and B). While the GPU computes on batch N (from buffer A), asynchronously transfer batch N+1 from CPU to GPU (into buffer B) on a separate CUDA stream. When batch N finishes, immediately start computing on buffer B while transferring batch N+2 into buffer A. Implementation: use non_blocking=True in tensor.to(device) and PyTorch DataLoader with pin_memory=True, num_workers>0, prefetch_factor=2. Effective batch time: max(compute, transfer) = max(15, 20) = 20ms instead of 35ms. To fully hide transfer: either reduce batch size (less data to transfer) or use faster PCIe (Gen5: 64 GB/s vs Gen4: 32 GB/s).

scenario: Your training loop on a single H100 spends 15ms per batch on GPU computation but 20ms waiting for the next batch to transfer from CPU to GPU. The GPU is idle 57% of the time. Explain the double-buffering technique to hide data transfer latency.
title: Double Buffering for Data Loading Overlap with GPU Compute

details.common_mistake: Only prefetching one micro-batch ahead. With 4 pipeline stages and network latency, a single prefetch may not fully hide the transfer time, especially if compute time per micro-batch varies across stages.
details.napkin_math: Without prefetch: 50ms compute + 5.1ms transfer = 55.1ms per stage per micro-batch. With prefetch: 50ms compute (transfer hidden). 4 stages x 8 micro-batches: without = 4 x 8 x 55.1 = 1763ms. With = 4 x 8 x 50 = 1600ms. 9.3% speedup.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-level prefetching: (1) Stage i starts transferring micro-batch N+1's activations to stage i+1 as soon as micro-batch N's forward pass completes. (2) Use a ring buffer of 2-3 activation slots per stage to allow multiple in-flight transfers. (3) Record CUDA events after each forward pass to trigger the next prefetch. (4) Key optimization: overlap the activation send with the current micro-batch's backward pass (which doesn't need the sent activations). Transfer time for 256MB at 400 Gbps: 256MB / 50GB/s = 5.1ms. If forward compute is 50ms per stage, prefetching hides the 5.1ms transfer completely within the previous micro-batch's compute.

scenario: In a 4-node pipeline-parallel setup with H100 GPUs connected via 400 Gbps InfiniBand, each pipeline stage sends activation tensors (256MB per micro-batch) to the next stage. Without prefetching, each stage waits for the activation transfer before starting compute. Design an activation prefetching scheme.
title: Prefetching Activations in Pipeline Parallelism Across Nodes

details.common_mistake: Assuming AllReduce time scales linearly with node count. Ring AllReduce time is 2(n-1)/n x M/B (nearly constant for large n), but in practice, cross-node AllReduce has much higher latency than intra-node NVLink AllReduce.
details.napkin_math: Hierarchical AR: Step 1: 8-GPU reduce-scatter on NVLink, 5.2GB / 8 = 650MB per GPU. Step 2: inter-node AllReduce of 650MB at 50 GB/s = 13ms. Step 3: intra-node all-gather, ~1ms. Total: ~14ms vs flat AllReduce 104ms. Overlap at 14ms becomes feasible against a 200ms backward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Three factors degrade overlap at 256 GPUs: (1) AllReduce latency increases: intra-node NVLink ring at 900 GB/s vs inter-node IB at 50 GB/s per link. For 5.2GB gradients: NVLink AllReduce ~6ms, IB AllReduce ~104ms. The 104ms AllReduce exceeds the backward pass time, making overlap impossible. (2) Network congestion: 32 nodes doing simultaneous AllReduce creates IB fabric contention, adding 10-30% overhead. (3) Bucket synchronization: 256 processes must synchronize bucket readiness, adding coordination latency. Fix: use hierarchical AllReduce (intra-node reduce first via NVLink, then inter-node AllReduce of reduced results). This cuts inter-node traffic by 8x.

scenario: Your DDP training achieves 92% overlap efficiency at 8 H100 GPUs (single node, NVLink) but only 68% at 256 H100 GPUs (32 nodes, InfiniBand). AllReduce time grows faster than expected. Diagnose why overlap degrades at scale.
title: Overlap Efficiency Degradation at Scale: 8 GPUs vs 256 GPUs

details.common_mistake: Assuming tensor parallelism AllReduces can be overlapped like DDP gradient AllReduces. In tensor parallelism, the AllReduce output is the input to the next computation — there is a strict data dependency.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, 8-way TP, 96 layers. Each layer: 2 AllReduces of ~160MB (hidden_size=8192, seq_len=2048, BF16). NVLink 900 GB/s: 160MB/900 = 0.18ms per AllReduce. 192 AllReduces x 0.18ms = 34.5ms total. Compute per layer: ~5ms. Communication is 7% of compute — small enough that partial overlap via sequence parallelism recovers most of it.
details.realistic_solution: Standard tensor parallelism AllReduces cannot be overlapped because each produces a partial sum that is needed before the next layer starts. However, two techniques partially address this: (1) Async ReduceScatter + AllGather decomposition: split AllReduce into ReduceScatter (output partial results while computing) + AllGather (reconstruct while starting next layer's computation). The AllGather can partially overlap with the next layer's input processing. (2) Sequence parallelism: overlap the sequence dimension's AllGather with computation by processing received chunks as they arrive. Megatron-LM uses this to overlap 30-40% of communication.

scenario: In tensor-parallel training of a 70B LLM across 8 H100 GPUs (NVLink), each transformer layer requires two AllReduce operations: one after the attention block and one after the MLP block. These AllReduces are on the critical path. Can they be overlapped with computation?
title: Tensor Parallelism AllReduce Overlap with Feedforward Computation

details.common_mistake: Only overlapping AllGather with computation for the current layer. The real optimization is prefetching: AllGathering the NEXT layer's parameters while computing the current layer.
details.napkin_math: 13B model, 40 layers. Per-layer params: 325M = 1.3GB BF16. AllGather across 64 GPUs at 50 GB/s effective IB: 1.3GB/50 = 26ms. Per-layer forward compute: ~30ms. Since compute > AllGather, prefetching hides it. Without prefetch: 30 + 26 = 56ms/layer. With prefetch: 30ms/layer. 1.87x speedup on forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: DeepSpeed's ZeRO-3 prefetch strategy: (1) Forward pass: while computing layer L, issue AllGather for layer L+1's parameters on a separate stream. When layer L finishes, L+1's parameters are already gathered. After layer L's forward pass, release layer L's gathered parameters (keeping only the local shard). (2) Backward pass: same prefetch in reverse — while computing layer L's backward, AllGather layer L-1's parameters. (3) Tune prefetch_count: how many layers ahead to prefetch. Default: 1 layer ahead. For variable-size layers, prefetch 2+ for small layers. (4) Use NCCL's async AllGather with CUDA events for synchronization. Result: communication is almost fully hidden if per-layer compute > AllGather time.

scenario: You train a 13B model using ZeRO Stage 3 (DeepSpeed) across 64 A100 GPUs. ZeRO-3 partitions parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs. Before each layer's forward pass, all parameters for that layer must be AllGathered. This adds communication to the forward pass (not just backward). Design the overlap strategy.
title: ZeRO Stage 3 Communication-Computation Overlap Strategy

details.common_mistake: Setting all streams to the same priority and relying on the GPU scheduler's default round-robin. This can cause communication kernels to preempt compute kernels that are on the critical path.
details.napkin_math: H100 has 132 SMs. NCCL AllReduce uses 8-16 SMs for reduction. Without priority: NCCL can steal 12% of SMs from compute. With priority: compute gets all 132 SMs, NCCL uses only idle SM slots. Net compute speedup: 5-12% for communication-heavy workloads.
details.realistic_solution: CUDA stream priorities: (1) Compute stream: highest priority (cudaStreamCreateWithPriority, priority 0 = highest on NVIDIA GPUs). Compute is always on the critical path. (2) Communication stream: medium priority. NCCL kernels need GPU resources (for data packing/unpacking and reduction) but should yield to compute. (3) H2D transfer stream: lowest priority. DMA engine handles most of the transfer; GPU involvement is minimal. Set with: cudaStreamCreateWithPriority(&stream, cudaStreamNonBlocking, priority). On H100, only 2 priority levels are hardware-supported, so effectively: {high: compute, low: communication + prefetch}. This ensures compute kernels are never preempted by NCCL reduction kernels.

scenario: You have a training loop with three CUDA streams: compute (default), AllReduce (communication), and data prefetch (H2D transfer). All three contend for GPU resources. You observe that AllReduce sometimes delays compute kernels. How do you prioritize?
title: CUDA Stream Priority for Communication vs Computation Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Applying aggressive compression (e.g., 1-bit SGD or top-k with 99% sparsity) without accounting for convergence slowdown. The training time saved per step can be lost to needing more steps to converge.
details.napkin_math: AllReduce for 175B x 4 bytes = 700GB at 50 GB/s = 14 seconds (non-overlapped). With PowerSGD 10x: 70GB / 50 = 1.4 seconds, now fits within 80ms backward per bucket. Convergence overhead: ~5% more steps. Net speedup: (14s - 1.4s) / 14s = 90% communication reduction, minus 5% convergence = 85% net improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Compression options: (1) FP16 gradients instead of FP32: 2x compression, virtually no convergence impact (already standard). AllReduce: 52ms -> fits in 80ms backward. (2) PowerSGD (rank-4 approximation): ~10x compression with <1% convergence impact for most models. AllReduce: ~10ms, easily hidden. (3) Top-k (1% sparsity): 100x compression but requires error feedback and typically needs 1.2-1.5x more steps to converge. (4) FP8 gradients (H100-specific): 4x compression, emerging technique with mixed convergence results. Recommendation: PowerSGD is the sweet spot — enough compression to make overlap feasible while maintaining convergence quality.

scenario: Your 175B model trained across 512 A100 GPUs has AllReduce time (104ms) that exceeds backward pass time (80ms). Even with perfect overlap, 24ms of communication is exposed. Gradient compression is proposed to reduce communication volume. Evaluate the tradeoff.
title: Gradient Compression to Improve Overlap Feasibility at Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming interleaved scheduling is strictly better than 1F1B. While it reduces the bubble, it increases point-to-point communication because non-contiguous stages require more cross-device tensor transfers.
details.napkin_math: 32-layer 70B model. 1F1B bubble: 27.3% x 2200ms = 600ms wasted. Interleaved v=2: 15.8% x 2200ms = 347ms wasted, but extra comms: 8 micro-batches x 4 extra sends x 5ms = 160ms. Net: 347 + 160 = 507ms vs 600ms. Marginal win. At v=4: 8.6% x 2200ms = 189ms + 320ms comms = 509ms. Diminishing returns.
details.realistic_solution: Interleaved scheduling with virtual pipeline stages (v): each device holds v chunks of layers. With k=4 physical stages and v=2 virtual stages per device: effective pipeline depth = k*v = 8 virtual stages, each processing 4 layers. Bubble fraction = (k-1)/(m*v + k-1). For m=8 micro-batches: standard 1F1B = 3/11 = 27.3%, interleaved (v=2) = 3/19 = 15.8%, interleaved (v=4) = 3/35 = 8.6%. However, communication increases by v-fold: with v=2, each micro-batch traverses the network 2x. On NVLink (low latency), this is acceptable. On InfiniBand (higher latency), the extra communication may negate bubble savings. Profile both configs to find the optimal v for your network topology.

scenario: The Megatron-LM team introduced interleaved pipeline scheduling where each device holds multiple non-contiguous pipeline stages. For a 32-layer model with 4 pipeline stages, each device handles 8 layers in an interleaved pattern (device 0: layers 0,4,8,...28). Evaluate how this reduces the pipeline bubble compared to 1F1B.
title: Interleaved Pipeline Schedules: Zero-Bubble Pipeline Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Running the optimizer step as a single operation after all AllReduce completes. This wastes the time between the first gradient bucket's AllReduce completion and the last bucket's completion.
details.napkin_math: 100 gradient shards. ReduceScatter per shard: 1ms. Optimizer step per shard: 0.5ms. AllGather per shard: 1ms. Serial: 100 x (1+0.5+1) = 250ms. Pipelined: 100ms (RS pipeline) + 0.5ms (last optimizer) + 1ms (last AG) = 101.5ms. 2.5x speedup.
details.realistic_solution: Yes — ReduceScatter + local optimizer step + AllGather pattern: (1) Replace AllReduce with ReduceScatter (each GPU gets its shard of reduced gradients). (2) As soon as a GPU receives its gradient shard from ReduceScatter, it can run the optimizer step for that shard immediately, even while other ReduceScatter operations are in progress. (3) After the optimizer updates the parameter shard, AllGather distributes the updated parameters. This pipeline: ReduceScatter(shard_i) -> Optimizer(shard_i) -> AllGather(shard_i) can run concurrently for different shards. DeepSpeed and FSDP implement this pattern, overlapping optimizer compute with communication.

scenario: In standard DDP, the optimizer step waits for AllReduce to complete on all gradients. With ZeRO-1, each GPU owns a shard of optimizer states. Can we overlap the optimizer step with ongoing AllReduce by processing shards as their gradients are reduced?
title: Overlapping AllReduce with Optimizer Step via Gradient Sharding

details.common_mistake: Using BACKWARD_PRE (most aggressive prefetch) with large models without considering memory overhead. BACKWARD_PRE fetches the next layer's full parameters before the current layer's backward finishes, requiring memory for two full layers simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: BACKWARD_POST overlap: AllGather ~3ms, backward compute ~8ms per layer. Overlap hides 3ms/8ms = 37.5% of communication. Total training time reduction vs NO_PREFETCH: ~25%. Memory overhead: 1.5GB (1 extra layer) vs 3GB (BACKWARD_PRE). The 25% speedup at 1.5GB cost is the best tradeoff.
details.realistic_solution: BACKWARD_PRE: fetches next FSDP unit's params during current backward. Doubles per-layer memory. BACKWARD_POST: fetches after current backward finishes but before waiting for result. Less aggressive, lower memory. NO_PREFETCH: waits until params are actually needed. For 30B model with 32 GPUs: per-GPU params in FSDP = 30B/32 = 937.5M. Each FSDP unit (1 layer, ~750M params) = 1.5GB BF16. BACKWARD_PRE: 2 x 1.5GB = 3GB extra. At 80GB H100 with 70GB occupied, 3GB causes OOM. Solution: use BACKWARD_POST (prefetch with lower memory), or use BACKWARD_PRE with limit_all_gathers=True (limits concurrent AllGathers to 2).

scenario: You use PyTorch FSDP to train a 30B model across 32 H100 GPUs. FSDP has three prefetch policies: BACKWARD_PRE, BACKWARD_POST, and NO_PREFETCH. With BACKWARD_PRE, memory spikes cause OOM. With NO_PREFETCH, training is 40% slower. Find the right configuration.
title: FSDP Prefetch Policy Tuning for Communication-Compute Overlap

details.common_mistake: Waiting for the entire KV cache to transfer before starting decode. A 2GB transfer over NVLink at 900 GB/s takes 2.2ms, during which the decode GPU is completely idle.
details.napkin_math: KV cache per layer (70B model, 2048 context, BF16): 2 x 128 x 2048 x 80_heads/80_layers x 2 bytes = 25.6MB. Transfer at 900 GB/s: 0.028ms. Decode at ~0.5ms/layer. Transfer is 18x faster than compute — perfect overlap.
details.realistic_solution: Streamed KV cache transfer: (1) Partition the KV cache by layer (e.g., 80 layers for a 70B model). (2) Transfer layer 0's KV cache (~25MB per layer). (3) As soon as layer 0's KV arrives, start decode for layer 0 while layer 1's KV is transferring. (4) Pipeline: transfer(layer_i+1) || decode(layer_i). Decode per layer: ~0.5ms. KV transfer per layer: 25MB / 900 GB/s = 0.028ms. Since decode >> transfer, the KV transfer is completely hidden after the first layer. Total time: 0.028ms (first transfer) + 80 x 0.5ms (decode) = 40ms vs sequential: 2.2ms + 40ms = 42.2ms. Savings: 5%. Small here but critical at high QPS where every ms matters for SLA.

scenario: In a disaggregated LLM serving system (separate prefill and decode GPUs), after prefill completes, the KV cache (2GB for a long context) must be transferred from the prefill GPU to the decode GPU via NVLink. During transfer, the decode GPU is idle. Design an overlap strategy.
title: Overlapping KV Cache Transfer with Decode Computation in Serving

details.common_mistake: Comparing only peak bandwidth numbers. H100 NVSwitch provides all-to-all full bisection bandwidth (any GPU can communicate with any other at full speed), while MI300X's Infinity Fabric topology may have different bandwidth depending on GPU pair proximity.
details.napkin_math: 70B in TP-8: 2 AllReduces/layer x 96 layers = 192 AllReduces per step. 160MB each at 450 GB/s (H100 NVLink): 0.36ms each, 69ms total. At variable 300-450 GB/s (MI300X IF): 0.36-0.53ms each, 69-102ms total. Variance adds 33ms worst case.
details.realistic_solution: Key differences for overlap: (1) H100 NVSwitch: flat topology, all pairs get 450 GB/s bidirectional. AllReduce is perfectly balanced. (2) MI300X Infinity Fabric: hierarchical — pairs within the same OAM module have higher bandwidth than cross-module pairs. This creates uneven AllReduce performance. (3) For overlap, consistency matters: if AllReduce latency varies by 30% across pairs, the overlap buffer must account for the worst case. H100's flat topology gives predictable AllReduce timing, making overlap scheduling easier. (4) MI300X compensates with 192GB VRAM — more model data stays resident, reducing communication frequency in ZeRO-3. (5) Recommendation: for TP (frequent, small AllReduces), H100 NVSwitch is better. For FSDP (infrequent, large AllGathers), MI300X's larger memory reduces communication need.

scenario: You are choosing between an 8x H100 DGX node (NVLink 900 GB/s bisection) and an 8x MI300X node (Infinity Fabric 896 GB/s bisection) for distributed training. Both have similar aggregate bandwidth. Analyze how the interconnect topology affects communication-computation overlap for a 70B LLM.
title: MI300X Infinity Fabric vs H100 NVLink for Communication Overlap

details.common_mistake: Assuming PyTorch DDP always creates a separate NCCL stream. Depending on the NCCL version and configuration, NCCL may run on the default stream if NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE is not set correctly.
details.napkin_math: Serialized: 200ms backward + 50ms AllReduce = 250ms per step. Overlapped (expected): max(200, 50) = 200ms. The missing overlap costs 50/250 = 20% throughput. Fixing NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE recovers this entire 20%.
details.realistic_solution: Check NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE environment variable. Before NCCL 2.19: default is 'PARALLEL', which uses separate streams. In some configurations, it can be 'GROUP', which serializes NCCL calls. Set NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=PARALLEL explicitly. Also check: (1) Is the CUDA device set correctly before NCCL initialization? (2) Are backward hooks registered correctly? (3) Is there an implicit cudaStreamSynchronize() between backward and AllReduce? In PyTorch DDP, gradient_as_bucket_view=True can sometimes force synchronization. Also verify with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO that NCCL is using the expected transport (NVLink vs PCIe) — PCIe fallback can serialize operations.

scenario: You set up DDP with gradient bucketing and NCCL on a separate CUDA stream. Nsight Systems profiling shows that the AllReduce kernels run sequentially with backward computation — no overlap. Both the compute and NCCL kernels appear on the same stream in the timeline. What went wrong?
title: Diagnosing Failed Overlap: NCCL Blocking on Compute Stream

details.common_mistake: Trying to overlap All-to-All with expert computation within the same layer. The All-to-All output IS the expert input — they cannot overlap within a single layer due to data dependency.
details.napkin_math: 32 MoE layers. Serial: 32 x (8+6) = 448ms. Pipelined: 32 x 8 = 256ms + 6ms (last expert) = 262ms. Speedup: 448/262 = 1.71x. Time saved: 186ms per training step. At 1000 steps: 186 seconds saved.
details.realistic_solution: Inter-layer overlap (pipeline the communication): (1) Split each MoE layer's All-to-All into dispatch (tokens to experts) and combine (expert outputs back). (2) While experts compute on layer L, start the dispatch All-to-All for layer L+1 simultaneously. This requires knowing L+1's routing decisions early — run the gating network (tiny MLP, <0.1ms) for L+1 during L's expert computation. (3) Double-buffer token assignments: two sets of dispatch buffers, alternating per layer. (4) Additionally, overlap the combine All-to-All of layer L with the non-MoE layers (attention) between L and L+1. Architecture: gate(L+1) || expert_compute(L) || dispatch_A2A(L+1) || combine_A2A(L). With 8ms A2A and 6ms compute + 0.1ms gate: serial = 14ms/layer, pipelined = max(8, 6.1) = 8ms/layer. 1.75x speedup.

scenario: You train a 1.8T Mixture-of-Experts model (128 experts, top-2 routing) across 128 H100 GPUs. Each MoE layer requires All-to-All communication to route tokens to their assigned expert GPUs. The All-to-All takes 8ms per MoE layer, and expert computation takes 6ms. With 32 MoE layers, communication dominates. Design an overlap architecture.
title: Expert Parallelism All-to-All Overlap in Mixture-of-Experts Training

details.common_mistake: Thinking the GPU must pause computation to handle PCIe data transfers. The DMA copy engine is an independent hardware unit that moves data without consuming compute resources.
details.napkin_math: H100 HBM3: 3.35 TB/s. PCIe Gen5 x16: 64 GB/s. Compute kernel BW: ~2.5 TB/s typical. PCIe uses 64/3350 = 1.9% of HBM bandwidth. Minimal contention — the DMA engine can operate at full PCIe speed without impacting compute.
details.realistic_solution: H100 has a dedicated DMA copy engine that operates independently from the 132 SMs. This enables three concurrent operations: (1) H2D transfer: DMA engine copies training data from host pinned memory to GPU HBM via PCIe Gen5 (64 GB/s). (2) Compute: SMs execute the current batch's forward/backward kernels. (3) D2H transfer: DMA engine copies results back to host. These three operations run simultaneously using separate CUDA streams. The H100 actually has two copy engines (one for each direction), so H2D and D2H can also overlap. Total overlap: compute, H2D, and D2H all concurrent. The only shared resource is HBM bandwidth — if all three compete, effective bandwidth per operation decreases.

scenario: An H100 GPU connected via PCIe Gen5 x16 has a DMA copy engine separate from its compute SMs. Explain how this hardware design enables overlapping data transfers with kernel execution.
title: PCIe DMA Engine Overlap for Host-Device Data Movement

details.common_mistake: Claiming 100% overlap because the two streams run concurrently for most of their duration. Overlap efficiency depends on how much communication is hidden behind computation.
details.napkin_math: If NCCL ended at 390ms (10ms after backward): exposed communication = 10ms. Overlap efficiency = 150ms / (150+10ms) = 93.8%. The 10ms exposure adds directly to step time. Every 1% of communication exposure = 1.5ms/step at this scale.
details.realistic_solution: Timeline analysis: Backward: [180ms, 380ms], duration = 200ms. NCCL: [200ms, 350ms], duration = 150ms. Overlap window (intersection): [200ms, 350ms], duration = 150ms. The NCCL AllReduce starts 20ms after backward (first bucket becomes ready) and finishes 30ms before backward ends. Communication fully overlapped: 150ms/150ms = 100% of NCCL time is hidden behind backward. Exposed communication: 0ms. But backward has 20ms before NCCL starts (no overlap possible — gradients not ready) and 30ms after NCCL finishes (backward still computing early layers). This means the first gradient bucket takes 20ms to fill — consider smaller first bucket. Overlap efficiency: 150ms/(150ms + 0ms exposed) = 100%. Total step time: 380ms (end of backward) + optimizer.

scenario: You profile a DDP training step with Nsight Systems and see: backward pass spans 180-380ms on the compute stream. NCCL AllReduce spans 200-350ms on the NCCL stream. Calculate the overlap efficiency and identify the exposed communication time.
title: Quantifying Overlap Efficiency with Nsight Systems Timeline Analysis

details.common_mistake: Maximizing micro-batch count without considering that smaller micro-batches reduce GPU utilization (lower arithmetic intensity, more kernel launch overhead).
details.napkin_math: m=32 wins. Effective throughput 0.62 vs m=4's 0.34 = 1.82x faster. Further increasing m to 64 hurts because GPU utilization drop outweighs bubble reduction. The knee is where d(GPU_eff)/dm = d(bubble_reduction)/dm.
details.realistic_solution: The optimal micro-batch count balances bubble ratio against per-micro-batch GPU efficiency. (1) GPU efficiency vs micro-batch size: H100 Tensor Cores need batch >= 64 for >80% utilization on typical matmuls. Below batch 32, utilization drops rapidly. (2) If global batch = 1024, and k=8 stages: m micro-batches of size 1024/m each. At m=4: batch 256 per micro-batch (high GPU efficiency ~95%), bubble 175%. At m=32: batch 32 per micro-batch (moderate GPU efficiency ~75%), bubble 21.9%. At m=64: batch 16 (low efficiency ~50%), bubble 10.9%. (3) Effective throughput = GPU_efficiency x (1 - bubble_fraction). m=4: 0.95 x 0.36 = 0.34. m=32: 0.75 x 0.82 = 0.62. m=64: 0.50 x 0.90 = 0.45. Optimal: m=32.

scenario: Your 8-stage pipeline trains a 175B model. With 4 micro-batches, the bubble ratio is (8-1)/4 = 175% overhead (more bubble than compute). With 32 micro-batches, it drops to (8-1)/32 = 21.9%. But increasing micro-batches requires reducing per-micro-batch size, which may hurt GPU compute efficiency. Find the optimal tradeoff.
title: Micro-Batch Size Impact on Pipeline Parallelism Bubble Ratio

details.common_mistake: Using the same AllReduce strategy for both sparse embedding gradients and dense MLP gradients. Sparse AllReduce (AllGather of indices + values) has very different performance characteristics than dense AllReduce.
details.napkin_math: MLP dense AllReduce: 8GB at 900 GB/s NVLink = 8.9ms. Embedding sparse AlltoAll: 500MB at 900 GB/s = 0.56ms. If overlapped: total = max(8.9, 0.56) = 8.9ms vs serial 9.46ms. Small savings, but the embedding optimizer starts 8.9ms earlier — pipeline win.
details.realistic_solution: Overlap strategy: (1) MLP backward finishes before embedding backward (MLP is on top of the network). Start dense AllReduce for MLP gradients immediately on NCCL stream 1. (2) Embedding backward produces sparse gradients (only ~1% of the table is accessed per batch). Use AlltoAll (not AllReduce) to route sparse gradients to the owning GPU on NCCL stream 2. (3) Both communications overlap with each other AND with any remaining embedding backward computation. (4) Key: sparse gradient communication is much smaller than dense. 50GB table with 1% sparsity: only 500MB of sparse gradients vs 8GB dense MLP gradients. The sparse AlltoAll finishes first, allowing the embedding optimizer to start while MLP AllReduce is still in progress.

scenario: Your recommendation model has a 50GB embedding table (table-parallel across 8 GPUs) and a 2B-parameter MLP (data-parallel across the same 8 GPUs). The embedding lookup produces sparse gradients, while the MLP produces dense gradients. Both need AllReduce. Can they overlap?
title: Overlapping Embedding Table AllReduce in Hybrid Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Applying GPU-optimized overlap strategies (flat AllReduce + bucketing) directly to TPU without considering the torus topology. Multi-hop AllReduce on a torus has different latency characteristics than NVSwitch.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e ICI: 1.6 Tbps = 200 GB/s per link. 4x4 torus AllReduce: 2 x 3/4 x M / 200 GB/s (two dimensions, ring formula). For M=1GB: 2 x 0.75 x 1/200 = 7.5ms. Compared to flat ring over 16 chips: 15/16 x 1/200 x 2 = 9.4ms. Torus is 20% faster.
details.realistic_solution: On TPU's 2D torus: (1) AllReduce is implemented as ReduceScatter + AllGather over the torus dimensions. Each dimension does a separate ring reduce. (2) For a 4x4 torus (16 TPUs): AllReduce in the X dimension (4 chips), then Y dimension (4 chips). Total latency proportional to chip_count_per_dim, not total chips. (3) XLA's SPMD partitioner automatically maps AllReduce to torus dimensions. (4) Overlap opportunity: XLA can overlap the Y-dimension AllReduce with computation if the next operation only needs the X-dimension reduction first. This is XLA's 'latency hiding' optimization. (5) Unlike GPU, TPUs handle communication overlap at the compiler level (XLA), not runtime level (CUDA streams). The programmer's job is to provide static graphs that XLA can analyze.

scenario: TPU v5e pods use ICI (Inter-Chip Interconnect) in a 2D torus topology with 1.6 Tbps bandwidth per link. Unlike NVIDIA's NVSwitch (all-to-all), the torus requires multi-hop communication for non-adjacent chips. How does this topology affect communication-computation overlap strategy for data-parallel training?
title: TPU v5e ICI Ring Topology and Communication Overlap Opportunities

details.common_mistake: Choosing activation recomputation purely based on memory savings without considering its impact on compute-communication overlap. Recomputation adds compute to the backward pass, which can improve overlap by making the backward pass longer than communication.
details.napkin_math: Memory savings from recomputation: 8 micro-batches x 2GB activations per micro-batch = 16GB freed. This can increase batch size by 2x on an 80GB H100. With 2x batch: forward 400ms, backward 400ms, recompute 400ms. But samples per step doubles. Throughput: 2x samples / 1.5x time = 1.33x improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Counterintuitive benefit: activation recomputation actually IMPROVES overlap. (1) Without recomputation: backward pass = 200ms, AllReduce = 150ms. Overlap ratio: 150/200 = 75%. (2) With recomputation: backward pass = 200ms (original) + 200ms (recompute forward) = 400ms. AllReduce = 150ms (unchanged). Overlap ratio: 150/400 = 100% (fully hidden). (3) Total time: without recomputation: max(200, 150) = 200ms (if fully overlapped). With recomputation: max(400, 150) = 400ms.
