When the RDMA buffer is 2KB-aligned (not 64KB-aligned), the first 62KB of the first page and the last portion of the buffer span partial pages. The HCA's DMA engine can only issue TLPs that don't cross page boundaries (PCIe spec requirement). A 4KB MTU packet that crosses a 64KB page boundary is split into two TLPs: one for the data before the boundary and one for the data after. Each TLP has 12-20 bytes of overhead. With 2KB alignment: every 64KB, one 4KB packet gets split into two TLPs. Impact: 4KB/64KB = 6.25% of packets are split, each incurring an extra TLP header (16 bytes) plus PCIe link layer overhead (2 bytes DLLP + 8 bytes framing). But the real cost is PCIe transaction ordering: split TLPs can't be reordered, creating pipeline bubbles in the HCA's DMA engine. Each bubble ≈ 100ns at PCIe Gen5. With 12.2M packets/sec × 6.25% × 100ns = 76.3ms of bubbles per second = 7.6% throughput loss. Fix: allocate RDMA buffers with cuMemAlloc aligned to 2MB (huge page size) using cudaMemAllocManaged with cudaMemAdvise for preferred location.

scenario: Your GPUDirect RDMA transfers on MI300X achieve only 35 GB/s instead of the expected 50 GB/s (400Gbps line rate). The GPU memory buffer starts at an address that is 2KB-aligned rather than 64KB-aligned. PCIe performance counters show excessive TLP (Transaction Layer Packet) splitting. Diagnose the alignment issue and its impact on RDMA throughput.
title: GPUDirect RDMA Page Table Alignment

details.common_mistake: Choosing RC for everything because 'reliable is always better.' RC requires O(N²) QP resources (one QP per connection pair), which doesn't scale to thousands of GPUs. Each QP consumes ~1KB of HCA memory, and QP state transitions are expensive.
details.napkin_math: RC QP memory: 512 GPUs × 4088 QPs × 1KB = 2GB across the cluster (4MB per GPU). UD QP memory: 4096 × 1KB = 4MB across entire cluster. 500× less. But at 512 GPUs, 4MB per GPU is fine. At 16,384 GPUs: RC would need 131K QPs per GPU = 128MB — hitting HCA limits. UD scales to 16K+ easily.
details.realistic_solution: RC (Reliable Connection): (1) Guarantees in-order delivery and automatic retransmission. (2) QP scaling: 512 GPUs × 511 peers × 8 rails = 2,087,424 QPs per cluster. Per GPU: 511 × 8 = 4,088 QPs × ~1KB = 4MB of HCA memory. Feasible on ConnectX-7 (256MB HCA memory). (3) Failure: if one QP errors (e.g., remote GPU crash), only that QP is affected. (4) Throughput: 50 GB/s per QP (line rate). UD (Unreliable Datagram): (1) No delivery guarantee — NCCL must handle retransmission in software. (2) QP scaling: O(N) — one QP per GPU handles all peers via multicast. 512 × 8 = 4,096 QPs total. (3) Failure: lost packets silently dropped. NCCL detects via timeout and retransmits. Higher software complexity. (4) Throughput: same line rate but with software retransmission overhead. (5) Advantage: supports multicast, enabling one-to-many broadcast with single send. For AllReduce on 512 H100s: Use RC for reduce-scatter/all-gather (data integrity critical, QP count manageable). Use UD+multicast for small broadcasts (parameter updates, control messages) where QP savings matter and occasional retransmission is tolerable. NCCL v2.18+ uses this hybrid approach.

scenario: InfiniBand offers two transport modes: Reliable Connection (RC) with guaranteed delivery and ordering, and Unreliable Datagram (UD) with no delivery guarantees. NCCL uses both: RC for point-to-point transfers and UD for some collective operations. Evaluate the tradeoffs for AllReduce on a 512-H100 cluster, considering QP scalability, failure handling, and throughput.
title: RDMA Reliable Connection vs Unreliable Datagram

details.common_mistake: Assuming on-demand paging for GPU memory works like CPU ODP. CPU ODP leverages virtual memory page faults, but GPU VRAM doesn't have a traditional MMU with page fault handling. GPUDirect RDMA ODP requires a different mechanism based on page table invalidation callbacks.
details.napkin_math: Without ODP: register 64 × 32MB buffers = 2GB pinned, inflexible. With ODP: full 192GB addressable, ~10ms first-use overhead. Page fault rate after warmup: 0 (steady-state buffers). PyTorch caching allocator fragmentation trigger: when free_memory < 10% (19.2GB on MI300X), allocation churn increases and ODP fault rate rises.
details.realistic_solution: Specification for GPU RDMA ODP: (1) Implicit MR: register the entire 192GB GPU VRAM as a single implicit Memory Region at startup. This establishes the HCA↔GPU PCIe BAR mapping for the full address range. Cost: one-time, ~50ms. (2) Page table callback: register nvidia_p2p_put_pages callback with the GPU driver. When PyTorch's caching allocator frees or reallocates a VRAM region, the callback notifies the HCA to invalidate those page table entries. (3) Lazy validation: when an RDMA operation references an invalidated page, the HCA traps to the kernel ODP handler, which calls nvidia_p2p_get_pages to re-establish the mapping. This adds ~10μs per page fault — amortized over subsequent accesses. (4) Prefault optimization: before starting AllReduce, NCCL calls ibv_advise_mr on the gradient buffer addresses, pre-faulting all pages into the HCA's MTT. Cost: 192GB / 2MB pages = 96K entries × 100ns = 9.6ms. (5) Memory pressure: if GPU memory is heavily fragmented, page faults during RDMA increase. Set a threshold: if fault rate exceeds 100/second, log a warning and pre-register active buffers. Expected performance: first AllReduce iteration incurs ~10ms of page faults. Subsequent iterations run at line rate (0 faults) as long as buffers aren't reallocated.

scenario: Traditional RDMA requires all memory to be pinned (non-swappable) and registered with the HCA before use. For a 192GB MI300X GPU, registering all HBM with the RDMA subsystem creates a rigid allocation that conflicts with PyTorch's dynamic memory allocator (caching allocator). Specify an on-demand paging (ODP) architecture for GPUDirect RDMA that allows dynamic GPU memory allocation without pre-registration.
title: RDMA Memory Registration with On-Demand Paging

details.common_mistake: Assuming GPUDirect RDMA and GPUDirect Storage use separate PCIe paths. On most server platforms, the NIC and NVMe SSDs share the same PCIe root complex or switch, creating bandwidth contention during concurrent operations.
details.napkin_math: PCIe contention: 50 + 28 = 78 GB/s demand on 57 GB/s bus = 1.37× oversubscription. AllReduce degradation: from 50 to 36.5 GB/s = 27% throughput loss. For 2GB AllReduce: normal = 40ms, degraded = 54.8ms. Extra 14.8ms per iteration during checkpoint window. Checkpoint duration: 192GB/20.5GB/s = 9.4s. Total wasted time: 9.4s × 14.8ms/200ms = 693ms of AllReduce overhead per checkpoint.
details.realistic_solution: On a typical MI300X server (e.g., Supermicro AS-8125GS): each GPU connects to a PCIe Gen5 x16 switch that also hosts its ConnectX-7 NIC and 2 NVMe SSDs. PCIe Gen5 x16: 64 GB/s per direction (theoretical), ~57 GB/s effective. AllReduce GPUDirect RDMA: GPU VRAM → PCIe → NIC. Requires ~50 GB/s (400Gbps NIC line rate) = 88% of PCIe bandwidth. Checkpoint GPUDirect Storage: GPU VRAM → PCIe → NVMe. Each NVMe Gen5: 14 GB/s. 2 SSDs = 28 GB/s = 49% of PCIe bandwidth. Total demand: 50 + 28 = 78 GB/s on a 57 GB/s link — 137% oversubscription! Result: AllReduce throughput drops to 57 × 50/78 = 36.5 GB/s (73% of normal). Checkpoint throughput: 57 × 28/78 = 20.5 GB/s (73% of normal). Both suffer proportionally. Mitigation: (1) Schedule checkpoints during forward-pass computation when NICs are idle. (2) Checkpoint only on a subset of GPUs (ZeRO-3 shards: only checkpoint 1/N of weights per GPU, reducing by 64×). (3) Use CPU-bounce buffer path for checkpoints: GPU→CPU→NVMe, trading latency for PCIe bandwidth isolation (CPU uses different PCIe root complex). (4) On MI300X with 192GB: checkpoint = 192GB per GPU. At 20.5 GB/s degraded: 192/20.5 = 9.4 seconds. With full NVMe bandwidth: 192/28 = 6.9 seconds. The 2.5 seconds of extra checkpoint time cascades into 2.5s × 64 GPUs of stalled AllReduce.

scenario: During training, a 64-MI300X cluster performs two types of bulk data transfer: (1) AllReduce gradients via GPUDirect RDMA (GPU→NIC→GPU), and (2) checkpoint saves via GPUDirect Storage (GPU→NVMe SSD). Both bypass CPU memory but share the PCIe bus. Analyze how concurrent checkpoint saves affect AllReduce throughput when both operations compete for PCIe bandwidth.
title: GPUDirect RDMA vs GPUDirect Storage Data Paths

details.common_mistake: Simple round-robin striping across NICs, which causes packet reordering since different rails have different latencies. RDMA RC transport interprets reordering as packet loss, triggering expensive go-back-N retransmission.
details.napkin_math: Single rail: 2GB / 50 GB/s = 40ms. 8 rails parallel: 2GB / (8 × 50) GB/s = 5ms (pure bandwidth). With AllReduce overhead: ~10.2ms. Speedup: 40ms/10.2ms = 3.92× (not 8× due to latency overhead in each rail's AllReduce). At N=64: per-rail AllReduce = 2 × 63/64 × 256MB / 50GB/s = 10.1ms ≈ same, because bandwidth term dominates.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-rail AllReduce design: (1) Data partitioning: divide the 2GB gradient into 8 equal partitions of 256MB. Assign each partition to a dedicated rail. Rail K handles gradient[K×256MB : (K+1)×256MB]. This eliminates reordering because each rail processes independent data — no cross-rail ordering dependency. (2) Per-rail AllReduce: each rail runs an independent ring AllReduce on its 256MB partition. With N=512 GPUs: each rail has 512 participants. Time per rail: 2 × 511/512 × 256MB / 50GB/s = 10.2ms. All 8 rails run simultaneously: total time = 10.2ms (not 8 × 10.2ms). (3) Rail failure handling: if Rail K fails, redistribute its 256MB across remaining 7 rails (256/7 = 36.6MB extra per rail). New per-rail data: 256 + 36.6 = 292.6MB. Time: 2 × 511/512 × 292.6MB / 50GB/s = 11.7ms. Degradation: 14.7% (vs 12.5% bandwidth loss — close to theoretical minimum). (4) Implementation: NCCL sets NCCL_NCHANNELS=8 (one channel per rail) and binds each channel to a specific NIC via NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0,mlx5_1,...,mlx5_7. (5) Consistency: after all 8 rail-level AllReduces complete, each GPU has the fully reduced gradient — no cross-rail synchronization needed because the partitions are disjoint.

scenario: Each H100 node has 8 ConnectX-7 NICs (8-rail design). Design the multi-path RDMA strategy for a single 2GB AllReduce operation that utilizes all 8 NICs simultaneously, addressing how to partition data across rails, handle rail failures, and maintain in-order delivery for the reduction operation.
title: RDMA Multi-Path with Bonded NICs

details.common_mistake: Lumping everything into 'network latency ~5μs.' The breakdown reveals that PCIe and DMA setup dominate for small messages, not the wire or switch. This is why RDMA latency doesn't improve linearly with faster link speeds.
details.napkin_math: 64B RDMA Write: ~1.2μs total. PCIe: 600ns (50%). HCA processing: 300ns (25%). Wire + switch: 94ns (8%). WQE/CQE overhead: 200ns (17%). For large messages (1MB): serialization dominates: 1MB / 50GB/s = 20μs wire time. PCIe: 1MB / 57GB/s = 17.5μs. Total ≈ 40μs (wire becomes 50% again due to store-and-forward effects).
details.realistic_solution: End-to-end breakdown for 64-byte RDMA Write via GPUDirect RDMA: (1) Work Request posting: CPU writes WQE to send queue via MMIO doorbell → 200ns. (2) HCA fetches WQE from host memory via DMA → 100ns. (3) HCA initiates PCIe read from GPU VRAM: PCIe Gen5 read request → 300ns (round-trip for 64B read with TLP). (4) HCA packetizes: adds IB headers (42 bytes for IB, ~80 for RoCE) → 50ns. (5) Link serialization: 106 bytes (64 payload + 42 header) / 50 GB/s = 2.12ns. (6) Switch forwarding: cut-through latency = ~90ns (Quantum-2 IB switch port-to-port). (7) Link serialization (switch to remote HCA): 2.12ns. (8) Remote HCA receives and processes: strips headers, validates ICRC → 100ns. (9) Remote HCA writes to remote GPU VRAM via PCIe: 300ns (PCIe write). (10) Remote HCA generates CQE on local CQ → 50ns (optional, for signaled completions). Total: 200 + 100 + 300 + 50 + 2 + 90 + 2 + 100 + 300 + 50 = 1,194ns ≈ 1.2μs. Measured InfiniBand Write latency for 64 bytes: ~1.3μs (close to our estimate). The wire itself (items 5-7) accounts for only 94ns = 7.9% of total latency. PCIe operations (items 3, 9) account for 600ns = 50%.

scenario: Trace the end-to-end latency of a single 64-byte RDMA Write from GPU A's VRAM to GPU B's VRAM across two H100 nodes connected by a single 400Gbps InfiniBand switch. Break down every component: GPU DMA initiation, PCIe traversal, HCA processing, link serialization, switch forwarding, and remote-side processing.
title: RDMA Latency Breakdown for a Single Write

details.common_mistake: Applying traffic shaping at the switch level only. Switch-level QoS (WFQ, strict priority) helps but doesn't prevent bursty traffic from entering the fabric. NIC-level shaping prevents congestion from forming in the first place by smoothing traffic at the source.
details.napkin_math: Job A unshaped: 400Gbps bursts every 200ms during AllReduce → 400Gbps × 60ms burst = 3GB instantaneous → switch buffer overflow. Job A shaped at 300Gbps with 32KB burst: max instantaneous rate = 300Gbps, spread over 60ms = 2.25GB smoothly. Job B guaranteed: 100Gbps × always available. Activation transfer: 8MB / (100Gbps/8) = 640μs — well within 2ms pipeline budget.
details.realistic_solution: NIC-level traffic shaping on ConnectX-7 with MI300X: (1) Rate limiting: configure per-QP rate limiters on Job A's AllReduce QPs. Set max rate = 300Gbps per NIC (75% of 400Gbps), reserving 100Gbps for Job B. ConnectX-7 supports 128 rate-limited QPs. NCCL configuration: NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION=4, each limited to 75Gbps. (2) Burst control: set maximum burst size to 32KB per QP using the HCA's token bucket shaper. This converts Job A's large 256MB bursts into a smooth stream of 32KB chunks, preventing instantaneous incast at switches. (3) Priority mapping: Job A uses SL0 (best effort), Job B uses SL4 (high priority). Configure the HCA's SL-to-VL mapping so SL4 maps to VL1 with guaranteed minimum bandwidth of 100Gbps. (4) Implementation: mlnx_qos -i mlx5_0 --rate_limit 300000 (Mbps) for Job A's port. For per-QP shaping: use ibv_modify_qp_rate_limit() with rate=75000 Mbps, burst=32768 bytes. (5) Monitoring: use ConnectX-7 telemetry counters: tx_pause_duration (should decrease for Job B's ports) and tx_bytes_phy per SL.

scenario: On a multi-tenant 256-MI300X cluster, two training jobs share the same physical network. Job A uses 128 GPUs for AllReduce and Job B uses 128 GPUs for pipeline-parallel training. Job A's bursty AllReduce traffic starves Job B's latency-sensitive activation transfers. Design NIC-level traffic shaping to ensure fairness without fabric-level changes.
title: NIC-Level Traffic Shaping for RDMA Fairness

details.common_mistake: Favoring iWARP because it eliminates PFC. While PFC-free operation is attractive, iWARP's reliance on TCP introduces per-connection state overhead and higher latency that makes it unsuitable for high-performance AllReduce at scale.
details.napkin_math: 1024 GPUs AllReduce overhead: RoCE = 2 × 1023 × 2μs = 4.1ms latency. iWARP = 2 × 1023 × 4μs = 8.2ms. Extra 4.1ms per iteration × 3600 iterations/hour = 14.8 seconds/hour wasted. iWARP TCP state: 8.4M connections × 2KB = 16.8GB — 65× more than RoCE QP state (256MB). Not feasible on current HCAs.
details.realistic_solution: iWARP drawbacks for ML: (1) Latency: iWARP adds TCP processing overhead even with hardware offload. Measured latency: 3-5μs vs RoCE's 1.5-2.5μs. For AllReduce with 2048 steps at N=1024: extra latency = 2048 × 2μs = 4ms per iteration. (2) Throughput: TCP segmentation and reassembly limits throughput to ~350Gbps on current hardware (vs 400Gbps for RoCE). 12.5% throughput penalty. (3) CPU overhead: while iWARP offloads TCP to hardware (TOE), the TCP state machine is inherently more complex than UDP. Connection setup: TCP 3-way handshake = 3 RTTs vs RoCE QP setup = 1 RTT. (4) Scalability: TCP maintains per-connection state (buffers, sequence numbers, congestion windows). For 1024 GPUs × 1023 connections × 8 rails = 8.4M TCP connections, each needing ~2KB state = 16.8GB of TOE memory — exceeding HCA capacity. (5) Advantage: no PFC needed, works over any Ethernet fabric, handles lossy networks gracefully. Verdict: iWARP is suitable for small clusters (<64 GPUs) or lossy WAN-connected training (cross-datacenter DiLoCo). RoCE v2 remains necessary for large-scale training where latency and throughput matter.

scenario: A cloud provider considers deploying iWARP (RDMA over TCP) instead of RoCE v2 (RDMA over UDP) for their multi-tenant ML training infrastructure. iWARP doesn't need PFC since TCP handles retransmission, eliminating the PFC deadlock risk. Evaluate iWARP's suitability for large-scale ML training compared to RoCE v2, considering latency, throughput, CPU overhead, and operational complexity.
title: iWARP vs RoCE v2 for ML Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming RDMA atomics scale with bandwidth. RDMA atomics are processed sequentially by the target HCA's atomic processing unit — there is no parallelism. Each atomic operation must read, compare, and write to a single memory location, and concurrent atomics to the same address are serialized.
details.napkin_math: Single lock CAS: 333K ops/sec total. 256 contenders: 333K/256 = 1.3K acquisitions/sec per worker. SGD at 1000 iter/sec needs 1000 lock acquisitions/sec per worker. Deficit: 1.3K vs 1000 — barely sufficient, and only with zero-contention lock usage. In practice: lock waiters spin on CAS, consuming RDMA bandwidth on failed attempts. 256 workers × 333K attempts/sec = 85.3M RDMA atomics/sec hitting one HCA port.
details.realistic_solution: RDMA CAS throughput to a single address: 1 / 3μs = 333K operations/sec, regardless of bandwidth. With 256 workers contending: each CAS attempt has 1/256 probability of success (only one wins). Expected attempts per successful acquisition: 256 (geometric distribution mean). Time per lock acquisition: 256 × 3μs = 768μs on average. Maximum lock turnover rate: 333K ops/sec / 256 contenders = ~1,302 lock acquisitions per second across the entire system. If each parameter update requires the lock for 10μs of critical section: effective throughput = 1/(768μs + 10μs) = 1,284 updates/sec. At this rate, 256 workers each get ~5 updates/sec — completely inadequate for SGD which needs 1000+ updates/sec per worker. Fix: (1) Eliminate distributed locking — use AllReduce (lock-free by design). (2) Use partitioned locks — 256 independent lock addresses, each worker acquires a different lock. Contention drops to 1 worker per lock = 333K ops/sec. (3) Use RDMA Write for parameter updates (no atomics needed if updates are commutative — gradient addition is commutative).

scenario: Your parameter server implementation uses RDMA Compare-and-Swap (CAS) atomics for distributed locking. Each of 256 H100 workers acquires a lock before updating shared parameters. Under high contention (all 256 workers trying to acquire the same lock simultaneously), each CAS takes 3μs. Calculate the maximum lock acquisition throughput and diagnose why RDMA atomics become a bottleneck at scale.
title: RDMA Atomic Operations for Distributed Locking

details.common_mistake: Evaluating UEC purely on paper specifications without considering the maturity gap. RoCE v2 and InfiniBand have 15+ years of production hardening, while UEC is pre-silicon. Paper specs always look better than deployed systems.
details.napkin_math: 8192 MI300X cluster: AllReduce with ECMP (RoCE): ~15% throughput loss from hash collisions at scale. AllReduce with packet spray (UEC): ~2% overhead from reordering. Net improvement: 13% throughput gain. Training cost for 70B model: $10M (estimate). 13% faster training: saves $1.3M. UEC's incremental NIC/switch cost: ~$2M for 8192-GPU cluster. Payback: 1.5 training runs.
details.realistic_solution: UEC key innovations and evaluation: (1) Packet spraying: distributes individual packets across all available paths, achieving perfect load balancing without ECMP hash collisions. Benefit: eliminates the hash polarization problem that causes 10-20% throughput loss with ECMP at >1024 GPUs. Concern: requires hardware reordering buffers at every receiver — each 400G port needs ~4MB of reorder buffer, adding to switch silicon cost. (2) Selective retransmission: retransmits only lost packets (vs RDMA RC's go-back-N which retransmits entire windows). Benefit: reduces retransmission overhead from O(window) to O(1). For AllReduce with 0.01% loss rate: RC retransmits ~655 extra packets per 256MB, selective retransmits ~65. 10× reduction. (3) Multi-path transport: single connection uses multiple physical paths natively. Eliminates the need for NCCL to manage per-rail QPs manually. Benefit: automatic failover and load balancing without application changes. Overall: UEC addresses real pain points, especially PFC elimination and vendor independence. For 8192 MI300X: UEC's packet spraying alone would improve AllReduce throughput by 15-25% vs ECMP-based RoCE v2. But timeline risk: UEC silicon expected 2026-2027, first production deployments 2028+. IB and RoCE will advance 2 generations by then.

scenario: The Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) is designing a new RDMA transport specifically for AI/ML workloads, addressing RoCE v2's PFC dependency and InfiniBand's vendor lock-in. UEC proposes packet spraying (per-packet load balancing), hardware-based selective retransmission, and multi-path transport. Evaluate UEC's architecture for a hypothetical 8192-MI300X training cluster compared to RoCE v2 and InfiniBand.
title: Ultra Ethernet Consortium for ML Training

details.common_mistake: Treating RDMA errors as fatal and restarting the entire job. At 1024 GPUs running for 90 days, the mean time between any RDMA error is ~4 hours (based on production data). Restarting from checkpoint on every error would spend more time restarting than training.
details.napkin_math: 90 days × 1024 GPUs: Tier 1 events: ~900. Recovery: 900 × 100ms = 90 seconds total. Tier 2 events: ~90. Recovery: 90 × 5s = 450 seconds = 7.5 minutes total. Tier 3 events: ~13. Recovery: 13 × 10min = 130 minutes. Total downtime: 138 minutes / 129,600 minutes = 0.11% — 99.89% uptime. Without tiered recovery (restart on every error): ~1003 restarts × 10 minutes = 167 hours of downtime = 7.7% — 8× worse.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-tier error recovery specification: Tier 1 — Transient errors (QP error, retransmission timeout, ~10/day): Detection: CQE with error status from ibv_poll_cq(). Recovery: (1) Reset the affected QP (RESET→INIT→RTR→RTS transition, ~1ms). (2) Re-register memory regions if MR was invalidated. (3) Retry the failed AllReduce from the current chunk. (4) Time budget: <100ms. No checkpoint rollback. NCCL handles this transparently via NCCL_IB_RETRY_CNT=7. Tier 2 — Path failures (cable disconnect, switch port failure, ~1/day): Detection: multiple QP timeouts on the same rail. Recovery: (1) Detect via IB subnet manager trap notifications. (2) Activate alternate path via APM (Automatic Path Migration) on InfiniBand — pre-configured during QP setup. (3) If no alternate path: redistribute traffic across remaining 7 rails (12.5% throughput loss). (4) Time budget: <5 seconds. (5) Alert ops team for cable replacement. Tier 3 — Node failure (GPU crash, HCA reset, ~1/week): Detection: NCCL timeout (NCCL_TIMEOUT=1800 seconds). Recovery: (1) Exclude failed node. (2) Load checkpoint on a spare node. (3) Re-establish all QP connections for the replacement node. (4) Resume training from last checkpoint. Time budget: <10 minutes. Checkpoint frequency: every 30 minutes (2GB checkpoint save takes ~40ms with GPUDirect Storage). Monitoring: per-QP error counters (ibv_query_qp), per-port symbol_error and link_downed counters, MTBF tracking per node.

scenario: A 90-day training run on 1024 H100s will inevitably experience RDMA transport errors: QP failures, path migration events, HCA resets, and cable disconnections. Specify the error recovery architecture that allows training to continue with minimal interruption, including error detection, automatic QP re-establishment, and checkpoint-based rollback criteria.
title: RDMA Error Recovery in Long-Running Training Jobs

details.common_mistake: Assuming GDRCopy is always faster than GPUDirect RDMA. GDRCopy's advantage is only for small messages where the overhead of posting RDMA work requests exceeds the data transfer time. For large transfers, GPUDirect RDMA's hardware DMA engine is faster.
details.napkin_math: Control messages per AllReduce iteration: ~128 ready flags + 128 completion signals = 256 messages × 64 bytes = 16KB total. GDRCopy: 256 × 1.4μs = 358μs (sequential). GPUDirect RDMA: 256 × 0.7μs = 179μs but requires CQ polling overhead. In practice: GDRCopy control plane runs on CPU while GPU does computation — the 358μs is fully hidden.
details.realistic_solution: GDRCopy path for 64-byte control message: CPU reads from GPU VRAM via mapped BAR1 region → ~1μs (PCIe read). CPU copies data to host buffer → ~10ns (L1 cache). CPU posts RDMA Send with inline data (data embedded in WQE, no separate DMA) → ~300ns. HCA sends 64-byte message → serialization + network = ~100ns. Total: ~1.4μs. GPUDirect RDMA path for 64-byte message: Post WQE specifying GPU VRAM source → 200ns. HCA fetches WQE → 100ns. HCA reads 64 bytes from GPU VRAM via PCIe → 300ns. HCA sends packet → ~100ns. Total: ~700ns. Wait — GPUDirect RDMA is actually faster? Yes, for 64-byte messages, GPUDirect RDMA with inline data is competitive. But: GPUDirect RDMA requires memory registration (MR setup) which is expensive (~2ms per region). GDRCopy uses a pre-established BAR mapping and avoids MR management. The real advantage: GDRCopy allows the CPU to read/write GPU memory synchronously without posting RDMA work requests, which is critical for NCCL's control plane where the CPU orchestrates buffer management. Latency comparison: GDRCopy = 1.4μs with CPU flexibility. GPUDirect RDMA = 0.7μs but requires async WR posting and CQ polling.

scenario: GDRCopy is a library that allows low-latency CPU access to GPU memory via a persistent BAR mapping. NCCL uses GDRCopy for small control messages (<8KB) instead of GPUDirect RDMA. For a 128-A100 cluster performing AllReduce, control messages include: buffer pointers, ready flags, and completion signals (~64 bytes each). Calculate the latency advantage of GDRCopy over GPUDirect RDMA for these small messages.
title: GDRCopy for Small RDMA Messages

details.common_mistake: Dismissing the O(N²) problem because 'memory is cheap.' At 16K GPUs with 8 rails, the QP count and connection setup time become operationally prohibitive — not because of memory cost but because of setup latency and HCA resource limits.
details.napkin_math: RC at 16K GPUs: 131K QPs/GPU × 128MB HCA memory = infeasible. DC at 16K GPUs: 8 QPs/GPU × 8KB HCA memory = trivial. DC context cache: 32 entries (hot peers) × 256 bytes = 8KB on HCA. Ring AllReduce accesses 2 peers repeatedly: 100% cache hit rate. All-to-All (MoE): accesses 16K peers with Zipf distribution — top 32 experts cover 80% of traffic, so cache hit rate ≈ 80%. Remaining 20% incur 5μs penalty per miss.
details.realistic_solution: Naive O(N²): 16,384 GPUs × 16,383 peers × 8 rails = 2.15 billion QPs. Per QP: ~1KB state on HCA. Per GPU: 16,383 × 8 = 131K QPs × 1KB = 128MB — exceeds ConnectX-7's 256MB HCA memory (QPs share with MRs, CQs, etc.). Connection setup: 131K QPs × 0.3ms/QP = 39.3 seconds — too slow for elastic scaling. Scalable architecture: (1) Shared Receive Queue (SRQ): all QPs on a port share one receive queue. Reduces receive buffer memory from O(N) to O(1) per port. (2) Dynamic Connected (DC) transport (Mellanox extension): single QP handles connections to all peers by swapping connection context on each message. Per GPU: 8 DC QPs (one per rail) instead of 131K. Memory: 8 × 1KB = 8KB vs 128MB. 16,000× reduction. (3) Connection caching: DC maintains an LRU cache of recently-used peer contexts. Cache hit = 0 overhead. Cache miss = ~5μs to fetch context from host memory. For ring AllReduce (each GPU talks to 2 neighbors): cache hit rate > 99%. (4) Hybrid: use DC for AllReduce (N peers, infrequent connection changes) and RC for pipeline-parallel (fixed peers, latency-critical). Estimate 16 RC QPs (pipeline) + 8 DC QPs (AllReduce) = 24 QPs per GPU × 1KB = 24KB. (5) Connection setup: 24 QPs × 0.3ms = 7.2ms (vs 39 seconds). 5,400× faster.

scenario: You are architecting the RDMA transport for a 16,384-MI300X GPU cluster (the scale of frontier model training). Traditional RDMA requires O(N²) QP connections for all-to-all communication. Calculate the total QP state memory, connection setup time, and propose an architecture that scales sub-quadratically while maintaining full AllReduce functionality.
title: RDMA Connection Scaling for 10K GPU Clusters

details.common_mistake: Assuming SR-IOV has zero overhead because it is 'hardware virtualization.' SR-IOV adds IOMMU address translation (1-3% throughput overhead), VF scheduling latency (100-500ns), and shares the physical NIC's processing resources across all VFs.
details.napkin_math: Bare-metal: 400 Gbps × 92% (IOMMU overhead) = 368 Gbps per NIC. SR-IOV with 2 VFs: 368/2 = 184 Gbps per VF (46% of bare-metal). SR-IOV with 4 VFs: 368/4 = 92 Gbps per VF (23%). For AllReduce at 90% bare-metal: need dedicated NIC per tenant. 8 NICs per MI300X → maximum 8 tenants with full RDMA performance.
details.realistic_solution: SR-IOV overhead analysis for RDMA: (1) IOMMU translation: each DMA operation goes through IOMMU page table walk. Impact: +100ns per DMA transaction = +200ns per RDMA Write (read source + write destination). For 4KB packets: 200ns / 82ns (serialization at 400G) = 2.4× latency overhead per packet. Throughput impact: 100ns / (82ns + 100ns) = 55% of time spent on IOMMU → 45% throughput = 180 Gbps. With IOMMU IOTLB cache hit (64-entry TLB): overhead drops to ~10ns → 92% throughput = 368 Gbps. (2) VF scheduling: the PF (Physical Function) arbitrates between VFs. With round-robin and N VFs: each VF gets 1/N of processing cycles. (3) Maximum tenants for 90% throughput: per VF bandwidth = 400Gbps × 0.92 (IOMMU) / N = target 360 Gbps (90%). Solving: N = 400 × 0.92 / 360 = 1.02 → N=1 only! This means a single VF achieves ~92% of bare-metal, and adding a second VF drops each to 46% — unacceptable. Solution: use separate physical NICs per tenant (possible on MI300X with 8 NICs), or use one NIC per tenant with dedicated VFs on dedicated PCIe virtual functions that have guaranteed bandwidth. With per-VF rate guarantees: 2 VFs × 200Gbps each = 400Gbps total, each achieving ~184 Gbps effective (92% × 200G) = 46% of bare-metal per VF.

scenario: A cloud provider wants to offer bare-metal RDMA performance to multiple tenants sharing a physical MI300X server. SR-IOV (Single Root I/O Virtualization) creates virtual NIC functions (VFs) from a physical ConnectX-7 NIC. Quantify the performance overhead of SR-IOV for RDMA compared to bare-metal, and specify the maximum number of tenants that can share one 400G NIC without degrading AllReduce throughput below 90% of bare-metal.
title: RDMA Performance Isolation with SR-IOV

details.common_mistake: Conflating CXL memory bandwidth with HBM bandwidth. CXL 3.0 over PCIe Gen6 provides ~128 GB/s per port — 26× less than H100's 3.35 TB/s HBM3. Using CXL memory for gradient buffers creates a massive bandwidth bottleneck for the GPU's DMA engine.
details.napkin_math: CXL bandwidth: 128 GB/s. NIC bandwidth: 50 GB/s. Ratio: 2.56× headroom — CXL can feed the NIC. But: GPU DMA from HBM at 3.35 TB/s fills NIC 67× faster than CXL. For 2GB gradient: HBM→NIC prefetch = 2GB/3350GB/s = 0.6ms. CXL→NIC prefetch = 2GB/128GB/s = 15.6ms. 26× slower prefetch, adding 15ms to AllReduce setup. Not worth the complexity.
details.realistic_solution: CXL memory for RDMA gradient buffers — analysis: (1) Bandwidth: CXL 3.0 via PCIe Gen6 x16 = 128 GB/s per direction. GPU reads gradients from CXL at 128 GB/s to fill NIC send buffers. NIC sends at 50 GB/s (400Gbps). CXL bandwidth (128 GB/s) >> NIC bandwidth (50 GB/s), so CXL is NOT the bottleneck for RDMA sends. Good. (2) Latency: CXL memory access = ~200ns vs HBM = ~300ns. CXL is actually lower latency for small random accesses (counterintuitive but correct — CXL memory is DRAM without the HBM interposer distance). But for sequential DMA (gradient transfer), HBM's 3.35 TB/s >> CXL's 128 GB/s, so HBM fills the NIC's DMA buffer 26× faster. (3) Coherency: CXL 3.0 provides hardware cache coherence between GPU and CXL memory. GPU writes gradients during backward pass, RDMA NIC reads them for AllReduce. Without CXL coherence: explicit flush needed (10-50μs). With CXL coherence: automatic, but coherence protocol adds ~50ns per cache line = ~50ns × (2GB / 64B cache lines) = 1.56 seconds — unacceptable for full gradient! Must use uncacheable (UC) memory mapping for gradient buffers, bypassing coherence. (4) Use case: CXL memory is valuable NOT for gradient buffers but for expanding optimizer state capacity. Adam optimizer for a 70B model needs 70B × 12 bytes = 840GB across GPUs. CXL pool can hold overflow optimizer state, accessed infrequently. Verdict: CXL for RDMA gradient buffers is architecturally unsound. CXL for optimizer state expansion is promising.

scenario: CXL (Compute Express Link) 3.0 enables memory pooling where a GPU can access remote DRAM attached to a CXL switch with ~200ns latency (vs ~300ns for local HBM). Some propose using CXL memory as an extended gradient buffer for AllReduce, allowing RDMA NICs to read gradients from CXL-attached memory instead of GPU HBM. Evaluate this architecture for a 512-H100 cluster, considering the latency, bandwidth, and coherency implications.
title: RDMA with CXL Memory Expansion for ML

details.common_mistake: Confusing AllReduce (which sums partial results) with AllGather (which concatenates shards). Column-parallel splits the weight matrix along the output dimension, so each GPU produces a complete partial output that must be summed, not concatenated.
details.napkin_math: For a 4-way TP MLP with hidden_dim=16384: each GPU holds a [16384, 4096] column shard (W shape is [H_in, H_out]; column-parallel splits H_out, so each shard is [H_in, H_out/4] = [16384, 4096]). Output per GPU is [batch, seq, 4096]. AllGather across 4 GPUs reconstructs [batch, seq, 16384].
details.realistic_solution: No collective is needed between the column-parallel layer and a subsequent row-parallel layer in Megatron's fused design. The column-parallel layer splits weights along columns (output dim), producing independent partial activations on each GPU. These feed directly into the row-parallel layer, which splits along rows (input dim). Only after the row-parallel layer is an AllReduce needed to sum the partial results. This fused column→row design eliminates one communication step per transformer block. If used standalone, a column-parallel layer would need an AllGather to reconstruct the full output tensor.

scenario: In Megatron-LM's column-parallel linear layer running on an 8×MI300X node, after each GPU computes its local partial output, what collective operation is required before the result can be used by the next layer, and why?
title: Column-Parallel Linear Layer Communication Pattern

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that AllReduce = ReduceScatter + AllGather, so the actual bytes on the wire is 2 × (N-1)/N × message_size, not just the message size. Also confusing HBM bandwidth with NVLink bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Per AllReduce: 2048 × 8192 × 2B = 33.6 MB. Ring cost: 2 × (7/8) × 33.6 = 58.8 MB. At 400 GB/s: 0.15 ms. Two per block × 80 blocks = 24 ms total.
details.realistic_solution: Each AllReduce sends a tensor of shape [2048, 8192] in BF16 = 2048 × 8192 × 2 = 33.6 MB. Two AllReduces per block = 67.2 MB message volume. Using ring AllReduce, actual bytes per GPU = 2 × (7/8) × 33.6 MB = 58.8 MB per AllReduce. With 8×MI300X connected via Infinity Fabric at ~400 GB/s bisection bandwidth, each AllReduce takes ~58.8 MB / 400 GB/s ≈ 0.15 ms. Two AllReduces ≈ 0.3 ms per block. With 80 layers, total TP communication ≈ 24 ms per forward pass. This is small relative to compute, confirming TP is communication-efficient within a node.

scenario: A Llama-70B transformer block has hidden_dim=8192 and runs with TP=8 on MI300X GPUs (5.3 TB/s HBM3). Each transformer block requires 2 AllReduce operations in the forward pass (one for attention, one for MLP). For a batch of 2048 tokens, estimate the per-block AllReduce communication volume and time.
title: TP Communication Volume for Transformer Block

details.common_mistake: Thinking that InfiniBand bandwidth (400 Gbps = 50 GB/s) is comparable to intra-node NVLink (900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU on H100). The 18× bandwidth gap makes cross-node TP devastating for throughput.
details.napkin_math: NVLink: 900 GB/s. InfiniBand: 50 GB/s. Ratio: 18×. 192 AllReduces × 0.85 ms extra latency = 163 ms wasted per forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: TP requires AllReduce after every attention and MLP block — 2 AllReduces per layer, executed synchronously. With 96 layers in a 175B model, that is 192 AllReduces per forward pass. Intra-node NVLink on H100 provides 900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU. Cross-node InfiniBand provides only 50 GB/s — an 18× slowdown on every collective. Each AllReduce that took 0.05 ms intra-node would take ~0.9 ms cross-node, adding ~170 ms of pure communication overhead per forward pass. Instead, use TP=8 within each node and PP=2 across nodes. Pipeline parallelism only communicates activations between stages (one send per microbatch boundary), which is far less frequent and tolerates higher latency.

scenario: Your team proposes using TP=16 across two 8-GPU nodes (one H100 node, one MI300X node) connected by 400 Gbps InfiniBand to train a 175B parameter model. Why is this almost certainly a bad idea, and what would you recommend instead?
title: Why TP Stays Within a Node

details.common_mistake: Mixing up which dimension is split. Column-parallel splits along H_out (each GPU gets full H_in but H_out/4). Row-parallel splits along H_in (each GPU gets H_in/4 but full H_out).
details.napkin_math: For H_in=H_out=8192, TP=4: Column-parallel shards are [8192, 2048] (8192×2048 = 16.78M params). Row-parallel shards are [2048, 8192] (16.78M params). Both are 16.78M params × 2B = 33.6 MB per GPU.
details.realistic_solution: Column-parallel: W is split along columns (output dimension). Each GPU holds W_i of shape [H_in, H_out/4]. Input x is replicated on all GPUs. Each GPU computes y_i = x @ W_i, producing shape [batch, H_out/4]. An AllGather concatenates these into the full [batch, H_out]. Row-parallel: W is split along rows (input dimension). Each GPU holds W_i of shape [H_in/4, H_out]. Input x must be split: each GPU gets x_i of shape [batch, H_in/4]. Each GPU computes y_i = x_i @ W_i, producing a partial sum of shape [batch, H_out]. An AllReduce sums these partials into the final result. Megatron pairs column→row to eliminate one collective: the column output is already naturally partitioned to serve as row input.

scenario: Explain the difference between column-parallel and row-parallel linear layers in Megatron-LM. For a weight matrix W of shape [H_in, H_out] split across 4 GPUs, what does each GPU hold, and what collective is needed after each?
title: Row-Parallel vs Column-Parallel Weight Splitting

details.common_mistake: Thinking sequence parallelism splits the model weights along the sequence dimension. It only splits the activations for non-TP operations (LayerNorm, Dropout), keeping TP for the GEMM operations unchanged.
details.napkin_math: Replicated activation per layer: 4 × 8192 × 8192 × 2B = 512 MB. With SP: 512/8 = 64 MB. Savings over 80 layers: (512-64) × 80 = 35.8 GB per GPU.
details.realistic_solution: Without sequence parallelism, LayerNorm and Dropout activations of shape [batch, seq, hidden] = [4, 8192, 8192] are replicated on all 8 GPUs. Each copy is 4 × 8192 × 8192 × 2B = 512 MB per layer. With 80 layers, that is 80 × 512 MB = 40 GB of replicated activations per GPU — wasted because each GPU holds identical copies. Sequence parallelism splits the sequence dimension across TP ranks for these operations. Each GPU processes seq_len/TP = 1024 tokens for LayerNorm/Dropout, reducing activation memory to 512/8 = 64 MB per layer, saving 87.5%. The key insight: between the column-parallel and row-parallel layers, activations are already partitioned. Sequence parallelism replaces the AllGather/ReduceScatter with communication that serves double duty — redistributing for TP while partitioning for LayerNorm.

scenario: Megatron-LM introduced sequence parallelism alongside tensor parallelism. LayerNorm and Dropout are not parallelized by standard TP and their activations are replicated across all TP ranks. For a 70B model with seq_len=8192, batch=4, hidden=8192, TP=8 on H100 GPUs, quantify the activation memory waste from replication and explain how sequence parallelism fixes it.
title: Sequence Parallelism in Megatron-LM

details.common_mistake: Only considering whether the model fits in memory. A single MI300X has 192 GB, so 140 GB weights fit, but you also need KV cache and activation memory. Also ignoring that TP=2 doubles available memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: TP=1: 5.3 TB/s, 140 GB weights → decode step = 140/5300 = 26 ms. TP=2: 10.6 TB/s, 70 GB/GPU → decode step ≈ 70/5300 + comms ≈ 13 + 8 = 21 ms. ~20% faster.
details.realistic_solution: Single MI300X (TP=1): 140 GB weights leave 52 GB for KV cache and activations. With long context (32K tokens, 80 layers, 64 KV heads, head_dim=128), KV cache = 2 × 32768 × 80 × 64 × 128 × 2B = 84 GB — exceeds remaining memory. So TP=1 fails for long context. TP=2 on MI300X: 384 GB total, 140 GB weights split = 70 GB per GPU, leaving 122 GB per GPU for KV cache. KV cache is also split across TP ranks, so each GPU holds 42 GB. Memory bandwidth doubles from 5.3 to 10.6 TB/s, nearly doubling decode throughput since decode is memory-bandwidth bound. The cost: each transformer block now needs 2 AllReduces over the inter-GPU link. On MI300X with Infinity Fabric at ~400 GB/s between GPUs, this adds ~0.1 ms per block × 80 blocks = 8 ms — modest vs the ~25 ms decode latency at TP=1.

scenario: You are deploying a 70B parameter model (BF16) for inference. You have access to MI300X GPUs (192 GB HBM3 each). The model weights alone are 140 GB. Should you use TP=1 with a single MI300X or TP=2 across two MI300X GPUs? Analyze the tradeoff.
title: TP Degree Selection for Inference

details.common_mistake: Thinking AllReduce and AllGather have very different costs. In a ring implementation, both transfer approximately 2(P-1)/P × M bytes total across the ring, making them nearly equal for large P.
details.napkin_math: M = 32 MB, P = 8. AllGather per GPU: 7/8 × 32 = 28 MB. AllReduce per GPU: 2 × 7/8 × 32 = 56 MB. AllReduce is 2× the traffic of AllGather.
details.realistic_solution: Ring AllGather: each GPU sends its local shard (M/P bytes) around the ring in P-1 steps. Total bytes per GPU = (P-1) × M/P ≈ M for large P. Ring AllReduce: equivalent to ReduceScatter + AllGather. Total bytes per GPU = 2 × (P-1)/P × M ≈ 2M for large P. So AllReduce costs roughly 2× AllGather. In Megatron: column-parallel forward uses AllGather (concatenate partial outputs), row-parallel forward uses AllReduce (sum partial results). In the backward pass, the collectives swap: column-parallel backward uses ReduceScatter, row-parallel backward uses AllReduce. The fused column→row design means you pay 1 AllReduce per MLP/Attention block in forward, and 1 AllReduce in backward = 2 AllReduces total per block per training step.

scenario: On an 8×MI300X node with Infinity Fabric interconnect, compare the communication volume of AllReduce and AllGather for a tensor of size M bytes across P GPUs using a ring algorithm. Which one does Megatron's row-parallel layer use, and which does the column-parallel layer use?
title: AllReduce vs AllGather Cost in TP

details.common_mistake: Assuming any TP degree works. Since each GPU must get an equal number of complete attention heads, TP must evenly divide the number of heads.
details.napkin_math: 32 heads ÷ TP=8 = 4 heads/GPU. 32 heads ÷ TP=6 = 5.33 → invalid. Valid TP values for 32 heads: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
details.realistic_solution: TP=8 with 32 heads: 32/8 = 4 heads per GPU. This works perfectly. TP=6 with 32 heads: 32/6 = 5.33 — not an integer. You cannot split an attention head across GPUs without fundamentally changing the computation (each head's Q, K, V projections and attention computation are tightly coupled). So TP must divide the head count evenly. Practically, TP is always a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8) because: (a) GPU counts per node are powers of 2, (b) NVLink topologies are optimized for power-of-2 groups, (c) head counts in modern models are always powers of 2 or multiples of common TP degrees. For GQA models with fewer KV heads (e.g., 8 KV heads), this further constrains TP to divide the KV head count, limiting TP to at most 8.

scenario: A model has 32 attention heads. Your cluster has 8 GPUs per node. Can you use TP=8? What about TP=6? Explain the constraint that attention heads place on TP degree.
title: TP and Attention Head Partitioning

details.common_mistake: Assuming TP=4 means each GPU holds exactly 1/4 of everything. While weights are split 4 ways, some parameters like embedding tables and final LayerNorms may be replicated, and optimizer states scale with the local parameter count.
details.napkin_math: TP=4: 30B/4 = 7.5B params per GPU. Weight only: 7.5B × 2B = 15 GB. Training total: 7.5B × 16B = 120 GB → exceeds A100-80GB.
details.realistic_solution: Weight memory per GPU: ~60 GB / 4 = 15 GB (BF16 weights split across TP ranks). Small components like positional embeddings and final LayerNorm are replicated but negligible (<100 MB). For AdamW mixed-precision training, per-parameter overhead is: FP32 master weight (4B) + FP32 momentum (4B) + FP32 variance (4B) + BF16 gradient (2B) = 14B per parameter, plus the 2B BF16 weight = 16B total. With 30B/4 = 7.5B params per GPU: 7.5B × 16B = 120 GB per GPU. This exceeds A100-80GB! Solutions: add ZeRO Stage 1 (partition optimizer states across DP ranks) or use activation checkpointing to reclaim memory from activations.

scenario: A 30B parameter model uses BF16 weights (60 GB total). You apply TP=4 across four A100-80GB GPUs. How much weight memory does each GPU hold? What about optimizer states during training with AdamW in mixed precision?
title: TP Memory Savings Calculation

details.common_mistake: Suggesting to simply reduce TP degree without considering that the model may not fit in memory with fewer GPUs. Also suggesting async AllReduce without understanding that TP AllReduces are on the critical path — next layer depends on the result.
details.napkin_math: Current comm time: 15% of step. FP8 comms: halve message size → ~7.5%. Overlap: recover ~3%. Net: ~4.5-6%. MFU improvement: 72% × (1 + 0.09) ≈ 78%.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy 1: Overlap communication with computation using CUDA streams. While AllReduce runs for one sub-layer (e.g., attention output), the independent Dropout/LayerNorm of the next sub-layer can execute concurrently. Megatron-LM's async TP does this, recovering 5-8% of the communication overhead. Strategy 2: Use FP8 for TP communication (available on H100 Transformer Engine). AllReduce message size drops by 2× vs BF16, halving communication time. The slight precision loss in the collective is acceptable because LayerNorm immediately follows, restoring numerical stability. Combined effect: 15% overhead → ~6-7% overhead, pushing MFU from 72% to ~78-80%. Additional option: switch from ring AllReduce to tree AllReduce on NVSwitch-connected H100s, reducing latency from O(P) to O(log P) steps.

scenario: Your TP=8 training job on H100 nodes shows 72% MFU (Model FLOP Utilization). Profiling reveals that AllReduce operations account for 15% of step time. Propose two concrete strategies to reduce TP communication overhead without changing the TP degree.
title: TP Bubble: Synchronization Overhead in Practice

details.common_mistake: Not realizing that KV heads constrain TP degree more than query heads. With only 8 KV heads, TP=16 would require splitting individual KV heads, which is architecturally invalid.
details.napkin_math: 64 Q-heads / TP=8 = 8 Q-heads per GPU. 8 KV-heads / TP=8 = 1 KV-head per GPU. Max TP = min(num_kv_heads, GPUs_per_node) = 8.
details.realistic_solution: With TP=8 and 8 KV heads: each GPU gets exactly 1 KV head and 64/8 = 8 query heads. The 8 query heads on each GPU all attend to the same single local KV head — no cross-GPU KV communication needed. This is clean and efficient. With TP=16 and 8 KV heads: 8/16 = 0.5 KV heads per GPU — impossible. You would need to either replicate KV heads (each pair of GPUs shares a KV head, wasting memory) or redesign the attention kernel to split within a KV head (complex, breaks the abstraction). In practice, TP degree for GQA models is capped at num_kv_heads. For Llama-3 70B, max practical TP = 8. To scale beyond 8-way parallelism within a node, combine TP=8 with context parallelism (split along sequence dimension for long contexts).

scenario: Llama-3 70B uses Grouped Query Attention with 64 query heads and 8 KV heads. You set TP=8 on MI300X GPUs. How are the KV heads distributed, and what problem arises if you try TP=16?
title: GQA Impact on Tensor Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Assuming TP is always better because it is more established. For MoE, expert parallelism is almost always preferred because experts are independent — there is no mathematical reason to split a single expert across GPUs.
details.napkin_math: With top-2 routing, each expert sees 2/8 = 25% of tokens. EP All-to-All: dispatches 2 × batch × hidden × 2B — equivalent in volume to TP's AllReduce (both are ~2 × batch × hidden × 2B). The advantage of EP is not reduced communication volume but elimination of synchronization barriers: experts compute independently after the All-to-All.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy A (TP=8 per expert): Each expert's FFN weights are split across all 8 GPUs. Every token requires 2 AllReduces per expert layer, regardless of which expert it is routed to. All 8 GPUs participate in every token's computation. Strategy B (Expert Parallelism): Each GPU holds one complete expert. Tokens are routed via All-to-All dispatch to the owning GPU, processed locally, then All-to-All collected back. Communication volume is comparable to TP's AllReduce (~2 × batch × hidden × 2B), but there is no synchronization barrier during compute — each GPU works independently. Strategy B wins because: (1) experts are embarrassingly parallel, (2) each GPU does a full GEMM (better utilization than tiny TP shards), (3) no barrier stall during compute. Expert parallelism is the standard for MoE (GShard, Switch Transformer, Mixtral).

scenario: You are training a Mixture-of-Experts model with 8 experts per layer, each expert having hidden_dim=4096. You have 8 H100 GPUs in a node. Compare two strategies: (A) TP=8 applied to each expert, or (B) Expert Parallelism where each GPU holds one complete expert. Which is superior and why?
title: TP vs Expert Parallelism for MoE Models

details.common_mistake: Assuming the embedding table must be replicated on all GPUs. This wastes memory and is unnecessary since each token only accesses one row.
details.napkin_math: Embedding table: 128K × 12288 × 2B = 3 GB. Per GPU with TP=8: 384 MB. Replicated: 3 GB × 8 = 24 GB wasted cluster-wide.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy 1 — Vocabulary Parallelism (Megatron default): Split the embedding table along the vocabulary dimension. Each GPU holds 128K/8 = 16K rows of shape [16K, 12288] = 384 MB. For a given token ID, only the GPU owning that vocabulary range does a lookup; others output zeros. An AllReduce sums across GPUs to produce the final embedding. Pros: Memory efficient, matches output layer (which reuses embedding weights). Cons: AllReduce for every forward pass on embeddings. Strategy 2 — Column Parallelism on embeddings: Split along hidden_dim. Each GPU holds [128K, 12288/8] = [128K, 1536] = 384 MB. Every GPU does a lookup (all rows are local), producing a partial embedding. An AllGather reconstructs the full hidden_dim. Pros: No GPU is idle during lookup. Cons: Does not align with the output projection's parallelism. Megatron uses Strategy 1 because the output linear layer (logits = hidden @ embed.T) naturally shares the same vocabulary partition, eliminating an extra communication step.

scenario: A large language model has a vocabulary of 128K tokens with hidden_dim=12288. The embedding table is 128K × 12288 × 2B = 3 GB in BF16. With TP=8, describe two valid strategies to parallelize the embedding table and their tradeoffs.
title: Embedding Table Parallelism Strategy

details.common_mistake: Assuming backward communication mirrors forward exactly. The backward pass through an AllReduce in the forward becomes a no-op (identity) in backward, while the forward identity (input replication) becomes an AllReduce in backward.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, hidden=8192, TP=8, batch×seq=8192: per AllReduce = 2 × 7/8 × 8192 × 8192 × 2B = 230 MB. 4 per block × 80 blocks = 320 AllReduces × 230 MB = 72 GB per step.
details.realistic_solution: Forward: Identity (replicate input) → Column-parallel GEMM → Row-parallel GEMM → AllReduce (sum partials). Backward (reverse order): AllReduce backward = Identity (gradients pass through unchanged). Row-parallel backward: local gradient GEMM, but need AllReduce on input gradient to get ∂L/∂x_row. Column-parallel backward: local gradient GEMM, but the gradient of the Identity (input replication) is AllReduce (sum gradients from all ranks). So the backward pass has: 1 AllReduce for gradient through the row-parallel input, and 1 AllReduce for gradient through the column-parallel input. Total per block per training step: Forward: 1 AllReduce (after row-parallel). Backward: 1 AllReduce (through column-parallel input). For a block with both Attention and MLP: 4 AllReduces total (2 forward + 2 backward). Communication volume per AllReduce = 2 × (P-1)/P × batch × seq × hidden × 2B.

scenario: In the forward pass of Megatron's fused column→row design, an AllReduce follows the row-parallel layer. What communication operations occur in the backward pass through the same two layers? Derive the total communication volume per block for a full training step.
title: Backward Pass Communication in TP

details.common_mistake: Assuming activation checkpointing only costs extra compute (recomputed FLOPs). In TP, recomputation also requires re-executing the AllReduce/AllGather collectives from the forward pass, increasing communication volume.
details.napkin_math: Without checkpointing: 4N AllReduces. With: 6N. For 80 layers: 320 → 480 AllReduces. At 0.15 ms each: 48 ms → 72 ms. But saved ~30 GB activation memory enables 2× batch size.
details.realistic_solution: With full activation checkpointing, only the input to each transformer block is saved. During backward, the entire forward pass is recomputed to regenerate intermediate activations. This recomputation includes the TP collectives: the AllReduce after row-parallel layers must be re-executed. For a model with N blocks, forward TP communication = 2N AllReduces (attention + MLP). Backward recomputation adds another 2N AllReduces. Backward's own gradient AllReduces add 2N more. Total: 6N AllReduces per step (vs 4N without checkpointing) — a 50% increase in TP communication. This is usually acceptable because: (1) TP communication is fast over NVLink, (2) recomputed collectives overlap with recomputed GEMMs, (3) the memory savings from checkpointing (often 5-10× activation memory reduction) enable larger batch sizes that amortize the overhead.

scenario: You enable full activation checkpointing on a TP=8 training job. During recomputation in the backward pass, which TP communication operations must be re-executed? Does activation checkpointing increase TP communication volume?
title: TP with Activation Checkpointing Interaction

details.common_mistake: Assuming that equal partition sizes guarantee equal execution time. In practice, GPU clock throttling, memory access patterns, and NCCL ring ordering create micro-imbalances.
details.napkin_math: 5% clock throttle on one MI300X: if MLP GEMM takes 0.5 ms, straggler takes 0.525 ms. Over 80 layers × 2 MLPs: 80 × 2 × 0.025 = 4 ms wasted per step. At 100 ms step time: 4% throughput loss.
details.realistic_solution: Even with perfect weight partitioning (each GPU holds exactly H_out/8 columns), several factors cause micro-imbalance: (1) Thermal throttling: MI300X GPUs in different physical positions experience different cooling, causing 2-5% clock frequency variation. The hottest GPU becomes the straggler in every AllReduce. (2) Memory alignment: depending on partition sizes, some GPU shards may have dimensions that align better with the memory controller's interleaving (e.g., multiples of 256 bytes), giving slightly better memory throughput. (3) NCCL ring ordering: the AllReduce ring topology means some GPUs start sending/receiving earlier. (4) OS jitter: interrupts and context switches on one GPU's host thread cause microsecond delays that compound over thousands of layers. Mitigation: ensure adequate cooling, use CUDA MPS to reduce context-switching, pin NCCL to optimal ring topologies with NCCL_RINGS environment variable.

scenario: A custom model architecture uses 48 attention heads. Your team deploys with TP=8 on MI300X GPUs. Each GPU gets 6 heads, which works. But profiling shows that the MLP layers have slightly uneven execution times across TP ranks. What could cause this imbalance in a correctly partitioned TP setup?
title: TP Load Imbalance from Uneven Head Counts

details.common_mistake: Placing TP groups across nodes. TP groups must be intra-node (using NVLink) because TP requires frequent synchronization. DP groups span across nodes (using InfiniBand) because gradient AllReduce is infrequent (once per step).
details.napkin_math: TP groups: 4 groups of 8 (intra-node). DP groups: 8 groups of 4 (inter-node). DP AllReduce: 17.5 GB × 2 × 0.75 / 50 GB/s = 525 ms (overlapped with backward).
details.realistic_solution: Layout: Node 0: GPUs [0-7] = TP group 0 (data-parallel rank 0). Node 1: GPUs [8-15] = TP group 1 (DP rank 1). Node 2: GPUs [16-23] = TP group 2 (DP rank 2). Node 3: GPUs [24-31] = TP group 3 (DP rank 3). TP communication (AllReduce per layer): happens within each node over NVLink (900 GB/s per GPU). DP communication (gradient AllReduce): GPU 0 communicates with GPUs 8, 16, 24; GPU 1 with GPUs 9, 17, 25; etc. This crosses nodes over InfiniBand (400 Gbps per node). DP gradient AllReduce happens once per training step, sending each GPU's local gradient shard. With TP=8, each GPU holds 1/8 of the model, so DP AllReduce message size = total_params/8 × 2B = 70B/8 × 2 = 17.5 GB. At 50 GB/s effective InfiniBand: 17.5 GB × 2 × (3/4) / 50 = 525 ms without overlap. With gradient bucketing and compute overlap, this is hidden behind the backward pass.

scenario: You have 32 H100 GPUs across 4 nodes (8 GPUs per node). You want to train a 70B model with TP=8 and DP=4. Draw the process group layout: which GPUs form TP groups, which form DP groups, and where does each type of communication occur?
title: TP + DP Hybrid Parallelism Layout

details.common_mistake: Assuming linear scaling — doubling TP should halve time. In reality, each GPU's GEMM shrinks (lower arithmetic intensity) while communication stays constant per collective, causing the compute-to-communication ratio to collapse.
details.napkin_math: hidden/TP threshold: 5120/8 = 640 — well below 2048. At TP=4: 5120/4 = 1280, borderline. 13B models are best at TP=2 or TP=4.
details.realistic_solution: For a 13B model (hidden=5120, 40 layers, 40 heads): TP=1: Each GEMM is large ([batch, 5120] × [5120, 20480]), achieving near-peak Tensor Core utilization. MFU ~55-60%. TP=2: GEMMs halve in one dimension, still large enough for good utilization. Comms are tiny on NVLink. MFU ~52-55%. TP=4: GEMMs are 1/4 size. Still reasonable. MFU ~45-50%. TP=8: Each GPU handles [batch, 5120] × [5120, 2560] — the output dimension is only 2560. For small batch sizes, this GEMM becomes memory-bound (low arithmetic intensity). Meanwhile, 2 AllReduces per block × 40 blocks = 80 AllReduces per forward pass. MFU drops to ~30-35%. The cliff hits between TP=4 and TP=8 for 13B models because the GEMM dimensions shrink below the Tensor Core efficiency threshold (~4096 in the smallest dimension). Rule of thumb: TP is efficient when hidden_dim / TP ≥ 2048.

scenario: Plot the expected MFU (Model FLOP Utilization) as TP degree increases from 1 to 8 on H100 NVLink nodes for a 13B parameter model. At what TP degree does efficiency drop sharply, and why?
title: TP Scaling Efficiency Cliff

details.common_mistake: Inserting an AllGather to reconstruct the full encoder output before cross-attention KV projection. This adds unnecessary communication and memory overhead.
details.napkin_math: Extra AllGather cost if not done correctly: enc_seq × hidden × 2B × (P-1)/P. For enc_seq=2048, hidden=4096, TP=4: 2048 × 4096 × 2 × 0.75 = 12.6 MB per layer. Avoided entirely with row-parallel KV projection.
details.realistic_solution: With Megatron-style TP, the encoder output is column-parallel partitioned: each GPU holds encoder_output_i of shape [enc_seq, hidden/4]. The cross-attention KV projections (W_K and W_V) can be applied as row-parallel operations: W_K is split along the input dimension (rows), matching the encoder output partition. Each GPU computes K_i = encoder_output_i @ W_K_i, producing partial keys of shape [enc_seq, head_dim × num_heads/4]. This is exactly the same pattern as self-attention: each GPU owns num_heads/4 heads and computes complete attention for those heads using its local KV partition. No extra communication is needed beyond the standard row-parallel AllReduce after the output projection. The encoder and decoder TP groups must be identical (same GPUs in the same order) for this to work — a constraint that Megatron enforces by construction.

scenario: You are applying TP to a T5-style encoder-decoder model where the decoder's cross-attention keys and values come from the encoder output. With TP=4, the encoder output is already partitioned across 4 GPUs. How do you handle the cross-attention KV projections without extra communication?
title: TP for Cross-Attention in Encoder-Decoder Models

details.common_mistake: Blaming NCCL bugs or hardware errors. The most common cause is non-deterministic floating-point reduction order in AllReduce, which accumulates different rounding errors across TP configurations.
details.napkin_math: BF16 has 7-8 bits mantissa → relative precision ~1/128 ≈ 0.8%. After 500 AllReduces with 4-way reduction, accumulated error ≈ sqrt(500) × 0.8% ≈ 17.9% relative — enough to perturb gradient direction in flat loss regions.
details.realistic_solution: Root causes (most to least likely): (1) AllReduce non-determinism: ring AllReduce sums elements in different orders than single-GPU reduction. FP32/BF16 addition is not associative — (a+b)+c ≠ a+(b+c) due to rounding. Over hundreds of steps, different reduction trees produce different accumulated errors. Fix: enable deterministic NCCL (NCCL_ALGO=Ring, fixed topology), or use Kahan summation in the optimizer. (2) Dropout seed mismatch: with TP, dropout masks must be identical across TP ranks for replicated regions (LayerNorm input) but independent for partitioned regions. Incorrect seeding causes divergent regularization. Fix: use Megatron's parallel RNG state management. (3) Gradient scaling interaction: loss scaling for mixed precision interacts differently with TP because gradients are AllReduced at different scales. Fix: ensure loss scaler state is synchronized. Debug approach: (a) Run TP=1 and TP=4 with dropout disabled and deterministic NCCL. (b) Compare activations layer-by-layer at step 1, 100, 200. (c) Identify the first layer where relative error exceeds 1e-5. (d) Check if it correlates with RNG-dependent ops.

scenario: After switching from TP=1 to TP=4 on MI300X, your 30B model's training loss diverges after 500 steps. Loss curves match perfectly for the first 200 steps, then gradually separate. What are the most likely causes, and how would you systematically debug this?
title: Debugging TP Numerical Divergence

details.common_mistake: Using the terms interchangeably. Sequence parallelism is tightly coupled with TP and only affects LayerNorm/Dropout activations. Context parallelism is an independent parallelism dimension that splits the attention computation itself across GPUs.
details.napkin_math: KV cache for 128K context, 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128, BF16: 2 × 128K × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 2 × 131072 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 42,949,672,960 bytes ≈ 40 GiB (42.9 GB) per GPU. With CP=4: ~10.7 GB per GPU.
details.realistic_solution: Sequence Parallelism (SP): Splits the sequence dimension ONLY for non-TP operations (LayerNorm, Dropout, residual connections). Each TP rank processes seq_len/TP tokens for these ops. The GEMM operations still use standard TP. SP is always used WITH TP and requires no additional GPUs — it reuses the TP group. Purpose: reduce activation memory from replicated LayerNorm/Dropout activations. Context Parallelism (CP) / Ring Attention: Splits the actual attention computation across GPUs along the sequence dimension. Each GPU holds seq_len/CP tokens and computes attention by ring-passing KV blocks. Requires dedicated GPUs beyond the TP group. Purpose: enable training with sequence lengths that exceed single-GPU memory (e.g., 128K+ tokens). When to use: SP is essentially free (no extra GPUs, minimal extra comms) — always use with TP. CP is needed when sequence length × hidden_dim × num_layers × bytes_per_element > available_GPU_memory for activations, typically at seq_len > 32K with large models.

scenario: Distinguish between Megatron's 'sequence parallelism' and 'context parallelism' (also called Ring Attention). Both split the sequence dimension, but they solve different problems. When would you use each?
title: Context Parallelism vs Sequence Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Assuming that PyTorch automatically overlaps communication with compute. By default, NCCL operations and CUDA kernels run on the same stream, serializing them.
details.napkin_math: Without overlap: GEMM=0.5ms + AllReduce=0.1ms = 0.6ms per block. With 70% overlap: 0.5 + 0.03 = 0.53ms. Over 80 blocks: 48ms → 42.4ms. MFU improvement: ~12%.
details.realistic_solution: To enable overlap, you need separate CUDA streams for compute and communication: (1) Create a dedicated NCCL stream (torch.cuda.Stream) for collective operations. (2) After the row-parallel GEMM, launch the AllReduce on the NCCL stream. (3) Meanwhile, on the default compute stream, begin the next layer's LayerNorm and dropout (these don't depend on the AllReduce result in Megatron's architecture with residual connections). (4) Synchronize (stream.wait_event) only before the operation that actually needs the AllReduce result. Implementation in Megatron: the _VocabParallelCrossEntropy and ColumnParallelLinear modules use torch.distributed async operations with custom autograd functions that insert stream synchronization at the right points. Key detail on A100: NVLink and SMs share the GPU's 2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. Heavy AllReduce can contend with GEMM memory reads, limiting actual overlap benefit to ~60-70% of theoretical. On H100, the dedicated copy engines reduce this contention.

scenario: On an 8×A100 DGX node with NVLink providing 600 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, your TP=8 training achieves only 45% MFU. Profiling shows zero overlap between AllReduce and GEMM operations. Describe the CUDA stream configuration needed to enable overlap.
title: TP Communication Overlap with NVLink

details.common_mistake: Only counting weight-loading time and ignoring attention compute. For 2048-token prefill, the operation is compute-bound, not memory-bound, so you need to estimate FLOP requirements.
details.napkin_math: Prefill FLOPs: 2 × 70B × 2048 = 287 TFLOPS. H100 effective: 693 TFLOPS. TP=4: 287/(4×693) = 103 ms compute + 6 ms comms = 109 ms. p99 with 30% margin: 142 ms < 200 ms.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill is compute-bound. FLOPs for prefill ≈ 2 × 70B × 2048 = 287 TFLOPS per request. H100 BF16 peak = 989 TFLOPS. Achievable utilization for prefill ≈ 70% → effective = 693 TFLOPS per GPU. Time with TP=1: 287T / 693T = 414 ms → exceeds 200 ms SLA. TP=2: 287T / (2 × 693T) = 207 ms. Close but p99 needs margin. TP=4: 287T / (4 × 693T) = 103 ms + TP overhead. TP overhead at TP=4: 2 AllReduces × 80 layers × (2048 × 8192 × 2B) / 900 GB/s ≈ 2 × 80 × 32MB / 900GB/s ≈ 5.7 ms. Total ≈ 109 ms — well within 200 ms. For p99 reliability (add 30% margin for tail latency from GC, scheduling, etc.): TP=4 at ~142 ms p99 meets the SLA. TP=2 at ~270 ms p99 fails. Minimum TP degree = 4.

scenario: You must serve a 70B BF16 model with a p99 time-to-first-token (TTFT) under 200ms for 2048-token prompts. H100 GPUs provide 3.35 TB/s HBM3 bandwidth and 900 GB/s NVLink. What is the minimum TP degree needed to meet this SLA?
title: TP Degree for Inference Latency SLA

details.common_mistake: Loading the full checkpoint on every GPU and then slicing — this requires 140 GB of CPU memory per process and is extremely slow for large models.
details.napkin_math: Full load approach: 140 GB × 8 processes = 1.12 TB CPU RAM. Pre-sharded: 17.5 GB × 1 process = 17.5 GB per GPU. Loading time at PCIe 5.0 (64 GB/s): 17.5/64 = 0.27 s vs 140/64 = 2.2 s.
details.realistic_solution: Two approaches: (1) Pre-sharded checkpoints (Megatron default): During training with TP=8, each rank saves its own shard as a separate file (e.g., model_tp0.pt through model_tp7.pt). Each file is ~17.5 GB. At inference, each GPU loads only its file — fast, memory-efficient, but checkpoint is TP-degree-specific. Changing TP requires a resharding script. (2) Consolidated checkpoint with lazy loading: Store one full checkpoint. Use torch.load with mmap=True (PyTorch 2.1+) or safetensors memory mapping. Each GPU memory-maps the full file but only materializes its shard into GPU memory by slicing the relevant rows/columns. OS page cache means only accessed pages are loaded from disk. Memory efficient but requires the filesystem to handle random reads well. Modern practice: store consolidated safetensors checkpoints (compatible with any TP degree) and shard on-the-fly using tensor_parallel metadata that records split dimensions.

scenario: When loading a 70B model checkpoint for TP=8 inference, each GPU needs only its shard of the weights. Describe how Megatron-style checkpoints store TP-sharded weights and the two approaches for loading them.
title: TP Weight Sharding Memory Layout

details.common_mistake: Using a single parallelism strategy. 405B parameters × 16 bytes (mixed precision training) = 6.48 TB — far exceeding any single node's memory. You need all three parallelism dimensions.
details.napkin_math: TP=8, PP=4, DP=4 = 128 GPUs. Per-GPU params: 405B/32 = 12.66B. With ZeRO-1: 88.6 GB/GPU < 192 GB. Throughput: ~31K tokens/s at 45% MFU.
details.realistic_solution: Model memory: 405B × 16B (AdamW mixed precision) = 6.48 TB. Per-node memory: 8 × 192 GB = 1.536 TB. Need at least 6.48/1.536 = 5 nodes for parameters alone. Layout: TP=8 (intra-node, exploit MI300X Infinity Fabric 400 GB/s), PP=4 (126 layers / 4 = ~32 layers per stage, across 4 nodes), DP=4 (4 pipeline replicas across remaining nodes). Total GPUs: 8 × 4 × 4 = 128. Memory per GPU: 405B / (8×4) × 16B = 405B/32 × 16B ≈ 202.5 GB. MI300X has 192 GB → tight! Enable ZeRO Stage 1 to partition optimizer states across DP=4: optimizer memory per GPU drops from 12.66B × 12B = 152 GB to 152/4 = 38 GB. Weight + gradient: 12.66B × 4B = 50.6 GB. Total per GPU: 38 + 50.6 = 88.6 GB. Activations + KV cache fit in remaining 103.4 GB with activation checkpointing. Throughput estimate: MI300X BF16 peak ≈ 1.3 PFLOPS. At 45% MFU (realistic with 3D parallelism): 128 × 1300 × 0.45 = 74.9 PFLOPS effective. FLOPs per token: 6 × 405B = 2.43 TFLOPS. Tokens per second: 74,900 / 2.43 = 30,823 tokens/s.

scenario: Design the complete parallelism layout for training a 405B parameter model (126 layers, hidden=16384, 128 heads) on 128 MI300X GPUs across 16 nodes (8 GPUs each). Specify TP, PP, and DP degrees, justify each choice, and estimate the training throughput.
title: TP + Pipeline Parallelism Interaction

details.common_mistake: Blindly switching to shortest-job-first (SJF) without recognizing that SJF can cause starvation of large training jobs — they may never run if small jobs keep arriving.
details.napkin_math: Without backfill: 3 inference jobs wait 4h each = 12 GPU-hours wasted waiting. With backfill: inference jobs start in <5 min, run for 10 min. Saved: 11.5 GPU-hours of wait time.
details.realistic_solution: Switch to a priority-based scheduler with backfill. Backfill scheduling (used by Slurm): the large 64-GPU job retains its priority, but while waiting for 64 GPUs to free up, the scheduler checks if any smaller jobs can complete before the large job's expected start time. If so, the small inference jobs (1 GPU, short runtime) run in the 'holes' without delaying the large job. This reduces average wait time for small jobs from hours to minutes while preserving FIFO ordering for large jobs. Key tradeoff: backfill requires runtime estimates. If a backfilled job exceeds its estimate, it gets preempted (killed), wasting its compute. Alternative: multi-level feedback queue — separate queues for interactive (inference, <1h), development (<8h), and production (>8h) with different priorities and GPU limits per queue.

scenario: Your ML platform uses FIFO scheduling for GPU jobs. A 64-GPU training job arrives and waits for resources while three 1-GPU inference jobs queue behind it. Average queue wait time is 4 hours. What scheduling policy would reduce this, and what tradeoff does it introduce?
title: GPU Scheduling: FIFO vs Shortest-Job-First

details.common_mistake: Assuming fragmentation is only about unused GPUs. The bigger issue is NVLink topology fragmentation — a 4-GPU job placed on GPUs {0,1,4,5} might get worse NVLink connectivity than {0,1,2,3}, impacting training throughput.
details.napkin_math: 10 nodes × 8 GPUs = 80 GPUs. Naive: 35% util = 28 GPUs active. Bin-packed: 70% util = 56 GPUs active. Equivalent to adding 3.5 more nodes of capacity for free.
details.realistic_solution: Naive allocation causes fragmentation: Node A has GPUs 0-3 used (one 4-GPU job), Node B has GPUs 0,2 used (two 1-GPU jobs). A new 2-GPU job goes to Node B GPUs 1,3 — but these are not NVLink-adjacent, degrading multi-GPU job performance. Meanwhile, Node A has 4 free GPUs but they are not considered because the scheduler checks nodes in order. Bin-packing strategies: (1) Best-fit decreasing: sort jobs by GPU count (largest first), assign each to the node with the least free GPUs that still fits. This consolidates small jobs onto fewer nodes, leaving full nodes free for large jobs. (2) Topology-aware packing: prefer allocations that preserve NVLink groups. On DGX H100 (4 NVLink groups of 2), assign 2-GPU jobs to NVLink pairs, 4-GPU jobs to NVLink quads. Result: GPU utilization rises from 35% to 65-75% because large jobs find contiguous allocations and small jobs are consolidated.

scenario: You manage a cluster of 8-GPU H100 nodes. Incoming jobs request 1, 2, 4, or 8 GPUs. Using naive allocation (assign jobs to the first node with free GPUs), you observe 35% average GPU utilization. Why, and how does bin-packing improve this?
title: Bin-Packing GPUs for Mixed Workloads

details.common_mistake: Assuming MIG can create arbitrary partition sizes. A100 supports specific MIG profiles: 1g.10gb, 2g.20gb, 3g.40gb, 4g.40gb, 7g.80gb. You cannot create a 5g or 6g partition.
details.napkin_math: 4 GPUs × 3 MIG instances = 12 instances. Each gets 20 GB memory, ~28.6% compute. Without MIG: 4 models max (1 per GPU) or time-slicing with interference.
details.realistic_solution: A100-80GB MIG profiles: 1g.10gb (1 SM partition, 10 GB), 2g.20gb (2 SMs, 20 GB), 3g.40gb (3 SMs, 40 GB), 7g.80gb (full GPU). For 7B models at 14 GB FP16: need at least 2g.20gb instances (20 GB provides 14 GB for weights + 6 GB for activations/KV cache). Each A100 can be split into: 3× 2g.20gb + 1× 1g.10gb (using 7 of 7 SM partitions, 70 of 80 GB). That gives 3 model slots per GPU × 4 GPUs = 12 slots — exactly matching the 12 models. The 1g.10gb partitions can serve smaller models (<3B) or run monitoring. Key benefits: (1) Hardware-level memory isolation — one model's OOM cannot crash others, (2) SM partitioning guarantees compute throughput — no time-slicing jitter, (3) Each MIG instance gets its own CUDA context and L2 cache partition. Tradeoff: each 2g.20gb partition has only 2/7 ≈ 28.6% of the GPU's compute, so throughput per model is ~3.5× lower than having the full GPU.

scenario: You have 4 A100-80GB GPUs and need to serve 12 different small models (each <7B parameters, ~14 GB in FP16). Using MIG, design a partitioning scheme that maximizes the number of concurrent model instances while ensuring performance isolation.
title: MIG Partitioning for Inference Multiplexing

details.common_mistake: Thinking the issue is just a slow node. The real problem is that without gang scheduling, some processes start and enter their first AllReduce barrier while others have not launched. This wastes GPU compute on the 31 started processes, which are blocked waiting for the straggler.
details.napkin_math: 32 GPUs idle for 10 min = 5.3 GPU-hours wasted per occurrence. If this happens 3× daily: 16 GPU-hours/day = $48/day at $3/GPU-hr. Gang scheduling eliminates this entirely.
details.realistic_solution: Gang scheduling ensures all processes of a distributed job are launched simultaneously (or not at all). Without it: 31 GPUs enter NCCL initialization and block on ncclCommInitRank waiting for all 32 ranks. If rank 31 waits 10 minutes for its GPU, the other 31 GPUs sit idle — wasting 31 × 10 = 310 GPU-minutes. With gang scheduling: the scheduler reserves all 32 GPUs atomically before launching any process. If 32 GPUs are not available, the job waits in the queue. No GPU is allocated until all are ready. Implementation: Slurm provides gang scheduling via sched/gang plugin. Kubernetes uses kube-batch or Volcano scheduler with PodGroup CRD that specifies minMember=32. The tradeoff: gang scheduling can reduce cluster utilization because large jobs hold back until their full allocation is available, while smaller jobs could have used those GPUs. Combining gang scheduling with backfill mitigates this.

scenario: A distributed training job using 32 GPUs across 4 nodes hangs intermittently. Investigation reveals that 31 of 32 processes start within seconds, but the last process sometimes waits 10+ minutes for its GPU allocation. What scheduling concept prevents this, and why is it critical for distributed training?
title: Gang Scheduling for Distributed Training

details.common_mistake: Enforcing hard quotas — Team A's 30 idle GPUs would sit unused while Team B's jobs wait. This wastes expensive GPU resources.
