details.napkin_math: 100 GPUs at $3/hr = $300/hr. 30 idle GPUs (hard quota) = $90/hr wasted. Fair-share with borrowing: ~$0/hr wasted. Annual savings: $90 × 8760 = $788K.
details.realistic_solution: Fair-share scheduling uses soft quotas with preemption priorities. When Team A underuses its share, Team B's jobs can borrow the excess GPUs (Team B gets 30 allocated + 30 borrowed = 60 GPUs). When Team A submits a large job needing its full 50 GPUs: the scheduler must reclaim 30 GPUs from Team B. Policies: (1) Graceful preemption: Team B's borrowing jobs receive SIGTERM with a grace period (e.g., 5 minutes) to checkpoint. After grace period, SIGKILL. Jobs restart when GPUs become available. (2) Priority drain: Team B's borrowing jobs continue until they finish or hit a time limit, but no new Team B jobs start on borrowed GPUs. New Team A jobs get next-free GPU. (3) Slurm implementation: QOS (Quality of Service) with GrpTRES=gpu=50 for Team A, UsageFactor tracking historical usage. Teams that underused their share get a priority boost (fair-share factor > 1.0). Teams that overused get deprioritized. This naturally balances toward target allocations over time windows.

scenario: Three teams share a 100-GPU H100 cluster with allocations: Team A (50%), Team B (30%), Team C (20%). Team A is only using 20 GPUs currently, while Team B has 40 GPUs worth of jobs queued. How should a fair-share scheduler handle this, and what happens when Team A suddenly submits a large job?
title: Fair-Share Scheduling Across Teams

details.common_mistake: Killing training jobs immediately — this wastes all compute since the last checkpoint (potentially hours of training).
details.napkin_math: 8 MI300X preemption: checkpoint 2 min + restart 1 min = 3 min SLA gap. Wasted training compute: 8 GPUs × 3 min = 24 GPU-min. Without checkpointing: 8 GPUs × 2 hr (since last checkpoint) = 16 GPU-hrs wasted.
details.realistic_solution: Tiered preemption strategy: (1) Check for checkpointable training jobs: use DMTCP or application-level checkpointing. Signal the 8 lowest-priority training processes to checkpoint (SIGUSR1). Give 2-minute deadline. Jobs write checkpoint to fast NVMe storage (MI300X nodes typically have local NVMe). After checkpoint, terminate and free GPUs. Total preemption time: ~2-3 minutes. (2) If inference SLA requires <1 minute: use NVIDIA MPS (Multi-Process Service) to temporarily share GPUs. The inference model loads onto GPUs already running training, gets priority SM scheduling. Training throughput drops ~40% but inference starts immediately. Once dedicated GPUs free up, migrate inference to dedicated allocation. (3) Prevention: reserve a small pool (8-16 GPUs) as 'burst capacity' for high-priority inference, never allocated to training. These GPUs serve inference immediately with zero preemption. Cost: 8 idle GPUs × $3/hr = $24/hr — cheap insurance for SLA compliance. Production systems (Google Borg, Microsoft Philly) use priority classes: inference=highest, interactive training=medium, batch training=lowest (preemptable).

scenario: Your GPU cluster serves both latency-sensitive inference and batch training workloads. A high-priority inference model needs 8 MI300X GPUs immediately, but all GPUs are running training jobs. Design a preemption strategy that minimizes wasted compute while meeting the inference SLA.
title: GPU Preemption for Priority Inference

details.common_mistake: Treating MIG and time-slicing as equivalent. Time-slicing provides no memory isolation (one workload can OOM and crash all others), while MIG provides hardware-level memory and compute partitioning.
details.napkin_math: A100 MIG max partitions: 7 × 1g.10gb. MPS: unlimited processes but shared 80 GB. Time-slicing: unlimited processes but 10-25 μs context switch per swap. For inference at 10 ms latency: time-slicing adds 0.1-0.25% overhead; MIG adds 0%.
details.realistic_solution: CUDA Time-Slicing: GPU context-switches between workloads. No memory isolation — all workloads share the full GPU memory space. Overhead: context switch takes 10-25 μs. Best for: development environments where isolation does not matter and workloads are bursty. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): Hardware partitioning of SMs and memory. Full isolation — each partition has its own memory controllers, L2 cache, and SM sets. No context switching overhead. Only available on A100/H100. Best for: production inference serving multiple independent models with strict SLA requirements. MPS (Multi-Process Service): CUDA contexts share GPU simultaneously via a daemon process. Partial isolation — separate address spaces but shared SMs and memory bandwidth. Low overhead (~5%). Best for: running multiple small training jobs or MPI ranks that collectively use the full GPU. Can over-subscribe SMs, causing unpredictable latency. Key distinction: MIG gives guaranteed resources (cannot be taken away), MPS shares resources (contention possible), time-slicing alternates resources (latency spikes during context switches).

scenario: Compare three GPU sharing mechanisms: CUDA time-slicing, MIG, and MPS. For each, explain the isolation guarantees, overhead, and best use case.
title: GPU Time-Slicing vs MIG vs MPS

details.common_mistake: Checkpointing too frequently (every 5 minutes) — large model checkpoints take significant time and bandwidth. Or too infrequently (every 2 hours) — losing nearly all progress on interruption.
details.napkin_math: Checkpoint: 10 s every 6 min = 2.8% overhead. Waste per interruption: 3 min average. Cost: spot saves $1,612/day vs $4.50/day wasted compute.
details.realistic_solution: Optimal checkpoint interval (Young's approximation): interval = sqrt(2 × mean_time_between_failures × checkpoint_cost). Checkpoint cost for 13B model: 13B × 2B (BF16) = 26 GB to write. At NVMe write speed of 3 GB/s: ~9 seconds. Plus optimizer states: 13B × 12B = 156 GB across 32 GPUs (ZeRO-sharded), so each GPU writes ~4.9 GB → 1.6 s. Total checkpoint time ≈ 10 seconds. MTBF = 2 hours = 7200 s. Optimal interval = sqrt(2 × 7200 × 10) = sqrt(144000) ≈ 380 seconds ≈ 6.3 minutes. Strategy: checkpoint every 6 minutes to local NVMe, async upload to S3 every 30 minutes. On 2-minute interruption warning: immediately checkpoint (10 s) and gracefully shut down. Expected wasted compute per interruption: 6/2 = 3 minutes average (half the checkpoint interval). At 3 interruptions/day: 9 GPU-minutes wasted. Cost savings: 32 GPUs × $3/hr × 0.7 discount × 24h = $1,612/day saved. Wasted compute cost: negligible.

scenario: You are training a 13B model on 32 MI300X spot instances at 70% discount. Spot interruptions occur on average every 2 hours with 2-minute warning. Design a checkpointing strategy that maximizes cost savings while minimizing wasted compute.
title: Spot Instance Strategy for Training Resilience

details.common_mistake: Flat quotas per team without considering job-size diversity. A team with a 100-GPU quota running one training job has very different needs than a team running 50 × 2-GPU experiments.
details.napkin_math: 500 H100s at $3/hr = 500 × $3 × 730 hrs/month = $1,095,000/month (~$1.1M/month). At 80% utilization (with fair-share): ~$876K productive compute. At 50% (poor scheduling): ~$547K productive. Good scheduling = ~$329K/month more value.
details.realistic_solution: Hierarchical quota design: Level 1 — Organization pool: 500 GPUs total with 10% (50 GPUs) reserved for burst capacity. Level 2 — Team quotas (soft limits): Large training teams (3 teams × 100 GPUs), Medium teams (3 teams × 50 GPUs), Small teams (2 teams × 25 GPUs). Total committed: 450 GPUs + 50 burst = 500. Scheduling policies: (1) Job classes with limits: interactive (max 8 GPUs, 4h wall time, highest priority), development (max 16 GPUs, 24h, medium priority), production (no GPU limit, 7d wall time, low priority but not preemptable), preemptable (any size, no time limit, lowest priority, uses idle GPUs). (2) Per-team sub-quotas: max 50% of team quota in production jobs (prevents one team from hogging their entire allocation with a single training run). (3) Anti-starvation: minimum 1 GPU guaranteed per team at all times. (4) Burst borrowing: when cluster utilization <70%, teams can exceed their quota by 50%. Safeguards: per-user daily GPU-hour caps, automatic job termination at wall time, GPU health checks before allocation.

scenario: You are designing the quota system for a new 500-GPU H100 cluster serving 8 ML teams. Some teams do large-scale training (100+ GPUs), others do small-scale experimentation (1-4 GPUs). Design the resource quota hierarchy, scheduling policies, and safeguards.
title: Multi-Tenant GPU Cluster Quota Design

details.common_mistake: Assuming all NVLink topologies are full mesh. While DGX H100 does use NVSwitch for all-to-all connectivity, DGX A100 had a hybrid topology where not all GPU pairs had direct NVLink connections. Also, NUMA node affinity (which CPU socket / PCIe root complex each GPU is attached to) matters for host-to-device transfer performance.
details.napkin_math: Cross-NUMA CPU-GPU transfer: ~20 GB/s vs same-NUMA: ~30 GB/s (PCIe 5.0). For a DataLoader pushing 1 GB/s of training data: same-NUMA overhead = 33 ms, cross-NUMA = 50 ms. 50% penalty per batch.
details.realistic_solution: On DGX H100 with NVSwitch: all 8 GPUs have full mesh NVLink connectivity (900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU pair). Any 4-GPU subset gets equal NVLink bandwidth for AllReduce. However, NUMA topology still matters. In a 2-socket system, GPUs 0-3 are typically on NUMA node 0 and GPUs 4-7 on NUMA node 1. A 4-GPU job on GPUs {0,1,4,5} spans NUMA nodes, meaning CPU-GPU data transfers for 2 GPUs cross the UPI/xGMI link between CPU sockets — adding ~50% latency for host-to-device copies. Best practice: prefer GPUs within the same NUMA node (GPUs {0,1,2,3} or {4,5,6,7}) for 4-GPU jobs. This optimizes: (a) DataLoader CPU-to-GPU transfers, (b) pinned memory allocation locality, (c) PCIe P2P if used alongside NVLink. Slurm implements this via gres/gpu with --gpu-bind=closest or CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES + numactl --cpunodebind.

scenario: A DGX H100 node has 8 GPUs connected via NVSwitch with full mesh NVLink. A 4-GPU distributed training job is scheduled. Does NVLink topology matter for placement on this node, or are all 4-GPU subsets equivalent?
title: Topology-Aware Scheduling on DGX H100

details.common_mistake: Thinking 30 + 35 = 65 GB < 80 GB so everything is fine. Forgetting that inference requires additional memory for activations, KV cache, and CUDA context that are not counted in model weight size.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 65 GB. Peak KV cache (both): 8 GB. Contexts + activations: 3 GB. Total peak: 76 GB / 80 GB = 95% utilization — one burst away from OOM.
details.realistic_solution: Model weights: 30 + 35 = 65 GB. But each model also needs: CUDA context overhead: ~500 MB per context. KV cache: at batch_size=32, seq_len=2048, 32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim=128, BF16: 2 × 32 × 2048 × 32 × 128 × 2B = 1 GB per model. Activation memory: ~500 MB per model during forward pass. Total per model: weights + 2 GB overhead. Combined: 65 + 4 = 69 GB — still fits in 80 GB, but with only 11 GB headroom. During peak traffic: batch sizes increase, KV cache grows with longer sequences. Model A at batch_size=128 with 4096-token sequences: KV cache grows to 4 GB. Model B similarly. Total: 65 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 74 GB. Approaching 80 GB, CUDA's memory allocator starts failing. Result: OOM (Out of Memory) error crashes both models, not just the one that triggered it — no isolation between CUDA contexts sharing a GPU. Fix: use MIG to partition the GPU with hardware memory isolation, or enforce memory limits in the serving framework.

scenario: A scheduler places two inference models on the same H100 GPU: Model A (30 GB) and Model B (35 GB). The GPU has 80 GB HBM3. Both models fit individually, but during peak traffic both receive concurrent requests. What happens and why?
title: GPU Memory Oversubscription Dangers

details.common_mistake: Assuming NCCL timeout means a network issue. In this case, the 4 GPUs have their CUDA contexts locked by stale processes, so the new training job's 4 ranks on that node cannot initialize CUDA, and the other 60 ranks block in ncclCommInitRank waiting for all 64.
details.napkin_math: 30-minute NCCL timeout × 60 working GPUs = 30 GPU-hours wasted. With epilogue cleanup: 0 waste. With health check: <1 min detection = 1 GPU-hour wasted.
details.realistic_solution: The chain of events: (1) Previous job on the node was killed but left zombie CUDA processes holding GPU memory. (2) Scheduler marked GPUs as 'free' based on job completion, not GPU state. (3) New job's 4 ranks on the affected node call torch.cuda.init() but fail (CUDA_ERROR_NOT_INITIALIZED or CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY). (4) These 4 ranks never call ncclCommInitRank. (5) The other 60 ranks block in ncclCommInitRank waiting for all 64. (6) After 30 minutes: NCCL timeout. Prevention: (a) Epilogue scripts: Slurm's task/cgroup plugin with TaskEpilog that runs nvidia-smi -r (GPU reset) or kills all processes with GPU contexts after each job. (b) Health checks: before allocating a GPU, run a quick CUDA initialization test (allocate and free 1 MB). If it fails, mark the GPU as 'draining' and schedule repair. (c) NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1: fail fast instead of waiting 30 minutes. Each rank detects the timeout quickly and reports which ranks are missing.

scenario: Your 64-GPU training job fails with NCCL timeout errors (default 30 minutes). The scheduler log shows all 64 GPUs were allocated, but 4 GPUs on one node had a prior job's cleanup process still running. How does a stale process cause NCCL timeout, and what scheduler improvement prevents this?
title: Scheduler Interaction with NCCL Timeout

details.common_mistake: Assuming you can just kill 16 processes. Distributed training has NCCL communicators that require all ranks to participate. Removing ranks requires reinitializing all communication groups.
details.napkin_math: Shrink 64→48: remove 2 nodes (16 GPUs). Checkpoint: 20 s. Re-rendezvous: 30 s. NCCL re-init: 60 s. Total: ~2 min. Throughput drops 25% but job continues vs. full restart (10+ min).
details.realistic_solution: Elastic training mechanics (TorchElastic/etcd-based): (1) Scheduler sends SIGTERM to 16 selected workers (preferring workers on the same node to maintain topology efficiency). (2) Surviving 48 workers detect membership change via the rendezvous backend (etcd or C10d store). (3) All 48 workers: save checkpoint, destroy current NCCL communicators, re-rendezvous with new world_size=48, re-initialize NCCL with new rank assignments, reload checkpoint, adjust learning rate (linear scaling rule: LR × 48/64 = 0.75× original LR), adjust batch size or gradient accumulation steps to maintain global batch size. (4) Training resumes. Total downtime: ~2-5 minutes (dominated by checkpoint I/O and NCCL re-initialization). Critical challenges: (a) TP groups must remain intact — you can only remove complete TP groups (e.g., 8 GPUs at a time if TP=8). (b) PP stages need rebalancing if a pipeline stage is removed. (c) DP degree changes require adjusting the learning rate schedule. TorchElastic handles DP-only elasticity well. TP/PP elasticity requires custom resharding logic.

scenario: Your scheduler supports elastic training: jobs can shrink or grow their GPU allocation dynamically. A 64-GPU training job is running when a higher-priority job needs 16 GPUs. Describe the mechanics of safely shrinking the training job to 48 GPUs without restarting from scratch.
title: Elastic Training with Dynamic GPU Scaling

details.common_mistake: Assuming low GPU utilization always means the user requested too many GPUs. Often the issue is CPU-bound data loading, inefficient kernels, or excessive synchronization.
details.napkin_math: 40% of cluster at 20% utilization: effective waste = 0.4 × 0.8 = 32% of cluster capacity. On 100 MI300X at $3/hr: $96/hr = $840K/year wasted.
details.realistic_solution: Cause 1: CPU-bound data preprocessing. The DataLoader cannot feed data fast enough, leaving GPUs idle between batches. GPU util cycles between 0% and 100%. Fix: increase num_workers, use prefetching, move preprocessing to GPU (DALI/cuDF), or use WebDataset for pre-processed shards. Cause 2: Excessive GPU memory requested but not used. User requests 1 full MI300X (192 GB) for a 3B model that uses 20 GB. GPU SM utilization may be fine per-batch but the remaining 172 GB is wasted. Fix: use MIG 3g.40gb partition, freeing 4/7 of the GPU for other jobs. Cause 3: Small model with large batch gaps. Inference serving with low QPS — GPU computes a forward pass in 5 ms but waits 200 ms between requests. Average utilization: 5/205 = 2.4%. Fix: (a) enable dynamic batching (wait up to 50 ms to collect multiple requests), (b) colocate multiple models on the same GPU, (c) switch to a smaller GPU or MIG partition. Right-sizing policy: jobs consistently below 30% utilization for >1 hour get flagged with a recommendation to reduce GPU allocation.

scenario: You observe that 40% of GPU jobs on your MI300X cluster show <20% GPU utilization (SM activity). List three common causes and the right-sizing action for each.
title: GPU Utilization Monitoring and Right-Sizing

details.common_mistake: Dedicating 128 GPUs exclusively for 14 days — this wastes GPUs during the team's inevitable downtime (debugging, job failures, re-queuing).
details.napkin_math: Llama 2 70B: 1.7M GPU-hours for 2T tokens. 1T tokens ≈ 850K GPU-hours. 128 GPUs × 14 days × 24h = 43K GPU-hours. Shortfall: 850K - 43K = 807K GPU-hours. Need ~2500 GPUs for 14-day deadline.
details.realistic_solution: Phase 1: Capacity planning. 70B model at 1T tokens: FLOPs = 6 × 70B × 1T = 420 PFLOP-days. 128 H100s at 989 TFLOPS BF16, 50% MFU: 128 × 990 × 0.5 = 63.4 PFLOPS effective. Time: 420,000 PFLOP / (63.4 PFLOPS × 86400 s/day) = 76.7 s? No: 420 × 10^18 / (63.4 × 10^15) = 6624 seconds = 1.84 hours. Wait, let me recalculate: 6 × 70 × 10^9 × 10^12 = 420 × 10^21 FLOPs total. Per second: 63.4 × 10^15. Time: 420 × 10^21 / 63.4 × 10^15 = 6624 × 10^0... That gives 6624 seconds = 110 minutes. This seems too fast. Recheck: the standard estimate is ~21 days on 128 H100s for 70B at 1T tokens. Using the empirical Llama 2 70B number: 1.7M GPU-hours for 2T tokens. For 1T tokens: 850K GPU-hours. With 128 GPUs: 850K/128 = 6640 hours = 277 days. Schedule: 128 GPUs is insufficient — need the full 200 GPUs. At 200 GPUs: 850K/200 = 4250 hours = 177 days. Still over 14 days. Resolution: the team needs to reduce scope (fewer tokens), use more GPUs, or accept a longer timeline. Scheduling plan: reserve 128 GPUs with guaranteed preemption priority, allow other users on remaining 72 GPUs, implement automatic checkpointing every 30 minutes, use the remaining 72 GPUs as burst capacity during off-peak hours (nights/weekends).

scenario: A research team needs their 70B model trained to 1T tokens before a conference deadline in 14 days. They estimate needing 128 H100 GPUs continuously. Your cluster has 200 H100 GPUs with other workloads. Design a scheduling plan that guarantees the deadline while maximizing cluster utilization for other users.
title: Scheduling Deadline-Aware Training Jobs

details.common_mistake: Shutting down GPUs entirely. A smarter approach is to reduce power per GPU (power capping) and prioritize high-efficiency workloads.
details.napkin_math: 700W → 500W per GPU: 29% power reduction, ~18% throughput loss. 256 GPUs at 500W: 128 kW vs 179.2 kW. Throughput per watt improves by (82/71) = 15%.
details.realistic_solution: Power management strategy: (1) Power cap GPUs: use nvidia-smi -pl to reduce power limit from 700W to 500W. At 500W, H100 loses ~15-20% throughput (the GPU throttles boost clocks but Tensor Cores still operate efficiently). New GPU power: 256 × 500W = 128 kW. Total with overhead at PUE 1.3: 128 × 1.3 + 40 (non-GPU) = 206 kW — under 1.5 MW easily. (2) Selective throttling: power-cap batch training jobs (latency-insensitive) to 400W while keeping inference GPUs at 700W. Training loses ~25% throughput; inference maintains SLA. (3) Workload consolidation: during power constraints, consolidate inference onto fewer GPUs with higher power budgets. Use remaining GPUs at reduced power for training. (4) Job deferral: delay new low-priority training jobs during peak thermal hours (2-6 PM), allowing the cluster to run fewer GPUs at higher efficiency. NVIDIA DCGM provides per-GPU power monitoring and dynamic power capping APIs that integrate with Slurm via job prolog/epilog scripts.

scenario: Your data center has a 2 MW power budget for 256 H100 GPUs (each 700W TDP). At full load: 256 × 700W = 179.2 kW for GPUs alone, plus ~90 kW for CPUs, networking, and cooling (PUE 1.3). Total: ~350 kW — well within budget. But during a heatwave, the cooling system can only reject 1.5 MW. How do you adjust GPU scheduling?
title: Power-Aware GPU Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Defragmenting by live-migrating GPU processes between nodes. GPU workloads cannot be live-migrated — the CUDA context is bound to a specific GPU's physical memory.
details.napkin_math: 22 free GPUs across 6 nodes: none has 8 free. Pack small jobs: 22 free GPUs could concentrate on 3 nodes (2 fully free + 1 with 6 free). Now the 16-GPU job fits on 2 free nodes.
details.realistic_solution: Prevention strategies (cannot cure fragmentation, must prevent it): (1) Reservation-based scheduling: when a large job is queued, the scheduler begins draining target nodes by not scheduling new small jobs on them. As existing jobs complete, GPUs free up contiguously. The large job starts when 2 nodes are fully free. Drain time = max remaining wall time of small jobs on the 2 least-loaded nodes. (2) Defrag-aware placement: always pack small jobs onto the fewest possible nodes (best-fit bin packing). When 6 × 1-GPU jobs arrive, place all 6 on one node instead of spreading across 6 nodes. This keeps other nodes fully free for large jobs. (3) Tiered node pools: designate 3 nodes for small jobs (≤4 GPUs) and 7 nodes for large jobs (>4 GPUs). Small jobs never fragment the large-job pool. Tradeoff: may have idle GPUs in the large-job pool when no large jobs are queued — mitigate with borrowing. (4) Compaction jobs: when fragmentation exceeds a threshold, checkpoint and restart small jobs, repacking them onto fewer nodes. Cost: ~2-5 minutes of downtime per affected job.

scenario: Your 10-node MI300X cluster (8 GPUs each, 80 total) currently has the following allocation: 6 nodes have 2-4 GPUs free each, totaling 22 free GPUs. A 16-GPU training job arrives but cannot be scheduled because no contiguous block of 16 GPUs exists (the job needs 2 full nodes). This is the 'GPU fragmentation problem.' Propose a scheduling policy to prevent this.
title: Fragmentation-Aware Scheduling Policy

details.common_mistake: Treating all GPUs as equivalent. An H100 is not interchangeable with an A100 — different memory (80GB vs 80GB), bandwidth (3.35 vs 2 TB/s), compute (990 vs 312 TFLOPS BF16), and interconnect (NVLink4 vs NVLink3).
details.napkin_math: 70B inference on MI300X: fits in 1 GPU (192 GB). On H100: needs TP=2 (2 GPUs). On A100: needs TP=2. Cost-per-query is lowest on MI300X for memory-bound decode.
details.realistic_solution: Federated scheduler architecture: (1) Job classification layer: parse job requirements — model size (determines memory needs), precision (FP8 → H100 preferred), training vs inference, TP degree requirements, estimated runtime. (2) Hardware matching: H100: best for FP8 training, Transformer Engine workloads, and large-scale TP (NVSwitch). MI300X: best for memory-heavy workloads (192 GB HBM3), large KV caches for long-context inference, and bandwidth-bound operations (5.3 TB/s). A100: best for smaller models, fine-tuning, and cost-sensitive batch inference. (3) Routing rules: job.model_size > 100B → H100 or MI300X (need HBM capacity). job.precision == FP8 → H100 only. job.context_length > 32K → MI300X (largest memory). job.type == fine-tuning AND model_size < 13B → A100 (cheapest). (4) Load balancing: if preferred cluster is >80% utilized, overflow to next-best cluster with a cost multiplier warning. (5) Data locality: prefer cluster closest to training data storage to minimize data transfer time. Cross-cluster training (spanning clusters) is generally impractical due to WAN latency.

scenario: Your organization has three GPU clusters: Cluster A (128 H100 in Region A), Cluster B (64 MI300X in Region B), Cluster C (256 A100 in Region C). Design a federated scheduling system that routes jobs to the optimal cluster based on job characteristics, hardware capabilities, and current load.
title: Multi-Cluster GPU Federation Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Killing the training job, wasting 1,504 GPU-hours of compute. Or waiting for it to finish, which could take another 24+ hours.
details.napkin_math: 1,504 GPU-hours at $3/hr = $4,512 of compute at risk. Checkpoint cost: 30 seconds × 32 GPUs = 0.27 GPU-hours = $0.80. Checkpoint + shrink preserves $4,512 and serves inference.
details.realistic_solution: Resolution strategy: (1) Checkpoint-and-shrink: signal the training job to checkpoint immediately (takes ~30s for a typical model). Then release 8 of its 32 GPUs to the P0 inference deployment. The training job resumes on 24 GPUs with adjusted data parallelism — throughput drops 25% but no compute is wasted. (2) If the inference deployment needs all 32 GPUs: checkpoint the training job, release all GPUs, start inference. Queue the training job for immediate restart at highest batch-training priority once additional GPUs are available from other low-priority jobs. (3) Prevention: implement priority aging — jobs running longer than their estimated time should not block higher-priority jobs. Set a maximum 'preemption protection window' (e.g., 4 hours) after which even running jobs can be preempted by checkpointing. (4) Slurm implementation: set PreemptMode=REQUEUE with GraceTime=300 (5 minutes for checkpointing). The training job is checkpointed, requeued at front of its priority class, and restarts when GPUs are available.

scenario: A high-priority inference deployment (P0) is queued behind a low-priority batch training job (P3) that has been running for 47 hours on 32 GPUs. The scheduler will not preempt the training job because it has accumulated 1,504 GPU-hours of compute. This is priority inversion. How do you resolve this without wasting the training compute?
title: Job Priority Inversion in GPU Clusters

details.common_mistake: Only monitoring GPU utilization. A GPU at 100% utilization can still be unhealthy (ECC errors, thermal throttling, driver issues).
details.napkin_math: A single undetected DBE corrupts model weights. If the corrupted model trains for 2 hours before detection: 2h × 128 GPUs = 256 GPU-hours wasted. Proactive monitoring: 0 waste.
details.realistic_solution: (1) ECC errors (DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_DBE_VOL): double-bit errors are uncorrectable and cause silent data corruption. Threshold: any DBE → immediately drain GPU. Single-bit errors >100/hour → schedule maintenance. (2) GPU temperature (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP): sustained temperatures above throttle point cause clock reduction. Threshold: >83°C sustained for >5 minutes on H100 → drain and check cooling. (3) PCIe/NVLink link errors: retransmissions indicate failing interconnect. Threshold: >10 retransmissions/second → drain for hardware inspection. (4) Memory utilization vs allocation: if a GPU shows 0% memory utilization but the scheduler thinks it is allocated, a job has crashed silently. Threshold: allocated GPU at 0% memory for >2 minutes → mark job as failed, reclaim GPU. (5) XID errors (nvidia-smi -q -d PAGE_RETIREMENT): GPU driver errors logged to dmesg. XID 48 (DBE) and XID 74 (NVLink error) are critical. Threshold: any XID 48/74 → drain immediately. Monitoring stack: DCGM exporter → Prometheus → AlertManager → Slurm health check script. Check frequency: every 30 seconds for temperature/utilization, every 5 minutes for ECC/XID.

scenario: List the five most important GPU health metrics a scheduler should monitor to proactively prevent job failures, and the threshold that should trigger removing a GPU from the schedulable pool.
title: GPU Health Monitoring for Scheduler Integration

details.common_mistake: Comparing raw throughput without considering that MIG lets you serve multiple models (or multiple instances) on one GPU. The cost metric should be tokens per dollar, not tokens per second.
details.napkin_math: Full A100: 240K tokens/$. MIG 3g.40gb: 204K tokens/$. Full GPU is 18% cheaper per token. MIG advantage: 2 independent models, hardware isolation.
details.realistic_solution: Full GPU: 200 tokens/s at $3/hr = 200 × 3600 = 720K tokens per $3 = 240K tokens per dollar. MIG 3g.40gb: 85 tokens/s. An A100 can run 2× 3g.40gb partitions (using 6 of 7 SM partitions). If both serve the same model: 170 tokens/s total at $3/hr = 170 × 3600 = 612K tokens per $3 = 204K tokens per dollar. So full GPU is ~18% more cost-efficient for throughput. But MIG wins if: (1) you need isolation between different models (each partition is independent), (2) your traffic is bursty — 50 QPS × 20 tokens average = 1000 tokens/s needed. One A100 (200 tok/s) is insufficient, you need 5 full A100s = $15/hr. With MIG, you still need 12 MIG partitions (85 tok/s each) = 6 A100s = $18/hr. Full GPU wins on cost. MIG wins when workloads are heterogeneous (different models), need isolation, or individual models are small enough to waste most of a full GPU's memory.

scenario: You serve a 7B model at 50 QPS. On a full A100-80GB, the model achieves 200 tokens/s decode throughput. A 3g.40gb MIG partition achieves 85 tokens/s. Compare the cost-per-token for full-GPU vs MIG deployment, assuming an A100 costs $3/hour.
title: MIG vs Full GPU for Inference Cost Optimization

details.common_mistake: Treating all nodes equally and spreading the job across IB and Ethernet nodes. The 4× bandwidth difference means Ethernet nodes become severe bottlenecks for gradient AllReduce.
details.napkin_math: IB AllReduce: 75 ms. Ethernet: 375 ms. Mixed (assuming slowest link dominates ring): 375 ms. Backward compute: ~500 ms. Ethernet overlap: 375/500 = 75% — some leaks into forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Network-aware scheduling policy: (1) Classify the job: 128 GPUs with DP=16 means 16 data-parallel groups. Each step, gradient AllReduce sends ~model_size bytes across DP groups. For a model with 1B params: AllReduce volume ≈ 2 × (15/16) × 2 GB = 3.75 GB per step. (2) Calculate communication time: On IB (400 Gbps = 50 GB/s effective): 3.75/50 = 75 ms. On Ethernet (100 Gbps = 10 GB/s effective): 3.75/10 = 375 ms — 5× slower. (3) Scheduling rule: the job MUST run entirely on IB nodes. It needs 128/8 = 16 nodes, but only 10 IB nodes exist (80 GPUs). Options: (a) Queue until 16 IB nodes are available (never — only 10 exist). (b) Reduce job to 80 GPUs (10 IB nodes), adjust DP=10. (c) Use 10 IB nodes + 6 Ethernet nodes, but pin TP/PP communication to IB and only use Ethernet for DP AllReduce (which can overlap with backward compute). The scheduler should expose network topology as a schedulable resource (Slurm features: ib=true/false) so users can specify constraints.

scenario: Your cluster has 20 nodes with 8 H100s each, but only 10 nodes have 400 Gbps InfiniBand (IB) while the other 10 have 100 Gbps Ethernet. A 128-GPU training job with DP=16 arrives. How should the scheduler consider network topology?
title: Scheduling Multi-Node Training with Network Constraints

details.common_mistake: Simply capping wall times at a short duration. This forces users to implement checkpointing and restart logic, increasing complexity and reducing user satisfaction.
details.napkin_math: 15% utilization on 7-day jobs: 85% waste. If 30% of cluster runs 7-day jobs: 0.3 × 0.85 = 25.5% cluster-wide waste. Right-sizing to 85% utilization recovers 0.30 × (0.85 - 0.15) = 0.30 × 0.70 = 21% cluster capacity.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-pronged approach: (1) Adaptive wall time: allow users to request up to 7 days but implement 'wall time right-sizing.' Track actual runtime distributions per user/job-type. If a user consistently finishes in 6 hours but requests 7 days, suggest (and eventually enforce) a 12-hour wall time with automatic requeue. (2) Shrink-to-fit: when a job completes early, immediately release GPUs. This sounds obvious but requires proper job exit detection — many frameworks leave zombie processes. Use job epilog scripts with nvidia-smi to verify GPU release. (3) Backfill with short wall times: Slurm's backfill scheduler can start short jobs in the 'shadow' of long reservations. To help backfill work, require runtime estimates (Slurm --time flag) and penalize inaccurate estimates (if a job runs 2× longer than estimated, lower the user's priority). (4) Time-boxing: Tier 1 (0-1h, highest priority, for inference/debugging), Tier 2 (1-8h, medium priority, for experiments), Tier 3 (8h-7d, lowest priority, preemptable). Tier 3 jobs must checkpoint every hour or risk being preempted without recovery.

scenario: Your MI300X cluster allows job wall times from 1 hour to 7 days. You observe that jobs with 7-day wall times have 15% actual runtime utilization (they finish early but reserved GPUs remain idle). Propose a wall time policy that improves cluster efficiency.
title: GPU Lease Duration and Scheduling Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Simple priority queuing across all GPU types. Each GPU type has different strengths, and placing a memory-bound workload on a compute-optimized GPU wastes its capabilities.
details.napkin_math: 70B decode on MI300X: 1 GPU (192 GB fits model). On H100: 2 GPUs (TP=2). On A100: 2 GPUs (TP=2). Cost ratio: MI300X 1× vs H100 2× vs A100 2×. MI300X wins for memory-bound inference.
details.realistic_solution: Affinity-based heterogeneous scheduler: (1) Job profiling: classify each job by resource bottleneck — compute-bound (training large models), memory-bound (long-context inference), or balanced (fine-tuning). (2) GPU affinity matrix: H100: best for FP8 training (Transformer Engine), compute-bound prefill, medium-batch inference. Affinity: training=0.9, inference=0.7, fine-tuning=0.6. MI300X: best for memory-bound decode (5.3 TB/s bandwidth, 192 GB capacity), long-context inference, large-batch training. Affinity: training=0.85, inference=0.95, fine-tuning=0.5. A100: best for fine-tuning (cost-effective), small model inference, data preprocessing. Affinity: training=0.5, inference=0.6, fine-tuning=0.9. (3) Scheduling algorithm: for each incoming job, compute score = affinity × (1 / queue_wait_time) × (1 / cost_per_gpu_hour) for each GPU type. Assign to highest-scoring GPU type with available capacity. (4) Cost normalization: normalize job accounting by GPU-equivalent-hours. 1 H100-hour = 3.17 A100-hours (990/312 TFLOPS ratio). Charge teams in normalized units so they are indifferent to GPU assignment. (5) Fallback: if preferred GPU type is full, allow placement on next-best type with a 10-minute queue wait before fallback triggers.

scenario: Your cluster has 3 GPU types: 32× H100 (80 GB, 989 TFLOPS BF16), 16× MI300X (192 GB, 1.3 PFLOPS BF16), and 64× A100 (80 GB, 312 TFLOPS BF16). Design a scheduler that maximizes fleet-wide throughput-per-dollar for a mixed workload of LLM training, LLM inference, and fine-tuning jobs.
title: Scheduling for Heterogeneous GPU Clusters

details.common_mistake: Configuring GPUs as generic resources without specifying types, which prevents heterogeneous GPU scheduling. Also forgetting to set SelectType to enable GPU-aware scheduling.
details.napkin_math: 10 nodes × 8 GPUs = 80 schedulable GPUs. With MIG 3g.40gb: 80 × 2 = 160 schedulable GPU instances. Resource tracking: 80 GPUs + 1280 CPU cores + 20 TB RAM.
details.realistic_solution: gres.conf (per node): Name=gpu Type=h100 File=/dev/nvidia[0-7] Count=8. This registers 8 H100 GPUs as schedulable resources. slurm.conf key entries: SelectType=select/cons_tres (enables GPU-aware scheduling), GresTypes=gpu (enable GPU GRES), SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory (schedule by core and memory), DefMemPerCPU=16000 (default 16 GB per CPU core), TaskPlugin=task/cgroup,task/affinity (enable cgroup isolation and CPU affinity), PrologFlags=Alloc (run prolog on allocation for GPU cleanup), TopologyPlugin=topology/tree (enable network topology awareness). Job submission: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:h100:4 (request 4 H100s), #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4, #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1, #SBATCH --gpu-bind=closest (bind each task to its nearest GPU). For MIG support, add: Name=gpu Type=h100_3g.40gb File=/dev/nvidia[0-7] Count=16 (2 MIG instances per GPU). The topology/tree plugin uses a topology.conf file defining switch hierarchy so multi-node jobs prefer nodes on the same leaf switch.

scenario: You are configuring Slurm for a new 10-node H100 cluster. Each node has 8 H100 GPUs, 2 TB RAM, and 128 CPU cores. Write the key slurm.conf and gres.conf entries needed to enable GPU-aware scheduling with topology awareness.
title: Slurm GPU Resource Configuration

details.common_mistake: Thinking Kubernetes natively understands GPUs. Without the device plugin, Kubernetes has no concept of GPU resources. The device plugin is a DaemonSet that registers GPU resources with the kubelet.
details.napkin_math: 8 GPUs per node. Pod requests 2: after allocation, node reports 6 available. Max pods with GPUs per node: 8/2 = 4 pods. No oversubscription by default.
details.realistic_solution: Sequence: (1) NVIDIA device plugin DaemonSet runs on every GPU node. On startup, it calls kubelet's Registration API to register 'nvidia.com/gpu' as an extended resource, reporting the count of available GPUs (e.g., 8 per node). (2) Pod spec requests nvidia.com/gpu: 2 in resources.limits. (3) kube-scheduler finds a node with ≥2 available nvidia.com/gpu resources and binds the pod. (4) kubelet calls the device plugin's Allocate() RPC with the device IDs of 2 selected GPUs. (5) The device plugin returns: container environment variables (NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=GPU-uuid1,GPU-uuid2), device mounts (/dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidia1), and volume mounts for NVIDIA driver libraries. (6) kubelet creates the container with these environment variables and device mounts. (7) The NVIDIA container runtime (nvidia-container-runtime) intercepts the container creation, reads NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, and sets up the GPU namespace so the container only sees 2 GPUs (appears as cuda:0 and cuda:1 inside the container). Important: GPU allocation is exclusive — a GPU assigned to one pod cannot be shared with another pod (unlike CPU, which is time-shared).

scenario: Explain how the NVIDIA GPU device plugin for Kubernetes works. When a pod requests nvidia.com/gpu: 2, what is the sequence of events from pod scheduling to GPU availability inside the container?
title: Kubernetes GPU Device Plugin Architecture

details.common_mistake: Using nodeSelector alone (too rigid, cannot express preferences) or forgetting tolerations (GPU nodes are typically tainted to prevent non-GPU pods from landing on them).
details.napkin_math: Misplacement on A100 instead of H100: no FP8 support → must fall back to BF16. Training throughput penalty: ~1.8× slower (990 vs 312 TFLOPS for FP8 vs A100 BF16). Cost of misplacement: $3/hr × 8 GPUs × 1.8× longer = $43.2/hr vs $24/hr.
details.realistic_solution: Pod spec: spec.affinity.nodeAffinity.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution with matchExpressions: key=accelerator-type, operator=In, values=[h100]. This hard requirement ensures only H100 nodes are considered. Tolerations: key=nvidia.com/gpu, operator=Exists, effect=NoSchedule — allows the pod to be scheduled on GPU-tainted nodes. Resource requests: resources.limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 8 (request all 8 GPUs for distributed training). resources.requests: cpu: 64, memory: 512Gi (ensure enough CPU and RAM for data loading). Additional labels for topology: topology.kubernetes.io/zone can be used to co-locate pods in the same data center zone for low-latency inter-node communication. For multi-node training, use a podAffinity rule with topologyKey=kubernetes.io/hostname to prefer co-locating pods on the same rack (labeled with a rack topology key). The NVIDIA GPU Operator automates node labeling (nvidia.com/gpu.product=NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3) and tainting.

scenario: Your Kubernetes cluster has two node types: gpu-h100 (8× H100, NVLink) and gpu-a100 (8× A100, NVLink). A training job requires H100s for FP8 support. Write the pod spec with node affinity, tolerations, and resource requests to ensure correct placement.
title: Node Affinity for GPU Topology in K8s

details.common_mistake: Thinking Kubernetes' default scheduler handles multi-pod atomicity. The default scheduler evaluates and binds pods independently — there is no concept of 'all or nothing' for a group of pods.
details.napkin_math: Without gang scheduling: 4 pods scheduled over 15 minutes. First 3 pods idle for 15 min × 3 × 8 GPUs = 360 GPU-minutes. With gang: 0 waste.
details.realistic_solution: Volcano introduces the PodGroup CRD (Custom Resource Definition) and a gang-scheduling plugin. Setup: (1) Create a PodGroup with minMember=4 (all 4 pods must be schedulable). (2) Each pod references the PodGroup via annotations: scheduling.volcano.sh/group-name=training-job-1. (3) Volcano's gang plugin: when a pod arrives, it checks if ALL pods in the PodGroup can be scheduled simultaneously. If not, none are scheduled — they wait. If yes, all are bound atomically. (4) Queue management: Volcano maintains job queues with fair-share scheduling. Jobs are evaluated as units, not individual pods. This prevents: (a) partial allocation deadlocks (Job A has 3/4 nodes, Job B has 1/4, neither can proceed), (b) GPU waste from partially-started distributed training, (c) NCCL timeout from staggered process launch. Alternative: Kubernetes 1.27+ has native PodSchedulingContext for DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation), which provides some gang-like semantics. But Volcano remains the production standard for ML workloads due to its mature queue management and fair-share scheduling. Kueue (from Google) is a newer alternative that integrates with Kubernetes' native scheduler.

scenario: You need to run a 32-GPU distributed training job across 4 Kubernetes nodes. Default kube-scheduler may schedule pods one at a time, leading to partial allocation where 3 nodes have pods but the 4th node does not have available GPUs. How does Volcano scheduler solve this?
title: Gang Scheduling in Kubernetes with Volcano

details.common_mistake: Assuming standard nvidia.com/gpu resource requests work with MIG. MIG instances are exposed as different resource types (e.g., nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb) and require specific device plugin configuration.
details.napkin_math: 4 A100s × 2 MIG-3g.40gb = 8 schedulable instances. Without MIG: 4 schedulable GPUs. 2× more pods can be served. Each pod gets 40 GB and ~42% compute.
details.realistic_solution: Setup: (1) Enable MIG on each GPU: nvidia-smi -i 0,1,2,3 -mig 1 (requires GPU reset). (2) Create MIG instances: nvidia-smi mig -i 0 -cgi 9,9 -C (creates 2× 3g.40gb GPU instances per GPU). Repeat for GPUs 1-3. Total: 8 MIG instances. (3) Configure the NVIDIA device plugin with MIG strategy: 'single' strategy (all MIG instances on a node must be the same profile) or 'mixed' strategy (different profiles per GPU). For this case, use 'single' with MIG_STRATEGY=single in the device plugin DaemonSet. (4) The device plugin discovers MIG instances and registers them as nvidia.com/gpu resources (in single strategy) or nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb (in mixed strategy). (5) Pod spec: resources.limits: nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb: 1 requests one MIG partition. The container sees a single GPU device with 40 GB memory and 3/7 compute capacity. Kubernetes RBAC can enforce which namespaces can request which MIG profiles. Operational consideration: changing MIG profiles requires draining the node, resetting GPUs, and reconfiguring — not dynamic. Plan MIG profiles based on workload mix.

scenario: You have a Kubernetes node with 4 A100-80GB GPUs and want to expose MIG partitions as schedulable resources. Each GPU should be split into 3g.40gb instances. Describe the configuration and how pods request specific MIG profiles.
title: MIG Partitioning in Kubernetes

details.common_mistake: Setting nvidia.com/gpu in resources.requests but not limits. For GPUs, requests and limits must be equal — there is no oversubscription. Setting only requests without limits has no effect.
details.napkin_math: 8-GPU node serving pods requesting 1 GPU each: max 8 pods regardless of utilization. With MIG 1g.10gb: max 56 pods (7 per GPU). With time-slicing (10 replicas per GPU): max 80 pods (but shared performance).
details.realistic_solution: GPUs are fundamentally different from CPU/memory: (1) Non-compressible: CPU can be time-shared (a pod using 'less than requested' still allows other pods to use the slack). GPU contexts are exclusive — a GPU assigned to a pod is fully reserved even if utilization is 0%. (2) No overcommit: CPU allows requests < limits, enabling oversubscription (schedule more pods than physical cores). GPU device plugin allocates whole devices, so requests = limits is enforced by design. If you request 2 GPUs, you get exactly 2 physical GPUs (or MIG instances). (3) No fractional allocation: CPU supports milliCPU (e.g., 500m = 0.5 cores). GPU has no equivalent — you get 0 or 1+ whole GPUs. Implications: (a) GPU bin-packing is coarser than CPU — you cannot request 0.5 GPU natively. (b) GPU utilization waste is harder to reclaim — an idle GPU in a running pod cannot be lent to another pod. (c) Solutions for fractional GPU: use MIG for hardware partitioning, or NVIDIA's MPS with time-slicing device plugin (beta) for software partitioning. The time-slicing plugin allows nvidia.com/gpu: 1 to map to a shared GPU slice.

scenario: In Kubernetes, CPU and memory support both 'requests' (scheduling guarantee) and 'limits' (hard cap). GPU resources only support 'limits.' Why this asymmetry, and what does it mean for GPU scheduling?
title: K8s Resource Limits vs Requests for GPU Workloads

details.common_mistake: Using a Kubernetes Deployment, which assigns random pod names, has no master-worker coordination, and does not handle failure semantics for distributed training (e.g., if one pod dies, should all pods restart?).
details.napkin_math: PyTorchJob setup: 1 master + 7 workers = 8 pods × 8 GPUs = 64 total. MASTER_ADDR=worker-0.svc. WORLD_SIZE=64. Rank auto-assigned 0-63.
details.realistic_solution: (A) Raw Deployment: creates independent replicas with no coordination. Each pod does not know the addresses of other pods, so you cannot configure MASTER_ADDR, WORLD_SIZE, or RANK dynamically. Not viable for distributed training without significant custom scripting. (B) Kubeflow PyTorchJob (recommended): creates a CRD with master and worker specs. It automatically: sets MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT, WORLD_SIZE, RANK for each pod. Uses a headless Service for DNS-based discovery (worker-0.training-svc, worker-1.training-svc). Supports elasticPolicy for TorchElastic integration. Handles restart semantics: if one worker fails, all workers are restarted (distributed training requires all ranks). (C) LeaderWorkerSet: Kubernetes native (alpha in 1.27). Similar to PyTorchJob but lighter-weight, no CRD installation needed. Supports leader-worker pattern with ordinal indexing. Less ML-specific (no automatic environment variable injection). For MI300X: ensure ROCm container images are used (not CUDA). The PyTorchJob spec needs: nvidia.com/gpu: 8 per pod (AMD GPUs still use the nvidia.com/gpu resource name with AMD's device plugin, or amd.com/gpu with AMD's plugin). Recommendation: Kubeflow PyTorchJob with Volcano scheduler for gang scheduling.

scenario: You need to run a 64-GPU PyTorch DDP training job across 8 Kubernetes nodes (8 GPUs each) using MI300X GPUs. Compare three orchestration approaches: (A) raw Kubernetes Deployment, (B) Kubeflow PyTorchJob, (C) LeaderWorkerSet. Which is most appropriate and why?
title: Multi-Node Training Job Orchestration in K8s

details.common_mistake: Relying solely on reactive autoscaling (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler + Cluster Autoscaler). By the time the HPA detects high load, requests the cluster autoscaler to add a node, and the node boots with GPU drivers, 5-7 minutes have passed — violating SLAs.
details.napkin_math: Warm pool cost: 2 H100 nodes × $24/hr = $48/hr = $1,152/day. SLA violation cost: 5 min downtime × 1000 req/s × $0.01/failed_req = $3,000 per incident. Break-even: 1 incident every 2.6 days.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-layer strategy: (1) Warm pool: maintain 1-2 GPU nodes in 'standby' — empty but running with GPU drivers loaded. Cost: $6-12/hr for 2 idle H100 nodes. When HPA scales up, pods land on warm nodes in <30 seconds. Cluster autoscaler replenishes the warm pool in the background. (2) Predictive scaling: use KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler) with custom metrics from traffic prediction. If traffic follows daily patterns (peak at 10 AM), pre-scale at 9:55 AM. (3) Overprovisioning with priority: create low-priority 'placeholder' pods that reserve GPU resources. When real workloads arrive, the placeholder pods are evicted (priority-based preemption), and real pods start immediately. The evicted placeholders trigger cluster autoscaler to add new nodes. (4) Multi-model serving: pack multiple models onto each GPU using NVIDIA Triton with model instances. Scale model replicas within existing GPUs before scaling GPU nodes. (5) Serverless fallback: route overflow traffic to a serverless GPU endpoint (AWS Inferentia, GCP Cloud Run GPU) during scale-up delays. Pay premium for burst but maintain SLA.

scenario: You run an inference service on Kubernetes with the cluster autoscaler. GPU node spin-up takes 5-7 minutes (vs 30 seconds for CPU nodes). How do you design autoscaling to handle traffic spikes without 5-minute cold starts?
title: GPU Node Autoscaling in Kubernetes

details.common_mistake: Trying to reduce image size by removing CUDA libraries — these are essential and incompressible. The real issue is image pull time and caching strategy.
details.napkin_math: 25 GB at 100 MB/s = 250 s (4.2 min) network + decompression. With pre-cached base (15 GB) + external data (10 GB): only 500 MB to pull = 5 s. 50× improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-pronged approach: (1) Layer caching with base images: split into base image (NVIDIA CUDA base + PyTorch = ~15 GB, changes rarely) and application layer (code + configs = ~500 MB, changes frequently). Use a private registry with layer-level caching. After first pull, only the small application layer needs pulling on updates. (2) Pre-pull DaemonSet: create a DaemonSet that pulls the large base image to all GPU nodes proactively. When a training pod starts, the 15 GB base layer is already cached. Only the ~500 MB app layer pulls = ~5 seconds at 100 MB/s. (3) Separate data from images: mount datasets and checkpoints as PersistentVolumes (NFS, CephFS, or cloud storage). This removes 10+ GB from the image. (4) Lazy image pulling with Stargz/SOCI: use eStargz format or AWS SOCI (Seekable OCI) to allow containers to start before the full image is pulled. Only needed layers are pulled on-demand. Startup drops to <30 seconds. (5) Registry placement: use a cluster-local registry (Harbor) or cloud registry in the same region. Cross-region pulls add 2-5× latency. Result: 25 GB image → 500 MB effective pull + pre-cached base → <30 second startup.

scenario: Your ML training container image is 25 GB (includes CUDA toolkit, PyTorch, datasets, and model checkpoints). Pod startup takes 8 minutes because each node must pull the full image. How do you reduce this to under 1 minute?
title: Container Image Optimization for GPU ML Workloads

details.common_mistake: Assuming Kubernetes pod networking automatically uses InfiniBand. Standard CNIs (Calico, Flannel, Cilium) only support TCP/IP over Ethernet. InfiniBand RDMA requires special CNI configuration and host networking.
details.napkin_math: TCP/IP: 15 GB/s (30% of wire speed). RDMA: 45 GB/s (90% of wire speed). 3× improvement. For 128-GPU training with 2 GB AllReduce: TCP = 133 ms, RDMA = 44 ms. Per-step savings: 89 ms.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck: NCCL over TCP/IP adds kernel network stack overhead. Data goes: GPU → PCIe → CPU memory → kernel TCP/IP stack → Ethernet NIC → switch → Ethernet NIC → kernel → CPU memory → PCIe → GPU. Each copy adds latency and CPU overhead. Fix: enable GPUDirect RDMA (GDR) + RDMA-capable CNI. Configuration: (1) Install Multus CNI to attach multiple network interfaces to pods. (2) Install RDMA/IB CNI (k8snetworkplumbingwg/sriov-network-device-plugin) to expose InfiniBand devices as schedulable resources (rdma/hca_devices). (3) Create NetworkAttachmentDefinition for the IB network. (4) Pod spec: annotations for Multus to attach IB interface, plus rdma/hca_devices: 1 in resources. (5) Enable hostNetwork: true as a simpler alternative — the pod uses the host's network stack directly, including IB devices. Tradeoff: loses network namespace isolation. (6) Set NCCL environment variables: NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0, NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5. With GPUDirect RDMA: data flows GPU → NVLink → IB NIC → switch → IB NIC → GPU. No CPU memory copies. Throughput: ~45 GB/s (90% of 50 GB/s theoretical).

scenario: Your Kubernetes training pods use standard pod networking (Calico CNI) and achieve only 15 GB/s between nodes for NCCL AllReduce, despite having 400 Gbps InfiniBand NICs. The theoretical maximum is 50 GB/s. Diagnose the bottleneck and describe the K8s configuration needed for full bandwidth.
title: RDMA and Host Networking for ML Training Pods

details.common_mistake: Expecting the 31 remaining pods to continue training. Without the crashed rank, NCCL operations will hang at the next collective, and all 31 pods will eventually hit NCCL timeout (wasting 31 GPUs for up to 30 minutes).
details.napkin_math: OOM → 31 pods idle for 30 min (NCCL timeout) = 15.5 GPU-hours wasted. With NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING: fail in ~1 min = 0.5 GPU-hours. With elastic: 0 GPU-hours (surviving ranks continue).
details.realistic_solution: Chain of events: (1) Pod killed by OOM killer → container exits with code 137. (2) The 31 remaining ranks call the next NCCL collective (e.g., AllReduce) and block waiting for rank from the dead pod. (3) After NCCL_TIMEOUT (default 30 min), all 31 ranks throw TimeoutError and crash. (4) PyTorchJob controller detects failed workers. Configuration for correct handling: (a) Set restartPolicy: OnFailure in the PyTorchJob spec. When any worker fails, the PyTorchJob controller restarts ALL workers (not just the failed one) because NCCL communicators must be re-initialized with all ranks. (b) Enable elastic training: set elasticPolicy.minReplicas and maxReplicas. With TorchElastic, surviving workers detect the failure via the rendezvous mechanism, checkpoint, and re-form with available ranks. (c) Set NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1 or use torch.distributed's init_process_group with timeout parameter to fail fast instead of waiting 30 minutes. (d) Fix the root cause: increase memory limits (likely the DataLoader or activation checkpointing needed), or reduce batch size to fit in the memory limit. (e) Always set resources.limits.memory generously for training pods — OOM during training is always worse than wasting memory.

scenario: A 32-GPU training job running as a Kubeflow PyTorchJob has one worker pod killed by the OOM killer (memory limit exceeded). The other 31 pods are still running. What happens next, and how should the PyTorchJob be configured to handle this correctly?
title: K8s Pod Failure Semantics for Distributed Training

details.common_mistake: Using a ReadWriteOnce PVC (only one pod can write). In distributed training, all 32 pods need to write their shard of the checkpoint simultaneously. Also using slow storage (standard HDD) for checkpoints, causing training to block during writes.
details.napkin_math: 26 GB checkpoint at NVMe speed (3 GB/s): 8.7 s. At CephFS (500 MB/s): 52 s. At EFS (100 MB/s): 260 s = 4.3 min — blocks training for 14% of checkpoint interval.
details.realistic_solution: Storage architecture: (1) Checkpoint volume: use ReadWriteMany (RWX) PersistentVolume backed by a parallel filesystem (CephFS, GlusterFS, or cloud equivalent like AWS EFS/FSx for Lustre). All 32 pods mount the same PVC and write their shards concurrently. Required throughput: 26 GB in <60 seconds = 433 MB/s aggregate. CephFS with 3 MDS nodes provides ~500 MB/s — sufficient. (2) Alternative — local NVMe + async sync: each pod writes its checkpoint shard to local NVMe (ephemeral storage, ~3 GB/s per node). A sidecar container async-copies checkpoints to S3/GCS in the background. Pros: near-zero training interruption. Cons: if node dies before sync, checkpoint is lost. (3) Capacity planning: 26 GB × (3 days × 24h × 2/hr) = 26 × 144 = 3.74 TB total. Keep only last 3 checkpoints (78 GB) and archive older ones to object storage. PVC size: 200 GB (3 checkpoints + headroom). (4) StorageClass: set reclaimPolicy=Retain (not Delete) so checkpoints survive pod deletion. Set volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer to ensure the PV is provisioned in the same zone as the GPU nodes.

scenario: Your 32-GPU Kubernetes training job produces 26 GB checkpoints every 30 minutes. The job runs for 3 days. Design the PersistentVolume configuration, considering performance, capacity, and cost.
title: Persistent Volume Strategy for Training Checkpoints

details.common_mistake: Thinking the GPU Operator only installs drivers. It manages the entire NVIDIA software stack as Kubernetes-native resources, including device plugin, container runtime, DCGM monitoring, MIG manager, and GFD (GPU Feature Discovery).
details.napkin_math: GPU Operator deployment: 1 Helm install, ~5 min. Manual setup per node: driver install (10 min) + toolkit (5 min) + config (10 min) = 25 min. For 100 nodes: 42 hrs manual vs 5 min automated.
details.realistic_solution: Manual installation (A): install NVIDIA driver on host OS, install nvidia-container-toolkit, deploy device plugin DaemonSet, deploy DCGM exporter separately, manually configure MIG, manually update drivers (requires node drain and reboot). Works but is fragile: driver version mismatches between nodes, manual update process, no self-healing. GPU Operator (B): deploys as a single Helm chart and manages: (1) NVIDIA driver (as a container or pre-installed detection), (2) nvidia-container-toolkit, (3) NVIDIA device plugin, (4) DCGM exporter (GPU metrics for Prometheus), (5) GPU Feature Discovery (labels nodes with GPU model, driver version, CUDA version, MIG capability), (6) MIG Manager (reconfigures MIG profiles via CRD without manual SSH), (7) Node Feature Discovery integration, (8) Validator (runs GPU health checks on node startup). Key advantage: when adding a new bare-metal node to the cluster, the GPU Operator automatically installs drivers and configures everything. No manual SSH needed. The Operator also handles driver upgrades by draining nodes, updating the driver pod, and uncordoning — fully automated. For production: always use GPU Operator. Manual installation only for air-gapped or highly customized environments.

scenario: Compare two approaches for managing NVIDIA drivers and tooling in a Kubernetes GPU cluster: (A) pre-installing drivers on the host OS of each node, or (B) using the NVIDIA GPU Operator. What does the GPU Operator manage that manual installation does not?
title: GPU Operator vs Manual Driver Management in K8s

details.common_mistake: Setting maxUnavailable=0 and expecting zero downtime. The gap comes from the new pod's startup time: pulling the container image, initializing CUDA context, and loading model weights into GPU memory takes 20-30 seconds, during which readiness probes fail.
details.napkin_math: Model load time: 20s (pull weights from S3) → 3s (load from local NVMe). CUDA context init: 2s. Warm-up inference: 1s. Total readiness: 25s → 6s. Gap with proper config: 0s (old pod serves until new is ready).
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: Kubernetes marks old pods for termination as soon as new pods are created, but new pods are not ready until model loading completes. Even with maxUnavailable=0, the old pod starts receiving SIGTERM while the new pod is still loading. Fix — multi-layer approach: (1) Readiness probe: configure an HTTP readiness probe that returns 200 only after the model is fully loaded and a warm-up inference has completed. initialDelaySeconds=30, periodSeconds=5. Kubernetes routes traffic only to ready pods. (2) Rolling update config: maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0. This creates the new pod first, waits for it to pass readiness, then terminates the old pod. (3) Pre-stop hook: add a preStop lifecycle hook with a 15-second sleep. This keeps the old pod in the Service endpoints for 15 seconds after SIGTERM, allowing in-flight requests to complete (graceful drain). (4) terminationGracePeriodSeconds=60: give the old pod enough time to finish processing long-running inference requests (LLM generation can take 10+ seconds). (5) Model pre-loading: use an init container that downloads the model to a shared emptyDir volume. The main container loads from local disk (fast) instead of pulling from remote storage.

scenario: Your ML platform auto-deploys new model versions as Kubernetes Deployments. A rolling update replaces old pods with new ones. During the rollout, you observe a 30-second gap where some requests fail (503 errors). Diagnose the root cause and design a zero-downtime deployment strategy for GPU inference pods.
title: K8s Scheduling Latency for Real-Time Inference

details.common_mistake: Assuming the tail is caused by insufficient capacity. Adding replicas does not help if the tail comes from JIT compilation, GC pauses, cold cache misses, or NUMA-remote memory accesses — the same outlier causes will appear on new replicas.
details.napkin_math: P50 = 45ms, P99 = 820ms. If 1% of requests hit a torch.compile recompilation at ~500ms + normal 45ms = 545ms, and another 0.5% hit NUMA-remote allocation adding 300ms, the blended P99 is ~820ms. Adding 2× replicas: P99 stays ~820ms because the same code paths trigger on every replica. Fixing JIT warmup: P99 drops to ~120ms (3× improvement with zero cost).
details.realistic_solution: The 18× ratio signals a multi-modal latency distribution, not simple overload. Investigate: (1) JIT recompilation — torch.compile graph breaks on rare input shapes cause 200-500ms spikes; (2) CUDA context switches when multiple models share a GPU; (3) PCIe contention from KV cache spills to host memory; (4) OS-level jitter — context switches, THP defragmentation, or NUMA-remote allocations. Profile with NVIDIA Nsight to correlate tail events with system interrupts. The fix is usually pinning CUDA contexts, pre-warming all input shapes, and disabling THP — not adding replicas.

scenario: Your LLM inference service on H100s reports a healthy P50 latency of 45ms but a P99 of 820ms — an 18× ratio. The team proposes adding more replicas. Why is P50-to-P99 divergence a poor signal for capacity planning, and what root causes should you investigate before scaling out?
title: P99 vs P50 Divergence Under Load

details.common_mistake: Applying Little's Law correctly but forgetting to account for the memory footprint of concurrent requests. Each in-flight request consumes KV cache memory, so the concurrency requirement directly constrains the batch size the GPU can support.
details.napkin_math: Little's Law: L = 500 × 0.08 = 40 concurrent. KV cache per request (70B, 2048 ctx, FP16): ~5.2 GB. Total: 40 × 5.2 = 208 GB > 192 GB MI300X. With GQA 8:1 ratio: 208 / 8 = 26 GB — fits easily. With FP8 KV cache: 208 / 2 = 104 GB — also fits.
details.realistic_solution: Little's Law: L = λ × W. Concurrency = 500 req/s × 0.08s = 40 concurrent requests. Each request's KV cache for a 70B model with 80 layers, 64 heads, 128 dim, 2048 context in FP16 = 80 × 64 × 128 × 2048 × 2 × 2 bytes = 5.24 GB. For 40 concurrent requests: 40 × 5.24 GB = ~210 GB of KV cache alone. MI300X has 192 GB HBM3 — this does not fit. You must either reduce context length, use GQA (which cuts KV cache by head ratio), apply PagedAttention to share pages, or quantize KV cache to INT8/FP8, cutting memory by 2×.

scenario: Your MI300X inference server handles requests with a mean latency of 80ms and you need to sustain 500 requests/second. Using Little's Law, how many concurrent requests must be in-flight, and what does this imply for GPU memory reserved for KV cache?
title: Little's Law for GPU Inference Throughput

details.common_mistake: Assuming hedging always cuts tail latency dramatically. If the tail is caused by a correlated issue (e.g., all replicas share the same NFS for model loading, or all hit GC at similar intervals), hedging provides no benefit because both copies experience the same delay.
details.napkin_math: Naive hedging: P99 improves from 450ms to ~250ms. Cost: 2× GPU compute = 2× fleet cost. Deadline hedging at P50=80ms: hedge ~50% of requests, ~25% extra compute. P99 improves to ~260ms. Cost per request: 1.25× base. ROI: 200ms latency reduction for 25% more compute vs 200ms for 100% more compute.
details.realistic_solution: For uncorrelated tail latency, hedged requests reduce P99 to approximately P99² of the original distribution. If P99 = 450ms comes from independent causes, hedged P99 ≈ original P99.8 — roughly 250ms for a typical log-normal distribution. But the cost is real: you double GPU utilization for every hedged request. If you hedge 100% of requests, you need 2× the GPU fleet. The practical approach: hedge only after a deadline — send the second copy only if the first hasn't responded within P50 (say 80ms). This hedges only ~50% of requests but catches nearly all tail events, costing ~25% extra compute instead of 100%.

scenario: Your 8-replica A100 inference cluster shows P99 latency of 450ms against a 200ms SLA. You propose hedged requests — sending each request to 2 replicas and taking the first response. What is the expected P99 improvement, and what is the cost in wasted GPU compute?
title: Hedged Requests in Distributed Inference

details.common_mistake: Sticking with round-robin because it seems 'fair'. Round-robin is oblivious to request cost — it can stack multiple long-generation requests on the same replica while others sit idle, creating head-of-line blocking.
details.napkin_math: Round-robin worst case: 3 long requests (500ms each) queued on one replica = 1500ms for the third request. JSQ: distributes across 16 replicas, max queue depth ~1, P99 ≈ single long request = 500ms. With iteration-level preemption: long requests chunked into 50ms iterations, short requests interleaved, P99 ≈ 120ms.
details.realistic_solution: Round-robin assigns by count, not by load. When request durations vary 10×, a replica may receive 3 long-generation requests back-to-back, each occupying 500ms, while other replicas finish short requests in 50ms. Switch to least-loaded or join-shortest-queue (JSQ) balancing: route each new request to the replica with the fewest in-flight tokens. Better still, use a token-aware scheduler like Orca's iteration-level scheduling, which preempts long requests to interleave short ones. With JSQ on MI300X: P99 drops from 900ms to ~200ms because no replica accumulates disproportionate load.

scenario: Your MI300X inference cluster uses round-robin load balancing across 16 replicas. P50 is 60ms but P99 spikes to 900ms. You discover that some requests are 10× longer than others due to variable output sequence lengths. Why does round-robin fail here, and what load-balancing strategy would you use instead?
title: Load Balancing Algorithms and Tail Latency

details.common_mistake: Assuming end-to-end P99 equals the sum of per-stage P99s. Tail latency compounds non-linearly across serial stages — the probability of at least one stage hitting its tail grows with the number of stages.
details.napkin_math: 4 stages, each P99=50ms. Naive sum: 4 × 50 = 200ms. Actual E2E P99: ~380ms because tail events correlate. P(all fast) = 0.99^4 = 96.06%, so E2E P96 ≈ sum of P50s = 4 × 30ms = 120ms, but E2E P99 ≈ 2-3 stages hitting tail = 380ms. With parallelization (2 stages overlapped): effective 3 serial stages, P99 ≈ 280ms.
details.realistic_solution: For 4 independent stages each with P99 = 50ms, the probability of ALL stages being fast (below P99) is 0.99^4 = 0.96. So the end-to-end P99 corresponds roughly to P96 of the individual stages — the tail bleeds into the median. Worse, if any stage has a heavy-tailed distribution (common for GPU inference with variable batch sizes), the compound tail is dominated by the worst stage. The fix: allocate tighter per-stage budgets using a tail budget. If end-to-end P99 target is 250ms total, allocate each stage a P99.75 budget (50ms for P99.75 ≈ 35ms for P99). Use async prefetching to overlap retrieval with embedding, converting 2 serial stages into 1 parallel stage. Monitor per-stage P99.9 independently.

scenario: Your production RAG pipeline has 4 serial stages: embedding (H100), retrieval (CPU), reranking (A100), and generation (MI300X). Each stage individually meets a P99 of 50ms. A product manager asks why the end-to-end P99 is 380ms instead of 200ms. Explain the tail amplification and propose a budget allocation strategy.
title: P999 Latency in Multi-Stage Pipelines

details.common_mistake: Trusting closed-loop benchmarks for latency SLAs. Closed-loop benchmarks (send request, wait for response, send next) systematically undercount tail latency because they reduce load during slow periods — exactly when tail latency matters most.
details.napkin_math: Target rate: 1000 req/s. One request takes 2000ms instead of 35ms. Closed-loop: misses ~2000 requests that would have queued. Reports: P99 = 35ms (only measures the fast ones). Open-loop: those 2000 requests waited 0-2000ms in queue. True P99 ≈ 500ms. Underestimation factor: 14×.
details.realistic_solution: Coordinated omission occurs when the measurement tool reduces its offered load during slow periods. If a request takes 2s instead of 35ms, a closed-loop benchmark skips ~57 requests that would have arrived during those 2s. Those 57 'phantom' requests — each of which would have experienced queueing delays — are never measured. The true P99 includes all requests that would have arrived at the intended rate. Fix: use open-loop benchmarking (send requests on a fixed schedule regardless of responses), or use Gil Tene's HDR Histogram with coordinated omission correction. In production, measure from the client side (including queue wait) not server side.

scenario: Your H100 inference benchmark reports P99 = 35ms, but production users complain of multi-second delays. You discover the benchmark tool pauses sending new requests while waiting for slow responses. Explain coordinated omission and how it masks true tail latency.
title: Coordinated Omission in Latency Measurement

details.common_mistake: Sending backup requests immediately (wasting 2× compute) or waiting too long (backup arrives after the SLA deadline). The threshold must be calibrated to the latency distribution — typically at P90 or P95.
details.napkin_math: 64 GPUs, P999 = 1.2s. Backup at P95 = 90ms. 5% of requests get backup. Extra compute: 5% × 90ms average wasted work = 4.5ms per request amortized. Fleet cost increase: 5% × (90ms / 45ms) = 10% additional GPU-seconds. P999 with backup: P999² ≈ P99.9999 of single GPU ≈ 150ms. Cost: 64 × $2/hr × 1.10 = $140.80/hr vs $128/hr baseline. ROI: 1050ms P999 reduction for $12.80/hr.
details.realistic_solution: Design: (1) Track running P50 and P95 per GPU using an exponentially weighted moving average. (2) If primary hasn't responded by P95 threshold (~90ms given P50=45ms), send backup to the least-loaded GPU. (3) On first response, send cancellation token to the other GPU via a side channel (CUDA event flag in shared memory for same-node, gRPC cancel for cross-node). (4) Adaptive threshold: if backup rate exceeds 10%, investigate root cause rather than masking it. Implementation on MI300X: use Infinity Fabric for same-node backup routing (400 GB/s, <1μs overhead). Cross-node via RoCE v2 adds 5μs. With 5% backup rate: P999 drops from 1.2s to ~150ms.

scenario: You serve a 13B model across 64 MI300X GPUs. Each request is routed to one GPU. Your SLA requires P999 < 200ms but current P999 is 1.2s. Design a backup-request system with specific thresholds, cancellation logic, and calculate the additional GPU cost.
title: Tail Tolerance with Backup Requests at Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming larger batches always increase latency. While queueing delay increases, the per-request compute cost decreases because weight loads are amortized across more requests. There is an optimal batch window that minimizes total latency.
details.napkin_math: Batch=4, window=20ms: wait=10ms, compute=12ms, total=22ms. P99 dominated by queue buildup under bursts: ~80ms. Batch=10, window=50ms: wait=25ms, compute=5ms, total=30ms. P99: queue is more predictable, ~55ms. GPU util: batch=4 → 4×12ms/20ms = 2.4x parallelism, batch=10 → 10×5ms/50ms = 1x per cycle but higher MBU.
details.realistic_solution: M/D/1 queue with 20ms batch window: avg wait = 10ms (half the window). Per-request compute at batch=4: decode takes 12ms per token (weights loaded once for 4 requests). Total = 10ms wait + 12ms compute = 22ms per request. With 50ms window: avg wait = 25ms. Per-request compute at batch=10: weights loaded once for 10 requests, decode = 5ms per token (memory bandwidth amortized). Total = 25ms + 5ms = 30ms average but P99 improves because: (1) larger batches have lower variance in compute time, (2) GPU utilization increases from 30% to 75%, reducing queueing from bursty arrivals. Optimal window: ~35ms, balancing wait time against amortization.

scenario: Your H100 inference server batches requests every 20ms to maximize throughput. At 200 req/s, the average batch size is 4 requests. Using M/D/1 queueing, calculate the expected waiting time and explain why increasing batch wait time to 50ms (average batch = 10) actually improves P99 latency despite higher queueing delay.
title: Queueing Theory Applied to GPU Batch Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Calculating P99 for a single token's 2-expert fan-out but forgetting that the batch waits for the slowest token across all 128 tokens. The batch P99 is far worse than single-token P99.
details.napkin_math: Per-token: P99 with 2 experts = 1-(1-0.01)^2 ≈ 2% tail rate. Batch of 128: P(≥1 tail) = 1-0.98^128 = 92%. Expected max latency ≈ P99.95 of single expert ≈ 45ms. With expert replication (2× hot experts): tail rate per expert halved, batch P99 ≈ 25ms. Infinity Fabric cost: 400 GB/s per MI300X link, expert weights ~2 GB, replication takes 5ms one-time.
details.realistic_solution: Single token: P(both experts < 20ms) = 0.99² = 0.9801. So per-token P99 ≈ P98 of single expert ≈ 18ms. But for 128 tokens across a batch: P(all 128 tokens fast) = 0.9801^128 = 0.079 — only 8% chance that no token hits tail. The batch P99 is dominated by the worst token, which will almost certainly have at least one expert hitting P99.9+, roughly 45ms. Mitigation: (1) Expert-parallel AllToAll overlapped with compute so no token blocks others; (2) speculative expert execution — run top-3 experts, use first 2 to respond; (3) expert replication — place hot experts on multiple GPUs via Infinity Fabric to reduce queuing at popular experts.

scenario: Your MoE model with 8 experts across 8 MI300X GPUs activates 2 experts per token. Each expert has P99 = 20ms. A single token's latency is determined by the slower of its 2 experts. For a batch of 128 tokens, each needing different expert pairs, what is the expected P99 of the full batch, and how do you mitigate the amplification?
title: Fan-Out Tail Amplification in Mixture-of-Experts

details.common_mistake: Dividing the budget equally (33ms each). Service tail distributions differ wildly — CPU services have tighter distributions, GPU inference has heavier tails. Equal allocation wastes budget on services that don't need it.
details.napkin_math: Equal split: 33ms each. Tokenizer only needs 8ms → 25ms wasted. Inference needs 85ms → 52ms over budget. Proportional: tokenizer 8%, inference 82%, post-proc 10%. Budgets: 8ms + 82ms + 10ms = 100ms. With 3-stage amplification factor ~1.08: need 92ms allocated, 8ms buffer. Alert at 80%: [5.6ms, 60ms, 8ms].
details.realistic_solution: Analyze empirical tail distributions: tokenizer P50=2ms, P99=8ms (tight); inference P50=40ms, P99=85ms (heavy tail); post-processing P50=3ms, P99=10ms (tight). Budget allocation weighted by tail heaviness: tokenizer=8ms, inference=80ms, post-processing=12ms, total=100ms. But tail amplification across 3 stages means we need ~15% headroom: set budgets to tokenizer=7ms, inference=75ms, post-processing=10ms = 92ms, leaving 8ms buffer. Alert thresholds: set at 80% of budget — tokenizer P99 > 5.6ms, inference P99 > 60ms, post-processing P99 > 8ms. Monitor P99.9 independently to catch emerging tail issues before they breach P99.

scenario: You are designing an ML serving architecture with 3 microservices in series: tokenizer (CPU), model inference (H100), and post-processing (CPU). End-to-end P99 target is 100ms. Each service has different tail characteristics. Specify the per-service latency budgets and the monitoring thresholds that trigger alerts.
title: Tail Latency Budgeting Across Microservices

details.common_mistake: Assuming the GPUs are the bottleneck. In a dual-socket system, each GPU is physically closer to one CPU socket. If the inference process runs on the wrong NUMA node, PCIe transfers cross the QPI/UPI interconnect, adding 40-60ms of latency.
details.napkin_math: Local NUMA: PCIe Gen4 x16 = 32 GB/s, latency = 30ms. Remote NUMA: crosses UPI at 10.4 GT/s, effective bandwidth halved to ~16 GB/s, latency = 30ms × 2 + UPI overhead = ~90ms. After NUMA pinning: all requests at 30ms. P99 drops from 90ms to 35ms.
details.realistic_solution: Each A100 is attached via PCIe Gen4 to one CPU socket. When the inference process allocates host memory on NUMA node 0 but the GPU is on NUMA node 1, every CPU-GPU transfer traverses the UPI link (Intel) or Infinity Fabric (AMD), adding ~50ns per cache line and causing 2-3× slowdown for data staging. The 50/50 split occurs because the OS scheduler randomly assigns threads to either NUMA node. Fix: (1) Pin each inference process to the correct NUMA node: `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./server --gpu=0`. (2) Set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES per process. (3) Use `nvidia-smi topo -m` to identify GPU-to-NUMA affinity. After pinning: bimodal distribution collapses to unimodal 30ms.

scenario: Your dual-socket inference server with 2 A100s shows bimodal latency: 50% of requests complete in 30ms, 50% in 90ms. Both GPUs are identical and equally loaded. What hardware topology issue explains this bimodal distribution, and how do you fix it?
title: NUMA Effects on Inference Tail Latency

details.common_mistake: Setting the timeout based on the worst case (long prompts) and applying it uniformly. This masks failures for short requests — a short request that takes 4.9s is clearly broken but passes the timeout check.
