Evaluate the consistency model and propose an architecture that guarantees eventual consistency with bounded divergence.
title: Feature Store Consistency Guarantees

details.common_mistake: Treating embeddings like scalar features and storing them as-is in Redis. At 3 KB per embedding and 50M entities, the memory requirement alone is 150 GB — exceeding single-node Redis and creating serialization bottlenecks.
details.napkin_math: FP32: 50M × 3,072 bytes = 150 GB storage. Network: 100 embeddings/req × 3 KB × 20K QPS = 6 GB/s. INT8: 50M × 768 bytes = 38.4 GB storage, 1.5 GB/s network. PCA-256 + INT8: 50M × 256 bytes = 12.5 GB, 512 MB/s network. GPU HBM (INT8, 768-dim): 38.4 GB on A100, lookup via tensor indexing in ~0.1ms. Winner: GPU-resident embeddings if inference is already on GPU.
details.realistic_solution: Redis struggles with large values. A 3 KB MGET for 100 embeddings transfers 300 KB per request — at 20K QPS, that's 6 GB/s of Redis network throughput, exceeding most instances' 10Gbps NIC (1.25 GB/s). Solutions: (1) Quantize embeddings to INT8: 768 bytes/embedding, 4× reduction → 38.4 GB storage, 1.5 GB/s throughput. Still tight. (2) Use a dedicated vector store (Milvus, Pinecone) with GPU-accelerated serving — these are optimized for embedding retrieval with batching and compression. (3) Reduce dimensionality via PCA to 256 dimensions (if downstream model tolerates it): 1 KB/embedding in FP32, or 256 bytes in INT8. (4) For highest throughput: load embeddings on GPU HBM — A100 80 GB fits 50M × 768 × 1 byte (INT8) = 38.4 GB with room for the model.

scenario: Your feature store needs to serve 768-dimensional embedding vectors as features for 50M entities. Each embedding is FP32 (3,072 bytes). The online store must handle 20K QPS with p99 < 5ms. Can Redis handle this workload, and what are the alternatives if not?
title: Embedding Feature Serving at Scale

details.common_mistake: Choosing Parquet because it's 'industry standard.' Parquet is columnar and excels at analytical queries (SELECT columns, filter rows), but for ML training you read entire records sequentially — a row-oriented format like TFRecord is more natural.
details.napkin_math: TFRecord sequential read: NVMe SSD at 7 GB/s per drive, 2 drives = 14 GB/s > 10 GB/s target. Parquet full-record read (binary blob): ~5 GB/s due to column reassembly overhead (30% penalty). From S3: TFRecord parallel shards (1,000 shards × 10 MB/s each) = 10 GB/s. Parquet from S3: similar with row group parallelism. Compression: Parquet Snappy on images ≈ 0.95× (images already compressed) — negligible benefit, 5% CPU overhead for decompression.
details.realistic_solution: TFRecord wins for this workload. Parquet's columnar layout means reading a full image record requires seeking across column chunks — for wide binary blobs (images), this creates random I/O. TFRecord stores records sequentially as length-prefixed protobufs, enabling pure sequential reads. However, the real differentiator is the I/O pattern: (1) TFRecord files are pre-sharded (e.g., 1,000 shards × 5 GB each), enabling embarrassingly parallel reads across 8 GPUs. (2) Parquet supports predicate pushdown and column pruning — irrelevant for image training where you read every pixel. (3) TFRecord with tf.data.TFRecordDataset supports deterministic shuffling via interleaved shards, while Parquet requires a shuffle buffer or pre-shuffle step. For tabular data, the analysis reverses — Parquet's column pruning (read 10 of 500 columns) gives 50× I/O reduction.

scenario: Your team must choose between Parquet and TFRecord for storing a 5 TB image classification dataset (10M images, 500 KB average). Training runs on 8× A100 GPUs. The data pipeline must sustain 10 GB/s aggregate read throughput to avoid GPU starvation. Compare the two formats for this workload.
title: Parquet vs TFRecord for Training Throughput

details.common_mistake: Assuming the savings is exactly 20/500 = 96%. This ignores Parquet metadata overhead, row group structure, and the fact that compression ratios differ between columnar and row layouts.
details.napkin_math: Row format (CSV): read 200 GB, compressed ~3× → 67 GB I/O. Column format (Parquet): read 20/500 columns = 8 GB, compressed ~5× → 1.6 GB I/O. Speedup: 67 / 1.6 = 42×. At 2 GB/s S3 throughput: CSV = 33 seconds, Parquet = 0.8 seconds. For iterative training (100 epochs): CSV = 55 minutes I/O, Parquet = 80 seconds I/O. Column pruning + compression = the two multipliers.
details.realistic_solution: Columnar formats store each column contiguously, enabling column pruning — reading only the 20 needed columns skips 96% of the data. For 200 GB uncompressed: Parquet reads ~8 GB of raw column data (200 GB × 20/500). But Parquet also compresses far better than row formats because adjacent values in a column are the same type and often have low entropy (e.g., a 'country' column with 200 unique values compresses to near-zero with dictionary encoding). Typical Parquet compression: 3-10× for tabular data. So 8 GB raw → ~1.5 GB compressed. CSV/TFRecord would read all 200 GB, compressed to ~60 GB. Effective I/O savings: 1.5 GB vs 60 GB = 40×, not just 25×.

scenario: A tabular dataset has 500 columns and 100M rows (200 GB uncompressed). Your training pipeline only uses 20 columns. How much I/O does a columnar format (Parquet) save versus a row format (CSV/TFRecord), and what enables this savings?
title: Columnar vs Row Format for Feature Tables

details.common_mistake: Choosing very small shards (10 MB) to maximize parallelism. This recreates the small-file problem — 50 TB / 10 MB = 5M shards, and each worker still opens/closes many files. Choosing very large shards (50 GB) causes imbalanced loading and wastes memory.
details.napkin_math: Individual files: 100M open() + stat() calls per epoch × 64 workers = 6.4B metadata ops. NFS metadata server: ~100K ops/s → 64,000 seconds = 17.8 hours just for metadata. WebDataset (250 MB shards): 200K open() calls per epoch × 64 workers = 12.8M ops → 128 seconds. Metadata overhead: 17.8 hrs → 2 min (500× improvement). Sequential read throughput: 200 GB/s aggregate (64 × 3.1 GB/s per H100 node NVMe) > training consumption rate.
details.realistic_solution: WebDataset packages images into tar archives (shards), converting millions of small-file operations into sequential reads of large files. This eliminates metadata server bottlenecks. Shard sizing: target 100-500 MB per shard. At 250 MB: 50 TB / 250 MB = 200K shards. Each of 64 workers gets 200K/64 = 3,125 shards. Workers stream through shards sequentially — one open() call per shard instead of thousands per shard's contents. Shuffling: inter-shard shuffle (randomize shard order per epoch) + intra-shard shuffle buffer (10K samples). NFS metadata: 200K file entries vs. 100M — 500× fewer metadata operations. Alternative: store shards on S3, stream via HTTP range requests — eliminates NFS entirely.

scenario: Your team trains a vision model on 100M images (50 TB) across 64 H100 GPUs on 8 nodes. The current pipeline uses individual image files on a shared NFS mount. Training throughput is 40% below target because the NFS metadata server is overwhelmed by 64 workers each opening thousands of small files. How does WebDataset solve this, and what shard size do you choose?
title: WebDataset for Distributed Training

details.common_mistake: Choosing maximum compression (Zstd level 19) to minimize storage and egress costs. High compression levels can make decompression CPU-bound, starving the GPUs of data and negating the I/O savings.
details.napkin_math: Storage costs (S3): uncompressed 10 TB × $0.023/GB/month = $230/month. Snappy 5 TB = $115/month. Zstd-3 2.86 TB = $66/month. Egress (5 epochs): uncompressed $4,500, Snappy $2,250, Zstd-3 $1,287. Total monthly (1 training run): uncompressed $4,730, Snappy $2,365, Zstd-3 $1,353. Savings: Zstd-3 saves 71% vs uncompressed.
details.realistic_solution: Snappy: ~2× compression ratio, decompression at 1.5 GB/s per core. 10 TB → 5 TB stored. Egress: 5 TB × 5 epochs × $0.09 = $2,250. Decompression throughput: 128 cores × 1.5 GB/s = 192 GB/s (not a bottleneck). Zstd (level 3): ~3.5× ratio, decompression at 1.0 GB/s per core. 10 TB → 2.86 TB. Egress: 2.86 TB × 5 × $0.09 = $1,287. Decompression: 128 × 1.0 = 128 GB/s (adequate). Uncompressed: 10 TB × 5 × $0.09 = $4,500. Best choice: Zstd level 3 — saves $3,213 vs uncompressed, decompression is not the bottleneck with 128 cores. Zstd level 19 would compress to 2.5 TB but decompresses at only 0.4 GB/s per core → 51 GB/s aggregate, potentially bottlenecking the pipeline.

scenario: Your 10 TB training dataset is stored as Parquet files on S3. You're choosing between Snappy, Zstd, and uncompressed. S3 egress costs $0.09/GB, and your training cluster has 128 CPU cores available for decompression alongside 8 A100 GPUs. The pipeline runs 5 epochs. Calculate the cost-performance tradeoff for each compression option.
title: Compression Tradeoffs for ML Data Pipelines

details.common_mistake: Blaming TFRecord as a 'bad format.' TFRecord is excellent for sequential access. The issue is that TFRecord lacks a built-in index — random access requires sequential scanning to find specific records.
details.napkin_math: Sequential scan for random 10K from 2 TB: worst case scan 2 TB at 2 GB/s = 1,000 seconds ≈ 17 min. Average case: scan ~50% = 8.5 min. Observed 45 min suggests S3 throttling or single-stream S3 (~200 MB/s → 2.8 hrs, closer to reported). With index: 10K seeks × ~50ms S3 GET each = 500 seconds, but parallelized 100-way: 5 seconds. With sharded files: random 10 shards × 2 GB each = 20 GB at 2 GB/s = 10 seconds.
details.realistic_solution: TFRecord stores records as sequential length-prefixed protocol buffers with no global index. To read record N, you must scan through records 0 to N-1 to find offset boundaries. For random 10K samples from 50M records, worst case requires scanning nearly the entire file. Fixes: (1) Build an external index file mapping record_id → byte_offset. Create by scanning once, storing offsets. Random access then becomes seek(offset) + read(record_length). (2) Shard the TFRecord into 1,000 files. Random sampling: pick 10 random shards, read 1K records from each. Much faster than scanning a monolithic file. (3) Use a format with built-in indexing: Parquet (row group offsets in footer), Lance (random access columnar), or Arrow IPC. (4) For this specific case, pre-compute the evaluation set as a separate small file.

scenario: A team stores their 2 TB NLP dataset as a single large TFRecord file. Training works fine (sequential streaming), but when they try to evaluate on a random 10K sample, it takes 45 minutes to read — almost as long as scanning the entire dataset. What storage format property causes this, and how do you fix it without duplicating the dataset?
title: Storage Format for Streaming vs Random Access

details.common_mistake: Increasing row group size to reduce the number of S3 GET requests. Larger row groups actually worsen the problem — with 2.5% column selectivity, you're reading 128 MB row groups but only using 3.2 MB of data from each. The wasted I/O is the bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: 128 MB row groups: useful data = 128 MB × 2.5% = 3.2 MB. Wasted I/O = 97.5%. S3 GETs per row group: 50 columns × 20ms = 1s overhead. 10 TB dataset / 128 MB = 78K row groups / 8 workers = 9,750 row groups each × 1s = 2.7 hours of pure GET overhead. With 16 MB row groups and coalesced reads: 50 columns now in ~3 S3 range requests × 20ms = 60ms per row group. 625K row groups / 8 = 78K × 60ms = 1.3 hours. Better: pre-filter columns into a 50-column projection file: 10 TB × 2.5% = 250 GB, sequential read.
details.realistic_solution: Parquet reads entire column chunks within a row group. With 128 MB row groups and 2,000 columns, each column chunk is ~64 KB. Reading 50 columns = 3.2 MB useful data per 128 MB row group. But the I/O pattern matters: Parquet issues separate S3 GET requests per column chunk (or coalesces nearby chunks). 50 column chunks × separate GET requests = 50 S3 round trips per row group (each ~20ms) = 1 second per row group in metadata + request overhead. Fix: reduce row group size to 8-16 MB. At 8 MB: each column chunk is ~4 KB, 50 columns = 200 KB per row group. More row groups but each is fast. Or: use Parquet's column chunk coalescing (read contiguous byte ranges) with columns sorted by access frequency. Best: switch to Lance or Arrow IPC formats that support vectorized I/O for high column selectivity workloads.

scenario: Your Parquet files use the default 128 MB row group size. Training on an 8× H100 cluster reads 50 columns out of 2,000 (2.5% column selectivity). Each worker processes one row group at a time. You notice that workers spend 60% of time waiting for I/O despite S3 bandwidth being underutilized. What's wrong with the row group size, and what should it be?
title: Parquet Row Group Sizing for ML Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming Delta Lake replaces Parquet. Delta Lake is built ON TOP of Parquet — it adds a transaction log (JSON/Parquet files in _delta_log/) that provides ACID semantics, but the underlying data files remain Parquet. The overhead is in the metadata layer, not the data format.
details.napkin_math: Raw Parquet update (1% change to 10 TB): rewrite 10 TB at 500 MB/s = 5.6 hours, cost: $45 in S3 PUT + compute. Delta Lake MERGE (1% change): rewrite affected files only ≈ 200 GB at 500 MB/s = 6.7 minutes, cost: $1.80. Time travel storage: 30 days × 200 GB/day = 6 TB of versioned files (vs 10 TB base). S3 cost: $0.023/GB × 16 TB = $368/month vs $230/month for raw Parquet. 60% more storage for full reproducibility + ACID.
details.realistic_solution: Delta Lake adds three properties raw Parquet lacks: (1) ACID transactions — concurrent writers are serialized via optimistic concurrency control on the transaction log. No more corrupted partial writes. (2) Time travel — every write creates a new version. `SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF 42` reproduces exactly the dataset used for training run 42. Versions are retained for a configurable period (default 30 days). (3) Incremental updates — UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE operations rewrite only affected Parquet files, not the entire dataset. For a 10 TB dataset with 1% daily changes, this writes 100 GB instead of 10 TB. Costs: transaction log overhead (~1 MB per 1,000 commits), listing _delta_log/ adds 100-500ms to first read, and small file problem from frequent updates requires periodic OPTIMIZE (compaction).

scenario: Your ML platform stores training datasets as raw Parquet files on S3. Teams frequently complain about: (1) broken training runs from concurrent writes corrupting files, (2) inability to reproduce past experiments because data changed, (3) slow dataset updates requiring full rewrites. You're evaluating Delta Lake as a replacement. What properties does it add over raw Parquet, and what are the performance costs?
title: Delta Lake vs Parquet for ML Versioning

details.common_mistake: Storing all modalities in a single Parquet file. Parquet handles binary blobs poorly — large variable-length columns (images, audio) destroy columnar compression benefits and create huge row groups that waste memory.
details.napkin_math: WebDataset (80 TB in 250 MB shards): 320K shards, sequential read at 10 GB/s = full scan in 2.2 hours. Text-only training still reads 80 TB. Separate files: text-only Parquet = 5 TB (tokenized), read in 8 minutes. But multimodal join adds 2s latency per batch for manifest lookup. Lance: text-only = 5 TB read (column pruning), full multimodal = 80 TB. No join overhead. Storage: WebDataset ≈ 80 TB (no compression benefit across modalities). Parquet text + TFRecord media ≈ 75 TB (text compresses 3×, media doesn't). Lance ≈ 76 TB.
details.realistic_solution: Analysis: (1) Separate files: text in Parquet (great compression, column pruning for text-only training), images in TFRecord shards, audio in TFRecord shards. Pro: each modality can be independently updated, compressed optimally, and versioned. Con: joining across modalities requires a manifest file and multi-stream coordination — complex data loader code, potential for misalignment. (2) WebDataset: each tar shard contains all modalities for a sample group. Pro: atomic samples, simple streaming, no join needed. Con: updating one modality requires rewriting entire shards. No column pruning — text-only training still reads images. (3) Lance: columnar format designed for ML with native support for variable-length binary data. Pro: column pruning across modalities, random access, versioning built-in. Con: newer format, smaller ecosystem. Winner depends on access pattern: WebDataset for full-sample training, Lance for modality-selective training, separate files for independent modality evolution.

scenario: You're building a multimodal training pipeline that ingests text (tokens), images (JPEG), audio (WAV), and metadata (JSON) for each sample. The dataset has 50M samples totaling 80 TB. Compare three storage strategies: (1) separate files per modality in Parquet/TFRecord, (2) everything packed into WebDataset tar shards, (3) a database approach (Lance format). Evaluate on training throughput, storage efficiency, and operational complexity.
title: Storage Format Selection for Multimodal Datasets

details.common_mistake: Using Parquet because 'it's the standard for data.' Parquet's columnar layout and row group metadata add overhead for a single-column dataset of fixed-width integers. The data is inherently row-oriented — each sample is a sequence of tokens read in order.
details.napkin_math: Raw binary: 200B tokens × 2 bytes = 400 GB. Read speed: memmap sequential = NVMe speed (7 GB/s per drive). One epoch I/O: 400 GB / 7 GB/s = 57 seconds. Parquet: 400 GB + 5% metadata = 420 GB, + Snappy compression (0.85×) = 357 GB stored, but decompression at 1.5 GB/s per core × 16 cores = 24 GB/s (bottleneck). Effective: 357 GB / 24 GB/s = 15s decompress, but latency per batch increases. Arrow IPC: 400 GB + 64 bytes header, memmap-able. Same speed as raw binary. Winner: raw binary for simplicity, Arrow IPC if you want schema validation.
details.realistic_solution: For pre-tokenized LLM data, raw binary (numpy memmap) wins. The data is a single column of fixed-width uint16 values with no schema complexity. Memmap: zero deserialization, direct memory access, perfect sequential read patterns. File size: 200B × 2 bytes = 400 GB. With memmap, the OS page cache handles caching — repeated epochs hit warm pages. No compression because: (1) uint16 tokens have high entropy (50K vocab, roughly uniform), compressing poorly (~0.85× ratio); (2) decompression burns CPU cycles that add latency without meaningful size reduction. Parquet overhead: row group metadata, column chunk headers, Thrift encoding for each row group = 5-10% overhead for zero benefit on a single-column uint16 dataset. Arrow IPC: reasonable middle ground — flat binary with schema metadata, supports memory mapping. Slight overhead for the schema header but negligible at scale.

scenario: You're pre-tokenizing a 10 TB text corpus (200B tokens) for LLM training. Each token is a uint16 (50K vocab). The tokenized output will be read thousands of times during training. Compare storing tokens as: (1) Parquet with Snappy compression, (2) raw binary files (numpy memmap), (3) Arrow IPC format. Optimize for training throughput on 8× H100s.
title: Tokenized Dataset Storage Format

details.common_mistake: Full dataset shuffle in memory: 4 TB doesn't fit in RAM on any single machine. Even distributed shuffle across 8 nodes (500 GB each) requires all-to-all communication that takes hours.
details.napkin_math: Shard shuffle (10K shards × 400 MB): time-to-first-batch = 400 MB / 7 GB/s = 57ms + buffer fill (10K samples × 4 KB = 40 MB) = 63ms. Throughput: 7 GB/s sustained. Index permutation: random 4 KB reads at 200K IOPS (NVMe) = 800 MB/s vs 7 GB/s sequential = 8.75× slower. Reservoir (R=10M): fill time = 10M × 4 KB / 7 GB/s = 5.7 seconds. Throughput after fill: 7 GB/s. Winner: shard shuffle — 63ms to first batch, full sequential throughput, acceptable randomness with pre-shuffled shards.
details.realistic_solution: Three approaches: (1) Shard shuffle (WebDataset): shuffle shard order, then shuffle within each shard's buffer. Quality: approximate — samples within a shard are always neighbors in the original data. Fix by pre-shuffling shards once. Time-to-first-batch: open first shard + fill shuffle buffer ≈ 2 seconds. (2) Index permutation (memmap): generate a random permutation of 2T indices, access tokens by permuted index. Quality: perfect global shuffle. But random access to memmap is catastrophic — each sample triggers a page fault at a random 4 KB page. 2T random 4 KB reads = no sequential I/O benefit. Time-to-first-batch: instant (generate permutation, first read), but sustained throughput collapses. (3) Streaming reservoir: read sequentially, maintain a reservoir of size R. Quality: depends on R — R = 10M gives good local randomness. Time-to-first-batch: fill reservoir first = R samples × read speed. Best hybrid: pre-shuffle the dataset once into shards, then shard-shuffle + buffer-shuffle per epoch.

scenario: Training a 70B LLM requires shuffling 2 trillion tokens across epochs for convergence. Your storage format must support efficient shuffling without loading the entire dataset into memory. The dataset is 4 TB (uint16 tokens). Compare chunk-based shuffling (WebDataset shards), index-based shuffling (memory-mapped arrays with permutation indices), and streaming shuffle (reservoir sampling). Which minimizes time-to-first-batch while maintaining statistical quality?
title: Storage Format Impact on Shuffle Performance

details.common_mistake: Picking one format and converting everything at once. A 5 PB migration takes weeks of compute, and if the target format has an unforeseen issue (e.g., poor performance for one workload type), you've spent enormous resources on a dead end.
details.napkin_math: Current: 5 PB × $0.023/GB/month = $115K/month. Post-optimization: Parquet compression (3×) on 2 PB tabular = 667 TB. WebDataset on 2.5 PB media = 2.5 PB (no compression benefit). Binary on 0.5 PB tokens = 0.5 PB. Total: 3.67 PB = $84K/month. Savings: $31K/month = $372K/year. GPU waste recovery: 30% of $500K/month GPU spend = $150K/month. Migration cost: ~$100K compute + 3 engineer-months (~$150K). Payback: 1.4 months. 6-month ROI: ($31K + $150K) × 6 - $250K = $836K net savings.
details.realistic_solution: Phase 1 (month 1): Audit — categorize 200 datasets by access pattern: (a) tabular/structured → Parquet, (b) sequential media (images, audio) → WebDataset/tar shards, (c) pre-tokenized text → raw binary/Arrow. No single format fits all. Standardize on 2-3 formats, not 1. Phase 2 (month 2): Build migration tooling — idempotent conversion pipelines with validation (row counts, checksums, sample spot-checks). Run on spot instances. Phase 3 (months 3-5): Migrate in priority order — start with highest-cost datasets (largest size × most GPU waste). Dual-write period: new data written in both old and new formats. Training pipelines updated with feature flags to switch formats. Phase 4 (month 6): Decommission old formats, enforce format governance via CI checks. Rollback: keep old format files for 30 days post-migration with lifecycle policies for automatic deletion. Total compute cost: 5 PB × $0.02/GB conversion ≈ $100K one-time.

scenario: Your organization has 5 PB of ML training data across 200 datasets in a mix of CSV, JSON, TFRecord, and Parquet formats. Storage costs $115K/month. Training pipelines waste 30% of GPU time on format conversion and inefficient reads. You're tasked with standardizing on a single format and migrating all data within 6 months. Design the migration strategy, format choice, and rollback plan.
title: Petabyte-Scale Format Migration Strategy

details.common_mistake: Writing individual log records to a database or object store. 500K writes/s exceeds most database throughput limits, and S3 PUT rate limits at 3,500 PUT/s per prefix — you'd need 143 prefixes just for write throughput.
details.napkin_math: Raw throughput: 3.5 GB/s × 86,400 s/day = 302 TB/day. With Parquet + Zstd (3× compression): 101 TB/day. S3 cost: 101 TB × 30 days × $0.023/GB = $69.7K/month. With S3 Intelligent Tiering (archive after 7 days): 7 days hot (101 × 7 = 707 TB × $0.023) + 23 days archive (101 × 23 = 2.3 PB × $0.004) = $16.3K + $9.3K = $25.6K/month. Savings vs all-hot: 63%. Kafka cluster: 50 brokers × $0.10/hr = $3,600/month. Total infrastructure: ~$30K/month for 3 PB/month of inference logs.
details.realistic_solution: Architecture: (1) Buffer logs in memory (ring buffer, 30-second window = 105 GB — too large). Instead, use a streaming aggregation: Kafka topics partitioned by inference server (50 partitions for 50 servers). Each partition handles 10K records/s = well within Kafka broker capacity. (2) Kafka consumers batch records and write to S3 as Parquet files every 60 seconds. Parquet is ideal here: prompts and responses compress 3-5× with dictionary + Zstd encoding (natural language has low entropy). Fixed-width metrics columns get excellent compression. (3) Partition S3 by date/hour for efficient time-range queries. File size: 60s × 3.5 GB/s / 3× compression = 70 GB/minute in Parquet files. (4) For real-time monitoring, maintain a 1-hour sliding window in Redis (summary statistics only, not raw logs). For fine-tuning data selection: query Parquet files with Athena/Presto, selecting by quality metrics.

scenario: Your LLM inference service on H100s generates 500K inference logs per second, each containing: prompt (variable length, ~2KB avg), response (variable length, ~4KB avg), latency metrics (fixed, 200 bytes), and token probabilities (variable, ~1KB avg). Total throughput: 3.5 GB/s. These logs must be stored for model monitoring, fine-tuning, and compliance. Design the storage format and pipeline to handle this throughput at minimal cost.
title: Storage Format for Streaming Inference Logs

details.common_mistake: Assuming DP-SGD is simply 'SGD plus noise' with negligible overhead. The bottleneck isn't the noise addition (one random tensor per parameter) — it's per-sample gradient computation, which prevents the batch-level gradient accumulation optimizations that make training fast.
details.napkin_math: Standard: 4 hours, batch size 64, 110M params × 4 bytes = 440 MB gradients. DP-SGD naive: 64 × 440 MB = 28.2 GB per-sample gradients (fits in H100 80 GB). Opacus optimized: ~3× memory overhead = 1.32 GB. Throughput overhead: 5× slower (per-sample clipping + noise). Training time: 4 hrs × 5 = 20 hours. Noise cost: 110M params × 4 bytes × 1 sample (Gaussian) per step ≈ negligible (440 MB/s at H100 memory bandwidth). Bottleneck: per-sample gradient computation, not noise.
details.realistic_solution: Standard SGD computes gradients for an entire mini-batch in one backward pass — the loss is averaged, and a single gradient tensor per parameter is produced. DP-SGD requires individual gradients for each sample in the batch to clip each one independently before averaging. For batch size 64: standard backprop produces 1 gradient per parameter, DP-SGD produces 64 gradients per parameter. This 64× memory increase forces either: (1) virtual batching — run batch_size=1 forward/backward 64 times sequentially, or (2) specialized implementations (Opacus, JAX vmap) that compute per-sample gradients via clever vectorization but still use 3-10× more memory. Opacus on H100: typically 3-8× slower than standard training due to per-sample gradient memory pressure and reduced batch size.

scenario: You're training a text classifier (BERT-base, 110M params) with DP-SGD on 8× H100 GPUs. Standard SGD training takes 4 hours. DP-SGD requires per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise addition. Estimate the training time overhead of DP-SGD compared to standard SGD, and identify the computational bottleneck.
title: DP-SGD Training Cost on H100

details.common_mistake: Dividing epsilon equally: 10.0 / 2,400 = 0.0042 per query. This epsilon is so small that every query result is drowned in noise and useless. Equal allocation ignores that some queries are more valuable than others.
details.napkin_math: Equal allocation: 10 / 2400 = 0.0042 per query → noise scale σ = sensitivity / 0.0042 ≈ 238× sensitivity. Useless. Tiered: training (ε=0.25): σ = sensitivity / 0.25 = 4× sensitivity. Accuracy loss ~15% — acceptable. SVT (ε=3.0 for 200 queries): each threshold query costs ε ≈ 0.015. Synthetic dataset (ε=2.0): one-time cost, unlimited queries after. Total: 5.0 + 3.0 + 2.0 = 10.0. Effective queries: 20 (high) + 200 (medium) + unlimited (low) vs 2,400 useless queries under equal allocation.
details.realistic_solution: Use a tiered allocation strategy: (1) Reserve 50% of budget (epsilon = 5.0) for high-priority queries (model training runs) — expect ~20/year, each gets epsilon = 0.25 (reasonable for DP-SGD). (2) Allocate 30% (epsilon = 3.0) for medium-priority queries (aggregate statistics) — expect ~200/year via the sparse vector technique (SVT), which answers above/below-threshold queries cheaply. SVT can answer 200 threshold queries for total epsilon = 3.0 by only 'paying' for queries that exceed the threshold. (3) Reserve 20% (epsilon = 2.0) for ad-hoc exploration with the private data synopsis — a one-time differentially private synthetic dataset that subsequent queries access for free (post-processing immunity). When budget exhausts: queries against the real data are blocked. Teams must use the synthetic dataset or wait for the next budget period. Implement a dashboard showing remaining budget and projected exhaustion date.

scenario: Your analytics platform lets ML teams query a sensitive medical dataset. The total privacy budget is epsilon = 10.0 for the year. Teams submit 200 queries per month (2,400/year). Each query trains a small model or computes aggregate statistics. How do you allocate the epsilon budget, and what happens when it's exhausted?
title: Epsilon Budget Allocation Across Queries

details.common_mistake: Concluding that differential privacy is fundamentally incompatible with LLMs. The issue is often the approach (DP-SGD on all parameters), not the concept. Fine-tuning all 1.5B parameters with DP-SGD requires massive noise injection because the sensitivity scales with model size.
details.napkin_math: DP-SGD full model: noise σ = C × √(2 ln(1.25/δ)) / (ε × batch_size). For C=1.0, ε=1.0, δ=1e-5, batch=256: factor = √(2 ln(1.25/1e-5)) = √(2 × ln(125000)) ≈ 4.84. σ = 1.0 × 4.84 / 256 ≈ 0.019 per param per step. 1.5B params × 0.019 noise ≈ 28.5M noise magnitude per step. DP-LoRA (10M params): same σ but gradient norm over 10M params — effective noise impact 150× smaller relative to signal. DP-LoRA training time: 5× standard LoRA. Cost: 8× H100 × 6 hours × $3.50/hr = $168 vs full DP-SGD: 8× H100 × 80 hours = $2,240.
details.realistic_solution: The noise in DP-SGD scales with the gradient clipping norm divided by batch size, multiplied by a factor dependent on epsilon. With 1.5B parameters, the gradient norm is large, requiring aggressive clipping that distorts learning signals. Alternatives: (1) DP-LoRA: freeze the base model, apply DP-SGD only to LoRA adapters (e.g., rank 16: 1.5B → ~10M trainable params). Sensitivity decreases by ~150× because gradients are over far fewer parameters. Expected accuracy at ε=1.0: 65-75%. (2) PATE: train an ensemble of teacher models on disjoint private data partitions, then use their aggregated (noisy) votes to label a public dataset for student training. Teachers never leave the private environment. (3) Pre-train on public medical text (PubMed, clinical trials), then DP fine-tune only the classifier head on private data — reducing trainable params to <1M. Expected accuracy: 80%+ at ε=1.0.

scenario: Your team fine-tunes GPT-2 (1.5B params) on private medical records using DP-SGD. At epsilon = 8.0 (moderate privacy), the model achieves 72% accuracy on medical NER. At epsilon = 1.0 (strong privacy), accuracy drops to 41% — barely above the 38% random baseline. The non-private baseline is 89%. Evaluate whether DP-SGD is viable for this use case and propose alternatives that achieve better privacy-utility tradeoff.
title: Privacy-Utility Tradeoff in LLM Fine-Tuning

details.common_mistake: Treating MIA accuracy as a direct measure of privacy loss. A 78% MIA accuracy doesn't mean 78% of training data is memorized — it means the model's loss distribution differs measurably between training members and non-members (overfitting signal).
details.napkin_math: MIA bound: ACC ≤ 0.5 + 0.5(1 - e^(-ε)). ε=0.1: ACC ≤ 54.8%. ε=1.0: ACC ≤ 81.6%. ε=3.0: ACC ≤ 97.5%. Wait — this means ε=3 allows MIA up to 97.5%? Yes, but practical MIA accuracy is always lower because the bound is worst-case. Empirically: ε=3 → MIA ~58%, ε=8 → MIA ~62%. Without DP: MIA 78% (observed). With aggressive regularization alone: MIA ~60%. DP-SGD (ε=8) + regularization: MIA ~55%, training overhead: 5×.
details.realistic_solution: MIA exploits the gap between training loss and test loss — overfit models assign lower loss to training examples. The 78% accuracy indicates significant memorization, particularly concerning for sensitive data. To bound MIA success: DP guarantees that for any individual sample, the model's output distribution changes by at most a factor of e^ε when that sample is included vs excluded. MIA accuracy is bounded by: ACC ≤ 0.5 + 0.5 × (1 - e^(-ε)). For ACC < 55%: 0.55 = 0.5 + 0.5(1 - e^(-ε)) → e^(-ε) > 0.9 → ε < 0.105. This is extremely tight — achieving ε ≈ 0.1 with DP-SGD typically destroys model utility. Practical middle ground: (1) DP-SGD with ε = 3-8 reduces MIA to 55-60% while maintaining utility; (2) combine with deduplication (remove near-duplicate training samples, which are most vulnerable to MIA); (3) regularization (dropout, weight decay) reduces memorization without formal privacy guarantees but practically reduces MIA accuracy to 55-65%.

scenario: An auditor runs a membership inference attack (MIA) against your production LLM and achieves 78% accuracy at distinguishing training data from non-training data (random baseline: 50%). The model was trained without DP. What does the 78% MIA accuracy tell you about memorization risk, and what epsilon would you need to reduce MIA accuracy to <55%?
title: Membership Inference Attack Defense

details.common_mistake: Assuming each release is independent and the total epsilon stays at 3.0. Each release on the same data compounds privacy loss. Basic composition: total ε = 12 × 3.0 = 36.0 — essentially no meaningful privacy guarantee.
details.napkin_math: Basic: 12 × 3 = 36 (loose). RDP (subsampling q=0.01, σ=1.0): per-step RDP(α=10) ≈ 0.005. Over T=100K steps × 12 releases: RDP(α=10) = 6.0. Convert: ε = 6.0 - ln(δ)/(α-1) = 6.0 + 11.5/9 = 7.28 at δ=1e-5. Budget of ε=15: 15/7.28 × 12 ≈ 24.7 releases possible. Monthly cadence: ~2 years before budget exhaustion. Re-collection cost at that point: depends on domain.
details.realistic_solution: Three composition theorems give different bounds: (1) Basic composition: ε_total = k × ε = 12 × 3 = 36. Very loose. (2) Advanced composition: ε_total = ε√(2k × ln(1/δ)) + k × ε(e^ε - 1). For k=12, ε=3, δ=1e-5: ε_total ≈ 3 × √(24 × 11.5) + 12 × 3 × (e³-1) ≈ 49.8 + 717 ≈ too loose (worse than basic for large ε). Advanced composition works better for small ε. (3) Renyi DP (RDP): track privacy loss as Renyi divergence, convert to (ε,δ)-DP at the end. For Gaussian mechanism with σ calibrated for ε=3: RDP gives ε_total ≈ 10.4 after 12 compositions — much tighter. Practical: with RDP accounting, budget of ε_total ≤ 15 allows 18-20 monthly releases before exhaustion. After that: either collect fresh data, or use a private synthetic dataset that doesn't consume additional budget (post-processing immunity).

scenario: Your ML team releases a new model version monthly, each trained with DP-SGD at epsilon = 3.0 on the same private dataset. After 12 monthly releases, what is the total privacy loss? Compare basic composition, advanced composition, and Renyi DP accounting. At what point must you refresh the dataset or stop releasing models?
title: DP Composition Across Multiple Model Releases

details.common_mistake: Relying solely on regex-based PII detection. Regex catches structured PII (emails: 99%, SSNs: 99%) but fails on unstructured PII (names in context: 70-80%, addresses without standard format: 60-70%). The 8% miss rate is an average — for names, it's 20-30%.
details.napkin_math: Regex only (92%): 80M PII leaked. Regex + NER (97%): 30M PII leaked. + Dedup removes 30% of corpus: 30M × 0.7 = 21M. + DP-SGD (ε=8): memorization probability per data point ~10⁻⁴. Expected extractable PII: 21M × 10⁻⁴ = 2,100 instances. + Output filtering (99.5% catch): 2,100 × 0.005 = ~10 instances might slip through in production. Cost of NER pipeline: 500M docs × 0.5ms/doc = 69 hours on 1 GPU. At $3/hr: $207. Worth it for 50M fewer leaked PII instances.
details.realistic_solution: Leaked PII: 500M docs × 2 PII/doc × 8% miss = 80M PII instances in training data. Defense-in-depth: (1) Layer 1 — Regex scrubbing for structured PII (emails, SSNs, phone numbers). Catch rate: ~99%. (2) Layer 2 — NER model (spaCy, Presidio) for names, addresses, organizations. Catch rate: ~90% for names, ~85% for addresses. Combined with regex: ~97% overall catch rate. (3) Layer 3 — DP-SGD training (ε=8) to prevent memorization of remaining PII. Even if PII exists in training data, DP bounds how much the model can memorize about any individual. (4) Layer 4 — Output filtering: regex + NER on model outputs to catch generated PII at inference time. (5) Layer 5 — Deduplication: remove near-duplicate documents (PII repeated across duplicates is most likely to be memorized). After all layers: residual risk = 500M × 2 × 0.03 × (1 - DP protection) ≈ negligible.

scenario: Before training an LLM on 500M web-scraped documents, you must remove PII (names, emails, phone numbers, SSNs, addresses). Your regex-based scrubber catches 92% of PII but misses 8%. With 500M documents averaging 2 PII instances each, how many PII instances leak through, and what's the defense-in-depth strategy?
title: PII Detection and Scrubbing Pipeline

details.common_mistake: Training the diffusion model with ε=1 and expecting high-quality images. DP-SGD on diffusion models is extremely expensive — hundreds of denoising steps, each requiring per-sample gradients. At ε=1, the noise overwhelms the learning signal and the synthetic images are blurry, anatomically incorrect, or mode-collapsed.
details.napkin_math: Full DP-SGD training (ε=10): 100K images, 100 epochs, batch 64 = 156K steps. Per-step cost with per-sample gradients: 8× standard. Total: 156K × 8 = 1.25M equivalent steps × 2s/step on H100 = 694 hours = $2,430 on H100. Pre-train + DP fine-tune: 50K public pre-train steps (standard) + 15K DP steps = 50K × 2s + 15K × 16s = 100K + 240K seconds = 94 hours = $329. Savings: 86%. Quality at ε=10 with pre-training: FID 25-40 (vs non-DP FID 15-20). Utility gap: ~3-5% accuracy drop on downstream tasks.
details.realistic_solution: Practical approach: (1) Pre-train the diffusion model on public chest X-ray datasets (CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR — already de-identified and publicly available). This learns general X-ray structure without privacy cost. (2) Fine-tune with DP-SGD (ε=8-10) on the private dataset for domain-specific features. Pre-training reduces the DP fine-tuning to ~10% of total training, dramatically reducing privacy cost. (3) Validation protocol: utility — train a downstream classifier on synthetic data, compare performance to classifier trained on real data (target: within 5% accuracy). Privacy — run membership inference attacks against the generator; pass if MIA accuracy < 55%. Also verify no training images are reproduced verbatim (nearest-neighbor check in embedding space). (4) Post-processing: DP guarantees compose with post-processing for free. Any filtering, augmentation, or curation of synthetic data doesn't increase privacy loss.

scenario: Your healthcare company wants to share a medical imaging dataset with external researchers without exposing patient data. You propose training a DP generative model (diffusion model with DP-SGD) to create synthetic X-rays. The original dataset has 100K images. What epsilon provides useful synthetic data, and how do you validate that the synthetic images are both private and medically useful?
title: DP Synthetic Data Generation

details.common_mistake: Claiming DP-SGD automatically satisfies right to erasure because 'the model didn't memorize individual data.' DP provides plausible deniability about whether a specific record was in the training set, but it doesn't remove the record's influence — the model's weights were still shaped by that data. Legal interpretations vary, and most DPAs (Data Protection Authorities) consider DP a mitigation, not a substitute for erasure.
details.napkin_math: Full retrain: 13B model, 1T tokens, 8× H100 for 250 hrs = 2,000 GPU-hrs × $3.50 = $7,000. Gradient ascent unlearning: 100 steps × 13B params × batch=1 ≈ 10 minutes on 8× H100 = 8 × (10/60) × $3.50 = $4.67. SISA (k=100): retrain 1 shard = $70. Inference overhead: 100 sub-models × 13B = 1.3T params at inference — use distillation to compress ensemble into one model periodically. At 1,000 erasure requests/year: full retrain = $7M, gradient ascent = $4,670, SISA = $70K. Winner: gradient ascent if legally acceptable, SISA if not.
details.realistic_solution: Three approaches: (1) Full retrain: remove the user's data and retrain from scratch. For a 13B model: ~2,000 H100-hours × $3.50/hr = $7,000 per erasure request. If 1% of users (100K) request erasure annually, this costs $700M — infeasible. (2) Approximate unlearning (machine unlearning): fine-tune the model to 'forget' the specific user's contribution. Methods: gradient ascent on the user's data for a few steps (reverses the training influence). Cost: ~10 minutes on 8× H100 = $4.67 per request. Risk: may not fully remove influence, and repeated unlearning degrades model quality. (3) SISA (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated) training: partition training data into k shards, train k sub-models, ensemble for inference. Erasure only requires retraining the shard containing the user's data. Cost: 1/k of full retrain. With k=100: $70 per request. Trade-off: ensemble inference is k× more expensive. (4) DP argument (ε=5): present to the DPA that the model provably cannot distinguish whether the user's data was included. May satisfy some regulators but not all.

scenario: A user invokes GDPR Article 17 (right to erasure) requesting removal of their data from your trained LLM. The model was trained with DP-SGD at ε=5. Does DP training satisfy the erasure requirement? If not, what's the cost of machine unlearning (retraining from scratch without that user's data) for a 13B parameter model, and what alternatives exist?
title: GDPR Right to Erasure with DP Training

details.common_mistake: Running all experiments on the private data and using advanced composition to get a tighter bound. Even with advanced composition, 50 experiments × ε=0.2 each gives total ε ≈ 3.2 — leaving only ε=6.8 for the final model. This wastes 32% of the budget on tuning.
details.napkin_math: Basic: 50 × 0.2 = 10 (entire budget). Advanced: √(50) × 0.2 × √(2 ln(1/δ)) ≈ 7.07 × 0.2 × 4.8 = 6.8 (68% of budget). RDP subsample: 50 × 0.07 = 3.5 (35% of budget). Exponential mechanism: 1.0 (10% of budget). Non-private transfer + 1 private run: ε = 10.0 for final model (100% efficient). Winner: non-private transfer. Tune on public data or without DP, then train once with DP using the best hyperparameters.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy: minimize private data usage during tuning. (1) Public proxy: tune hyperparameters on a public dataset from a similar domain. Learning rate, clipping norm, and noise multiplier transfer reasonably well across similar tasks. Cost: zero privacy. (2) Subsample tuning: run experiments on 10% of the private data. Privacy amplification by subsampling reduces per-experiment privacy cost by ~3×. Total: 50 × (ε=0.07) ≈ ε=3.5 via RDP. (3) Private selection: run all experiments and use the exponential mechanism to privately select the best hyperparameters. Cost: ε=1.0 for the selection step, independent of the number of configurations (only depends on the sensitivity of the quality score). This is the theoretically optimal approach. (4) Transfer from non-private training: train the model without DP first to find good hyperparameters (LR, batch size, architecture), then add DP noise calibrated to those hyperparameters. The non-private runs don't touch the privacy budget because you don't release those models.

scenario: Hyperparameter tuning for DP-SGD requires running many training experiments. Each experiment on the private data consumes privacy budget. With a total budget of ε=10, running 50 hyperparameter configurations via basic composition leaves only ε=0.2 per run — too noisy to be useful. How do you tune hyperparameters without exhausting the privacy budget?
title: DP-SGD Hyperparameter Tuning Without Spending Privacy Budget

details.common_mistake: Counting only parameter memory (7B × 2 bytes = 14GB) and forgetting that forward pass stores all intermediate activations for gradient computation. A 7B transformer with full activation storage can require 60-80GB of activations alone at batch=32, seq=2048.
details.napkin_math: Residual stream: 32 × 2048 × 4096 × 32 × 2B ≈ 34GB. Attention matrices: 32 × 32 × 2048² × 32 × 2B ≈ 64GB. Total ≈ 98GB >> 80GB HBM. Must use activation checkpointing or reduce batch.
details.realistic_solution: Estimate per-layer activation cost: for each transformer block, store Q/K/V projections, attention scores, MLP intermediates ≈ 12 × seq_len × d_model × batch × 2 bytes. For 7B model: 32 layers × 2048 × 4096 × 32 × 2 ≈ 34GB just for residual stream. Add attention matrices: 32 layers × 32 heads × 2048² × 32 × 2 bytes ≈ 64GB. Total exceeds 80GB. Enable activation checkpointing to trade recompute for memory.

scenario: You are training a 7B parameter transformer on H100 (80GB HBM, 3.35TB/s) with batch size 32 and sequence length 2048. The model uses mixed precision (BF16). Activation checkpointing is not enabled. Your job is to estimate whether activations fit in memory before the backward pass begins.
title: Estimating activation memory for backward pass on H100 with large batch

details.common_mistake: Assuming torch.compile works transparently on all PyTorch code. Dynamic control flow (if/else on tensor values, data-dependent shapes, Python-level conditionals on tensor content) causes graph breaks that force fallback to eager mode for each subgraph, eliminating fusion benefits.
details.napkin_math: Each graph break adds ~0.5-2ms overhead (kernel launch + Python interpreter). 47 breaks × 1ms ≈ 47ms per step. At 200ms total step time, breaks consume 23% of runtime, explaining why only 8% speedup is seen instead of 35%.
details.realistic_solution: Use torch.compile(model, dynamic=True) to handle dynamic shapes without retracing. Refactor the custom attention mask to use torch.where() or masked_fill() instead of Python branching. For truly unavoidable breaks, use fullgraph=False and profile which breaks cost the most with TORCH_LOGS='recompiles'. Target: reduce to <5 breaks per forward pass.

scenario: You apply torch.compile to a ViT-L training loop on H100 but the speedup is only 8% instead of the expected 35%. Using TORCH_LOGS='graph_breaks', you see 47 breaks per forward pass. The model uses a custom attention mask that branches on the input tensor's shape at runtime.
title: Debugging a graph break in torch.compile during transformer training

details.common_mistake: Computing exp(x) directly in FP16 before subtracting the max, causing inf values. In the backward pass, recomputing softmax from scratch instead of saving it from the forward pass, wasting memory bandwidth on MI300X's 5.3TB/s fabric.
details.napkin_math: Saving softmax (N × C × 4 bytes FP32) vs recomputing: for batch=512, C=50000, saving costs 512×50000×4=102MB. Recompute costs 1 extra forward pass ≈ +15% step time. At 5.3TB/s, loading 102MB takes 0.019ms — saving is clearly worth it.
details.realistic_solution: In forward: save softmax output (not logits) using ctx.save_for_backward. Compute log-sum-exp with the max-subtraction trick: m = max(x), output = log(sum(exp(x-m))) + m. In backward: grad_input = softmax - (1 if label else 0), which requires only the saved softmax. Mark ctx.mark_non_differentiable() for any integer indices.

scenario: You are implementing a custom cross-entropy variant that fuses the softmax and log-sum-exp into a single CUDA kernel for MI300X (192GB, 5.3TB/s). The forward pass computes log(sum(exp(x))) but naively overflows in FP16. You need to implement the backward pass using torch.autograd.Function.
title: Implementing a numerically stable custom backward pass for a fused loss function

details.common_mistake: Not understanding that torch.compile (via TorchDynamo) traces and compiles a specialized graph for each unique set of tensor shapes it encounters. A new batch size triggers retracing and recompilation, causing the observed stalls.
details.napkin_math: TorchInductor compilation takes 30-90 seconds for large models. If seen once: fine. If triggered every 100 steps due to shape variation, overhead is 90s/100steps × 1000steps = 900s of pure compile time — more than the training itself for short runs.
details.realistic_solution: Use torch.compile(model, dynamic=True) to generate shape-generic code. Alternatively, bucket batch sizes into 2-3 discrete values and always pad to the nearest bucket — this caps recompilations to the number of buckets. Monitor with TORCH_LOGS='recompiles' to confirm fixes work.

scenario: A team trains a model on A100 (312 TFLOPS, 2TB/s) with variable batch sizes from a data loader that pads batches differently each step. After enabling torch.compile, they notice periodic 3-5 second stalls every few hundred steps and GPU utilization drops to 0% during these windows.
title: Understanding why torch.compile retraces after dynamic batch size changes

details.common_mistake: Assuming activation checkpointing is 'free' because MI300X has high bandwidth. The cost is a full extra forward pass per checkpointed segment, adding ~33% to total training FLOPs. Teams often checkpoint every block when checkpointing every other block is sufficient.
details.napkin_math: 70B params FP16 = 140GB total / 8 devices = 17.5GB params. Adam states (FP32 params + m + v) = 3 × 70B × 4B / 8 = 105GB/device. Activations with full checkpoint = 140GB. With every-other-block checkpoint ≈ 70GB. Total: 17.5 + 105 + 70 ≈ 192.5GB — fits just within MI300X.
details.realistic_solution: Checkpoint every other transformer block: saves ~50% of activation memory (70GB → 35GB), reducing total device memory from 140GB to ~105GB, which fits within 192GB alongside 140GB of parameters + optimizer states (70B × 2 bytes params + 70B × 8 bytes Adam states = 700GB distributed across 8 devices = 87.5GB/device). The recompute cost is ~17% extra forward FLOPs.

scenario: You are pretraining a 70B parameter model on MI300X (192GB, 5.3TB/s) with pipeline parallelism across 8 nodes. Without activation checkpointing, peak activation memory is 140GB per device, exceeding the 192GB limit when accounting for parameters and optimizer states. You need to determine the compute overhead of checkpointing every other transformer block.
title: Quantifying activation checkpointing trade-off for LLM pretraining on MI300X

details.common_mistake: Implementing the CUDA kernel but wrapping it in a regular Python function, preventing autograd from computing gradients through it. Alternatively, trying to use .detach() in the middle of the computation and manually backpropagating, which breaks the gradient tape.
details.napkin_math: NeRF ray marching: 512 rays × 256 samples × 8 feature dims = 1M operations. On H100 at 989 TFLOPS, the forward kernel takes <1ms. The backward kernel (adjoint) is typically 1.5-2× more expensive due to scatter operations, so expect <2ms. Total gradient step per image batch: ~5-10ms.
details.realistic_solution: Subclass torch.autograd.Function. In forward(), call the CUDA kernel via a loaded extension and use ctx.save_for_backward() for needed intermediates. In backward(), implement the analytical gradient of the ray-marching operation and call the adjoint CUDA kernel. Register with @staticmethod and use apply() at call sites. Use gradcheck() with double precision to validate correctness.

scenario: You are building a differentiable neural radiance field (NeRF) renderer that requires a custom ray-marching operation on H100 (989 TFLOPS FP16, 3.35TB/s). The operation is not expressible as composition of standard PyTorch ops and requires a hand-written CUDA kernel. You need to integrate it into the autograd graph.
title: Designing a custom autograd function for a differentiable rendering operation

details.common_mistake: Using torch.jit.trace on a model with data-dependent control flow. Tracing records the execution path for a specific input and silently bakes that path into the graph, causing incorrect results on inputs that follow different branches.
details.napkin_math: BERT-base forward at batch=32, seq=128 on A100: eager ≈ 8ms, torch.compile ≈ 4.5ms (44% speedup from kernel fusion). torch.jit.trace ≈ 5ms. For an inference service at 1000 QPS: compile saves (8-4.5)ms × 1000 = 3.5 GPU-seconds/second, meaning ~3.5 fewer A100s needed at scale.
details.realistic_solution: Use torch.compile for the transformer backbone (handles dynamic shapes natively, best performance on A100 via TorchInductor). Use torch.jit.script for the post-processing logic with control flow (script captures all branches symbolically). Alternatively, factor the model so the traced portion has no branching. Validate with torch.jit.verify_usages() and test across diverse inputs.

scenario: Your team has an A100-based inference cluster serving a BERT-based NLP model. You need to choose between torch.jit.trace, torch.jit.script, and torch.compile for production deployment. The model has some data-dependent control flow in its tokenizer post-processing but the core transformer is static.
title: Tracing vs. capture: choosing between torch.jit.trace and torch.compile for production

details.common_mistake: Calling loss.backward(retain_graph=True) in a loop to accumulate gradient statistics without understanding that each call accumulates gradients by adding to .grad instead of replacing them. Also failing to clear the graph between Fisher estimation steps and training steps, causing memory to grow unboundedly.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-152 activations for retained graph at batch=32: ~6GB. Second-order graph (for Hessian-vector products) roughly doubles this to ~12GB. MI300X has 192GB — fits easily, but on A100 (80GB) this can be tight when combined with Adam states (3×60M params×4bytes=720MB) and activations.
details.realistic_solution: For K-FAC, use torch.autograd.grad() with create_graph=True for computing the Fisher-vector product, which returns gradient tensors without accumulating into .grad. Track graph memory explicitly: the retained graph for ResNet-152 at batch=32 holds ~8GB. Implement Fisher block updates every k=100 steps to amortize the memory cost. Zero gradients with model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) to free grad tensors.

scenario: You are implementing K-FAC (Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature) on MI300X (192GB, 5.3TB/s) for training a ResNet-152. K-FAC requires computing Fisher information matrix blocks, which necessitates retaining the computational graph after backward() to compute second-order derivatives. Memory usage explodes unexpectedly.
title: Memory layout of autograd computational graph for second-order optimization on MI300X

details.common_mistake: Using torch.argsort() and indexing with it, expecting gradients to flow. Since argsort returns integer indices, PyTorch cannot propagate gradients through the indexing operation. The model trains but the ranking loss gradient is always zero, silently.
details.napkin_math: NeuralSort for N=100 items: O(N²) comparisons = 10,000 ops. On TPU v4 at ~275 TFLOPS, this is negligible. The pairwise comparison matrix (100×100×batch_size×4 bytes) = 100×100×512×4 = 20MB per batch — fits in TPU HBM easily.
details.realistic_solution: Use a soft-sort approximation: NeuralSort (parameterized softmax of pairwise comparisons) or SoftRank. Implement via a custom autograd Function: forward computes the permutation matrix (differentiable), backward uses the chain rule through the soft permutation. Alternatively, use ListNet loss which converts rankings to probability distributions over permutations, which is naturally differentiable.

scenario: You are implementing a differentiable ranking loss for a recommendation system on TPU v4. Standard torch.sort() is not differentiable (the backward pass produces zero gradients). Your loss function needs to rank items by predicted score and compute NDCG, which requires gradients to flow back to the scoring model.
title: Differentiating through a sort operation for learning-to-rank on TPU

details.common_mistake: Calling scaler.step() and scaler.update() after every micro-batch instead of after the full accumulation. With FP16 (not BF16), gradient scaling must be skipped during accumulation steps. With BF16 on MI300X (no need for loss scaling), teams still copy FP16 patterns and introduce scaling artifacts.
details.napkin_math: BF16 range: ±3.4×10³⁸ (same as FP32). FP16 range: ±65504. Loss values of O(1), gradients of O(0.01): FP16 needs scaling to avoid underflow; BF16 does not. Gradient accumulation over 8 steps scales gradients by 8× — with FP16 loss scaling of 65536, effective scale = 65536×8 = 524288, potentially causing overflow.
details.realistic_solution: For BF16 on MI300X/ROCm: do not use GradScaler — BF16 has 8 exponent bits and doesn't need dynamic loss scaling. For gradient accumulation: call optimizer.step() only after all micro-batches, use with autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16). Check if MI300X ROCm driver requires autocast(device_type='hip'). Clip gradients with torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0) before optimizer.step().

scenario: You are training a 13B model on MI300X (192GB, 5.3TB/s) with gradient accumulation over 8 micro-batches to simulate an effective batch size of 512. You use torch.cuda.amp.autocast() for BF16 training. Gradients are exploding and loss is NaN after ~1000 steps.
title: Managing gradient accumulation with mixed precision and autocast on MI300X

details.common_mistake: Storing references to loss tensors or intermediate activations in a Python list (e.g., losses.append(loss) for logging) without detaching them first. Each loss tensor holds a reference to the entire computational graph for that step, preventing garbage collection.
details.napkin_math: A single forward pass for a 1B param model creates ~4GB of activation nodes in the graph. If stored in a list and not freed, after 400 steps: 400 × 4GB = 1.6TB of cumulative references to graphs, with only the actual live memory of ~4GB visible — but the gc cannot collect until references drop, so effective peak is much higher.
details.realistic_solution: Always detach tensors before storing for logging: losses.append(loss.item()) or losses.append(loss.detach().cpu()). Use torch.cuda.memory_summary() to identify the leak source. Profile with torch.cuda.memory_snapshot(). The fundamental rule: once backward() is called, the graph is freed. If you store a tensor before backward(), you keep the graph alive.

scenario: A junior engineer runs a training loop on A100 (80GB) and observes GPU memory growing by ~200MB per step. After 400 steps the process crashes with OOM. The loss is computed correctly and backward() is called each step. The engineer cannot identify the leak.
title: Understanding the autograd graph lifecycle and preventing memory leaks

details.common_mistake: Wrapping the entire attention function (including KV projection) in checkpoint, causing KV projections to be recomputed for every window during backward even though they could be cached. The sliding-window design shares KV states across windows but checkpointing destroys this sharing.
details.napkin_math: Attention scores for 100K tokens: 100K × 100K × 2 bytes = 20GB per layer. With 32 layers: 640GB — obviously cannot store all. KV projections: 100K × 8192 × 2 × 2 bytes = 3.2GB per layer, 102GB total. Checkpointing only attention scores (recompute) saves 640GB; keeping KV (12% overhead) avoids the 3× recompute penalty.
details.realistic_solution: Split the checkpointed region: pre-compute and save KV projections outside the checkpointed block (they are memory-cheap), checkpoint only the attention score computation (memory-expensive: O(seq_len²)). Use checkpoint with use_reentrant=False for better gradient correctness with nested checkpoints. Verify with torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks() that the right tensors are being offloaded vs retained.

scenario: You have a custom sliding-window attention mechanism for processing 100K-token sequences on H100 (80GB). Standard torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint() wraps your attention block, but you notice the recompute during backward is 3× slower than the original forward because it also recomputes the KV cache generation that should be shared across windows.
title: Implementing gradient checkpointing for a custom attention mechanism

details.common_mistake: Treating torch.compile as a black box. Engineers cannot explain why the expert routing (top-k selection + scatter) is creating separate kernels rather than being fused with the expert computation, missing the opportunity to guide the compiler.
details.napkin_math: MoE routing: for 1024 tokens, 8 experts, top-2 routing: topk over 1024×8 = 8192 values, scatter to expert buffers. Each kernel launch overhead: ~5μs on H100. If 3 separate kernels vs 1 fused: 15μs vs 5μs per step. At 1000 steps/sec: 10ms/sec = 1% overhead — small, but compounds in sequence-parallel setups.
details.realistic_solution: Use torch._dynamo.explain(model)(inputs) to inspect captured graphs. Use TORCH_LOGS='output_code' to see generated Triton kernels. Identify that torch.topk() followed by scatter creates a graph break or inhibits fusion. Replace with torch._C._VariableFunctions.topk (same) but wrapped in a custom operator registered via torch.library.custom_op to give TorchInductor a fusion hint. Alternatively, use Triton kernels directly for the routing logic.

scenario: You are optimizing inference for a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model on H100. torch.compile generates a graph but the TorchInductor-generated CUDA kernels are slower than hand-written ones. You need to inspect the fx.Graph to understand what operations are being fused and which are not.
title: Analyzing the computational graph captured by TorchDynamo for a complex model

details.common_mistake: Using in-place operations on tensors that are inputs to other operations still in the graph. PyTorch's autograd tracks version counters; an in-place op increments the version. If a saved tensor's version at use-time differs from its version at save-time, PyTorch raises this error — but only when the backward pass actually reaches that node, explaining intermittent behavior.
details.napkin_math: In-place ReLU saves 0 bytes of new allocation (overwrites existing tensor) but corrupts backward. Out-of-place ReLU requires 0 bytes for a view — in modern PyTorch, F.relu creates a view where possible. Net memory cost of switching to out-of-place: 0 bytes extra. The 'optimization' was never real.
details.realistic_solution: Replace x.relu_() with F.relu(x) (out-of-place). The memory savings from in-place ops are marginal for ReLU (no new allocation, just overwrite). Reserve in-place ops for cases where you are certain the tensor is no longer needed as a backward input: e.g., in-place updates to buffers not in the compute graph. Use torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) to get a stack trace pointing to the exact in-place operation.

scenario: A team migrates a model from numpy to PyTorch on A100. They use in-place ReLU (x.relu_()) for memory efficiency. During training, they get a RuntimeError: 'one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation'. This error appears intermittently, only with certain batch sizes.
title: Handling in-place operations and their effect on the autograd graph

details.common_mistake: Computing the full N×N similarity matrix as a dense tensor, materializing 4096×4096×512_dims × 4 bytes = 32GB just for the similarity scores, plus 32GB for the gradient of that matrix, plus all other activations — totaling >100GB for this one operation alone.
details.napkin_math: Full similarity matrix: 4096×4096×4 bytes = 64MB (just float matrix). But each embedding is dim=512: similarity computation requires 4096²×512 intermediate FLOPs. Backward through softmax of 4096-way softmax requires storing 4096×4096 attention-like weights = 64MB × 2 (grad) = 128MB — manageable. OOM is actually from encoder activations for all 4096 samples, not the matrix itself: 4096 images × ViT-L activations ≈ 40GB.
details.realistic_solution: Use GradCache or MoCo-style gradient chunking: split the batch into chunks of size K (e.g., K=256), compute similarity in chunks, accumulate gradients without materializing the full N×N matrix. The memory cost becomes O(N×K) instead of O(N²). Alternatively, use in-batch hard-negative mining that only materializes top-k pairs per anchor. On MI300X, K=512 reduces similarity matrix memory from 32GB to 2GB while maintaining full effective batch size.

scenario: You train a CLIP-style vision-language model on MI300X (192GB, 5.3TB/s). The contrastive loss requires computing similarity between all N×N image-text pairs in a batch. With N=4096, the similarity matrix is 4096×4096 pairs. The backward pass through the loss OOMs even though MI300X has 192GB.
title: Optimizing backward pass memory for a contrastive learning model on MI300X

details.common_mistake: Not handling the degenerate case where the gradient magnitude |∇f| approaches 0, causing division by zero in the backward pass. This is a silent bug because forward values are unaffected, but backward gradients explode when the SDF is evaluated near medial axis points where |∇f| ≈ 0.
details.napkin_math: Probability of a random 3D point being within epsilon=1e-3 of the medial axis ≈ O(surface_area × epsilon). For typical shapes: ~1% of samples per batch. At batch=10000 samples: 100 degenerate points per step × gradient of ∞ → NaN propagates through the full batch gradient in ~500 steps.
details.realistic_solution: Add an epsilon clamp in the backward: grad_magnitude = torch.clamp(torch.norm(input_grad, dim=-1, keepdim=True), min=1e-6). Use torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) to find the exact backward step producing NaN. Register a gradient hook on the custom function output to log max gradient magnitude per step. Consider replacing 1/|∇f| with the Eikonal loss formulation that penalizes |∇f|=1 without division.

scenario: A team implements a custom signed distance function (SDF) layer for 3D shape learning on H100. After 500 training steps, gradients become NaN. The forward pass looks correct and loss values are normal. The custom backward involves computing 1/|∇f| (inverse gradient magnitude) which can be numerically unstable.
title: Diagnosing NaN gradients in a deep network with custom autograd operations

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to reverse-mode AD (jacrev) even when the output dimension is much smaller than the input dimension, or using neither and instead manually running 10 separate backward passes. For Jacobian of shape (10 outputs × 3 spatial inputs), the correct choice is forward-mode (jacfwd) with 3 tangent vectors, not 10 reverse passes.
details.napkin_math: PINN training step: 10K collocation points. jacrev (10 passes): 10 × 5ms/pass = 50ms. jacfwd (3 passes): 3 × 5ms/pass = 15ms. At 10K steps: (50-15)ms × 10K = 350 seconds saved per training run. On H100, full Jacobian computation with jacfwd: 15ms/step × 100K steps = 25 minutes for Jacobian computation alone.
details.realistic_solution: For Jacobian of shape (m outputs × n inputs): use jacfwd if n < m (forward-mode: n passes), use jacrev if m < n (reverse-mode: m passes). Here n=3 spatial inputs, m=10 outputs: use jacfwd with 3 tangent vectors. torch.func.jacfwd computes the full 10×3 Jacobian in 3 JVP (Jacobian-vector product) calls. jacrev would require 10 VJP calls. Speedup: 3/10 = 3× fewer passes.

scenario: You are training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) that requires computing the full Jacobian of a 10-output model with respect to 3 spatial inputs (∂u/∂x, ∂u/∂y, ∂u/∂z) at every training step on H100. The model has 10M parameters. You need to choose between torch.func.jacfwd (forward-mode) and torch.func.jacrev (reverse-mode).
title: Comparing forward-mode vs reverse-mode AD for Jacobian computation on H100

details.common_mistake: Attempting to capture CUDA graphs for the full autoregressive loop, including the KV cache update. CUDA graphs require static tensor shapes and memory addresses. The KV cache grows with each token, changing tensor shapes, making the naive approach fail with CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS or incorrect results.
details.napkin_math: GPT-2 XL (1.5B params) single-token decode: without CUDA graphs ≈ 15ms (kernel launch overhead dominates at batch=1). With CUDA graphs ≈ 3ms (5× speedup). KV cache for max_len=2048: 2048 × 25 layers × 16 heads × 64 dim × 2 (K+V) × 2 bytes = 200MB — static allocation is fine on A100.
details.realistic_solution: Pre-allocate a fixed-size KV cache tensor (max_seq_len × n_heads × d_head × 2 bytes × n_layers) and use in-place writes via slice assignment: kv_cache[:, :, :, :cur_len] = new_kv. This keeps tensor addresses static. Capture the single-step decode function (not the full generation loop) using torch.cuda.graph.capture(). The Python loop over positions remains outside the graph. Validate with torch.cuda.check_error() after warmup.

scenario: You are deploying a GPT-2 XL inference service on A100 (312 TFLOPS, 2TB/s). At batch=1, the model achieves only 40% GPU utilization because kernel launch overhead dominates. CUDA graphs can replay a pre-captured sequence of kernels without Python overhead. You need to implement CUDA graph capture for autoregressive generation.
title: Autograd graph capture for CUDA graphs on A100 for inference acceleration

details.common_mistake: Not using ddp_model.no_sync() context manager during micro-batch accumulation steps. Without no_sync(), DDP triggers an AllReduce after every backward() call, including the intermediate micro-batch steps. This averages gradients over the wrong effective batch size (64 instead of 256 per GPU), and the gradient averaging is applied 4 times instead of once.
details.napkin_math: AllReduce data volume: each GPU sends its gradient shard. For 8-GPU AllReduce, each GPU sends data to all others. Total data transferred per GPU: (N-1)/N × data × 2 (ring). Total across all GPUs: N × (N-1)/N × data × 2 = 2(N-1) × data. For N=8, data=2GB: 2×7×2GB = 28GB... but the question asks total bytes transferred across the network: each of 8 GPUs sends 2GB: 8 GPUs × 2GB = 16GB transferred (not 8GB which would be if each GPU only sends once — ring AllReduce requires each GPU to send 2×(N-1)/N × D = 1.75 × 2GB = 3.5GB, × 8 GPUs = 28GB total network traffic, but unique data = 16GB).
details.realistic_solution: 8 GPUs × 2GB gradient each = 16GB total gradient data transferred (not 8GB). Total network bytes in ring AllReduce = 2×(N-1)/N×D per GPU × N GPUs = 2×7×2GB = 28GB network traffic.

scenario: You are using PyTorch DDP across 8 MI300X GPUs with gradient accumulation over 4 micro-batches. Effective batch size should be 8 GPUs × 4 micro-batches × 64 samples = 2048. But validation loss is worse than the 8-GPU baseline without accumulation, suggesting gradients are not being averaged correctly.
title: Gradient accumulation correctness with DDP and autograd on MI300X

details.common_mistake: Applying torchvision transforms after detaching the image tensor (treating augmentation as a preprocessing step), which stops gradient flow from the discriminator loss back through augmentations to the generator. The GAN cannot learn augmentation-robust features.
details.napkin_math: grid_sample for random crop at resolution 256×256, batch=64: input 64×3×256×256, grid 64×256×256×2. Memory: 64×3×256×256×4 = 50MB + 64×256×256×2×4 = 32MB. FLOP cost: O(batch × H × W × 4) for bilinear interp = 4M ops. At H100 989 TFLOPS: <0.01ms — negligible, worth it for full gradient flow.
details.realistic_solution: Implement augmentations as differentiable tensor operations: random crop via grid_sample with bilinear interpolation (differentiable), color jitter via tensor arithmetic (multiply/add), cutout via masked_fill with a learnable or random mask. Keep requires_grad=True throughout. For the generator path, ensure the augmented image remains in the computation graph. Use kornia library which provides differentiable augmentations as nn.Module layers.

scenario: You are implementing differentiable augmentation (DiffAugment) for a GAN training pipeline on H100. The discriminator loss must backpropagate through random cropping, color jitter, and cutout operations. Standard torchvision transforms do not participate in autograd.
title: Designing a differentiable data augmentation pipeline for training on H100

details.common_mistake: Using model.parameters() with requires_grad=False on frozen layers but still running frozen layers inside the normal forward pass without torch.no_grad(), causing PyTorch to build the computational graph for frozen layers anyway and store their activations for a backward pass that never uses them.
details.napkin_math: BERT-large: 24 layers. Frozen 20 layers' activations: 20/24 × total activation memory. At batch=32, seq=512: total activations ≈ 8GB. Frozen layer activations that can be freed: 20/24 × 8GB ≈ 6.7GB. New total: 72GB - 6.7GB ≈ 65GB. Fits comfortably within 80GB with headroom for optimizer states of trainable params only.
details.realistic_solution: Wrap frozen layers in with torch.no_grad(): within forward(), or use model.backbone.requires_grad_(False) which correctly sets requires_grad=False on all parameters AND prevents gradient tracking during forward. The latter is preferred as it also disables autograd graph construction for those layers. Verify with any(p.requires_grad for p in model.backbone.parameters()) == False.

scenario: You are fine-tuning only the last 4 transformer blocks of a 24-layer BERT-large on A100 (80GB). The backbone (first 20 layers) should be frozen. Current training uses 72GB, close to the 80GB limit, and you need to reduce memory usage.
title: Selective gradient computation using requires_grad and no_grad for fine-tuning

details.common_mistake: Storing the full computational graph for all 5 inner loop steps with retain_graph=True, keeping 5× the normal activation memory. Also using high-order finite differences instead of exact second-order gradients, which is both inaccurate and more expensive.
details.napkin_math: MAML memory cost: 5 inner steps × activation memory per step × 2 (for create_graph). 50M param model, batch=32: activations ≈ 4GB/step. MAML: 5 steps × 4GB × 2 = 40GB (matches observed). FOMAML: 1 step stored = 4GB. iMAML: O(1) steps stored via conjugate gradient = <1GB. Choose based on task sensitivity to second-order terms.
details.realistic_solution: Use torch.autograd.grad() with create_graph=True to compute inner loop gradients, then update parameters using functional forms (higher library or manual parameter dictionary) rather than in-place updates (which break the graph). Consider first-order MAML (FOMAML) that ignores second-order terms — often achieves 95% of MAML performance at 1/5 the cost. Or use implicit differentiation (iMAML) which avoids unrolling the inner loop entirely.

scenario: You implement Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) on H100. MAML requires differentiating through the inner loop optimization steps — computing second-order gradients (gradients of gradients). Your implementation using loss.backward(create_graph=True) is 8× slower than expected and uses 40GB for a 50M parameter model with 5 inner steps.
title: Implementing double backward for meta-learning with MAML on H100

details.common_mistake: Not registering the custom op with TorchDynamo's allow-list. By default, unknown Python callables or C++ extensions cause graph breaks because TorchDynamo cannot symbolically trace through them. Teams assume the custom op will be treated like any other torch op.
details.napkin_math: Without registration: every attention call (32 transformer layers) causes a graph break. TorchInductor optimizes within each subgraph but cannot fuse across breaks. Lost fusion opportunities: Q/K/V projection + attention could be 1 kernel; instead it is 4+ separate kernels. H100 fusion benefit: 4 kernels × 5μs launch overhead vs 1 kernel = 15μs saved × 32 layers = 480μs per step.
details.realistic_solution: Register the custom op using torch.library: define torch.ops.custom_ext.attention_fwd with a schema via torch.library.Library and use torch.library.impl_abstract() to provide a shape-inference function for TorchDynamo. This allows Dynamo to trace through the op symbolically without needing to execute it. Alternatively, use torch._dynamo.allow_in_graph(custom_func) for simpler cases where you want Dynamo to treat the function as an opaque leaf.

scenario: You have a custom CUDA extension for a specialized attention variant on H100 that calls torch.ops.custom_ext.attention_fwd(). After wrapping the model with torch.compile, you get a graph break at every custom op call. The compiler cannot trace through the custom extension's C++ dispatch.
title: Understanding graph break costs in torch.compile for a custom CUDA extension

details.common_mistake: Only testing that backward() runs without error, not verifying that the computed gradients match the numerical Jacobian. Silent gradient errors (wrong but non-NaN gradients) lead to models that train without errors but converge to suboptimal solutions.
details.napkin_math: gradcheck runs 2×n_inputs finite difference evaluations (forward + perturbation for each element). For a beam search with batch=2, beam_width=4, seq_len=10: input size = 2×4×10×vocab_size. With vocab=1000: 2×4×10×1000 = 80K input elements → 160K forward passes. At 1ms each: 160 seconds. Reduce input size to batch=1, beam=2, seq=3, vocab=10 for testing — 120 forward passes in 0.1 seconds.
details.realistic_solution: Use torch.autograd.gradcheck(func, inputs, eps=1e-6, atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-3, dtype=torch.float64) to compare analytical gradients against finite differences. Use double precision (float64) to minimize numerical error in the finite difference baseline. For second-order: use torch.autograd.gradgradcheck(). If gradcheck fails, use check_grad_dtypes=True to diagnose type issues, and examine individual Jacobian elements with torch.autograd.functional.jacobian().

scenario: You have implemented a custom differentiable beam search decoder for sequence generation on A100. The operation involves a differentiable top-k selection with soft attention over beam hypotheses.
