Before deploying to production training, you need to verify the backward pass is analytically correct.
title: Autograd correctness testing with gradcheck and gradgradcheck

details.common_mistake: Treating MI300X as a single homogeneous compute die. Engineers assume uniform memory latency across all 192 GB because the HBM pool is presented as a flat address space.
details.napkin_math: 8 XCDs x 24 GB HBM3 = 192 GB total. Die-to-die Infinity Fabric bandwidth ~896 GB/s aggregate. Local XCD HBM access ~5.3 TB/s peak / 8 XCDs = ~660 GB/s per XCD local; cross-XCD adds 1-2 fabric hops.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X is composed of 8 XCDs (Compute Dies) plus 4 MCD (Memory Cache Dies) connected via AMD Infinity Fabric on an interposer. Each XCD has its own L2 cache and direct HBM attachment through the MCDs. The OS and runtime see 192 GB unified but NUMA distance between XCDs varies by fabric hop count.

scenario: A colleague claims the MI300X is a monolithic die with a large HBM pool. Correct their mental model and describe the actual physical topology.
title: MI300X XCD Count and Die Topology

details.common_mistake: Blaming HBM bandwidth immediately. Engineers add more parallelism across XCDs hoping to spread load, but this actually increases cross-die traffic on Infinity Fabric.
details.napkin_math: Local HBM3 ~660 GB/s per XCD. Cross-XCD via Infinity Fabric adds ~1.5-2x latency penalty. For a 128 GB KV cache striped across 8 XCDs, each decode step fetches ~16 GB/XCD locally vs ~112 GB crossing the fabric — a 7x cross-fabric pressure multiplier.
details.realistic_solution: The attention pattern may be causing KV-cache accesses that span multiple XCDs. If the KV cache for a single sequence is striped across XCDs, each token generation requires cross-fabric reads. Pin KV cache allocation to a single XCD's local HBM region using ROCm's NUMA-aware allocator.

scenario: You are profiling a transformer inference kernel on MI300X and see unexpectedly high latency on attention heads. What chiplet-level bottleneck should you investigate first?
title: Chiplet Die-to-Die Bandwidth vs HBM Bandwidth

details.common_mistake: Assuming monolithic is always faster because there are no interconnect hops. This ignores that defect density makes large dies exponentially costly to manufacture.
details.napkin_math: D₀=0.1/cm², α=2 (clustering). Y_mono = (1 + 0.1×6/2)^-2 = (1.3)^-2 ≈ 59%. Y_chiplet = (1 + 0.1×1.5/2)^-2 = (1.075)^-2 ≈ 86%. 4-chiplet system: P(all 4 good) = 0.86^4 ≈ 55%, but bad dies are discarded individually making bin yield economics far better.
details.realistic_solution: Die yield follows Poisson: Y ≈ (1 + D₀A/α)^(-α). At D₀=0.1 defects/cm², a 600mm² die yields ~47% while a 150mm² die yields ~86%. Four 150mm² chiplets cost ~1.7x less per working unit. The performance penalty is only paid for cross-chiplet traffic, which good partitioning minimizes by keeping hot data paths within a single die.

scenario: Your team is deciding between a monolithic 600mm² die vs a 4-chiplet design of 150mm² dies for a next-gen ML accelerator. What yield and performance arguments should you present?
title: Yield-Performance Tradeoff in Chiplet Design

details.common_mistake: Comparing aggregate bandwidth numbers directly. MI300X's 5.3 TB/s is the sum across all XCDs; each XCD sees only a fraction. H100's 3.35 TB/s is monolithic — every SM can access it equally.
details.napkin_math: MI300X per-XCD local BW: 5.3 TB/s / 8 ≈ 662 GB/s. H100 monolithic BW: 3.35 TB/s. If 30% of MI300X accesses are cross-XCD at 2x penalty, effective BW ≈ 662×0.7 + 331×0.3 = 463 + 99 = 562 GB/s per XCD — below H100's flat 3.35 TB/s available to all SMs.
details.realistic_solution: Profile with rocprof to measure cross-XCD fabric traffic. Check if weight matrices are allocated NUMA-locally per XCD. Use hipMemAdvise(HIP_MEM_ADVISE_SET_PREFERRED_LOCATION) to pin tensors. For tensor parallel workloads, partition model layers such that each XCD owns complete weight shards, minimizing all-reduce hops across the Infinity Fabric.

scenario: A distributed training run on MI300X shows 15% lower MFU than expected on H100 despite MI300X having higher raw bandwidth. Describe your NUMA diagnosis methodology.
title: NUMA Effects in MI300X Multi-XCD Workloads

details.common_mistake: Assuming cache coherency is handled transparently across XCDs like within a single GPU SM cluster. Writes from one XCD's L2 are not automatically visible to another XCD's L2 without explicit fences.
details.napkin_math: Each XCD L2 is ~4 MB. An all-reduce across 8 XCDs on a 1 GB gradient requires 8 passes through the Infinity Fabric. Without fences, stale L2 reads can produce incorrect gradients. Fence overhead: ~200ns per barrier × 8 XCDs × 1000 steps = 1.6ms extra per iteration on a typical training step.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X Infinity Fabric provides coherency at the HBM level, not L2 level. Intermediate reduction buffers in L2 require explicit __threadfence_system() barriers before cross-XCD reads. Allocate reduction scratch space in global HBM (not L2-resident) and use atomic operations that flush to the coherency point. ROCm's rccl library handles this via ring-reduce with fabric-level fences.

scenario: You are designing a custom all-reduce kernel for MI300X that shares intermediate reduction buffers across XCDs. What coherency constraints must you enforce?
title: Coherency Domains Across XCDs

details.common_mistake: Believing unified memory eliminates all data movement cost. The physical data still traverses Infinity Fabric or PCIe; unified memory just removes explicit memcpy calls and programmer-managed staging buffers.
details.napkin_math: MI300X Infinity Fabric CPU-GPU BW: ~500 GB/s (bidirectional). PCIe 5.0 (discrete): ~128 GB/s. For a 1 GB batch: unified memory migration ~2ms vs explicit HtoD ~8ms via PCIe. But page-fault driven migration of 4KB pages at 10µs each = 10µs × (1GB/4KB) = 2.5 seconds worst case — always prefetch or prefault.
details.realistic_solution: On MI300X APU configurations, CPU and GPU share HBM via Infinity Fabric with coherent access. For preprocessing data that fits in HBM (~192 GB), zero-copy works well if the access pattern is sequential. But CPU random access into GPU-mapped pages triggers page migration with ~10µs overhead per fault. Pin frequently-accessed preprocessing buffers to CPU-local DRAM and only move inference input batches to HBM explicitly.

scenario: An inference pipeline uses CPU preprocessing feeding into MI300X compute. A teammate proposes using unified memory to eliminate explicit CPU-GPU copies. What are the performance implications?
title: APU Unified Memory and Zero-Copy Data Paths

details.common_mistake: Assuming bandwidth scales linearly: 4 XCDs = 4x single-XCD bandwidth. This ignores interposer congestion, shared bus arbitration, and the fact that cross-XCD traffic competes for the same physical wires.
details.napkin_math: Theoretical: 8 XCDs × 662 GB/s = 5.3 TB/s. Measured peak on stream benchmark: ~4.2 TB/s ≈ 79% efficiency. Coherency overhead at 8-way: ~8% of fabric bandwidth. Crossbar arbitration: ~13% overhead. Net: 5.3 × 0.79 ≈ 4.2 TB/s matches observed.
details.realistic_solution: Interposer bandwidth scales sublinearly due to: (1) shared crossbar arbitration latency increasing with N², (2) physical wire density limits on the silicon interposer, (3) coherency traffic consuming a fraction of aggregate bandwidth. Empirically, 8-XCD systems like MI300X achieve ~70-80% of theoretical peak aggregate bandwidth on uniform workloads.

scenario: You are benchmarking a 4-XCD chiplet system and notice that aggregate bandwidth scales sublinearly with XCD count. Explain the physical mechanism and quantify the expected scaling.
title: Interposer Bandwidth Scaling Laws

details.common_mistake: Using a single roofline with 5.3 TB/s as the memory bandwidth ceiling. This overstates achievable bandwidth for any single kernel because no single XCD can access the full aggregate bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: MI300X compute ceiling: 1307 TFLOPS FP16 (peak). Local XCD BW ceiling: 662 GB/s. Arithmetic intensity crossover: 1307×10¹² / 662×10⁹ = 1974 FLOPs/byte. H100 crossover: 989×10¹² / 3350×10⁹ = 295 FLOPs/byte. MI300X is far more compute-bound per XCD — memory-bound kernels are relatively more penalized.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X needs a three-tier roofline: (1) local XCD HBM: 662 GB/s ceiling, (2) cross-XCD fabric: ~300 GB/s effective for random cross-die access, (3) host: ~500 GB/s via Infinity Fabric. Kernels should be tuned against the local-XCD roofline. H100's single-tier 3.35 TB/s is more predictable — memory-bound kernels saturate a flat ceiling regardless of which SMs run them.

scenario: Construct a roofline model for MI300X that accounts for the NUMA bandwidth hierarchy: local XCD HBM, cross-XCD Infinity Fabric, and host DRAM. How does this affect kernel tuning versus H100?
title: Chiplet vs Monolithic Roofline Model

details.common_mistake: Comparing peak bandwidth numbers without accounting for latency. Infinity Fabric is on-package (sub-100ns); NVLink 4.0 is chip-to-chip via physical connectors (~1-2µs). For small-message collectives, latency dominates bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Small message all-reduce latency: MI300X 8-XCD ~0.5µs vs NVLink H100×8 ~8µs = 16x faster. Large message (10 GB): MI300X fabric ~10GB/896GB/s ≈ 11ms vs NVLink ~10GB/900GB/s ≈ 11ms — bandwidth-equivalent but MI300X all 8 in one package, no PCIe or cable overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Infinity Fabric intra-package latency: ~50-100ns. NVLink 4.0 latency: ~1-2µs. For all-reduce on small gradients (<1 MB), MI300X's 8-XCD collective is ~20x lower latency than NVLink. For large gradients (>1 GB), bandwidth matters more: NVLink 4.0 per-link 900 GB/s (8-GPU NVSwitch) vs MI300X Infinity Fabric 896 GB/s — roughly equal bandwidth but fundamentally different use cases (inter-node vs intra-package).

scenario: An engineer argues that MI300X's intra-package Infinity Fabric is equivalent to NVLink 4.0 between H100s for collective communication. Evaluate this claim quantitatively.
title: Die-to-Die Link Latency vs NVLink Comparison

details.common_mistake: Round-robin distributing weight shards across all XCDs. This maximizes memory utilization but ensures every matrix multiplication requires cross-XCD fabric reads during the partial sum accumulation phase.
details.napkin_math: 70B params FP16 = 140 GB. 8 XCDs × 24 GB = 192 GB. Per XCD: 140/8 = 17.5 GB weights + activations. Layer-local strategy: ~2 GB activations cross-XCD per pipeline boundary vs weight all-gather of 17.5 GB per layer in tensor-parallel. Pipeline boundary traffic: 2 GB × 7 boundaries = 14 GB vs tensor-parallel: 17.5 GB × 80 layers = 1.4 TB fabric traffic per forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Partition by layer groups: assign consecutive transformer layers (e.g., layers 0-9) to XCDs 0-1, layers 10-19 to XCDs 2-3, etc. Within each layer group, keep both weight matrices and activation buffers on the same XCD pair. Use pipeline parallelism between XCD groups rather than tensor parallelism across all 8. Cross-XCD traffic is then only activation tensors at pipeline stage boundaries (much smaller than weights).

scenario: You are deploying a 70B parameter model on a single MI300X (192 GB). Design the tensor parallelism partitioning strategy that maximizes XCD-local memory access.
title: Tensor Parallelism Partitioning for XCD Locality

details.common_mistake: Assuming each MCD serves exactly two XCDs in a symmetric 2:1 mapping. The actual topology has non-uniform proximity due to physical interposer layout.
details.napkin_math: 4 MCDs × 48 GB = 192 GB. Aggregate HBM3 BW: 5.3 TB/s → 1.325 TB/s per MCD. XCD-to-local-MCD: 1 hop ~50ns. XCD-to-remote-MCD: 2 hops ~100ns. Bandwidth penalty for remote access: ~15-20% throughput reduction due to arbitration.
details.realistic_solution: Each MCD manages a 48 GB HBM3 stack partition. XCDs are arranged in two rows of 4 on the interposer. XCDs nearest to an MCD have lower fabric hop count (~1 hop) while diagonal XCDs have 2+ hops. AMD's NUMA-aware memory allocator (ROCm NUMA) attempts to place tensors on HBM closest to the XCD that will process them, but this requires explicit hints via hipMemAdvise.

scenario: How are the 4 Memory Cache Dies (MCDs) in MI300X physically connected to the 8 XCDs, and what does this mean for memory access symmetry?
title: HBM3 Stack Partitioning Across MCDs

details.common_mistake: Assuming XCDs are fully independent and isolated like separate GPUs. XCDs share the coherency fabric, HBM controller arbitration, and the L3 cache domain, creating side-channel and performance interference risks.
details.napkin_math: 8 tenants × 24 GB = 192 GB, memory isolation is straightforward. Fabric bandwidth isolation: 896 GB/s total fabric / 8 tenants = 112 GB/s guaranteed per tenant, but cross-tenant coherency traffic can consume an additional 10-15% overhead from snoops even with isolation.
details.realistic_solution: XCD isolation requires: (1) page table separation enforced by IOMMU per XCD, (2) bandwidth QoS on Infinity Fabric to prevent one tenant's XCD from starving others, (3) HBM partition tables in MCDs to enforce memory isolation. AMD's CDX (Compute Die eXtension) spec provides hardware isolation primitives but full tenant isolation requires hypervisor support that is not yet standardized in ROCm.

scenario: A cloud provider wants to offer 1/8 MI300X slices (one XCD per tenant) for smaller inference workloads. What architectural challenges arise from XCD-level multi-tenancy?
title: Chiplet Architecture and Multi-Tenant Isolation

details.common_mistake: Assuming thermal throttling is uniform across all chiplets since they share a TDP budget. Each XCD has independent voltage regulators and thermal sensors, causing workload-dependent thermal gradients.
details.napkin_math: MI300X TDP: 750W across 8 XCDs = 93.75W average per XCD. Compute-bound XCD (FFN): ~110W. Memory-bound XCD (attention): ~70W. Thermal margin before throttle: 110W/93.75W = 1.17x headroom. At 600W package limit during throttle: (600W - 70W×4 attention XCDs) / 4 compute XCDs = (600-280)/4 = 80W per compute XCD, forcing ~15% frequency reduction.
details.realistic_solution: Non-uniform throttling indicates workload imbalance across XCDs. XCDs processing attention heads (memory-bound, lower power) run cooler than XCDs running FFN layers (compute-bound, higher power). The MI300X package thermal management allows individual XCD DVFS. Rebalance layer assignments to distribute power more uniformly, or use ROCm's power management API to cap per-XCD TDP.

scenario: During sustained inference on MI300X, you observe that XCD thermal throttling is non-uniform — some XCDs throttle at 600W TDP while others remain at full frequency. Diagnose the root cause.
title: Power Delivery Across Chiplet Dies

details.common_mistake: Arbitrarily ordering XCDs 0-7 in the logical ring. This can place non-adjacent XCDs as ring neighbors, maximizing cross-interposer fabric hops and degrading allreduce bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: 8-XCD ring all-reduce: 2×(N-1)/N × BW per link. With optimal ring (all single-hop, 896 GB/s fabric): 2×7/8 × 896 = 1,568 GB/s effective. With random ring (avg 1.8 hops): 2×7/8 × (896/1.8) ≈ 871 GB/s — 44% degradation from non-topology-aware ring ordering.
details.realistic_solution: Map the physical XCD layout (2×4 grid on interposer) to a ring that only traverses adjacent edges. Optimal ring follows a Hamiltonian path on the 2×4 grid: XCD0→XCD1→XCD2→XCD3→XCD7→XCD6→XCD5→XCD4→XCD0. This ensures every ring step is a single fabric hop. RCCL auto-detects this topology via the Infinity Fabric topology discovery API.

scenario: Design an optimal ring-allreduce topology for MI300X's 8 XCDs given the physical Infinity Fabric layout. How does the physical topology constrain the logical ring order?
title: Infinity Fabric Topology and All-Reduce Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Using simple sequential prefetch (prefetch next token's KV block). Autoregressive decode with top-p sampling has unpredictable next-token positions, making sequential prefetch ineffective for KV indices.
details.napkin_math: KV cache fetch latency: remote XCD 100ns + HBM access ~200ns = 300ns per KV block. Compute per token (attention + FFN): ~500µs for 70B model on MI300X. Prefetch overlap window: 500µs / 0.3µs = 1667 KV blocks can be prefetched during compute. Top-4 speculation: 4 × 300ns = 1.2µs prefetch cost vs 300ns × K miss penalty avoided.
details.realistic_solution: Use speculative prefetch: during the compute phase of token T, launch async DMA transfers from remote XCDs for KV blocks of the top-K most likely next tokens (determined by logit distribution at T-1). With K=4 and speculation accuracy ~60%, ~60% of KV fetches arrive before decode begins. This overlaps 100ns Infinity Fabric latency with ~500µs compute for typical sequence lengths.

scenario: LLM decode on MI300X is memory-bandwidth-limited. Propose a cross-XCD prefetch strategy that hides Infinity Fabric latency for KV-cache access during autoregressive generation.
title: Cross-Die Prefetching for LLM Decode

details.common_mistake: Pre-loading all 1000 adapters into GPU memory. At 13 MB each (rank-16, 13B base), 1000 adapters = 13 GB — feasible but wasteful when only 50 are active.
details.napkin_math: 1000 adapters × 13 MB = 13 GB total. Active pool (50 adapters, matching scenario): 650 MB. Cache hit rate for top-50 adapters (power law, 80/20 rule): ~95% of requests. Miss cost: 13 MB / 16 GB/s (PCIe 4.0) = 0.8ms per miss. At 1000 RPS with 5% miss rate: 50 misses/sec × 0.8ms = 40ms total eviction latency/sec spread across requests — 0.04ms average overhead per request.
details.realistic_solution: Use paged adapter management: maintain a GPU-resident adapter pool of 50 slots (650 MB, covering the peak active count). Evict LRU adapters to CPU pinned memory (latency ~0.8ms for 13 MB at PCIe 4.0 16 GB/s). On cache miss, evict LRU and load from CPU. For the 50 concurrently active adapters, group requests by adapter to minimize swaps. Track adapter hotness via request frequency; top-50 hot adapters never evict (covers ~95% of traffic in power-law distribution).

scenario: You are building a multi-adapter serving system to handle 1000 LoRA adapters on a cluster of 8 H100s. Only 50 adapters are active at any given time. Design the paged adapter memory management system (S-LoRA style) and calculate the memory overhead.
title: Adapter Serving Infrastructure: S-LoRA Paged Memory Design

details.common_mistake: Calculating LoRA memory as just the adapter parameters. Engineers forget that the frozen base model weights must still reside in GPU memory, and optimizer states are needed for the trainable adapter parameters.
details.napkin_math: LoRA trainable params: 2 × 16 × 4096 × 32 layers = 4,194,304 ≈ 4.19M. Adapter memory: 4.19M × 4 bytes (FP32) = 16.8 MB. Base model BF16: 14 GB. Adapter Adam states: 33.6 MB. Activations (batch=4, seq=2048): ~2 GB. Total: 14 + 0.017 + 0.034 + 2 ≈ 16.1 GB. H100 has 80 GB — 5× headroom for larger batches.
details.realistic_solution: Full fine-tune 7B (FP32): 7B × 4 bytes = 28 GB weights + 56 GB optimizer (Adam: 2 moments × 28 GB) + activations = ~120 GB — exceeds H100. LoRA rank-16: trainable params = 2 × rank × d_model × num_layers = 2 × 16 × 4096 × 32 = 4.19M params. Adapter memory: 4.19M × 4B = 16.8 MB weights + 33.6 MB optimizer. Frozen base (BF16): 7B × 2B = 14 GB. Total: ~14.05 GB — easily fits.

scenario: You need to fine-tune a 7B parameter base model using LoRA on a single H100 (80 GB). Calculate the memory budget for rank-16 LoRA vs full fine-tuning.
title: LoRA Rank Selection and Memory Budget

details.common_mistake: Thinking QLoRA reduces the LoRA adapter training to 4-bit. Adapter weights themselves remain in BF16 for numerical stability; only the frozen base model is quantized to NF4.
details.napkin_math: 70B × 4 bits / 8 bits/byte = 35 GB NF4. Double quantization: saves ~0.5 bits per parameter (quantizes the quantization constants), reducing to ~35 × (3.5/4) ≈ 30.6 GB. Rank-16 LoRA BF16 adapters: 2 × 16 × 8192 × 80 × 2B = 84 MB. Activations (batch=2, seq=2048): ~6 GB. Total: 30.6 + 0.084 + 6 ≈ 36.7 GB. Two H100s provide 160 GB — fine-tune with batch=16 or serve multiple LoRA variants simultaneously.
details.realistic_solution: QLoRA quantizes the frozen 70B base model to NF4 (4-bit Normal Float): 70B × 0.5 bytes = 35 GB. Double quantization further reduces size by quantizing the quantization constants themselves — saving roughly 0.5 bits per parameter, bringing the model to approximately 30.6 GB (not halving to 17.5 GB). LoRA adapters remain in BF16. With rank-16: 2 × 16 × 8192 × 80 layers × 2 bytes = 84 MB adapters. Paged optimizer in CPU RAM handles rare Adam state spikes. Total GPU: ~30.6 GB base + 84 MB adapters + 6 GB activations ≈ 36.7 GB — fits on one H100 with headroom.

scenario: Explain how QLoRA fits a 70B parameter model fine-tuning on two H100s (160 GB total) and calculate the actual memory footprint.
title: QLoRA 4-bit Quantization Memory Arithmetic

details.common_mistake: Loading each adapter separately with its own copy of the base model weights. This requires 50 × 26 GB = 1.3 TB — impossible on any single node.
details.napkin_math: 13B base BF16: 26 GB. Rank-16 adapter: 2 × 16 × 5120 × 40 = 6.5M params × 2B = 13 MB per adapter. 50 adapters: 650 MB. Total: 26.65 GB on H100 80 GB — 53 GB free for KV cache. KV cache per request: 40 layers × 2 × 5120 × seq_len × 2B. At seq=4096: 40 × 2 × 5120 × 4096 × 2B = 3.3 GB/request → ~16 concurrent requests in remaining memory.
details.realistic_solution: Share the base model: one 13B BF16 copy = 26 GB. All 50 rank-16 adapters: 50 × (2 × 16 × 5120 × 40 layers × 2B) = 50 × 105 MB = 5.25 GB. Total: 26 + 5.25 = 31.25 GB — fits on one H100. For batching, group requests by adapter (adapter-aware batching): requests using the same adapter are batched together to avoid adapter switching overhead between tokens. Use S-LoRA-style paged adapter management for adapters not fitting in GPU memory.

scenario: Your serving system hosts 50 different LoRA adapters (rank-16) on top of a shared 13B base model. Design the memory layout and batching strategy for serving multiple adapters concurrently.
title: Multi-Adapter Batching and Shared Base Model

details.common_mistake: Running all four PPO models (policy, reference, reward, critic) simultaneously on all GPUs. This 4x memory multiplication is the primary reason RLHF is prohibitively expensive when not architected carefully.
details.napkin_math: 7B policy (BF16 + Adam FP32): 14 GB + 56 GB optimizer = 70 GB. 7B reference (BF16, frozen): 14 GB. 1B reward model (BF16): 2 GB. 7B critic (BF16 + Adam): 70 GB. Total naive: 156 GB → 2 H100s for policy, 1 for reference, 0.5 for reward, 2 for critic. Tensor parallel over 8×H100: 156 GB / 8 = 19.5 GB/GPU — fits with memory for KV cache.
details.realistic_solution: PPO-RLHF requires: (1) policy model (trained), (2) reference model (frozen, for KL penalty), (3) reward model, (4) critic/value model. Strategy: colocate reference and policy on same GPUs (reference is frozen, no optimizer states); run reward model on separate GPU subset only during rollout phase; use frozen reference in inference mode to halve its memory. 8×H100: policy+optimizer on 4 GPUs (tensor parallel), reference on same 4 GPUs (frozen, no optimizer = 2x less memory), reward on 2 GPUs, critic on 2 GPUs.

scenario: Design the infrastructure for PPO-based RLHF on a 7B policy model. Specify the four required models, their roles, and how to schedule them efficiently across an 8×H100 node.
title: RLHF Infrastructure: PPO Training Pipeline Architecture

details.common_mistake: Stopping training at a fixed step count regardless of reward model signal quality. Engineers set reward thresholds without monitoring KL divergence from the reference policy, missing the onset of reward hacking.
details.napkin_math: KL budget: 0.1 nats/token. At seq_len=512: total KL budget = 51.2 nats per sequence. KL increase rate: ~0.01 nats/PPO step typical. Steps to budget: 51.2 / 0.01 = 5120 steps before KL cap. With KL penalty coefficient β=0.01: reward penalty = 0.01 × KL = 0.01 × 51.2 = 0.512 reward units. If reward model range is 0-5, this 0.5 penalty is meaningful but not dominant — insufficient, increase β to 0.1.
details.realistic_solution: Reward hacking manifests as high reward + high KL from reference + low human preference. Infrastructure mitigations: (1) monitor KL(policy || reference) per training step — set hard KL budget (e.g., 0.1 nats); (2) checkpoint policy every 500 steps and run periodic human preference eval; (3) use constitutional AI reward ensemble (multiple reward models) to reduce single-model gaming; (4) implement reward model uncertainty estimation to detect out-of-distribution outputs.

scenario: After 3000 PPO steps, your RLHF-trained model achieves high reward scores but produces outputs that human raters find unhelpful or repetitive. Diagnose the reward hacking and propose infrastructure-level mitigations.
title: Reward Hacking Detection in RLHF Systems

details.common_mistake: Always merging adapters into base weights for zero inference overhead. Merging destroys the ability to switch adapters per request and requires storing 100 separate model copies.
details.napkin_math: 100 adapters rank-16 (13B base): 100 × 13 MB = 1.3 GB. H100 80 GB — 1.3 GB adapters + 26 GB base = 27.3 GB. 52 GB remaining for KV cache → strategy C is optimal. 100 merged copies: 100 × 26 GB = 2.6 TB — needs 33 H100s. Strategy A only viable when single adapter serves 80% of traffic.
details.realistic_solution: (A) Merge: zero inference overhead, but requires 100 × base_model_size storage and separate deployment per adapter — optimal when one customer has very high traffic (>1000 RPS) and dedicated serving. (B) Dynamic loading: adapter loaded/unloaded per request — ~50ms swap latency, optimal for long-tail adapters with <1 RPS each. (C) All-in-memory: zero swap latency, requires 100 × adapter_size in HBM — optimal for up to ~100 rank-16 adapters (100 × 13 MB = 1.3 GB on H100 80 GB — easily feasible).

scenario: You have 100 LoRA adapters for customer-specific fine-tunes. Compare three serving strategies: (A) merge adapters into base weights, (B) dynamic adapter loading, (C) keep all adapters in GPU memory. When is each optimal?
title: LoRA Adapter Merging and Serving Tradeoffs

details.common_mistake: Dividing total memory by 8 GPUs and assuming each GPU holds 1/8 of everything. Adapter parameters must be replicated across all tensor-parallel workers (not sharded) to enable gradient synchronization, creating a memory asymmetry.
details.napkin_math: 70B / 8 GPUs (TP) = 8.75B params/GPU × 2B (BF16) = 17.5 GB. Rank-64 adapters: 2 × 64 × 8192 × 80 layers × 2B = 167 MB per GPU (replicated, not sharded). Adapter Adam: 335 MB. Activations (batch=2): ~6 GB. Total per GPU: 17.5 + 0.167 + 0.335 + 6 = 24.0 GB. 80 GB H100: 56 GB free for larger batches.
details.realistic_solution: Tensor parallel shards the frozen base model (70B / 8 = 8.75B params per GPU = 17.5 GB BF16). LoRA adapters are replicated on all GPUs (not sharded) because each GPU computes a partial matrix product and the adapter modifies the full output. Adapter size rank-64: 2 × 64 × 8192 × 80 × 2B = 167 MB per GPU. Adam states for adapters: 335 MB per GPU. Per-GPU total: 17.5 GB base + 167 MB adapters + 335 MB optimizer + 6 GB activations ≈ 24 GB. Binding constraint: base model shards.

scenario: Fine-tuning a 70B model with LoRA rank-64 across 8 H100s. Calculate the per-GPU memory breakdown for tensor-parallel LoRA training and identify the binding constraint.
title: PEFT Memory Budget Across Parallelism Strategies

details.common_mistake: Assuming prefix KV cache sharing works across adapters with the same system prompt. The same input produces different KV values when processed through different LoRA adapters because the adapted attention projection weights change the key/value computation.
details.napkin_math: KV cache per sequence (13B, rank-16, seq=2048): 40 layers × 2 × 5120 × 2048 × 2B = 1.67 GB. Without prefix sharing: 50 users × 1.67 GB = 83.5 GB — exceeds H100. With prefix sharing (1000-token shared prefix): shared portion = 40 × 2 × 5120 × 1000 × 2B = 0.82 GB × 50 = 41 GB without sharing vs 0.82 GB with perfect sharing. Multi-adapter kills this sharing.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache values are computed as K = xW_K + x(A_K B_K) where A_K, B_K are adapter matrices. Different adapters produce different K, V values for identical inputs — prefix sharing is only valid within the same adapter. In a 50-adapter system, prefix cache hit rate drops from ~70% (single adapter) to ~1-2% (random adapter assignment). Mitigation: adapter-aware request routing to maximize same-adapter batching and restore prefix cache hits.

scenario: Your multi-adapter serving system uses PagedAttention. Explain why KV cache pages cannot be shared across different LoRA adapters and quantify the memory overhead.
title: Adapter-Aware KV Cache Management

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the inference cost of the judge LLM in RLAIF. A GPT-4-class judge generating 100 preference labels costs ~$0.01, making RLAIF appear cheap per sample — but RLHF requires 10K-100K labeled comparisons, and the total cost compounds quickly.
details.napkin_math: RLHF human labels: 10K × $0.10 = $1,000. RLAIF (GPT-4): 10K × (avg 500 tokens × $0.01/1K tokens) = 10K × $0.005 = $50. Training: 8×H100 × 4 hours × $4/GPU-hr = $128. Total RLHF: $1,128. Total RLAIF: $178. RLAIF saves $950 (84%). At 100K comparisons: RLHF=$10,128 vs RLAIF=$628 — 16x savings.
details.realistic_solution: RLHF: 10K human comparisons × $0.10/comparison = $1,000 labeling cost + GPU training (~$500 for 7B on 8×H100 for 1000 PPO steps). RLAIF with GPT-4-turbo judge: 10K AI comparisons × $0.005/comparison = $50 + same training cost. RLAIF is 20x cheaper on labeling. Crossover: RLAIF is preferred when judge LLM quality is sufficient (>85% agreement with human raters). For safety-critical applications, human labels remain necessary regardless of cost.

scenario: Compare the infrastructure cost of RLHF with human feedback vs RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback using a judge LLM) for fine-tuning a 7B assistant model. What is the crossover point where RLAIF becomes cost-effective?
title: RLHF vs RLAIF Infrastructure Cost Comparison

details.common_mistake: Assuming per-user LoRA is infeasible at 10M users due to storage. Storage is not the constraint — it is the impossibility of training individual adapters without sufficient per-user data.
details.napkin_math: Rank-4 adapter (13B): 2 × 4 × 5120 × 40 × 2B = 3.3 MB. 10M users × 3.3 MB = 33 TB storage. At $0.023/GB/month (S3): 33TB × $0.023 = $759/month storage. Serving: load adapter per request — 3.3 MB from S3 at 500 MB/s = 6.6ms load latency. Cache hot adapters in GPU memory: 100 hot adapters × 3.3 MB = 330 MB — negligible, cache top-1000 adapters covering 80% of traffic (power law).
details.realistic_solution: Prompt personalization: zero storage overhead, works with 0 training examples (user description in system prompt), but bounded by context window — 500 token user profile consumes 25% of 2048-token context, degrading generalization. Per-user LoRA: requires 100-1000 user interactions to train a meaningful adapter (rank-4: only 3.25 MB storage per user × 10M = 32.5 TB total storage). Break-even: users with >500 interactions benefit from LoRA; sparse users (<100 interactions) should use prompt personalization.

scenario: A consumer product has 10 million users and wants personalized LLM behavior. Compare per-user LoRA adapters vs long system prompt personalization. At what scale does each approach break down?
title: Personalization at Scale: Per-User LoRA vs Prompt Engineering

details.common_mistake: Increasing the learning rate to escape the plateau where loss instability appears. This worsens gradient magnitude, further destabilizing LoRA weight updates.
details.napkin_math: Effective batch size: 4 × 16 = 64. LR for LoRA: typically 1e-4 to 3e-4 (10x higher than full fine-tune). Gradient norm before clip: if >10, indicates rank collapse. Rank collapse condition: when singular values of AB concentrate ratio > 10:1. Monitor via SVD of adapter weights every 100 steps. Dropout 0.1 on LoRA reduces rank collapse probability by ~40% empirically.
details.realistic_solution: LoRA gradient instability with high gradient accumulation often results from rank collapse: the low-rank matrices A and B align their singular vectors, causing the adapter update to concentrate on a single direction. Mitigation: (1) add LoRA dropout (0.1) to regularize adapter directions; (2) reduce accumulation steps (effective batch size too large for the rank), or use smaller learning rate with warmup; (3) initialize B to zero (standard LoRA) but verify this is not being overridden. Gradient clipping at 1.0 is essential for LoRA.

scenario: A LoRA fine-tuning run shows loss instability and gradient explosions after 500 steps despite using AdamW. The batch size is 4 with gradient accumulation over 16 steps. Diagnose the issue.
title: Gradient Accumulation in LoRA Training Stability

details.common_mistake: Setting rank as high as memory allows (rank-256 or higher) assuming more rank = better performance. The intrinsic dimensionality of fine-tuning tasks is typically low (rank 8-32 captures 90%+ of task-specific signal).
details.napkin_math: 34B model adapter sizes (d_model=8192, 48 layers): Rank-4: 2×4×8192×48×2B = 6.3 MB. Rank-16: 25.2 MB. Rank-64: 100.7 MB. Rank-256: 402.7 MB. Performance on HumanEval code: rank-4→rank-16: +8% pass@1. rank-16→rank-64: +2%. rank-64→rank-256: +0.3%. Marginal gain per doubling drops exponentially after rank-32 for most tasks.
details.realistic_solution: Use spectral analysis: train with rank-256, then analyze singular value decomposition of the learned AB matrix. The number of singular values above a threshold (e.g., 5% of max) gives the effective rank. For most NLP tasks, effective rank is 4-32. Beyond rank-64, performance gains are <0.5% on standard benchmarks but memory and compute scale linearly. Use rank-16 for production, rank-64 for maximum quality, rank-4 for resource-constrained fine-tuning.

scenario: You are tuning LoRA rank for a code generation task on a 34B model. Describe the methodology for selecting optimal rank and the diminishing returns beyond rank-64.
title: LoRA Rank Sensitivity Analysis

details.common_mistake: Averaging LoRA adapter gradients directly (FedAvg on adapter parameters). Without differential privacy, gradient averaging can leak training data through gradient inversion attacks, violating HIPAA.
details.napkin_math: Rank-4 adapter params: 2×4×4096×32 = 1.05M. Full fine-tune 7B: 7B params. DP noise budget: for same ε=1 guarantee, noise ∝ √(params). √(7B/1.05M) = √6667 ≈ 82x. DP-LoRA requires 82x less noise than DP full fine-tune for same privacy budget → 82x better utility at identical privacy level. Communication: 1.05M × 4B = 4.2 MB per round vs 7B × 4B = 28 GB for full gradients.
details.realistic_solution: Use DP-LoRA: each hospital trains a local rank-4 adapter with Gaussian noise added to gradients before transmission (ε=1.0, δ=10⁻⁵). Central server aggregates noisy adapter updates via FedAvg. Noise scale: σ = C√(2ln(1.25/δ))/ε × √T where T=rounds, C=gradient clip norm. Key insight: LoRA's small parameter count (vs full fine-tune) dramatically reduces noise needed for the same DP guarantee — rank-4 has 4000x fewer parameters than 7B full fine-tune, requiring 4000x less noise for same ε.

scenario: A healthcare company wants to fine-tune a medical LLM across 50 hospitals without sharing patient data. Design a federated LoRA training system with differential privacy guarantees.
title: Federated LoRA Training for Privacy-Preserving Adaptation

details.common_mistake: Implementing token-level routing with a separate learned router per layer, ignoring that 8 adapters per layer × 32 layers = 256 routing decisions per forward pass, each requiring its own compute.
details.napkin_math: Single rank-16 adapter per layer: 2×16×4096 = 131K params × 2B = 256 KB. 32 layers single adapter: 131K × 32 = 4.19M params × 2B = 8.4 MB. 8 MoLoRA adapters: 8 × 4.19M × 2B = 67.1 MB for adapters. Router: 32 × (4096×256 + 256×8) = 32 × 1.05M = 33.6M params → 67.1 MB. Total MoLoRA overhead: 134 MB vs 8.4 MB single adapter = 16× more memory but routes each token to its specialized adapter.
details.realistic_solution: MoLoRA uses a lightweight router (2-layer MLP, 256 hidden) that maps input embeddings to a soft assignment over K=8 adapters. Top-2 routing with load balancing loss (like MoE). Forward pass: for each token, compute 2 adapter outputs and sum. Memory: 8 rank-16 adapters per layer × 32 layers = 256 adapter matrices = 8× single-adapter memory (67.1 MB total vs 8.4 MB). Inference overhead: router (256 params per layer, negligible) + 2 adapter forward passes per token. Net overhead: 2× single-adapter compute, 8× memory.

scenario: Design a mixture-of-adapters system where each input token is routed to one of 8 specialized LoRA adapters. Analyze the computational overhead and routing mechanism.
title: Mixture of LoRA Experts (MoLoRA) Architecture

details.common_mistake: Saying the split is purely about memory — both phases need HBM, so memory alone doesn't explain the split. The real driver is compute vs. memory-bandwidth utilization profiles being fundamentally different.
details.napkin_math: H100 compute-to-bandwidth ratio: 989e12 / 3.35e12 = ~295 FLOP/byte ridge point. Prefill for 4096-token input on 70B model: 2×70e9×4096 = 573 TFLOPs of compute, weight reads ~140 GB → ~4,096 FLOP/byte — firmly compute-bound. Single decode step: 2×70e9×1 = 140 GFLOPs, weight reads ~140 GB → 1 FLOP/byte — firmly bandwidth-bound.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill is compute-bound: it processes all input tokens simultaneously as a large matrix multiply (high arithmetic intensity ~300 FLOP/byte on H100 at long context). Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: it streams the full model weight matrix once per generated token to produce a single token (arithmetic intensity ~1-2 FLOP/byte). Mixing them on the same GPU forces a compromise: prefill under-utilizes the 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth while decode under-utilizes 989 TFLOPS of compute. Disaggregation lets each pool run at its natural bottleneck, improving overall cluster utilization by 30-50% in practice.

scenario: A colleague asks why disaggregated serving splits prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools rather than running both phases on every GPU. Explain the core motivation and what hardware characteristic makes the two phases incompatible on shared capacity.
title: Prefill-Decode Split Rationale

details.common_mistake: Forgetting GQA reduces KV heads from 96 to 8, causing a 12x overcount of transfer size. Also forgetting the factor-of-2 for key AND value tensors.
details.napkin_math: 2 × 8 × 128 × 4096 × 96 × 2 = 1,610,612,736 bytes ≈ 1.5 GiB (1.61 GB). 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s. 1.61 GB / 50 GB/s ≈ 32ms. For a 1k-token prompt the prefill itself on H100 takes ~10ms, so KV transfer adds ~3× overhead — a significant TTFT penalty at this network speed.
details.realistic_solution: KV-cache size = 2 (K+V) × num_kv_heads × head_dim × seq_len × num_layers × bytes_per_element. With GQA: 2 × 8 × 128 × 4096 × 96 × 2 bytes = 1.61 GB. At 400 Gbps (50 GB/s effective): 1.61 GB / 50 GB/s = ~32ms. Yes, this is on the critical path for TTFT since decode cannot start until the KV-cache arrives.

scenario: After prefill finishes on a prefill GPU, the KV-cache for a 4096-token request (using a 70B model with 96 layers, GQA with 8 KV heads, head dim 128, FP16) must be transferred to a decode GPU over 400 Gbps InfiniBand HDR. Calculate the transfer size and the resulting transfer latency. Is this on the critical path for TTFT?
title: KV-Cache Transfer Bandwidth Budget

details.common_mistake: Treating TTFT and TPOT as independent — migrating capacity to prefill directly lengthens decode queues, increasing TPOT for all in-flight requests, not just new ones. The queuing is coupled.
details.napkin_math: If prefill pool processes 200k tokens/s and decode pool generates 80k tokens/s, decode is the bottleneck. Moving 1 GPU from decode (saves ~10k tokens/s decode capacity) to prefill (gains ~25k tokens/s prefill capacity) widens the bottleneck. Correct direction: move prefill GPUs to decode until the ratio equalizes at target utilization ρ < 0.8. On MI300X (5.3 TB/s, 192 GB): decode throughput = 5.3e12/140e9 = 37.8 tok/s — 1.58× H100; larger KV pool means more concurrent sequences before decode saturates, shifting the breakeven pool ratio in favor of fewer decode GPUs.
details.realistic_solution: Moving GPUs from decode to prefill reduces prefill queue depth and TTFT, but each decode GPU now serves more concurrent in-flight sequences. TPOT degrades because decode is already memory-bandwidth-bound: adding sequences increases HBM reads per step proportionally. The right signal is the ratio of prefill throughput (tokens/s processed) to decode throughput (tokens/s generated). If prefill throughput >> decode throughput, the bottleneck is decode and migrating to prefill worsens TPOT. Track P99 of both SLOs independently and model the system as two coupled M/D/c queues — find the pool split where both P99s are met with maximum total throughput.

scenario: Your disaggregated serving cluster has separate TTFT and TPOT SLOs: TTFT < 500 ms, TPOT < 50 ms per token. During a load spike the prefill queue grows. An engineer proposes migrating two decode GPUs to the prefill pool to reduce TTFT. Analyze the tradeoff — what does this fix, what does it break, and what metric do you use to decide the right pool ratio?
title: TTFT vs TPOT SLO Tension

details.common_mistake: Blaming network congestion or KV transfer failures. The correlation with decode memory utilization is the key signal — network errors would show different patterns.
details.napkin_math: If a decode GPU has 80 GB HBM, model weights for 70B at FP16 = 140 GB (needs 2 GPUs for tensor parallel), so per-GPU weight footprint ≈ 70 GB. Free KV pool ≈ 10 GB. At 4096 tokens, the true KV cache per request = 2 × 8 × 128 × 4096 × 96 × 2B ≈ 1.61 GB, and with TP=2 per GPU = ~0.8 GB per GPU. The pool holds ~10GB / 0.8GB ≈ 12 concurrent sequences. Throttle at 10 slots (83% watermark) to prevent stall.
details.realistic_solution: When all decode GPUs are at high memory utilization, new KV-cache blocks from completed prefills cannot be placed — the decode pool has no free HBM to accept the transfer. The prefill GPU finishes work and then waits, holding the request in limbo (the 'prefill stall'). The prefill GPU is effectively blocked: it cannot start the next prefill because the current request's KV-cache has nowhere to go. The fix is back-pressure signaling: the decode pool advertises free KV-block capacity to the prefill scheduler. The prefill scheduler throttles new prefills when decode-side free capacity falls below a threshold (e.g., 2× the max KV size of a single request). This converts a hard stall into a controlled queue.

scenario: After deploying disaggregated serving, you observe that TTFT is fine at P50 (120 ms) but P99 TTFT spikes to 4 seconds intermittently. Profiling shows the spikes correlate with periods when all decode GPUs have high memory utilization. There are no network errors. Diagnose the root cause and propose a fix.
title: Prefill Stall During Decode Migration

details.common_mistake: Setting chunk size based on memory only, ignoring that multiple chunks serialized across multiple prefill GPUs introduces queuing delay between chunks — the inter-chunk scheduling latency can dominate TTFT for long inputs.
details.napkin_math: H100 prefill throughput for 70B: ~200k tokens/s (compute-bound at long seq). 32k tokens / 200k tokens/s = 160 ms for a single-chunk prefill — just under SLO. But 64×512-token chunks: each chunk has lower arithmetic intensity, GPU runs at ~50% efficiency → 400 ms total. Dynamic chunk size ≥ 4096 restores efficiency: 32k/4096 = 8 chunks × ~20 ms = 160 ms.
details.realistic_solution: For a 32k-token input with 512-token chunks, you need 64 chunks. If each chunk takes ~5 ms on H100 and there is 1 ms inter-chunk scheduling overhead, total prefill time = 64 × 6 ms = 384 ms — already over the 200 ms SLO. Solution: (1) Scale chunk size dynamically with input length: for inputs > 8k tokens, increase chunk size to saturate the GPU (H100 prefill compute is saturated around 2048-4096 tokens for 70B models). (2) Use parallel chunked prefill: split chunks across multiple prefill GPUs with a ring-allreduce over partial attention scores. (3) Set chunk size to 2048 for inputs > 8k, giving 32k/2048 = 16 chunks × 6 ms = 96 ms — within SLO.

scenario: Your disaggregated prefill cluster uses chunked prefill to prevent long requests from monopolizing a GPU. You set a fixed chunk size of 512 tokens. A product requirement says TTFT must be under 200 ms for all requests regardless of input length. Design the chunk scheduling policy that satisfies this SLO for inputs up to 32k tokens on H100.
title: Chunked Prefill Scheduling Window

details.common_mistake: Choosing MI300X purely for memory capacity without accounting for the fact that decode throughput scales with memory bandwidth, not capacity — more sequences only helps if bandwidth can keep up.
details.napkin_math: Decode tok/s = HBM_bandwidth / model_size_bytes. H100: 3.35e12 / 140e9 = 23.9 tok/s (single GPU, but TP=2 needed so use 2×). MI300X: 5.3e12 / 140e9 = 37.8 tok/s (single GPU). MI300X delivers 1.58× more tokens/s per GPU and 5.2× more concurrent sequences per GPU-unit vs H100 TP=2 pair. TCO favors MI300X for memory-bound decode.
details.realistic_solution: Model weights for 70B FP16 = 140 GB. H100: 140 GB exceeds 80 GB → needs tensor parallelism (TP=2, two H100s), leaving each GPU with 80-70=10 GB for KV. MI300X: 192 GB fits entire model on one GPU with 52 GB free for KV. KV per sequence at 4096 tokens (96 layers, 8 KV heads GQA, head_dim 128, FP16) ≈ 384 MB. H100 (10 GB KV pool): ~26 sequences. MI300X (52 GB KV pool): ~135 sequences. Token throughput (bandwidth-limited): H100 pair at 2×3.35 TB/s = 6.7 TB/s / 140 GB = 47.8 tokens/s per sequence × 26 = 1243 tok/s aggregate. MI300X at 5.3 TB/s / 140 GB = 37.8 tokens/s single sequence × 135 = 5103 tok/s aggregate. MI300X wins on aggregate throughput per GPU-unit for decode, especially when eliminating TP communication overhead.

scenario: You are choosing the GPU for your decode pool in a disaggregated serving deployment for a 70B FP16 model. Compare H100 SXM5 (80 GB, 3.35 TB/s) and MI300X (192 GB, 5.3 TB/s) for the decode role. Compute the maximum concurrent sequences each can serve at 4096-token context, and the single-stream token generation throughput. Which is better for decode and why?
title: MI300X KV Pool Sizing vs H100

details.common_mistake: Using CPU/memory utilization as the leading indicator — decode is GPU-bound and CPU metrics lag or are irrelevant. Using instantaneous TPOT P50 instead of a leading queue metric.
details.napkin_math: If peak traffic grows at 20% per minute and queue fills in 90 s, leading indicator at 70% capacity fires at 90×0.7/1.0 = 63 s before saturation. Warm-up = 90 s. Net: we're 63 s early but warm-up takes 90 s, so we still have a 27 s exposure window vs 90 s before — a 70% reduction in SLO violation duration.
details.realistic_solution: TPOT is a lagging indicator — by the time it degrades, the decode queue is already backed up. The leading indicator is decode queue depth (number of in-flight sequences waiting for their next token step). When this exceeds a threshold — e.g., 80% of the decode pool's maximum concurrent sequence capacity — autoscaling triggers immediately. A secondary signal is the ratio of prefill completions per second to decode token emissions per second: if prefill output rate > decode absorption rate, the decode queue will grow. Set the autoscale trigger at queue_depth > 0.7 × max_capacity. GPU warm-up takes ~90 s (model load + NCCL init). Old SLO violation window: 180 s. With leading indicator at 70% queue depth, trigger fires ~30 s before degradation onset. New violation window: max(0, 90 - 30) = 60 s — a 67% reduction. On MI300X decode nodes (192 GB HBM), the larger KV pool (52 GB vs 10 GB on H100 TP=1) increases time-to-saturation, giving more lead time before the leading indicator fires.

scenario: Your decode pool autoscales based on average TPOT over a 60-second window. During traffic ramps, TPOT degrades for 2-3 minutes before new decode instances warm up and register. Propose a leading indicator metric that would trigger autoscaling before TPOT degrades, and quantify the improvement in worst-case SLO violation duration.
title: Decode Pool Autoscaling Lag

details.common_mistake: Approving it unconditionally based on the 2× transfer speedup without accounting for decompression cost on the decode GPU and accuracy impact on long-generation tasks.
details.napkin_math: 400 Gbps network: 384 MB transfer = 7.7 ms. With INT8 2×: 3.9 ms savings. But 200-token decode with 0.2 ms/step decompression overhead = 40 ms added TPOT. Breakeven: 3.9 ms TTFT improvement / 40 ms TPOT degradation = net negative for TPOT-sensitive workloads. At 100 Gbps (25 GB/s): same 384 MB takes 15.4 ms, savings = 7.7 ms, still net negative at 200 tokens.
details.realistic_solution: Benefits: KV transfer halved (e.g., 7.7 ms → 3.8 ms for the Q62001 scenario), reducing TTFT. Each decode step reads KV from HBM: INT8 KV halves KV read bandwidth, increasing decode throughput on bandwidth-bound GPUs. Costs: (1) Compression adds latency at end of prefill (~0.5-1 ms for CUDA kernel, negligible). (2) Decompression per decode step adds ~0.1-0.2 ms per step — on a 200-token output this is 20-40 ms extra TPOT overhead. (3) Quantization error in KV accumulates over long generations — INT8 KV causes measurable quality degradation at 1k+ output tokens. Net-positive when: output length is short (<200 tokens), TTFT is the binding SLO (not TPOT), and network is the bottleneck (< 200 Gbps). Net-negative when: long outputs, TPOT-sensitive workloads, or high-bandwidth network (400+ Gbps) where transfer latency is already small.

scenario: Your team proposes compressing the KV-cache before transferring it from prefill to decode GPUs (e.g., quantizing KV from FP16 to INT8 or FP8). The expected compression ratio is 2×, halving transfer time. Evaluate this proposal: what does it improve, what does it cost, and under what conditions is it net-positive?
title: Cross-Pool KV Compression Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Placing the draft model on the prefill nodes — prefill nodes are sized for compute-bound workloads and will be underutilized for the memory-bound draft decode steps. Also ignoring that speculation rejection requires re-running target model decode, which changes the scheduling contract.
details.napkin_math: Draft model (7B) token throughput on MI300X: 5.3e12 / 14e9 = 378 tok/s. Target verify pass: same cost as 1 decode step but processes γ+1=5 tokens as a small prefill → ~5× cheaper per token vs sequential. Expected speedup with γ=4 and acceptance rate α=0.8: E[tokens/step] = (1-α^(γ+1))/(1-α) = (1-0.32768)/0.2 = 3.36. Throughput gain: 3.36× fewer target model calls. Net: ~2.5× end-to-end TPOT improvement after draft overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Optimal placement: co-locate the 7B draft model on each decode node alongside the 70B target model. MI300X has 192 GB — 70B target (140 GB) + 7B draft (14 GB) = 154 GB, fits with 38 GB for KV. Draft runs γ=4 steps autonomously on the decode node, producing 4 candidate tokens. Target model verifies in one forward pass (also on decode node). Accepted tokens skip target decode steps; rejected tokens revert. KV-cache interaction: draft model and target model maintain separate KV caches; accepted tokens' target-model KV entries are written, draft KV is discarded. New failure modes: (1) Draft-target KV desynchronization if preemption occurs mid-speculation — requires atomic speculation rollback. (2) Speculative decoding changes batch composition unpredictably, breaking the fixed-size decode step assumption used by the prefill-to-decode scheduling contract. (3) Rejection rate spikes under distribution shift, wasting compute without throughput gain.

scenario: You want to add speculative decoding (draft model + target model verification) to a disaggregated serving system. The target model is 70B on MI300X decode nodes; the draft model is 7B. Design the placement architecture: where does the draft model run, how does the KV-cache interaction work, and what new failure modes does this introduce vs. non-disaggregated speculative decoding?
title: Speculative Decoding in Disaggregated Architecture

details.common_mistake: Storing prefix caches on prefill nodes — a cache hit still requires transferring the prefix KV to the decode node, paying the same network cost. Storing on decode nodes avoids this transfer but requires routing requests to the decode node holding the cache.
details.napkin_math: Prefix KV cache size (2048 tokens, same GQA params): 2×8×128×2048×96×2B = 805,306,368 bytes ≈ 768 MB (0.75 GiB). With 38 GB free KV pool on MI300X: 38,000 MB / 768 MB ≈ 49 cacheable prefixes per decode node. With consistent hashing across 10 decode nodes: ~490 total cached prefixes. At 1000 RPS with 60% hit rate = 600 cache hits/s avoiding 768 MB transfers each. Bandwidth saved: 600 × 768 MB/s = 461 GB/s of InfiniBand bandwidth freed.
details.realistic_solution: Optimal placement: store prefix KV-caches on decode nodes. On a cache hit, the request skips prefill entirely for the cached prefix, and decode can start immediately without any KV transfer. The prefill node only processes the new suffix tokens. Routing policy: hash the prefix to a consistent decode node (consistent hashing), so all requests with the same prefix land on the same decode node. Invalidation: LRU eviction when KV pool utilization > 85% watermark. TTFT savings: assume prefix = 2048 tokens of a 2560-token request. Prefill for 2048 tokens at 200k tok/s = 10.2 ms; KV transfer for 2048 tokens (768 MB) at 50 GB/s = 15.4 ms. Cache hit saves ~25.6 ms. At 60% hit rate, E[TTFT savings] = 0.6 × 25.6 ms = 15.4 ms per request.

scenario: Your service adds prompt caching: if a request shares a prefix with a recently processed request, the KV-cache for that prefix is reused. Design the cache placement policy in a disaggregated architecture. Should prefix KV-caches be stored on prefill nodes, decode nodes, or a shared storage tier? Specify the invalidation policy and quantify expected TTFT savings at 60% prefix hit rate.
title: Prefill-Decode Affinity and Context Caching

details.common_mistake: Attributing the slowdown to CPU-GPU synchronization overhead or Python scheduler latency. The real cause is PCIe bandwidth saturation during KV swap-in competing with weight reads during decode.
details.napkin_math: KV swap-in rate (PCIe): 64 GB/s. 192 MB KV for 2048-token sequence: 3 ms swap time. Normally decode step time = model_size / HBM_bw = 140 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 41.8 ms. During swap, effective HBM bandwidth drops to ~2 TB/s (PCIe contention): step time = 140/2000 = 70 ms. Ratio: 70/41.8 = 1.67×. For full 192 MB swap affecting 3 ms window with 41.8 ms/step: first token post-preemption incurs 3 ms + 41.8 ms vs normal 41.8 ms = 1.07× overhead. Doesn't match 8× — the real mechanism is page-fault stalls if using demand paging. Full KV not pre-fetched: each token decode triggers page faults for its own KV pages → stall per fault × 20 pages = 8× plausible.
details.realistic_solution: When a preempted sequence resumes, its KV-cache must be swapped back from CPU DRAM to GPU HBM over PCIe (typically 64 GB/s). During the swap, the decode kernel is also reading model weights from HBM (140 GB for 70B model × decode step = streaming weights). The PCIe bus saturates during the KV swap-in, stalling the HBM DMA engine because both operations compete for HBM write bandwidth. The GPU cannot begin the decode kernel until the KV-cache is resident in HBM. For 20 tokens, the KV-cache grows by 20 × (frame size per token), each token requiring a PCIe read before it can be used. Fix: (1) Use asynchronous KV swap with double-buffering — begin swapping the KV-cache for a sequence one step before it is scheduled to resume. (2) Reduce swap frequency by increasing HBM KV pool (use MI300X 192 GB). (3) Use NVLink-attached CPU memory pools (Grace Hopper) where swap bandwidth is 900 GB/s vs 64 GB/s PCIe.

scenario: Under heavy load, your decode scheduler preempts low-priority in-flight sequences by swapping their KV-cache to CPU DRAM to free HBM for new high-priority requests. Users report that preempted requests, when resumed, have TPOT 8× higher than normal for the first 20 tokens before recovering. Explain the exact mechanism causing this and how to fix it.
title: Decode Preemption and KV Swap

details.common_mistake: Using total model size in the roofline instead of per-layer FLOPs and memory accesses. The roofline is applied per-operation, not across the whole forward pass.
details.napkin_math: H100 ridge point: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOP/byte. Arithmetic intensity for prefill (B=1, S=512): (2 × 13e9 × 512) / (13e9 × 2 bytes) = 512. Compute-bound since 512 > 295. For S=32: intensity = 32 < 295 → memory-bound. Crossover sequence length: S* = 295 × (2 bytes × 13e9) / (2 × 13e9) = 295 tokens. So prefill is compute-bound for any sequence ≥ 295 tokens at B=1.
details.realistic_solution: For attention and MLP layers combined in a transformer, the dominant operation is GEMMs. For a single forward pass with batch size B and sequence length S: FLOPs = 2 × N_params × B × S (approximate for transformer). Memory reads ≈ N_params bytes × 2 (FP16) + activation memory. The ridge point of H100 is ~295 FLOP/byte. Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes = (2 × 13e9 × B × S) / (26e9 + activations). For S=1 (pure decode): intensity = 2B/(2+ε) ≈ B FLOP/byte. For S=512 (prefill batch B=1): intensity = 512 FLOP/byte >> 295 → compute-bound. Crossover at intensity = 295: B×S ≈ 295 → B=1 is compute-bound for S ≥ 295 tokens. For S=512, any batch size makes prefill compute-bound.

scenario: On an H100 SXM5 running prefill for a 13B parameter FP16 model (hidden dim 5120, 40 layers), you want to choose the batch size that maximizes GPU utilization without hurting TTFT. At what batch size does the prefill become compute-bound vs. memory-bandwidth-bound? Show the calculation using the roofline model.
title: Optimal Prefill Batch Size for TTFT

details.common_mistake: Assuming full bisection bandwidth is available — 2:1 oversubscription halves the effective bandwidth for cross-switch traffic, and not all prefill-to-decode transfers are local to the same ToR switch.
details.napkin_math: Aggregate KV bandwidth: 500 × 384e6 = 192e9 bytes/s = 192 GB/s. 64 prefill nodes: 192/64 = 3 GB/s per node average. 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s per link. Per-node utilization: 3/50 = 6% — well within limits. Spine bisection (2:1): 25 GB/s effective. 3 GB/s << 25 GB/s. Network is NOT a bottleneck at uniform load. Hot-spot scenario: if 10% of requests go to 1 node: 50 × 384 MB/s = 19.2 GB/s — still < 50 GB/s per link. System is safe up to ~130 req/s per prefill node.
details.realistic_solution: Total KV transfer bandwidth demand: 500 req/s × 384 MB = 192 GB/s. With 64 prefill nodes each sending at most 192/64 = 3 GB/s — well within 400 Gbps (50 GB/s) per link. However, with 2:1 oversubscription, spine bandwidth = 400 Gbps × (number of leaf uplinks) / 2. If all prefill nodes are on different ToR switches from decode nodes (worst case), all traffic crosses the spine. Effective spine bandwidth per node-pair ≈ 25 GB/s. 3 GB/s << 25 GB/s — not a bottleneck in this scenario. However, if a single prefill node is saturating (doing 500 req/s itself): 500 × 384 MB = 192 GB/s from one node — exceeds 50 GB/s link rate by 3.8×. Solution: load-balance requests across prefill nodes. Max per-node KV egress should be < 40 GB/s (80% of link rate). At 384 MB per transfer, one node can handle 40/0.384 ≈ 104 req/s. Require at least 500/104 = 5 prefill nodes minimum to avoid link saturation.

scenario: You are deploying a disaggregated serving cluster with 64 prefill H100s and 128 decode MI300Xs connected over a two-tier fat-tree InfiniBand network (400 Gbps per link, 2:1 oversubscription at the spine). At peak load, 500 requests/s each transfer 384 MB of KV-cache from prefill to decode. Determine whether the network is a bottleneck, and design a mitigation if it is.
title: Network Topology for KV Transfer at Scale

details.common_mistake: Adding more decode GPUs to fix the imbalance — this treats the symptom, not the cause. The root cause is that round-robin ignores output length heterogeneity, causing long-running sequences to cluster.
details.napkin_math: Assume 10 decode MI300X GPUs, 38 GB KV pool each. 380 GB total KV. Round-robin at 500 req/s: each GPU gets 50 req/s. If 10% are long (2000 tok × 384MB/4096tok = 188 MB each): 5 long req/s per GPU × 188 MB = 940 MB/s KV accumulation; at steady state with mean 10s long jobs: 9.4 GB pinned. 10% short (50 tok): frees in 0.1s. Imbalance variance depends on burst pattern — binomial variance in long-job assignment → hot GPU gets 3σ = 3×√(50×0.1×0.9) = 3×2.1 = 6.3 extra long jobs → 6.3 × 188 MB = 1.2 GB extra pressure.
details.realistic_solution: Round-robin does not account for output length variance. A 2000-token output occupies a KV slot for 2000 steps; a 50-token output frees its slot in 50 steps. If requests arrive in bursts where long outputs cluster on the same GPU (e.g., during batch processing jobs), those GPUs fill up while others stay empty. Solutions: (1) Least-loaded-first assignment at transfer time: assign each new KV to the decode GPU with the most free HBM KV blocks. (2) Work-stealing: decode GPUs at <30% utilization advertise capacity; overloaded GPUs migrate completed KV sequences mid-flight to underloaded neighbors (requires live KV transfer over InfiniBand — same mechanism as prefill→decode transfer). (3) Output length prediction: use a draft model or heuristic to estimate output length at prefill time and bin requests into short/long queues served by different decode GPU subsets.

scenario: Your decode pool uses static round-robin assignment: each incoming prefill completion is assigned to the next decode GPU in sequence. You observe that some decode GPUs are at 95% memory utilization while others sit at 40%. Users with long outputs (>2000 tokens) report degraded TPOT. Root-cause this imbalance and propose a work-stealing or rebalancing mechanism.
title: Variable Output Length and Decode Pool Imbalance

details.common_mistake: Comparing raw TFLOPS directly without noting that TPU v5e's peak is for systolic array operations with specific matrix tile sizes, and that XLA compilation adds per-shape compilation latency that hurts dynamic input lengths.
details.napkin_math: Cost comparison: TPU v5e ~$1.20/chip-hour vs H100 ~$3.50/GPU-hour. Prefill throughput ratio: H100/TPU = 989/197 = 5.02×. Cost efficiency: H100 costs 3.50/989 = $0.00354/TFLOPS-hour. TPU v5e: 1.20/197 = $0.00609/TFLOPS-hour. H100 is actually more cost-efficient per TFLOP. TPU v5e advantage only if workload perfectly fits systolic tile sizes and uses XLA fusion aggressively.
details.realistic_solution: 7B BF16 model = 14 GB. TPU v5e chip: 16 GB — fits with 2 GB spare (very tight for activations at long context). A 4-chip node has 64 GB total. Prefill compute: 197 TFLOPS BF16 per chip vs H100's 989 TFLOPS. TPU v5e is 5× slower per chip in raw compute but much cheaper. For compute-bound prefill at S=1024: H100 latency = 2×7e9×1024/(989e12) = 14.5 ms. TPU v5e = 2×7e9×1024/(197e12) = 72.8 ms — 5× slower. KV transfer cost from TPU to H100 decode: same InfiniBand cost. Operational constraints: (1) XLA requires static input shapes or re-compilation for each new shape — dynamic sequence lengths cause XLA retracing storms. (2) TPU→GPU KV transfer requires format conversion (BF16→FP16 or vice versa). (3) JAX/XLA ecosystem doesn't integrate with vLLM serving stack natively. Not recommended unless cost is the primary driver and TTFT SLO > 500 ms.

scenario: Your team proposes using TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16, 1600 GB/s HBM bandwidth, 16 GB HBM per chip, 4 chips per node) exclusively for the prefill pool, with H100 for decode. For a 7B BF16 model, evaluate whether TPU v5e is a better prefill accelerator than H100 and identify the practical constraints that could make this combination operationally painful.
title: TPU v5e as Prefill Accelerator

details.common_mistake: Padding all requests to the maximum length in a batch — a batch with one 8192-token request and seven 50-token requests wastes 98.8% of compute on padding for the short requests.
details.napkin_math: Throughput without bucketing (naive padding to max): batch of 8 requests padded to 8192: useful compute = (50+50+50+50+50+50+50+8192) / (8 × 8192) = 8542/65536 = 13%. With bucketing ([0,128] bucket for 7 short + separate [2048,8192] for 1 long): short batch useful compute = 7×50 / (7×128) = 350/896 = 39%. Long batch: 100%. Overall throughput: ~3× improvement vs naive padding.
details.realistic_solution: Length-bucketed batching: sort incoming requests into length buckets (e.g., [0,512], [512,2048], [2048,8192]). Batch requests within the same bucket together. Short requests are padded at most 10× (50→512), not 163× (50→8192). Within each bucket, use continuous batching to avoid waiting for a full batch. TTFT bound: a 50-token request in the [0,512] bucket is padded to 512 → prefill cost = 512-token prefill. Minimum TTFT (no padding, single request) = 50-token prefill. Ratio: 512/50 = 10.24 — within 3× is too tight for this bucket design. Tighten to [0,128], [128,512], [512,2048], [2048,8192] → max padding 128/50 = 2.56× within the first bucket. TTFT variation now within 3× for all buckets. Router assigns each request to the lowest bucket that fits its length, dispatches to the prefill node with the shallowest queue for that bucket.

scenario: Requests arrive at a router with variable input lengths (50–8192 tokens, Zipf-distributed). Your prefill pool has 8 H100s. Design a batching strategy that maximizes prefill throughput while bounding TTFT variation to within 3× of minimum TTFT. Specifically address length-based bucketing vs. continuous batching.
title: Batching Strategy Across Prefill Nodes

details.common_mistake: Checkpointing the full KV-cache every N tokens — this floods the network. The smarter approach is to recognize that prefill can be replayed cheaply and only the incremental generated tokens need checkpointing.
details.napkin_math: 200 sequences, avg 100 generated tokens each at checkpoint: 200 × 100 tokens × 2 bytes = 40 KB checkpoint. Checkpointing every 10 tokens at 50 tok/s per sequence: 5 checkpoints/s per sequence × 200 sequences = 1000 checkpoint writes/s. At 40 KB each cumulative: steady-state checkpoint write rate = 200 seq × 10 tokens × 2 bytes / 10 steps = 400 bytes/s per sequence — negligible. Full KV checkpoint (alternative): 200 × 192 MB = 38.4 GB every 10 tokens — 38.4 GB / 10 tokens × 50 tok/s = 192 GB/s — saturates all available bandwidth. Token ID checkpoint: 4000× cheaper. On MI300X with 192 GB HBM: KV pool ≈ 52 GB per GPU → 52 GB / 192 MB per request = 270 concurrent sequences before any preemption is needed — 10× more than H100 before swap pressure occurs.
details.realistic_solution: KV-cache is decomposable: prompt KV + generation KV. Prompt KV can always be regenerated by re-running prefill on the original prompt (which is stored in the request router). Generation KV for tokens already emitted can be regenerated by re-running decode on those tokens deterministically (temperature=0) or stored as compressed token IDs. Checkpoint strategy: store generated token IDs (not KV-cache) to a low-latency key-value store (e.g., Redis on the same rack) every 10 tokens. Token IDs for 200 sequences × max 2000 tokens × 2 bytes = 800 KB — trivially small. On failure: (1) Router detects decode node down via heartbeat (<1 s). (2) Recovery node loads model weights (90 s cold start, or 0 s if warm standby). (3) Re-runs prefill for all 200 prompts on prefill nodes (parallel, 200 × ~10 ms = 10 ms if batched). (4) Re-runs decode for checkpointed tokens (deterministic, fast — same as normal decode). Total recovery: 90 s cold / 5 s warm (prefill replay) + decode replay time. Warm standby decode node reduces to ~15 s recovery.

scenario: A decode GPU fails mid-generation for 200 in-flight sequences. You want to recover without dropping requests and with minimal TPOT disruption. The KV-cache for all 200 sequences was only on the failed GPU's HBM. Design a fault-tolerance architecture for decode nodes that allows recovery, specifying what state must be checkpointed, at what frequency, and what the recovery latency looks like.
title: Graceful Decode Node Failure During Generation

details.common_mistake: Saying continuous batching just 'keeps the GPU busy' without explaining the mechanism. The key is the per-step insertion point, not simply avoiding idle time.
details.napkin_math: Static batching efficiency: if batch size = 32 and sequences have uniform geometric output length with mean μ=200 tokens, the expected idle time per batch = time waiting for slowest sequence. With geometric distribution, max of 32 geometric(1/200) RVs ≈ 200 × ln(32) = 200 × 3.47 = 694 tokens before batch ends. GPU runs at 100% for first 200 tokens on avg, then partially idle as sequences complete. Wasted steps ≈ 50%. Continuous batching: GPU always has ≈ 32 active sequences, near 100% occupancy. Throughput improvement: ~2×.
details.realistic_solution: Static batching waits until a full batch of new sequences is available before starting a decode run; all sequences must finish before the next batch starts. This means the GPU is idle after sequences of varying length finish, waiting for the slowest sequence. Continuous batching inserts new sequences into the running batch at each decode step boundary. The key event: at the end of each decode step, the scheduler checks for completed sequences (those that emitted EOS) and newly arrived KV-caches from prefill. It evicts completed slots and inserts new sequences in a single atomic swap. This maximizes GPU occupancy because the batch size stays approximately constant throughout the decode pool's lifetime. In a disaggregated system, KV-caches arrive from prefill nodes asynchronously; continuous batching is the mechanism that absorbs this asynchrony without GPU stalls.

scenario: Explain why continuous batching (also called iteration-level scheduling) significantly improves decode GPU utilization compared to static batching, specifically in the context of a disaggregated serving system where new sequences arrive from the prefill pool asynchronously. What is the key scheduling event that enables continuous batching?
title: Continuous vs. Static Batching in Decode Pool

details.common_mistake: Statically partitioning pools per model — 5 dedicated pools waste capacity when models have non-simultaneous peaks. The answer involves dynamic pool multiplexing with priority-based isolation.
details.napkin_math: MI300X decode node (192 GB): 140B model TP=2 (280 GB across 2 GPUs, 140 GB each) + KV pool = 192-140 = 52 GB KV per GPU. 70B model on 1 GPU: 140 GB fits, 52 GB KV. 34B: 68 GB, 124 GB KV. 13B: 26 GB, 166 GB KV. 7B: 14 GB, 178 GB KV. 6 × 7B models on one GPU: 84 GB weights + shared KV pool of 108 GB. Total GPU count for baseline reserved capacity: 70B needs 10 decode GPUs at 500 RPS; scaling linearly, full 5-model platform ≈ 35 decode GPUs + 15 prefill H100s.
details.realistic_solution: Use a two-level architecture: (1) Physical pools: prefill pool (H100s optimized for compute) and decode pool (MI300X for memory capacity). Both pools are shared across models. (2) Logical isolation via virtual queues per model with reserved + burstable capacity. Each model gets a reserved capacity slice (e.g., 20% for each of 5 models) and can burst into unused capacity. (3) Model loading: maintain all models hot on decode nodes using fractional GPU allocation. 140B requires TP=2 on MI300X (140 GB < 192 GB each, 2 GPUs for safety margin). 7B fits in 14 GB — multiplex 6 instances per MI300X GPU. (4) KV-cache isolation: per-tenant KV namespaces with HBM quotas enforced by the PagedAttention block allocator. Blocks are tagged with tenant ID; cross-tenant block reuse is disabled. (5) Capacity allocation: weighted fair queuing at the prefill scheduler; decode assignments respect per-model KV quotas. A load spike on the 70B model can consume up to 150% of its reserved capacity (burst) but triggers autoscaling before consuming 200%.

scenario: You run a platform serving 5 different LLM models (7B, 13B, 34B, 70B, 140B) to thousands of tenants with different SLOs. Design the full disaggregated serving architecture: how do you partition prefill and decode pools across models, handle model loading, manage KV-cache isolation between tenants, and set capacity allocation rules that prevent one model's load spike from impacting SLOs of others?
title: Multi-Model Disaggregated Serving Isolation

details.common_mistake: Tuning batch size to fix compute utilization — the real bottleneck is PCIe, and increasing batch size only increases PCIe pressure further if inputs are being transferred per-batch.
details.napkin_math: If model is 175B FP16 = 350 GB > 4 × 80 GB = 320 GB. Cannot fit in TP=4. Must page. Paging rate: each forward pass needs all 350 GB of weights. At 150k tok/s and 512 tok/sequence: 293 forward passes/s × 350 GB = 102 TB/s of weight reads needed. H100 HBM: 3.35 TB/s × 4 = 13.4 TB/s. PCIe: 32 GB/s — 3000× bottleneck if paging over PCIe. Diagnosis confirmed. Solution: use FP8 quantization (175 GB, fits in 320 GB TP=4) or model parallelism with NVLink.
details.realistic_solution: PCIe at 90% utilization is the bottleneck. At 512-token sequences with FP16 tokens (embedding dim=8192 for a large model), input activations per request = 512 × 8192 × 2 bytes = 8.4 MB. At 150k tok/s, input transfer rate = 150e3/512 × 8.4 MB = 4.4 GB/s — not enough to saturate PCIe. The bottleneck is likely KV-cache output transfer to CPU pinned memory (pre-transfer staging before InfiniBand send). At 150k tokens/s output with 384 MB per 4096-token sequence: for 512-token sequences, KV = 384/8 = 48 MB. At 300 completions/s: 300 × 48 MB = 14.4 GB/s — close to PCIe 4.0 x16 limit of 32 GB/s but not over. Re-examine: are weight tensors being reloaded from CPU? Suspect the model doesn't fit in 80 GB H100 and is paging weights over PCIe. 80 GB < model_size means PCIe is streaming weights. Fix: use tensor-parallel across all 4 H100s (total 320 GB) so weights fit in HBM, eliminating PCIe weight paging.

scenario: Your prefill pool of 4 H100s is processing at 150k tokens/s aggregate, but expected throughput is 400k tokens/s (4 × 100k tok/s per GPU). Profiling shows GPU compute utilization at 35% and PCIe transfer utilization at 90%. All requests have sequence lengths of 512 tokens. Diagnose the bottleneck and fix it.
title: Prefill Throughput Saturation Diagnosis

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that the radix tree stores the prefix KV once per unique prefix, not once per user. Also forgetting that the total KV = prefix KV + suffix KV per request.
details.napkin_math: Per-token KV size (GQA): 2 × 8 heads × 128 dim × 96 layers × 2 bytes = 393,216 bytes = 384 KB/token. 512-token prefix: 512 × 384 KB = 192 MB. 128-token suffix: 128 × 384 KB = 48 MB. No sharing: 240 MB × N = 52 GB → N = 216. With sharing: 200 prefixes × 192 MB = 38.4 GB prefix store. Suffix pool: 13.6 GB / 48 MB = 283. Concurrent: 283 (+31%).
details.realistic_solution: Without prefix sharing: each request stores full 640-token KV (512 system prompt + 128 user). KV per token (70B, GQA 8 heads, head_dim 128, 96 layers, FP16): 2×8×128×1×96×2 = 393,216 bytes ≈ 0.375 MB/token. Full request KV: 640 × 0.375 MB = 240 MB. 52 GB / 240 MB = 216 concurrent requests. With prefix sharing: prefix KV (512 tokens) stored once per unique system prompt. 200 system prompts × 512 tokens × 0.375 MB = 38.4 GB for all prefix caches. Remaining for user suffix KV: 52 - 38.4 = 13.6 GB. User suffix KV: 128 tokens × 0.375 MB = 48 MB per request. 13.6 GB / 48 MB = 283 concurrent user suffix KV slots. Total concurrent requests: 283 (limited by suffix KV). Improvement: 283 vs 216 = 31% more concurrent requests. Memory saved: 200 × 50 users × 512 tokens × 0.375 MB × (1 - 1/50) = 196 × 50 × 192 MB = 188 GB if unshared vs 38.4 GB shared — but constrained by 52 GB pool anyway.

scenario: Your serving system (SGLang-style) uses a radix tree to manage prefix KV-cache sharing. You have 200 active system prompts, each used by ~50 users simultaneously, with 512-token system prompts and 128-token user suffixes. On MI300X (192 GB, model=70B at 140 GB, 52 GB KV pool), compute how much HBM is saved by shared prefix caching vs. no sharing, and determine the maximum number of concurrent requests the KV pool can support with vs. without sharing.
title: KV-Cache Radix Tree for Prefix Sharing

details.common_mistake: Attributing tail TPOT to memory bandwidth variability or thermal throttling — these cause 10-20% variance, not 8×. The 8× ratio points to head-of-line blocking from large batches of co-scheduled long-output requests.
details.napkin_math: H100 decode step time for 70B: 140 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 41.8 ms/step. Short request (50 tokens): total time = 50 × 41.8 ms = 2.09 s if no priority. With priority, short request waits at most 2 steps behind other short requests: wait = 2 × 41.8 ms = 83.6 ms + 50 × 41.8 ms for own decode = 2.17 s. The priority helps TPOT (per-step wait), not total time. P99 TPOT: without priority — step time inflated by large batch ≈ 42 ms × (B/B_short) overhead. With priority, short requests always find a batch slot within 1-2 steps: TPOT wait reduced from 7+ steps to ≤2 steps → P99 TPOT: 2 × 42 = 84 ms vs 280 ms = 3.3× improvement.
details.realistic_solution: When long-output requests accumulate in the batch, they hold KV-cache slots for hundreds of steps. At high occupancy (e.g., 90% of KV pool used by long requests), each decode step processes a large batch. The H100 is bandwidth-bound at decode: at batch size B, step time = max(model_weight_read / HBM_bw, compute). With many long requests in batch, step time is ~constant at ~42 ms (140 GB / 3.35 TB/s for 70B). Short requests entering this batch wait for each step the same as long requests — no priority. A short request that generates 50 tokens spends 50 × step_time = 50 × 42 ms = 2.1 s if unlucky enough to enter when batch is saturated. Fix: separate decode queues for short vs. long outputs. Short-output queue (predicted ≤50 tokens) gets absolute priority: the scheduler reserves 20% of batch slots for short requests. When short-output queue is non-empty, long requests cannot fill those slots. Result: P99 TPOT for short requests drops from 280 ms to ~50 ms (2 batch-lengths of wait + 1 step). P99 for long requests may increase slightly (5-10%).

scenario: Your decode pool shows P50 TPOT of 35 ms and P99 TPOT of 280 ms — an 8× tail ratio. The workload mix is 70% short-output requests (≤50 tokens) and 30% long-output requests (500–2000 tokens). The decode GPU is an H100.
