Identify the mechanism causing the tail and design a priority scheduling intervention with quantified impact.
title: Tail Latency of Decode Under Mixed Workloads

details.common_mistake: Saying disaggregation is always better or always worse. The break-even depends on the workload mix: when the workload is dominated by short requests (low compute/bandwidth ratio variance), colocation is simpler and competitive.
details.napkin_math: 13B FP16 prefill, 4096 tokens, H100: 2×13e9×4096/989e12 = 107.6 ms. SLO = 100 ms: colocation fails for long inputs. Disaggregated prefill with chunked (3840 tok chunk): 2×13e9×3840/989e12 ≈ 100.8 ms — still slightly over. Need TP=2 prefill: 107.6/2 = 53.8 ms — safely within 100 ms SLO with KV transfer. Cost: 2 H100s per long prefill. Break-even: at 300 RPS × 30% long = 90 long req/s, dedicate 90 × 2 GPUs × 0.054 s = 9.7 GPU-equivalents to prefill. 32-9.7 = 22.3 GPUs for decode. Throughput: 22.3 × 24 tok/s (H100 decode) × 512 output = 273 k tok/s. Colocation at same 300 RPS: 32 × (24 tok/s per GPU × 512) = 393 k tok/s but TTFT SLO violated. Disaggregation is mandatory above minimum long-input load.
details.realistic_solution: Collocated (32 H100s, each doing prefill+decode): Each GPU serves mixed workload. TTFT for short requests (256 tokens, 13B model): 2×13e9×256/(989e12) = 6.7 ms — trivially within SLO. Long prefill (4096 tokens): 2×13e9×4096/(989e12) = 107 ms — exceeds 100 ms TTFT SLO! Colocation fails for long inputs. Disaggregated: 8 H100 prefill + 24 H100 decode (1:3 ratio for 70/30 split). Long prefill on dedicated prefill GPU: 107 ms (borderline). Need chunked prefill to get under 100 ms: chunk to 3840 tokens → 100 ms. KV transfer adds 3.8 ms (2×8×128×4096×40×2 = 160 MB for 13B with GQA, at 50 GB/s). Total TTFT: ~104 ms — still slightly over. Fix: use H100 SXM5 burst mode or reduce model to FP8 for prefill. Break-even point: at <300 RPS with 30% long requests, colocation is operationally simpler and meets all SLOs except long-input TTFT. Above 300 RPS, disaggregation's ability to independently scale prefill/decode provides 40% more throughput.

scenario: Your team is deciding whether to adopt disaggregated serving or stick with colocated serving for a new 13B FP16 model deployment. Workload: 70% short input/output (input ≤256, output ≤64), 30% long input/long output (input 4096, output 512). TTFT SLO: 100 ms. TPOT SLO: 40 ms. H100 cluster of 32 GPUs. Perform a break-even analysis: at what request rate does disaggregation outperform colocation on cluster throughput, accounting for the KV transfer overhead?
title: Disaggregation vs. Colocation Break-Even Analysis

details.common_mistake: Assuming TP=2 always gives 2× throughput — TP requires AllReduce after each layer's GEMM, and at small batch sizes the communication overhead dominates.
details.napkin_math: H100 TP=2: each GPU reads 70 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 20.9 ms/step. MI300X TP=1: 140 GB / 5.3 TB/s = 26.4 ms/step. AllReduce at batch=1, 2-way NVLink (600 GB/s bidi = 300 GB/s per direction): message = 16 KB, latency = 16e3/300e9 = 53 ns × 96 layers = 5.1 μs — 0.02% of step time. AllReduce only becomes bottleneck at batch ≥ 10,000 (2 MB × 96 layers = 192 MB AllReduce, latency 0.64 ms ≈ 3% overhead).
details.realistic_solution: TP=2 H100 decode: each GPU holds half the weights (70 GB). Decode step: each GPU reads 70 GB from HBM at 3.35 TB/s = 20.9 ms. After each GEMM (96 layers), an AllReduce across 2 GPUs via NVLink: message size = batch_size × hidden_dim × 2 bytes. At batch=1, hidden_dim=8192: 1 × 8192 × 2 = 16 KB. NVLink AllReduce latency = 16 KB / (600 GB/s / 2) = 0.05 μs — negligible. At batch=128: 128 × 8192 × 2 = 2 MB. AllReduce = 2 MB / 300 GB/s = 6.7 μs per layer × 96 layers = 0.64 ms — still small vs 20.9 ms. TP=1 MI300X: reads 140 GB at 5.3 TB/s = 26.4 ms. No AllReduce. Per-token latency: TP=2 H100 = 20.9 ms (weight read dominates, AllReduce negligible). TP=1 MI300X = 26.4 ms. H100 TP=2 is 21% faster per token but requires 2 GPUs. Per-GPU-cost: MI300X is better (26.4 ms per single GPU vs 41.8 ms total for the H100 pair? No: TP=2 H100 step = 20.9 ms, requires 2 GPU-steps). Throughput: H100 TP=2: 1/0.0209 = 47.8 tok/s using 2 GPUs. MI300X TP=1: 1/0.0264 = 37.9 tok/s using 1 GPU. Per GPU: H100 23.9 tok/s vs MI300X 37.9 tok/s — MI300X wins per GPU.

scenario: You are scaling a 70B FP16 decode cluster using tensor parallelism. Compare the per-token decode latency and aggregate throughput for TP=2 H100s vs. TP=1 MI300X at the same model. Show where AllReduce communication overhead becomes the bottleneck, assuming NVLink (600 GB/s bidirectional) between TP peers.
title: Decode Throughput Scaling with Tensor Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Optimizing GPU count without accounting for the fact that prefill and decode have different utilization bounds — decode at 90%+ utilization causes queuing latency explosions, so you must size to 70-80% utilization.
details.napkin_math: Prefill load: 3203 tok/s. H100 prefill capacity: 200k tok/s. GPUs needed: ceil(3203/150k) = 1 (at 75% util: 150k tok/s). Decode load: 800 tok/s output. Average decode time per request (short): 64 tok × 26.4 ms/tok = 1.69 s; (long): 512 × 26.4 ms = 13.5 s. Concurrent sequences at steady state (Little's Law): λ × W. Short: 1.39 × 1.69 = 2.3. Long: 1.39 × 13.5 = 18.8. Total: 21 concurrent sequences. MI300X holds 135 sequences. 1 MI300X is sufficient at this load! Cost: 1 H100 + 1 MI300X = $3.50 + $4.50 = $8/hr = $0.0008/request. Scale: at 100k req/hr (27.8 req/s), concurrent sequences = 210 → 2 MI300X; 10 H100 prefill. Cost: 10×$3.50 + 2×$4.50 = $44/hr.
details.realistic_solution: Step 1: Characterize load. 10k req/hr = 2.78 req/s. Short: 1.39 req/s × 256 input = 356 tok/s prefill, 1.39 × 64 = 89 tok/s decode. Long: 1.39 × 2048 = 2847 tok/s prefill, 1.39 × 512 = 711 tok/s decode. Total: prefill = 3203 tok/s, decode = 800 tok/s. Step 2: Capacity per GPU. H100 prefill: 200k tok/s per GPU (compute-bound, 70B, mixed lengths). Required prefill GPUs at 75% util: 3203 / (200k × 0.75) = 0.021 GPUs — trivially 1 GPU handles this load. MI300X decode: 37.8 tok/s per sequence, concurrent sequences = 135 per MI300X. At 800 tok/s and 512 avg output (0.78 s per sequence): concurrent sequences = 800 × 0.78 = 624 sequences. MI300X needed: 624/135 = 4.6 → 5 MI300X at 75% util. Step 3: Cost. 1 H100 × $3.50/hr + 5 MI300X × $4.50/hr = $3.50 + $22.50 = $26/hr. Cost per request: $26/hr / 10k req/hr = $0.0026/request. Validate SLOs: TTFT for long (2048 tok): 2048/200k = 10.2 ms << 200 ms. TPOT: 5 MI300X serving 624 sequences: step time = 140 GB / 5.3 TB/s = 26.4 ms < 50 ms. Both SLOs met.

scenario: Build a cost model for a disaggregated serving deployment at 10,000 requests/hour, 70B FP16 model, mixed workload (50% short: 256 input/64 output; 50% long: 2048 input/512 output). GPU costs: H100 at $3.50/hr, MI300X at $4.50/hr. Determine the optimal prefill (H100) to decode (MI300X) pool ratio that minimizes cost while meeting TTFT < 200 ms and TPOT < 50 ms. Show all work.
title: Disaggregated Serving Cost Model

details.common_mistake: Treating DLRM as a standard dense neural network. The embedding lookup pathway is entirely memory-access-bound (random sparse reads), while the dense MLP pathway is compute-bound — conflating them leads to incorrect bottleneck analysis.
details.napkin_math: Typical DLRM at Meta scale: embedding tables = 10-100 TB total, each table entry = 64-dimensional FP32 vector = 256 bytes. A single recommendation request looks up ~500 sparse features across ~100 embedding tables. Memory accessed per request: 500 × 256 bytes = 128 KB. At 1M QPS: 128 KB × 1e6 = 128 GB/s of embedding memory bandwidth. Dense MLP: ~1 GFLOP per request. Ratio: 128 GB/s memory vs 1 TFLOP/s compute — embedding lookup is 100× more bandwidth-intensive per FLOP.
details.realistic_solution: DLRM has two pathways: (1) Sparse pathway: categorical features (user ID, item ID, context features) are mapped through embedding tables via lookup operations. Each lookup is an irregular memory access into a table that can be TB-scale — entirely memory-bandwidth- and DRAM-latency-bound. (2) Dense pathway: continuous features (CTR history, dwell time) pass through a bottom MLP (Dense → ReLU → Dense). Output is a dense vector. Fusion: the sparse embedding outputs and bottom MLP output are combined via second-order feature interaction (dot products between all pairs of feature vectors, producing an interaction matrix). The resulting interaction features concatenate with the bottom MLP output and feed into a top MLP that outputs a ranking score.

scenario: Describe the DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model) architecture. What are the two distinct compute pathways, why are they architecturally separate, and what operation fuses their outputs?
title: DLRM Architecture Overview

details.common_mistake: Sharding by table size alone — putting large tables on CPU and small tables on GPU. The correct criterion is access frequency (hot tables) and lookup-to-size ratio (tables with high QPS per byte).
details.napkin_math: 128 A100s × 80 GB = 10.24 TB HBM. Reserve 20% for activations/gradients: 8.2 TB usable for embeddings. If top-10 hot tables sum to 8 TB: fit on GPU. CPU DRAM: 128 nodes × 512 GB = 65 TB capacity (ample). CPU lookup latency: ~100 μs (DRAM latency + memory bus). GPU lookup latency: ~5 μs (HBM access + CUDA kernel). For P99 < 10 ms serving, CPU lookups must be pipelined to hide latency: start CPU lookups asynchronously while GPU handles dense pathway.
details.realistic_solution: Partition tables by access frequency × embedding dimension (i.e., bandwidth demand per second). Hot tables — those accessed in every request or with high lookup frequency — belong on GPU HBM for low-latency access (A100 HBM: 2 TB/s). Cold tables (accessed in <10% of requests) go to CPU DRAM (DDR5: ~50 GB/s aggregate across CPUs). For tables that exceed single-GPU capacity: row-wise sharding (each GPU holds a contiguous range of rows) minimizes cross-GPU communication for any single lookup. For small hot tables that fit in GPU HBM: replicate on all GPUs to eliminate all-to-all communication for those lookups. Final strategy: (1) Sort tables by QPS × row_size_bytes. (2) Place top tables on GPU until 80% of cluster HBM is used (10 TB × 0.8 = 8 TB). (3) Remaining on CPU DRAM with prefetch pipeline. (4) Replicate tables < 100 MB on all 128 GPUs if they appear in every request.

scenario: You have 50 embedding tables with sizes ranging from 1 GB to 2 TB (total 20 TB). You must shard them across 128 A100 GPUs (80 GB each), with 10 TB fitting in GPU HBM across the cluster. The remaining 10 TB must live in CPU DRAM. Design the sharding strategy to minimize P99 lookup latency. What determines which tables go to GPU vs CPU?
title: TB-Scale Embedding Table Sharding

details.common_mistake: Allocating equal latency budgets to each stage. Retrieval operates on 100,000× more candidates than re-ranking; its per-candidate budget must be 100,000× smaller, pushing it toward approximate methods (ANN search, hashing).
details.napkin_math: Ranking stage (1k candidates, DLRM): each candidate requires ~1 GFLOP + 128 KB embedding lookups. 1k candidates: 1 TFLOP compute + 128 MB embedding reads. A100 at 312 TFLOPS: compute = 1e12/312e12 = 3.2 ms. Embedding reads at 2 TB/s: 128 MB/2000 = 0.064 ms. Total: ~5 ms per batch of 1k — well within 80 ms budget. Pre-ranking on CPU (10k, small 2-layer MLP ~10 MFLOP/candidate): 10k × 10 MFLOPs = 100 GFLOPs. CPU at 2 TFLOPS: 50 ms — over budget. Need GPU for pre-ranking too: 100 GFLOPs / 312 TFLOPS = 0.32 ms.
details.realistic_solution: Latency budget allocation (principles): Retrieval must scan 1B candidates in minimal time → use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search (e.g., FAISS, ScaNN) on vector embeddings. Budget: 20 ms. Pre-ranking: 10k candidates, simple model (2-layer MLP, no embedding lookups). GPU batch scoring. Budget: 15 ms. Ranking: 1k candidates, full DLRM with all embedding lookups and deep MLP. Most expensive per-candidate. Budget: 80 ms (dominant stage). Re-ranking: 100 candidates, rule-based + light contextual model. CPU. Budget: 20 ms. Overhead (network, feature fetch): 15 ms. Total: 150 ms. GPU acceleration most valuable at Ranking: 1k × full DLRM forward pass. Pre-ranking can run on CPU at 10k candidates if model is small enough. Retrieval: GPU-accelerated FAISS/HNSW for ANN — critical for 1B-scale.

scenario: A social platform's recommendation pipeline has 4 stages: (1) Retrieval: 1B candidates → 10k, (2) Pre-ranking: 10k → 1k, (3) Ranking: 1k → 100, (4) Re-ranking: 100 → 10 final results. Total end-to-end SLO is 150 ms. Allocate latency budgets across stages and identify which stage most benefits from GPU acceleration vs. CPU/approximate methods.
title: Multi-Stage Ranking Latency Budget

details.common_mistake: Trying to optimize the NCCL all-to-all implementation without addressing the root cause: the sharding strategy forces every GPU to communicate with every other GPU for every batch.
details.napkin_math: All-to-all volume: 64 GPUs, batch=2048, 100 embedding tables, dim=64, FP32: each GPU sends (2048/64) × 100 × 64 × 4 bytes = 32 × 25600 bytes = 819 KB to each other GPU. Total per GPU: 819 KB × 63 = 51 MB. Bandwidth needed: at 80% overlap with compute: 51 MB / (step_time × 0.2) = 51 MB / 2 ms = 25.5 GB/s. A100 NVLink: 600 GB/s — ample. But 64-GPU cluster may span multiple nodes. Cross-node InfiniBand at 200 Gbps (25 GB/s): 51 MB / 25 GB/s = 2 ms for all-to-all — dominates 1 ms compute step. Hybrid sharding: replicate top-20 tables (< 100 MB each) → eliminates 20% of all-to-all volume.
details.realistic_solution: In DLRM training, embedding tables are sharded across GPUs (model parallelism for embeddings) while input batches are replicated across GPUs (data parallelism for MLPs). Each GPU in the batch needs embedding rows that live on different GPUs — this creates an all-to-all: each of N GPUs sends to each of N GPUs. Volume: batch_size × embedding_dim × num_tables bytes per collective. At 64 GPUs, all-to-all scales as O(N²) in communication pairs. Fix: (1) Embedding table placement optimization: group tables accessed together by the same requests onto the same GPU, reducing inter-GPU communication to only tables that span GPU boundaries. (2) Hybrid sharding: replicate small hot tables on all GPUs (row-wise for large, replicated for small). This converts all-to-all to all-gather for replicated tables (O(N) vs O(N²) scaling). (3) Reduce embedding dimension: use 64-dim instead of 256-dim embeddings where accuracy permits (4× reduction in all-to-all volume).

scenario: Your DLRM training cluster (64 A100s) shows that GPU utilization during embedding forward passes is 8% while MLP backward passes reach 90%. Profiling shows an all-to-all collective taking 85% of the embedding step time. Explain the root cause and propose an architectural change to reduce all-to-all volume.
title: Embedding Lookup All-to-All Communication

details.common_mistake: Blaming network latency or feature pipeline delays. The issue is cold-start for new items/users created during the event, not update frequency for existing items.
details.napkin_math: Event duration: 60 minutes. New items created: 10,000 (product catalog update). Each with 0 training examples at launch. 10-minute update batch: only items with ≥1 interaction in the last 10 min get gradient updates. At launch, new items have ~0 impressions in first 10 min (not surfaced → not clicked → no data). Dead loop: cold items not surfaced → not trained → stay cold. CTR impact: 10k cold items × 0% recall × 15% of impressions = 1.5% absolute CTR drop. Content embedding fallback: new items get content_sim score → shown → get clicks → join training data within 2 update cycles (20 min).
details.realistic_solution: During a product launch or viral event: (1) New items appear with no historical embeddings — they are assigned random or zero initialization. The model has no signal for new item IDs → systematically under-ranks them. (2) New users (event-driven signups) also have cold-start embeddings. (3) Existing item embeddings become stale: the distribution of how users interact with items shifts rapidly (e.g., a viral post gets 1000× more views than its historical embedding was trained on). 10-minute updates help for items that existed before the event, but new item/user IDs are never in the update batch until they have sufficient interaction data. Fix: (1) Cold-start fallback: for items with <N impressions, use content-based features (text/image embeddings) instead of learned ID embeddings. (2) Reduce new-item embedding initialization latency: on item creation, immediately compute a content embedding and use it as the initial embedding value. (3) For viral items: trigger immediate retraining of that item's embedding row when impression velocity exceeds a threshold (e.g., 100 impressions in 5 minutes).

scenario: Your recommendation model does online learning: embedding tables are updated every 10 minutes using the last batch of user interactions. Product team reports CTR dropping 15% during major events (product launches, viral moments) that last 30-60 minutes. The model updates within 10 minutes, but the degradation persists. Diagnose why 10-minute update frequency is insufficient for this failure mode.
title: Online Learning Staleness and Embedding Drift

details.common_mistake: Computing FLOPs per feature pair without accounting for the batch dimension, then comparing to peak TFLOPS without checking memory access to determine the actual bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Interaction FLOPs: 2048 × 27 × 27 × 64 × 2 = 191.1 MFLOPs. Memory access: read 27 vecs × 64 dim × 4 bytes × 2048 = 14.2 MB input; write 351 × 4 × 2048 = 2.88 MB output. AI = 191e6 / 17e6 = 11.2 FLOP/byte. A100: 312 TFLOPS / 2 TB/s = 156 FLOP/byte ridge. Memory-bound (11.2 << 156). Expected throughput: A100 memory bandwidth 2 TB/s × (191 MFLOPs / 17 MB) limited by memory: time = 17 MB / 2 TB/s = 8.5 μs per batch. Compare to compute peak: 191 MFLOPs / 312 TFLOPS = 0.6 μs. Memory dominates: 14× memory-bound.
details.realistic_solution: FLOPs per sample: n×n dot products each of size d=64: n² × 2d = 27² × 128 = 93,312 FLOPs. For batch=2048: 2048 × 93,312 = 191 MFLOPs. Memory: input is 2048 × 27 × 64 × 4 bytes (FP32) = 14.2 MB. Output (upper triangle, 2048 × 351 × 4 bytes) = 2.9 MB. Total memory: ~17 MB. Arithmetic intensity: 191 MFLOPs / 17 MB = 11.2 FLOP/byte. A100 ridge point: 312 TFLOPS / 2 TB/s = 156 FLOP/byte. Since 11.2 << 156, the interaction layer is strongly memory-bandwidth-bound. Optimization: fuse the dot product computation with the embedding output to avoid re-reading the embedding vectors from HBM, increasing effective arithmetic intensity.

scenario: DLRM's feature interaction layer computes dot products between all pairs of n=27 feature vectors (each 64-dimensional). This produces an n×n interaction matrix, of which the upper triangle (n*(n-1)/2 = 351 values) is used. For a batch of 2048 samples, compute the FLOPs for the interaction layer and determine whether this layer is compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound on an A100.
title: Feature Interaction Layer Arithmetic Intensity

details.common_mistake: Attributing the issue to learning rate being too high for hot embeddings. The actual cause is stale gradient accumulation: hot embeddings are updated by multiple workers simultaneously, causing conflicting stale gradient application.
details.napkin_math: Hot item accessed by 20 workers/step. SGD update per worker: Δw = -η × g_i. Total update in one step: -η × Σ g_i ≈ -20η × E[g] (if gradients are correlated for hot items). Effective LR = 20η. If η = 0.01 for convergence of medium items: hot items see effective LR = 0.2 → oscillation/divergence. Adagrad: LR_effective = η / √(Σ g²). After T steps, for hot items Σ g² ≈ 20T × E[g²] vs medium items T × E[g²]. Effective LR ratio: √(20) ≈ 4.5× lower for hot items. Normalizes the discrepancy.
details.realistic_solution: High-frequency items are accessed by many of the 64 workers simultaneously. Each worker computes a gradient for that embedding row based on a stale copy (the parameter server sends the embedding value at the start of the step, then multiple workers update it asynchronously). The effective learning rate for hot embeddings = η × (number of concurrent updates) — it scales with access frequency. For items accessed by 20 of 64 workers per step, the effective update magnitude is 20× intended. Fix: (1) Use Adagrad or Adam for embedding updates: these adapt the learning rate per-row based on accumulated squared gradients, automatically reducing updates for frequently-accessed rows. (2) Gradient accumulation with synchronous updates: for hot embedding rows (access freq > threshold), synchronize gradients before applying (reduce scatter pattern). (3) Frequency-aware clipping: clip embedding gradient norms by sqrt(access_frequency) to normalize effective update magnitude.

scenario: In your DLRM training cluster, 64 GPUs perform data-parallel training. Each GPU sees a different mini-batch and computes gradients for different sparse embedding rows. You use parameter servers to aggregate embedding updates. After a week of training, you notice that high-frequency item embeddings (accessed >10k times/hour) have 3× higher loss than medium-frequency items. Hypothesize the cause and specify the fix in terms of optimizer and update protocol changes.
title: Embedding Table Update Consistency in Distributed Training

details.common_mistake: Sizing the cache based on total table size (100 TB) and concluding caching is impossible. Zipf access means a tiny fraction of rows captures most lookups — the cache size needed for high hit rate is far smaller than total table size.
details.napkin_math: Zipf(α=1.2), N=1M rows: fraction of accesses covered by top-f fraction of items ≈ 1 - (1-f)^(1-α+1) for α<2 ... use empirical: top 1% ≈ 26%, top 5% ≈ 48%, top 10% ≈ 60%, top 20% ≈ 72%. Cache 10% × 1M = 100k rows × 100 tables × 256 bytes = 2.56 GB. 1 TB cache holds 100% of top-10% rows per table. Hit rate: 60%. To reach 90% hit rate: need top-30% ≈ cache 300k rows × 100 tables × 256 bytes = 7.68 GB. Well within 1 TB.
details.realistic_solution: Zipf α=1.2: the top-k fraction f(k) of items captures fraction C(k) of all accesses. For α=1.2, the top 1% of items (10k rows per table) captures ~30% of lookups; top 10% captures ~60%. Cache 10% of each table's rows by access frequency: 100 tables × 1M rows × 10% = 10M rows × 64 dim × 4 bytes = 2.56 GB per table slice × 100 = 256 GB — fits in 1 TB cache. Expected hit rate: ~60% for Zipf α=1.2 at 10% cache. Cache miss handling: on miss, fetch from DRAM (100 TB total) — latency 100 μs vs 5 μs for HBM hit. At 2M QPS and 60% hit rate: 800k misses/s. DRAM bandwidth needed: 800k × 100 tables × 64 × 4 × 0.4 (miss fraction per table) = 800k × 25.6 KB = 20.5 TB/s — exceeds DRAM. Must use distributed DRAM across many nodes: 20.5 TB/s / 50 GB/s per node = 410 nodes. OR: increase cache hit rate to 90% (cache top 20% of rows: 512 GB). At 90%: 200k misses/s × 25.6 KB = 5.1 TB/s — 102 nodes.

scenario: Your social platform serves 500M daily active users, with peak QPS of 2M recommendation requests/second. Each request requires embedding lookups across 100 tables (avg 1M rows, 64-dim FP32). Table access follows a Zipf distribution (α=1.2). Design a multi-tier caching strategy for embedding vectors and calculate the cache hit rate achievable with a 1 TB L2 cache (GPU HBM cluster), assuming Zipf access patterns.
title: Social-Scale Serving QPS and Caching Strategy

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT4 is always inferior to FP16 for accuracy — for cold embeddings with sparse training signal, INT4 may be fine because those rows have high uncertainty anyway. Also forgetting that embedding quantization affects lookup output fed into the MLP, not just storage.
details.napkin_math: FP32: 50 TB. FP16: 25 TB (-50%). INT8: 12.5 TB (-75%). INT4: 6.25 TB (-87.5%). Mixed strategy: 20%×FP16 + 60%×INT8 + 20%×INT4 = 10 TB × (1/2) + 30 TB × (1/4) + 10 TB × (1/8) = 5 + 7.5 + 1.25 = 13.75 TB. Bandwidth reduction: same ratios. Hot embedding bandwidth: was 10 TB × access_rate, now 5 TB × access_rate — 2× more headroom for hot row serving.
details.realistic_solution: FP16: 2× compression (50 TB → 25 TB). Precision loss minimal for well-trained embeddings (range typically ±3σ, FP16 has 3 decimal digits precision). Bandwidth: 2× reduction. Recommended for hot embeddings (high-quality training signal). INT8: 4× compression (50 TB → 12.5 TB). Per-row quantization (each row has its own scale/zero-point). Quantization error: ~0.4% relative to FP32 range. Known to cause <0.1% CTR regression on well-trained tables. Recommended for medium-frequency embeddings. INT4: 8× compression (50 TB → 6.25 TB). Quantization error ~1-2% per lookup. For cold embeddings (rare items, few training examples): the trained FP32 value itself is noisy — INT4 adds no meaningful degradation. For hot embeddings: noticeable quality degradation. Recommended only for cold (tail) embeddings. Strategy: FP16 for top-20% hot rows, INT8 for middle-60%, INT4 for bottom-20% cold. Effective compression: 0.2/2 + 0.6/4 + 0.2/8 = 0.1 + 0.15 + 0.025 = 3.64× compression → 50 TB becomes 13.7 TB.

scenario: Your 50 TB embedding table cluster stores all embeddings in FP32. You want to reduce storage and memory bandwidth without retraining from scratch. Compare FP16, INT8, and INT4 quantization for embeddings: what is the accuracy impact mechanism for each, what is the bandwidth reduction, and which is preferred for the hot/cold split?
title: Mixed-Precision Embedding Tables

details.common_mistake: Blaming the ranking model's MLP weights. The bias is in the embedding space — popular items have better-trained embeddings because they appear as negatives more often, making them universally high-similarity.
details.napkin_math: Item popularity: Zipf(α=1.0). Top 0.1% = 1k items out of 1M. Fraction of in-batch negatives they represent: proportional to popularity → top 0.1% appear in ~10% of batches as negatives at α=1.0. 10% of gradient steps update their embeddings as negatives. For 100B training examples: 10B gradient updates to top 1k items vs 100M for median item (100× more updates). Well-trained vs poorly-trained embeddings: 100× training signal → 10× lower embedding variance → sharper recommendations. Logit correction: score_corrected = score - β × log(freq_i / avg_freq). At β=1: popular item score reduced by log(10k) = 4.6 nats ≈ enough to reduce top-0.1% from 40% to ~15% of recommendations.
details.realistic_solution: In-batch negatives: for a batch of B items, each positive pair (user, item_i) uses the other B-1 items as negatives. Popular items appear in the batch more often (proportional to their frequency in training data). An item appearing K× more frequently serves as a negative K× more often — its embedding is pushed away from all other items K× more. This makes popular items' embeddings 'universally repellent' in a counterintuitive way — BUT simultaneously, popular items appear as positives K× more often too, pulling their embeddings toward the users who do interact with them. Net effect: popular items dominate the learned embedding space because they receive disproportionately more gradient updates, leading to sharper, better-calibrated embeddings that the ranking MLP learns to prefer. Debiasing: (1) Logit adjustment: subtract log(item_frequency) from the ranking score at inference time (frequency-based logit correction). (2) Popularity-stratified sampling: oversample rare items as negatives to equalize training signal. (3) Hard negative mining: use items with high predicted score but no interaction as negatives, forcing the model to distinguish similar items rather than just popular ones.

scenario: Your recommendation model is trained with in-batch negatives (other items in the same batch serve as negatives for each positive pair). At 1M QPS serving, you observe a popularity bias: the top-0.1% most popular items account for 40% of recommendations even though they represent 3% of catalog impressions. Diagnose why in-batch negatives cause this bias and propose a debiasing technique.
title: Negative Sampling Bias in Recommendation Training

details.common_mistake: Proposing DLRM for retrieval because it captures feature interactions. DLRM requires both user and item features simultaneously — it cannot precompute item representations, making it O(candidates × model_cost) at inference, infeasible for 1B candidates.
details.napkin_math: Two-tower retrieval: user tower = 10M-param MLP → ~1 ms. FAISS HNSW search over 1B items: ~10 ms at 95% recall@100. Total: 11 ms. DLRM retrieval (1B candidates): 1B × (10 μs per DLRM forward pass) = 10,000 s. Not feasible. Storage: 1B × 64 × 4 = 256 GB for FP32 item embeddings. With INT8: 64 GB — fits in cluster HBM. ANN index overhead (HNSW): ~10× base embedding size = 640 GB FP32 / 160 GB INT8.
details.realistic_solution: Two-tower: user tower and item tower compute independent embeddings. Item embeddings precomputed and indexed (e.g., FAISS). At serving: compute user embedding (1 tower forward pass, ~1 ms) + ANN search over 1B items (~10 ms with HNSW/FAISS). Total: ~11 ms per request regardless of catalog size. Storage: 1B items × 64-dim × 4 bytes = 256 GB for item index. Feature interactions: only between user and item via dot product/cosine similarity — no cross-feature interactions within a request. DLRM at retrieval: requires full forward pass for each candidate pair (user, item). 1B candidates × 1 μs per candidate = 1000 seconds — completely infeasible. Conclusion: two-tower is mandatory for retrieval due to O(1) serving cost via precomputed item embeddings. DLRM is appropriate only for ranking (1k candidates) where full pairwise computation is feasible within latency budget.

scenario: Compare two-tower (dual encoder) models and DLRM for the retrieval stage of a recommendation pipeline (1B candidates → 10k). Evaluate on: (1) serving latency at 1M QPS, (2) ability to support feature interactions at retrieval, (3) storage cost for precomputed item embeddings. Which is appropriate for retrieval vs. ranking?
title: Two-Tower Model vs. DLRM for Retrieval

details.common_mistake: Trying to optimize the DAG computation speed. The bottleneck is not compute but the streaming event bus read latency — pulling from Kafka/Kinesis at P99 adds 30+ ms of tail latency from consumer lag.
details.napkin_math: Current P99: 5 ms (batch features) + 45 ms (real-time) = 50 ms total feature assembly. Real-time DAG: 10 nodes, Kafka consumer P99 = 30 ms, computation = 5 ms, serialization = 10 ms. After pre-aggregation: Redis GET P99 = 1 ms. New P99: 5 + 1 = 6 ms for feature assembly. Model inference: 9 ms (ranking 1k candidates). Total: 6 + 9 = 15 ms. Cache write throughput needed: DAU 500M users × 10 events/user/hour = 5M events/s cache writes. At 1 KB per user state: 5 MB/s writes to Redis — trivial.
details.realistic_solution: The streaming event bus adds ~40 ms of P99 latency (Kafka consumer group lag + deserialization). Fix: move real-time feature aggregation to a push-based architecture. (1) Pre-aggregate: run the 10-node DAG continuously as events arrive, maintaining a stateful user feature cache (e.g., Redis Streams or RocksDB). When a user triggers a recommendation request, the aggregated features are already computed and cached — lookup latency = O(1) cache read, ~1 ms P99. (2) Incremental update: on each user event (click, view, search), push an update to the user feature cache with the new aggregated values. The cache serves as a low-latency snapshot of the aggregation DAG output. (3) Fallback: for new users with no cache entry, use batch pre-computed features from the feature store (5 ms). P99 after change: 5 ms (feature store) + 1 ms (real-time cache) + 9 ms (model inference) = 15 ms — meets SLO.

scenario: Your recommendation model uses 200 features, 150 of which are pre-computed (served from a feature store with 5 ms P99) and 50 are real-time (computed on-the-fly from the last 5 minutes of user activity). The real-time features require reading from a streaming event bus and running a 10-node aggregation DAG. P99 feature assembly time is 45 ms. You need to reduce it to under 15 ms to meet the end-to-end SLO. Design the architecture change.
title: Real-Time Feature Pipeline Latency

details.common_mistake: Thinking gradient accumulation for sparse tensors works like dense: accumulate for N steps, then update. For sparse tensors, naive accumulation materializes all gradient indices from all N steps into a single sparse tensor — the number of unique indices grows with N steps, consuming O(N × batch_size × indices_per_sample) memory.
details.napkin_math: Sparse grad memory per step: 2048 samples × 500 sparse features × (8 byte index + 256 byte grad) = 2048 × 500 × 264 = 270 MB per step. 16 steps: 4.3 GB. With model (140 GB shard) + activations (estimate 20 GB) + optimizer states (280 GB for Adam on 140 GB shard) — already over 192 GB budget. Apply-immediately: memory for sparse grads = 270 MB (1 step) — 16× reduction, frees 4 GB.
details.realistic_solution: Sparse embedding gradients are indexed: each training sample touches a specific subset of embedding rows. With 16-step accumulation, the accumulated sparse gradient contains indices from 16 batches, each with batch_size × num_sparse_features unique rows. If batch_size=2048 and each sample touches 500 sparse features, one step produces 2048 × 500 = 1M gradient entries. 16 steps: 16M entries × (index: 8 bytes + gradient: 64 dim × 4 bytes) = 16M × 264 bytes = 4.2 GB per GPU just for sparse gradient accumulation. MI300X 192 GB: with 140 GB model shards and 4.2 GB sparse grads × 16 accumulation = 67 GB → total 207 GB > 192 GB. Fix: (1) Use immediate sparse gradient application (not accumulation): after each micro-step, immediately apply the sparse gradient update to the embedding table (embedding_table[indices] += lr × grad). This keeps memory O(1 step) instead of O(N steps). Dense gradients (MLP) still accumulate normally. (2) Alternatively: deduplicate indices within each step and average gradients for repeated indices before accumulation.

scenario: You are training a DLRM on 128 MI300X GPUs (192 GB each, 5.3 TB/s HBM). Gradient accumulation is set to 16 steps. You observe that memory usage for sparse gradient tensors grows unboundedly during accumulation, eventually OOMing at step 12. Diagnose the cause and fix it without reducing accumulation steps or batch size.
title: Gradient Accumulation for Sparse Embedding Training

details.common_mistake: Treating cold start as solely an exploration problem (multi-armed bandit). The embedding cold start is a representation problem — even with exploration, you can't train a useful embedding without initial signal.
details.napkin_math: Content embedding projection: pretrained CLIP text embedding (512 dim) → projection MLP (512 → 64) → DLRM embedding space. Training data: all items with >100 interactions (well-trained ID embeddings + content embeddings available). If catalog has 10M items and 50% have >100 interactions: 5M training pairs. Projection MLP is tiny (~200k params), trains in minutes. At serving: new item embedding = projection(content_features). Expected quality: 70-80% of fully-trained embedding quality after first recommendation batch.
details.realistic_solution: (1) Content-based initialization: use the item's metadata (title text, image, category) to compute a content embedding (e.g., from a pretrained language or vision model). Map this to the DLRM embedding space via a learned projection trained on items that have both content and ID embeddings. New item immediately gets a meaningful embedding based on content similarity to existing items. (2) Cluster-based initialization: assign the new item to the nearest cluster centroid (k-means over existing embeddings) based on content features. Initialize the new embedding to that centroid. (3) Meta-learning / warm-up: maintain a 'meta-embedder' — a small model trained to produce good initial embeddings for items with few interactions (few-shot). When a new item gets its first 5-10 interactions, the meta-embedder produces a refined embedding that is used as the starting point for full gradient training.

scenario: A new item is added to your catalog. It has no interaction history. Your DLRM assigns it a random embedding initialization. Explain the 'cold start problem' and describe three industry approaches to initialize new item embeddings more effectively without waiting for organic training data.
title: Cold Start for New Item Embeddings

details.common_mistake: Applying data parallelism uniformly — data parallelism for 100 TB embeddings requires all-to-all communication that scales poorly. The embeddings need model parallelism, while the MLP needs data parallelism.
details.napkin_math: MLP backward all-reduce: 10B params × 2 bytes × 2 (gradient buffer) = 40 GB total. Ring-allreduce on 512 GPUs: each sends/receives 40 GB × 2 × (N-1)/N / N ≈ 40 GB / 512 = 78 MB. At 400 Gbps: 78 MB / 50 GB/s = 1.56 ms — fast. Embedding all-to-all: 512 GPUs × batch=4096 × 500 features × 256 bytes = 256 GB exchanged per step. At 400 Gbps (50 GB/s): 256 GB / 50 = 5.12 s — too slow! Must reduce: use 8-bit embedding gradients (64 GB / 50 GB/s = 1.28 s) or reduce batch to 256 (16 GB / 50 GB/s = 0.32 s). With batch=256: throughput = 256 × 512 / 0.32 s = 409k samples/s.
details.realistic_solution: Hybrid parallelism: (1) Embedding model parallelism: 100 TB / (512 H100s × 80 GB + 512 CPU nodes × 2 TB) = 100 TB / (40.96 TB GPU + 1024 TB CPU). Hot embeddings on GPU HBM (40.96 TB fits ~41% of tables by frequency). Cold embeddings on CPU DRAM. Row-wise sharding: each GPU/CPU holds a disjoint row range per table. (2) MLP data parallelism: 10B params at FP16 = 20 GB — fits on a single H100 with room for activations. Replicate MLP across all 512 H100s. Data-parallel batches: 512 replicas × batch_size_per_replica. (3) Gradient sync: MLP: standard all-reduce across 512 GPUs (NCCL ring-allreduce, ~20 GB / 512 GPUs = 39 MB each, ~39 ms on 400 Gbps). Embeddings: sparse row-wise updates sent to the GPU/CPU holding that row (parameter server pattern, no all-reduce needed). (4) Throughput: assume each H100 processes 4096 samples/step at 10 ms/step (dominated by embedding all-to-all): 4096 × 512 / 0.010 = 209M samples/s aggregate. Realistic with communication: ~50M samples/s.

scenario: Design the full training parallelism strategy for a DLRM with 100 TB of embedding tables and a 10B parameter dense MLP. You have 512 H100s (80 GB each) and 512 CPU nodes (2 TB DRAM each). Specify: embedding sharding strategy, MLP parallelism, gradient synchronization protocol, and expected training throughput in samples/second.
title: Model Parallelism Strategy for 100TB Embedding Cluster

details.common_mistake: The naive concatenation approach is order-agnostic if the MLP doesn't see positional information, and it grows the bottom MLP input 50× — these are the problems. Many engineers spot the positional issue but miss the memory/compute scaling problem.
details.napkin_math: Naive: bottom MLP input = 64 × 50 = 3200 dims. First MLP layer (3200 → 512): 3200 × 512 = 1.64M params × 4 bytes = 6.6 MB per layer. FLOPs per sample: 2 × 3200 × 512 = 3.28 MFLOPs vs original 2 × 64 × 512 = 65k FLOPs — 50× more. Attention session encoder: 50 items × 64 dim, self-attention cost per sample = 4 × 50² × 64 = 640k FLOPs. Output: 64 dim — same as original. Total overhead: 640k FLOPs vs 3.28M FLOPs for naive. 5× less compute, same expressiveness.
details.realistic_solution: Problems with naive concatenation: (1) Order is not encoded — item 1 and item 50 in the session are treated identically unless positional encodings are added. (2) Input dimension scales with session length (3200 vs 64), requiring the bottom MLP to have 50× more parameters and compute for this feature alone. (3) All 50 items must be looked up (50 embedding reads) even for users with short sessions (wasteful). Better architecture: (1) Self-attention session encoder: apply a lightweight Transformer (1-2 layers, attention over 50-item sequence) to produce a single 64-dim session embedding. The Transformer handles ordering naturally via positional embeddings. (2) Pooling with attention weights: compute attention-weighted sum of item embeddings with a query vector derived from the target item. This is equivalent to a one-layer cross-attention (much cheaper than self-attention). (3) Recurrent encoding: GRU over item embeddings → final hidden state as session embedding (O(T) compute, O(1) output). All approaches produce a single 64-dim session embedding fed into the existing DLRM pipeline — no change to bottom MLP input size.

scenario: You want to add temporal sequence features to your DLRM: the last 50 items a user interacted with (their session history). Naive approach: concatenate 50 item embeddings (each 64-dim) as a 3200-dim feature vector, passing it into the bottom MLP. Identify the architectural problems with this approach and design a better session encoding.
title: Session-Based Recommendation Temporal Features

details.common_mistake: Choosing (A) purely because it's fresher, without accounting for the serving latency increase during swap and the P99 latency SLO violation risk at 100k QPS.
details.napkin_math: CTR decay model: CTR(t) = CTR_0 × (1 - 0.005 × t_minutes). Strategy A avg staleness: 10ms → 0.000167 min → CTR loss: 0.0008%. Negligible. Strategy B avg staleness: 2.5 min → CTR loss: 1.25%. At 2% baseline CTR: loss = 0.025% absolute. Revenue: 0.025% × 100k QPS × $0.001/impression × 86400s = $2,160/day (not $2.16M). Strategy A swap overhead: 20 ms every 10 ms = 200% overhead → non-starter. Strategy A with 1s batch: swap every 1s, 0.02ms swap time → 2% overhead. Viable.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy A: Model updated every 1000 requests / 100k QPS = 0.01 seconds = every 10 ms. At 2s update latency, during those 2s: 200k requests served on stale model. During swap: 20 ms serving latency increase affects all in-flight requests. P99 latency during swap: baseline P99 + 20 ms. Swaps happen every 10 ms — system is in 'swap' state 2× → constant elevated latency. CTR: ~0.01 min staleness average = essentially fresh. Strategy B: max staleness = 5 minutes = 2.5% CTR decay on average. CTR loss = 0.05% absolute. Revenue impact: 0.05% × 100k QPS × $0.001/click × 86400s = $4,320/day. Verdict: Strategy A is unsustainable at 100k QPS. Fix: increase batch to 100k requests (1 second batch) and use zero-downtime weight swap (double-buffering). Then swap every 1s with atomic swap <1ms overhead. Or use Strategy B with 1-minute updates instead of 5-minute.

scenario: You can deploy one of two update strategies: (A) Synchronous online learning — every 1000 requests update the model and immediately swap it into serving (update latency: 2 seconds, serving latency increase: +20 ms during swap). (B) Asynchronous shadow updates — model updates accumulate in shadow weights, applied every 5 minutes via atomic weight swap (no serving latency impact). At 100k QPS, evaluate the CTR impact of each strategy, considering that recommendation quality decays 0.5% per minute of staleness.
title: Serving Latency vs. Model Freshness Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Assuming better retrieval always improves ranking quality. The issue is that the ranking model was trained on the old retrieval's candidate distribution, and changing that distribution breaks ranking model calibration.
details.napkin_math: Old system: 72% recall → 72 true positives in top-100 (on average). Ranking selects top-10 from 100: NDCG@10 = 0.38. New system: 81% recall → 81 true positives in top-100. Expected NDCG@10 should improve (more true positives to choose from). Actual: 0.35. Drop = 0.03 NDCG units. Explanation: 9 new true positives added to candidate set, but 9 borderline items added too. Ranking model mis-ranks: 4 borderline items rank above true positives in top-10. DCG loss: sum(1/log2(rank+1)) for misplaced items. At ranks 1-10: placing 4 wrong items at ranks 3-6 causes DCG drop of ~0.06 (more than the gain from 9 extra true positives in top-100).
details.realistic_solution: The ranking model is trained on candidates that come from the old retrieval model. Its training negatives are items that the old retrieval model surfaced. When the retrieval model changes, it surfaces different candidates — potentially items the ranking model has never seen as negatives. The ranking model cannot correctly score these out-of-distribution candidates because its decision boundary was trained on the old retrieval's item distribution. Specifically: the new retrieval model may surface more 'borderline relevant' items (it retrieves harder, more semantically similar items). The ranking model sees these as confusing — it assigns them scores similar to positives because they look like positives but aren't. NDCG@10 drops because the ranking model places these borderline-relevant items above true positives. Fix: (1) Retrain the ranking model with candidates from the new retrieval model. (2) Use a staged rollout: A/B test with the ranking model retrained on the new retrieval distribution before full deployment.

scenario: Your retrieval model optimizes for Recall@100 (does the ground-truth item appear in the top-100 retrieved?). The ranking model then re-orders these 100. After a model upgrade, Recall@100 improves from 72% to 81%, but end-to-end NDCG@10 (quality of the final top-10) drops from 0.38 to 0.35. Explain the mechanism that allows better retrieval recall to worsen final ranking quality.
title: Recall@K vs. NDCG Tradeoff in Retrieval Optimization

details.common_mistake: Choosing the largest dimension that fits without considering that embedding capacity scales logarithmically with dimension — going from 128 to 256 dims doubles storage but provides far less than 2× improvement in representational capacity for a fixed catalog size.
details.napkin_math: Storage per dim: 100M × 4 bytes = 400 MB. Dim choices: 16→6.4 GB, 32→12.8 GB, 64→25.6 GB, 128→51.2 GB, 256→102.4 GB. 512 GB budget: any of these fit easily. Max dim in budget: 512 GB / 400 MB = 1280 (ignore dims > 256 due to diminishing returns). Representational capacity: dim=64 gives 64-dimensional space for 100M items → avg angle between random vectors ≈ 90° (orthogonal) for up to ~2^64 items — more than sufficient. Going to dim=256: marginal capacity gain ≈ 0, but 4× storage cost.
details.realistic_solution: Storage: 100M items × dim × 4 bytes (FP32) = dim × 400 MB. At 512 GB: max dim = 512 GB / 400 MB = 1280. But in practice, use 20% headroom: 512 × 0.8 = 409.6 GB / 400 MB = 1024-dim would be the absolute max. Practical recommendation: 256-dim uses 100 GB (20% of cluster HBM). Capacity argument: for a catalog of N items, the minimum dimension needed to represent all pairwise relationships is O(log N) — the intrinsic dimensionality. For 100M items: log₂(100M) ≈ 27 dimensions would theoretically suffice for perfect orthogonal separation. In practice, embedding dimensions of 64-128 are sufficient for most recommendation tasks; going beyond 256 shows diminishing returns unless interaction features are extremely high-dimensional. Choice: 64-dim (uses 25 GB) is often optimal by the information-theoretic argument, leaving 487 GB for other model components.

scenario: You have a catalog of 100M items and must choose an embedding dimension (options: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256) for the item embedding table. The table must fit in 512 GB of GPU HBM across a cluster. Compute the maximum embedding dimension that fits, and explain the relationship between embedding dimension and model capacity using the intrinsic dimensionality argument.
title: Embedding Dimension Selection and Capacity

details.common_mistake: Caching at the response level without considering that recommendation lists should be refreshed after user interactions (clicks, skips) — a staleness-unaware cache degrades CTR by serving stale lists after user feedback events.
details.napkin_math: 500k QPS × 9ms = 4,500,000 GPU-ms/s = 4,500 GPU-seconds/s → need 4,500 GPUs continuously. With 63% cache hit: 185k QPS × 9ms = 1,665,000 GPU-ms/s → 1,665 GPUs. 1 GPU handles 1000ms/9ms ≈ 111 RPS. Savings: 2,835 GPUs × $3.50/hr = $9,922/hr. At $3.50/GPU-hr, cache saves ~63% GPU cost for serving.
details.realistic_solution: Two-level cache: (1) Hot result cache: cache the full ranked recommendation list per user, keyed by (user_id, context_hash). TTL: 30 seconds, but with event-based invalidation — invalidate immediately on any user interaction event (click, skip, dwell > 5s). (2) Invalidation mechanism: user interaction events are streamed to a lightweight invalidation service that deletes the cache entry for that user. Cache hit rate: 70% of requests are re-requests within 30s with <2% change. If 90% of those are passive (no interaction), cache serves 70% × 90% = 63% of requests. GPU load reduction: 63% fewer requests to the ranking model. From 500k QPS to 185k QPS on GPU. GPU savings: 63% reduction. Cache storage: 500k active users × avg list 10 items × 8 bytes item_id = 40 MB — trivial.

scenario: Your recommendation serving system at 500k QPS is spending 70% of GPU time on requests from users who visited within the last 30 seconds (re-requests from rapid page scrolling). The per-user recommendation list changes less than 2% between re-requests. Design a result caching layer and quantify the GPU load reduction, accounting for cache invalidation triggers.
title: Request Deduplication and Result Caching in Rec Serving

details.common_mistake: Saying DLRM is fine on TPU because the dense MLP is compute-bound. The embedding lookups are irregular memory accesses (sparse, non-sequential) — TPUs are optimized for dense matrix operations via systolic arrays and perform poorly on irregular sparse access patterns.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e pod: 256 × 197 TFLOPS = 50.4 PFLOPS BF16. Dense MLP (5B params, batch=262k): FLOPs = 2 × 5e9 × 262144 = 2.6 PFLOPS per step. Time at 50% MFU: 2.6P / (50.4P × 0.5) = 103 ms/step. Embedding lookup: 500 GB / (256 chips × 1.6 TB/s) = 1.2 ms if sequential. But random access: effective BW drops to ~10% = 0.12 TB/s per chip → 500 GB / (256 × 0.12 TB/s) = 16 ms — still faster than MLP. However TPU's XLA compiler cannot fuse irregular scatter-gather → kernel launch overhead per embedding table lookup: 10 μs × 100 tables × 256 chips = 256 ms overhead alone. CPU offload eliminates this.
details.realistic_solution: MLP components (bottom MLP, top MLP, feature interaction): all are dense matrix operations → perfect fit for TPU systolic arrays. Expected MFU (model FLOP utilization) > 50%. Embedding lookup components: sparse, random-access reads from large tables. TPU HBM controllers are optimized for streaming sequential access, not random scatter-gather. Sparse embedding lookups on TPU can be 10-50× slower than on GPU due to irregular access patterns inefficiency in the systolic architecture. Key modification: offload embedding lookups from TPU to CPU/host memory. Use the 'embedding CPU offload' pattern: CPUs handle embedding lookups (sending batched index requests), TPUs handle all dense operations. Communication bridge: embedding vectors are sent from CPU to TPU via PCIe/custom interconnect before each forward pass. This hybrid CPU+TPU architecture (used in Meta's ZION platform equivalent for Google) is the only practical way to run DLRM on TPUs at scale. Embedding placement: 500 GB fits in cluster CPU DRAM (256 hosts × 512 GB each = 128 TB available).

scenario: Your team proposes training DLRM on a TPU v5e pod (256 chips × 197 TFLOPS BF16, 1.6 TB/s per chip HBM, 16 GB per chip). The embedding tables total 500 GB; the dense MLP is 5B params. Specify which DLRM components map well to TPU and which do not, and identify the key architectural modification required to make DLRM TPU-trainable.
title: DLRM Training on TPU v5e Pod

details.common_mistake: Saying positional embeddings always help. For users with highly diverse, non-sequential browsing (random exploration), positional encoding overfits to arbitrary orderings in training data.
details.napkin_math: SASRec with T=50 positions, dim=64: positional embedding table = 50 × 64 × 4 bytes = 12.8 KB — negligible. Attention over 50-item sequence: O(T²) = 2500 operations per head per sample. With 2 heads: 5000 ops × 64 dim × batch=2048 = 655 MFLOPs. Compare to pooling: 50 × 64 × 2048 = 6.5 MFLOPs. 100× more FLOPs for attention, but Recall@10 gain of 15% — worth it for sequential-heavy user segments.
details.realistic_solution: Positional embeddings encode the recency and order of items in a session. In sequential recommendation, a user's recent items (position N-1, N-2) are stronger predictors of next intent than older items. Without positional embeddings, all-position pooling treats 'viewed 5 minutes ago' and 'viewed 3 days ago' identically — losing the recency signal. SASRec with learned positional embeddings achieves 10-20% Recall@10 improvement over average pooling on standard benchmarks (Amazon review datasets) because attention can learn to weight recent positions more heavily. Hurt generalization: users with random exploratory behavior (e.g., browsing unrelated categories sequentially) — the model learns spurious temporal correlations. If 'sport shoes → kitchen appliances → sport shoes' appears in training as a pattern (because of a random co-occurrence), the model over-fits to that position 1→position 3 pattern. Mitigation: train with dropout over positional embeddings (randomly drop positions during training), forcing the model to rely on content when position is unavailable.

scenario: Explain why adding positional embeddings to a session sequence in a recommendation model (e.g., SASRec-style self-attention) typically improves next-item prediction accuracy compared to unordered pooling, and describe one scenario where positional information hurts generalization.
title: Learned Positional Embeddings for Sequence Modeling

details.common_mistake: Proposing static replication of all top-10k rows on all 16 nodes upfront — this works but doesn't adapt to changes in access patterns (popularity changes over time as new users become active).
details.napkin_math: Hot row lookup rate: assume 2M QPS × 500 sparse features = 1B lookups/s total. 80% = 800M lookups/s to 10k hot rows. 2 nodes at 200k lookup/s each: 400k/s capacity — 2000× under-provisioned! Even with 16 nodes: 3.2M/s — still 250× under. Real fix: a single 'hot row' must be cached in L2/L3 GPU cache across all nodes. At 256 bytes/row × 10k rows = 2.56 MB — fits in L2 cache (A100 L2 = 40 MB). Cached hot row lookup latency = L2 hit time (~50 ns vs ~250 ns HBM). Effective throughput: 16 nodes × (40 MB L2 / 256 bytes × 1B lookups/s) = 16 × 156M = 2.5B lookups/s. Sufficient for 800M hot lookups/s with 3× headroom.
details.realistic_solution: Dynamic hot-row replication: (1) Monitor per-row access frequency on a sliding 10-minute window. Rows exceeding 100 lookups/minute are promoted to 'hot' status. (2) Hot rows are replicated to all serving nodes asynchronously (gossip-based or central coordinator push). Replication lag: <5 seconds for hot rows (small data). (3) Routing: a consistent hash ring normally assigns rows to nodes. For replicated hot rows, the router uses load-aware routing — send to the least-loaded node among all nodes holding that row. (4) Invalidation: on embedding update (online learning), broadcast updates for hot rows to all replicas before marking the update complete. Read throughput improvement: currently 2 nodes serve 80% of lookups (10k hot rows on 2 nodes). Each A100 can serve 200k lookups/s (random HBM access at 2 TB/s / 256 bytes per row). 2 nodes: 400k lookups/s at 80% load = 320k effective. After replication to all 16 nodes: 16 × 200k × 0.8 = 2.56M lookups/s. Improvement: 2.56M / 320k = 8× for hot rows.

scenario: Your recommendation serving cluster has 16 A100 serving nodes, each with an embedding table shard. Profiling shows that the top-10k rows (out of 50M total) in the user-ID embedding table receive 80% of all lookups. These 10k rows create a hotspot on 2 nodes (they share a row range). Design a dynamic hot-row replication scheme and compute the read throughput improvement.
title: Embedding Table Hot Row Replication for Serving

details.common_mistake: Treating diversity as a purely algorithmic problem and adding diversity post-hoc via random item injection. The root cause is that the ranking model learned to exploit user interest clusters, creating a feedback loop.
details.napkin_math: MMR diversity penalty: assume top-100 items from ranking, greedily select 10 with MMR λ=0.85. For each position i, we skip items with cosine_sim > 0.7 to any already-selected item. In a cluster-heavy distribution: ~20% of top-100 items are near-duplicates (cosine_sim > 0.7). MMR filters these: instead of selecting positions 1-10 purely by score, 2 of the top 10 are replaced by diverse items at positions 11-20 in the ranked list. CTR impact: positions 11-20 avg score ≈ 95% of top-10 avg score. CTR drop = 2/10 × (1-0.95) = 1% — exactly at budget. Diversity score: 2 diverse items in top-10 → 20% category diversity improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: the new ranking model has higher capacity (more parameters, better feature interactions). It learned that users who clicked item type A in the last session are very likely to click similar A items again. It exploits this short-term signal (recency bias) by flooding the feed with A-type items. This is a reward hacking problem: CTR is a short-term metric; the model maximizes it at the expense of long-term engagement. Feedback loop: high-CTR homogeneous feeds → user only sees A-type content → click history becomes all-A → model further concentrates on A → diversity collapses. Re-ranking intervention: Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR): given a ranked list of N candidates, iteratively select the next item that maximizes: λ × relevance_score - (1-λ) × max_similarity_to_already_selected. At λ=0.85: 85% weight on relevance, 15% on diversity. This ensures no two consecutive top-10 items share >70% embedding similarity. Expected CTR impact: -0.8% (within 1% budget). Expected diversity score: +25% (partial recovery from -40%). Additional fix: add session-diversity reward to training objective: penalize sequences with >3 items from the same category.

scenario: After deploying a new ranking model with higher CTR (+3%), users report that their feed feels 'repetitive' (content diversity score drops 40%). A/B test shows 7-day retention drops 5% despite the CTR gain. Diagnose the system-level cause of this diversity collapse and propose a re-ranking intervention that recovers diversity without sacrificing more than 1% CTR.
title: Diversity vs Relevance Tradeoff in Re-ranking

details.common_mistake: Designing for year-3 scale at launch — over-engineering. Or designing only for launch and requiring full architecture replacement at scale. The question asks for a staged evolution plan.
details.napkin_math: Launch serving: 500k QPS × 9ms/request = 4,500,000 GPU-ms/s = 4,500 GPUs for ranking. 1 GPU handles ~111 RPS. With 2× headroom: 9,000 GPUs. Cost: 9,000 × $3.50/hr = $31,500/hr = $275M/year. Scale: 5M QPS × 9ms = 45,000 GPUs or ~28,900 MI300X (higher throughput from larger HBM). Training at scale: 512 H100 × $3.50/hr = $1,792/hr for training jobs. Total year-3 infra: ~$20M/year for the recommendation stack.
details.realistic_solution: Launch (100M users, 500k QPS): Retrieval: Two-tower model, FAISS HNSW index on 100M items (256 GB INT8). Deployed on 4 A100 nodes (CPU for FAISS, GPU for user tower). Pre-ranking: small 2-layer MLP, CPU-based, 10k→1k. Ranking: DLRM with 10 embedding tables totaling 500 GB, 1B param MLP. Re-ranking: MMR on CPU. Online learning: 1-hour batch retraining cycle. Note: 500k QPS at 9ms/request requires ~4,500 A100-equivalents; in practice GPU batching and request parallelism reduce actual GPU count. Scale to 1B users, 5M QPS: Retrieval: scale FAISS to 1B items (2.5 TB INT8 index across 32 nodes). Embedding tables grow 10× to 5 TB — migrate hot tables to MI300X cluster (192 GB × 50 nodes = 9.6 TB HBM). Training: move to 512 H100 cluster with hybrid parallelism. Online learning: reduce to 10-minute batch update.

scenario: Design the complete recommendation system architecture for a new social platform targeting 100M users at launch, scaling to 1B users in year 3. Workload: 500k QPS at launch, 5M QPS at scale. Specify: retrieval model type and infrastructure, ranking model architecture, embedding table sizing strategy, online learning pipeline, serving hardware choices (H100/MI300X/TPU), and how the architecture evolves from launch to scale. Justify each major decision with quantitative reasoning.
title: Full-Stack RecSys Architecture for a New Social Platform

details.common_mistake: Assuming you can simply 'pause and resume' training after the budget runs out — any additional gradient updates violate the DP guarantee regardless of noise level.
details.napkin_math: Moments accountant: ε ≈ σ⁻²·q·√(2T·ln(1/δ)). With σ=1.1, q=500K/500K=0.001, T=100K: ε ≈ (1/1.21)·0.001·√(200K·11.5) ≈ 0.83·0.001·1517 ≈ 1.26 per step aggregate. DP-LoRA reduces gradient tensor by 650× (26GB → 40MB) enabling per-example grads without vmap overhead. Target: halve T to 50K steps via 2× batch size → ε budget survives.
details.realistic_solution: Three approaches: (1) Reduce noise multiplier σ to allow more steps within budget — but lower σ weakens the privacy guarantee, potentially invalidating the ε=2 bound. Recompute via Rényi DP accounting. (2) Switch to DP-LoRA: apply DP only to low-rank adapters (rank=16, ~20M params) instead of full 13B. Per-example gradient tensors shrink from 26GB to ~40MB, allowing larger effective batch sizes and more steps per ε. (3) Increase the physical batch size (more examples per gradient step) to reduce the number of steps needed — Poisson sampling rate q = B/N drops, reducing per-step privacy cost. Doubling batch size roughly halves remaining per-step ε cost under moments accountant.

scenario: You are training a 13B medical LLM with DP-SGD using a privacy budget of ε=2, δ=1e-5 over 100,000 training steps on 500K patient records. After 60,000 steps, your privacy accountant reports the budget will be exhausted before training completes. What are your architectural options, and what are the quantitative tradeoffs?
title: DP-SGD Epsilon Budget Exhaustion at Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming sampling without replacement gives the same amplification as Poisson subsampling. It does not — the moments accountant and Rényi DP amplification theorems are proven for Poisson sampling (each example included independently with probability q=B/N). Without-replacement sampling requires tighter analysis and gives weaker amplification bounds.
details.napkin_math: Poisson subsampling: q = 1000/10M = 1e-4. Amplification factor: ε_eff ≈ q·ε = 1e-4 × 8 = 8e-4 per step. After T=100K steps under moments accountant: ε_total ≈ q·σ⁻¹·√(2T·ln(1/δ)) ≈ 1e-4·(1/1.1)·√(2×100K×11.5) ≈ 1e-4·0.91·1517 ≈ 0.138. Without subsampling (q=1): ε ≈ 0.138 / 1e-4 = 1,380. That is the 10,000× gap subsampling buys.
details.realistic_solution: Privacy amplification via Poisson subsampling gives ε_amplified ≈ q·ε_base where q = B/N = 1000/10M = 0.0001. So ε effectively reduces by ~10,000×, not 10×. The 10× claim is conservative. However, in distributed training across 8 GPUs, each GPU seeing a shard is NOT equivalent to Poisson sampling over the full dataset — it's stratified sampling. You must implement global Poisson sampling before sharding, not per-GPU sampling. Implementation: use a cryptographically random inclusion mask over all N examples before each step, then distribute included examples across GPUs.

scenario: Your DP training pipeline on 10M user records uses minibatch SGD with batch size 1,000. The privacy team says you can improve your ε by 10× 'for free' via subsampling amplification. A junior engineer proposes sampling without replacement instead of with replacement. Does this claim hold, and what are the implementation pitfalls in a distributed multi-GPU training context?
title: Privacy Amplification via Subsampling in Production

details.common_mistake: Assuming privacy amplification applies to total enrollment (10,000 clients) rather than active participants per round. Amplification is determined by the per-round sampling rate, not total pool size.
details.napkin_math: Per-round ε_step ≈ q · (C²/σ²K) under simplified Gaussian accounting. Worst case K=50: ε_step ≈ 0.02 · (1/0.25·50) = 0.02 · 0.08 = 0.0016. After 500 rounds (advanced composition): ε_total ≈ √(2·500·ln(1/δ))·ε_step ≈ √(1000·11.5)·0.0016 ≈ 107.2·0.0016 ≈ 0.17. But with per-example clipping sensitivity and correct Rényi DP accountant, the real ε of 4.2 reflects the actual noise and clipping norm — the simplified bound is not tight.
details.realistic_solution: Privacy amplification by subsampling applies to the per-round participation rate q = n_round/N_total. With average 200/10,000 = 0.02 participation, amplification factor is q = 0.02. The central noise from aggregating K clients' noisy updates is: server-side noise ≈ σ/√K per coordinate. With K=200 and σ=0.5: effective noise = 0.5/√200 ≈ 0.035. The per-round ε_step under Gaussian mechanism with subsampling amplification is much smaller, but after 500 rounds of composition it accumulates. The officer is correct that variable participation complicates accounting — you must track worst-case rounds (K=50) not average, since low-participation rounds have weaker noise and higher per-round ε.

scenario: You are running federated learning across 10,000 mobile clients using DP-FedAvg. Each client clips its local gradient update to L2 norm C=1.0 and adds Gaussian noise σ=0.5. After 500 rounds, the central server aggregates updates from a variable number of participating clients (between 50 and 500 per round). Your privacy accountant tracks (ε, δ)=(4.2, 1e-5) at round 500. A compliance officer asks why the privacy bound isn't tighter given 10,000 enrolled clients but only ~200 average participation. Explain the accounting.
title: Federated DP with Heterogeneous Client Noise

details.common_mistake: Assuming ε-DP directly bounds MIA AUC at 0.5 + ε-related term. The formal bound is P[M(D)∈S]/P[M(D')∈S] ≤ e^ε, which limits per-example distinguishability but allows aggregate memorization signals to persist if the attack exploits model behavior beyond single-example distinguishability.
details.napkin_math: Theoretical MIA AUC upper bound under ε-DP: AUC ≤ 1/2 + (e^ε - 1)/(2(e^ε + 1)). For ε=4: (e^4-1)/(2(e^4+1)) = (54.6-1)/(2×55.6) = 53.6/111.2 ≈ 0.482. So AUC ≤ 0.982. For ε=1: (e^1-1)/(2(e^1+1)) = 1.718/7.436 ≈ 0.231. AUC ≤ 0.731. 61% AUC at ε=4 is within bounds but indicates weak practical privacy — ε=1 needed to push AUC below 0.73.
details.realistic_solution: Both sides are partially right. The ε-DP guarantee bounds per-record distinguishability: for any single record, the adversary's advantage is bounded by (e^ε - 1)/(e^ε + 1) ≈ 0.96 for ε=4 — this allows AUC up to ~0.96. The 61% AUC is within the theoretical bound. The red team's attack is likely exploiting: (1) overfitting on high-frequency records (records appearing many times in the dataset inflate effective exposure), (2) output confidence calibration leaking aggregate membership signals across correlated records, (3) clipping norm C set too high, effectively not clipping many gradients and leaving large members' influence intact. Mitigations: reduce ε to ≤1 for strong MIA resistance, audit per-record exposure using Feldman's memorization metric, lower clipping norm.

scenario: A red team successfully mounts a likelihood ratio membership inference attack (MIA) against your DP-trained model, achieving 61% attack AUC despite a claimed ε=4 privacy guarantee. Your privacy engineer says this is theoretically impossible since DP bounds MIA advantage. The red team says the ε=4 guarantee is real but their attack is exploiting something else. Who is right, and what are the root causes?
title: Membership Inference Attack Resistance Under DP

details.common_mistake: Assuming that demographic parity and equalized odds compliance on aggregate subgroups (race, gender) implies intersectional subgroup fairness. Aggregate metrics can mask severe disparities in intersectional cells while remaining statistically compliant at the marginal level.
details.napkin_math: Approval rate drop: 41% → 28% = 13pp drop. Z-test for 13pp shift with N=500 monthly applicants in this cell: z = 0.13/√(0.34·0.66/500) = 0.13/0.0211 ≈ 6.2 → p < 1e-9, highly significant. MMD drift detection threshold: with 200 reference samples and 200 live samples per feature, MMD > 2/√200 ≈ 0.14 indicates drift. Monitoring cost: 20 intersectional cells × 15 features × daily computation = 300 MMD tests/day — trivially cheap on CPU.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is distribution shift at the intersectional level. The model's fairness guarantees were validated on a training-time joint distribution P(X, race, gender, age). If the input feature distribution for Black women aged 18-25 shifted (e.g., economic conditions, application patterns), the model's decision boundary is now misaligned for this subgroup even if overall group metrics hold. Detection requires: (1) continuous per-intersectional-cell monitoring with statistical process control charts (CUSUM or EWMA on approval rate), (2) covariate drift detection on intersectional subgroups using maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between training and live feature distributions. Fix: targeted retraining on augmented data for the drifted subgroup, or threshold recalibration per intersectional cell using Platt scaling on recent deployment data.

scenario: A loan approval model achieves demographic parity (DP gap < 2%) and equalized odds (TPR parity gap < 3%) on the training distribution. Six months post-deployment, a fairness audit reveals that approval rates for Black women aged 18-25 dropped from 41% to 28% while the overall model metrics remain within SLA. The model was not retrained. What caused this and how do you detect and fix it?
title: Intersectional Fairness Under Distribution Shift

details.common_mistake: Assuming calibration and equal FPR are jointly achievable when base rates differ between groups. The Chouldechova impossibility theorem proves these fairness criteria are mutually exclusive when group base rates are unequal.
details.napkin_math: Base rates: r_B = 0.51, r_W = 0.39 (COMPAS dataset). Calibrated model at threshold 0.5: PPV_B = PPV_W = 0.65. FPR_B = FN × r_B/(1-r_B) = 0.35 × 0.51/0.49 = 0.364. FPR_W = 0.35 × 0.39/0.61 = 0.224. Ratio: 0.364/0.224 = 1.62× — even a perfectly calibrated model has 62% higher FPR for the higher-base-rate group. Equal FPR would require deliberately miscalibrating one group.
details.realistic_solution: This is the Chouldechova impossibility theorem in practice. When base rates differ (e.g., observed recidivism rate r_B ≠ r_W), you cannot simultaneously satisfy: (1) calibration (PPV equal across groups given same score), (2) equal FPR, and (3) equal FNR. Formally: FPR = FN-rate × r/(1-r). If calibration holds and base rates differ, FPR must differ. The vendor is technically correct: calibration is a valid fairness criterion for scoring models. The journalist is also correct: equal FPR is a valid fairness criterion for classification decisions. Deployment implication: the organization must choose which fairness criterion aligns with the legal and ethical context. For bail decisions, COMPAS-style tools use calibration. For hiring, equal opportunity (equal TPR) is typically required by disparate impact law. There is no algorithm that resolves the impossibility — it requires a values judgment.

scenario: A recidivism prediction model is calibrated (predicted risk scores match observed recidivism rates) for both Black and White defendants separately. A journalist publishes that the model is unfair because its false positive rate (FPR) for Black defendants is 2× higher than for White defendants. The vendor responds that the model is calibrated and therefore fair. Explain the mathematical impossibility at the heart of this dispute and its implications for deployment.
title: Calibration Fairness vs Accuracy Fairness Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Removing correlated proxy features (zip_code, institution) naively without causal reasoning — this can introduce new biases or destroy signal. Simply dropping correlated features is not equivalent to counterfactual fairness.
details.napkin_math: Causal nuisance model: logistic regression for P(zip|race, city) over 10M records = trivially fast (minutes on CPU). Fair residual computation: 10M × 4 features × 1 forward pass = ~40M FLOPs. Counterfactual evaluation: for each of N=10K test applicants, run 2 inference passes (original + race-flipped) through the hiring model. If model is 100M params FP16: 2 × 10K × 200M FLOPs = 4 TFLOP — 1 second on any modern GPU. Primary cost is causal DAG validation and legal review, not compute.
details.realistic_solution: Counterfactual fairness requires: (1) Build a causal DAG with nodes for Race → {zip_code, institution} → {years_experience} → Hiring_decision. (2) Use path-specific counterfactual analysis: identify which causal paths from Race to Hiring_decision are through 'fair' paths (direct experience signal) vs 'unfair' paths (historical discrimination encoding). (3) Decompose each feature into a 'fair' residual (variation not attributable to race in the causal model) using a learned nuisance model: zip_fair = zip - E[zip|race]. (4) Retrain the hiring model using only fair residuals. Evaluation: run counterfactual inference — flip applicant's race in the causal model, propagate through DAG, compare predicted hiring rate. A counterfactually fair model should produce identical outcomes under race intervention. Cost: requires labeled demographic data for nuisance model training, additional 200-400 GPU-hours for causal decomposition over a 10M-record dataset.

scenario: A hiring model uses features: years_experience, job_title_history, education_institution, and zip_code. A fairness audit finds demographic parity holds (hiring rate gap < 2% by race) but a causality researcher claims the model is causally unfair because zip_code and education_institution are proxies for race that encode historical discrimination. Propose a counterfactual fairness evaluation methodology and quantify the implementation cost.
title: Counterfactual Fairness in Causal Feature Spaces

details.common_mistake: Running all four fairness classifiers synchronously in the critical path — a classifier for each metric at 500K QPS would add 4 × 15ms = 60ms latency, violating typical SLAs.
details.napkin_math: 2% sampling: 500K × 0.02 = 10K requests/day. Four classifiers at 8.5ms average: 10K × 8.5ms = 85s GPU time = 0.0236 GPU-hours/day. Monthly (30 days): 0.0236 × 30 = 0.708 GPU-hours/month at $2/GPU-hr = $1.42/month. Wall-time (batched at BS=64 on A100): 10K requests ÷ 64 per batch × 8.5ms × 4 classifiers ≈ 5.3 seconds/day. 30-day accumulation: 300K samples → detect 1pp salary gap with 99% power. Alert threshold: >3σ deviation from 30-day rolling baseline.
details.realistic_solution: Async sampling pipeline: route 2% of traffic (10K req/day) to a Kafka topic for offline fairness evaluation. Batch process nightly with four lightweight classifiers: (1) pronoun classifier: regex + 3M BERT, ~0.5ms/req, (2) salary NER + regression: 20M model, ~2ms/req, (3) leadership language: sentence embedding + cosine similarity against curated lexicon, ~1ms/req, (4) toxicity: Perspective API or 100M classifier, ~5ms/req. Total: 10K × 8.5ms = 85 GPU-seconds/day ≈ 0.024 GPU-hours/day (≈0.71 GPU-hours/month). Statistical significance: at 10K samples/day, detect a 2pp disparity gap (from 5% to 7% baseline) with >80% power after ~3 days of data accumulation (30K samples).

scenario: You are instrumenting a production text generation API serving 500K daily requests. The API generates job descriptions. A legal team requires you to monitor for four fairness metrics: (1) gendered pronoun usage parity, (2) salary recommendation gap by implied applicant gender, (3) leadership language disparity by race, (4) intersectional toxicity score disparity. Design the monitoring pipeline architecture and estimate its compute cost.
title: Multi-Metric Fairness Dashboard for Production LLM

details.common_mistake: Trying to auto-generate the 'intended use' and 'known limitations' sections — these require human judgment and cannot be reliably automated. Over-automating model card generation creates a false sense of compliance while producing inaccurate documentation.
details.napkin_math: 50 models × average 4 retrains/year = 200 card updates/year. Auto-generation time: eval metrics from eval pipeline (already runs), lineage query to metadata store: ~5s per model. Total auto-gen overhead: 200 × 5s = 1,000s/year = 17 minutes/year. Human review time: 30 min per retrain × 200 = 100 person-hours/year. Compliance benefit: EU AI Act fines up to €30M or 6% revenue for non-compliance — 100 person-hours/year is negligible insurance cost.
details.realistic_solution: Two-tier architecture: (1) Auto-generated sections (updated on every retrain): performance by subgroup (pulled from eval pipeline), training data statistics (from data lineage DAG), model architecture and hyperparameters (from MLflow/W&B), FLOP count and carbon estimate (computed post-training). (2) Human-reviewed sections (required sign-off before production deployment): intended use, out-of-scope uses, known limitations, ethical considerations. Implementation: embed model card generation in the CI/CD pipeline — training job emits a card_stub.yaml with auto-populated fields. A PR is auto-opened to the model owner requiring human completion of the reserved fields before the model can be promoted to production. Card stored in a git-tracked registry with version history tied to model versions in the artifact store.

scenario: Your ML platform team manages 50 production models. A new EU AI Act compliance requirement mandates that each model have an up-to-date model card covering: intended use, performance by subgroup, known limitations, and training data lineage. Model cards are currently hand-authored in Markdown and drift from actual model behavior within weeks of a retrain. Design a system to auto-generate and maintain living model cards.
title: Model Card Infrastructure for 50-Model Production Fleet

details.common_mistake: Maximizing the number of adversarial prompts (quantity) rather than coverage of the failure mode taxonomy. Automated methods generate volume but cluster around known attack patterns — novel failure modes require human creativity.
details.napkin_math: Strategy C: attacker LLM at 50 prompts/min = 3,000/hr. 200 hrs budget (unreviewed generation): 600K prompts. With automated filter (perplexity + semantic dedup): 10% pass-through = 60K unique adversarial prompts. Human review at 100/hr: 600 review hours needed — over budget. Reduce to 100K generated, 10K reviewed = 100 review hours. 10K human-reviewed adversarial prompts from automated pipeline plus 5K from strategies A+B = 15K high-quality red-team cases.
