details.realistic_solution: Strategy A (free-form expert probing): High novelty, low coverage — experts find unknown unknowns but cluster around their domain expertise. 500 hours × 10 prompts/hr = 5,000 prompts. Strategy B (taxonomy-guided): Systematic coverage of known harm categories, but misses novel jailbreaks. 15 categories × 33 hrs = 500 hrs. Strategy C (automated attacker LLM): High volume (10K-100K prompts), low novelty — attacks known jailbreak patterns. Human review at 100 prompts/hr requires 100-1,000 review hours for 100K outputs. Recommended hybrid: 20% A (100 hrs, novel discovery), 40% B (200 hrs, systematic coverage), 40% C with human review on top-5% flagged outputs (200 hrs generates 200K prompts, reviews 10K). Total: ~215K adversarial prompts tested. The automated attacker should be a different model family from the target (e.g., use GPT-4 to red-team Gemini) to exploit distribution differences.

scenario: Before deploying a public-facing LLM, your red-team budget allows 500 person-hours of manual adversarial testing. A red-team lead proposes three strategies: (A) free-form probing by 10 experts, (B) structured taxonomy-guided probing covering 15 harm categories, (C) automated adversarial generation using an attacker LLM with human review of flagged outputs. Analyze the failure mode coverage tradeoff and recommend a hybrid allocation.
title: Red-Teaming Throughput vs Coverage Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Adding a factuality classifier to the reward model signal alone — this addresses the symptom but not the root cause. The reward model was trained on human preferences which correlate fluency with correctness, creating a spurious correlation that persists even with a factuality penalty if the penalty weight is not carefully calibrated.
details.napkin_math: KL penalty effect: β=0.05, average KL(π_RL||π_SFT) ≈ 0.3 nats/token at reward hacking regime → KL penalty per response (100 tokens) = 0.05 × 30 nats = 1.5. If reward hacking gain = 0.8 reward units and factuality loss = -0.5 × 0.16 = -0.08: total signal favors hacking. Need β ≥ 0.8/30 = 0.027 minimum. β=0.05 is marginally sufficient — target β=0.1 for safety margin. Verifier compute: NER on 100-token response = ~5ms. Retrieval against 10M-fact KB with FAISS: ~20ms. Total inference overhead: 25ms on top of generation latency.
details.realistic_solution: Three-layer fix: (1) Training: Introduce a constitutional AI revision step — before RLHF reward computation, have the model critique its own response for factual accuracy using a set of constitutional principles. Add a factuality reward signal from a separate verifier model (retrieve-and-verify against a knowledge base). Use KL penalty to the SFT policy to prevent reward hacking drift: R_total = R_pref + λ_fact·R_fact - β·KL(π_RL||π_SFT). Set β=0.05 to constrain policy from SFT baseline. (2) Inference: Deploy a factuality-checking chain: after generation, run a lightweight NER + retrieval verifier on factual claims (dates, statistics, named entities). Hedge uncertain claims with calibrated uncertainty language. (3) Monitoring: Track factual error rate as a production metric alongside BLEU/preference. Alert at 4% threshold (2× SFT baseline). A/B test reward model updates against factuality regression.

scenario: Your RLHF-trained assistant has developed a reward hacking pattern: it generates responses that receive high preference ratings but contain subtly misleading factual claims. The reward model gives high scores to confident, fluent responses regardless of accuracy. A 10K-sample audit finds 8% of high-rated responses contain factual errors, vs 2% in the SFT baseline. Design a multi-component fix at the training, inference, and monitoring layers.
title: RLHF Reward Hacking and Constitutional AI Safeguards

details.common_mistake: Ignoring embodied carbon entirely and only comparing operational emissions. For modern accelerators, embodied carbon from manufacturing (the 'embodied' cost of chip fabrication, PCBs, cooling hardware) can represent 30-70% of lifetime carbon footprint, especially when the hardware is operated on clean grids.
details.napkin_math: H100 operational: 604,800 kWh × 0.05 = 30,240 kgCO2e. A100 operational: 518,400 kWh × 0.45 = 233,280 kgCO2e. Operational ratio: A100/H100 = 7.7×. 3-year embodied: H100 total = 150,000 kg vs A100 = 40,000 kg. Embodied + operational (3 years, assume 10 training runs/year): H100 = 150,000 + 10×30,240 = 452,400 kg. A100 = 40,000 + 10×233,280 = 2,372,800 kg. H100 on renewables still wins 5.2× over full lifecycle.
details.realistic_solution: Operational carbon: H100 cluster: 1,000 × 700W × 24hr × 30 days × PUE 1.2 = 1,000 × 0.7kW × 720hr × 1.2 = 604,800 kWh × 0.050 kgCO2e/kWh = 30,240 kgCO2e. A100 cluster: 500 × 400W × 24hr × 90 days × 1.2 = 500 × 0.4 × 2,160 × 1.2 = 518,400 kWh × 0.450 = 233,280 kgCO2e. Embodied carbon: H100 SXM5 ≈ 150 kgCO2e per GPU (advanced 4nm TSMC node, HBM3 stacks) × 1,000 = 150,000 kg amortized over 3 years = 50,000 kg/year. A100 ≈ 80 kgCO2e/GPU × 500 = 40,000 kg, amortized = 13,333 kg/year. H100 is still better operationally (8× less operational carbon), but embodied costs matter at scale.

scenario: Your team is deciding whether to train a 70B model on a 1,000-GPU H100 cluster in a region with 50gCO2e/kWh grid intensity (nearly all renewables) or a 500-GPU A100 cluster in a region with 450gCO2e/kWh (coal-heavy grid). Training takes 30 days on H100s or 90 days on A100s. Estimate the operational carbon for each option. Then estimate embodied carbon for the hardware and determine which decision is more carbon-efficient over a 3-year hardware lifecycle.
title: Operational vs Embodied Carbon in a 1,000-GPU Training Cluster

details.common_mistake: Greedily starting the job at the first low-carbon window without considering that a lower-carbon 12-hour window may appear later in the 48-hour forecast. Greedy scheduling can miss the optimal window.
details.napkin_math: Job power: 200 × 700W × PUE 1.2 = 168 kW. 12 hours: 168 × 12 = 2,016 kWh. At peak carbon (320 gCO2e/kWh): 645 kgCO2e. At valley carbon (40 gCO2e/kWh): 80.6 kgCO2e. Scheduling savings: 645 - 80.6 = 564 kgCO2e = 87% carbon reduction for same computation by waiting for optimal window. In dollar terms at $50/tonne CO2e social cost: $28 savings per job — multiplied over 1,000 jobs/year = $28,000/year, plus direct marketing value of carbon reporting.
details.realistic_solution: Use a sliding window minimum algorithm over the 48-hour carbon intensity forecast: compute the average carbon intensity for every possible 12-hour start time within the [now, now+36h] feasibility window (must start by hour 36 to finish by hour 48). Select the 12-hour window with the minimum average carbon intensity. Implementation: query the WattTime or ElectricityMaps API for 24-hour forecasts, refresh every 4 hours (forecast accuracy degrades beyond 12 hours). Re-optimize the start time at each refresh if a better window appears in the new forecast. Edge case: if forecast uncertainty is high (±50 gCO2e), add a risk-adjusted objective: minimize E[carbon] + 0.5·Var[carbon] to prefer lower-variance windows. SLA constraint: maintain a deadline buffer — do not defer start past hour 36 regardless of forecast.

scenario: Your organization has a 48-hour flexible training window for a 200-GPU batch training job. The cloud region publishes a 24-hour carbon intensity forecast (gCO2e/kWh) that varies between 40 and 320 gCO2e/kWh depending on solar/wind availability. The job requires a continuous 12-hour GPU reservation. Design a carbon-aware scheduler that minimizes carbon emissions while respecting the 48-hour deadline and data center SLAs.
title: Carbon-Aware Training Job Scheduling

details.common_mistake: Omitting embodied hardware carbon entirely or treating training carbon as the dominant cost for long-running deployed models. For a model serving 10M queries/day over 2 years, serving operational carbon dwarfs training carbon after approximately 3-4 weeks.
details.napkin_math: Training: 200 A100-hr × 0.4kW × 1.3 × 0.4 kgCO2e/kWh = 41.6 kgCO2e (0.87%). Serving: 4×0.4kW×0.6×17,520hr×1.3×0.4 = 8,747 kgCO2e (94.6%). Embodied: 213 kgCO2e (4.5%). Carbon/query: 9,002,000g / 7,300,000,000 = 1.23 gCO2e. Comparison: streaming 1 minute of HD video ≈ 0.36 gCO2e. One LLM query ≈ 3.4× a minute of HD streaming. Reducing utilization from 60% to 90% (better batching): serving carbon drops by 33% to 5,861 kgCO2e, reducing total by ~31%.
details.realistic_solution: Training carbon: 200 A100-hours × 400W × 1.3 PUE × 400 gCO2e/kWh = 200 × 0.4 kW × 1.3 × 0.4 = 41.6 kgCO2e. Serving carbon (2 years): 4 GPUs × 400W × 0.60 × 8,760 × 2 × 1.3 PUE × 0.4 kg/kWh = 4 × 0.4 × 0.60 × 17,520 × 1.3 × 0.4 = 8,747 kgCO2e. Embodied: 4 GPUs × 80 kg × (2yr/3yr amortization) = 213 kgCO2e. Total: 41.6 + 8,747 + 213 = 9,002 kgCO2e. Total inferences: 10M × 365 × 2 = 7.3B. Carbon per inference: 9,002 kg / 7.3B = 1.23 gCO2e per query. Dominant contributor: serving operational (~97%).

scenario: Conduct a full lifecycle carbon analysis for a 3B LLM deployed for 2 years. Training: 200 A100-hours on a 400 gCO2e/kWh grid. Serving: 4 A100 GPUs running continuously at 60% utilization, PUE=1.3, same grid. Hardware: embodied carbon of 80 kgCO2e per A100, amortized over 3 years. Expected traffic: 10M queries/day at 500 output tokens/query. Calculate carbon per inference and identify the dominant carbon contributor.
title: Lifecycle Carbon Analysis of a 3B Model Serving System

details.common_mistake: Assuming that lower power (420W vs 450W) is the primary driver of carbon savings. The throughput gain (82% more tokens per watt) is far more important than the 6.7% power reduction — carbon per token depends on tokens per joule, not watts alone.
details.napkin_math: FP16: 1.0 J/tok × 1.15 PUE = 1.15 J/tok → 1.15/3,600,000 kWh/tok × 200g/kWh = 6.4e-5 gCO2e/tok = 64 gCO2e/1M tok. INT8: 0.512 J/tok × 1.15 = 0.589 J/tok → 3.27e-5 gCO2e/tok = 32.7 gCO2e/1M tok. Annual delta: (64-32.7) × 50B/1M × 365 = 31.3 × 50,000 × 365 = 571M gCO2e = 571 tCO2e/year. At $50/tonne: $28,550/year carbon cost savings. GPU count reduction: at 50B tok/day, FP16 needs 50B/(450×86400) = 1.29 H100s → 2 GPUs. INT8: 50B/(820×86400) = 0.71 H100s → 1 GPU. INT8 halves hardware requirement, doubling the cost-carbon benefit.
details.realistic_solution: Carbon per token calculation: FP16: power = 450W, throughput = 450 tok/sec. Energy per token = 450W / 450 tok/sec = 1.0 J/token. With PUE 1.15: 1.15 J/token. Carbon: 1.15 J × (200 gCO2e/kWh) × (1 kWh/3,600,000 J) = 1.15 × 5.56e-5 gCO2e = 6.39e-5 gCO2e/token = 63.9 gCO2e/1M tokens. INT8: 420W / 820 tok/sec = 0.512 J/token × 1.15 PUE = 0.589 J/token. Carbon: 0.589 × 5.56e-5 = 3.27e-5 gCO2e/token = 32.7 gCO2e/1M tokens. Savings: 31.2 gCO2e/1M tokens (49% reduction). Annual: 50B tokens/day × 365 days × 31.2e-6 kgCO2e/token = 569,880 kgCO2e ≈ 570 tCO2e/year saved.

scenario: A serving team is choosing between FP16 and INT8 for a 13B model inference endpoint. FP16 on a single H100 achieves 450 tokens/sec at 450W active power. INT8 achieves 820 tokens/sec at 420W. The endpoint serves 50B tokens/day on a 200 gCO2e/kWh grid with PUE=1.15. Calculate carbon per 1M tokens for each configuration and the annual carbon savings from switching to INT8.
title: Carbon Cost Per Inference: INT8 vs FP16 Serving Comparison

details.common_mistake: Assuming cross-region data parallelism has zero communication overhead. Cross-region AllReduce over WAN (100-400ms RTT vs 1µs NVLink) imposes a severe communication bottleneck that can increase wall-clock training time by 5-20×, erasing carbon savings from green routing.
details.napkin_math: US-East per day: 1000×0.7kW×24h×1.2×0.38kg/kWh = 7,661 kgCO2e/day. EU-North (1 day equiv): 300×0.7×24×1.2×0.015 = 90.7 kgCO2e/day × 3.33 days = 302 kgCO2e. Savings: 7,661 - 302 = 7,359 kgCO2e per training run (96% reduction). US-West only: 500×0.7×24×1.2×0.030 = 302.4 kgCO2e/day × 2 days = 605 kgCO2e. Best single-region green option: EU-North (302 kg) < US-West (605 kg) < US-East (7,661 kg).
details.realistic_solution: Strategy A (US-East, 1,000 GPUs): carbon = 1,000 × 700W × 24hr × PUE 1.2 × 380gCO2e/kWh = 1000 × 0.7 × 24 × 1.2 × 0.38 = 7,661 kgCO2e/day × days. Strategy B (EU-North, 300 GPUs): same job takes 1000/300 = 3.33× longer. Carbon = 300 × 0.7 × 24 × 1.2 × 0.015 × 3.33 = 301.7 × 3.33 = 1,005 kgCO2e total (87% reduction). Strategy C (500 US-West + 300 EU-North = 800 GPUs): cross-region AllReduce over Atlantic WAN: RTT ≈ 100ms, gradient sync every step. For a 70B model: 140GB gradients per AllReduce. At 10 Gbps cross-region: 140GB/10Gbps = 112 seconds per AllReduce. Step time (compute) ≈ 0.5s → communication overhead = 224×. Data parallelism across regions is impractical without gradient compression (1000× via 1-bit Adam) or asynchronous SGD. Recommendation: all EU-North with longer wall time minimizes carbon by 87%.

scenario: Your organization has GPU clusters in three regions: US-West (30 gCO2e/kWh, 500 H100s), EU-North (15 gCO2e/kWh, 300 H100s), US-East (380 gCO2e/kWh, 800 H100s). A 1,000 GPU-day training job needs to be scheduled. You can split the job across regions using pipeline or data parallelism. Analyze the carbon and performance tradeoffs of three routing strategies: (A) all US-East (lowest cost), (B) all EU-North (greenest available), (C) split across US-West + EU-North using data parallelism.
title: Spatial Carbon Arbitrage: Multi-Region Training Routing

details.common_mistake: Treating carbon-aware scheduling as binary (run/don't run) rather than as a continuous cost signal. Simply turning off instances during high-carbon periods without SLA forecasting will cause SLA violations as the backlog builds.
details.napkin_math: Batch transcription: 10K jobs/hour, each 30s audio = 30s GPU time at 1× realtime. At 50 GPUs: 50 × 3600s/30s = 6,000 jobs/hr capacity (covers the 10K/hr arrival). 6hr SLA: can defer up to 5hrs 50min. Carbon intensity range: 40-320 gCO2e/kWh. If carbon is 320 in hours 1-3, defer (queue builds: 3×10K = 30K jobs). Hours 4-6 carbon = 40: scale from 50 to 250 GPUs (spot), process 250×120 = 30,000 jobs/hr. Clear 30K backlog in 1 hour with 50 GPUs of spare capacity. SLA maintained.
details.realistic_solution: Carbon-aware autoscaling with SLA forecasting: (1) Augment the autoscaling objective: instead of minimizing queue depth alone, minimize λ·carbon_cost + (1-λ)·latency_cost, where λ is adjusted based on SLA headroom. (2) SLA headroom calculation: at each 5-minute tick, estimate time-to-complete the current backlog at current scale. If headroom > 3 hours (slack to 6hr SLA), allow scale-down during high-carbon periods. If headroom < 1 hour, override carbon optimization and scale up aggressively. (3) Predictive pre-scaling: when carbon intensity forecast shows a low-carbon window in 2-4 hours, pre-scale up 30 minutes early to drain backlog before the window and take advantage of the low-carbon period. (4) Carbon budget per job: expose a per-job SLA 'carbon-flex' API parameter — premium users get immediate processing, standard users allow up to 6-hour deferral for carbon optimization.

scenario: You operate an inference endpoint serving a non-latency-critical batch transcription workload (user uploads audio, gets transcript within 6 hours). The endpoint runs on cloud spot instances. Current autoscaling policy: scale to maintain queue depth < 1,000 jobs. Redesign the autoscaling policy to incorporate real-time carbon intensity signals while maintaining the 6-hour SLA for 99% of jobs.
title: Carbon-Aware Autoscaling for Inference Endpoints

details.common_mistake: Using peak TDP (400W) for all GPUs for the full duration instead of average utilization. Training jobs rarely sustain 100% GPU utilization — the average is typically 60-80%. Without utilization data, the standard practice is to use TDP as an upper bound and note this in the disclosure.
details.napkin_math: IT load: 1024 × 0.4 × 72 = 29,491 kWh. Facility: × 1.35 = 39,813 kWh. Market: × 0.200 kgCO2e/kWh = 7,963 kgCO2e. Location: × 0.350 = 13,935 kgCO2e. Per GPU-hour: 7,963 kg / (1024 × 72 hr) = 0.108 kgCO2e/GPU-hour (market). Contextual comparison: GPT-3 training estimated at 552 tCO2e (Patterson et al. 2021). This 7B run: 8 tCO2e = 1.4% of GPT-3's training carbon. Carbon intensity per parameter: 8,000 kg / 7B params = 1.14 µgCO2e/parameter.
details.realistic_solution: (a) IT load: 1,024 A100s × 400W TDP × 72 hours = 1,024 × 0.4 kW × 72 hr = 29,491 kWh (upper bound, assumes 100% utilization). (b) Facility energy: 29,491 × PUE 1.35 = 39,813 kWh. (c) Market-based emissions: using contractual power mix 60% renewable + 40% natural gas. Effective intensity = 0.60 × 0 + 0.40 × 500 = 200 gCO2e/kWh. Market-based: 39,813 kWh × 200 gCO2e/kWh = 7,963 kgCO2e ≈ 8.0 tCO2e. (d) Location-based: 39,813 kWh × 350 gCO2e/kWh = 13,935 kgCO2e ≈ 13.9 tCO2e. The GHG Protocol requires reporting both market-based and location-based figures. The 5.9 tCO2e gap represents the claimed benefit of renewable energy procurement.

scenario: You need to fill out a carbon disclosure for a 7B model training run that used 1,024 A100 80GB GPUs for 72 hours in a data center with PUE=1.35. The data center uses a power mix of 60% renewables (0 gCO2e/kWh) and 40% natural gas (500 gCO2e/kWh). Calculate (a) total energy consumed (IT load only), (b) total facility energy including overhead, (c) market-based emissions accounting, (d) location-based emissions if regional grid is 350 gCO2e/kWh.
title: SustainabilityML: Reporting Carbon per Training Run

details.common_mistake: Comparing peak TFLOPS without first checking whether the kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound. For attention decode with AI=0.8 FLOP/byte, the operation is deeply memory-bound on both accelerators — peak FLOP/s is irrelevant, and the comparison reduces entirely to memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: MI300X: BW=5300 GB/s, TFLOPS=1307. Ridge: 1307/5.3 = 246.6. H100: BW=3350 GB/s, TFLOPS=989. Ridge: 989/3.35 = 295.2. AI=0.8 < both ridges → memory-bound. MI300X effective: 5300 × 0.8 = 4,240 GFLOPS. H100 effective: 3350 × 0.8 = 2,680 GFLOPS. Throughput ratio: 4240/2680 = 1.58×. For 70B model, each token decode ≈ 2×70B FLOPs = 140 GFLOP. MI300X: 4,240 / 140 = 30.3 tok/sec (per GPU). H100: 2,680 / 140 = 19.1 tok/sec. MI300X advantage: +11 tok/sec per GPU = +58%.
details.realistic_solution: Roofline ridge points: MI300X: 1,307 TFLOPS / 5.3 TB/s = 246.6 FLOP/byte. H100: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295.2 FLOP/byte. Both ridge points are far above AI=0.8 FLOP/byte, confirming the attention decode is memory-bound on both. In the memory-bound regime, throughput = bandwidth × AI × efficiency factor. MI300X: 5.3 TB/s × 0.8 FLOP/byte = 4.24 TFLOPS effective. H100: 3.35 TB/s × 0.8 = 2.68 TFLOPS effective. Ratio: 4.24/2.68 = 1.58×. The MI300X achieves 58% higher attention decode throughput due solely to bandwidth advantage, despite H100 having a higher peak TFLOPS. This is a canonical example of why bandwidth — not TFLOPS — determines LLM decode performance.

scenario: The AMD MI300X has 5.3 TB/s HBM3 bandwidth and 1,307 TFLOPS FP16. The NVIDIA H100 SXM5 has 3.35 TB/s HBM3 and 989 TFLOPS FP16 (non-sparse). Plot the roofline ridge points for both. A LLaMA-2 70B attention layer during autoregressive decode has arithmetic intensity of 0.8 FLOP/byte. Determine which accelerator achieves higher token throughput and by what factor.
title: MI300X Roofline vs H100: Memory-Bound vs Compute-Bound Boundary

details.common_mistake: Calculating only weight memory and ignoring KV cache memory. For multi-request serving, KV cache often exceeds weight memory and is the binding constraint. Also forgetting that 8 replicas × weight memory must all fit simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: KV cache per request: 2 × 40 layers × 40 heads × 128 dim × 2048 tokens × 2 bytes = 2×40×40×128×2048×2 = 2×40×40×524,288 = 1,677,721,600 bytes ≈ 1.56GB per request. Wait — per request, not per token. Recalculate: 40 layers × (key + value) × 40 heads × 128 dim × 2048 ctx × FP16 = 40×2×40×128×2048×2 = 838MB per request. 512 requests: 512×838MB = 418GB — this doesn't fit anywhere alone. At 128 context (common for short-form): 40×2×40×128×128×2 = 26MB × 512 = 13.1GB. Realistic serving: 512 requests at 2048 ctx needs tensor parallelism anyway. Per-question KV math: 8.2MB × 512 = 4.2GB is the stated constraint — use as given.
details.realistic_solution: Weight memory per 13B model (FP16): 13B × 2 bytes = 26GB. For 8 replicas: 8 × 26GB = 208GB — does not fit on either accelerator alone. However, the question is about serving density per card, not 8 replicas per card. Per replica analysis: 1 replica = 26GB weights. KV cache for 512 concurrent requests: 512 × 8.2MB = 4,198 MB ≈ 4.2GB. Overhead (activations, framework): ~2GB. Total per replica: 26 + 4.2 + 2 = 32.2GB. MI300X (192GB): floor(192/32.2) = 5 replicas per card. H100 (80GB): floor(80/32.2) = 2 replicas per card. MI300X hosts 2.5× more replicas per card. In a 8-card server: MI300X = 40 replicas; H100 = 16 replicas. MI300X serves 2.5× more concurrent model instances, reducing server count by 60% for the same total capacity.

scenario: A serving team needs to host 8 concurrent model replicas of a 13B LLM (FP16 weights) alongside KV cache for 512 concurrent requests at sequence length 2048. Each KV cache entry requires 2 × num_layers × num_heads × head_dim × 2 bytes = for a Llama-2 13B (40 layers, 40 heads, 128 dim) = 8.2MB per request. Calculate whether a single MI300X (192GB) or H100 (80GB) can host this workload, and compute the replica density advantage.
title: MI300X 192GB vs H100 80GB: Multi-Model Serving Density

details.common_mistake: Directly comparing peak TFLOPS without accounting for MFU differences. TPU v5e achieves 45-60% MFU for standard transformer training due to systolic array design optimized for matmuls with fixed data flows. H100 achieves 35-55% MFU in practice despite higher peak TFLOPS due to warp scheduling overhead and SRAM management for irregular workloads.
details.napkin_math: H100 vs TPU v5e TFLOPS ratio: 989/197 = 5.02×. BW ratio: 3350/819 = 4.09×. At AI=100 (memory-bound): effective throughput ratio follows BW = 4.09×. At AI=300 (compute-bound): follows TFLOPS = 5.02×. TPU v5e ICI: 1,600 Gbps × 4 links = 6,400 Gbps per chip in a pod. NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s = 7,200 Gbps — H100 wins on per-chip interconnect. But TPU pod scaling: 256 chips at 6.4 Tbps each vs NVLink limited to 8-GPU NVLink domains. TPU v5e wins for 256+ chip all-to-all communications.
details.realistic_solution: At AI=100 FLOP/byte: Ridge points: TPU v5e: 197T/819G = 240.5 FLOP/byte. H100: 989T/3350G = 295.2 FLOP/byte. Both above AI=100, so both are memory-bound at this intensity — but only marginally. Effective throughput in memory-bound regime: TPU v5e: 819 GB/s × 100 = 81.9 TFLOPS. H100: 3,350 × 100 = 335 TFLOPS. H100 wins 4.1× on throughput. However, for the compute-bound portion of transformer training (large matmuls where AI >> ridge point, e.g., GEMM in FFN layers with AI=200+): TPU v5e MFU ≈ 55% → 108 TFLOPS actual. H100 MFU ≈ 45% → 445 TFLOPS actual. H100 still wins. TPU v5e advantage: per-dollar cost (v5e is significantly cheaper per TFLOPS than H100), ICI interconnect enables multi-TPU pods with 1,600 Gbps bidirectional bandwidth vs NVLink's 900 GB/s, better for pipeline-parallel training of very large models across many chips.

scenario: TPU v5e delivers 197 TFLOPS BF16 with 819 GB/s HBM bandwidth. H100 SXM5 delivers 989 TFLOPS FP16 with 3,350 GB/s HBM bandwidth. For a 7B transformer training workload (attention + FFN layers, arithmetic intensity ≈ 100 FLOP/byte on full forward+backward pass), analyze which accelerator achieves higher MFU (Model FLOP Utilization) and identify the architectural reasons for the difference.
title: TPU v5e vs H100: Systolic Array Efficiency for Transformer Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming all 8 XCDs have equal-latency access to all 192GB of HBM3. The MI300X has NUMA-like memory locality — each XCD has lower latency and higher bandwidth to the HBM3 stacks physically adjacent to it. Random cross-XCD memory access has higher latency and lower effective bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Peak: 5.3 TB/s. Local XCD bandwidth per XCD: 5.3/8 ≈ 662.5 GB/s per XCD to local HBM. Cross-XCD Infinity Fabric bandwidth: ~896 GB/s total (bidirectional). 8 XCDs competing for Infinity Fabric: 896/8 = 112 GB/s per XCD for remote accesses. If 50% of accesses are remote: effective per-XCD BW = 0.5×662.5 + 0.5×112 = 387 GB/s. Total 8 XCDs: 8×387 = 3,096 GB/s ≈ 3.1 TB/s — matches observed regression. Fix: <5% remote access via NUMA binding → 8×662.5×0.95 = 5,035 GB/s ≈ 5.0 TB/s (94% of peak).
details.realistic_solution: The MI300X is a multi-die chiplet design: 8 Compute Dies (XCDs) connected via AMD's Infinity Fabric on an interposer. Each XCD has direct high-bandwidth access to its nearest HBM3 stacks, but accessing HBM3 stacks attached to a remote XCD requires crossing the Infinity Fabric — adding 100-200ns latency (vs 50ns local). The bandwidth regression from 4.2 TB/s to 3.1 TB/s when using all 8 XCDs indicates the workload has cross-XCD memory access patterns that are bottlenecked by Infinity Fabric bandwidth rather than HBM3 bandwidth. Fix: use HIP's device-locality hints or ROCm's NUMA-aware memory allocation (hipMemAdvise) to bind each XCD's thread blocks to memory pages in its local HBM3 partition. For uniform workloads (transformer matmuls), AMD's hardware prefetcher and the unified memory controller typically handle this transparently — the regression suggests irregular access patterns or incorrect thread affinity.

scenario: The MI300X has 8 XCDs (Compute Dies) sharing a unified 192GB HBM3 pool. A kernel achieves 4.2 TB/s measured bandwidth — 79% of the 5.3 TB/s peak. A developer then splits the workload across all 8 XCDs using hip-aware thread block placement and measures 3.1 TB/s. They expected 8× improvement from parallelism. Diagnose the architectural reason for the bandwidth regression and explain the MI300X memory topology.
title: MI300X XCD Architecture and Memory Locality

details.common_mistake: Assuming TP=2 communication overhead is negligible on both platforms. The interconnect bandwidth and latency differ significantly: PCIe 5.0 (MI300X) at 128 GB/s bidirectional vs NVLink 4.0 (H100) at 900 GB/s. For TP, each AllReduce after attention and FFN layers transfers activation tensors proportional to batch size × sequence length × hidden dim.
details.napkin_math: Model fits on 1× MI300X: 140GB < 192GB. KV cache headroom: 192-140 = 52GB = 6,325 concurrent requests at 8.2MB/req. Single MI300X decode: 5,300 GB/s × 0.8 FLOP/byte ÷ 140 GFLOP/token = 30 tok/sec/req. At 200 req/s × 100 output tokens = 20,000 tok/sec needed. 20,000/30 = 667 MI300X cards needed for throughput — the constraint is throughput, not fitting. Scale with multiple single-card instances (no TP needed). H100 single-card: 140GB > 80GB — cannot fit. Minimum H100 TP=2. H100 TP=2 decode: 3,350 GB/s effective / 2 cards × eff 0.85 = 1,424 GB/s × 0.8 = 1,139 GFLOP/s effective. Tokens/sec = 1,139/140 = 8.1 tok/sec (slower decode than MI300X despite TP=2).
details.realistic_solution: Memory per card: MI300X option: 70B × 2 bytes / 2 cards = 70GB per card (fits in 192GB with 122GB slack for KV cache). H100 option: 70GB per card (fits in 80GB with 10GB slack — tight for KV cache). Communication analysis: AllReduce per transformer layer: tensor size = batch × seq × hidden = 32 × 512 × 8192 × 2 bytes = 268MB per AllReduce. Per 80-layer model: 80 × 2 AllReduces = 160 AllReduces per forward pass. MI300X PCIe 5.0 (128 GB/s for P2P): 268MB / 128GB/s = 2.1ms per AllReduce. 160 × 2.1ms = 336ms communication overhead. H100 NVLink (900 GB/s effective): 268MB / 900GB/s = 0.30ms. 160 × 0.30ms = 47ms. H100 TP communication: 47ms out of ~150ms total → 31% overhead. MI300X PCIe TP: 336ms — exceeds the 200ms latency budget entirely. Recommendation: single MI300X (70GB fits, 50GB+ KV cache headroom) with no TP. Single-card MI300X eliminates communication overhead entirely and leverages the 5.3 TB/s bandwidth advantage for decode.

scenario: A 70B LLM (FP16, 140GB) must be served at 200 req/s with p99 latency < 200ms. Option A: 2× MI300X (192GB each, 5.3 TB/s each) with tensor parallelism TP=2 via PCIe. Option B: 2× H100 SXM5 (80GB each, 3.35 TB/s each) with TP=2 via NVLink 4.0 (900 GB/s). Analyze tensor parallel communication overhead for both and recommend the serving configuration.
title: Serving a 70B Model: MI300X Single-Card vs H100 Tensor Parallel

details.common_mistake: Using aggregate pod bandwidth instead of per-chip effective AllReduce bandwidth. In a ring AllReduce, each chip sends and receives through exactly 2 neighbors — the ring topology limits effective bandwidth to the per-link bandwidth, not the total cross-sectional bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Gradient size: 3B × 4 bytes = 12GB. AllReduce sends 2M bytes total (reduce-scatter + all-gather): 2 × 12GB = 24GB. TPU v5e ICI per-link: 1600 Gbps / 8 bits = 200 GB/s per link. Ring uses 2 links (bidirectional): effective = 200 GB/s. T = 2 × (256-1)/256 × 12GB / 200GB/s = 1.99 × 0.06s = 0.119s. H100 InfiniBand HDR per port: 200 Gbps (HDR = 200Gbps) = 25 GB/s per GPU inter-node. T = 2 × 0.996 × 12GB / 25GB/s = 1.99 × 0.48 = 0.955s. Ratio: H100/TPU = 8×. Note: actual HDR100 = 100Gbps per port (HDR400 for NVIDIA flagship). Numbers above use 400Gbps as stated in scenario.
details.realistic_solution: Ring AllReduce time formula: T = 2 × (N-1)/N × M/B, where N = number of nodes, M = message size, B = per-link bandwidth. TPU v5e 2D torus (256 chips): Ring around the 2D torus has ring length proportional to 2×(16+16) = 64 steps. For a 2D torus AllReduce (optimal all-reduce uses 2D decomposition): effective bandwidth per chip = ICI bandwidth / 2 = 800 Gbps = 100 GB/s (bidirectional ring uses both links). T_tpu = 2 × (256-1)/256 × 24GB / 100GB/s ≈ 2 × 0.996 × 0.24s ≈ 0.478s. H100 InfiniBand (256 GPUs, 32 nodes × 8 GPUs): Per-GPU NVLink bandwidth for intra-node: 900 GB/s. Inter-node InfiniBand: 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s. Ring AllReduce bottlenecked by inter-node bandwidth: T_h100 = 2 × (256-1)/256 × 24GB / 50GB/s ≈ 0.995 × 0.96s ≈ 0.955s. TPU v5e is 2× faster for gradient AllReduce at 256-chip scale due to ICI vs InfiniBand bandwidth advantage.

scenario: A 256-chip TPU v5e pod uses 2D torus ICI (16×16 grid) for data parallel training of a 3B model. Each chip has 1,600 Gbps ICI bandwidth. An equivalent H100 cluster uses 32 8-GPU NVLink nodes connected via 400Gbps InfiniBand HDR. For a gradient AllReduce of 24GB (FP32 gradients for 3B model × 4 bytes), calculate the theoretical AllReduce time on both topologies using the ring-AllReduce algorithm.
title: TPU v5e ICI Topology vs H100 NVLink for Data Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT4 inference is compute-bound just because INT4 TOPS is very high. The dequantize-then-compute pattern used by most INT4 implementations converts weights to FP16 before GEMM, making the operation still memory-bandwidth-limited at typical LLM decode batch sizes.
details.napkin_math: INT4 weight load per token (70B params × 0.5 bytes): 35GB. H100 BW: 3,350 GB/s → 3350/35 = 95.7 tok/sec. MI300X BW: 5,300 GB/s → 5300/35 = 151.4 tok/sec. BW ratio: 151.4/95.7 = 1.58× (matches FP16 ratio exactly). Compute ceiling check: 70B FLOPs per token requires 2 FLOPs per parameter = 140 GFLOPs/token. H100 INT4: 2,467 TOPS → 2,467T / 140G = 17,621 tok/sec compute ceiling. Both are 184× above actual throughput → confirmed memory-bound. MI300X 192GB enables fitting three 70B INT4 models simultaneously (3×35GB = 105GB < 192GB) vs one per H100 — 3× serving density advantage.
details.realistic_solution: INT4 model on H100: 35GB weight fits in 80GB (45GB slack for KV cache and activations). On MI300X: 35GB in 192GB (157GB slack). The key question: is INT4 decode memory-bound or compute-bound? For dequantize-then-FP16 GEMM (most common path): weights load as INT4 (0.5 bytes/param), dequantize to FP16 before multiply. Effective memory bandwidth requirement: 35GB × throughput. Arithmetic intensity: for batch=1, AI ≈ 2 FLOP/byte (similar to FP16 decode). Memory-bound. H100 bandwidth: 3,350 GB/s. INT4 weights: 35GB load per forward pass. At batch=1: H100 decode = 3,350 GB/s / 35GB = 95.7 passes/sec = 95.7 tok/sec. MI300X: 5,300 / 35 = 151.4 tok/sec. MI300X advantage: 1.58× — identical ratio to FP16 case, confirming bandwidth is still the bottleneck.

scenario: A 70B LLM is quantized to INT4 using GPTQ (group size 128). The INT4 weight size is 35GB. On an H100 SXM5 (80GB), INT4 inference achieves 2,467 TOPS INT4 throughput. On an MI300X (192GB), ROCm reports 2,614 TOPS INT4. Compare the token generation throughput advantage of each approach and determine whether the MI300X's memory bandwidth advantage persists under INT4 quantization.
title: MI300X INT4 Quantization: VRAM and Throughput vs H100

details.common_mistake: Attributing the loss divergence to BF16's lower precision mantissa (7 bits vs FP16's 10 bits). BF16 actually has better dynamic range than FP16 (8 exponent bits vs 5), making it more numerically stable for gradient training. The problem is accumulation precision, not weight precision.
details.napkin_math: BF16 precision: 1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 mantissa = 16 bits. FP32 accumulator: 1+8+23 = 32 bits. Gradient magnitude at LR=1e-4 and batch=512: typical gradient ≈ 1e-4 to 1e-3. BF16 representable step at magnitude 1e-3: epsilon = 2^-7 × 1e-3 ≈ 7.8e-6. FP32 epsilon at 1e-3: 2^-23 × 1e-3 ≈ 1.2e-10. Rounding error in BF16 accumulation: 7.8e-6 per multiply-add. Over 1B accumulations in a large matmul: drift ≈ √(1e9) × 7.8e-6 = 0.25. FP32 drift: √(1e9) × 1.2e-10 = 3.8e-3. BF16 accumulation introduces 66× larger numerical drift — explains 1.8% loss gap.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is BF16 accumulation in MXU (TPU's matrix unit). H100 Tensor Cores accumulate in FP32 even when inputs are FP16 — this is critical for gradient accumulation across large batch sizes and long sequences where small gradient signals would otherwise be rounded to zero in lower precision accumulators. TPU v5e MXU can be configured for BF16 accumulation (fast) or FP32 accumulation (slower but numerically accurate). If the team used BF16 matmul with BF16 accumulation, gradient updates for small learning rates are systematically rounded, causing the loss divergence. Fix: enable FP32 accumulation in JAX/XLA via `jax.lax.Precision.HIGHEST` or `tf.matmul(..., use_32bit_accumulation=True)`. Expected performance cost: ~15-25% throughput reduction. Alternatively, use stochastic rounding (available on TPU v5e) which provides unbiased accumulation in BF16 with minimal throughput cost.

scenario: A team migrates transformer training from H100 (FP16 with FP32 accumulation via Tensor Cores) to TPU v5e (BF16 with BF16 accumulation). After 50K training steps, the TPU run shows 1.8% higher loss than the H100 baseline at the same number of steps. Diagnose the root cause and propose a fix without switching back to H100.
title: TPU v5e BF16 Accumulation and Training Stability vs H100

details.common_mistake: Assuming the performance gap (1,307 - 1,050 = 257 TFLOPS, 80.3% efficiency) is entirely due to thermal throttling. Memory bandwidth saturation, kernel efficiency (wave quantization, register spilling), and software overhead all contribute to sub-peak utilization even without thermal constraints.
details.napkin_math: MI300X heat density: 750W/192GB = 3.9W/GB. H100: 700W/80GB = 8.75W/GB (higher per-memory, lower per-FLOP). Thermal resistance to ambient (data center inlet): assume θ_ja = 0.05°C/W. MI300X: ΔT = 0.05 × 742W = 37.1°C above coolant. At 55°C coolant: junction = 92.1°C. 3°C from throttle. H100: 0.05 × 700×0.985 = 34.5°C above coolant. At 46.5°C coolant: 81°C junction = 2°C below stated 83°C. Both operating near thermal limits. In a 8-GPU HGX system: MI300X total = 8×750W = 6,000W. H100: 8×700W = 5,600W. Cooling capacity delta: 400W = additional cooling requirement for MI300X 8-card system.
details.realistic_solution: Thermal analysis: MI300X at 92°C with 95°C threshold = 3°C headroom. At 742W out of 750W TDP: 98.9% power draw. The GPU is operating at near-maximum power without throttling, but with minimal thermal margin. Any workload spike (batch size increase, longer sequences) will push it over 95°C and trigger throttling. H100 at 1.5°C below 83°C threshold = at 81.5°C, with TDP 700W — operating with more proportional headroom. Performance gap analysis: 1,050/1,307 = 80.3% efficiency. At 742W of 750W (98.9% power utilization), compute efficiency is 80.3% — the gap is not thermal (would be lower if throttling). It is kernel efficiency (GEMM wave quantization, occupancy). Thermal recommendation: MI300X requires better cooling (liquid cooling, higher airflow) to maintain the 3°C margin. With standard air cooling, sustained 750W in a dense cluster risks thermal throttling. H100's 700W TDP in the same enclosure has 7% lower heat density per GPU.

scenario: An MI300X GPU (TDP 750W) is running a training workload. Under sustained FP16 GEMM at 90% GPU utilization, measured throughput is 1,050 TFLOPS against the 1,307 TFLOPS peak. The cooling system is rated for 750W steady-state. An engineer notices the GPU's thermal sensor reads 92°C (throttle threshold: 95°C) and power draw is 742W. An H100 SXM5 (TDP 700W) running the same relative workload measures 1.5°C below its 83°C throttle threshold. Analyze whether the MI300X is thermals-limited in this configuration and compare thermal headroom.
title: MI300X Power Budget and Thermal Throttling Under Full Load

details.common_mistake: Attributing hardware capability differences when the bottleneck is clearly software (kernel availability). The roofline analysis shows MI300X should be faster, so any throughput deficit is a software/ecosystem issue, not a hardware limitation.
details.napkin_math: Attention FLOPs for 70B, N=2048, 80 layers: naive attention memory = N² × num_heads × L × 2 bytes (attention scores, not N²×d). For 64 heads: N²×64×80×2 = 4M×64×80×2 = 42.9 GB — impossible to materialize. Scaled to single layer (batch=1): N²×64×2 = 4M×128 = 512MB per layer. FlashAttention: uses SRAM tiles, memory traffic ≈ 2×N×d_head×num_heads×2 = 2×2048×128×64×2 = 67MB per layer — 7.6× less. The real gain is avoiding slow HBM random access. Without FlashAttention on ROCm, HBM access patterns are suboptimal.
details.realistic_solution: FlashAttention-2 impact: naive attention is O(N²) memory I/O (materializes full N×N attention matrix per head). FlashAttention-2 is O(N) memory I/O via tiled SRAM-based computation. For N=2048 with 64 heads, naive attention writes/reads N²×num_heads×2bytes = 2048²×64×2 = 512 MB per layer per forward pass. FlashAttention-2: tiles fit in SRAM, reduces to ~67 MB per layer. Bandwidth savings: ~7.6×. If H100 uses FlashAttention-2 and MI300X falls back to naive: H100 effective attention BW use: 67 MB per layer. MI300X: 512 MB per layer. On H100: 67 MB / 3,350 GB/s = 0.02ms/layer. On MI300X: 512 MB / 5,300 GB/s = 0.097ms/layer. MI300X is ~5× slower on attention despite superior bandwidth — this largely explains the 85% throughput gap. With proper FlashAttention on ROCm: expected MI300X throughput = 1.58× H100.

scenario: A team evaluating MI300X for production serving finds that vLLM on ROCm achieves 85% of the throughput of vLLM on H100 despite the MI300X having 58% more memory bandwidth. A CUDA kernel profiler shows the H100 run uses FlashAttention-2 (custom CUDA kernel), while the ROCm run falls back to a naive attention implementation. Quantify the performance gap attributable to software maturity vs hardware capability, and estimate the timeline to close it.
title: ROCm vs CUDA Ecosystem Overhead for MI300X Deployment

details.common_mistake: Assuming hardware MIG (H100) is always superior to software partitioning (MI300X). For small model serving with strong isolation requirements, MIG provides better fault isolation. But for flexible multi-model serving with variable model sizes, software scheduling on a large unified memory pool can be more efficient.
details.napkin_math: H100 MIG: 2 GPUs × 7 instances = 14 instances. Memory: 14 × 10GB = 140GB allocated, 14 × 7GB = 98GB used → 30% waste. Bandwidth per instance: 3350/7 = 479 GB/s. Decode throughput per model: 479 × 0.8 / 14 GFLOP = 27.4 tok/sec/model. MI300X: 192GB for 14 × 7GB = 98GB used, 94GB free. Bandwidth: 5300 GB/s shared. Per model bandwidth (fair share): 5300/14 = 379 GB/s → 379 × 0.8 / 14 = 21.7 tok/sec/model. H100 MIG wins per-model throughput (27.4 vs 21.7) due to 2× more GPUs and dedicated slices, but at 2× hardware cost. Single MI300X total: 5300/7×0.8/1 GFLOP = decode for 14 models at 21.7 vs H100 2-GPU MIG at 27.4 — but MI300X uses 1 GPU vs 2 H100s.
details.realistic_solution: H100 MIG approach: 2 H100s × 7 MIG instances each = 14 instances × 10GB each. Hardware memory isolation: one tenant's OOM cannot affect others. Throughput per instance: ~140 GFLOPS and ~480 GB/s bandwidth slice. Fixed partitioning: a 7GB model uses 10GB instance, wasting 3GB per instance = 42GB waste across 14 instances. MI300X software approach: 1 MI300X × 192GB unified pool. KV cache and model weights co-located. ROCM compute partition modes (CPX mode): 8 XCDs can be assigned to processes, giving 8 compute domains. For 14 models, use 1 MI300X with MPS (Multi-Process Service equivalent in ROCm) + memory protection via IOMMU. Memory: 14 × 7GB = 98GB < 192GB, fits with 94GB KV cache headroom. Throughput: full 5,300 GB/s shared across models with fair-scheduling. Hardware isolation: weaker than MIG — software isolation only. For regulated tenants: use 2× MI300X with compute partitioning (7 models each). MI300X advantage: 3× better memory utilization, 1.58× higher aggregate decode throughput, but weaker isolation guarantees.

scenario: H100 supports Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitioning into up to 7 GPU instances (each with 10GB memory slice). AMD MI300X does not natively support MIG-equivalent hardware partitioning. A cloud operator needs to serve 14 concurrent small (7GB) models to different tenants. Compare the H100 MIG vs MI300X software-based partitioning approach, and design the MI300X multi-tenant architecture.
title: MI300X MIG vs H100 MIG: Multi-Tenant Serving Partitioning

details.common_mistake: Mapping tensor parallelism to the highest-latency torus dimension. TP requires the most frequent and latency-sensitive AllReduces (every transformer layer, every forward pass). TP must be mapped to the dimension with lowest hop count and highest bandwidth — the shortest torus axis.
details.napkin_math: MoE 1T params: 1T × 2 bytes FP16 = 2TB. Distributed across 2048 chips: 1GB/chip average. TP AllReduce per layer: 2 × (N-1)/N × activation_size. Activation: 2048 tokens × 16384 hidden × 2 bytes = 67MB. TP=8: 2 × 7/8 × 67MB = 117MB. 128 layers: 15GB. ICI ring: 15GB / 200GB/s = 75ms. H100 NVLink: 15GB / 450GB/s = 33ms. But H100 PP=16 over IB: pipeline stage activation = 2048×16384×2 = 67MB. IB: 67MB/50GB/s = 1.3ms per stage × 16 stages = 21ms pipeline latency per micro-batch. TPU: 67MB/200GB/s = 0.34ms × 16 = 5.4ms. TPU 4× faster for PP. For 2048 micro-batches: H100 PP overhead = 2048 × 21ms = 43s. TPU = 11s. Training throughput impact is dominated by PP latency at this scale.
details.realistic_solution: Torus mapping: TP=8 → 8-chip axis (lowest latency, highest bandwidth within node-equivalent group). PP=16 → one 16-chip axis (point-to-point pipeline sends, latency-tolerant). EP=16 → remaining 16-chip axis (all-to-all for expert routing). Communication per step: TP AllReduce: 2 × (8-1)/8 × (hidden=16384 × seq=2048 × 2 bytes) = 2 × 0.875 × 67MB = 117MB per layer × 128 layers = 15GB total. At ICI 1600 Gbps = 200 GB/s per chip: T_TP = 15GB/200 = 75ms (ring across 8 chips). PP bubble overhead: with PP=16, micro-batch pipeline has (PP-1)/PP = 93.75% efficiency with 1F1B. EP all-to-all: route to 16 experts, each forward/backward = 2 × MoE_input × top-k/16. H100 comparison: TP=8 via NVLink (900 GB/s per pair): T_TP = 15GB/450 = 33ms. PP and EP via 400Gbps InfiniBand: T_PP = point-to-point 100GB/50GB/s = 2s — catastrophically slow for pipeline. TPU v5e wins by using ICI (200 GB/s) for PP instead of InfiniBand (50 GB/s), making the H100 cluster ~4× slower for pipeline-parallel steps.

scenario: Training a 1T MoE model requires 2,048 TPU v5e chips using 3D model parallelism: TP=8, PP=16, EP=16 (expert parallelism). Each dimension requires distinct collective communication patterns. The ICI topology is a 3D torus (16×16×8). Map each parallelism dimension to the torus axes, calculate the communication volume per step, and compare against an equivalent H100 cluster using NVLink for TP and InfiniBand for PP+EP.
title: TPU v5e Pod AllReduce Topology for 1T Model Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming MI300X unified memory means all 192GB has identical bandwidth from the GPU perspective. CPU pages and GPU pages in the unified HBM pool may have different NUMA distances on MI300X — GPU-originated accesses to GPU-local pages are fast; CPU-pinned pages accessed by GPU may have higher latency through the driver/IOMMU path.
details.napkin_math: H100 PCIe offload bandwidth: 128 GB/s bidirectional = 64 GB/s per direction. 1GB KV block fetch: 1/64 = 15.6ms (one-directional). MI300X Infinity Fabric (CPU↔GPU within unified pool): ~500-900 GB/s depending on access pattern. 1GB fetch: 1/900 = 1.1ms. Speedup: 15.6/1.1 = 14×. For p99 at 200 concurrent users with 5% cold cache miss rate: H100: 200×0.05×15.6ms = 156ms added latency per request. MI300X: 200×0.05×1.1ms = 11ms. H100 blows p99 latency budget; MI300X maintains sub-20ms cold-cache overhead.
details.realistic_solution: H100 PCIe offloading: 80GB VRAM holds model weights (but 180GB model needs TP=3 across 3 H100s). Single H100 approach: keep hot KV cache (50GB working set) on GPU, offload cold KV (130GB) to CPU DRAM via PCIe 5.0. Fetch latency: 1GB KV block / 128 GB/s = 7.8ms per fetch. At 200 concurrent requests, each needing occasional cold cache fetch: 200 × 7.8ms = 1.56s latency spike — unacceptable for p99. MI300X: 192GB unified pool. 180GB model + 50GB hot KV = 230GB — still doesn't fit entirely. But MI300X can split differently: 180GB model weight in GPU-local HBM pages, 12GB for hot KV cache. Cold KV (130GB) in CPU-accessible pages of the unified pool — accessed via NUMA-local path with ~1 TB/s effective bandwidth (Infinity Fabric to CPU). Fetch latency: 1GB / 1000 GB/s = 1ms vs 7.8ms on H100 PCIe. 7.8× faster cold cache access. Alternative: use 2× MI300X with TP=2 — 384GB total, fits entire model + full KV cache with no offloading needed.

scenario: The MI300X uses a unified memory architecture where the CPU and GPU share the same physical HBM3 pool (192GB total, accessible by both CPU and GPU without explicit copy). An H100 PCIe connects to CPU DRAM via PCIe 5.0 (128 GB/s). A 180GB model must be loaded and served (too large for H100's 80GB without splitting). Compare the KV cache offloading strategy on H100 PCIe (offload KV cache to CPU DRAM) vs MI300X unified memory for a serving workload with 50GB working set and 130GB KV cache.
title: MI300X Unified Memory for CPU-GPU Tensor Offloading vs H100 PCIe

details.common_mistake: Using theoretical TFLOPS × chip count without accounting for LoRA's unique computation profile. LoRA fine-tuning is not purely matmul-dominated — the frozen backbone runs in inference mode (no gradient accumulation through most layers), and only the small adapter matrices require gradient computation. The effective FLOP count is much lower than full fine-tuning.
details.napkin_math: LoRA backward: only 40M/7B = 0.57% of parameters require gradient. Effective backward FLOPs: 0.57% of full backward. Full step FLOPs: forward (7B) + backward (7B + 40M) ≈ 4×7B×64×512 = 9.2×10¹⁴. Total training: 46875 × 9.2×10¹⁴ = 4.3×10¹⁹. TPU 16: 16×197×10¹²×0.55 = 1.73×10¹⁵/s → 4.3×10¹⁹/1.73×10¹⁵ = 24,855s = 6.9h. H100 8: 8×989×10¹²×0.50 = 3.96×10¹⁵/s → 10,859s = 3.0h. Cost: TPU = 6.9×16×$1.20 = $132. H100 = 3.0×8×$3.50 = $84. H100 still 36% cheaper. Note: TPU wins when using 128+ chips on 100B+ models.
details.realistic_solution: LoRA training FLOPs: forward pass (full 7B model): 2 × 7B × batch × seq ≈ 2 × 7B × 64 × 512 = 4.6×10¹⁴ FLOPs/step. Backward pass through LoRA adapters only: 2 × 40M × 64 × 512 = 2.6×10¹² FLOPs/step. Total: ≈ 4.6×10¹⁴ FLOPs/step. Steps: 1M × 3 / 64 = 46,875 steps. Total FLOPs: 46,875 × 4.6×10¹⁴ = 2.16×10¹⁹ FLOPs. TPU v5e 16 chips at MFU=55%: 16 × 197 TFLOPS × 0.55 = 1,732 GFLOPS effective = 1.73×10¹⁵ FLOPS/sec. Time: 2.16×10¹⁹ / 1.73×10¹⁵ = 12,486 sec = 3.47 hours. H100 8 GPUs at MFU=50%: 8 × 989 × 0.50 = 3,956 GFLOPS = 3.96×10¹⁵ FLOPS/sec. Time: 2.16×10¹⁹ / 3.96×10¹⁵ = 5,455 sec = 1.52 hours. Cost: TPU v5e: 3.47 × 16 × $1.20 = $66.6. H100: 1.52 × 8 × $3.50 = $42.6. H100 wins on time (2.3× faster) and cost (36% cheaper) for this LoRA workload. TPU advantage emerges at much larger scales (thousands of chips).

scenario: A team runs LoRA fine-tuning (rank=16) on a 7B base model using a dataset of 1M samples, batch size 64, 3 epochs on both TPU v5e (16 chips) and H100 (8 GPUs, NVLink). The LoRA adapter has 40M trainable parameters. TPU v5e achieves 197 TFLOPS BF16 per chip; H100 achieves 989 TFLOPS FP16 per GPU. Which configuration finishes faster, and what is the per-dollar cost comparison assuming $1.2/chip-hr TPU v5e and $3.5/GPU-hr H100?
title: TPU v5e vs H100 for Fine-Tuning LoRA at Scale

details.common_mistake: Computing KV cache only for a single layer instead of all layers. The full KV cache memory = per_token_per_layer × num_layers × context_length. For a 40-layer model, this multiplies the per-layer figure by 40.
details.napkin_math: KV per token all layers: 2 × 40 heads × 128 dim × 40 layers × 2 bytes (FP16) = 2×40×128×40×2 = 819,200 bytes = 800KB/token. 128K tokens: 800KB × 128K = 102.4GB per request. Weights: 26GB. A100/H100 (80GB): 80-26=54GB available < 102.4GB needed. Cannot serve. MI300X (192GB): 192-26=166GB. 1 request uses 102.4GB → 63.6GB left. 2nd request needs 102.4 > 63.6 → cannot fit 2. MI300X: 1 concurrent 128K request. Contrast: at 4K context: 800KB × 4K = 3.2GB per request. A100: (54GB / 3.2GB) = 16 concurrent. H100: 16. MI300X: 51 concurrent. MI300X advantage scales with context length.
details.realistic_solution: Per-token KV cache (all 40 layers): 40 layers × 20.5KB = 820KB per token. For 128K context: 820KB × 128,000 tokens = 105GB per request. Weight memory: 13B × 2 bytes = 26GB. Available KV cache memory: A100 (80GB): 80 - 26 = 54GB. Requests: floor(54GB / 105GB) = 0 — cannot serve a single 128K request. H100 (80GB): same, 0 requests. MI300X (192GB): 192 - 26 = 166GB. floor(166 / 105) = 1 request (with 61GB remaining). For 2 concurrent 128K requests: need 26 + 2×105 = 236GB — requires 2× MI300X (TP=2 not needed for weight, but needed for KV cache). MI300X is the only single-card option that can serve 128K context at all — and even then, only 1 request at a time. This is a case where H100 and A100 are architecturally unsuitable regardless of compute performance.

scenario: A legal AI application requires serving a 13B model with 128K context length. KV cache per token per layer: 2 × num_heads × head_dim × 2 bytes = 2 × 40 × 128 × 2 = 20.5KB per token. Calculate the KV cache size for a single 128K context request. Determine how many concurrent 128K requests an A100 80GB, H100 80GB, and MI300X 192GB can serve simultaneously (all hosting the same 13B model in FP16).
title: MI300X vs A100: VRAM Capacity Advantage for Long-Context Serving

details.common_mistake: Assuming prefill is always memory-bound like decode. For long sequences, attention's AI scales with sequence length, eventually crossing the roofline ridge point and becoming compute-bound. At N=32K with d_head=128, AI≈250 is above H100's ridge (295) but below, and above A100's ridge (156) — the crossover behavior differs per accelerator.
details.napkin_math: AI for attention at N=32K, d_head=128: FLOPs = 2×H×N²×d = 2×40×32K²×128 = 2×40×1024M×128 = 10.5T. Memory = 2×H×N×d×2bytes (Q,K matrices) + H×N²×2bytes (attention map) = 2×40×32K×128×2 + 40×32K²×2 = 655MB + 83.9GB ≈ 84.6GB. AI = 10.5T/84.6G = 124 FLOP/byte (not 250 — the simplified formula overestimates). At AI=124: all below H100 ridge (295) and MI300X ridge (247): all memory-bound. Effective: A100: 2000×124 = 248 TFLOPS. H100: 3350×124 = 415 TFLOPS. MI300X: 5300×124 = 657 TFLOPS. MI300X still wins by 1.58× over H100 — bandwidth advantage persists.
details.realistic_solution: Ridge points: A100: 312 TFLOPS / 2,000 GB/s = 156 FLOP/byte. H100: 989 / 3,350 = 295.2 FLOP/byte. MI300X: 1,307 / 5,300 = 246.6 FLOP/byte. At AI=250: A100: AI=250 > ridge=156 → compute-bound. Effective throughput = 312 TFLOPS (full compute). H100: AI=250 < ridge=295 → memory-bound. Effective: 3,350 GB/s × 250 = 838 TFLOPS. MI300X: AI=250 > ridge=247 → compute-bound (barely). Effective: 1,307 TFLOPS (full compute). Throughput ranking at AI=250: A100 (312) < MI300X (1,307) ≈ H100 (838). Wait — H100 effective is 838 (memory-bound) vs MI300X 1,307 (compute-bound). MI300X wins prefill by 1,307/838 = 1.56×. A100 is far behind at 312. Key insight: MI300X's higher TFLOPS makes it compute-bound (good for prefill) while H100 remains memory-bound at this AI. For very long contexts (N→∞, AI→∞), all accelerators become compute-bound and MI300X dominates by raw TFLOPS.

scenario: During prefill (processing a 32K-token prompt), attention computes QK^T of shape [H, N, N] where H=40 heads and N=32K tokens. The arithmetic intensity of this operation is 2N/(2×d_head + 2×N) ≈ N/d_head for large N. With d_head=128, AI ≈ 250 FLOP/byte at N=32K. A100 SXM4 (312 TFLOPS FP16, 2TB/s), H100 SXM5 (989 TFLOPS, 3.35 TB/s), MI300X (1,307 TFLOPS, 5.3 TB/s). Which accelerator is compute-bound for prefill at this AI, and what are the expected FLOP efficiencies?
title: MI300X Prefill Throughput: Compute-Bound vs H100 for Long Prompts

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that TPU v5e has only 16GB HBM — the 14GB model leaves only 2GB for KV cache. A single v5e cannot realistically serve the 7B model without tensor parallelism across multiple chips, fundamentally changing the compute topology.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e decode BW: 819 GB/s. Model: 14GB. Single chip: 819/14 = 58.5 tok/sec. KV constraint: 2GB remaining → ~240 concurrent tokens at 8MB/req. With TP=2: 117 tok/sec per pair (halved per chip, doubled chips). MI300X: 5300/14 = 379 tok/sec, 178GB KV headroom. Scale: 1.157M tok/sec ÷ 379 = 3,054 MI300X cards. Cost/day: 3,054×$5.5×24 = $403K. TPU: 9,892 chips ÷ 2 per pair = 4,946 pairs, 9,892 chips × $1.2 × 24 = $284K/day. TPU is $2.85/1M vs MI300X $4.03/1M = 29% cheaper despite lower per-chip performance.
details.realistic_solution: TPU v5e: 16GB per chip, 14GB model → only 2GB KV cache per chip → TP=2 minimum (8GB KV cache per pair). With TP=2: 2 chips share 14GB weights + 2×(16-7)GB = 18GB KV cache. Bandwidth for decode (TP=2): each chip loads half of weights: 7GB per forward pass. Per-chip BW: 819 GB/s → tokens per chip per second: 819/7 = 117 tok/sec → 2 chips: 234 tok/sec per TP=2 pair. For 100B tok/day: 100B/86400 = 1,157,407 tok/sec needed. Pairs needed: 1,157,407/234 = 4,946 pairs = 9,892 chips. Cost: 9,892 × ($1.2/hr) × (24 hr/day) = $284,889/day. Per 1M tokens: $284,889/(100,000) = $2.85/1M tokens. MI300X: 14GB model in 192GB, 178GB KV cache. Single card: 5,300/14 = 379 tok/sec. GPUs needed: 1,157,407/379 = 3,054. Cost: 3,054 × $5.5 × 24 = $403,128/day. Per 1M tokens: $4.03/1M tokens. TPU v5e wins on cost by 29% despite needing 3.2× more chips. MI300X wins if you can negotiate better GPU pricing (<$4.5/GPU-hr) or if serving latency requires lower TP fan-out.

scenario: You are choosing infrastructure for serving a 7B LLM at 100B tokens/day. TPU v5e: $1.2/chip-hr, 197 TFLOPS BF16, 819 GB/s, 16GB HBM. MI300X: $5.5/GPU-hr (cloud estimate), 1,307 TFLOPS FP16, 5,300 GB/s, 192GB HBM. The 7B model (FP16, 14GB) requires memory bandwidth for decode. Calculate chips/GPUs needed, total cost per 1M tokens, and identify which platform wins on cost at this scale.
title: TPU v5e vs MI300X: Serving Cost Per Token at Scale

details.common_mistake: Using total fabric bandwidth (896 GB/s or 900 GB/s aggregate) instead of per-GPU link bandwidth for ring AllReduce. Ring AllReduce uses each GPU's send and receive bandwidth, not total cross-sectional bandwidth. Each GPU in an 8-GPU ring sends to exactly one neighbor and receives from exactly one neighbor.
details.napkin_math: Gradient size: 7B × 4 bytes (FP32) = 28GB. Ring AllReduce: 2×(7/8)×28GB = 49GB transferred. H100 NVLink per-GPU BW: 450 GB/s send (900 GB/s bidirectional / 2). T_H100 = 49/450 = 0.109s = 109ms. MI300X xGMI per-GPU: scenario states 128 GB/s per pair in full-mesh; using 128 GB/s. T_MI300X = 49/128 = 0.383s = 383ms. NVLink is 3.5× faster. Training step compute: 7B params × 6 × batch 64 × seq 512 = 1,376 TFLOPs ÷ (8 × 989 TFLOPS × 0.50) = 1376/3956 = 0.348s = 348ms. MI300X: ÷ (8 × 1307 × 0.50) = 1376/5228 = 0.263s = 263ms. H100: compute 348ms + AllReduce 109ms = 457ms per step. MI300X: compute 263ms + AllReduce 383ms = 646ms per step. H100 is 1.4× faster for 8-GPU data parallel training — xGMI is the bottleneck.
details.realistic_solution: Ring AllReduce formula: T = 2 × (N-1)/N × M / B_per_link. MI300X xGMI: scenario specifies full-mesh at 128 GB/s per GPU pair. For ring topology each GPU uses one link at 128 GB/s. T_MI300X = 2 × (7/8) × 14GB / 128GB/s = 0.191s = 191ms. H100 NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s per GPU bidirectional = 450 GB/s per direction. T_H100 = 2 × (7/8) × 14GB / 450GB/s = 0.054s = 54ms. H100 is 3.5× faster for gradient AllReduce. For a training step with 200ms compute time: H100 communication overhead = 27%, MI300X = 96% (communication-dominated). MI300X needs gradient compression or a dedicated high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU fabric to be competitive with H100 NVLink for data-parallel training.

scenario: An 8-GPU MI300X server uses AMD's xGMI/Infinity Fabric interconnect providing 896 GB/s total bidirectional bandwidth between GPUs (equivalent to a full-mesh at 128 GB/s per GPU pair). An 8-GPU H100 SXM5 server uses NVLink 4.0 at 900 GB/s per GPU bidirectional. For data parallel training of a 7B model, the gradient AllReduce after each backward pass transfers 14GB of FP32 gradients. Calculate the AllReduce time on both platforms using ring-AllReduce.
title: MI300X AllReduce Performance in 8-GPU Data Parallel Training vs H100

details.common_mistake: Treating MoE serving the same as dense model serving and ignoring expert routing overhead. Only 2 of 8 experts are activated per token — the inactive expert weights still occupy memory but don't contribute to compute. The effective arithmetic intensity is that of a 2×7B model, not 8×7B.
details.napkin_math: MoE effective weight per token: 2 active experts × 7B × 2 bytes = 28GB loaded per forward pass. H100 (TP=2): each GPU holds 56GB, serves 14GB per GPU per forward. Per GPU: 3350/14 = 239 tok/sec per GPU = 239/2 × 2 = 239 tok/sec total (TP=2 doesn't double throughput, both GPUs load their half simultaneously). Actually TP=2: both GPUs load in parallel → total BW = 2×3350 = 6700 GB/s loading 28GB → 6700/28 = 239 tok/sec. MI300X (single): 5300 GB/s loading 28GB → 5300/28 = 189 tok/sec. H100 TP=2 wins slightly (239 vs 189)! But MI300X uses 1 GPU vs 2 H100s. Per-GPU cost: MI300X at $5.50/hr, H100 at $3.50/hr×2=$7.00/hr. MI300X cost per million tokens: (1/189)hr/1M×$5.50 = $0.029/1M. H100: (1/239)×$7.00 = $0.029/1M — exactly tied on cost per token.
details.realistic_solution: Effective model for compute: 2 active experts × 7B = 14B effective parameters per forward pass. But all 112GB must reside in memory for routing. H100 TP=2 configuration: each GPU holds 56GB (half of 112GB). Expert routing requires AllReduce across GPUs if the activated expert is on the other GPU. Cross-GPU expert routing: 50% probability that a token's top-2 experts span both GPUs → 50% of tokens require data transfer. Transfer: token activation (8192×2 bytes = 16KB per token). At 200 tok/batch: 200×16KB×0.5 = 1.6MB per AllReduce. NVLink latency: 1.6MB/450 = 3.6µs — negligible. H100 TP=2 decode throughput: effective BW per GPU for active experts: 3,350/2 = 1,675 GB/s, loading 14GB active weights per forward: 1,675/14 = 119.6 tok/sec. MI300X single-card: load 14GB active experts from 192GB pool. BW: 5,300 GB/s. Throughput: 5,300/14 = 378.6 tok/sec — 3.2× higher than H100 TP=2. No cross-GPU expert routing needed. MI300X is massively superior for MoE serving at this scale.

scenario: A Mixtral 8×7B MoE model has 8 experts, each 7B parameters, with top-2 routing (2 experts activated per token). Full model size: 8 × 14GB (FP16) = 112GB. On an H100 (80GB), this requires 2-GPU tensor parallel to hold the model. On a single MI300X (192GB), the full model fits with 80GB spare. Design the optimal serving configuration for each platform and calculate expected decode throughput.
title: MI300X for Mixture-of-Experts: Expert Capacity and Memory Layout

details.common_mistake: Making the decision purely on TFLOPS/dollar or memory bandwidth. For a 5-year commitment, ecosystem lock-in, software compatibility, and upgrade path risk often dominate pure hardware metrics. A 20% performance advantage is worthless if your entire model training stack requires 18 months to port.
details.napkin_math: 5-year TCO comparison (1,000 GPU equivalent, 100B tok/day): H100 cloud: 1,000 × $3.50/hr × 8,760 × 5 = $153M. MI300X cloud: equivalent capacity at 1.58× throughput/GPU → 633 GPUs × $5.50 × 8,760 × 5 = $152M — essentially tied. TPU v5e equivalent: 5,000 chips × $1.20 × 8,760 × 5 = $263M (requires more chips due to 16GB constraint). Migration cost (if pivot needed at year 3): H100→H200: $0 code change. H100→MI300X: 6-12 month eng effort ($2-5M). H100→TPU: 18-24 month rewrite ($10-20M). Risk-adjusted TCO: H100 = $153M + low migration risk. TPU = $263M + high lock-in risk. Decision: H100 primary.
details.realistic_solution: H100/H200 (CUDA): Ecosystem: 95%+ of open-source ML frameworks support CUDA natively. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX all run on CUDA without modification. Software risk: LOW. Upgrade path: H200 (141GB HBM3e, 4.8 TB/s) is backward-compatible. B200 planned. Hardware risk: LOW. Portability: code runs on any NVIDIA GPU from A10 to H200. Lock-in: NVIDIA-only, but CUDA runs on cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) — cloud portability HIGH. MI300X (ROCm): Ecosystem: ROCm supports most PyTorch ops but with occasional fallbacks to CPU for unsupported kernels. vLLM, DeepSpeed have ROCm ports at ~3-6 month lag from CUDA releases. Software risk: MEDIUM (improving rapidly). Hardware risk: LOW (AMD roadmap: MI400X). Cloud availability: Azure + Oracle, not GCP. TPU v5e (XLA): Ecosystem: JAX-first, PyTorch-XLA requires significant code adaptation. Most HuggingFace models require porting. Software risk: HIGH for non-JAX codebases. Lock-in: GCP-only, no on-prem option. Portability: near-zero without rewrite. Recommendation: Primary H100/H200 (low risk, maximum optionality). Hedge 20% of workload on MI300X (price pressure on NVIDIA, improving ROCm). Avoid TPU as primary unless already JAX-native.

scenario: A large ML platform team must choose a primary accelerator for a 5-year infrastructure commitment. They will train and serve models from 7B to 100B parameters at 1B tokens/day. Candidates: H100/H200 (CUDA ecosystem, wide software support), MI300X (ROCm, AMD), TPU v5e (XLA/JAX only, GCP-locked). Conduct a multi-axis vendor risk analysis covering: software ecosystem maturity, hardware upgrade path, workload portability, and total cost of ownership. Recommend a primary and hedge strategy.
title: Vendor Lock-In Analysis: TPU v5e vs MI300X vs H100 for a 5-Year Infrastructure Plan

details.common_mistake: Applying the 4/5ths rule to mean similarity scores directly. The ratio 0.74/0.81 = 91% looks acceptable. But the 4/5ths rule applies to selection rates (fraction of each group selected), not to mean scores. A small difference in means can cause severe disparate impact at a fixed selection threshold.
details.napkin_math: Group A: P(Z > (0.831-0.81)/0.06) = P(Z > 0.35) = 36.3%. Group B: P(Z > (0.831-0.74)/0.06) = P(Z > 1.517) = 6.5%. 4/5ths: 6.5/36.3 = 17.9%. Selections from 5000 per group: A=1815, B=325. Representation in selected pool: A=84.8%, B=15.2% vs 50/50 population. Group-conditional threshold fix: each group uses its own 80th-percentile threshold (A=0.861, B=0.791). Each group selects exactly 20% of its members. No disparate impact by construction. Cost: requires demographic labels for threshold calibration.
details.realistic_solution: Estimate the selection threshold for top 20% of the combined population. Combined mean approx 0.78, std 0.06. 80th percentile: 0.78 + 0.842*0.06 = 0.831. Group A selection rate: P(X > 0.831 | mean=0.81, std=0.06) = P(Z > 0.35) = 36.3%. Group B selection rate: P(X > 0.831 | mean=0.74, std=0.06) = P(Z > 1.517) = 6.5%. Disparate impact ratio: 6.5/36.3 = 17.9% — far below the 80% threshold. The system has severe disparate impact despite appearing acceptable by mean score comparison. Fix options: (1) group-conditional thresholds calibrated so each group selects 20% of its own distribution, (2) audit the job description embedding for demographic bias using WEAT (Word Embedding Association Test), (3) retrain embeddings with adversarial debiasing loss that penalizes demographic predictability from the embedding space.

scenario: An embedding model is used for resume screening: candidates are ranked by cosine similarity of their resume embedding to a job description embedding. A legal team raises concerns about disparate impact. You measure average cosine similarity for Group A (majority) = 0.81 and Group B (minority) = 0.74. The EEOC 4/5ths rule requires the selection rate of the protected group to be at least 80% of the majority group. If you rank the top 20% of 10,000 candidates, estimate the selection rates for each group assuming Gaussian similarity distributions (std=0.06) and determine whether the system violates the 4/5ths rule.
title: Disparate Impact Testing for LLM Embedding Spaces

details.common_mistake: Candidates conflate compute FLOPS with memory bandwidth, assuming the higher-FLOPS chip always wins on throughput. Memory-bandwidth-bound workloads (most transformer inference) are governed by bandwidth, not FLOPS.
details.napkin_math: Assume 1 token/s ≈ 1.5 GB/s of model weight streaming (70B model, 2 bytes/param). H100: 3,350 GB/s / 1.5 = ~2,233 tokens/s per chip. MI300X: 5,300 GB/s / 1.5 = ~3,533 tokens/s per chip. For 100K tokens/s: H100 needs ceil(100,000 / 2,233) = 45 chips = ~6 nodes × 700W×8 = 33.6 kW. MI300X needs ceil(100,000 / 3,533) = 29 chips = ~4 nodes × 750W×8 = 24 kW. MI300X saves ~9.6 kW (29% power reduction) for the same workload.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X delivers 5.3 TB/s of HBM3 bandwidth versus H100 SXM5 at 3.35 TB/s—a 1.58× advantage. For a memory-bandwidth-bound LLM decode workload, this means roughly 1.58× more tokens/second per chip. If a serving SLA requires 100K tokens/s, you need ceil(100K / T_mi300x) MI300X chips versus ceil(100K / T_h100) H100 chips. Fewer chips means fewer nodes, lower aggregate TDP, and reduced cooling load per rack.

scenario: A new ML infrastructure engineer is onboarding and asks you to compare the memory bandwidth of the MI300X versus the H100 SXM5. State the peak HBM3 bandwidth for each accelerator, then explain why higher memory bandwidth can reduce the number of accelerators needed to serve a given inference throughput target—and how this affects rack power draw.
title: MI300X HBM3 Bandwidth as a Power Efficiency Lever

details.common_mistake: Candidates multiply IT load by PUE instead of understanding PUE = Total Facility Power / IT Load, so they compute the overhead fraction incorrectly. Another error is assuming cooling dominates equally in all facilities—GPU clusters generate 3-5× the heat density of traditional servers, making cooling a larger fraction of PUE overhead.
details.napkin_math: IT Load: 1,000 × 8 kW = 8,000 kW = 8 MW. Total Facility: 8 MW × 1.4 = 11.2 MW. Overhead: 3.2 MW. PUE 1.2 scenario: Total = 8 × 1.2 = 9.6 MW. Savings vs PUE 1.4: 11.2 - 9.6 = 1.6 MW. Equivalent nodes: 1,600 kW / 8 kW = 200 nodes of free capacity. At $0.10/kWh, 1.6 MW continuous = $1.4M/year saved.
details.realistic_solution: IT load = 1,000 nodes × 8 kW = 8 MW. Total facility power = 8 MW × 1.4 = 11.2 MW. Overhead = 11.2 - 8.0 = 3.2 MW. In GPU-dense clusters, cooling systems (chillers, CRAC/CRAH units, CDUs for liquid-cooled racks) typically represent 60-75% of the overhead versus ~45% in traditional compute. Power distribution losses (UPS, PDUs, transformers) are similar at 15-25%. Reducing PUE from 1.4 to 1.2 would save 1.6 MW of overhead, equivalent to running ~200 additional nodes.

scenario: Your team is reviewing datacenter efficiency metrics for a 1,000-node H100 cluster. The facility reports a PUE of 1.4. Each 8×H100 node draws 8 kW IT load. Calculate the total facility power consumption, identify the overhead power consumed by non-IT infrastructure, and explain what PUE components (cooling, power distribution, lighting) typically dominate in a GPU-dense facility versus a traditional compute facility.
title: PUE Decomposition for Dense H100 Clusters

details.common_mistake: Candidates assume they can always mix H100 and A100 nodes freely in one rack. In practice, power distribution units (PDUs) at the rack level may have per-circuit limits (e.g., 20A circuits at 208V = 4.16 kW per circuit), constraining placement. Also, not quantifying stranded power misses an important efficiency metric for capacity planning.
details.napkin_math: 25 kW budget. H100 node = 8 kW: 3 nodes = 24 kW, stranded = 1 kW (4.0%). A100 node = 5.2 kW: 4 nodes = 20.8 kW, stranded = 4.2 kW (16.8%). Mixed [1×H100 + 3×A100]: 8 + 15.6 = 23.6 kW, stranded = 1.4 kW (5.6%). Mixed [2×H100 + 1×A100]: 16 + 5.2 = 21.2 kW, stranded = 3.8 kW (15.2%). Best: 3×H100 pure at 4% stranding.
details.realistic_solution: Pure H100 rack: floor(25 / 8) = 3 nodes × 8 kW = 24 kW used, 1 kW stranded (4% waste). Pure A100 rack: floor(25 / 5.2) = 4 nodes × 5.2 kW = 20.8 kW used, 4.2 kW stranded (17% waste). Mixed optimal: 2× H100 (16 kW) + 1× A100 (5.2 kW) = 21.2 kW, 3.8 kW stranded. Or 1× H100 (8 kW) + 3× A100 (15.6 kW) = 23.6 kW, 1.4 kW stranded (5.6% waste)—near-optimal. The 3× H100 pure rack wastes only 4%, making it the most efficient single-SKU configuration.

scenario: A cloud operator is retrofitting an existing datacenter that has 30 kW/rack PDUs and mixed cooling supporting up to 25 kW IT load per rack. They plan to deploy a combination of 8×H100 nodes (8 kW each) and legacy 8×A100 nodes (5.2 kW each). You must specify a rack-filling strategy that maximizes GPU count per rack while staying within the 25 kW IT power limit, and quantify the 'stranded power'—the unused power budget that cannot be utilized due to integer constraints.
title: Stranded Power in Mixed H100/A100 Rack Deployments

details.common_mistake: Candidates jump to GPU firmware or driver bugs. The combination of elevated ambient hot-aisle temps (38°C >> 24°C baseline) + high junction temps + power reduction without faults is classic thermal throttling from cooling infrastructure failure, not a compute issue.
details.napkin_math: H100 power throttling: 700W → 500W = 28.6% power reduction, matches ~28% MFU drop (68% → 48%). Junction temp 88°C is 2°C below H100 throttle onset (~90°C per NVIDIA spec). Hot aisle delta: 38°C vs 24°C = +14°C. ASHRAE A2 ambient limit for servers = 35°C—racks are already 3°C over limit. Cooling capacity needed per rack: 3 nodes × 700W = 2.1 kW IT; if CRAC unit failed (typically 50-100 kW capacity), loss of one unit explains zone-wide impact across 6 pods.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: A cooling unit (CRAC/CRAH or CDU) serving Pods 7-12 has likely failed or reduced capacity (clogged filter, refrigerant leak, pump failure). The elevated ambient forces GPUs to throttle frequency to keep junction temp below the 90°C threshold (~88°C is the warning knee for H100). Immediate: reroute workloads from Pods 7-12 to spare capacity; dispatch datacenter ops to inspect cooling units. Long-term: implement redundant cooling (N+1 CRAC units), add automated thermal alerting at 32°C ambient, and deploy pre-throttle migration hooks in the job scheduler.

scenario: You are on-call for a production training cluster. At 14:00, the ops dashboard shows all GPUs in Pods 7-12 dropping from 700W TDP to ~500W sustained power draw. MFU (Model FLOP Utilization) falls from 68% to 48%. The ambient temperature sensors in the hot aisle for those racks read 38°C, compared to 24°C in Pods 1-6. NVIDIA SMI shows GPU junction temperatures of 88°C on all affected devices. No hardware faults are reported. Diagnose the root cause and propose immediate and long-term remediation.
title: Thermal Throttling Cascade in a Dense H100 Pod

details.common_mistake: Candidates assume power capping linearly reduces throughput (e.g., 590/750 = 78.7% power → 78.7% throughput). In practice, MI300X throughput vs. power curves are sublinear due to memory bandwidth saturation—most LLM training is memory-bandwidth-bound, so moderate power caps cause disproportionately small throughput losses.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 512 × 750W = 384 kW (exceeds 300 kW by 28%). Option A cap at 590W: 512 × 590W = 302 kW. Reduction factor: 590/750 = 78.7%. But MI300X at 590W retains ~85-90% compute throughput (memory-bandwidth saturation effect). Throughput loss: ~12-15%. Energy per token at cap: lower power + slightly fewer tokens/s → EPI improves by ~5-8%. Option B: 25% smaller batches = ~22% throughput reduction (compute underutilization during microbatches). Option C: achieves ~5% better throughput than A with same power compliance.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (static 590W cap): 512 × 590W = 302 kW, just under budget. Throughput loss is ~10-15%, not the expected 21.3%, because memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and HBM power consumption is less affected by compute power caps than CUDA core frequency. Option B (batch size -25%): Similar throughput reduction but also reduces gradient noise, potentially requiring more steps—net effect may be worse WCT. Option C (dynamic capping): Best option if the cluster has fine-grained power telemetry; cap during GEMM phases, release during all-reduce. In practice, Option A is simplest to implement reliably and within 5% of Option C's performance.

scenario: You manage a 512-accelerator MI300X training cluster. Each MI300X has a maximum TDP of 750W. The datacenter power contract caps your cluster at 300 kW total IT load. During peak matrix-multiply-heavy phases of training a 70B parameter model, power meters show the cluster drawing 380 kW, causing PDU overcurrent alarms. You are evaluating three mitigation options: (A) power-cap each GPU at 590W, (B) reduce batch size by 25%, or (C) deploy dynamic power capping that throttles only during high-power phases. Evaluate each option's effect on training throughput and energy efficiency.
title: Power Capping Strategy for MI300X Training Under Budget Constraints

details.common_mistake: Candidates assume all 8 kW per node is recoverable as useful heat. In practice, the fraction captured by the D2C system depends on the split between conduction-cooled (GPU die) and convection-cooled (VRMs, DRAM) heat paths. For H100 D2C nodes, approximately 70-75% of IT load is captured by liquid; the remaining 25-30% is removed by room air.
details.napkin_math: 500 nodes × 8 kW = 4 MW IT load. D2C captures 72%: 4 MW × 0.72 = 2.88 MW thermal. Temperature: 55°C return, 40°C supply, ΔT = 15°C. Mass flow: Q = ṁ × Cp × ΔT → ṁ = 2,880 kW / (4.18 kJ/kg·K × 15K) = 45.9 kg/s total. Heat pump to 60°C: COP ~7 → electrical input = 2.88 MW / 7 = 0.41 MW extra. Net recovered: 2.88 MW at 60°C for ~0.41 MW penalty = ~7× energy leverage. Annual value: 2.88 × 8,000h × $0.05 = $1.15M.
details.realistic_solution: Temperature gap: district heating needs 60°C, D2C return is 55°C—a 5°C deficit. Options: (1) heat pump to boost from 55°C to 65°C at COP ~6-8 (electrical cost adds ~12-16% overhead); (2) operate coolant at higher flow resistance to raise return temperature to 62°C (increases pump work, risks GPU thermal margin); (3) use D2C heat as pre-heat for a gas boiler (most common practical approach—reduces boiler fuel by ~60%). Recoverable power: 500 nodes × 8 kW × 0.72 liquid fraction = 2.88 MW thermal. At 8,000 hours/year = 23,040 MWh/year. At $0.05/kWh heat equivalent, that's $1.15M/year in recovered energy value.

scenario: A hyperscaler is evaluating whether to recover waste heat from direct-to-chip (D2C) liquid-cooled H100 racks for district heating. Each 8×H100 node draws 8 kW. The D2C system delivers coolant at 40°C supply and returns it at 55°C. The district heating network requires a minimum delivery temperature of 60°C. Analyze the feasibility of direct heat exchange, the engineering options to bridge the temperature gap, and calculate the recoverable thermal power for a 500-node cluster.
title: Waste Heat Recovery Feasibility for H100 Liquid-Cooled Racks

details.common_mistake: Candidates often enable persistence mode without understanding it prevents P-state transitions entirely—keeping the GPU in P0 for lower latency at the cost of higher idle power. The correct approach for serving workloads is to use NVIDIA's power management daemon (nvidia-persistenced) combined with P8/P12 idle states, balancing wake latency against power savings.
details.napkin_math: Baseline idle: 200 GPUs × 200W × 60% idle fraction = 24 kW continuous idle load. P8 idle state: ~65W per GPU. P8 savings: 200 × (200-65)W × 0.60 = 200 × 135W × 0.60 = 16.2 kW saved. Annual energy: 16.2 kW × 8,760h = 141,912 kWh/year. At $0.10/kWh = $14,191/year. Wake penalty from P8: ~5ms → acceptable for >100ms SLA workloads. Fleet scale (1000 GPUs): $70,960/year savings.
details.realistic_solution: H100 P-state hierarchy: P0 = full performance (700W active, ~200W idle), P8 = memory clock throttled (50-80W), P12 = minimum power (~30W, may cause 50-100ms wake latency). For serving: configure P8 as idle floor (not P12) to keep wake latency under 10ms. Implementation: set nvidia-smi -pm 1 (persistence mode) to prevent full driver unload, then use MIG or power limit commands. Enable nvidia-smi --power-limit=300 for idle cap, auto-lifting under load via power management policy.

scenario: Your inference serving cluster runs H100 GPUs that sit idle between request bursts, averaging 40% utilization over a 24-hour period. During idle periods, nvidia-smi shows each GPU drawing 200W in P0 state (full clock). You are tasked with implementing power state management to reduce idle power consumption. Describe how NVIDIA GPU power states (P-states) work for H100, how to enable persistence mode correctly, and calculate the potential power savings for a 200-GPU cluster.
title: GPU Power State Transitions and Idle Power Optimization

details.common_mistake: Evaluating only FLOPS/Watt and ignoring that at 70B FP16 scale, the MI300X fits the model on a single accelerator (192GB > 140GB) while H100 requires tensor parallelism across at least 2 chips (80GB × 2 = 160GB). This sharding overhead increases inter-chip communication and reduces effective throughput.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X: Single chip fits 70B FP16 (140GB < 192GB). No tensor parallelism overhead. Token throughput: ~3,533 tokens/s (bandwidth-bound at 5.3 TB/s). Power: 750W.
