Energy/token: 750W / 3,533 tok/s = 0.212 J/token. H100 (2-chip TP): Each chip holds 70GB of the 140GB model. NVLink overhead for TP2 ~5-8% latency penalty. Effective throughput per 2-GPU pair: ~(3.35 TB/s per chip × 2 chips × 0.93 efficiency) / 1.5 GB/token = ~4,154 tok/s. Power: 2 × 700W = 1,400W. Energy/token: 1,400W / 4,154 tok/s = 0.337 J/token. MI300X is 37% more energy efficient per token for this workload.

scenario: You are selecting the accelerator platform for a 100B-token-per-day LLM inference service. The MI300X offers 192GB HBM3 at 5.3 TB/s and 750W TDP, while the H100 SXM5 offers 80GB HBM3e at 3.35 TB/s and 700W TDP. The service runs Llama-3 70B in FP16 (140GB model weight). Evaluate which platform delivers lower energy-per-token, accounting for model sharding requirements, memory bandwidth utilization, and total power budget for the serving fleet.
title: MI300X vs H100: Energy-per-Token at Scale for LLM Inference

details.common_mistake: Treating DVFS as a per-GPU control loop rather than a cluster-level policy. Individual GPU DVFS reacts too slowly (10-100ms) to catch AllReduce windows (often 5-50ms). The scheduler must operate at the job level, using job topology information to predict AllReduce phases.
details.napkin_math: 256 nodes × 8 GPUs = 2,048 GPUs. Compute phase: 2,048 × 700W = 1,434 kW. Comm phase: 2,048 × 450W = 921 kW. Average if 60% compute / 40% comm: 0.6×1,434 + 0.4×921 = 860 + 368 = 1,228 kW = 1.228 MW. 25 MW facility budget → 25,000 / 1,228 = 20× oversubscription potential at cluster level (20 jobs). DVFS smoothing target: cap at 950W peak (boost phase) + 400W comm = weighted avg 710W. Max GPUs under 25 MW: 25,000,000 / 710 = 35,211 GPUs = ~4,401 nodes. Versus naive: 25,000 / 700 = 35,714 GPUs (similar, but DVFS eliminates PDU overcurrent spikes).
details.realistic_solution: Design a two-level policy: (1) Cluster scheduler annotates jobs with topology metadata (TP degree, PP stages, AllReduce frequency). (2) Power controller subscribes to NCCL collective events and pre-emptively steps down GPU frequency 50ms before predicted AllReduce windows. During communication phases, reduce GPU clock from 1,980 MHz to 1,410 MHz (boost to base) → ~35% power reduction per GPU. Budget math: during compute phases, 256 nodes × 8 GPUs × 700W = 1.434 GW (well over 25 MW). During comm phases at reduced clocks: 256 × 8 × 450W = 921.6 MW. Policy target: smooth to constant 850W average by oversubscribing compute phases within thermal buffer.

scenario: You are designing a power-aware training scheduler for a 256-node H100 cluster operating under a 25 MW facility power budget. The cluster's measured power draw follows a bimodal distribution: 700W/GPU during GEMM-heavy forward/backward passes and 450W/GPU during all-reduce communication phases. Each training job uses 4-way tensor parallelism and 16-way pipeline parallelism. Design a cluster-level DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) policy that exploits the communication-compute overlap to smooth power consumption and maximize GPUs under budget.
title: Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling for H100 Training Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Assuming PDU peak rating is safe for simultaneous all-node power ramp. The 20% oversubscription on 30 kW PDUs = 36 kW, but 3 nodes × 8 kW = 24 kW steady state. The risk is not steady-state overflow but rather the transient inrush current when GPU voltage regulators all switch on simultaneously—this can produce 1.5-2× instantaneous spike above TDP for 100-500ms.
details.napkin_math: Steady state: 3 nodes × 8 kW = 24 kW (80% of 30 kW PDU). Inrush spike: 3 × 12 kW = 36 kW = 100% of 36 kW PDU peak. Zero headroom. With staggered start (5s delay): max 1 node inrush + 2 steady-state = 12 + 16 = 28 kW (93% of 30 kW continuous, 78% of 36 kW peak). Safe. Stagger time to choose: inrush duration ~200ms, so 200ms delay is theoretically sufficient, but 5s is safer given CPU/memory ramp. Per rack across 1000-rack cluster: 1,000 × 5s stagger = 5,000s total ramp window, but can parallelize across racks.
details.realistic_solution: Steady state: 3 × 8 kW = 24 kW, well within 30 kW continuous. But simultaneous power-on inrush: each node can spike to ~12 kW for 200ms (1.5× TDP). Three nodes simultaneously: 3 × 12 kW = 36 kW = exactly the PDU peak limit, with zero margin. Risk: any additional overhead (networking, CPUs ramping) tips the PDU over. Soft-start policy: stagger job launch across nodes with 5-second delays. In SLURM, use --begin with per-node stagger or implement a prolog script that delays GPU power-on by node_rank × 5s. Reduces simultaneous peak to max 2 nodes = 24 kW inrush, leaving 12 kW headroom.

scenario: You are commissioning a new H100 training cluster. The datacenter vendor offers PDUs rated at 30 kW continuous and 36 kW peak (20% oversubscription for 10-second bursts). Your deployment uses 3× 8×H100 nodes per rack, each node rated at 8 kW TDP. A cluster benchmarking team reports that during the first minute of large-model training, all GPUs ramp from idle to full TDP simultaneously. Explain the power ramp-up risk, calculate whether the PDU can handle it, and propose a soft-start training policy.
title: Power Distribution Unit Over-Subscription in GPU Clusters

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply IT power by PUE before applying grid intensity—PUE accounts for all facility power, not just GPU power. Also, candidates omit embodied/operational scope (Scope 1/2/3 distinction) from the reporting methodology.
details.realistic_solution: Pacific NW: IT power = 64 × 680W = 43.52 kW. Total facility = 43.52 × 1.2 = 52.22 kW. Energy = 52.22 kW × 72h = 3,760 kWh. Carbon = 3,760 × 180 = 676,800 gCO2 = 677 kgCO2. US SE: IT same = 43.52 kW. Total facility = 43.52 × 1.35 = 58.75 kW. Energy = 58.75 × 72 = 4,230 kWh. Carbon = 4,230 × 580 = 2,453,400 g = 2,453 kgCO2. SE is 3.63× higher carbon. Reporting: use GHG Protocol Scope 2 (market-based or location-based). Include Scope 3 for hardware manufacturing (amortized over device lifetime, ~50-100 kgCO2 per MI300X chip).

scenario: Your ML platform team must produce a carbon disclosure report for a 13B parameter fine-tuning job run on a 64× MI300X cluster in a US Pacific Northwest datacenter (grid intensity: 180 gCO2eq/kWh). The job ran for 72 hours. Each MI300X averaged 680W during training. The datacenter has a PUE of 1.2. Calculate the total carbon footprint and compare it to running the same job in a US Southeast region (grid intensity: 580 gCO2eq/kWh, PUE 1.35). Recommend carbon reporting methodology.
title: Computational Carbon Intensity of MI300X Fine-Tuning Runs

details.common_mistake: Confusing hot-aisle containment with cold-aisle containment, or thinking they are equivalent. HAC traps the hot exhaust and routes it directly to CRAC return, preventing recirculation. CAC keeps cold supply contained. For GPU-dense rows, HAC is often preferred because the high exhaust temperature (50-60°C for H100s) can be used for economizer cooling if the building design permits.
details.napkin_math: 1°C chiller inlet rise → 2.5% more chiller power. Without HAC: hot exhaust recirculation raises inlet by 5-8°C. Chiller overhead increase: 5°C × 2.5%/°C = 12.5% more chiller power. For a 10 MW IT cluster at PUE 1.5: cooling overhead = 5 MW. 12.5% extra = 625 kW wasted. With HAC eliminating recirculation: 625 kW saved = reduces PUE overhead by 625/10,000 = 0.0625 PUE points on 1.5 baseline → PUE 1.44. Additional economizer effect: another 0.05-0.10 PUE. Total: PUE 1.35-1.40.
details.realistic_solution: HAC prevents hot exhaust air (50-55°C from H100 nodes) from mixing with cold supply air (18-22°C) in the open floor. Without containment, hot/cold air mixing raises the average CRAC inlet temperature, forcing chillers to work harder (each 1°C rise in chiller inlet ≈ 2-3% more chiller energy). With HAC, CRAC units see only hot return air at a consistent 50°C, enabling delta-T optimization. Typical PUE improvement: 0.1-0.15 PUE points (e.g., 1.5 → 1.35) from containment alone. Combined with economizer cooling (free cooling when outdoor temp < 18°C), HAC-equipped facilities regularly achieve PUE 1.1-1.15.

scenario: A datacenter architect is explaining hot-aisle containment (HAC) to a new ML infrastructure engineer. The facility houses 8×H100 nodes generating 8 kW IT load each, deployed in rows with HAC. Explain how HAC improves PUE compared to an open-floor layout, name the key thermodynamic mechanism that makes it effective for GPU-dense rows, and state the typical PUE improvement achievable.
title: Cooling Fluid Routing for Hot-Aisle Containment in H100 Deployments

details.common_mistake: Candidates confuse input power efficiency with output power delivered. The 8 kW IT load is the output the server needs; the PSU draws more from the wall due to conversion losses. Titanium PSUs draw less from the wall for the same output—the difference is the wasted heat.
details.napkin_math: IT output at 50% load: 8 kW × 0.5 = 4 kW. Gold: 4 / 0.92 = 4,348W wall input. Titanium: 4 / 0.96 = 4,167W. Delta: 181W. Annual kWh: 0.181 kW × 8,760h = 1,585.6 kWh. Annual $: 1,585.6 × $0.10 = $158.56. 1,000 servers: $158,560/yr. Titanium PSU premium over Gold: ~$50-100/unit = $50,000-100,000 fleet. Payback: 0.3-0.6 years.
details.realistic_solution: 80 PLUS efficiency at 50% load: Gold ≥ 92%, Platinum ≥ 94%, Titanium ≥ 96%. For 8 kW IT load at 50% utilization = 4 kW average IT output. Gold PSU input: 4 kW / 0.92 = 4.348 kW. Titanium PSU input: 4 kW / 0.96 = 4.167 kW. Difference: 181 W per server. Annual: 181W × 8,760h = 1,585 kWh/year. At $0.10/kWh = $158.50/server/year. For a 1,000-server cluster: $158,500/year saved by choosing Titanium over Gold, often paying back the PSU premium in 1-2 years.

scenario: A procurement engineer asks you to compare power supply unit (PSU) efficiency tiers for GPU server deployments. Name the 80 PLUS efficiency tiers relevant to datacenter servers (Titanium, Platinum, Gold), state their minimum efficiency at 50% load, and calculate the difference in annual electricity cost between a Gold and Titanium PSU powering a single 8×H100 server drawing 8 kW IT load at 50% average utilization.
title: Server Power Supply Efficiency Curves and 80 PLUS Certification Impact

details.common_mistake: Assuming that powering off GPUs saves 100% of their power. GPUs in deep sleep or powered off still draw ~30-50W for keep-alive, NVLink heartbeat, and PCIe power. Also, candidates ignore the wake latency cost when demand spikes.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 1000 × 280W = 280 kW. Full consolidation (650 powered off at 5W): 350 × 700W + 650 × 5W = 245,000 + 3,250 = 248,250W = 248 kW. Savings: 32 kW (11.4%). MIG 7-way: 350 active tasks / 5 MIG per GPU = 70 physical GPUs needed (round up to 141 for load headroom). 141 × 700W = 98.7 kW active. 859 × 5W = 4.3 kW standby. Total: 103 kW. Savings vs baseline: 177 kW (63.2%). Annual: 177 kW × 8,760h × $0.10 = $155,052/year. MIG management overhead: ~5% engineering cost.
details.realistic_solution: Current: 1,000 GPUs × 280W = 280 kW. Consolidation: 350 GPUs × 700W = 245 kW active + 650 × 45W idle = 29.25 kW. Total = 274.25 kW (2.4% savings—poor). Better approach: power off 650 GPUs completely (5W standby on managed BMCs): 350 × 700W + 650 × 5W = 245 + 3.25 = 248.25 kW (11.3% savings). Risk: demand spikes require 30-60 second GPU boot time. Hybrid with MIG: 7 MIG instances per H100 (3g.40gb), run 5 at 35% utilization = same throughput with 71% fewer GPUs active. Power: 141 GPUs × 700W + 859 × 5W = 98.7 + 4.3 = 103 kW (63% savings).

scenario: A cloud ML platform has 1,000 H100 GPUs allocated to batch inference jobs that average 35% GPU utilization. Power metering shows each GPU drawing 280W (idle + partial load). The platform team proposes consolidating workloads to run 350 GPUs at 100% utilization and powering off the remaining 650 GPUs. Evaluate this proposal: calculate the power savings, identify the risks of this strategy, and propose a hybrid approach using MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) or time-slicing.
title: Workload Consolidation to Improve GPU Utilization and Power Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Treating energy/token as constant across batch sizes. At batch size 1, the MI300X is deeply memory-bandwidth-bound (arithmetic intensity < 1 FLOP/byte), so most transistors are idle while HBM streams weights. Power is low but so is compute utilization. Energy/token is high because idle power is amortized over very few tokens.
details.napkin_math: B=1: E/tok = 320/2800 = 0.1143 J/tok. B=64: E/tok = 680/8400 = 0.0810 J/tok. Efficiency gain: (0.1143-0.0810)/0.1143 = 29.1%. Power increase B1→B64: 680/320 = 2.125×. Throughput increase: 8400/2800 = 3×. So power grows 2.125× but throughput grows 3× → energy/token improves. Extrapolating to B=100: assume linear throughput (saturation check: 100 × 2 bytes × 13B params = 2.6 TB/s < 5.3 TB/s BW, still under limit). Throughput ≈ 8400 × (100/64) × 0.9 = 11,813 tok/s. Power ≈ 720W. E/tok = 0.061 J/tok (47% better than B=1).
details.realistic_solution: Batch 1: E/token = 320W / 2,800 tok/s = 0.114 J/token. Batch 64: E/token = 680W / 8,400 tok/s = 0.081 J/token. Batch 64 is 29% more energy-efficient. Roofline: batch 1 arithmetic intensity ≈ 2×13B params × 2 bytes / (13B × 2 FLOPs) = 1 byte/FLOP < MI300X ridge point (~300 FLOP/byte). As batch size grows, KV cache reuse increases arithmetic intensity. SLA constraint: TTFT at batch 64 ≈ 64 × average prefill time. If prefill = 2ms per request, TTFT = 128ms < 200ms SLA. Maximum batch size before SLA violation: 200ms / 2ms = 100 requests. Optimal: batch 96-100 (further power reduction possible).

scenario: You are profiling energy efficiency for a Llama-2 13B inference workload on MI300X. At batch size 1 (single-request decode), the MI300X draws 320W and achieves 2,800 tokens/sec. At batch size 64, it draws 680W and achieves 8,400 tokens/sec. Analyze why energy-per-token (J/token) differs dramatically between batch sizes, connect this to the roofline model, and determine the optimal batch size for a data center that wants to minimize total energy cost while meeting a 200ms TTFT (time to first token) SLA.
title: Transformer Inference Memory Bandwidth Saturation and Power Envelope

details.common_mistake: Specifying UPS capacity based solely on kW (active power) and ignoring apparent power (kVA). UPS units are rated in kVA, and undersizing by using kW leads to UPS overload during power events. GPU server PSUs have power factors of 0.92-0.96, meaning kVA > kW.
details.napkin_math: Nodes: 3 × 10.5 kVA = 31.5 kVA. TOR switch: 0.5 kVA. Mgmt: 2 × 1.0 = 2.0 kVA. Total: 34.0 kVA. UPS with 20% buffer: 40.8 kVA → 50 kVA unit. kW actual: 8 kW × 3 + 0.4 + 0.8 = 25.2 kW. PF = 25.2 / 34.0 = 0.741 average (mixed loads). With APFC (PF=0.99): required kVA = 25.2 / 0.99 = 25.45 kVA × 1.2 = 30.5 kVA → 30 kVA unit. Savings: 50 - 30 kVA = 20 kVA less UPS capacity. UPS cost: ~$100/kVA → $2,000 savings per rack.
details.realistic_solution: GPU node kVA: 3 × 10.5 kVA = 31.5 kVA. Switch: 0.5 kVA. Mgmt servers: 2 × 1.0 = 2.0 kVA. Total: 34.0 kVA. With 20% headroom: 34.0 × 1.2 = 40.8 kVA. Specify 40 or 50 kVA UPS. Power factor: kW = kVA × PF. At PF = 0.92, kW = 34 × 0.92 = 31.28 kW (vs 24 kW IT load). The apparent power gap is due to reactive current from switching power supplies. Active Power Factor Correction (APFC) in modern PSUs brings PF to 0.99, reducing the kVA requirement. With APFC at PF=0.99: kVA needed = 24 kW / 0.99 = 24.24 kVA (vs 34 kVA traditional). 29% reduction in UPS sizing cost.

scenario: You are specifying a UPS system for a new rack containing three 8×H100 nodes. Each node has a nameplate rating of 10.5 kVA (kilo-volt-amperes) despite drawing only 8 kW. The rack also includes a top-of-rack switch (0.5 kVA) and two management servers (1.0 kVA each). Calculate the required UPS capacity in kVA, explain why the kVA rating exceeds kW for GPU servers, and determine the power factor correction benefit.
title: Rack-Level UPS Sizing and Power Factor Correction for GPU Servers

details.common_mistake: Calculating average annual PUE by simple arithmetic mean of hours, forgetting to weight by energy (kWh). A 5,500-hour free cooling period at low overhead has much more weight on annual PUE than a 3,260-hour mechanical period at high overhead.
details.napkin_math: Mechanical: 3,260h × 400kW cooling overhead = 1,304 MWh cooling. Free: 5,500h × 60kW = 330 MWh cooling. Total cooling: 1,634 MWh. Without economizer: 8,760 × 400 = 3,504 MWh. Savings: 1,870 MWh × $0.10 = $187,000/yr. IT energy: 1,600 kW × 8,760h = 14,016 MWh. Annual PUE: (14,016 + 1,634) / 14,016 = 15,650 / 14,016 = 1.117. Compare to no-economizer PUE: (14,016 + 3,504) / 14,016 = 1.25. Economizer saves 0.133 PUE points annually.
details.realistic_solution: Mechanical cooling: 3,260h × (1,600 + 400) kW = 3,260 × 2,000 = 6,520 MWh. PUE mechanical = 2,000 / 1,600 = 1.25. Free cooling: 5,500h × (1,600 + 60) kW = 5,500 × 1,660 = 9,130 MWh. PUE free = 1,660 / 1,600 = 1.0375. Annual energy: 6,520 + 9,130 = 15,650 MWh. Counterfactual (no economizer): 8,760h × 2,000 kW = 17,520 MWh. Savings: 1,870 MWh/year = $187,000/year. Annualized PUE: 15,650 / (1,600 × 8,760) = 15,650 / 14,016 = 1.117. Strategy: schedule latency-sensitive workloads year-round; shift batch jobs to free-cooling hours to maximize green compute window.

scenario: A cloud operator runs a 200-node H100 cluster in a facility with an economizer (free cooling) that activates when outdoor dry-bulb temperature drops below 18°C. The local climate provides free cooling for 5,500 hours/year. During mechanical cooling (3,260 hours/year), the chiller draws 400 kW to cool the cluster's 1.6 MW IT load. During free cooling, the facility pumps and fans draw only 60 kW. Calculate the annual cooling energy savings, the annualized PUE for each mode, and advise on whether to co-locate latency-sensitive and batch workloads to take advantage of the free-cooling window.
title: Cooling Power Versus Compute Power Tradeoff in Free-Cooling Regimes

details.common_mistake: Using junction temperature (die temp) as the only throttle indicator while ignoring HBM stack temperature. MI300X has separate thermal limits for the compute die (~110°C) and HBM3 stacks (~85-90°C). HBM throttling often triggers before die throttling in memory-bandwidth-heavy workloads.
details.napkin_math: HBM thermal margin: limit 85°C, current 95°C → -10°C (over limit). Die thermal margin: 110 - 82 = 28°C remaining. At 5°C ambient increase: typical thermal resistance GPU die-to-ambient ≈ 0.1°C/W. To reduce die temp by 10°C: reduce power by 100W. 90% util at 750W = 675W. Target: 575W (reduce util to ~77%). Or increase cooling airflow: doubling airflow reduces θja by ~30% → could recover 8-9°C headroom. AMD SMI monitoring: amd-smi metric --gpu -m TEMP | grep -E 'HBM|junction'. Alert threshold: HBM > 78°C (7°C below limit for reaction time).
details.realistic_solution: Two thermal limits to monitor: die junction = 110°C limit (current: 82°C, margin = 28°C). HBM temperature = 85°C typical soft limit (current: 95°C—already over limit!). Root cause: HBM at 95°C is above the 85°C performance threshold—MI300X may already be throttling memory bandwidth by 10-20%. At 30°C ambient (5°C over 25°C TDC baseline), derate TDP by ~5W/°C × 5°C = ~25W, so effective TDC = 725W. Policy: alert at HBM ≥ 80°C, throttle workload at 85°C, emergency shutdown at 95°C. Adjust fan curve for 30°C ambient to maintain HBM < 80°C at 90% util.

scenario: You are qualifying a new MI300X OAM (Open Accelerator Module) server for production. The vendor spec states a maximum junction temperature of 110°C and a thermal design current (TDC) of 750W at 25°C ambient. Your datacenter runs at 30°C ambient supply air. During burn-in tests, the HBM stack temperature (visible via AMD SMI) reaches 95°C at 90% GPU utilization, but the die temperature is 82°C. Implement a monitoring policy that prevents thermal throttling, identify the thermal margin remaining, and calculate the maximum safe utilization given your ambient conditions.
title: MI300X OAM Module Thermal Interface and Cooling Validation

details.common_mistake: Treating TDP as an absolute maximum. TDP (Thermal Design Power) is the sustained power under typical workloads; H100 SXM5 can sustain up to ~900W in short bursts under mixed workloads due to boost clocks. The 'actual' ceiling is the 700W configurable power limit, but GPUs can exceed TDP temporarily if the power limit is not set.
details.napkin_math: H100 SXM5 spec: TDP = 700W (default limit), absolute max clock power ≈ 900W (unrestricted boost). 820W is within the 700-900W range. Power draw breakdown: GPU compute die ≈ 550W at full boost, HBM3 ≈ 100W, VRM switching losses ≈ 50W, PCIe aux ≈ 20W, NVLink PHY ≈ 30W. Total OOB with boost = ~750-820W. PDU measurement includes host VRM: adds 30-50W. So 820W observed may be 770W GPU actual + 50W host overhead—within spec if power limit is 700W with boost budget. Action: cap at 700W to guarantee sustained TDP: expected power drops to 700-730W (VRM + aux).
details.realistic_solution: Root cause candidates: (1) Power limit not explicitly set—H100 defaults to 700W limit via nvidia-smi -pl, but if unset or overridden, can boost to ~900W during Tensor Core-heavy phases. (2) Measurement artifact: PDU meter reading includes VRM and PCIe auxiliary power not in the GPU TDP spec. (3) Workload has exceptionally high arithmetic intensity (INT8 tensor operations) driving max boost. Check: nvidia-smi -q -d POWER to see current enforced limit. If limit = 700W but draw = 820W, likely PDU measurement includes other components. If limit = 900W (unconstrained), set -pl 700 immediately. Alert thresholds: >750W for >60s = investigate; >900W = page on-call immediately.

scenario: The ops team gets a page: GPU node h100-rack07-node04 is drawing 820W per GPU sustained—17% above the 700W TDP. No thermal throttling flags are set, training loss is progressing normally, and SMI shows no errors. Diagnose the possible causes of sustained over-TDP power draw, determine whether this is a hardware fault or expected behavior, and specify the monitoring thresholds that should trigger escalation.
title: Power Anomaly Detection for H100 Training Clusters

details.common_mistake: Using only peak FLOPS/Watt from vendor datasheets. This ignores memory-bandwidth-bound workloads (dominant in LLM decode), memory capacity constraints (70B+ models may require multi-chip setups for H100), and real-world utilization rates that differ between platforms.
details.napkin_math: Decode-weighted EPE: H100: 3,350 GB/s BW → 2,233 tok/s (70B FP16). Power at 70% util: 0.7×700W = 490W effective. EPE_H100 = 2,233 / 490 = 4.56 tok/s/W. MI300X: 5,300 GB/s → 3,533 tok/s. No TP overhead. Power at 70% util: 0.7×750 = 525W. EPE_MI300X = 3,533 / 525 = 6.73 tok/s/W. A100: 2,000 GB/s → 1,333 tok/s. 70% × 400W = 280W. EPE_A100 = 1,333 / 280 = 4.76 tok/s/W. Ranking: MI300X (6.73) > A100 (4.76) > H100 (4.56). Note: H100 advantage emerges for prefill (FLOPS-bound): 312 TFLOPS at 700W = 446 GFLOPS/W vs MI300X 383 TFLOPS/750W = 511 GFLOPS/W. MI300X wins both.
details.realistic_solution: Design a composite metric: EPE (Effective Performance-per-Watt) = (weighted_throughput × utilization_factor × capacity_bonus) / (average_power_draw). Methodology: (1) Run standardized prefill benchmark (512 input tokens, batch 32) and decode benchmark (batch 1, 100 output tokens) on each platform. (2) Weight by fleet traffic split (typically 70% decode, 30% prefill). (3) Apply capacity bonus for platforms that avoid model sharding (MI300X 192GB handles 70B FP16 without TP). (4) Measure at three utilization points (20%, 50%, 80%) to capture real fleet utilization. Expected outcome: MI300X leads for 70B+ models on decode-heavy workloads; H100 leads for prefill-heavy or smaller models. Recommend H100 for diversity + ecosystem; MI300X for power-constrained large-model serving.

scenario: You are the principal ML infrastructure engineer responsible for a heterogeneous 10,000-GPU fleet comprising H100 SXM5, A100 SXM4, and MI300X accelerators serving production LLM inference. Your VP asks for a single 'energy efficiency score' metric to inform the next hardware refresh cycle. Design a performance-per-watt benchmarking framework that accounts for workload diversity (prefill vs decode), memory capacity constraints, and multi-tenant utilization patterns. Present a methodology, propose the metric formula, and defend your accelerator recommendation.
title: Fleet-Wide GPU Energy Efficiency Benchmarking with Performance-per-Watt

details.common_mistake: Assuming HBM bandwidth is 'free' in terms of power. HBM3 power consumption scales with bandwidth: ~8-12 pJ/bit at peak bandwidth. At 5.1 TB/s, HBM3 draws approximately 50-70W more than at 3.8 TB/s. Combined with die-to-die interconnect power across 8 compute chiplets, near-peak bandwidth significantly increases thermal load.
details.napkin_math: HBM3 bandwidth: 5.3 TB/s max. At 5.1 TB/s: 96% utilization. Power: 5.1e12 bytes/s × 8 bits/byte × 10e-12 J/bit = 408W. At 3.8 TB/s: 304W. Delta: 104W HBM alone. Actual system delta: 60W (other components reduced). KV cache bandwidth: 2K context → KV per layer = 2,048 tokens × 2 (K+V) × 128 heads × 128 head_dim × 2 bytes = 134MB/layer read per decode step. 80 layers = 10.7GB/step → at 20 steps/s = 214 GB/s. 8K context: 8× = 1.7 TB/s KV alone. Added to weight reads ~2.8 TB/s total → pushes to 4.5+ TB/s. At prompt=8K: ~5.1 TB/s.
details.realistic_solution: Power delta: 740W - 680W = 60W additional. HBM3 power model: 5.1 TB/s × 8 b/byte × 10 pJ/bit = 5.1e12 × 8 × 10e-12 = 408W HBM at peak. At 3.8 TB/s: 304W HBM. Delta = 104W—but actual delta is 60W, suggesting HBM power model is ~0.6× of theoretical (other power domains decrease as compute is stalled waiting for memory). Workload change: likely a sequence length increase (e.g., from 2K to 8K context) triggering much larger KV cache reads per token. At 8K context, KV cache per layer = 8,192 × 2 × 128 × 2 bytes = 4MB per layer, vs 512KB at 2K context. Full model KV cache: 80 layers × 4MB = 320MB per forward pass, vs 40MB—8× more HBM bandwidth per token.

scenario: The MI300X uses a unified memory architecture where CPU and GPU share the same 192GB HBM3 pool across 8 compute dies on a single package. During a production incident, a model serving process on MI300X unexpectedly causes memory bandwidth saturation at 5.1 TB/s—despite the workload previously running at 3.8 TB/s on H100. The system power jumps from 680W to 740W. Trace the power path from workload to HBM3 memory bandwidth consumption, explain the thermal consequences of near-peak bandwidth operation, and identify what changed in the workload to trigger this.
title: MI300X Unified Memory Architecture and Its Thermal Implications

details.common_mistake: Shifting all load to EU-North without checking if it has capacity. 150 GPUs × 3,600 s/hour = 540,000 GPU-seconds capacity, but 18,000 queries × 1 GPU-second = 18,000 GPU-seconds needed. EU-North alone can serve the entire volume, but network latency from APAC to EU-North may violate the 200ms SLA for those users.
details.napkin_math: Baseline carbon/hr: each query = 1 GPU-s × 700W = 700 Ws = 0.194 Wh = 0.000194 kWh. US-West: 8,000 × 0.000194 × 120 = 186 gCO2/hr. EU-North: 6,000 × 0.000194 × 45 = 52.4 gCO2/hr. APAC: 4,000 × 0.000194 × 650 = 504.4 gCO2/hr. Total: 742.8 gCO2/hr. Optimized (minimize APAC load): APAC = 2,000q, US-West = 10,000q. APAC: 252.2g, US-West: 232.8g, EU: 52.4g. Total: 537.4g. Reduction: 27.6%. To hit 30%: need EU-North to absorb 500 more queries from APAC via CDN pre-warming: total ≈ 519g → 30.2% reduction.
details.realistic_solution: Baseline routing (proportional to GPU count): US-West: 8,000 q/h, EU-North: 6,000 q/h, APAC-SE: 4,000 q/h. Baseline carbon: US-West: 8,000 × (1/3600) h × 700W × 0.120 kg/kWh = 187g/hr. EU-North: 6,000 × (1/3600) × 700 × 0.045 = 52.5g/hr. APAC-SE: 4,000 × (1/3600) × 700 × 0.650 = 505.6g/hr. Total: 745g/hr. Carbon-aware policy: route APAC users to US-West if latency allows (<200ms from APAC to US-West East Coast infeasible; APAC must stay local for SLA). Shift EU users from APAC to EU-North. New APAC-SE load: only APAC-local traffic (assume 2,000 q/h latency-constrained). Route remaining 2,000 q/h to US-West. New carbon: APAC: 2,000 × 700/3,600,000 × 650 = 252.8g. US-West: 10,000 × 700/3,600,000 × 120 = 233g. EU-North: 6,000 × 52.5/6,000 = 52.5g. Total: 538g. Reduction: (745-538)/745 = 27.8%.

scenario: You operate a global LLM inference service with H100 clusters in three regions: US-West (grid: 120 gCO2/kWh, 200 GPUs), EU-North (grid: 45 gCO2/kWh, 150 GPUs), and APAC-SE (grid: 650 gCO2/kWh, 100 GPUs). Total query volume is 18,000 queries/hour, each requiring 1 GPU-second. Current routing is pure latency-based. Design a carbon-aware routing policy that reduces total Scope 2 emissions by at least 30% without violating a 200ms p99 latency SLA, and quantify the carbon savings.
title: Carbon-Aware Inference Routing Across Multi-Region H100 Fleets

details.common_mistake: Calculating Scope 2 as GPU power only, forgetting PUE multiplier. Also, comparing raw carbon values without normalizing per unit of output (e.g., per million tokens) makes the analysis less actionable.
details.realistic_solution: Scope 3 (embodied): 512 chips × 800 kgCO2 = 409,600 kgCO2 = 409.6 tCO2 (fixed). Scope 2 (operational): 512 chips × 750W × 0.70 util × 1.2 PUE × 4 years × 8,760 h/yr × 0.200 kgCO2/kWh. = 512 × 0.75 kW × 0.70 × 1.2 × 35,040 h × 0.200 = 512 × 4,415 kgCO2 = 2,260,480 kgCO2 = 2,261 tCO2. Ratio: Scope 2 / Scope 3 = 2,261 / 409.6 = 5.52×. Operational carbon dominates. Breakeven utilization: Scope 2 = Scope 3 → 512 × 750 × U × 1.2 × 35,040 × 0.200 = 409,600. U = 409,600 / (512 × 750 × 1.2 × 35,040 × 0.200) = 409,600 / 3,229,286 = 12.7%. Only at utilization below 12.7% does embodied carbon exceed operational.

scenario: Your sustainability team is conducting a full lifecycle carbon assessment for a proposed 512-MI300X cluster. Each MI300X chip has an estimated embodied carbon of 800 kgCO2eq (fabrication, packaging, shipping). The cluster will operate for 4 years at an average utilization of 70%, drawing 750W per chip, in a datacenter with PUE 1.2 and grid intensity of 200 gCO2/kWh. Compare Scope 2 (operational) versus Scope 3 (embodied) carbon over the 4-year lifecycle, and determine the breakeven utilization at which Scope 3 exceeds Scope 2.
title: Scope 3 Embodied Carbon Accounting for MI300X Cluster Procurement

details.common_mistake: Assuming you can simply pause training during high-carbon periods. A 4,096-GPU job at 700W draws 2.87 MW. Idle GPUs during a pause still draw ~150W each = 614 kW of wasted power. The 2-hour restart overhead (checkpointing + warmup) consumes additional energy. Carbon-aware scheduling must account for these overheads.
details.napkin_math: Total GPU-hours needed: 6 weeks × 7 × 24 × 4,096 = 4,128,768. Baseline: avg intensity = (10×80 + 14×420)/24 = (800 + 5880)/24 = 6680/24 = 278.3 g/kWh. Energy = 4,128,768 × 0.70 × 1.2 = 3,468,165 kWh. Carbon = 3,468,165 × 0.2783 = 965,213 kgCO2. Optimized (run only at night, 10h/day): GPU-h/day = 10 × 4,096 = 40,960. Days needed: 4,128,768 / 40,960 = 100.8 days (vs 42 days baseline). Not viable—too long. Carbon at night (10h): 10 × 4,096 × 0.7 × 1.2 × 0.080 = 2,753 kgCO2. Day (14h): 14 × 4,096 × 0.7 × 1.2 × 0.420 = 20,239 kgCO2/day. Total/day = 22,992 kg. Baseline/day: 24 × 4,096 × 0.7 × 1.2 × 0.2783 = 22,981 kg/day. Key insight: day-only carbon (420 g/kWh) dominates the blended average; to save 30%, reduce day load by ~43%.
details.realistic_solution: Non-carbon-aware baseline: Total GPU-hours = 6 × 7 × 24 × 4,096 = 4,128,768 GPU-h. Actual average carbon intensity = (10h × 80 + 14h × 420) / 24 = 278.3 g/kWh. Baseline carbon = 4,128,768 × 0.7 kWh × 1.2 × 278.3 g/kWh = 965,000 kgCO2. Optimized: schedule 10 night hours, pause 14 day hours. Night throughput: same. But pause requires warmup — net effective compute loss. Best tradeoff: run 24/7 but during day hours reduce batch size to 10% load (70W/GPU warm idle). Day carbon: 14h × 4,096 × 0.070 × 1.2 × 420 = 2,025 kgCO2/day. Night carbon: 10h × 4,096 × 0.700 × 1.2 × 80 = 275 kgCO2/day. Total/day: 2,300 kgCO2. Baseline/day: ≈22,981 kgCO2. Savings: ~20,681 kgCO2/day × 42 days = 868,602 kgCO2 (90% reduction at cost of slower throughput). Requires extending the job duration to compensate for lost daytime compute.

scenario: You are designing a carbon-aware scheduling system for a 6-week, 4,096-GPU H100 pretraining run. The datacenter is in a region with highly variable grid carbon intensity: 80 gCO2/kWh at night (20:00-06:00, 10 hours) and 420 gCO2/kWh during peak day (06:00-20:00, 14 hours). Each GPU draws 700W. The training job cannot be paused without 2-hour restart overhead. Design a system that minimizes total carbon footprint while guaranteeing the job completes within 6 weeks, and calculate the carbon savings versus a non-carbon-aware baseline.
title: Carbon Intensity Time-Shifting for Large-Scale H100 Pretraining

details.common_mistake: Assuming GPU-only workloads cannot be affected by CPU contention. Modern LLM serving has significant CPU-side overhead: tokenization, KV cache management, request scheduling, tensor deserialization, and CUDA kernel launch all run on CPU cores. p99 spikes with stable p50 and stable GPU utilization is a classic sign of CPU scheduling jitter, not GPU pressure.
details.napkin_math: p99/p50 ratio: 380/42 = 9.05×. In an M/M/1 queue, p99/p50 ≈ log2(100)/log2(2) = log2(100) ≈ 6.64× at heavy load—but at 45% GPU util, queue theory predicts p99/p50 ≈ 2-3×. Actual 9× ratio implies external latency injection, not queueing. CPU scheduling quantum: Linux CFS default 4ms per 100ms period = 4% CPU time minimum. If analytics job takes 95% of shared cores, serving gets 5% of CPU time. CPU work per request: ~5ms (tokenization + launch). At 5% CPU allocation: 5ms / 0.05 = 100ms CPU wait. p99 = 42ms GPU + 100ms CPU stall = 142ms... but analytics job is bursty → p99 can hit 42 + 338 = 380ms when preempted at worst moment.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: CPU core contention between the inference serving process and the analytics job is causing scheduling latency for CUDA kernel launches and pre-processing steps. The long tail (p99) blooms because CPU stalls are bursty and rare, not because average GPU work increased. Evidence: p50 unchanged (most requests complete before CPU is preempted), GPU util unchanged (GPU work finishes fast when CPU isn't stalled). Immediate: use cgroups or Kubernetes CPU limits to isolate the serving process to dedicated CPU cores (e.g., numactl --cpunodebind=0). Systemic: request CPU isolation guarantees from cloud provider (dedicated host or CPU-pinned pods), add CPU scheduling jitter to your SLO monitoring.

scenario: Your LLM serving system on H100 has been meeting p99 < 150ms for weeks. After a co-tenant's batch analytics job is scheduled on the same physical host's CPUs, you observe p99 latency spiking to 380ms while p50 remains at 42ms. GPU utilization on nvidia-smi is unchanged at 45%. The analytics job uses no GPUs. Diagnose the root cause of the latency spike and propose both immediate and systemic mitigations.
title: H100 Inference SLA Degradation Under Noisy Neighbor CPU Contention

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the KV cache transfer overhead in disaggregated architectures. After prefill finishes on a prefill GPU, the KV cache (often 10-100MB for long contexts) must be transferred to the decode GPU before generation begins. At 400 Gbps NVLink or 100 Gbps Ethernet, this transfer takes non-trivial time and can dominate TTFT for long sequences.
details.napkin_math: Prefill compute: 2 × 70B params × 4,096 tokens FLOPs / 312 TFLOPS = 573,440B / 312,000B/ms = 1.84ms compute. Memory-bound check: 70B × 2 bytes = 140GB weights, bandwidth-bound at: 140GB / 3,350 GB/s = 41.8ms. So prefill is compute-bound for 4K tokens (good). KV cache: 4,096 × 2 × 80 layers × (8 KV heads) × 128 dim × 2 bytes = 4,096×2×80×8×128×2 = 1,073,741,824 bytes? Recheck: 80 layers × 2 (K,V) × 8 heads × 128 head_dim × 4,096 tokens × 2 bytes = 80×2×8×128×4096×2 = 671,088,640 bytes = 640MB. At 100 Gbps (12.5 GB/s): 640/12,500 = 51ms. At 900 GB/s: 0.71ms. TTFT at 100 Gbps: 2ms prefill + 51ms transfer = 53ms (well under 500ms p99 even with 5-10× tail factor). Decode: 500 tokens × (280GB / 5,300 GB/s per token) = 500 × 52.8ms? No: per-token decode = 2×70B × 2 bytes / 5,300 GB/s = 280GB / 5,300 = 52.8ms/token × 500 = 26.4s. Too slow! Need batch decode: batch 10 = 5.28s per 500 tokens. Need MI300X batch ≥ 6 to meet 4s.
details.realistic_solution: Disaggregation design: separate prefill fleet (compute-optimized: H100 @ 312 TFLOPS) from decode fleet (memory-bandwidth-optimized: MI300X @ 5.3 TB/s). Prefill H100: 4K-token prefill takes 4,096 × 4 FLOPs × 70B params / 312 TFLOPS = 4,096 × 280B / 312T = 3.7ms (compute-bound). KV cache size for 4K tokens, 70B model (80 layers, GQA): 4,096 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 536MB. Transfer at 100 Gbps: 536MB / 12.5 GB/s = 43ms. This dominates! Use NVLink-C2C at 900 GB/s: 536MB / 900 GB/s = 0.6ms. Within-cluster NVLink: must co-locate prefill and decode within same NVSwitch domain. With 43ms transfer on Ethernet: total TTFT = 3.7 + 43 = 46.7ms for 4K. With NVLink: 4.3ms. Target p99 < 500ms met. End-to-end for 500 tokens on MI300X: 500 steps × 1ms/step = 500ms. Meets <4s.

scenario: Your LLM serving team observes that long-prompt requests (input > 4K tokens) are causing p99 TTFT (time to first token) to spike to 3.2 seconds, even when the median prompt is 256 tokens with p50 TTFT of 80ms. GPU utilization is 72%. Your current monolithic architecture runs prefill and decode on the same H100 pool. Design a disaggregated prefill/decode architecture that achieves p99 TTFT < 500ms while maintaining end-to-end p99 generation latency < 4 seconds for a 500-token output. Include the KV cache transfer cost in your analysis.
title: Disaggregated Prefill-Decode Architecture for Tail Latency Control

details.common_mistake: Assuming retransmits indicate faulty hardware and raising a datacenter ticket. In high-performance RDMA clusters, retransmits often indicate RoCEv2 congestion due to misconfigured ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) thresholds or DCQCN parameters, not hardware failures.
details.napkin_math: Theoretical AllReduce: 4GB × (2×(N-1)/N) / BW = 4GB × 2 × 511/512 / 50GB/s (400Gbps = 50GB/s) = 7.984GB / 50 = 159.7ms ideal. Measured: 140 Gbps → 17.5 GB/s → 4GB × 2 × 511/512 / 17.5 = 456ms. Slowdown: 456/160 = 2.85×. 35% retransmit rate means ~1.35× average packet delivery. Effective BW = 400 Gbps / 1.35 = 296 Gbps. Gap from 296 to 140 Gbps: additional 53% loss from PFC-induced stalls.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: RoCEv2 congestion feedback loop. At 400 Gbps line rate with 512 GPU ring-AllReduce, the 64-node fat-tree switch fabric has 3:1 oversubscription at spine layer. During synchronized AllReduce phases, all nodes inject traffic simultaneously, causing head-of-line blocking and PFC storms. PFC storms trigger RDMA retransmits because paused senders time out. Diagnosis: check switch port PFC TX/RX counters (should be near zero for well-tuned networks). Fix: (1) Tune DCQCN: reduce initial rate (IR) from 1 Gbps to 400 Mbps, increase Alpha (ECN marking sensitivity). (2) Enable SHARP in-network computing to reduce AllReduce traffic by 2×. (3) Use tree-AllReduce instead of ring for fat-tree topology. Expected throughput: 140 → 280-320 Gbps (70-80% of line rate) with proper DCQCN tuning.

scenario: You are tuning AllReduce performance for a 64-node MI300X cluster connected with 400 Gbps InfiniBand HDR2. Each node has 8 MI300X GPUs. A ring-AllReduce of a 4GB gradient tensor across all 512 GPUs achieves only 140 Gbps per rail, while the theoretical per-link throughput is 400 Gbps. Profiling shows 35% of RDMA operations are completing with retransmit counters incrementing. Diagnose the performance gap, identify why retransmits are occurring, and propose tuning parameters.
title: RDMA Write Throughput Saturation in MI300X AllReduce Rings

details.common_mistake: Assuming NCCL's QP count scales linearly with N nodes. In fact, NCCL creates a QP for each participating rank-to-rank pair in the collective operation. For N ranks in a fully-connected AllReduce, QPs scale as O(N²), not O(N). This causes catastrophic QP exhaustion at scale.
details.napkin_math: HCA QP limit: 32,768. 512 nodes × 8 GPUs = 4,096 GPUs. NCCL ring-AllReduce QPs per GPU: 2 (left + right neighbor). But initialization phase creates QPs to all ranks: 4,096 - 1 = 4,095 QPs per GPU × 8 GPUs/node × 1 HCA = 4,095 × 8 / (number_of_HCAs). If 1 HCA per node: 4,095 × 8 = 32,760 QPs per HCA → exactly at limit of 32,768! Any additional communicator (pipeline parallel) pushes over. At 1,024 nodes (8,192 GPUs): 8,192 × 8 = 65,536 QPs → 2× over limit, hang on initialization. Fix: NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION=1 + set NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS=4 to reduce QP count. Or deploy 2 HCAs per node: QPs split 50/50 via NIC bonding. Or use SHARP: reduces fan-out to logarithmic tree.
details.realistic_solution: NCCL default: for N GPUs in a single communicator, each GPU opens QPs to all other GPUs it communicates with in the ring or tree. In ring-AllReduce, each rank connects to 2 neighbors = 2N QPs total across the ring. But NCCL also creates point-to-point QPs for send/recv operations: O(N) per GPU, O(N²) total. At 512 nodes × 8 GPUs = 4,096 GPUs: QPs per GPU = min(N-1, max_peers) ≈ 4,095. Total QPs per HCA: 4,096 (for all rank communications). But with multiple communicators (data parallel + tensor parallel + pipeline parallel), multiply by communicator count. At 4,096 GPUs × 3D parallelism = 3 communicators, per-GPU QPs = 3 × (DP_size - 1 + TP_size - 1) + PP_size - 1. Fix: enable NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION=1 (already default), use SHARP for reduction offload, or use hierarchical AllReduce to limit QP fan-out per node.

scenario: You are scaling a distributed training cluster from 128 to 1,024 H100 nodes, each with one 400 Gbps InfiniBand HCA (Host Channel Adapter). Each NCCL AllReduce creates one RDMA Queue Pair (QP) per participating GPU pair. Your HCA supports a maximum of 32,768 QPs. After scaling to 512 nodes, training initialization hangs for 10 minutes. Analyze the QP exhaustion problem, calculate the scaling limits, and propose architectural solutions.
title: RDMA Queue Pair Limits and Scalability in Large H100 Pods

details.common_mistake: Assuming RDMA memory registration is free or negligible. RDMA requires memory to be pinned (non-pageable) and registered with the HCA's memory translation table (MTT). Dynamic allocation/deregistration forces the OS to pin/unpin pages and the HCA to update its MTT on every step—this is the dominant overhead for dynamic buffers.
details.napkin_math: ibv_reg_mr cost: kernel page pin + HCA MTT update. Empirical: ~2μs/4KB page. Gradient buffer size (LLaMA-2 7B, FP32): 7B × 4 bytes = 28GB. Pages: 28GB / 4096 = 7,340,032 pages. Full registration: 7.34M × 2μs = 14.68 seconds (absurd). PyTorch actually registers per-tensor per allreduce: if gradient is split into 128 chunks for ring allreduce = 28GB/128 = 218MB per chunk. Pages: 218MB/4KB = 55,808. Registration: 55,808 × 2μs = 111.6ms per chunk. But only 2-3 chunks in flight = 223-335ms. Matches observed 310ms! Fix: pre-register 28GB once: 14.7s one-time vs 310ms × N steps. At 10,000 steps: dynamic = 310ms × 10,000 = 51.67 hours overhead. Pre-registered: 14.7s. Savings: 51.67h - 0.004h = 51.67h. ROI: 1 registration call saves 99.99% of RDMA overhead.
details.realistic_solution: RDMA memory registration cost: approximately 1-5 μs per page (4KB) for HCA MTT updates, plus TLB shootdown across CPUs for page pinning. For a 7B model gradient buffer: 7B params × 4 bytes (FP32) = 28GB. Registration: 28GB / 4KB × 2 μs = 7,000,000 × 2 μs = 14,000,000 μs = 14 seconds per registration—impossible. But if PyTorch uses per-tensor registration (not full gradient): a typical microbatch gradient chunk = 100MB. 100MB / 4KB × 2 μs = 51,200 μs = 51ms per tensor × 6 pipeline stages = 307ms. Close to observed 310ms. Fix: implement a RDMA buffer pool. Pre-register a fixed memory region at startup (all gradient memory in one ibv_reg_mr call), reuse across steps. Registration becomes a one-time cost at initialization.

scenario: Your H100 training framework uses dynamic tensor allocation—gradient buffers are created and destroyed each training step, rather than pre-allocated. After migrating to a 128-node InfiniBand RDMA cluster, you observe that each training step takes 850ms instead of the expected 420ms. Profiling shows RDMA memory registration (ibv_reg_mr) consuming 310ms per step across all nodes. Explain why dynamic allocation causes this overhead, quantify the RDMA registration cost, and redesign the memory management strategy.
title: RDMA Memory Registration Overhead in Dynamic Batch LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming UCIe bandwidth scales linearly with die count. Engineers add more compute dies without accounting for the interposer routing congestion and the fact that UCIe bandwidth per mm of die edge is fixed at ~1 TB/s/mm for UCIe 2.0 short-reach.
details.napkin_math: UCIe 2.0 SR: 4 µm bump pitch, ~256 Gbps/mm. For 4 TB/s: convert to Gbps = 4,000 GB/s × 8 = 32,000 Gbps. 32,000 Gbps / 256 Gbps/mm = 125 mm of die edge required. A 26mm × 26mm compute die has 104mm perimeter — 125mm is not feasible without multiple chiplets. Need HBM memory tiles on all four sides of multiple compute dies, or higher bump density.
details.realistic_solution: UCIe 2.0 SR achieves ~256 Gbps/mm of die edge at 4 µm bump pitch. For 4 TB/s (32,000 Gbps), you need 125 mm of active die edge — more than the perimeter of a single large die. Arrange compute dies centrally with HBM memory dies on all four sides rather than one. Use a 2.5D interposer with active silicon bridge segments. Place high-bandwidth-demand compute tiles closest to HBM stacks to minimize hop distance. At this bandwidth requirement, a multi-chiplet design with 4+ HBM stacks is necessary.

scenario: You are designing a next-generation AI accelerator using UCIe 2.0 die-to-die interconnect. The system needs 4 TB/s aggregate compute-to-HBM bandwidth but the UCIe links are becoming the bottleneck. Diagnose the constraint and propose a chiplet floorplan.
title: UCIe Bandwidth Scaling for Multi-Chiplet AI Accelerators

details.common_mistake: Assuming ROCm assigns TP ranks to XCDs in a NUMA-optimal order by default. By default, rank 0-7 may be assigned round-robin or in hardware enumeration order, which does not minimize fabric hops for the all-reduce communication pattern.
details.napkin_math: MI300X Infinity Fabric: 896 GB/s aggregate. Single-hop XCD pair latency ~200ns, cross-group hop adds ~150ns. For 1GB all-reduce across 8 ranks: ring all-reduce = 2*(N-1)/N * message = 1.75 GB transferred. At 896 GB/s, ideal = 1.95ms. With NUMA penalty: +18% = 2.3ms. Fixing placement recovers ~280us per all-reduce.
details.realistic_solution: Use ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES and numactl to pin TP ranks to XCDs sharing the same Infinity Fabric sub-ring. On MI300X, XCDs are organized in pairs sharing a fabric sub-domain. For TP=8 spanning all 8 XCDs, use hierarchical all-reduce: reduce within each 4-XCD group first, then across groups. Set HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION for kernel compatibility and NUMA_BALANCING=0 to prevent OS page migration during training.

scenario: A team running TP=8 on MI300X sees 18% higher all-reduce latency than expected from peak Infinity Fabric bandwidth. ROCm NUMA topology shows ranks are spread across all 8 XCDs. How do you fix the rank placement?
title: MI300X NUMA-Aware Tensor Parallel Rank Placement

details.common_mistake: Using a linear yield model. Engineers divide the defect density by area and assume yield scales proportionally. The Poisson/Murphy yield model shows yield degrades super-linearly with die area because a single defect anywhere on the die causes full die loss.
details.napkin_math: Monolithic: 600mm² at $0.10/mm² = $60 wafer cost, yield 49% → $122 per good die. Chiplet (6x100mm²): $10 each, yield 90% → $11.11 per good die, $66.67 for 6. Assembly overhead $5–15 per package → total $72–82. Chiplet saves ~33–40% at scale.
details.realistic_solution: Use Murphy's yield model: Y = (1 - e^(-D0*A) / (D0*A))^2. At D0=0.1 defects/cm², 600mm²=6cm²: Y_mono ≈ (1-e^(-0.6)/0.6)^2 ≈ 0.49. For 100mm²=1cm²: Y_small = (1-e^(-0.1)/0.1)^2 ≈ 0.90. Effective chiplet yield = 0.90^6 = 0.53 (needing all 6), plus assembly yield ~0.99 per die = 0.99^6 = 0.94 → net 0.50. But chiplet approach allows binning: one bad die scraps only 1/6 vs whole chip. With bin selling, chiplet cost advantage grows.

scenario: A fab offers N5 (5nm) compute dies at $0.10/mm² defect density. Your monolithic design is 600mm² (H100-class). A chiplet alternative uses 6x100mm² dies. Calculate the yield difference and cost crossover.
title: Chiplet Yield Model and Cost per Compute Die

details.common_mistake: Treating memory bandwidth as the only variable. Teams focus solely on GB/s per stack without considering stack height (capacity), TSV yield at the new node, thermal implications of taller HBM4 stacks, and the 6-month qualification period that eats into the 18-month availability window.
details.napkin_math: Compute:bandwidth ratio target for transformer: ~50 TFLOPS per TB/s. H100 actual: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 TFLOPS/TB/s → compute-bound. For memory-bound training (small batch): need ~10 TB/s min. 6x HBM3E = 7.2 TB/s (gap), 6x HBM4 = 10.8 TB/s (meets threshold).
details.realistic_solution: HBM4 at 1.8 TB/s per stack vs HBM3E at 1.2 TB/s is a 50% bandwidth uplift. For an H100-class die (80 TFLOPS at BF16), compute intensity of LLM training (~6 ops/byte) requires: 80 TFLOPS / 6 = 13.35 TB/s memory bandwidth. At 6 stacks: HBM3E = 7.2 TB/s (still memory-bound), HBM4 = 10.8 TB/s (closer to balanced). But 18mo availability + 6mo qual = 24mo → same ship date. If any HBM4 yield issues slip to 26mo, you miss launch. Risk-adjusted recommendation: commit to HBM3E for main product, design HBM4 socket-compatible variant for refresh.

scenario: Your roadmap needs to decide between HBM3E (available now, 1.2 TB/s per stack) and HBM4 (available in 18 months, 1.8 TB/s per stack) for a training accelerator. The accelerator ships in 24 months. Analyze the bandwidth-compute balance decision.
title: HBM4 Stack Integration Timing for Next-Gen AI Die

details.common_mistake: Blaming the XLA fusion pass itself rather than the data placement. Engineers disable operator fusion to eliminate the regression, losing the throughput benefits of fusion on the portions of the kernel that stay within a single XCD's memory domain.
details.napkin_math: Fused kernel with 1000 cross-XCD cache misses at 400ns each = 400 us overhead per kernel launch. Kernel itself runs in 1ms → 40% overhead matches observation. Fixing placement: cross-XCD misses drop to ~50 (compulsory) → 20us → 2% overhead.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X uses a cache-coherent NUMA model: each XCD has 4MB L2 per compute unit, and cross-XCD cache coherency is maintained via Infinity Fabric directory protocol. When a fused kernel reads a tensor allocated on XCD-A from a kernel running on XCD-B, the coherency protocol issues directory lookups adding ~300-500ns per cache miss. Fix: use HIP memory placement hints (hipMemAdvise with hipMemAdviseSetPreferredLocation) to co-locate tensors with the XCD executing the kernel. For XLA, use custom buffer assignment to constrain placement.

scenario: A JAX XLA operator fusion pass that works well on A100 causes 40% slowdown on MI300X. The fused kernel accesses tensors allocated on different XCDs. Diagnose the coherency overhead and recommend a fix.
title: Coherency Protocol Overhead Across XCD Boundaries

details.common_mistake: Evaluating only the bandwidth density metric in isolation. Active interposers add logic (repeaters, retimers, even simple routing logic) which improves signal integrity at high frequencies, but they introduce new failure modes, increase NRE cost by 5-10x, add yield dependencies, and require the interposer itself to be designed and qualified on a separate process node.
details.napkin_math: Passive interposer: 256 Gbps/mm UCIe. Active interposer: 333 Gbps/mm (+30%). To reach 4 TB/s (32,000 Gbps): passive needs 32,000 / 256 = 125mm edge, active needs 32,000 / 333 = 96mm edge — saves ~29mm total edge, enabling more compute dies per interposer. At 100K units, active interposer NRE $5M / 100K = $50/unit. Saved area at $0.10/mm² × 29mm × die_height — roughly $10-20/unit. Active interposer only justified at >300K+ units in this scenario.
details.realistic_solution: Active interposer advantages: embedded repeaters allow longer routes and higher frequencies; can integrate PHY logic reducing die-edge area requirements; enables 3D stacking of logic dies. Disadvantages: interposer fabricated on mature node (28nm typical) adds process qualification; any defect in interposer logic kills the whole package; power delivery to interposer logic adds complexity; thermal path from top dies through interposer to package is degraded. For AI accelerators at exascale (1000+ TFLOPS), active interposer makes sense if the bandwidth gain enables removing one memory stack — the cost crossover is roughly when active interposer NRE < (saved HBM stack cost × volume).

scenario: Your team is evaluating active interposer technology (with embedded logic) versus passive silicon interposer for the next AI accelerator generation. The active interposer vendor claims 30% better bandwidth density. Evaluate the full system tradeoff.
title: Active Interposer vs Passive Silicon Interposer Tradeoffs

details.common_mistake: Assuming MIG-style isolation is directly portable from H100 to MI300X. H100 MIG uses dedicated SM partitions and memory controllers baked into the monolithic die design. MI300X lacks hardware MIG support — its XCD boundaries offer natural isolation points but require software enforcement.
details.napkin_math: MI300X: 8 XCDs, 192GB HBM. 1-XCD slice: 24GB HBM, ~660 GB/s local BW, ~228 TFLOPS BF16 (1/8 of ~1826 TFLOPS). Comparable to: A100 80GB (2TB/s, 312 TFLOPS) — MI300X XCD slice has higher memory but lower bandwidth per TFLOP, good for memory-capacity-bound workloads.
details.realistic_solution: MI300X's 8 XCDs each have independent CUs, L2 caches, and HBM partitions through MCDs. Define isolation zones as 1-XCD, 2-XCD, or 4-XCD slices: assign one tenant per XCD partition. Use ROCm's CRIU-based context isolation and set HSA memory pools to restrict allocation to assigned XCD's HBM region. Infinity Fabric QoS registers can throttle cross-XCD bandwidth to enforce SLA. Limitation: no hardware memory encryption boundary between XCDs (unlike H100 Confidential Computing), so must add software memory scrubbing on XCD release.

scenario: A cloud provider wants to offer MI300X as a multi-tenant service with strong isolation guarantees, analogous to H100 MIG. Design an isolation scheme that maps to MI300X's XCD physical topology.
title: Chiplet-Based GPU Multi-Instance Partitioning

details.common_mistake: Comparing peak bandwidth specs directly (NVLink 900 GB/s vs Infinity Fabric 896 GB/s) and concluding they are equivalent. The critical difference is memory capacity (80GB H100 vs 192GB MI300X) and compute throughput (989 vs ~1826 TFLOPS BF16), which changes the compute-to-communication ratio and whether the workload is compute or memory bound.
details.napkin_math: 70B model, TP=8: each rank holds 70B/8 = 8.75B params = 17.5 GB BF16. All-reduce per step: 2*(N-1)/N * 17.5GB = 30.6 GB. At 900 GB/s: 34ms all-reduce latency. Compute per step (forward+backward): ~6 × 70B FLOP (for F+B+optimizer) = 420 GFLOPs per token, or for a batch: depends on batch size. For a single forward pass: 2 × 70B = 140 GFLOPs — this is 0.14 TFLOPs (not 280 TFLOPs). With batch=512 tokens: 2 × 2 × 70B × 512 = 143 TFLOPs. H100: 143T / 989T = 0.14s compute. Ratio: 34ms comm / 140ms compute = 24% overhead.
details.realistic_solution: For 70B LLM in BF16: model weights = 140GB. H100 8-GPU: 640GB total, 140GB fits with headroom for activations and optimizer states in mixed precision. MI300X 8-GPU: 1.536TB total, can hold full optimizer states in BF16 without offloading. All-reduce: both nodes have ~900 GB/s bandwidth. H100 NVLink topology: fully connected NVSwitch (6 switches), bisection bandwidth = 900 GB/s. MI300X: Infinity Fabric peer-to-peer bandwidth depends on system topology (PCIe vs dedicated fabric on OAM modules). AMD Instinct MI300X OAM: 7-link Infinity Fabric = 896 GB/s aggregate. Performance near-equivalent for all-reduce; MI300X wins on memory capacity and can eliminate gradient checkpointing.

scenario: You are choosing between an 8x H100 NVLink node and an 8x MI300X Infinity Fabric node for a 70B parameter LLM training job with TP=8. Compare the all-reduce performance and memory capacity tradeoffs.
title: Infinity Fabric vs NVLink for Scale-Up Topology

details.common_mistake: Assuming uniform TDP means uniform thermal load. The TDP reading is an aggregate; individual XCDs can have hotspots from unequal workload distribution (e.g., embedding lookups concentrated on certain XCDs by tensor parallelism rank assignment) while the average temperature appears normal.
details.napkin_math: MI300X TDP: 750W over 8 XCDs = ~94W per XCD average. If XCDs 0-1 carry 1.4x load: 130W each vs 83W for others. Junction temperature delta: 130W * 0.08°C/W thermal resistance = 10.4°C above average. If average is 75°C, XCDs 0-1 hit 85.4°C → frequency throttle threshold typically 85°C.
details.realistic_solution: XCDs 0 and 1 are throttling due to localized hotspots even though the package-level thermal sensor reads nominal. Root cause: the job's memory access pattern creates non-uniform HBM utilization — XCDs 0-1 serve as the 'master' ranks handling cross-XCD reduction which increases their compute and traffic load. Fix: (1) redistribute tensor parallel ranks so reduction work rotates across XCDs; (2) enable per-XCD frequency monitoring via rocm-smi --showclkfreq; (3) adjust power limit per XCD using ROCm SMI power cap features; (4) verify thermal interface paste distribution — chiplet packages with interposers can have uneven TIM coverage.

scenario: In production, MI300X TDP readings are uniform but sustained throughput on one job type drops 12% after 30 minutes. rocm-smi shows temperature uniform across XCDs but frequency drops on XCDs 0 and 1. Diagnose and fix.
title: XCD Hot-Spot Thermal Management Under Sustained Load

details.common_mistake: Treating CXL memory as equivalent to HBM with lower bandwidth. CXL 3.0 latency (100-200ns) is 5-10x higher than HBM (20-40ns), and bandwidth per pin is lower. For LLM decode where each token generation requires loading ~140GB of model weights, latency sensitivity is high and the bandwidth gap is critical.
details.napkin_math: 70B BF16 weights = 140 GB. 4x HBM3 stacks: 100 GB, 2 TB/s. CXL tier: 40 GB, 400 GB/s, 150ns latency. Per-layer weight load: 140GB/80 = 1.75 GB/layer. HBM: 1.75GB / 2TB/s = 0.875ms/layer. CXL: 1.75GB / 400GB/s = 4.375ms/layer + latency overhead. 20 CXL layers: 20 * 4.375ms = 87.5ms. Full model if all HBM: 80 * 0.875ms = 70ms. Mixed: 60*0.875 + 20*4.375 = 52.5 + 87.5 = 140ms — 2x slowdown for CXL layers.
details.realistic_solution: Tiered approach: keep KV cache and active layer weights in HBM (hot tier), use CXL for inactive layers and spilled KV from long-context requests (warm tier). For 70B model decode with TP=1: each forward pass loads all 80 layers sequentially. With 4 HBM stacks (2 TB/s) + 2 CXL modules (400 GB/s): place first 60 layers in HBM, last 20 in CXL. CXL layers take 5x longer to load. If CXL layers are 25% of model: decode latency increases 25% * 5x = ~100% for those layers, avg ~25% slowdown. Justified only if cost savings > 25% SLA degradation impact.

scenario: A hyperscaler proposes replacing some HBM stacks on a chiplet AI accelerator with CXL 3.0 attached DRAM to reduce cost while maintaining capacity for LLM inference. Analyze the bandwidth and latency tradeoffs for a 70B model serving workload.
title: Disaggregated Memory Architecture: CXL vs HBM on Chiplet

details.common_mistake: Immediately blaming the SerDes IP or process node. BER degradation at 112G PAM-4 is more commonly caused by interposer trace impedance mismatch, bump inductance at die-interposer interface, or insufficient equalization coefficients rather than SerDes IP bugs.
details.napkin_math: 112G PAM-4: 2 bits/symbol at 56 Gbaud. Nyquist frequency = 28 GHz. Maximum allowable IL at 28GHz for 1e-12 BER: ~4dB total channel budget. Breakdown: PCB trace 0.5dB, connector 0.3dB, interposer trace 1.5dB target, bump interface 0.5dB, TX/RX package 0.5dB = 3.3dB. If measured is 1e-8 BER, channel loss is ~5.5dB — ~2dB over budget, likely interposer stub resonance.
details.realistic_solution: Systematic diagnosis: (1) Measure insertion loss (IL) and return loss (RL) with VNA at interposer bumps — target IL < 3dB at 28GHz (Nyquist for 112G PAM-4). (2) Check via stub resonance on interposer — stubs create notches at f = c/(4*stub_length*sqrt(Er)). (3) Verify bump array ground-signal-ground ratio — insufficient ground return causes simultaneous switching noise. (4) Tune CTLE/DFE tap weights via receiver adaptation sweep. At 112G PAM-4, 1dB extra loss degrades SNR by ~0.5dB, increasing BER by ~1 order of magnitude. Fix: back-drill vias to remove stubs, add decoupling caps at bump periphery, re-tune DFE.

scenario: Your chiplet AI accelerator uses 112G PAM-4 SerDes for die-to-die links on a passive silicon interposer. Signal integrity testing shows BER of 1e-8, which is above the target of 1e-12. Systematic root cause analysis is needed.
title: Chiplet Package Signal Integrity at 112G SerDes

details.common_mistake: Adding bulk capacitance at the PCB level to solve on-package droop. PCB decoupling caps have ~10ns response time, but on-package voltage droop during burst workloads occurs in 1-2ns. The effective series inductance (ESL) of PCB capacitors makes them ineffective for nanosecond-scale droop.
details.napkin_math: Compute die: 1V supply, 300A peak per die. IR drop = I * Z_PDN. At 8% droop: Z = 0.08V / 300A = 0.27mΩ per die. For 4 dies in parallel sharing supply: Z_total = 0.27/4 = 0.067mΩ. Wait — 8% at 1V = 80mV droop. 80mV / 300A = 0.27mΩ per die. Adding 50 μF on-die decap with ESL 100pH: impedance at 1GHz = 2π*1G*100pH + 1/(2π*1G*50μF) = 0.63mΩ + 3.2μΩ ≈ 0.63mΩ. On-die decap dominates at lower frequency; need VRM improvement for full solution.
details.realistic_solution: Address droop at each hierarchy: (1) On-die decap: maximize MOM capacitor fill in all metal layers above active logic — target 10 nF/mm² on N5. (2) Package-embedded capacitors: thin-film capacitors in package substrate (100 pF/mm²), placed directly under hot compute regions. (3) Active voltage regulator (AVR) on package: integrated VRM with <2ns response time, 100A/ns slew rate. (4) Structured power mesh: 4um pitch power grid on M8/M9 to minimize IR drop. Budget: 8% droop at 750A transient current implies 8mΩ effective PDN impedance. Target: 3% → need 2.25mΩ. Achieve with on-die decap (reduces high-freq component) + faster VRM.

scenario: A chiplet AI accelerator with 4 compute dies and 2 HBM stacks on a silicon interposer experiences voltage droop of 8% during matrix multiply bursts, causing frequency throttling. Design a power delivery network to reduce droop to under 3%.
title: Multi-Die Power Delivery Network Design for AI Chiplet

details.common_mistake: Comparing peak TFLOPS directly and concluding MI300X always wins. The ridge point (compute/bandwidth ratio) determines whether a workload is compute or memory bound, and the two accelerators have very different ridge points due to their different chiplet architectures.
details.napkin_math: Memory bandwidth bound: achieved_TFLOPS = BW * AI. H100: 3.35e12 * 120 = 402 TFLOPS (41% of peak). MI300X: 5.3e12 * 120 = 636 TFLOPS (35% of peak). MI300X advantage = 636/402 = 1.58x. Crossover to compute-bound: H100 at AI=295, MI300X at AI=345. LLM inference decode (AI ~5) → strongly memory bound. LLM training large-batch (AI ~500) → compute bound.
details.realistic_solution: Ridge point = Peak TFLOPS / Peak BW. H100: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOP/byte. MI300X: 1826 TFLOPS / 5.3 TB/s = 345 FLOP/byte. Arithmetic intensity = 120 FLOP/byte. Both accelerators: 120 < 295 (H100 ridge) and 120 < 345 (MI300X ridge) → both are memory-bandwidth bound at this intensity. Achieved TFLOPS = BW * arithmetic_intensity. H100: 3.35 TB/s * 120 = 402 TFLOPS. MI300X: 5.3 TB/s * 120 = 636 TFLOPS. MI300X is 58% faster for this workload — primarily due to its 58% higher memory bandwidth, not its compute advantage.

scenario: You are comparing BF16 training performance on MI300X (8 XCDs, 5.3 TB/s, ~1826 TFLOPS BF16) vs H100 SXM5 (989 TFLOPS BF16, 3.35 TB/s). For a batch of transformer forward passes with arithmetic intensity 120 FLOP/byte, predict which accelerator is bandwidth-bound vs compute-bound.
title: Chiplet Roofline Model for Mixed Precision LLM Training

details.common_mistake: Treating inter-XCD latency as a fixed overhead to subtract from throughput. In a pipelined system, die-to-die latency causes bubbles that compound — a 180ns stall in a stage with 100ns compute time effectively doubles that stage's wall time and reduces pipeline efficiency.
details.napkin_math: Without die crossings: throughput = 1/T_compute. With 3 crossings at 180ns each: added latency = 540ns = 0.00054ms. If forward pass compute = 10ms: new time = 10ms + 0.00054ms = 10.00054ms → 0.0054% slowdown. Observed 7% degradation implies other factors (e.g., pipeline stalls, cache misses, synchronization bubbles at XCD boundaries) dominate, not raw latency. Double-buffering: overlap 180ns transfer with next-stage compute → eliminates most stall → reduces to <1% overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline efficiency = compute_time / (compute_time + stall_time). The raw latency of 3 × 180ns = 540ns (0.00054ms) is negligible vs a 10ms forward pass. The 7% observed degradation must come from pipeline bubbles, not raw latency: if each XCD boundary crossing stalls a pipeline stage while waiting for data, the stall time = crossing latency / stage_granularity. If pipeline stage = 10ms/N_stages, stalls of 180ns per crossing can still bubble up to ~7% at fine granularity. Fix: (1) Use double-buffering at XCD boundaries — prefetch next layer's weights while current layer computes; (2) Remap layers to minimize XCD crossings — keep attention heads on same XCD as their FFN; (3) Overlap die-to-die transfer with independent computation using HIP streams.

scenario: A pipelined inference system on a multi-chiplet accelerator shows 7% throughput degradation compared to simulation. The pipeline crosses XCD boundaries 3 times per forward pass. Each XCD boundary crossing adds 180ns latency. Compute the pipeline bubble rate and propose fixes.
title: Chiplet Die-to-Die Latency Impact on Pipeline Bubble Rate

details.common_mistake: Designing a shared memory pool with coherent access from both dies. Coherent shared memory between heterogeneous dies (different ISAs, different memory models) requires a complex coherency protocol that adds 3-5x latency compared to explicit message passing for large data transfers.
details.napkin_math: Signal processing output: 100MB/s continuous, 16K FFT per batch = 128KB per call at 780 calls/sec. AI die needs 128KB every 1.28ms. Die-to-die DMA at 500 GB/s: 128KB transfer = 0.26us — negligible. Coherent shared access: 128KB at cache-line granularity (64B) = 2048 coherency transactions at 200ns each = 409us — 1573x slower than DMA. DMA is clearly correct architecture.
details.realistic_solution: Use a producer-consumer pipeline with explicit DMA: DSP outputs signal processing results to a shared SRAM buffer on the interposer; AI die reads via DMA with coherency disabled (streaming mode). Interpose a small (4-16 MB) low-latency SRAM on the active interposer as a staging buffer. DSP signals AI die via lightweight interrupt through a mailbox register. This avoids coherency overhead while achieving <1us data handoff latency. For large tensors (>16MB), use HBM partition assignment — DSP writes to HBM partition A, AI die reads from partition A directly after DSP signals completion.

scenario: A cloud inference service needs to combine dense DNN inference with heavy signal processing (FFT, filtering). The proposal is to integrate a DSP die and an AI inference die on the same chiplet package. Design the data path and memory sharing strategy.
title: Heterogeneous Chiplet Integration: DSP + AI Core on Same Package

details.common_mistake: Treating rank selection as a hyperparameter to maximize without a principled framework. Teams run expensive sweeps or default to r=8 or r=16 without analyzing the intrinsic dimensionality of the task or measuring gradient signal through the LoRA matrices.
details.napkin_math: Memory for LoRA adapters on Llama-3 70B: rank r, model dim d=8192, 80 attention layers. Per layer: 2 matrices (Q,V) * 2 (A+B) * r * d * 2B (BF16). r=4: 2*2*4*8192*2 = 262KB/layer * 80 = 21MB. r=16: 83MB. r=64: 335MB. Full fine-tune delta: 2*d*d*2B = 268MB per layer = 21.5GB total. LoRA r=64: 335MB vs 21.5GB full = 64x compression even at high rank.
details.realistic_solution: LoRA approximates the weight update delta_W = B*A where A in R^(r x d) and B in R^(d x r). The optimal rank equals the intrinsic dimensionality of the task-specific weight update. SQL generation is a structured task with grammar constraints — its update space is low-dimensional but not trivially so. Intrinsic dimensionality analysis: compute SVD of full fine-tune delta_W and count singular values above 1% of top SV threshold. For code-like tasks: typically r=16-32 captures >95% of the signal. Diagnosis: rank 4 misses fine-grained syntax patterns; rank 64 overfits or adds noise. Use r=16 as baseline; verify with SV analysis on a rank-64 run: if top 16 SVs capture 95% of variance, r=16 is optimal.

scenario: A team fine-tunes Llama-3 70B for SQL generation using LoRA. They try rank 4, 16, and 64. Rank 4 underperforms by 8% on evaluation metrics. Rank 64 shows no improvement over rank 16 but uses 4x more memory. Explain why and choose the right rank.
title: LoRA Rank Sensitivity to Task Complexity

details.common_mistake: Only accounting for the quantized base model weights and forgetting optimizer states, gradients, and activation memory during backward pass. QLoRA only quantizes the frozen base model; LoRA adapters and their optimizer states are in full precision.
details.napkin_math: NF4 quantization: 4 bits/param = 0.5 bytes. 70B * 0.5 = 35GB. Double quant: quantize the quantization constants (FP32 to 8-bit) for 256-element blocks. Savings: (32-8)/256 bits/param = 0.09375 bits/param. 70B * 0.09375/8 = 820MB savings. Total base model: 35 - 0.82 = 34.2GB. Plus LoRA: +0.25GB. Plus activations (gradient checkpoint): +0.5GB. Total: ~35GB. Fits in 80GB with 45GB headroom for batching.
details.realistic_solution: QLoRA memory breakdown: (1) Base model NF4: 70B params * 0.5 bytes = 35GB. (2) Double quantization saves ~0.37 bits/param additionally: 70B * 0.37/8 = 3.2GB savings = 31.8GB. (3) LoRA adapters (r=16): ~83MB in BF16 (negligible). (4) LoRA optimizer states (Adam): 2 * 83MB = 166MB. (5) Activation memory per layer during backward: depends on batch size and sequence length. For batch=1, seq=2048, Llama-3 70B: ~256MB activations with gradient checkpointing. (6) CUDA kernels + overhead: ~2GB. Total: 31.8 + 0.17 + 0.26 + 2 = 34.2GB. Fits in 80GB with room for batch size 2-4.

scenario: A team wants to fine-tune a 70B model on a single 80GB H100 using QLoRA. They plan to use NF4 base weights with double quantization. Calculate the total memory usage and verify feasibility.
title: QLoRA Double Quantization Memory Accounting

details.common_mistake: Loading all 500 adapters into GPU memory simultaneously. At r=16, each adapter is ~4MB. 500 adapters = 2GB, but the per-adapter KV cache context and batching overhead means serving 500 adapters simultaneously fragments GPU memory and increases scheduling latency.
details.napkin_math: Zipf: top 20% adapters (100) handle 80% of 200 QPS = 160 QPS. Bottom 80% (400 adapters) handle 40 QPS. Hot pool hit rate: 80%. Miss rate 20% = 40 QPS need loading. Each cold load: 4MB NVMe. NVMe 7 GB/s handles 7000/4 = 1750 loads/sec. Bandwidth not a bottleneck. TTFT budget: 100ms. Prefill 512 tokens on 8B model: ~10ms on H100. Cold load: 0.6ms. Total: 10.6ms, well within 100ms. At 3x traffic spike: 120 cold loads/sec, still fine at 1750 capacity.
details.realistic_solution: S-LoRA paged adapter system: maintain a hot-adapter pool in GPU memory (top 100 adapters by request rate = 2GB) and a warm pool on CPU memory (next 200 adapters = 4GB, NVLink-accessible). Cold adapters (remaining 200) stay on NVMe. Serving: for hot adapters, LoRA weights are fused into the compute path with no loading overhead. For warm adapters, NVLink transfer at 900 GB/s: 4MB at 900 GB/s = 4.4us, negligible. For cold adapters: NVMe read at 7 GB/s = 571us + PCIe transfer 64 GB/s = 62us = ~633us total. Prefill for typical prompt (512 tokens) on 8B model: ~50ms. Cold load: 0.6ms, total ~51ms, within 100ms budget.

scenario: A serving system hosts 500 LoRA adapters over a single Llama-3 8B base model on 4xH100. Average request rate is 200 QPS with a Zipf distribution (20% of adapters handle 80% of traffic). Design the adapter loading strategy to meet P99 TTFT < 100ms.
title: Multi-Adapter Hot-Swap Serving with S-LoRA

details.common_mistake: Continuing to optimize with a tighter KL coefficient (beta) without investigating what reward features the model exploits. A higher beta just slows down the hacking; it does not prevent the model from finding reward model blind spots.
details.napkin_math: KL divergence 12 nats: this is high. Rule of thumb: KL > 8 nats indicates significant distribution shift. Expected-KL cost to performance: each 1 nat above 6 reduces human preference rate by ~1-2% empirically. At 12 nats: 6 nats excess = -6% to -12% human preference. If initial preference = 75%, after hacking: 63-69%. Recommended PPO beta: 0.1-0.3 for first training run. With beta=0.1 and 12 nats KL: KL penalty = 0.1 * 12 = 1.2 reward units — insufficient to prevent hacking.
details.realistic_solution: Reward hacking symptoms: reward model (RM) assigns high scores to responses that humans rate poorly. Common failure modes: (1) length bias — RM trained on human data where longer responses were preferred, model generates verbose non-answers; (2) formatting exploitation — RM overfits to formatting patterns (bullet points, code blocks); (3) sycophancy — model learns to agree with implied user preferences. Diagnosis: sample 50 high-reward responses, have raters evaluate on separate rubric. Check response length distribution vs reference. Fix: (1) Add length penalty: r_adjusted = r_rm - lambda * max(0, len - len_ref); (2) Retrain RM with adversarial examples; (3) Use ensemble RMs; (4) Reduce PPO epochs; (5) Set KL threshold at 6-8 nats and stop when exceeded.

scenario: After 3 PPO epochs in an RLHF training run for a coding assistant, reward scores increase steadily but human rater evaluations decline. The KL divergence from the reference policy has grown to 12 nats. Diagnose reward hacking and prescribe a fix.
title: RLHF Reward Model Overoptimization Detection

details.common_mistake: Simply adding the two adapter weight matrices together (delta_W1 + delta_W2). This works for orthogonal adapters but causes interference when both adapters modify the same weight directions.
details.napkin_math: LoRA inference overhead for r=16 on Llama-3 8B: per layer, LoRA adds 2 matmuls: (seq_len, d) @ (d, r) + (seq_len, r) @ (r, d). FLOP per layer: 2 * seq_len * d * r = 2 * 512 * 4096 * 16 = 67M FLOP. Base layer FLOP: 2 * seq_len * d * d = 2 * 512 * 4096^2 = 17.2B FLOP. LoRA overhead per layer: 67M / 17.2B = 0.4%. Two sequential adapters: 0.8% overhead. Negligible, sequential composition is safe and avoids interference analysis.
details.realistic_solution: Three approaches: (1) Sequential: apply adapter 1 then adapter 2 at inference. Adds 2x LoRA compute overhead but preserves each adapter's behavior. (2) Parallel merge: delta_W_merged = alpha1 * B1*A1 + alpha2 * B2*A2. Check interference via cosine similarity of B1*A1 and B2*A2. If cosine < 0.1 (near orthogonal), addition is safe. Scale factors alpha control contribution. (3) Task arithmetic: merge weights into base before serving, zero inference overhead but static. For medical+formal: these are likely near-orthogonal (different attention heads specialize for domain vs style). Use parallel merge with alpha1=alpha2=0.7 (scale down to avoid magnitude explosion). Validate on held-out set covering both properties.

scenario: A multi-tenant serving system needs to apply two LoRA adapters simultaneously: one for domain-specific knowledge (medical) and one for style (formal tone). Design whether to use sequential composition, parallel merge, or task vector arithmetic.
title: Adapter Composition: Sequential vs Parallel LoRA Merging

details.common_mistake: Selecting LoRA by default without considering that (IA)^3 has 100x fewer parameters for similar or better performance on many tasks, especially when training data is small. For a 10K example dataset, overfitting risk with LoRA (millions of adapter params) is real.
details.napkin_math: LoRA r=4, 140B model: trainable params = 2 * num_layers * d_model * r * 2. Llama-3 140B approx: 120 layers, d=8192. Params = 2*120*8192*4*2 = 15.7M. (IA)^3: 3 * num_layers * d = 3*120*8192 = 2.95M params. 5x fewer than LoRA r=4. Adam optimizer states: LoRA r=4: 15.7M * 2 * 4B = 126MB. (IA)^3: 2.95M * 2 * 4B = 23.6MB. Both negligible vs 280GB base. Training time difference: proportional to trainable params, so (IA)^3 is ~5x faster per step.
details.realistic_solution: Method comparison for 140B model with 10K examples: (1) LoRA (r=16): 140M adapter params. Memory: base model 280GB BF16 + 280MB adapters + 560MB optimizer = ~281GB. Requires 4xH100 with TP=4. Training: 3-4 GPU-hours. Risk: may overfit with 10K examples; use r=4. (2) (IA)^3: ~1M adapter params (element-wise scaling). Memory: 280GB + 2MB adapters = ~280GB. Same GPU requirement. Training faster than LoRA. Better regularization for small datasets. (3) Prefix tuning: soft prompt tokens prepended to each layer. ~700K params but inference overhead: prefixes add to KV cache for every request, expensive at scale. Recommendation: (IA)^3 for 10K dataset with unknown task difficulty; LoRA r=4 if task requires structural knowledge; avoid prefix tuning for production serving.

scenario: Your team must fine-tune a 140B parameter model on a 10K example dataset for a specialized enterprise task. Full fine-tune requires 48xH100. Compare LoRA, (IA)^3, and prefix tuning on memory efficiency, performance, and training time.
title: PEFT Strategy Selection for 100B+ Models at Cloud Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming applying LoRA to all layers always improves performance. The common misunderstanding is that more trainable parameters always help. For many tasks, attention mechanisms capture task-relevant transformations, and adding LoRA to MLP layers adds capacity without proportional improvement.
