details.napkin_math: Mistral 7B, r=8: Q+V only: 2 * 32 * 4096 * 8 * 2 = 4.19M params. All-linear (Q,K,V,O + gate,up,down) — correct LoRA params per linear layer = r*(d_in + d_out). For attn [4096,4096]: r*(4096+4096)=65,536 per matrix × 4 matrices × 32 layers = 8.39M. MLP [4096,14336]: r*(4096+14336)=147,456 per matrix × 3 matrices × 32 layers = 14.15M. Total all-linear ≈ 8.39M + 14.15M = 22.5M params. ~5.4× more than Q+V. GPU memory delta: 22.5M * 2B (BF16) = 45MB — still small. Training time delta: 5.4× more gradient computation.
details.realistic_solution: LoRA module selection for Mistral 7B: standard (Q+V only): 2 matrices × 32 layers × d=4096 × r. All-linear (Q,K,V,O,gate,up,down): 7 matrices × 32 layers. Memory scaling: ~5× more params for all-linear. For classification tasks, the final MLP layers are most task-critical, so adding LoRA to MLP is more valuable than for generation tasks. Research finding: for classification and extraction tasks, Q+V+down_proj covers 90%+ of performance of all-linear at ~50% the parameter count. For generation/instruction-following: Q+V+up_proj captures attention-MLP interaction. Ablation test: start with Q+V, measure validation performance, add MLP matrices, check if improvement exceeds 0.5% practical significance threshold.

scenario: A team fine-tuning Mistral 7B for classification debates whether to apply LoRA to only Q and V projections (standard practice) versus all linear layers including MLP. Calculate the parameter count difference and performance implications.
title: LoRA Target Module Selection: Q/K/V/O vs All Linear Layers

details.common_mistake: Using the same size model as the policy for the reward model. A 70B RM would require 16xA100 just to serve, consuming more compute than the policy training itself. Empirically, RM performance scales with data quality more than model size.
details.napkin_math: 7B model forward pass at 512 tokens on A100: ~12ms. Single A100: 1000/12 = 83 QPS serial. With continuous batching (batch=8): effective throughput ~200 QPS per A100. 2xA100 TP=2: 200 QPS. 4xA100 in 2 separate TP=2 instances: 400 QPS. To hit 500 QPS: need 6xA100 or use FP8 on 4xA100 for 1.5x throughput boost: 400 * 1.5 = 600 QPS. FP8 inference on A100 is feasible for RM scoring (lower precision acceptable for ranking).
details.realistic_solution: RM sizing: empirical finding is that RM performance plateaus at 10-20% of policy model size for typical RLHF tasks. Use 7B RM on 2xA100 in TP=2 (14GB per GPU for BF16 + KV cache). Architecture: take a pretrained 7B model, replace next-token prediction head with a scalar output head (single linear layer: d_model to 1). Training: binary cross-entropy or Bradley-Terry loss on human preference pairs. Serving for 500 QPS: 7B model on 2xA100, BF16, sequence length 512. With continuous batching at batch=16: ~120 QPS per GPU pair = 240 QPS for 2 serving instances. For 500 QPS: need 3 pairs = 6xA100. With 4xA100 budget: use 2xA100 for serving (240 QPS) and queue the remaining requests, or serve at BF16 vs FP8 for higher throughput.

scenario: Design a reward model (RM) for an RLHF pipeline fine-tuning a 70B policy model. The RM needs to score completions at 500 QPS during PPO rollouts. Budget: 4xA100. Specify the RM model size, architecture, and serving strategy.
title: Reward Model Architecture for RLHF at Scale

details.common_mistake: Assuming frozen base weights prevent catastrophic forgetting. The LoRA adapters themselves can accumulate task interference across monthly updates if each new adapter is merged additively into the base, causing the effective base to drift from the original.
details.napkin_math: 4 months of updates, 15% degradation = ~3.75% per update. EWC regularization cost: compute Fisher information matrix of 15M LoRA params = 15M * 4B (FP32 FIM diagonal) = 60MB storage per checkpoint. Negligible. Replay 5% of 3 previous months: if monthly dataset = 10K examples, replay = 0.05 * 30K = 1500 examples. Adds ~15% to training time. Expected forgetting with replay: <0.5%/month empirically.
details.realistic_solution: Frozen base prevents catastrophic forgetting of base knowledge. But if the deployment pattern merges adapters into the base (for efficiency) and then trains new adapters on top of the merged base, the frozen base is different each month and gradually drifts. Fix A (no merge): maintain versioned separate adapters, serve them in ensemble. Fix B (merge with regularization): when merging adapter n, add EWC (Elastic Weight Consolidation) penalty for parameters important to previous tasks. Fix C (adapter capacity): train each monthly adapter to be orthogonal to previous adapters using Gram-Schmidt on the LoRA B matrices. Fix D (replay): include 5% of old task data in each monthly training run. Most practical: Fix D with 5% replay buffer sampled from each of the 4 previous months.

scenario: A production LLM is updated monthly with new LoRA adapters trained on fresh data. After 4 months, benchmark performance on original tasks has degraded 15% even though the base model weights are frozen. Diagnose the continual learning failure.
title: Continual Adaptation: Catastrophic Forgetting in LoRA Updates

details.common_mistake: Reducing the clip ratio to stabilize training without investigating the value function separately. PPO uses a value function baseline to reduce variance; if the value function is poorly calibrated, even a tight clip ratio will not prevent reward collapse.
details.napkin_math: PPO clip ratio epsilon=0.2 allows up to 20% policy ratio change per step. For LLMs this is typically too aggressive. Recommended: epsilon=0.1 for 7B models, epsilon=0.05 for 70B models. Value function lr ratio: value_lr = 10x * policy_lr is common. At policy_lr=1e-6: value_lr=1e-5. Value loss should converge within 100 steps if architecture is correct. High value loss (>0.5 after 500 steps) indicates the value head architecture is too shallow. Add 1-2 hidden layers to the value MLP.
details.realistic_solution: Reward collapse in PPO has two causes: (1) Policy updates too large (fix: reduce epsilon or learning rate); (2) Value function divergence making advantage estimates unreliable (fix: separate value function learning rate, add value loss clipping). If value loss is high while policy loss is stable, the bottleneck is the value function. In RLHF with an LLM, the value head is a small MLP added to the last layer that often needs more updates than the policy. Fix: (1) Use separate optimizers: policy lr=1e-6, value lr=1e-5; (2) Run value function warmup for 5 epochs before starting policy updates; (3) Add value loss clipping: clip(V - V_old, -eps_v, +eps_v) with eps_v=0.5; (4) Normalize advantages: (A - mean(A)) / (std(A) + 1e-8). Reduce clip epsilon from 0.2 to 0.1 only if policy updates are confirmed too large.

scenario: An RLHF PPO training run shows high reward variance with frequent reward collapses every 200 steps. The policy loss is stable but value function loss is high. The clip ratio epsilon is currently 0.2. Diagnose and tune.
title: PPO Clip Ratio Tuning for RLHF Stability

details.common_mistake: Using simple gradient averaging across tasks and assuming the highest-loss task will eventually converge. Summarization and QA may have gradients that directly conflict with code generation in the shared LoRA parameter space, causing the code task to regress.
details.napkin_math: PCGrad overhead: compute gradient dot products across all task pairs. 3 tasks = 3 pairs. Gradient vector size = LoRA params = 15M floats (r=8 on 7B). Dot product: 15M FLOP = negligible (H100 does this in 15us). PCGrad projection: 3 * 15M FLOP per pair = 135M FLOP/step vs forward pass ~42B FLOP = 0.3% overhead. MoLoRA: 3x adapter memory = 3 * 30MB = 90MB + router (tiny MLP per layer = 32 * 4096 * 3 = 393K params = 786KB). Total MoLoRA overhead: ~90MB memory + 1.5% compute for router.
details.realistic_solution: Gradient conflict diagnosis: compute cosine similarity between task gradients at the LoRA parameters at step 500. If cos(g_code, g_summarization) < -0.3, they are conflicting. Methods to resolve: (1) PCGrad (Project Conflicting Gradients): project each task's gradient onto the orthogonal complement of conflicting gradients. Reduces interference without requiring separate adapters. (2) GradNorm: dynamically reweight task losses to equalize gradient magnitudes. (3) Mixture of LoRA Experts (MoLoRA): add a router layer that selects which LoRA adapter to apply per token per layer. (4) Task-specific learning rates: use lower lr for saturating tasks and higher for underfitting. MoLoRA is most robust for 3+ tasks with conflicting gradients but doubles serving memory.

scenario: A single LoRA adapter is trained simultaneously on 3 tasks: summarization, code generation, and QA. Training loss for code generation increases after step 500 while the other tasks improve. Gradient conflict analysis is needed.
title: Multi-Task LoRA Training with Gradient Conflict Resolution

details.common_mistake: Assuming DPO is always cheaper than PPO. DPO requires the reference model to be loaded simultaneously with the policy for computing log-probability ratios. For 70B models, this means 2x model memory, often requiring more GPUs than PPO with a shared reference policy.
details.napkin_math: DPO training time: 200K preference pairs, batch=32, 70B model. Both policy and reference forward: 2 * 200K * 512 * 2 * 70B FLOP = 1.79 EFLOP. 32xH100 at 989 TFLOPS at 40% MFU: 12.7 PFLOPS. Time: 1.79E18 / 12.7E15 = 141 seconds per step. Hmm, recalculate: 200K samples total. Per-sample FLOP = 2 * seq * params * 2 = 2 * 512 * 70e9 * 2 = 143T FLOP (both ref+policy). 200K * 143T = 28.6 EFLOP. At 12.7 PFLOPS: 28.6E18 / 12.7E15 = 2252 seconds = 37.5 min per epoch. 3 epochs: 1.9 hours — very fast on 32xH100.
details.realistic_solution: DPO memory: policy (140GB BF16) + reference model (140GB BF16) + optimizer (280GB for AdamW) = 560GB minimum. Requires ~14xH100. PPO memory: policy (140GB) + value head (~1GB) + reward model (14GB for 7B RM) + reference (frozen copy at FP8, ~70GB): ~225GB total, about 3xH100 for models. PPO is more GPU-efficient per GPU but requires more infrastructure complexity (rollout server, RM server, PPO trainer). At 32xH100 budget: DPO uses 14 GPUs leaving 18 for larger batch sizes. PPO uses 8 GPUs for models + rollout infrastructure, enabling larger effective batch. DPO training on 200K pairs at 32xH100: ~2-3 days. PPO: ~5-7 days due to rollout generation overhead. Recommendation: DPO for budget-constrained simpler implementation; PPO for iterative online alignment with real user feedback.

scenario: A team must choose between DPO and PPO for aligning a 70B model. Budget: 32xH100 for 1 week. Preference dataset: 200K pairs. Compare compute cost, stability, and expected alignment quality.
title: DPO vs PPO Infrastructure Cost for Alignment at 70B Scale

details.common_mistake: Storing only the latest version of each adapter and relying on retraining to recover the previous version. This makes rollback take hours rather than minutes, violating SLA requirements for incident response.
details.napkin_math: Adapter v22 storage: 4MB in S3. S3 download at 1 Gbps: 4MB/125MB/s = 32ms. At 10 Gbps: 3.2ms. CPU-to-GPU PCIe transfer (PCIe 4.0 x16 = 32 GB/s): 4MB/32GB/s = 0.125ms. Total hot-swap: <50ms. With S-LoRA paged system, old adapter pages evicted and new pages loaded atomically between batches. Zero-downtime rollback achievable.
details.realistic_solution: Adapter versioning system: (1) Object store (S3/GCS) stores all adapter versions in serialized format (safetensors): ~4MB per adapter per version. 100 adapters * 10 versions = 1GB storage, trivial cost. (2) Serving system maintains in-memory adapter cache and version manifest JSON. (3) Rollback API: PATCH /adapters/{adapter_id}/active_version triggers: (a) Load v22 from S3 to serving node CPU memory (4MB, <100ms over 10 Gbps), (b) Hot-swap in GPU memory via paged adapter swapping, (c) Update version manifest, (d) Emit rollback metrics. Total rollback time: S3 fetch 100ms + CPU-GPU copy 4ms + manifest update 1ms = <200ms. For 5-minute SLA: metric anomaly detection (1min) + triage (2min) + rollback execution (0.2min) = 3.2min. Feasible. (4) Blue-green adapter deployment: run v22 and v23 on separate pods, route 1% traffic to v23, automated canary analysis for 24h before full rollout.

scenario: A production system serving 100 LoRA adapters rolls out new adapter updates weekly. A deployment of adapter v23 causes a 5% increase in user complaint rate. Design the rollback system to revert v23 to v22 within 5 minutes.
title: Adapter Versioning and Rollback in Production ML Systems

details.common_mistake: Distilling the full 70B adapted model into a smaller model. Full distillation (70B teacher to 7B student) takes weeks and may not preserve adapter-specific knowledge if the student lacks enough capacity for both base and adapter knowledge.
details.napkin_math: 70B model TTFT at 512-token prompt on 4xH100 TP=4: prefill FLOP = 2 * seq_len * model_params = 2 * 512 * 70e9 = 71.7T FLOP. At 4xH100 effective 1600 TFLOPS: 71.7T / 1600T = 44.8ms. Close to 50ms but tight. 7B student: 2 * 512 * 7e9 = 7.17T FLOP. At 1xH100 400 TFLOPS: 17.9ms. Well under 50ms. With speculative decoding: effective TTFT similar to 7B-only for first batch.
details.realistic_solution: Adapter-aware distillation strategy: (1) Merge the LoRA adapter into the 70B base weights: W_merged = W_base + alpha * B*A. This creates a 70B specialized model. (2) Use the merged 70B as teacher to distill a 7B student with KL divergence loss, only on the adapter's target domain data. The student learns the merged behavior without needing to separately handle base + adapter. (3) Alternatively, train a 7B student with LoRA using the 70B adapted model as teacher — the 7B+LoRA serves as the production model. (4) For maximum latency reduction: speculative decoding with 7B adapted student as draft and 70B as verifier. Draft latency: 7B at ~5ms/token. Verification batch: 4 tokens per 70B call at 20ms. Accept rate ~80%: effective throughput = 4*0.8/20ms = 0.16 tokens/ms = 6.4x speedup over 70B alone.

scenario: A latency-sensitive serving system has a 70B base model with a domain LoRA adapter (r=16) but cannot meet P95 TTFT < 50ms. Propose an adapter distillation strategy to reduce latency while preserving adapter quality.
title: LoRA Adapter Distillation for Latency-Sensitive Serving

details.common_mistake: Applying rules of thumb about full fine-tuning data requirements to LoRA. Full fine-tuning of 8B parameters requires thousands of examples to avoid overfitting. LoRA adapts only millions of parameters, dramatically lowering the data requirement.
details.napkin_math: LoRA r=8 on Llama-3 8B (d=4096, 32 layers, Q+V): trainable params = 2 * 32 * 2 * 4096 * 8 = 4.2M. Data-to-params ratio with 500 examples at avg 512 tokens: 500 * 512 = 256K training tokens. Tokens per trainable param: 256K / 4.2M = 0.061. This appears low, but LoRA overfit risk is buffered by the frozen pretrained weights providing implicit regularization. Practical threshold: 50K tokens (100 examples at 512 tokens) is empirically sufficient for style adaptation.
details.realistic_solution: LoRA data efficiency: since LoRA r=8 trains ~6M parameters (vs 8B base), the effective parameter-to-data ratio is 6M/500 = 12K params/example. For full fine-tune: 8B/500 = 16M params/example — severe overfitting risk. LoRA is fine with 500 examples if: (1) Examples are representative of the target distribution; (2) Regularization is applied (weight decay 0.01, dropout 0.05 on LoRA layers); (3) Evaluate on a held-out set (80/20 split = 400 train, 100 eval). Expected performance: 500 high-quality examples typically suffices for style transfer and domain terminology adaptation. Insufficient for: entirely new factual knowledge not in pretraining data. For pharmaceutical regs: most factual content exists in pretraining; LoRA helps with format and style. 500 examples is viable.

scenario: A team wants to fine-tune Llama-3 8B for pharmaceutical regulatory documents. They have 500 examples. A colleague argues they need at least 10K examples for LoRA to be effective. Who is right?
title: LoRA Training Data Efficiency: Minimum Viable Dataset Size

details.common_mistake: Sizing the prefill pool based on average load without a queuing model. Average utilization of 80% sounds fine but at P95, queue depth causes TTFT to exceed SLO. Engineers omit the M/D/1 or M/M/1 queuing term from the sizing calculation.
details.napkin_math: Assuming 8B model. Service time per request: 16.5ms. Target P95 TTFT: 200ms. M/M/1 queue: E[W] = rho / (mu * (1-rho)) where mu = 1/service_time. For E[W] + service_time < 200ms: rho/(60*(1-rho)) + 1/60 < 0.2. rho/(60-60*rho) < 0.183. rho < 0.183*(60-60*rho). rho < 11 - 11*rho. 12*rho < 11. rho < 0.917. At 500 RPS: need mu > 500/0.917 = 545 RPS. At 60 RPS/H100: 545/60 = 9.1 H100s. Round up to 10, plus 2 spare = 12 H100s.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill throughput per H100: 512-token prompt on 8B model = 2*512*8B = 8.19T FLOP. H100 at 989 TFLOPS, ~50% MFU = 989 TFLOPS effective. Time = 8.19T/495T = 16.5ms per request. Throughput per H100 = 1000/16.5 = 60 req/sec. For 500 RPS: 500/60 = 8.3 H100s (raw compute). But with queuing: for M/M/1 queue, P95 latency = -ln(1-0.95) / (mu - lambda) where mu = service rate, lambda = arrival rate. For 95th percentile TTFT < 200ms and service time 16.5ms: need utilization rho < 1 - (16.5ms / 200ms) = 0.92 approximately. At rho=0.9: 9/0.9 = 10 H100s minimum. Add 20% headroom: 12 H100s. Use 70B model: service time 10x longer, need 80-100 H100s for prefill pool.

scenario: A disaggregated serving system handles 500 RPS with average prompt length 512 tokens and P95 TTFT SLO of 200ms. How many H100s do you need in the prefill pool?
title: Prefill Pool GPU Count Formula for TTFT SLO

details.common_mistake: Applying general-purpose compression (LZ4, Zstd) to KV cache tensors. KV caches are floating point tensors with low compressibility under entropy coding — typical compression ratios are only 1.1-1.3x. The compute overhead of compression often exceeds the transfer savings.
details.napkin_math: 70B model KV cache for 512 tokens: layers=80, heads=64, head_dim=128. KV cache = 2 * 80 * 64 * 128 * 512 * 2B = 1,342,177,280 bytes = 1.25 GiB (1.34 GB). At 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s: 1.34GB / 50 GB/s = 26.8ms. But stated 3.2ms — implies this is for a smaller model or fewer heads. At 3.2ms: effective bandwidth = 1.34GB/3.2ms = 419 GB/s. With INT8 compression: 0.67GB at 419 GB/s = 1.6ms. TTFT improvement: 3.2ms - 1.6ms = 1.6ms saved.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache compression strategies: (1) Quantization: KV caches can be quantized to INT8 without significant quality loss (attention scores are softmax-normalized, less sensitive to quantization). INT8 KV = 2× compression, halves transfer size. (2) Cross-layer sharing (CLA): many adjacent layers have nearly identical KV patterns. Share KV cache across every 2 layers: 2× reduction in cache size at cost of minor quality degradation. (3) Head pruning: not all attention heads carry equal information across layers. Drop bottom 20% of heads by attention entropy variance: 20% reduction with <0.5% quality impact. Combined: INT8 (2×) + 20% head pruning (1.25×) = 2.5× compression. Transfer time: 3.2ms / 2.5 = 1.28ms. TTFT overhead drops from 16% to 6.4%. (4) Speculative KV: decode GPU speculatively starts generation with a partial KV cache (first 8 layers), receives remaining layers asynchronously — hides transfer behind compute.

scenario: In a disaggregated serving cluster, KV-cache transfer from prefill to decode GPUs uses 400 Gbps InfiniBand. A 70B model with 512-token prompt has KV cache that takes 3.2ms to transfer, adding 16% to TTFT. Design a compression scheme to reduce transfer time.
title: KV-Cache Transfer Compression to Reduce Network Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Using FIFO scheduling in the decode pool. Long requests that arrive first or early block short requests from completing, inflating P99 tail latency. FIFO is fair but not latency-optimal for mixed workloads.
details.napkin_math: Decode pool with 8xH100. At 100 tok/sec per request per H100 decode: each H100 handles ~80 requests in continuous batch (memory limited). 2000-token request occupies one slot for 20 seconds. 50-token request: 0.5 seconds. FIFO at 10% long: if 8 slots, probability all 8 are occupied by long requests: 0.1^8 = negligible. But if long requests arrive in bursts: FIFO P99 = time for long request to complete = 20 seconds. With preemption at 50-token quantum: P99 for short requests = wait for one quantum of long request + own decode = 50/100 = 0.5s + 0.5s = 1s vs 20s FIFO. 20x P99 improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-queue scheduling for decode pool: (1) Length prediction: at the end of prefill, use a lightweight length predictor (trained on prompt features) to estimate output length. Accuracy ~70% for broad buckets (short <50, medium 50-500, long 500+). (2) Preemptive multi-queue: assign requests to priority queues by predicted length. Short requests run at highest priority. Long requests are preempted after N tokens (configurable threshold) if short requests are waiting. (3) Preemption strategy: when a short request arrives and decode pool is full with a long request, pause the long request (checkpoint KV cache position + generated tokens), migrate to lower-priority queue. Resume when short requests clear. KV cache migration cost: negligible if within same GPU (just update scheduler state). (4) Max token budget per scheduling quantum: long requests get 50 tokens per quantum before yielding. Short requests run to completion.

scenario: A disaggregated decode pool processes requests with highly variable output lengths: 10% of requests generate 2000+ tokens (long-tail). These long requests occupy decode GPU slots for 40x longer than median requests, causing P99 TTOT to spike. Design a scheduling policy.
title: Decode Pool Scaling Policy Under Variable Output Length

details.common_mistake: Restarting all 200 requests from scratch (re-prefill). For requests that have already generated 1000+ tokens, re-prefill adds 5-10 seconds of latency and 1000 tokens of wasted compute. At 200 requests, this wastes significant GPU-hours and breaks user SLA.
details.napkin_math: 200 requests, average position 500 tokens. KV cache per request at 500 tokens (70B model): 2*80*64*128*500*2B = 1,310,720,000 bytes = 1.22 GiB (1.31 GB) per request. Total KV for 200 requests: 200 * 1.31 GB = 262 GB. Replication to secondary node: requires 262 GB free in secondary, or selective replication of top-K by token count. Checkpoint to NVMe (7 GB/s): 262 GB / 7 = 37.4 seconds per checkpoint — too slow for real-time. DRAM checkpoint: 262 GB to 3.35TB/s HBM copy = 0.078s. Feasible. PCIe 32 GB/s: 262GB / 32 = 8.2 seconds per checkpoint. Too slow if done synchronously — use async checkpoint every 100 tokens.
details.realistic_solution: Recovery hierarchy: (1) KV cache replication: if KV caches are replicated to a secondary decode node or a KV cache store (e.g., vLLM's distributed KV store or DistServe's KV migration), failover is instant. Cost: 2× KV cache memory across cluster. (2) Checkpoint-based recovery: periodically checkpoint KV caches to NVMe or DRAM (every 100 tokens). On failure: restore from last checkpoint, replay only since last checkpoint. At 100-token checkpoint granularity: worst case replay = 100 tokens per request. For 200 requests: 200 × 100 × decode_time = manageable. (3) Prefix cache reuse: for requests with unique KV caches (no prefix sharing), re-prefill is unavoidable. Minimize cost: batch re-prefill of all 200 requests on available prefill nodes, using their already-generated tokens as context. (4) Client-side retry: include generated tokens so far in retry request header; model continues from exact position. Requires streaming token delivery to client so partial output is already sent.

scenario: A decode node fails mid-generation with 200 active requests, each at different token positions (50-1500 tokens generated). The KV cache for these requests is in the failed node's GPU memory. Design a recovery protocol to restore service without full request re-execution.
title: Fault Tolerance for In-Flight Requests During Decode Node Failure

details.common_mistake: Setting prefill:decode ratio based on prompt:output token counts alone (256:512 = 1:2). Prefill compute scales as O(seq_len^2) due to attention, while decode is O(1) per token. The compute imbalance is not 1:2 — it requires roofline analysis of each phase.
details.napkin_math: Prefill H100 capacity: 36ms/request = 27.8 req/sec. Decode H100 capacity (batch=64, 512 output tokens): 64 requests * 512 tokens / 1531 tok/sec = 21.4 sec per batch. So each decode H100 handles 64/21.4 = 3 req/sec (serial). But pipelining: 64 requests complete at 0.33s each = 194 req/sec per decode H100 in continuous batching. So decode:prefill capacity ratio = 194/27.8 = 7. Optimal ratio: 1 prefill : 7 decode H100s. Rounding: 1:6 or 1:8 in 2x increments.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill compute (TTFT phase): FLOP for 256-token prompt on 70B = 2 * 256 * 70B = 35.8T FLOP. Prefill is compute-bound on H100 (arithmetic intensity > 295 FLOP/byte). Prefill throughput: 35.8T / 989T = 36ms per request. Decode compute per token: 2 * 70B = 140B FLOP per token. Decode is memory-bound (arithmetic intensity ~2 FLOP/byte at batch=1). Decode throughput per token: 70B * 2B / 3.35TB/s = 41.8ms. For 512 output tokens: 512 * 41.8ms = 21.4 seconds total decode time (single stream). In continuous batching at batch=64: decode throughput scales: 64 requests share 41.8ms per token step = 64 tok/step / 41.8ms = 1531 tok/sec per H100. Per request at 512 tokens: 512/1531 = 0.33 seconds. Ratio: prefill 36ms vs decode 334ms per request = 1:9.3. Prefill:decode ratio should be approximately 1:9 (1 prefill GPU per 9 decode GPUs). In practice: 1:4 to 1:8 due to variable traffic and batching efficiency.

scenario: A disaggregated serving fleet runs a 70B model. Traffic analysis shows average prompt length 256 tokens and average output length 512 tokens. Determine the optimal prefill:decode GPU ratio to maximize GPU utilization.
title: Prefill-Decode Ratio Optimization for LLM Serving Fleet

details.common_mistake: Maximizing chunk size to minimize TTFT, not considering that large chunks starve decode tokens from being processed, increasing token generation latency (TPOT) for already-running requests. The tradeoff between TTFT and TPOT depends on the SLO priorities.
details.napkin_math: H100 prefill throughput at different chunk sizes: chunk_size * 2 * model_params FLOP / H100 TFLOPS. 70B model: chunk=128: 2*128*70B = 17.9T FLOP / 989T = 18.1ms. chunk=256: 36.1ms. chunk=512: 72.2ms. chunk=1024: 144.4ms. Scheduling overhead per chunk (kernel launch, memory allocation): ~0.5ms. For 2048-token prompt: total TTFT = (2048/chunk) * (compute + overhead). At chunk=512: 4 * 72.7 = 290.8ms. At chunk=1024: 2 * 144.9 = 289.8ms — nearly same. At chunk=2048 (single): 288.8ms — minimal benefit over 1024. Use chunk=512 for best interleaving with decode.
details.realistic_solution: Chunked prefill tradeoff: small chunks (64-256 tokens) interleave decode work frequently, keeping TPOT low but adding scheduling overhead per chunk. Large chunks (512-2048) reduce overhead but block decode tokens for longer. Optimal chunk size formula: chunk_size = sqrt(decode_batch_size * decode_time_per_token / scheduling_overhead). In practice, chunk_size 512-1024 is optimal for most workloads. For 2048-token prompt: at chunk=256: 8 chunks * (256-token prefill time + scheduling_overhead). At chunk=512: 4 chunks * 512-token prefill time. With H100, 512-token chunk prefill time on 70B: 2*512*70B/989T = 72.5ms. 4 chunks: 4*72.5 = 290ms TTFT. At chunk=256: 2*256*70B/989T = 36.3ms. 8 chunks: 8*36.3 = 290ms. Same! But scheduling overhead favors larger chunks. Optimal: 512-1024 for 70B. For smaller models: chunk=256-512.

scenario: A disaggregated serving system uses chunked prefill to interleave prefill and decode work on prefill GPUs. The chunk size is currently 256 tokens. Requests with 2048-token prompts show poor TTFT due to 8 chunks. Analyze the chunk size tradeoff and find the optimal value.
title: Chunked Prefill Optimal Chunk Size Selection

details.common_mistake: Assuming doubling link bandwidth directly halves transfer time. This only holds if the bottleneck is bandwidth, not latency. InfiniBand fabric latency is 1-2us per hop, and multiple hops through the fat-tree switch fabric can add 3-10us. For small KV caches, latency dominates; for large KV caches, bandwidth dominates.
details.napkin_math: NVLink within DGX-H100: 900 GB/s per GPU. KV transfer 7B/512 tokens: 134MB / 900 GB/s = 0.15ms. vs HDR InfiniBand: 2.68ms. NVLink is 18x faster. But co-location reduces disaggregation flexibility (prefill and decode share physical GPU, losing the ability to independently scale each pool). Break-even: if KV transfer latency > 1ms and re-routing overhead > 0.5ms, co-location on NVLink wins. For 70B model with 1.64GB KV: InfiniBand HDR = 32.8ms + latency, NDR = 16.4ms + latency. Both are too slow for 100ms TTFT — must use KV compression or smaller model.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache size analysis: for 70B model, 512-token prompt: 1.64GB (calculated earlier). At 400 Gbps = 50 GB/s: transfer = 1.64/50 = 32.8ms. At 800 Gbps: 16.4ms. Both much larger than stated 4ms. Stated 4ms suggests smaller model (7B) or shorter prompt. 7B model, 512 tokens: 2*32*32*128*512*2B = 134MB. At 400 Gbps: 134MB/50GB/s = 2.68ms + fabric latency ~1.5ms = 4.18ms — matches! NDR upgrade: 134MB / 100 GB/s = 1.34ms + 1.5ms = 2.84ms. Saves 1.34ms. Cost of NDR upgrade: ~$30K per port. Benefit: 1.34ms reduction. If P99 TTFT target is 100ms, this is 1.3% improvement — marginal. Alternative: co-locate prefill and decode on same DGX node using NVLink (600 GB/s bidirectional per GPU pair): 134MB / 600 GB/s = 0.22ms. Zero network cost, 18x faster than HDR.

scenario: A disaggregated serving cluster has prefill nodes and decode nodes in separate racks, connected via 400 Gbps InfiniBand HDR. KV cache transfer adds 4ms P99 latency. The network team proposes moving to InfiniBand NDR (800 Gbps). Calculate the benefit and propose an alternative if the upgrade is cost-prohibitive.
title: KV Cache Network Topology for High-Bandwidth Transfer

details.common_mistake: Using reactive autoscaling with a fixed threshold (e.g., scale up when GPU utilization > 80%). By the time GPU utilization exceeds 80%, the queue is already building and latency violations are imminent. The 90-second provisioning lag makes reactive scaling too slow for transient spikes.
details.napkin_math: Traffic spike: 2x for 3 minutes = 180 seconds. With 90s provisioning: first 90s of spike unmitigated. At 2x traffic, utilization jumps from 70% to 140% — 40% excess. At 40% excess: queue grows at 0.4 * arrival_rate. Over 90 seconds: queue depth = 0.4 * 500 RPS * 90s = 18,000 requests queued. Average wait = queue_depth / service_rate = 18000 / 500 = 36 seconds added latency. P99 TTFT: baseline 200ms + 36s = unacceptable. With warm pool (15s switch): only 15s unmitigated: queue = 0.4 * 500 * 15 = 3000 requests. Wait = 3000/500 = 6 seconds. Still high. Need warm pool for full 2x capacity: 2x warm pool = expensive but guarantees SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Predictive autoscaling strategies: (1) Time-series forecasting: train a model (e.g., LSTM or Prophet) on historical traffic patterns. Forecast 5-minute ahead traffic. Pre-provision decode nodes 90 seconds before predicted spike onset. (2) Warm pool: maintain N spare pre-provisioned decode nodes in standby (model loaded, not serving). Switch warm nodes to active in <5 seconds. Cost: N * GPU_cost * idle_time. For 5% traffic variance: keep 10% spare warm capacity. (3) Hybrid reactive + predictive: predictive handles known patterns (daily/weekly), reactive handles anomalies via warm pool. (4) Gradual scale-up: start provisioning at 60% utilization (before 80% threshold) to overlap provisioning with the pre-spike window. For 70B on H100: model load = 80 seconds (280GB / 3.35TB/s). Pre-load model at boot, keep model in CPU RAM for fast GPU transfer (280GB at PCIe 32 GB/s = 8.75s). Reduces scale-up time from 90s to ~15s.

scenario: A disaggregated serving autoscaler takes 90 seconds to provision a new decode node (container start + model load). Traffic spikes of 2x baseline lasting 3 minutes cause P99 latency violations for the first 90 seconds. Design a predictive autoscaling strategy.
title: Disaggregated Serving Autoscaler Response Time Analysis

details.common_mistake: Storing the shared prefix KV cache in the prefill node's local GPU memory. When prefill nodes scale horizontally, each node stores its own copy, wasting memory. The cache also evicts under memory pressure, causing frequent recomputation.
details.napkin_math: 1024-token shared prefix KV cache (70B): 2*80*64*128*1024*2B = 2,684,354,560 bytes = 2.5 GiB (2.68 GB). Local cache on H100 (80GB): reserve 40GB for KV cache of active requests, 30GB for shared prefix cache: 30GB/2.68GB = 11 prefixes storable. Cache hit rate for top-11 prefixes in production: ~85-95% depending on product. Per-request savings at 95% hit rate: prefill skip + KV transfer savings. At 500 RPS: ROI is excellent.
details.realistic_solution: Distributed prefix KV store architecture: (1) Centralized KV store: use a dedicated high-bandwidth memory node (e.g., 2×H100 with 160GB HBM as shared KV store). Shared prefix KV cache (1024 tokens, 70B): 2.68 GB. Fits easily. Transfer: 2.68 GB at 400 Gbps = 53.6ms — too slow for interactive. (2) Local cache per prefill node: each prefill node caches the top-K most common shared prefixes in HBM. For K=11 prefixes at 2.68GB each: 29.5GB. H100 has 80GB — feasible for K=10-14 prefixes. Cache hit: skip prefix prefill entirely. Cache miss: compute and cache. (3) Bloom filter for cache presence check: 64-byte prefix hash lookup in bloom filter → determine if local cache hit or compute needed. Cache hit rate for system prompt: >95% in steady state. Prefill savings: 1024-token prefix skip saves 2×1024×70B/989T = 145ms per request with 95% hit rate.

scenario: A disaggregated serving system receives many requests sharing a common 1024-token system prompt. Without caching, each request re-computes the system prompt KV cache during prefill. Design a distributed KV cache store to serve the shared prefix.
title: Context Caching with Disaggregated KV Stores

details.common_mistake: Comparing only TFLOPS between H100 and MI300X for decode. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound at small batch sizes, not compute bound. The relevant comparison metric is GB/s per dollar, not TFLOPS per dollar.
details.napkin_math: Cost per million output tokens: H100 single (can't fit 70B alone). H100 TP=2: 2 GPUs * $3/hr = $6/hr. Decode at batch=128: H100 TP=2 gets ~2*3.35TB/s*0.93/140GB/token * 128 batch = 6,126 tok/sec effective. MI300X single: 5.3TB/s/140GB*128 = 4,846 tok/sec at batch=128. H100 TP=2: $6/hr for 6,126 tok/sec = $0.000272/token. MI300X: $4/hr for 4,846 tok/sec = $0.000229/token. MI300X is 16% cheaper per token for 70B decode. Definitive recommendation: MI300X for 70B decode pools.
details.realistic_solution: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: throughput proportional to HBM bandwidth. H100 decode tokens/sec per GPU: bandwidth / model_bytes_per_token = 3.35TB/s / (70B*2B) = 3.35e12 / 140e9 = 23.9 tok/sec at batch=1. MI300X: 5.3TB/s / 140GB = 37.9 tok/sec at batch=1. At large batches, both scale roughly proportionally with bandwidth. Cost comparison: H100 pair (TP=2) at $6/hr vs MI300X single at $4/hr. For single-GPU batch decode, MI300X 19% more cost-efficient. Memory capacity advantage: MI300X 192GB vs H100 80GB. 70B model weights: 140GB BF16. H100: needs 2×H100 (TP=2) for 70B decode. MI300X: fits on single GPU with 52GB KV headroom. H100 pair: $6/hr at TP=2. MI300X single: $4/hr. MI300X wins decisively for 70B decode.

scenario: Your team is choosing between H100 SXM5 (80GB, 3.35 TB/s) and MI300X (192GB, 5.3 TB/s) for the decode pool of a 70B disaggregated serving cluster. Cost: H100 ~$3/hr, MI300X ~$4/hr. Compare cost-per-token and memory capacity advantages.
title: MI300X vs H100 Decode Pool Economics

details.common_mistake: Using a single FIFO queue for all requests regardless of SLA tier. Premium requests wait behind standard requests, violating the P99 < 100ms SLA even when total load is within capacity.
details.napkin_math: Premium SLA: P99 TTFT < 100ms. Service time per request (8B, 512 token prompt): 16.5ms. Queue wait for P99 < 83.5ms. M/D/1 queue: P99 wait < 83.5ms requires rho < 0.83 for dedicated pool of 3 GPUs at 60 RPS each = 180 RPS premium capacity. If premium RPS < 0.83 * 180 = 149 RPS, SLA met. Standard SLA: P99 < 500ms. Queue wait budget: 500 - 16.5 = 483.5ms. At 7 GPUs + 3 overflow from premium: standard capacity = 420 RPS. Sustainable standard load < 0.85 * 420 = 357 RPS. Total system capacity: 149 premium + 357 standard = 506 RPS.
details.realistic_solution: Priority-aware routing: (1) Dedicated pool partition: reserve 3/10 GPUs for premium-only traffic. Remaining 7 for standard + overflow premium. Premium queue: FIFO with preemption. Standard queue: FIFO. (2) Admission control: premium requests bypass the standard queue. When premium pool is full (>90% utilization), route premium overflow to standard pool with priority interrupt. (3) Work-stealing: when premium pool is idle, it processes standard queue to avoid GPU waste. (4) Queue depth monitoring: premium queue target depth < 2 requests (to ensure <100ms wait). Standard queue can have depth up to 20 (SLA allows 500ms wait = 10 * 50ms avg service time). (5) Load shedding: when standard queue > 50 requests, return HTTP 503 to standard tier clients with retry-after header. Premium tier never load-sheds.

scenario: A disaggregated serving gateway receives requests with two SLA tiers: premium (P99 TTFT < 100ms) and standard (P99 TTFT < 500ms). Prefill pool has 10 GPUs. Design a routing policy that satisfies both SLAs.
title: SLA-Aware Request Routing Between Prefill and Decode Pools

details.common_mistake: Running draft and target models on the same GPU pool and treating speculative decoding as a drop-in optimization. The synchronization overhead between draft and target inference steps can negate the speedup if not carefully pipelined, especially in a disaggregated setting with network round-trips.
details.napkin_math: Speculative decoding speedup: without spec decoding, 70B decode = 1 target call per token. With spec decoding (K=4, alpha=0.8): 3.36 tokens per target call. Target call takes: verify K tokens = 2*4*70B/989T = 0.57ms + overhead ~5ms = 5.57ms. Without: 70B single-token decode memory-bound: 140GB / 3.35TB/s = 41.8ms. Speedup: 41.8 / (5.57ms / 3.36) = 41.8 / 1.66 = 25.2x per target GPU. Actual speedup limited by draft generation speed: 7B draft at 5ms per step for 4 tokens = 20ms per round. Target verification: 5.57ms. Total round: 25.57ms for 3.36 tokens = 7.6ms/token. vs 70B no spec: 41.8ms/token. Speedup: 5.5x. More realistic than theoretical 25x.
details.realistic_solution: Disaggregated speculative decoding flow: (1) Request arrives at gateway: routed to draft pool for token generation. (2) Draft pool generates K=4 draft tokens (7B model, ~5ms per step). (3) Draft tokens + original KV cache sent to target pool in a single batch. (4) Target pool verifies K draft tokens in parallel (70B prefill-like operation on K tokens): 2*K*70B FLOP = 2*4*70B = 560B FLOP. At 989 TFLOPS: 0.57ms. (5) Acceptance sampling: expected accept rate ~75-80% for same-domain drafts. Expected accepted tokens per target call = K * alpha^avg where alpha = acceptance rate. At K=4, alpha=0.8: E[accepted] = (1 - 0.8^5)/(1-0.8) = 3.36 tokens. (6) Target returns accepted tokens + 1 bonus token. Draft continues with corrected KV state. Network overhead: 4 draft tokens per round trip to target = 4 * 2B = 8 bytes — negligible. KV delta: only the new KV for K tokens must be synchronized. Resource sizing: 1 target GPU (70B) supports ~10 draft GPUs (7B) given 10x compute ratio. 7B draft: 10 tok/sec single stream. 70B target verifies 3.36 accepted tokens per call at ~20ms: 3.36/(20ms) = 168 tok/sec effective.

scenario: Design a speculative decoding architecture integrated into a disaggregated serving system. The draft model is 7B, the target model is 70B. Both have separate pools. Design the request flow, acceptance sampling protocol, and resource sizing.
title: Speculative Decoding in Disaggregated Architecture: Draft Pool Design

details.common_mistake: Monitoring only aggregate TTFT and TPOT without separating prefill and decode pool metrics. When TTFT degrades, it could be a prefill pool CPU-bound issue, a KV transfer bottleneck, or a decode pool full condition causing new requests to wait for available decode slots.
details.napkin_math: Debugging workflow: TTFT high + prefill_queue_depth high + prefill_compute_utilization high: scale up prefill pool. TTFT high + kv_transfer_latency high: investigate network (check InfiniBand utilization, check KV size, enable compression). TTFT high + decode_queue_depth high + decode_batch_size low: decode pool undersized (requests backlogged). TPOT high + decode_batch_size at max + decode memory bandwidth at 100%: memory-bound decode, need more decode GPUs or smaller model. TPOT high + decode_batch_size low: scheduling inefficiency, check batching configuration.
details.realistic_solution: Disaggregated serving metric taxonomy: Prefill pool: (1) prefill_queue_depth — number of requests waiting for prefill. High = prefill pool undersized. (2) prefill_compute_utilization — GPU MFU during prefill. Low (<50%) = inefficient batching. High (>90%) = pool undersized. (3) ttft_prefill_only_ms — TTFT excluding KV transfer, pure prefill time. KV transfer: (4) kv_transfer_latency_ms — end-to-end KV cache transfer time. Spike = network congestion or large KV caches. (5) kv_transfer_bandwidth_gbps — actual vs available InfiniBand. Decode pool: (6) decode_queue_depth — requests waiting for decode slot. High = decode pool undersized. (7) tpot_ms — time per output token. High = memory bandwidth saturated. (8) decode_batch_size_avg — should be close to max configured. Low = underutilization. Aggregated: (9) e2e_ttft_p95, e2e_ttft_p99. (10) tpot_p95. (11) kv_store_hit_rate — for prefix caching.

scenario: You are onboarding an SRE to a disaggregated serving system. They ask what the key operational metrics are and how to distinguish prefill-pool problems from decode-pool problems in the dashboard. Describe the metric taxonomy.
title: Disaggregated Serving Observability: Key Metrics Dashboard

details.common_mistake: Using fixed-size batches with padding to the longest sequence. At 60% waste, effective compute utilization is 40% of peak. Engineers may attempt to set a maximum sequence length limit to reduce padding, but this simply discards long requests rather than handling them efficiently.
details.napkin_math: Naive padding at 60% waste: effective compute = 40% of H100 989 TFLOPS = 396 TFLOPS. With sequence packing at 95% efficiency: effective compute = 95% * 989 = 939 TFLOPS. Throughput improvement: 939/396 = 2.37x. Packing overhead: sorting O(n log n) + bin-packing heuristic O(n). At 1000 requests per batch: negligible. Flash Attention 2 with varlen: no performance penalty vs padded (actually faster due to skipping padding computation). Implementation: use flash_attn_varlen_func with cu_seqlens.
details.realistic_solution: Variable-length batching strategies: (1) Sequence packing (Flash Attention 2 style): pack multiple variable-length sequences into a single attention operation up to a token budget (e.g., 4096 tokens per batch). No padding between sequences — use cu_seqlens tensor to track sequence boundaries. The 2D attention mask prevents cross-sequence attention. Pack sequences greedily: sort by length descending, fill each bin with remaining capacity. Packing efficiency: 90-95% vs 40% with naive padding. (2) Bucketed batching: sort requests into length buckets (e.g., 0-256, 256-512, 512-1024, 1024-2048, 2048-4096). Each bucket forms its own batch padded to bucket maximum. Buckets balance utilization vs latency. (3) Dynamic batching with timeout: collect requests for 10ms, then dispatch the most efficient batch. Short requests: high-density packing. Long requests (>1024): smaller batch to avoid memory OOM.

scenario: A prefill pool is processing requests with highly variable prompt lengths (32 to 4096 tokens). Padding short prompts to the longest in the batch wastes 60% of compute. Design a batch composition strategy to maximize GPU utilization.
title: Prefill Batch Composition for Throughput Maximization

details.common_mistake: Reducing the maximum context length to avoid preemptions. This limits the product's capabilities and does not address the root cause: the KV cache allocator does not account for the growth of existing requests' KV caches as they generate more tokens.
details.napkin_math: H100 80GB: 70B model at BF16 = 140GB — needs TP=2. Wait, for decode with KV: if using FP8 weights: 70GB weights + 10GB KV headroom. Or: run smaller model. Assume 8B model: 16GB BF16. KV cache available: 80 - 16 - 4 (overhead) = 60GB. KV per token (8B, 32 layers, 32 heads, 128 head_dim): 2*32*32*128*1*2B = 524KB/token. 60GB / 524KB = 114,503 tokens of KV capacity. At batch=128 requests with avg 2K context: 128*2K = 262K tokens needed. Exceeds capacity — need to run TP=2 or use INT8 KV (2x capacity) or limit batch size to 57 requests.
details.realistic_solution: vLLM KV cache preemption analysis: KV cache is paged (PagedAttention). Each page = 16 tokens. At 95% utilization with 4K token requests arriving: the new request needs 4K/16 = 256 pages for prefill KV. Plus existing requests are generating tokens and consuming more pages. The preemption cascade: (1) New long request pre-allocated 256 pages; (2) Existing decode requests' page tables overflow; (3) vLLM preempts lowest-priority decode request, swaps KV pages to CPU DRAM. Preemption cost: swap 70B model KV for a 2K-token request = 2*80*64*128*2K*2B = 6.7GB. At PCIe 32 GB/s: 0.21 seconds of disruption per preemption. Fix: (1) Implement admission control: reject new requests when GPU memory is above 85% to prevent cascade. (2) Reserve 10% of KV pages for existing request growth: only admit new request if remaining_pages > request_max_output_tokens * pages_per_token. (3) Use KV cache compression (INT8) to effectively double cache size.

scenario: A decode pool running vLLM shows increasing preemptions when long-context requests arrive (>4K tokens). KV cache utilization is at 95% when preemptions begin. GPU memory is 80GB H100. Analyze the eviction cascade and propose a fix.
title: KV Cache Eviction Policy for Decode Pool Memory Management

details.common_mistake: Comparing only raw GPU compute costs without including: engineering time to build and maintain the disaggregated system, redundancy costs for high availability, bandwidth costs for KV cache transfer, and the opportunity cost of not using that engineering time for product development.
details.napkin_math: Build variable compute cost: 1B tokens / (23.9 tok/sec × 3600 × 24 × 30) = 16.2 H100-months. At $3/hr: 16.2 × 720 hrs × $3 = $34,992/month GPU compute. True variable cost per million tokens ≈ $34.99/M, not $0.03/M. Break-even analysis: build fixed = ~$52K/month (engineering + infrastructure). Build total = $52K + $35K compute = $87K/month. Buy = $900/month at $0.90/M. Managed API wins at 1B tokens/month by 97×. Break-even: ~500B tokens/month (build ≈ $87K + scale compute vs buy at $450K).
details.realistic_solution: Build cost analysis: GPU cost: 1B tokens/month / (H100 decode 23.9 tok/sec × 3600 × 24 × 30) = 16.2 H100-months. At $3/hr H100: 16.2 × 720 × $3 = $34,992/month for compute. Add: 2× redundancy = $70K. InfiniBand networking: ~$82K/month. Engineering: 2 FTEs at $250K/year = $41.7K/month. Total build: ~$194K/month. Buy cost: Together AI pricing ~$0.90 per million output tokens (Llama-3 70B). 1B tokens: $900/month. Managed API wins at this scale by 215×. Build makes sense at: 1T tokens/month ($900K managed) vs build: ~$200K + engineering. Break-even: ~500B tokens/month. Conclusion: below 100B tokens/month, use managed API; above 500B tokens/month, build is cost-effective.

scenario: A startup is considering building a disaggregated LLM serving system vs using a managed inference API (e.g., Bedrock, Together AI). Monthly traffic: 1B output tokens. Model: Llama-3 70B. Perform a build vs buy cost analysis.
title: Disaggregated Serving Cost Model: Build vs Buy

details.common_mistake: Implementing token-bucket rate limiting at the request level without KV cache memory quotas. Rate limiting prevents request flooding but does not prevent a single tenant with large requests (long context) from monopolizing KV cache memory and causing other tenants' cache evictions.
details.napkin_math: 10 tenants, 60GB KV cache. Baseline: 6GB per tenant. Max context per tenant: 6GB / (524KB/token for 8B model) = 11,450 tokens max outstanding context per tenant. For 70B: 6GB / (2*80*64*128*2B/1000 = 2.62MB/token) = 2290 tokens max. At 10 requests per tenant with 200-token context: 10 * 200 * 2.62MB = 5.24GB per tenant — just under 6GB quota. Burst allowance (10GB): 10 * 400-token context = 4GB OK. Prevents tenant monopolization while allowing reasonable bursting.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-tenant KV cache isolation: (1) Per-tenant KV page quotas: allocate a fixed fraction of KV cache pages to each tenant. With 10 tenants and 60GB KV capacity: 6GB per tenant baseline. Allow burst up to 10GB with work-stealing from idle tenants. Implemented via tenant_id tag on KV page allocations. (2) Hierarchical fair queuing: maintain per-tenant decode queues. Scheduler processes queues in round-robin weighted by tenant SLA tier. Premium tenants get 2x weight. (3) Admission control per tenant: when tenant KV quota is exhausted, new requests from that tenant are queued (not preempting other tenants' live KV caches). (4) KV cache eviction scope: when a tenant's quota is full, evict only from that tenant's KV pages using LRU within the tenant's pages. Never evict another tenant's pages for a different tenant's benefit. (5) Cross-tenant prefix sharing: if two tenants share a common system prompt, store one copy and reference-count it — deducted proportionally from each tenant's quota.

scenario: A shared disaggregated serving cluster handles requests from 10 enterprise tenants. Tenant A's large batch of 10K requests floods the KV cache store, causing tenant B's requests to be preempted and delayed. Design a multi-tenant KV cache isolation scheme.
title: Multi-Tenant KV Cache Isolation in Disaggregated Serving

details.common_mistake: Assuming the 1% slow requests are simply longer sequences requiring more memory. In continuous batching, all requests in a batch proceed token-by-token together — a single slow operation delays the entire batch, not just the slow request.
details.napkin_math: Batch of 128 requests, 127 have 512 context, 1 has 10K context. Memory bandwidth per step: normal request KV load = 2*32*32*128*512*2B = 268MB. 10K context request: 268MB * 20 = 5.36GB. Total batch KV load per step: 127*268MB + 1*5360MB = 34GB + 5.36GB = 39.4GB. At 3.35TB/s: 39.4GB/3350GB = 11.8ms per step. Without 10K request: 34GB/3350GB = 10.1ms. The single long-context request adds only 1.7ms (17% overhead), not 3x. 3x TPOT points to KV swap (PCIe bottleneck) rather than sequence length.
details.realistic_solution: In continuous batching, the token generation step for all batched requests completes together (synchronized per-step). If 1% of requests have 3x higher TPOT, it means those requests are in a batch where the per-step compute takes 3x longer. Possible causes: (1) Long sequence KV cache access: requests with 10K+ context tokens require loading more KV pages per step, increasing memory bandwidth consumption beyond HBM capacity for that batch. (2) CPU-offloaded KV: if some KV pages were swapped to CPU DRAM and not yet restored, the GPU stalls waiting for PCIe transfer. (3) Kernel launch serialization: if certain requests trigger fallback kernels (e.g., unsupported attention patterns), those kernels serialize on the GPU. Diagnosis: check (a) per-request context length distribution for the slow 1%; (b) KV cache swap metrics; (c) CUDA kernel timeline for serialization. Fix: (1) If long context: separate long-context requests into a dedicated decode pool with smaller batch size; (2) If KV swap: increase KV cache capacity or reduce batch size; (3) If kernel fallback: update attention implementation.

scenario: Decode pool P99 TPOT is 3x higher than median TPOT. Profiling shows most requests complete in 40ms/token but 1% take 120ms/token. GPU utilization shows no idle time. Diagnose the straggler cause.
title: Decode Straggler Detection in Large Batch Disaggregated Serving

details.common_mistake: Comparing TPU v5e TFLOPS (197) to H100 TFLOPS (989) and concluding TPU v5e is 5x slower for prefill. Prefill is compute-bound, so TFLOPS comparison is relevant — but TPU v5e is designed for batch training efficiency, not low-latency single-request prefill. The XLA compilation model adds overhead.
details.napkin_math: TPU v5e for prefill, cost: $1.20/hr on Google Cloud for v5e-1 (1 chip). H100 $3/hr. Cost per TFLOP: TPU v5e $1.20/197 = $0.0061/TFLOP-hr. H100: $3/989 = $0.00303/TFLOP-hr. H100 is actually 2x more cost-efficient per TFLOP. TPU v5e advantage only if using v5e pods with high MFU on large batches. In practice: TPU v5e is not cost-effective for disaggregated prefill vs H100 unless GPU availability is constrained.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill analysis on TPU v5e: for a 512-token prompt on 70B model: 2*512*70B = 71.7T FLOP. TPU v5e at 197 TFLOPS: 71.7T/197T = 364ms per request. H100 at 989 TFLOPS: 72ms. TPU v5e is 5x slower per request in isolation. BUT: TPU v5e is designed for high-throughput batched inference. In batched prefill: TPU v5e throughput scales well due to systolic array. Batch of 64, 512-token prompts: 64*71.7T = 4.6P FLOP. TPU v5e: 4.6P/197T = 23.4 seconds for batch. H100: 4.6P/989T = 4.65 seconds. H100 still 5x faster. Integration challenges: (1) KV cache format: TPU uses bf16 by default; decode H100 may expect different format — conversion overhead. (2) Network transfer: TPU is on Google Cloud; H100 on custom on-prem or AWS — cross-cloud KV transfer is high-latency. (3) XLA compilation: TPU requires JAX/TF; vLLM decode uses PyTorch — need a translation layer. Verdict: TPU v5e for prefill only makes sense if dramatically cheaper than H100 and latency SLO is relaxed (>1s TTFT).

scenario: A team proposes using TPU v5e (197 TFLOPS BF16, 800 GB/s) for prefill nodes and H100 for decode nodes in a disaggregated 70B serving system. Analyze whether TPU v5e is prefill-optimal and identify the integration challenges.
title: Disaggregated Serving with TPU v5e Prefill Nodes

details.common_mistake: Migrating all requests atomically by checkpointing all KV caches simultaneously. For a node at 95% KV utilization with batch=128 requests, migrating 128 * average_kv_size simultaneously can take 10+ seconds, causing a service interruption.
details.napkin_math: Overloaded nodes: 3 nodes at 95% KV utilization. Batch per node: ~128 requests. Total to migrate to restore balance: migrate until 70% utilization. Migration needed: (95-70)% * 3 nodes = 75% of one node's requests = ~96 requests. At 10 requests/sec: 9.6 seconds to complete migration. During migration: 96 requests experience 5.4ms pause each. Impact on user experience: 5.4ms interruption during ongoing decode = imperceptible (decode steps are typically 40ms anyway). TPOT blip: one step takes 45.4ms vs 40ms = 13.5% slower for migrated requests for one step.
details.realistic_solution: Incremental request migration protocol: (1) Identify migration candidates: select requests from overloaded nodes ordered by lowest token-position (recently arrived, least KV to migrate). (2) Per-request migration: for request R at token position T: (a) Pause R's decode slot on source node (one step boundary); (b) Transfer KV cache: T tokens * kv_size_per_token to destination node over InfiniBand; (c) Register R with destination decode scheduler; (d) Resume R on destination. Migration time per request: for 512-token context in 8B model: 268MB at 50 GB/s InfiniBand = 5.4ms per request. (3) Throttled migration: migrate N requests per second where N is chosen to not saturate InfiniBand. At 10 requests/sec: InfiniBand load = 10 * 268MB = 2.68 GB/s (5% of 50 GB/s). Very manageable. (4) Drain and redirect: after migrating 30% of requests from overloaded nodes, re-route new requests to underloaded nodes. (5) Target: equalize utilization to 65-70% across all nodes.

scenario: A decode pool has 8 nodes with unequal KV cache utilization: nodes 1-3 at 95%, nodes 4-8 at 50%. You need to migrate live decode requests from nodes 1-3 to nodes 4-8 without dropping requests. Design the live migration protocol.
title: Request Migration Between Decode Nodes for Load Balancing

details.common_mistake: Assuming higher TP always improves decode performance. TP reduces per-GPU memory bandwidth requirement but adds all-reduce communication overhead per decode step. At small batch sizes, the all-reduce latency can exceed the compute time, making higher TP counterproductive.
details.napkin_math: Summary: TP=1 MI300X: 37.9 tok/sec, $0.0000293/token. TP=2 H100: 47.9 tok/sec, $6/hr = $0.0000348/token. TP=4 H100: 95.7 tok/sec, $12/hr = $0.0000348/token. MI300X single is most cost-efficient. TP=4 doubles throughput vs MI300X but costs 3x more. Use case: if low latency (not throughput) is needed, TP=4 H100 provides lowest TPOT via higher parallel bandwidth. If cost efficiency matters most, MI300X wins.
details.realistic_solution: Decode throughput analysis per TP degree: TP=1 on MI300X: memory-bound decode at 5.3 TB/s / 140GB (70B BF16) = 37.9 tok/sec per stream. KV cache: 192-140 = 52GB available. TP=2 on 2xH100: each GPU holds 70GB model shard. Effective BW = 2 * 3.35 = 6.7 TB/s for model weights. tok/sec = 6.7TB/140GB = 47.9 tok/sec. But all-reduce latency per step: 2 * (N-1)/N * message_size / NVLink_BW = 2 * 0.5 * small_message / 900GB/s. For TP=2 attention reduce: message = 2 * seq_len * hidden * 2B = 2 * 1 * 8192 * 2 = 32KB. All-reduce: 32KB / 900GB/s = 0.036us — negligible. TP=2 wins over MI300X single in throughput. TP=4 on 4xH100: BW = 4 * 3.35 = 13.4 TB/s effective. tok/sec = 13.4TB/140GB = 95.7 tok/sec. All-reduce for TP=4: 3 * 32KB / 900GB/s = 0.107us — still negligible. TP=4 wins on throughput. But cost: TP=4 requires 4 GPUs at $12/hr vs MI300X at $4/hr. Cost per token: TP=4: $12/hr / (95.7 * 3600) = $0.000035/token. MI300X: $4/(37.9*3600) = $0.0000293/token. MI300X is cheaper per token.

scenario: A 70B model decode pool can use TP=1 (192GB MI300X single GPU), TP=2 (2xH100 NVLink), or TP=4 (4xH100 NVLink). Analyze how TP degree affects decode throughput and latency per token.
title: Decode Pool Tensor Parallelism Degree Selection

details.common_mistake: Assuming adding new requests to a continuous batch is free. Each new request added to the batch increases the per-step memory bandwidth consumption (more KV pages to load), which slows the decode step for all requests already in the batch, increasing their TPOT.
details.napkin_math: Per-step KV bandwidth: 90 requests avg 1K context * 524KB/token = 47.2GB. Model load: 16GB (8B BF16). Total: 63.2GB / 3.35TB/s = 18.9ms/step. Adding 15 requests avg 512 context: +15*512*524KB = +4GB. New total: 67.2GB / 3.35TB = 20.1ms/step. TPOT inflation: +1.2ms = +6.3% for existing requests. To keep TPOT inflation <5%: add at most 11 requests (11*512*524KB = 2.9GB, +8.7% of 47.2GB KV: 63.2+2.9=66.1GB, 19.7ms, +4.2% inflation).
details.realistic_solution: TPOT impact of batch size increase: decode is memory-bandwidth bound. Per-step time = (total KV bytes + model bytes) / HBM bandwidth. Model bytes are fixed per step. KV bytes per step = sum of all requests' context lengths * kv_size_per_token. Adding 15 new requests (avg 512 tokens context): delta_KV = 15 * 512 * kv_per_token. For 8B model: 15 * 512 * (2*32*32*128*2B) = 15 * 512 * 524KB = 4GB extra KV per step. At 3.35 TB/s: +1.19ms per step. If baseline step is 40ms: +3% TPOT inflation for all 90 existing requests. Fairness policy: to maintain SLA for existing requests, limit batch expansion rate. Add at most N new requests where N satisfies: (N * avg_context * kv_per_token) / HBM_BW < TPOT_slack_ms. This is the TPOT budget constraint for admission control.

scenario: In a continuous batching decode pool, 10 requests complete their generation while 90 ongoing requests are mid-decode. The scheduler adds 15 new requests to the next step. Explain the fairness implications and identify when new request additions cause TPOT inflation for existing requests.
title: Continuous Batching Micro-Batch Scheduling for TPOT Fairness

details.common_mistake: Focusing on average utilization metrics when diagnosing tail latency. P99 is determined by rare worst-case events, not average behavior. Low average utilization does not preclude tail latency from queue bursts, garbage collection pauses, or OS jitter.
details.napkin_math: P99/P50 ratio: 800ms/120ms = 6.67x. This is high — for a well-tuned system, P99/P50 < 3x. Sources of 6.67x tail: (a) GIL jitter: 50ms at P99 vs 2ms avg = 25x amplification. Probability of GIL jitter at P99: 1% of requests. (b) Memory allocation: cudaMalloc at P99: 200ms vs <1ms typical. (c) Cross-rack network retransmit: InfiniBand packet drop at P99 adds 100ms retransmit timer. Likely cause: combination of GIL jitter + cudaMalloc. Fix: use torch.cuda.memory.caching_allocator_alloc, increase PyTorch memory pool, async scheduler to avoid GIL blocking.
details.realistic_solution: Tail latency diagnostic framework for disaggregated serving: (1) Decompose TTFT into phases: time in prefill queue + prefill compute + KV transfer + decode queue wait. Use distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) to get per-phase latencies. P99 of each phase: is one phase responsible for most P99 TTFT? (2) Check software overhead: Python GIL jitter in vLLM scheduler can add 5-50ms per scheduling cycle. Profile scheduler with py-spy: is scheduler holding GIL during token generation? (3) GPU kernel launch latency: CUDA context switches between prefill and decode batches can add 1-5ms. Check with Nsight Systems. (4) TCP/gRPC timeout and retry: if decode node sends back-pressure via gRPC stream, the client might have a 100ms retry timer. Check gRPC retry logs. (5) Memory allocation jitter: cudaMalloc is slow and non-deterministic. Is P99 correlated with memory allocation events? Use pre-allocated memory pools. (6) OS scheduler interference: Python process scheduled off-CPU during batch formation. Use SCHED_FIFO for serving threads on dedicated cores.

scenario: A disaggregated serving system P99 TTFT is 800ms, P50 is 120ms. The engineering team has checked GPU utilization (70%), queue depth (low), and network bandwidth (40% utilized). Nothing obvious is wrong. Provide a systematic diagnostic framework.
title: Disaggregated Serving Tail Latency Root Cause Framework

details.common_mistake: Using a simple HTTP health check (server is up and responding) as the readiness signal. The server can respond to health checks immediately after startup while still performing JIT compilation, making health checks insufficient as readiness signals.
details.napkin_math: CUDA graph capture for 70B on H100: graph capture per batch size = 5-10 seconds (JIT traces all ops). For batch sizes 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128: 8 * 7.5s = 60 seconds warmup. Total startup: model load (80s) + warmup (60s) = 140 seconds before ready. At 1 pod scale-up per minute during traffic spike: 140s gap where incoming traffic may hit cold pods. Solution: maintain warm-standby pool with models pre-loaded; scale from standby pool (only need 60s warmup) not from scratch.
details.realistic_solution: Deployment readiness lifecycle for prefill nodes: (1) Startup phase: load model weights (8B: ~5s, 70B: ~80s); (2) Warmup phase: run dummy forward passes at all expected batch sizes and sequence lengths to trigger CUDA graph capture and cuBLAS kernel selection. Duration: 10-30 seconds for sequence lengths 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048. (3) Readiness check: node emits ready signal after warmup completion. Kubernetes readinessProbe: use exec probe that checks a local file written by the server after warmup. (4) Load balancer integration: Kubernetes readinessProbe failure excludes pod from Service endpoints. New pod starts traffic only after readiness probe succeeds. (5) Canary deployment: first route 1% traffic to warm pod, verify P99 latency within 10% of baseline, then increase to 100%. Implementation: vLLM's --enable-prefix-caching and --max-num-seqs should be specified at startup; warmup script runs representative prompts at each sequence length.

scenario: A newly deployed prefill node takes 45 seconds to serve its first request due to JIT compilation and CUDA graph capture. During this time, the load balancer routes traffic to the node anyway, causing 45 seconds of 30x higher latency. Design the deployment readiness lifecycle.
title: Prefill Warmup and JIT Compilation Latency at Service Start

details.common_mistake: Treating partial failure as binary (system works or fails) and attempting to maintain full functionality for all requests, resulting in all requests being degraded. A better approach: triage requests by SLA tier and maintain full service for high-priority users while gracefully degrading for low-priority.
details.napkin_math: Normal: 500 RPS, 70B decode, 350 decode slots. After 30% failure: 245 decode slots. If premium is 20% of load: 100 RPS premium, 400 RPS standard. New standard capacity: 245 - 100 = 145 RPS. Standard at 145/400 = 36% of normal. Fallback: route 200 standard RPS to 8B model (5x faster): 8B handles 5x more throughput per slot. Effectively 200 RPS * 1/5 = 40 slot-equivalents. Total: 145 + 40 = 185 RPS standard. Standard capacity restored to 185/400 = 46% of normal. Significantly better than dropping all standard requests.
details.realistic_solution: Graceful degradation protocol: (1) Immediate detection: decode pool health monitor detects 30% node loss within 10 seconds (health check interval). (2) Capacity recomputation: new capacity = 70% of baseline. If baseline handles 500 RPS, new capacity = 350 RPS. (3) Triage by SLA tier: (a) Premium tier (typically 20% of requests): serve at full SLA — 100 RPS if premium is 20% of 500. Within 350 RPS capacity. (b) Standard tier: rate-limit to available capacity after premium: 350 - 100 = 250 RPS for standard (reduced from 400 RPS baseline). Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 5s for excess standard requests. (4) Model fallback: if 70B is under pressure, route low-priority requests to a smaller model (8B) running on the same nodes. 8B decode is 5x faster, increasing effective capacity. (5) Output length capping: for standard tier during degradation, cap max_tokens to 256 instead of 1024. This 4x reduces decode slots usage, partially compensating for lost capacity. (6) Customer communication: trigger status page incident update.

scenario: A disaggregated serving cluster loses 30% of its decode pool due to a network partition. The remaining 70% of decode capacity cannot serve all requests. Design a graceful degradation strategy that maintains service for as many users as possible.
title: Disaggregated Serving Graceful Degradation Under Partial Failure

details.common_mistake: Sharding all tables uniformly across all GPUs. This ignores hot-row imbalance: the largest tables have power-law access distributions where top 0.1% of rows receive 10% of lookups. Uniform sharding puts hot rows on arbitrary shards, causing all-to-all traffic and load imbalance.
details.napkin_math: 512GB table, 8 GPUs: 512/8 = 64GB per GPU. Fits in 80GB with 16GB headroom for KV and compute. All-to-all traffic per batch: DLRM lookup batch of 4K samples, avg 100 lookups per sample, 400K total. Per shard: 400K/8 = 50K lookups. Each lookup is 64*4B = 256B. Total embedding output: 400K * 256B = 100MB per batch. All-to-all reduce: 100MB * (8-1)/8 = 87.5MB per batch. At 400 Gbps InfiniBand: 87.5MB / 50GB/s = 1.75ms. Manageable for a 10ms budget batch step.
details.realistic_solution: Hybrid sharding strategy: (1) Table-wise sharding: each table assigned to a GPU group. Large table (512GB): requires 512/80 = 6.4 GPUs minimum. Assign to 8 GPUs (10% overhead). Row-wise shard: split 2B rows into 8 shards of 250M rows each. (2) Column-wise sharding: for tables that are tall but narrow, column sharding is better — keeps all rows on each GPU, shards embedding dimensions. For 512GB table, row-wise is better (balanced row access). (3) Hot row replication: identify top-1K hot rows via access logs. Replicate these rows to all 8 shards in the GPU group. Lookups for hot rows: local, no network. Cold rows: routed to responsible shard via consistent hashing. (4) Column-parallel for dense tables: tables used in upper layers of ranking where all embeddings needed per request — column-parallel reduces per-request all-to-all.

scenario: A production recommendation system has 50 embedding tables totaling 10TB. The largest table has 2B rows x 64-dim float32 (512GB). You have 128 GPUs each with 80GB HBM. Design the sharding strategy.
title: Embedding Table Sharding Strategy for 10TB Feature Space

details.common_mistake: Flushing the entire embedding cache on every update cycle. With 128MB L2 cache and updates every 5 minutes, full cache flush every 5 minutes eliminates the cache hit rate benefit entirely, causing 100% cache miss rate after each update and spiking embedding lookup latency.
details.napkin_math: L2 cache: 128MB, 64-dim float32 embeddings = 256B each. Cache capacity: 128MB / 256B = 500K rows. With 2B total rows: cache holds 500K/2B = 0.025% of table. Cache hit rate for popular items: following Zipf distribution, top 0.025% items receive ~15% of traffic — so cache hit rate ~15% at steady state. With 1% update rate per cycle: 20M updated rows. Probability that a cached row is updated: 20M updated / 2B total * 500K cached = 5K stale rows per cache. Bloom filter check: 5K stale hits per cycle / 500K cache = 1% cache entries are stale. This matches observed 15% * 10% stale served = 1.5% if hot rows are more likely updated (biased toward high-traffic items).
details.realistic_solution: Selective cache invalidation: (1) Track which embedding rows were updated in each training cycle. Online learning typically updates <1% of rows per cycle (sparse gradient updates). Tag updated rows with a version number. (2) Lazy invalidation: serving replicas check embedding version on cache hit. If cached version < current_version, re-fetch from parameter server. Version check: O(1) hash lookup in a 'dirty set' (bloom filter of updated row IDs). Bloom filter for 1% of 2B rows = 20M updated rows: ~20MB at 1% false positive rate. (3) Version broadcast: parameter server broadcasts a compact dirty-set (bloom filter) to all serving replicas after each update cycle. Serving replicas load the bloom filter (20MB) atomically: <1ms to apply. (4) Eviction-aware update: prioritize updating cache entries for rows in the dirty set. Background thread checks dirty set and evicts stale entries asynchronously.

scenario: A recommendation system updates item embeddings every 5 minutes via online learning. The serving system caches embeddings in L2 cache (128MB per serving replica). After an update cycle, 15% of requests use stale embeddings for 3-8 minutes. Diagnose and fix.
title: Online Learning Embedding Staleness and Cache Invalidation

details.common_mistake: Allocating latency budget equally across stages (33ms each). Retrieval is embarrassingly parallel and can be very fast. Heavy ranking is the accuracy bottleneck and should receive the most budget. Equal allocation wastes budget on fast stages and under-allocates to the quality-critical stage.
details.napkin_math: Heavy ranker 50M params, batch=500: FLOP = 500 * 50M * 2 (inference, not training) = 50B FLOP. H100 at 989 TFLOPS: 0.050ms compute. Actual cost dominated by: (1) Embedding lookups: 500 items * 20 embedding tables * 256B = 2.56MB bandwidth. At 3.35TB/s: 0.76µs. (2) Feature interaction: 500 * n_features^2 matmul. If n_features=200: 40M FLOP / 989T = 40ns. (3) DNN forward 50M: 50B FLOP = 0.05ms. Total heavy ranker: ~1ms compute, 15ms for batch formation + feature preprocessing + Python overhead + network. Budget of 50ms is comfortable.
details.realistic_solution: Latency budget allocation: Retrieval (ANN search, 1M candidates to 10K): HNSW or FAISS at 1M items, 128-dim vectors. On GPU: 1ms. Allocate 5ms (5× headroom for network, sorting). Light ranking (10K candidates to 500): run a small 2-layer MLP (0.5M params) scoring 10K items. At H100: 10K × 0.5M × 2 FLOP = 10B FLOP / 989T = 0.01ms. Including embedding lookup: 10K lookups × 256B = 2.5MB at 3.35TB/s = 0.75µs. Allocate 20ms for light ranker (includes embedding table lookups, feature engineering). Heavy ranking (500 candidates): run a large cross-feature DNN (50M params). 500 × 50M × 2 FLOP = 50B FLOP / 989T = 0.05ms compute. Dominant cost: embedding lookups for 500 items, feature interaction layers. Allocate 50ms. Buffer: 25ms for serialization, network, runtime overhead. Total: 5 + 20 + 50 + 25 = 100ms.

scenario: A recommendation pipeline has a 100ms total latency SLO. It runs: retrieval (ANN search), light ranking (score 10K candidates), and heavy ranking (score 500 candidates). Allocate the latency budget and specify the model sizes for each stage.
title: Multi-Stage Ranking Latency Budget Decomposition

details.common_mistake: Treating all 200 features as equally time-sensitive and either pre-computing everything (staleness for real-time features) or computing everything at serving time (unnecessary latency for slow-changing features). Feature freshness requirements are highly heterogeneous.
details.napkin_math: Feature lookup time breakdown: Redis GET for 150 hourly features (batched): 1 network RTT + 150 hash lookups = 1ms. Session store GET for 50 real-time features: streaming consumer maintains in-memory session cache (HashMap): 0.1ms. Feature encoding to float tensor: 200 features * 4B = 800B + one-hot encoding. Total: 2ms. Without pre-computation (compute all 200 features from raw logs): stream join across 5 Kafka topics, 10ms P50, 50ms P99. Pre-computation clearly wins for hourly+ features.
details.realistic_solution: Tiered feature architecture: (1) Static features (pre-computed, refreshed daily): user demographics, item metadata, historical statistics. Store in Redis/RocksDB. Latency: 0.5ms lookup. (2) Hourly features (pre-computed, refreshed hourly): item popularity counts, user preference histograms, collaborative filtering embeddings. Store in Redis. Staleness: 0-60 minutes. Acceptable for popularity signals. (3) Real-time features (computed at serving time): current session behavior (last 5 clicked items), real-time inventory status, time-of-day. Compute from streaming pipeline output (Kafka consumer reading session events). Latency: 1-2ms to query session store. (4) Near-real-time features (micro-batch, refreshed every 1 minute): aggregate session signals (click rate in last 10 minutes). Pre-computed by a Flink streaming job, served from feature store with 1-minute staleness. Total feature fetch latency: 0.5ms static + 0.5ms hourly + 1.5ms real-time = 2.5ms. Without pre-computation (all real-time): 8-12ms. Pre-computing saves 5-10ms of the 100ms budget.

scenario: A recommendation system uses 200 features per (user, item) pair. 50 features change in real-time (e.g., current session behavior). 150 features change hourly (e.g., item popularity). Evaluate pre-computing all features vs computing in real-time for latency and freshness.
title: Feature Freshness vs Serving Latency: Pre-Compute vs Real-Time

details.common_mistake: Loading full friend activity lists at request time from a graph database. For a user with 200 friends, this requires 200 graph traversals + activity lookups, which at 1ms per traversal = 200ms sequential, or with parallelism: 10ms+ for 200 async calls. Both violate the 50ms budget.
details.napkin_math: Social embedding storage: 1B users * 128 * 4B = 512GB. Redis cluster at 16GB per node: 32 nodes for 512GB. At 10K QPS, 1 lookup per request: 10K GET/sec per Redis cluster. Redis handles 100K+ GET/sec single node: well within 10K QPS across 32 nodes. Latency: P99 Redis GET = 1ms (including network RTT on same rack). Hourly aggregation job: 1B users * 200 friends * 1 event/hour = 200B events/hour. Flink at 10M events/sec: 200B / 3600 / 10M = 5.6 hours to process 1B users. Too slow for hourly refresh — need to parallelize Flink job to 100 workers: 3.4 minutes. Feasible.
details.realistic_solution: Pre-aggregated social signals: (1) Offline aggregation job (hourly): for each user U, compute a compact social signal vector: weighted sum of friend item embeddings clicked in last 24h. Result: one 128-dim vector per user (social_embedding). Size: 1B users * 128 * 4B = 512GB. Store in distributed key-value store (RocksDB or Redis cluster). (2) At serving time: single lookup for user's social_embedding (1 Redis GET, 1ms). Use social_embedding as an additional input feature to the ranking model — no per-friend lookup needed. (3) Real-time social signal (for high-recency): maintain a streaming counter of friend activity in last 1 hour. Flink job aggregates Kafka events per user. Serves 'recent_friend_activity_count' as a scalar feature. Lookup: 1ms. (4) Total social feature latency: 2ms for pre-aggregated embedding + recency count. Fits within 50ms budget. Trade-off: social embedding is hourly stale. For friend-based freshness: use real-time recency signal to boost content where recent_friend_activity_count > 0.

scenario: A social recommendation system incorporates friend activity into item scores: items liked by friends score higher. The social graph has 1B users with avg 200 friends each. Friend-aware scoring at request time requires loading friend activity lists. Design the architecture for 10K QPS at P99 < 50ms.
title: Social Graph Embedding Update Frequency for Friend-Aware Rec

details.common_mistake: Attributing poor offline-to-online transfer to online feature mismatch without investigating the training distribution. Uniform random negatives create an unrealistically easy training problem — the model learns to distinguish positive items from random items in the full catalog, but at serving time it must distinguish from items that were already retrieved and ranked, which are much harder negatives.
details.napkin_math: Batch size 4K (2K positive pairs + 2K items as in-batch negatives). In-batch negative ratio: each positive pair sees 2K-1 negatives. Total positive:negative ratio = 1:1999. Random negatives (same batch size): 1:1 positive:negative ratio — easy. In-batch negatives: 1999x harder training signal. Expected AUC improvement: in-batch negatives typically improve AUC by 5-10 points on retrieval tasks (1-tower to 2-tower with in-batch: +8 AUC reported in literature). Online improvement proportional: 5% -> 15-20% expected after fix.
