details.realistic_solution: The correct architectural decision is to choose **FastFusion-CNN** for the initial launch, as the system is severely memory-bandwidth bound, not compute-bound. The Jetson AGX Orin's memory bandwidth is the hard physical constraint that makes DenseViT non-viable at 8K/30FPS.

scenario: You are the lead ML Systems Architect for a self-driving car company. Your team is upgrading the main forward-facing camera from a 4K sensor to a new 8K sensor to improve long-range object detection. The perception stack runs on a Jetson AGX Orin, and you have a hard real-time deadline of 33ms per frame (30 FPS).
title: The 8K Sensor Upgrade Dilemma

details.common_mistake: Engineers often fall into one of two traps: 1) 'ViT is the future, so we must use it everywhere,' completely ignoring the astronomical, budget-breaking compute cost on edge hardware. 2) 'CNNs are the only thing that works on edge,' which is an overly conservative stance that cedes future performance advantages to competitors and ignores modern hybrid and sparse architectures.
details.napkin_math: A naive ViT processes images in patches. For a 2MP image with 16x16 patches, sequence length N is 7812. Self-attention complexity is O(N^2). Attention score matrix is 7812^2 = 61M elements. Reading this 61MB matrix per head at Orin's 204.8 GB/s bandwidth takes 61MB / 204.8GB/s = 0.3ms. With 12 heads and 12 layers, just loading attention matrices takes 0.3ms * 144 = 43ms. Misses 33ms budget instantly.
details.realistic_solution: A Principal-level solution avoids dogmatic choices and proposes a pragmatic, hybrid, and data-driven approach.

scenario: You are the new Principal ML Systems Engineer at 'NüVuro', an EV startup aiming to build a unified perception stack for its 2028 model year, moving beyond the current generation's collection of disparate, hand-tuned CNNs. The entire system, processing feeds from 8 surround-view cameras, must run on a single automotive-grade SoC with hard real-time constraints.
title: The Unified Automotive Perception Stack Design

details.common_mistake: Suggesting incremental, insufficient fixes like 'prune the existing models more' or 'try a slightly smaller backbone.' These fail to address the core architectural flaw: the lack of early, cross-sensor fusion and the massive overhead of running eight separate models. Another common mistake is to suggest more powerful hardware, ignoring the strict power, thermal, and cost constraints of an automotive platform.
details.napkin_math: Let's quantify the waste of the old system and the gains of the new one. The Orin's memory bandwidth is 204.8 GB/s. A lightweight model (e.g., 50MB) must be loaded 8 times. Memory traffic = 8 models * 50MB = 400MB per frame. Time to load weights = 400MB / 204.8 GB/s ≈ 2ms. More importantly, each of the 8 inferences is a separate kernel launch sequence, adding microseconds of CPU overhead each time, and preventing the GPU from being saturated with a single, large, efficient computation. For the new system, let's say our distilled BEV model is 200MB. We load it once: 200MB / 204.8 GB/s ≈ 1ms. The key is that the entire compute workload is now one large graph. The arithmetic intensity skyrockets. An AGX Orin at 45W can sustain ~200 INT8 TOPS. The previous 8 small models likely had low arithmetic intensity, making them memory-bound and achieving maybe 30% of peak TOPS (60 TOPS). The new unified model is a large, dense computation, much more likely to be compute-bound and hit 70-80% of peak (140-160 TOPS). This >2x increase in effective compute utilization is what allows us to meet the 33ms deadline, even with a more complex model.
details.realistic_solution: The 'N-model' approach is fundamentally flawed. The solution is to move to a single, unified architecture that performs early fusion, is optimized via distillation, and is deployed with hardware-aware compilation.

scenario: You are the lead architect for an autonomous trucking company. Your current perception system uses eight 1080p cameras feeding into a central Jetson AGX Orin, which has a 60W thermal design power (TDP) limit. The current architecture runs eight separate, lightweight classification models, one per camera, and then attempts a late fusion of their outputs. This design has a 150ms end-to-end latency, catastrophically missing the 33ms hard real-time deadline for object detection. The system already consumes 55W, leaving no room for a new LiDAR processing pipeline that engineering insists is necessary. Propose a new system architecture from scratch that can meet the latency and power budget while also accommodating the future LiDAR stream. Justify your first three architectural decisions with quantitative reasoning.
title: The 360° Vision System Latency Collapse

details.common_mistake: The most common L5 answer is 'use a much smaller model.' This ignores the product requirement for a certain level of reasoning quality that the 1B model provides. Another incorrect path is 'batch the sensor inputs,' which makes no sense for a single, real-time braking event. A purely software-based engineer might miss the hardware-specific nature of the bottleneck: that it's not about FLOPs, but about the memory wall hit on every single token generation.
details.napkin_math: Let's analyze the bottleneck. A 1B parameter model (INT8) has 1 GB of weights. A Hailo-8 has extremely fast on-chip SRAM, but let's assume a more typical edge system-level memory bandwidth of ~2.5 GB/s to access the full model if it doesn't fit entirely on-chip. Time to load weights = 1 GB / 2.5 GB/s = 400ms. This is the absolute wall, proving the model *must* live in on-chip memory. Even with it on-chip, let's say internal BW is 100GB/s. Loading 1GB for every token is 10ms. This is the real bottleneck. Now, let's model speculative decoding with k=5. The draft model (100M params, 100MB) runs in ~1ms. The verifier (1B params) runs once to check 5 tokens, taking its ~10ms. Total time for 5 tokens ≈ 11ms. Average time per token ≈ 2.2ms. This is a ~5x speedup that breaks the memory wall. Fusing the attention kernel might save another 20-30% off the 10ms verification time, bringing it to 7ms. Total time for 5 tokens is now ~8ms. This is well within the 15ms budget and provides the required rationale.
details.realistic_solution: The core problem is the memory wall of auto-regressive decoding. We hit a latency floor determined by loading the model weights for every single token. The plan must break this sequential dependency.

scenario: As the Staff Engineer for a new active safety feature, you've been asked to design a system that uses a 1B-parameter LLM to generate a human-readable rationale *before* an Automated Emergency Braking (AEB) event occurs. The rationale (e.g., 'pedestrian detected, high speed, braking now') is for logging and future analysis. The entire AEB decision loop has a hard real-time budget of 33ms. The team has already quantized the 1B model to INT8 and deployed it to a Hailo-8-like accelerator (26 TOPS, on-chip SRAM). However, initial tests show that generating even the first few tokens takes over 100ms. The sequential, auto-regressive nature of the LLM is the bottleneck. The VP of Engineering wants a concrete, three-point plan to get the rationale generation latency under 15ms. What is your proposal?
title: The Speculative Braking Rationale Failure

details.common_mistake: Engineers often fixate on the 'peak TOPS' marketing number. They assume the 275 TOPS 'Big Core' chip must be better than the 26 TOPS 'Heterogeneous' chip. This ignores the reality that performance is dictated by the *lesser* of compute or memory bandwidth. A chip with immense compute is useless if it's constantly stalled waiting for data from slow memory (the 'Memory Wall'). This also ignores the critical TOPS/W metric, especially in a power-constrained environment like a vehicle.
details.napkin_math: Target: ViT with 500 GOPs, 10 GB memory access/inference. Orin provides 204.8 GB/s. Reading 10 GB alone takes 10GB / 204.8 GB/s = 48.8ms. We already miss the 30 FPS (33ms) deadline without even computing! Compute at 275 TOPS takes 500G / 275T = 1.8ms. The AI is 500G / 10GB = 50 Ops/Byte, far below Orin's 1342 ridge point. To fix this, cache activations in SRAM or use a CNN with higher AI.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to recognize that system performance is a function of both the hardware's capabilities and the workload's demands. A Vision Transformer, especially on high-resolution camera data, is fundamentally a memory-intensive architecture. The self-attention mechanism requires large matrix multiplications (Q, K, V) that often exceed on-chip cache, leading to significant memory traffic.

scenario: You are the new Principal Engineer designing the perception compute module for a next-generation autonomous truck. The current system uses a power-hungry 150W automotive GPU. Your mandate is to drastically reduce cost and power for the new platform, targeting a total power budget of 45W and a 30 FPS processing rate for a challenging new multi-camera vision model.
title: The Automotive Roofline Dilemma

details.common_mistake: A purely model-centric answer, e.g., 'I would quantize the model to INT8 and prune it.' While correct, this is insufficient. This L4-level answer ignores that even a smaller model will be fundamentally memory-bound on this hardware, and fails to propose the necessary system-level architectural changes to overcome the I/O bottleneck, which is the dominant factor for generative models on edge devices.
details.napkin_math: Orin total bandwidth: 204.8 GB/s. 70% is used, leaving 30% (61.4 GB/s) for the LLM. Generating 5 tokens in 33ms means 151 tokens/sec. Time per token is 33ms / 5 = 6.6ms. In auto-regressive generation, weights are loaded per token. Max weight size we can load in 6.6ms at 61.4 GB/s is 6.6ms * 61.4 GB/s = 405 MB. Even quantized to 4-bit (0.5B/param), the max model size is ~800M parameters, not a 7B LLM.
details.realistic_solution: The core problem is that generative inference on edge devices is almost always limited by memory bandwidth, not compute. The latency to load the model's weights from DRAM for every single generated token exceeds the entire time budget. Therefore, the architecture must focus on amortizing this I/O cost.

scenario: You are the lead ML Systems Architect for a new ADAS platform. The current system, running on a Jetson AGX Orin, handles standard perception (object detection, lane keeping) and consumes ~70% of the device's compute and power budget. A new 'look-ahead' feature, which requires a 3-billion parameter Vision-Language Model (VLM) to interpret complex urban scenes, has been mandated. The VLM must generate a 5-token textual analysis of the scene within the existing 33ms hard real-time perception loop budget. The VLM is too large and slow for naive deployment. Propose a full-stack system architecture, from the model itself to the inference runtime, that makes this feature feasible. Justify your first three architectural decisions with quantitative reasoning.
title: The ADAS Look-Ahead Dilemma

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on total FLOPs, parameter count, or theoretical model accuracy. A model with fewer FLOPs can be slower and less power-efficient if its architecture creates memory-bound operators that underutilize the GPU's compute units. Another common mistake is assuming the chip's advertised 'Peak TOPS' is achievable for any workload; in reality, it's only achievable by compute-bound workloads.
details.napkin_math: At 30W, Orin downclocks to ~137 INT8 TOPS and ~100 GB/s bandwidth. Design A requires 10 T-ops, AI = 500. Design B requires 5 T-ops, AI = 50. Ridge point is 137 TOPS / 100 GB/s = 1370 Ops/Byte. Both are memory bound! A takes 10T / 500 = 20GB data movement. B takes 5T / 50 = 100GB. Time for A: 20GB / 100 GB/s = 200ms. Time for B: 100GB / 100 GB/s = 1000ms. Design A is 5x faster due to higher AI.
details.realistic_solution: The decision cannot be based on FLOPs alone, but on how efficiently each architecture uses the hardware. The correct KPI is **Achieved TOPS-per-Watt**, which measures the actual realized computational throughput against the power consumed.

scenario: You are the lead architect for the perception system of a new Level 3 autonomous vehicle. Your team is debating two competing designs for the core perception stack, which must run on a Jetson AGX Orin-class processor with a strict 30W thermal design power (TDP) budget and meet a 33ms per-frame deadline.
title: The Autonomous Perception Stack Fork

details.common_mistake: The most common L4/L5 answer is to immediately jump to Quantization-Aware Training (QAT). QAT is a powerful tool, but it's a brute-force solution that requires an expensive and slow retraining pipeline. A Staff+ engineer must first diagnose the root cause, which QAT might fix but won't explain. Another common mistake is suggesting a fallback to FP16, without first calculating if it's even feasible within the strict latency and power budgets of the edge device.
details.napkin_math: Orin FP32 performance is ~68 TFLOPS. A 5 TFLOP model takes 5T / 68T = 73.5ms (misses 33ms budget). pure FP16 yields ~137 TFLOPS, taking 5T / 137T = 36.5ms (still misses). Mixed precision targets 80% INT8 (275 TOPS) and 20% FP16 (137 TFLOPS). Compute time = (4T / 275T) + (1T / 137T) = 14.5ms + 7.3ms = 21.8ms. Adding 100MB / 204.8 GB/s = 0.5ms memory read, total latency is ~22ms. We hit 30 FPS!
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a dynamic range mismatch. The headlight glare introduces extreme outlier activation values that were not present in the daytime-heavy calibration dataset. Standard PTQ calculates a narrow scaling factor from this limited data, causing the high-intensity glare values to be 'clipped' to the maximum INT8 value (127). This clipping saturates entire feature maps, destroying the subtle, low-intensity information needed to detect a distant pedestrian in the darker parts of the scene.

scenario: You are the ML Systems Architect for the perception team at a leading autonomous vehicle company. Your team must deploy a new, larger SOTA object detection model (from a FP32 baseline) onto the fleet's existing hardware, a Jetson AGX Orin-based ECU with a hard 33ms latency budget for the perception stage.
title: The Night-Drive Quantization Collapse

details.common_mistake: Engineers often propose a single solution like 'just quantize to INT8' or 'prune the model'. These are necessary but completely insufficient. A senior engineer might suggest combining pruning and quantization. However, an L6+ candidate must recognize this is a multi-faceted systems problem where different parts of the model's execution (vision encoding vs. text decoding) have different bottlenecks. They must propose a *holistic architecture* that combines model size reduction, I/O-aware algorithms for encoding, and specialized techniques for accelerating autoregressive decoding, understanding that just shrinking the model won't solve the memory bandwidth issues inherent in attention and generation.
details.napkin_math: Let's evaluate a 7B VLM. Weights in 4-bit INT take 3.5GB. Memory bandwidth is 204.8 GB/s. For generation (batch size 1), every token requires loading the full 3.5GB model. Time per token = 3.5GB / 204.8GB/s = 17ms. Compute is minimal: 7B * 2 ops = 14 GOPs, taking 14G / 275T = 0.05ms. Max generation speed is 1000ms / 17ms ≈ 58 tokens/s. A 50-token response takes 0.85s, ensuring instantaneous feel.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is a multi-pillar strategy that attacks the problem from model design down to algorithmic optimization, acknowledging different bottlenecks at each stage.

scenario: You are the tech lead for the 'In-Cabin AI' team at a major automaker. Management wants to ship a new 'AI Copilot' feature—a vision-language model (VLM) that understands the driver-facing camera and voice commands—to the entire fleet via an Over-the-Air (OTA) update. The problem: the fleet's hardware is a fixed target, an automotive-grade SoC equivalent to a Jetson AGX Orin (275 INT8 TOPS, 32 GB LPDDR5 RAM). This hardware is already running the existing perception stack, leaving a strict budget of 15W of power and a 500ms end-to-end latency budget for the VLM to respond to a query like 'Is my blind spot clear?'. The baseline model from R&D is a 7B parameter Transformer-based VLM. A naive, unoptimized deployment is over 100x too slow and exceeds the power budget by 20x. Your VP says this feature is non-negotiable for competitive reasons. Formulate a multi-stage optimization strategy to make this deployment feasible. What are the first three architectural pillars of your plan, and why? For each, provide a napkin-math estimate of the expected improvement.
title: The Impossible OTA Update: Architecting a Generative VLM for an Automotive SoC

details.common_mistake: Engineers often fixate on the peak TOPS of the most powerful chip (the Orin), assuming more is always better. They might select Proposal A and argue that the high peak TOPS provides 'future-proofing' or can 'brute-force' the problem. This ignores the reality that a significant portion of the workload is memory-bound and cannot utilize the peak compute, leading to catastrophic power inefficiency. They fail to treat power and arithmetic intensity as primary design constraints.
details.napkin_math: Monolithic GPU at 30W: Orin NX draws ~25W, leaves ~5W for CPU/sensors. Idle power ~8W even when not inferring. Heterogeneous: DLA core ~5W for perception (24/7), GPU ~15W burst for planning. Idle: DLA 5W + CPU 3W = 8W vs GPU 25W always-on. Utilization: GPU idle 70% of time wastes 0.7*25W=17.5W. Heterogeneous saves ~60% energy over duty cycle.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to advocate for a modified version of **Proposal B (Heterogeneous)**, or a hybrid. The core insight is that a single, monolithic GPU is deeply inefficient for a mixed workload under a strict power budget.

scenario: You are the Lead ML Systems Architect at a new EV company designing a Level 3 autonomous driving system. Your team is finalizing the central compute module, which has a strict, passively-cooled thermal design power (TDP) of 30W.
title: The Autonomous Vehicle Power-Performance Paradox

details.common_mistake: A junior engineer would propose a single solution, like 'Let's just prune the model by 85%,' without considering the massive risk to model accuracy or the engineering cost of extensive retraining. A senior engineer might suggest a few techniques, but a principal-level answer must present a risk-managed portfolio of optimizations, ordered logically from safest to riskiest, and justify the sequencing based on quantitative estimates of return on investment.
details.napkin_math: We need to get from 200ms to 33ms, a speedup of ~6x.
details.realistic_solution: A principal-level response involves a phased strategy that tackles different sources of latency in order of increasing risk and engineering cost.

scenario: You are the new Principal ML Systems Engineer for a luxury EV company. Your flagship sedan, which shipped to customers in 2023, needs to receive a new 'Autonomous Valet' feature via an over-the-air (OTA) update. This feature requires a state-of-the-art Transformer-based BEV (Bird's-Eye-View) perception model for safe navigation in tight parking structures.
title: The Autonomous Valet Retrofit

details.common_mistake: Picking Chip B because it has higher peak TOPS on the datasheet. This is a classic trap of ignoring the memory system and the workload's characteristics. An engineer making this mistake fails to analyze the system's Arithmetic Intensity, assumes advertised TOPS are always achievable, and doesn't understand that for a memory-bound model, excess compute is uselessly idle, generating zero effective TOPS/W.
details.napkin_math: Datacenter GPU (e.g., A100 downclocked) has 2000 GB/s BW and 312 TFLOPS. Ridge point: 312T / 2000GB/s = 156 Ops/Byte. Jetson Orin has 204.8 GB/s and 275 INT8 TOPS. Orin Ridge point: 275T / 204.8GB/s = 1342 Ops/Byte. If the Gen-1 model has an AI of 300, it's compute-bound on the GPU (300 > 156), but heavily memory-bound on Orin (300 < 1342). On Orin, throughput crashes to 300 * 204.8 = 61 TOPS.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to analyze the workloads against the hardware capabilities, not just look at peak datasheet numbers. The architect must recognize this is a system co-design problem.

scenario: You are the Lead ML Systems Architect for a self-driving truck company. The Gen-1 prototype meets its 30 FPS perception deadline using a down-clocked datacenter GPU, but it consumes 200W and requires a liquid cooling system. For the Gen-2 production vehicle, the system must fit in a passive, air-cooled enclosure with a strict Thermal Design Power (TDP) budget of 60W.
title: The Autonomous Freeway Thermal Throttling Crisis

details.common_mistake: Focusing solely on peak TOPS. An engineer might incorrectly choose the next-gen 550 TOPS GPU, assuming that more peak FLOPS directly translates to more performance. This ignores the fact that if a workload is memory-bound, the extra compute cores will just sit idle, starved for data. They are not considering the performance-per-watt implications.
details.napkin_math: Orin specs: 275 INT8 TOPS, 204.8 GB/s. Ridge point = 275T / 204.8GB/s = 1342 Ops/Byte. With AI = 100 Ops/Byte, the new model is memory-bound. Effective compute throughput is capped at AI * Bandwidth = 100 Ops/Byte * 204.8 GB/s = 20.48 TOPS. To process a 1 T-op frame takes 1T / 20.48T = 48.8ms, blowing past the 33ms budget. To hit 33ms, we need to increase AI or reduce total operations to 0.67 T-ops.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to recognize this is a roofline problem where the new model is memory-bandwidth bound. The BEV-Transformer's lower arithmetic intensity means it cannot take advantage of the Orin's massive compute power; it's limited by the speed of HBM.

scenario: You are the Principal ML Systems Engineer for an autonomous trucking company. Your current fleet uses a perception system built on the Jetson AGX Orin, which comfortably meets its 33ms end-to-end latency budget. Your modeling team has just developed a new, much safer, BEV-Transformer model that reduces accident risk by 5%. However, when you benchmark this new model, it badly misses the 33ms deadline. `tegrastats` shows the Orin's GPU is pegged at 100%, but the model's arithmetic intensity is known to be significantly lower than the previous-generation CNNs.
title: The Autonomous Fleet Compute Upgrade

details.common_mistake: An L5-level answer is to propose incremental optimizations: 'We'll switch to a more efficient MobileNetV3 backbone, apply aggressive INT8 quantization, and use depthwise separable convolutions.' While these are good practices, they offer linear, not step-function, improvements. A 10-20% efficiency gain is plausible, but a 40% capability increase within the *same* power budget is not. This approach fails to address the core problem: the monolithic 'always-on' compute model has hit a wall.
details.napkin_math: 8 cameras at 6MP = 48MP per frame. At 3 bytes/pixel (RGB), that's 144MB per frame. Over Orin's 204.8 GB/s memory bus, just transferring the raw input takes 144MB / 204.8GB/s = 0.7ms. A standard CNN taking 100 GOPs/img yields 8 * 100G = 800 GOPs. At 275 TOPS, compute is 800G / 275T = 2.9ms. Total base time is 3.6ms, leaving plenty of 33ms budget, meaning 55W power draw can be reduced via underclocking.
details.realistic_solution: The correct L6+ approach is to abandon the monolithic paradigm and propose a **conditional compute architecture**, likely a **Mixture of Experts (MoE)**. The core insight is that not all driving scenes are equally complex; you don't need to run your most powerful, power-hungry model on an empty highway.

scenario: You are the new Tech Lead for the perception team at a leading autonomous vehicle company. Your current system, built on a Jetson AGX Orin, uses a large, monolithic CNN to fuse data from eight 6-megapixel cameras. This model consumes 55W of the SoC's 60W thermal design power (TDP), leaving no room for growth. The product team wants to add three major new features, including cyclist hand-signal detection and construction zone awareness. Your team estimates this requires a 40% increase in model FLOPs to hit the required accuracy targets for these long-tail events. A hardware change is not possible for two years due to supply chain commitments. Propose a novel software and model architecture for the next-generation perception stack that meets the product requirements without violating the hard 60W power constraint. What are your first three architectural decisions, and how do you justify them with quantitative reasoning?
title: The Autonomous Perception Power Wall

details.common_mistake: The most common junior-level response is to blame the quantization tool (e.g., 'TensorRT must have a bug') or to suggest simply reverting to the FP16 model, which would miss the hard real-time latency budget and is not a viable long-term solution. Another mistake is to suggest only retraining with more night-time data, without addressing the fundamental architectural flaw in the quantization process itself.
details.napkin_math: Let's quantify why the saturation happened. An FP16 tensor has a massive dynamic range (from ~6e-5 to 65504). INT8's range is a fixed [-128, 127]. PTQ calibration finds a scaling factor `S` to map the typical FP16 activation range to the INT8 range. Assume the daytime calibration data has a typical max activation value of `A_fp16_day = 2.0` in the first layer. The calibrator sets `S = 127 / 2.0 = 63.5`.
details.realistic_solution: A Staff-level engineer must go beyond a simple fix and propose a systemic defense-in-depth strategy.

scenario: You are the ML Systems Architect for a leading autonomous vehicle company. Your team has just developed a new HDR-capable (High Dynamic Range) pedestrian detection model. To meet the 33ms real-time deadline on the vehicle's Jetson AGX Orin compute module, the model was quantized from FP16 to INT8 using Post-Training Quantization (PTQ). The quantized model passed all extensive simulation tests, which used a standard daytime driving dataset for calibration. However, during a fleet-wide field test, a critical failure occurs: at night, when an oncoming car's headlights create a sudden, bright flare, the system fails to detect a pedestrian stepping off the curb. Analysis of the captured sensor data reveals that during the flare event, the activation values in the first three convolutional layers of the model saturate, clamping to the INT8 maximum value of 127. Propose a robust, multi-layered architectural strategy to resolve this immediate crisis and prevent this entire class of 'data-dependent quantization failures' from recurring.
title: The Headlight Flare Catastrophe

details.common_mistake: Proposing only incremental optimizations like vanilla quantization or unstructured pruning. These are necessary but insufficient for the 15x performance gap. Another common mistake is to suggest abandoning the ViT, which ignores the strategic requirement, or to focus on only one technique (like quantization) without a holistic architectural vision. An L3 might suggest a bigger GPU, which isn't an option in a car.
details.napkin_math: ViT 2B params = 2GB (INT8). Eight 640x480 images = 2.45MP. For patch size 16x16, sequence length N = 2.45M / 256 = 9570. Memory load per inference: 2GB weights. Orin BW is 204.8 GB/s. Weight load time: 2GB / 204.8GB/s = 9.7ms. Attention matrix (N^2) = 9570^2 = 91MB per layer/head. Loading this dominates. 12 layers * 12 heads * 91MB = 13GB data movement. 13GB / 204.8 = 63ms. Misses 33ms budget totally.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is a multi-stage architectural redesign that attacks the computational complexity at its source, demonstrating a grasp of architectural trade-offs beyond simple optimization.

scenario: You are the new Principal Engineer for the 'Perception v5' team at a leading autonomous vehicle company. The current v4 system uses a dozen specialized CNNs for tasks like pedestrian detection, lane finding, and sign recognition.
title: The Autonomous Vision Unification Dilemma

details.common_mistake: Engineers often fall into one of two traps. The first is architectural purity: 'We must switch to a pure Vision Transformer (ViT) because it's state-of-the-art,' ignoring the catastrophic mismatch between a ViT's quadratic scaling in attention and the fixed power/memory budget of an edge device. The second trap is excessive conservatism: 'Transformers are too slow for the edge, we can only use CNNs,' which misses the opportunity to use hybrid models, NAS, or techniques like Mixture-of-Experts to gain Transformer-like capabilities within an edge-friendly envelope.
details.napkin_math: **1. Justifying Depthwise Convolution:** A standard 3x3 convolution with 256 input channels and 256 output channels has a computational cost proportional to `3*3*256 * 256 = 589,824`. A depthwise separable version has a cost of `(3*3*256) + (1*1*256*256) = 2,304 + 65,536 = 67,840`. This is an **8.7x reduction in FLOPs** for that single layer, creating significant power and latency headroom across the entire network.
details.realistic_solution: A Staff-level architect would propose a pragmatic, multi-phase roadmap that de-risks the transition and delivers value at each stage.

scenario: You are the new Lead ML Systems Architect for a flagship autonomous vehicle program. The current perception system, built on a fleet of ResNet-based CNNs, is hitting a hard compute and power wall on its NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin ECU. It consumes the entire 30W power budget and can barely maintain the 33ms per-frame deadline.
title: The Perception Platform Redesign

details.common_mistake: Engineers often propose a single technique in isolation, like 'we'll just use 8-bit quantization.' They fail to recognize that no single optimization can bridge this massive performance gap. Another common mistake is to only focus on model compression (pruning/distillation) without considering the algorithmic and kernel-level changes required to fundamentally reduce latency, like altering the decoding strategy itself.
details.napkin_math: 500M parameter Transformer in INT8 = 0.5GB. Memory bandwidth on Orin is 204.8 GB/s. Reading weights per token takes 0.5GB / 204.8GB/s = 2.44ms. Compute for 1 token: 500M * 2 ops = 1 GOP. At 275 TOPS, compute time is 1G / 275T = 0.003ms. Heavily memory bound! To speed this up, we apply KV-caching and process a batch of 10 sequence steps at once, amortizing the 2.44ms weight load across 10 tokens.
details.realistic_solution: A multi-stage approach is required, as the performance gap is too large for any single technique. The plan must attack the model, the algorithm, and the kernel execution.

scenario: You are the Lead ML Systems Engineer at an automotive supplier. Your team has developed a powerful 500M parameter Transformer model for a new 'Driver Intention' feature, which predicts if a driver is about to turn or change lanes based on in-cabin video. The cloud-trained model achieves 99.5% accuracy. However, deploying it on the vehicle's edge NPU results in a latency of 500ms per frame, which is completely unacceptable for real-time safety (target is 33ms). Propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline across the model, algorithm, and hardware levels to achieve the 15x speedup required without dropping accuracy below 98%.
title: The Over-Budget Driver Intention Model

details.common_mistake: The most common and dangerous mistake is to blame the training data or the algorithm, suggesting a full retraining cycle ('We need more night images in our training set'). This is a slow, expensive, and incorrect guess. Another common mistake is to immediately revert to FP16, which fixes the symptom but doesn't solve the underlying systemic issue with the quantization process, guaranteeing it will happen again with a different model or scenario.
details.napkin_math: Current FP16 model: 4 TFLOPs. Orin FP16 is ~137 TFLOPS. Compute time = 4T / 137T = 29.2ms. Weight memory (100MB) read = 100MB / 204.8 GB/s = 0.5ms. Total ~29.7ms (barely under 33ms). Mixed-precision: 90% INT8 (275 TOPS), 10% FP16. Compute drops to (3.6T / 275T) + (0.4T / 137T) = 13ms + 2.9ms = 15.9ms. Weights shrink to 55MB (0.26ms). New total = 16.1ms, saving ~13ms and significantly cutting power draw.
details.realistic_solution: The physical root cause is almost certainly **activation overflow due to calibration data mismatch**. The headlights create a high dynamic range (HDR) scene that is not present in the original calibration dataset. The pixel values from the headlights and their reflections are orders of magnitude brighter than typical 'daytime' or 'ambient night' scenes. This causes the activation values in the early layers of the neural network to spike, exceeding the [min, max] range observed during calibration. When these large activation values are quantized to INT8's limited [-128, 127] range, they are 'clipped' to the maximum value, destroying the fine-grained information needed to identify the cones. The network effectively becomes 'blinded by the light'.

scenario: You are the tech lead for the perception team at a leading autonomous vehicle company. Your team has successfully deployed an FP16 vision model on the car's Jetson AGX Orin, meeting the 30 FPS (33ms) deadline. To reduce power and free up compute for sensor fusion, you lead the effort to quantize the model to INT8. The model passes all simulation tests and regression benchmarks. However, during on-track testing, a catastrophic failure emerges: the car completely fails to detect traffic cones at night, but only when its own headlights are on. The FP16 model handled this scenario perfectly. The team is blocked, and pressure is mounting from the safety organization. Propose a systematic plan to diagnose this failure. What is the most likely physical root cause, and how would you redesign your team's quantization and deployment architecture to prevent this entire class of failures in the future?
title: The Headlight Blindness Catastrophe

details.common_mistake: The most common mistake is proposing a linear, naive application of tools without considering the dependencies and the scale of the problem. For example, starting with pruning a 100B model is computationally infeasible and will destroy its accuracy. Another mistake is assuming a compiler like TensorRT can magically solve the problem; operator fusion is a final-mile optimization, not a solution for a 10,000x model size gap. Finally, many engineers might miss the autoregressive nature of the problem and focus only on single-pass latency, completely failing to budget for the sequential token generation that would blow the latency budget.
details.napkin_math: Let's assume the final distilled, pruned, and quantized student model has 500M parameters (INT8 = 500 MB weights) and the hazard description requires generating 8 tokens.
details.realistic_solution: A successful plan requires a multi-stage strategy that treats the problem as one of progressive model reduction and targeted optimization, where each stage enables the next.

scenario: You are the Lead ML Systems Engineer for the autonomous driving unit at a major automaker. Your company has just trained a groundbreaking 100B-parameter, multi-modal Vision-Language Model (VLM) in the cloud. This 'Driver-VLM' achieves state-of-the-art hazard prediction by processing sensor streams and generating descriptive text of potential dangers. However, you need to deploy this VLM on the vehicle's embedded compute platform, which has only 16 GB of shared memory and a strict 50ms latency budget. What is the optimal strategy to deploy this system on the edge?
title: The Autonomous 'Cloud-to-Edge' VLM Deployment

details.common_mistake: A junior engineer might immediately suggest 'Just use Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)'. This is a valid tool, but it's a brute-force solution, not a diagnosis. It doesn't explain *why* PTQ failed, is computationally expensive, and may not even converge if the underlying issue is extreme. Another common mistake is to blame the calibration dataset without a specific hypothesis, leading to a vague 'let's just collect more fog data' plan, which wastes valuable time.
details.napkin_math:
The core constraint is the 33ms (30 FPS) latency budget on the Jetson AGX Orin. Let's assume our ViT requires 5 Trillion Operations per inference.

1. **FP32 inference time:**
   - Orin FP32 peak: ~5.3 TFLOPS (GPU)
   - Time = 5 TOps / 5.3 TFLOPS ≈ 943ms → **way over budget** (need INT8)

2. **INT8 inference time:**
   - Orin INT8 peak: ~275 TOPS
   - Time = 5 TOps / 275 TOPS ≈ 18ms → **within 33ms budget** ✓

3. **The quantization dilemma:**
   - FP32 dynamic range: ±3.4 × 10³⁸ with ~7 decimal digits precision
   - INT8 dynamic range: [−128, 127] — only 256 discrete levels
   - If calibration data is all clear-weather, the scale factor s = (max_activation − min_activation) / 255 is tuned for "normal" activations
   - Fog activations with low contrast may cluster in a tiny sub-range, getting quantized to just 2–3 INT8 levels → information destroyed

4. **Fix cost (QAT):**
   - QAT requires ~10–20% of original training compute
   - If original training was 1000 GPU-hours, QAT ≈ 100–200 GPU-hours
   - But the real fix is mixed-precision: keep fog-sensitive layers (Softmax, final attention) in FP16 while keeping bulk compute in INT8
   - FP16 layers add ~5ms overhead → total ≈ 23ms, still within 33ms budget
details.realistic_solution: The core issue is almost certainly catastrophic activation clipping. The low-contrast features in foggy images likely push activation values in certain layers outside the narrow dynamic range captured during calibration on 'clean' data. The Softmax and GELU activations in ViTs are particularly prone to producing extreme outliers that get saturated in INT8, destroying the model's ability to discern fine-grained features.

scenario: You are the tech lead for the perception team at a major automotive company. Your team's new ViT-based pedestrian detector, running in FP32, achieves 99.5% accuracy on your validation set. To meet the production hardware budget, the model must be quantized. After a standard post-training static quantization (PTQ) to INT8, the overall accuracy drops slightly to 98%, which seems acceptable. However, during fleet validation, you discover a catastrophic failure: the INT8 model's accuracy on pedestrians in foggy conditions has plummeted to 35%.
title: The Foggy Road Catastrophe

details.common_mistake: Immediately choosing the Vision Transformer 'because it's state-of-the-art' without considering the physics of the hardware. A junior answer is qualitative; a senior answer is quantitative. Another mistake is to propose a lengthy empirical bake-off without a guiding hypothesis, wasting months of engineering time. The goal is to predict the outcome with high confidence using math.
details.napkin_math: Goal: Prove the Hybrid CNN is viable and the ViT is not, based on the Orin's 33ms latency budget. Orin memory bandwidth is 204.8 GB/s. Max data transfer strictly bound by physics in 33ms = 204.8 GB/s * 0.033s = 6.75 GB. The ViT requires 8 GB of memory traffic per frame, meaning it will take at least 8 / 204.8 = 39ms strictly bound by memory physics, failing the 33ms budget regardless of compute optimizations. The Hybrid CNN requires 1 GB (takes ~5ms memory time) and 500 GOPs (takes ~1.8ms at 275 TOPS), easily fitting the 33ms budget.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to immediately analyze both proposed architectures through the lens of the Roofline Model, specifically by estimating their Arithmetic Intensity (AI) relative to the Jetson AGX Orin's hardware capabilities. The path chosen must respect the physics of the device.

scenario: You are the new lead architect for the perception team at a major autonomous vehicle company. Our current fleet runs on a Jetson AGX Orin with a 60W thermal design power (TDP) and uses a mature, highly-optimized CNN-based model for object detection. This system reliably hits its 33ms end-to-end latency budget. However, to advance our autonomous capabilities, we must improve detection of small, distant objects and performance in dense, cluttered scenes. Your team has two competing proposals for the next-generation model: Proposal A is a deeper Hybrid CNN requiring 500 GOPs and 1 GB of memory traffic per frame. Proposal B is a high-resolution Vision Transformer (ViT) requiring 300 GOPs but 8 GB of memory traffic per frame due to large self-attention maps. Which proposal is viable within the 33ms latency budget?
title: The Autonomous Perception Horizon

details.common_mistake: Relying on FLOPs as the sole proxy for latency. A lower-FLOP CNN can be slower than a higher-FLOP ViT if the CNN's architecture (e.g., many depthwise separable convolutions with low arithmetic intensity) is memory-bound on the target hardware, while the ViT's dense matrix multiplies are compute-bound. Another mistake is assuming cloud performance translates directly to the edge, ignoring the quadratic scaling of self-attention on large sensor images and the much more constrained memory system of an automotive SoC.
details.napkin_math: The fundamental flaw in the FLOPs analysis is revealed by a Roofline analysis of the AGX Orin.
details.realistic_solution: The junior engineers' analysis is flawed because it ignores the **Roofline Model** and the concept of **Arithmetic Intensity (AI)**. The core challenge is not total FLOPs, but whether the architecture can actually use the 275 TOPS of the SoC, which is determined by the memory system's ability to feed the compute units.

scenario: You are the Lead ML Systems Architect for a top-tier automotive company. Your current perception system, based on a highly-optimized CNN (similar to EfficientNet-B5), is hitting accuracy limits on long-tail scenarios like occluded pedestrians and unusual weather. An offline prototype using a Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture shows a 5% mAP improvement, which the product team desperately wants.
title: The Autonomous Perception Stack Redesign: Transformer Systems Cost

details.common_mistake: Engineers often suggest unrealistic solutions like 'upgrade the hardware' (which is forbidden) or only focus on one area, like aggressive quantization, without a holistic plan. Another common mistake is mis-ordering the plan, for example, trying to apply speculative decoding before fixing the core attention bottleneck, which yields minimal gains. They might also incorrectly calculate the impact of an optimization, confusing compute-bound vs. memory-bound effects.
details.napkin_math: 15 CNNs process independently. Assume each uses 2 GOPs and reads 10MB of weights. Total compute: 30 GOPs. Sequential execution memory load: 15 * 10MB = 150MB. Read time: 150MB / 204.8 GB/s = 0.73ms. Compute time: 30G / 275T = 0.1ms. Kernel launch overhead dominates: 15 models * 50 layers * 0.05ms = 37.5ms. Fusing them into one shared-backbone architecture eliminates launches, reaching the <25ms target.
details.realistic_solution: A successful plan requires a systematic approach, starting with the biggest sources of waste and moving to more sophisticated techniques. The correct order is crucial because the effectiveness of later stages depends on the success of earlier ones.

scenario: You are the new technical lead for the perception team at a leading autonomous vehicle company. The current system is a complex web of 15+ specialized CNNs (for object detection, lane segmentation, sign recognition, etc.) running on a Jetson AGX Orin. This system is stable and meets its 33ms end-to-end latency budget, with the perception stack consuming 25ms of that budget. The research team has developed a new unified Transformer-based model that significantly improves accuracy but takes 200ms per inference. Formulate a systematic plan to optimize this new model to meet the <25ms latency budget on the same hardware.
title: The Autonomous Stack Consolidation

details.common_mistake: "The CPU is fast, so it must be the complexity of the pixel transformation or some OS overhead." This often overlooks the cost of memory accesses.
details.napkin_math: - L1 cache hit: ~1-4 CPU cycles | - L2 cache hit: ~10-20 CPU cycles | - L3 cache hit (if present): ~40-80 CPU cycles | - DRAM access (cache miss): ~100-300 CPU cycles
details.realistic_solution: The most common reason for this slowdown is **cache misses**. A 10MB image buffer is significantly larger than typical L1 (e.g., 32KB-128KB) and often L2 (e.g., 256KB-1MB) caches on edge ARM processors. When the CPU tries to access data that is not in its L1 or L2 cache, it incurs a cache miss. This forces the CPU to fetch data from the slower main memory (DRAM), which can take hundreds of CPU cycles. If the access pattern is not perfectly sequential or if other processes evict data from the cache, the problem is exacerbated, leading to a "cache miss storm." The CPU spends a disproportionate amount of time waiting for data rather than computing.

scenario: You're writing a pre-processing routine for an image classification model on an embedded Linux device. A simple loop that iterates over a 10MB image buffer, applying a pixel-wise transformation, is running much slower than expected, even on a high-frequency ARM core. The core is rated for 2.0 GHz. What's a common reason for such a slowdown in data-intensive loops, even on fast CPUs?
title: The Unexpected Cache Miss Storm

details.common_mistake: Assuming that "model memory footprint" only refers to the weights, and that quantization applies uniformly to all data within the inference pipeline.
details.napkin_math: *   **Model:** A typical ResNet-50 might have ~25 MB of FP32 weights. | *   **Expected INT8 Weights:** 25 MB / 4 = 6.25 MB. | *   **Peak Activations (FP32):** For a 224x224x3 input, a common intermediate layer might produce a 14x14x1024 feature map. In FP32, this is 14 * 14 * 1024 * 4 bytes ≈ 0.8 MB. If multiple such large activation maps need to be held, or if they are FP16/FP32, they add up. | *   **Scratchpad:** A convolution operation might temporarily require memory equivalent to several input/output feature maps. | *   **Total observed:** If weights are 6.25MB, but activations/buffers add 5-10MB and runtime adds 2-3MB, the total could be 13-19MB, which is only ~1.3x-1.9x smaller than the FP32 version's 25MB weights + similar activation/buffer/runtime overhead (e.g., 25MB + 15MB = 40MB for FP32 vs 15MB for INT8 total).
details.realistic_solution:
While model weights often see a near 4x reduction from FP32 to INT8, the *total* memory footprint during inference includes much more:
  1.  **Intermediate Activations:** The tensors produced by each layer (activations) often need to be stored, at least temporarily. These might remain in higher precision (e.g., FP16 or even FP32, depending on the operator and hardware support) for numerical stability or performance reasons, or they might be explicitly de-quantized/re-quantized between layers, consuming more memory than expected.
  2.  **Input/Output Buffers:** The input image/data and the final output tensors (e.g., bounding boxes, class probabilities) also occupy memory.
  3.  **Scratchpad/Workspace Memory:** Many ML operations (e.g., convolutions using `im2col`, matrix multiplications) require temporary scratchpad buffers for intermediate calculations or data reordering. These buffers can be significant and might operate in higher precision.
  4.  **Runtime Overhead:** The ML inference engine itself (e.g., TFLite, ONNX Runtime), its internal data structures, graph representation, and operating system overhead consume RAM.
  5.  **Look-up Tables (LUTs):** For certain quantized operations or post-processing steps (e.g., de-quantization, activation functions), LUTs might be used, adding to memory.

scenario: You've successfully quantized your FP32 object detection model to INT8 for deployment on an edge device, expecting a 4x reduction in model memory footprint (weights). However, after deployment, you notice the total RAM usage during inference is only reduced by about 2x-2.5x compared to the FP32 version. What explains this discrepancy, and what other components contribute significantly to the overall memory footprint?
title: The Bloated INT8 Model

details.common_mistake: "Model weights are 2.1 MB. At 30 FPS that's 63 MB/s. Trivial compared to 25.6 GB/s." This only counts weight reads and ignores activation memory traffic, which dominates for segmentation models that produce large spatial feature maps.
details.napkin_math: GPU bandwidth need: 1.8 GB/s out of 25.6 GB/s = 7%. System total: 9.3 GB/s = 36%. Comfortable on average. But ISP bursts at 8 GB/s for 2ms during frame readout → instantaneous demand = 8 + 1.8 + 2 + 1.5 = 13.3 GB/s = 52%. Still under peak, but memory controller queuing adds ~1ms latency to GPU requests during ISP bursts. Fix: schedule inference to start 5ms after ISP frame capture completes, avoiding the burst overlap.
details.realistic_solution: Segmentation models have high activation-to-weight ratios because they maintain spatial resolution through the network.

scenario: Your edge device has LPDDR4x memory with 25.6 GB/s bandwidth, shared between the CPU, GPU, ISP, and display controller. You need to run a segmentation model (DeepLabv3-MobileNetV2, 2.7 GFLOPs, 2.1M params INT8) at 30 FPS on the GPU. The ISP consumes 4 GB/s for 1080p camera processing, and the display controller uses 2 GB/s. Estimate whether you have enough DRAM bandwidth for 30 FPS inference.
title: DRAM Bandwidth for 30 FPS Inference

details.common_mistake: "4 cameras × 1080p × 30 FPS — just multiply frame size by 4. It's a few hundred MB." This counts only the raw frames and ignores the pipeline buffers, model weights, tracking state, and GPU memory fragmentation that dominate real memory usage.
details.napkin_math: Memory capacity: 3.0 GB / 16 GB = 19%. Safe. Memory bandwidth: 4 cameras × 30 FPS × (3.1 MB decode + 4.9 MB resize + ~20 MB inference activations) = 4 × 30 × 28 = 3360 MB/s = 3.36 GB/s. Orin NX bandwidth: 102.4 GB/s. Bandwidth utilization: ~3.3%. Also safe. The system could handle 12+ cameras before hitting either limit. Practical limit: GPU compute (4 × YOLOv8n at 30 FPS = 120 inferences/sec × ~3ms each = 360ms/s of GPU time — 36% GPU utilization).
details.realistic_solution: Build a complete memory budget. Per-stream: decode buffers (2x 3.1 MB NV12 = 6.2 MB), resize buffer (1.2 MB), YOLOv8n weights (6.3 MB, shared), inference activations (~50 MB), DeepSORT tracker state (128-dim embeddings x 200 tracks = ~0.1 MB). Total per-stream unique: ~57.5 MB. Four streams: 4 x 57.5 + 6.3 (shared weights) = 236.3 MB. Add CUDA context (~300 MB), TensorRT engine cache (~200 MB), OS overhead (~1 GB). Grand total: ~1.7 GB. At 3 GB / 16 GB = 19% memory utilization, the system is safe. The real limit is GPU compute: 120 inferences/sec at 3ms each = 36% GPU utilization.

scenario: Your edge device (Jetson Orin NX, 16 GB LPDDR5) processes 4 camera streams simultaneously for a warehouse tracking system. Each camera delivers 1080p (1920×1080) at 30 FPS in NV12 format. The pipeline for each stream: decode → resize to 640×640 → run YOLOv8n → track (DeepSORT with ReID embeddings). Estimate the total memory footprint and determine if 16 GB is sufficient.
title: Memory for Multi-Camera Tracking

details.common_mistake: "The USB bus is saturated." USB3 has 5 Gbps bandwidth — a 1080p frame at 6 MB and TPU transfers of ~1 MB per inference together use only ~200 MB/s, well under the 625 MB/s USB3 limit.
details.napkin_math: LPDDR4 bus: 3.2 GB/s shared. Camera DMA: 30 FPS × 6 MB = 180 MB/s (5.6% of bus). CPU preprocessing DMA: ~180 MB/s read + 60 MB/s write = 240 MB/s (7.5%). TPU DMA: 1 MB in + 0.1 MB out per inference × 60 inferences/sec = 66 MB/s (2%). Total: 486 MB/s (15% of bus). Bandwidth isn't the issue — **latency is**. Each 6 MB camera burst holds the bus for 1.9ms. During that burst, the TPU stalls. With 30 bursts/sec, the TPU sees ~57ms of stalls per second → 10ms inference includes ~2ms of DMA stalls (8ms compute + 2ms stall). Reducing to 720p: 0.8ms bursts → <1ms stalls/inference → ~8.5ms total.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck isn't USB bandwidth — it's **DMA controller contention on the shared LPDDR4 bus**. Both the USB3 host controller (VL805 on Pi CM4) and the CPU use DMA to access main memory. The camera's DMA writes 6 MB frames into a ring buffer in DRAM. The CPU's DMA reads those frames, preprocesses them, and writes the result to a USB3 output buffer for the TPU. The TPU's DMA reads input tensors and writes output tensors. All four DMA streams compete for the same 3.2 GB/s LPDDR4 bus. The BCM2711's memory controller uses round-robin arbitration with no QoS priority. When the camera DMA fires a burst write (6 MB at 3.2 GB/s = 1.9ms bus hold), it blocks the TPU's DMA read for that entire burst, adding up to 1.9ms of stall to inference. The fix: (1) reduce camera resolution to 720p (2.7 MB frames → 0.8ms bursts), (2) use the Pi's VideoCore GPU for preprocessing (separate DMA path), (3) pin TPU transfers to a dedicated USB controller if available.

scenario: Your edge AI system runs on a Raspberry Pi CM4 (BCM2711, 4× Cortex-A72, LPDDR4 at 3.2 GB/s shared bandwidth). You attach a Coral USB TPU for inference and a USB3 camera for input. In isolation, the camera captures at 30 FPS and the TPU infers in 8ms. When both run simultaneously, camera frames drop to 18 FPS and TPU inference spikes to 10ms. Neither device is individually saturating the bus. What is happening?
title: The DMA Contention Blind Spot

details.common_mistake: "Use a faster I2C clock (1 MHz Fast-mode Plus)." Even at 1 MHz, the fundamental protocol overhead remains — I2C is a serial bus with per-byte acknowledgment.
details.napkin_math: I2C at 400 kHz = ~40 KB/s raw bit rate. But protocol overhead (start, address, ack, stop) means an 8-byte sensor read takes ~30 bytes on the wire. $30 \times 8 \text{ bits} / 400,000 = 0.6\text{ms}$ per sensor. For 8 sensors sequentially: $8 \times 0.6\text{ms} = 4.8\text{ms}$ just in bus time. Add OS context switching and driver overhead (~1.4ms per read), and you hit ~16ms total. The model expects a 10ms update rate but the data takes 16ms to collect. The ML pipeline is starved by the physical bus architecture.
details.realistic_solution: The model's accuracy drops because it is receiving stale, temporally smeared features. The GPU is perfectly capable of running the sensor fusion model at 100 Hz, but the I2C bus acts as a severe bottleneck. I2C requires addressing the device, sending a register address, waiting for the sensor to convert, and reading the bytes back — all sequentially. If reading 8 sensors takes 16ms, the first sensor's data is 16ms older than the last sensor's data by the time the tensor is formed. The ML model was likely trained on perfectly synchronized, instantaneous snapshots of the environment. In production, it receives a "smeared" snapshot, destroying the temporal correlations between sensors that the model relies on. The fix is to decouple the sensor reads from the CPU/GPU using a dedicated microcontroller (or PRU/sensor hub) that reads the sensors concurrently via SPI or parallel I2C buses, buffers them, and DMA-transfers a perfectly coherent snapshot to the ML model's input tensor memory at exactly 100 Hz.

scenario: Your edge AI system reads data from 8 environmental sensors via I2C at 400 kHz. Your sensor fusion model expects 100 Hz input data (10ms intervals), but the I2C bus overhead limits you to 60 Hz. How does the I2C sensor polling rate limit the ML model's input freshness, and why does this bus bottleneck cause the model's accuracy to drop despite the GPU running at full speed?
title: The MMIO Sensor Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: "The DSP isn't fast enough" or "The model is still too large." While these can be issues, fitting the model in SRAM suggests a different problem.
details.napkin_math: A DSP running at 500MHz might have 4 MAC units, achieving 2 GMAC/s. If each MAC operation requires 2 bytes (INT8 weight + INT8 activation) and writes 1 byte (INT32 accumulator), this is 5 bytes/MAC. For 2 GMAC/s, it needs 10 GB/s of memory bandwidth. A 4MB SRAM might have an internal bus running at 200MHz with a 64-bit width, yielding 1.6 GB/s. This stark mismatch indicates a memory bottleneck.
details.realistic_solution: The likely bottleneck is **memory bandwidth**, specifically the **internal memory bandwidth** of the SRAM or the bandwidth between the DSP and the SRAM. Even if data resides in fast on-chip memory, the rate at which the DSP can *access* that data might be insufficient for the computational throughput it can achieve. Convolutional layers, for instance, involve frequent reads of weights and activations, and if the memory interface cannot feed the DSP's ALUs fast enough, the DSP will stall, waiting for data. This is a common characteristic of compute-bound tasks becoming memory-bound due to inefficient data movement.

scenario: You've highly optimized and quantized a neural network to fit entirely within the 4MB on-chip SRAM of an edge microcontroller with a powerful DSP. However, despite the model fitting perfectly and the DSP running at a high clock frequency, its inference latency is still much higher than your theoretical calculations based purely on FLOPs. What's a likely bottleneck, and how would you diagnose it?
title: The Data Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: "The SD card is slow to load the model." The model is already loaded. The problem is what the OS does *during* inference.
details.napkin_math: GPU Memory Bandwidth = 25 GB/s. SD Card Bandwidth = 0.025 GB/s. Swapping reduces your memory throughput by a factor of 1,000x. If a layer takes 4ms to read from RAM, it takes 4,000ms to read from an SD card.
details.realistic_solution: The erratic latency is caused by Linux swap thrashing. The 4GB model plus the OS, CUDA runtime, and kernel buffers exceed 4GB of physical RAM. Linux silently evicts pages to the SD card swap file. During inference, when a layer's weights have been swapped out, the GPU stalls while the CPU fetches the page from the SD card at 25 MB/s — 1000x slower than RAM's 25 GB/s. A single swapped 4MB weight tensor takes 160ms to reload instead of 0.16ms. The fix: reduce the model to fit in RAM (INT8 quantization halves it to 2GB), disable swap entirely (`swapoff`), or upgrade to 8GB hardware. Never rely on swap for inference workloads.

scenario: You deploy a 4GB model to a Jetson Nano that has exactly 4GB of physical RAM. You enable a 4GB Linux Swap File on the SD card to prevent OOM crashes. The model loads successfully. However, when the inference runs, the latency is completely erratic—sometimes it takes 50ms, sometimes it takes 4,000ms. The CPU and GPU are barely being utilized during the 4,000ms spikes. Why?
title: The Swap File Latency Cliff

details.common_mistake: "The eMMC is slower than spec." The raw bandwidth is fine — the overhead is elsewhere.
details.napkin_math: Sequential read: 200MB / 300MB/s = 0.67s. The missing 2.3s is execution overhead. TensorRT deserialization on a Cortex-M4 or Orin CPU involves memory allocation and PCIe/system bus transfers. Moving 200MB to Orin's DRAM at 204.8 GB/s is instant (0.001s). But CUDA context initialization takes ~300ms. JIT compiling/optimizing un-cached engine layers easily eats 1.5s. Flash fragmentation adds the remaining 0.5s.
details.realistic_solution: The 300 MB/s spec is for large sequential reads. Model loading involves: (1) filesystem overhead — ext4 metadata lookups, inode traversal, and block allocation table reads add ~200ms, (2) the model file is fragmented on a well-used eMMC — random 4K reads drop to ~20 MB/s, adding ~500ms, (3) TensorRT engine deserialization — parsing the serialized engine, allocating CUDA memory, and building the execution context takes ~1.5s for a 200 MB engine, (4) CUDA context initialization on first use adds ~300ms. The fix: (a) store the model on a dedicated, defragmented partition, (b) use `mmap()` to map the weight file so pages load on demand during the first inference rather than all at once, (c) keep a lightweight fallback model (~20 MB, loads in <200ms) that serves immediately while the full model loads in a background thread.

scenario: Your edge device loads a 200 MB model from eMMC flash into DRAM at boot. The eMMC spec says 300 MB/s sequential read, so you expect a 0.67-second load time. In practice, first inference takes over 3 seconds. Where did the other 2.3 seconds go?
title: The eMMC Cold Start

details.common_mistake: "Tracking state is just a few kilobytes — it's never a concern." This is true for 10-20 objects but breaks down at scale with rich per-object state.
details.napkin_math: 500 active tracks: 446 KB total. 2000 lost tracks: 1.78 MB total. Total: 2.23 MB. Matching bandwidth: 50 detections × 2500 tracks × 512 bytes = 64 MB/frame × 30 FPS = **1.92 GB/s** — that's 3.7% of the RB5's 51.2 GB/s LPDDR5 bandwidth, just for tracking. With spatial indexing (average 50 candidates per detection): 50 × 50 × 512 = 1.28 MB/frame → 38.4 MB/s (50× reduction).
details.realistic_solution: Per-track memory: 16 + 8 + 324 + 512 + 32 = **892 bytes**. At 500 tracks: 500 × 892 = **446 KB**. At 2500 total tracks, it's **2.23 MB**. That's indeed small compared to a 40 MB model. But the real cost is in the operations, not the storage: without spatial indexing, computing embedding distances requires streaming 512 bytes per track for every detection. At 30 FPS, this burns 1.92 GB/s of memory bandwidth, bottlenecking the system.

scenario: Your warehouse robot uses a Qualcomm RB5 (15 TOPS, 8 GB LPDDR5) to track inventory items on shelves. During a busy warehouse scan, the tracker maintains state for up to 500 objects simultaneously. Each track stores: bounding box (16 bytes), velocity vector (8 bytes), Kalman filter state (9×9 float matrix = 324 bytes), appearance embedding (128 floats = 512 bytes), and metadata (track ID, age, confidence = 32 bytes). Your colleague says 'tracking memory is negligible compared to the model.' Is that true, and when does it become a problem?
title: The Object Tracking Memory Budget

details.common_mistake: "Performance scales linearly with TOPS." This assumes the workload is compute-bound on both platforms, which is almost never true for the same model on different hardware.
details.napkin_math: RTX 4090: 1 TB/s BW, 1321 TOPS. Orin NX: 102.4 GB/s BW, 100 TOPS. BW ratio: 9.8×. TOPS ratio: 13.2×. YOLOv8-L at AI=600: 4090 attainable = 600 TOPS, Orin attainable = 61.4 TOPS → compute ratio = 9.8× (matches BW ratio, confirming memory-bound). Expected FPS scaling: 60 / 9.8 = 6.1 FPS (compute-only). Actual 8 FPS suggests TensorRT on Orin achieves better layer fusion (reducing memory traffic). Colleague's estimate of 4.5 FPS was wrong because they used peak TOPS ratio instead of bandwidth ratio.
details.realistic_solution: The colleague's estimate is wrong because both platforms are memory-bound, not compute-bound. YOLOv8-L has high arithmetic intensity (~600 FLOPs/byte), but on both platforms it exceeds the ridge point, making it memory-bandwidth-bound during many layers. The correct scaling factor is the bandwidth ratio (1000/102.4 = 9.8x), not the TOPS ratio (1321/100 = 13.2x). Expected FPS: 60/9.8 = 6.1 FPS. The actual 8 FPS exceeds this because TensorRT on the Orin achieves superior layer fusion, reducing total memory traffic. The lesson: always determine your bottleneck (compute vs memory) before scaling performance estimates across hardware.

scenario: Your team developed a YOLOv8-L model that runs at 60 FPS on a desktop RTX 4090 (1 TB/s GDDR6X bandwidth, 1321 TOPS INT8). You need to deploy the same model on a Jetson Orin NX (102.4 GB/s LPDDR5, 100 TOPS INT8). Your colleague calculates: 'The Orin has 100/1321 = 7.6% of the 4090's compute, so we'll get 60 × 0.076 = 4.5 FPS.' But the actual result is 8 FPS. Why is the colleague's estimate wrong in both directions — too pessimistic about compute, too optimistic about the real bottleneck?
title: The Edge GPU Memory Bandwidth

details.common_mistake: "The model has a memory leak — switch to a different framework." The model itself is stateless between inferences. The leak is in the surrounding infrastructure.
details.napkin_math: 3-day inference count: 30 FPS × 259,200s = 7.78M inferences. Python fragmentation at 500 bytes/inference: 3.89 GB (primary culprit). DMA leak at 1/hour: 72 × 4.1 MB = 295 MB. Engine cache: ~200 MB. Total: ~4.4 GB leak → 1.8 + 4.4 = 6.2 GB (close to observed 7.2 GB). C++ inference eliminates ~3.9 GB. Fixed resolution eliminates ~200 MB. DMA fix eliminates ~295 MB. With all fixes: stable at ~2.0 GB indefinitely.
details.realistic_solution: Multiple subtle sources compound over 3 days: (1) **TensorRT engine cache** — the TDA4VM's TIDL runtime caches optimized execution plans. Each unique input shape triggers a new cache entry. If the camera occasionally delivers frames at slightly different resolutions (e.g., during USB bandwidth negotiation or ISP reconfiguration), each unique resolution creates a new cached plan. At ~2 MB per plan, 100 unique resolutions over 3 days = 200 MB. (2) **Python garbage collection fragmentation** — if using Python (common with TFLite/ONNX), the CPython allocator requests memory from the OS in 256 KB arenas but never returns them. Small temporary allocations (bounding box lists, confidence arrays) fragment these arenas. After millions of inferences: 3 days × 86400s × 30 FPS = 7.8M inferences. Even 100 bytes of fragmentation per inference = 780 MB. (3) **DMA buffer leak** — the V4L2 camera driver allocates DMA buffers for each frame. If the application doesn't properly release buffers back to the driver (e.g., missing `VIDIOC_QBUF` call on an error path), each leaked buffer is 1920×1080×2 (NV12) = 4.1 MB. One leak per hour = 72 buffers = 295 MB over 3 days. (4) **Syslog file descriptors** — if the inference process opens log files without closing them (or appends to an in-memory log), file descriptor table and kernel buffer cache grow.

scenario: Your TI TDA4VM-based dashcam runs a lane detection model 24/7. Memory usage starts at 1.8 GB after boot (of 8 GB total). After 3 days of continuous operation, memory usage reaches 7.2 GB and the OOM killer terminates the inference process. The model is loaded once at startup and never reloaded. The input pipeline processes frames in a fixed-size ring buffer. Where is the 5.4 GB leak coming from?
title: The Inference Memory Leak

details.common_mistake: "The model files aren't being freed — add explicit `del model` calls." The model weights are freed correctly. The leak is in the runtime, not the model.
details.napkin_math: Three models loaded simultaneously: 45 MB. Available RAM after OS: ~6.5 GB. Models as % of available RAM: 0.7% — trivially small. Leak rate: 50 MB/day. Time to OOM without fix: (6,500 - 45 - 5,500 base) / 50 = 19 days (the 3-day observation was with a higher detection rate in a busy store). With all models pre-loaded: leak rate = 0. Memory overhead: 45 MB constant. The "optimization" of dynamic loading actually caused a worse outcome than the "wasteful" approach of keeping everything loaded.
details.realistic_solution: The Qualcomm SNPE (Snapdragon Neural Processing Engine) runtime allocates **intermediate activation buffers** on the Hexagon DSP's shared memory (ION/DMA-BUF allocations) each time a model is loaded. When the model is unloaded, SNPE releases the model weights but **doesn't fully release the DSP's scratch memory allocations**. This is a known behavior in several edge ML runtimes — the runtime keeps a memory pool for fast re-allocation, but the pool grows monotonically because each load/unload cycle fragments the pool slightly differently.

scenario: Your edge device (Qualcomm RB5, 8 GB RAM, Hexagon DSP) runs a multi-model pipeline: a person detector, then a pose estimator, then an action classifier. To save memory, you load and unload models on demand — detector runs continuously, pose estimator loads when a person is detected, action classifier loads when pose is extracted. After 3 days of continuous operation, the device OOM-kills the inference process. Memory monitoring shows a steady climb of 50 MB/day, even though each model is only 15 MB. What's leaking?
title: The Repeated Model Loading Memory Leak

details.common_mistake: "Confusing software-level 'zero-copy' (avoiding `memcpy()` in C++) with hardware-level cache coherency."
details.napkin_math: Flushing 10MB of image data from a CPU's L2 cache to main DDR memory over a standard mobile memory bus might take `2-3 milliseconds`. If your total inference budget is only `10ms`, that invisible cache flush operation just consumed 30% of your entire real-time budget before the NPU even fired its first transistor.
details.realistic_solution: You hit a cache flush/invalidate penalty. The CPU operates on data in its fast L1/L2 caches. When you tell the NPU (via a DMA engine) to read from a specific physical RAM address using a 'zero-copy' pointer, the NPU bypasses the CPU cache and reads directly from main DDR memory. If the CPU has recently written the image data but hasn't flushed its L1 cache back to main memory, the NPU will read stale, garbage data. To prevent this, the OS must issue a cache flush instruction before the NPU starts, forcing the CPU to write all dirty cache lines out to DDR.

scenario: You are optimizing an Edge TPU pipeline on a Coral Dev Board. You use a 'zero-copy' memory pointer to pass a tensor from the CPU directly to the NPU's input buffer. However, the system profiler shows a massive latency spike right before inference begins. If the pointer was passed directly, why is there still a latency spike?
title: The Zero-Copy Illusion

details.common_mistake: "4 GB is way more than 760 MB — there's no problem." This ignores peak memory, concurrent allocations, and fragmentation.
details.napkin_math: Naive: 360 MB weights + 600 MB peak activations + 400 MB TensorRT workspace = 1.36 GB. With shared allocator: activations drop to ~350 MB (sequential reuse). With backbone sharing: weights drop to ~280 MB. With temporal multiplexing: peak concurrent memory = ~800 MB. Headroom in 4 GB: 3.2 GB free for sensor buffers and growth.
details.realistic_solution: The 760 MB is the *minimum* — it ignores peak activation memory during concurrent execution. When detection and depth estimation run simultaneously, their activation buffers peak at ~600 MB combined (not 400 MB, because peaks overlap). Plus TensorRT workspace memory (~200 MB per engine). Real peak: ~1.2 GB. The strategy: (1) **Shared tensor allocator** — use a single CUDA memory pool (like TensorRT's `IGpuAllocator`) that reuses activation buffers between sequential stages. Detection's output buffer becomes tracking's input buffer without a copy. (2) **Temporal multiplexing** — depth estimation doesn't need to run every frame. Run it at 10 FPS (every 3rd frame) and reuse its memory during off-frames for other models. (3) **Backbone sharing** — if detection and depth share a ResNet backbone, load the backbone weights once and run both heads on the shared features. This saves 60+ MB of duplicated weights. (4) **Memory-mapped weights** — mmap the planning model's weights so they're paged in only when the planning module runs (every 100ms), freeing physical RAM between invocations.

scenario: Your autonomous vehicle runs four models concurrently: detection (YOLOv8-L, 80 MB weights), tracking (DeepSORT, 30 MB), depth estimation (MiDaS, 200 MB), and path planning (custom, 50 MB). Total: 360 MB of weights plus ~400 MB of activation buffers. Your Jetson AGX Orin has 32 GB DRAM, but after the OS and sensor pipelines, only 4 GB is available for ML. How do you fit 760 MB of ML workload into 4 GB with room for growth?
title: The Multi-Model Memory Sharing

details.common_mistake: "The model is leaking memory" or "Activations are too large." The weights are static and activations are small for a single-token decode step. The growing cost is something else.
details.napkin_math: Phi-3-mini KV-cache: 393 KB/token. At 2048 tokens: 786 MB. At 4096 tokens: 1.57 GB. With INT4 KV quantization: 196 MB at 2048 tokens. Memory budget on 8 GB Orin NX: 8 GB - 3.5 GB (OS) - 1.5 GB (weights) = 3 GB for KV-cache. Max tokens without quantization: 3 GB / 393 KB = ~7,800 tokens. With INT4 KV: ~31,000 tokens. KV quantization is mandatory for edge LLMs.
details.realistic_solution: The KV-cache. During autoregressive generation, the model stores the key and value tensors for every token generated so far, across every layer. For Phi-3-mini (32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim=96): KV-cache per token = 2 (K+V) × 32 layers × 32 heads × 96 dim × 2 bytes (FP16) = 393 KB per token. At turn 15 of a conversation with ~2000 tokens of context: 2000 × 393 KB = **786 MB**. Add the model weights (1.5 GB), OS and sensor overhead (~3.5 GB on the 8 GB Orin NX), and you're at 5.8 GB — dangerously close to the 8 GB limit. By turn 20 (~3000 tokens): KV-cache = 1.15 GB, total = 6.2 GB. A spike in OS memory usage (camera ISP burst) pushes you over the edge.

scenario: You're deploying a 3B parameter small language model (Phi-3-mini) on a Jetson Orin NX with 8 GB DRAM. The model weights in INT4 are 1.5 GB. Your colleague says 'plenty of room — we have 6.5 GB free.' The first few conversation turns work fine, but at turn 15 the system crashes with an OOM error. What's consuming the memory?
title: The Edge LLM Memory Wall

details.common_mistake: "A 2D grid is simple and cheap." This ignores the update rate, temporal history, and bandwidth implications of a high-resolution, high-frequency map.
details.napkin_math: Full grid: 4M cells × 9 bytes = 36 MB. With 10-frame history: 360 MB. Random access bandwidth amplification: 45 MB/s logical → 320 MB/s physical (7.1× amplification). Cache miss penalty: 50ms/s of CPU stall. Sparse representation (10% occupancy): 3.6 MB (fits L2), random access drops to 32 MB/s physical. Multi-resolution: 12.2 MB base, 122 MB with history — 66% memory reduction.
details.realistic_solution: Grid dimensions: 200m / 0.1m = 2000 cells per axis. Total cells: 2000 × 2000 = **4 million cells**. Per-cell storage: 4 + 4 + 1 = **9 bytes**. Single frame map: 4M × 9 = **36 MB**.

scenario: Your autonomous mining truck uses a Jetson AGX Orin (64 GB DRAM, 204.8 GB/s) to build a real-time occupancy grid map of its surroundings. The map covers a 200m × 200m area at 10cm resolution, updated at 10 Hz from LiDAR. Each cell stores: occupancy probability (1 float = 4 bytes), height (1 float = 4 bytes), and terrain class (1 byte). Your colleague says 'it's just a 2D array — memory is trivial.' Quantify the actual memory and bandwidth requirements, and identify when the map becomes the system bottleneck.
title: The Occupancy Grid Map Memory

details.common_mistake: "The brownout corrupted the model file on disk." But the checksum is fine — the on-disk model is intact. The corruption is in volatile memory.
details.napkin_math: Brownout: 85V AC for 200ms. PSU holdup: ~100ms at full load. LPDDR4 voltage droop: 1.1V → 1.0V (below 1.06V JEDEC minimum). Bit flip rate at 1.0V: ~0.001% of cells. Model size: 50 MB = 400M bits. Corrupted bits: ~4000. Supercapacitor holdup: 10F × 5V² / 2 / 5W = 25s. Cost: $5. Model reload time: 250ms. Weight CRC32 check: 0.25ms per 1 MB block. Full model verification: 50 × 0.25ms = 12.5ms.
details.realistic_solution: The Movidius VPU loads model weights from eMMC into LPDDR4 DRAM at boot. During the 200ms brownout, the AC input drops to 85V. The power supply unit (PSU) has bulk capacitors that maintain the 5V rail for ~100ms, but the voltage droops to 4.6V before the AC recovers. The 1.1V LPDDR4 supply (derived from the 5V rail via a buck converter) droops to ~1.0V. LPDDR4 requires a minimum of 1.06V for reliable operation (JEDEC spec). At 1.0V, DRAM cells with the weakest retention (those storing '1' with the least charge) flip to '0'. This corrupts a small fraction of bits — perhaps 0.001% of the 50 MB model weights, or ~500 bytes.

scenario: Your Intel Movidius-based industrial inspection system is deployed in a rural factory with unstable power. After a brief brownout (voltage sag to 85V AC for 200ms), the system continues running but starts classifying every part as 'defective' — a 100% false positive rate. A full power cycle fixes it. The model file on eMMC is intact (checksum matches). What happened to the model in RAM?
title: The Brownout Weight Corruption: Memory Hierarchy Design

details.common_mistake: "Assuming that because both models have the same number of parameters, their memory footprint will scale identically when the input size changes."
details.napkin_math: At 224x224 with 16x16 patches, you have `(224/16)^2 = 196 patches`. The attention matrix size is proportional to `196^2 = ~38,416` elements. At 448x448, you have `(448/16)^2 = 784 patches`. The attention matrix size jumps to `784^2 = ~614,656` elements. A 16x explosion in intermediate activation memory purely from the attention mechanism.
details.realistic_solution: You hit the quadratic memory wall of self-attention. A CNN's activation memory grows *linearly* with the number of input pixels. A Vision Transformer splits the image into patches (tokens) and computes self-attention across all of them. The memory required to store the self-attention matrix scales quadratically ($O(N^2)$) with the number of patches. By doubling the resolution, you quadrupled the number of patches, which increased the attention memory requirement by 16x, instantly blowing out the edge device's RAM.

scenario: You decide to replace a standard CNN with a Vision Transformer (ViT) for a drone's obstacle avoidance system. The ViT has the exact same number of parameters as the CNN. However, when you increase the input camera resolution from 224x224 to 448x448 to see smaller wires, the CNN runs slightly slower, but the ViT completely crashes with an Out-of-Memory (OOM) error. Why?
title: The Transformer Patch Limit

details.common_mistake: "The model inference is too slow." PointPillars on an Orin GPU takes ~15ms. The 100ms budget has plenty of room for a 15ms model. The bottleneck is in the *data preparation*, not the model.
details.napkin_math: Voxel grid: 432 × 496 × 32 points × 24 bytes = 164.5 MB. Memory traffic for voxelization (random scatter): 164.5 MB at ~5 GB/s effective = 33ms (CPU) vs 8ms (GPU at ~20 GB/s). Total pipeline: CPU voxelization = 48ms (20 Hz). GPU voxelization = 23ms (43 Hz capable, 4.3× headroom). The lesson: in point cloud pipelines, preprocessing is 2-3× more expensive than inference. Optimize the data path, not just the model.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck is point cloud preprocessing, not model inference. Voxelizing 1.2M points (5 sweeps x 240K) involves random memory scatter operations — each point maps to a random voxel location. CPU-based voxelization achieves only ~5 GB/s effective bandwidth (random access pattern) vs 204.8 GB/s peak, taking ~33ms. PointPillars inference itself is only 15ms. Total with CPU voxelization: 33ms + 15ms = 48ms (20 Hz). The fix: move voxelization to the GPU using CUDA kernels (hash-based scatter), which achieves ~20 GB/s effective random access. GPU voxelization takes 8ms, dropping total pipeline to 23ms (43 Hz capable, 4.3x headroom).
