details.common_mistake: Assuming the NPU is simply too slow at prefill compared to the CPU's vector extensions.
details.napkin_math: KV cache size for 2048 tokens = 2048 * 32 layers * 32 heads * 128 dim * 2 bytes * 2 (K+V) = ~1 GB. PCIe Gen4 x4 effective bandwidth = ~8 GB/s. Reading 1GB over PCIe takes 125ms. If accessed token-by-token during decode: 128 tokens * 125ms = 16 seconds! Even with aggressive caching, reading it once takes 125ms, plus synchronization overhead per layer. If CPU decode is local, 1GB at 100GB/s = 10ms per token -> 1.28s total decode.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is the massive communication overhead of migrating the KV cache between discrete memory spaces. When prefill runs on the NPU, it generates the KV cache for the 2048-token prompt in the NPU's local memory. To perform decoding on the CPU, this KV cache must either be copied to system RAM in bulk, or accessed by the CPU over the PCIe bus during every single decode step. If the software stack doesn't explicitly migrate the KV cache, the CPU reads the 1GB tensor over the PCIe bus 128 times (once per generated token). This turns a high-bandwidth local memory read into a high-latency, low-bandwidth cross-device read, completely destroying any compute time saved during prefill. The solution is to either keep both phases on the same device, or perform a single, explicit bulk DMA transfer of the KV cache from NPU to CPU RAM immediately after prefill.

scenario: On an AI PC, you map the compute-heavy Prefill phase to the discrete NPU (45 TOPS) and the memory-bound Decode phase to the CPU (100 GB/s RAM). End-to-end latency for a 2048-token prompt and 128-token generation is 4.5 seconds. Running purely on the CPU takes only 2.0 seconds.
title: Asymmetric Offload PCIe Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Pushing the full 150MB model to all devices simultaneously using a standard cloud-based pub/sub trigger.
details.napkin_math: Full update cost: 150MB * 50,000 = 7.5TB data. At $0.10/GB = $750. Delta update (typical 10% size) = 15MB * 50,000 = 750GB ($75). Bootloop cost without fallback: 1% of 50,000 = 500 devices * $150 truck roll = $75,000. Fallback mechanism saves $75,000 per bad deployment.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a phased canary rollout with binary delta updates and an A/B partition fallback mechanism. First, the model registry generates a binary patch (delta) between V1 and V2, reducing payload size significantly. Second, deploy to a 1% canary fleet, monitoring for bootloops or inference crashes for 24 hours. The edge device uses an A/B partition scheme: it downloads the delta, applies it to the inactive B partition, and sets a watchdog timer. If the model fails to load or crashes within 5 minutes, the device automatically reboots into the known-good A partition, averting a truck roll. This trades off immediate fleet-wide deployment for high reliability and low bandwidth costs.

scenario: You manage 50,000 smart dashcams connected via 3G cellular (average 1 Mbps downlink). A new 150MB object detection model needs deployment. A previous faulty update caused a 1% device bootloop rate, requiring $150 manual truck rolls per device. You must design a safe update mechanism that minimizes cellular costs and mitigates catastrophic failure risk.
title: Fleet OTA Update Strategy

details.common_mistake: Attempting to sample and send a small percentage of full images to the cloud for central drift analysis.
details.napkin_math: Sending 10 raw images/day: 10 * 5MB = 50MB/device/day. 50MB * 10,000 = 500 GB/day (fails HIPAA and saturates 20Kbps link taking 5.5 hours/device). Edge telemetry: 1KB/day/device * 10,000 = 10MB/day fleet-wide. Transmitting 1KB over 20 Kbps takes 0.4 seconds.
details.realistic_solution: Push drift detection compute to the edge by calculating distribution metrics locally. Instead of raw data, the edge device computes lightweight statistical signatures of the input data and model outputs. Extract the mean and variance of intermediate CNN embeddings, and the entropy of the final softmax layer. The device aggregates these metrics over a sliding window (e.g., 24 hours) and calculates the Wasserstein distance against a locally stored baseline distribution from the training set. It then transmits only a 1KB telemetry payload containing these summary statistics and drift scores to the cloud. This trades off centralized raw-data visibility for strict privacy compliance and ultra-low bandwidth utilization.

scenario: You have 10,000 portable ultrasound devices operating in rural clinics. They run an edge CNN for anomaly detection. Due to HIPAA and severe bandwidth limits (20 Kbps uplink), you cannot send the 5MB DICOM images to the cloud. You must design a system to detect data drift (e.g., sensor degradation or new population demographics) within 7 days of occurrence.
title: Disconnected Drift Detection

details.common_mistake: Using a swapfile on the SD card to fit both models into memory, severely degrading system performance.
details.napkin_math: Memory required: 0.5GB (OS) + 1.2GB (Model A) + 1.2GB (Model B) = 2.9GB. Physical RAM = 2.0GB. Deficit = 0.9GB. Swap latency on SD card (reads at ~20MB/s) for 0.9GB would stall inference for 45 seconds per swap, missing the 30fps (33ms) requirement entirely. Multiplexing (swapping models in RAM from eMMC at 200MB/s) takes ~6 seconds of downtime per swap.
details.realistic_solution: Implement time-multiplexed shadow testing or a fleet-wide fractional deployment. Since simultaneous execution exceeds physical memory, the system must trade temporal resolution for safe testing. The edge inference engine is reconfigured to load Model A, process frames for 5 seconds, flush it, load Model B, and process frames for 5 seconds. Alternatively, if dropping frames is unacceptable, abandon single-device shadow mode and use fleet-level A/B testing, where 50% of devices run Model A and 50% run Model B, comparing aggregate metrics in the cloud. Time-multiplexing trades latency/throughput for exact input parity; A/B testing trades exact input parity for continuous throughput.

scenario: You are deploying a new vision model to a fleet of Jetson Nanos (2GB RAM). The host OS and camera buffer consume 0.5GB. The current production model requires 1.2GB of RAM. You want to run the new 1.2GB model in shadow mode to compare inference results on live data, but running both simultaneously causes an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
title: Shadow Mode on Tight Edge Memory

details.common_mistake: Adding a larger memory buffer to queue frames during thermal throttling.
details.napkin_math: Standard model latency at 800MHz = 20ms. Throttled to 300MHz (2.66x slower) = 20 * 2.66 = 53.3ms. Frame budget = 33.3ms. Deficit = 20ms per frame. Fallback INT8 model latency at 800MHz = 10ms. Throttled to 300MHz = 10 * 2.66 = 26.6ms. 26.6ms < 33.3ms budget, ensuring no frames are dropped.
details.realistic_solution: Implement thermal-aware dynamic model switching. The MLOps runtime must monitor SoC temperature and NPU frequency as primary observability metrics. When the telemetry indicates throttling (e.g., NPU drops to 300MHz), the system intercepts the event and dynamically hot-swaps the primary FP16 model for a pre-loaded, heavily quantized (INT8) or structurally pruned "fallback" model. This trades off inference accuracy (e.g., 2-3% mAP drop) for latency guarantees, maintaining the critical 33ms frame budget. Once the temperature drops below a hysteresis threshold (e.g., 75°C), the system restores the high-accuracy model.

scenario: Agricultural drones process crop images at 30 FPS (33.3ms budget). The NPU runs at 800MHz with 20ms inference latency. At 45°C ambient temperatures, the SoC reaches 85°C and thermally throttles the NPU to 300MHz. Inference latency spikes, causing frame buffer overflows, lost frames, and erratic navigation. You must ensure continuous system reliability.
title: Thermal Throttling Runtime Adaptation

details.common_mistake: Attempting to push a rollback command or binary patch via the acoustic modem when failures are detected.
details.napkin_math: Acoustic modem bandwidth: 100 bits per second = 12.5 Bytes/sec. Model size = 50MB. Time to transmit rollback model = 50,000,000 / 12.5 = 4,000,000 seconds (~46 days). Remote rollback is mathematically impossible during a 4-hour mission. Dual storage requires 100MB flash, costing pennies but saving a $500,000 AUV.
details.realistic_solution: Design an autonomous on-device watchdog and dual-bank model storage. The edge device stores both Model V1 (known-good) and Model V2 (new) in flash memory. A deterministic supervisory control loop monitors the ML system's outputs. If the watchdog detects anomalous ML behavior—defined by domain-specific heuristics, such as >5 erratic stops within 10 minutes or consecutive bounding box outputs with extremely low confidence—it triggers a local incident response. The system automatically shifts the model pointer back to V1 and restarts the inference service. This trades storage space (holding two models) for absolute fault tolerance in disconnected environments.

scenario: You deploy a new obstacle avoidance model to deep-sea Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs). Missions last 4 hours. The only communication is an acoustic modem at 100 bps. If the new model hallucinates obstacles, the AUV halts and aborts the mission. Remote debugging or rollback during the mission is impossible due to the bandwidth. How do you design the reliability layer?
title: Zero-Connectivity Autonomous Rollback

details.common_mistake: Packaging all compiled targets into a single "fat binary" container so the edge device can select the right one at runtime.
details.napkin_math: Fat binary size: 15MB (Coral) + 30MB (Jetson) + 20MB (Hexagon) = 65MB. Thin binary = 15-30MB. If Gen 1 devices have 32MB of free flash storage remaining, downloading a 65MB fat binary results in 100% deployment failure (OOM storage). Target-specific resolution ensures the 15MB file fits comfortably.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a target-aware Model Registry with hardware-specific compilation in the CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline takes the PyTorch artifact, exports to ONNX, and branches into three compilation paths: EdgeTPU Compiler (INT8), TensorRT (FP16), and Qualcomm SNPE (INT8). The registry tags each resulting artifact with `model_version`, `target_hw`, and `precision`. During the OTA check-in, the edge device sends its hardware manifest (e.g., `hw: coral_edgetpu`). The registry dynamically resolves this to the exact thin binary required. This trades pipeline complexity (maintaining N compilation toolchains) for edge storage efficiency and reduced network transfer times.

scenario: Your consumer hardware startup has 1 million active devices across 3 generations. Gen 1 uses a Coral EdgeTPU (INT8), Gen 2 uses Jetson Nano (FP16), Gen 3 uses Snapdragon Hexagon (INT8/FP16). You train a single PyTorch model. You must design a CI/CD pipeline and registry to update all devices over unmetered WiFi without exhausting device storage.
title: Heterogeneous Edge Model Registry

details.common_mistake: Running the test longer or randomly assigning more users to smooth out the variance.
details.napkin_math: Between-home variance (σ) is $50/month. Model impact (δ) is expected to be $5/month. For a two-sample test with 80% power (z_β=0.84) and α=0.05 (z_α/2=1.96): N per group = 2 × (1.96+0.84)² × 50² / 5² = 2 × 7.84 × 100 = 1,568 homes per group (~3,200 total). Within-home variance (day-to-day) is only $5/month. Switchback testing reduces the required N: 2 × 7.84 × 5² / 5² = 2 × 7.84 ≈ 16 per group — roughly 100× fewer devices needed, or equivalently, dramatically higher statistical power with the same sample size.
details.realistic_solution: Use Switchback (Crossover) Testing or Stratified Sampling based on edge-computed embeddings. In a switchback design, each individual edge device alternates between Model A (Control) and Model B (Treatment) in randomized blocks (e.g., daily or weekly). The device acts as its own control, completely isolating the environmental variance (climate, house size) from the model performance. Alternatively, edge devices can locally compute a 'climate/usage embedding' and send it to the cloud, allowing the MLOps platform to pair similar homes into matched A/B cohorts. This trades off temporal correlation risks (e.g., weather changing day-to-day) for a massive reduction in cross-sectional variance.

scenario: You are deploying a new RL-based energy-saving model to 100,000 smart HVAC controllers. You want to run an A/B test to measure energy savings. However, household energy usage varies wildly based on climate (e.g., Arizona vs. Alaska) and insulation. A standard randomized 50/50 split yields massive variance, hiding the model's actual impact.
title: Skewed Edge A/B Testing

details.common_mistake: Streaming all frames that triggered an 'intruder' detection directly to the cloud, congesting the network.
details.napkin_math: 10 false positives/hr * 2MB = 20MB/hr. If 100 cameras at a site trigger simultaneously (e.g., a lighting change), that's 200MB. At 500 KB/s, uploading takes 400 seconds, killing the network. Metadata approach: 100 cameras * 1KB = 100KB. Takes 0.2 seconds to upload. Engineers selectively pull only 5 representative frames (10MB) over 20 seconds, preserving 99% of bandwidth.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a local ring buffer combined with metadata-driven triggered uploads. The edge device continuously saves the last N frames to a local disk ring buffer. When an inference occurs, the device uploads only a lightweight metadata JSON (1KB) containing the bounding boxes, confidence scores, and activation entropies. The cloud MLOps platform analyzes these metadata streams. If a specific prediction is deemed highly suspicious (e.g., a massive drop in confidence compared to historical data, or a request from a debugging engineer), the cloud sends a targeted fetch command to the edge. The edge then retrieves the specific 2MB frame from the ring buffer and uploads it during off-peak hours or via a rate-limited background thread.

scenario: You oversee 5,000 enterprise security cameras. After deploying Model V3, incident reports indicate a 10x spike in false positives for 'intruder detection'. You need raw images to debug the issue, but 1080p frames are 2MB, and the upload bandwidth per site is capped at 500 KB/s. Saturating this link disrupts standard security feeds.
title: Bandwidth-Aware Edge Debugging

details.common_mistake: Investigating OS thread scheduling, NUMA effects, or thermal throttling during acceleration.
details.napkin_math: Normal 100GbE PHY latency ~ 100-200ns. RS-FEC adds ~250ns base latency, but heavy symbol correction introduces pipeline stalls at the hardware level, pushing latency to 50us. At 100Gbps (12.5GB/s), a 50us stall delays 625KB of buffered data per spike.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose PHY-level Forward Error Correction (FEC) intervention due to Electromagnetic Interference (EMI). 100GbE over PAM4 requires FEC (like RS-FEC) to maintain link integrity. When the electric motors draw massive current, they generate high EMI, degrading signal integrity on the copper DACs and causing a high Bit Error Rate (BER). The MAC layer recovers the data using FEC, which prevents OS-visible packet loss but adds significant processing latency (correcting symbols takes time). The solution is to replace copper DACs with Active Optical Cables (AOCs) which are immune to EMI.

scenario: An onboard ML system in an electric mining haul truck uses 100GbE PAM4 copper DAC cables to connect a sensor-fusion node to an inference accelerator. Throughput remains at 80Gbps, but interconnect latency randomly spikes from 500ns to 50us whenever the truck's main electric drive motors accelerate. OS reports 0 dropped packets.
title: Harsh Environment Signal Degradation

details.common_mistake: Blaming the GNN's graph partitioning and attempting to manually re-partition the graph.
details.napkin_math: In a 9-group Dragonfly, each group has 1 direct link to every other group. Traffic from Group A to Group B uses 1 link (100Gbps). With VLB, Group A can route to Group B via the 7 other groups. Effective bandwidth = 1 direct link + 7 indirect paths = 8 * 100Gbps = 800Gbps. Static routing leaves 700Gbps of potential bandwidth unused.
details.realistic_solution: Identify the failure of static minimal routing in a Dragonfly topology. Dragonfly relies on high-radix routers and sparse global links. If static minimal (shortest-path) routing is used, an adversarial traffic pattern (like a GNN where one chassis communicates heavily with exactly one other chassis) will bottleneck on the single dedicated global link between those two chassis. The solution is to enable Adaptive Routing (AR) or Valiant Load Balancing (VLB), which routes traffic non-minimally through intermediate chassis to utilize idle global links and increase effective bisection bandwidth.

scenario: A specialized edge cluster for autonomous vehicle fleet management uses a miniature Dragonfly topology connecting 72 nodes across 9 chassis (8 nodes per chassis). Intra-chassis links are 200Gbps; inter-chassis optical links are 100Gbps. A distributed graph neural network (GNN) inference task causes massive congestion on a single inter-chassis link, while other optical links sit at 0% utilization.
title: Adversarial Traffic on Edge Dragonfly

details.common_mistake: Assuming the storage array's NVMe controllers are internally bottlenecked at 100Gbps.
details.napkin_math: 4 flows mapping across 4 links. Output port = hash(flow_i) % 4. If all hashes result in the same modulo (e.g., 0), all traffic goes to Link 0. Maximum throughput = 1 link * 100Gbps = 100Gbps. Wasted bandwidth = 3 links * 100Gbps = 300Gbps. System operates at 25% efficiency.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) hash polarization/collision. ECMP distributes traffic across parallel links by hashing packet header fields (typically 5-tuple: Src IP, Dst IP, Protocol, Src Port, Dst Port). If the 4 inference servers connect to a single IP/Port on the storage array and use fixed source ports, or if the switch's hash algorithm only checks IP addresses, the hashes for all 4 flows compute to the same output port modulo 4. The solution is to vary the source ports (multiplexing flows), use a deeper hashing algorithm, or implement flowlet switching.

scenario: An edge storage rack uses 4 parallel 100GbE links between a Top-of-Rack (ToR) switch and a dense NVMe-oF storage array to provide 400Gbps aggregate bandwidth. However, when 4 edge inference servers pull 100Gbps video streams simultaneously, total throughput caps at 100Gbps. One specific 100GbE link shows 100% utilization while the other 3 show near 0%.
title: ECMP Hash Polarization in Edge Storage

details.common_mistake: Assuming the memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and trying to quantize the depthwise weights to INT4.
details.napkin_math: Systolic array capacity: 16x16 = 256 MAC units. Standard 1x1 conv mapping (Input Channels x Output Channels): perfectly fills the 16x16 grid. Depthwise conv mapping: 1 Input Channel -> 1 Output Channel. Active MACs per cycle = 1x16 (if spatial mapped 1D) or just 1x1. If mapped naively on the channel dimension, utilization = 16 / 256 = 6.25%.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a fundamental mismatch between the model's arithmetic intensity and the systolic array's spatial architecture. Depthwise convolutions process each input channel independently, meaning there is zero data reuse across channels. A 16x16 systolic array typically maps input channels to one dimension and output channels to the other. For a depthwise convolution, only 1 out of 16 rows/columns is active, wasting the rest of the array. To resolve this, you must co-design the architecture: either modify the model to use grouped convolutions (where group size matches the array dimension, e.g., 16) to restore channel reuse, or rewrite the compiler's scheduling dataflow to map spatial dimensions (width/height tiles) to the systolic grid instead of channels during depthwise layers.

scenario: You are deploying a MobileNetV2-based object detector on a custom edge NPU featuring a 16x16 systolic array (peak 512 MACs/cycle). The NPU has 2MB of SRAM and runs at 500 MHz. Profiling reveals that the standard 1x1 convolutions achieve 85% array utilization, but the 3x3 depthwise convolutions drop to roughly 6% utilization, causing the overall inference latency to miss the 15ms target by taking 42ms.
title: NPU Underutilization in Depthwise Convolutions

details.common_mistake: Adding more pipeline registers to fix the clock frequency, which worsens area and power.
details.napkin_math: Memory bandwidth needed at INT8: 15M weights * 1 byte * 30 FPS = 450 MB/s per read (often read multiple times if not cached perfectly). INT4 reduces this to 225 MB/s. DSP slice dynamic power is typically 0.1-0.2x the power of an equivalent LUT-based multiplier. By unpacking INT4->INT8 locally, we save ~1W of LUT switching power.
details.realistic_solution: The routing congestion and frequency drop occur because the FPGA's hardened DSP slices are natively designed for 8x8 or 18x18 bit arithmetic. When you explicitly force INT4 MAC operations, the synthesis tool often bypasses the hardened, power-efficient DSP slices and implements the INT4 multipliers using general-purpose LUTs (Look-Up Tables) and distributed routing. This consumes massive programmable logic area, causing routing congestion, dropping the clock frequency, and spiking dynamic power. The hardware-software co-design solution is to store the weights in DRAM as INT4 (to save the critical memory bandwidth), but unpack them to INT8 on-the-fly inside the FPGA's BRAM/registers right before computation. This allows the compute engine to utilize the hardened INT8 DSP slices efficiently while still achieving the 50% bandwidth reduction.

scenario: You are designing an FPGA-based accelerator for a 2W smart camera. The system needs to run a 15-million parameter CNN at 30 FPS. To fit the tight 1.5 GB/s LPDDR4 bandwidth budget, you quantize the model weights to INT4. However, after synthesis, the FPGA routing is severely congested, clock frequency drops from 300MHz to 120MHz, and power consumption exceeds 3W, despite using fewer bits.
title: FPGA DSP Slice Mapping for INT4

details.common_mistake: Downsampling the input image to 1080p, sacrificing the required detection accuracy for small objects.
details.napkin_math: Early layer input size: 3840 x 2160 x 3 channels * 1 byte (INT8) = 24.8 MB. SRAM = 4 MB. In WS dataflow, computing 32 output channels might require streaming the 24.8 MB input map multiple times if it doesn't fit in SRAM. 24.8 MB * 60 FPS = 1.48 GB/s just for one read. If read 10 times due to capacity misses, it's 14.8 GB/s just for layer 1, saturating the 25.6 GB/s bus quickly.
details.realistic_solution: The Weight-Stationary (WS) dataflow keeps weights pinned in the Processing Element (PE) registers while streaming activations from DRAM through the array. For a 4K image, the input activations of the early layers are massive, while the weight matrices (e.g., 3x3x3 x 32 = 864 bytes) are tiny. The 4MB SRAM cannot hold the entire 4K feature map, forcing the ASIC to constantly spill and reload activations from DRAM for every output channel computation. The solution is to reconfigure the compiler to use an Output-Stationary (OS) or Row-Stationary (RS) dataflow for the early layers. By tiling the massive input activations and keeping the intermediate output sums stationary in the PEs, you drastically reduce DRAM read/writes for the heavy feature maps. WS should only be used in later layers where channels are deep and spatial resolution is small.

scenario: You are programming an autonomous drone's custom ASIC to run a 4K (3840x2160) object detection CNN at 60 FPS. The ASIC has 4MB of on-chip SRAM and a peak DRAM bandwidth of 25.6 GB/s. The compiler defaults to a Weight-Stationary (WS) dataflow. In early layers, the ASIC achieves only 12 FPS, and power monitoring shows the DRAM interface drawing maximum power.
title: Dataflow Bottleneck in High-Res Drone NPU

details.common_mistake: Overclocking the MCU or aggressively pruning the model, which hurts accuracy and battery life.
details.napkin_math: Theoretical compute: 13 channels * scalar MAC = 13 cycles. Padded compute: 16 channels / 4 (SIMD quad MAC) = 4 cycles. Time reduction is 13/4 = 3.25x speedup. At 168MHz, each cycle = 5.95ns. Latency drops from 180ms to ~55ms, and with slight loop unrolling, comfortably hits the <50ms target.
details.realistic_solution: The Cortex-M4 DSP extensions (like SMLAD) perform dual 16-bit or quad 8-bit MAC operations in a single cycle, but they strictly require data to be 4-byte aligned in memory, and the inner loop dimension (usually channels) must be a multiple of 4. Because the input feature has 13 bands (channels), the CMSIS-NN optimized kernels cannot fully pack the SIMD registers and fall back to the unoptimized scalar C implementation, processing one MAC per cycle instead of four. The co-design solution is to pad the input features from 13 to 16 bands (filling the extra bands with zeros) and ensure all intermediate layer channel counts are multiples of 4. This slightly increases the theoretical FLOPs but allows the compiler to map the operations to the SIMD DSP instructions, yielding a near 4x speedup.

scenario: You are deploying a keyword spotting CNN on an ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller (features DSP extensions, 32-bit SIMD MAC instructions, 256KB SRAM, 120MHz). The input is a 13-band MFCC spectrogram. Using an INT8 quantized model, inference takes 180ms per window, missing the 50ms real-time deadline. Profiler shows the CMSIS-NN library is executing standard scalar instructions instead of packed SIMD.
title: MCU SIMD Alignment for Audio CNNs

details.common_mistake: Trying to increase the NPU clock speed or adding more SRAM capacity to the NPU.
details.napkin_math: NPU Peak Compute: 10 TOPS. SRAM Bandwidth: 400 GB/s. LSTM Arithmetic Intensity: 2 OPs / 1 Byte = 2 OPs/Byte. Max achievable compute = 400 GB/s * 2 OPs/Byte = 800 GOPs = 0.8 TOPS. Utilization = 0.8 / 10 = 8% maximum (often lower due to overhead). To hit 10 TOPS, required intensity = 10,000 GOPs / 400 GB/s = 25 OPs/Byte.
details.realistic_solution: The LSTM model running at batch size 1 is entirely memory-bandwidth bound due to low arithmetic intensity. An LSTM requires reading the entire weight matrix for every single token (packet payload byte) processed. The arithmetic intensity is approximately 1 MAC (2 operations) per 1 byte of weight read. With an SRAM bandwidth of 400 GB/s, the theoretical maximum throughput is 400 GigaMACs/s (0.8 TOPS), meaning 92% of the 10 TOPS compute array is starved of data. To fix this, you must co-design the algorithm/architecture: replace the LSTM with a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) or a small Transformer over a sliding window of packets. These architectures allow spatial parallelization and weight reuse across the sequence dimension, significantly raising the arithmetic intensity and allowing the hardware to utilize its 10 TOPS compute array.

scenario: A SmartNIC embedded with a 10 TOPS (INT8) NPU is designed to perform line-rate deep packet inspection at 100 Gbps. The security team deployed an LSTM-based anomaly detection model (batch size 1 per flow). The NPU has 8MB of SRAM with 400 GB/s internal bandwidth. Despite the 10 TOPS rating, the NPU drops 45% of packets, and utilization sits at just 4%.
title: SmartNIC NPU Arithmetic Intensity Mismatch

details.common_mistake: Compressing the image data over the USB bus using JPEG, which introduces latency and compression artifacts ruining the super-resolution.
details.napkin_math: 1080p image = 1920x1080x3 = 6,220,800 bytes (~6.22 MB). USB 3.0 practical bandwidth ~400 MB/s. At 30 FPS, raw input is ~186.6 MB/s. However, with a deep network (e.g., receptive field of 64 pixels), a 128x128 tile needs a 256x256 input patch. Area ratio = 65536 / 16384 = 4x redundancy. 186.6 MB/s * 4 (input) + output transfers easily exceeds the 400 MB/s limit, dropping framerate to ~4 FPS.
details.realistic_solution: The severe bottleneck is the redundant PCIe/USB host-to-device data transfer caused by naive spatial tiling. Because convolutions have receptive fields, splitting an image into spatial tiles requires overlapping 'halos' to prevent edge artifacts. In a deep U-Net, this halo grows exponentially with depth. If the host tiles the input, it must transmit the massive overlapping regions repeatedly, saturating the USB 3.0 bandwidth. The co-design solution is 'Fused Layer Execution' or 'Depth-First Scheduling' inside the compiler. Instead of host-side tiling, send the entire image (or large chunks) to the TPU's DRAM. The TPU compiler should be configured to tile the computation internally inside the 8MB SRAM, calculating a tile all the way through the depth of the network before evicting. This keeps the intermediate halo exchanges entirely within the high-bandwidth on-chip SRAM, drastically reducing USB I/O.

scenario: You are deploying a U-Net based super-resolution model on a Google Edge TPU (8MB SRAM, 4 TOPS, USB 3.0 interface). To fit the 1080p input image, the host CPU spatially tiles the image into 16x16 overlapping patches and sends them to the TPU sequentially. The system targets 30 FPS but only achieves 4 FPS. USB bandwidth monitoring shows 1.8 GB/s of sustained bidirectional transfer.
title: Edge TPU Spatial Tiling Overhead

details.common_mistake: Quantizing the model weights further to INT4, which won't fix the attention phase bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Weights: 8GB read per token. KV Cache: 1GB read per token. Total read per token = 9GB. Max theoretical throughput = 204 GB/s / 9 GB/token = 22.6 tokens/sec. Actual is 8 due to overhead. If we use GQA (8x reduction in KV) + INT8 KV (2x reduction), KV cache drops to 1GB / 16 = 62.5 MB. Now memory read per token is ~8.06 GB. Max throughput rises to 204 / 8.06 = 25.3 tokens/sec, and L2 thrashing is mitigated for the KV portion.
details.realistic_solution: During auto-regressive decoding, the attention mechanism must read the entire KV cache from DRAM for every single generated token. Even though the 1GB KV cache easily fits in the 64GB unified memory, it is vastly larger than the 8MB L2 cache. This causes a complete L2 cache eviction on every token step, forcing the GPU to pull the 1GB cache across the 204 GB/s memory bus repeatedly. The solution requires algorithmic-hardware co-design: implement Grouped Query Attention (GQA) or Multi-Query Attention (MQA) combined with KV cache quantization (INT8/INT4) or Flash-Decoding. By reducing the size of the KV cache by 4-8x, you lower the DRAM bandwidth requirement per token step, and using Flash-Decoding splits the KV cache across thread blocks to maximize SRAM reuse, significantly improving tokens/sec.

scenario: You are deploying an 8-billion parameter LLM on a Jetson AGX Orin (64GB unified memory, 204 GB/s bandwidth) for a local coding assistant. Token generation is heavily bandwidth-bound, achieving only 8 tokens/sec. The model weights take 8GB (INT8). The KV cache for a 4096-token context takes about 1GB. The GPU has an 8MB L2 cache. Profiling shows massive L2 cache thrashing during the attention phase of decode.
title: Edge GPU LLM KV Cache Thrashing

details.common_mistake: Upgrading to a faster NPU or reducing the batch size to lower latency, ignoring the I/O bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: 16 streams * 1920*1080 pixels * 3 channels * 30fps = ~2.98 GB/s of raw RGB data. PCIe Gen3 x4 real-world bandwidth is ~3.2 GB/s. Transmitting uncompressed frames consumes 93% of the bus, causing severe queueing delays.
details.realistic_solution: The system is bottlenecked by the PCIe memory hierarchy. You must redesign the architecture to use 'Zero-Copy' and edge-native decoding. Instead of the host CPU decoding video and sending uncompressed RGB frames over PCIe, pass the compressed H.264/H.265 streams directly to the NPU's hardware video decoder (if available) or a unified memory space. Furthermore, fuse preprocessing (resize, normalize) directly into the early layers of the NPU graph so the massive uncompressed data remains entirely in the NPU's high-bandwidth local SRAM/LPDDR, avoiding costly round-trips to the host CPU's main memory.

scenario: You are architecting a retail edge server processing 16 concurrent 1080p video streams at 30fps. The system uses a host CPU connected to an edge NPU via PCIe Gen3 x4 (theoretical 3.9 GB/s). Inference latency spikes to 200ms when all streams are active, despite the NPU reporting only 40% compute utilization. Memory profiling shows 99% PCIe bus saturation.
title: Multi-Camera NPU PCIe Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Attempting to use DMA to page weights from Flash to SRAM on demand, which still incurs the massive Flash power penalty.
details.napkin_math: Reading from Flash costs ~20 pJ/bit, while SRAM costs ~2 pJ/bit. A 1.2MB model = 9.6M bits. Flash read per inference: 9.6M * 20pJ = 192 uJ. At 50 inferences/sec, memory fetches alone consume 9.6mW > 5mW total budget.
details.realistic_solution: The excessive power drain is caused by fetching weights from high-latency, high-power Flash memory for every inference. To meet the 5mW requirements, you must architect the system to fit entirely within the 512KB SRAM. Apply INT8 Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) or Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) to compress the 1.2MB model down to ~300KB. Pin these quantized weights permanently in SRAM. Design a ring buffer in the remaining 200KB SRAM for audio feature extraction and intermediate activations, ensuring absolute zero Flash memory accesses during the steady-state inference loop.

scenario: You are designing an always-on keyword spotting system for a smartwatch with a strict 5mW active power budget. The microcontroller has 512KB of SRAM and 4MB of eXecute-In-Place (XIP) Flash memory. Your float32 audio model is 1.2MB. Initial testing shows the system drawing 15mW during inference, draining the battery in hours.
title: Wearable SRAM Weight Pinning

details.common_mistake: Reducing the vocabulary size or hidden dimension of the model, which degrades quality without solving the dynamic scaling issue.
details.napkin_math: 3B model = 3GB (INT8). KV cache for 2000 tokens (fp16, d_model=3072, 32 layers) = 2*2*3072*32 * 2000 = ~786MB. Total footprint = 3.78GB. Generating 1 token requires reading 3.78GB. At 51.2 GB/s, max theoretical throughput is 51.2 / 3.78 = 13.5 tok/sec. Dropping to 3 tok/sec implies OS swapping.
details.realistic_solution: The performance cliff is due to the KV cache exceeding the NPU/GPU's localized SRAM tier and competing with the OS for unified DRAM, causing severe page thrashing. To fix this, you must change the architecture to aggressively manage memory locality. First, implement 4-bit KV cache quantization to reduce the footprint by 75%. Second, implement a chunked attention mechanism (like Flash-Decoding) that loads smaller blocks of the KV cache into the fast SRAM compute cores, performing local reductions before a final global reduction, minimizing DRAM round-trips and avoiding OS-level page faults.

scenario: Deploying a 3B parameter LLM on a premium smartphone (8GB unified LPDDR5 RAM at 51.2 GB/s). Initially, text generation achieves 18 tokens/sec. However, when the context window reaches 2000 tokens, generation speed plummets to 3 tokens/sec, and the OS occasionally kills the background app.
title: On-Device LLM KV Cache Spilling

details.common_mistake: Writing a background garbage collection thread to defragment memory, which would ruin real-time 60fps latency guarantees.
details.napkin_math: At 60fps, dynamic sequence lengths generate ~150 variable-sized allocations per frame. 150 * 60 * 60 * 45 = ~24.3 million allocations over 45 mins. A 15% fragmentation waste on 2.5GB used = 375MB scattered in tiny holes, failing contiguous 5MB tensor requests.
details.realistic_solution: The system is suffering from catastrophic memory fragmentation caused by standard `malloc`/`free` handling variable-sized tensor allocations over long periods. The architecture must be redesigned to use a static Memory Pool or Arena Allocator. Perform an offline analysis of the model's computational graph to determine the maximum liveness footprint (the peak memory required at any point in the graph). Pre-allocate a single, contiguous block of memory (e.g., 50MB) at startup. Reuse offsets within this arena for intermediate activations, guaranteeing zero fragmentation and O(1) allocation time.

scenario: An AR headset runs continuous hand-tracking and SLAM. After 45 minutes of operation, the system crashes with a `std::bad_alloc` OOM error. Diagnostics show 1.2GB of physical RAM is still technically 'free' out of the 4GB total, but tensor allocation latency has spiked from 1us to 3ms right before the crash.
title: AR Glasses Memory Fragmentation

details.common_mistake: Lowering the CPU priority of the LiDAR thread, which doesn't stop the cache eviction when the thread actually is scheduled to run.
details.napkin_math: ViT needs 8MB working set; LiDAR needs 12MB. 8+12 = 20MB > 16MB L3. Thrashing causes DRAM trips (100ns vs 15ns L3). 10,000 memory accesses * 85ns penalty = 0.85ms per layer * 32 layers = ~27ms extra latency.
details.realistic_solution: The degradation is caused by cache contention and thrashing in the shared L3 cache and DRAM bus. The CPU's random memory access patterns for LiDAR preprocessing are evicting the NPU's localized tensor data. The architectural solution requires strict memory isolation. Implement Cache Quality of Service (QoS) / Cache Allocation Technology (CAT) to hard-partition the L3 cache (e.g., 8MB locked for NPU, 8MB for CPU). Additionally, map the NPU's large intermediate activation buffers as 'non-cacheable' to bypass the L3 entirely, forcing them directly to LPDDR5 via DMA, preserving the L3 for latency-sensitive weights.

scenario: You are designing an automotive ADAS SoC with an 8-core CPU, a shared 16MB L3 cache, and a discrete NPU sharing LPDDR5 DRAM. When running a Vision Transformer (ViT) on the NPU in isolation, latency is 15ms. When simultaneously running LiDAR point-cloud preprocessing on the CPU, the ViT latency degrades to 42ms.
title: ADAS SoC L3 Cache Contention

details.common_mistake: Applying channel pruning or weight quantization, which reduces compute and weight footprint but barely impacts the massive activation memory bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: 4K image * 32 channels * 2 bytes (fp16) = ~530MB activation size for early layers. Transferring 530MB to/from DRAM at 25 GB/s takes ~42ms per layer. For 4 early layers, that's 168ms of pure DRAM wait time, explaining the 200ms latency.
details.realistic_solution: The model is severely memory-bandwidth bound due to low arithmetic intensity in the early high-resolution layers. The intermediate activations vastly exceed the 4MB SRAM, causing continuous spilling to DRAM. You must architect a 'fused layer tiling' (depth-first) memory strategy. Instead of computing layer 1 entirely and writing to DRAM, then reading back for layer 2, divide the 4K image into smaller spatial patches (e.g., 256x256). Push each patch through multiple layers sequentially, keeping all intermediate activations strictly within the 4MB SRAM, and only write the heavily downsampled output back to DRAM.

scenario: A drone is running a high-resolution (4K) object detection CNN on a custom edge accelerator. Processing takes 200ms per frame. The accelerator has 4MB of SRAM and LPDDR4 memory with 25 GB/s bandwidth. Hardware monitors show the compute units (MACs) are only 18% utilized.
title: Drone Fused Layer Tiling

details.common_mistake: Multi-threading the CPU's YUV to RGB conversion, which might speed up compute but still incurs the massive 12ms memory copy penalty.
details.napkin_math: 12MP in RGB = 36MB. CPU copying 36MB at 3 GB/s DMA takes 12ms. YUV420 is 1.5 bytes/pixel = 18MB. By skipping the CPU conversion and copy, we save 30ms, bringing latency from 40ms down to 10ms.
details.realistic_solution: The architecture is bottlenecked by inefficient memory movement and format conversions across the memory hierarchy (ISP -> Main RAM -> CPU Cache -> Main RAM -> NPU RAM). The solution is a zero-copy, edge-native pipeline. First, allocate a contiguous dmabuf (Direct Memory Access buffer) shared between the ISP and NPU MMUs. Configure the ISP to write the YUV420 frames directly into this buffer. Second, retrain the NPU model to natively ingest YUV420 channels, or add a hardware-accelerated 1x1 convolution at the start of the NPU graph to handle the YUV-to-RGB conversion, completely bypassing the CPU and extra RAM roundtrips.

scenario: A smart camera pipeline processes 12MP (4000x3000) frames. The Image Signal Processor (ISP) outputs YUV420. The CPU converts this to RGB (takes 18ms), copies it to the NPU's reserved memory (takes 12ms), and the NPU runs inference (takes 10ms). Total latency is 40ms, failing the 33ms (30fps) requirement.
title: Smart Camera Zero-Copy Pipeline

details.common_mistake: Assuming fewer MACs always means faster inference, and trying to prune MobileNet further to improve FPS.
details.napkin_math:
NPU Ridge Point: (2 * 10^12 OPS) / (4 * 10^9 B/s) = 500 OPS/B.
MobileNet AI: 0.6 GOPS / 30MB = 20 OPS/B (Memory Bound). Inference time = 30MB / 4 GB/s = 7.5ms (133 FPS).
VGG AI: 8 GOPS / 12MB = 666 OPS/B (Compute Bound). Inference time = 8 GOPS / 2 TOPS = 4.0ms (250 FPS).
VGG easily meets the 200 FPS (5ms) requirement.
details.realistic_solution: The NPU performance is strictly governed by the Roofline model. The NPU's ridge point (the Arithmetic Intensity where compute-bound meets memory-bound) is 500 OPS/Byte. MobileNetV2 relies heavily on depthwise separable convolutions which lack data reuse, giving it a very low arithmetic intensity that makes it severely memory-bound. VGG uses dense convolutions with high data reuse, pushing its AI well above the ridge point, thus achieving near-peak TOPS. To get 200+ FPS, you must choose the VGG model, or heavily optimize MobileNet's memory bandwidth by fusing depthwise and pointwise layers to shift its Arithmetic Intensity to the right on the Roofline plot.

scenario: You are porting an image classifier to an Edge NPU with 2 TOPS (INT8) peak compute and 4 GB/s memory bandwidth. A custom VGG-like model has 8 GOPS and requires 12MB of memory traffic per inference. MobileNetV2 has only 0.6 GOPS but requires 30MB of memory traffic due to unfused depthwise layers. Surprisingly, MobileNetV2 yields 133 FPS, while the larger VGG model yields 250 FPS. Optimize the model choice to achieve a strict 200+ FPS requirement.
title: MobileNet vs VGG NPU Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Focusing solely on the 20% increase in GOPS and assuming the INT8 model will draw more total energy because it requires more operations.
details.napkin_math:
GPU efficiency: 2 TFLOPS / 4W = 500 GFLOPS/W. 
GPU Frame Energy: 10 GOPS / 500 GFLOPS/W = 0.02 Joules = 20 mJ.
NPU efficiency: 8 TOPS / 1W = 8000 GOPS/W. 
NPU Frame Energy: 12 GOPS / 8000 GOPS/W = 0.0015 Joules = 1.5 mJ.
At 30 FPS, GPU draws 0.6W average, NPU draws 0.045W average. The NPU saves 0.555W continuously.
details.realistic_solution: Although the INT8 model requires 20% more operations (12 GOPS vs 10 GOPS), the NPU's power efficiency (TOPS/Watt) is vastly superior to the GPU. We must calculate the energy consumed per frame for both accelerators to determine the battery drain. The GPU consumes 20mJ per frame, while the NPU consumes only 1.5mJ per frame. Despite the compute overhead from quantization scaling layers, the INT8 NPU is over 13x more energy-efficient per frame. For a battery-constrained edge device, the NPU is the only viable choice to maximize flight time.

scenario: A battery-powered drone runs obstacle avoidance at 30 FPS. The model requires 10 GOPS/frame. The SoC has an FP16 GPU (2 TFLOPS peak, drawing 4W) and an INT8 NPU (8 TOPS peak, drawing 1W). Quantizing the model to INT8 increases the required compute to 12 GOPS due to quantization-aware scaling layers, and drops accuracy by 1%. The product manager suggests using the GPU to avoid the 20% compute penalty and accuracy drop. Evaluate the impact on flight time to justify your architectural choice.
title: Drone Power-Precision Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Assuming the NPU compute units are overheating or underutilized due to software bugs, and trying to optimize the matrix multiplication kernels.
details.napkin_math:
Decoding 1 token requires loading 1GB (weights) + 0.128GB (KV cache) = 1.128GB.
Max memory-bound throughput = 25 GB/s / 1.128 GB/token = 22.16 tokens/s.
Compute required per token: ~4 GOPS. Compute ceiling = 50 TOPS / 4 GOPS = 12,500 tokens/s.
The system is operating exactly at its theoretical memory bandwidth limit (22 tokens/s).
details.realistic_solution: The decoding phase of an LLM is heavily memory-bound because it operates with an effective batch size of 1. For every single generated token, the entire 1GB of model weights must be streamed from DRAM, plus the KV cache. The theoretical maximum decoding speed is dictated entirely by memory bandwidth, not compute TOPS. The roofline ceiling is strictly enforced by the 25 GB/s bus. To optimize decoding on the edge, you must reduce memory traffic. Techniques include Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) to shrink the KV cache, or Speculative Decoding, which evaluates multiple tokens per weight load, artificially increasing the batch size and Arithmetic Intensity.

scenario: You are deploying a 2B parameter LLM (INT4, 1GB weights) on an edge device with a 50 TOPS NPU and 25 GB/s memory bandwidth. During the prefill phase (prompt length 1024), you achieve 200 tokens/s. During decoding, token generation drops abruptly to 22 tokens/s. The KV cache size averages 128MB during decoding. Diagnose the bottleneck and propose an optimization strategy.
title: LLM KV Cache Bandwidth Ceiling

details.common_mistake: Attempting to prune the MatMul weights to reduce the 4 GOPS, assuming the model is too large for the 2 TOPS NPU.
details.napkin_math:
Current memory time = 20MB / 4 GB/s = 5ms (max 200 QPS).
Compute time = 4 GOPS / 2 TOPS = 2ms (max 500 QPS).
Ridge point = 2 TOPS / 4 GB/s = 500 OPS/Byte.
Current AI = 4 GOPS / 20MB = 200 OPS/Byte (Memory Bound).
To hit 500 QPS, we need memory time <= 2ms, meaning max traffic = 2ms * 4 GB/s = 8MB. Fusing operators removes the 15MB of intermediate read/writes, reducing traffic to 5MB. New memory time = 1.25ms. Workload becomes compute-bound at 2ms (500 QPS).
details.realistic_solution: The low QPS is a classic symptom of a memory-bound workload on the Roofline model. Un-fused operations force the accelerator to write intermediate activations back to DRAM and read them again for the next layer, destroying Arithmetic Intensity. At 20MB per inference, the memory bandwidth limits the system to 200 QPS. By fusing the MatMul, LayerNorm, and GELU into a single kernel, the intermediate results stay in the NPU's SRAM (scratchpad). This drastically reduces DRAM traffic, shifting the workload to the right on the Roofline plot towards the compute-bound regime. Reducing traffic to 5MB per inference allows the system to hit the compute ceiling of 500 QPS.

scenario: An edge TPU runs a custom Transformer encoder for anomaly detection. SLA requires 500 inferences/sec (QPS). The NPU has 2 TOPS compute and 4 GB/s memory bandwidth. The model requires 4 GOPS per inference. Currently, the system maxes out at 200 QPS. Profiling shows unfused MatMul, LayerNorm, and GELU operations are causing 20MB of intermediate activation read/writes to DRAM per inference. Design an optimization to meet the SLA.
title: Operator Fusion for Arithmetic Intensity

details.common_mistake: Assuming that since peak compute (64 GOPS) and total operations (100 MOPS) remain the same, quantization will not improve inference time if the device was compute-bound.
details.napkin_math:
Ridge Point (both FP32/INT8) = 64 GOPS / 12.8 GB/s = 5 OPS/B.
FP32 Model AI = 100 MOPS / 50 MB = 2 OPS/B (Memory Bound). 
FP32 Mem Time = 50MB / 12.8 GB/s = 3.9ms.
INT8 Model AI = 100 MOPS / 12.5 MB = 8 OPS/B (Compute Bound). 
INT8 Compute Time = 100 MOPS / 64 GOPS = 1.56ms.
Inference time drops from 3.9ms to 1.56ms, and the bottleneck shifts from memory bandwidth to compute.
details.realistic_solution: Quantization affects both the Y-axis (peak compute) and X-axis (Arithmetic Intensity) of the Roofline model. In FP32, the workload has a very low Arithmetic Intensity and is heavily memory-bound, resulting in high latency due to the 50MB data transfer. Quantizing to INT8 reduces the data transfer by 4x. Because the operation count stays the same, the Arithmetic Intensity increases by 4x. This shift pushes the workload past the ridge point on the Roofline plot, changing it from a memory-bound workload to a compute-bound workload, drastically reducing inference time.

scenario: Optimizing a dense neural network on an edge DSP. DSP specs: FP32 peak is 64 GFLOPS, INT8 peak is 64 GOPS. Memory bandwidth is 12.8 GB/s for both data types. The FP32 model requires 100 MOPS per inference and loads 50MB of weights/activations. You quantize the model to INT8 (data footprint becomes 12.5MB, operations remain 100 MOPS). Calculate the inference time before and after quantization, and identify how the bottleneck shifts.
title: Quantization Roofline Shift

details.common_mistake: Calculating compute time only (40 GOPS / 5 TOPS = 0.008ms) and assuming both batching strategies will easily meet the 15ms SLA.
details.napkin_math:
Batch=1 (Sequential): Data = 20MB (Weights) + 1MB (Acts) = 21MB. 
Mem time = 21MB / 5 GB/s = 4.2ms per stream. Compute time = 10 GOPS / 5 TOPS = 0.002ms. 
Total time for 4 streams = 4 * max(4.2ms, 0.002ms) = 16.8ms (Fails 15ms SLA).
Batch=4 (Batched): Data = 20MB (Weights) + 4 * 1MB (Acts) = 24MB. 
Mem time = 24MB / 5 GB/s = 4.8ms. Compute time = 40 GOPS / 5 TOPS = 0.008ms. 
Total time = max(4.8ms, 0.008ms) = 4.8ms (Passes 15ms SLA).
details.realistic_solution: Batching fundamentally alters Arithmetic Intensity by reusing loaded weights across multiple inputs. For Batch=1, the 20MB weights are loaded 4 separate times from DRAM, making the workload highly memory-bound and exceeding the SLA due to cumulative memory transfer latency. For Batch=4, the 20MB weights are loaded only once, shifting the workload's Arithmetic Intensity significantly higher. The total execution time for Batch=4 is dictated by a single memory load, which easily meets the 15ms SLA for all streams.

scenario: A smart home hub processes 4 concurrent audio streams using an NLP intent model. The model requires 10 GOPS, 20MB of weights, and 1MB of activations per stream. The NPU has 5 TOPS compute and 5 GB/s memory bandwidth. You can execute them sequentially (Batch=1, 4 times) or batch them together (Batch=4, 1 time). The latency SLA is 15ms total for all streams to finish. Evaluate both strategies using the roofline model to determine which meets the SLA.
title: Hardware-Aware Batching for Edge NLP

details.common_mistake: Agreeing to upgrade the NPU because 99% utilization typically implies a compute-bound bottleneck in isolated microbenchmarks.
details.napkin_math:
Total Bandwidth Demand = CPU (2 GB/s) + NPU (5 GB/s) + GPU (15 GB/s) = 22 GB/s.
Available SoC Bandwidth = 17 GB/s.
Deficit = 5 GB/s. The memory controller will stall requests, artificially inflating the execution time of all accelerators. The NPU's 99% utilization is likely due to stall cycles waiting on memory (memory-bound), not actual compute saturation.
details.realistic_solution: Upgrading the NPU will not increase the system FPS because the SoC is facing a global memory bandwidth bottleneck, not an isolated compute bottleneck. While the NPU might be fully utilized locally, the CPU, NPU, and GPU are concurrently demanding a total of 22 GB/s from a shared bus that can only provide 17 GB/s. The bus is over-subscribed by 129%, causing severe memory throttling across all components. Upgrading the NPU's compute capacity (TOPS) does nothing to alleviate the bandwidth starvation. You must optimize the memory traffic—specifically the GPU's massive 15 GB/s demand—via quantization, layer fusion, or smaller input resolutions.

scenario: An edge vision system targets 30 FPS. The pipeline runs concurrently: 1) CPU decodes frame (demands 2 GB/s BW), 2) NPU runs Object Detection (demands 5 GB/s BW), 3) GPU runs depth estimation (demands 15 GB/s BW). The CPU, NPU, and GPU share a unified LPDDR4 memory bus with a peak bandwidth of 17 GB/s. The system is currently dropping frames. A junior engineer notes the NPU is at 99% compute utilization and suggests upgrading to an NPU with 2x the TOPS. Evaluate this proposal.
title: Shared Bus Bottleneck in SoC Pipelines

details.common_mistake: Calculating only the compute power (0.5 GOPS / 10 TOPS/W = 0.05 mW) and concluding the model perfectly fits the budget, completely ignoring the DRAM access energy.
details.napkin_math:
Compute power: 5 M-Ops * 100 Hz = 500 MOPS = 0.5 GOPS.
Compute power draw = 0.5 GOPS / 10,000 GOPS/W (10 TOPS/W) = 0.00005 W = 0.05 mW.
Memory bandwidth: 2MB * 100 Hz = 200 MB/s.
Assuming typical LPDDR DRAM access costs ~100 pJ/byte:
Memory power draw = 200 * 10^6 bytes/s * 100 * 10^-12 J/byte = 0.02 W = 20 mW.
Total power = 0.05 mW + 20 mW = 20.05 mW. This is 4x the strict 5mW budget.
details.realistic_solution: The compute power alone is minimal (0.05 mW) and easily fits the budget, but the true failure point is the memory access energy. Fetching data from off-chip DRAM consumes orders of magnitude more energy per byte than on-chip SRAM or the compute operations themselves. Streaming 2MB of weights from DRAM at 100 Hz draws 20 mW, which is 4x the entire device power budget. The Transformer model is completely infeasible not because of compute operations, but because the memory-bound nature of the larger weights catastrophically breaches the energy roofline.

scenario: A wearable health monitor runs an anomaly model continuously. The power budget is strictly 5mW. The SoC has an efficient NPU (10 TOPS/W) and 1MB of SRAM. A proposed Transformer-based model requires 5 M-Operations per inference at 100 Hz, and 2MB of weights. Because it exceeds SRAM, the weights must be streamed from off-chip DRAM for every inference. Evaluate if the new model fits within the 5mW budget.
title: SRAM vs DRAM Energy Roofline

details.common_mistake: Streaming raw inference latencies or logs to a centralized cloud observability platform for evaluation.
details.napkin_math: Streaming raw logs: 50,000 devices * 25 inferences/sec * 50 bytes = 62.5 MB/sec global ingest (expensive, clogs uplink). Local aggregation: 1 payload per device every 5 mins = 100 bytes / 300s = 0.33 bytes/sec per device. Global ingest drops to ~16.5 KB/sec.
details.realistic_solution: Implement an edge-evaluated canary deployment with aggregated local telemetry. Instead of streaming raw inference logs, the edge device calculates a rolling 5-minute P99 latency and OOM/frame-drop counter locally. If the local P99 exceeds an 80ms threshold or frame drops exceed 1%, the device automatically switches its symlink to the cached previous model (stored in an A/B partition) and sends a lightweight 1KB 'rollback event' to the cloud. The cloud control plane monitors these events; if more than 5% of the canary group reports a rollback, the global rollout is automatically halted.

scenario: You are deploying a 25MB object detection update to 50,000 cellular-connected dashcams (1 Mbps uplink max). A memory leak in the new inference engine causes latencies to creep from 40ms to 150ms over 2 hours, dropping frames. You need an observability system to detect this and safely rollback without saturating the cellular network.
title: Fleet-wide Rollback under Bandwidth Constraints

details.common_mistake: Aggressively downsampling or JPEG-compressing the images to 10KB to send to the cloud.
details.napkin_math: Raw image: 2,000,000 bytes. Uncompressed embedding: 128 float32 = 512 bytes. Projected sketch: 4 float32 = 16 bytes. Softmax entropy + metadata = 12 bytes. Total payload: 28 bytes per inference. At 5 inferences/sec = 140 bytes/sec, easily fitting the 10 KB/s budget (1.4% utilization).
details.realistic_solution: Compute a lightweight statistical sketch of the data distribution directly on the edge. Extract a bottleneck feature layer (e.g., a 128-dimensional embedding) and project it down to a 4-dimensional vector using a pre-deployed random projection matrix (Locality Sensitive Hashing) or PCA. Send this 4-d sketch alongside the softmax entropy and basic image stats (mean brightness). The cloud maintains a running Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test or Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) on these sketches against the baseline training set sketches to trigger retraining alerts.

scenario: 1,000 agricultural drones run offline crop inspection using a CNN. Satellite uplink is strictly limited to 10 KB/s per drone. Seasonal lighting changes cause silent accuracy degradation. Sending raw 2MB RGB images for cloud-side validation is impossible. You must optimize the observability payload to monitor data drift.
title: Ultra-Low Bandwidth Drift Detection

details.common_mistake: Running a background thread that polls OS temperature and CPU frequency at the frame rate (30Hz).
details.napkin_math: Polling overhead: 30 calls/sec * 1ms CPU time = 30ms/sec overhead (3% of CPU). Event-driven callback: 1 interrupt every few seconds = ~0 overhead. Circular buffer: 100 elements * 4 bytes (float32) = 400 bytes RAM. Flash write on drop: 404 bytes per jitter event.
details.realistic_solution: Use an event-driven, piggybacked observability architecture. Instead of polling, register a callback for the OS `THERMAL_EVENT` broadcast to update a cached thermal state variable. To correlate temperature with jitter, maintain a lightweight lock-free circular buffer of the last 100 inference latencies in memory. When a frame drops (latency > 33ms), dump the buffer along with the last known thermal state to flash storage for asynchronous upload when the device is charging and connected to Wi-Fi.

scenario: Smart glasses run a hand-tracking model at 30 FPS (33ms budget) on an XR2 chip. Users report intermittent jitter. Profiling reveals the device hits 85°C, thermal throttles the DSP, pushing inference to 45ms. Polling the OS temperature API at 30Hz consumes 5% CPU, worsening the heat.
title: Debugging Thermal Throttling Cascades

details.common_mistake: Attempting to compress both models into RAM/Flash or doing a shadow run which causes an Out-Of-Memory brick.
details.napkin_math: Flash required for dual-model: 19.5MB (Fails). Flash for A/B partitioning: 8MB + max(6MB, 5.5MB) = 14MB (Leaves 2MB for logs). Recovery network cost: 6MB download @ 10 Mbps = ~4.8 seconds to fetch V1 upon critical failure.
details.realistic_solution: Since 8MB + 6MB + 5.5MB = 19.5MB (>16MB), you must partition the fleet into mutually exclusive A and B groups at the cloud registry. To ensure safe deployment without a local fallback model, utilize a hardware watchdog timer and an algorithmic minimal fallback in the OS (e.g., simple 'bump-and-turn'). If V2 faults or times out, the watchdog resets the device, the OS boots into safe mode using the algorithmic fallback, navigates to the dock, and triggers an OTA network fetch to download V1 from the registry.

scenario: 500,000 autonomous vacuums run on an MCU with 16MB of total flash storage. The OS takes 8MB. The current navigation model (V1) is 6MB. The new model (V2) is 5.5MB. You want to run a fleet-wide A/B test but cannot fit both models on disk to do a shadow deployment or instant fallback.
title: Safe A/B Testing on Storage-Constrained Edge

details.common_mistake: Using an edge OpenTelemetry agent to independently emit spans to an observability backend over a separate network connection.
details.napkin_math: Edge-emitted spans: 1 extra HTTP request (TLS + payload) = ~30-50ms blocking I/O if not perfectly async. Header injection: 3 timestamps (8 bytes each) + 16-byte TraceID = 40 bytes added to the existing payload. String formatting takes <0.1ms. Zero additional network connections.
details.realistic_solution: Implement W3C Trace Context propagation natively within the inference pipeline. Generate a 16-byte TraceID at the edge upon frame capture. Instead of making separate network calls to emit spans, inject the TraceID and local timestamps (capture_time, detection_end, queue_start) directly into the HTTP headers of the crop payload sent to the cloud classifier. The cloud service, possessing abundant resources, strips these headers, computes the edge durations, appends its own inference/DB spans, and asynchronously flushes the complete unified trace to the observability backend.

scenario: Retail cameras run an edge SSD detector (20ms), crop items, and send them to a cloud ViT classifier via an API. The end-to-end SLA is 500ms. P99 latency is spiking to 1200ms. You need to implement distributed tracing to isolate the bottleneck without adding more than 2ms overhead to the edge critical path.
title: Tracing Latency in Hybrid Edge-Cloud Pipelines

details.common_mistake: Assuming that doing 5x more local compute per round will inevitably burn more total battery life.
details.napkin_math: Compute per epoch = 5mJ * 1000 = 5J. Comms per round = 10MB * 500mJ/MB * 2 (upload+download) = 10J. Baseline (1 epoch): 5J compute + 10J comms = 15J/round. Total = 15J * 200 rounds = 3000J. Proposal (5 epochs): 25J compute + 10J comms = 35J/round. Total = 35J * 80 rounds = 2800J. The proposal saves 200J per device.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the energy per round for both strategies, then multiply by the number of rounds to find the total energy footprint. In Federated Learning, communication (transmitting weights) is often significantly more expensive than local computation. By doing more local work (epochs) per round, you reduce the total number of global syncs required. You must evaluate the sum of compute and communication energy over the entire convergence lifecycle. The proposal with 5 epochs actually saves total energy because the massive reduction in communication rounds more than offsets the increase in local compute.

scenario: You are deploying a 10MB Federated Learning model on 100,000 edge devices. Local training costs 5mJ per batch (1,000 batches/epoch). Network transmission costs 500mJ/MB. The baseline uses 1 local epoch per round, converging in 200 rounds. A new proposal uses 5 local epochs per round, converging in 80 rounds. Evaluate the total energy cost per device to reach convergence.
title: Federated Learning Energy Optimization

details.common_mistake: Believing race-to-sleep is always optimal because it maximizes the time spent in the low-power static state.
details.napkin_math: Race-to-Sleep: 10ms active (1.5W dyn + 0.5W static = 2.0W) + 6.6ms sleep (0.5W). Avg Power = ((10 * 2.0) + (6.6 * 0.5)) / 16.6 = 23.3 / 16.6 = 1.4W (Exceeds 1.2W TDP). DVFS: Freq drops to 0.6x, so time is 10/0.6 = 16.6ms. Voltage drops to 0.6x. P_dyn = 1.5W * (0.6)^2 * (0.6) = 0.324W. Total Power = 0.324W + 0.5W = 0.824W (Safely under 1.2W TDP).
details.realistic_solution: Use the CMOS power equation (P_dyn ∝ V^2 * f) to analyze DVFS. Race-to-sleep averages the high active power with the low sleep power, but due to the V^2 factor, lowering frequency and voltage yields cubic power savings for the dynamic portion. DVFS stretches the execution to fill the deadline but drastically reduces dynamic power. In heavily thermally constrained edge environments, DVFS keeps the device well under the thermal limit without dropping frames, whereas race-to-sleep violates the TDP.

scenario: An AR headset runs a hand-tracking CNN at 60 FPS (16.6ms budget). At max frequency (1.0 GHz, 1.0V), inference takes 10ms. Dynamic power is 1.5W and static power is 0.5W. The headset has a strict thermal design power (TDP) limit of 1.2W. You must evaluate Race-to-Sleep (run at max clock, then sleep) vs DVFS (downclock to 0.6 GHz, 0.6V) to meet the TDP constraint.
title: AR Glasses Thermal Management via DVFS

details.common_mistake: Only calculating operational energy savings and ignoring the embodied carbon cost of manufacturing the new edge hardware.
details.napkin_math: Power saved = 6W - 2W = 4W per camera. Annual energy saved = 4W * 24h * 365d = 35,040 Wh = 35.04 kWh. Annual carbon saved = 35.04 kWh * 0.4 kgCO2/kWh = 14.016 kg CO2e/year. Payback period = Embodied Carbon / Annual Savings = 20 kg / 14.016 kg/yr = 1.42 years.
details.realistic_solution: Perform a lifecycle carbon assessment. Calculate the operational energy saved by eliminating the continuous video stream, convert it to carbon emissions using the grid's specific carbon intensity, and divide the embodied carbon of the new hardware by the annual operational carbon savings. The edge deployment is highly sustainable and justified if the carbon payback period is significantly shorter than the hardware's expected 3-5 year lifespan.

scenario: A smart city operates 10,000 traffic cameras sending 1080p video to a cloud server. The continuous network transmission draws 6W per camera. A proposal suggests upgrading to edge AI modules (embodied carbon: 20 kg CO2e each) that draw 2W to process video locally and only transmit 1KB/s of metadata. The local grid carbon intensity is 400 gCO2/kWh. Evaluate the carbon payback period of this edge upgrade.
title: Smart Camera Carbon Payback Period

details.common_mistake: Assuming a 10% frequency reduction only yields a 10% power reduction, which would fail to bring the system under the 200W budget.
details.napkin_math: Current total = 3*50 + 65 = 215W (15W over budget). Reduce perception freq by 10% (0.9x). New latency = 20ms / 0.9 = 22.2ms (meets 33.3ms deadline). New dynamic power = 40W * (0.9)^3 = 29.16W. New node power = 29.16W + 10W = 39.16W. Savings per node = 10.84W. Total savings = 32.52W. New total = 3*39.16 + 65 = 182.48W (Safely under 200W).
details.realistic_solution: Applying a uniform 10% DVFS step to the perception nodes leverages the non-linear relationship between frequency/voltage and dynamic power. Since inference latency increases linearly but dynamic power decreases cubically (P ∝ V^2 * f), you can harvest massive power savings with minimal latency impact. By downclocking the perception nodes, the system safely absorbs the planning node's power spike while still comfortably meeting the 33.3ms deadline required for 30 FPS.

scenario: An autonomous vehicle edge cluster has 4 identical SoC nodes with a shared physical power budget of 200W. Normally, 3 perception nodes use 50W each (40W dynamic, 10W static) running at 30 FPS (20ms latency), and 1 planning node uses 30W. A routing failure causes the planning node to spike to 65W. Evaluate applying a 10% frequency reduction (and 10% voltage reduction) to the 3 perception nodes to prevent a system shutdown while maintaining 30 FPS.
title: Autonomous Vehicle Dynamic Power Capping

details.common_mistake: Optimizing solely for the AI chip's power consumption without considering the massive baseline power draw of the drone's mechanical systems.
details.napkin_math: FP16 Total Power = 250W + 30W = 280W. Flight Time = 150 Wh / 280W = 0.535 hours. Distance = 0.535 * Speed_V. INT8 Total Power = 250W + 10W = 260W. Flight Time = 150 Wh / 260W = 0.576 hours. Distance = 0.576 * (0.8 * Speed_V) = 0.461 * Speed_V. FP16 covers 16% more distance despite higher compute power.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the total flight time for both configurations based on total system power (motors + compute). Then calculate the relative distance covered, factoring in the slower flight speed of the INT8 configuration. In robotics and drones, optimizing edge compute power is counterproductive if it significantly increases the runtime of the massive mechanical power draw. The FP16 model uses more compute power but allows faster flight, resulting in a net increase in total inspection distance.

scenario: A drone performs powerline inspection. The battery is 150 Wh. The motors draw 250W. Running the vision model in FP16 draws 30W at 30 FPS. Quantizing the model to INT8 reduces chip power to 10W, but due to slight accuracy degradation, the drone must fly 20% slower to capture more overlapping frames for reliable detection. Evaluate which precision maximizes the total distance inspected.
title: Drone Edge Compute vs Flight Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on the per-token inference cost and ignoring the continuous static power draw and hardware amortization of the edge server.
details.napkin_math: Cloud: 20k tokens/day * 365 = 7.3M tokens/yr. 3-year tokens = 21.9M. Cloud Cost = 21.9 * $0.50 = $10.95 over 3 years. Edge: CapEx = $1500. Power = 150W * 24h * 365d * 3yrs = 3942 kWh. Power Cost = 3942 * $0.12 = $473.04. Edge TCO = $1500 + $473.04 = $1973.04 over 3 years. Cloud ($10.95) is massively cheaper.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the operational cost of the cloud API over 3 years based on daily token volume. Compare this to the sum of the edge server's CapEx and its 3-year operational power cost. For low-utilization, bursty edge deployments, the static power draw and upfront hardware amortization vastly outweigh the per-token cost of centralized cloud serving. The cloud deployment is orders of magnitude cheaper.

scenario: A retail chain evaluates adding a local voice assistant to 5,000 stores. Cloud API serving costs $0.50 per 1M tokens. Alternatively, an edge server costs $1,500 CapEx (amortized over 3 years), draws 150W continuously, and electricity costs $0.12/kWh. Average usage per store is 20,000 tokens per day. Evaluate the 3-year Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) per store to decide between edge and cloud.
title: Retail Edge vs Cloud LLM TCO

details.common_mistake: Assuming speculative decoding uses more energy because it runs two models and draws higher peak power (5W total).
details.napkin_math: Standard: 10 tok/s = 100ms/token. Energy = 4W * 0.1s = 0.4 J/token. Speculative: Draft 4 tokens takes 100ms (1W * 0.1s = 0.1 J). Verification takes 100ms (4W * 0.1s = 0.4 J). Total step energy = 0.5 J. Tokens accepted per step = 2.5. Energy per token = 0.5 J / 2.5 tok = 0.2 J/token. Speculative decoding cuts energy consumption in half.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the energy consumed per token for standard generation. For speculative decoding, calculate the total energy per step (drafting + parallel verification) and divide by the expected number of accepted tokens per step. Speculative decoding not only reduces latency but can significantly improve energy efficiency on battery-constrained devices, provided the acceptance rate is high enough to offset the draft model's overhead and the higher peak power draw.

scenario: A smartphone runs a 3B parameter LLM locally. Standard autoregressive generation draws 4W and produces 10 tokens/sec. Speculative decoding uses a 100M draft model (draws 1W) and verifies using the 3B model (draws 4W). A verification step takes 100ms, evaluates 4 draft tokens in parallel, and has an average acceptance rate of 2.5 tokens per step. Evaluate the energy efficiency (Joules per token) of both methods.
title: Mobile Speculative Decoding Energy Efficiency

details.common_mistake: Choosing the power-gated mode solely because 0.05W is much lower than 0.5W, ignoring the massive energy penalty of the wake-up phase.
details.napkin_math: Cycle = 200ms. Active = 10ms. Clock-gated: Wake=1ms, Sleep=189ms. Energy = (10ms*2.5W) + (1ms*1.0W) + (189ms*0.5W) = 25 + 1 + 94.5 = 120.5 mJ. Power-gated: Wake=40ms, Sleep=150ms. Energy = (10ms*2.5W) + (40ms*1.5W) + (150ms*0.05W) = 25 + 60 + 7.5 = 92.5 mJ. Power-gated saves 28 mJ per cycle.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the energy consumed over a single 200ms duty cycle for both sleep states. Break the cycle into active time, wake time, and sleep time. Power gating has a much lower static draw but incurs a significant energy penalty during its long wake-up sequence. The optimal state depends entirely on whether the idle duration is longer than the break-even time of the deep sleep penalty. In this case, the duty cycle is long enough that power gating saves more energy.

scenario: An industrial IoT sensor runs an anomaly model every 200ms. Inference takes 10ms on an edge TPU (2.5W active). In "clock-gated" mode, it uses 0.5W and wakes in 1ms (drawing 1.0W during wake). In "power-gated" mode, it uses 0.05W but takes 40ms to wake (drawing 1.5W during wake). Evaluate which sleep state minimizes average energy consumption per cycle.
title: IoT Edge TPU Sleep State Optimization

details.common_mistake: Assuming reducing FLOPs always reduces energy proportionally. In memory-bound regimes, data movement dominates total energy.
details.napkin_math: At AI=15: mem_E = 15×0.5/(20+15×0.5) = 27% compute, 73% memory. Team A saves 40%×27% ≈ 11%. Team B saves 67%×73% ≈ 49%.
details.realistic_solution: Ridge point = 20/0.5 = 40 FLOPs/byte. Team A: Reduces compute energy by 40%, but sparse access patterns may increase memory traffic (irregular access defeats caching). If memory traffic stays constant, they save 40% of compute energy but the workload at AI=15 is memory-bound — compute is only ~27% of total energy. Net saving: ~11%. Team B: Fusion triples data reuse, reducing memory accesses by ~3x. At AI=15, memory dominates (~73% of energy). Reducing memory energy by 67% saves ~49% of total energy. Team B wins decisively because the workload is memory-energy-bound, making memory optimization far more impactful than FLOP reduction.

scenario: Two teams optimize inference energy for an edge vision model. Team A reduces FLOPs by 40% via pruning (but adds sparse memory accesses). Team B fuses 5 consecutive layers to increase arithmetic intensity from 15 to 45 FLOPs/byte without reducing total FLOPs. Which saves more energy on a chip with 20 pJ/byte DRAM and 0.5 pJ/FLOP?
title: Energy Optimization Strategy Selection

details.common_mistake: Using larger kernels to increase RF. Dilated 3×3 convolutions achieve the same RF as larger kernels with far fewer parameters — critical for edge deployment budgets.
details.napkin_math: A: RF=17, 1.8MB. B: RF=25, 3.2MB (over budget). C: RF=19, 1.5MB. C wins: better RF than A at lower size. Dilated convs = free RF expansion.
details.realistic_solution: Option A: RF=17 covers 13% of the 128px input. Within budget (1.8M params ≈ 1.8M × 2B = 3.6MB in FP16, but with INT8 quantization = 1.8MB). Marginal RF coverage for full-image classification. Option B: RF=25 (19.5% coverage) is better but 3.2M params = 3.2MB in INT8, exceeding 2MB budget. Eliminated. Option C: Dilated convolutions expand RF without adding parameters or reducing spatial resolution. Dilation=2 on a 3×3 kernel gives effective 5×5 RF per layer without 5×5 parameter cost. RF=19 with only 1.5M params = 1.5MB in INT8. Well within budget with better RF than Option A. Option C is the clear winner: it achieves a larger RF than Option A with ~17% fewer parameters by using dilated convolutions. The key insight is that dilated convolutions are 'free RF expansion' — same parameter cost as regular convolutions but with multiplicatively larger receptive fields.

scenario: An edge device with 2MB model budget needs to classify 128×128 images. Option A: 8 layers of 3×3 convs (RF=17, 1.8M params). Option B: 4 layers of 7×7 convs (RF=25, 3.2M params, exceeds budget). Option C: 5 layers of 3×3 convs + 2 dilated convs (dilation=2, RF=19, 1.5M params). Which achieves the best RF within budget?
title: Receptive Field vs Model Size Trade-off for Edge Deployment

details.common_mistake: Using 'stop and hover' as the only fallback for a drone. At 1/10K failure rate and 30Hz inference, the drone would stop every 5 minutes — operationally unacceptable.
details.napkin_math: Primary failure: 1/10K. Secondary failure: 1/5K. Both fail simultaneously (if independent): 1/50M. Conservative fusion: near-zero unsafe failures at 2x compute cost.
details.realistic_solution: Option C (parallel execution, conservative fusion) is the only acceptable answer for safety-critical systems. Option A (stop and hover) is safe but operationally degrading — if the drone stops every time the primary model is uncertain, it becomes unusable in novel environments (construction zones, unusual weather). 1 in 10K failures with continuous inference (~30 Hz) means a failure every ~5.5 minutes. Option B (simpler model on synthetic data) introduces its own failure modes — synthetic data may not cover real-world edge cases, and the simpler model may be confidently wrong on scenarios the primary model correctly flags as uncertain. Option C runs both models on every frame. The system takes the more conservative prediction (e.g., if either model detects an obstacle, avoid it). This provides: (1) redundancy — both must fail simultaneously for system failure, (2) safety — conservative fusion errs on the side of caution, (3) continuous operation — the drone never needs to stop, it just uses the safer prediction. Cost: 2x compute, which is acceptable for safety-critical applications.

scenario: An autonomous drone uses an onboard ML model for obstacle avoidance. The model occasionally fails (1 in 10K inferences) when encountering novel objects not in training data. Option A: heuristic fallback (stop and hover). Option B: simpler model trained on synthetic data covering more scenarios. Option C: always run both models and take the more conservative action. Which strategy for a safety-critical system?
title: Designing Fallback for an Autonomous System

details.common_mistake: Assuming compute (TFLOPS) is the bottleneck for generation, ignoring that LLM decoding on GPUs is almost entirely bound by memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: FP16 size = 7B * 2B = 14GB. Bandwidth = 320GB/s. Time to read weights = 14GB / 320GB/s = 43.7ms/token. BS=1 yields 22.8 tokens/s. BS=8 yields 183 tokens/s overall (22.8 per sequence), as computation overhead is mathematically negligible.
details.realistic_solution: For auto-regressive decoding, the workload is overwhelmingly memory-bandwidth bound. A 7B model tightly fits the 16GB T4. At batch size 1, the GPU reads 14GB per token, heavily underutilizing compute. At batch size 8, it reads the identical 14GB but processes 8 tokens simultaneously. The optimal tradeoff favors batch size 8 to dramatically multiply overall throughput without significantly impacting individual per-token generation latency.

scenario: Deploying a 7B parameter LLM on an edge server with a single T4 GPU (16GB GDDR6, 320GB/s). The system must serve requests at minimum latency. Analyze the tradeoff between running batch size 1 versus batch size 8 for auto-regressive decoding.
title: Edge New 0001

details.common_mistake: Believing that lowering GOPs always results in an exactly proportional reduction in latency, without checking the memory bandwidth floor.
details.napkin_math: Standard: 100 GOPs / 275 TOPS = 0.36ms. Memory: 10MB / 200 GB/s = 0.05ms. Time = 0.36ms (Compute bound). Depthwise: 10 GOPs / 275 TOPS = 0.036ms. Memory: 10MB / 200 GB/s = 0.05ms. Time = 0.05ms (Memory bound). Depthwise is 7.2x faster.
details.realistic_solution: Depthwise convolutions dramatically reduce operations but maintain the same parameter footprint for spatial weights, significantly lowering arithmetic intensity.
