Re-ranking 1000 items with O(N log N) sorting: 1000 * 10 ≈ 10,000 operations. With complex fairness constraints, an LP solver on 1000 items takes ~25-40ms (violates SLA).
Truncating to top 100 items: LP solver on 100 items takes ~1-2ms. 40ms (rank) + 2ms (re-rank) = 42ms. Leaves 18ms for overhead, safely meeting the 60ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: We must trade off theoretical perfect parity across the entire candidate pool for strict latency compliance. An in-processing approach (modifying the ranker's loss function) adds zero latency but is notoriously unstable for exposure equity. We choose a post-processing approach, but restrict the optimization space. Instead of re-ranking all 1,000 candidates (O(N log N) or O(N^2)), we take the top 100 items from the ranker. We apply a deterministic greedy algorithm or a lightweight linear program to select the final 10 items such that creator demographic constraints are met while maximizing the sum of predicted CTRs. Reducing N from 1000 to 100 drops the re-ranking latency from ~25ms down to <2ms, safely fitting within the remaining 20ms latency budget.

scenario: An e-commerce recommendation engine serves 20,000 QPS. The candidate generator returns 1,000 items, and the ranker scores them in 40ms. The total system p99 latency SLA is 60ms. The current system exhibits extreme popularity bias, starving new/minority creators. You must enforce demographic parity (exposure equity) for creators in the final top-10 list.
title: Low-Latency Multi-Objective Recommendation Debiasing System

details.common_mistake: Assuming FP8 has uniform dynamic range and attributing the NaN to a learning rate that is too high for quantized training.
details.napkin_math: In FP8 (E4M3), max value is (1 + 6/8) * 2^(15-7) = 1.75 * 256 = 448. A gradient of 800 exceeds this, causing NaN on H100. FP8 E5M2 max value is (1 + 3/4) * 2^(31-15) = 1.75 * 65536 = 114,688. Wait, E5M2 exponent bias is 15. Max exp is 30. 30-15=15. 2^15 = 32768. 1.75 * 32768 = 57,344. Gradient 800 fits in E5M2. Use E5M2 for backward pass gradients to prevent overflow.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a mismatch in FP8 encoding formats. FP8 has two standard formats: E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) and E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits). You used E4M3 for both the forward and backward passes. E4M3 provides higher precision (needed for activations/weights) but has a maximum representable value of 448. When gradients hit ~800.0, E4M3 overflows, producing NaNs. The fix is to use E4M3 for the forward pass (activations and weights) and E5M2 for the backward pass (gradients), as E5M2 sacrifices precision for a much larger dynamic range (max value 57,344), comfortably accommodating the gradient norms.

scenario: You are migrating a 70B parameter LLM fine-tuning pipeline from FP16 to FP8 on H100 GPUs to double throughput to 4,000 tokens/sec/GPU. The forward pass works perfectly, but during the backward pass in QAT, the loss immediately spikes to NaN after 15 steps. The gradient norms are roughly ~800.0 before the crash. What caused this catastrophic failure?
title: FP8 Gradient Casting Overflow Crisis

details.common_mistake: Assuming the tokenizer vocabulary distribution caused the issue or that INT8 inherently lacks the precision for complex syntax.
details.napkin_math: English Max Act = 15.0. INT8 Scale = 15.0 / 127 = 0.118 per bin. German Max Act = 120.0. With static scale, 120.0 is clipped to 15.0 (losing 87.5% of the signal magnitude). If calibrated on German: Scale = 120.0 / 127 = 0.94 per bin, meaning English activations (max 15.0) only use 15.0 / 0.94 = 16 bins (3-4 bits of precision), degrading English.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is uncalibrated activation outliers. Large language models exhibit massive activation outliers in specific feed-forward channels. Your PTQ calibration dataset used 5,000 English Wikipedia articles, so the static quantization scales for activations were set based on English outlier magnitudes. German and Code inputs route through different network pathways, producing activation outliers up to 10x larger than English ones in specific channels. Because the PTQ ranges were statically fixed to the English maximums, these cross-lingual outliers were severely clipped, destroying the signal. The solution is either SmoothQuant (migrating activation difficulty to weights) or using dynamic per-token activation quantization.

scenario: A globally deployed 30B LLM is quantized using INT8 W8A8 PTQ. English generation latency drops from 45ms/token to 22ms/token with <0.5% perplexity degradation. However, telemetry shows that German and Code generation outputs are producing gibberish, with perplexity spiking by 400%. Your calibration dataset consisted of 5,000 Wikipedia articles. Why did quantization break specific languages?
title: Cross-Lingual PTQ Activation Outliers

details.common_mistake: Assuming the CPU lacks INT8 vector instructions (VNNI) or that memory bandwidth is the bottleneck due to cache thrashing.
details.napkin_math: Symmetric MAC: 1 instruction (VPMADDUBSW). Asymmetric MAC: W*X (1 inst) + row_sum(W)*Zx (1 inst) + col_sum(X)*Zw (1 inst) + precomputed_term. Execution time per layer increases by roughly ~3x in instruction count, turning a 1ms FP32 layer into a 0.33ms (INT8 sym) or a 1.2ms (INT8 asym) layer.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is the computational overhead of asymmetric quantization zero-points. CPU SIMD instructions (like AVX-512 VNNI) are optimized for INT8 dot products. However, with asymmetric quantization, the matrix multiplication expands: (W - Zw) * (X - Zx) = W*X - W*Zx - X*Zw + Zw*Zx. While Zw*Zx can be precomputed, the cross terms (W*Zx and X*Zw) require a reduction across the rows/columns at runtime. This forces the CPU to execute multiple additional instructions (accumulations and broadcasts) per MAC, destroying the throughput. Switching to symmetric quantization (zero-point = 0) eliminates these cross terms, allowing direct use of high-throughput VNNI DP4A instructions, restoring QPS to >20,000.

scenario: You quantize a recommendation model's MLP layers to INT8 to deploy on Intel Xeon CPUs. Model size drops from 4GB to 1GB. However, CPU inference throughput drops from 12,000 QPS (FP32) to 5,500 QPS (INT8). Profiling shows the CPU is 100% utilized and not memory-bound. You used asymmetric per-tensor quantization (min/max). Why is the smaller INT8 model slower than FP32?
title: Asymmetric Quantization Throughput Collapse

details.common_mistake: Believing that QAT actually stores the model in INT8 during training, and attributing the OOM to a memory leak in the data loader.
details.napkin_math: 15B params. Standard FP16 FT: Weights 30GB + Adam (FP32) 120GB = 150GB (usually sharded via FSDP to ~18.75GB/GPU) + 30GB activations = ~45GB per GPU after sharding. QAT adds: FP32 shadow weights (60GB total, ~7.5GB/GPU sharded) + INT8 fake weights (15GB total, ~2GB/GPU) + FakeQuant activation copies (~25GB/GPU overhead). Total per GPU: 45GB + 7.5GB + 2GB + 25GB = ~79.5GB -> OOM.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is the maintenance of FP32 'shadow weights' alongside the fake-quantization graph. In QAT, gradients cannot flow through discrete INT8 steps (due to zero derivatives), so the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) is used. This requires keeping the continuous FP32 weights to accumulate small gradient updates. During the forward pass, the framework must store both the FP32 weights AND the simulated INT8 weights (FakeQuant), plus the FP32 optimizer states (Adam requires two FP32 tensors per parameter — momentum and variance — totaling 120GB for 15B parameters). Furthermore, FakeQuant nodes inject additional activation tensors into the computation graph that must be saved for the backward pass, dramatically increasing the activation memory footprint.

scenario: You initiate Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) for a 15B parameter vision-language model on an 8x80GB A100 node. Standard FP16 fine-tuning takes 45GB VRAM per GPU. When you enable INT8 QAT, you expect memory to drop or stay constant, but it spikes to 82GB per GPU, causing an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error. What is causing this massive memory inflation?
title: The QAT Shadow Weight OOM

details.common_mistake: Assuming the calibration dataset lacked acoustic diversity, leading to clipping of speech outliers.
details.napkin_math: Global max = 50.0. Per-tensor INT8 scale = 50.0 / 127 = 0.393. Channel 0 range is [-0.1, 0.1]. Number of representable bins for Channel 0 = (0.1 - (-0.1)) / 0.393 = 0.5 bins. All weights in Channel 0 quantize to exactly 0. 100% information loss for that channel.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is applying per-tensor quantization to Depthwise Convolutions. In standard convolutions, weights are mixed across input channels, keeping dynamic ranges relatively uniform. In Depthwise Convolutions, each channel is convolved independently. The network learns wildly different weight magnitudes for different channels (e.g., channel 0 might have a range of [-0.1, 0.1] while channel 120 has [-50.0, 50.0]). With per-tensor quantization, a single scale factor is calculated based on the global maximum (50.0). Small-magnitude channels are entirely squashed to zero because their entire range falls within a single quantization bin, destroying critical acoustic features. The fix is per-channel quantization for the weights.

scenario: You deploy an INT8 quantized Conformer acoustic model for global speech recognition. The pipeline processes 5,000 hours of audio daily. After switching from FP32 to INT8 using per-tensor PTQ, the Word Error Rate (WER) jumps from 4.2% to 28.5%. Standard Convs show no degradation, but the Depthwise Convolution layers exhibit massive activation errors. Why?
title: Depthwise Conv Per-Tensor Collapse

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT8 simply doesn't have enough bits to store 16,000 unique token representations, leading to hash collisions in attention.
details.napkin_math: Max token outlier magnitude = 12.0. INT8 Step size = 12.0 / 127 = 0.094. High-frequency RoPE rotation alters values by ~0.02. Since 0.02 < 0.094/2 (the rounding threshold), the rotation is rounded away (quantized delta = 0). Tokens at pos 10,000 and 15,000 become positionally indistinguishable.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is the destructive interaction between INT8 quantization and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) when quantizing *after* rotation. RoPE injects positional information by rotating the Query and Key vectors. For long contexts, high-frequency dimensions encode fine-grained distances and have very small activation amplitudes. Conversely, LLMs have massive magnitude outliers in specific hidden dimensions. If you apply RoPE and then quantize to INT8 per-tensor or per-token, the large outliers force a large quantization step size. The small-amplitude high-frequency RoPE rotations are rounded to zero, completely erasing long-range positional information. The fix is either to quantize the KV cache *before* applying RoPE (applying RoPE dynamically during attention) or use RoPE-aware per-channel quantization.

scenario: To increase serving batch size from 32 to 128, you quantize the KV cache of a 7B LLM to INT8, saving 12GB of VRAM. Short-context tasks (1k tokens) maintain 99% accuracy. However, a 16k-token needle-in-a-haystack passkey test completely fails, dropping from 100% to 4% accuracy. What interaction destroyed the long-context retrieval?
title: Long-Context KV Cache RoPE Failure

details.common_mistake: Blaming the PCIe bus transfer time for hiding the compute speedup, or assuming the model is completely memory-bandwidth bound.
details.napkin_math: ResNet-152 has ~150 Conv+BN blocks. INT8 Conv takes 0.02ms (150 * 0.02 = 3ms). Unfolded overhead: Dequantize (0.01ms) + FP32 BN (0.05ms) + Quantize (0.01ms) = 0.07ms per block. 150 * 0.07ms = 10.5ms overhead. Total INT8 = 13.5ms. FP32 Conv (0.08ms) + FP32 BN (0.01ms folded) = ~13.5ms. The Quant/Dequant overhead equals the FP32 compute time.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a failure to fold Batch Normalization (BN) layers into the Convolutional layers before quantization. In FP32, Conv -> BN -> ReLU is executed sequentially. If BN is not mathematically folded into the Conv weights/biases before the INT8 conversion, the graph compiler is forced to execute: INT8 Conv -> Dequantize to FP32 -> FP32 BN -> Quantize to INT8 -> INT8 ReLU. The massive overhead of inserting hundreds of Quantize/Dequantize nodes and executing memory-bound BN operations in FP32 completely erases the compute savings of the INT8 Convolutions. Folding BN updates the Conv weights (W_new = W * gamma / std) and biases, allowing pure INT8 execution.

scenario: You deploy an INT8 ResNet-152 image embedding model via TensorRT. Despite the INT8 weights bringing the memory down from 230MB to 58MB, the end-to-end latency is 14ms per image—exactly the same as the FP32 model. The hardware has dedicated INT8 matrix multipliers (Tensor Cores) capable of 4x speedups. Why is there zero latency improvement?
title: The Unfolded BatchNorm Latency Trap

details.common_mistake: Applying W8A8 quantization to reduce weights and compute, which degrades accuracy and doesn't maximize generation token throughput since generation is memory-bandwidth bound.
details.napkin_math: FP16 weights: 70B * 2 bytes = 140GB (OOM on 96GB node). INT4 weights: 70B * 0.5 bytes = 35GB. VRAM remaining: 96GB - 35GB = 61GB. KV Cache per token (Llama-2 70B GQA): 80 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 dim * 2 (K+V) * 2 bytes = 327KB/token. 61GB allows for ~186,000 tokens in the KV cache, easily supporting high concurrency.
details.realistic_solution: Implement Weight-Only Post-Training Quantization (e.g., AWQ or GPTQ) down to 4-bit (INT4). In autoregressive generation, the process is heavily memory-bandwidth bound (batch size of 1 per step implies reading the entire weight matrix to generate a single token). By quantizing weights to INT4 and keeping activations in FP16 (W4A16), you reduce the memory footprint to fit within the 96GB limit with plenty of room for the KV cache, while drastically reducing the bytes read from VRAM per token, directly accelerating generation throughput. A calibration set must be used during the PTQ process to protect salient weights, minimizing the perplexity degradation typically seen in uniform 4-bit quantization.

scenario: You need to deploy a 70B parameter LLM for a global chatbot service. The hardware budget strictly limits you to a single node with 4x A10G (24GB VRAM each, 96GB total). The throughput requirement is 500 tokens/sec. The model in FP16 requires ~140GB just for weights. How do you architect the deployment to meet memory constraints while maximizing generation throughput?
title: Serving 70B LLMs on Single Node

details.common_mistake: Assuming all FP8 formats are interchangeable and applying E5M2 uniformly to maximize dynamic range, destroying the mantissa precision needed for forward-pass inference.
details.napkin_math: E5M2 has 2 mantissa bits: 2^2 = 4 fractional values per bin, max value ~57344. E4M3 has 3 mantissa bits: 2^3 = 8 fractional values per bin (double the precision), max value ~448. Inference activations rarely exceed 448 (especially with LayerNorm), making E4M3 the mathematically superior choice for reducing quantization noise in the forward pass.
details.realistic_solution: The architecture must selectively utilize the two distinct FP8 formats: E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) and E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits). E5M2 provides a larger dynamic range (like FP16) which is highly beneficial for gradient representation during training. However, for inference (weights and forward activations), dynamic range is less critical than precision. The solution is to cast weights and activations to E4M3, which provides an extra bit of mantissa (higher precision), effectively preserving the model's accuracy. Furthermore, per-tensor or per-channel scaling factors must be computed during calibration to map the FP16 values into the representable range of E4M3.

scenario: Migrating a dense 100B transformer to Hopper H100 GPUs, the infrastructure team switches the serving engine to use FP8 to double the MAC throughput (target: 8000 QPS). They blindly cast all FP16 weights and activations to the E5M2 FP8 format. Benchmarks show the target throughput is reached, but the model's accuracy drops catastrophically (MMLU score drops from 72% to 45%).
title: Hopper FP8 Format Mismatch

details.common_mistake: Aggressively quantizing the model weights further to INT3 or INT2, which degrades accuracy but fails to solve the OOM because the KV cache is the actual memory bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Assume 60 layers, 64 heads, 128 head dim. FP16 KV cache per token: 60 * 64 * 128 * 2 (K+V) * 2 bytes = ~1.96 MB/token. For 64k context: 1.96 MB * 65536 = 128 GB per request! Across 20 requests = 2.56 TB (impossible on 160GB total VRAM). Using Grouped Query Attention (GQA, e.g. 8 KV heads) reduces this to 16 GB/req. Still, 20 reqs = 320GB. Quantizing KV to INT8 (1 byte) halves it to 160GB, and using INT4 KV cache (0.5 bytes) brings it to 80GB, fitting comfortably within the 160GB VRAM budget.
details.realistic_solution: The architectural requirement is to implement KV Cache Quantization. While weights are INT4, the KV cache (storing past keys and values for attention) is likely defaulting to FP16. At long context lengths, the KV cache footprint grows linearly and surpasses the weight footprint. By quantizing the KV cache dynamically to INT8 (or FP8 on supported hardware) using techniques like per-token or per-channel asymmetric quantization, you halve the memory required per token. This allows the system to support the required 64k context at 20+ concurrency without OOMing, while maintaining long-context retrieval accuracy.

scenario: You are serving a 34B parameter code generation model with a massive 64k token context window on 2x A100 (80GB) GPUs. The model weights are quantized to INT4 (occupying ~17GB). At a concurrency of just 20 requests, the system hits Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors and crashes, even though compute utilization is below 40%.
title: Long-Context VRAM Exhaustion

details.common_mistake: Switching back to FP16 or Mixed Precision, which immediately violates the strict 5W power budget and edge NPU silicon constraints (which may only have INT8 ALUs).
details.napkin_math: Edge NPU budget: 5W. FP32 MAC energy ~ 3.7pJ. INT8 MAC energy ~ 0.2pJ (18x lower). 50M params * 30 FPS * ~100 MACs/param = 150 GigaMACs/sec. FP32 power = 150G * 3.7pJ = 0.55W (compute only, memory is 10x higher, easily exceeding 5W). INT8 compute power = 150G * 0.2pJ = 0.03W. Thus, INT8 is physically required to stay under the thermal envelope.
details.realistic_solution: Architect a Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) pipeline. PTQ fails because static calibration cannot adequately capture and mitigate the clipping errors from activation outliers in the compact vision model. QAT simulates the quantization effects (clipping and rounding) during the training forward pass using FakeQuant nodes. The gradients are approximated using the Straight-Through Estimator (STE). By fine-tuning the model for a few epochs with QAT, the weights adjust to accommodate the restricted INT8 dynamic range, effectively pushing the Pareto curve to recover the mAP to ~0.80 while strictly maintaining the INT8 data paths for the 5W edge deployment.

scenario: An autonomous delivery drone runs a 50M parameter object detection model at 30 FPS. To meet the 5W power limit of the edge NPU, the model must execute entirely in INT8. Standard Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) achieves the power and latency targets, but the mAP (mean Average Precision) drops from 0.82 to 0.65, causing missed detections of pedestrians.
title: Recovering Edge Vision Accuracy

details.common_mistake: Using dynamic per-token activation quantization without addressing the channel outliers, which adds severe runtime overhead and still struggles with channel-wise variance.
details.napkin_math: A100 FP16 dense peak is 312 TFLOPS. INT8 dense peak is 624 TOPS (2x compute speedup). If an activation channel has max value 500 and median 5, an INT8 range [-127, 127] gives a scale of 500/127 = 3.93. The median 5 becomes 5/3.93 = 1.27 (rounded to 1), losing massive precision. SmoothQuant scales the 500 down to ~50, reducing the scale factor to 0.39, preserving the precision of the median values.
details.realistic_solution: Implement SmoothQuant or a similar mathematically equivalent transformation. In LLMs, activation outliers are highly systematic (they appear in specific channels across all tokens), while weights are relatively uniform. Standard per-tensor activation quantization clips these outliers or destroys the precision of non-outliers. SmoothQuant introduces a per-channel scaling factor that mathematically migrates the quantization difficulty from the activations to the weights. By dividing the activation channels by a scale factor and multiplying the corresponding weight channels by the same factor (Y = (X / S) * (W * S)), you smooth out the activations. Both weights and activations are then easily quantized to INT8 statically, allowing full use of INT8 Tensor Cores without runtime quantization overhead or accuracy loss.

scenario: You are deploying a 13B LLM for a high-throughput summarization task. To maximize compute efficiency on A100s, you target W8A8 (INT8 weights and activations) utilizing INT8 Tensor Cores. However, standard W8A8 PTQ causes zero-shot accuracy to plummet by 25%. Analysis shows massive, systematic outliers in specific activation channels (up to 100x the median value).
title: Systematic Activation Outliers

details.common_mistake: Attempting to quantize the MLP weights, which does nothing to solve the All-to-All network bandwidth bottleneck caused by the massive embedding vector transfers.
details.napkin_math: 10,000 QPS. Assume 200 features per request, embedding dimension 128. Payload per request = 200 * 128 * 4 bytes (FP32) = 102.4 KB. All-to-All transfer for 8 GPUs: each GPU sends 7/8 of its embeddings = ~89.6 KB per request. At 10K QPS per GPU: 89.6 KB * 10K = 896 MB/s per GPU outbound. With NVLink A100 (600 GB/s), bandwidth is not the issue — latency from small-message overhead dominates. At 10K QPS burst: All-to-All latency ~45ms at P99 due to message scheduling and synchronization across 8 GPUs. Compressing to INT8 reduces payload per request to 200 * 128 * 1 = 25.6 KB (4x reduction). All-to-All data volume drops to 224 MB/s per GPU. Fewer bytes per message means faster serialization and less bus contention: P99 latency drops to ~11ms. Total per-step: 5ms compute + 11ms comm = 16ms, well under 30ms budget.
details.realistic_solution: Architect a solution applying Row-wise PTQ or QAT to the embedding tables, compressing them from FP32 to INT8 or INT4. In DLRM model parallelism, GPUs look up embeddings locally and then must exchange them (All-to-All) to assemble the full feature vector before the top MLP. By storing and transmitting the embeddings in INT8, you immediately reduce the network payload by 4x. The vectors are only dequantized to FP16/FP32 immediately before the top MLP compute phase. Row-wise quantization (calculating scale/zero-point per embedding vector) is critical here because embedding vectors have highly independent distributions; per-tensor quantization would destroy recommendation accuracy.

scenario: A Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) uses a 200GB embedding table sharded across 8 GPUs (25GB per GPU) via model parallelism. At 10,000 QPS, the P99 latency is 60ms (budget is 30ms). Profiling reveals that the compute time is only 5ms; the bottleneck is the All-to-All network communication transferring gathered FP32 embedding vectors across the PCIe/NVLink bus.
title: RecSys Network Bottlenecks

details.common_mistake: Increasing the number of calibration samples of the same short-sentence dataset, which fails to capture the long-context activation distributions.
details.napkin_math: If max activation for length 10 is 15.0, static scale is 15.0/127 = 0.118. For length 500, attention sums grow, max activation hits 60.0. Using the static scale of 0.118, the INT8 value would need to be 60.0 / 0.118 = 508, which clips to 127. The dequantized value is 127 * 0.118 = 15.0. An error of 45.0 (75% error) is injected into the residual stream per layer, destroying the representation.
details.realistic_solution: The architecture suffers from calibration distribution mismatch. In transformers, activation magnitudes (especially in attention layers and residual streams) scale with sequence length. Static ranges `[-max, max]` calculated on 10-token sequences are far too narrow for 500-token sequences, leading to severe clipping of valid activations. The solution is twofold: 1) Re-calibrate the static PTQ using a representative dataset that matches production sequence lengths (legal documents), and 2) If variance remains high, shift the architecture from Static PTQ to Dynamic Activation Quantization, where the scale/zero-point for activations are calculated on-the-fly per token at runtime, trading a slight compute overhead for robustness against sequence length variance.

scenario: A transformer translation model runs W8A8 static PTQ at 200 QPS. The static calibration was done on a dataset of short conversational sentences (avg 10 tokens). In production, the model receives complex legal documents (avg 500 tokens). Latency is optimal (40ms), but the BLEU score on production data drops by 15 points due to severe activation clipping.
title: Static Calibration Distribution Shift

details.common_mistake: Quantizing the universal artifact to INT8, which wastes the specialized FP8 tensor cores and higher precision capabilities of the H100 GPUs.
details.napkin_math: A10G INT8 TOPS = 250. H100 FP8 TOPS = 3,958. If forced to INT8, H100 falls back to INT8 TOPS (1,979), leaving ~2,000 TOPS unused. By using hardware-aware JIT quantization, 300 H100s provide 300 * 3958 = 1,187,400 TFLOPS (~1.18 ExaFLOPS), while 700 A10Gs provide 700 * 250 = 175,000 TFLOPS (175 PetaOPS). Total fleet compute is optimized, and artifact storage is kept to 1 model * 50B * 2 bytes = 100GB (plus <1GB for calibration metadata).
details.realistic_solution: Design a Just-In-Time (JIT) quantization architecture or a universal precision-aware artifact. Store the base model weights in the registry in BF16 (or a highly compressed format like FP4 with metadata if storage is the absolute bottleneck, though BF16 is standard). During the deployment phase (container initialization), the inference server queries the local hardware topology. If an H100 is detected, the server dynamically applies FP8 (E4M3) PTQ using pre-computed calibration scales stored as lightweight metadata in the artifact. If an A10G is detected, it applies INT8 SmoothQuant using its respective pre-computed scales. This decouples the representation from the artifact, maximizing hardware-specific TOPS while maintaining a single source of truth.

scenario: You manage a global serving fleet of 1,000 GPUs for a 50B parameter model. 300 are H100s (FP8 capable), and 700 are older A10Gs (only INT8 capable). You must deploy a single model artifact from CI/CD to simplify versioning, but you need to maximize hardware utilization to hit 50,000 QPS fleet-wide. Storing multiple 50GB artifacts in the registry is prohibited.
title: Mixed-Precision Fleet Integration

details.common_mistake: Assuming that increasing batch size linearly increases throughput until you run out of compute TFLOPS.
details.napkin_math: A100 Ridge Point: 312 TFLOPS / 2 TB/s ≈ 156 FLOPs/byte. 70B model in FP16 = 140GB weights. Distributed across 4 GPUs = 35GB/GPU. Max BW = 2 TB/s per GPU. Weight load time = 35GB / 2TB/s = 17.5ms per token. At BS=1, I = 2. At BS=64, I = 128 (still on the memory-bound slope!). KV Cache for BS=64 at 2k context = 64 (batch) * 2 (K+V) * 80 layers * 8 heads * 128 dim * 2000 seq_len * 2 bytes ≈ 41.9 GB. Total VRAM used: 35GB (weights) + 41.9GB (KV) + activations. You are out of VRAM before hitting the compute ridge.
details.realistic_solution: The decode phase of LLM generation is fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. At batch size 1, you must read the entire 140GB model from HBM to generate a single token, resulting in an extremely low arithmetic intensity (I ≈ 2 FLOPs/byte). As you increase batch size, you reuse the weights across multiple requests, increasing arithmetic intensity (I ≈ 2 * B). This moves the workload to the right on the Roofline model. However, increasing batch size also increases the KV cache size. Before you ever reach the compute-bound ridge point, you hit a memory capacity bound. The KV cache fills the remaining VRAM, forcing the system to either swap to CPU memory (shattering bandwidth) or recompute, which destroys latency. The plateau occurs because the system becomes bottlenecked by KV cache paging overheads and memory fragmentation, not ALU limits.

scenario: You are optimizing a Llama-70B serving cluster on 4x 80GB A100 GPUs. At batch size 1, the decode phase achieves 18 tokens/s per user. To hit a throughput target of 2000 tokens/s, the team proposes aggressively increasing the batch size to 256. However, at batch size 64, latency already spikes beyond the 100ms/token SLA, and throughput plateaus. Explain this bottleneck using the roofline model.
title: LLM Decode Batch Size Limits

details.common_mistake: Assuming that because hardware TOPS increase by 4x, the workload execution speed will scale proportionally.
details.napkin_math: Original FP16: 10ms total latency (9ms memory transfer, 1ms compute). INT8 halves memory transfer: 9ms / 2 = 4.5ms. INT8 compute is 4x faster: 1ms / 4 = 0.25ms. Add 0.5ms quantization overhead. New latency = 4.5 + 0.25 + 0.5 = 5.25ms. Expected speedup: 10 / 5.25 ≈ 1.9x. If actual is only 1.18x (8.4ms), kernel launch overheads (~3ms total) are dominating the critical path.
details.realistic_solution: RNNs process tokens sequentially, requiring the entire weight matrix to be loaded from HBM for every token. This makes them heavily memory-bandwidth bound (Arithmetic Intensity I ≈ 2 FLOPs/byte). When you move from FP16 to INT8, you halve the memory traffic, which theoretically doubles the speed of the memory-bound portion. However, the 4x increase in compute TOPS is completely irrelevant because the ALUs were already starving for data; raising the compute ceiling doesn't help a workload stuck on the memory bandwidth slope. Furthermore, the 18% actual improvement (instead of 50%) is due to two factors: 1) Quantization/dequantization overheads inject new compute operations that disrupt memory access pipelining, and 2) the workload is likely hitting kernel launch latency limits or PCIe overheads, meaning it is no longer just bandwidth-bound, but latency-bound.

scenario: Your team quantizes an RNN-based sequence model from FP16 to INT8. The target accelerator provides 4x more INT8 TOPS than FP16 TFLOPS, and the memory footprint is halved. The team expects a 3x-4x latency reduction, but the end-to-end latency only improves by 18%. Identify the discrepancy using workload characteristics.
title: The Quantization Roofline Paradox

details.common_mistake: Explaining that FlashAttention reduces memory footprint without connecting it to arithmetic intensity and HBM bandwidth ceilings.
details.napkin_math: Seq len N=32768, heads=32. Standard attention reads/writes O(N^2) to HBM. N^2 matrix = 32768 * 32768 * 2 bytes ≈ 2.1 GB per head. For 32 heads, that's 67 GB of HBM traffic per layer just for attention scores. FlashAttention only reads/writes O(N * d) to HBM. 32768 * 128 * 2 bytes ≈ 8 MB per head. HBM traffic drops from 67 GB to ~256 MB. Arithmetic intensity shifts from I ≈ 1 to I ≈ 128, moving from bandwidth-starved to compute-saturated.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention materializes the massive N x N attention score matrix to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). For N=32k, this requires reading and writing gigabytes of data per layer, forcing the operation deep into the memory-bandwidth bound region of the Roofline model. FlashAttention uses tiling to fuse the Softmax and matrix multiplications, keeping the intermediate N x N matrix entirely in fast, on-chip SRAM. By doing so, it drastically reduces HBM reads/writes. Even though the backward pass recomputes the forward pass (increasing total FLOPs), the Arithmetic Intensity (FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic) increases by orders of magnitude. The workload shifts from the memory-bound slope to the compute-bound ceiling. Because SRAM bandwidth is terabytes per second faster than HBM, the ALUs are finally kept fed, resulting in a 4x speedup despite the extra math.

scenario: While training a foundation model with a 32k context window, standard attention consumes 65% of the step time. You implement FlashAttention, which actually increases the total number of FLOPs performed by ~15% due to recomputation in the backward pass. Despite doing more math, the attention phase executes 4x faster. Explain the physical hardware mechanism enabling this.
title: Recomputation and Arithmetic Intensity

details.common_mistake: Blaming the routing network's compute overhead or network communication latency without analyzing the memory bandwidth degradation.
details.napkin_math: Dense 30B: Batch size 64. Weights read = 60GB (FP16). FLOPs = 2 * 30B * 64 = 3.84 TFLOPs. Intensity I = 3.84e12 / 60e9 = 64 FLOPs/byte. MoE 8x10B (2 active): Batch size 64. Assume all 8 experts are hit across the batch. Weights read = 160GB (80B params). FLOPs = 2 * 20B * 64 = 2.56 TFLOPs. Intensity I = 2.56e12 / 160e9 = 16 FLOPs/byte. The MoE model requires 2.6x more memory bandwidth per step, reducing throughput by ~30-60% depending on HBM limits.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck is the drastic reduction in effective Arithmetic Intensity. In a dense model, the 30B parameters are loaded from HBM once and applied to all 64 tokens in the batch. In the MoE model, tokens route to different experts. To process the batch, the hardware must load the weights for all activated experts. At batch size 64, it is highly probable that almost all experts (80B parameters total) are activated by at least one token. Therefore, the system loads ~80B parameters from HBM to do the math for 64 tokens, whereas the dense model loads 30B parameters for 64 tokens. The MoE model's arithmetic intensity is significantly lower, pushing it further down the memory-bound slope of the Roofline model. The hardware spends more time waiting for HBM reads, resulting in lower throughput despite fewer total FLOPs.

scenario: You are replacing a 30B parameter dense LLM with an 8x10B Mixture of Experts (MoE) model. The MoE model routes each token to 2 experts, resulting in roughly 20B active parameters per token. Since 20B < 30B, the MoE model requires fewer FLOPs per token. However, during serving at a batch size of 64, the MoE model's decode throughput (tokens/sec) is 30% lower than the dense model on the same hardware. Why?
title: MoE vs Dense Arithmetic Intensity

details.common_mistake: Assuming GPUs are always better due to higher bandwidth, or putting the whole model on CPU because of capacity.
details.napkin_math: MLP compute: 15,000 QPS * 50M FLOPs/query = 750 GFLOPs (trivial for GPU, slow on CPU). Embeddings: 200 features/query * 15,000 QPS = 3M lookups/sec. Each lookup fetches 128 bytes. Total bandwidth = 3M * 128B = 384 MB/s. This is tiny compared to peak bandwidth! The bottleneck is memory capacity (600GB > 80GB) and transaction latency. CPU DDR5 handles millions of random accesses well and has 2TB capacity. PCIe Gen4 x16 gives 32 GB/s, easily handling the 384 MB/s gathered vectors passed to the GPU.
details.realistic_solution: DLRMs exhibit a split-personality Roofline profile. The MLP layers are dense matrix multiplications with high arithmetic intensity, placing them firmly in the compute-bound regime where GPUs excel. Conversely, the embedding lookups are highly sparse, requiring random memory accesses. They have an arithmetic intensity of practically zero (just a gather/sum operation) and are bound by memory capacity and memory latency/transaction rate, not peak sequential bandwidth. Upgrading to 80GB GPUs requires sharding the 600GB tables across 8+ GPUs, incurring massive PCIe/NVLink all-to-all communication overheads that will bottleneck the 30k QPS target. The optimal L6+ architecture is heterogeneous: host the 600GB embedding tables on the high-capacity CPU memory (which has sufficient transaction rate for sparse lookups), and pipeline the gathered dense vectors over PCIe to the GPU to execute the compute-bound MLP.

scenario: Your massive click-through rate (CTR) model processes 15,000 QPS. It consists of 600GB of sparse embedding tables and a dense 6-layer MLP. To scale to 30,000 QPS, you must choose between upgrading to GPUs with 3.2 TB/s HBM (but only 80GB capacity per GPU), or moving to dual-socket CPUs with 12 channels of DDR5 (300 GB/s) and 2TB of capacity. Evaluate the tradeoffs using roofline principles.
title: DLRM Heterogeneous Bottlenecks

details.common_mistake: Agreeing that low-FLOP operations don't impact execution time, ignoring the memory bandwidth wall.
details.napkin_math: Tensor size: 10MB (FP16). Unfused (4 ops): Each op reads 10MB and writes 10MB. Total HBM traffic = 4 * 20MB = 80MB. At 1 TB/s HBM bandwidth, time = 80us. Fused (1 op): Read 10MB, compute all 4 ops in SRAM, write 10MB. Total HBM traffic = 20MB. Time = 20us. Add kernel launch overhead (~5us per launch). Unfused = 80us + (4 * 5us) = 100us. Fused = 20us + 5us = 25us. Speedup is 4x on that 40% of the model.
details.realistic_solution: Execution time is dictated by the Roofline model, not just total FLOPs. Element-wise operations have an Arithmetic Intensity of roughly 0.5 to 1 FLOPs/byte, placing them deep in the memory-bandwidth bound regime. Every individual kernel call (LayerNorm, ReLU, etc.) must read the activation tensor from HBM, perform a trivial calculation, and write it back to HBM. The hardware's ALUs sit idle waiting for memory. By fusing these four operations into a single kernel, the tensor is read from HBM once into SRAM, all four operations are computed in registers, and the result is written back to HBM once. This reduces HBM traffic by a factor of 4, directly reducing execution time for this block by up to 75%, while also eliminating three kernel launch overheads. The low FLOP count is exactly *why* they take so long relative to their math—they are entirely bandwidth-bound.

scenario: Optimizing a real-time speech recognition model, profiling shows 40% of inference time is spent in a sequence of element-wise operations (LayerNorm -> ReLU -> Dropout -> Scale). A junior engineer argues that fusing these kernels won't improve performance because these operations account for less than 1% of the model's total FLOPs. Counter this argument quantitatively.
title: Kernel Fusion Roofline Shift

details.common_mistake: Assuming latency scales strictly with FLOPs, or missing the quadratic sequence length scaling of attention mechanisms in the UNet.
details.napkin_math: At 512x512, downsampled by 8 in latent space = 64x64 latent. Sequence length N = 4096. Attention matrix size = 4096 * 4096 * 2 bytes ≈ 33 MB per head. At 1024x1024, latent is 128x128. Sequence length N = 16384. Attention matrix size = 16384 * 16384 * 2 bytes ≈ 536 MB per head. Traffic increases by 16x. If attention was 20% of the latency at 512x512 (e.g., 20ms out of 100ms) and convolutions were 80% (80ms). New conv time = 80 * 4 = 320ms. New attention time = 20 * 16 = 320ms (assuming bandwidth bound). Total latency = 640ms. 640 / 100 = 6.4x increase. With HBM thrashing, this easily hits 9x.
details.realistic_solution: The bottleneck lies in the self-attention layers within the diffusion UNet. When resolution doubles (512 to 1024), the sequence length (N = H * W) of the flattened feature maps increases by 4x. Standard self-attention has O(N^2) memory complexity for the attention matrix. Therefore, the memory read/write traffic for the attention scores increases by 16x! This massive explosion in memory traffic violently shifts the arithmetic intensity of the attention layers to the left. A workload that was previously sitting comfortably near the compute-bound ridge point at 512x512 suddenly falls off the cliff into the severely memory-bandwidth bound regime at 1024x1024. The 9x latency increase is a blend of the 4x compute increase in convolutional layers and the 16x memory latency increase in the attention layers.

scenario: You are upgrading a text-to-image diffusion model from generating 512x512 images to 1024x1024 images. The pixel count increases by 4x, and the theoretical FLOPs increase by ~4.5x. However, your profiling on A100 GPUs shows that latency per denoising step increases by nearly 9x. Diagnose the architectural bottleneck causing this super-linear scaling.
title: Diffusion Resolution Scaling Cliff

details.common_mistake: Relying on OS-level Unified Memory (UVM) or mmap to automatically page the KV cache from NVMe to HBM, which causes severe thread blocking and unpredictable latency spikes.
details.napkin_math: 1M tokens KV cache = 1M * 32 layers * 8 KV heads * 128 dim * 4 bytes (FP16 K+V) = 131GB. With 80GB HBM, only ~40GB is available for KV cache after model weights. We must page ~90GB. To sustain 10 tokens/sec, the attention operation needs to process 1M tokens per 100ms. PCIe Gen5 x16 bandwidth = 64GB/s. We can transfer 6.4GB per 100ms step. Therefore, we cannot fetch the entire 131GB per token; we must use a Ring Attention or FlashAttention-style block-wise compute that keeps older blocks in Host DRAM and only streams them into HBM in chunks of <6.4GB during the attention pass.
details.realistic_solution: Design an explicit, software-managed 3-tier memory hierarchy (NVMe -> Host DRAM -> HBM). Divide the KV cache into fixed-size block chunks (e.g., 256 tokens). Pin a sliding window of the most recent blocks in HBM. As generation proceeds, use dedicated background CUDA streams to prefetch upcoming KV blocks from Host DRAM via PCIe, while simultaneously evicting older blocks. Use Host DRAM as an L2 cache, pulling from NVMe asynchronously via io_uring or SPDK to bypass OS page cache overhead. Compute and I/O must be perfectly overlapped.

scenario: You are designing an inference engine to serve a 1-million context window Llama-3 8B model. The hardware is a single node with 8x H100 (80GB) GPUs, 2TB Host DRAM, and 4x Gen5 NVMe drives. The KV cache for a single request exceeds the available HBM. Design a paging architecture to stream KV cache across the memory hierarchy while maintaining at least 10 tokens/sec decoding speed.
title: Massive Context KV Cache Paging

details.common_mistake: Assuming a memory leak in Python/PyTorch and adding garbage collection calls, or simply reducing the max batch size without addressing the underlying allocation pattern.
details.napkin_math: Assume batch size 64. Pre-allocating max length (8000 tokens) naively requires 8000 * 64 * 125KB (approx per token KV) = 64GB (which leaves almost no room for the model weights on an 80GB GPU). Dynamic allocation of varying sizes (e.g., 100 to 8000) causes gaps. If 45GB is allocated but fragmented into 50MB chunks, an attempt to allocate a contiguous 1GB tensor for a new long sequence fails. With a block size of 16 tokens (approx 2MB), a 40GB KV pool provides 20,000 perfectly reusable slots, ensuring 100% utilization regardless of sequence length variance.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is severe external and internal memory fragmentation. Contiguous memory allocators (like PyTorch's default caching allocator) struggle when allocating and freeing variable-sized KV cache tensors over long periods. When a large contiguous block is requested for an 8000-token sequence, the allocator fails because available memory is scattered in small chunks. The architectural fix is to implement a paged memory manager (e.g., PagedAttention). Pre-allocate a single massive contiguous block of HBM at startup. Divide it into fixed-size physical blocks (e.g., 16 or 32 tokens). Maintain a page table mapping logical token blocks to physical blocks, completely eliminating external fragmentation and bounding internal fragmentation to <1 block per request.

scenario: Your dynamic batching LLM server runs perfectly for the first 6 hours, processing requests with varying lengths (100 to 8000 tokens). However, around hour 12, the service consistently crashes with CUDA OOM, despite Prometheus metrics showing the theoretical peak memory usage never exceeding 45GB on an 80GB A100 GPU. Diagnose the root cause and architect a robust memory management subsystem.
title: Long-Running Inference OOM Death

details.common_mistake: Attempting to load entire rows of the attention matrix into shared memory, which exceeds the strict physical limits of SRAM per Streaming Multiprocessor (SM).
details.napkin_math: Naive intermediate QK^T size: 131,072 * 131,072 * 2 bytes (FP16) = ~34.3 GB per head. Reading/writing this to HBM at 2 TB/s (A100 spec) takes 34.3 / 2000 * 2 = 0.0343 seconds (34.3 ms) per layer. While 34.3 ms sounds small, over 96 layers this becomes ~3.3 seconds per token just for memory transfers, yielding terrible MFU. An A100 has 164 KB of shared memory per SM. We can choose a block size of 128x128. Block of K (128x128x2 bytes = 32 KB) and V (32 KB) fit comfortably in the 164 KB SRAM, leaving room for Q blocks and intermediate register spills, keeping all O(N^2) operations on-chip.
details.realistic_solution: The architecture must implement hardware-aware block tiling (similar to FlashAttention). The intermediate N x N attention matrix (Q*K^T) is too large to materialize in HBM, let alone SRAM. We must tile the computation into blocks that fit entirely within the SM's shared memory (SRAM). Load a block of K and V into SRAM. Then, stream blocks of Q from HBM to SRAM, compute the partial attention scores, update the running maximum and denominator for the softmax (using the online safe softmax trick), multiply by V, and accumulate the result in registers. Finally, write the output block back to HBM. This reduces HBM accesses from O(N^2) to O(N).

scenario: You are writing a custom fused CUDA kernel for a novel sliding-window attention mechanism used in DNA sequence modeling (seq_len=131,072). The naive PyTorch implementation achieves only 5% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) because it is entirely memory-bandwidth bound. Architect the memory access pattern utilizing registers, SRAM (Shared Memory), and HBM to maximize arithmetic intensity.
title: SRAM Tiling for Custom Attention

details.common_mistake: Focusing on optimizing the attention kernel or upgrading the CPU, ignoring that batch size 1 MoE decoding is fundamentally bottlenecked by HBM memory bandwidth for weight loading.
details.napkin_math: 8x7B MoE. Total params = 56B (~112GB in FP16). Active params per token (2 experts + dense layers) = ~14B params = 28GB in FP16. HBM bandwidth on an A100 is ~2000 GB/s. Time to read 28GB = 28 / 2000 = 14ms per token. 1000ms / 14ms = ~71 tokens/sec theoretical max, but overheads drop this to 8-10. Quantizing weights to 4-bit reduces active payload to 7GB. 7 / 2000 = 3.5ms per token, raising the theoretical ceiling to 285 tokens/sec, easily meeting the 40 tokens/sec SLA.
details.realistic_solution: At batch size 1, autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound (low arithmetic intensity). For an MoE, each token routes to a subset of experts (e.g., 2 out of 8). The GPU must fetch the weights of these specific experts from HBM to SRAM for every single token. To hit the SLA, we must increase arithmetic intensity or reduce memory footprint. Solutions: 1) Implement continuous batching to serve multiple requests concurrently, amortizing the cost of fetching expert weights across multiple tokens. 2) If strictly single-user, apply 4-bit weight-only quantization (e.g., AWQ/GPTQ) to reduce the HBM read volume by 4x. 3) Implement speculative decoding, which processes multiple tokens in a single forward pass, fetching the massive expert weights once for a batch of draft tokens.

scenario: Your startup is serving an 8x7B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model for code generation. At batch size 1 (interactive local testing), the token generation rate is 8 tokens/sec, far below the 40 tokens/sec SLA. Profiling reveals the GPU compute units are idle 90% of the time. Evaluate the memory hierarchy bottleneck and propose an architectural solution to hit the SLA.
title: MoE Weight Fetching Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Synchronously copying adapters from Host DRAM to GPU HBM on every request using standard `cudaMemcpy`, which blocks the compute stream and violates the 200ms SLA during burst traffic.
details.napkin_math: 10,000 adapters * 50MB = 500GB total size (exceeds 80GB HBM). Base model = 26GB. PCIe Gen5 x16 bandwidth = 64GB/s. Transferring a 50MB adapter takes 50MB / 64GB/s = ~0.78ms. A typical forward pass for the base model takes ~20ms. Since 0.78ms << 20ms, the PCIe transfer of the adapter can be completely hidden behind the compute of the previous batch, provided async streams and pinned memory are used.
details.realistic_solution: Design a 3-tier caching architecture: HBM (L1), Pinned Host DRAM (L2), and NVMe (L3). The 13B base model takes ~26GB (FP16). Allocate 40GB of HBM as an LRU cache for the hottest ~800 adapters. Allocate 500GB of pinned Host DRAM for the remaining 9,200 adapters. Crucially, use separate CUDA streams for compute and memory transfers. When a request arrives for an un-cached adapter, trigger an async DMA transfer from Pinned DRAM to HBM over PCIe. Batch requests by adapter ID. While the DMA transfer occurs, the compute stream processes requests for already-cached adapters. This perfectly overlaps PCIe memory bandwidth with GPU compute.

scenario: You must serve 10,000 distinct LoRA adapters for a 13B base model on a single H100 (80GB). Each adapter is 50MB. The traffic follows a heavy-tailed Zipfian distribution. The strict latency SLA is 200ms per request. Architect a multi-tier memory hierarchy to route and swap adapters without stalling the base model compute pipeline.
title: High-Density LoRA Adapter Swapping

details.common_mistake: Relying on OS-level page faults (mmap) to pull embeddings from NVMe directly, resulting in massive I/O amplification, thread blocking, and missing the 50ms p99 SLA.
details.napkin_math: 10,000 QPS * 100 features per request = 1M embedding lookups/sec. NVMe random read IOPS per drive is ~1M, so 8 drives yield 8M IOPS (sufficient throughput). NVMe latency is ~10-50us. DRAM latency is ~100ns. HBM latency is ~1us (but massive bandwidth). If cache hit rates are 80% L1, 15% L2, 5% L3: we do 50,000 NVMe reads/sec. 50k reads * 128 bytes (embedding size) = 6.4 MB/s PCIe traffic, which is trivial. The latency is dominated by the 5% NVMe lookups (~50us), comfortably fitting within the 50ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a software-managed, explicitly tiered embedding cache. HBM acts as L1 (caching the top 5% hottest embeddings, ~300GB across 8 GPUs). Host DRAM acts as L2 (caching the next 30%, ~1.5TB). NVMe acts as L3 (storing all 5TB). Use a hash-based routing mechanism to shard requests across GPUs. For L3 (NVMe) lookups, bypass the OS page cache entirely using `O_DIRECT` and async I/O (io_uring) to eliminate memory copies and CPU overhead. Implement a background prefetching thread that predicts upcoming lookups (e.g., using user session context) to promote embeddings from NVMe -> DRAM -> HBM before the forward pass requires them.

scenario: Your recommendation system uses an enormous Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) with 5TB of embedding tables. The hardware is a single node with 8x A100 (80GB) GPUs, 2TB Host RAM, and 8x 3.2TB NVMe drives. You need to process 10,000 QPS with p99 latency < 50ms. Architect the embedding lookup system across this memory hierarchy.
title: Multi-Tier Embedding Lookups

details.common_mistake: Offloading all activations to Host CPU RAM indiscriminately, which bottlenecks on PCIe Gen4 bandwidth and severely degrades training speed.
details.napkin_math: 1 volume = 512^3 pixels = 134M pixels. A single 32-channel FP32 activation tensor = 134M * 32 * 4 bytes = 17.1GB. PCIe Gen4 x16 bandwidth = 32GB/s. Offloading one such tensor takes 17.1 / 32 = ~0.53 seconds. If we offload 5 such tensors, it takes 2.65s (bottlenecking the 1.5 iter/sec goal). By selectively discarding and recomputing ReLU/Norm (which takes <10ms to recompute but 0.5s to transfer) and only offloading the bottleneck convolutions, we stay under the 80GB HBM limit and bypass the PCIe bottleneck.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a heterogeneous activation management strategy based on the arithmetic intensity of each layer type. The architecture must evaluate layer characteristics: Convolutional layers are compute-heavy but produce relatively small activations. Normalization and Activation layers (e.g., BatchNorm, ReLU) are compute-light but memory-bandwidth heavy (large activations). Strategy: Use Activation Checkpointing (recompute) for memory-heavy/compute-light layers, saving massive HBM without much compute penalty. For compute-heavy layers, asynchronously offload the activations to Host DRAM over PCIe using dedicated CUDA streams, overlapping the transfer with the computation of subsequent layers.

scenario: Training a 3D UNet on 512x512x512 CT scans (batch size 1) requires 180GB for forward pass activations, but you only have an 80GB A100 GPU. Using full activation checkpointing (recomputing all layers) drops throughput to 0.5 iter/sec. Goal is 1.5 iter/sec. Propose a hybrid memory architecture balancing recompute and PCIe offloading.
title: 3D CNN Activation Checkpointing

details.common_mistake: Loading the model in FP16 and assuming the OS will gracefully swap to the NVMe SSD, which drops token generation speed from 20 tokens/sec to <1 token/sec due to SSD latency.
details.napkin_math: Available Memory = 10GB. 8B model at 4-bit = 8 billion * 0.5 bytes = 4.0GB + metadata = ~4.5GB. Memory bandwidth is 100GB/s. Generating 1 token requires reading all weights. 100GB/s / 4.5GB = 22.2 tokens/sec theoretical maximum, which perfectly aligns with the 20 tokens/sec SLA. KV Cache calculation: 32,000 tokens * 32 layers * 8 heads * 128 dim * 2 bytes (FP16) * 2 (K+V) = 4,194,304,000 bytes (~4.2GB). Quantizing to 8-bit halves this to 2.1GB, leaving a 2.4GB safety buffer for IDE spikes.
details.realistic_solution: With Unified Memory, the CPU and GPU share the same physical RAM, but exceeding physical capacity invokes swap space (SSD), which destroys LLM inference speed. Total available RAM = 16GB - 6GB (OS) = 10GB. An 8B model in FP16 requires 16GB (OOM). The architecture must aggressively compress both weights and KV cache. Step 1: Quantize weights to 4-bit (e.g., AWQ/GGUF), reducing weight footprint to ~4.5GB. Step 2: Quantize the KV cache to 8-bit. A 32k context KV cache in FP16 takes ~4.2GB. At 8-bit, it takes ~2.1GB. Total memory footprint: 4.5GB (weights) + 2.1GB (KV) + 1GB (workspace) = 7.6GB. This fits safely under the 10GB limit, avoiding SSD swap.

scenario: Deploying a local 8B parameter coding assistant on an Apple Silicon laptop with a Unified Memory Architecture (16GB RAM, 100GB/s bandwidth). The OS and IDE constantly consume 6GB. The target is 20 tokens/sec, supporting a 32,000 token context window. Architect the precision and memory layout to prevent catastrophic SSD swapping.
title: Edge LLM Unified Memory Sizing

details.common_mistake: Assuming operator fusion always strictly reduces memory traffic without side effects like register pressure.
details.napkin_math:
Unfused: 100M * 4 bytes = 400MB per read/write. 4 ops = 4 reads, 4 writes. Total traffic = 3.2GB. 3.2GB / 32 GB/s = 100ms.
Fused (Expected): 1 read, 1 write. Total traffic = 800MB. 800MB / 32 GB/s = 25ms.
Fused (Actual): Spilling causes ~12 uncoalesced reads/writes per element. Traffic = 4.8GB. Uncoalesced access drops effective bandwidth to ~32 GB/s. 4.8GB / 32 GB/s = 150ms.
details.realistic_solution: The failure is caused by catastrophic register spilling. While operator fusion theoretically increases arithmetic intensity by keeping intermediate values in registers, fusing too many operations (or operations with high variable counts) exceeds the physical register file size per thread block. When registers are exhausted, the compiler spills variables to local memory, which is physically backed by the slow HBM. Because these spills are often uncoalesced, the effective memory bandwidth drops significantly below the theoretical maximum. The workload, already possessing low arithmetic intensity, is now pinned against a severely degraded memory bandwidth ceiling on the Roofline model.

scenario: You are optimizing a custom inference chip (32 GB/s HBM, 16 TFLOPS). You fuse a sequence of 4 element-wise operations (Add, Mul, ReLU, Add) operating on a 100M element FP32 tensor. Unfused latency was 100ms. You expected fusion to drop latency to 25ms by eliminating HBM roundtrips. Instead, the fused kernel takes 150ms. Profiling shows ALU utilization is < 5%.
title: The Operator Fusion Trap

details.common_mistake: Calculating latency using only theoretical MACs and peak TOPS, ignoring the Roofline memory wall.
details.napkin_math:
NPU Ridge Point: 4 TOPS / 20 GB/s = 200 MACs/byte.
Standard Conv: 2.5 GMACs / 5MB = 500 MACs/byte. (Compute bound: 2.5 GMACs / 4 TOPS = 0.625ms. Actual 1.25ms implies ~50% ALU utilization).
Depthwise Conv: 0.3 GMACs / 5MB = 60 MACs/byte. (Memory bound: 5MB / 20 GB/s = 0.25ms theoretical). The degradation to 2.5ms means effective bandwidth collapsed to 2 GB/s due to poor NPU DMA utilization with depthwise access patterns.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a massive drop in arithmetic intensity, shifting the workload from compute-bound to severely memory-bound. Standard convolutions heavily reuse weights and activations, resulting in high arithmetic intensity that allows the NPU to approach its 4 TOPS ceiling. Depthwise convolutions, however, only apply one filter per input channel, resulting in an arithmetic intensity of roughly 1 MAC/byte. On the Roofline model, the NPU's ridge point is 200 MACs/byte (4 TOPS / 20 GB/s). Depthwise convolutions operate far to the left of the ridge point. The NPU is starved for data, and the overhead of fragmented memory access patterns for depthwise operations further degrades effective bandwidth.

scenario: Your mobile vision team replaced standard 3x3 convolutions with depthwise separable convolutions in a custom ResNet, reducing theoretical compute from 2.5 GMACs to 0.3 GMACs per frame. Deployed on an edge NPU (4 TOPS, 20 GB/s bandwidth), latency surprisingly degraded from 1.25ms to 2.5ms. The memory footprint (5MB of activations/weights) remained identical.
title: Depthwise Separable Disappointment

details.common_mistake: Assuming a 3x TFLOPS upgrade will uniformly speed up all phases of LLM generation.
details.napkin_math:
Prefill (Compute Bound): A100 Compute = 286 TFLOPs / 312 TFLOPS = 916ms. H100 Compute = 286 TFLOPs / 989 TFLOPS = 289ms (~3.1x).
Decode (Memory Bound): 70B FP16 weights = 140GB. A100 Memory Time = 140GB / 2.0 TB/s = 70ms. H100 Memory Time = 140 GB / 3.35 TB/s = 42ms (~1.67x).
details.realistic_solution: There is no bug; this is a textbook demonstration of the Roofline model. LLM generation consists of two distinct phases with radically different arithmetic intensities. The prefill phase performs a matrix-matrix multiplication (weights * sequence of tokens), resulting in high arithmetic intensity. It sits on the flat, compute-bound ceiling of the Roofline. Therefore, prefill scales perfectly with the 3.1x increase in TFLOPS (989/312). The decode phase, however, performs a matrix-vector multiplication (weights * 1 token), which has an arithmetic intensity of ~1 FLOP/byte. It sits entirely on the sloped, memory-bandwidth-bound section of the Roofline. Decode latency is purely dictated by memory bandwidth, scaling exactly with the 1.67x increase in HBM bandwidth (3.35/2.0).

scenario: You upgraded an LLM serving cluster from A100 (312 TFLOPS, 2 TB/s) to H100 (989 TFLOPS, 3.35 TB/s). For a 70B parameter model at batch size 1, the prefill phase latency (2048 tokens) dropped from 916ms to 295ms (3.1x speedup). However, decode latency per token only dropped from 70ms to 42ms (1.6x speedup). The team suspects a PyTorch bug.
title: The H100 Speedup Discrepancy

details.common_mistake: Assuming FlashAttention is always faster because it eliminates HBM reads/writes, regardless of sequence length.
details.napkin_math: Sequence length 196, dim 1024. Standard attention matrix is 196*196*2B (FP16) = 76.8KB. This tiny matrix easily fits entirely in the A100's 40MB L2 cache. FlashAttention avoids HBM roundtrips by fusing ops in SRAM, but since 76KB doesn't spill to the 2TB/s HBM anyway, the memory savings are moot. The extra FLOPs overhead actually makes it slower for small sequences.
details.realistic_solution: FlashAttention optimizes the memory roofline by tiling the attention matrix to avoid writing the O(N^2) intermediate attention matrix to HBM. It trades memory bandwidth for extra compute (recomputation in backward, and extra ALU instructions for tiling/scaling in forward). However, for very short sequence lengths like 196, the attention matrix is extremely small. It fits entirely within the A100's massive 40MB L2 cache. Therefore, standard attention is not HBM-bandwidth bound; it runs at L2 cache bandwidth speeds (~5-10 TB/s). Because the memory bottleneck FlashAttention solves doesn't exist for this workload, you only incur the extra ALU overhead, shifting the workload up the compute ceiling and increasing latency.

scenario: You serve a Vision Transformer on an A100 (40MB L2 cache, 2TB/s HBM). The sequence length is 196 (14x14 patches), with embedding dim 1024. Standard PyTorch attention takes 0.8ms. You upgrade to FlashAttention-2, expecting a 2x speedup by eliminating HBM read/writes. Instead, latency increases to 1.2ms.
title: The FlashAttention Paradox

details.common_mistake: Assuming workload throughput scales linearly with core clock frequency (compute capacity) for all deep learning tasks.
details.napkin_math:
A100 Ridge Point = 312 TFLOPS / 2 TB/s = 156 FLOPs/Byte.
Whisper BS=1 Decode Arithmetic Intensity ≈ 2 FLOPs/Byte.
2 << 156. The workload is completely memory-bound.
Underclocked Ridge Point = (312 * 0.6) / 2 TB/s = 93 FLOPs/Byte.
2 << 93. The workload remains completely memory-bound, so throughput is unaffected.
details.realistic_solution: The Whisper workload at batch size 1 has an extremely low arithmetic intensity (dominated by memory fetches for autoregressive decoding), placing it far to the left of the Roofline ridge point. It is entirely memory-bandwidth bound. The GPU ALUs spend the vast majority of their time idle, waiting for data from HBM. Lowering the core clock reduces the horizontal compute ceiling of the Roofline model but leaves the sloped memory bandwidth ceiling unchanged. Because the workload's operating point is on the slope, dropping the compute ceiling has almost zero effect on performance. However, power consumption scales roughly with voltage^2 * frequency, resulting in massive power savings with no latency penalty.

scenario: To save datacenter power, you underclock the GPU cores of an A100 cluster running Whisper (audio transcription) at batch size 1. You drop the core clock by 40% (1410 MHz -> 846 MHz), reducing peak TFLOPS by 40%. You expect a 40% drop in throughput. Surprisingly, throughput only drops by 1%, while GPU power consumption drops by 35%.
title: The Power-Clock Anomaly

details.common_mistake: Ignoring intermediate activation sizes and assuming theoretical peak NPU TOPS can be reached regardless of SRAM capacity.
details.napkin_math:
4K Image (3840x2160) = 8.3M pixels.
Activations (e.g., 64 channels, FP16) = 8.3M * 64 * 2 bytes = 1.06 GB per layer.
1.06 GB >> 2MB SRAM.
For a 10-layer model, memory traffic = 10 * 1.06 GB (read) + 10 * 1.06 GB (write) ≈ 20 GB.
Time spent on memory = 20 GB / 30 GB/s = 666ms (or 333ms if fused partially). Compute time = 10ms. Total time is dominated by memory IO.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is aggressive SRAM spilling to main memory. A 4K feature map with even a modest number of channels is massive. Because the intermediate activations far exceed the NPU's 2MB SRAM, every layer must write its output to main memory and the next layer must read it back. This drops the arithmetic intensity of the model drastically. The workload hits the bandwidth roofline ceiling of the mobile SoC. The NPU ALUs process the data almost instantly but then sit idle waiting hundreds of milliseconds for the memory controller to fetch the next layer's inputs from LPDDR.

scenario: Deploying a 4K Super-Resolution model on a mobile SoC (NPU: 10 TOPS, 30 GB/s main memory bandwidth, 2MB NPU SRAM). The model requires 100 GMACs per frame. Based on 10 TOPS, expected latency is 10ms (100 FPS). Actual latency is 333ms (3 FPS). Profiling shows NPU ALU utilization is below 3%.
title: Mobile NPU Utilization Collapse

details.common_mistake: Assuming memory bandwidth scales linearly with precision reduction without accounting for ALU unpacking overhead or hardware fetch limits.
details.napkin_math:
FP16: 26GB / 1 TB/s = 26ms.
INT8: 13GB / 1 TB/s = 13ms.
INT4: 6.5GB / 1 TB/s = 6.5ms (Memory theoretical).
BUT, Unpacking INT4 requires ~5 instructions per weight. 13B weights = 65 G-Ops. Due to dependency chains and register pressure in the unpacking kernel, effective ALU utilization is low, taking ~12ms. max(6.5ms, 12ms) = 12ms.
details.realistic_solution: The workload experienced a bottleneck shift on the Roofline model. At FP16 and INT8, the decode phase was strictly memory-bandwidth bound, so halving the weight size halved the latency. However, standard GPUs do not have native 4-bit memory load instructions; they load 32-bit or 8-bit registers. INT4 weights must be explicitly unpacked and dequantized into FP16 using bitwise shifts and masks on the ALUs before the matrix multiplication can occur. This decompression requires significant compute instructions per byte. At INT4, the compute required for unpacking exceeds the time saved by fetching fewer bytes, shifting the workload from the memory-bandwidth slope to the compute-bound ceiling for the unpacking kernel.

scenario: Serving Llama-2 13B on an RTX 4090 (1 TB/s bandwidth). FP16 decode latency is 26ms/token. You apply INT8 weight-only quantization, and latency drops to 13ms/token. Next, you apply INT4 weight-only quantization, expecting latency to drop to 6.5ms. Instead, latency plateaus at 12ms/token.
title: The INT4 Quantization Plateau

details.common_mistake: Assuming increasing batch size strictly increases arithmetic intensity and throughput without encountering architectural memory cliffs.
details.napkin_math:
KV Cache per token = 2KB (assuming specific hidden dim/layers).
BS=16, Seq=1024: 16 * 1024 * 2KB = 32MB. 32MB < 40MB (Fits in L2 @ 5 TB/s).
BS=128, Seq=1024: 128 * 1024 * 2KB = 256MB. 256MB >> 40MB (Spills to HBM @ 2 TB/s).
Bandwidth drops by over 2.5x. Arithmetic intensity increase from batching weights doesn't offset the massive latency penalty of reading 256MB from HBM for every generation step.
details.realistic_solution: The system hit an L2 cache capacity cliff, causing the effective memory bandwidth roofline to collapse. At smaller batch sizes, the entire KV cache for the batch fits within the A100's massive 40MB L2 cache. The attention mechanism can read the KV cache at L2 bandwidth speeds (~5 TB/s). When the batch size is increased to 128, the KV cache size exceeds the L2 capacity. The KV cache spills into HBM. Because attention is a memory-bound operation, forcing it to fetch from HBM (2 TB/s) instead of L2 drops the effective bandwidth by over 2.5x. The roofline ceiling shifts downward abruptly, throttling the throughput despite the higher batch size.

scenario: Serving an LLM on an A100 (40MB L2 cache, 2TB/s HBM). At batch size 16 (Sequence Length = 1024), throughput is 500 tokens/s. To maximize throughput, you increase batch size to 128. You expect throughput to scale linearly as arithmetic intensity increases. Instead, throughput drops to 300 tokens/s.
title: The KV Cache Roofline Collapse

details.common_mistake: Assuming the GPU is simply overloaded and decreasing the maximum batch size to reduce compute pressure.
details.napkin_math: Compute time for 4k prefill = ~150ms. Decode time = ~20ms. Synchronous iteration time = max(150, 20) = 150ms (SLA violation). Chunked to 512 tokens: Chunk compute = ~18ms. Iteration time = max(18, 20) = 20ms (SLA met).
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the latency: Continuous batching mixes prefill and decode phases in the same forward pass. A 4k-token prefill requires massive matrix multiplications, taking ~150ms of compute. Because the GPU executes the batch synchronously, the decode steps for all other requests in the batch are blocked until the 150ms prefill completes, violating the 50ms TPOT SLA. The architectural requirement is to implement Chunked Prefill (e.g., Sarathi or Piggybacking). By chunking the 4k prompt into segments of 512 tokens, the prefill compute is bounded to ~20ms per step. This allows decode steps to interleave, keeping the step latency below 45ms and satisfying the TPOT SLA while slightly increasing TTFT.

scenario: You operate a multi-turn chat service using a 13B model on A100 GPUs. The business SLA mandates a Time Between Tokens (TPOT) of < 50ms to ensure smooth text generation. With continuous batching enabled, average TPOT is 25ms. However, P99 TPOT frequently spikes to 200ms+. Telemetry shows these spikes correlate exactly with new users submitting long prompts (e.g., 4k tokens) into the system.
title: Continuous Batching Decode Spikes

details.common_mistake: Increasing the number of draft tokens generated per step (e.g., from 5 to 10) to increase the potential acceptance yield.
details.napkin_math: Current: T_step = 50ms + 30ms = 80ms. Yield = 2.5 tokens. TPOT = 80 / 2.5 = 32ms. (Worse than 30ms base). Proposed (<1B draft): T_draft = 2ms * 5 = 10ms. T_step = 10ms + 30ms = 40ms. Yield = 2.5. TPOT = 40 / 2.5 = 16ms (SLA met).
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the speculative decoding latency: T_step = (T_draft * K) + T_verify. The draft model takes 10ms per token (50ms/5). The verify step takes 30ms. Total step latency = 80ms. With an expected acceptance rate E(N) of 1.5 tokens + 1 guaranteed token = 2.5 tokens per step. The effective TPOT = 80ms / 2.5 tokens = 32ms. Speculative decoding only works if T_draft is negligible or E(N) is exceptionally high. A 7B model is architecturally too large/slow for a 70B target. You must replace the 7B draft model with a much smaller <1B model (T_draft < 2ms), or eliminate the draft model entirely by using Medusa/EAGLE heads attached directly to the 70B model, reducing T_draft to 0.

scenario: You are optimizing a code generation API using a 70B target model with a strict TPOT SLA of < 25ms. Currently, the target model achieves 30ms TPOT. To accelerate it, you deploy a 7B draft model for speculative decoding. The draft model generates 5 tokens in 50ms. The target model verifies them in 30ms. The domain acceptance rate is 1.5 tokens per step. The resulting TPOT worsens to 32ms.
title: Speculative Decoding Economics

details.common_mistake: Adding more GPUs to increase total VRAM, or reducing the model's precision to INT4 to fit the batch size.
details.napkin_math: KV cache per token for Llama-2 13B (40 layers, 40 KV heads, head_dim=128, FP16): 2 (K+V) × 40 × 40 × 128 × 2 bytes = 819,200 bytes ≈ 800 KB per token. This already accounts for all layers. Block size 512 tokens = 512 × 800 KB = 400 MB per block. For batch=128 requests (avg 80 tokens each): reserved = 128 blocks × 400 MB = 50 GB. Actual needed: 128 × 80 × 800 KB = 8 GB. Wasted: 42 GB — causes OOM on an 80 GB GPU (model weights ~26 GB + 50 GB reserved = 76 GB, no room for activations). Block size 16: each request needs ceil(80/16) = 5 blocks × 16 × 800 KB = 64 MB. Total reserved: 128 × 64 MB = 8.2 GB ≈ actual usage. Problem solved without extra hardware.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the memory allocation latency and capacity. The architectural failure is massive internal memory fragmentation. With a block size of 512 tokens, every request, regardless of its actual length, reserves a minimum of one full block. Since the average request is 80 tokens, 432 tokens of KV cache memory per request are pre-allocated but completely wasted. This is an 84% memory waste. The architecture requirement is to reduce the PagedAttention block size to 16 or 32 tokens. This drastically reduces internal fragmentation, freeing up enough VRAM to easily support the required batch size of 128 without buying more hardware.

scenario: You are designing a high-throughput translation API. The system requires a batch size of 128 to meet the 2000 QPS throughput SLA. Average prompt + generation length is 80 tokens. You configure PagedAttention with a block size of 512 tokens to minimize pointer overhead. The system constantly OOMs at a batch size of just 32, failing the throughput requirement.
title: Paged Attention Internal Fragmentation

details.common_mistake: Assuming the prefill compute is bottlenecked and buying faster GPUs for the prefill cluster.
details.napkin_math: KV Cache size per token = 2 (K,V) * 80 layers * 8 heads * 128 dim * 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes (~327 KB). For 10,000 tokens = 3.27 GB. Network speed = 100 Gbps = 12.5 GB/s. Transfer latency = 3.27 GB / 10 GB/s (effective) = 327ms. Total TTFT = 150ms + 327ms = 477ms.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the end-to-end TTFT latency: Client TTFT = Prefill Compute + KV Cache Network Transfer + Initial Decode Step + Network RTT. The hidden bottleneck is the KV cache transfer. Llama-3 70B has 80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim. A 10k token prompt generates ~3.27 GB of KV cache. Over a 100 Gbps (12.5 GB/s theoretical, ~10 GB/s actual) network, transferring this cache takes ~327ms. 150ms compute + 327ms transfer = 477ms TTFT. To fix this architecture, you must upgrade the inter-node network to Infiniband (400 Gbps / 800 Gbps) with RDMA to reduce transfer time to <50ms, or abandon disaggregation for long-context requests and route them to single nodes.

scenario: To optimize your Llama-3 70B serving cluster, you implement disaggregated architecture: separating Prefill (Compute-bound) onto A100s and Decode (Memory-bound) onto H100s. For a 10k token prompt, the Prefill TTFT is 150ms and Decode TPOT is 20ms. However, end-to-end TTFT measured by the client spikes to ~400ms. The nodes are connected via a 100 Gbps Ethernet network.
title: Disaggregated Prefill Network Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Optimizing the CPU RAM speed or trying to compress the KV cache using standard ZIP/LZ4 algorithms before transfer.
details.napkin_math: KV size: 50,000 tokens * 327 KB/token (Llama-3 70B) = 16.35 GB. PCIe Gen4 x16 effective bandwidth = ~26 GB/s. Transfer time = 16.35 GB / 26 GB/s = 628ms. 628ms + 50ms (user prompt prefill) = 678ms > 500ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the cached TTFT latency: TTFT = KV Cache PCIe Load Time + User Prompt Prefill + Decode Step. The 50k token system prompt generates a ~16.3 GB KV cache for a 70B model. PCIe Gen4 x16 has a theoretical max bandwidth of 32 GB/s (realistically ~26 GB/s). Transferring 16.3 GB takes ~620ms. The architecture is bound by PCIe bandwidth, not compute. To meet the 500ms SLA, the architecture must change: the shared 50k KV cache must be pinned as a resident block directly in GPU VRAM (sacrificing some batch size capacity), or the model must use Multi-Query Attention/Grouped-Query Attention to drastically reduce the absolute size of the KV cache, or upgrade to PCIe Gen5 / NVLink.

scenario: You are building a multi-tenant RAG application using a 70B model. Every request shares a massive 50k token system prompt. TTFT SLA is 500ms. Standard prefill takes 1.5s. You implement RadixAttention prompt caching, storing the 50k KV cache on host CPU RAM (NVMe offload) and loading it on demand over PCIe Gen4 x16. The TTFT drops, but only to ~700ms, failing the 500ms SLA.
title: Prompt Caching PCIe Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Attempting to optimize compute with FlashAttention or fusing CUDA kernels, which only helps compute-bound workloads.
details.napkin_math: Model size = 70 billion parameters * 2 bytes (FP16) = 140 GB. Hardware bandwidth = 2 * 2.0 TB/s = 4.0 TB/s. Minimum physical time to read weights = 140 GB / 4000 GB/s = 0.035 seconds = 35ms. 35ms > 20ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the decode step latency: In autoregressive generation (batch size 1), the operation is entirely Memory Bandwidth Bound. For every single token generated, the entire 140 GB model weight matrix must be read from HBM to SRAM. Compute time is negligible. T_token = Model_Size / Total_Memory_Bandwidth. 140 GB / 4000 GB/s = 35ms. It is physically impossible to hit 20ms on this hardware in FP16. The architectural requirement is to either quantize the model weights to INT8/INT4 (reducing weights to 70GB/35GB -> 23ms/11ms latency), or double the hardware footprint to 4x A100s to aggregate 6.0 TB/s of memory bandwidth.

scenario: You deploy a 70B parameter model (FP16) for a real-time voice agent. Target TPOT is 20ms. The model is deployed on 2x A100 80GB GPUs (Tensor Parallelism, 2 TB/s bandwidth each). Even with a batch size of 1, the best TPOT achieved is ~48ms, severely violating the 20ms requirement.
title: Memory Bandwidth Bound Decode

details.common_mistake: Blaming continuous batching overhead and reverting to static batching, or trying to optimize the TPOT slightly.
details.napkin_math: Prefill = 1s. Generate 1000 tokens at 30ms TPOT = 30s. Total request time = 31s. With max batch size 8, throughput is 8 requests / 31s = 0.258 QPS. Incoming rate is 2 QPS. Deficit = 1.74 requests/sec added to queue. After 10 mins (600s), queue has 600 * 1.74 = 1044 requests. A new request waits 1044 / 0.258 QPS = 4046 seconds (~67 mins) before processing.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose latency using Queueing Theory: End-to-End Latency = Queue Time + Prefill Time + (Tokens * TPOT). Service time per request = 1s + (1000 * 30ms) = 31 seconds. With a max batch size of 8, the system's maximum service rate (mu) = 8 requests / 31 seconds = 0.258 QPS. The arrival rate (lambda) is 2 QPS. Because lambda > mu (2 > 0.258), the system is in a queueing death spiral; the queue grows infinitely. The architecture must be redesigned to increase capacity: either scale horizontally by adding 8x more replicas (2 / 0.258 = 7.7), or implement KV cache quantization (e.g., FP8/INT4) to safely increase the max batch size from 8 to 64 on the existing node.

scenario: Your summarization service handles exactly 2 QPS. Prompts are 8k tokens, outputs are 1k tokens. The business SLA is 45s end-to-end latency. You cap the batch size at 8 to strictly prevent KV cache OOMs. TPOT is a flat 30ms. Prefill is 1s. Under sustained 2 QPS load, P99 latency slowly climbs to over 5 minutes.
title: Continuous Batching Queueing Death Spiral

details.common_mistake: Assuming FlashAttention reduces compute complexity, and trying to tune the block size to speed up the operation.
