Total Quebec = 123 + 250 (transfer) = 373 kg. Net savings: 2,795 - 373 = 2,422 kg CO2 (87% reduction). Verdict: the migration IS worth it because the 25× difference in carbon intensity overwhelms the transfer overhead. However, if the carbon intensity difference were only 2×, the transfer cost could negate the savings.

scenario: Your carbon-aware scheduler routes training jobs to the region with the lowest carbon intensity at any given moment. Today it wants to move a 256-GPU training job from Virginia (500 gCO2/kWh, 10ms to training data) to Quebec (20 gCO2/kWh, 80ms to training data). The model trains on a 50TB dataset stored in Virginia. Evaluate whether this migration actually reduces net carbon.
title: The Green AI Paradox

details.common_mistake: Comparing only the GPU cost and choosing centralized because it is 28% cheaper. The latency analysis reveals that centralized cannot meet the SLA for distant users, which may cost far more in lost users than the 28% savings.
details.napkin_math: Centralized cost: 64 × $2.50 × 730 = $116,800/mo. Distributed cost: 64 × $3.20 × 730 = $149,504/mo. Premium: $32,704/mo (28%). SLA compliance: Centralized serves ~75% of users within SLA. Distributed serves ~100%. Revenue risk: 250K users × $0.50 = $125K/mo lost revenue >> $33K infra premium. Distributed wins on total cost of ownership.
details.realistic_solution: Centralized (US-East): 64 GPUs = 16 inference replicas (4 GPUs each). Latency for nearby users (US/Canada, RTT ~20ms): 20 + 150 = 170ms. PASS. Latency for European users (RTT ~80ms): 80 + 150 = 230ms. PASS. Latency for Asian users (RTT ~150ms): 150 + 150 = 300ms. BORDERLINE. Latency for Australian users (RTT ~200ms): 200 + 150 = 350ms. FAIL. Monthly cost: 64 × $2.50 × 730h = $116,800. Distributed (8 regions): 8 GPUs per region = 2 replicas each. Latency: all users within 30ms of nearest cluster → 30 + 150 = 180ms. All PASS. Monthly cost: 64 × $3.20 × 730h = $149,504. Premium: $32,704/month (28%). But: centralized fails SLA for ~25% of users (Asia-Pacific, Oceania, Africa). If each failed-SLA user represents $0.50/month in revenue and you have 1M users, failing 250K users costs $125K/month — far exceeding the $33K infrastructure premium. Recommendation: Distributed, with the caveat that 2 replicas per region provides minimal redundancy. Consider 6 regions with slightly larger clusters.

scenario: You serve a real-time translation model to users across 40 countries. Option A: one large centralized cluster of 64 H100s in US-East ($2.50/GPU-hour). Option B: 8 small regional clusters of 8 H100s each ($3.20/GPU-hour, 28% premium for regional pricing). Total GPU count is the same (64). The model requires 4 H100s for tensor parallelism. Your P95 latency target is 300ms and inference takes 150ms. Evaluate both architectures.
title: The Inference Placement Decision

details.common_mistake: Confusing parameter count with training compute. A 70B model does not automatically exceed the threshold — it depends on how long it was trained and at what efficiency. Also, some engineers ignore the threshold entirely, assuming it only applies to companies like OpenAI.
details.realistic_solution: Training compute: H100 peak FP16 = 989 TFLOPS. Effective FLOPS = 989 × 0.40 MFU = 395.6 TFLOPS per GPU. Total compute = 2,048 GPUs × 395.6 TFLOPS × 90 days × 86,400 s/day = 2,048 × 395.6 × 10^12 × 7,776,000 = 6.3 × 10^24 FLOPs. This is BELOW the 10^25 threshold (by ~37%). The model does not trigger systemic risk obligations. However: it is close enough that adding 60% more training (e.g., training for 144 days, or using 3,200 GPUs) would cross the line. Implications: (1) You avoid the most onerous obligations (red-teaming, incident reporting, cybersecurity measures). (2) You still must comply with basic GPAI obligations (technical documentation, copyright compliance, training data summary). (3) Strategic consideration: if you plan to scale up, design your compliance infrastructure now because the next model will likely cross the threshold.

scenario: The EU AI Act defines 'General-Purpose AI' (GPAI) models with additional obligations for those trained with more than 10^25 FLOPs (the 'systemic risk' threshold). Your company trained a 70B parameter model using 2,048 H100 GPUs for 90 days at 40% MFU. Does this model exceed the systemic risk threshold? Evaluate the implications for your deployment strategy.
title: The GPAI Threshold Debate

details.common_mistake: Planning to run the entire datacenter on solar and being surprised when 16 hours/day require grid power. Also, treating training and inference identically — inference cannot be deferred, but training can be scheduled to follow solar availability.
details.napkin_math: Solar-only training: Cost = $51,200/day = $18.7M/year. Training capacity: 160 MWh/day. 24/7 training (grid at night): Cost = $80,000/day = $29.2M/year. Training capacity: 480 MWh/day. Cost per training MWh: Solar-schedule: $18.7M / (160 × 365) = $320/MWh. 24/7 with grid: $29.2M / (480 × 365) = $167/MWh. Paradox: running 24/7 is cheaper PER UNIT of training because the inference grid cost is fixed regardless. The marginal cost of night training is only $0.09/kWh = $90/MWh.
details.realistic_solution: Power budget analysis: Inference (24/7): 30 MW × 24h = 720 MWh/day. Training max: 20 MW × 24h = 480 MWh/day. Solar available: 50 MW × 8h = 400 MWh/day. Strategy: During solar hours (8h): Run inference (30 MW from solar) + training at max (20 MW from solar). Total: 50 MW solar, 0 MW grid. Cost: 400 MWh × $0.02 = $8,000. During night (16h): Run inference only (30 MW from grid). No training. Cost: 30 MW × 16h × $0.09 = $43,200. Daily cost: $8,000 + $43,200 = $51,200. Training throughput: 20 MW × 8h = 160 MWh/day (33% of 24/7 max). Alternative (run training 24/7 on grid at night): Night cost with training: (30+20) MW × 16h × $0.09 = $72,000. Daily total: $8,000 + $72,000 = $80,000. Extra cost for 24/7 training: $28,800/day ($10.5M/year) for 67% more training throughput. Decision: depends on whether training speed or cost efficiency is the priority.

scenario: A company builds a 50 MW GPU datacenter co-located with a solar farm in Arizona. Solar produces 50 MW for 8 hours/day (capacity factor 33%) and 0 MW at night. Grid backup costs $0.09/kWh vs $0.02/kWh for solar. You run both latency-sensitive inference (30 MW, must run 24/7) and batch training (variable, up to 20 MW, can be deferred). Evaluate power scheduling strategies to minimize cost while maintaining inference availability.
title: The Renewable Intermittency Trap

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to 'all users must get the same model for fairness' without quantifying the actual quality-latency tradeoff. Also ignoring that the 70B model served from US to Asia would have 150ms+ RTT added, potentially making the total experience worse than a local 13B model.
details.napkin_math: Option 1 (centralized 70B): TTFT = 450ms for Asia (40% users). Average global TTFT = 0.6×300 + 0.4×450 = 360ms. Option 2 (regional 13B): TTFT = 90ms for Asia. Average = 0.6×300 + 0.4×90 = 216ms. Quality hit: ~15% for 40% of users. Option 3 (hybrid): TTFT = 198ms for Asia. Average = 0.6×300 + 0.4×198 = 259ms. Quality hit: ~5% for 40% of users (only on the 30% hard queries). Option 3 dominates: best quality-adjusted latency.
details.realistic_solution: Option 1: Same model (70B) for all — route Asian users to US. TTFT for Asian users: 150ms RTT + 300ms prefill = 450ms. Quality: identical to US/EU users. Cost: no additional infra, but cross-Pacific bandwidth costs for 40% of traffic. Option 2: Regional models — 70B in US/EU, 13B in Asia. TTFT for Asian users: 10ms RTT + 80ms prefill = 90ms. Quality: lower (13B vs 70B, roughly 85% as good on benchmarks). Cost: 2×H100 in Asia (~$7K/month). Option 3: Hybrid — route easy queries to 13B locally, hard queries to 70B in US. TTFT: 90ms for easy (70% of queries), 450ms for hard (30%). Average TTFT: 0.7×90 + 0.3×450 = 198ms. Quality: ~95% of always-70B (easy queries are equally good on both models). Recommendation: Option 3 (hybrid routing) — best balance of latency, quality, and cost. The 5× latency improvement for 70% of queries with negligible quality loss is the winning tradeoff. Implement a lightweight query classifier (runs in <5ms) to route between models.

scenario: You serve a global chat application. US and EU regions have 8×H100 clusters running a 70B model (300ms TTFT, high quality). Your new Asia-Pacific region only has 2×H100 (budget constraint), which can only run a 13B model (80ms TTFT, lower quality). 40% of your users are in Asia-Pacific. Your PM asks: should all users get the same model, or should Asian users get the smaller, faster model? Evaluate the tradeoffs.
title: The Regional Model Routing Decision

details.common_mistake: Only considering checkpoint frequency without accounting for the cost of lost work on failure. Also ignoring that remote replication competes for the same network bandwidth used for training communication.
details.napkin_math: (A) Local only: P(failure in 30 days) = 1-(0.999^30) = 2.96%. Expected loss: 0.0296 × 15 days (average) = 0.44 days. But catastrophic risk: 3% chance of losing ALL 30 days. (B) Remote 6h: max loss = 6h. Expected: 0.0296 × 3h = 0.089 hours. Storage: 200GB × 4/day × 30 = 24 TB. (C) Remote 1h: max loss = 1h. Expected: 0.0296 × 0.5h = 0.015 hours. Storage: 200GB × 24/day × 30 = 144 TB = $3,312/mo. Training compute cost: 512 × $2.50/h × 720h = $921,600. Storage cost is 0.36% of compute — trivially worth it.
details.realistic_solution: (A) Local only, hourly: Checkpoint write: 200 GB to NVMe at 5 GB/s = 40s. On datacenter failure: ALL progress lost (local storage is in the failed DC). Expected work lost over 30 days: 30 × 0.001 = 3% chance of total loss = 0.03 × 30 = 0.9 expected days lost. But if the DC fails, you lose EVERYTHING — the loss distribution is bimodal (0 or 30 days). (B) Local hourly + remote every 6h: Remote transfer: 200 GB / 12.5 GB/s = 16 seconds. On DC failure, maximum work lost = 6 hours. Expected lost work: 30 × 0.001 × 3h (average) = 0.09 hours. Remote transfer bandwidth cost: 16s every 6h = 0.07% of link capacity — negligible. (C) Remote every hour: Transfer: 16s per hour = 0.44% of link capacity. On DC failure, max work lost = 1 hour. Expected: 30 × 0.001 × 0.5h = 0.015 hours. Bandwidth impact: minimal. Recommendation: Option C — remote hourly checkpoints. The 16 seconds of network usage per hour is trivial, and reducing max work loss from 'total' to '1 hour' is transformative for a 30-day job. The real cost is storage: 200 GB × 24 checkpoints/day × 30 days = 144 TB of remote checkpoint storage (at $0.023/GB/month on S3 = $3,312/month).

scenario: You are training a critical 100B parameter model on 512 H100 GPUs in a single datacenter. The checkpoint is 200 GB (FP16 weights + optimizer states). Training takes 30 days. Your datacenter has a 0.1% daily probability of a full outage (power, cooling, or network failure). Evaluate checkpoint strategies: (A) local checkpoints every hour, (B) local every hour + remote replication to another region (100 Gbps link, 40ms RTT) every 6 hours, (C) remote replication every hour.
title: The Multi-Region Checkpoint Strategy

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to count both read and write traffic, or using element count instead of byte count for the memory term.
details.napkin_math: FLOPs = 2 × 4096³ ≈ 137 GFLOP. Bytes = 3 × 4096² × 2 ≈ 100 MB. AI = 137G / 0.1G ≈ 1370 FLOP/byte. Ridge = 312T / 2T = 156. 1370 >> 156 → compute-bound.
details.realistic_solution: FLOPs = 2 × 4096³ ≈ 137.4 GFLOP. Memory traffic = read A + read B + write C = 3 × 4096² × 2 bytes = 100.7 MB. Arithmetic intensity = 137.4 GFLOP / 0.1007 GB ≈ 1364 FLOP/byte. A100 ridge point = 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOP/byte. Since 1364 >> 156, this is solidly compute-bound. Large matmuls are the bread and butter of GPU utilization — this is why Transformers map so well to GPUs.

scenario: You are computing a square matrix multiply C = A × B where A and B are 4096×4096 FP16 matrices on an A100. Estimate the arithmetic intensity and determine whether this operation is compute-bound or memory-bound.
title: Matrix Multiply Arithmetic Intensity on A100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply by 2 for both K and V tensors, or ignoring that model weights also consume memory.
details.napkin_math: KV per request: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 4096 × 2 bytes = 2.15 GB. Weights = 14 GB. Free VRAM ≈ 64 GB. Fits ≈ 64/2.15 ≈ 29 concurrent requests.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache per request = 2 (K+V) × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 dim × 4096 tokens × 2 bytes = 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 4096 × 2 = 2.15 GB. Model weights at FP16 = 7B × 2 = 14 GB. Available for KV = 80 - 14 - ~2 overhead = 64 GB. Concurrent requests = 64 / 2.15 ≈ 29 requests. This is why KV cache is the primary bottleneck in LLM serving throughput.

scenario: You are serving a 7B-parameter LLM (32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim=128) with a context window of 4096 tokens in FP16. Estimate the KV cache memory per request and how many concurrent requests fit on an A100-80GB alongside the model weights.
title: KV Cache Memory for 7B Model Serving

details.common_mistake: Assuming quantization gives a 4× speedup because 'INT8 is 4× smaller than FP32.' The baseline here is FP16, so the reduction is 2×.
details.napkin_math: FP16: 13B × 2B = 26 GB. INT8: 13B × 1B = 13 GB. Bandwidth saving = 2×. Decode is memory-bound → throughput ≈ 2 × 40 = ~80 tok/s.
details.realistic_solution: In memory-bound decode, throughput scales linearly with bytes-per-parameter reduction. FP16 = 2 bytes/param, INT8 = 1 byte/param, so memory traffic halves. Model size drops from 26 GB to 13 GB. Since decode is bandwidth-bound, throughput roughly doubles to ~80 tokens/s. In practice, you get slightly less due to dequantization overhead and activation memory, but 1.7-1.9× is realistic.

scenario: Your 13B-parameter model in FP16 achieves 40 tokens/s on an A100 during decode, which is memory-bandwidth-bound. You quantize to INT8. Estimate the new throughput assuming decode remains memory-bound.
title: INT8 Quantization Serving Throughput Gain

details.common_mistake: Forgetting the PUE multiplier. The cooling and networking overhead adds 30% on top of the raw GPU power draw.
details.realistic_solution: GPU power = 64 × 300W = 19.2 kW. With PUE 1.3, total facility power = 19.2 × 1.3 = 24.96 kW. Energy = 24.96 kW × 72 h = 1797 kWh. Cost = 1797 × $0.10 = $179.70. This is just electricity — total TCO including GPU depreciation, networking, and staffing is typically 3-5× higher. For context, a 1000-GPU run for 30 days would cost ~$28K in electricity alone.

scenario: You train a model on 64 A100 GPUs for 72 hours. Each A100 draws 300W at full load, and the data center PUE is 1.3. At $0.10/kWh, estimate the total electricity cost of this training run.
title: Energy Cost of a Training Run

details.common_mistake: Using total bandwidth instead of per-link bandwidth, or forgetting the 2×(N-1)/N factor in ring AllReduce.
details.napkin_math: Data moved = 2 × (7/8) × 2 GB = 3.5 GB. NVLink per-direction: 300 GB/s. Time = 3.5/300 ≈ 12 ms.
details.realistic_solution: Ring AllReduce transfers 2 × (N-1)/N × data_size across the ring. With N=8: 2 × 7/8 × 2 GB = 3.5 GB total data moved. Each GPU sends/receives on one link at a time. Effective bandwidth per direction ≈ 300 GB/s (half of bidirectional 600 GB/s). Time = 3.5 GB / 300 GB/s ≈ 11.7 ms. In practice, overhead from chunking and synchronization adds ~20%, so expect ~14 ms.

scenario: You are training with data parallelism across 8 A100 GPUs connected via NVLink at 600 GB/s bidirectional. The gradient buffer is 2 GB (1B-parameter model in FP16). Estimate the ring AllReduce communication time.
title: Ring AllReduce Communication Time

details.common_mistake: Using bidirectional bandwidth as if it were available in one direction. PCIe Gen5 x16 is 64 GB/s bidirectional but only 32 GB/s in each direction.
details.napkin_math: PCIe: 10 GB / 32 GB/s = 312 ms. NVLink: 10 GB / 450 GB/s = 22 ms. Ratio: 14× faster on NVLink.
details.realistic_solution: PCIe Gen5: 10 GB / 32 GB/s = 312 ms. NVLink 4.0: 10 GB / 450 GB/s = 22 ms. NVLink is ~14× faster for this transfer. This is why intra-node tensor parallelism requires NVLink — splitting a single matrix multiply across GPUs connected only by PCIe would make the communication overhead dominate. The rule of thumb: use NVLink for tight coupling (tensor parallelism), PCIe for loose coupling (data parallelism across nodes).

scenario: You need to transfer a 10 GB tensor shard between two GPUs. Compare the transfer time using PCIe Gen5 x16 (64 GB/s bidirectional, 32 GB/s per direction) versus NVLink 4.0 (900 GB/s bidirectional, 450 GB/s per direction).
title: PCIe vs NVLink Model Shard Transfer

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that on-prem costs include power, cooling, and networking — typically 1.5-2× the raw GPU cost over its lifetime. Also forgetting utilization: idle GPUs still cost money.
details.napkin_math: On-prem: $15K/36mo + 50% overhead = $625/mo. Cloud: 0.8 × 720h × $2.50 = $1,440/mo. Savings = $815/mo. Break-even = $15K / $815 ≈ 18 months.
details.realistic_solution: On-prem monthly cost: $15,000 / 36 months = $417/mo depreciation. Add ~50% overhead (power, cooling, staff) = $625/mo total. Cloud monthly cost at 80% util: 0.80 × 24h × 30d × $2.50 = $1,440/mo. Break-even: $15,000 / ($1,440 - $625) ≈ 18.4 months. After ~18 months, owning is cheaper IF you maintain 80% utilization. Below ~45% utilization, cloud is always cheaper over 3 years.

scenario: An A100-80GB costs $15,000 and has a 3-year useful life. Cloud A100 instances cost $2.50/GPU-hour. Assuming 80% average utilization on-prem, estimate the break-even point in months.
title: Buy vs Rent GPU Break-Even

details.common_mistake: Treating decode attention like training attention. During decode, you compute Q×K^T for a single query against the entire KV cache, which has very low reuse.
details.napkin_math: FLOPs ≈ 2 × 2 × 2048 × 128 = 1M. Bytes: read K+V = 2 × 2048 × 128 × 2 = 1 MB. AI = 1 FLOP/byte. Ridge = 156. Massively memory-bound.
details.realistic_solution: FLOPs: Q×K^T = 2 × 1 × 2048 × 128 = 524K FLOP. Then softmax×V = 2 × 1 × 128 × 2048 = 524K FLOP. Total ≈ 1M FLOP. Memory: read K (2048×128×2B = 512KB) + read V (512KB) + read Q (256B) + write output (256B) ≈ 1 MB. AI = 1M FLOP / 1 MB = 1 FLOP/byte. A100 ridge = 156. Since 1 << 156, decode attention is extremely memory-bound. This is the fundamental reason decode is slow and why FlashDecoding and speculative decoding exist.

scenario: During autoregressive decode of a single token, the attention query is 1×128 and the KV cache is 2048×128, both FP16. Estimate the arithmetic intensity of this single-token attention and classify it on the A100 roofline.
title: Self-Attention Arithmetic Intensity During Decode

details.common_mistake: Thinking checkpointing eliminates all activation memory. You still store activations at checkpoint boundaries — you just recompute the rest during backward.
details.napkin_math: No ckpt: 24 × 512 MB = 12.3 GB. Ckpt every 4: 6 boundaries × 512 MB + 4 active × 512 MB = 3.1 + 2.0 = 5.1 GB. Saves ~59%, costs ~33% extra compute.
details.realistic_solution: Without checkpointing: 24 layers × 512 MB = 12.3 GB. With checkpointing every 4 layers: store activations at 6 boundaries (layers 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20) = 6 × 512 MB = 3.1 GB. Plus the 4 layers of activations being recomputed in the current segment = 4 × 512 MB = 2 GB. Peak = 3.1 + 2.0 = 5.1 GB. Savings = ~59%. The trade-off: ~33% extra compute from recomputation (recompute forward for each segment during backward pass).

scenario: A 24-layer Transformer with batch size 32, sequence length 2048, hidden dimension 4096 stores activations in FP16. Without checkpointing, each layer stores ~512 MB of activations. Estimate total activation memory with and without checkpointing (checkpoint every 4 layers).
title: Activation Checkpointing Memory Savings

details.common_mistake: Confusing per-request throughput with system throughput. Batching dramatically increases system throughput and, in memory-bound decode phases, can even improve per-request latency slightly by fully utilizing memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: B=1: 50 tok/s total. B=32: 32 × 60 = 1920 tok/s total. Throughput gain = 38.4×. Per-request latency: 1/50 sec (20ms) vs 1/60 sec (16.6ms) → slight latency improvement per token, though queuing delay might be added before generation.
details.realistic_solution: Batch=1: 50 tok/s system throughput, 50 tok/s per-request (20ms/token). Batch=32: total system throughput = 32 × 60 = 1920 tok/s (since decode is memory-bound, batching amortizes weight loading). Per-request: each request gets 60 tok/s, lowering token generation latency to 16.6ms. System throughput gain: 1920/50 = 38.4×. Time-to-first-token may increase due to queuing, but per-token latency improves. At batch=32, each decode step loads weights once but computes 32 outputs, achieving near-linear throughput scaling in the memory-bound regime.

scenario: An inference server processes requests at 50 tokens/s per request with batch size 1. With continuous batching, batch size grows to 32 and per-request throughput increases to 60 tokens/s. Estimate the throughput gain and per-request latency impact.
title: Continuous Batching Throughput vs Latency

details.common_mistake: Only counting the reads. Each unfused kernel writes its output to HBM AND the next kernel reads it back — so each intermediate result incurs a write + read round trip.
details.napkin_math: Tensor = 32 × 2048 × 4096 × 2B = 512 MB. Unfused: 6 × 512 = 3072 MB. Fused: 2 × 512 = 1024 MB. Saves 2048 MB → 3× less traffic. Time saved per call: 2 GB / 2 TB/s = 1 ms.
details.realistic_solution: Tensor size = 32 × 2048 × 4096 × 2 bytes = 512 MB. Unfused: 3 reads + 3 writes = 6 × 512 MB = 3072 MB total HBM traffic. Fused: 1 read + 1 write = 2 × 512 MB = 1024 MB. Savings = 2048 MB, a 3× reduction in memory traffic. On A100 at 2 TB/s, this saves 2048 MB / 2000 GB/s ≈ 1 ms per invocation. Over thousands of iterations, this compounds to minutes of training time saved.

scenario: A sequence of LayerNorm → GELU → Dropout on a tensor of shape (32, 2048, 4096) in FP16 launches 3 separate CUDA kernels. Each kernel reads from and writes to HBM. Estimate the memory traffic saved by fusing these into one kernel.
title: Kernel Fusion Memory Bandwidth Savings

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that the 10.2 kW is the server total (CPU + GPU + fans + networking), not just the GPUs. Also forgetting that you often can't fill a rack to 100% of power capacity.
details.napkin_math: 20 kW / 10.2 kW = 1.96 → fits 1 server = 8 H100 GPUs per standard rack. Need 40+ kW racks for 16+ GPUs.
details.realistic_solution: Servers per rack = floor(20 kW / 10.2 kW) = 1 server with room to spare (10.2 kW used, 9.8 kW spare), but practically only 1 DGX-style server fits due to power constraints. That's 8 GPUs per rack. Modern AI racks are moving to 40-100 kW to fit 2-4 servers (16-32 GPUs). This is why power density is a first-class constraint: you can afford the GPUs but can't cool them in a standard facility.

scenario: A standard data center rack supports 20 kW. Each H100 SXM server (8 GPUs) draws 10.2 kW total. How many H100 servers fit in one rack, and what is the GPU density per rack?
title: GPU Rack Power Density Limit

details.common_mistake: Thinking elementwise operations can saturate the GPU's FLOP throughput. They are almost always memory-bound because they do exactly 1 operation per element loaded.
details.napkin_math: FLOPs = 100M. Bytes = 2 × 100M × 2 = 400 MB. AI = 0.25 FLOP/byte. Perf = 0.25 × 2 TB/s = 0.5 TFLOPS (0.16% of peak).
details.realistic_solution: FLOPs = 100M (one comparison per element). Memory = read 100M × 2 bytes + write 100M × 2 bytes = 400 MB. AI = 100M FLOP / 400 MB = 0.25 FLOP/byte. A100 ridge = 156 FLOP/byte. At 0.25 FLOP/byte, achievable TFLOPS = 0.25 × 2.0 TB/s = 500 GFLOPS = 0.5 TFLOPS. That's 0.16% of peak 312 TFLOPS. This is why kernel fusion matters — fusing ReLU into a matmul avoids the separate HBM round trip entirely.

scenario: You apply ReLU activation to a tensor of 100M FP16 elements on an A100. Estimate the arithmetic intensity and determine the maximum achievable TFLOPS for this operation.
title: Roofline Classification of Elementwise Operations

details.common_mistake: Forgetting the quantization metadata overhead (scales and zero-points per group) which adds ~0.5 bits/param for typical group sizes of 128.
details.napkin_math: FP16: 70B × 2 = 140 GB. INT8: 70B × 1 = 70 GB. INT4+overhead: 70B × 0.5625 = 39.4 GB. None fit in 24 GB. Need ≤~40B params for single 24GB GPU at INT4.
details.realistic_solution: FP16: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB — needs 2× H100s. INT8: 70B × 1 byte = 70 GB — still too large. INT4 with overhead: 70B × (4 + 0.5) bits / 8 = 70B × 0.5625 bytes = 39.4 GB — still too large for 24 GB. With 3-bit GPTQ or aggressive compression: 70B × 0.4375 = 30.6 GB — still tight. Realistically, 70B models need ~35-40 GB at INT4, so you need at least 2× 24GB GPUs. A 34B model at INT4 ≈ 19 GB, which fits with room for KV cache.

scenario: A 70B-parameter model needs to run on a consumer GPU with 24 GB VRAM. Estimate the memory footprint at FP16, INT8, and INT4 (with group quantization overhead of ~0.5 bits/param). Can it fit at INT4?
title: 4-Bit Quantization for Consumer GPU Deployment

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to account for both input and output tokens separately, or confusing per-request throughput with aggregate throughput.
details.napkin_math: Tokens/hr = 2000 × 3600 = 7.2M. Cost/1M = $3.50 / 7.2 = $0.49. With 2× redundancy and overhead: ~$1.50-2.50/1M tokens in production.
details.realistic_solution: Tokens per hour = 2000 tok/s × 3600 s = 7.2M tokens. Cost per 1M tokens = $3.50 / 7.2 = $0.49/1M tokens. For context, this is the marginal compute cost only — you also need input processing (cheaper, higher throughput), redundancy (typically 2× for availability), load balancing, and engineering overhead. Real-world pricing is typically 3-5× marginal cost. This is why OpenAI charges ~$2-15/1M output tokens depending on model size.

scenario: Your H100 instance costs $3.50/hour and serves a 70B model at 2000 output tokens/s aggregate throughput. Estimate the cost per 1M output tokens.
title: Cost Per 1M Tokens Served

details.common_mistake: Thinking tensor parallelism splits the weights and that's it. Each TP shard produces a partial result that must be AllReduced to get the correct output.
details.napkin_math: Output per layer = 2048 × 4096 × 2B = 16 MB. AllReduce: 2 × (3/4) × 16 = 24 MB. 32 layers → 768 MB. Over NVLink (300 GB/s): 2.6 ms total.
details.realistic_solution: In Megatron-style TP, the first linear is column-parallel (each GPU has 4096×4096 shard) and the second is row-parallel (each GPU has 4096×4096 shard). After the second linear, an AllReduce of the output is needed. Output shape = (batch × seq, 4096). For batch=1, seq=2048: output = 2048 × 4096 × 2 bytes = 16 MB. AllReduce volume = 2 × (3/4) × 16 MB = 24 MB per layer forward. With 32 layers, total = 768 MB. This is why TP needs NVLink — 768 MB / 300 GB/s = 2.6 ms overhead for the forward pass alone.

scenario: A Transformer MLP layer has weight matrices of shape (4096, 16384) and (16384, 4096) in FP16. You split across 4 GPUs using tensor parallelism. Estimate the AllReduce volume per layer per forward pass.
title: Tensor Parallelism Communication Volume

details.common_mistake: Checkpointing too frequently wastes time on I/O; too infrequently means losing hours of work on failure. The classic square-root formula gives the optimum.
details.napkin_math: t_opt = sqrt(2 × 240 × 5) = sqrt(2400) ≈ 49 min. Ckpt overhead: 5/49 ≈ 10%. Waste per failure: 49/2 = 25 min. Total overhead ≈ 20%.
details.realistic_solution: The optimal checkpoint interval follows: t_opt = sqrt(2 × MTBF × t_ckpt). t_opt = sqrt(2 × 240 min × 5 min) = sqrt(2400) ≈ 49 minutes. At this interval: checkpoint overhead = 5/49 ≈ 10.2% of training time. Expected wasted work per failure = t_opt/2 = 24.5 minutes. Total overhead ≈ checkpoint_cost + expected_waste/MTBF = 10.2% + (24.5/240) = 10.2% + 10.2% ≈ 20.4%. Without checkpointing, you'd lose on average 2 hours per failure = 50% waste.

scenario: A 256-GPU training cluster has a mean-time-between-failures (MTBF) of 4 hours. Writing a full checkpoint takes 5 minutes and stalls training. Estimate the optimal checkpoint interval to minimize wasted compute.
title: Optimal Checkpointing Interval

details.common_mistake: Only counting the FP16 weights (6 GB) and thinking it fits easily. Adam mixed-precision needs FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance on top of FP16 working copies.
details.napkin_math: 16 bytes/param for Adam mixed-precision. 3B × 16 = 48 GB. A100-80GB has 32 GB left for activations. Tight but fits for moderate batch sizes with checkpointing.
details.realistic_solution: FP16 weights: 3B × 2 = 6 GB. FP16 gradients: 3B × 2 = 6 GB. FP32 master weights: 3B × 4 = 12 GB. FP32 momentum (Adam): 3B × 4 = 12 GB. FP32 variance (Adam): 3B × 4 = 12 GB. Total model state = 48 GB. This leaves 80 - 48 = 32 GB for activations, KV cache, and framework overhead. With batch size 8, seq_len 2048, activation checkpointing is likely needed. Per-parameter cost: 48 GB / 3B = 16 bytes/param — the well-known Adam mixed-precision constant.

scenario: You want to train a 3B-parameter model with Adam optimizer in mixed precision (FP16 weights + FP32 optimizer states). Estimate the minimum GPU memory needed just for model state (no activations), and determine if it fits on a single A100-80GB.
title: Mixed-Precision Training Memory Budget

details.common_mistake: Assuming hierarchical AllReduce is as fast as flat AllReduce. The cross-rack link becomes the bottleneck in a two-level reduction.
details.napkin_math: Single-rack: 4 GB / 900 GB/s ≈ 4.4 ms for the bottleneck step, total ~8.8 ms. Two-rack hierarchical: Intra-rack ReduceScatter (3.9 ms) + Cross-rack AllReduce of 0.5 GB chunks (10 ms) + Intra-rack AllGather (3.9 ms) ≈ 17.8 ms. ~2× slower than single-rack.
details.realistic_solution: Single-rack (8 GPUs, NVSwitch): AllReduce time ≈ 2 × (7/8) × 4 GB / 900 GB/s = 7.8 ms. Two-rack hierarchical: Step 1: intra-rack ReduceScatter (each GPU ends up with a 0.5 GB chunk): (7/8) × 4 GB / 900 GB/s = 3.9 ms. Step 2: cross-rack AllReduce of the 0.5 GB chunks over IB: 2 × (1/2) × 0.5 GB / 50 GB/s = 10 ms. Step 3: intra-rack AllGather: (7/8) × 4 GB / 900 GB/s = 3.9 ms. Total ≈ 3.9 + 10 + 3.9 = 17.8 ms. This 2.2× slowdown is why topology-aware placement puts tightly-coupled GPU groups within the same rack.

scenario: Intra-rack NVSwitch provides 900 GB/s between GPUs. Cross-rack InfiniBand NDR provides 50 GB/s per link. For a 4 GB gradient AllReduce across 2 racks (8 GPUs each), estimate the time difference vs. a single-rack AllReduce.
title: Cross-Rack AllReduce Latency Impact

details.common_mistake: Applying voltage reduction linearly. Dynamic power scales with V² × f, so reducing voltage has a cubic effect on power (V² × V-proportional-frequency = V³).
details.napkin_math: P ∝ V²f ∝ V³ (since f ∝ V). P' = 250 × 0.85³ = 250 × 0.614 = 153.5W. 39% power savings for 15% perf loss. Perf/watt improves 1.38×.
details.realistic_solution: P_dyn = C × V² × f. With V' = 0.85V and f' = 0.85f (frequency proportional to voltage): P' = C × (0.85V)² × (0.85f) = C × V² × f × 0.85³ = 250 × 0.6141 = 153.5W. Power drops by 38.6% while performance drops by only 15%. This cubic relationship is why DVFS (dynamic voltage-frequency scaling) is so effective. Performance per watt actually improves: 85% performance at 61.4% power = 1.38× better perf/W.

scenario: An accelerator runs at 1.0V and 1.5 GHz, consuming 250W dynamic power. If you reduce voltage by 15% to 0.85V (and frequency drops proportionally to 1.275 GHz), estimate the new dynamic power.
title: Voltage Scaling and Dynamic Power

details.common_mistake: Comparing only peak TFLOPS. If your workload is below the ridge point, bandwidth matters more than compute.
details.napkin_math: A100 ridge = 156. H100 ridge = 295. At AI=200: A100 hits peak 312 TF. H100 is BW-limited: 200 × 3.35 = 670 TF. Speedup = 2.15× (not the expected 3.17×).
details.realistic_solution: A100 ridge = 312T / 2.0T = 156 FLOP/byte. H100 ridge = 989T / 3.35T = 295 FLOP/byte. At AI = 200: A100 is compute-bound (200 > 156), achieves 312 TFLOPS. H100 is memory-bound (200 < 295), achieves 200 × 3.35 = 670 TFLOPS. H100 speedup = 670/312 = 2.15×. Note: despite H100 having 3.17× more peak FLOPS, you only get 2.15× for this workload because it lands in H100's memory-bound region. To get full 3.17× speedup, you need AI > 295 FLOP/byte.

scenario: Compare the ridge points of H100 (989 TFLOPS FP16, 3.35 TB/s) and A100 (312 TFLOPS FP16, 2.0 TB/s). For a kernel with arithmetic intensity of 200 FLOP/byte, which GPU gives higher speedup and by how much?
title: H100 vs A100 Roofline Comparison

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for compilation overhead. Short runs or debugging sessions may be slower with torch.compile.
details.napkin_math: Save 35 ms/step. Break-even: 45s / 0.035s = 1,286 steps. For 10K steps: save 305s (25%). For 100 steps: 4.5× slower (compilation dominates).
details.realistic_solution: Savings per step = 120 - 85 = 35 ms. Break-even steps = 45,000 ms / 35 ms = 1,286 steps. After 1,286 steps, compilation has paid for itself. For 10,000 steps: uncompiled = 10,000 × 120 ms = 1,200 s. Compiled = 45 + 10,000 × 85 ms = 45 + 850 = 895 s. Net savings = 305 s (25.4%). For a 100-step debug run: uncompiled = 12 s, compiled = 45 + 8.5 = 53.5 s — 4.5× slower. Rule of thumb: compile for production training, not for debugging.

scenario: torch.compile traces and compiles a model graph in 45 seconds but reduces per-step time from 120 ms to 85 ms. For a training run of 10,000 steps, estimate the break-even point and total time savings.
title: torch.compile Warm-Up vs Steady-State

details.common_mistake: Dividing requests/s by a single-request throughput. Little's Law properly accounts for concurrency: L = λW (queue length = arrival rate × wait time).
details.napkin_math: L = λW = 500 × 0.2 = 100 concurrent requests. GPUs = ceil(100/8) = 13. With 20% headroom: 16 GPUs.
details.realistic_solution: By Little's Law: L = λ × W = 500 req/s × 0.2 s = 100 concurrent requests. GPUs needed = ceil(100 / 8) = 13 GPUs. Add 20% headroom for traffic spikes: 16 GPUs. This assumes uniform request distribution. In practice, with Poisson arrivals, you need more headroom — at 80% utilization target: 100 / 0.8 / 8 = 16 GPUs, matching our headroom estimate. Below 60% utilization, queuing delay is negligible; above 80%, tail latency explodes.

scenario: Your service receives 500 requests/s. Average request latency is 200 ms. Each GPU can handle 8 concurrent requests. How many GPUs do you need to serve this traffic without queuing?
title: Little's Law for GPU Inference Server Sizing

details.common_mistake: Blaming GPU underutilization or insufficient batching. The real issue is prefill (compute-bound, long) stealing GPU cycles from decode (memory-bound, latency-sensitive).
details.napkin_math: Prefill for 4K tokens: attention requires 4 × N² × d FLOPs per head per layer. For N=4096, d=128, this is 4 × 16.7M × 128 = ~8.6 billion FLOPs per head per layer. Summed across heads and layers, a single prefill can block SMs for tens or hundreds of milliseconds, causing decode stalls.
details.realistic_solution: This is prefill-decode interference. Long-context prefill operations are compute-heavy and monopolize SMs, starving concurrent decode requests of compute time. Solutions: (1) Disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools — prefill GPUs optimize for throughput, decode GPUs optimize for latency. (2) Chunked prefill: break long prefills into fixed-size chunks interleaved with decode steps, bounding worst-case decode latency. (3) Priority scheduling: preempt prefill to service decode requests at SLA boundaries. Splitwise and DistServe architectures address this systematically.

scenario: Your LLM inference server shows bimodal latency: most requests complete at p50=80ms per token but p99=450ms. GPU utilization is consistently 85%. Logs show that high-latency events correlate with bursts of new long-context requests arriving while short decode requests are in-flight.
title: Diagnosing Prefill-Decode Interference

details.common_mistake: Assuming low utilization means you need a larger batch. nvidia-smi 'utilization' measures the fraction of time at least one kernel is running, not compute efficiency. 40% means the GPU is idle 60% of the time.
details.napkin_math: Data loading at 100 ms/batch + 150 ms GPU compute = 250 ms cycle. GPU active = 150/250 = 60%. Adding 40 ms of kernel launch overhead → 150/290 = 52%. Close to the observed 40%.
details.realistic_solution: The most likely cause is CPU-bound data loading or preprocessing creating pipeline bubbles. While the GPU waits for the next batch, utilization drops to 0%. Other possibilities: (1) Excessive CPU-GPU synchronization points (e.g., .item() calls in the training loop). (2) Small kernels with high launch overhead — many tiny ops instead of fused kernels. (3) Data transfer bottleneck on PCIe. Diagnosis: profile with nsys/Nsight to see the timeline. Fix: use multi-worker data loading (num_workers=4-8), pin_memory=True, prefetch_factor=2, and ensure no synchronization points in the hot loop.

scenario: Your training job runs a fully-packed batch but nvidia-smi reports only 40% GPU utilization. The model is a Transformer with standard attention. GPU memory is 70% used. What is the most likely root cause?
title: GPU Shows 40% Utilization Despite Full Batch

details.common_mistake: Assuming a memory leak in the training loop code. While possible, the most common cause in PyTorch is accumulating computation graph history.
details.napkin_math: Each retained backward graph for a Transformer step ≈ 500 MB-2 GB. After 500 steps without detaching: 500 × 500 MB = 250 GB → OOM long before step 500.
details.realistic_solution: The most likely cause is retaining computation graphs across steps — typically from storing loss tensors without calling .detach() or .item(). Each stored tensor keeps the entire backward graph alive, accumulating memory linearly. Common culprits: (1) Appending loss.item() is correct, but appending loss (without .item()) retains the graph. (2) Metrics tracking that stores tensors instead of scalars. (3) Learning rate schedulers or custom callbacks holding tensor references. (4) Less commonly: CUDA caching allocator fragmentation, which grows as different tensor sizes are allocated/freed. Debug: torch.cuda.memory_summary() shows reserved vs. allocated — a growing gap suggests fragmentation; growing allocated suggests retained references.

scenario: Your training run starts fine but OOMs at step 500. The model, batch size, and sequence length haven't changed. Memory usage has been gradually climbing since step 1. What is the most likely cause?
title: OOM at Step 500 but Not Step 1

details.common_mistake: Trusting perplexity as a sufficient proxy for task performance. Perplexity measures average next-token prediction, which can mask catastrophic failures on specific knowledge-intensive tasks.
details.napkin_math: 7B model has 32 layers. If 4 layers are 'knowledge layers' responsible for 80% of factual accuracy, keeping those in FP16 costs only 4/32 × 7 GB = 0.875 GB extra but may recover most accuracy.
details.realistic_solution: Quantization error distributes unevenly across weight matrices. Layers responsible for factual recall (early MLP layers encoding knowledge, attention heads specializing in entity resolution) may lose critical precision. Perplexity averages over all tokens, masking that rare factual tokens are disproportionately affected. The fix: (1) Use mixed-precision quantization — keep knowledge-critical layers in FP16, quantize attention and normalization layers to INT8. (2) Evaluate on task-specific metrics, not just perplexity. (3) Consider GPTQ or AWQ which use calibration data to minimize task-relevant quantization error. (4) Sensitivity analysis: quantize one layer at a time and measure per-layer impact on your specific task.

scenario: You quantize a 7B model to INT8. Perplexity degrades by only 0.3 (acceptable). However, on your specific RAG application, factual accuracy drops from 89% to 71%. The benchmark suite shows minimal degradation. Analyze why application-level metrics diverge from perplexity.
title: When INT8 Quantization Hurts More Than It Helps

details.common_mistake: Thinking more pipeline stages always improve throughput. More stages mean smaller per-stage compute but proportionally more bubble time.
details.napkin_math: A: bubble = 3/19 = 15.8%, time = 190 ms. B: bubble = 7/39 = 17.9%, time = 195 ms. To get <10% bubble with 8 stages: need M ≥ 63 micro-batches.
details.realistic_solution: Bubble fraction = (P-1) / (P-1+M) where P=stages, M=micro-batches. Config A: 4 stages, 16 micro-batches: bubble = 3/(3+16) = 15.8%. Total time = (16+3) × 10 = 190 ms. Config B: 8 stages, 32 micro-batches: bubble = 7/(7+32) = 17.9%. Total time = (32+7) × 5 = 195 ms. Despite 2× more micro-batches, Config B has higher bubble overhead and slightly higher total time. The key insight: bubble fraction is (P-1)/(M+P-1). To keep it below 10%, you need M ≥ 9P. More stages require proportionally more micro-batches, which increases memory for in-flight activations.

scenario: You implement pipeline parallelism with 4 stages and 16 micro-batches. Each micro-batch takes 10 ms per stage. Analyze the bubble overhead and compare with an alternative of 8 stages and 32 micro-batches (each micro-batch now takes 5 ms per stage).
title: Pipeline Parallelism Bubble Overhead Analysis

details.common_mistake: Blaming hardware errors or data corruption. NaN after LR warmup is almost always a numerical stability issue triggered by the sudden transition to peak learning rate.
details.napkin_math: FP16 max = 65504. If a gradient hits 70000, it becomes Inf. One Inf in a sum → NaN. BF16 max = 3.4e38, same as FP32 — eliminates this class of bug entirely.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: FP16 overflow during the backward pass. During warmup, small LR produces small gradients that stay within FP16 range (max ~65504). At peak LR, gradient magnitudes increase and exceed FP16 dynamic range, producing Inf → NaN propagation. The loss scaler should catch this, but may be too aggressive. Fixes: (1) Reduce initial loss scale or increase scale_growth_interval. (2) Enable gradient clipping before the optimizer step. (3) Use BF16 instead of FP16 — BF16 has the same exponent range as FP32, eliminating overflow. (4) Reduce peak LR. (5) Extend warmup period for gentler LR ramp.

scenario: Your distributed training run produces NaN gradients 200 steps into training, right after learning rate warmup completes and LR reaches its peak. Loss was decreasing normally during warmup. The model uses mixed-precision training with FP16 forward/backward and FP32 optimizer.
title: NaN Gradients Appearing After Learning Rate Warmup

details.common_mistake: Blaming faulty hardware since specific pairs are consistently slow. The deterministic nature actually points to a routing issue, not a hardware issue.
details.napkin_math: With 8 equal-cost paths, probability of 2 flows colliding = 1/8. With 16 flows: expected collisions ≈ 16²/(2×8) = 16. Birthday paradox makes hotspots inevitable at scale.
details.realistic_solution: This is an ECMP hash collision. ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) routing uses a hash of the flow 5-tuple to select among equal-cost paths. If multiple heavy flows hash to the same path, that link becomes a hotspot while parallel links sit idle. The 45% average but 95% peak confirms this — traffic is unevenly distributed. Fixes: (1) Use adaptive routing (e.g., InfiniBand AR) that dynamically selects paths based on congestion. (2) Flowlet switching to re-hash flows at packet-gap boundaries. (3) Add entropy to flow headers (vary source ports). (4) Topology-aware job placement to avoid flows that hash to the same spine links.

scenario: In a 64-node training cluster with a fat-tree network, 4 specific node pairs consistently show 3× higher AllReduce latency than others. All links are healthy. The pattern is deterministic — the same pairs are always slow. Network utilization averages 45% but some links show 95%.
title: ECMP Hash Collision Causing Training Slowdown

details.common_mistake: Simply comparing hourly rates. You must account for wasted compute from preemptions and the cost of frequent checkpointing.
details.napkin_math: Spot: ~122h total clock time × $1.10 = $135. On-demand: 100h × $3.50 = $350. Savings: 61%. Break-even: spot is cheaper if preemption overhead < (3.50-1.10)/3.50 = 69% of training time.
details.realistic_solution: On-demand: 100h × $3.50 = $350. Spot analysis: MTBF = 2h. Optimal checkpoint interval = sqrt(2 × 120min × 3min) = 26.8 min. Overhead per cycle: checkpoint = 3/26.8 = 11.2%. Wasted work per preemption = 26.8/2 = 13.4 min. Preemptions in 100h effective compute: ~50. Total wasted = 50 × 13.4 min = 670 min = 11.2h. Checkpoint overhead = 11.2% × 100h = 11.2h. Real clock time = 100 + 11.2 + 11.2 = 122.4h. Spot cost = 122.4 × $1.10 = $134.64. Savings = $350 - $135 = $215 (61% savings). Spot is clearly worth it IF your framework supports preemption gracefully.

scenario: On-demand H100 instances cost $3.50/hr. Spot instances cost $1.10/hr but get preempted on average every 2 hours. Your training step takes 500 ms and checkpointing takes 3 minutes. Analyze whether spot instances are cost-effective for a 100-hour training run.
title: Spot Instance Strategy for Fault-Tolerant Training

details.common_mistake: Only comparing carbon intensity without accounting for the extra energy from cross-region overhead. Moving workloads to green regions has a transfer cost.
details.napkin_math: A(day): 8h × 1.15 × 50 = 460 units. B: 8h × 350 = 2800 units. A saves 84%. But if A spills to night: 4×1.15×50 + 4×1.15×400 = 2070. Only 26% savings.
details.realistic_solution: Region A daytime: 8h × Power × 50 gCO2/kWh. Region B: 8h × Power × 350 gCO2/kWh. Region A with transfer overhead: 8h × 1.15 × Power × 50 = 460 × Power gCO2. Region B: 8h × Power × 350 = 2800 × Power gCO2. Region A saves 2800-460 = 2340 × Power gCO2 (83.6% reduction). Even with 15% overhead, solar daytime is vastly better. But: if the job runs into nighttime in Region A: 4h × 1.15P × 50 + 4h × 1.15P × 400 = 230P + 1840P = 2070P gCO2. Still better than Region B's 2800P but the gap narrows to 26%. The insight: carbon-aware scheduling helps most when green windows fully cover job duration.

scenario: Your cluster spans two regions: Region A (solar-heavy, 50 gCO2/kWh daytime, 400 gCO2/kWh nighttime) and Region B (natural gas, constant 350 gCO2/kWh). A training job takes 8 hours. Analyze the carbon tradeoff of running during Region A's daytime vs. Region B anytime, considering a 15% compute overhead from cross-region data transfer.
title: Carbon-Aware Scheduling Tradeoff

details.common_mistake: Defaulting to LRU because it works for CPU caches. Inference serving has different access patterns — a request being 'old' doesn't mean it's less valuable.
details.napkin_math: 50 requests × 2 GB KV each = 100 GB. Evicting 5 requests frees 10 GB. If those 5 were 90% complete, you waste 5 × 0.9 × 200ms = 900ms of compute. Minimum-completion-threshold prevents this.
details.realistic_solution: LRU: Simple but suboptimal. A long-running request near completion may be evicted, wasting all the tokens already generated. Shortest-remaining: Better for individual request completion but may starve new requests if all active requests are long. Prefix-sharing: Preserves shared prefixes (e.g., system prompts) that benefit multiple requests, maximizing cache utility per byte. The best approach depends on workload: for chatbots (shared system prompts), prefix-sharing wins. For diverse API traffic, LRU with a minimum-tokens-generated threshold prevents wasting near-complete requests. vLLM's PagedAttention uses a more sophisticated approach: evict at the page granularity, preferring pages unique to single requests over shared pages.

scenario: Your inference server runs out of KV cache memory with 50 active requests. You must evict some cached context to admit new requests. Analyze the tradeoff between LRU eviction (evict least-recently-used request's context), shortest-remaining eviction (evict requests closest to completion), and prefix-sharing eviction (evict requests that share the least common prefix with others).
title: KV Cache Eviction Under Memory Pressure

details.common_mistake: Equating FLOPs with wall-clock time. On modern GPUs, memory bandwidth is often the bottleneck, not compute. Extra FLOPs that avoid HBM round-trips are essentially 'free.'
details.napkin_math: Standard: write/read N² matrix = 2048² × 2B = 8 MB per head. Round-trip HBM traffic = 16 MB (write + read). At 2 TB/s: 16 MB / 2 TB/s = 8 μs. Flash: stays in SRAM, zero HBM traffic for intermediates. Extra FLOPs ~1 μs. Avoided traffic saves ~8 μs. Net win: 7 μs per head.
details.realistic_solution: Standard attention materializes the N×N attention matrix to HBM: O(N²) memory reads/writes. FlashAttention tiles the computation, keeping Q, K, V blocks in SRAM (192 KB on A100) and never materializing the full matrix. This trades extra FLOPs (recomputing softmax statistics in backward) for eliminating O(N²) HBM traffic. On A100: 312 TFLOPS compute but only 2 TB/s bandwidth. The attention matrix for seq_len=2048 = 2048² × 2 bytes = 8 MB per head per layer. Writing and reading this 8 MB costs 8 MB / 2 TB/s = 4 μs, but the extra recomputation FLOPs cost << 1 μs at 312 TFLOPS. The memory wall makes the recomputation essentially free. This is the roofline model in action: in the memory-bound regime, adding compute costs nothing.

scenario: FlashAttention performs more total FLOPs than standard attention (due to recomputation in the backward pass) yet runs 2-4× faster on GPU. A colleague claims 'doing more compute can't possibly be faster.' Analyze why this counter-intuitive result holds.
title: Why FlashAttention is Faster Despite More FLOPs

details.common_mistake: Blaming network congestion or a single faulty GPU. The random rotation of the slowest GPU rules out a single hardware fault.
details.napkin_math: P(any GPU delayed) = 1 - (1-p)^128. If p=0.5% per step per GPU: P(straggler) = 1 - 0.995^128 = 47%. Nearly every other step has a straggler.
details.realistic_solution: This is the straggler problem caused by OS-level interference (jitter). In synchronous training, all GPUs must synchronize at the AllReduce barrier — the slowest GPU determines step time. With 128 GPUs, the probability of at least one experiencing a delay (context switch, page fault, network interrupt, ECC memory scrub, GPU thermal throttling) is high. A single GPU delayed by 200ms delays all 128. Root causes: (1) CPU interrupts during data loading. (2) NUMA memory access misalignment. (3) GPU thermal throttling (one GPU in a hot spot). (4) ECC error detection/correction pauses. Fixes: CPU pinning, NUMA-aware allocation, disabling hyperthreading, using NCCL ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING, and setting cudaDeviceScheduleBlockingSync.

scenario: Your 128-GPU synchronous data parallel training shows step times oscillating between 350ms and 800ms with no pattern. Average GPU utilization is 91% but the slowest GPU per step varies randomly. The cluster is homogeneous (same GPU model, same network). What is happening?
title: Diagnosing Stragglers in Synchronous Training

details.common_mistake: Thinking torch.compile compiles once. Dynamic shapes (varying sequence lengths, batch sizes) trigger recompilation, and each compiled graph is cached — consuming memory.
details.napkin_math: Each compiled graph: 50-500 MB. 20 unique shapes = 1-10 GB of compiled cache. Recompile time: 5-30s per graph. If shapes repeat, amortizes over time; if not, the overhead is constant.
details.realistic_solution: torch.compile traces a graph specialized to specific tensor shapes. When a new shape arrives, it triggers recompilation (expensive: seconds to tens of seconds). In inference serving, varying request lengths produce diverse shapes, causing a 'recompilation storm.' Fixes: (1) Use torch.compile(dynamic=True) to generate shape-generic kernels (slight perf loss but no recompilation). (2) Pad inputs to a small set of bucket sizes (e.g., 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048) so only 5 graphs are compiled. (3) Set torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit to cap memory. (4) Pre-warm the cache with representative shapes during server startup. The fundamental tradeoff: specialized kernels are faster but shape-specific; generic kernels are slower but compile once.

scenario: After enabling torch.compile, your inference server's latency spikes to 5× normal every few minutes before returning to baseline. GPU memory gradually increases. Profiling shows the compiler is triggered repeatedly. What causes this and how do you fix it?
title: torch.compile Recompilation Storm

details.common_mistake: Assuming p99 of a chain equals the sum of individual p99s. In reality, the probability of at least one stage being slow increases multiplicatively.
details.napkin_math: P(all 3 stages < p99) = 0.99³ = 97%. Pipeline p99 ≈ individual p97. If p99.9 = 200ms per stage: P(any > 200ms) = 1 - 0.999³ = 0.3%. Pipeline p99 includes tail spikes from any stage.
details.realistic_solution: For sequential stages, the end-to-end p99 is NOT the sum of individual p99s. If each stage hits p99 independently with P=0.01, the probability ALL three are fast (below p99) = 0.99³ = 0.97. So p99 of the pipeline ≈ p97 of the sum. But worse: when one stage is slow, it often shifts to a much higher percentile (p99 might be 50ms but p99.9 might be 200ms). The compound effect: P(any stage > p99.9) = 1 - 0.999³ = 0.3%. This means the pipeline's p99 approaches max(individual p99.9 + 2×normal). Mitigations: (1) Hedged requests — send to two replicas, take the first response. (2) Timeout-and-retry with budget. (3) Async pipeline stages with queuing. (4) Set per-stage latency budgets that sum to the SLA.

scenario: Your serving pipeline chains 3 models (embedding → retrieval → generation). Each model independently achieves p99=50ms. But the end-to-end pipeline p99 is 280ms, far exceeding the expected 150ms (3×50ms). Analyze why tail latencies compound super-linearly.
title: Tail Latency Sources in Multi-Model Serving

details.common_mistake: Only optimizing for electricity cost. The GPU lease cost (depreciation + rental) usually dominates, so slowing down the GPU to save power increases total cost.
details.napkin_math: 700W: $0.084 elec + $4 lease = $4.08/hr, 36K steps/hr. $0.000113/step. 400W: $0.048 + $4 = $4.05/hr, 26.7K steps/hr. $0.000152/step. 700W is 25% cheaper per step.
details.realistic_solution: At 700W: step=100ms, power=$0.12 × 0.7kW = $0.084/hr electricity. Lease = $4/hr. Total/step = (100ms/3.6M ms) × ($4.084) = $0.000113. At 400W: step=135ms, power=$0.12 × 0.4kW = $0.048/hr electricity. Lease = $4/hr. Total/step = (135ms/3.6M ms) × ($4.048) = $0.000152. The 700W setting is 25% cheaper per step despite higher electricity! The lease dominates: $4/hr vs $0.05-0.08/hr electricity. Power capping only makes sense when electricity is the dominant cost (e.g., owned hardware fully depreciated) or when hitting thermal limits. At $0.12/kWh, the break-even is when lease < $0.20/hr — essentially only for fully-owned, depreciated hardware.

scenario: Your H100 cluster allows per-GPU power capping via nvidia-smi. At 700W (default), training step takes 100ms. At 400W, the step takes 135ms. You pay $0.12/kWh for electricity and $4/GPU-hr for the lease. Analyze the cost-optimal power cap.
title: Optimal Power Cap for Training Cost Minimization

details.common_mistake: Trying to optimize these operations in isolation. The solution is to eliminate the HBM round-trips by fusing these memory-bound ops with adjacent compute-bound ops.
details.napkin_math: Unfused: 3 ops × 2 passes (r+w) = 6 HBM transactions. Fused: 1 op × 2 passes = 2 transactions. 3× less traffic → ~3× faster. 35% of step × 67% reduction = 23% total speedup.
details.realistic_solution: These operations are deeply memory-bound (AI < 1 FLOP/byte) — optimizing their compute is pointless since they spend >95% of time waiting for memory. Strategy: (1) Kernel fusion: fuse BatchNorm + ReLU + Dropout into a single kernel (1 read + 1 write instead of 3×(read+write), saving ~67% of memory traffic). (2) Use torch.compile which automatically fuses elementwise ops. (3) Replace BatchNorm with LayerNorm or RMSNorm which fuse better with attention operations. (4) Enable CUDA graphs to eliminate kernel launch overhead between small ops. Expected result: fusing 3-4 elementwise ops reduces their combined time by 60-70%, cutting total step time by 35% × 65% ≈ 23%.

scenario: Profiling reveals that 35% of your training step time is spent in batch normalization and elementwise operations, despite these accounting for only 2% of total FLOPs. You are on an A100 GPU. Design an optimization strategy to reduce this overhead by at least 50%.
title: Optimizing a Memory-Bound Training Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Only optimizing one dimension (e.g., just quantizing weights). Maximum throughput requires simultaneous optimization of model memory, KV cache memory, and batching efficiency.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: ~208 users. +INT8 weights: 260. +PagedAttention: 364. +TP instead of replication: 434. Compounding optimizations: ~2.1x improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Current: 13B × 2B = 26 GB weights per GPU. KV cache = (80-26-2 overhead) = 52 GB / ~1 GB per user = 52 users per GPU. Across 4 GPUs = 208 users. Optimizations: (1) INT8 quantization: weights = 13 GB, freeing 13 GB extra per GPU for KV cache. Users per GPU: 65, total = 260. (2) Add PagedAttention (vLLM): reduces KV fragmentation waste from ~30% to ~2%, effectively allowing 1.4× more users = 364. (3) Use tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs instead of replication, with INT4 weights: single copy of INT4 weights split across 4 GPUs = ~2 GB overhead per GPU, KV space = ~76 GB per GPU. Total KV = 304 GB. At ~0.7 GB/user with INT8 KV: 434 concurrent users. Net: ~2.1× improvement from combined optimization.

scenario: You have 4× A100-80GB GPUs serving a 13B-parameter chatbot. Current config: FP16 weights replicated on each GPU, handling ~208 concurrent users. Your SLA requires p99 < 200ms per token. Design optimizations to maximize concurrent users within the same hardware and SLA.
title: Maximizing Concurrent Users on Fixed GPU Budget

details.common_mistake: Using maximum tensor parallelism across all 64 GPUs. TP requires all-to-all communication every layer and is only efficient over NVLink (intra-node).
details.napkin_math: 480 GB state. TP=4, PP=2: per-GPU = 480/8 = 60 GB. With ZeRO-1 on DP=8: optimizer sharded → ~21 GB. Leaves 59 GB for activations. TP-4 AllReduce volume is 1.5x tensor size vs 1.75x for TP-8.
details.realistic_solution: Constraints: TP must stay intra-node (NVLink). DP and PP can span nodes (InfiniBand). 480 GB model state / 8 GPUs per TP group = 60 GB per GPU — fits in 80 GB with room for activations. Config: TP=8 (within each node), PP=1, DP=8 (across 8 nodes). But 60 GB/GPU leaves only 20 GB for activations — tight. Alternative: TP=4, PP=2, DP=8. Model state = 480/(4×2) = 60 GB per GPU (same). But TP=4 has lower communication overhead: ring AllReduce volume drops from 1.75x to 1.5x tensor size. PP=2 splits model across 2 nodes in a pipeline, adding ~15 ms bubble per micro-batch. Best config: TP=4, PP=2, DP=8 balances memory, communication, and pipeline efficiency. Use ZeRO-1 to shard optimizer states across DP ranks, reducing per-GPU memory from 60 GB to ~21 GB.

scenario: You must train a 30B-parameter model on 64 H100 GPUs (8 nodes × 8 GPUs). Intra-node NVLink: 900 GB/s. Inter-node InfiniBand: 400 Gb/s. Adam mixed-precision requires 16 bytes/param = 480 GB total model state. Design the optimal (TP, PP, DP) configuration.
title: Choosing 3D Parallelism Configuration

details.common_mistake: Trying to optimize decode when the bottleneck is prefill. TTFT is dominated by the initial forward pass over the entire prompt, which is compute-bound.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 1.2s prefill for 2048 tokens. FP8: 0.6s. Prefix cache (50% cached): 0.3s. TP=2: 0.15s. Pick FP8 + prefix → 0.3s < 500ms SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Prefill optimization strategy: (1) FP8 inference: H100 FP8 = 1979 TFLOPS vs 989 FP16. Near 2× prefill speedup for negligible quality loss. TTFT → ~600ms. (2) Chunked prefill: process prompt in 512-token chunks, allowing decode of other requests between chunks. Doesn't reduce absolute TTFT but improves p99 by preventing long prefills from blocking short ones. (3) Speculative prefill with early KV caching: for common prefixes (system prompts), cache the KV states. If 1024 of 2048 tokens are cached prefix, you only prefill 1024 tokens → 50% TTFT reduction. (4) Tensor parallelism: split across 2 GPUs to halve prefill compute. With FP8 + prefix caching: TTFT ≈ 600ms × 0.5 = 300ms. Combined: FP8 + prefix caching achieves <500ms SLA.

scenario: Your chatbot's time-to-first-token (TTFT) averages 1.2s for 2048-token prompts on H100. The SLA requires TTFT < 500ms. Decode throughput is acceptable. Design an optimization plan targeting the prefill phase specifically.
title: Optimizing Time-to-First-Token for Interactive Chat

details.common_mistake: Just adding more network bandwidth. Often the bottleneck is protocol overhead, topology, or lack of overlap — not raw bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Gradient compression: 8 GB → 0.8 GB. AllReduce time: 10× faster. Overlap 70%: only 30% exposed. Net: 40% × (1/10) × 0.3 = 1.2% overhead. Well under 15%.
details.realistic_solution: Current: 40% overhead. Target: <15%. Strategy stack: (1) Gradient compression (PowerSGD or TopK): compress 8 GB → 800 MB (10× reduction, ~1% accuracy impact). AllReduce time drops ~10×. (2) Overlap communication with computation: start AllReduce for layer N's gradients while computing backward for layer N-1. With good overlap, 50-80% of AllReduce is hidden. (3) Hierarchical AllReduce: intra-rack reduce (NVSwitch, fast), then inter-rack AllReduce (smaller data). (4) FP16 gradient AllReduce instead of FP32: halves volume (use loss scaling to maintain precision). Combined: compression 10× + overlap 70% of remaining → effective overhead = 40% / 10 × 0.3 = 1.2%. Even just compression + overlap: 40% × 0.1 × 0.3 = 1.2%. Either approach achieves <15%.

scenario: Your 256-GPU training cluster (32 nodes across 4 racks) spends 40% of step time in AllReduce over InfiniBand NDR (400 Gb/s per port). Gradient size is 8 GB. Design optimizations to reduce communication overhead below 15%.
title: Reducing AllReduce Bottleneck in Cross-Rack Training

details.common_mistake: Either over-provisioning with all reserved instances (paying for idle capacity) or under-provisioning with all on-demand (paying premium at peak).
details.napkin_math: Reserve base = 2-8 GPUs. On-demand peak = 12-18 GPUs for ~12h/day. Sweet spot: reserve 6 GPUs ($78,840/yr) + on-demand burst ($50K) = ~$129K vs all-on-demand ($263K) or all-reserved ($263K).
details.realistic_solution: Peak GPUs needed = 1000/50 = 20. Trough = 100/50 = 2. Strategy: reserve enough for the sustained baseline, use on-demand for bursts. If trough lasts 12h and peak lasts 12h (simplified): reserve 2 GPUs (always needed): 2 × $1.50 × 8760h = $26,280/yr. On-demand for peak delta: average additional GPUs during peak hours ≈ (20-2)/2 × 12h (triangle approximation) = 9 extra GPUs × 12h × 365d × $3 = $118,260. Total = $144,540. Optimized: reserve ~8 GPUs (covers ~80% of traffic hours): 8 × $1.50 × 8760 = $105,120. On-demand: ~6 GPUs × 6h/day × 365 × $3 = $39,420. Total = $144,540. Analysis shows reserve 6-8 GPUs is optimal. Adding autoscaling with 2-minute spin-up + predictive scaling reduces on-demand waste by ~30%.

scenario: Your LLM service has traffic that varies 10× between peak (1000 req/s) and trough (100 req/s) over 24 hours. Each GPU handles 50 req/s. On-demand GPUs cost $3/hr, reserved (1-year) cost $1.50/hr. Design the optimal fleet composition to minimize annual cost while meeting peak demand.
title: Right-Sizing an Inference Fleet for Variable Traffic

details.common_mistake: Uniformly quantizing all layers to INT4. Different layers have different sensitivity — attention projection layers are more sensitive than MLP layers.
details.napkin_math: 70B model breakdown: MLP ~56B params (INT4) = 28 GB, Attention ~10.5B (INT8) = 10.5 GB, Embeddings ~3.5B (FP16) = 7 GB. Total: ~45.5 GB (3.1× compression from 140 GB FP16). BW savings: 3.1×. Throughput: 800 × 2.5 = 2000 tok/s. Quality: <1% degradation with AWQ calibration.
details.realistic_solution: Step 1: Profile layer sensitivity — quantize each layer independently and measure perplexity impact. Typically: embedding layers = very sensitive (keep FP16), attention QKV = medium sensitivity (INT8), MLP up/down/gate = low sensitivity (INT4), LayerNorm = keep FP16 (tiny memory footprint). Step 2: Apply mixed scheme. Rough breakdown for 70B: embeddings (FP16) = 2 GB, attention (INT8) = 10 GB, MLP (INT4) = 12 GB, other (FP16) = 1 GB. Total ≈ 25 GB vs 140 GB FP16. Step 3: Memory-bound decode throughput scales ≈ proportionally to weight reduction: 140/25 = 5.6× potential speedup. Realistic with overhead: 4×. New throughput: 800 × 4 = 3200 tok/s. Well above 2000 target with room for conservative quantization where needed. Step 4: Use calibration data from your domain to select per-layer bit widths with AWQ.

scenario: You serve a 70B model on 2× H100 GPUs. FP16 achieves baseline quality but only 800 tok/s aggregate. Your target is 2000 tok/s with <1% quality degradation on your evaluation suite. Design a mixed-precision quantization strategy.
title: Designing a Mixed-Precision Serving Strategy

details.common_mistake: Simply checkpointing more frequently. With 8-minute stall and 30-minute MTBF, increasing frequency makes overhead worse.
details.napkin_math: Async ckpt: 30s stall. ZeRO: 2.8 GB/GPU. Interval: sqrt(2 × 30 × 0.5) = 5.5 min. Overhead: 9% + 9% = 18%. With buddy ckpt (MTBF→60min): 12.9%. Under 15% target.
details.realistic_solution: Problem: synchronous checkpoint takes 8 min out of every 30-min MTBF = 27% overhead just from checkpointing, plus ~50% of inter-checkpoint work is lost on failure. Solution stack: (1) Asynchronous checkpointing: snapshot state to CPU/host memory (fast, <30s) then write to persistent storage in background. GPU stall drops from 8 min to 30s. (2) Reduce checkpoint size with ZeRO: each GPU only checkpoints its optimizer shard (175B / 1000 = 175M params × 16 bytes = 2.8 GB per GPU vs 2.8 TB total). (3) Local SSD checkpoint first, then replicate to remote storage. (4) With t_ckpt=0.5 min, optimal interval = sqrt(2 × 30 × 0.5) = 5.5 min. Overhead: ckpt = 0.5/5.5 = 9%. Wasted work = 5.5/(2×30) = 9.2%. Total = 18.2%. Add in-memory redundancy (buddy checkpointing): MTBF effectively doubles to 60 min. New overhead: sqrt(2×60×0.5) = 7.7 min interval. Waste = 6.5% (checkpointing) + 6.4% (wasted work) = 12.9%.

scenario: Your 1000-GPU training cluster has MTBF of 30 minutes. Full synchronous checkpoint of a 175B model takes 8 minutes and stalls all GPUs. Current wasted compute is estimated at 45%. Design a checkpointing strategy to reduce waste below 15%.
title: Optimizing Checkpoint Strategy for 1000-GPU Training

details.common_mistake: Focusing on compute optimization when decode is memory-bound. The tiny kernels aren't slow because of compute — they're slow because each one triggers an HBM round-trip and kernel launch overhead.
details.napkin_math: 100 kernel launches × 10μs = 1ms overhead per step. CUDA graphs: 0. Fusion: 3 HBM round-trips → 1 = 3× for fused ops. FlashDecoding: 2× for long sequences. Net decode speedup: 2-3×.
details.realistic_solution: Decode optimization plan: (1) CUDA Graphs: capture the entire decode step as a single graph. Eliminates per-kernel launch overhead (~10μs × 100s of kernels = 1-2ms saved per step). This alone can give 10-20% speedup. (2) Aggressive operator fusion for decode path: fuse all elementwise ops (LayerNorm → Linear → GELU → Linear → Residual) into mega-kernels. torch.compile with mode='max-autotune' enables this. (3) Custom CUDA kernel for decode attention: FlashDecoding parallelizes across the KV cache sequence dimension, maximizing memory bandwidth utilization. (4) KV cache in contiguous memory (PagedAttention compatible with CUDA Graphs): reduces scattered memory access. (5) INT8 KV cache: halves memory traffic for attention. Combined: CUDA graphs (15%) + fusion (20%) + FlashDecoding (30%) + INT8 KV (40% for attention) → decode throughput ~2-3×.

scenario: Your torch.compile'd model achieves 85% of peak TFLOPS during prefill but only 15% during decode. Decode dominates total latency for long outputs. Profile shows hundreds of tiny elementwise kernels during decode with high launch overhead. Design a compilation optimization strategy for decode.
title: Optimizing a Compiled Inference Graph for Throughput

details.common_mistake: Only considering hardware power reduction. The full solution space includes model efficiency, scheduling, and energy source.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 195 gCO2 / 1M tokens. Power cap H100 to 400W: throughput drops ~10% but power drops 43%, reducing energy/token by ~36% -> 124 gCO2. Carbon-aware scheduling: shift workloads to times/regions with 200 gCO2/kWh (50% reduction in carbon intensity) -> 62 gCO2. Target of 100 gCO2 met safely.
details.realistic_solution: The baseline is 195 gCO2 per 1M tokens. To hit the 100 gCO2 budget, we must optimize both hardware power efficiency and energy source carbon intensity. (1) Power Capping: Capping the H100 at 400W reduces power consumption by 43% while throughput only drops by ~10% (as it enters the more efficient region of the voltage-frequency curve). This reduces energy per token, bringing emissions to ~124 gCO2 / 1M tokens. (2) Carbon-aware Scheduling: By shifting flexible batch workloads to regions or times where the grid carbon intensity is lower (e.g., 200 gCO2/kWh instead of 400 gCO2/kWh), we halve the remaining emissions, reaching ~62 gCO2 / 1M tokens, safely meeting the 100 gCO2 budget.

scenario: Your organization commits to a carbon budget of 100 gCO2 per 1M output tokens. Current infrastructure (H100 at 700W, grid at 400 gCO2/kWh) produces 195 gCO2/1M tokens. Design an optimization plan to meet the carbon target without reducing throughput.
title: Maximizing Tokens-per-Watt for Sustainable Inference

details.common_mistake: Confusing HBM2e and HBM3 specs, or mixing up bandwidth with capacity. A100 and H100 both have 80GB but very different bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: A100: 2.0 TB/s HBM2e. H100: 3.35 TB/s HBM3. Ratio: 3.35/2.0 = 1.68x bandwidth improvement across generations.
details.realistic_solution: The A100 delivers 2.0 TB/s of HBM2e bandwidth, while the H100 delivers 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 bandwidth — a 1.68x improvement. This matters because many LLM inference workloads are memory-bandwidth-bound (not compute-bound), so the H100's 1.68x bandwidth gain translates almost directly to 1.68x faster token generation for autoregressive decoding. The compute improvement is even larger (989 vs 312 TFLOPS = 3.17x), meaning the H100 shifts the roofline knee further right, making more workloads compute-bound.

scenario: What is the peak HBM2e memory bandwidth of an NVIDIA A100-80GB GPU, and how does it compare to the H100's HBM3 bandwidth?
title: HBM Bandwidth Ceiling on A100

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that arithmetic intensity is FLOPS per byte transferred, not per element. Also confusing FP16 (2 bytes) with FP32 (4 bytes).
details.realistic_solution: Arithmetic intensity (AI) = FLOPs / Bytes transferred. Units: FLOP/Byte. For y = Wx with W being 4096×4096 FP16: FLOPs = 2 × 4096 × 4096 = 33,554,432 (multiply-add counted as 2 ops). Bytes moved = W (33,554,432 bytes) + x (8,192 bytes) + y (8,192 bytes) = 33,570,816 bytes. AI = 33.55M / 33.57M ≈ 1.0 FLOP/Byte. This is well below the A100's ridge point of 156 FLOP/Byte (312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s), confirming that matrix-vector multiplies are deeply memory-bound — the fundamental reason autoregressive decoding is slow.

scenario: Define arithmetic intensity and state its units. What is the arithmetic intensity of a matrix-vector multiply y = Wx where W is 4096×4096 in FP16?
title: Arithmetic Intensity Definition

details.common_mistake: Forgetting INT4 is half a byte (4 bits = 0.5 bytes), leading to wrong memory estimates. Also neglecting quantization overhead (scales, zero-points) which adds ~0.5-2% extra memory.
details.napkin_math: 70B × 4B = 280GB (FP32). 70B × 2B = 140GB (FP16). 70B × 1B = 70GB (INT8). 70B × 0.5B = 35GB (INT4). Memory halves with each precision step.
details.realistic_solution: FP32 = 4 bytes, FP16/BF16 = 2 bytes, INT8 = 1 byte, INT4 = 0.5 bytes. For a 70B model: FP32 = 70B × 4 = 280 GB. FP16 = 70B × 2 = 140 GB. INT8 = 70B × 1 = 70 GB. INT4 = 70B × 0.5 = 35 GB. This is why quantization is transformative for deployment: a 70B model that requires 2× A100-80GB in FP16 fits on a single A100-80GB in INT8, or a single 48GB GPU in INT4. The key insight is that each halving of precision halves the memory and doubles the effective memory bandwidth (since the same TB/s moves twice as many parameters).

scenario: How many bytes does a single model parameter consume in FP32, FP16, INT8, and INT4 formats? What is the total VRAM for a 70B parameter model in each?
title: Bytes per Parameter Across Precisions

details.common_mistake: Confusing power (watts, instantaneous) with energy (watt-hours, cumulative). Also forgetting that real-world power draw averages 70-85% of TDP, not 100%.
details.napkin_math: 400W × 24h = 9.6 kWh/day. At $0.10/kWh = $0.96/day per GPU. 1024-GPU cluster: $0.96 × 1024 × 30 ≈ $29.5K/month electricity.
details.realistic_solution: Energy = Power × Time. At full TDP: 400W × 24h = 9,600 Wh = 9.6 kWh. Cost: 9.6 × $0.10 = $0.96/day per GPU. At realistic 80% average utilization: 320W × 24h = 7.68 kWh = $0.77/day. For a 1024-GPU cluster running 30 days: 1024 × 9.6 × 30 = 294,912 kWh = $29,491/month in electricity alone. Adding cooling overhead (PUE ≈ 1.2), total energy cost becomes $35,389/month. This is why hyperscalers locate data centers near cheap hydroelectric power.

scenario: An A100 GPU has a TDP of 400W. How much energy (in kWh) does a single A100 consume running at full power for 24 hours? What does this cost at $0.10/kWh?
title: TDP and Energy Cost of GPU Hours

details.common_mistake: Quoting unidirectional bandwidth as total, or confusing NVLink per-link bandwidth with total aggregate bandwidth across all links.
details.napkin_math: NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s bidir. PCIe Gen5 x16: 64 GB/s bidir. Ratio: 14x. Gradient sync for 7B (14GB FP16): PCIe ~440ms, NVLink ~31ms.
details.realistic_solution: NVLink 4.0 on H100 provides 900 GB/s total bidirectional bandwidth (18 links × 50 GB/s each). PCIe Gen5 x16 provides ~64 GB/s bidirectional (32 GB/s each direction). The ratio is 900/64 ≈ 14x. This gap is critical for data-parallel training: after each backward pass, all GPUs must synchronize gradients via AllReduce. For a 7B model, gradients are 14 GB in FP16. Over PCIe: 14 GB / 32 GB/s ≈ 440 ms. Over NVLink: 14 GB / 450 GB/s ≈ 31 ms (using half the bidirectional bandwidth in ring allreduce). NVLink makes gradient sync fast enough to overlap with computation; PCIe cannot.

scenario: What is the bidirectional bandwidth of NVLink 4.0 (as found in H100 DGX systems) vs PCIe Gen5 x16? Why does this gap matter for multi-GPU training?
title: NVLink vs PCIe Bandwidth Gap

details.common_mistake: Confusing tensor parallelism with pipeline parallelism. TP splits individual layers (intra-layer), PP splits groups of layers (inter-layer), DP replicates the full model.
details.napkin_math: For a 175B model on 512 GPUs: typical config is DP=64, TP=4, PP=2. 64×4×2 = 512. TP=4 within a node (NVLink), PP=2 across nodes, DP=64 across the cluster.
details.realistic_solution: Data Parallelism (DP): replicates the entire model on each GPU; partitions the training batch across GPUs. Each GPU processes different data, then gradients are synchronized via AllReduce. Tensor Parallelism (TP): splits individual weight matrices within a single layer across GPUs. A single matrix multiply is distributed (e.g., column-parallel linear layers). Requires high-bandwidth interconnect (NVLink) because GPUs exchange activations every layer. Pipeline Parallelism (PP): partitions the model's layers into sequential stages across GPUs. GPU 0 runs layers 1-10, GPU 1 runs layers 11-20, etc. Introduces pipeline bubbles but needs only point-to-point communication between adjacent stages.

scenario: Name the three primary axes of parallelism used in distributed LLM training and state what each axis partitions across GPUs.
title: Three Axes of Parallelism

details.common_mistake: Computing the ridge point for FP32 instead of FP16 Tensor Cores, or using the wrong bandwidth number (DRAM vs cache).
details.napkin_math: A100: 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOP/Byte. H100: 989 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s = 295 FLOP/Byte. Higher ridge = more operations need to reach compute saturation.
details.realistic_solution: Ridge point = Peak Compute / Peak Bandwidth = 312 TFLOPS / 2.0 TB/s = 156 FLOP/Byte. This means: if your kernel's arithmetic intensity is below 156 FLOP/Byte, it is memory-bandwidth-bound (performance limited by how fast data can be fed to the cores). If above 156, it is compute-bound (performance limited by FLOPS). Most inference workloads (batch=1 attention, small-batch MLP) have AI of 1-10 FLOP/Byte — deeply memory-bound. Training with large batches pushes GEMM operations to AI of 500-2000, well into the compute-bound regime. The H100's ridge point is 989/3.35 = 295 FLOP/Byte.

scenario: Calculate the ridge point (in FLOP/Byte) of the A100 for FP16 Tensor Core operations. What does this number physically mean?
title: The A100 Ridge Point

details.common_mistake: Assuming electricity is the dominant cost. In reality, hardware amortization (GPU depreciation) dominates cloud GPU pricing at 50-60% of the total.
details.napkin_math: A100 server ~$200K / (3yr × 8760h × 8 GPUs) = $0.95/GPU-hr hardware cost. Electricity: 400W × $0.06/kWh × 1.2 PUE = $0.029/hr. Margin + ops doubles the base cost → $3.00/hr.
details.realistic_solution: Approximate decomposition of a $3.00/GPU-hour A100 instance: Hardware amortization: ~$1.50-1.80 (50-60%). An A100 GPU costs ~$15K, server total ~$200K for 8 GPUs. Over 3 years = $200K / (3×8760h×8) ≈ $0.95/GPU-hour for hardware alone, but cloud providers add margin. Electricity: ~$0.30-0.45 (10-15%). 400W × $0.06/kWh = $0.024/h raw power, but PUE of 1.2 and facility costs push this up. Networking + storage: ~$0.15-0.30 (5-10%). Facility + cooling: ~$0.15-0.30 (5-10%). Staff + operations: ~$0.15-0.30 (5-10%). Cloud provider margin: ~$0.30-0.60 (10-20%). Understanding this breakdown reveals why spot instances (50-70% discount) exist — the hardware depreciates whether it runs or not.
