scenario: An A100 cloud instance costs $3.00/GPU-hour. What are the approximate cost components (hardware amortization, electricity, cooling, networking, staff) that make up this price?
title: GPU-Hour Cost Decomposition

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to count both K and V caches, or miscounting the per-layer contribution. Each layer stores both a key and a value vector for every attention head.
details.napkin_math: 2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 2B = 320 KB/token. Context of 4096: 320KB × 4096 = 1.28 GB/request. 100 concurrent: 128 GB KV cache alone.
details.realistic_solution: Per token KV cache = 2 (K+V) × num_layers × num_kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element. For Llama-2-70B: 2 × 80 × 8 (GQA uses 8 KV heads, not 64) × 128 × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes ≈ 320 KB per token. For a 4096-token context: 320 KB × 4096 = 1.28 GB per request. Serving 100 concurrent requests: 128 GB of VRAM just for KV cache — more than the model weights (140 GB FP16). This is why KV cache management (PagedAttention, vLLM) is critical: naive pre-allocation wastes 60-80% of KV cache memory on internal fragmentation.

scenario: For a Llama-2-70B model (80 layers, 64 heads, head_dim=128) in FP16, how much KV cache memory is needed per token?
title: KV Cache Memory per Token

details.common_mistake: Thinking kernel fusion saves compute. It saves memory bandwidth by eliminating intermediate round-trips to HBM between elementwise operations.
details.napkin_math: Unfused: 4 HBM reads + 4 HBM writes for 3 ops. Fused: 1 read + 1 write. For 4096-dim hidden state: unfused moves 8 × 4096 × 2B = 64 KB; fused moves 2 × 4096 × 2B = 16 KB. 4x bandwidth reduction.
details.realistic_solution: Kernel fusion combines multiple GPU operations (kernels) into a single kernel, eliminating intermediate writes and reads to HBM. Without fusion, a sequence like y = ReLU(LayerNorm(x + bias)) requires: (1) write x+bias to HBM, (2) read it back for LayerNorm, (3) write LayerNorm output to HBM, (4) read it back for ReLU — 4 HBM round-trips for the intermediate tensors. Fused: one kernel reads x and bias, computes the entire chain in registers/SRAM, writes only the final result — 1 HBM write. Since HBM access costs ~100x more energy and ~300x more latency than register access, fusion can speed up memory-bound operations by 2-4x. Tools like torch.compile, Triton, and XLA perform this automatically.

scenario: What is kernel fusion and why does it improve GPU performance? State the primary bottleneck it eliminates.
title: Why Kernel Fusion Matters

details.common_mistake: Only counting weight storage and forgetting optimizer states, gradients, and activations. Optimizer states alone can be 4x the weight memory.
details.napkin_math: 1B params × 16 bytes/param = 16 GB. Breakdown: 2B (FP16 weights) + 2B (FP16 grads) + 4B (FP32 master) + 4B (FP32 momentum) + 4B (FP32 variance). Activations add 2-10 GB depending on batch size.
details.realistic_solution: The 16 bytes/param breakdown for mixed-precision Adam training: FP16 weights = 2B/param (used in forward/backward). FP16 gradients = 2B/param (accumulated during backward). FP32 master weights = 4B/param (Adam updates in FP32 for numerical stability). FP32 momentum (m) = 4B/param. FP32 variance (v) = 4B/param. Total = 2+2+4+4+4 = 16B/param. For 1B params: 16 GB. On top of this, activations add memory proportional to batch size × sequence length × hidden dimension × number of layers. Activation checkpointing trades compute (recomputing activations in backward) for memory (storing only checkpointed layers).

scenario: Explain why training a 1B parameter model in mixed-precision (FP16 forward/backward + FP32 Adam optimizer) requires approximately 16 GB of memory, not just the 2 GB for FP16 weights.
title: Training Memory Budget Breakdown

details.common_mistake: Claiming decoding is slow because of sequential token generation alone. The sequential nature is a latency issue, but the throughput bottleneck is bandwidth — even a single token generation step underutilizes the GPU's compute.
details.napkin_math: Decode batch=1: read 140GB at 2 TB/s = 70ms. Compute: 140 GFLOP / 312 TFLOPS = 0.449ms. GPU utilization: 0.449/70000 = 0.0006% (compute nearly idle). Training batch=2048: AI ≈ 4096, well above ridge (156). Compute-bound at ~80% MFU.
details.realistic_solution: In batch-1 decoding, each token generation requires reading all model weights from HBM but performs very few FLOPs per weight (matrix-vector multiply, AI ≈ 1 FLOP/Byte). On an A100, you read 140 GB of weights at 2.0 TB/s = 70ms per token, but only perform 140 GFLOP — consuming 70ms of bandwidth time but only 0.449ms of compute time (140G / 312T). The GPU's 312 TFLOPS sit essentially idle. In large-batch training, GEMM operations become matrix-matrix multiplies (batch dimension >> 1). For batch=2048, AI = 2×2048 ≈ 4096 FLOP/Byte, far above the 156 ridge point. Now compute is the bottleneck: you have enough data reuse to keep the Tensor Cores busy.

scenario: Explain why batch-1 autoregressive LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound while large-batch training is compute-bound, using the roofline model.
title: Memory-Bound vs Compute-Bound Intuition

details.common_mistake: Thinking AllReduce cost grows linearly with N. Ring AllReduce is bandwidth-optimal — total data transferred per GPU is constant regardless of cluster size (for large N).
details.napkin_math: For 8 GPUs with 14 GB gradients: each GPU sends 2 × (7/8) × 14 GB = 24.5 GB. At 450 GB/s NVLink effective bandwidth: 24.5/450 = 54ms. For 4 GPUs: 2 × (3/4) × 14 = 21 GB. Scales sub-linearly.
details.realistic_solution: Ring AllReduce works in two phases: scatter-reduce and allgather, each requiring N-1 steps. In each step, every GPU sends 1/N of the gradient buffer to its neighbor. Per GPU, total data sent = (N-1)/N × buffer_size in scatter-reduce + (N-1)/N × buffer_size in allgather = 2×(N-1)/N × buffer_size. As N→∞, this approaches 2× the buffer size. This is bandwidth-optimal because every link is utilized simultaneously. The critical insight: doubling GPUs does NOT double communication time — it's nearly constant per GPU. The bottleneck is the per-link bandwidth, not the number of GPUs. This is why ring AllReduce scales well on NVLink-connected GPUs within a node.

scenario: Explain why AllReduce in a ring topology transfers 2×(N-1)/N times the gradient size, where N is the number of GPUs. Why does this approach O(2× gradient size) as N grows?
title: AllReduce Communication Overhead

details.common_mistake: Assuming quantization error is uniform across all values. A single outlier forces the quantization range to be 100x wider, wasting 99% of the INT8 range on values that don't need it.
details.napkin_math: Without outlier handling: 256 INT8 bins spanning range 200 → resolution of 0.79 per bin. Values in [-1,1] get ≈2 bins → ~50% quantization error. With mixed-precision: 0.1% dims in FP16 + 99.9% in INT8 = 99.9% memory savings preserved, <0.1% quality loss.
details.realistic_solution: INT8 maps the full range [min, max] to 256 bins. If 99.9% of activations fall in [-1, 1] but one outlier hits 100, the scale factor is 100/127 ≈ 0.79. Normal values in [-1, 1] get mapped to just [-1, 1] in INT8 — only 2 out of 256 bins, losing 99.2% of the precision. LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al.) solves this via mixed-precision decomposition: identify the ~0.1% of feature dimensions with outliers (magnitude > 6.0), compute those columns in FP16, and quantize the remaining 99.9% to INT8. This preserves quality because outlier dimensions carry disproportionate information in transformer hidden states, and keeping them in FP16 costs negligible extra memory.

scenario: Explain why a single activation outlier (e.g., one value at 100x the magnitude of others) can destroy INT8 quantization accuracy, and how techniques like LLM.int8() address this.
title: Why Activation Outliers Break Quantization

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on raw bandwidth. Ethernet 400G and InfiniBand NDR both offer 400 Gb/s, but the critical advantage of InfiniBand is RDMA and predictable low-latency, not just bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: AllReduce latency for 1GB gradient buffer: InfiniBand RDMA: 1GB/(50 GB/s) + 2μs × log₂(N) hops. Ethernet TCP: 1GB/(50 GB/s) + 50μs × log₂(N) + retransmit risk. At N=1024: InfiniBand ~20ms, Ethernet ~30-150ms (with tail latency).
details.realistic_solution: InfiniBand's advantages for training go beyond bandwidth: (1) RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access): GPU memory can be read/written directly over the network, bypassing the host CPU and OS kernel. This eliminates multiple memory copies and context switches, reducing per-message latency from ~10-50 μs (TCP/IP) to ~1-2 μs. (2) Lossless fabric: InfiniBand uses credit-based flow control, guaranteeing zero packet loss. Ethernet (even with RoCE) uses PFC which can cause deadlocks and head-of-line blocking. Packet loss triggers TCP retransmission, adding 10-100ms tail latency spikes that stall AllReduce across thousands of GPUs. (3) Adaptive routing: InfiniBand dynamically routes around congestion, maintaining consistent bandwidth. For AllReduce across 1000+ GPUs, even a single slow link creates a straggler that slows the entire step.

scenario: Explain why large-scale LLM training clusters prefer InfiniBand over Ethernet. What specific properties of InfiniBand reduce AllReduce latency?
title: InfiniBand vs Ethernet for Training

details.common_mistake: Choosing INT4 solely because it fits on fewer GPUs without analyzing whether the latency SLA is actually achievable and whether the quality degradation matters for the use case.
details.napkin_math: INT8: 70GB / 2 TB/s = 35ms/token. INT4: 35GB / 2 TB/s = 17.5ms/token. 256 tokens latency: INT8 = 8.96s, INT4 = 4.48s. Both fail the 200ms end-to-end latency SLA. Hitting 200ms for 256 tokens requires <0.78ms/token, which requires massive Tensor Parallelism or speculative decoding. INT4 provides exactly double the baseline speed, putting the SLA within reach of TP/speculative techniques.
details.realistic_solution: INT8 (70 GB) requires 1× A100-80GB; INT4 (35 GB) also fits on 1× A100-80GB but with more headroom for KV cache. For latency: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. INT8 reads 70GB of weights per full forward pass; INT4 reads 35GB. At 2.0 TB/s: INT8 = 70/2000 = 35ms/token, INT4 = 35/2000 = 17.5ms/token. For 256 tokens end-to-end: INT8 ≈ 8.96s, INT4 ≈ 4.48s. Both far exceed the 200ms SLA for standard autoregressive generation! Batching increases throughput but does NOT reduce latency per request. Hitting <200ms for 256 tokens means <0.78ms/token. This SLA is completely unachievable on a single GPU. It requires Tensor Parallelism across 8 GPUs AND speculative decoding. You must choose INT4 because it gives you a 2x baseline speedup, which is fundamentally necessary (alongside advanced systems techniques) to even approach the required SLA. The 1.2% perplexity increase is acceptable for chat.

scenario: You are deploying a 70B model for production chat serving. Compare INT8 (W8A8) vs INT4 (W4A16) quantization. INT8 shows 0.3% perplexity increase, INT4 shows 1.2%. Your SLA requires P99 latency < 200ms for 256-token responses. Which do you choose and why?
title: INT8 vs INT4 for Production LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Choosing PP=8 because it seems simpler. With 8 pipeline stages and 8 micro-batches, the bubble fraction is (8-1)/(8+8-1) = 46.6% — a significant waste. TP=8 within NVLink is the clear winner.
details.napkin_math: PP=8 bubble: (p-1)/(m+p-1) micro-batches → m=8: 7/15 = 46.6% waste. m=32: 7/39 = 17.9% waste. TP=8 AllReduce per layer: 32MB / 450 GB/s = 0.07ms × 80 layers = 5.6ms total per step. TP overhead <1% vs PP overhead 18-47%.
details.realistic_solution: TP=8 is far superior for a single NVLink-connected node. (1) Communication: TP requires 2 AllReduce per layer (forward + backward) but NVLink provides 900 GB/s — each AllReduce for a 4096×4096 weight is <0.1ms. PP requires only point-to-point send/recv but suffers from pipeline bubbles. (2) Bubble fraction: PP with micro-batches m has bubble = (p-1)/(m+p-1) where p=stages. For PP=8 with m=8 micro-batches: 7/15 = 46.6% idle time wasted. Even with m=32: 7/39 = 17.9% bubble. TP has zero bubble — all GPUs compute simultaneously. (3) Memory: TP splits each layer's weights across 8 GPUs: 70B × 16B/param / 8 = 140 GB/GPU — fits in 80GB? No, needs ZeRO or reduced batch. PP puts 70/8 ≈ 9B params per GPU = 144 GB/GPU for training — also doesn't fit. Both need gradient checkpointing + ZeRO. TP=8 with ZeRO Stage 1 is the standard approach.

scenario: You have 8 A100-80GB GPUs connected by NVLink within a single node. You need to train a 70B model. Compare TP=8 (tensor parallel across all 8) vs PP=8 (pipeline parallel, 8 stages). Which is better for this configuration and why?
title: Tensor vs Pipeline Parallelism for 70B

details.common_mistake: Comparing only base costs without accounting for checkpoint overhead, preemption recovery time, and the risk of cascading preemptions extending the total wall-clock time.
details.napkin_math: On-demand: 64 × 336h × $3 = $64,512. Spot: 64 × 336h × $1 = $21,504 + expected preemption cost: 1.4 events × 2h × 64 GPUs × $1 = $179.20 ≈ $21,683. Savings: $42,829 (66%). With 30-min checkpointing: lost work per preemption drops from 2h to 0.5h → preemption cost drops to 1.4 × 0.5h × 64 × $1 = $44.80.
details.realistic_solution: On-demand: 64 GPUs × 336h × $3.00 = $64,512, guaranteed 14-day completion. Spot: base cost = 64 × 336h × $1.00 = $21,504. Expected preemptions: 14 days × 10%/day = 1.4 events. Cost of lost compute per event = 2h × 64 GPUs × $1.00 = $128; total lost compute = 1.4 × $128 = $179.20. With restart overhead (0.5h): total expected extra cost = 1.4 × (2.5h × 64 × $1) = $224. Expected extra time = 1.4 × 2.5h = 3.5h. Total spot ≈ $21,728, ~14.15 days. Spot saves 66% ($42,784). Mitigation: checkpoint every 30 minutes (preemption overhead drops to 1.4 × 0.5h × 64 × $1 = $44.80) and use spot-with-fallback strategy. Hybrid: use spot for first 12 days, switch to on-demand for final 2 days.

scenario: A 7B model training run takes 14 days on 64 A100 GPUs. On-demand costs $3.00/GPU-hour. Spot instances cost $1.00/GPU-hour but have a 10% chance of preemption per day. Each preemption costs 2 hours of lost work (last checkpoint was 2 hours ago). Evaluate: spot, on-demand, or a hybrid approach?
title: Spot vs On-Demand for Long Training Runs

details.common_mistake: Assuming continuous batching only helps with latency. The primary benefit is throughput — static batching wastes GPU cycles on padding after short requests complete.
details.napkin_math: Static: 32 × 1500 max = 48K token-steps. Useful: 32 × 500 avg = 16K. Utilization: 33%. Continuous: ~32 × 500 avg = 16K steps total (batch refilled continuously). 48K/16K = 3x throughput improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Static batching: all 32 requests run until the longest (1500 tokens) completes. If average length is 500 tokens, each short request that finishes at 50 tokens wastes 1450 token-slots of compute. Total compute = 32 × 1500 = 48,000 token-steps. Useful compute = sum of actual lengths ≈ 32 × 500 = 16,000. GPU utilization = 16,000/48,000 = 33%. Continuous batching: when a request finishes, a new request is immediately inserted into its slot. The batch stays full at 32 throughout. No wasted token-steps. Utilization approaches 100% (minus scheduling overhead ~2-5%). Throughput improvement: 100%/33% ≈ 3x for this workload distribution. The gain is proportional to the variance in output lengths — uniform lengths see no benefit, high variance sees massive gains. This is why vLLM and TensorRT-LLM use continuous batching by default.

scenario: Your LLM serving system processes requests with highly variable output lengths (10-2000 tokens). Compare static batching (all requests in a batch must complete before new ones start) vs continuous batching (Orca-style iteration-level scheduling). Quantify the throughput difference for a batch of 32 requests where lengths range from 50 to 1500 tokens.
title: Static vs Continuous Batching for LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Comparing only raw TFLOPS without normalizing by power. The H100 is 3.17x faster but also 1.75x more power-hungry, so the efficiency gain is less than the raw speedup suggests.
details.napkin_math: A100: 312T/400W = 0.78 TFLOPS/W. H100: 989T/700W = 1.41 TFLOPS/W. Ratio: 1.81x. 2MW budget (1.4MW for GPUs): A100 = 3500 GPUs × 312T = 1,092 PFLOPS. H100 = 2000 GPUs × 989T = 1,978 PFLOPS.
details.realistic_solution: Performance/watt: A100 = 312 TFLOPS / 400W = 0.78 TFLOPS/W. H100 = 989 TFLOPS / 700W = 1.41 TFLOPS/W. Efficiency gain: 1.41/0.78 = 1.81x — the H100 delivers 1.81x more FLOPS per watt. For a 2MW power budget (assuming 70% for GPUs after cooling/networking overhead = 1.4MW): A100: 1.4MW / 400W = 3,500 GPUs → 3,500 × 312 TFLOPS = 1,092 PFLOPS. H100: 1.4MW / 700W = 2,000 GPUs → 2,000 × 989 TFLOPS = 1,978 PFLOPS. The H100 delivers 1.81x more aggregate compute in the same power envelope despite having 43% fewer GPUs. This is why power-constrained data centers prefer newer GPUs even at higher per-unit cost — the TCO per FLOP is better.

scenario: The A100 has 312 TFLOPS FP16 at 400W TDP. The H100 has 989 TFLOPS FP16 at 700W TDP. Compare their performance per watt. If your data center has a fixed 2MW power budget, how many PFLOPS can you achieve with each?
title: A100 vs H100 Performance per Watt

details.common_mistake: Choosing offloading because 'memory is cheap on CPU' without accounting for the PCIe bandwidth bottleneck. 20 GB over 32 GB/s PCIe takes 625ms — potentially longer than recomputation.
details.napkin_math: Offload: 40 GB / 32 GB/s = 1.25s added per step. On 3s base: 42% overhead. Recompute: 33% extra FLOPS on 3s step = 1.0s. Recompute wins: 33% < 42%. Breakeven: offload wins when base step T satisfies 1.33T > T + 1.25s -> 0.33T > 1.25s -> T > 3.78s.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (Offloading): Transfer 20 GB to CPU and back = 40 GB total over PCIe Gen4 (32 GB/s) = 1.25 seconds per training step. If a forward+backward pass takes 3 seconds, offloading adds 1.25s = 42% overhead. Option B (Recomputation): Checkpoint every other layer. Recompute activations during backward adds ~33% compute overhead. On a 3-second step: adds 1.0 second = 33% overhead. Option B wins at 33% vs 42% overhead. The crossover point where offloading wins: when per-step compute time is very high (>3.78s) making the fixed 1.25s PCIe cost relatively small.

scenario: You're training a 13B model on a single A100-80GB. Activations consume 45 GB, exceeding available memory after weights and optimizer states (using 55 GB). Compare two solutions: (A) offload 20 GB of activations to CPU RAM via PCIe Gen4 (32 GB/s), or (B) use activation checkpointing to recompute activations during backward pass (adds ~33% compute overhead).
title: CPU Offloading vs Activation Recomputation

details.common_mistake: Treating cross-node bandwidth the same as intra-node bandwidth. NVLink is 18x faster than InfiniBand — running TP across the slow link decimates training throughput.
details.napkin_math: TP=16: 80 cross-node AllReduces × 128MB. Each takes ~5.12ms (AllReduce multiplier). 80 × 5.12ms = 409.6ms non-overlappable. TP=8+DP=2: 0ms cross-node TP + DP sync overlapped with backward. NVLink/IB ratio: 900/50 = 18x. TP cross-node adds massive latency per layer.
details.realistic_solution: TP=16 across 2 nodes: every layer requires 2 AllReduce operations (forward + backward). For hidden_dim=8192, FP16, micro-batch=4, seq=2048: the full activation tensor is 4 × 2048 × 8192 × 2B = 128 MB. With 80 layers: 160 AllReduces per step, half crossing the IB link. Cross-node AllReduce of 128 MB at 50 GB/s (using 2× multiplier for AllReduce): 2 × 128 MB / 50 = ~5.12ms each × 80 cross-node = 409.6ms. NVLink AllReduce: 2 × 128 MB / 450 = 0.57ms × 80 = 45.6ms. Total TP=16 comm: 455.2ms. TP=8+DP=2: TP AllReduce is NVLink-only: 0.57ms × 160 = 91.2ms. DP gradient sync: 14 GB over IB at 50 GB/s = 280ms, but overlaps with backward pass. Net exposed comm: ~91.2ms + 20ms residual DP sync = 111.2ms. TP=8+DP=2 exposes significantly less non-overlappable communication. TP across nodes is worse because TP communication cannot be overlapped with compute.

scenario: A team proposes TP=16 across two 8-GPU DGX H100 nodes (NVLink within node: 900 GB/s, InfiniBand between nodes: 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s). Compare this to TP=8 within a node + DP=2 across nodes. Quantify the communication overhead of each.
title: Tensor Parallelism Within vs Across Nodes

details.common_mistake: Assuming monolithic prefill is always better because it maximizes compute utilization. It blocks all decode requests for the duration of prefill, causing latency spikes for concurrent users.
details.napkin_math: Monolithic: 2 × 70B × 32K = 4.48 PFLOP / 156 TFLOPS (50% MFU) = 28.7s. Decode stall: 28.7s for all users. Chunked (4K): 3.6s per chunk, 8 chunks. Max decode stall: 3.6s (8x improvement). Throughput cost: ~10%.
details.realistic_solution: Monolithic prefill for 32K tokens on a 70B model (INT8): prefill is compute-bound with AI >> ridge point. FLOPs ≈ 2 × 70B × 32K = 4.48 PFLOP. On A100 at 50% MFU: 4.48P / 156T = 28.7 seconds. During this time, all 100 concurrent decode requests stall — their P99 latency spikes to 28.7s + their decode time. Chunked prefill (4K chunks): each chunk takes 28.7 × (4K/32K) = 3.6 seconds. Between chunks, decode 1-2 iterations for waiting users (~70ms each). Total prefill time increases to ~32s (3.6s × 8 chunks + decode interleaving), but decode users see max stall of 3.6s instead of 28.7s. Throughput impact: ~10% lower prefill throughput due to context switching overhead, but P99 decode latency improves 8x. For production with SLAs, chunked prefill is essential. The sweet spot for chunk size balances compute efficiency (larger chunks) against decode latency (smaller chunks).

scenario: A serving system receives a 32K-token prompt. Compare monolithic prefill (process all 32K tokens at once) vs chunked prefill (process in 4K chunks, interleaving decode requests between chunks). Your system serves 100 concurrent users. Evaluate latency and throughput tradeoffs.
title: Prefill Chunking vs Monolithic Prefill

details.common_mistake: Always choosing compiled mode without considering cold start, dynamic shapes, or the amortization window. Compilation is wasted if the model is reloaded frequently or inputs have highly variable shapes.
details.napkin_math: Save 17ms/request. Compile cost: 120s = 7,059 requests to break even. At 10K req/hr: amortized in 42 min. 24h savings: (240K - 7K) × 17ms = 3,960s = $3.30/day/replica.
details.realistic_solution: Speedup per request: 45ms - 28ms = 17ms saved. Compilation cost: 120 seconds = 120,000ms. Break-even: 120,000 / 17 = 7,059 requests to amortize. At 10K req/hour, break-even in 42 minutes. Over 24 hours: savings = (24h × 10K/h - 7,059) × 17ms = 232,941 × 17ms = 3,960 seconds = 66 minutes of GPU time saved. At $3/GPU-hr: saves $3.30/day per replica. When compilation DOESN'T pay: (1) Short-lived serverless functions restarting every 15 minutes — never amortizes. (2) Dynamic input shapes (variable sequence lengths without padding) — torch.compile recompiles for each new shape, potentially adding seconds of overhead per unique shape. (3) Models with data-dependent control flow (early exit, mixture of experts routing) — graph breaks force partial compilation with diminished gains. (4) Debugging/development — compiled tracebacks are opaque.

scenario: You have a transformer model in PyTorch eager mode averaging 45ms per forward pass. torch.compile with mode='reduce-overhead' achieves 28ms but adds 120 seconds of compilation time on first call. Your serving endpoint handles 10K requests/hour. Evaluate when compilation pays for itself and identify scenarios where it doesn't.
title: Eager vs Compiled Execution for Inference

details.common_mistake: Always choosing GPU preprocessing without considering that GPU memory and compute used for preprocessing reduces what's available for training. Also, random augmentation cannot be pre-computed for all epochs.
details.napkin_math: A: 40% idle → 20% idle, 1.25x speedup, +$0.50/hr. B: 40% idle → ~2% idle, 1.6x speedup, +0 cost. C: 40% idle → 0%, 1.67x speedup, +2-10x storage. B gives best cost-performance.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (64 CPUs): Doubles preprocessing throughput. If 32 cores → 40% idle, 64 cores → ~20% idle (Amdahl's Law: speedup = 1/(0.6 + 0.4/2) = 1.25x overall). Cost: ~$0.50/hr for 32 extra vCPUs. Reduces wall time from T to 0.8T. Option B (GPU DALI): Moves preprocessing to GPU, eliminating CPU→GPU data copy latency. GPU preprocessing is 10-50x faster than CPU for image operations. Training time: ~0.62T (eliminates 38% of the 40% idle, some overhead). Cost: zero extra — uses same GPU. Caveat: uses 2-5 GB VRAM for preprocessing buffers. Option C (Pre-process offline): Eliminates runtime preprocessing entirely. Training time: 0.6T (removes all CPU preprocessing wait). Cost: 2-10x storage (augmented copies), plus offline preprocessing compute. Only works for deterministic augmentation — random crop/flip must still be applied online. Best approach: B for random augmentations (GPU handles them in the pipeline), C for expensive fixed transforms (tokenization, feature extraction). Avoid A unless GPU memory is critically constrained.

scenario: Your image classification training pipeline spends 40% of wall-clock time waiting for data preprocessing (resize, augment, normalize) on 32 CPU cores. The GPU sits idle during this time. Compare: (A) double the CPU cores to 64, (B) move preprocessing to GPU using DALI/torchvision on CUDA, (C) pre-process the entire dataset offline and store as pre-augmented shards.
title: GPU vs CPU Data Preprocessing for Training

details.common_mistake: Comparing on-prem at 100% utilization against cloud at 100% utilization. Real on-prem runs at 60-80% utilization; cloud is pay-per-use. The break-even depends critically on utilization.
details.napkin_math: Cloud (70% util): 64 × 8760 × 0.7 × $3 × 3yr = $3.53M. On-prem: $1.6M + $150K ops = $1.75M. Savings: $1.78M (50%). Break-even: $1.75M / $5.04M = 34.7% utilization.
details.realistic_solution: Cloud cost at 70% utilization: 64 GPUs × 8,760h/yr × 0.70 × $3.00 × 3 years = $3,532,032. On-prem: $1.6M hardware + $50K × 3 ops = $1.75M, plus residual value (~$200K after 3 years for 2-year-old GPUs). Net on-prem: $1.55M. On-prem is over 2x cheaper at 70% utilization. Break-even utilization: on-prem cost $1.75M = cloud cost at break-even. Cloud cost = 64 × 8760 × U × $3 × 3 = $5,045,760 × U. Break-even: $1,750,000 / $5,045,760 = 34.7% utilization. Below 35% utilization, cloud wins. Above 35%, on-prem wins. Real-world factors: on-prem requires 6-12 month lead time for procurement, staff expertise, facility space. Cloud provides elasticity — burst to 256 GPUs for a week, impossible with on-prem. Hybrid approach: on-prem for baseline steady-state load + cloud for bursting.

scenario: Your team needs 64 A100-80GB GPUs for 3 years. Compare: (A) buy 8× DGX A100 nodes ($200K each = $1.6M upfront) with $50K/year operational costs (power, cooling, staff), vs (B) rent 64 A100 GPUs on-demand at $3.00/GPU-hour. Assume 70% average utilization. At what utilization does on-prem break even?
title: On-Prem vs Cloud GPU Cluster Economics

details.common_mistake: Optimizing for the same metric in both use cases. Real-time chatbots need low P99 latency (user experience), while batch pipelines need maximum throughput (cost efficiency). Conflating these leads to poor system design.
details.napkin_math: Chatbot: 900ms P99 = 1.8s for 2-token word → 33 WPM perceived, below 50 WPM readability threshold. 450ms P99 = 67 WPM — acceptable. Batch: Config B saves 10K×500/800 vs /500 = 1.04h = $3.12/run. At 10 runs/day: $31.20/day savings.
details.realistic_solution: For the chatbot: P99 of 450ms/token means 1 in 100 users sees ~450ms between tokens — noticeable but acceptable (human reading speed is ~250ms/word). P99 of 900ms/token creates visible lag that frustrates users. Choose config A (P99=450ms). User satisfaction depends on tail latency, not average. For batch summarization: processing 10,000 documents. Config A: 10K docs × ~500 tokens avg / 500 tok/s = 10,000s ≈ 2.78 hours. Config B: 10K × 500 / 800 = 6,250s ≈ 1.74 hours. Config B saves 1.04 hours = $3.12 at $3/GPU-hr. Tail latency is irrelevant — no human waits for individual documents. Choose config B. The key insight: latency and throughput are fundamentally at odds in serving systems. Higher batching improves throughput (better GPU utilization) but increases queuing delay (worse tail latency). You must choose based on the workload's sensitivity to latency vs cost.

scenario: Your LLM serving system shows P50 latency of 80ms/token but P99 of 450ms/token. Throughput is 500 tokens/sec. A new batching configuration increases throughput to 800 tokens/sec but P99 rises to 900ms/token. Evaluate which configuration is better for (a) a real-time chatbot and (b) a batch document summarization pipeline.
title: Latency Optimization vs Throughput Optimization

details.common_mistake: Assuming you need batch=156 to hit the ridge point. The relationship between batch size and AI is roughly linear for GEMM (y=Wx becomes Y=WX where X has batch columns), so batch ≈ ridge point, but this ignores that not all operations are GEMM.
details.napkin_math: AI at batch B ≈ B FLOP/Byte for large GEMM. Ridge at 156 → need batch ≥ 156. Throughput: batch=1 = 143 tok/s, batch=156 = 156/0.014s = 11,143 tok/s. 78x throughput gain, 2x latency increase.
details.realistic_solution: For a matrix-vector multiply y=Wx (batch=1): AI = 2×d / (d×2 + 2) ≈ 1 FLOP/Byte (for d=4096, FP16). For matrix-matrix Y=WX with batch B: FLOPs = 2×d×d×B, Bytes = d×d×2 + d×B×2 + d×B×2. For large d: AI ≈ 2×d×B / (d×2) = B FLOP/Byte. To reach ridge: B ≥ 156. So batch ≈ 156 on A100. On H100 (ridge=295): batch ≈ 295. Latency impact: batch=1 at bandwidth limit = 14 GB / 2 TB/s = 7ms per token. Batch=156: same 7ms for reading weights (amortized) + compute time 156× more FLOPs = 2 × 7B × 156 / 312T = 7ms. Total ≈ 14ms for 156 tokens = 0.09ms/token effective — a 78x throughput improvement. But per-request latency increases from 7ms to 14ms (2x worse) because each request waits for the batch.

scenario: You are serving a 7B FP16 model on an A100. Each forward pass for batch=1 has AI ≈ 1 FLOP/Byte. The ridge point is 156 FLOP/Byte. What minimum batch size pushes the main GEMM operations into the compute-bound regime? What are the latency implications?
title: Batch Size to Reach Compute-Bound Regime

details.common_mistake: Deploying each adapter as a separate model instance — that would require 200 × 70B model copies, consuming petabytes of VRAM. LoRA's whole point is that adapters share the base model.
details.napkin_math: Adapter size: 4 × 2 × 8192 × 16 × 2B × 80 layers = 167.7 MB each. 200 adapters = 33.5 GB total. Base model: 70 GB INT8. 20 replicas × 2 GPUs = 40 GPUs vs 400 without sharing. 10x GPU reduction.
details.realistic_solution: Architecture: shared base model with hot-swappable LoRA adapters. (1) Base model deployment: 70B INT8 = 70 GB per replica. Use TP=2 across 2 A100-80GB (35 GB/GPU, leaving 45 GB for KV cache and adapters). (2) LoRA adapter size: rank=16, 4 projections per layer, 80 layers. Per adapter: 4 projections × 2 matrices × (8192 × 16) params × 2B × 80 layers = 167.7 MB FP16. All 200 adapters: 33.5 GB — fits in host RAM with GPU-side caching. (3) Adapter scheduling: keep top-20 adapters (~90% traffic) in GPU memory permanently (20 × 167.7 MB = 3.35 GB). Remaining adapters loaded on-demand from CPU (PCIe: 167.7 MB / 32 GB/s = 5.2ms — well within SLA). (4) Capacity planning: 5K req/s with continuous batching, batch=64 per replica. Per replica throughput: ~250 req/s. Need 5000/250 = 20 replicas = 40 A100 GPUs. Without LoRA sharing: 200 models × 2 GPUs = 400 GPUs. LoRA sharing saves 360 GPUs (90% reduction).

scenario: You need to serve 200 fine-tuned variants of a 70B base model, each with LoRA adapters (rank=16, applied to Q,K,V,O projections). Total traffic is 5K requests/sec with uneven distribution (top 10 adapters get 80% of traffic). Design a serving architecture that minimizes GPU cost while meeting P99 < 300ms TTFT.
title: Multi-LoRA Serving Architecture

details.common_mistake: Relying solely on checkpoint-restart for every failure. At 1024 GPUs with MTBF of 2-4h, restarting the entire job every failure wastes 30-50% of training time.
details.napkin_math: MTBF per GPU: ~20,000h. System MTBF: 20,000/1024 ≈ 19.5h (but correlated failures reduce this to 2-4h). 32 spares: 32/1024 = 3.1% cost. Async checkpoint: 700 GB local NVMe write at 3.2 TB/s = 0.22s stall every 2h = 0.003% overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-layer resilience design: (1) Hot spare pool: keep 32 spare GPUs (3.1% overhead). When a GPU fails, remap its work to a spare within 30 seconds. The failed GPU's data-parallel rank is replaced; its gradient contribution comes from the spare running the same model shard. (2) Elastic data parallelism: DP dimension can shrink/grow without stopping training. If a spare is unavailable, reduce DP from 128 to 127 — throughput drops 0.8% until replacement. Training continues without restart. (3) Asynchronous checkpointing: checkpoint to NVMe SSDs local to each node (3.2 TB/s aggregate for 128 nodes), then async copy to shared storage. Checkpoint takes 700 GB / 3.2 TB/s = 0.22 seconds for the local write (training stall), plus background network copy. (4) In-memory redundancy: replicate optimizer states across DP ranks (already inherent in ZeRO Stage 1). A failed GPU's optimizer shard is reconstructed from its DP peer in <1 second. (5) Monitoring: heartbeat every 500ms, failure detected in 1s, spare activated in 30s. Total throughput overhead: 3.1% (spares) + 0.5% (async checkpoint) + 0.3% (heartbeat) ≈ 3.9% < 5% budget.

scenario: Design a fault-tolerant training system for a 175B model on 1024 GPUs where individual GPU failures occur every 2-4 hours. Requirements: (1) training must not stop for single GPU failures, (2) maximum 5% throughput overhead for fault tolerance, (3) checkpoint recovery in under 10 minutes.
title: Resilient 1024-GPU Training System

details.common_mistake: Statically assigning GPUs to models and scaling by adding more replicas. This fragments the GPU pool and leads to utilization of 30-40% because each model's traffic pattern is different.
details.napkin_math: 48 GPUs × 80 GB = 3.84 TB total VRAM. 15 models INT8 ≈ 500 GB. Average 2.5 model copies per GPU at 70% util. Cold start: 70 GB / 7 GB/s NVMe = 10s. Co-locate: 80 GB fits 1×70B or 5×7B + KV cache.
details.realistic_solution: Design: (1) Model registry + weight cache: all 15 model weights stored on a shared NVMe tier (total ≈ 500 GB INT8). Each GPU has 80 GB VRAM; can hold one 70B model or multiple smaller models. Weights cached in GPU memory with LRU eviction. (2) Request router: incoming requests are classified by model, routed to a GPU that already has the model loaded (cache hit) or to the least-loaded GPU (cache miss triggers load). (3) Dynamic packing: small models (7B = 7 GB INT8) can co-locate on a single GPU. Pack up to 10× 7B models per GPU with separate CUDA streams, or 1× 70B model. The router tracks per-GPU memory utilization and co-locates compatible models. (4) Cold start budget: loading 70B INT8 (70 GB) from NVMe SSD at 7 GB/s = 10 seconds. From network storage at 3 GB/s = 23 seconds. Both under 60s. Pre-warm top-5 models on dedicated GPUs. (5) Graceful degradation: when all GPUs are saturated, queue requests with priority (paying tier first), return estimated wait time, and optionally route to a smaller model for approximate answers. (6) Autoscaler: monitors request queue depth per model, scales replicas up (load model on idle GPU) or down (evict cold model) every 30 seconds.

scenario: Design a serving gateway for a company running 15 LLMs (7B to 70B) across 48 A100-80GB GPUs. Requirements: (1) auto-scale models based on traffic, (2) cold start for any model < 60 seconds, (3) overall GPU utilization > 70%, (4) graceful degradation when capacity is exhausted.
title: Multi-Model Serving Gateway Design

details.common_mistake: Choosing TP=8 and PP=64 without considering that PP=64 creates massive pipeline bubbles and underutilizes the fast NVLink interconnect within each node.
details.napkin_math: TP=8: NVLink AllReduce ~5ms/step. PP=4: bubble (4-1)/32 = 9.375% with m=32 micro-batches of size 4. DP=16: gradient sync 10.9 GB / 50 GB/s = 0.22s (overlapped). Total overhead: ~9.375% bubble + ~2% TP comm + ~1% residual DP = ~12.4%.
details.realistic_solution: Configuration: TP=8, PP=4, DP=16 (8×4×16 = 512). Justification: (1) TP=8 within each node: uses NVLink (900 GB/s). 175B/4 PP stages = ~44B params per stage. TP=8 splits each stage: 44B/8 = 5.5B params/GPU = 11 GB FP16 weights per GPU. With mixed-precision training overhead (16B/param for optimizer): 5.5B × 16 = 88 GB — tight fit on 80 GB. Need ZeRO Stage 1 to partition optimizer across DP ranks, reducing per-GPU optimizer memory 16x. Result: ~11 GB weights + 88/16 = 5.5 GB optimizer = 16.5 GB + activations. (2) PP=4 across 4 consecutive nodes: 175B / 4 = ~44B params per stage. Pipeline bubble: (4-1)/m where m = micro-batches. Local batch = global batch 2048 / DP=16 = 128 samples per DP rank. With m=32 micro-batches of size 4: bubble = 3/32 = 9.375%. (3) DP=16 across the 16 groups of 4 nodes: gradient AllReduce over InfiniBand. Gradients per DP rank = 175B × 2B / (8 TP × 4 PP) = 10.9 GB. AllReduce over 16 ranks at 50 GB/s: ~0.44 seconds (overlapped with backward). (4) Micro-batch: global batch 2048 / DP=16 = 128 samples per DP rank. PP with m=32 micro-batches of size 4 each. Sequence length 2048 × hidden 12288 × 4 ≈ 200 MB activations per micro-batch — manageable with activation checkpointing.

scenario: You have 512 H100 GPUs across 64 nodes (8 GPUs/node, NVLink within node, 400Gb/s InfiniBand between nodes). Design the parallelism configuration (DP, TP, PP, micro-batch size) to train a 175B GPT-style model with global batch size 2048 and sequence length 2048. Justify each dimension.
title: 3D Parallelism Configuration for 175B

details.common_mistake: Streaming directly from S3 to GPUs, assuming network bandwidth is sufficient. S3 GET throughput has per-prefix limits and added latency that can cause starvation at 500K tok/sec.
details.napkin_math: 500K tok/s × 2B = 1 MB/s aggregate read bandwidth — trivial. 4 TB dataset / 128 nodes = 31 GB/node local. 4 TB at 2 bytes/token = 2T tokens. 2T tokens = 1 epoch. Training time: 2T / 500K = 4M sec ≈ 46 days.
details.realistic_solution: Three-tier pipeline: (1) S3 → NVMe staging: pre-fetch tokenized shards from S3 to local NVMe SSDs on each node. 8 TB dataset at 2 bytes/token = 4 TB raw storage. Each of 128 nodes stores 4 TB / 128 = 31 GB locally — fits easily. Pre-fetch next shards into buffer. S3 download at 10 Gbps per node = 1.25 GB/s; full 31 GB subset in 31/1.25 = ~25 seconds per node (parallel). (2) NVMe → host RAM buffer: memory-mapped shards with 4-shard read-ahead. At 500K tok/s across 1024 GPUs: each GPU needs 500K/1024 = 488 tok/s × 2B = ~1 KB/s — trivial bandwidth. The challenge is random access for shuffling. (3) Deterministic shuffle with resumability: use a seeded permutation of shard indices. Each DP rank reads shards in a deterministic order based on (epoch, rank, seed). On failure recovery, the dataloader reads the last consumed shard index from the checkpoint and resumes from shard N+1. No re-shuffling needed. Exactly-once: each shard is assigned to exactly one DP rank per epoch via round-robin on the shuffled shard list. (4) Capacity: 2T tokens / 500K per sec = 4M seconds = 46.3 days. Dataset is 2T tokens (4 TB) → exactly 1 epoch. Shard size: 512 MB each → 8,000 shards. Each GPU processes 8,000 / 1024 ≈ 8 shards per epoch.

scenario: Design a data pipeline to feed a 1024-GPU training cluster processing 2 trillion tokens for a pre-training run. The cluster consumes tokens at 500K tokens/sec. Raw data is 8 TB of deduplicated, cleaned text stored as tokenized shards on S3. Requirements: zero data starvation, exactly-once epoch ordering, resumability after failures.
title: Trillion-Token Data Pipeline Architecture

details.common_mistake: Only monitoring loss and GPU utilization. These catch obvious failures but miss subtle issues like learning rate schedule bugs, data pipeline stalls, slow stragglers, or thermal throttling that wastes 10-20% of compute.
details.napkin_math: 256 GPUs × 10 metrics × 1 sample/10s = 256 samples/sec → 22M samples/day. At 100 bytes each: 2.2 GB/day raw metrics. 21-day run: 46 GB total. MFU target: 50% on H100 = 256 × 989T × 0.5 = 126.6 PFLOPS effective.
details.realistic_solution: Four-layer monitoring stack: (1) Hardware layer (60s detection): per-GPU metrics every 10s — temperature, power draw, HBM utilization, ECC error count, NVLink/IB link status. Alert: temperature > 83°C (throttling), ECC errors > 0 (impending failure), any link down. Use DCGM exporter → Prometheus → PagerDuty. (2) Communication layer: per-step AllReduce time, per-rank gradient norm, straggler detection (any rank > 2σ from mean step time). Alert: AllReduce time > 2x baseline (network degradation), step time variance > 20% (straggler). (3) Training dynamics layer (5-min detection): loss (per-step + 100-step EMA), gradient norm (global + per-layer), learning rate, batch throughput (samples/sec), MFU = actual_FLOPS / theoretical_peak. Alert: loss spike > 3σ from EMA, gradient norm > 10x baseline, MFU drop > 15%. Compute MFU: actual_tokens_per_sec × 6 × model_params / (num_GPUs × peak_FLOPS). (4) Data pipeline layer: dataloader queue depth, prefetch buffer occupancy, disk I/O wait. Alert: queue depth = 0 (starvation). Dashboard: real-time panel with loss curve + grad norm + MFU + GPU temps, plus a Gantt-chart view showing per-step breakdown (forward/backward/allreduce/idle) for identifying bottlenecks.

scenario: Design a monitoring system for a 256-GPU training run of a 70B model expected to take 21 days. Requirements: detect hardware failures within 60 seconds, detect training instability (loss spikes, gradient explosions) within 5 minutes, provide MFU tracking, and support post-mortem analysis. What metrics, alerts, and dashboards do you build?
title: Training Observability Dashboard Design

details.common_mistake: Allocating all remaining memory after model weights to KV cache without reserving space for activations, CUDA context, and memory fragmentation. This causes OOM under load.
details.napkin_math: Model: 35 GB/GPU. KV budget: 42 GB/GPU. KV per token (TP=2): 160 KB/GPU. Max tokens: 42 GB / 160 KB = 262,144 tokens total across the sequence. Need: 256 × 4096 = 1.05M. Deficit: ~786K tokens. Supports only 64 concurrent requests. INT8 KV cache doubles capacity to 524K → still fails 256 concurrent.
details.realistic_solution: Memory budget: (1) Model weights (INT8): 70B × 1B = 70 GB, split TP=2: 35 GB/GPU. (2) CUDA context + framework overhead: ~2 GB/GPU. (3) Activation workspace: for batch=256, seq=4096, hidden=8192: chunked prefill (chunk=512): 256 × 512 × 8192 × 2B = 2 GB. Split TP=2: 1 GB/GPU. (4) Available for KV cache: 80 - 35 - 2 - 1 = 42 GB/GPU. (5) KV cache per token: 2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 2B = 320 KB total. Split TP=2: 160 KB/GPU per token. (6) Max tokens in KV cache: 42 GB / 160 KB = 262,144 tokens total maximum length. (7) 256 requests × 4096 tokens = 1,048,576 tokens needed. Available: 262K — only supports 64 concurrent requests at full context! Binding constraint: KV cache. Solutions: (a) use INT8 KV cache (halves to 80 KB/token → 524K tokens, supports 128 concurrent), (b) reduce max context to 1024 (supports 256 concurrency), or scale out TP to TP=8.

scenario: Design the memory allocation strategy for serving Llama-2-70B on 2× A100-80GB (TP=2) with a target of 256 concurrent requests at 4096 max context length. You have 160 GB total VRAM. Specify exactly how memory is divided between model weights, KV cache, activations, and system overhead. Identify the binding constraint.
title: Memory Budget for High-Concurrency LLM Serving

details.common_mistake: Proposing a flat switched fabric without calculating the number of switch ports needed. 256 nodes with single-port connections need a 256-port switch — which doesn't exist in InfiniBand. Multi-tier fat-tree is required.
details.napkin_math: 256 nodes → 8 leaf switches (32 nodes each) + 32 spine switches. 40 total switches × 64 ports = 2,560 ports. Bisection: 8 × 32 × 50 GB/s = 12.8 TB/s. AllReduce 1 GB: ~5ms hierarchical (NVLink + IB). Cost: ~$800K switches.
details.realistic_solution: Design: 2-tier fat-tree with InfiniBand NDR (400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s per port). (1) Leaf layer: each of 256 nodes connects to a leaf switch. Use 64-port NDR switches. Each leaf switch connects 32 nodes (downlinks) + 32 uplinks to spine. Need 256/32 = 8 leaf switches. (2) Spine layer: 32 uplinks per leaf × 8 leaves = 256 total uplinks. Distribute across spine switches: with 64-port spines, each spine connects to all 8 leaves (8 downlinks) + unused ports. Need 256/8 = 32 spine switches. (3) Bisection bandwidth: 8 leaves × 32 uplinks × 50 GB/s = 12.8 TB/s total. Per-node bisection: 50 GB/s — full line rate, non-blocking. (4) AllReduce latency for 1 GB: A flat ring AllReduce across 256 nodes requires 2(N-1) steps. Time = 2 × (255/256) × 1 GB / 50 GB/s = ~40ms. This strictly violates the 5ms requirement. However, using hierarchical AllReduce (intra-node NVLink, then inter-node IB) drastically cuts this time. Intra-node reduce-scatter: 2 × (7/8) × 1 GB / 900 GB/s = ~1.9ms. Inter-node ring: 2 × (255/256) × (1 GB / 8) / 50 GB/s = ~5ms. Intra-node all-gather: ~1.9ms. Utilizing in-network reduction (SHARP) on the InfiniBand switches avoids the 5ms ring penalty, bringing the total well under the 5ms requirement. (5) Total hardware: 8 leaf + 32 spine = 40 switches × ~$20K = $800K networking cost.

scenario: Design the network topology for a 2048 H100 GPU training cluster (256 nodes × 8 GPUs). The cluster must support AllReduce across all GPUs with < 5ms latency for 1 GB payloads and non-blocking any-to-any communication. Specify the switch topology, link speeds, and total switch port count.
title: Network Topology for 2048-GPU Training Cluster

details.common_mistake: Using traditional air cooling for H100-class density. At 50 kW/rack, air cooling requires impossibly high airflow. Liquid cooling is mandatory above ~25-30 kW/rack.
details.napkin_math: 1000 H100 × 700W = 700 kW GPU power. 125 nodes × 10.2 kW = 1.275 MW IT. Total facility: IT 1.275 MW + cooling 0.08 MW + distribution losses 0.06 MW + misc 0.01 MW = 1.425 MW. PUE = 1.425/1.275 = 1.118 ≤ 1.15. UPS: 1.275 MW × 10 min = 212.5 kWh battery. 32 racks at 40.8 kW each.
details.realistic_solution: Design: (1) Cooling: direct-to-chip liquid cooling (rear-door heat exchangers or cold plates). Each H100 SXM at 700W generates ~95% of heat through the GPU die. Cold plates with 40°C supply water remove heat directly, no air gap. Facility cooling: cooling towers or dry coolers (free cooling when ambient < 35°C). This achieves cooling PUE contribution of 0.05-0.08 (vs 0.3-0.5 for air). (2) Power distribution: utility feed → 2× 1.5 MVA transformers (N+1) → medium-voltage switchgear → PDUs → rack-level busway. Each rack: 40.8 kW / 208V 3-phase = 113A per rack. Use 60A circuits × 3 per rack for N+1 within rack. Total racks: 125 nodes / 4 nodes per rack = 32 racks (at 40.8 kW/rack). (3) UPS: 3× 750 kVA UPS modules (N+1) with 10-minute battery backup for graceful checkpoint + shutdown. Battery bank: 1.275 MW × 10 min = 212.5 kWh → ~250 kWh with efficiency losses. (4) PUE calculation: IT load 1.275 MW + cooling 0.08 MW + power distribution losses 0.06 MW + lighting/misc 0.01 MW = total 1.425 MW. PUE = 1.425/1.275 = 1.118 < 1.15 requirement met.

scenario: Design the power and cooling architecture for a 1000 H100 GPU data center (125 DGX nodes, each at 10.2 kW). Total IT load is 1.275 MW. Requirements: PUE < 1.15, support for 50 kW/rack density, and N+1 redundancy on all power paths. Specify the cooling technology, power distribution, and UPS configuration.
title: Power and Cooling for a 1000-GPU Cluster

details.common_mistake: Assuming speculative decoding always gives K× speedup. The actual speedup depends on the acceptance rate and the overhead of running the draft model. With 70% acceptance rate and K=5, expected accepted tokens is less than 5.
details.napkin_math: Expected accepted tokens (finite K=5): (1-0.7^6)/(1-0.7) = (1-0.1176)/0.3 = 2.94/round. Draft cost: 5 × 1ms = 5ms. Target verify: 35ms (INT8 70 GB / 2 TB/s). Round time: 40ms for 2.94 tokens = 13.6ms/token vs 35ms/token baseline. Speedup: 35/13.6 = 2.57x.
details.realistic_solution: Design: (1) Memory allocation on A100-80GB: target model INT8 = 70 GB. Draft model FP16 = 2 GB. KV cache budget: 80 - 70 - 2 - 2 (overhead) = 6 GB. At 320 KB/token for 70B KV cache: 6 GB / 320 KB = 19,200 tokens max context — sufficient for most use cases. (2) Speculative decoding flow: draft model generates K=5 tokens autoregressively (5 forward passes). Target model verifies all 5 in one forward pass (parallel verification). On rejection at position i, discard tokens i+1..K and resample from target distribution at position i. (3) Expected speedup: with acceptance rate α=0.7 and finite K=5, expected tokens per speculation round = (1−α^(K+1))/(1−α) = (1−0.7^6)/0.3 = 0.8824/0.3 ≈ 2.94 tokens per round (geometric series truncated at K). Draft overhead: 5ms total for K=5. Target verify: 35ms. Total round time: 40ms for 2.94 tokens → 13.6ms/token. Baseline: 35ms/token. Speedup = 35/13.6 ≈ 2.57x. (4) Optimization: increase K for higher α models (if α=0.85, K=5: (1−0.85^6)/0.15 = 0.6228/0.15 ≈ 4.15 tokens/round).

scenario: Design a speculative decoding system for a 70B target model using a 1B draft model. Both run on the same A100-80GB. The draft model proposes K=5 candidate tokens per step. The target model verifies all K tokens in a single forward pass. Calculate the expected speedup assuming 70% draft acceptance rate and specify memory allocation.
title: Speculative Decoding Architecture

details.common_mistake: Treating MoE like a dense model and using standard TP/PP. MoE requires expert parallelism — distributing experts across GPUs — which introduces all-to-all communication patterns fundamentally different from AllReduce.
details.napkin_math: All-to-all per layer: 65K tokens × 2 routes × 8KB / 8 GPUs = 128 MB/GPU. NVLink: 256 MB / 450 GB/s = 0.57ms × 32 layers = 18ms forward. DP sync: 26 GB / 50 GB/s = 0.52s (overlapped). Expert routing overhead: ~18%.
details.realistic_solution: Configuration: EP=8 (expert parallel), DP=8 (8 nodes). Each GPU in an EP group holds 1 of the 8 experts per layer. Shared layers (attention, embeddings) are replicated across all 8 GPUs in the EP group (via DP). (1) Expert placement: within each node (8 GPUs, NVLink), each GPU holds a different expert for all 32 MoE layers. The model has 47B total params: ~13B shared and 34B MoE params. Each GPU holds 1/8th of the MoE params (4.25B params) = 8.5 GB. Shared attention params: ~13B = 26 GB. Per-GPU: 8.5 + 26 = 34.5 GB weights + optimizer states. (2) All-to-all communication: top-2 routing means each token goes to 2 of 8 experts. Tokens must be dispatched to the correct GPU. For batch=32, seq=2048: 32 × 2048 = 65,536 tokens × 2 copies = 131,072 token-expert pairs. Each token's hidden state: 4096 × 2B = 8 KB. All-to-all volume per layer: 131,072 × 8 KB / 8 GPUs = 128 MB per GPU sent + 128 MB received. Over NVLink (450 GB/s effective): 256 MB / 450 = 0.57ms per layer × 32 layers = 18.2ms per forward. (3) Cross-node DP gradient sync: shared attention params (13B × 2B = 26 GB) AllReduce over IB: 26 GB / 50 GB/s × 2 = 1.04s (overlapped with backward). (4) Total comm overhead: ~36ms (all-to-all forward+backward) + residual DP sync. With 200ms compute per step: 36/200 = 18% communication overhead for expert routing.

scenario: Design the parallelism strategy for training a Mixtral-style 8×7B MoE model (47B total params, top-2 routing, 8 experts per layer) on 64 H100 GPUs across 8 nodes. The model has 32 transformer layers with MoE FFN. Specify how to partition experts, handle the all-to-all communication for token routing, and estimate communication overhead.
title: Expert Parallelism for MoE Training

details.common_mistake: Running tokenization as a single-threaded preprocessing step, creating a bottleneck. At 500K tokens/core, you need 20 cores just for tokenization, and the pipeline must handle backpressure from the training loop.
details.napkin_math: Online: 10M tok/s / 500K tok/core = 20 cores needed. Ring buffer: 100M tokens × 2B = 200 MB. Offline (preferred): 4 TB pre-tokenized dataset, read at 20 MB/s — any SSD handles this.
details.realistic_solution: Architecture: (1) Pre-tokenize offline and store as binary token IDs (preferred): tokenize the entire dataset once, store as memory-mapped numpy arrays of uint16 (128K vocab fits in uint16). Storage: 2 bytes/token × 2T tokens = 4 TB. This eliminates runtime tokenization entirely. Loading 10M tokens/sec × 2 bytes = 20 MB/s — trivial bandwidth. (2) If online tokenization is required (streaming data): parallelize across 24 CPU cores (10M / 500K = 20, plus 20% overhead). Use a multi-process tokenizer pool with shared-memory ring buffers. Architecture: raw text → chunker (split on sentence boundaries to avoid cross-chunk BPE issues) → 24 tokenizer workers (each with its own BPE model loaded) → merge buffer (reorders chunks) → batched tensor output → GPU via DMA. (3) Backpressure handling: ring buffer between tokenizer pool and GPU dataloader holds 10 seconds of tokens (10M × 10 = 100M tokens × 2B = 200 MB). If GPUs consume faster than tokenizers produce, stall detected and alert fired. (4) Memory layout: pack tokenized sequences into fixed-length chunks (2048 or 4096 tokens) with attention mask. Use packing (concatenate short sequences with separator tokens) to avoid padding waste — increases effective throughput by 15-30% for variable-length inputs.

scenario: Design a tokenization pipeline that converts raw text to tokens at 10M tokens/sec to feed a 512-GPU training cluster. The tokenizer is BPE with 128K vocabulary (like Llama-3). Raw text arrives as UTF-8 from a decompression stage at 200 MB/s. Tokenization is CPU-bound at 500K tokens/sec per core. Specify the architecture to achieve 10M tokens/sec throughput.
title: Real-Time Tokenization Pipeline at Scale

details.common_mistake: Blaming the model or GPU for slow inference. P50 is fine (150ms), so the model and GPU are healthy. The P99 spike points to queuing or scheduling issues, not compute.
details.napkin_math: Long prompt (32K tokens) prefill: 2 × 70B × 32K / (312T × 2 GPUs × 0.5) = 14.3s. Short prompt (512 tokens): 0.22s. If 5% of requests are 32K: P99 ≈ 14.3s queuing. Chunked (512 tokens): max block time = 0.22s.
details.realistic_solution: The 27x gap between P50 and P99 TTFT with only 65% GPU utilization points to request queuing behind long-context prefills. Root cause: a small fraction of requests have very long prompts (e.g., 32K tokens). Prefill is compute-bound and takes proportional time: 32K tokens on 70B INT8 ≈ 2 × 70B × 32K FLOPs / (2 × 312T × 0.5 MFU) = 14.3 seconds total prefill. Without chunked prefill, this long request blocks the GPU for 14.3s, causing all queued requests to wait. Even with 65% average utilization, these occasional long prefills create head-of-line blocking. Fix: (1) implement chunked prefill (chunk_size=512) to interleave decode requests, (2) add a priority queue that promotes short-context requests, (3) set a max prompt length or route long prompts to dedicated capacity. Expected result: P99 drops from 4s to ~500ms.

scenario: Your LLM serving system shows P50 TTFT (time to first token) of 150ms but P99 spikes to 4 seconds. GPU utilization averages 65%. The model is 70B INT8 on 2× A100 with TP=2. No code changes were made recently. Diagnose the root cause.
title: TTFT Latency Spike Diagnosis

details.common_mistake: Looking at GPU utilization and concluding the GPUs are fine. High GPU utilization with low throughput means the GPUs are busy waiting on communication, not computing. The 'utilization' metric includes time spent in NCCL communication kernels.
details.napkin_math: Original: 45K tok/s. AllReduce for 7B model (14 GB FP16) over 16 DP ranks at 50 GB/s: ~0.56s. With degraded link at 25 GB/s: ~1.12s. Extra 0.56s on a ~1.5s step → throughput drops to 45K × 1.5/2.06 = 32.7K tok/s (≈28K with additional congestion).
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: a degraded InfiniBand link between two nodes. The symptoms are diagnostic: (1) all GPUs show 95%+ utilization — because NCCL AllReduce kernels (which are GPU-executed) show as 'GPU busy' even when they're waiting for network data. (2) 38% throughput drop ≈ the fraction of step time now spent in communication. With DP=16 across IB, gradient AllReduce is on the critical path. A degraded link (e.g., one port dropped from NDR 400 Gb/s to HDR 200 Gb/s due to a cable issue, or a port flapped to a slower speed) would double the AllReduce time for the ranks communicating through that link. Since AllReduce is synchronous across all 16 DP ranks, the slowest link determines overall throughput. Diagnosis: (1) check `ibstat` on all nodes for link speed/state, (2) run NCCL all-reduce benchmark between each pair of nodes to find the slow link, (3) check switch port error counters for CRC errors or symbol errors indicating a bad cable/transceiver.

scenario: Your 128-GPU training run (16 nodes × 8 GPUs, TP=8 within node, DP=16 across nodes) suddenly drops from 45K tokens/sec to 28K tokens/sec — a 38% throughput loss. GPU utilization remains at 95%+ on all GPUs. No OOM errors. Loss continues to decrease normally. What is happening?
title: Sudden Training Throughput Drop

details.common_mistake: Thinking evaluation should use LESS memory than training because there are no optimizer states or gradients. While those are freed, evaluation often uses MORE activation memory because gradient checkpointing is disabled during eval.
details.napkin_math: Training activations (checkpointed every 2 layers): 16 × 32/2 × 2048 × 4096 × 2B = 4.3 GB. Eval activations (no checkpointing): 16 × 32 × 2048 × 4096 × 2B × 3 (with FFN) = 25.8 GB. Difference: 21.5 GB — enough to push past 80 GB limit.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: gradient checkpointing is active during training but automatically disabled during model.eval(). During training with gradient checkpointing: only activations at checkpoint boundaries are stored (e.g., every 2nd layer). Intermediate activations are recomputed during backward. This reduces activation memory from O(L × B × S × H) to O(sqrt(L) × B × S × H). During evaluation: no backward pass is needed, so frameworks skip gradient checkpointing. But if you're computing perplexity or doing evaluation with gradients (e.g., for gradient-based analysis), the model stores ALL activations for ALL layers simultaneously because there's no recomputation happening. For 7B model, batch=16, seq=2048, hidden=4096, 32 layers: full activations = 32 × 16 × 2048 × 4096 × 2B ≈ 8.6 GB (just attention, actual is 3-4x with intermediate FFN). With checkpointing every 2 layers: ~0.54 GB. Fix: (1) wrap eval in torch.no_grad() (already done?), (2) reduce eval batch size, (3) force gradient checkpointing during eval, (4) use torch.inference_mode() which skips autograd overhead entirely.

scenario: Your 7B model trains fine on an A100-80GB with batch_size=16, seq_len=2048. But when you run evaluation (same batch size, same sequence length), you get a CUDA OOM error. Training uses mixed-precision with gradient checkpointing. No evaluation-specific code changes. Why?
title: OOM During Evaluation but Not Training

details.common_mistake: Blaming the learning rate schedule or model architecture. The warmup phase worked (loss decreased), so the model CAN learn. The plateau after warmup with healthy gradients suggests the optimization is stuck, not that the model is broken.
details.napkin_math: Expected loss decrease: ~0.1 per 1000 steps for a healthy 3B run. Plateau = 0.0 decrease over 5000 steps. Probability of genuine plateau at step 1000 for a 3B model: <0.1%. Data cycling: if buffer=1000 samples and dataset=1M, model sees 0.1% of data → memorizes quickly, cannot generalize.
details.realistic_solution: Most likely root cause: a data pipeline bug causing the model to see the same data repeatedly. During warmup (first 1000 steps), the dataloader's buffer was filling and serving fresh data. After the buffer filled, a shuffle/seed bug causes it to cycle through the same small subset. The model memorizes this subset (loss decreases initially) then cannot learn further (plateau). Diagnosis steps: (1) Log actual sample IDs per batch — check for repeated patterns. (2) Monitor training loss AND validation loss. If train loss plateaus but val loss doesn't change, it's not a data issue. If both plateau, it IS data. (3) Check dataloader shuffle seed — is it reset every epoch? A common bug: setting seed=42 at every epoch restart causes identical ordering. (4) Check num_workers > 0 with persistent_workers=True — this can cause workers to cache and reuse the same samples. (5) Less likely: gradient accumulation bug where gradients are accumulated but never applied (loss stays constant because weights never update). Check that optimizer.step() is called every accumulation_steps, not every step.

scenario: Your 3B model's training loss decreases normally during the first 1000 steps (warmup phase), then completely plateaus at a high loss value for the next 5000 steps despite the learning rate schedule continuing normally. GPU utilization is 100%. Gradient norms look healthy (no explosion or vanishing). What is wrong?
title: Loss Plateau After Learning Rate Warmup

details.common_mistake: Suspecting a software issue (cron job, log rotation) because the time correlation seems too coincidental for hardware. But the 11 AM - 3 PM window correlates with peak ambient temperature, which is a hardware signal.
details.napkin_math: GPU clock: 1410 MHz → 1200 MHz = 15% reduction. Thermal headroom: 83°C throttle - 75°C night = 8°C margin. Daytime: ambient +8°C → junction hits 83°C → throttle. Power limit 350W/400W: 12.5% power cut → ~5°C junction temp drop → no throttle → net +3% vs current daytime.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: thermal throttling due to elevated ambient temperature during peak daytime hours. The data center's cooling system struggles to maintain inlet temperature during hot afternoons, especially if it's summer or the facility uses economizer (free cooling) mode. When GPU junction temperature exceeds 83°C (A100 throttle point), the GPU reduces clock frequency to prevent thermal damage, directly reducing FLOPS. At 98% utilization, the GPU is fully busy — just at a lower clock. Diagnosis: (1) Check GPU temperature logs — nvidia-smi shows temp hitting 83-87°C during the day vs 70-75°C at night. (2) Check clock frequencies — GPU clock drops from 1410 MHz to ~1200 MHz (15% reduction matches the throughput drop). (3) Check facility CRAC (computer room air conditioning) inlet temperature — likely rising from 20°C to 28°C during peak hours. Fix: (1) lower GPU power limit to 350W (reduces peak temp by ~5°C with ~8% performance loss, but eliminates throttling for net gain), (2) request the facility lower the cold aisle temperature setpoint, (3) add supplemental cooling (rear-door heat exchangers), (4) long-term: migrate to direct liquid cooling which is immune to ambient temperature fluctuations.

scenario: Your 64-GPU training cluster consistently shows 15% lower throughput between 11 AM and 3 PM compared to nighttime performance. GPU utilization stays at 98%. No other jobs are running. The cluster is in a shared data center facility. What is happening?
title: Mysterious 15% Throughput Drop at Noon

details.common_mistake: Choosing 3-way replication for simplicity without calculating the massive storage cost. At 700 GB per checkpoint × 3 copies × 12 checkpoints/day = 25.2 TB/day of raw writes — erasure coding nearly halves this.
details.napkin_math: Replication 3x: 700 GB × 3 = 2.1 TB/checkpoint. EC 10+4: 700 × 1.4 = 980 GB/checkpoint. Daily (12 ckpts): replication = 25.2 TB, EC = 11.8 TB. Annual storage written: (25.2-11.8) × 365 = 4,891 TB difference. At $0.02/GB/month: 4,891 TB × 1,024 GB/TB × $0.02/GB/month × 12 months/year ≈ $1.20M/year saved.
details.realistic_solution: Replication (3x): storage overhead = 3x. Each 700 GB checkpoint requires 2.1 TB of storage. Write throughput: 3 parallel writes of 700 GB. At 10 GB/s per storage node: 700 GB / 10 = 70 seconds, all 3 replicas written in parallel = 70s total. Survives 2 failures (any 2 of 3 copies can fail, 1 remains). Recovery: copy 700 GB from surviving replica = 70s. Erasure coding (10+4): storage overhead = 1.4x (14/10). Each 700 GB checkpoint requires 980 GB. Write throughput: split 700 GB into 10 chunks of 70 GB, compute 4 parity chunks of 70 GB each. Write 14 × 70 GB chunks in parallel. Encoding compute: ~2 seconds (CPU-bound, Reed-Solomon is fast). Write: 70 GB / 10 GB/s = 7 seconds per chunk (parallel across 14 nodes). Total: ~9 seconds — faster than replication because each node writes less data. Survives any 4 failures (out of 14 chunks). Recovery: read 10 chunks (70 GB × 10 = 700 GB), decode 2 missing chunks in ~2s. Total recovery: 9s read + 2s decode = 11s. Erasure coding wins: 52% less storage (980 GB vs 2.1 TB), faster writes (9s vs 70s), higher fault tolerance (4 failures vs 2), slightly more complex recovery. At $0.02/GB/month, annual storage savings ≈ $1.20M/year.

scenario: Your 512-GPU training cluster writes 700 GB checkpoints every 2 hours to a distributed filesystem. The storage system must survive 2 simultaneous disk failures. Compare 3-way replication (store 3 copies) vs Reed-Solomon erasure coding (10+4 scheme: 10 data + 4 parity chunks). Evaluate storage overhead, write throughput, and recovery time.
title: Replication vs Erasure Coding for Checkpoint Storage

details.common_mistake: Failing to correctly align units (TFLOPS vs TB/s) or misinterpreting the ridge point threshold, concluding it is compute-bound.
details.napkin_math: A100 Peak Compute = 312 TFLOPS. A100 Peak Bandwidth = 2.0 TB/s. Ridge Point = 312e12 / 2.0e12 = 156 FLOPs/byte. Layer OI = 100 FLOPs/byte. Since 100 < 156, the layer is strictly memory-bound.
details.realistic_solution: To determine the bottleneck, calculate the hardware's ridge point, which is the ratio of peak compute to peak memory bandwidth. If the layer's operational intensity is below this ridge point, it is memory-bound; if above, it is compute-bound. Comparing the layer's 100 FLOPs/byte against the A100's ridge point reveals the operational bottleneck.

scenario: A dense matrix multiplication layer is profiled on an A100 80GB GPU. You need to calculate the operational intensity ridge point for the hardware to determine if the layer will be memory-bound or compute-bound, given a theoretical 100 FLOPs per byte for the specific layer.
title: Global New 0001

details.common_mistake: Assuming 1 byte per parameter for FP16 or forgetting to account for the actual memory bandwidth of the T4 (320GB/s).
details.napkin_math: Weights Memory = 7B parameters * 2 bytes = 14GB. Fits in 16GB T4. Read Time = Memory Size / Bandwidth = 14GB / 320GB/s = 0.04375 seconds (43.75 ms).
details.realistic_solution: First, establish the memory footprint of the weights using the rule of thumb that 1 billion parameters in FP16 equates to roughly 2GB. Check if it fits within the 16GB limit. Then, apply the T4's memory bandwidth to find the theoretical minimum duration to load the entire model from GDDR6 memory to the compute cores.

scenario: You are attempting to load and run a 7B parameter LLM in FP16 precision on a standard T4 16GB GPU. You need to calculate the memory required for the weights and determine the absolute minimum time required to read these weights from memory once.
title: Global New 0002

details.common_mistake: Calculating token speed using peak TFLOPS instead of memory bandwidth, which ignores the memory-bound nature of autoregressive decoding.
details.napkin_math: FP16 size = 40B * 2B = 80GB. INT8 size = 40B * 1B = 40GB. Memory savings = 40GB. Max Decoding Speed = 3.35 TB/s / 40GB = 3350GB/s / 40GB = 83.75 tokens/second.
details.realistic_solution: Quantizing from 16-bit to 8-bit halves the parameter memory footprint, allowing larger models or larger batches to fit in VRAM. During autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, the entire model must be read from memory for every single token generated. The theoretical max tokens per second is the memory bandwidth divided by the model size.

scenario: A 40B parameter model is quantized from FP16 to INT8 to run on a single H100 80GB GPU. Calculate the memory savings achieved by quantization and the maximum theoretical decoding speed per token, assuming inference is strictly memory-bandwidth bound.
title: Global New 0003

details.common_mistake: Failing to round up the GPU count correctly, or miscalculating the NVLink transfer time by mixing up megabytes and gigabytes.
details.napkin_math: 175B * 2 bytes = 350GB. 350GB / 80GB = 4.375 GPUs -> requires 5 GPUs (practically 8 for power-of-2). NVLink transfer time = 12MB / 600GB/s = 0.012GB / 600GB/s = 0.00002s (20 microseconds).
details.realistic_solution: Calculate the FP16 memory footprint and divide by the GPU memory capacity to find the minimum GPU count. Tensor parallelism requires massive inter-GPU communication, heavily relying on NVLink. The transfer time is calculated by dividing the activation payload size by the NVLink bandwidth.

scenario: You must serve a 175B parameter model in FP16 across multiple A100 80GB GPUs using Tensor Parallelism. Calculate the minimum number of GPUs required just to hold the weights, and find the time to transfer a 12MB activation tensor between GPUs via NVLink.
title: Global New 0004

details.common_mistake: Using 400 GB/s instead of 400 Gbps (Gigabits per second), leading to an 8x underestimation of the delay time.
details.napkin_math: IB NDR = 400Gbps = 50GB/s. Activation size = 250MB = 0.25GB. Transfer delay = 0.25GB / 50GB/s = 0.005 seconds (5 milliseconds).
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline parallelism involves sending activations forward and gradients backward across node boundaries. The network bandwidth limits this transfer. By taking the activation tensor size and dividing it by the IB NDR bandwidth, you can find the transmission delay that contributes to the pipeline bubble.

scenario: Two H100 nodes are operating in a pipeline parallel setup connected via InfiniBand NDR. Calculate the pipeline bubble delay added by transferring a 250MB intermediate activation tensor between the two nodes over the network.
title: Global New 0005

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the 30% utilization factor or failing to correctly convert TFLOPS (10^12) into standard FLOPs for the division.
details.napkin_math: V100 Effective = 125 TFLOPS * 0.3 = 37.5e12 FLOPS. V100 Time = 1e21 / 37.5e12 = 26.66e6 seconds = 7407 hours. A100 Effective = 312 TFLOPS * 0.3 = 93.6e12 FLOPS. A100 Time = 1e21 / 93.6e12 = 10.68e6 seconds = 2967 hours. Difference = 4440 hours.
details.realistic_solution: To model the cost and time of training, apply the utilization factor to the peak theoretical FLOPS for both GPUs. Then, divide the total required FLOPs by the effective continuous FLOPS rate of each GPU to find the total training time in seconds, converting to hours to find the time saved.

scenario: A large training job requires exactly 10^21 FLOPs. Assuming a constant 30% utilization of peak theoretical FLOPs, calculate the difference in total training hours when using a single V100 32GB versus a single A100 80GB.
title: Global New 0006

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to subtract the base model weights from the total VRAM, incorrectly assuming all 80GB can be used for the KV cache.
details.napkin_math: Model size = 30B * 2B = 60GB. Remaining VRAM = 80GB - 60GB = 20GB. KV cache capacity = 20GB / 1MB/token = 20,000MB / 1MB = 20,000 tokens.
details.realistic_solution: Memory capacity sets a hard ceiling on concurrent serving. First, determine the size of the model weights in VRAM. Subtract this from the total GPU memory to find the residual memory available for the KV cache. Divide this residual memory by the per-token KV cache size to find the token capacity.

scenario: You are serving a 30B parameter FP16 model on a single H100 80GB GPU. Determine the available memory for KV cache and calculate how many total tokens can be stored concurrently if each token requires exactly 1MB of KV cache memory.
title: Global New 0008

details.common_mistake: Using the V100's HBM2 bandwidth (900GB/s) instead of the PCIe Gen4 bandwidth (32GB/s) to calculate data transfer latency.
details.napkin_math: Compute time = 20e9 FLOPs / 125e12 FLOPS = 0.00016s (0.16 ms). Transfer time = 2GB / 32GB/s = 0.0625s (62.5 ms). 62.5 ms >> 0.16 ms, making this heavily I/O bound over PCIe.
details.realistic_solution: When weights are not resident on the GPU, interconnect bandwidth dominates latency. Calculate the compute time based on V100 peak TFLOPS and compare it to the data transfer time over PCIe Gen4. The slower of the two represents the primary bottleneck dictated by the roofline model.

scenario: A convolution layer requires 2GB of weights and 20 GFLOPs of compute. Weights are offloaded to CPU memory and must be streamed over PCIe Gen4 to a V100 GPU for execution. Calculate the total time and identify the primary bottleneck.
title: Global New 0009

details.common_mistake: Assuming parameters are 32-bit (FP32) or 16-bit (FP16), dividing the available bytes by 4 or 2 respectively.
details.napkin_math: Total SRAM = 256KB. Reserved = 100KB. Available for weights = 256KB - 100KB = 156KB. Since 1 INT8 parameter = 1 Byte, Max Parameters = 156,000.
details.realistic_solution: Microcontrollers lack complex memory hierarchies and operate strictly within SRAM limits. Deduct the memory required for the OS and dynamic activations from the total SRAM. The remaining memory is the capacity for the model weights, which directly translates to INT8 parameter count.

scenario: A tiny keyword spotting model is being deployed to a Cortex-M4 microcontroller with 256KB of SRAM. If 100KB is strictly reserved for the OS and activations, calculate the absolute maximum number of INT8 parameters the model can have.
title: Global New 0010

details.common_mistake: Calculating INT4 memory as 4 bytes instead of 4 bits (0.5 bytes), leading to the incorrect conclusion that INT4 also fails to fit.
details.napkin_math: FP16 Memory = 14B * 2B = 28GB (Fails: 28 > 16). INT4 Memory = 14B * 0.5B = 7GB (Fits). Throughput = T4 Bandwidth / INT4 Size = 320GB/s / 7GB = 45.7 tokens/sec.
details.realistic_solution: FP16 requires 2 bytes per parameter, exceeding the T4's 16GB capacity. INT4 quantization compresses each parameter to 0.5 bytes, easily fitting into VRAM. Throughput for single-batch autoregressive generation is computed by dividing memory bandwidth by the quantized model size.

scenario: You want to deploy a 14B parameter model on a 16GB T4. Explain why FP16 fails. Then, assuming you use INT4 quantization, calculate the memory required for the weights and compute the max theoretical token generation throughput.
title: Global New 0011

details.common_mistake: Using the A100 NVLink speed (600GB/s) instead of the H100 NVLink speed (900GB/s) to calculate the pipeline stage delay.
details.napkin_math: Total weights = 120B * 2B = 240GB. Per-GPU footprint = 240GB / 4 = 60GB. Activation transfer delay = 150MB / 900GB/s = 0.15GB / 900GB/s = 0.000166s (0.166 ms).
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline parallelism divides layers across GPUs, splitting the weight memory linearly. Calculate the total model size in FP16, then divide by the number of GPUs. The transfer latency between pipeline stages depends on the activation size and the NVLink bandwidth between adjacent GPUs.

scenario: A 120B parameter model in FP16 is partitioned evenly across 4 H100 GPUs using Pipeline Parallelism. Calculate the per-GPU weight memory footprint. Then compute the transfer delay if 150MB activations are sent between stages via NVLink.
title: Global New 0012

details.common_mistake: Neglecting the All-Reduce data volume formula and just assuming 1x tensor size, or confusing the 50GB/s IB speed with the 600GB/s NVLink speed.
details.napkin_math: Ring All-Reduce volume = 2 * (2-1)/2 * 2GB = 2 * 0.5 * 2GB = 2GB total transferred per node. Time = 2GB / 50GB/s (IB NDR) = 0.04 seconds (40 ms).
details.realistic_solution: In a standard Ring All-Reduce, each node sends and receives a total data volume equal to 2 * (N-1)/N * Tensor Size. For exactly 2 nodes, this formula simplifies. Divide the resulting data volume by the InfiniBand NDR bandwidth to determine the total synchronization time.

scenario: In a multi-node A100 cluster, gradients must be synchronized across nodes. Using a ring all-reduce algorithm over IB NDR, calculate the theoretical time to synchronize a 2GB gradient tensor between exactly 2 nodes.
title: Global New 0013

details.common_mistake: Failing to convert seconds to hours before applying the $40 rate, resulting in an absurdly high cost estimate.
details.napkin_math: Total seconds = 1,500,000 tokens / 200 tokens/sec = 7500 seconds. Total hours = 7500 / 3600 = 2.0833 hours. Total Cost = 2.0833 hours * $40/hour = $83.33.
details.realistic_solution: Cost modeling for serving requires translating tokens per second into time, and then time into dollars. First, calculate the total time in seconds required to generate 1.5 million tokens. Convert this duration to hours, and multiply by the hourly rate of the H100 instance.

scenario: You are hosting a model on an H100 instance that costs $40 per hour. The model sustains a generation rate of 200 tokens/sec. Calculate the exact dollar cost incurred to generate exactly 1.5 million tokens at continuous full load.
title: Global New 0014

details.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply by the PUE or forgetting to include the host system overhead, leading to a serious underestimation of datacenter power.
details.napkin_math: GPU Power = 8 * 400W = 3200W. IT Load = 3200W + 1000W = 4200W (4.2kW). Total Facility Power = IT Load * PUE = 4200W * 1.25 = 5250W (5.25kW).
details.realistic_solution: Total IT load is the sum of the power consumed by all GPUs and the host system. The Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) accounts for overhead like cooling and power delivery. Multiply the total IT load by the PUE to get the total facility power draw for the rack.

scenario: A datacenter rack is populated with an 8x A100 GPU server. Each A100 consumes 400W at peak, and the host system (CPU/RAM/fans) consumes an additional 1000W. If the datacenter PUE is 1.25, calculate the total facility power drawn by this single rack.
title: Global New 0015

details.common_mistake: Adding the KV cache size to the weights before dividing by bandwidth; for standard generation, weights are the primary memory bottleneck, not KV reads.
