(2) Fusion strategy — CoreML aggressively fuses Conv+BN+ReLU into single ops, QNN is more conservative. (3) Cost modeling — compilers decide whether running an op on NPU vs CPU is worth the DMA transfer cost differently. QNN's 7 CPU fallback layers add only 1.5ms of compute but 2.1ms of DMA transfers (3 boundaries). Debug: export per-layer delegation logs from each compiler, identify the specific unsupported ops, and replace them with universally-supported alternatives.

scenario: You export the same ONNX model to three mobile NPU compilers: Apple's CoreML compiler (for ANE), Qualcomm's QNN compiler (for Hexagon), and MediaTek's NeuroPilot compiler (for APU). The model has 45 layers. CoreML maps 44 layers to the ANE, QNN maps 38 layers, and NeuroPilot maps 41 layers. The unmapped layers fall back to CPU. Why do three compilers targeting three NPUs produce different partitioning decisions from the same ONNX graph, and how do you debug this?
title: The NPU Compiler Black Box

details.common_mistake: "Use ONNX Runtime — it abstracts all hardware." ONNX Runtime provides a common API, but each backend (CoreML EP, QNN EP, NNAPI EP) still has different operator coverage, quantization requirements, and performance characteristics. Abstraction hides the differences but doesn't eliminate them.
details.napkin_math: Without abstraction: 5 platforms × 10 models × 4 updates/year = 200 compilation+testing cycles/year. At 2 hours each: 400 engineer-hours/year. With automated pipeline: 200 cycles × 15 min (automated) = 50 hours of compute + 40 hours of manual intervention for failures (20% failure rate). Savings: 310 engineer-hours/year × $150/hr = **$46.5K/year**. Device farm cost: $5K/month (BrowserStack/Firebase Test Lab). Net savings: $46.5K - $60K = -$13.5K in Year 1 (investment), +$46.5K/year from Year 2 onward as the model count grows.
details.realistic_solution: Build a three-layer architecture: (1) Model layer — design models using only universally-supported ops (a 'portable op set' that works on ANE, Hexagon, Ethos, APU, and TPU). (2) Compilation layer — automated pipeline that compiles from ONNX to each platform's native format, runs validation tests on a device farm, and flags regressions. (3) Deployment layer — A/B testing and rollback per device family. Cost: 200 compilation cycles/year automated at 15 min each vs 2 hours manual. Year 1 investment: -$13.5K. Year 2+ savings: $46.5K/year as model count grows. The key: test on real hardware, not just simulators.

scenario: You're the ML platform lead at a major app company. You need to decide your on-device ML strategy for the next 3 years. Apple is pushing the ANE (fixed-function, proprietary), Qualcomm is pushing Hexagon (programmable DSP + NPU), Google is building custom TPU cores in Tensor chips, Samsung is licensing ARM Ethos NPUs, and MediaTek is integrating custom APUs. How do you build a model deployment pipeline that survives this hardware fragmentation without maintaining 5 separate codepaths?
title: The Mobile AI Chip Roadmap Bet

details.common_mistake: "The CPU-NPU synchronization overhead." While synchronization exists, the primary bottleneck for large data transfers is often the physical data movement itself.
details.napkin_math: A 1080p image (1920x1080) with 3 channels, FP32, is $1920 \times 1080 \times 3 \times 4 \text{ bytes} \approx 24.8 \text{ MB}$. If the interconnect bandwidth between CPU and NPU is effectively 10 GB/s, the transfer would take $\frac{24.8 MB}{10 GB/s} = \frac{24.8 \times 10^6 \text{ bytes}}{10 \times 10^9 \text{ bytes/s}} \approx 2.48 \text{ ms}$. This 2.48ms is *pure transfer time* and adds directly to end-to-end latency, often unnoticed if not explicitly profiled. If the bandwidth is lower or under contention, this time increases.
details.realistic_solution: The likely bottleneck is the **SoC interconnect** (e.g., ARM's AMBA AXI bus or proprietary interconnects like Qualcomm's NoC - Network on Chip). When the CPU finishes preprocessing, the resulting image tensor (e.g., FP32 or INT8) must be transferred from CPU-visible DRAM to the NPU's local memory or cache for inference. This data transfer is not instantaneous and consumes valuable time, especially for high-resolution images or large tensors. The interconnect has finite bandwidth and latency, and contention from other SoC components (GPU, display controller, modem) can further degrade performance.

scenario: You are profiling a real-time semantic segmentation model on a mobile SoC. The pipeline consists of two main stages: complex image preprocessing on the CPU (e.g., tone mapping, color space conversion) followed by neural network inference on the NPU. You observe that the end-to-end latency is significantly higher than the sum of CPU preprocessing time and NPU inference time. What SoC-level component is likely causing this discrepancy, and how would you quantify its impact?
title: The Interconnect Choke Point

details.common_mistake: "The Java Garbage Collector is pausing the threads." While GC causes pauses, a 3x consistent variance on CPU execution points to hardware asymmetry.
details.napkin_math: Big Core: 3.0 GHz, 4-wide decode, massive L2 cache. LITTLE Core: 1.8 GHz, 2-wide decode, tiny cache. The raw architectural difference is roughly 2.5x to 3x in IPC (Instructions Per Clock). 50ms * 3 = 150ms.
details.realistic_solution: ARM big.LITTLE has two core types: big cores (3.0 GHz, 4-wide decode, large L2) and LITTLE cores (1.8 GHz, 2-wide decode, tiny L2). The OS scheduler may place your threads on any core. When all 4 threads land on big cores: 50ms. When 1-2 threads land on LITTLE cores: that thread takes ~150ms (3x slower due to IPC + cache differences), and the whole inference waits for the slowest thread. Fix: use Android's pthread_setaffinity or Java's Process.setThreadPriority with CPU affinity masks to pin ML threads exclusively to big cores. This eliminates the P99 spike entirely.

scenario: Your Android app runs an OCR model entirely on the CPU (using XNNPACK). You spawn 4 threads to match the 4 cores of the device. The average latency is 50ms. However, the 99th percentile (P99) latency is a massive 150ms, causing noticeable UI stutter. The device is not thermal throttling. What architectural feature of mobile CPUs causes this massive latency variance?
title: The Asymmetric Multiprocessing (Big.LITTLE) Stutter

details.common_mistake: "Just implement it as a TFLite custom op, which will run on the CPU." While this addresses the API integration, it fails to solve the critical performance issue.
details.napkin_math: If the CPU execution of the custom op takes 20ms, and the target is <5ms, a 4-5x speedup is needed. A typical NPU/DSP can offer 10-100x speedup for suitable operations compared to a single CPU core, making custom kernel development a viable path if the operation maps well to the accelerator's architecture (e.g., matrix multiplications, element-wise operations, reductions).
details.realistic_solution: Accelerating a critical custom operator requires deep integration with the vendor's hardware acceleration stack and often involves low-level engineering:

scenario: You're integrating a novel graph neural network (GNN) model on a specific Android device with a proprietary NPU (e.g., a custom Google Tensor NPU or Qualcomm Hexagon DSP). The GNN has a custom aggregation operator not natively supported by TensorFlow Lite or the vendor's NPU SDK. Running this operator on the CPU causes a 20ms latency spike, making the overall model too slow. How would you approach accelerating this custom operator?
title: The "Unaccelerated Custom Op" Dilemma

details.common_mistake: "You didn't flush the CPU cache." The CPU isn't touching this memory—it's a direct ISP to NPU transfer. The issue is between the hardware blocks.
details.napkin_math: An ISP might process a frame in 10ms. The final DMA flush to RAM takes 0.5ms. If the CPU signals the NPU in 0.1ms, the NPU reads memory that is 400 microseconds out of date, destroying the spatial consistency of the image tensor.
details.realistic_solution: You forgot a hardware sync fence between the ISP's DMA write and the NPU's DMA read. The ISP signals 'frame complete' to the CPU before its final DMA flush finishes (0.5ms remaining). The CPU immediately signals the NPU, which reads partially-written memory — the bottom portion of the image contains stale data from the previous frame, corrupting the ML input tensor. Fix: insert an Android SyncFence or iOS Metal Event between ISP output and NPU input. The fence guarantees all DMA writes are visible in DRAM before the NPU begins reading. Cost: <10us latency, zero CPU involvement.

scenario: Your AR headset uses a dedicated Image Signal Processor (ISP) and an NPU. You want zero-copy memory between them. You allocate a hardware buffer. The ISP writes a frame to it, then the NPU reads it. It works, but occasionally the ML model outputs complete garbage. The image visually looks fine if you save it to disk right after the ISP finishes. What hardware synchronization mechanism did you forget?
title: The ISP/NPU Hardware Synchronization

details.common_mistake: Suggesting running a multi-billion parameter Vision-Language Model (VLM) on-device using standard 4-bit quantization (which still violates the 50MB RAM constraint by orders of magnitude), or relying on DOM/accessibility trees which are notoriously unreliable and not universally implemented across all iOS apps.
details.napkin_math: - Memory: 15M parameters quantized to INT4 = ~7.5MB. | - Activations: Downsampled 512x512 image input → peak activation memory is 256 x 256 x 16 channels x 2 bytes (FP16) = ~2MB. | - Context/OS Buffer: ~5MB. | - Total RAM Footprint: ~14.5MB (safely under the 50MB constraint). | - Latency: The ANE computes ~11-35 TOPS. A 15M parameter forward pass is ~0.5 GFLOPs. Compute time is bounded by memory bandwidth. At ~50GB/s unified memory bandwidth, transferring 7 MB of vision encoder weights from DRAM to NPU SRAM takes 7 MB / 25.6 GB/s LPDDR5 bandwidth = 0.27 ms. Total end-to-end latency: 12 ms vision encoding + 0.27 ms weight transfer + 8 ms text grounding + 2 ms action mapping = 22.3 ms, well within the 100 ms interaction budget.
details.realistic_solution: Use an asymmetric cascaded architecture. An ultra-small, specialized CoreML model (e.g., a MobileNetV4-based encoder paired with a lightweight transformer decoder, ~15M parameters) continuously runs on the ANE to output bounding boxes and semantic embeddings for UI elements. It relies solely on pixels, bypassing the accessibility tree. For the handoff protocol, instead of sending the raw screenshot to the cloud (which introduces latency and privacy risks), the on-device model generates a highly compressed semantic embedding grid (e.g., 16x16 tokens) of the screen. Only this grid and the user's audio transcript are securely handed off to the Apple Intelligence cloud nodes, drastically reducing bandwidth and preserving user privacy.

scenario: We're implementing a Ferret-UI-inspired agentic system where Siri can perform actions based on what the user is currently looking at on their screen. The vision-language model needs to ground user commands (e.g., 'Click the second checkout button') to explicit x,y coordinates. The constraint: this grounding model must reside entirely in-memory with a peak RAM footprint under 50MB, execute in <10ms on the Apple Neural Engine (ANE), and support seamless handoff to Private Cloud Compute for complex reasoning. How do you design the on-device grounding architecture and the handoff protocol?
title: Zero-Shot UI Action Grounding

details.common_mistake: Using standard vector databases like FAISS or HNSW locally. HNSW has massive, unpredictable memory overhead for its graph structure and indexing latency spikes that will trigger iOS watchdog terminations. Furthermore, applying standard Laplace noise to raw text embeddings degrades local utility to the point of uselessness.
details.napkin_math: - **Memory:** Model: 10M params @ INT8 = **10MB**. | - **Index Storage:** 100,000 local items * 64-dim * 1-byte (PQ) = **6.4MB** on disk (mmap'd, zero RAM footprint). | - **Active RAM:** 10MB (model) + 2MB (activations) + 1MB (PQ centroids in RAM) = **13MB total RAM**. | - **Latency:** Embedding extraction = **~4ms** on ANE. Dot product of query against 100,000 64-dim INT8 vectors = 6.4M MACs. AMX throughput is ~2 TMACs/s. Compute time for the search is **< 0.1ms**. Total latency = **~4.1ms**.
details.realistic_solution: Implement a direct-to-flash Product Quantization (PQ) index. The embedding model is an ultra-lite dual-encoder (~10M parameters, INT8). The vector index uses memory-mapped (mmap) files backed by NVMe flash storage, completely bypassing the RAM limit for storage. The ANE handles the embedding extraction, while the Apple Matrix AMX coprocessor handles the PQ asymmetric distance calculations. For telemetry, we use DP-FTRL (Differential Privacy Follow-The-Regularized-Leader). We never send embeddings or text. We calculate local gradients on-device using a tiny federated learning task, clip the gradients, add Gaussian noise (ensuring strict LDP), and only send the noisy gradients to the server.

scenario: Siri needs to proactively suggest contextual actions based on a user's local message history, photos, and app usage. We want to update a semantic index dynamically on-device, but we must guarantee strict Local Differential Privacy (LDP) before any aggregated telemetry (to improve the global model) leaves the device. The entire indexing and query pipeline must consume <50MB of RAM and <10ms latency per query. How do you architect the local vector store, the CoreML embedding pipeline, and the LDP mechanism?
title: Local-Local RAG & On-Device Telemetry

details.common_mistake: Proposing a "small" LLM (like TinyLlama or MobileLLM) with KV caching. Even a 1-billion parameter model quantized to 2-bit takes ~250MB, completely destroying the 50MB budget and forcing background apps to be evicted from memory.
details.napkin_math: - Model Size: 20M parameters. Core weights in INT4 = 10MB. | - Context State: 5 interactions * 512 float16 values = ~5KB (completely negligible). | - Activations: For a short sequence (seq_len=32): 32 * 256 (hidden) * 2 bytes = ~16KB. | - Total RAM Footprint: ~10.1MB. | - Latency: 20M params per token. For 32 tokens = ~1.2 GFLOPs. With ANE memory bandwidth at ~50GB/s, fetching 10MB of weights takes 0.2ms. Compute overhead is ~0.1ms. Total end-to-end routing decision takes < 1ms, ensuring zero user-perceptible delay before OS execution or cloud handoff begins.
details.realistic_solution: Frame the routing not as generative text, but as an Intent Classification and Entity Extraction (NER) task. Use an extreme-quantized CNN-RNN hybrid or a distilled ALBERT-style architecture (~20M parameters). Context is NOT maintained by a KV cache; instead, we use a fixed-size running state vector (e.g., 512-dim) updated via a lightweight GRU/LSTM cell after each turn. The graph is compiled directly to CoreML, utilizing mixed-precision: INT4 weight-only quantization for the feed-forward layers and INT8 for the recurrent activations, fully hardware-accelerated by the ANE.

scenario: We need an on-device 'Router' model that listens to every user invocation and decides in <10ms whether the query can be handled entirely locally (e.g., toggling a setting) or if it requires handing off to Apple Intelligence in the cloud. The router must maintain semantic context of the last 5 interactions, fit strictly under 50MB RAM, and operate seamlessly with the Neural Engine. How do you design the model architecture, context management, and extreme quantization strategy?
title: The Semantic Router

details.common_mistake: Thinking iOS natively supports PyTorch or that you just need to install a PyTorch pip package on the iPhone.
details.napkin_math: - A MobileNetV2 (3.4M params) in PyTorch FP32: 3.4M x 4 bytes = **13.6 MB** | - CoreML auto-converts to FP16 during export: 3.4M x 2 bytes = **6.8 MB** (2x smaller) | - CoreML compiler then fuses ops (Conv+BN+ReLU) and maps to Neural Engine instructions | - => Same model goes from 13.6 MB generic weights to a 6.8 MB hardware-optimized package that runs on the A17 Pro's 35 TOPS Neural Engine instead of the CPU
details.realistic_solution: No. The raw PyTorch model must be converted into Apple's proprietary CoreML format (`.mlpackage` or `.mlmodel`) so that the iOS operating system can automatically route the operations to the Neural Engine, GPU, or CPU.

scenario: If you train a model in PyTorch, can you deploy the raw `.pt` or `.pth` file directly into a native iOS Swift application?
title: CoreML vs PyTorch

details.common_mistake: Worrying about the network connection dropping or the UI freezing.
details.napkin_math: - On-device LLM inference draws ~3W sustained on an A17 Pro SoC | - Battery capacity: 4,000 mAh x 3.7V = **14.8 Wh** | - Drain rate at 3W: 811 mA = **20% of battery per hour** | - iOS grants background tasks only ~30 seconds of execution time | - => At 3W for 30s the model consumes 0.025 Wh per cycle, but the watchdog kills any process sustaining >80% CPU utilization beyond ~180s — the thermal and power budget makes continuous background LLM inference physically impossible
details.realistic_solution: The iOS Watchdog Timer. iOS aggressively monitors background apps for memory and CPU usage. Background execution limits: 30 seconds for most tasks, 3 minutes for audio processing (with Background Modes entitlement). A 7B LLM at INT4 = 3.5 GB weights + 0.5 GB KV-cache = 4 GB. iPhone 16 Pro has 8 GB total, ~5 GB available. In foreground: 4 GB fits. In background: iOS reclaims memory aggressively. Any app using >50% of physical RAM gets jetsammed (killed) within seconds. Even with smaller models (1B = 500 MB INT4), sustained CPU/GPU usage >80% for >30 seconds in background triggers the watchdog. Solutions: (1) pause inference when backgrounded and resume in foreground, (2) use background audio session for short summarization bursts (<10s), (3) offload to a local server process via network extension (exempt from watchdog), (4) use on-device APIs (Apple Intelligence) that run in a system process exempt from app limits.

scenario: You are designing an iOS app that runs an LLM to summarize incoming audio while the app is in the background (user is looking at the home screen). What is the primary risk of running heavy ML inference in the background?
title: Background Inference Limits

details.common_mistake: "Show a progress bar instead of a spinner." A progress bar is better UX, but 70 seconds is too long regardless of visual feedback.
details.napkin_math: User attention span for a new app launch is ~2-5 seconds. A 70-second block is 14-35x longer than the tolerance threshold of a typical mobile user.
details.realistic_solution: The architecture has a **Synchronous Dependency on the Critical Path**. The app forces users to wait for sequential download, validation, and compilation before any functionality is available. The fix is a **Progressive Launch Architecture**: ship a tiny fallback model (~3 MB) in the app bundle for instant value, while downloading and compiling the high-quality model in the background.

scenario: A user downloads your new LLM-powered translation app. Upon first launch, the app shows a spinner for 70 seconds while it prepares the model. Based on the launch timeline, why are you seeing a 95% abandonment rate?
title: The Launch Blocker

details.common_mistake: "The NPU is slow — use a bigger model." The NPU compute is fine. The overhead is in the data movement.
details.napkin_math: Each NPU-CPU-NPU round-trip costs ~2.4ms in DMA overhead. With 2 such bounces, you spend 4.8ms just moving data—roughly 32% of your 15ms total budget—without doing any significant math.
details.realistic_solution: You are hitting **Graph Partitioning Overhead**. Each unsupported operator forces the graph to 'ping-pong' data from the NPU to the CPU and back via DMA. This incurs a latency tax for the transfer and leaves the NPU idle while the CPU processes the single op. The fix is to eliminate partition boundaries by replacing unsupported ops with approximations (e.g., Sigmoid approximation for GELU) or static-shape equivalents.

scenario: You are deploying a model to a mobile NPU. The math should only take 10ms, but the actual inference latency is 15ms. You find two unsupported operators in your graph. Based on the DMA flow, why are these two ops causing a 50% latency penalty?
title: The Operator Gap

details.common_mistake: "The model is too big — quantize it." Quantization helps, but the real issue is that the camera ISP's memory allocation is invisible to your app and uncontrollable.
details.napkin_math: Total Memory = 1.5 GB (OS) + 1.2 GB (ISP) + 0.82 GB (App) = 3.52 GB. This is dangerously close to the 4 GB limit. Any background task (like a notification or a message) will push the system over the edge.
details.realistic_solution: You are hitting a **Shared Resource RAM Collision**. The camera ISP service runs in a separate process but shares the same physical RAM pool. During photo capture, the ISP HDR pipeline can consume >1.2 GB. When combined with the OS and your app, total demand exceeds 4 GB, and the OS kills the app to protect the camera. The fix is to use **mmap** for weights (allowing OS eviction), reduce camera resolution during inference, or sequentialize the capture and ML phases.

scenario: Your AR app crashes with a 'SIGKILL' (Jetsam kill) when users take a high-resolution photo, even though your app is only using 822 MB of its 2 GB memory limit. Based on the RAM diagram, what is the 'invisible' resource consumer causing the OS to kill your process?
title: The Jetsam Guillotine

details.common_mistake: "The phone is defective" or "Add a cooling fan." You can't attach a fan to a user's phone. The phone is working exactly as designed — DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) protects the SoC from thermal damage.
details.napkin_math: Sustained TOPS is typically ~50% of Peak. If your model requires 100% of peak TOPS to hit 30 FPS, you are guaranteed to drop to 15 FPS once the thermal envelope is saturated (~60 seconds).
details.realistic_solution: You are hitting the **Sustained Thermal Envelope**. Mobile SoCs support high TOPS only for short "bursts." For continuous inference, the device throttles to its sustained thermal design power (sTDP), often 40-60% of peak. The fix is to target sustained performance (e.g., design for 20 TOPS, not 45 TOPS peak), implement adaptive frame rates based on `ThermalState`, or use the NPU instead of the GPU to halve heat generation.

scenario: Your mobile model runs at 30 FPS during internal demos, but users complain that it slows down to 12 FPS after a minute of use. Based on the performance timeline, what physical protection mechanism is engaging inside the smartphone?
title: The Burst Benchmarking Illusion

details.common_mistake: "Run the models in parallel on different cores." The phone has one NPU — parallel execution doesn't help. And you'd still waste 24 MB of memory.
details.napkin_math: 3 tasks with MobileNetV3 (12MB weights). Independent execution: 3 * 12MB = 36MB RAM, and 3 * 2 TFLOPs = 6 TFLOPs compute. Shared backbone: Features extracted once (12MB RAM, 2 TFLOPs), then branched to 3 light heads. Saves 24MB RAM and cuts compute by 66%, dropping per-frame latency from 18ms to 8ms.
details.realistic_solution: You have **Backbone Redundancy**. The app loads three identical copies of the backbone weights and computes the same features three times per frame. The fix is a **Multi-Task Architecture with Shared Backbone**: load the backbone once (12 MB), run it once (6ms), and branch into three lightweight task heads. This reduces memory by 64% and latency by 40%.

scenario: Your mobile app has three different computer vision features (Face Detection, Face Mesh, and Segmentation). All three use the same MobileNetV3 backbone. Based on the VRAM diagram, what is the 'efficiency gap' in your model loading strategy?
title: The Backbone Bloat

details.common_mistake: "Check battery level before training." Battery checks don't prevent interruptions like OS kills or reboots.
details.napkin_math: If 60% of layers are v2.0 and 40% are v1.0, the feature map distribution from Layer 2 will not match the weights expected by Layer 3, leading to catastrophic error propagation.
details.realistic_solution: You have a **Frankenstein Model** caused by non-atomic updates. The pipeline wrote the updated model directly to the active file. If interrupted, the file contains a mix of new and old layers, which is numerically invalid. The fix is **Atomic Promotion (Shadow Copy)**: download/train the model in a temporary directory, and only after validation is complete, use an atomic `rename()` call to replace the active model file.

scenario: During a background model update on a user's phone, the device suddenly reboots. Upon next launch, the app doesn't crash, but the ML model produces nonsensical 'garbage' outputs. Based on the file-write diagram, what state is the model file in?
title: The Frankenstein Model

details.common_mistake: "The model needs to be quantized to INT8 so it uses less power." The model's compute cost is negligible; the power is being burned by the hardware state required to execute it.
details.napkin_math: Basal AP power is ~80 mW. DSP power is ~1 mW. By failing to delegate to the AOD, you are using 80x more power than necessary just to keep the lights on for a simple task.
details.realistic_solution: You are suffering from **Application Processor Wake-Lock Tax**. To run the model on the main CPU, the OS must hold a wake-lock, powering up the high-power CPU rails and DDR RAM. This prevents the phone from entering Deep Sleep. The fix is to push always-on models down to the **Always-On Domain (AOD) / DSP**, which reads the microphone directly into tiny SRAM and only wakes the main AP if the wake-word is detected.

scenario: You deploy a simple wake-word detection model. Even though the model uses very little CPU, users report that the app is the top battery consumer on their device. Based on the power domain diagram, where is the energy going?
title: The CPU Wake-Lock Tax

details.common_mistake: "The game is stealing NPU cycles." The game uses the GPU, not the NPU. They are separate physical cores.
details.napkin_math: A phone can only dissipate ~3-5 Watts sustained. If a 3D game pulls 4 Watts, the NPU is left with <1 Watt of thermal margin, triggering immediate frequency capping.
details.realistic_solution: You are hitting **Global Thermal Throttling**. In a mobile SoC, all cores share the same silicon die and thermal envelope. When the GPU generates massive heat from a game, the system's DVFS controller downclocks *the entire SoC*—including the NPU—to stay within safe skin-temperature limits. The fix is to use hyper-optimized, low-power models that can still meet deadlines even when the SoC is forced into its lowest frequency state.

scenario: Your real-time translation app works perfectly until the user starts a 3D game in picture-in-picture mode. Suddenly, your NPU translation latency triples. Based on the SoC diagram, why is the game affecting the NPU speed?
title: The Silicon Shared Oven

details.common_mistake: "Retrain the model to be even smaller." The model's 3 mW is already negligible compared to the system overhead.
details.napkin_math: Radio: 800 mW × 10s (wake + tail) × 12 times/hr = 26.7 mWh. Model: 3 mW × 1 hr = 3 mWh. The radio wake is ~9x more expensive than the actual ML work.
details.realistic_solution: You are hitting the **Radio Wake Overhead**. The cellular radio consumes ~800 mW every time it wakes from idle. Waking it every 5 minutes for a tiny payload prevents the radio from staying in its low-power state. The fix is **Batching and Delegation**: buffer results locally and upload once per hour, and use the OS's low-power activity co-processor (like Apple's M-series) instead of a custom always-on CPU loop.

scenario: You optimize your activity-tracking model down to 3 mW. However, the app still drains the battery by 10% per hour because it uploads labels to your server every 5 minutes. Based on the power breakdown, where is your optimization effort being wasted?
title: The Radio Energy Wall

details.common_mistake: "The phone is thermal throttling." While heat is a factor, the immediate drop is due to memory bus physics.
details.napkin_math: 4K display = 3840 * 2160 * 4 bytes (RGBA) = 33MB per frame. At 120Hz, display refresh alone consumes 33MB * 120 = 4.0 GB/s bandwidth. The GPU rendering adds another 4-8 GB/s. On a phone with 50 GB/s total RAM bandwidth, this steals 20% capacity. NPU misses deadlines because memory channels are saturated.
details.realistic_solution: You are suffering from **Memory Bus Contention**. In a Unified Memory Architecture (UMA), the Display Controller, GPU, and NPU all share the same LPDDR5 bus. A 120Hz display must refresh the framebuffer twice as often as a 60Hz one, consuming a massive slice of the total bandwidth. The memory controller prioritizes the display to prevent tearing, starving the bandwidth-hungry NPU. The fix is to drop the refresh rate to 60Hz during heavy AR features or reduce NPU precision to INT8 to halve its bandwidth needs.

scenario: Your AR app runs a real-time style transfer model. When the user upgrades to a Pro phone with a 120Hz 'ProMotion' display, the NPU inference suddenly starts stuttering and missing deadlines. Based on the UMA diagram, why is a faster screen slowing down your AI?
title: The UMA Bandwidth Wall

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on peak TOPS without considering power. The Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 advertises 73 TOPS but at similar power, so raw TOPS alone does not determine which chip is better for a battery-constrained workload.
details.napkin_math: A17 Pro ANE: 35 TOPS / 5W = 7 TOPS/W. At 18.5 Wh battery, running the ANE at full power drains the battery in ~3.7 hours.
details.realistic_solution: 35 TOPS / 5W = 7 TOPS/W. On a mobile device, the binding constraint is the battery, not peak compute. A chip that delivers 7 TOPS/W means each watt of battery power yields 7 trillion INT8 operations per second. This is the metric that determines how many inferences you can run before the battery dies.

scenario: Your team is evaluating mobile SoCs for an always-on image classification app. The Apple A17 Pro advertises 35 TOPS from its Neural Engine at a sustained power draw of approximately 5W. What is the compute efficiency in TOPS per watt, and why does this metric matter more than raw TOPS for a mobile device?
title: The ANE Efficiency Advantage

details.common_mistake: Confusing the compressed HEIF/JPEG output size (a few MB per photo) with the raw sensor bandwidth. The ISP must handle the full uncompressed firehose before any compression occurs.
details.napkin_math: 48MP x 2 bytes x 30 fps = 2.88 GB/s raw sensor bandwidth. This rivals the LPDDR5X memory bandwidth of the entire SoC.
details.realistic_solution: 48 million pixels x 2 bytes (10-bit packed into 16-bit) x 30 fps = 2.88 GB/s. This is why mobile SoCs need dedicated high-bandwidth MIPI CSI interfaces and why the ISP is a critical bottleneck, not the CPU or GPU.

scenario: A modern flagship phone has a 48MP camera sensor shooting 10-bit RAW at 30 fps burst mode. Before any ISP processing or compression, what is the raw data bandwidth flowing from the sensor to the SoC?
title: The 48MP Camera Firehose

details.common_mistake: Estimating based on JPEG file sizes (a few MB total) rather than the uncompressed tensor representation that the training loop actually requires in memory.
details.napkin_math: Images = 1000*224*224*3*4B = 602MB. Model (25M INT8) = 25MB. Gradients + Adam Optimizer (FP32) = 25M*8B = 200MB. Forward activations for batch size 32 = ~100MB. Total RAM needed = 602 + 25 + 200 + 100 = 927MB. This easily fits inside the 8GB unified memory of the iPhone 15 Pro, leaving 7GB+ for iOS.
details.realistic_solution: 1,000 images x 224 x 224 x 3 channels x 4 bytes (FP32) = 602 MB. This is significant but fits in 8GB alongside a quantized model. However, training also needs gradients and optimizer states, which can 2-3x the memory pressure.

scenario: You want to fine-tune a mobile vision model on-device using 1,000 user photos preprocessed to 224x224 RGB tensors in FP32. How much memory does this training dataset occupy, and does it fit comfortably in the 8GB unified memory of an iPhone 15 Pro alongside the model?
title: The On-Device Fine-Tuning Data Budget

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT4 is always a free win. The 1.5 GB savings is real, but INT4 quantization can cause significant accuracy degradation on tasks requiring precise numerical reasoning, and not all layers quantize equally well.
details.napkin_math: INT8: 3B x 1 byte = 3.0 GB. INT4: 3B x 0.5 bytes = 1.5 GB. Savings = 1.5 GB. Fits in 8 GB with room for KV cache + OS.
details.realistic_solution: INT4 halves the weight memory: 3B x 0.5 bytes = 1.5 GB, saving 1.5 GB compared to INT8. This freed memory can hold a KV cache of ~1,500 tokens at FP16 for a 7B-class model. The risk is accuracy loss, especially in embedding and attention output layers.

scenario: Your team wants to deploy a 3B parameter language model on a phone with 8GB unified memory. The INT8 version is 3 GB. A colleague proposes INT4 quantization to free memory for the KV cache. How much memory does the INT4 model save, and what is the primary risk?
title: The INT4 Quantization Payoff

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that 5W is only the ANE power draw. The display, radios, and OS consume another 2-3W minimum, so actual battery life is much shorter than the naive calculation suggests.
details.napkin_math: Inference only: 18.5 Wh / 5W = 3.7h. With system overhead: 18.5 Wh / 8W = 2.3h. At 5 fps (1/6 duty cycle): ~1W inference + 3W system = 4W, giving 18.5/4 = 4.6h. Still short of 8h.
details.realistic_solution: 18.5 Wh / 5W = 3.7 hours from inference alone. Adding display and OS overhead (~3W), total draw is ~8W, giving only ~2.3 hours. The 8-hour target is physically impossible without reducing inference frequency (e.g., 5 fps instead of 30 fps, cutting power to ~1W).

scenario: A mobile health app runs continuous pose estimation at 30 fps, consuming 5W sustained on the ANE. The phone has an 18.5 Wh battery. The product manager wants the app to run for 8 hours. Is this feasible with inference alone, ignoring all other phone functions?
title: The Battery Inference Budget

details.common_mistake: Guessing a 2-3x reduction. The actual savings scale with the number of output channels and are much larger, which is why MobileNet achieved near-ResNet accuracy with 8-9x fewer FLOPs.
details.napkin_math: Standard: C_in x C_out x K^2 = 256 x 256 x 9 = 590K MACs. DW-sep: C_in x K^2 + C_in x C_out = 2.3K + 65.5K = 67.8K MACs. Savings: ~8.7x.
details.realistic_solution: Standard 3x3 conv: 256 x 256 x 9 = 589,824 MACs per position. Depthwise separable: (256 x 9) + (256 x 256) = 2,304 + 65,536 = 67,840 MACs. Ratio: 589,824 / 67,840 = 8.7x reduction.

scenario: You are porting a server-side image classifier to mobile. The heaviest layer is a standard 3x3 convolution with 256 input and 256 output channels. A colleague suggests replacing it with a depthwise separable convolution. By what factor does this reduce the multiply-accumulate operations per spatial position?
title: The Depthwise Separable Convolution Dividend

details.common_mistake: Treating the embedding table as a trivially small lookup. For LLMs, the embedding and unembedding layers can be a significant fraction of total memory, and they are often the hardest to quantize aggressively.
details.napkin_math: Embedding table: 32K x 4096 x 2B = 262 MB. Fraction of 3.5 GB model: 262/3500 = 7.5%. Un-quantizable overhead.
details.realistic_solution: 32,000 x 4,096 x 2 bytes = 262 MB. This is 262/3500 = 7.5% of the INT4 model. If the embeddings must stay at FP16 while other layers go to INT4, the effective compression ratio of the full model is worse than advertised.

scenario: A mobile LLM uses a 32K token vocabulary with a 4096-dimensional embedding layer stored in FP16. How large is the embedding table, and what fraction of a 3.5 GB INT4 model does it represent if the embeddings cannot be quantized below FP16 without severe quality loss?
title: The Vocabulary Embedding Tax

details.common_mistake: Assuming speculative decoding simply adds the two models' speeds. The key insight is that the large model verifies all 4 draft tokens in a single forward pass (same cost as generating 1 token), so you get multiple tokens for the price of one verification.
details.napkin_math: Main 7B speed: 5 tok/s = 200ms/tok. Draft 150M speed: 20 tok/s = 50ms/tok. Generating 4 draft tokens takes 4 * 50ms = 200ms. Target model verifies these 4 tokens in a single batch pass (memory bandwidth bound) taking ~200ms. Total time = 400ms. 3 draft accepted + 1 verified = 4 tokens per 400ms. Effective speed = 10 tok/s (2x speedup).
details.realistic_solution: Draft time: 4 tokens / 20 tok/s = 0.2s. Verification: 1 forward pass of large model = 0.2s. Total: 0.4s for 4 accepted tokens (3 accepted + 1 from verification). Effective: 4/0.4 = 10 tok/s, a 2x speedup over the baseline 5 tok/s.

scenario: On a mobile device, your main 7B LLM generates at 5 tokens/second (memory-bandwidth-bound). You add a 150M draft model that runs at 20 tokens/second. The draft model proposes 4 tokens at a time, and on average 3 are accepted by the verifier. What is the effective token throughput with speculative decoding?
title: The Speculative Decoding Gambit

details.common_mistake: Confusing megabits (Mb) with megabytes (MB). 50 Mbps = 6.25 MB/s, not 50 MB/s. Also, ignoring that cellular connections are bursty and real throughput is often 30-50% of advertised speeds.
details.napkin_math: LTE Speed = 50 Mbps / 8 = 6.25 MB/s. Model size = 4 GB = 4096 MB. Download time = 4096 / 6.25 = 655 seconds (~10.9 mins). Metered cost = 4 GB * $10/GB = $40. Strategy: Require WiFi for the 4GB payload. For future updates, ship INT4 LoRA adapters (~50MB), which download in 8 seconds and cost only $0.50 on cellular.
details.realistic_solution: 4 GB / 6.25 MB/s = 640 seconds = 10.7 minutes at peak. Real-world with overhead: 15-20 minutes. Strategy: (1) Ship a base model in the app bundle, (2) download full model over WiFi only with user consent, (3) use delta updates for model version upgrades (~5-10% of full size), (4) stream initial layers while downloading the rest.

scenario: Your app needs to deliver a 4 GB INT4 language model to users over cellular. The median LTE download speed is 50 Mbps. A product review flags that users on metered data plans will be unhappy. Calculate the download time and propose a deployment strategy that respects mobile network constraints.
title: The Cellular Model Delivery Problem

details.common_mistake: Only considering a single device's upload cost (~500 MB/day), which seems manageable. The system-level cost across all participating devices reveals the true infrastructure burden.
details.napkin_math: Daily upload: 50 MB x 1,000 x 10 = 500 GB. Per device: 500 MB/day upload. With 10x compression: 50 GB total, 50 MB per device. Upload time at 10 Mbps: 4s per round compressed vs 40s uncompressed.
details.realistic_solution: 50 MB x 1,000 devices x 10 rounds = 500 GB uploaded per day. At median mobile upload speed of 10 Mbps (1.25 MB/s), each device spends 50/1.25 = 40 seconds per upload. With gradient compression (10-100x), this drops to 5-50 GB/day. Techniques: top-k sparsification, quantized gradients, or sending only significant parameter deltas.

scenario: You are designing a federated learning system for a mobile keyboard app. Each training round involves 1,000 devices uploading a 50 MB model diff. The system runs 10 rounds per day. Calculate the total daily upload bandwidth and explain why naive federated learning is infeasible at scale without compression.
title: The Federated Learning Upload Bill

details.common_mistake: Using naive (linear) composition and concluding that differential privacy is useless for frequent queries. Advanced composition via the moments accountant or Renyi DP gives a much tighter bound, making practical deployments feasible.
details.napkin_math: Naive: 100 queries x eps=1 = eps_total=100. Advanced (sqrt): sqrt(100) x 1 = eps_total~10. With Renyi DP: potentially eps_total~7-8. To stay under eps_total=5, limit to ~25 queries/day.
details.realistic_solution: Naive composition: total epsilon = 100 x 1 = 100 (no meaningful privacy). Advanced composition (square-root law): total epsilon scales as roughly sqrt(100) x 1 = 10. With Renyi DP accounting, even tighter bounds are achievable. Practical implication: use the moments accountant, batch correlated queries, and set a daily privacy budget (e.g., epsilon=5) that limits total queries.

scenario: A mobile health app uses differential privacy with epsilon=1 per query. The analytics team wants to run 100 on-device queries per day against a user's data. Using basic composition, the daily privacy budget would be epsilon=100, which provides almost no privacy. How does advanced composition improve this, and what is the practical implication for query budgeting?
title: The Privacy Budget Drain

details.common_mistake: Assuming gradient checkpointing is free. It trades memory for compute by recomputing activations during the backward pass, typically adding 30-40% wall-clock time. On a battery-powered device, this also means 30-40% more energy per training step.
details.napkin_math: Full activations: 32 layers x 4 x 512 x 4096 x 2B = 537 MB. Checkpointed (5 layers): 5 x 17 MB = 84 MB. Savings: 453 MB. Compute cost: ~33% more FLOPs for backward pass.
details.realistic_solution: Without checkpointing: 537 MB activations across 32 layers. With gradient checkpointing (store every sqrt(32)=5-6 layers): ~84 MB activations, saving ~450 MB. The cost: ~33% more compute (recomputing activations for non-checkpointed layers during backward). On a 5W device, this means ~1.65W extra per training step, but the 450 MB savings is critical to fitting in memory.

scenario: You are implementing on-device fine-tuning of a 32-layer transformer on a phone with 8 GB memory. With batch size 4, sequence length 512, and hidden dimension 4096 in FP16, the activation memory for backpropagation across all layers is ~537 MB. The model weights (INT4) are 3.5 GB. Together with KV cache and OS, memory is critically tight. How does gradient checkpointing help, and what does it cost?
title: The On-Device Training Memory Crisis

details.common_mistake: Confusing active compute parameters with memory footprint. On a server with fast NVMe, you can page experts in and out. On a mobile device, NAND flash is 1000x slower than DRAM, so all experts must reside in memory to avoid catastrophic latency spikes.
details.napkin_math: All experts: 8 x 500M x 0.5B = 2.0 GB (must be in DRAM). Active per token: 2 x 500M x 0.5B = 0.5 GB. Flash paging penalty: 0.5 GB / 500 MB/s = 1 second per cold expert load. Unacceptable for real-time generation.
details.realistic_solution: Total model memory: 4B x 0.5 bytes (INT4) = 2.0 GB for all experts. Even though only 0.5 GB is active per token, the routing decision changes per token, so all experts must be resident in DRAM. You cannot page from flash (200-500 MB/s) fast enough; loading a cold expert from NAND would add 1-2 seconds of latency per token. The 2 GB footprint fits in 8 GB, but the team's 0.5 GB claim is misleading.

scenario: A research team proposes deploying a Mixture of Experts model on mobile: 8 experts of 500M parameters each (4B total) in INT4, with top-2 routing so only 1B parameters are active per token. They claim it fits in 8 GB because only 0.5 GB of active experts need to be in memory. Explain why this reasoning is flawed for mobile deployment.
title: The Mobile MoE Memory Illusion

details.common_mistake: Only counting model weights and forgetting the optimizer states, gradients, and activations required for the RL training loop. The reward model also needs inference activations, even though it is not being trained.
details.napkin_math: Policy (INT4): 1.5 GB. Reward (INT8): 1.0 GB. LoRA optimizer: 0.4 GB. Activations: 0.4 GB. OS: 1.5 GB. Total: 4.8 GB / 8 GB = 60% utilization. Full fine-tuning would add 3B × 8 bytes = 24 GB optimizer states. Impossible.
details.realistic_solution: Policy weights: 1.5 GB. Reward model: 1.0 GB. Policy optimizer (AdamW states for LoRA, ~50M trainable params): 50M x 8 bytes = 400 MB. Policy activations + gradients: ~300 MB (with checkpointing). Reward inference activations: ~100 MB. OS + framework overhead: ~1.5 GB. Total: ~4.8 GB. Fits in 8 GB, but barely. Must use LoRA (not full fine-tuning) and gradient checkpointing.

scenario: You are implementing on-device RLHF for a mobile assistant. The policy model is 3B params (INT4 = 1.5 GB) and you need a 1B parameter reward model (INT8 = 1 GB) to score responses. Both must be in memory simultaneously during training. On a device with 8 GB unified memory, is this feasible? What are the memory stacks involved?
title: The On-Device RLHF Memory Wall

details.common_mistake: Storing raw input data (images, text) in the replay buffer instead of compact embeddings. A single 224x224 image in FP32 is 600 KB, while its 768-dim FP16 embedding is only 1.5 KB, a 400x compression that makes replay buffers feasible on mobile.
details.napkin_math: Per sample: 768 dims x 2 bytes + 64 bytes metadata = 1,600 bytes. Buffer: 10K x 1.6 KB = 16 MB. Compare: 10K raw images at 600 KB = 6 GB. Embedding replay is 375x more memory-efficient.
details.realistic_solution: Buffer size: 10,000 x (768 x 2 + 64) = 10,000 x 1,600 bytes = 16 MB. Eviction policy: (1) Hard cap at 16 MB / 10K samples, (2) reservoir sampling to maintain distribution representativeness, (3) priority eviction based on prediction confidence (remove easy examples first), (4) class-balanced eviction to prevent catastrophic forgetting of rare categories.

scenario: You are designing a continuous learning system for a mobile recommendation model. The system maintains a replay buffer of 10,000 past interactions stored as 768-dimensional FP16 embeddings plus 64 bytes of metadata per sample. Calculate the buffer size and design a memory-aware eviction policy that prevents unbounded growth on a memory-constrained device.
title: The Replay Buffer Memory Budget

details.common_mistake: Only considering per-device bandwidth (10 MB / 300s = 33 KB/s, trivial). The aggregate server-side cost is the real engineering challenge: 1M concurrent downloads create a massive egress bill and bandwidth requirement.
details.napkin_math: Aggregate BW: 10 MB x 1M / 300s = 33 GB/s. Daily egress: 10 MB x 1M x 288 = 2,880 TB. Cost at $0.08/GB: $230K/day. With delta compression (20x): 1.65 GB/s, $11.5K/day.
details.realistic_solution: Server egress: 10 MB x 1M devices / 300s = 33 GB/s sustained. At cloud egress pricing ($0.08/GB), this costs 10 MB x 1M x 288 syncs/day = 2,880 TB/day = $230,400/day. Solutions: (1) CDN edge caching for shared adapter updates, (2) push-based delta updates (only changed bytes, ~500 KB), (3) staggered sync windows (not all at once), (4) peer-to-peer gossip for nearby devices.

scenario: Your mobile app personalizes a model using 10 MB LoRA adapters synced from the cloud every 5 minutes. The app has 1 million active users. Calculate the server-side egress bandwidth required and propose a scalable distribution architecture.
title: The Million-Device Adapter Sync Storm

details.common_mistake: Assuming compression is lossless. Top-k sparsification discards 90% of gradient components, which can slow convergence by 2-5x in rounds needed, partially offsetting the communication savings. The net benefit depends on whether communication or computation is the bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Uncompressed: 100 devices x 50 MB = 5 GB/round. Compressed (10x): 500 MB/round. Upload time: 5 MB / 1.25 MB/s = 4s vs 40s. If convergence needs 2.5x rounds: total = 500 MB x 250 = 125 GB vs 5 GB x 100 = 500 GB. 4x total savings.
details.realistic_solution: Uncompressed: 100 x 50 MB = 5 GB per round. With 10x compression: 100 x 5 MB = 500 MB per round. At 10 Mbps upload, each device takes 4 seconds instead of 40 seconds. Trade-off: convergence may require 2-3x more rounds (200-300 vs 100), but total communication drops from 500 GB to 100-150 GB across the full training run. Net win if upload bandwidth is the bottleneck.

scenario: In your federated learning system, 100 mobile devices each produce a 50 MB gradient update per round. The team applies 10x gradient compression (top-k sparsification + quantization). Calculate the per-round upload volume and analyze the convergence trade-off of aggressive compression.
title: The Federated Gradient Compression Trade-Off

details.common_mistake: Sending the full 500 MB teacher model to the device. The student does not need the full teacher; it needs the teacher's soft labels or a compressed delta of the teacher's behavior on the student's local data distribution.
details.napkin_math: Full teacher: 500 MB (exceeds budget). Delta: 500 MB x 5% = 25 MB (fits). Soft labels (top-32): 10K x 32 x 4B = 1.3 MB (fits easily). Monthly WiFi + daily delta: 25 MB/day = 750 MB/month cellular. Soft labels: 1.3 MB/day = 39 MB/month.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy: (1) Delta compression of teacher weights: ~5% of full model = 25 MB, fits in 100 MB budget. (2) Alternatively, send soft-label distillation targets: for 10K local samples x 32K vocab x FP16, this is too large. Better: send only top-32 logits per sample = 10K x 32 x 4 bytes = 1.3 MB. (3) Hybrid: monthly full sync over WiFi (500 MB), daily delta sync over cellular (25 MB). Budget: 25 MB/day << 100 MB limit.

scenario: You run on-device knowledge distillation: a 500 MB teacher model in the cloud periodically pushes updates to guide a 50 MB on-device student. The user has a 100 MB daily cellular data budget. Design a sync protocol that keeps the student model fresh without exceeding the data budget.
title: The Model Distillation Sync Budget

details.common_mistake: Only checking a single whole-file hash, which catches corruption but requires re-downloading the entire 4 GB model. Chunk-level checksums allow surgical repair of only the corrupted chunks.
details.napkin_math: Checksum storage: 4,000 chunks x 32 bytes = 128 KB (0.003% overhead). Verification time: 4 GB / 2 GB/s read = 2s. Repair: 3 MB re-download vs 4 GB full re-download = 1,333x bandwidth savings.
details.realistic_solution: Chunk-level integrity: store a SHA-256 hash (32 bytes) for each 1 MB chunk. Total overhead: 4,000 x 32 bytes = 128 KB (negligible). On startup, verify all chunks in parallel using the ANE or GPU idle cycles (~2 seconds for 4 GB at 2 GB/s read speed). If 3 chunks fail, re-download only 3 MB instead of 4 GB. Additionally, store a Merkle tree root hash for tamper detection.

scenario: After an OS update, users report that your on-device LLM produces nonsensical outputs. Investigation reveals that 3 of the 4,000 one-megabyte weight file chunks were silently corrupted during the filesystem migration. Design a verification system that detects such corruption before inference begins.
title: The Silent Model Corruption Problem

details.common_mistake: Ignoring thermal throttling entirely and having the app stutter or crash when throughput drops. Another mistake is statically reducing quality at app launch, wasting the initial thermal headroom.
details.napkin_math: Peak: 35 TOPS at 5W. Throttled: 35 × 3/5 = 21 TOPS at 3W (60% throughput). Frame budget: full model needs 30 TOPS for 30fps. At 21 TOPS, max sustainable is ~21 fps. Switching to medium model (15 TOPS for 30fps) restores 30fps under throttling.
details.realistic_solution: Throttled throughput: 35 × (3/5) = 21 TOPS (60% of peak). Adaptive strategy: (1) Monitor thermal state via OS APIs, (2) maintain 3 model tiers: full (35 TOPS, 30fps), medium (21 TOPS, 20fps with smaller input resolution), lite (14 TOPS, 15fps with aggressive pruning), (3) smooth transitions over 2-3 seconds to avoid visual jarring, (4) predictive throttling: start reducing quality 30s before expected thermal limit based on temperature trajectory.

scenario: Your mobile AR app runs a real-time segmentation model on the A17 Pro ANE at 35 TOPS. After 10 minutes of sustained use, the thermal management system throttles power from 5W to 3W. The ANE throughput drops proportionally. Design an adaptive inference strategy that maintains acceptable user experience under thermal constraints.
title: The Thermal Throttling Adaptation Loop

details.common_mistake: Assuming the ANE is inherently slow at Transformer architectures or blindly restricting execution to the GPU, ignoring the massive memory synchronization overhead caused by CPU fallback.
details.napkin_math: Initial Latency (140ms) = ANE Time (10ms) + CPU Time (30ms) + Context Switches. If a 12-layer ViT switches between ANE and CPU twice per layer (24 switches) at ~4ms memory sync overhead each, sync alone costs ~96ms. Fixing operations eliminates sync overhead, yielding ~15ms total latency.
details.realistic_solution: Use the Core ML Performance Report to identify ANE-unsupported operations (e.g., dynamic shapes, Einsum, or specific GELU variants) forcing CPU fallback. Refactor the PyTorch/TensorFlow source to use static shapes and supported primitives (e.g., replacing Einsum with standard matmuls), allowing the entire graph to compile for ANE.

scenario: A mobile team ports a Vision Transformer (ViT-Base) to Core ML for an iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS ANE). They expect high efficiency, but Instruments profiling reveals a latency of 140ms per frame. The trace shows execution constantly ping-ponging between the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) and the CPU. What is the architectural root cause of this execution pattern, and how can it be analyzed and resolved to achieve target performance?
title: Diagnosing Core ML ANE Fallback

details.common_mistake: Candidates often calculate the ANE compute time but forget to add both the two-way context switch penalty (ANE -> CPU -> ANE) and the CPU execution time, or they incorrectly assume 100% ANE utilization.
details.napkin_math: Peak ANE = 35 TOPS. Assume 40% efficiency = 14 TOPS (14,000 GOPS). ANE compute for 99% of model (1.98 GOPS) = 1.98 / 14000 = ~0.14 ms. CPU fallback = ~1.5 ms. ANE-to-CPU context switches (2 ways) = 2 * 0.5 ms = 1.0 ms. Total per-frame latency = 0.14 + 1.5 + 1.0 = 2.64 ms. Max throughput = 1000 ms / 2.64 ms = 378 FPS.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate effective ANE throughput, add the compute time, the CPU execution time, and the two context switch penalties. ANE compute time is negligible but context switching dominates the latency.

scenario: You are deploying a custom vision model via CoreML on an iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro chip). The model requires 2 GOPS per frame. The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) provides 35 TOPS of peak performance. Due to an unsupported custom activation function in the middle of the network, CoreML is forced to fall back to the CPU for that specific layer. The CPU takes 1.5ms to process this layer, but the ANE-to-CPU synchronization and memory copy takes 0.5ms each way. Assuming the ANE achieves 40% of its peak utilization on the supported layers (which account for 99.9% of the GOPS), calculate the total end-to-end latency for a single frame and the maximum sustainable FPS.
title: CoreML Execution Fallback Latency

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT8 quantization on GPU is the primary fix, while completely ignoring the massive latency penalties associated with intermediate tensor transfers between ANE and GPU.
details.napkin_math: ANE<->GPU transfer overhead ≈ 1.5ms per switch. With 4 attention blocks causing fallbacks, that's 8 switches per frame = 12ms pure overhead. Frame budget at 60 FPS = 16.6ms. The overhead alone consumes 72% of the budget. Eliminating switches drops latency from 25ms to ~13ms.
details.realistic_solution: Rewriting the attention blocks to use ANE-friendly operations (e.g., swapping Einsum for standard 1x1 convolutions and static shapes) to ensure the entire computation graph executes on the ANE. This completely eliminates ANE-GPU context switching overhead, achieving the sub-16.6ms latency target.

scenario: You are deploying a 15M parameter Vision Transformer (ViT) for real-time video processing (60 FPS) on an iPhone 14 Pro (A16 Bionic). Initial CoreML profiling shows the model takes 25ms per frame, missing the 16.6ms budget. The trace reveals frequent context switching between the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) and the GPU because the ANE does not natively support the specific 'Einsum' and dynamic reshape operations used in your attention blocks. Evaluate the trade-offs of the following optimization paths: 1) Quantizing the model to INT8 to accelerate GPU execution, 2) Rewriting the attention blocks using 1x1 convolutions to force full ANE execution, or 3) Manually partitioning the model to run the CNN backbone on ANE and attention heads on GPU.
title: CoreML ViT ANE Fallback Evaluation

details.common_mistake: Assuming that simply enabling a hardware delegate like NNAPI will universally improve performance, ignoring the severe latency and power penalties of graph partitioning and CPU fallback.
details.napkin_math: Partial NPU delegation fragments the model into subgraphs. NPU compute = 15ms, CPU fallback = 25ms. Switching subgraphs incurs driver overhead (2ms) and RAM copy (12MB / 10GB/s = 1.2ms) ~ 3.2ms per switch. With 4 context switches, overhead = 12.8ms. Total latency = 15 + 25 + 12.8 = 52.8ms. Fix: Use supported ops.
details.realistic_solution: Replace the unsupported Swish and GatherNd ops with standard TFLite built-ins (e.g., HardSwish and basic Gather) supported by NNAPI. Retrain the model to map the entire graph to a single NPU subgraph, eliminating synchronization overhead and meeting both latency (~15ms) and power (<1.0W) budgets.

scenario: You are deploying a 12MB computer vision model for real-time video processing (30 FPS) on Android devices via TensorFlow Lite. CPU execution yields 50ms/frame. You enable the NNAPI delegate to leverage the NPU, but latency surprisingly increases to 54ms/frame. Profiling reveals the model is partitioned into 5 subgraphs because of an unsupported custom Swish activation and a GatherNd op, causing constant CPU-NPU synchronization. The GPU delegate achieves 28ms/frame but draws 2.2W, exceeding your 1.5W thermal budget. Evaluate the trade-offs and justify a design decision to meet both the 33ms latency and 1.5W power constraints.
title: TFLite Delegate Graph Partitioning Trade-offs

details.common_mistake: Assuming the NPU hardware is thermally throttling or that NNAPI initialization overhead dominates, without checking for operator fallback.
details.napkin_math: 1 unsupported op in the middle creates 3 subgraphs (NPU -> CPU -> NPU). Compute time: NPU (4ms) + CPU (1ms) = 5ms. Memory copy is fast, but kernel synchronization and context switch overhead is ~15ms per transition. Total Latency = 5ms compute + (2 transitions * 15ms overhead) = 35ms.
details.realistic_solution: Profile the TFLite execution to detect subgraph partitioning. An unsupported operator in the middle of the network forces a fallback to the CPU, splitting the graph and introducing massive synchronization overhead. Replace the unsupported op so the entire model compiles into a single NPU subgraph.

scenario: Your team deploys a 5MB MobileNetV3-based model to Android via TFLite. On a Snapdragon 8 Gen 1 device, 4-thread CPU inference takes 18ms. You enable the NNAPI delegate to leverage the NPU, expecting sub-5ms latency. Instead, overall latency jumps to 35ms and battery drain increases. Profiling reveals the model outputs correct results, but performance is strictly worse than the CPU baseline.
title: Diagnosing TFLite NNAPI Delegate Subgraph Fallback

details.common_mistake: Candidates correctly calculate the raw compute time reduction but forget to account for the memory synchronization and context switching overhead at each subgraph boundary.
details.napkin_math:
Original CPU compute = 20ms.
GPU compute portion = 18ms / 6x speedup = 3ms.
CPU fallback compute portion = 2ms.
Transitions between 9 subgraphs = 8 context switches.
Context switch overhead = 8 * 2ms = 16ms.
Total Latency = 3ms (GPU) + 2ms (CPU) + 16ms (Overhead) = 21ms.
details.realistic_solution: The new end-to-end latency is 21ms, which is actually slower than the CPU-only baseline. To fix this, you must either replace the unsupported custom ops with standard GPU-supported ops, or move them to the very end of the model to reduce the number of subgraphs to exactly 2.

scenario: You are deploying a custom object detection model using TFLite on an Android phone. The model runs entirely on the Snapdragon CPU in 20ms. You enable the GPU delegate, which accelerates 90% of the model's operations (by original CPU time) by a factor of 6x. However, 4 interspersed custom operations are not supported by the GPU delegate, causing TFLite to partition the graph into 9 subgraphs (5 GPU, 4 CPU). If each CPU-GPU context switch (tensor copy and synchronization) takes 2ms, what is the expected new end-to-end latency?
title: TFLite Delegate Subgraph Partitioning Overhead

details.common_mistake: Choosing ViT because it's 'newer' without considering the hardware constraints. Mobile NPUs are optimized for regular, channel-wise operations like depthwise separable convolutions — not the dynamic attention patterns in ViT.
details.napkin_math: MobileNetV2: ~300M MACs (~600M FLOPs), peak activations ~1 MB (fits SRAM). On 8 TOPS NPU: 600M FLOPs / 8 TFLOPS = 0.075 ms theoretical, but real-world NPU utilization is ~5-10% due to operator dispatch, data marshalling, and memory stalls. Realistic latency: ~2-3 ms. Mobile ViT: ~1 GFLOP with attention scores for 196 patches = 196^2 x 2B = ~75 KB per head x 12 heads = 0.9 MB (fits SRAM, but irregular access pattern). Dynamic shapes in attention prevent NPU kernel fusion. Realistic latency: ~40 ms due to NPU fallback to CPU for attention ops.
details.realistic_solution: MobileNetV2 wins on this hardware for several reasons: (1) Depthwise separable convolutions map perfectly to NPU hardware (fixed 3×3 or 5×5 kernels, regular memory access). (2) The activation tensors are small at each layer (pooling reduces spatial dimensions progressively), fitting in the 2 MB SRAM. (3) INT8 quantization is straightforward for conv layers (well-studied, minimal accuracy loss). Mobile ViT challenges: (1) Self-attention requires dynamic memory allocation for the $S \times S$ score matrix, which NPU compilers handle poorly. (2) Softmax and LayerNorm require FP16/FP32, forcing mixed-precision execution and NPU-to-CPU fallback. (3) Attention is memory-bandwidth-bound — wasteful on an NPU designed for high-compute-intensity convolutions. (4) Quantizing attention to INT8 often degrades quality more than quantizing convolutions.

scenario: You are deploying a real-time object detection model on a mobile phone with a Qualcomm NPU (8 TOPS INT8, 2 MB SRAM). Compare deploying a MobileNetV2-based detector vs a Mobile ViT model of equivalent accuracy. Which architecture is better suited to this hardware, and why?
title: Edge Vision Model: CNN vs ViT Deployment

details.common_mistake: Blaming thermal throttling alone. 'The SoC gets hot under full load.' Thermal effects contribute but are not the primary cause, and they would affect all architectures equally — they wouldn't make this specific NAS-found architecture worse than alternatives.
details.napkin_math: Isolated NPU: 50 GB/s bandwidth. NAS-selected arch compute: 4.0ms (memory-bound depthwise convs). Overhead: 80 ops × 0.05ms = 4.0ms. Total isolated = 8.0ms. Under contention (15 GB/s): memory-bound ops slow 3.3x (4.0ms × 3.3 = 13.2ms), plus cascading DMA stalls (~4.8ms). Total = 13.2 + 4.0 + 4.8 = 22.0ms. Alt arch (dense convs, compute-bound): 7.0ms compute + 20 ops × 0.05ms overhead = 8.0ms. Under contention: 7.0ms + 1.0ms = 8.0ms (unaffected).
details.realistic_solution: The NAS latency predictor has a fundamental blind spot: it profiles operators in isolation on the NPU, but the production deployment shares the SoC's resources with other workloads. Three specific failures occur: (1) Memory bandwidth contention — the NAS-selected architecture uses depthwise separable convolutions with large spatial dimensions that are memory-bandwidth-bound. In isolation, they get full LPDDR5 bandwidth (~50 GB/s). When the ISP and GPU are also active, available bandwidth drops to ~15 GB/s, and memory-bound operators slow down 3.3x while compute-bound operators are unaffected. A NAS that accounted for contention would prefer compute-bound operators (dense convolutions, attention). (2) The NPU has a DMA engine that overlaps data loading with compute; under contention, DMA stalls cascade through the operator pipeline. (3) The NAS explored architectures with many small operators (higher accuracy per FLOP), but each operator has fixed dispatch overhead on the NPU runtime (~0.05ms), and 80 operators × 0.05ms = 4.0ms of overhead alone. The fix: profile the latency LUT under realistic concurrent load, penalize memory-bandwidth-bound operators, and add an operator-count penalty to the NAS reward function.

scenario: You are using hardware-aware NAS to find an optimal architecture for a mobile vision model targeting a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 NPU. The NAS uses a latency lookup table (LUT) built by profiling individual operators (convolutions, depthwise separable convolutions, attention blocks) in isolation. After 500 GPU-hours of search, the top architecture achieves the predicted 8ms latency on the NPU — but only when run in isolation. When deployed inside the full camera pipeline (which also runs ISP processing, object tracking, and UI rendering on the same SoC), actual latency balloons to 22ms. The NAS found the wrong architecture. Why?
title: The NAS Latency Predictor Blind Spot

details.common_mistake: Routing completely to the local model when the network is detected as poor, sacrificing quality for all requests during that period.
details.napkin_math: Cloud path P50 latency = 100ms (RTT) + 80ms (compute) = 180ms (Cloud wins). Local fallback path max latency = 150ms (wait threshold) + 250ms (NPU compute) = 400ms. The P99 is hard-bounded at 400ms regardless of network spikes.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the end-to-end latency: $T_{e2e} = T_{network} + T_{cloud\_compute}$ for the cloud path, and $T_{e2e} = T_{local\_load} + T_{local\_compute}$ for the edge path. To bound the P99 latency strictly at 400ms, the local fallback must finish by 400ms. Since the local model takes 250ms to execute, we must trigger it no later than $400ms - 250ms = 150ms$ into the request. Architecture: Dispatch the request to the cloud at $T=0$. Set an asynchronous timer for 150ms. If the cloud hasn't returned a full response by $T=150ms$, launch the local NPU inference in parallel (hedged request). Whichever finishes first is returned to the user, and the other is canceled. This maximizes cloud usage (high quality) for the majority of requests where network RTT is fast, while strictly capping tail latency via the local NPU.

scenario: A mobile voice translation app requires a strict <400ms end-to-end latency SLA. The cloud-based 10B parameter model has 80ms compute latency, but mobile network RTT is highly variable (P50 100ms, P99 800ms). The local 1B parameter on-device model takes 250ms on the NPU but yields lower translation quality (BLEU score drops by 4 points).
title: Hedged Edge-Cloud Model Routing

details.common_mistake: Switching to a lower-precision or smaller GPU model upon throttling, which permanently degrades visual quality.
details.napkin_math: Synchronous throttled: $1000 / (5 + 10 + 25) = 25$ FPS (violates 30 FPS SLA). Pipelined throttled throughput: $1000 / \max(5, 10, 25) = 1000 / 25 = 40$ FPS capacity. Since $40 > 30$, the 30 FPS SLA is maintained.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose latency into synchronous end-to-end time vs. pipeline throughput. In a synchronous architecture, $T_{frame} = T_{ISP} + T_{NPU} + T_{GPU}$. When throttled, $T_{frame} = 5 + 10 + 25 = 40ms$, yielding $1000/40 = 25$ FPS. To fix this without dropping model quality, decouple the stages into an asynchronous pipeline using bounded queues (ring buffers) between the ISP, NPU, and GPU. In a pipelined architecture, throughput is determined by the bottleneck stage: $T_{bottleneck} = \max(T_{ISP}, T_{NPU}, T_{GPU})$. Even under thermal throttling, the slowest stage (GPU) takes 25ms. Since $25ms < 33.3ms$, the system can process a new frame every 25ms (40 FPS capacity), easily meeting the 30 FPS SLA. The tradeoff is that end-to-end latency increases to ~75ms (frames are delayed by 2-3 frames), but rendering frame rate remains perfectly smooth.

scenario: A mobile AR application processes video at 30 FPS (33.3ms per frame SLA). The synchronous vision pipeline is: ISP extraction (5ms) -> NPU Object Detection (10ms) -> GPU Style Transfer (15ms). Total latency = 30ms. After 5 minutes, thermal throttling drops GPU clock speed by 40%, increasing Style Transfer to 25ms. Total synchronous latency becomes 40ms, causing massive frame drops.
title: Thermal-Aware On-Device Pipelining

details.common_mistake: Increasing the sensor sampling interval to 10Hz to save battery, which destroys the model's ability to detect high-frequency fall signatures.
details.napkin_math: Unbatched (per second): 50 CPU wakeups. CPU active time = $50 \times (15ms + 2ms) = 850ms$ per second (85% duty cycle). Batched (800ms window): $1.25$ wakeups per second. CPU active time = $1.25 \times (15ms + 8ms) = 28.75ms$ per second (2.8% duty cycle). Battery drain from CPU compute is reduced by ~30x.
details.realistic_solution: Decompose the end-to-end latency and power profile: $T_{e2e} = T_{buffer} + T_{wake} + T_{batch\_compute}$. To minimize CPU active time, we must maximize the buffering window (batch size) without violating the 1000ms SLA. Architecturally, buffer the raw sensor data in the ultra-low-power DSP/sensor hub for 800ms. This accumulates a batch of 40 samples (800ms / 20ms). The CPU wakes up ($T_{wake} = 15ms$) and processes the batch. Due to CPU SIMD vectorization and cache locality, batch compute scales sub-linearly: $T_{batch\_compute}$ for 40 samples takes 8ms (vs $40 \times 2ms = 80ms$). Total worst-case latency is $800ms + 15ms + 8ms = 823ms < 1000ms$. This dramatically reduces the CPU duty cycle while maintaining high-frequency data fidelity.

scenario: A smartwatch continuously monitors accelerometer data at 50Hz (every 20ms) to detect falls. A 2MB MLP runs on the CPU for inference. SLA requires fall detection within 1000ms of the physical event. Waking the CPU from sleep takes 15ms, and unbatched inference takes 2ms. Running inference every 20ms keeps the CPU awake 85% of the time, draining the battery in hours.
title: Battery-Aware Sensor Batching

details.common_mistake: Assuming the draft model is too slow, when in reality a 100M model on a modern mobile CPU can generate tokens extremely fast.
details.napkin_math:
Baseline target: 1000ms / 15 = 66ms/token.
Draft step (4 tokens): CPU takes 4 * 10ms = 40ms.
Target validation (4 tokens): NPU takes 70ms.
Hardware Sync overhead (CPU->NPU->CPU): 150ms per step.
Total time per step: 40 + 70 + 150 = 260ms.
Accepted tokens per step: 1 (base) + (4 * 0.65) = 3.6 tokens.
Theoretical speed: 3.6 tokens / 0.26s = ~13.8 tok/s. Additional overheads (buffer allocation, cache invalidation, driver scheduling jitter) add ~37ms per step, bringing effective speed down to 3.6 / 0.297s ≈ 10 tok/s as observed.
details.realistic_solution: The performance regression is caused by the heterogeneous compute synchronization overhead between the CPU and the NPU. Speculative decoding requires the draft model (CPU) to send its generated token IDs and KV data to the target model (NPU) for validation. Mobile SoCs do not have cache-coherent unified memory between the CPU and the NPU in the same way server GPUs do. The OS must perform expensive cross-device buffer synchronizations, cache flushes, and driver API calls for every single speculative step. This latency completely negates the compute savings of skipping target model decode steps.

scenario: You implement speculative decoding on a flagship phone to accelerate a 4B target model (running on the NPU at 15 tok/s). You use a 100M draft model running on the CPU. Despite achieving a strong draft acceptance rate of 65% (gamma=4), the overall effective throughput drops from 15 tok/s to 10 tok/s.
title: Speculative Decoding Performance Regression

details.common_mistake: Assuming the device ran out of RAM and started swapping to flash storage, which would cause a much more erratic latency profile.
details.napkin_math:
For a standard head dimension of 64 (FP16): 1024 tokens * 64 dim * 2 bytes = 128KB. If the GPU's max shared memory is 32KB, the tile cannot fit. 
Standard Attention Memory Traffic at 1025 tokens: Read K (1025*64*2 = 131KB), Read V (131KB), Write Logits (1025*2 = 2KB) = ~264KB per head, per layer, per token. Across 32 layers and 8 heads, this is ~67MB of DRAM traffic per token just for attention, bottlenecking the GPU.
details.realistic_solution: The step-function increase in latency is caused by a hardware-specific FlashAttention tile size limit. Mobile GPUs have strictly limited threadgroup shared memory (e.g., 32KB per workgroup). The FlashAttention kernel is heavily optimized to keep the K and V blocks in this fast SRAM. At exactly 1024 tokens, the required tile size for the sequence length exceeds the maximum shared memory allocation for the shader. The inference engine's fallback mechanism silently switches to a standard, unoptimized attention kernel, which requires O(N) reads and writes to the slower LPDDR5 DRAM for every single token generated.

scenario: A local mobile chat app runs a 2B parameter model using a mobile GPU. Decode latency is perfectly stable at 35ms/token. However, exactly when the conversation history reaches 1024 tokens, decode latency instantly jumps to 110ms/token and remains there. Device thermals are normal and there is no OS memory paging.
title: The Context Length Latency Spike

details.common_mistake: Assuming the decode phase is slowing down due to the larger KV cache, which contradicts the constant decode speed metric.
details.napkin_math: Prefill compute roughly scales as O(N^2) for attention. Turn 1 (100 tokens): 100^2 = 10,000 operations. Turn 10 (2000 tokens): 2000^2 = 4,000,000 operations. The attention compute workload increased by 400x. If the base prefill compute (linear layers + attention) took 150ms, the quadratic scaling of the attention component easily drives the latency to 4.5 seconds for 2000 tokens when recomputed entirely.
details.realistic_solution: The degradation is caused by KV-cache recomputation. Without a persistent, appendable KV-cache, each turn recomputes attention for all prior tokens. Turn 1: prefill 100 tokens, attention matrix = 100 * 100 = 10K elements. Turn 10: prefill 2,000 accumulated tokens, matrix = 2,000 * 2,000 = 4M elements (400x more computation). For a 3B model (32 layers, 32 heads, d_head=128): KV-cache at 2K tokens = 32 * 32 * 2 * 2000 * 128 * 2 bytes (FP16) = 1.05 GB. On Pixel 8 Pro (LPDDR5, 51.2 GB/s): prefill 100 tokens = 12 ms. Prefill 2,000 tokens = 240 ms (20x slower, quadratic scaling). Fix: implement a ring-buffer KV-cache that persists across turns. Allocate 1 GB contiguous buffer at app start. Each new turn appends only new tokens KV pairs (~50 KB per turn). TTFT drops from 240 ms to 15 ms at turn 10.

scenario: In a mobile voice assistant using a 3B LLM, the 1st turn (100 tokens) has a TTFT of 150ms. By the 10th turn (accumulated 2000 tokens), TTFT degrades to 4500ms. Decode speed remains perfectly constant at 18 tok/s throughout all turns. The profiler shows 0% thermal throttling.
title: Multi-Turn Chat Degradation

details.common_mistake: Assuming the target model struggles to generate code and requires more compute per token.
details.napkin_math:
Target-only latency: 1000ms / 12 = 83ms/token. 
Speculative step (4 draft tokens): Draft generation takes 4 * 10ms = 40ms. Target validation takes 90ms. Total step time = 130ms. 
If acceptance rate is 5%, expected accepted tokens per step = 1 (the forced correction token) + 0.05*4 = ~1.2 tokens. 
Effective latency = 130ms / 1.2 tokens = 108ms/token. 
Throughput = 1000 / 108 = 9.2 tok/s. However, each rejection forces an additional full target-model pass to generate the correction token, adding ~90ms of non-productive overhead per step. With ~3.8 of 4 draft tokens rejected per step, rejection overhead = 3.8 * (90ms / 4) ≈ 85ms extra per step. Adjusted effective latency = (130 + 85)ms / 1.2 tokens = 179ms/token → throughput ≈ 5.6 tok/s, consistent with the observed 6 tok/s.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a catastrophic drop in the draft model's acceptance rate due to a domain shift. The heavily pruned 60M draft model was likely distilled exclusively on natural language data to save space on-device, meaning it lacks basic Python syntax knowledge. When generating code, the draft model consistently guesses wrong (acceptance rate near 0%). Consequently, the system pays the latency penalty for the draft model's generation AND the target model's validation, but rejects almost all draft tokens. Each rejection forces an additional target-model forward pass to emit the correction token, adding substantial overhead on top of the wasted draft generation time. This makes speculative decoding strictly slower than running the target model alone at 12 tok/s.

scenario: Your speculative decoding setup (3B Target, 60M Draft) yields 25 tok/s for general chat on-device. When a user asks the app to generate a Python script, throughput suddenly drops to 6 tok/s. Disabling speculative decoding entirely restores Python generation to a flat 12 tok/s.
title: The Code Generation Stall

details.common_mistake: Assuming the NPU ran out of compute ALUs, when in reality decode is almost entirely memory-bound, not compute-bound.
details.napkin_math:
INT4 3B model = 1.5GB weights. At 20 tok/s, weight bandwidth = 1.5GB * 20 = 30 GB/s (near the ~34 GB/s max of LPDDR5). 
At BS=2, we need to read 1.5GB of weights + 2 separate KV caches. If the scattered reads drop effective bandwidth to 18 GB/s due to DRAM page misses, the max decode speed becomes 18 GB/s / 1.5 GB = 12 tok/s total. Divided by 2 tasks, each task gets exactly 6 tok/s.
details.realistic_solution: The system hits a severe memory bandwidth wall. At batch size 1, the LLM streams the 1.5GB of quantized weights from LPDDR5 perfectly linearly. At batch size 2, the continuous batching engine must fetch the KV cache for two completely disparate sequences simultaneously. This disrupts the contiguous memory access patterns. The mobile memory controller experiences high page miss rates in the DRAM banks, causing the effective memory bandwidth utilization to drop precipitously. Total throughput decreases because the memory bus is stalling.

scenario: Your mobile OS runs a 3B LLM (INT4 quantized). A foreground chat runs at 20 tok/s (batch size 1). When the OS schedules a background notification summarizer to run concurrently (batch size 2), the total system throughput plummets to 12 tok/s (6 tok/s per task), rather than achieving higher total throughput.
