title: The Background Batching Bottleneck

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT8 memory fetches are slower than FP16 memory fetches.
details.napkin_math: For a 4B model, assume 36 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head_dim=128. With a 1000-token context: INT8 KV cache per layer = 2 × 8 × 128 × 1000 × 1 byte = 2 MB. Total across 36 layers = 72 MB (INT8), vs 144 MB (FP16) — saving ~72 MB, though the scenario's 600 MB savings implies a longer context or larger head config. Dequantization overhead per layer: read 2 MB (INT8) + write 4 MB (FP16 intermediate) = 6 MB. At 30 GB/s LPDDR bandwidth: 0.2 ms per layer. Across 36 layers: 7.2 ms. Kernel launch overhead on mobile (~0.2 ms per extra dequant kernel × 36 layers): ~7.2 ms. Total added latency ≈ 14–20 ms per token, explaining the increase from 35 ms to 55 ms.
details.realistic_solution: The latency increase is caused by the lack of native INT8-to-FP16 mixed-precision attention support on the mobile NPU. To perform the attention mechanism, the inference engine must insert an explicit dequantization kernel that reads the INT8 KV cache, casts it back to FP16, and writes it to an intermediate buffer in SRAM (or DRAM) before the actual attention kernel can run. This extra kernel launch, combined with the intermediate memory round-trip on every single decode step, adds pure latency overhead that stalls the NPU.

scenario: To fit a 4B model in 4GB of mobile RAM, you quantize the KV cache from FP16 to INT8, successfully saving 600MB. However, you observe that decode latency increases from 35ms per token to 55ms per token, and overall NPU utilization drops from 80% to 50%.
title: The INT8 KV Cache Penalty

details.common_mistake: Assuming the GPU is struggling to read from non-contiguous memory blocks due to cache misses.
details.napkin_math:
2000 tokens / 16 block size = 125 blocks. 
32 layers * 125 blocks = 4,000 separate buffer bindings per token generated. 
If the mobile graphics driver takes 0.02ms per descriptor binding, 4000 * 0.02ms = 80ms of pure CPU overhead per token. 
Because the OS scheduler preempts the thread, this latency is highly erratic, causing the observed 40-180ms jitter.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is CPU-bound driver API overhead. Mobile GPUs lack the advanced hardware scatter-gather Memory Management Units (MMUs) found in data center GPUs. To emulate PagedAttention, the inference engine must bind hundreds of separate memory descriptors (one for each 16-token block) to the GPU command buffer for every layer, on every token. Submitting these tiny, fragmented buffer bindings overwhelms the Android graphics driver (e.g., Vulkan/OpenCL), causing the CPU to bottleneck the GPU. The GPU sits idle waiting for the CPU to construct and submit the command buffers.

scenario: You port a PagedAttention implementation to an Android flagship to prevent KV cache fragmentation. With a block size of 16, a 2000-token prompt causes severe decode latency jitter (varying wildly from 40ms to 180ms per token) and massive CPU overhead (peaking at 100% on one core), even though the LLM is running entirely on the GPU.
title: The PagedAttention System Call Trap

details.common_mistake: Adding the peak power of both models (0.8W + 1.2W + 0.8W system = 2.8W) and concluding it instantly violates the TDP.
details.napkin_math:
Eye-tracking: 5ms * 30 frames = 150ms active/sec. Energy = 0.8W * 0.15s = 0.12 Joules.
Hand-tracking: 15ms * 30 frames = 450ms active/sec. Energy = 1.2W * 0.45s = 0.54 Joules.
Idle time: 1000ms - 150ms - 450ms = 400ms. Idle energy = 0.1W * 0.40s = 0.04 Joules.
Total ML Energy/sec = 0.12 + 0.54 + 0.04 = 0.70 Joules (0.7W average).
Baseline system power = 0.8W.
Total average power = 0.8W + 0.7W = 1.50W. This exactly meets the 1.5W TDP limit.
details.realistic_solution: To determine if the thermal envelope is violated, we must calculate the time-averaged power consumption over a 1-second window, as thermal limits (TDP) on mobile devices are bound by sustained heat dissipation rather than instantaneous spikes. First, calculate the duty cycle (active time per second) for each model at 30Hz. The eye tracker runs for 150ms/sec, and the hand tracker runs for 450ms/sec. The NPU is active for 600ms total and idle for 400ms. We sum the energy consumed during these states and add the continuous baseline system power. The total average power comes out to 1.5W exactly, meaning it perfectly hits the thermal limit without exceeding it, assuming perfect scheduling without overlap.

scenario: Your team is designing ML pipelines for AR glasses. To prevent skin burns, the device has a strict continuous thermal dissipation limit (TDP) of 1.5W. The baseline OS and display draw a constant 0.8W. You need to run an eye-tracking CNN (5ms execution time at 800mW active power) and a hand-tracking transformer (15ms execution time at 1.2W active power). Both models must run at 30Hz. The ML accelerator draws 100mW when idle.
title: AR Glasses Thermal Budgeting

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the 5G communication energy, which heavily dominates the local compute energy in modern FL workloads.
details.napkin_math:
Local compute per device: 100 Joules.
Comm energy per device: 500MB * 0.5 J/MB = 250 Joules.
Total energy per device = 350 Joules.
Total for 1M devices = 350,000,000 Joules.
Convert to kWh: 350,000,000 J / 3,600,000 J/kWh = 97.22 kWh.
Device Carbon = 97.22 kWh * 400 gCO2/kWh = 38,888 gCO2 = ~38.9 kg CO2.
Cloud Carbon = 50 kWh * 50 gCO2/kWh = 2,500 gCO2 = 2.5 kg CO2.
Total Carbon = 38.9 + 2.5 = 41.4 kg CO2.
details.realistic_solution: In mobile Federated Learning, the energy bottleneck is rarely the local compute; it is almost always the radio transmission cost for large model weights. To find the total carbon footprint, we must quantify the energy used by the 1 million devices (compute + 5G communication) and the energy used by the cloud aggregator. We calculate the local energy in Joules, convert it to kWh (since 1 kWh = 3.6 million Joules), and multiply by the local grid's carbon intensity. Then we add the cloud's carbon footprint. The communication energy (250J) dwarfs the compute (100J). The total system footprint is 38.8 kg CO2 local + 2.5 kg CO2 cloud = 41.3 kg CO2 daily.

scenario: You are evaluating Federated Learning (FL) vs Centralized Cloud training. 1,000,000 mobile devices perform 1 FL epoch daily. Local compute takes 100 Joules/device. Each device uploads/downloads a 500MB payload over 5G (0.5 Joules/MB). Cloud aggregation uses 50 kWh total. The average device grid carbon intensity is 400 gCO2/kWh, while the cloud datacenter uses renewable energy at 50 gCO2/kWh. We need to calculate the total daily carbon footprint of the FL approach.
title: Federated Learning Carbon Trade-offs

details.common_mistake: Calculating battery capacity incorrectly (ignoring voltage) or forgetting to average the LPDDR memory spike over the 1-second window.
details.napkin_math:
Battery Capacity = 3000 mAh * 3.8V = 11,400 mWh.
DSP continuous power = 4 mW.
Memory flush duty cycle = 10ms / 1000ms = 0.01 (1%).
Average memory power = 200 mW * 0.01 = 2 mW.
Total average system power = 4 mW + 2 mW = 6 mW.
Energy consumed in 24 hours = 6 mW * 24 h = 144 mWh.
Percentage drained = (144 mWh / 11,400 mWh) * 100 = 1.26%.
details.realistic_solution: To calculate battery drain percentage, we first need the total energy capacity of the battery in Watt-hours (Wh). A battery's capacity in mAh must be multiplied by its nominal voltage to get mWh. Next, we determine the average power consumption of the DSP approach. While the DSP uses 4mW continuously, the periodic 10ms memory wake-ups at 200mW add a time-averaged power overhead. We sum the continuous DSP power and the duty-cycled memory power to find the true average power. Finally, we multiply this average power by 24 hours to get the total energy consumed in mWh, and divide by the battery capacity to find the percentage. The DSP approach drains about 1.26% of the battery, making it highly efficient for an always-on task.

scenario: A smartphone has a 3000mAh battery operating at 3.8V. We are deploying an always-on wake-word model. Running it on the main CPU consumes a continuous 40mW. Offloading to a dedicated DSP consumes only 4mW continuously, but requires waking up the main LPDDR memory for 10ms every 1 second to flush audio buffers, consuming 200mW during that 10ms spike. Calculate the percentage of battery drained over 24 hours for the DSP approach.
title: Always-On Wake Word Battery Drain

details.common_mistake: Assuming that because dynamic power drops by 75%, the total energy per token will also drastically decrease, ignoring the increased execution time and static power leakage.
details.napkin_math:
Max Freq:
Time per token = 4GB / 50GB/s = 0.08s (80ms).
Total Power = 4W (dynamic) + 1W (static) = 5W.
Energy per token = 5W * 0.08s = 0.40 Joules.

Half Freq:
Time per token = 4GB / 25GB/s = 0.16s (160ms).
Total Power = 1W (dynamic) + 1W (static) = 2W.
Energy per token = 2W * 0.16s = 0.32 Joules.
Energy saved per token = 0.40 - 0.32 = 0.08 Joules (20% savings).
details.realistic_solution: Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) reduces dynamic power significantly (proportional to V^2 * f), but it also increases the time required to complete a fixed workload (like generating one token). Because mobile SoCs have static power components (leakage current, display, background OS) that remain constant regardless of the ML workload's frequency, running slower means this static power is drawn for a longer duration. To evaluate the trade-off, we calculate the total energy (Joules = Watts * seconds) per token for both states. At max frequency, total energy is 0.40J per token. At half frequency, the time doubles to 160ms, resulting in 0.32J per token. Downclocking saves energy here, but less than the power drop suggests due to the static power penalty.

scenario: Running a 4GB mobile LLM at max memory frequency (50GB/s bandwidth) draws 4W dynamic power for RAM and 1W static system power, taking 80ms per token. To save battery, you propose dropping frequency by 50%. Due to V^2f scaling, RAM dynamic power drops to 1W, but bandwidth drops to 25GB/s. The 1W static system power remains constant. Calculate the energy per token for both the max frequency and 50% frequency states to determine if downclocking actually saves energy.
title: LLM DVFS and Static Power Wall

details.common_mistake: Focusing only on the high NPU power (1.5W) and assuming on-device ML is worse, failing to factor in the massive energy savings from the 5G radio step-down.
details.napkin_math:
Option A Power (Native 4K) = 3.0W (5G) + 0.9W (Decoder) = 3.9W.
Option B Power (ML Super-Res) = 0.8W (5G) + 0.5W (Decoder) + 1.5W (NPU) = 2.8W.
Power Savings = 3.9W - 2.8W = 1.1W.
Movie duration = 2 hours = 7200 seconds.
Total Energy Saved = 1.1 Watts * 7200 seconds = 7,920 Joules.
details.realistic_solution: In mobile systems, radio transmission (especially 5G) is one of the most power-hungry components. Offloading bandwidth to local compute (like ML super-resolution) is a classic energy optimization technique if the local compute is highly efficient. We evaluate this by comparing the sum of subsystem power draws for both options. Option A (Native 4K) relies heavily on the 5G modem, resulting in a total system power of 3.9W. Option B utilizes the NPU but drastically reduces the 5G and decoding power, resulting in a total system power of 2.8W. By multiplying the power difference by the total duration of the movie in seconds, we can quantify the exact energy savings in Joules.

scenario: A mobile app plays a 2-hour 4K movie. Option A: Stream native 4K. The 5G radio draws 3.0W for 4K bandwidth, and the hardware decoder draws 0.9W. Option B: Stream 1080p and use an on-device NPU for ML super-resolution to 4K. The 5G radio draws 0.8W for 1080p, the decoder draws 0.5W, and the NPU draws 1.5W for 60FPS upscaling. Calculate the total energy saved (in Joules) by using the ML super-resolution approach over the 2-hour movie.
title: Super-Res NPU vs 5G Streaming Energy

details.common_mistake: Calculating throughput purely based on the 4.0W burst without realizing the duty cycle is constrained by the 1.0W cool-down floor.
details.napkin_math:
Max energy per minute = 2.5W * 60s = 150 Joules.
Let T_burst = time spent at 4.0W, T_cool = time spent at 1.0W.
T_burst + T_cool = 60s.
Energy equation: (4.0 * T_burst) + (1.0 * T_cool) = 150.
Substitute T_cool: 4.0 * T_burst + 1.0 * (60 - T_burst) = 150.
3.0 * T_burst + 60 = 150.
3.0 * T_burst = 90  =>  T_burst = 30 seconds.
The device can run the ViT for 30 seconds per minute.
Throughput = 30 seconds * 30 FPS = 900 images per minute.
details.realistic_solution: Mobile thermal management relies on managing energy over a sliding window. The device can burst above its TDP (4.0W > 2.5W) as long as it compensates with a low-power cool-down phase (1.0W) such that the integral of power over the window (energy) equals the TDP's maximum energy allowance. For a 60-second window, the maximum allowed energy is 150 Joules. We set up an equation where the time spent bursting plus the time spent cooling equals 60 seconds, and their combined energy equals 150 Joules. Solving this gives the maximum allowable burst time per minute. Multiplying this burst time by the model's FPS yields the maximum sustained throughput.

scenario: A smartphone indexes local photos using a Vision Transformer. The SoC has a 2.5W continuous TDP. The ViT runs at 30 FPS, consuming 4.0W (burst mode). To prevent overheating, the thermal governor enforces a rule: the 1-minute average power cannot exceed the 2.5W TDP. When not bursting, the SoC enters a cool-down state drawing 1.0W (processing 0 FPS). Calculate the maximum number of images the device can index per minute without violating the thermal limit.
title: Thermal Throttling in Background Indexing

details.common_mistake: Only comparing the device energy to the cloud server energy, forgetting that the cloud approach also costs the device radio and idle energy.
details.napkin_math:
On-Device Approach:
Device Energy = 5W * 2.5s = 12.5 Joules.
Total System Energy = 12.5 Joules.

Cloud Approach:
Device Radio Energy = 2.0W * 0.5s = 1.0 Joules.
Device Idle Wait Energy = 0.5W * 1.0s = 0.5 Joules.
Total Device Energy = 1.5 Joules.
Cloud Server Energy = 50 tokens * 0.05 J/token = 2.5 Joules.
Total System Energy = 1.5J + 2.5J = 4.0 Joules.

Difference = 12.5J - 4.0J = 8.5 Joules more energy used by the on-device approach.
details.realistic_solution: To determine the true energy efficiency of edge vs cloud LLM serving, we must calculate the end-to-end energy for both scenarios. For the on-device approach, all energy is consumed locally by the SoC (NPU and memory bandwidth). For the cloud approach, the energy is split: the mobile device spends energy transmitting the prompt and keeping the radio active waiting for the response, while the datacenter spends energy computing the tokens. We calculate the Joules for each component. The local generation uses 12.5 Joules. The cloud generation uses 1.5 Joules locally and 2.5 Joules in the datacenter, totaling 4.0 Joules. The on-device approach actually consumes 8.5 Joules more total system energy.

scenario: Generating 50 tokens using an on-device 7B model takes 2.5 seconds at 5W (NPU + Memory). Alternatively, an API call to a cloud server takes 0.5s of 5G active radio time at 2.0W, followed by 1.0s of idle waiting for the response at 0.5W. The cloud server itself consumes 0.05 Joules per token. Compare the total system energy (Device + Cloud) of both approaches. How much more total energy (in Joules) does the on-device approach use compared to the cloud approach?
title: On-Device vs Cloud LLM Energy Cost

details.common_mistake: Assuming latency is always exactly `Compute / TOPS` and ignoring the critical impact of memory bandwidth limits.
details.napkin_math: Compute bound time: 10 GOPs / 275 TOPS = 0.036ms. Assume the layer reads 50MB of data. At 100GB/s bandwidth, BW time = 50MB / 100 GB/s = 0.5ms. 0.5ms > 0.036ms. Arithmetic intensity = 10 GOPs / 50MB = 200 OP/byte.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is a massive compute utilization drop caused by the layer being severely memory-bandwidth bound. While the NPU has 275 TOPS, it cannot compute faster than data is fed to it. The low arithmetic intensity (ratio of compute to memory access) of this specific layer prevents the NPU from reaching peak TOPS. The root cause is memory bandwidth bottlenecking the execution pipeline.

scenario: An Orin device (275 TOPS) runs a ResNet-style model. A specific layer requires 10 Giga-Operations (GOPs). Instead of taking the expected ~0.036ms, the layer takes 0.5ms. Profiling shows 100% memory read utilization but very low compute usage.
title: Mobile New 0001

details.common_mistake: Believing latency strictly scales down linearly with FLOP count and ignoring compiler alignment and SIMD rules.
details.napkin_math: 16-ch SIMD: 16 MACs = 8 cycles (2 MACs/cycle). 13-ch scalar: 13 MACs * 2 cycles/MAC = 26 cycles. Latency ratio = 26 / 8 = 3.25x latency multiplier despite 13 < 16.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of higher latency for fewer channels points to a compiler alignment fallback. Libraries like CMSIS-NN optimize for multiples of 4 channels using SIMD instructions (e.g., SMLAD) to perform 2 MACs per cycle. With 13 channels, the compiler falls back to a scalar unrolled loop, taking multiple cycles per MAC. The root cause is the abandonment of vectorization due to unaligned channel counts.

scenario: A Cortex-M4 (168MHz) runs a 1D convolution with 13 input channels. The latency is 3x higher than an identically structured layer with 16 channels, despite doing 20% fewer theoretical MACs. Profiling shows high core active time.
title: Mobile New 0002

details.common_mistake: Assuming all standard framework activation functions are implemented in hardware by mobile NPU vendors.
details.napkin_math: NPU Conv: 2ms. Tensor: 10MB. DRAM copy NPU->CPU: 10MB / 10GB/s = 1ms. CPU SiLU: 10M elements * 20 cycles / 2GHz = 100ms. CPU->NPU copy: 1ms. Total per layer: 104ms. For 8 layers = 832ms total latency.
details.realistic_solution: The massive latency spike and high CPU utilization are symptoms of operator fallback. The NPU compiler does not natively support the SiLU activation. Consequently, the execution graph fractures: the NPU computes the convolution, copies the tensor back to system DRAM, the CPU computes SiLU, and copies it back to the NPU. This CPU execution and memory roundtrip completely destroys performance.

scenario: An image segmentation model runs perfectly on a mobile NPU in 20ms. You replace the ReLU activations with SiLU to boost accuracy. Suddenly, latency spikes to 850ms, and the SoC CPU usage maxes out to 100%.
title: Mobile New 0003

details.common_mistake: Offloading every neural network to the NPU/GPU regardless of the model size and fixed communication overheads.
details.napkin_math: Compute time: 50K MACs / 100 GFLOPS (NPU) = 0.5us. NPU Wake/Interrupt overhead: 2000us. Total NPU = 2000.5us (~2.0ms). CPU compute: 50K MACs / 10 GFLOPS (CPU) = 5us. Overhead = 0. Total CPU = 5us. 5us << 2000us.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of a weaker CPU outperforming a powerful NPU on a tiny model indicates that dispatch and synchronization overheads are dominating the latency. The time required for the CPU to construct the command buffer, wake up the NPU via an interrupt, and synchronize memory far exceeds the actual computation time. For extremely small models, the CPU can just compute the result directly from its L1 cache in less time.

scenario: A 50KB dense model is deployed on a mobile SoC. When executed on the NPU, it takes 2.5ms per inference. When forced to run on the much weaker Cortex-A CPU, it takes only 0.8ms. The NPU utilization remains under 5%.
title: Mobile New 0004

details.common_mistake: Assuming Depthwise convolutions are always universally faster just because their total MAC count is lower.
details.napkin_math: Pointwise reuse: 1 byte read feeds 64 MACs. Depthwise reuse: 1 byte read feeds 9 MACs. Depthwise memory traffic = 10M MACs / 9 OP/byte = 1.11MB. BW = 1GB/s. Time = 1.11MB/1GB/s = 1.11ms + overhead = 1.5ms.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is higher latency for a layer with 10x less compute. The cause is the lack of data reuse in Depthwise convolutions. While a Pointwise conv reuses the same input activation across multiple output channels, a Depthwise conv reads an input patch, multiplies it by a filter, and never reuses it. This causes the NPU's MACs to starve while waiting for LPDDR memory fetches.

scenario: A mobile NPU profiles a 3x3 Depthwise Convolution (10M MACs) taking 1.5ms, while a 1x1 Pointwise Convolution (100M MACs) takes 0.5ms. The Depthwise layer shows severe memory stalls despite doing 10x fewer ops.
title: Mobile New 0005

details.common_mistake: Sizing microcontrollers based only on model weight size without accounting for peak activation footprint.
details.napkin_math: SRAM: 256KB. Weights: 200KB. OS: 16KB. Available: 40KB. New activation: 64KB. Spill: 24KB. SRAM latency: 1 cycle. Flash latency: 15 cycles. 24KB fetched repeatedly from flash per loop causes 15x slowdown on that layer.
details.realistic_solution: The 10x latency spike and flash read surge are symptoms of activation spilling. The 200KB model leaves only 56KB of SRAM for the OS, stack, and intermediate activations. The higher resolution input produces a larger intermediate tensor that overflows the remaining SRAM. The system is forced to swap activations to external flash memory, which is orders of magnitude slower than SRAM.

scenario: Running a 200KB INT8 model on a Cortex-M4 with 256KB SRAM. Inference normally takes 50ms, but suddenly spikes to 500ms on a specific high-resolution input. Flash memory read counters show massive spikes.
title: Mobile New 0006

details.common_mistake: Ignoring weight-pinning pragmas in compiler deployment resulting in redundant DRAM fetching.
details.napkin_math: Model: 10MB. 60 FPS. BW = 600MB/s. LPDDR energy cost: ~100 pJ/bit = 800 pJ/byte. SRAM energy: ~5 pJ/bit. Energy diff: 750 pJ/byte * 600 MB/s = 0.45 Joules/sec = 0.45W wasted just on redundant memory traffic.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is severe power draw and DRAM saturation on a small model. The root cause is the failure to pin the model weights into the NPU's dedicated SRAM. Because the NPU treats the weights as volatile per inference, it streams the entire 10MB from off-chip LPDDR memory for every frame. LPDDR access consumes massive amounts of dynamic energy compared to on-chip SRAM.

scenario: A 10MB model on a mobile NPU consumes an unexpected 2W of power. Profiling shows compute blocks are efficient, but the DRAM interface is completely saturated, reading the same 10MB weights repeatedly for every frame.
title: Mobile New 0008

details.common_mistake: Assuming DMA automatically hides memory latency without structuring the software pipeline to overlap operations.
details.napkin_math: Single buffer: T_total = T_dma (10k cycles) + T_compute (10k cycles) = 20k cycles. Ping-pong buffer: T_total = max(T_dma, T_compute) = 10k cycles (plus small fill/drain overhead). Missing this doubles the latency (20k vs 10k).
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is high latency with the CPU idling during memory transfers. The root cause is the failure to implement double-buffering (ping-pong buffering). The software uses a single buffer: it asks DMA to fetch data, blocks the CPU until done, then computes. It should fetch buffer B while computing buffer A to overlap memory access with computation.

scenario: A Cortex-M4 uses DMA to load memory tiles for a conv layer. Latency is double the theoretical minimum. The CPU sleep profile shows the core is entirely blocked waiting for the DMA transfer to complete before computing.
title: Mobile New 0009

details.common_mistake: Allocating monolithic buffers for sequence processing and ignoring hardware tile size limits.
details.napkin_math: Seq=100 KV size: 200KB (fits in 256KB SRAM). Access cost: O(N). Seq=1000 KV size: 2MB. SRAM miss rate explodes. 1000 queries * 2MB read per query = 2GB DRAM traffic per layer. 2GB / 100GB/s = 20ms per layer, a 100x jump.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is quadratic latency scaling in an attention layer, indicating a failure in KV cache tiling strategy. As the sequence length increases, the size of the Keys and Values exceeds the fast SRAM tile size. Because the software doesn't implement block-wise attention (like FlashAttention) properly, it repeatedly evicts and fetches the KV tensors from slow DRAM for every query token.

scenario: Running an LLM on Orin with KV cache tiling. As sequence length grows from 100 to 1000, latency increases by a factor of 100 instead of 10. Profiling shows massive SRAM evictions during the attention mechanism.
title: Mobile New 0010

details.common_mistake: Assuming that shrinking the model file size automatically triggers quantized integer execution on the hardware.
details.napkin_math: Storage: 10MB FP32 -> 2.5MB INT8. Compute: 100M FP32 MACs = 10ms. Since the engine inserts dequantize nodes (INT8 -> FP32), it executes 100M FP32 MACs + dequant overhead. 10ms + 1ms overhead = ~11ms latency.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of unchanged latency with fully saturated FP32 ALUs indicates the occurrence of fake quantization or a lack of native INT8 operator support. The model weights are stored in INT8 (saving disk/RAM space) but are cast back to FP32 at runtime before the actual multiply-accumulate operations. The CPU executes FP32 math, thereby nullifying any expected compute speedup.

scenario: You quantize a MobileNet to INT8. The model size drops by 4x, but inference latency on the mobile CPU remains identical to the FP32 version. Profiling reveals the CPU's floating-point vector units are fully saturated.
title: Mobile New 0011

details.common_mistake: Using INT8 data types for both the operands and the accumulator to save register space.
details.napkin_math: INT8 range: -128 to 127. MAC operation: 50 * 50 = 2500. 2500 > 127. In INT8 accumulator, 2500 saturates to 127. Summing 100 such values: 250000. In INT32 it's 250000, perfectly safe. In INT8 it stays clipped at 127.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of outputs uniformly pegging to 127 is a classic sign of accumulator overflow. When performing dot products of INT8 values, the sum can quickly exceed the 8-bit maximum (127). The DSP must accumulate intermediate MACs into a wider register (INT32). If the compiler or custom kernel erroneously sets the accumulator to INT8, every sum clips immediately.

scenario: A custom INT8 inference engine on a DSP runs fast but accuracy drops to zero. You notice all the intermediate output tensors are saturated exactly to the value of 127. The FP32 model does not have this issue.
title: Mobile New 0012

details.common_mistake: Assuming asymmetric quantization only affects the offline calibration phase without penalizing runtime compute.
details.napkin_math: Symmetric MAC: sum(W × X). Asymmetric MAC expands to: sum(W×X) - Z_x×sum(W) - Z_w×sum(X) + N×Z_w×Z_x. The terms Z_x×sum(W) and N×Z_w×Z_x are constants precomputed offline into the bias. Only Z_w×sum(X) requires runtime computation: 1 accumulate per input row (not per MAC). For a 3×3 kernel over 32 channels, this adds 32 additions per output position vs 288 MACs — roughly 11% overhead, not 3 extra ops per MAC.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of increased latency and instruction count stems from the mathematical overhead of asymmetric quantization. Symmetric quantization has a zero-point of 0, simplifying the dot product. Asymmetric introduces a non-zero zero-point, and the full expansion is sum(W×X) − Z_x×sum(W) − Z_w×sum(X) + N×Z_w×Z_x. Importantly, Z_x×sum(W) and N×Z_w×Z_x are constant per channel or tensor and can be precomputed offline and folded into the bias, adding zero runtime cost. The only runtime overhead is Z_w×sum(X), which requires one additional accumulation per input row (not per MAC). If a 25% latency increase is observed, it is likely caused by a non-optimized fallback path (e.g., lack of SIMD support for zero-point arithmetic on this CPU) rather than the theoretical asymptotic cost.

scenario: Switching from symmetric to asymmetric INT8 quantization on a mobile CPU recovers accuracy, but profiling shows a 25% increase in total latency and higher instruction counts per convolution loop.
title: Mobile New 0013

details.common_mistake: Ignoring the bandwidth and allocation cost of continuous type conversion nodes in mixed-precision networks.
details.napkin_math: All-INT16 latency: 50ms. Mixed: Conv (INT8) takes 2ms instead of 3ms. But Cast (INT8->INT16) for 5MB tensor at 5GB/s memory BW takes 1ms. If there are 30 alternating layers, casting overhead adds 30ms. Total = 2ms*30 + 30ms = 90ms > 50ms.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of performance degradation below the baseline is caused by the overhead of type casting and memory reallocation between operations. Because the layers alternate between INT8 and INT16, the runtime inserts 'Cast' nodes. These nodes require reading the INT8 tensor, converting it to INT16, and writing it to a newly allocated buffer, saturating memory bandwidth.

scenario: A mobile network uses mixed-precision (INT8 for Conv, INT16 for complex activations). Performance degrades below that of an all-INT16 model. Execution trace shows hundreds of small memory allocation events between layers.
title: Mobile New 0014

details.common_mistake: Looking only at total theoretical FLOPs and assuming scalar parameter fetching is mathematically 'free'.
details.napkin_math: Per-tensor: 1 scale (4B) in register. Per-channel for 4096 channels: 4096 scales = 16KB to fetch per layer. At 10GB/s, 16KB takes 1.6us to fetch. Over 100 layers, this plus the pipeline bubble resets adds significant latency.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of vector stalls and higher latency is caused by the memory and pipeline overhead of applying unique scale factors per channel. In per-tensor, one scale factor is kept in a register. In per-channel, the DSP must fetch a new scale and zero-point for every output channel from memory, causing L1 cache misses and stalling the tightly pipelined vector MAC instructions.

scenario: Applying per-channel INT8 quantization to a DSP preserves accuracy but causes vector ALUs to stall frequently. Latency is 30% higher compared to per-tensor quantization, even though the MAC count is identical.
title: Mobile New 0015

details.common_mistake: Compressing model weights in deployment bundles to save download size without accounting for initialization CPU cost.
details.napkin_math: Decompression throughput on weak mobile CPU: ~5MB/s. File size: 20MB. Time = 20MB / 5MB/s = 4.0 seconds just to inflate. Zero-copy mmap (uncompressed in APK) time = 20MB / 2GB/s (RAM speed) = 0.01 seconds.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of a massive initialization delay is caused by the OS decompressing the model file from the APK into system memory before the TFLite interpreter can map it. Because the model is compressed, the system cannot use zero-copy `mmap`. It must allocate 20MB of RAM and run a CPU-intensive inflation algorithm, causing a UI thread stall.

scenario: A mobile app includes a 20MB TFLite model compressed in a standard Android APK (ZIP). The inference runs in 50ms, but the UI freezes for 4 seconds every time the model is initialized for the first time.
title: Mobile New 0016

details.common_mistake: Using default pre-compiled framework binaries instead of compiling custom minimal runtimes for edge devices.
details.napkin_math: Model size = 2MB. TF Lite full shared library = ~5MB. Full PyTorch static lib = ~110MB. 110MB + 2MB = 112MB. Selective build drops unused ops, reducing runtime lib to ~800KB. 2MB + 800KB = 2.8MB, easily fitting the 32MB flash.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of an enormously bloated binary despite a tiny model is caused by static linking of the entire ML framework (e.g., TensorFlow/PyTorch) and all its dependencies. The compiler pulled in operator kernels for every possible mathematical function, image processing library, and RPC framework, instead of using a selective build that only links the ops required by the specific model.

scenario: You deploy a tiny 2MB keyword spotting model to an IoT device. However, the final compiled binary executable is 115MB, completely blowing past the device's 32MB storage limit.
title: Mobile New 0017

details.common_mistake: Looking only at aggregate free memory and assuming mobile OS heaps are perfectly defragmented.
details.napkin_math: Required contiguous block: 50MB. Available RAM: 120MB. Memory state: 120 isolated 1MB blocks scattered across the heap. Max contiguous size = 1MB. 50MB > 1MB. `malloc(50MB)` searches heap, fails, returns NULL.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of an OOM error despite seemingly adequate total free memory is caused by memory fragmentation. The inference engine requires contiguous memory blocks (either physical for NPU DMA, or virtual depending on OS limits) to load large tensors. If the 120MB free RAM is heavily fragmented into tiny chunks by other background processes, the OS cannot allocate a single 50MB contiguous block.

scenario: You load a 50MB model on a smartwatch showing 120MB of free RAM. During initialization, the `malloc` call fails, throwing an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error, crashing the app.
title: Mobile New 0018

details.common_mistake: Assuming logical model updates map directly to minimal binary diffs without ensuring fixed memory offsets.
details.napkin_math: Model has 10M parameters. Weight 0 changed. Offset of Weight 1 shifts by 4 bytes. bsdiff compares old File[4:end] vs new File[8:end]. Every single byte mismatches. Delta size = uncompressed remainder = 98MB instead of 4 Bytes.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of a massive delta file for a tiny model change is caused by flatbuffer/protobuf memory alignment shifts or global ZIP compression. If you insert or change a value that alters the byte offsets of the subsequent tensors, or if the entire model is bundled in a newly compressed ZIP, the binary diff algorithm (like bsdiff) sees almost every byte in the file as modified.

scenario: An app updates a deployed 100MB model over the air (OTA) using binary deltas. You changed just one bias value in the model. The resulting OTA delta file is still 98MB, consuming massive user bandwidth.
title: Mobile New 0019

details.common_mistake: Optimizing neural network MACs for power while ignoring the extreme energy cost of off-chip memory.
details.napkin_math: 100MB * 30 FPS = 3GB/s bandwidth. LPDDR4 energy: ~100 pJ/bit = 800 pJ/byte. 3GB/s * 800 pJ/byte = 2.4 Joules/sec = 2.4 Watts just for DRAM access. Total system power 5W, meaning memory consumes ~50% of the entire budget.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is severe battery drain despite low compute utilization. The cause is the massive energy cost of DRAM access. Fetching weights/activations from off-chip LPDDR consumes orders of magnitude more energy per byte than SRAM or ALUs. A 100MB model running at 30 FPS requires massive bandwidth, turning the memory subsystem into a severe power bottleneck.

scenario: An AR headset's battery drains in 30 minutes. Profiling shows the NPU is only 20% utilized, computing efficiently, but system power draw is 5W. The model reads 100MB of data from RAM per frame at 30 FPS.
title: Mobile New 0021

details.common_mistake: Running continuous polling loops on microcontrollers instead of event-driven interrupts.
details.napkin_math: Battery = 1000mAh. Required life = 30 days (720 hrs). Target current = 1000/720 = 1.38mA. M4 active at 168 MHz = ~25mA. 25mA * 24hrs = 600mAh/day. 1000mAh / 600 = 1.6 days. Sleep state current (10uA) is required 95% of the time.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of rapid battery depletion in an always-on device points to a failure to manage processor sleep states. The Cortex-M4 is running continuously at full clock speed to poll the microphone and run the model. Because the active duty cycle is 100%, the dynamic power draw remains at peak. The system should use a lower clock or hardware timer interrupts to sleep between audio chunks.

scenario: A smart speaker uses a Cortex-M4 for always-on wake-word detection. Instead of lasting 30 days on battery, it dies in 2 days. The CPU runs the detection loop at 168MHz every 10ms, never entering deep sleep.
title: Mobile New 0022

details.common_mistake: Assuming total power consumption is strictly a function of clock frequency and utilization, ignoring thermal leakage.
details.napkin_math: Total Power = Dynamic + Leakage. At 25C: P_dyn = 2.5W, P_leak = 0.5W (Total 3W). At 85C: P_dyn = 2.5W, but P_leak increases exponentially by ~4x to 2.0W. Total Power = 2.5W + 2.0W = 4.5W. Workload is identical, power is 50% higher.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of power draw increasing over time for a constant workload is caused by temperature-induced leakage current. As the SoC computes, it generates heat. As silicon temperature rises, transistor subthreshold leakage power increases exponentially. This creates a feedback loop: higher temp -> higher leakage -> higher power -> higher temp, increasing total Watts without any extra compute.

scenario: A mobile SoC runs a heavy generation model. In the first minute, the SoC draws 3W. After 10 minutes, despite doing the exact same number of MACs per second, the power draw creeps up to 4.5W.
title: Mobile New 0023

details.common_mistake: Treating the ML model execution as the only power consumer and ignoring the data pipeline overhead.
details.napkin_math: 4K 60FPS: 3840*2160*3 bytes * 60 = 1.5 GB/s. CPU read + CPU write + NPU read = 4.5 GB/s bandwidth. LPDDR energy: 800 pJ/byte. 4.5 GB/s * 800 pJ/byte = 3.6W peak theoretical memory power, accounting for the baseline 1.5W drain.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of high baseline power draw is caused by inefficient data routing and CPU-based image preprocessing. Routing 4K video through the CPU and main DRAM bus requires immense bandwidth and CPU cycles. The camera's Image Signal Processor (ISP) should be configured to directly write resized, cropped RGB frames into the NPU's SRAM/Memory via hardware DMA, bypassing the CPU entirely.

scenario: A drone's vision system consumes 1.5W before the NPU even starts inferencing. Profiling shows the image pipeline routing 4K 60FPS camera frames to the main CPU, resizing them, and then copying them to NPU memory.
title: Mobile New 0024

details.common_mistake: Processing continuous sensor streams at full frame rates regardless of information entropy.
details.napkin_math: Always on: 2W * 24hrs = 48 Watt-hours/day. Motion gated: ISP motion check = 50mW. If motion is 1% of the day, NPU runs 14 minutes. Total energy = (0.05W * 24h) + (2W * 0.24h) = 1.2 + 0.48 = 1.68 Watt-hours/day. Battery life extends 28x.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is constant high power consumption regardless of semantic content. The root cause is redundant inference processing. The system is running the full heavy CNN on every single frame, even if the pixels haven't changed. Implementing a cheap frame-differencing algorithm or a tiny motion-detection cascade could gate the heavy NPU execution, saving massive amounts of power.

scenario: A security camera runs object detection at 30 FPS. The NPU draws a steady 2W. The scene is an empty hallway with no movement 99% of the time, yet the battery drains just as fast as during a busy period.
title: Mobile New 0025

details.common_mistake: Assuming low ambient room temperature guarantees peak sustained performance without active cooling.
details.napkin_math: Power = C * V^2 * f. If f halves, V can drop by ~1.2x. Power reduction = 1.2^2 * 2 = 2.88x. Latency is inversely proportional to f: Latency = compute_cycles / f. When f drops from 1GHz to 500MHz, latency goes from 15ms to 30ms.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of a sudden, discrete doubling of latency indicates thermal throttling via Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS). Continuous full-utilization generates significant heat. Once the silicon die hits its maximum junction temperature (Tjmax), the hardware thermal controller aggressively halves the clock frequency to drop dynamic power and prevent physical silicon damage.

scenario: An Orin system continuously runs a tracking pipeline. After exactly 4 minutes, the end-to-end latency abruptly jumps from 15ms to 30ms. The ambient temperature is 25C, but the device enclosure is warm.
title: Mobile New 0026

details.common_mistake: Designing mobile ML models strictly against silicon thermal limits while ignoring user-ergonomic skin limits.
details.napkin_math: Die Tjmax = 85C. Skin limit = 42C. Thermal resistance die-to-skin (R_th) = 10 C/W. Room temp = 25C. Max allowable power = (42C - 25C) / 10 C/W = 1.7W limit. If NPU draws 4W, OS must throttle it by ~60-70% to hit the 1.7W budget.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of severe throttling while the internal die is safe is caused by the skin temperature limit constraint. Mobile devices must remain comfortable and safe to touch (typically capped at ~42-45C surface temp). Even if the silicon can safely operate at 85C, the thermal management system detects the chassis heating up and artificially limits power to maintain ergonomic safety.

scenario: A flagship smartphone runs a 3D generative model. Internal die temperature is completely safe at 50C, but the OS suddenly throttles the NPU clock by 70%, degrading performance to a crawl.
title: Mobile New 0027

details.common_mistake: Validating continuous performance benchmarks using short 5-minute runs on passively cooled devices.
details.napkin_math: Heat capacity Q = m * c * dT. Chassis mass = 100g. c = 0.9 J/gK. dT = 20K. Q = 1800 Joules. At 3W power, time to saturate = 1800J / 3W = 600s = 10 minutes. After 10 mins, it relies purely on convection (e.g., 0.75W max dissipation), dropping FPS by 4x.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of gradual, continuous performance degradation is caused by thermal saturation (heat soaking). In passive cooling, there are no fans to expel heat; the device relies entirely on the thermal capacitance of its chassis. Once the chassis absorbs its maximum heat capacity, it can only dissipate heat via convection. The OS continually drops frequency to match the low convection rate.

scenario: A passively cooled AR headset runs perfectly in a 10-minute test. In a 1-hour test, the frame rate steadily drops from 60 FPS to 15 FPS. Profiling shows frequency steps dropping continuously.
title: Mobile New 0028

details.common_mistake: Ignoring seasonal ambient temperature fluctuations when deploying edge AI in non-climate-controlled environments.
details.napkin_math: T_die = T_ambient + (Power * R_thermal). R_thermal = 3 C/W. Power = 25W. Night: T_die = 15C + (25*3) = 90C (Safe). Day: T_die = 35C + (25*3) = 110C. 110C > Tjmax (105C), triggering instantaneous hardware shutdown.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of random hardware resets during high ambient temperatures is a protective thermal shutdown (PROCHOT). When ambient temperature rises, the baseline cooling efficiency drops. If the NPU and CPU run heavily, the die temperature skyrockets past Tjmax (e.g., 105C). To prevent literal silicon melting, the hardware triggers a hard electrical power cut, causing kernel panics/resets.

scenario: An edge server in a closed metal box processes IP cameras. It works well at night (15C ambient) but restarts randomly during the day (35C ambient). Logs show kernel panics with no software errors.
title: Mobile New 0029

details.common_mistake: Assuming concurrent model serving on edge devices only competes for compute TOPS, ignoring the shared memory bus.
details.napkin_math: Video model BW: 10GB/s. SoC Max BW: 12GB/s. Audio model BW: 50MB/s. Average BW is fine, but instantaneous bursts delay Audio fetches. Audio deadline = 20ms. Wait in memory queue = 15ms. Compute = 10ms. 25ms > 20ms (Deadline missed).
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of an isolated model failing deadlines when paired with another is memory bandwidth contention. The Video Upscaler reads and writes massive high-resolution frames from LPDDR, saturating the system memory bus. The Audio model, while computationally light, requires rapid, real-time fetching of weights and audio buffers. The memory controller queues the audio requests behind the massive video bursts, causing latency spikes.

scenario: Two models (Audio Wake-Word and Video Upscaling) run flawlessly in isolation. When run concurrently, the Audio model misses deadlines and stutters, despite CPU and NPU utilization both being under 60%.
title: Mobile New 0031

details.common_mistake: Profiling and serving models in isolated benchmark apps without simulating foreground UI thread interference.
details.napkin_math: Normal compute: 15ms. UI render cycle: 16.6ms (60FPS). Scroll event triggers 3 back-to-back UI frames taking CPU priority. ML thread is preempted for 3 * 16.6 = 50ms. Total ML latency = 15ms compute + 50ms wait + OS overhead = 80ms spike.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of jittery ML latency during user interaction is caused by OS context switching and thread priority starvation. The mobile OS prioritizes the UI thread (usually 60Hz or 120Hz rendering) to maintain a smooth user experience. When scrolling, the OS preempts the background ML worker threads, pushing them off the CPU cores, heavily delaying tensor operations or NPU dispatch commands.

scenario: An on-device translation model averages 15ms per token. However, when the user scrolls quickly through the UI, token latency becomes extremely jittery, spiking up to 80ms randomly.
title: Mobile New 0032

details.common_mistake: Believing that total theoretical FLOPs alone determine latency, ignoring memory roundtrips and missed compiler fusions.
details.napkin_math: Fused kernel: 1 Read, 1 Write (20MB total). Unfused: Conv (1R,1W), BN (1R,1W), ReLU (1R,1W) = 60MB total. At 50GB/s BW, 60MB takes 1.2ms. Add kernel launch overheads (3 kernels * 0.2ms = 0.6ms), total is 1.8ms.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom is multiple kernel dispatches and heavily inflated latency, caused by operator fusion failure in the compiler. Because BN and ReLU weren't fused into the Convolution kernel, the GPU must write the intermediate Conv output to VRAM, read it back for BN, write it out, and read it for ReLU. This causes massive memory roundtrips and triple the kernel launch overhead.

scenario: A mobile GPU compiles a Conv-BatchNorm-ReLU block. Instead of a single kernel taking 0.5ms, the profiler shows three distinct kernels executing, and total latency is 1.8ms.
title: Mobile New 0033

details.common_mistake: Converting models between frameworks without explicitly aligning and optimizing the tensor memory format for the target backend.
details.napkin_math: Layer payload: 10MB. Transpose requires moving 10MB out of cache in non-contiguous strides. Transpose BW efficiency is often ~10%. At 1GB/s effective BW, transpose takes 10ms. Across 20 layers, injected transposes add 200ms of pure overhead.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom of massive time spent in non-compute operations is a layout mismatch issue (NCHW vs. NHWC). PyTorch defaults to NCHW (channels first), while TFLite and many mobile DSPs natively optimize for NHWC (channels last) to exploit SIMD vector lanes. The compiler automatically injects a layout transpose before and after every hardware-accelerated op, thrashing memory.

scenario: A PyTorch model is converted to TFLite for a mobile DSP. Profiling shows that 40% of the total execution time is spent executing `Transpose` or `Permute` operations that do not exist in the original PyTorch code.
title: Mobile New 0035

details.common_mistake: Assuming ANE speedup is only from higher TOPS rating, without understanding that ANE has dedicated depthwise convolution hardware units (not tensor cores) and that Core ML's ANE backend performs operation fusion that the GPU backend cannot.
details.napkin_math: MobileNetV3-Large: 0.22 GFLOPs. ANE 35 TOPS: 0.22G/35T = 6.3μs theoretical. Practical 1.8ms: 285× overhead (scheduling, memory DMA, fixed ANE pipeline latency). GPU 4.2ms with 6-core Apple GPU (est. 2 TFLOPS FP16): 0.22G/2T = 0.11ms theoretical. Practical 4.2ms: 38× overhead. ANE is 2.3× faster despite 4.2ms/1.8ms ratio. Core ML Instruments: ANE shows 16 operations for entire MobileNetV3 vs 160+ Metal kernels on GPU. Operation-count reduction is the key.
details.realistic_solution: A17 Pro ANE: 35 TOPS, optimized for CNN inference with hardware support for depthwise conv, BN fusion, and activation. GPU: 6-core Apple GPU, excellent for dense matmul but depthwise ops run on shader cores. For MobileNetV3: depthwise layers run on dedicated ANE spatial processing units at near-peak TOPS; pointwise 1×1 layers also mapped efficiently. ANE also fuses depthwise + BN + H-swish into a single operation. GPU overhead: H-swish requires two Metal shaders (relu6 + multiply), each adding latency. Core ML ANE compiler fuses the full MBConv block into ~3 ANE operations vs 10+ GPU kernels.

scenario: You are profiling MobileNetV3-Large (0.22 GFLOPs) on an iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS NPU, 8GB RAM) using Core ML. The model runs in 4.2ms on the GPU backend but only 1.8ms on the Neural Engine (ANE) backend. Analyze why the ANE is 2.3× faster despite having a different compute architecture, and identify which operations benefit most.
title: Analyze MobileNetV3 latency on A17 Pro ANE vs GPU execution path

details.common_mistake: Comparing models only by FLOPs without considering that Hexagon NPU has different TOPS efficiency for depthwise vs pointwise operations, and that the activation function (H-swish vs ReLU6) significantly affects NPU mapping efficiency.
details.napkin_math: Single inference energy: power × time. MV3-Large on Hexagon: ~1.2ms, NPU power ~0.4W (partial load) → energy = 0.4W × 1.2ms = 0.48 mJ. EfficientNet-Lite0: ~1.5ms, power ~0.5W → 0.75 mJ. MV3 is 1.56× more energy efficient despite similar accuracy. Battery impact: 1000 inferences/day. MV3: 1000 × 0.48mJ = 0.48J. Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 phone battery: 15Wh = 54,000J. Daily ML inference drain: 0.48/54,000 = 0.00089% battery. Negligible in isolation; matters at 100K inferences/day (~50mJ vs 75mJ → still 0.1% battery).
details.realistic_solution: Hexagon NPU HTP (Hyper Tensor Processor): native support for depthwise conv, 1×1 pointwise, INT8/INT4. H-swish in MobileNetV3 must be decomposed to relu6(x+3)/6 × x — two operations on HTP. EfficientNet-Lite0 uses ReLU6 — direct HTP support, single operation. Despite 0.13 GFLOPs fewer, MobileNetV3-Large may be slower on Hexagon due to H-swish overhead. Energy: Hexagon NPU ~2W at full utilization; at 0.35G/45T = 0.78% utilization → ~0.016W for Lite0. At 0.22G/45T = 0.49% → ~0.01W for MV3. Difference: 0.006W — negligible. Profile with Qualcomm AI Hub to get actual numbers.

scenario: You are evaluating EfficientNet-Lite0 (75.1% top-1, 0.35 GFLOPs) vs MobileNetV3-Large (75.2% top-1, 0.22 GFLOPs) on a Samsung Galaxy S24 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU). Analyze energy consumption per inference on the Hexagon DSP vs Qualcomm Adreno 750 GPU path using the QNN SDK.
title: Analyze EfficientNet-Lite0 vs MobileNetV3 accuracy-energy tradeoff on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Assuming the entire accuracy drop is from FP16 quantization precision when the primary cause is often Swish activation approximation in Core ML's ANE mapping, where the sigmoid component is approximated by a 4th-degree polynomial.
details.napkin_math: EfficientNet-B0: 16 MBConv blocks with SE. Swish sigmoid approximation error: FP16 sigmoid(x) for x in [-5, 5] vs FP32: max error ~0.002. Per SE block: sigmoid(FC(GAP(x))). With 2 FC layers and sigmoid, error accumulates. 16 blocks × 2 SE FC operations × 0.002 error ≈ 0.064 total propagated error (rough upper bound). For ImageNet top-1, a 0.06 logit shift can cause ~1-2pp accuracy drop. Remaining 0.3pp likely from FP16 BN and conv precision. Verify: replace Swish with Sigmoid(x) × x using ct.ops.sigmoid() — Core ML maps this directly.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnosis steps: (1) Run Core ML in FP32 mode (computeUnits=.cpuOnly) — if accuracy recovers to 76.8%, the issue is compute unit precision, not conversion. (2) Use coremltools to inspect the converted graph; Swish (x × sigmoid(x)) may be approximated as x × hardsigmoid(x) by Core ML's ANE mapper. (3) Check SE block global average pooling — Core ML FP16 GAP on small spatial dims (7×7) can lose precision. Fix: use ct.convert() with minimum_deployment_target=ct.target.iOS17 for improved Swish handling; or replace Swish with ReLU6 via fine-tuning (EfficientNet-Lite approach).

scenario: After converting EfficientNet-B0 from PyTorch FP32 to Core ML FP16 for A17 Pro, top-1 accuracy drops from 77.1% to 74.8% on a 500-image test set. The model uses Swish (SiLU) activations and SE blocks. Diagnose the sources of the 2.3pp accuracy regression.
title: Diagnose accuracy regression after Core ML conversion of EfficientNet-B0 for A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Assuming on-device training follows the same compute/memory tradeoffs as cloud training; ignoring that backpropagation through depthwise layers on ANE is not natively supported and falls back to CPU, making depthwise backward passes 10× slower than forward on A17 Pro.
details.napkin_math: Attention FLOPs: standard 3×3 conv at resolution 96×96×14 heads: 2×96²×14² = 2×9216×196 = 3,612,672 ≈ 3.6M FLOPs. For expansion at 960 channels: 2×960×1280×7² = 2×960×1280×49 = 120,422,400 ≈ 120M FLOPs.
details.realistic_solution: Attention FLOPs at 96×96 with 14 heads: 2×96²×14² = 3.6M. Expansion conv 960→1280 at 7×7: 2×960×1280×49 = 120M FLOPs.

scenario: You are designing an on-device personalization system that fine-tunes the last 3 MBConv blocks of MobileNetV3 on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB RAM) using 50 labeled images per class. Evaluate whether depthwise separable convolutions or standard convolutions in these final blocks better balance training speed and accuracy for on-device learning.
title: Evaluate depthwise separable vs standard conv for on-device training on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Choosing MobileNetV3 because it has fewest FLOPs without profiling ANE performance; H-swish requires sigmoid approximation on ANE while ReLU6 (used by Lite4 and MV2) maps directly, potentially making Lite4 faster despite more FLOPs.
details.napkin_math: Food-101 fine-tuning benefit over ImageNet: typically +8-12pp for domain-specific fine-tuning. Lite4 base 80.4% → fine-tuned ~91%. A17 Pro ANE at 35 TOPS. Lite4: 0.571G/35T = 16.3μs theoretical → practical ~3.5ms (215× scheduling overhead). MV3-Large: 0.22G/35T = 6.3μs → practical ~2.1ms (333× overhead; H-swish adds overhead). MV2-1.4×: 0.582G/35T = 16.6μs → practical ~2.8ms (169× overhead). User-facing: all under 5ms → invisible latency. Choose on accuracy: Lite4 wins.
details.realistic_solution: ANE mapping quality: EfficientNet-Lite4 and MobileNetV2-1.4× use ReLU6 — native ANE support, full fusion. MobileNetV3 uses H-swish — ANE approximates with hardsigmoid, adds 1 extra op per activation. Estimate: Lite4 ANE latency ~3.5ms (published by Apple ML Research); MV2-1.4× ~2.8ms; MV3-Large ~2.1ms (fewer FLOPs despite activation overhead). Accuracy on food-101 after fine-tuning: Lite4 ~91%, MV3-Large ~87%, MV2 ~85%. Decision: Lite4 for accuracy-critical use, MV3-Large for latency-critical. At 3.5ms, Lite4 easily handles 30 FPS (33ms budget).

scenario: You must pick a backbone for an iOS app that classifies food items (101 categories) running on iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro). Candidates: EfficientNet-Lite4 (0.571 GFLOPs, 80.4% top-1, ReLU6), MobileNetV3-Large 1.0× (0.22 GFLOPs, 75.2% top-1, H-swish), and MobileNetV2-1.4× (0.582 GFLOPs, 74.7% top-1, ReLU6). Evaluate for Core ML ANE deployment on A17 Pro.
title: Evaluate EfficientNet-Lite vs MobileNetV3 for CoreML ANE deployment accuracy-latency

details.common_mistake: Explaining only that mobile models are 'smaller and faster' without conveying the actual user experience stakes (3ms vs 200ms is invisible vs perceptible; 1% battery vs 10% battery matters) or that A17 Pro ANE changes the tradeoff.
details.napkin_math: A17 Pro ANE power: ~1W at full load. MobileNetV3 at 30 FPS: 30 × 2ms = 60ms/sec active = 6% duty cycle → 0.06W inference power. ResNet-50 alternative at 100ms/frame: 30 × 100ms = 3,000ms/sec — impossible at 30 FPS (need 10× slower FPS or 10× more power). MobileNetV3 enables real-time at 30 FPS; ResNet-50 limited to 10 FPS at same power. Battery per hour: 0.06W × 3600 sec = 216 J. iPhone 15 Pro battery: 13Wh = 46,800J. MobileNet: 0.46% battery/hr for continuous real-time inference.
details.realistic_solution: Frame it as: large cloud models (ResNet-50: 100ms on ANE) feel laggy for real-time camera features. MobileNetV3 at 2ms is imperceptible. The A17 Pro's Neural Engine (35 TOPS) is specifically designed to run these efficient models; it's 10× more power-efficient than the GPU for CNN inference. Accuracy: MobileNetV3 vs ResNet-50 is 75% vs 76% on ImageNet — 1% gap on academic benchmarks often disappears with app-specific fine-tuning. Battery: a 2ms inference at 30 FPS draws ~0.1% battery per hour vs 200ms inference drawing 10% per hour.

scenario: An iOS product manager asks why the team is using 'MobileNet' instead of the more accurate model from the ML paper they just read. Explain why efficient CNN architectures exist for mobile, the A17 Pro's role, and how to think about the accuracy-speed-battery tradeoff for user-facing features on iPhone 15 Pro.
title: Fluency: explain MobileNet-family tradeoffs to an iOS product manager

details.common_mistake: Assuming Hexagon HTP maps the expand-depthwise-project sequence as three separate kernel calls, when modern Hexagon HTP (v73) supports operation fusion across the entire MBConv block into a single accelerated op.
details.napkin_math: Hexagon HTP v73 SRAM: 4MB scratchpad. MBConv intermediate tensor at C=160, t=6, spatial 7×7: 960 × 7 × 7 × 1B (INT8) = 47KB. Fits in SRAM. At C=320, t=6, spatial 7×7: 1920 × 49 = 94KB — still fits. All MobileNetV2 stages fit in HTP SRAM. Tiling consideration: HTP processes in chunks of 32 channels × 4×4 spatial tiles. 960 channels / 32 = 30 tiles: 30 HTP dispatch cycles. vs t=4: 640/32 = 20 cycles → 33% fewer dispatches. At 45 TOPS, each dispatch ~1ns: 30 vs 20 ns per block — negligible absolute, but across 17 blocks × 30 FPS = meaningful.
details.realistic_solution: Hexagon HTP v73 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3): supports Conv2D, DepthwiseConv2D, BatchNorm, ReLU6 as fused operation. MBConv block: expand (1×1 + BN + ReLU6) + depthwise (3×3 + BN + ReLU6) + project (1×1 + BN) → fused into 1 HTP dispatch. Expansion ratio t=6 for Hexagon: intermediate channel count should be ≤512 for optimal HTP SRAM tiling. For input C=32, t=6 → 192 channels: fine. For C=160, t=6 → 960 channels: may exceed HTP tile budget, causing split. Recommend t=4 for high-channel stages (C>128) when targeting Hexagon, reducing FLOPs by 33% with <1pp accuracy loss.

scenario: A mobile ML engineer on your team is new to Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 45 TOPS). They ask how an inverted residual block from MobileNetV2 maps to Hexagon HTP operations and whether the expansion ratio t=6 is optimal for Hexagon. Explain the mapping and optimal configuration.
title: Fluency: describe inverted residual block execution on Qualcomm Hexagon NPU

details.common_mistake: Fine-tuning with PyTorch's default Swish/SiLU activation and then trying to convert directly to Core ML ANE — the ANE does not support torch.nn.SiLU directly and coremltools may produce a 'compute units: CPU_AND_GPU' fall-through instead of ANE execution.
details.napkin_math: Fine-tuning 10K images, 50 epochs, batch=32. Steps: 10K/32 × 50 = 15,625 steps. MobileNetV3-Large backward: ~0.66 GFLOPs (3× forward FLOPs). Per step: 32 × 0.66G = 21G FLOPs. On M3 Mac (15 TFLOPS): 21G/15T = 1.4ms/step. Total: 15,625 × 1.4ms = 21.9 sec fine-tuning. Core ML conversion: ~30 seconds. A17 Pro ANE inference with Hardswish: ~1.9ms (vs 2.1ms with H-swish approx). SiLU → Hardswish accuracy impact: <0.3pp on custom 5-class task (distribution shift dominates). Total pipeline: 5 minutes including validation.
details.realistic_solution: ANE compatibility: replace SiLU with nn.Hardswish() before or during fine-tuning (very close approximation, <0.5pp accuracy impact). Pipeline: (1) Load timm MobileNetV3-Large pretrained; (2) Replace SiLU → Hardswish; (3) Fine-tune 50 epochs with AdamW, LR=1e-4, cosine schedule; (4) Export: model.eval(); traced = torch.jit.trace(model, example_input); (5) coremltools.convert(traced, compute_units=ct.ComputeUnit.ALL, minimum_deployment_target=ct.target.iOS17); (6) Verify with Xcode Instruments that model runs on ANE. Test: ct.models.MLModel.predict() and check compute_device in metadata.

scenario: You need to fine-tune a pre-trained MobileNetV3-Large on a 5-class custom dataset (2,000 images per class) and deploy it to iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro) via Core ML. The deployment must use the Neural Engine for <3ms inference. Implement the full training and conversion pipeline with ANE-compatibility constraints.
title: Implement MobileNetV3 fine-tuning pipeline for Core ML deployment on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Using the generic ONNX → QNN conversion without disabling dynamic shapes, which prevents Hexagon HTP graph compilation and forces fallback to CPU; SE blocks with dynamic GAP also need static shape specification.
details.napkin_math: EfficientNet-B0 INT8 on Hexagon HTP: 0.39G GOPS / 45 TOPS = 8.7μs theoretical. Published QNN benchmark: ~1.5ms batch=1. Overhead factor: 172×. Model weights INT8: 5.3M × 1B = 5.3MB. Hexagon HTP SRAM: ~8MB → entire model fits on-chip. SE block FC layers: 16 × C²/4 FLOPs = 16 × (varying C² terms) ≈ 5M FLOPs total. SE as % of total: 5M/390M = 1.3% FLOPs. HTP dispatch overhead for 16 SE blocks: 16 × 2 FC layers × 0.1ms overhead = 3.2ms if not fused. Critical: ensure SE GAP + FC1 + FC2 + sigmoid + multiply are fused in QNN context.
details.realistic_solution: QNN conversion: (1) Export PyTorch → ONNX with static shapes (batch=1, input=1×3×224×224, opset=13); (2) Replace SiLU with approximation: hardswish or x × hardtanh(x+3,0,6)/6 (QNN-supported); (3) qnn-onnx-converter --input_network model.onnx --output_path model.cpp; (4) qnn-net-run with --backend libQnnHtp.so; (5) SE blocks: Hexagon HTP supports GlobalAveragePool as a native op. Verify latency < 3ms with qnn-net-run --duration 1000. If SE blocks cause issues, use qnn-model-lib-generator to inspect per-layer dispatch.

scenario: You are deploying EfficientNet-B0 (5.3M params, 0.39 GFLOPs) to a Samsung Galaxy S24 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Hexagon NPU, 45 TOPS) using the QNN SDK for offline deployment. The model has Swish (SiLU) activations and SE blocks. Implement the compilation pipeline with Hexagon-specific optimizations.
title: Implement EfficientNet-B0 for Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Hexagon NPU via QNN SDK

details.common_mistake: Projecting B3 latency from B0 by multiplying by FLOP ratio (1.8/0.39 = 4.6×) and concluding it takes 4.6 × 1.5ms = 6.9ms; ignoring that resolution scaling changes the NPU tiling strategy and that intermediate feature map sizes may exceed Hexagon HTP on-chip SRAM.
details.napkin_math: B0 → B3 scaling factors: depth 1.2^3=1.73×, width 1.1^3=1.33×, resolution 1.15^3=1.52× (224→300 ≈ 1.34× actually). FLOPs: 0.39 × 2³ = 3.1× (using 2^φ rule) → 1.2 GFLOPs (actual B3: 1.8 GFLOPs, close). Resolution 300 vs 224: (300/224)² = 1.79× spatial overhead. Hexagon at B3: 1.5ms × 1.8G/0.39G FLOPs ratio (if purely compute-bound) × 1.15 tiling factor = 8.8ms. Memory: B3 max activation 38×38×192 = 277KB — fits HTP SRAM (8MB). Bottleneck is compute + tiling, not memory.
details.realistic_solution: B3 feature maps: stage 1 at 150×150 (vs B0 112×112), intermediate maps proportionally larger. Hexagon HTP SRAM ~8MB. B3 peak activation: ~96×19×19 (stage 6) = 34.6KB × 1B → still fits. Resolution increase: HTP spatial tiling becomes less efficient at 300×300 vs 224×224 — tile count scales as (300/224)² = 1.79×. Latency scaling: 1.5ms × 4.6× FLOPs × 1.2× (tiling overhead) = 8.3ms → exceeds 5ms SLA. Break point: B2 (260×260, 1.0 GFLOPs). B2: 1.5 × (1.0/0.39) × 1.1 = 4.2ms — just under 5ms. B3 fails the SLA.

scenario: Your team successfully deploys EfficientNet-B0 on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (B0: 224×224, 0.39 GFLOPs). A PM requests scaling to B3 (300×300, 1.8 GFLOPs) for better accuracy without changing the SLA of <5ms. Demonstrate mastery by analyzing whether B3 fits the SLA and why compound scaling breaks down for mobile NPU deployment beyond a certain φ.
title: Mastery: explain compound scaling failure modes for mobile deployment

details.common_mistake: Treating SE removal as always beneficial for mobile without profiling; on A17 Pro ANE, SE blocks add ~0.2ms to a 2ms model — a 10% overhead worth 1pp accuracy. On Hexagon, SE may add 1.5ms if not properly fused — a 100% overhead clearly not worth it.
details.napkin_math: MV3-Large SE stats: 15 SE blocks (selected stages). C values: 16, 24, 40, 80, 112, 160 (varying). Total SE FLOPs: Σ(2×C²/4 × 2) for each stage ≈ 3M FLOPs. % of total 0.22G: 1.4%. A17 Pro ANE: 35 TOPS. 3M FLOPs / 35T = 0.086μs compute. Practical ANE overhead (scheduling): ~0.2ms for 15 separate small FC dispatches. If fused: 15 × 0.013ms = 0.2ms. Total inference 2.1ms → SE adds 10%. Hexagon: 45 TOPS. Same 3M FLOPs = 0.067μs compute. If 12 unfused dispatches: 12 × 0.1ms = 1.2ms. SE-free model: 1.5ms total. SE cost on Hexagon: 80% latency overhead for 1.4% FLOPs — remove SE for Hexagon deployment.
details.realistic_solution: A17 Pro ANE: SE blocks fully supported; GAP + two FC + sigmoid + scale are fused into a single ANE operation. Overhead: ~0.2ms for all SE blocks in MV3-Large. Accuracy gain: ~1.5pp. Worth keeping. Hexagon HTP v73: SE partially fused. GAP as native op, FC1+FC2+ReLU6+Hardsigmoid as fused block, final multiply is separate. If QNN compiler fuses properly: overhead ~0.3ms. If not fused: 12 separate dispatches × 0.1ms = 1.2ms overhead. Profile with qnn-net-run --profiling. Recommendation: keep SE for ANE; profile before deciding for Hexagon; consider SE reduction ratio r=8 to halve SE FLOPs.

scenario: MobileNetV3 uses SE blocks with reduction ratio r=4. The A17 Pro ANE and Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Hexagon NPU have different handling of SE blocks. Demonstrate mastery by analyzing SE block execution on each platform, quantifying the latency overhead, and recommending whether to include or remove SE for each platform.
title: Mastery: MobileNetV3 SE block impact on A17 Pro ANE vs Hexagon NPU

details.common_mistake: Reducing the expansion ratio uniformly across all layers from t=6 to t=4, which reduces accuracy by ~1.5pp unnecessarily; the memory spike only occurs in early large-spatial layers and can be addressed with selective expansion ratio reduction.
details.napkin_math: Hexagon HTP SRAM: ~8MB. MV2 peak activation without double-buffer: 56×56×192 = 602KB. With t=4: 56×56×128 = 401KB. Memory savings: 201KB. Double-buffer: 602 × 2 = 1.2MB for t=6, still fits in 8MB with room for weights (3.4M params = 3.4MB INT8). Total with t=6: 3.4MB weights + 1.2MB activations = 4.6MB < 8MB. No actual overflow! Investigate profiler: the 4ms might be the optimized path already. Check if spike is transient (FFT buffer) not persistent. Actual fix may be in QNN context memory management.
details.realistic_solution: Apply non-uniform expansion ratios: early stages (large spatial dims, 56×56 and 28×28) use t=4; later stages (14×14 and 7×7) keep t=6. Memory for bottleneck_2: t=6 → 56×56×192×1B = 602KB. At t=4 → 56×56×128×1B = 401KB. Total peak reduction: from ~1.5MB to ~0.9MB across early stages. Hexagon HTP SRAM: 8MB — the single activation still fits! Actual problem may be multi-buffering for pipeline. Check QNN profiler: if HTP is double-buffering (input + output in SRAM simultaneously), peak = 602 + 602 = 1.2MB. Use t=5 as compromise: 56×56×160×1B = 501KB × 2 = 1MB.

scenario: MobileNetV2 with expansion ratio t=6 achieves 72ms on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 using TFLite GPU delegate, but only 4ms on Hexagon HTP. The HTP version hits a memory spike at the bottleneck_2_expand layer (input 56×56×32, output 56×56×192). You need to reduce peak activation memory to prevent HTP SRAM overflow while maintaining >72% top-1 accuracy.
title: Optimize MobileNetV2 expansion ratio for Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Hexagon HTP memory

details.common_mistake: Simply reducing inference frequency from 30 FPS to 15 FPS, which cuts battery in half but noticeably degrades AR experience; missing that 30 FPS inference is over-provisioned (model accuracy doesn't benefit from 30 Hz for most objects) and that ANE can use power gating between inferences.
details.napkin_math: Current: 30 FPS × 2ms active ANE = 60ms active / 1000ms = 6% duty cycle. A17 Pro ANE power: ~1.5W active, 0.01W idle. Power = 0.06 × 1.5 + 0.94 × 0.01 = 0.09 + 0.0094 = 0.099W. Plus GPU/CPU overhead for pre/post-processing: ~0.3W total system. At 8% battery/hr: 8% × 15Wh = 1.2Wh/hr = 1.2W. Check: system is drawing 1.2W at 30 FPS. Target 4%: 0.6W. Need 50% power reduction. Adaptive 10 FPS: duty cycle 2%, ANE power = 0.02 × 1.5 = 0.03W. Pre/post at 10 FPS: ~0.1W. Total: 0.13W → 0.87% battery/hr. Exceeds target.
details.realistic_solution: Optimizations: (1) Adaptive inference rate: use CoreMotion to detect camera motion — if static (<0.1°/sec rotation), reduce to 5 FPS; if moderate, 15 FPS; if fast pan, 30 FPS. Average rate drops to ~10 FPS. (2) Enable ANE power gating: ensure model uses computeUnits=.neuralEngine (not .all) so A17 CPU/GPU shut down between inferences. (3) Warm model once, cache MLModel instance (avoid re-loading). (4) Use Core ML's MLComputePlan to profile which operations fall to CPU. Expected: 10 FPS average × 2ms × 35 TOPS active power + idle between → ~2.5% battery/hr.

scenario: An iOS AR application runs EfficientNet-Lite0 (0.35 GFLOPs) at 30 FPS continuously on A17 Pro for object recognition in the camera viewfinder. Battery drain is 8% per hour. Target is < 4% per hour. Optimize the inference pipeline without changing the model architecture.
title: Optimize EfficientNet-Lite0 for continuous inference battery life on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Shipping a pre-compiled MLModelc package for a specific device, which is large (>50MB compiled) and locks to a specific iOS version; the correct approach is to ship the .mlmodel file and let iOS compile on-device at first use, which takes <1 second on A17 Pro.
details.napkin_math: Model size: 5.4MB INT8. OTA download: at 20 Mbps LTE: 5.4MB × 8 / 20M = 2.16 seconds download. gzipped: 4MB → 1.6 seconds. A17 Pro compilation: MLModel.compileModel typically 300–800ms for MobileNetV3-class models (Apple documentation). Total: 1.6s + 0.5s = 2.1s setup time slightly over 2s target. Optimization: delta update (only changed weights) using MobileNetV3 fine-tune diff ≈ 2MB → 0.8s download + 0.5s compile = 1.3s total. Pre-cache on Wi-Fi: background download eliminates user-perceived latency entirely.
details.realistic_solution: Pipeline: (1) Ship .mlpackage (not .mlmodelc) via CDN: 5.4MB INT8 compressed (~4MB gzipped); (2) On download, iOS calls MLModel.compileModel(at:) asynchronously — A17 Pro compilation: ~500ms; (3) Store compiled .mlmodelc in Application Support; (4) Atomic swap: compile to temp path, validate with single inference, then rename; (5) Fallback: keep previous .mlmodelc, if new model validation fails (exception or accuracy check fails), revert to previous; (6) Background download + compile using BackgroundTasks framework. Model version check via JSON manifest. User impact: zero — compilation is background, served from compiled cache after first launch.

scenario: You need to ship a MobileNetV3-Large model update to iPhone 15 Pro users (A17 Pro) via OTA, with the model compiled for ANE execution. The update is 5.4MB (INT8 weights). Realize the delivery and on-device compilation pipeline that ensures < 2 seconds setup time and fallback to previous model on compilation failure.
title: Realization: ship MobileNetV3 model update OTA with Core ML compilation on device

details.common_mistake: Running both models sequentially on the Hexagon NPU, totaling ~3ms, when the CPU and NPU can execute in parallel — reducing wall-clock time from 3ms sequential to 2ms parallel for the ensemble.
details.napkin_math: MV3-Small: 0.056G / 45 TOPS = 1.2μs theoretical → practical ~0.5ms. Lite0: 0.35G / 45 TOPS = 7.8μs theoretical → practical ~2ms. Sequential: 2.5ms. Parallel: 2ms. Ensemble merge: two 1000-dim softmax vectors on Kryo: 2000 FP32 additions = 2000/3.3G ops = 0.6μs (negligible). Total pipeline: image → parallel NPU inference (2ms) → CPU merge (0.001ms) → result: 2.001ms. 4× headroom vs 8ms SLA. Power: both models at once: Hexagon ~0.8W + scheduling overhead. At 2ms per frame (30 FPS): 2ms × 30 / 1000ms = 6% duty cycle → 0.8 × 0.06 = 0.048W NPU.
details.realistic_solution: Heterogeneous split: (1) MobileNetV3-Small → Hexagon HTP (0.056G FLOPs, ~0.5ms); (2) EfficientNet-Lite0 → Hexagon HTP sequentially after or (better) run EfficientNet-Lite0 on Hexagon and MV3-Small on Kryo DSP or Adreno GPU concurrently. QNN supports multi-core scheduling: set QNN_PROPERTY_GROUP to enable concurrent NPU + GPU. Ensemble merge: on CPU (Cortex-A78, fast for 2×1000 softmax addition). If HTP queue can accept both simultaneously: total latency = max(0.5ms, 2ms) = 2ms. Sequential: 0.5 + 2 = 2.5ms. Parallel: 2ms. Well under 8ms SLA.

scenario: You need to run an ensemble of MobileNetV3-Small (0.056 GFLOPs) + EfficientNet-Lite0 (0.35 GFLOPs) simultaneously on a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 device for a high-accuracy classification feature. Total latency must be <8ms with results merged. Realize the heterogeneous compute split between Hexagon NPU (45 TOPS) and Kryo CPU (3.3 GHz).
title: Realization: build multi-model CNN ensemble on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 with CPU+NPU split

details.common_mistake: Including bias parameters in the count when MobileNetV2 uses no bias (bias=False) in conv layers — all normalization is done by BatchNorm which has its own γ,β parameters; counting BN parameters as conv parameters.
details.napkin_math: Standard 3×3 conv 32→16 at 112×112: FLOPs = 2 × 32 × 16 × 9 × 112 × 112 = 2 × 32 × 16 × 9 × 12,544 = 2 × 57,802,752 = 115,605,504 ≈ 115.6M FLOPs (not 102M — 102M would require ~88 for the kernel×spatial product instead of 9×12544=112,896).

scenario: You are reviewing a MobileNetV2 implementation on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3. The first bottleneck block has input 112×112×32, expansion t=1 (no expand for first block), 3×3 depthwise at 32 channels, and project 32→16. Calculate the exact parameter count and FLOPs for this block and explain why t=1 is used only in the first block.
title: Recall depthwise separable convolution parameter count for MobileNetV2 first block

details.common_mistake: Specifying accuracy as top-1 on ImageNet rather than on the AR-specific 50-class dataset; failing to specify ANE compatibility constraints (no custom ops, activation functions limited to ANE-supported set) that are required to hit the 3ms latency target.
details.napkin_math: Battery constraint: 4% per hour. iPhone 15 Pro battery: 13Wh. 4% = 0.52Wh/hr = 0.52W. ANE active at 2ms inference, 30 FPS: duty cycle = 2ms × 30 / 1000ms = 6%. ANE power: 1.5W × 6% = 0.09W. System overhead (CPU, display, camera): ~0.4W. Total: 0.49W < 0.52W target — just fits. If inference is 3ms (hitting upper limit): 9% duty cycle → 0.135W ANE → 0.535W total → slightly over. Therefore: <2ms ANE inference is a hard requirement derived from battery spec, not just latency SLA.
details.realistic_solution: Spec: (1) Architecture: MobileNetV3-Large or EfficientNet-Lite family; (2) FLOPs: ≤0.4 GFLOPs (ANE achieves <2ms at this FLOP count, with 1ms headroom); (3) Accuracy: >85% top-1 on held-out 50-class AR dataset (not ImageNet); (4) ANE constraints: activations must be ReLU6, Hardswish, or Sigmoid only; all layer shapes static at compile time; no custom ops; min iOS 17; (5) Memory: model size ≤10MB INT8 (A17 Pro ANE model cache limit); (6) Latency target: <2ms ANE measured with Core ML Instruments; (7) Battery: <4% per hour at 30 FPS = <0.6W total inference power; (8) Test: 500 AR-context images, 5 lighting conditions, 3 occlusion levels.

scenario: You are writing the model specification for a real-time AR object recognition feature on iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS ANE, 8GB RAM). The feature must run at 30 FPS with <3ms inference latency, <4% battery drain/hr, and >85% top-1 accuracy on a 50-class AR object dataset. Write a complete technical specification.
title: Specification: define mobile CNN requirements for real-time AR on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Maintaining two separate training checkpoints for iOS and Android rather than a single canonical PyTorch checkpoint with platform-specific export pipelines; this leads to divergent model versions and reproducibility issues.
details.napkin_math: Model artifacts per version: PyTorch checkpoint: 21.6MB (FP32, 5.4M params × 4B). Core ML INT8 .mlpackage: ~6MB. QNN serialized INT8: ~7MB. CDN storage per version: 35MB. At 10 versions/year: 350MB CDN storage = $0.007/month (S3 standard). Download bandwidth: 1M active users × 1 update/month × 6MB (mobile downloads compressed model) = 6TB/month = $138/month CDN egress. Validation pipeline: 500 images × 2 platforms × 10 versions = 10,000 model inferences. At 2ms each: 20 seconds total CI validation time.
details.realistic_solution: Spec: (1) Single source of truth: PyTorch FP32 checkpoint with architecture flag (ACTIVATION: hardswish for cross-platform compatibility, no SE blocks); (2) Export artifacts: .mlpackage for iOS, .serialized_bin for QNN; (3) Versioning: semantic versioning model_v{major}.{minor}.{patch} — major=architecture change, minor=fine-tune data update, patch=quantization calibration update; (4) Validation gate: both exports must pass accuracy within 1% of PyTorch baseline on 500-image canonical test set before release; (5) Artifacts stored in S3 with SHA256 checksums; (6) A/B test framework: device-side version selection via remote config with automatic rollback if error rate increases >5%.

scenario: Your team needs to deploy a MobileNetV3-Large variant on both iPhone 15 Pro (A17 Pro, Core ML) and Samsung Galaxy S24 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, QNN). The models share the same PyTorch weights but must be optimized for each platform. Write the specification for the model packaging, versioning, and validation pipeline.
title: Specification: model format and versioning requirements for cross-platform mobile CNN deployment

details.common_mistake: Summing model sizes and concluding the total fits because 2+1.5+0.8=4.3GB 'barely' exceeds the limit, without accounting for runtime overhead: iOS framework overhead (~200MB), KV caches, image decode buffers, and the fact that models are loaded into memory with alignment padding.
details.napkin_math: Model memory: 2+1.5+0.8=4.3GB. iOS overhead: 200MB. Image buffer (1080p): 1920*1080*4=8MB. KV cache: negligible (~6MB). Total peak: 4.508GB — exceeds 4GB limit by 508MB. Hot-swap vision: during vision phase: 2+0.2+0.008=2.208GB (safe). During NLP phase: 1.5+0.8+0.2+0.008=2.508GB (safe).
