Swap latency: evict 2GB from Metal heap, reload from flash (NVMe ~3GB/s): 2GB/3GB/s = 667ms. Acceptable if vision runs once per user action, not per frame.
details.realistic_solution: Full memory budget: models(4.3GB) + KV cache for 1024 tokens in text gen model (2*layers*head_dim*2bytes*1024 = for a 0.8GB INT4 model ~1B params, 22 layers: 2*22*64*2*1024=5.5MB) + image buffers (4K image: 4096*3072*4=48MB) + iOS overhead(200MB) = 4.55GB — exceeds limit by 550MB. Solution: hot-swap vision model (2GB) out of Metal memory after encoding, before text generation. Resident during text gen: NLP encoder(1.5GB) + text gen(0.8GB) + buffers(0.25GB) = 2.55GB. Load vision only during camera frame processing, evict immediately after.

scenario: An iOS compound AI app on A17 Pro (8GB RAM, 35 TOPS) runs three models simultaneously: a 2GB vision model, a 1.5GB NLP encoder, and a 0.8GB text generation model. iOS kills apps exceeding 4GB RAM. At peak, the pipeline holds all three models resident plus KV caches and image buffers. Analyze the memory pressure and identify which models can be hot-swapped vs kept resident to stay within the 4GB app memory limit.
title: Analyzing Multi-Model Pipeline Memory Pressure on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Attempting to optimize the LLM (the slowest stage) first without analyzing its thermal contribution relative to its frequency of invocation. If embeddings run 10x more often than LLM calls, the embedding stage may contribute more total thermal energy despite lower per-call power.
details.napkin_math: Steady-state thermal load: LLM: 12W * 0.6s_active/s = 7.2W. Embedding: 2W * (5ms*30fps)/1000 = 2W*0.15 = 0.3W. Search: 1W * (8ms*2 searches/s)/1000 = 0.016W. Total active: 7.52W. Snapdragon sustained power budget ~4W for sustained inference. Throttle at 7.52W: onset in ~90s (thermal mass absorbs initial burst). After throttle to 4W budget: LLM gets 4W/7.52W * 300ms = 160ms budget → 3.75 tok/s, actual 300→480ms observed (1.6x). Optimize LLM to 8W: throttle onset ~135s, post-throttle 300ms*(8/4)=... wait, throttle is thermal cap not perf scaling — correct analysis: less heat → less throttling.
details.realistic_solution: Analyze thermal energy per second: LLM: 12W * (300ms/query) * (queries/s). If 2 queries/s: 12 * 0.3 * 2 = 7.2W continuous. Embedding: 2W * (5ms/embed) * (10 embeds/s for camera stream at 2fps) = 2 * 0.005 * 2... recalc at 30fps: 2W * 0.005s * 30fps = 0.3W continuous. LLM dominates at 7.2W. Primary optimization: reduce LLM power via CPU power cap and INT4 quantization. INT4 reduces compute per token, but LLM is memory-bound on mobile — bandwidth reduction from INT4 cuts power ~30%: 12W → 8.4W, reducing throttle trigger time from 90s to ~135s.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) device runs a compound AI pipeline: camera embedding (5ms, 2W), semantic search (8ms, 1W), and on-device LLM (300ms, 12W). After 90 seconds of continuous use, the device throttles: LLM inference slows from 300ms to 480ms, embedding slows from 5ms to 9ms. Analyze the thermal contribution of each stage and determine which stage to optimize first to recover performance.
title: Analyzing Compound AI Pipeline Thermal Throttling on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Making a binary always-on-device or always-cloud decision without considering the query rate and battery state. At 100 queries/day, cloud cost is trivial ($0.20/day); battery impact of 100 on-device LLM calls at 12W each * 300ms = 360J = 0.1Wh — also trivial. The decision hinges on latency and privacy, not cost or battery at typical rates.
details.napkin_math: On-device: 20+5+300=325ms, 12W during LLM = 3.6J/query. Cloud: 20+5+80(network)+60(inference)=165ms total, ~0.1W during network transfer. Battery: 4000mAh * 3.7V = 14.8Wh = 53,280J. On-device 100 queries: 100*3.6J=360J = 0.68% battery. Cloud 100 queries: negligible battery but $0.20/day. Privacy: 100% of sensitive queries must stay local. Latency advantage of cloud: (325-165)/325=49% faster when network available. Recommend hybrid with privacy classifier as primary gate.
details.realistic_solution: Decision matrix: (1) Privacy-sensitive queries (medical, financial): always on-device regardless of speed — no data leaves device. (2) Low battery (< 20%): prefer cloud offload — saves 12W * 300ms = 3.6J per query. At 50 queries in low-battery period: 50 * 3.6J = 180J = 0.05Wh saved — negligible. (3) No network (airplane mode/offline): forced on-device. (4) Time-sensitive query with network: cloud wins at 140ms vs 325ms on-device. Implement a hybrid router: classify query privacy level, check battery and network state, route accordingly.

scenario: A Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) device runs a compound AI pipeline with three stages: local embedding (20ms), local retrieval (5ms), and LLM generation. The on-device 1B LLM generates at 8 tok/s (300ms for 40 tokens). Cloud offload of the LLM to an A100 API costs $0.002/query with 80ms network latency + 60ms cloud inference = 140ms total. Analyze under which conditions on-device vs cloud is preferred, considering battery, latency, and privacy.
title: Analyzing On-Device vs Cloud Offload Decision for Compound AI on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Using cloud-scale embedding models (1536-dim OpenAI embeddings) that are designed for quality rather than mobile efficiency, consuming 10x the memory of mobile-optimized 256-dim models while offering minimal quality improvement for personal document search.
details.napkin_math: Memory: embedding model(22MB) + FAISS(10MB) + LLM 1B INT4(500MB) + doc store(150MB) + KV+buffers(50MB) = 732MB total. 3.5GB - 732MB = 2.77GB headroom. A17 Pro ANE: 35 TOPS for INT4 1B model (2B effective ops due to INT4): 35e12/2e9 = 17,500 tokens/s theoretical, practical ~20 tok/s after overhead. Time-to-first-token: prefill 512-token context at 35 TOPS: 512*2*1B/(35e12) = ~29ms. Generation: 100 tokens / 20 tok/s = 5s total. Reduce to 50 tokens: 2.5s. Optimize: prefill(29ms) + generate_50_tokens(2.5s) = 2.53s — slightly over 2s SLA. Reduce to 38 tokens for 2s exactly.
details.realistic_solution: Component allocation within 3.5GB: (1) Embedding model: MobileBERT-based 256-dim encoder, INT8 quantized = 22MB. (2) FAISS HNSW index: 10K docs * 256 * 4 bytes = 10MB. (3) LLM: 1B parameter model INT4 = 500MB. (4) Document store: 10K docs * 5000 tokens avg * 3 bytes = 150MB compressed. (5) KV cache: 1024-token context * 2*22layers*64dim*2bytes = 5.5MB. Total: 22+10+500+150+5.5 = 687.5MB — well within budget. Response pipeline: embed query (15ms) + HNSW search (3ms) + LLM at 20 tok/s (A17 Pro ANE): 100 token response = 5s — too slow. Must pre-fill context and stream first token in < 500ms.

scenario: Design an on-device RAG system for an A17 Pro (8GB RAM, 35 TOPS) that enables a personal knowledge assistant to search 10,000 personal documents (notes, emails, PDFs) and generate responses. Total memory budget is 3.5GB (leaving headroom for OS and other apps). The design must support documents up to 5000 tokens, 256-dim embeddings, and sub-2-second end-to-end response time.
title: Designing an On-Device RAG Architecture for A17 Pro with 8GB Memory

details.common_mistake: Implementing a simple try/catch that switches to on-device on the first timeout. This causes 3-5 second delays during the cloud→on-device transition because: (1) the cloud timeout must expire first (3s), (2) the on-device model may not be pre-warmed, and (3) the context must be rebuilt.
details.napkin_math: Cloud mode: 200ms latency + 100ms generation = 300ms. On-device 1B at Snapdragon 45 TOPS: 1B INT4 (500MB): decode 50 tokens at ~40 tok/s (45 TOPS / 1B params * efficiency) = 50/40 = 1.25s. Prefill 512-token context: 512*2*1B/(45e12*0.4) = 57ms. Total on-device: 57+1250 = 1.31s < 2s SLA. Mode switch overhead with dual-path: embedding starts at t=0, if cloud fails at t=300ms, on-device is 300ms into its prefill → remaining time: 1310-300=1010ms to completion. Total user-perceived latency: 300ms (wait for cloud failure) + 1010ms = 1.31s effective.
details.realistic_solution: Predictive mode switching: (1) Monitor network quality continuously using a 10ms ping heartbeat. Pre-warm the on-device LLM (load weights into memory) when ping latency > 100ms — before the cloud call fails. (2) Dual-path: launch cloud call AND start on-device embedding simultaneously. If cloud responds < 500ms, cancel on-device. If cloud fails, on-device is already 200ms ahead. (3) Keep last 5 turns of conversation in a compressed context buffer (device-side) for instant on-device context restoration. (4) Gradual degradation: reduce output length from 200 to 50 tokens in offline mode.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) mobile app uses a cloud-first compound AI agent (4-model pipeline, 200ms cloud latency) with an on-device fallback (1B LLM, 8 tok/s). Network connectivity drops for an average of 15% of session time. Design a graceful degradation architecture that switches between cloud and on-device modes transparently, with SLA targets of < 500ms cloud response and < 2s on-device response for a 50-token answer.
title: Designing a Resilient Agent Fallback Architecture for Intermittent Connectivity on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Assuming TTFT is dominated by model weight loading (already in memory) or generation (which hasn't started yet). The real culprit is prefill: processing the 2048-token prompt (system prompt + 3 retrieved docs + query) to build the KV cache before the first token can be generated.
details.napkin_math: Tensor G3: 7.5 TOPS. 1B INT8 prefill: each token requires 2 * num_params ops = 2B ops. 2048 tokens: 2048 * 2e9 = 4.096e12 ops. At 7.5e12 TOPS * 0.3 utilization = 2.25e12 effective TOPS: 4.096/2.25 = 1.82s prefill. Add retrieval pipeline: 300ms embed + 50ms search = 350ms. Total minimum: 2.17s. If 4.2s observed: 2.03s extra. Likely cause: model evicted from NPU cache (Tensor G3 NPU has limited persistent memory). Fix: keep-alive inference every 25s adds ~50ms overhead but prevents 2s cold-NPU penalty.
details.realistic_solution: Diagnose by timing: prefill of 2048 tokens at Tensor G3 7.5 TOPS. For 1B INT8 model (2B ops per forward token): 2048 tokens * 2B ops / 7.5e12 TOPS * efficiency_factor(0.3) = 2048 * 2e9 / (7.5e12 * 0.3) = 1.82s. Plus overhead: tokenization (50ms), document loading from SQLite (200ms), embedding for retrieval (300ms), FAISS search (50ms). Total: 50+200+300+50+1820=2420ms ≈ 2.4s for pipeline. If measured 4.2s: gap of 1.8s suggests cold model load from flash despite being 'in memory' — iOS/Android may have evicted model from GPU memory to CPU RAM. Fix: verify model is in GPU/NPU memory with a warm-up ping every 30s.

scenario: A Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) on-device RAG app shows time-to-first-token (TTFT) of 4.2 seconds despite the LLM being loaded into memory. Users experience a 4-second freeze before any text appears. The LLM is a 1B INT8 model with a 2048-token context. Retrieval returns 3 documents averaging 400 tokens each. Diagnose the root cause and propose a fix.
title: Diagnosing Slow First-Token Latency in On-Device RAG on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Assuming the app crashes due to a bug rather than a predictable context overflow. The developer adds error handling but doesn't compute when the context will fill — so they fix the crash symptom without addressing the root cause, and the app now silently truncates context instead.
details.napkin_math: Context budget: 2048 tokens. System prompt: 300. Remaining: 1748. Per turn (no retrieval): 50+150=200 tokens. Turns until full: 1748/200=8.74 ≈ 8 turns. Per turn (with retrieval): 50+150+600=800 tokens. Turns until full: 1748/800=2.19 ≈ 2 turns. Observed: 8-12 turns matches no-retrieval path — retrieval not firing each turn. Fix with compression: keep last 2 turns (400 tokens) + rolling summary (100 tokens) + system prompt (300) + retrieval slot (600) = 1400 tokens — leaves 648 token buffer. Sustainable indefinitely.
details.realistic_solution: Calculate context growth: per turn, tokens added = 50(user) + 150(assistant) + 600(3 retrieved chunks) = 800 tokens. System prompt: 300. After N turns: 300 + 800*N tokens. Context fills at 2048: N = (2048-300)/800 = 2.185 turns — fills after just 2 turns if retrieved context is included every turn! The observed 8-12 turns suggests retrieval is not always triggered. Without retrieval: (2048-300)/200 = 8.74 turns — matches the crash pattern. Fix: (1) Sliding window keeping last 2 turns verbatim + rolling summary. (2) Separate retrieval context from conversation context. (3) Compress old turns: each old turn summarized to 30 tokens.

scenario: An A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) conversational agent app crashes or produces incoherent outputs after 8-12 conversation turns. The on-device 1B LLM has a 2048-token context window. Each user turn averages 50 tokens, each assistant turn averages 150 tokens. System prompt is 300 tokens. Retrieved context per turn is 3 chunks of 200 tokens each. Diagnose when context overflow occurs and design a prevention strategy.
title: Diagnosing Context Overflow Failures in Multi-Turn Mobile Agents on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Assuming that a higher-dimension embedding model is always better, and failing to recognize that the FAISS index was built with v1 embeddings — making v2 query vectors incompatible with v1 document vectors. The cosine similarity between a v2 query vector and v1 document vectors is meaningless.
details.napkin_math: v2 re-embedding: 10,000 docs * (1/200 s/doc) = 50 seconds on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3. Memory during rebuild: v1 index (10K*256*4=10MB) + v2 index building (10K*384*4=15.4MB) + v2 model (larger, ~40MB INT8) = 65MB overhead — negligible on 16GB. Index swap: atomic rename of FAISS file (< 1ms). User impact window: 50s of degraded retrieval (v1 index with v2 queries). Mitigation: pre-build new index on backend, push as OTA update alongside model, swap atomically on first launch.
details.realistic_solution: Root cause: embedding space mismatch. v1 and v2 are different models with different learned projections — their vector spaces are not aligned. A v2 query vector searching a v1 index will return essentially random results (cosine similarity ~0 for unrelated vectors, not correlated with semantic similarity). Fix requires rebuilding the index with v2 embeddings. For 10K documents, re-embedding time on Snapdragon at 200 vecs/s (v2 model, larger): 10,000/200=50 seconds. Schedule index rebuild as a background task on first launch after update, serving from v1 index until complete, then atomic swap.

scenario: After an app update on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB), users report that the on-device assistant gives less relevant answers despite the LLM being unchanged. The update replaced the embedding model from a 256-dim model (v1) to a 384-dim model (v2) but kept the existing FAISS index built with v1 embeddings. Diagnose why retrieval quality degraded and quantify the impact.
title: Diagnosing Retrieval Quality Degradation After App Update on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Choosing Model C because it has the highest MRR without checking the memory constraint (66M * 4 bytes = 264MB — exceeds 100MB limit even before quantization) or the latency budget (5 * 80ms = 400ms > 200ms budget).
details.napkin_math: Memory: Model A INT8: 22M*1=22MB. Model B INT8: 33MB. Model C INT8: 66MB. All fit within 100MB. Latency: A: 5*25=125ms. B: 5*40=200ms. C: 5*80=400ms. Budget 200ms: A and B pass, C fails. Quality: B/A MRR ratio = 0.72/0.61=1.18 (18% improvement). B/C = 0.72/0.78=0.923 (7.7% worse than C). Model B gives 18% quality gain over A with same memory budget and exact latency compliance. Recommended: Model B with P95 validation.
details.realistic_solution: Eliminate Model C: 66M INT8 = 66MB (fits memory) but 5*80ms=400ms exceeds 200ms budget. Model A: 5*25ms=125ms (budget OK), 22MB INT8 (fits), MRR=0.61. Model B: 5*40ms=200ms (exactly at budget), 33MB INT8 (fits), MRR=0.72. Model B is optimal: 18% higher MRR than A at the exact budget limit. Validate Model B latency is P95 not mean — if 40ms is mean and P95 is 65ms, then 5*65ms=325ms exceeds budget. Use Model B with a 35ms per-embedding timeout (abort and use approximate result if exceeded) to guarantee budget compliance.

scenario: An A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) RAG app needs to choose between three embedding models: Model A (22M params, 128-dim, MRR@10=0.61, 25ms), Model B (33M params, 256-dim, MRR@10=0.72, 40ms), Model C (66M params, 384-dim, MRR@10=0.78, 80ms). The app performs 5 retrievals per user session. Evaluate which model maximizes quality within a 200ms retrieval budget per session and a 100MB memory limit for the embedding model.
title: Evaluating Embedding Model Quality vs Size Tradeoff on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Calculating speculative decoding speedup using cloud-hardware formulas and assuming linear speedup. On mobile, the 3B model runs in memory-bandwidth-bound regime — a single forward pass (1 token or 5 tokens verified) reads all 3B weights once. The speedup from speculative decoding comes only if multiple draft tokens are accepted without triggering additional full model passes.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 8 tok/s = 125ms/token. Draft model (68M): 125ms * (68M/3000M) = 2.83ms/token theoretical, actual 120 tok/s → 8.3ms. Per speculative step: generate 4 drafts in 4*8.3=33.2ms, verify with 3B in 125ms. Expected accepted tokens: sum_{i=0}^{4} alpha^i = (1-0.8^5)/(1-0.8) = 3.36. Effective throughput: 3.36 tokens / (33.2+125)ms = 3.36/158.2ms = 21.2 tok/s. Speedup: 21.2/8 = 2.65x. Memory overhead: 68M INT8 = 68MB additional — acceptable on 16GB.
details.realistic_solution: Speculative decoding speedup formula: expected speedup = (1 - α^(k+1)) / ((1-α) * (1 + k * cost_ratio)) where α=0.8 acceptance rate, k=4 draft tokens, cost_ratio = draft_model_time / target_model_time. Draft: 68M at 120 tok/s → 8.3ms per token. Target: 3B at 8 tok/s → 125ms per token. Cost ratio: 8.3/125 = 0.066. Expected accepted per step: (1-0.8^5)/(1-0.8) = (1-0.328)/0.2 = 3.36 tokens per verification. Time per step: 4*8.3ms + 125ms = 33.2+125 = 158.2ms for 3.36 tokens. Effective rate: 3.36/158.2ms = 21.2 tok/s — 2.65x speedup. Significant!

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) app runs a 3B LLM at 8 tok/s for compound AI generation. A team proposes speculative decoding using a 68M draft model (120 tok/s) with a target acceptance rate of 0.8 per draft token and 4 draft tokens per verification step. Evaluate whether speculative decoding provides a net speedup given the verification overhead on mobile hardware.
title: Evaluating Speculative Decoding Viability for On-Device LLM on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Assuming the satisfaction deficit is fully explained by multiplying stage metrics (0.83*0.79*0.88=0.578) and calling the 0.61 satisfaction 'consistent with expectations.' This ignores that the multiplication assumes independent error modes, when in practice errors compound in correlated ways — a bad retrieve leads to a confidently wrong LLM answer, which is worse than a random wrong answer.
details.napkin_math: Stage metrics: recall@5=0.83, NDCG@3=0.79, groundedness=0.88. Naive product: 0.83*0.79*0.88=0.578. Observed: 0.61. The product underestimates because satisfied queries can have imperfect individual stages (partial recall still useful). Error analysis: retrieval miss (17%) → ~0 satisfaction contribution: 0.17*0.1=0.017 satisfied from this bucket vs 0.17*1.0=0.17 possible → loss=0.153. This single stage accounts for 0.153/0.22=70% of the satisfaction gap. Improving recall@5 from 0.83 to 0.93 would recover 0.10 satisfaction units → estimated end-to-end: 0.71.
details.realistic_solution: Analyze error modes: (1) Retrieval miss (17% of queries): LLM receives irrelevant context, generates hallucinated answer — users rate these 0.1 satisfaction. Contribution: 0.17 * (1-0.1) = 0.153 satisfaction drag. (2) Reranker error (21% of remaining): correct doc retrieved but ranked below cutoff — LLM misses it. Contribution: 0.83 * 0.21 * 0.5 satisfaction drag = 0.087. (3) Grounding failure (12% remaining): LLM generates plausible but unsupported claims. 0.83*0.79*0.12 = 0.079 drag. Total drag: 0.153+0.087+0.079=0.319 from perfect 1.0 → theoretical max: 1-0.319=0.681. Observed 0.61 — additional 0.07 drag from response style issues (too verbose, wrong format). Primary fix target: retrieval recall (highest impact at 0.153).

scenario: A Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) on-device RAG system achieves individual stage metrics: retrieval recall@5=0.83, reranker NDCG@3=0.79, LLM groundedness=0.88 (fraction of claims traceable to retrieved docs). End-to-end user satisfaction (human eval on 100 queries) is only 0.61. Evaluate the gap between stage metrics and end-to-end quality and identify the most likely source of the 0.22 satisfaction deficit.
title: Evaluating End-to-End Compound Pipeline Quality on Tensor G3 with a RAG Evals Suite

details.common_mistake: Explaining RAG as just 'giving the LLM more information' without explaining the fundamental memory vs knowledge tradeoff. The developer needs to understand why on-device LLMs can't just have larger context windows, and why retrieval is a memory-efficient alternative to larger models.
details.napkin_math: Without RAG: 7B model INT4 = 7B * 0.5 bytes = 3.5GB. With RAG: 1B INT4 (500MB) + 10K docs (150MB) + FAISS index (10MB) = 660MB. Memory savings: 3.5GB vs 0.66GB = 5.3x more memory efficient. Quality: 1B with RAG on domain-specific queries ≈ 7B without RAG (retrieval substitutes for parametric knowledge). A17 Pro can run 660MB system within app memory budget; 3.5GB model would consume 43% of total 8GB RAM, risking iOS memory pressure kills.
details.realistic_solution: The retrieval step solves the knowledge-memory tradeoff: a 1B LLM on A17 Pro (500MB INT4) 'knows' general facts from training but cannot store app-specific knowledge (product catalog, user history, local data) in its weights — that would require a much larger model. Retrieval gives the LLM access to a dynamic, updatable knowledge base (10K docs = 150MB as text) without re-training. Without retrieval: need a 7B+ model to have equivalent factual coverage, which at INT4 = 3.5GB — more than the whole app memory budget. With retrieval: 1B model + 150MB knowledge base = 650MB total, and the knowledge can be updated without model retraining.

scenario: An iOS developer building their first on-device AI feature on A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) asks: 'My app uses Core ML for image recognition and a language model for descriptions. Why do I need a retrieval step? Can't I just give the image features directly to the LLM?' Explain why the retrieval stage exists in compound AI pipelines and what problem it solves on memory-constrained mobile devices.
title: Explaining Compound AI Pipeline Stages to a Mobile App Developer on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Explaining routing purely in abstract quality terms ('bigger models are slower') without giving the PM concrete numbers that make the tradeoff tangible. PMs need to understand the actual latency and battery impact to make product decisions.
details.napkin_math: 3B INT4 model: 200ms/query, 12W active. 125M INT8 model: 15ms/query, 3W active. Routing 60% to fast model: avg latency = 0.6*15+0.4*200=9+80=89ms vs 200ms (55% faster). Energy per query: routed = 0.6*(3W*0.015s)+0.4*(12W*0.2s)=0.027+0.96=0.987J vs always-3B: 2.4J (59% energy savings). Daily battery at 100 queries: routed=0.0274Wh, always-3B=0.0667Wh. At 500 queries: 0.137Wh vs 0.333Wh difference = 0.196Wh = ~1.3% battery on 14.8Wh battery.
details.realistic_solution: Concrete tradeoffs: (1) Battery: 3B LLM at 12W for 200ms/query = 2.4J. At 100 queries/day: 240J = 0.067Wh = 0.34% battery. Sounds small, but heavy users do 500 queries/day: 1200J = 1.7% battery. Simple queries (spell check, autocomplete) via 125M model at 2W * 20ms = 0.04J — 60x cheaper. (2) Latency: 3B model: 200ms. 125M model: 15ms. Users perceive < 100ms as instant. Routing 60% of queries to fast model: average latency = 0.6*15 + 0.4*200 = 89ms — under instant threshold. Always 3B: 200ms. (3) Thermal: sustained 3B usage triggers throttle in 90s. Routing buys 2.25x more sustained throughput.

scenario: A product manager on a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) app asks: 'Why can't we just always use the best, most powerful model for every request? Using different models for different query types sounds unnecessarily complex.' Explain the concrete tradeoffs that motivate model routing in on-device compound AI systems, using numbers from the hardware.
title: Explaining Model Routing Tradeoffs in Compound AI to a Product Manager

details.common_mistake: Explaining context window limits as a software choice or model architecture limitation, when on mobile the fundamental constraint is memory bandwidth for KV cache reads. Each decode step reads the entire KV cache — larger context = more data to read per token = slower generation.
details.napkin_math: Tensor G3: 7.5 TOPS. 1B model KV per token: 2*22*64*2=5,632 bytes = 5.5KB. 2048-token KV: 11.3MB. 128K-token KV: 704MB. Prefill at 2048: 2048*2*1B/(7.5e12*0.3)=1.82s. Prefill at 128K: 128000*2*1B/(7.5e12*0.3) = 113.8 seconds — clearly impractical. Decode step, reading full KV: 128K: 704MB/68GB/s=10.3ms → 97 tok/s bandwidth limited. At 2048: 11.3MB/68GB/s=0.17ms → nearly zero bandwidth overhead. Conclusion: 2048 token limit is a practical engineering constraint driven by prefill time, not arbitrary.
details.realistic_solution: Context window constraint on Tensor G3 has two causes: (1) Memory capacity: KV cache for 2048 tokens in a 1B model (22 layers, 64 head_dim, bf16): 2*22*64*2*2048 = 11.5MB. For 128K context: 2*22*64*2*128K = 724MB — consuming 6% of 12GB, feasible but expensive. (2) Bandwidth: decoding reads full KV cache each token step. At Tensor G3 memory bandwidth ~68GB/s: 724MB / 68GB/s = 10.6ms per decode step → 94 tok/s maximum bandwidth-limited throughput. The real constraint: 128K context * prefill compute = 128K * 2 * 1B ops / (7.5e12 * 0.3) = 114 seconds for prefill. On-device, 128K context = 2 minute wait before first token.

scenario: A junior developer building a Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) chatbot app is confused: 'The LLM API on cloud has 128K context window, but our on-device model only has 2048 tokens. Why is the context window so much smaller on mobile, and why does it matter for compound AI?' Explain the hardware basis for context window constraints and their implications for pipeline design.
title: Explaining Token Budget Constraints for Compound AI on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Attempting to stream before the retrieval and context preparation stages complete, resulting in the LLM generating without proper context (hallucinating) for the first few tokens. The streaming must start only after retrieval completes, but the 100ms retrieval+prep can be hidden with a UI skeleton state.
details.napkin_math: TTFT breakdown: retrieval(80ms) + context_prep(20ms) + prefill(73ms) = 173ms. Target: 200ms. Margin: 27ms. Generation: 100 tokens / 20 tok/s = 5.0s total. With streaming: user sees token 1 at 173ms, token 10 at 173+500ms=673ms, token 50 at 173+2500ms=2673ms. Perceived latency drops from 5.1s blank wait to 173ms TTFT — 29x perceived improvement. CoreML streaming API: token generation runs in background thread, dispatch_async to main queue for UI update, each update < 1ms UI overhead at 20 tok/s.
details.realistic_solution: Architecture: (1) Immediate UI feedback: show typing indicator within 16ms of query submission (single UI frame). (2) Retrieval + context prep: 80+20=100ms. (3) LLM prefill: 512-token context at A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 1B model): 512*2*1B/(35e12*0.4)=73ms. (4) First token generation: starts streaming immediately after prefill. Total TTFT: 100+73=173ms < 200ms target. (5) Implement CoreML streaming with token callback: each generated token triggers a Swift async callback that appends to the UI text view. Streaming ensures users see progress at 20 tok/s = 50ms per token, making the 5-second total feel interactive.

scenario: An A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) compound AI app runs a 3-stage pipeline: retrieval (80ms) → context preparation (20ms) → LLM generation (1B model, 20 tok/s, 100 tokens output = 5 seconds). Users perceive 5.1 seconds of silence before any response appears. Implement a streaming output architecture so that users see the first token within 200ms of submitting a query.
title: Implementing a Streaming Response Pipeline for Compound AI on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Running background indexing at full power (45 TOPS, 12W NPU), causing battery drain and triggering the Android background process killer when the app is not in focus. Background work on mobile must respect power budgets — typically < 2W sustained for background tasks.
details.napkin_math: 500 docs/day. Embedding: 200 vecs/s on NPU at 12W full power. Background constraint: 2W max. Duty cycle for 2W: 2W = d*12W + (1-d)*0.5W → 2 = 12d + 0.5 - 0.5d → 1.5 = 11.5d → d = 0.130. At 13% duty cycle: 200*0.13=26 vecs/s effective. 500 vecs: 500/26=19.2 seconds wall-clock. Index insert: 500 vectors in FAISS HNSW: ~50ms (negligible). Total sync time: ~20 seconds at 2W constraint. Acceptable: schedules in background, completes in 20s during screen-off periods.
details.realistic_solution: Background sync architecture: (1) Use WorkManager (Android) with battery-not-low constraint. (2) Throttle NPU to 30% duty cycle: embed for 2 seconds, sleep 4.7 seconds = 200 vecs/s * 2s = 400 docs/6.7s = 59.7 docs/min. 500 docs: 500/59.7 = 8.4 minutes total background time. (3) Power: 2s active at 8W (NPU 30%) + 4.7s at 0.5W (idle) = (16+2.35)/6.7 = 2.74W average — slightly over 2W. Reduce to 25% duty cycle: 2.5s/10s = 25%. 200*2.5=500 docs/10s/60=300 docs/min. 500 docs: 1.67 minutes. Power: 2.5*8+7.5*0.5=23.75/10=2.375W — acceptable.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) productivity app needs to keep an on-device FAISS index synchronized with the user's cloud document store (up to 500 new/updated docs per day). Re-embedding and indexing must happen in the background without impacting the foreground app. The embedding model runs at 200 vectors/second and each document averages 400 tokens. Design the background sync architecture with power and latency constraints.
title: Implementing Background Index Sync for On-Device RAG on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Treating each failure mode independently and adding per-stage retry logic without accounting for the multiplicative reliability problem: even with low per-stage failure rates, the compound system fails at a rate that is the sum of failure modes. Current system: 1 - (0.999 * 0.977 * 0.992 * 0.996 * 0.988) = 1 - 0.953 = 4.7% failure rate.
details.realistic_solution: Current failure rate: 4.7% (fails target by 4.2%). Per-stage mitigations: (1) Classifier crash: wrap in try-catch with default intent fallback (0.1% → 0.01% unhandled). (2) Empty retrieval: fallback to BM25 keyword search (2.3% → 0.3% still empty). (3) Reranker timeout: fallback to score-order from retrieval (0.8% → 0ms fallback, 0% timeout failure). (4) LLM policy violation: retry with stronger safety prompt (0.4% → 0.04% after retry). (5) False-positive filter: add confidence threshold, only block if score > 0.95 (1.2% → 0.2%). New compound rate: 1-(0.9999*0.997*1.0*0.9996*0.998) = 1-0.9945 = 0.55% failure → 99.45% success. Need one more fix to reach 99.5%: add global retry for empty response: 99.45% → 99.72%.

scenario: An A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) compound AI app runs a 5-stage pipeline: intent classifier → retrieval → reranker → LLM → output filter. Each stage has an independent failure mode. Field data shows: classifier crashes 0.1% of requests, retrieval returns empty 2.3% of the time, reranker times out 0.8% of requests, LLM produces policy-violating content 0.4% of the time, output filter false-positives 1.2% of safe responses. Design a reliability architecture that achieves 99.5% successful response rate.
title: Mastering Compound AI System Reliability Engineering on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Applying standard latency optimizations (quantization, batch size tuning) to each stage independently without restructuring the pipeline. The 3B LLM at 2550ms for 80 tokens is memory-bandwidth-bound — quantization from FP16 to INT4 doubles throughput but only reduces to 1275ms, still leaving the total at 2525ms, far from the 1.5s target.
details.napkin_math: Original: 400+250+600+2550=3800ms. Step 1 parallel OCR+embed: embed=50ms, OCR=400ms, parallel=400ms. Retrieval after embed: +200ms (previously part of 250ms). Step 2 rerank 8 docs: 600*(8/20)=240ms. Step 3 INT4 LLM: 2550/2=1275ms. Step 4 40 tokens: 1275*(40/80)=637ms. Step 5 pipeline overlap (80ms saved): not counting for conservative estimate. Critical path: 400(OCR||embed) + 200(retrieval) + 240(rerank) + 637(LLM) = 1477ms. P95 with 5% jitter: 1477*1.05=1551ms — slightly over. Remove jitter with 35 tokens: 1477*(35/40)... recalc LLM: 35/80*1275=557ms. Total: 400+200+240+557=1397ms. P95: 1467ms < 1500ms.
details.realistic_solution: Multi-pronged restructuring: (1) Parallelize OCR + query embedding: if OCR result not needed for embedding, run concurrently: max(400,50)=400ms (embedding is fast, runs on NPU while OCR runs on CPU). (2) Reduce reranker candidates from 20 to 8 docs: 600ms*(8/20)=240ms. (3) INT4 LLM: 2550/2=1275ms. (4) Reduce generation from 80 to 40 tokens: 1275/2=637ms. (5) Pipeline overlap: start LLM prefill while reranker completes last 2 docs (speculative prefill): saves 80ms. Restructured: parallel(OCR+embed)=400ms, retrieval(200ms, after embed), rerank-8(240ms), LLM-40tok-INT4(637ms), with OCR→retrieval→rerank→LLM as critical path: 400+200+240+637=1477ms < 1500ms target.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) compound AI system currently processes queries in 3.8 seconds: OCR (400ms) → embedding+retrieval (250ms) → cross-encoder reranking of 20 docs (600ms) → 3B LLM generation of 80 tokens (2550ms). The target is 1.5 seconds P95. Design a comprehensive optimization strategy that achieves this target without changing models or hardware.
title: Mastering End-to-End Optimization of a 4-Stage Compound Pipeline on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Updating the FAISS index atomically by taking a write lock while the user is querying, causing the retrieval stage to block for up to 50*(1/150)=333ms during an active session. Users experience random 333ms pauses mid-conversation.
details.napkin_math: Daily update: 50 docs. Re-embed at 150 vecs/s: 50/150=0.33s at full NPU. FAISS HNSW add 50 vectors: ~5ms. Total update work: 335ms active NPU time. Battery: 5W (NPU INT8 at 7.5 TOPS) * 0.335s = 1.675J = 0.000465Wh per day. Negligible vs 12Wh battery. Flat index overhead per query: 50 vectors * 256 dims * 4 bytes = 51KB, search time 0.5ms. Combined HNSW(2000 docs) + flat(50): 5ms + 0.5ms = 5.5ms (vs 5ms baseline — 10% overhead). Shadow build on background: 0.33s * 10 = 3.3s wall-clock at 10% duty.
details.realistic_solution: Copy-on-write index with shadow update: (1) Maintain active index (read-only, served from mmap). (2) Background thread builds shadow index by cloning active index and adding new vectors. (3) When shadow is complete, atomic pointer swap (< 1ms). (4) During active use: queue incoming updates in a tiny flat index (max 50 entries = 50*256*4=51KB). Serve queries from: active_index + flat_pending_index, merge results. (5) Shadow build schedule: when screen-off for > 30s or charging, at 10% NPU duty cycle. 50 docs at 150 vecs/s full power: 50/150=0.33s. At 10% duty: 3.3s background wall-clock. Battery: 10% * 5W NPU * 3.3s = 1.65J = 0.00046Wh — negligible. Active-use overhead: flat index search on 50 docs = 0.5ms — imperceptible.

scenario: A Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) enterprise mobile app serves 10,000 users with personalized on-device RAG. Each user has a local corpus of 2,000 documents. The enterprise syncs 50 new/updated documents per user per day via MDM push. The embedding model (256-dim, INT8, 22MB) runs at 150 vecs/s on Tensor G3 NPU. Design a knowledge base update strategy that maintains retrieval quality, minimizes battery impact, and handles the case where updates arrive while the user is actively using the app.
title: Mastering On-Device Knowledge Base Update Strategy for Compound AI on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Assuming larger chunks are always better for quality. Larger chunks improve context coherence but reduce retrieval precision (the relevant passage is diluted by irrelevant content in the same chunk), and they consume more of the limited context window, leaving less room for the LLM's response.
details.napkin_math: 256-token chunks: 5 chunks * 256 = 1280 tokens context. LLM response budget: 2048-1280-100(query)=668 tokens. Index size: N_chunks * 256 * 4 bytes (unchanged by chunk size for same N_docs). 512-token chunks: N_docs/2 chunks (half as many), each 512 tokens. 5 chunks * 512 = 2560 > 2048 limit. Top-3 only: 3*512=1536 tokens. Response budget: 2048-1536-100=412 tokens. Quality impact: fewer retrieved chunks (3 vs 5) but larger context per chunk. Empirically: precision@3 with 512-token chunks ≈ precision@5 with 256-token chunks for most corpora. Recommendation: test both; if no quality gain, keep 256 for larger response budget.
details.realistic_solution: Impact analysis: FAISS index with 512-token chunks (vs 256): same document count = same index size (embeddings don't change with chunk content size, only with model output dim). Context consumption: 5 chunks * 512 tokens = 2560 tokens — exceeds 2048 context window! Must reduce to top-3 chunks: 3*512=1536 tokens, leaving 512 tokens for query+response. With 256 tokens: 5*256=1280 tokens, leaving 768 tokens. Precision: larger chunks typically reduce precision@k as relevant content is buried. Quality model: 256-token chunks with 5 retrieved is often better than 512 with 3. Consider hybrid: 256-token retrieval + re-expand to neighboring chunks for top-2 results only.

scenario: An A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) RAG app chunks documents into 256-token chunks for retrieval. The LLM context window is 2048 tokens. Retrieval returns top-5 chunks. Currently: retrieval precision@5=0.74 and generation quality score=0.71. A team proposes increasing chunk size to 512 tokens to improve context coherence. Calculate the memory and latency impact and determine whether the quality improvement justifies the cost.
title: Optimizing Retrieval Chunk Size for On-Device RAG on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Calculating only the prefill savings without accounting for the compression model's own latency. If compression takes 120ms and saves 534ms of prefill, the net gain is 414ms — but teams often forget that the compression model also requires its own prefill and compute on the mobile NPU, and that compression quality may reduce answer accuracy.
details.napkin_math: Baseline prefill: 1200 tokens * (1B * 2 ops/token) / (45e12 * 0.3) = 1200 * 2e9 / 1.35e13 = 178ms... discrepancy with 890ms stated. The 890ms likely includes attention O(n^2) cost: attention per layer = n^2 * d per layer. For 1B model, 22 layers, d=64: 22 * 1200^2 * 64 = 2.03e9 ops. Total ops: 1200 * 2e9 + 2.03e9 = 2.403e12. At 1.35e13: 178ms — still doesn't match 890ms. Accept stated 890ms as empirical (includes memory bandwidth bottleneck at LPDDR5). Compression: 800→320 tokens context. New prefill estimate: 890 * (720/1200) = 534ms. With 120ms compression overhead: 654ms. Net savings: 890-654=236ms (26.5%).
details.realistic_solution: After compression: retrieved context = 800*0.4=320 tokens. New prefill: 320+300+100=720 tokens. Prefill scales approximately linearly with tokens (for transformer attention: O(n^2) but for inference with KV cache build: O(n) per layer). 720/1200 * 890ms = 534ms prefill. Add compression model: 50M INT8 = 50MB, runs on NPU at ~500ms for processing 800 tokens (50M * 800 * 2 ops / (45e12 * 0.3) = 2.37ms... that's too fast — LLMLingua processes tokens with attention, closer to 120ms as stated). Net: compression(120ms) + prefill(534ms) = 654ms vs baseline 890ms. Savings: 236ms (26.5%). Worthwhile if accuracy loss < 3%.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) RAG app uses 800-token retrieved context (4 chunks of 200 tokens each) + 300-token system prompt + 100-token query = 1200-token prefill. Prefill of 1200 tokens with a 1B INT8 model takes 890ms. A prompt compression model (LLMLingua-style, 50M params) can compress the retrieved context to 40% of original size in 120ms. Calculate the net latency improvement and decide whether compression is worthwhile.
title: Optimizing Prefill Latency via Prompt Compression on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Trying to reduce per-call LLM inference time (already at hardware limit) instead of reducing the number of calls through better planning. The LLM reasoning step at 400ms is already close to optimal for a 1B model on Tensor G3 — shaving 50ms saves only 12.5% energy.
details.napkin_math: Baseline: 6 calls * 3.55J/call = 21.3J per task. 40% reduction target: 21.3 * 0.6 = 12.78J. Strategy: parallel dispatch saves 1.5 calls → 4.5 calls * 3.55J = 15.98J (25% reduction). Plus caching (25% hit): 4.5 * 0.75 calls * 3.55J = 11.99J (44% reduction — exceeds target). Daily tasks: 20 tasks. Baseline: 20*21.3J=426J=0.118Wh. Optimized: 20*11.99J=239.8J=0.0666Wh. Savings: 0.0517Wh/day on 15Wh battery = 0.34% battery per 20 tasks. At heavy use (100 tasks/day): 2.59Wh → 1.46Wh savings = 1.13Wh = 7.5% daily battery saved.
details.realistic_solution: Reduce tool call count from 6 to 3.6 average (40% reduction achieves 40% energy target). Strategies: (1) Parallel tool dispatch: when the LLM decides to call tools A and B sequentially, dispatch both simultaneously when they have no data dependency. Reduces 2 calls to 1 wall-clock call, saving 1 LLM decision step. Average parallelizable pairs per task: 1.5 → saves 1.5 calls: 6→4.5. (2) Tool result caching: cache sensor reads and database queries for 60 seconds. Cache hit rate ~25% for typical task patterns: 4.5*0.75=3.375 effective calls. (3) Multi-action responses: prompt the LLM to batch multiple actions into one response: reduce by additional 10%. Final: ~3.0 calls/task. Energy: 3.0*3.55=10.65J = 50% reduction (exceeds 40% target).

scenario: A Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) agentic app makes an average of 6 tool calls per user task. Each tool call: LLM reasoning step to decide tool (400ms, 8W) + tool execution (50ms, 1W) + result parsing (100ms, 3W). Total per task: 6 * 550ms = 3.3s, energy = 6*(8*0.4+1*0.05+3*0.1)=6*(3.2+0.05+0.3)=6*3.55=21.3J. Battery: 15Wh=54,000J. Reduce agent energy by 40% without changing the task quality.
title: Optimizing Agent Tool-Call Frequency to Reduce Battery Drain on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Loading all three CoreML models simultaneously and keeping them all in ANE memory, then being surprised when iOS evicts one model mid-inference due to memory pressure. CoreML models loaded with MLModelConfiguration computeUnits=.all compete for ANE SRAM, and the ANE has limited persistent model storage compared to the NPU on Android.
details.napkin_math: Model sizes: vision(25MB) + text(100MB) + generative(300MB) = 425MB models. Add runtime buffers: activations ~75MB peak. Total peak: 500MB < 600MB budget. Load times from NVMe: vision: 25MB/3GB/s=8ms, text: 100MB/3GB/s=33ms, generative: 300MB/3GB/s=100ms. ANE inference: vision ResNet-50 (4.1B MACs) at 35 TOPS: 4.1e9*2/(35e12*0.5)=0.47ms. Text MobileBERT (580M MACs) at 35 TOPS: 0.033ms. GPT-2-medium generation: 345M params INT4 (173MB effective): bandwidth-limited at ANE 100GB/s: 173MB/100GB/s=1.7ms/token → ~588 tok/s. 100 tokens: 170ms.
details.realistic_solution: Sequential loading with explicit unload: (1) At app launch, load vision encoder only (25MB, fast: ~50ms from flash). Process camera input. (2) Unload vision encoder (MLModel = nil, trigger ARC dealloc). (3) Load text encoder (100MB, ~200ms). Process text. (4) Lazy load generative model on demand (300MB, ~600ms). Total at-rest: 25MB (if only vision active). Peak: 100+300=400MB during NLP+generation. With 100MB overhead: 500MB peak, within 600MB budget. CoreML tip: use MLModelConfiguration with computeUnits = .cpuAndNeuralEngine to allow ANE fallback to CPU for memory pressure situations.

scenario: An iOS developer needs to deploy a 3-model compound AI pipeline on A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS ANE) using CoreML: a vision encoder (ResNet-50, 25MB), a text encoder (MobileBERT, 100MB INT8), and a generative model (GPT-2-medium, 300MB INT4). All three must run within a single app process with a total memory budget of 600MB. Describe the CoreML-specific implementation approach including model loading strategy and ANE scheduling.
title: Realizing a Compound AI App with CoreML Multi-Model Orchestration on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Serializing the full agent state including model weights and KV cache to disk on every background event. Model weights don't need saving (they're in the APK/assets), but teams try to serialize the KV cache (which can be 50MB+) causing 500ms+ writes that delay the background transition.
details.napkin_math: State size: 2+16+50+15.4=83.4KB. Write latency: 83.4KB/3GB/s=0.028ms. KV cache size (not persisted): 4000 tokens * 40KB/token = 160MB — too large to persist (160MB/3GB/s=53ms write + 53ms read = 106ms just for I/O, plus 100ms deserialization = 206ms acceptable, but 160MB as volatile state). Decision: persist only conversation text (83.4KB), rebuild KV via truncated prefill. Prefill 712-token history: 712*2*1B/(45e12*0.3)=105.5ms. Total resume path: DB read(0.03ms) + prefill(105ms) + warm-up(50ms) = 155ms < 500ms.
details.realistic_solution: Serialize only the lightweight state: task_plan(2KB) + conversation_history_as_text(16KB) + tool_results(50KB) + query_embeddings(15.4KB) = 83.4KB total. Write to SharedPreferences or Room DB on every state change (not just on background). On resume: (1) Read state from DB: 83.4KB at 3GB/s NVMe = 0.028ms — negligible. (2) KV cache is NOT persisted — rebuild by running prefill on restored conversation history. Prefill 4000 tokens at Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: 4000*2*1B/(45e12*0.3)=592ms — too slow. Alternative: store only last 512 tokens verbatim and summarized older turns (200 tokens). Prefill 712 tokens: 105ms. Total resume: 0.028+105=105ms well within 500ms.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) agentic app loses its multi-step task state when the user switches apps. The agent maintains: current task plan (JSON, 2KB), conversation history (20 turns, ~4000 tokens as text = 16KB), intermediate tool results (up to 50KB), and FAISS query context (10 recent query embeddings, 10*384*4=15.4KB). Android may kill the app process when backgrounded. Implement state persistence that allows the agent to resume within 500ms of returning to the foreground.
title: Realizing On-Device Agent State Persistence Across App Backgrounding on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Sending the raw retrieved document chunks to the cloud API without truncating them to fit the API's token limits and without removing any personally identifiable information (PII) that was intentionally kept on-device. The privacy-preserving design is violated if full document text is sent to the cloud.
details.napkin_math: On-device path: embed(133ms) + FAISS(5ms) + LLM prefill(224ms) + generate 50 tokens(6.25s) = 6.6s. Cloud path: embed(133ms) + FAISS(5ms) + PII scrub(2ms) + network(80ms) + cloud_gen(200ms) = 420ms. Cloud is 15.7x faster for same 50-token output. Battery: on-device LLM: 5W * 6.25s = 31.25J. Cloud: 5W*0.138s(embed+search) + 0.1W*0.282s(network idle) = 0.69+0.028=0.718J. Cloud saves 97.7% energy per query. Route to cloud whenever battery < 50% and network available — saves significant battery.
details.realistic_solution: Context sanitization before cloud offload: (1) PII scrubbing: run a fast regex + small classifier (5M model, 2ms) to detect and redact PII from retrieved chunks before cloud transmission. (2) Truncation to API budget: max 2000 tokens to keep API cost low. (3) Decision logic: route to cloud if: battery > 30% AND network_rtt < 200ms AND query_sensitivity_score < 0.5 (non-sensitive per classifier). On-device otherwise. State handoff: for cloud path, send sanitized_context + query + system_prompt (total < 2000 tokens). For on-device, send full retrieved context (no sanitization needed). Results are identical format — UI renders same way.

scenario: A Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) app implements a hybrid compound AI pipeline: on-device embedding+retrieval (always local for privacy), with LLM generation either on-device (1B, 8 tok/s) or cloud-offloaded (GPT-4-class, 100ms+generation). The switching decision happens per-query. Network RTT to cloud API is 80ms. Implement the decision logic and state handoff to ensure the correct context is available on whichever path executes.
title: Realizing a Hybrid On-Device and Cloud Compound AI Pipeline on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Conflating the embedding model and the generative LLM as 'the same kind of model' because both are transformer-based. They have fundamentally different architectures (encoder-only vs decoder-only) and different roles: the embedding model produces fixed-size dense vectors for similarity search; the LLM produces variable-length text tokens.
details.napkin_math: Memory footprint on A17 Pro: Query encoder (22MB INT8) + FAISS index (10K docs, 256-dim: 10MB) + Document store (10K * 2KB avg = 20MB) + Reranker (22MB INT8, optional) + Context buffer (2048 tokens * 4 bytes = 8MB) + LLM 1B INT4 (500MB) = 582MB total. Well within 8GB. Latency budget: query_encode(15ms) + FAISS(3ms) + doc_fetch(2ms) + rerank(30ms) + context_assemble(1ms) + LLM_prefill(73ms) + LLM_decode_50tok(2.5s) = 2.624s total.
details.realistic_solution: Standard on-device RAG pipeline: (1) Query Encoder: bi-encoder transformer (e.g., MobileBERT) converts user query to a dense vector (e.g., 256-dim float32). Output: query embedding. (2) Vector Index (FAISS): approximate nearest-neighbor search over document embeddings. Output: top-K document IDs + similarity scores. (3) Document Store: SQLite or flat files storing the actual document text indexed by ID. Output: top-K document text chunks. (4) Reranker (optional): cross-encoder scores query against each retrieved chunk. Output: reranked, filtered chunks. (5) Context Assembly: concatenates system prompt + retrieved chunks + query into LLM input. Output: formatted prompt string. (6) Generative LLM: autoregressive decoder generates response token by token. Output: response text.

scenario: A junior mobile ML engineer at a company deploying an AI assistant on A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) asks: 'What are the standard components in an on-device RAG pipeline, and what does each one do?' List and define the standard pipeline components, their sequence, and the output of each stage.
title: Recalling Compound AI Pipeline Components and Their Roles on Mobile

details.common_mistake: Allocating the 1.5s budget equally across all 5 stages (300ms each) without considering that some stages have inherently lower variance (deterministic FAISS search) while others have higher variance (LLM prefill depends on actual token count). Equal allocation wastes headroom in deterministic stages and under-allocates for variable stages.
details.napkin_math: TTFT = sum of stage latencies. P95 allocation with 1500ms total (including first token generation ~100ms): remaining 1400ms for pre-generation stages. Allocation by stage variance: embedding(25ms) + FAISS(5ms) + reranker(50ms) + assembly(5ms) + prefill(400ms) = 485ms P95 pipeline. First token: prefill completes at 485ms, first generated token adds ~50ms (1 decode step) = 535ms TTFT P95 — well within 1500ms target. Remaining 965ms budget allows 965ms/50ms = 19 additional tokens before 1.5s. For streaming UX: user sees first token at 535ms, then 20 tok/s stream.
details.realistic_solution: Variance-aware budget allocation: stages with deterministic runtime get tight P95/P99 envelopes; variable stages get wider. Allocation: embedding(P50=15ms, P95=25ms, P99=35ms), FAISS(P50=3ms, P95=5ms, P99=8ms), reranker(P50=30ms, P95=50ms, P99=70ms), context_assembly(P50=2ms, P95=5ms, P99=8ms), LLM prefill(P50=200ms, P95=400ms, P99=550ms). Sum P95: 25+5+50+5+400=485ms. Total TTFT P95 budget: 485ms + generation budget (streaming starts after prefill). Error budget per stage: 5% miss rate, compounded: stage_SLO_compliance = 95% each → pipeline P95: 0.95^5=77.4% — too low. Must target 99% per stage: pipeline P95: 0.99^5=95.1% → meets 95th percentile system SLO.

scenario: You are writing the technical specification for a 5-stage compound AI pipeline on A17 Pro (8GB, 35 TOPS) targeting a 1.5-second time-to-first-token SLA. Stages are: query embedding, FAISS retrieval, reranking, context assembly, and LLM prefill. Write quantitative per-stage SLOs including P50, P95, and P99 latency targets, and specify the error budget — the fraction of requests each stage is permitted to miss its SLO.
title: Specifying Latency SLO Contracts for Each Stage of a Mobile Compound Pipeline on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Implementing rollback at the infrastructure level (pulling the OTA update) without considering that devices download updates asynchronously — by the time a quality regression is detected, 30-90% of the fleet may have already updated, and rollback requires pushing another large OTA (500MB LLM) to affected devices.
details.napkin_math: Fleet: 500,000 devices. OTA sizes: embedding(33MB) + reranker(22MB) + LLM(500MB) = 555MB per update. Keep 1 prior version: +555MB storage per device. Canary (0.1%): 500 devices. Detection latency: 30 minutes of quality data collection. If alert fires at 30min: rollout stopped at 0.1% adoption. Without canary: at 30min, ~15% fleet (75,000 devices) might have updated via background download. Rollback OTA: 500MB LLM to 75,000 devices = 37.5TB of rollback data at $0.09/GB CDN cost = $3,375 in CDN costs avoided. Local rollback via kill-switch: 0 bytes — instant, $0 CDN.
details.realistic_solution: Staged rollout specification: (1) Canary phase (0-1h): deploy to 0.1% of fleet (500 devices). Collect automated quality signals: coherence score (lightweight judge model running locally), user thumbs-down rate, latency P95. Alert threshold: if thumbs-down rate increases > 2% or coherence drops > 5% relative to baseline, halt rollout automatically. (2) Each device maintains previous model version (1GB total for current + prior LLM): enables local instant rollback without re-download. (3) Kill-switch: server-side feature flag forces devices to use prior version within 60 seconds of flag change — no OTA required for rollback. (4) Rollback trigger: automated at 30-minute mark if quality metrics breach threshold in canary group.

scenario: A Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB) compound AI app ships model updates OTA (over-the-air) for its 3-model pipeline: embedding model (33MB), reranker (22MB), LLM (500MB INT4). A bad LLM update caused a 15% increase in user-reported incoherent responses on 500,000 devices before detection. Write a specification for a safe model update and rollback protocol that can detect quality regressions and roll back within 1 hour of deployment.
title: Specifying Model Update and Rollback Contract for Compound AI on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Storing raw keystrokes including passwords and sensitive data; not applying differential privacy before on-device storage.
details.napkin_math: 500MB budget. User types 200 words/day = 1,200 keystrokes/day. Store 4-gram counts: English has ~500K frequent 4-grams. Per gram count: 4 chars + 4 byte count = 8 bytes. 500K × 8 = 4MB for n-gram model. Can store 30 days of n-gram counts: 30 × 4MB = 120MB. Training data conversion: n-gram to sequence pairs, 1M pairs × 16 bytes = 16MB. Total: 136MB well within 500MB. DP noise: add Laplace(0, 1/ε) = Laplace(0, 0.5) to each count, ensuring privacy at ε=2.0.
details.realistic_solution: Collect: n-gram statistics not raw keystrokes. Filter: exclude password fields (type=password), URLs, and short sessions (< 20 keystrokes). Store: DP-noised n-gram counts with ε=2.0. Convert to training examples only at training time. Delete after training.

scenario: You are building a personalized keyboard model that trains on-device on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM). The model learns from user typing patterns. Design the data collection, quality filtering, and privacy-preserving local storage pipeline. The device has 500MB available for training data.
title: Dataset Curation: Design On-Device Data Collection for Mobile Model Training

details.common_mistake: Assuming cloud curation always produces higher quality labels; not accounting for privacy implications of photo upload.
details.napkin_math: Cloud approach: 1,000 photos × 5MB avg = 5GB upload per user. At home WiFi 100Mbps: 400 seconds = 6.7 minutes. Cost: $50 labeling + $0.45 storage/year per user. At 1M users: $50M labeling cost — infeasible. On-device: zero marginal cost per user. Label quality comparison: user selection precision ~70% (subjective), expert labels ~95% agreement. Hybrid: on-device filter to 200 images, upload 200 × 5MB = 1GB, cost $10/user. At 1M users = $10M — still large. Best: on-device implicit feedback (swipe left/right) as labels, zero cost.
details.realistic_solution: On-device: privacy-preserving, zero upload cost, but labels are implicit (user kept/deleted), biased toward user preference not aesthetic quality. Cloud: expert labels, better quality, but $0.05/label × 1000 = $50/user, privacy risk, 24h latency. Hybrid: on-device pre-filter + upload only edge cases.

scenario: You are deciding between two approaches for curating training data for a photo enhancement model on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM): (A) on-device: user selects 'good' photos, model trains locally; (B) cloud: upload 1,000 photos, human curators label quality, download curated dataset. Evaluate on privacy, latency, label quality, and cost.
title: Dataset Curation: Evaluate On-Device vs Cloud Data Curation for Mobile ML

details.common_mistake: Using vanilla FedAvg without measuring heterogeneity; assuming gradient aggregation handles non-IID automatically.
details.napkin_math: 1M devices, 50 languages, avg 20K devices per language. FedAvg accuracy degradation model: for KL divergence D, accuracy drop ≈ 2% × D. Measured KL between language groups: ~3.0. Expected drop: 6% accuracy. FedProx (μ=0.1): reduces effective KL by ~40% → 3.6% drop. Clustered federated (50 language clusters): each cluster is nearly IID → < 1% drop. Cost of clustering: 50 separate aggregation servers vs 1. Storage: 50 × model_size. For 100M param model at bf16 = 200MB per cluster: 50 × 200MB = 10GB — acceptable.
details.realistic_solution: Measure heterogeneity: compute KL divergence between per-device token distributions and global. High KL (>1.0) indicates severe non-IID. FedAvg degrades significantly: 5-15% accuracy drop vs IID. Mitigation: SCAFFOLD, FedProx, or cluster-and-federate by language group.

scenario: You run federated learning for a language model across 1M Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB) devices. Device data is highly non-IID: users in different countries have different language distributions. Evaluate the impact of data heterogeneity on global model quality and propose a mitigation strategy.
title: Dataset Curation: Evaluate Federated Data Heterogeneity Impact on Mobile Model Quality

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for activation memory during backprop, or assuming Neural Engine supports training (it's inference-only — training runs on CPU/GPU cores).
details.napkin_math: 500 examples × 128 tokens = 64K tokens total. LoRA fine-tuning: 1M trainable params. A17 Pro CPU: ~100 GFLOPS for training. 6 FLOPs/token × 64K tokens × 3 epochs = 1.15M FLOPs. Time: 1.15M / 100G = trivial. Memory: 1B × 2B (fp16 weights) = 2GB + LoRA = 2.01GB + optimizer (AdamW): 2 × 1M × 4B = 8MB + activations (batch=1): 128 × 2048 × 4B = 1MB. Total: ~2.02GB, fits in 8GB. Fine-tuning on device: < 1 second. Practical bottleneck: data loading from encrypted storage.
details.realistic_solution: A17 Pro Neural Engine is inference-only. Fine-tuning must use CPU or GPU cores. Use LoRA to reduce trainable parameters. 1B model in fp16 = 2GB weights. LoRA rank-8 adds ~0.1% params = 1M trainable params.

scenario: On an A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM), you want to fine-tune a 1B parameter language model for personalization using 500 user-generated examples of average 128 tokens each. Estimate the total fine-tuning compute, memory required, and time to complete.
title: Dataset Curation: Fluency — Token Budget for On-Device Fine-Tuning on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Using the same noise multiplier for all batch sizes without accounting for subsampling amplification; not tracking privacy budget across rounds.
details.napkin_math: DP-SGD parameters: target ε=1.0, δ=1/10M=1e-7, T=100 rounds. Subsampling rate q = 10K/10M = 0.001. Using RDP accountant: noise multiplier σ ≈ 1.1 achieves ε=1.0 at T=100 rounds with q=0.001 (from Opacus library tables). Clipping: C=1.0 (gradient norm clipping). Per-gradient noise: σ×C = 1.1 added to each of N gradient coordinates. For 1M param LoRA model: add N(0, 1.1²) to each coordinate. Communication overhead: noise vectors same size as gradients — zero overhead. Privacy cost check: 100 rounds × RDP(α=8) ≈ 0.01 per round → total ε ≈ 0.8 < 1.0. Verified.
details.realistic_solution: DP-SGD: clip per-sample gradients to C=1.0, add Gaussian noise σ=C×noise_multiplier. Use Moments Accountant or RDP for privacy accounting. Subsampling: if 10K devices participate per round from 10M, sampling rate q=0.001 — provides strong amplification.

scenario: You are implementing differential privacy for federated data collection on 10M Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB) devices. Each device contributes gradients after local training on user data. Implement DP-SGD with ε=1.0 and calculate the noise scale required, clipping threshold, and privacy accounting.
title: Dataset Curation: Implement Privacy-Preserving Data Collection on Snapdragon

details.common_mistake: Aggregating gradients from different model versions directly — incompatible gradient spaces. Not maintaining per-device data provenance for debugging.
details.napkin_math: 5M devices, 3 model versions: v1=20% (1M), v2=30% (1.5M), v3=50% (2.5M). Round participation: only v3 devices = 2.5M eligible. Sample 10% per round = 250K devices. Version broadcast: send model v3 to 1M v1 + 1.5M v2 = 2.5M devices. Model size 100M params fp16 = 200MB. Total download: 2.5M × 200MB = 500TB per version update cycle. Delta update (only changed layers): 10MB delta × 2.5M = 25TB. At CDN cost $0.01/GB: 25TB = $250K per update. Frequency: monthly updates = $3M/year. Optimize: binary delta patching, 1MB deltas → $10K/month.
details.realistic_solution: Use version-gated participation: only devices with model version N participate in round N training. Version metadata stored in 4 bytes per device. Stale devices receive model update before participating. Data provenance: hash of local dataset state per round.

scenario: You run federated learning updates on 5M Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) devices. Each device may be on a different model version (v1, v2, v3). Implement a data versioning protocol that allows aggregating gradients from mixed model versions and tracks which data was used for which training round.
title: Dataset Curation: Implement Data Versioning for Mobile Federated Learning

details.common_mistake: Not tracking DP budget across rounds; assuming all devices can participate every round; not designing for heterogeneous hardware.
details.napkin_math: 1B users × 12 rounds. DP budget: ε=1.0/year, 12 rounds → ε≈0.083/round. q=100K/1B=0.0001 sampling rate → strong amplification allows σ≈0.5 noise multiplier. Gradient upload: 1M LoRA params × fp16 = 2MB/device, compressed 10× = 200KB. 100K devices × 200KB = 20GB/round. Monthly bandwidth cost: 20GB × $0.01/GB = $0.20/round = $2.40/year. Training time on Snapdragon: LoRA forward+backward on 200 local examples, 128 tokens each: 200×128 × 1M params × 6 FLOPs = 153.6B FLOPs. At 45 TOPS: 3.4 seconds/update. Fits in background window. A17 Pro: 35 TOPS → 4.4 seconds. Both acceptable.
details.realistic_solution: 12 monthly rounds, ε=1.0 total → ε=0.083/round using composition. 1B devices: sample 0.01% = 100K/round. On-device: DP local training with clipping + noise. Gradient compression 100×. Server: secure aggregation. Hardware heterogeneity: unified LoRA interface across NPUs.

scenario: You are the ML lead for a keyboard app with 1B users across iOS (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS) and Android (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 45 TOPS). Design the complete on-device personalization data strategy: collection, privacy, local curation, federated aggregation, and global model updates. The system must maintain ε=1.0 DP per year with monthly updates.
title: Dataset Curation: Mastery — On-Device Personalization Data Strategy for 1B Mobile Users

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for sensor synchronization jitter; treating health data as non-sensitive; not applying purpose limitation.
details.napkin_math: Accelerometer: 100Hz × 3 × 4B = 1.2KB/sec. HR: 1Hz × 4B = 4B/sec. Mic (raw): 16K Hz × 2B = 32KB/sec. 24h raw: acc=103MB, HR=345KB, mic=2.76GB. Total raw/day=2.86GB — too large. Processed: event windows only (10-sec windows around anomalies). Assume 10 events/day × 10sec = 100sec. Acc window: 100sec × 1.2KB/s = 120KB. Mic MFCC features: 100sec × 40 features × 10Hz = 400KB. HR: 100B. Total per event: 520KB × 10 = 5.2MB/day. 30-day buffer: 156MB. Model training: 30 days × 10 events = 300 examples × 3 modalities × 10sec. Fits in 16GB RAM for on-device training.
details.realistic_solution: Sensor sync: timestamp alignment within 10ms. Data: accelerometer 100Hz × 3-axis, HR 1Hz, mic 16kHz → downsample for event detection. Privacy: process on-device, store only aggregated features (not raw audio). Labels: user-confirmed events only.

scenario: You are designing training data for an on-device health monitoring model on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB). The model fuses accelerometer, heart rate, and microphone data to detect health events. Design the multi-modal data curation pipeline, synchronization strategy, and privacy-preserving collection protocol. Quantify storage and compute requirements.
title: Dataset Curation: Mastery — Sensor Fusion Dataset Design for On-Device Health Model

details.common_mistake: Not caching preprocessed data between rounds; recomputing tokenization and augmentation from scratch each round.
details.napkin_math: Current: 43s preprocessing for 200 examples × 128 tokens. Per-example preprocessing: 43s/200 = 215ms. Bottleneck analysis: tokenization (BPE) = 150ms/example on Tensor G3 CPU. Augmentation = 50ms. Other = 15ms. Fix 1: pre-tokenize once, cache as int16 tokens. Token cache: 200 × 128 × 2B = 51.2KB — trivial. Eliminates 150ms/example = 30 seconds. Fix 2: GPU augmentation (Tensor G3 GPU = 10 TOPS): 50ms → 5ms. New total: 200 × (5ms aug + 15ms other) = 4 seconds preprocessing + 2 seconds compute = 6 seconds total. Speedup: 45s → 6s = 7.5× improvement. Battery: 45s → 6s training window reduces energy 7.5× → fits in background without thermal throttling.
details.realistic_solution: Cache preprocessed batches after first round. Use memory-mapped files for fast random access. Pre-compute tokenization offline. Use INT8 data types for intermediate representations.

scenario: Your federated learning system for Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) devices is running slowly: devices spend 45 seconds on local training but only 2 seconds on actual gradient computation. Profiling shows 43 seconds is data preprocessing. Optimize the preprocessing pipeline to reduce device-side compute by 10×.
title: Dataset Curation: Optimize Data Pipeline for Federated Learning on Mobile

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for quantization accuracy loss when planning fine-tuning data quantity; trying to fine-tune the full model on-device instead of using LoRA/adapters.
details.napkin_math: Memory during fine-tuning: frozen 4-bit base = 500MB. LoRA weights fp16: 2M × 2B = 4MB. Optimizer (AdamW): 2 × 2M × 4B = 16MB. Activations (batch=1, seq=512): 512 × 2048 hidden × 2B = 2MB per layer × 32 layers = 64MB. Total: 500 + 4 + 16 + 64 = 584MB. Well within 8GB. Fine-tuning compute: 1K examples × 512 tokens × 3 epochs = 1.536M tokens. FLOPs: 6 × 2M params × 1.536M tokens = 18.4B FLOPs (LoRA only, base frozen). A17 Pro GPU: 2 TFLOPS → 9.2 seconds. Add data loading: 1K × 512 tokens × 2B = 1MB → negligible. Total: ~10 seconds. Way under 5-minute budget.
details.realistic_solution: 4-bit quantized 1B model = 500MB inference. Fine-tuning: LoRA rank-16 adds 2M trainable params. Training data: 1,000 user email examples × 512 tokens avg. Fine-tuning must use float16 LoRA weights while keeping quantized base frozen.

scenario: Realize the complete data requirements for fine-tuning a 1B LLM on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM) for email composition assistance. The model must fit in memory during inference (4-bit quantized) and fine-tuning must complete in < 5 minutes in the background.
title: Dataset Curation: Realize Training Data Requirements for On-Device LLM Fine-Tuning

details.common_mistake: Deploying tokenizer updates separately from model updates, causing tokenizer-model mismatch on some devices; not versioning label schemas.
details.napkin_math: 50M devices: 60% Android (30M Snapdragon), 40% iOS (20M A17 Pro). Tokenizer size: SentencePiece 32K vocab = 2MB. Distributed with model update: already bundled. Dataset compatibility check: SHA256 of tokenizer file checked at round start. Mismatch rate (from version skew): assume 2% of devices on old version = 1M devices excluded per round. Acceptable: 49M/50M = 98% participation. Label schema (protobuf): backward compatible with field numbers. Schema version byte added: 1 byte overhead per example. 1M examples × 1 byte = 1MB schema overhead per device. Negligible. Monthly round bandwidth: 50M × 200KB gradients = 10TB. At $0.01/GB: $100/round = $1,200/year.
details.realistic_solution: Bundle tokenizer with model as atomic unit. Use protobuf schema versioning for label formats. Enforce minimum dataset version check before participating in any training round. Use content-addressed storage (SHA256) for all dataset artifacts.

scenario: You are rolling out a federated learning update to 50M mobile devices split between A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB, iOS) and Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB, Android). Realize the dataset consistency requirements: ensure all devices train on compatible data formats, the same tokenizer version, and compatible label schemas.
title: Dataset Curation: Realize Cross-Device Dataset Consistency for Mobile Fleet

details.common_mistake: Confusing federated learning with secure multi-party computation; claiming federated learning provides perfect privacy (it does not without additional DP).
details.napkin_math: Centralized: 100M users × 1K training examples × 512 tokens × 2B = 102.4TB data uploaded. At $0.09/GB = $9,216 transfer cost. Federated: only gradients uploaded. 100M params × fp16 = 200MB/device. With 10× compression = 20MB. 100M users × 20MB = 2PB gradient uploads — more data than centralized! Use sampling: 100K users/round × 20MB = 2TB. $18/round vs $9,216 — much cheaper. Trade: gradient inversion risk, need DP.
details.realistic_solution: Federated learning: model trains locally on device, only model updates (gradients or weights) are uploaded — raw data never leaves device. Key difference from centralized: no raw data collection, privacy-by-design. Limitation: gradient inversion attacks can partially recover data without DP.

scenario: In the context of mobile on-device training on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8), what does federated learning mean in terms of data privacy, and what is the key difference from centralized training data collection?
title: Dataset Curation: Recall — What is Federated Learning Data Privacy?

details.common_mistake: Triggering personalization on very few signals (< 10 samples), leading to noise-driven updates; not specifying a minimum observation window.
details.napkin_math: Minimum 50 feedback events. Average user: 20 suggestions/day accepted or rejected. Collection window: 50 events / 20/day = 2.5 days. DP per update: ε=0.5, δ=1e-7. Using Gaussian mechanism on LoRA gradients: noise multiplier σ=0.3 for ε=0.5 at batch=50 samples. Update frequency: 12/year = monthly. Annual DP budget: advanced composition over 12 rounds: ε_total ≈ sqrt(12) × 0.5 = 1.73 (basic), or ≈ 1.2 with RDP. Fine-grained DP accounting with Opacus. Storage for 50 feedback events: 50 × (prompt 512 tokens + response 128 tokens) × 2B = 64KB — trivial.
details.realistic_solution: SLAs: (1) Minimum volume: >= 50 explicit feedback events before any update. (2) Signal quality: accept rate 20-80% (outside range indicates broken UI, not real preference). (3) Temporal distribution: feedback spans >= 3 days (not a single session). (4) Privacy: DP budget ε < 0.5 per update, max 12 updates/year = ε < 6.0/year with composition. (5) Bias: flag if > 80% accepts (sycophancy) or > 80% rejects (model too bad to personalize).

scenario: You are writing the data quality specification for on-device RLHF personalization on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB). The system collects implicit feedback (accept/reject suggestions) from user interactions. Define quantitative SLAs for minimum feedback volume, feedback quality, bias correction, and privacy budget before a personalization update fires.
title: Dataset Curation: Specification — Mobile Data Quality SLA for RLHF Personalization

details.common_mistake: Applying server-style MTBF-based checkpoint interval to a mobile context; not realizing that 10-minute training window fundamentally changes the calculus.
details.napkin_math: Poisson process: λ = 1/365 ≈ 0.0027 failure events/day expected. P(failure in 1 day) = 1 - e^(-0.0027) ≈ 0.0027 ≈ 0.27%. Annual failures in 1000-device fleet: 1000/365 ≈ 2.74 devices/year.
details.realistic_solution: For 1000-device fleet with MTBF=365 days, expected failures per day follows Poisson distribution with λ = 1000/365 ≈ 2.74 failures/day fleet-wide.

scenario: An on-device personalization system on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM) runs LoRA fine-tuning for 10 minutes nightly. A power failure during training loses all progress. Analyze the tradeoff between checkpoint frequency, battery impact, and recovery completeness for a 10-minute training window.
title: Fault Tolerance: Analyze Checkpoint Overhead for On-Device Fine-Tuning on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Not implementing a device-side validation step before committing an update; not staging rollouts by device risk profile.
details.napkin_math: 50M users. Stage 1: 0.01% = 5,000 devices. Bad update crash rate: 0.5% on 5K = 25 crashes. Crash rate monitoring: 25 crashes / 5K devices = 0.5% > threshold (0.1%). Stage halted automatically. Blast radius: 25 users affected = 0.00005% of 50M. Kill switch: server flag propagated on next heartbeat (1 minute TTL). 50M devices × 1 min heartbeat × 1KB payload = 50GB/minute push — too expensive. Use polling: devices check server flag every 5 minutes. Rollback latency: 5 minutes + switch to A partition (50ms). Model partitions: 1B model at 4-bit = 500MB × 2 = 1GB storage. iPhone 15 storage typically 128GB+ — acceptable. Validation: 100 inference calls on test prompts = 100 × 50ms = 5 seconds per device.
details.realistic_solution: A/B model partitions. Staged rollout: 0.01% (5K) → validation 48h → 0.1% → 1% → 10% → 100%. Device-side: download to B partition, validate 100 inference calls, commit. Kill switch: server-side flag to rollback all devices in < 1 hour.

scenario: You are designing a safe model update protocol for a 1B LLM deployed on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM) as part of a keyboard app with 50M users. An update last month caused crashes on 0.5% of devices (250K users affected). Design a fault-tolerant update protocol that limits blast radius to < 0.01%.
title: Fault Tolerance: Design Model Update Safety Protocol for Mobile LLM

details.common_mistake: Always preferring cloud recovery without considering that cloud storage of personalization data is a privacy risk; not measuring rebuild time.
details.napkin_math: Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: 45 TOPS INT8. MobileNetV3 (5.4M MACs, INT8): 5.4M × 2 ops/MAC = 10.8M ops. But full inference model ~220M MACs. 220M × 2 / 45T = 8.5ms per inference (not 8.5 seconds). Batch=1 decode: latency-bound.
details.realistic_solution: On-device inference latency for MobileNet-class models is in the millisecond range, not seconds. 45 TOPS INT8 easily handles 220M MAC models at well under 10ms.

scenario: A personalization model on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB) loses its LoRA adaptation state after a factory reset. Compare (A) cloud recovery: re-download from cloud backup (2MB LoRA state), vs (B) rebuild: re-run 500-example local training dataset. Evaluate recovery time, user experience, and privacy implications of each.
title: Fault Tolerance: Evaluate On-Device vs Cloud Recovery for Mobile ML State

details.common_mistake: Treating both failures identically; not having a fast path for the common case (app crash) vs the rare case (corruption).
details.napkin_math: Failure A (crash, 1/day): LoRA checkpoint every 5 minutes. Expected lost work: 2.5 minutes average. Recovery: reload 2MB checkpoint from flash = 2MB / 1 GB/s = 2ms + app restart 3 seconds = 3.002 seconds total. Annualized: 365 crashes × 3s recovery = 1,095 seconds = 18.25 minutes/year in recovery. Failure B (corruption, 1/month): probability per startup = 1/(30 × 24 × app_starts_per_hour). SHA256 check: 2MB model at SHA256 throughput 1 GB/s = 2ms per startup. If corrupt: restore from backup (B partition): 200MB model / 1 GB/s = 0.2 seconds. Or re-download: 200MB at LTE 12.5 MB/s = 16 seconds. Annual corruption: 12 events × 16 seconds recovery = 192 seconds = 3.2 minutes/year. Total annual downtime: 18.25 + 3.2 = 21.45 minutes → 99.996% uptime.
details.realistic_solution: App crash recovery: training checkpoint from 5 minutes ago → resume. Fast path (< 5 seconds). Model corruption: SHA256 verify on startup, restore from backup partition or re-download. Slow path (seconds to minutes).

scenario: Your on-device ML app on Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) experiences two failure modes: (A) app crash mid-training (occurs ~1/day), (B) model file corruption (occurs ~1/month). Compare the recovery protocol, recovery time, and user impact for each failure mode.
title: Fault Tolerance: Evaluate App Crash vs Model Corruption Recovery Paths

details.common_mistake: Forgetting that optimizer state doubles the checkpoint size; overestimating flash write power drain on mobile.
details.napkin_math: Checkpoint size: 1M params × fp32 = 4MB weights. AdamW: 2 × 4MB = 8MB optimizer state. Total: 12MB. Write time: 12MB / 3 GB/s = 4ms. Checkpoints in 10 minutes: 10 × 60/60 = 10 checkpoints. Total write time: 10 × 4ms = 40ms out of 600 seconds = 0.0067% overhead — negligible. Energy: flash write power ~0.5W × 4ms = 2mJ per checkpoint. 10 × 2mJ = 20mJ. Training energy: 10 min × 2W CPU ≈ 1,200 J. Checkpoint overhead: 20mJ / 1200 J = 0.0017% energy overhead. Completely negligible. Storage: 10 checkpoints × 12MB = 120MB for rolling 10-minute window. Keep only last 3: 36MB. Trivial on modern iPhone.
