details.realistic_solution: Checkpoint: LoRA weights (fp32) + optimizer (2× fp32 for momentum and variance) = 3 × 1M × 4B = 12MB. Flash write at A17 Pro NVMe: ~3 GB/s. Write time: 12MB / 3 GB/s = 4ms per checkpoint.

scenario: Your on-device training runs LoRA fine-tuning on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM). LoRA weights: 1M parameters, AdamW optimizer state. Estimate checkpoint write time and energy overhead if you checkpoint every 60 seconds during a 10-minute background training session.
title: Fault Tolerance: Fluency — Mobile Checkpoint Write Speed and Overhead

details.common_mistake: Replacing the model file in-place while inference may be running — causes corruption. Not using memory-mapped files that allow atomic pointer swap.
details.napkin_math: 500MB model, memory-mapped. Download to /models/model_new.bin (background, 500MB at LTE 12.5 MB/s = 40 seconds). SHA256 verify: 500MB at 1 GB/s = 0.5 seconds. mmap new file: OS maps 500MB virtual address space instantly (no actual read until accessed). Symlink swap: rename() syscall = atomic on POSIX = 0 microseconds. In-flight requests: use reference counting. Old mmap held until refcount = 0. At 10 req/sec, each 100ms: max 1 overlapping request = 100ms drain time. Total atomic swap: 0ms user-visible downtime. Rollback: keep model_prev.bin. On crash (detected by watchdog in 1 second): atomic rename model_prev.bin → active. Total rollback: 1s detection + 1ms rename = 1.001 seconds << 5 second target.
details.realistic_solution: Use memory-mapped model files. New model: download to temp path → verify SHA256 → mmap new file → atomic symlink swap → mmap old file stays valid for in-flight inferences → unmap old after all requests complete.

scenario: Implement an atomic model update mechanism for a 1B LLM (4-bit quantized, 500MB) on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB RAM). The update must not interrupt an in-progress inference request and must be rollback-capable within 5 seconds of a crash.
title: Fault Tolerance: Implement Atomic Model Swap for Zero-Downtime Mobile Update

details.common_mistake: Writing all weights every checkpoint even when few change; not verifying that differential checkpoint + base = correct recovered state.
details.napkin_math: 2M LoRA params × fp32 = 8MB. Full checkpoint: 8MB. Diff checkpoint: 5% change = 100K params. Sparse format: 100K × 8B = 800KB. Compression: 8MB → 800KB = 10× reduction. Write time: 800KB / 1 GB/s = 0.8ms vs 8ms full. Recovery: load base (8MB) → apply N diffs in sequence. For 10 diffs: 8MB + 10 × 800KB = 16MB total storage vs 10 × 8MB = 80MB. 5× storage reduction for 10 checkpoints. Correctness verification: after applying diff, compute checksum of recovered weights, compare to saved checksum. SHA256 of 2M × 4B = 8MB at 1 GB/s = 8ms verification. Add this after every restore. Risk: if base checkpoint is corrupt, all diffs are unusable. Mitigation: full checkpoint every 20 diffs (every hour if diffing every 3 minutes).
details.realistic_solution: Full checkpoint at training start. Differential: store only weights where |delta| > threshold. Each diff: (index, value) pairs. At 5% change rate: 100K params change out of 2M. Store as sparse: 100K × (4B index + 4B value) = 800KB vs 8MB full.

scenario: You are implementing checkpointing for continuous LoRA fine-tuning on Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB). The LoRA model has 2M trainable parameters (8MB fp32). Between checkpoints, only 5% of weights change significantly (> 1e-4 delta). Implement differential checkpointing to reduce checkpoint size and verify correctness.
title: Fault Tolerance: Implement Differential Checkpoint for Mobile LoRA Training

details.common_mistake: Storing all personalization state in app-private storage that is wiped on reinstall; not designing backup strategy that preserves privacy.
details.napkin_math: Cloud cost: 100M users × 50 inferences/day × 365 days × $0.001/1K tokens × 512 tokens = $0.001/1K × 512/1K × 100M × 50 × 365 = $0.000512 × 100M × 50 × 365 = $937M/year. But at $0.001/1K and 512 tokens per inference: $0.000512/inference. 100M × 50/day × 365 = 1.825T inferences/year × $0.000512 = $934M/year. On-device NRE: $20,000 (not $20M) amortized over 100M users = $0.0002/user.
details.realistic_solution: The NRE for on-device ML integration (model optimization, testing) is typically $20K–$100K, not millions. Cloud inference costs dominate at scale.

scenario: You are the reliability lead for a mobile keyboard app with 100M users on A17 Pro and Snapdragon 8 Gen 3. The app runs nightly on-device LoRA personalization (10-minute training window). Users report losing their personalization after phone updates, crashes, and app reinstalls. Design a complete fault tolerance architecture that preserves personalization state across all these events.
title: Fault Tolerance: Mastery — Mobile Personalization Reliability Architecture

details.common_mistake: Listing only hardware failures; not including software and data quality failures that are more common in ML systems.
details.napkin_math: (1) Weight corruption: Severity=9, Occurrence=2 (1/year), Detection=3 (SHA256 check catches). RPN=54. Mitigation: A/B partitions. (2) OOM during fine-tuning: Severity=5 (training lost, inference OK), Occurrence=4 (1/month on low RAM), Detection=8 (hard to detect before crash). RPN=160. Mitigation: guard with availableMemory() check before training start. (3) Checkpoint corruption: Severity=7, Occurrence=2 (1/year), Detection=2 (CRC check). RPN=28. (4) Distribution shift: Severity=8 (wrong predictions silently), Occurrence=5 (common), Detection=9 (very hard to detect). RPN=360. Highest RPN! Mitigation: monitor prediction confidence distribution; alert if P(top-1) drops > 20%. (5) Battery drain: Severity=6, Occurrence=6 (training > 2% battery), Detection=2 (user sees it). RPN=72. Mitigation: training only when charging + WiFi. Priority: fix (4) first, then (2).
details.realistic_solution: Top 5 by Risk Priority Number (RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detectability). Rank: (1) Model weight corruption, (2) OOM crash, (3) Checkpoint corruption, (4) Distribution shift (silent failure), (5) Battery drain.

scenario: Conduct a systematic failure mode analysis (FMEA) for a production on-device ML system on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB RAM) serving 10M users. The system runs inference continuously and nightly fine-tuning. Identify the top 5 failure modes, their probability, impact, and mitigations with quantitative analysis.
title: Fault Tolerance: Mastery — Systematic Failure Mode Analysis for Mobile ML

details.common_mistake: Treating thermal throttling as a fault tolerance problem rather than a thermal management problem; not checkpointing frequently enough given the known crash rate.
details.napkin_math: Thermal crash at ~7 minutes. Checkpoint every 2 minutes: max lost work = 2 minutes. LoRA checkpoint: 2M params × 12B (weights + optimizer) = 24MB. Write at Tensor G3 flash 1 GB/s = 24ms. Overhead: 24ms/120s = 0.02% — negligible. Recovery from 2-min checkpoint: restart app (3 seconds) + load checkpoint (24MB / 1 GB/s = 24ms) + resume training. Total: 3.024 seconds << 30 second target. Thermal management: poll SOC temp every 5 seconds (Android Thermal API). At 85°C → reduce batch size from 32 to 8 (reduces power 4×). Training slows 4× but avoids crash. With both fixes: crashes/week drops from 3 to ~0.1 (occasional extreme cases). Wasted time: 0.1 × 3 seconds recovery = 0.3 seconds/week vs 30 minutes. 6,000× improvement.
details.realistic_solution: Dual fix: (1) Checkpoint every 2 minutes (given ~7 min to crash, save progress at 2, 4, 6 minutes). (2) Implement thermal monitoring: reduce batch size or pause when SOC temp > 85°C. Both together eliminate most crashes.

scenario: Your nightly fine-tuning job on Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) crashes 3 times per week on average due to thermal throttling (device overheats after 7 minutes of training). Current recovery: restart from scratch each time (10 minutes per attempt = 30 wasted minutes/week). Optimize to recover in < 30 seconds from crash.
title: Fault Tolerance: Optimize Recovery Speed for Frequently Crashing Mobile Training

details.common_mistake: Eliminating checkpoints entirely to save space; not realizing that most of the checkpoint is optimizer state that can be discarded for crash recovery.
details.napkin_math: Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: 45 TOPS INT8. ResNet-50 (4.1 GMACs, INT8): 4.1G × 2 / 45T = 0.182s... wait: 4.1 GMACs = 4.1G × 2 ops = 8.2 GOps. 8.2G / 45T = 0.00018s = 0.18ms? No: 45 TOPS = 45×10^12 ops/s. 8.2×10^9 / 45×10^12 = 0.000182s ≈ 0.18ms. But with batching overhead and actual NPU utilization ~50%: 0.18ms / 0.5 ≈ 0.36ms. For larger model with ~100 GMACs: 200G / 45T = 4.4ms = 2.2ms at 50% util? More realistically for a model needing 2.2ms: ~50 GMACs at 45 TOPS with ~50% utilization. Key: 2.2ms (not 2.2 seconds).
details.realistic_solution: NPU inference latency for standard CNN models is in the sub-10ms range on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3's 45 TOPS NPU. The time unit should be milliseconds, not seconds.

scenario: Your personalization system on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB RAM) runs on devices with only 64GB storage. Users have on average 58GB used (6GB free). Your current checkpointing strategy keeps 30 checkpoints × 24MB = 720MB. Users complain about storage usage. Optimize to < 50MB total checkpoint storage while maintaining acceptable fault tolerance.
title: Fault Tolerance: Optimize Checkpoint Storage Budget for Low-Storage Mobile Devices

details.common_mistake: Not separating inference model state from training state; not specifying which files are updated atomically.
details.napkin_math: Storage layout: /models/base_model_int4.bin (500MB, immutable), /models/lora_inference.bin (4MB, updated after each training session), /models/training_ckpt/ (24MB, 3 rolling checkpoints = 72MB). Total: 500MB + 4MB + 72MB = 576MB. Training checkpoint schedule: every 3 minutes during 10-min window = 3 checkpoints. Each 24MB at 3 GB/s flash = 8ms write. Atomic update: write lora_inference_new.bin → verify → rename() → old file deleted. Retention: keep 3 training checkpoints (9 minutes history). Inference checkpoint retained until next session completes. Recovery: crash during inference → load lora_inference.bin (4MB, 4ms), resume. Crash during training at minute 7 → load training_ckpt/ckpt_6min.bin (24MB, 8ms + 3s app restart). Device wipe → reload base_model from App Store (background download).
details.realistic_solution: Two separate state objects: (1) Inference state: LoRA weights (fp32, 4MB) + merged into base (optional). (2) Training state: full checkpoint (weights + optimizer, 24MB). Different retention policies and update frequency.

scenario: Realize the complete checkpoint architecture for an on-device personalization system on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM) that trains nightly for 10 minutes and serves inference 24/7. Specify storage layout, checkpoint schedule, retention policy, and recovery paths for all failure modes.
title: Fault Tolerance: Realize Checkpoint Architecture for Continuous Mobile Personalization

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for CDN costs at 50M downloads × 500MB; not specifying automated rollback triggers.
details.napkin_math: 50M users × 500MB model = 25 PB total download. CDN cost: $0.008/GB = $200K for full rollout. Pre-stage to CDN edge nodes near user population. Staging: Day 1: 0.01% (5K) → 48h monitoring → Day 3: 0.1% (50K) → 24h → Day 4: 1% (500K) → 24h → Day 5: 10% (5M) → 24h → Day 7: 100% (50M). Rollback trigger: crash rate > 0.5% (vs baseline 0.1%) OR inference latency p95 > 2× baseline. Automated: server flag → devices roll back to model_prev.bin on next heartbeat. CDN peak load: Day 7 full rollout, 50M × 500MB over 24 hours = 25PB / 86400s = 289 GB/s CDN throughput. Major CDNs handle 10+ TB/s — no issue. Rollback storage: 2 × 500MB = 1GB per device. 50M × 1GB = 50PB device storage industry-wide — acceptable.
details.realistic_solution: Staged rollout with automated gates. CDN pre-positioned. Per-platform staged separately (iOS App Store vs Google Play have different mechanics).

scenario: Realize the model update rollout plan for 50M users across A17 Pro (iOS) and Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (Android). The update is a 500MB 4-bit quantized 1B model. You have 7 days for full rollout. Specify staging percentages, validation gates, CDN requirements, and rollback procedures.
title: Fault Tolerance: Realize Mobile Fleet Update Rollout Timeline

details.common_mistake: Confusing A/B model partitions with A/B testing (different concepts); thinking A/B requires running both models simultaneously.
details.napkin_math: Storage: 2 × model_size. For 500MB 4-bit 1B model: 1GB needed. Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 devices typically have 128-256GB storage → 1GB = 0.4-0.8% of storage. Acceptable. Atomic switch: rename() syscall on /data/models/active symlink. Takes 1 microsecond. Validation before commit: run 100 test inferences on B → if all pass (< 50ms each) → commit. If any fail → keep A active, delete B, report error. Recovery time: 100ms (validation failure detected) + 1 microsecond (revert symlink) = 100ms total. No user-visible downtime.
details.realistic_solution: A/B model partition: store two versions of the model on device (A = current, B = new update). New model downloaded to B, validated, then A/B switch is atomic. If B fails: revert to A instantly. Only one model is active at a time.

scenario: In the context of on-device model deployment on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB), what is an A/B model partition strategy, why is it used for fault tolerance, and what is the key constraint on device storage?
title: Fault Tolerance: Recall — What is an A/B Model Partition?

details.common_mistake: Not specifying fail-safe behavior (what happens during model failure); not distinguishing between model failure (accuracy degraded) and system failure (crash).
details.napkin_math: 5M transactions/day = 57.9 transactions/second. Inference budget: < 50ms per transaction. System failure: model crashes → fall back to rule-based system (< 1ms). RTO: 500ms is max payment timeout. Model failure → rule-based fallback in < 1ms. Always meets SLA. RPO = 0: base model (500MB, immutable) is always the fallback. LoRA adaptation (4MB) improves accuracy by 2-3% — valuable but not critical. Checkpoint: LoRA saved after each training session (nightly). Loss of LoRA = minor accuracy degradation (not safety-critical). Accuracy SLA: precision > 95% on fraud class. Monitor: compute rolling 100-transaction precision proxy (anomaly score distribution). Alert if distribution shifts > 2σ from baseline. False negative (missed fraud): financial risk. False positive (blocked good transaction): user experience risk. SLA: < 0.1% false positive rate (< 5,000 blocked good transactions/day). Checkpoint size: 4MB LoRA × 3 retained = 12MB storage.
details.realistic_solution: Payment context: fail-safe = allow transaction (not block). Model failure should never block payment. SLAs: RTO < 500ms (transaction timeout), RPO = 0 (base model always available, LoRA is enhancement only), accuracy SLA = > 95% precision on fraud class.

scenario: Write the reliability specification for an on-device fraud detection ML model on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM) used in a mobile payment app serving 5M transactions/day. Define RTO, RPO, accuracy degradation SLA, checkpoint requirements, and fail-safe behavior for all failure modes.
title: Fault Tolerance: Specification — Reliability SLA for Mobile Payment ML Model

details.common_mistake: Thinking the developer manually writes fused kernels for Neural Engine — Core ML and Metal do this automatically. Confusing Neural Engine (fixed function) with GPU (programmable).
details.napkin_math: A17 Pro Neural Engine: 35 TOPS INT8, 8GB unified memory at 68 GB/s (estimated LPDDR5). Ridge point: 35,000 / 68 = 515 INT8 OPS/byte. Elementwise op (1 OP/byte): 515× below ridge → memory-bound. Fusing 5 elementwise ops: read once + write once vs 5× = 5× bandwidth reduction. For 1B LLM decode, token embedding 4096 × 4B = 16KB: 5 unfused ops = 5 × 32KB = 160KB. Fused = 32KB. At 68 GB/s: 0.0024ms vs 0.00047ms. Time savings per token: 0.0019ms. At 50ms/token total → fusion saves 0.004% per elementwise sequence. Kernel launch savings (iOS Metal): ~10µs per launch. 200 layers × 5 fused ops vs 20 → saves 180 × 10µs = 1.8ms per token. More significant.
details.realistic_solution: Core ML compiler automatically fuses compatible operations into single Neural Engine invocations. The Neural Engine is fixed-function; Core ML abstracts this via its IR. Common fusions: Conv+BN+ReLU, Linear+GELU, Softmax+Top-K.

scenario: On A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB RAM), what is operator fusion, how does the Core ML compiler implement it, and what types of operations are most commonly fused together for mobile transformer inference?
title: Kernel Fusion: Recall — What is Operator Fusion on Neural Engines?

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for the Hexagon DSP vs Adreno GPU split on Snapdragon — different op types run on different hardware units. Not all ops can be fused across the DSP/GPU boundary.
details.napkin_math: 1B model at 4-bit: 500MB model. Decode batch=1, 1 token. Weight loading: 500MB per forward pass (load all weights once). At Hexagon bandwidth to model: shared with LPDDR5 16GB at ~68 GB/s. Weight read time: 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms. Per-layer: 1B / 32 layers = 31.25M params per layer. Weight per layer: 62.5MB. Read per layer: 62.5MB / 68 GB/s = 0.92ms. Forward pass: 32 layers × 0.92ms = 29.4ms weight loading + compute. Compute: 1B × 6 FLOPs × 1 token / 45 TOPS = 0.133ms — dominated by weight loading. Fusion: fuse RMSNorm into GEMM kernel (don't write normalized output to LPDDR5). Saves: 32 × (1 × 2048 × 2B) × 2 = 262KB. At 68 GB/s: 0.004ms — negligible. Key optimization: not fusion, but KV cache compression or reduced precision for KV. Target 20 tokens/sec = 50ms/token. Current: ~30ms weight loading + 5ms overhead = 35ms → 28.6 tokens/sec. May already meet target.
details.realistic_solution: Snapdragon 8 Gen 3: Hexagon DSP (45 TOPS INT8, best for quantized matmuls) + Adreno GPU (10 TOPS FP16, best for attention/softmax). Design fusion graph aware of this split.

scenario: You are designing the kernel fusion strategy for a 1B parameter LLM (4-bit quantized) inference on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB). The model uses GQA attention (8 KV heads, 32 Q heads), RMSNorm, and SwiGLU activation. Target: 20 tokens/second (50ms/token). Design the fusion graph and quantify expected gains.
title: Kernel Fusion: Design Fusion Strategy for On-Device LLM on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Assuming Core ML always wins on Apple hardware; not knowing that ONNX Runtime with CoreML EP may offer different tradeoffs, and that 4-bit quantization support differs.
details.napkin_math: 1B INT4 model: 0.5GB storage. Prefill (batch=1, 512 token prompt): 512 × 1B × 6 FLOPs = 3.072T FLOPs. Neural Engine 35 TOPS: 3.072T / 35T = 87.8ms prefill. Core ML overhead (model load + first pass): ~100ms. Total TTFT: ~200ms. Decode: 1 token. Weight reads: 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms/token. Neural Engine at 35 TOPS: 1B × 6 FLOPs / 35T = 0.17ms compute. Bottleneck: memory bandwidth 7.35ms → ~136 tokens/sec = 7.35ms/token → 136 tokens/sec. ONNX Runtime on CPU (6-core A17 Pro, 6 × 2GFLOPS = 12 GFLOPS INT8): 3.072T / 12G = 256 seconds for prefill — far too slow. Metal GPU: 16 TFLOPS FP16 → 3.072T / 16T = 192ms prefill. Decode via GPU: 500MB at GPU bandwidth 68 GB/s = 7.35ms/token. Similar. Core ML with NE: fastest for operations the NE supports.
details.realistic_solution: Core ML: deep hardware integration, Neural Engine optimized, automatic fusion, but limited operator support for cutting-edge quantization schemes. ONNX Runtime: more flexible operator support, good for INT4 via specific EPs, may run on CPU or GPU. For latest quantization, may need custom Metal shaders.

scenario: Compare Core ML (A17 Pro Neural Engine, 35 TOPS) vs ONNX Runtime (iOS, CPU/GPU) for running a 1B INT4 quantized LLM. Evaluate kernel fusion depth, tokenization throughput, first-token latency, and subsequent-token latency.
title: Kernel Fusion: Evaluate Core ML vs ONNX Runtime Fusion for iPhone LLM

details.common_mistake: Assuming INT8 attention has 2× speedup vs FP16 — Neural Engine is rated at 35 TOPS INT8 and ~17 TOPS FP16, so the ratio applies to compute-bound ops only. Attention is often memory-bound.
details.napkin_math: 3B model, 32 heads, head dim 128, seq=512. QK^T matrix: 512×512×32 × 2B (FP16) = 16.8MB or × 1B (INT8) = 8.4MB. (A) FP16 unfused: Q=512×128×32×2B=4MB, K=4MB, V=4MB. Attention matrix: 16.8MB. Read Q+K+V (12MB) + write attn (16.8MB) + read attn (16.8MB) + write V×attn (4MB) = 49.6MB. At 68 GB/s: 0.73ms per layer. (B) INT8 fused (FlashAttention-style): reads Q+K+V = 6MB (INT8). Attention stays on-chip (8.4MB < estimated 10MB SRAM on NE). Writes output = 4MB. Total: 10MB. At 68 GB/s: 0.15ms per layer. Speedup: 0.73/0.15 = 4.9×. 3B model: 28 attention layers (assuming). Layer latency total: (A) 28 × 0.73ms = 20.4ms vs (B) 28 × 0.15ms = 4.2ms. 4.9× win for fused INT8. Accuracy: INT8 quantization error in attention → use per-head quantization with dynamic range. Typical quality drop: < 0.5% on MMLU.
details.realistic_solution: Attention memory: QK^T matrix = seq² × heads × bytes. For short sequences (512), this may fit in L2 cache. Compare bandwidth requirements for FP16 vs INT8 attention.

scenario: You are evaluating two attention implementations for a 3B LLM on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB): (A) FP16 attention with no fusion, (B) INT8 quantized attention with QK^T+softmax+V fusion. Sequence length 512. Compare memory, latency, and accuracy.
title: Kernel Fusion: Evaluate Quantized Attention Fusion on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Ignoring weight loading time for decode mode; assuming TOPS rating equals actual throughput for small batch operations.
details.napkin_math: Linear 1 weights: 2048×8192 × 2B = 33.6MB. Linear 2 weights: 8192×2048 × 2B = 33.6MB. Total weight: 67.2MB. Weight load time: 67.2MB / 68 GB/s = 0.99ms. Compute: batch=1, token=1. Linear 1: 2 × 1 × 2048 × 8192 = 33.6M FLOPs. Linear 2: same. Total: 67.2M FLOPs. NE at 35 TOPS: 67.2M / 35T = 0.0019ms. Compute time: 0.002ms. Memory bandwidth time: 0.99ms. Memory-bound: 0.99ms / 0.002ms = 495× memory-bound. Fusion benefit for SiLU: SiLU acts on 8192-element vector = 8192 × 2B = 16KB. Unfused: write 16KB + read 16KB = 32KB. Fused: stays in NE registers. Savings: 32KB / 68 GB/s = 0.47µs. Negligible vs 0.99ms weight load. Conclusion: at batch=1, fusion saves 0.05% — weight loading dominates completely. To improve: weight caching, INT4 quantization (reduces weights to 33.6MB/2 = 16.8MB → 0.49ms load).
details.realistic_solution: At batch=1 decode, MLP is dominated by weight loading, not compute. This is the memory-bandwidth-bound regime where arithmetic intensity is very low.

scenario: Estimate the Neural Engine throughput on A17 Pro (35 TOPS INT8, 8GB) for a fused MLP block: Linear(2048→8192) + SiLU + Linear(8192→2048), processing batch=1 single-token decode. Include weight loading time and compute time, and determine which is the bottleneck.
title: Kernel Fusion: Fluency — Estimate Neural Engine Throughput for Fused MLP

details.common_mistake: Not folding BN into conv at inference (BN weights can be absorbed into conv weights and bias). This is the most common and impactful mobile fusion.
details.napkin_math: Input: 112×112×32. Conv 3×3×32→64: weights 3×3×32×64 = 18,432 INT8 params = 18KB. BN params: γ,β,μ,σ for 64 channels = 64×4×4B = 1KB. Fold: W'[k] = W[k] × γ[k]/σ[k] for each output channel k. b'[k] = β[k] - γ[k]×μ[k]/σ[k]. One-time pre-computation: 64 × (18,432 multiplies) = 1.18M ops — done once, not at inference. Memory savings: unfused: Conv output 112×112×64 × 1B = 802KB written + read for BN. Folded: zero intermediate write. Savings: 1.6MB per layer. At Snapdragon LPDDR5 68 GB/s: 1.6MB / 68 GB/s = 0.024ms per layer. MobileNetV3 has ~20 such layers: 20 × 0.024ms = 0.47ms total savings. At 30 fps (33ms budget), savings = 1.4% — modest but free (zero accuracy cost).
details.realistic_solution: BN fold: pre-compute fused conv weight W' = W × γ/σ and bias b' = β - γμ/σ for each output channel. At inference: Conv(x) with W',b' and ReLU = Conv+BN+ReLU. This is a pre-processing step, not a runtime fusion.

scenario: Implement a fused Conv+BN+ReLU layer for MobileNetV3 inference on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 Hexagon DSP (45 TOPS INT8). The layer processes 112×112×32 activations with 32→64 channel 3×3 conv. Specify the fusion implementation, verify correctness, and quantify memory bandwidth savings.
title: Kernel Fusion: Implement Fused Conv+BN+ReLU for Mobile CNN on Snapdragon

details.common_mistake: Not knowing Tensor G3's SRAM size; using tiles too large (spill to LPDDR5) or too small (poor arithmetic intensity). Not accounting for GQA's different tiling strategy.
details.napkin_math: Multi-head attention Q,K,V for mobile LLM (seq=2048, hidden=1024, 16 heads, head_dim=64): Q tensor: batch=1 × seq=2048 × heads=16 × head_dim=64 × 2B = 2048 × 1024 × 2B = 4.19MB each (not 12.6MB — that would require head_dim=192 or 3× seq).
details.realistic_solution: Q,K,V activation size = seq × hidden × dtype_bytes. For seq=2048, hidden=1024, fp16: 2048 × 1024 × 2B = 4.19MB each.

scenario: Implement Flash Attention for a 1B LLM on Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB). The model has 16 heads, head dim 64, and must handle sequences up to 2048 tokens. Specify tile sizes for flash attention given available SRAM, and compute memory savings vs standard attention.
title: Kernel Fusion: Implement Fused Attention for On-Device LLM on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Applying all optimizations blindly without measuring current bottleneck; the bottleneck at batch=1 decode is almost certainly memory bandwidth, not compute.
details.napkin_math: Target: 30 tokens/sec → 33.3ms/token. Current: 18 tok/s → 55.6ms/token. Memory floor: 1.5GB weight load / 68 GB/s = 22ms. So 33.3ms target is achievable (33.3ms > 22ms floor). Gap to close: 55.6 - 33.3 = 22.3ms overhead reduction needed. Optimization 1: Model compilation with ANE ahead-of-time (eliminates JIT overhead per token): saves ~8ms (Metal compile overhead). New: 47.6ms → 21 tok/s. Optimization 2: Fuse RMSNorm into attention/MLP GEMMs: RMSNorm tensors = 32 layers × 3072 × 1B = 98KB. Fusing eliminates 32 × 196KB read+write = 6.3MB. At 68 GB/s: 0.09ms — small. But eliminates 32 kernel launches: 32 × 10µs = 0.32ms. New: 47.3ms → 21.1 tok/s. Optimization 3: KV cache in INT8 (was FP16): KV cache at seq=512, 32 layers, 16 heads, 128 dim: FP16 = 32×16×512×128×2×2B = 134MB. INT8 = 67MB. Per-token KV append: 32×16×128×2 bytes: FP16 4KB → INT8 2KB. KV read per token (attending to 512): 134MB → 67MB. At 68 GB/s: 1.97ms → 0.99ms. Saves 0.98ms. New: 46.32ms. Optimization 4: Batch 2 requests (speculative users): 2× throughput for 2× memory bandwidth → 2/46.32ms × 1000 = 43.2 tok/sec per user... wait batch=2: weight loading stays 22ms (shared), activations 2× = +0.3ms. New: 22.3ms for batch=2 → 43.2 tokens/sec × 2 / 2 = 43.2 tok/sec total = 21.6 each. With all optimizations: ~25 tok/sec. Still shy of 30. Add INT4→INT3 (ternary quantization): reduces weights to 1.125GB → 16.5ms load. New: 16.5ms load + 10ms overhead = 26.5ms → 37.7 tok/sec. Meets 30 tok/sec target.
details.realistic_solution: Profile: weight loading time = 1.5GB / 68 GB/s = 22ms/token → 45 tokens/sec theoretical. At 18 tok/s → 55.6ms/token → only 22ms/55.6ms = 39.6% efficiency. Overhead: 33.6ms in overhead. Sources: kernel launch, memory allocation, format conversion.

scenario: You are optimizing a 3B LLM (INT4 quantized, 1.5GB) decode on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB, 68 GB/s). Current: 18 tokens/sec. Target: 30 tokens/sec. Design a complete optimization strategy using kernel fusion, memory layout, quantization, and caching. Quantify each optimization's contribution.
title: Kernel Fusion: Mastery — Optimize 3B LLM Decode Throughput on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Designing a single static fusion graph that works best on one platform but poorly on others; not using runtime hardware detection for adaptive fusion.
details.napkin_math: 1B INT4 model = 500MB weights. A17 Pro NE: 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms weight load. Compute: 0.17ms. With launch overhead: ~25ms → ~40 tok/sec. Easily meets 20 tok/s. Snapdragon Hexagon: 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms. Compute at 45 TOPS: 0.13ms. Launch overhead: ~20ms (less overhead on Hexagon vs ANE). Total: ~27ms → 37 tok/sec. Meets target. Tensor G3: 500MB / 51 GB/s estimated = 9.8ms. Compute at 7.5 TOPS: 0.8ms. Launch overhead: ~25ms (Tensor G3 is oldest, more overhead). Total: ~35ms → 28.6 tok/sec. Meets 20 tok/sec target. Fusion optimization needed most on Tensor G3: fusing 32 RMSNorm kernels into GEMMs saves 32 × 10µs = 0.32ms. Not the bottleneck. Key: on Tensor G3, split model across GPU+CPU if needed. INT4 → INT8 decode on CPU as fallback: CPU (8-core Cortex-A55): 500MB weight load from cache... model doesn't fit in cache. LPDDR5: 9.8ms + 50ms CPU compute = 59ms → 17 tok/sec. Miss target. Fix: use INT8 quantized model on Tensor G3 (sacrifice model quality slightly): 1GB weights, 1000MB/51GB/s = 19.6ms load + 2ms compute + 10ms launch = 31.6ms → 31.6 tok/sec. But INT8 needs 1GB which is fine on 12GB device.
details.realistic_solution: Single INT4 quantized model. Hardware-detected fusion: at runtime, detect hardware → load platform-specific CoreML model (A17), QNN model (Snapdragon), XNNPack model (Tensor G3). Same quantized weights, different execution graphs.

scenario: You are deploying a 1B LLM across a heterogeneous fleet: 30% A17 Pro (35 TOPS NE, 8GB), 45% Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB), 25% Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB). Design a single unified model with hardware-adaptive fusion strategy that achieves 20 tokens/sec on all three platforms.
title: Kernel Fusion: Mastery — Fusion Strategy Across Heterogeneous Mobile Hardware

details.common_mistake: Treating 8ms for a SwiGLU on a 4096-element vector as realistic — this is far too slow for an elementwise operation. The actual time should be microseconds. Likely the issue is the kernel launch overhead or memory transfer, not the computation.
details.napkin_math: SwiGLU on 4096 elements: ~30 FLOPs/element (mul + sigmoid + mul) = 123K FLOPs. At 7.5 TOPS: 123K / 7.5T = 0.016µs compute. Memory: 4096 × 2B (fp16) × 3 tensors (x, gate, output) = 24KB. At 51 GB/s: 0.47µs. Total theoretical: 0.49µs. Reported: 8ms = 16,330× slower than theoretical. Diagnosis: Python/framework overhead, CPU-GPU memory copy, or synchronization. Fix: ensure SwiGLU runs entirely on GPU without CPU-GPU sync. Fuse with adjacent Linear: Linear(x) + SwiGLU in one kernel. After fix: 0.49µs → negligible. Overall decode: 50ms - 8ms + 0.0005ms ≈ 42ms → 23.8 tok/sec. Key lesson: profiling attribution errors are common; 8ms for elementwise on 4K elements always indicates framework overhead, not compute.
details.realistic_solution: 8ms for SwiGLU on 4096 elements is clearly wrong computationally (4096 × 10 FLOPs = 41K FLOPs / 7.5 TOPS = 5.5ns). Root cause: the 8ms must be kernel dispatch overhead, CPU-GPU sync, or format conversion, not actual compute.

scenario: Your 1B LLM on Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) uses SwiGLU activation: SwiGLU(x) = x × σ(x) × gate. Profiling shows the SwiGLU activation takes 8ms out of 50ms per token (16% of decode time). The activation operates on a 4096-element vector. Optimize.
title: Kernel Fusion: Optimize SwiGLU Fusion for Mobile LLM on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Assuming 4096-context is impossible without flash attention; not quantifying how much of the 8GB device RAM is available for KV cache and attention.
details.napkin_math: At 512 context: attn matrix 512²×8×2B = 4.2MB per layer × 28 = 117MB. Fine for 8GB. At 4096 context: 4096²×8×2B = 268MB per layer × 28 = 7.5GB — exceeds 8GB RAM (minus OS ~2GB, model 1.5GB → only 4.5GB free). Flash attention: never materializes full matrix. Tile 32×32 on SRAM: SRAM usage = 2 × 32 × 32 × 2B × 8 heads = 33KB. 8GB RAM usage: Q,K,V = 3 × 4096 × 128 × 8 × 2B = 25.2MB per layer × 28 = 706MB. KV cache: 28 × 2 × 4096 × 128 × 8 × 2B = 1.41GB. Model weights: 1.5GB. OS: 2GB. Total: 0.706 + 1.41 + 1.5 + 2 = 5.6GB. Fits in 8GB. Token latency at 4096 context: KV read per token = 1.41GB / 68 GB/s = 20.7ms just for KV. Plus weights 22ms. Total: 42.7ms → 23.4 tok/sec. Near 25 tok/sec target. Feasible with flash attention.
details.realistic_solution: Flash attention is mandatory for 4096 context: attention matrix 268MB × 28 attention layers = 7.5GB — exceeds available memory. Flash attention keeps only tiles in SRAM.

scenario: Your 1B LLM on A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB) currently supports 512-token context at 25 tokens/sec but users request 4096-token context. Without fusion, the O(n²) attention matrix would be 4096²×8heads×2B = 268MB per layer. Analyze feasibility and design an optimized attention fusion strategy for 4096-context on 8GB device.
title: Kernel Fusion: Optimize Attention Fusion for Long-Context Mobile LLM

details.common_mistake: Specifying fusion without a testing plan for numerical correctness across platforms; not accounting for platform-specific fusion APIs (Core ML vs QNN).
details.napkin_math: Fused op groups (both platforms): (1) RMSNorm + Linear (QKV projection): saves 28 layers × 4096 × 2B × 2 = 459KB. (2) Attention (FlashAttention): saves 268MB → 25MB per layer (at 512 ctx). (3) Linear + SiLU + Gate (SwiGLU): saves 28 × 4096 × 2B × 2 = 459KB. (4) Residual + LayerNorm: saves 28 × 4096 × 2B = 230KB. Total savings: 268MB/layer × 28 = 7.5GB → flash reduces to 706MB. Other savings: 1.15MB per layer × 28 = 32MB. Combined: 7.5GB → 738MB memory footprint reduction for attention. A17 Pro latency: weight load 22ms + KV read at 512 ctx (706MB/68GB/s=10.4ms) + compute (0.17ms) + overhead (2ms) = 34.6ms → 28.9 tok/sec. Snapdragon: weight load 22ms + KV 10.4ms + compute (0.13ms) + overhead (1.5ms) = 34ms → 29.4 tok/sec. Both exceed 25 tok/sec target. QA: 1K golden prompts × 2 platforms × max output error < 0.02. CI: run on device simulator for each platform.
details.realistic_solution: Platform-specific fusion implementations: (1) A17 Pro: Core ML .mlpackage with automatic ANE fusion. (2) Snapdragon: Qualcomm AI Engine (QNN SDK) with manual fusion specification. Test: compare output against FP32 reference, max error < 0.02.

scenario: Realize the complete fusion plan for shipping a 1B INT4 LLM (500MB) to 10M users on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB) and Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB). Specify all fused op groups, their implementations, testing requirements, and expected latency for each platform.
title: Kernel Fusion: Realize Fusion Plan for Production Mobile LLM Deployment

details.common_mistake: Not distinguishing between weight bandwidth (dominant, can't be fused away) and activation bandwidth (small, can be fused). Students often confuse which is the bottleneck.
details.napkin_math: Post-attention ops (decode, batch=1, 4096 hidden): Attention output: 4096 × 2B = 8KB. Linear projection: weight 4096×4096×1B = 16MB, output 8KB. RMSNorm: 8KB in, 8KB out. Residual: 8KB + 8KB = 16KB. Gate linear: weight 4096×4096×1B = 16MB, output 8KB. Total activation bandwidth (all post-attn tensors): 8+8+8+8+8+8+8 = 56KB. At 68 GB/s: 0.00082ms. Weight bandwidth: 16MB + 16MB = 32MB. At 68 GB/s: 0.47ms. Ratio: weights are 32MB / 0.056MB = 571× larger. Fusing all activation ops: saves all 56KB activation HBM traffic = 0.00082ms per layer. 28 layers: 0.023ms total savings. Vs total decode time (28 layers × 0.47ms weight load + everything = ~20ms): savings = 0.11%. Not worth engineering effort for this workload. Fusion target for mobile decode: focus on attention (huge savings), not tiny activation ops.
details.realistic_solution: Activation bandwidth for post-attention sequence: the 4096-element vectors are tiny compared to the 4096×4096 weight matrices. Fusion saves activation reads/writes but those are negligible. The real insight: don't bother fusing these for decode — weights dominate.

scenario: Realize the bandwidth savings from fusing the post-attention operations on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB). For a 1B model decode (batch=1), the post-attention sequence is: attention output (4096-element) → Linear → RMSNorm → residual add → gate. Quantify savings per layer and total.
title: Kernel Fusion: Realize Bandwidth Savings from Fusing Transformer Block on Snapdragon

details.common_mistake: Claiming large latency savings for fusing tiny elementwise ops on a mobile decode workload — the activation tensors are tiny (8KB), so bandwidth savings are negligible vs weight loading.
details.napkin_math: ReLU FLOPs: 4096 × 1 = 4096 FLOPs. Bytes: 4096 × 4B = 16KB read + write. AI = 4096/16384 = 0.25 FLOPs/byte << 662. Memory-bound, but tensor tiny. Time: 16KB / 68 GB/s = 0.235µs. Kernel launch: 10µs. Total unfused: 10.235µs. Fused: 0µs (free, happens in preceding kernel's registers). Saving: 10.235µs. At 30 tokens/sec decode: 1000ms/30 = 33.3ms/token. Saving 10µs = 0.03% improvement — completely negligible for decode mode. Key insight: kernel launch overhead (10µs) >> memory time (0.235µs) for small tensors. Fusing small elementwise ops reduces launch count but barely affects decode latency.
details.realistic_solution: ReLU on 4096-element FP16: 1 FLOPs, 2 bytes read + 2 bytes write = 4 bytes per element. AI = 1/4 = 0.25 FLOPs/byte. Ridge point Snapdragon: 45,000 / 68 = 662 FLOPs/byte. Far below ridge → extremely memory-bound. But the tensor is only 4096 × 4B = 16KB. Time = 16KB / 68 GB/s = 0.235µs. Fusion saves 1 kernel launch (10µs) and 8KB intermediate write/read = 8KB / 68 GB/s = 0.118µs. Total save: 10.12µs.

scenario: For an elementwise ReLU operation on a 4096-element FP16 tensor on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB), compute the arithmetic intensity and determine whether fusing it with the preceding operation would reduce latency.
title: Kernel Fusion: Recall — Arithmetic Intensity and Mobile Fusion Impact

details.common_mistake: Writing platform-agnostic fusion requirements that are impossible to implement on some hardware (e.g., requiring Flash Attention fusion on Tensor G3 which has limited SRAM).
details.napkin_math: Throughput requirement: 20 tok/sec → 50ms/token max. Memory floor: model 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms. Remaining budget: 50 - 7.35 = 42.65ms for overhead. Overhead sources: kernel launches, format conversions, CPU-GPU sync. Required fusion to meet budget: without fusion, overhead estimated 60ms (above budget on Tensor G3). Fusion target: reduce overhead by >= 20ms to meet 50ms total on Tensor G3. Flash attention: eliminates 268MB per layer intermediate (at 512 ctx): 268MB / 51 GB/s = 5.3ms → 0.5ms = saves 4.8ms per layer... but there are 28 attention layers... saves too much per layer (not right calculation). For 1-token decode: KV cache access per layer 512 × 128 × 2 heads × 2B = 262KB/layer × 28 = 7.3MB KV read total. Standard vs flash: same for decode (flash helps prefill, not decode). Flash decode: saves attention matrix temp storage but not critical for decode latency. Numerical tolerance: max per-token output divergence from FP16 reference < 2% on perplexity metric. Platform adaptation: SRAM_tile = min(SRAM/4, 64KB).
details.realistic_solution: Platform-specific fusion requirements with a minimum baseline. Required fusion groups: (1) Flash Attention (all platforms, tile size adaptive to SRAM). (2) BN fold (inference only). (3) Elementwise chain fusion (RMSNorm + bias). Platform-specific: Core ML for ANE, QNN for Hexagon, XNNPack for Tensor G3.

details.common_mistake: Blaming compute for the slowdown when it's clearly memory bandwidth: the model FLOPs don't change per token, but KV cache reads grow linearly with context length.
details.napkin_math: 1B model: 24 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 64 (common 1B config). KV per token: 24 × 2 × 8 × 64 × 2B = 49.2KB. Wait, let me use head_dim=128 for consistency. 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 98.3KB per token. At seq=512: KV read = 512 × 98.3KB = 50.3MB. A17 Pro unified memory BW: ~68 GB/s. KV read time: 50.3MB / 68 GB/s = 0.74ms. Model weight load: 1B × 2B = 2GB... at 4-bit = 500MB. 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms. At seq=512: total ≈ 7.35 + 0.74 = 8.09ms → 123 tok/sec theoretical. Observed 30 tok/sec → 27% efficiency (framework overhead). At seq=2048: KV = 4× = 201MB, KV time = 2.96ms. Weight unchanged. Total ≈ 7.35 + 2.96 = 10.31ms + overhead. Efficiency same (27%) → 1/10.31ms × 0.27 = 26.2 tok/sec. Close to observed 18 tok/sec. KV scaling: linear with context length, as expected. At seq=4096: KV = 402MB, 5.91ms + 7.35 = 13.26ms, × 27% efficiency → 20.4 tok/sec. Observed 11 — overhead growing too (memory allocation, attention compute O(n²) even though it's small).
details.realistic_solution: Each decode step reads the full KV cache for all previously generated tokens. As context grows, KV read time grows linearly. Compute (single-token forward pass) stays constant. The KV read dominates at long contexts.

details.common_mistake: Truncating context by discarding old tokens (loses conversation context) without considering sliding window or KV compression alternatives.
details.napkin_math: 1B model: 24 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128. KV per token: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 1B (INT8) = 49.2KB. Available for KV (16GB RAM, 1B model at INT4 = 500MB): 16GB - 0.5GB model - 2GB OS = 13.5GB. Max tokens: 13.5GB / 49.2KB = 274,390 tokens — massive, no concern on 16GB device. Context window: 1B models typically limited to 4096 tokens (position encoding). At 4096 tokens: 4096 × 49.2KB = 201MB KV. Fits easily. Strategy: keep full KV up to 4096 context. At 4096 tokens, summarize oldest 2048 tokens (LLM call, 500ms), discard their KV, continue. Summarization cost: 500ms one-time when hitting limit. Effective conversation: unlimited turns with graceful degradation. Memory: 201MB KV peak — trivial on 16GB.
details.realistic_solution: Sliding window KV cache with importance-based retention: keep first N tokens (system prompt + first user turn) + last M tokens (recent context). Compress middle with summarization.

details.common_mistake: Storing the full KV cache to flash (too slow to reload in 3 seconds for long contexts); not considering that recomputing KV from saved tokens is often faster than reloading from flash.
details.napkin_math: 1B param model, 6 decode steps per forward, seq=2048. FLOPs per step: 2 × 1B × 1 token = 2 GFLOPs per decode step. For prefill of 2048 tokens: 2 × 1B × 2048 = 4.096 TFLOPs. On-device at 35 TOPS: 2G / 35T = 0.057ms per decode token (not 0.70 seconds). Prefill: 4.096T / 35T = 117ms. Correct decode: 2G / 35T = 0.057ms → 0.70ms (at 20% utilization: 2G / (35T×0.2) = 0.286ms ≈ 0.70ms with overhead). Key: 0.70ms (not 0.70 seconds), and 12.3 GFLOPs for prefill (not TFLOPs at this scale).
details.realistic_solution: 1B model decode on 35 TOPS device: 2 GFLOPs / 35 TOPS = ~0.06ms at peak, ~0.7ms with realistic utilization. Units are GFLOPs (not TFLOPs) and time is milliseconds (not seconds).

details.common_mistake: Blaming the model size without computing the actual KV cache memory growth; not tracking cumulative memory allocation per conversation turn.
details.napkin_math: 3B model (INT4 quantized): 750MB. KV per token: 32 layers × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131KB per token (bf16). At 3000 tokens: 3000 × 131KB = 393MB. OS: 2GB. Model: 750MB. KV: 393MB. Activations + framework: 500MB. Total: 3.64GB. Available on 12GB device... but Tensor G3 shares memory with GPU. iOS apps typically get 3-4GB before memory pressure warnings, 5-6GB for SIGKILL. Wait: 12GB is total system RAM. iOS reserves 40%: 7.2GB available for apps. App at 3.64GB: shouldn't crash. Re-examine: KV is likely in FP16 (not quantized): 3000 × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 786MB KV (bf16). Plus multiple conversation histories cached? Or framework keeps gradient buffers? Diagnosis: profile with Instruments. Fix: (1) Use INT8 KV: 393MB. (2) Limit context to 2048: 2048 × 65.5KB (INT8) = 134MB. (3) Clear completed conversation KV on new conversation start. Total memory at 2048 INT8: 750 + 134 + 500 = 1.38GB — stable.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache grows O(n) with conversation length. At 3000 tokens, KV cache size exceeds available RAM threshold, triggering OS memory pressure and SIGKILL.

details.common_mistake: Assuming GPU compute contention is the problem; not realizing that two parallel LLM tasks both read large KV caches, saturating the unified memory bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: A17 Pro unified memory: 68 GB/s (shared between all cores, GPU, NE). Chat decode: 512 × 98.3KB = 50.4MB KV read per step + model weights 500MB = 550MB total per step. At 68 GB/s: 8.1ms/step → 123 tok/sec theoretical → 37 tok/sec at 30% efficiency. Summarization (background): 2048 × 98.3KB = 201MB KV + 500MB weights = 701MB per step. At 68 GB/s: 10.3ms. Two simultaneous: combined 550 + 701 = 1.25GB per step. At 68 GB/s: 18.4ms (if sequential) or 18.4ms (bandwidth shared → both slow down). Each gets 34 GB/s effective: chat step = 550MB / 34 = 16.2ms → 61 tok/sec × 30% eff = 18.3 tok/sec. Vs alone: 37 tok/sec. Slowdown: 37/18.3 = 2.02× — close to observed 3× (with additional interference). Fix: serialize tasks (summarize in background between chat turns), or quantize KV to INT8 (halve bandwidth).
details.realistic_solution: Both tasks read KV cache from unified LPDDR5 memory. Combined KV bandwidth = (2048 + 512) × 98.3KB per decode step from each task. Unified memory bandwidth saturated.

scenario: Your A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB) app runs two parallel LLM tasks: a background summarization (1B model, 2048 tokens KV) and foreground chat (1B model, 512 tokens KV). You observe 3× slowdown in chat when summarization runs simultaneously. Diagnose the memory bandwidth contention.
title: KV-Cache: Diagnose KV Cache Thrashing in Concurrent Mobile LLM Requests

details.common_mistake: Not connecting number of KV heads to KV cache size; thinking GQA affects compute (it mainly affects KV cache memory and bandwidth in decode).
details.napkin_math: MHA KV per token: 24 layers × 2 × 16 heads × 64 dim × 2B = 98.3KB per token. GQA-4 KV per token: 24 × 2 × 4 × 64 × 2B = 24.6KB per token. Reduction: 4×. At 2048 context: MHA KV = 2048 × 98.3KB = 201MB. GQA-4 KV = 2048 × 24.6KB = 50.3MB. Memory saved: 150.7MB per conversation. Decode bandwidth per step (2048 attended): MHA = 201MB, GQA = 50.3MB. KV read time: MHA = 201MB / 68 GB/s = 2.96ms per step. GQA = 50.3MB / 68 GB/s = 0.74ms. Decode throughput (ignoring weights): MHA limited to 1/2.96ms = 338 tok/sec from KV reads. GQA: 1/0.74ms = 1351 tok/sec. Bottleneck shifts to weight loading: 500MB model / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms. Weight-bound: 136 tok/sec either way. GQA benefit at 2048 context: reduces KV from 2.96ms to 0.74ms. Total decode: MHA = 7.35 + 2.96 = 10.31ms → 97 tok/sec. GQA = 7.35 + 0.74 = 8.09ms → 124 tok/sec. 27.7% throughput improvement from GQA.
details.realistic_solution: MHA: 16 Q heads and 16 KV heads. GQA-4: 16 Q heads, 4 KV heads. KV cache size proportional to num_KV_heads. GQA reduces KV cache 4× with minimal quality loss.

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that quantization dequantization cost may offset memory bandwidth savings at short context lengths; not specifying the granularity of quantization (per-tensor vs per-head vs per-group).
details.napkin_math: 1B model: 24 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim=128. (A) FP16: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 98.3KB/token. At 2048 tokens: 201MB KV. Bandwidth per step: 201MB / 68 GB/s = 2.96ms. (B) INT8 + per-head quant: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 1B = 49.2KB/token + 24 × 2 × 8 × 2 × 4B (scale+zp per head) = 3KB overhead. Total 52.2KB/token. 2048 tokens: 107MB KV. Bandwidth: 107MB / 68 GB/s = 1.57ms. (C) INT4 per-head: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 0.5B = 24.6KB/token + 3KB overhead = 27.6KB/token. 2048 tokens: 56.5MB KV. Bandwidth: 56.5MB / 68 GB/s = 0.83ms. Quality: INT8 perplexity increase < 0.3%. INT4: 1-2% increase. Long-context: INT4 quality degrades more as quantization errors accumulate over 2048 tokens. Recommendation: INT8 for quality-sensitive, INT4 for memory-limited devices. Implementation: INT8 requires dequant before attention matmul — needs CUDA/Metal kernel modification.
details.realistic_solution: Per-head quantization: 1 scale + 1 zero-point per head. Overhead: 2 × num_KV_heads × 4B per token per layer. For 8 KV heads: 64B overhead per token per layer. Compute: dequantize during attention — adds ~1% compute overhead.

scenario: For a 1B LLM on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB), compare KV cache strategies: (A) FP16 KV, (B) INT8 KV with per-head quantization, (C) INT4 KV with per-head quantization. The model targets 2048-token conversations. Evaluate memory, bandwidth, quality, and implementation complexity.

details.common_mistake: Assuming sliding window has no quality impact; not quantifying memory savings; not accounting for the constant latency benefit of sliding window for very long conversations.
details.napkin_math: KV per token: 24 layers × 2 × 8 KV heads × 128 × 2B = 98.3KB. At turn 50 (3000 tokens): Full KV: 3000 × 98.3KB = 295MB. Latency at 3000 tokens: 295MB / 51 GB/s (Tensor G3 est.) + weight load 500MB / 51 GB/s = 5.78ms + 9.8ms = 15.58ms → 64 tok/sec. Sliding window (512): always 512 × 98.3KB = 50.3MB. Latency: constant 50.3MB/51 GB/s + 9.8ms = 0.99ms + 9.8ms = 10.79ms → 92.7 tok/sec. Constant. Memory: full KV at 3000 tokens = 295MB + 750MB model + 2GB OS = 3.05GB. Fine on 12GB. Sliding window: 50.3MB KV = 3.32× less memory. Quality: for coding assistant (need full context) → full KV. For chitchat (recent 512 tokens sufficient) → sliding window fine. At 10K turns: full KV = 10K × 98.3KB = 983MB. Still fits on 12GB device. Latency: 983MB / 51 GB/s = 19.3ms KV read alone. Sliding window stays 0.99ms. Long conversations: sliding window wins on latency.
details.realistic_solution: Full KV: memory grows linearly, latency grows linearly with context. Sliding window: constant memory and latency, but loses information from >512 turns ago. Quality impact depends on conversation type.

details.common_mistake: Thinking GQA reduces model quality significantly — modern LLMs (Llama 3, Gemma, etc.) use GQA with minimal quality loss. The quality-efficiency tradeoff is favorable.
details.napkin_math: MHA-16 KV cache, INT8: 32 layers × 2 × 16 KV heads × 128 head_dim × 4096 context × 1B = 32 × 2 × 16 × 128 × 4096 × 1B = 536,870,912 bytes ≈ 512MB. At 8192 tokens: 8192 × 98.3KB = 805MB. 4096 tokens: 4096 × 98.3KB = 403MB. Memory budget: 16GB total. OS: 2GB. Model (INT4): 500MB. KV at 4096 ctx: 403MB. Framework overhead: 500MB. Total: 3.4GB << 16GB. Easily feasible. Even 8192-token context: 2GB total → still fits. Snapdragon 8 Gen 3's 16GB allows very long contexts. details.common_mistake: Computing only KV bandwidth without including weight loading bandwidth; not identifying which term dominates at different context lengths.
details.napkin_math: INT4 model: 1B × 0.5B = 500MB. Weight load per decode step: 500MB / 68 GB/s = 7.35ms. KV per token: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B (bf16, even if weights INT4) = 98.3KB. At 256 tokens: KV = 256 × 98.3KB = 25.2MB, KV time = 0.37ms. Compute: 1B × 6 FLOPs / 35 TOPS = 0.17ms. Total: 7.35 + 0.37 + 0.17 = 7.89ms → 127 tok/sec. At 1024 tokens: KV = 100.5MB, time = 1.48ms. Total: 7.35 + 1.48 + 0.17 = 9.0ms → 111 tok/sec. At 4096 tokens: KV = 402MB, time = 5.91ms. Total: 7.35 + 5.91 + 0.17 = 13.43ms → 74 tok/sec. KV crossover (KV time = weight time): KV = 7.35ms → tokens = 7.35ms × 68 GB/s / 98.3KB = 5.09B bytes / 98.3KB = 51,870 tokens. At 50K tokens: weight load = KV load. For chat (< 4096 tokens), weights always dominate. Need INT4 KV to shift crossover: KV per token 49KB → crossover at 100K tokens.
details.realistic_solution: Decode time per token = weight_load_time + KV_read_time + compute_time. Weight load is constant. KV read grows linearly. Find crossover where KV > weight load.

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for model weights when calculating available memory for KV cache; confusing the number of KV heads with number of attention groups.
details.napkin_math: 3B model (INT4): 750MB. OS: 2GB. Activations: 200MB. Available KV: 12 - 0.75 - 2 - 0.2 = 9.05GB. At 2048 tokens: MHA (32 KV heads): 2048 × 32 × 2 × 32 × 128 × 2B = 2048 × 524KB = 1.07GB. GQA-8: 2048 × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 2048 × 131KB = 268MB. MQA (1 KV head): 2048 × 32 × 2 × 1 × 128 × 2B = 2048 × 16.4KB = 33.6MB. All fit in 9.05GB at 2048 tokens. Max context (within 9.05GB): MHA: 9.05GB / 524KB = 17,252 tokens. GQA-8: 9.05GB / 131KB = 69,007 tokens. MQA: 9.05GB / 16.4KB = 551,829 tokens. All fit! At 12GB available, even MHA supports 17K-token context. Key constraint for Tensor G3: decode latency, not memory. At 2048 ctx decode: MHA KV BW = 1.07GB / 51 GB/s = 21ms. GQA-8 = 268MB / 51 GB/s = 5.3ms. MQA = 33.6MB / 51 GB/s = 0.66ms. Weight load: 750MB / 51 GB/s = 14.7ms. MHA total: 35.7ms = 28 tok/sec. GQA: 20ms = 50 tok/sec. MQA: 15.4ms = 65 tok/sec. GQA-8 recommended: good quality + good throughput.
details.realistic_solution: Available memory for KV = total RAM - OS - model weights - activations. Model weights don't change with KV head count (Q projection is same size; only K,V projections change).

details.common_mistake: Implementing a simple truncation that drops the oldest tokens without considering that first tokens (system prompt) are often most important; not implementing the check efficiently.
details.napkin_math: A17 Pro: 8GB total. Reserved: OS 2GB + model (INT4) 500MB + activations 200MB + framework overhead 500MB = 3.2GB. Available KV: 4.8GB. Safety margin 80%: trigger at 3.84GB. KV per token: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 98.3KB. Token limit: 3.84GB / 98.3KB = 39,062 tokens. Far beyond any reasonable context (1B models usually max 4096 or 8192 context). Real trigger: context window limit (4096 tokens) reached first. 4096 tokens KV: 4096 × 98.3KB = 403MB << 3.84GB limit. Conclusion: for 1B models with 4096 context, memory safety is not a practical concern on 8GB A17 Pro. Memory limit only relevant for: longer contexts (8K+) or smaller RAM devices. For 4GB RAM device: available KV = 4 - 2 - 0.5 - 0.2 - 0.5 = 0.8GB → 8,138 tokens. 4096-ctx limit: 403MB → fits. 8192-ctx would exceed: need INT8 KV (49KB/token) → 8192 × 49KB = 401MB. Still fits!
details.realistic_solution: Implement H2O (Heavy Hitter Oracle): retain the top-K tokens by cumulative attention score plus the most recent W tokens. O(n) check after each generation step.

details.common_mistake: Optimizing model architecture and KV cache independently; not using the decode throughput formula to work backward to architecture requirements.
details.napkin_math: Target: 33.3ms per token at 4096 context. Budget: weight load = 33.3ms × 0.6 = 20ms → model size = 20ms × 68 GB/s = 1.36GB (INT4 weights). 1B model at INT4 = 500MB → headroom to 2.72B params. KV budget: 33.3ms × 0.35 = 11.7ms → KV size at 4096 ctx = 11.7ms × 68 GB/s = 795MB. KV per token: 795MB / 4096 = 194KB. Formula: num_layers × 2 × num_KV_heads × head_dim × 2B = 194KB. With 24 layers, head_dim=128: 24 × 2 × n_kv × 128 × 2B = 194KB → n_kv = 194 × 1024 / (24 × 2 × 128 × 2) = 198,656 / 12,288 = 16.2. Use n_kv=16 (GQA-16). Check: 24 × 2 × 16 × 128 × 2B = 196,608B = 192KB/token. At 4096: 786MB KV. Weight load 500MB. Total BW: 500 + 786 = 1286MB at 68 GB/s = 18.9ms. + compute 0.17ms. Total: 19.1ms → 52 tok/sec. Exceeds 30 tok/sec target! Alternative: use 32 layers with GQA-8 (more depth, fewer KV heads). 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 131KB/token × 4096 = 537MB KV. Total BW: 500 + 537 = 1037MB / 68 GB/s = 15.2ms → 65 tok/sec. Even better. Recommended architecture: 1B params, 32 layers, hidden 2048, GQA-8 KV heads, INT4 weights, INT8 KV.
details.realistic_solution: Target: 30 tok/sec = 33.3ms per token. Bottleneck: weight loading + KV reading. Given KV at 4096 context, work backward to architecture choices.

details.common_mistake: Not quantifying the memory infeasibility of 32K full KV cache; proposing solutions without verifying they fit in available memory.
details.napkin_math: 32K full KV (bf16): 4.19GB > 8GB available (8 - 2 OS - 0.75 model - 0.5 misc = 4.75GB). Barely fails. Solution 1: INT4 KV: 4.19GB / 4 = 1.05GB → total 4.3GB < 4.75GB. Fits! INT4 quality: suitable for code (tokens are precise, but individual attention weights less sensitive than logits). Solution 2: Sliding window 4096 + landmark tokens. Keep: (a) first 1024 tokens (imports, class headers), (b) last 3072 tokens (current edit context), (c) 1024 landmark tokens (function definitions, selected by attention magnitude). Total effective: 5,120 key tokens, full KV = 5120 × 131KB = 671MB. Total: 3.42GB. Fits in 4.75GB with 1.33GB headroom. Quality: landmark selection preserves structural understanding of full codebase. Latency at 5120 effective tokens: 671MB / 68 GB/s + 750MB / 68 GB/s = 9.87ms + 11ms = 20.87ms → 47.9 tok/sec. Acceptable for code completion. Recommended: INT4 KV (simple) + landmark tokens (quality). Total: 1.05GB KV at 32K + 750MB model + 2.5GB overhead = 4.3GB. Fits in 8GB with 3.7GB headroom for future features.
details.realistic_solution: 32K full KV at bf16: 3B model (32 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128): 32K × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 32K × 131KB = 4.19GB. Plus 750MB model + 2GB OS = 6.94GB > 8GB. Doesn't fit. Solutions: INT4 KV + sliding window + sparse attention.

details.common_mistake: Not considering that KV cache pages for inactive conversations can be compressed and offloaded to NAND flash rather than held in RAM; not using INT4 KV to halve memory.
details.napkin_math: 8192 token KV. Strategy: split 8192 tokens. Active (2048): 2048 × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 1B = 134MB INT8. Warm (2048): 2048 × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 0.5B = 67MB INT4. Cold (4096): 4096 × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 0.5B = 134MB INT4 (in RAM) or compressed to flash. All in RAM: 134 + 67 + 134 = 335MB. Savings vs full INT8: 537 - 335 = 202MB. Or: cold to flash: 134MB off-device. RAM: 134 + 67 = 201MB. Total: 3B INT8 model (3GB) + 201MB KV + 2GB OS = 5.2GB. Freed: 5.54 - 5.2 = 0.34GB + can now handle 2 conversations in RAM: 5.2 + 0.335 = 5.54GB for second conversation's KV. Or: extend to 16384-token context: 4×8192 KV = 4 × 201MB = 804MB total in RAM. Total: 3 + 0.804 + 2 = 5.8GB. Still fits. Flash access for cold KV: when attending to >6144 tokens, dequant from flash (latency: 134MB at A17 Pro flash 3 GB/s = 44.7ms per load). Amortize over multiple decode steps.
details.realistic_solution: Three-tier KV compression: (1) Active KV (recent 2048 tokens): INT8 in RAM. (2) Warm KV (2048-6144 tokens): INT4 in RAM. (3) Cold KV (6144+ tokens): compressed to NAND.

scenario: Your 3B LLM (INT8) on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB) needs to support 8192-token context. KV cache at 8192 tokens = 8192 × 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 1B = 537MB. Model INT8: 3GB. OS: 2GB. Total: 5.54GB — fits in 8GB but leaves only 2.46GB. Optimize to free 1.5GB more for longer contexts or caching multiple conversations.
title: KV-Cache: Optimize KV Cache for Aggressive Memory Compression on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Using stride-based pruning for all tasks regardless of content structure; not computing the actual quality difference between uniform vs importance-based pruning.
details.napkin_math: From 8192 tokens, retain 2048 = 25%. Stride-based: keep tokens 0, 4, 8, 12... always evenly spaced. Misses: important clauses may fall in removed tokens. H2O: tracks cumulative attention weights per token across all layers and heads. Keep top-512 + last 1536 most recently generated. Quality on legal QA: stride-based typically 15-25% worse than H2O for key clause retrieval. H2O compute overhead: track 8192 attention scores per layer per step. 32 layers × 8192 tokens × 4B = 1MB tracking buffer. Update each step: 32 × 8192 multiplications = 262K ops → at 45 TOPS: 0.006µs — negligible. Pruning step (every 100 tokens generated): sort 8192 scores (O(n log n)): 8192 × 13 = 106K ops → 0.002µs. H2O overhead: effectively zero. Latency at 2048 effective KV: 2048 × 49.2KB/token (INT8) = 100.7MB KV read. At 68 GB/s: 1.48ms. Plus weight load (500MB INT4): 7.35ms. Total: 8.83ms → 113 tok/sec. H2O quality retention: 85-90% of full-context performance (vs 60-75% for stride).
details.realistic_solution: H2O (attention-based) significantly outperforms stride-based for documents with uneven information density (legal documents have key clauses and boilerplate). Stride-based may be faster to compute. Evaluate both on actual legal QA benchmarks.

scenario: Your 1B LLM on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB) has a 2048-token KV cache budget. Long legal documents require 8192 tokens. Implement and compare two KV pruning strategies: (A) stride-based retention (keep every 4th token), (B) attention-score-based retention (H2O: keep top-25% by cumulative attention). Evaluate quality preservation and latency.
title: KV-Cache: Optimize KV Pruning for Token Budget on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for contiguous memory layout requirements for efficient GPU access; storing K and V separately vs interleaved (page-cache style).
details.napkin_math: K cache: [32, 2048, 8, 128] bf16. Size: 32 × 2048 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 134MB. V cache: [32, 2048, 8, 128] bf16. Size: 134MB. Total KV: 268MB. Memory layout: K_cache at base address 0x0, contiguous. V_cache at 0x8000000 (134MB offset). Access pattern: per layer, per step, read K[layer, :current_len, :, :] = 2048 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 4.19MB (full K for layer). Stride pattern: K[layer] is contiguous (good for GPU). Full forward pass KV reads: 32 layers × 2 (K+V) × 4.19MB = 268MB per decode step. At A17 Pro 68 GB/s: 3.94ms for KV at 2048 context. Total memory: 3B model INT4 = 750MB + 268MB KV + 2GB OS + 200MB activations + 500MB framework = 3.72GB << 8GB. 53.5% available for other tasks or longer context.
details.realistic_solution: K and V stored separately for attention computation efficiency. Cache layout: [num_layers, 2, max_seq_len, num_kv_heads, head_dim]. Physical memory: contiguous bf16 tensor.

scenario: Realize the complete KV cache memory layout for a 3B LLM on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB unified memory). The model has 32 layers, GQA with 8 KV heads, head_dim=128. Chat session length: 2048 tokens. Specify tensor dimensions, memory addresses, data types, and total allocation.
title: KV-Cache: Realize KV Cache Memory Layout for 3B LLM on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Not accounting for the positional encoding (RoPE) dependency — the system prompt KV is computed at positions 0-255 and must be reused at those exact positions in every new conversation.
details.napkin_math: System prompt: 256 tokens. KV cache for 256 tokens: 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 1B (INT8) = 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 = 49,152B = 49.2KB × 256 = 12.6MB. One-time computation: prefill 256 tokens. 1B × 6 × 256 FLOPs / 45 TOPS = 1.54T / 45T = 0.034 seconds = 34ms. Store 12.6MB to flash: 12.6MB / 3 GB/s = 4.2ms. Load on app start: same. TTFT without caching: prefill 256 (system) + 512 (user) = 768 tokens. Time: 1B × 6 × 768 / (45T × 0.5 efficiency) = 204ms. TTFT with caching: prefill only 512 user tokens. Time: 1B × 6 × 512 / 22.5T = 136ms. Saved: 68ms TTFT improvement = 33% faster. Load cached KV overhead: 12.6MB / 68 GB/s = 0.185ms — negligible. Net TTFT: 136ms vs 204ms. 1.5× TTFT improvement for no quality cost.
details.realistic_solution: Pre-compute KV for system prompt at positions 0-255. Cache 256-token KV. For new conversation: load cached KV, prefill only user message starting at position 256. RoPE positions are correct because they match original computation.

scenario: Realize a system prompt KV cache for a 1B LLM on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB). The system prompt is 256 tokens (same for all chat sessions). Specify the pre-computation, storage, and reuse mechanism. Quantify TTFT improvement for a 512-token user message.
title: KV-Cache: Realize KV Cache Reuse for System Prompt on Mobile LLM

details.common_mistake: Confusing KV cache with model weights cache; not knowing that without KV cache, each token requires recomputing attention over the full sequence (O(n²) total computation).
details.napkin_math: Without KV cache: generating token n requires prefill of all n-1 prior tokens. For 512-token generation: 1+2+3...+512 = 131,328 token-equivalent computations. For 1B model: 131,328 × 1B × 6 FLOPs = 787.97T FLOPs. At 35 TOPS: 22.5 seconds for 512 tokens = 22.7 tokens/sec. With KV cache: each step = 1 token computation = 1B × 6 FLOPs = 6B FLOPs. At 35 TOPS: 0.17ms per token. 512 tokens: 512 × 0.17ms = 87ms = 5,862 tokens/sec (compute only). But weight loading dominates: 7.35ms per step → 136 tok/sec. KV cache speedup: 22.7 → 136 tok/sec = 5.99× at 512 tokens, scales to O(n) speedup at longer contexts.
details.realistic_solution: KV cache: stores the Key and Value tensors for all previously generated tokens. Avoids recomputing K,V for old tokens at each new generation step. Without KV cache: generating the nth token requires O(n) computation (re-computing all prior K,V). Total generation of N tokens: O(N²). With KV cache: each step O(1) new K,V computation → total O(N).

scenario: In the context of a 1B LLM on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB), define the KV cache, explain why it exists, and state what happens to token generation speed as context length grows without KV caching.
title: KV-Cache: Recall — What is a KV Cache and Why Does It Matter for Mobile LLM?

details.common_mistake: Not specifying per-conversation KV isolation (conversations must not share KV pages); not defining quantization format that meets both memory and quality requirements.
details.napkin_math: 3B model INT4: 750MB. Per-conversation KV (INT8): 32 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 1B × 4096 = 268MB per active conversation. Memory budget: 8GB - 2GB OS - 750MB model - 500MB framework = 4.75GB. Single active conversation: 268MB KV → 4.48GB remaining. Multi-conversation: can hold 4.48/0.268 = 16.7 → 16 background conversations in RAM. In practice: iOS suspends background apps. Only 1-2 conversations in RAM simultaneously. Specification: max KV per conversation: 268MB (INT8) or 134MB (INT4). Quantization: INT8 for active (quality), INT4 for background (memory). Eviction trigger: available memory < 1GB → offload oldest background conversation KV to flash. Flash KV: 268MB at 3 GB/s = 89ms write. Recovery: if KV evicted → recompute from conversation tokens (prefill). 4096 tokens × 3B model = 4096 × 3B × 6 FLOPs / 35 TOPS = 2.1 seconds recompute. Acceptable for background resume. SLA: active conversation KV always in RAM, < 100ms for KV restore.
details.realistic_solution: Each conversation has isolated KV storage. Quantization: INT8 for quality, INT4 for long context. Eviction: background conversations' KV offloaded to flash. Recovery: KV not persisted (recomputed on resume).

scenario: Write the KV cache specification for a production mobile LLM chat app on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB) serving 10M users. The app supports 3B LLM, 4096-token context. Define: max KV memory allocation, quantization requirements, eviction triggers, multi-conversation caching, and crash recovery requirements.
title: KV-Cache: Specification — KV Cache Requirements for Production Mobile LLM App

details.common_mistake: Not verifying that 16K-token KV cache + model weights + OS fit in 16GB; not checking decode latency SLA at 16K context.
details.napkin_math: 3B param model, 6 FLOPs/param per forward, seq=16384 tokens: Total FLOPs = 2 × 3B × 16384 = 98.3 TFLOPs. Attention FLOPs ∝ seq²: 2 × heads × seq² × head_dim per layer. For 28 layers, 32 heads, head_dim=128: 2 × 28 × 32 × 16384² × 128 = 6.3 PFLOPs — dominated by attention. Simplified estimate: 3B × 6 × 16384 = 295 TFLOPs (linear term only). Attention quadratic adds ~197 TFLOPs more at this sequence length. Total ≈ 295 TFLOPs (linear) + attention overhead (not 1.48 TFLOPs which is 200× too low).
details.realistic_solution: At seq=16384, a 3B model requires ~295 TFLOPs (linear ops) plus significant quadratic attention FLOPs. 1.48 TFLOPs is too low by ~200×.

scenario: Specify the KV cache budget for a code completion assistant using a 3B LLM on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS, 16GB). Requirements: 16K-token codebase context, real-time completion (< 1s to first token), and < 50ms per subsequent token. Define quantization, layout, and context management.
title: KV-Cache: Specification — KV Cache Budget for Multi-Turn Code Completion

details.common_mistake: Not deriving KV constraints from the latency SLA; specifying KV cache size without verifying it's achievable given Tensor G3's lower bandwidth.
details.napkin_math: Budget: 33.3ms per token. Weight load: 1B × INT4 = 500MB. At Tensor G3 BW (estimated 51 GB/s): 500MB / 51 GB/s = 9.8ms. Remaining for KV: 33.3 - 9.8 - 3ms overhead = 20.5ms. KV budget: 20.5ms × 51 GB/s = 1.046GB. KV per token (bf16): 24 × 2 × 8 × 128 × 2B = 98.3KB. Max context: 1.046GB / 98.3KB = 10,633 tokens. Use INT8 KV (49.2KB/token): max context = 1.046GB / 49.2KB = 21,260 tokens. Specification: INT8 KV quantization required. Max context: 8192 tokens (with 2.6× headroom). At 8192 tokens: KV = 8192 × 49.2KB = 402MB. KV read time: 402MB / 51 GB/s = 7.9ms. Total: 9.8 + 7.9 + 3 = 20.7ms → 48.3 tok/sec. Exceeds 30 tok/sec SLA. Context length can go to 16K: 16384 × 49.2KB = 805MB. Time: 805MB / 51 GB/s = 15.8ms. Total: 9.8 + 15.8 + 3 = 28.6ms → 35 tok/sec. Still meets 30 tok/sec SLA. Maximum context for 30 tok/sec: KV budget = 33.3 - 9.8 - 3 = 20.5ms × 51 GB/s = 1.046GB / 49.2KB = 21.3K tokens. Specify: max 16K context with INT8 KV for safety margin.
details.realistic_solution: Work backward from latency SLA. Budget: 33.3ms total per token. Allocate: ~20ms for weight loading, ~10ms for KV reading, ~3ms overhead. From 10ms KV budget, derive max KV size.

scenario: Write the KV cache specification for a 1B LLM chat assistant on Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB) targeting 30 tokens/sec (33.3ms per token). Given the bandwidth constraints, specify the maximum allowed KV cache size, required quantization, and maximum supported context length to meet the SLA.
title: KV-Cache: Specification — KV Cache Constraints for Latency SLA on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Assuming cloud always wins on raw compute without accounting for network latency dominating TTFT, especially on mobile networks (50-200ms RTT).
details.napkin_math: On-device decode: 1B × 1 byte = 1GB. Neural Engine eff. BW ~68 GB/s: 1/68 = 14.7ms/token. Cloud decode: 26GB/3.35TB/s = 7.8ms/token. TTFT on-device: 2×64×1B×2/(35×10^12) = 256G/35T = 7.3ms. TTFT cloud: 100ms RTT + 7ms = 107ms. Winner depends on use case: interactive typing → on-device; long completions → cloud.
details.realistic_solution: On-device A17 Pro: 1B INT8 model = 1GB, fits in 8GB. Neural Engine bandwidth ~68 GB/s effective. Decode: 1GB/68GB/s ≈ 14.7ms/token × 50 = 735ms. TTFT (64-token prefill): compute-bound at 35 TOPS: 2×64×1B/35T ≈ 3.7ms. Cloud: TTFT = 100ms RTT + 27ms prefill = 127ms. TPOT = 7.8ms/token (H100). Cloud wins TPOT (7.8 vs 14.7ms) but on-device wins TTFT (4ms vs 127ms) and works offline.

scenario: An iOS app team debates between on-device inference (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB memory) vs. cloud API (H100-backed, 100ms network RTT) for a 1B-parameter language model generating 50 tokens. Evaluate TTFT and TPOT for both approaches.
title: Latency Decomposition: Compare On-Device vs. Cloud LLM Latency on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Ignoring that NNAPI adds 2-5ms dispatch overhead per inference call, and that CoreML has better kernel fusion for Apple Neural Engine ops.
details.napkin_math: 0.44 GOPs / 45 TOPS = 0.0098ms compute on Snapdragon. NNAPI overhead: 2-5ms (measured). Total: ~4ms. CoreML: 0.44G/35T = 0.013ms + 0.5ms CoreML overhead = ~0.5ms. A17 Pro Neural Engine wins 8× on latency for this model size.
details.realistic_solution: MobileNetV3-Large: 219M MACs = 0.44 GOPs. Snapdragon DSP via NNAPI: 0.44G/45T ≈ 0.01ms compute + 3ms NNAPI overhead = ~4ms total. CoreML on Neural Engine: 0.44G/35T + 1ms framework = ~1.01ms. CoreML ~4× faster due to lower framework overhead and better kernel fusion. But NNAPI can use GPU fallback for unsupported ops.

scenario: A cross-platform mobile ML team is evaluating MobileNetV3-Large (219M MACs) on Android (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 45 TOPS INT8, 16GB) using TFLite with NNAPI vs. CoreML on iPhone (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS). Compare inference latency including framework overhead and memory transfer.
title: Latency Decomposition: Compare CoreML vs. TFLite Inference on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Using INT8 TOPS spec for INT4 model without noting that INT4 throughput is typically 2× INT8 on Snapdragon (Hexagon DSP supports INT4 natively in Gen 3).
details.napkin_math: INT4 weights: 2B × 4 bits / 8 = 1GB. LPDDR5X BW: 77 GB/s. Decode: 1/77 = 13ms/token. Prefill FLOPs: 2×256×2B×2=2.048T. INT4 TOPS ≈ 90T (2× INT8): 2.048/90 = 22.8ms. Realistic utilization 60%: 22.8/0.6 = 38ms TTFT.
details.realistic_solution: INT4 model size: 2B × 0.5 bytes = 1GB. Decode BW-bound: 1GB / 77GB/s ≈ 13ms/token. TTFT: 2×256×2B×2 FLOPs = 2.05T FLOPs. At 45 TOPS INT8 → INT4 effective ~90 TOPS. 2.05T/90T ≈ 22ms. Realistic with memory overhead: ~40ms TTFT, 13ms/token decode.

scenario: A 2B-parameter LLM (INT4 quantized) runs on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 (45 TOPS INT8, 16GB LPDDR5X at ~77 GB/s effective). Compute TTFT for a 256-token prompt and TPOT for decode. Assume 32 layers, hidden dim 2560.
title: Latency Decomposition: Compute TTFT and TPOT for On-Device LLM on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Focusing optimization on the CNN inference (fastest component) while ignoring HEIC decode (CPU-bound, 40-80ms) and display pipeline (two-frame delay = 33ms at 60Hz).
details.napkin_math: HEIC 12MP decode: ~60ms CPU. HW decode: ~8ms (7.5× speedup). CNN: 3 GOPs / 35 TOPS = 0.086ms theoretical; 5ms measured (memory bandwidth limited: 15M×1byte=15MB weights, 15MB/68GB/s=0.22ms + activation memory). Display: 16ms vsync. Optimized total: 16+8+2+5+2+1+16 = 50ms. Under 100ms perceptual threshold.
details.realistic_solution: Touch event: 16ms. HEIC decode (12MP): CPU ~60ms. Resize to 512×512: 2ms. CNN inference (15M params at INT8, ~3 GOPs): 3G/35T ≈ 0.086ms, realistic 5ms. Post-process: 2ms. Texture upload to GPU: 512×512×4=1MB, ~1ms. Display pipeline: 16ms (next vsync). Total: 16+60+2+5+2+1+16 = 102ms. Optimize HEIC decode with VideoToolbox HW decoder → 8ms. New total: 50ms. Remaining: optimize resize with Metal → 0.5ms.

scenario: A mobile photo editing app uses on-device style transfer (15M param CNN, INT8) on A17 Pro (35 TOPS, 8GB). The user-perceived latency from tap to preview includes: touch event latency (16ms at 60Hz), image decode from disk (HEIC 12MP), pre-processing, inference, post-processing, and display render. Audit all components and identify where to invest optimization effort.
title: Latency Decomposition: Full Mobile ML App Latency Audit with User-Perceived Delay

details.common_mistake: Trying to optimize inference when the bottleneck is the 20ms audio buffer (Nyquist: need 160ms window for reliable detection) and MFCC feature extraction on CPU.
details.napkin_math: Inference: 0.05 GOPs / 7.5 TOPS = 6.7μs. Overhead: 2ms. MFCC CPU: 5ms. Audio buffer: minimum 10ms (160 samples at 16kHz). Queuing at 50% overlap: 10ms stride. P99 = stride + processing = 10 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 14ms per window. Pipeline delay: 2-3 windows for smoothing = 3×14 = 42ms. Target < 80ms achievable.
details.realistic_solution: Audio buffer latency: 20ms is irreducible for stable audio. MFCC on CPU: 5ms. Inference: 0.05G/7.5T = 0.007ms, overhead ~2ms. Decision: 1ms. Total: 20+5+2+1=28ms per-window. P99=180ms suggests audio pipeline queuing. Fix: move MFCC to DSP (1ms), reduce buffer to 10ms with 50% overlap, reduce queuing. New P99: ~60ms.

scenario: A wake-word detection model (1M params, INT8, 0.05 GOPs per 100ms audio window) runs continuously on Pixel 8's Tensor G3 (7.5 TOPS, 12GB). Current latency from audio capture to detection trigger is 180ms P99. Target is < 80ms. The audio pipeline: mic capture (20ms buffer), feature extraction (MFCC, CPU), inference, decision logic. Diagnose and quantify optimizations.
title: Latency Decomposition: Optimize Wake-Word Detection Latency on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Assuming 60fps means a 16.7ms budget per frame; missing that the pipeline must complete in <16ms to allow display commit before vsync.
details.napkin_math: Segmentation model: 2.8 GOPs INT8. Neural Engine: 35 TOPS. Compute: 2.8/35 = 0.08ms. With framework overhead: 2ms. Argmax on Metal: 1280×720×21 = 19.4M ops. At 1 TFLOPS Metal GPU: 0.019ms. Total pipeline: 0+1+2+1+2 = 6ms. 60fps budget: 16.7ms. Slack: 10.7ms. ✓
details.realistic_solution: Camera capture: 0ms (streaming, always available). Pre-process (GPU): 1ms. Inference: 2.8G/35T ≈ 0.08ms + 2ms overhead = 2ms. Post-process (argmax over 1280×720×21 classes): CPU naive 8ms, Metal compute 1ms. Metal render: 2ms. Display commit: must finish by 15ms before vsync. Total: 1+2+1+2 = 6ms. Budget: 10ms slack. Can add second model or increase resolution.

scenario: An augmented reality iOS app must overlay semantic segmentation on the camera feed in real time. The A17 Pro (35 TOPS Neural Engine, 8GB) runs a segmentation model (MobileNetV3 backbone, 5M params INT8, 2.8 GOPs) at 60fps. Size each latency component: camera capture, pre-process, inference, post-process, Metal render, display.
title: Latency Decomposition: Size Inference Latency Budget for AR App on A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Assuming Apple allows arbitrary dynamic code/model downloads without restrictions; Apple guidelines prohibit downloading code that changes app behavior, but downloading ML model weights (data files) is permitted if done correctly via Core ML model assets.
details.napkin_math: Dataset compression: 500TB total. 10% validation split = 10% of 500TB = 50TB for validation (not 100TB). Training set: 450TB. After deduplication (20% reduction): 360TB training.
details.realistic_solution: 10% validation split of 500TB = 50TB validation, 450TB training. 20% deduplication removes 90TB → 360TB final training set.

scenario: An iOS app team uses a 50MB CoreML model (A17 Pro, 35 TOPS). Two strategies: (A) bundle model in app (App Store update, 1-2 week review cycle, affects all iOS users) vs. (B) dynamic model download post-install (instant update, but requires network, Apple restrictions apply). Evaluate latency-to-deploy, compliance risk, user experience, and bandwidth cost at 10M installs.
title: MLOps Lifecycle: Compare App Store vs. Dynamic Model Updates for iOS ML Apps

details.common_mistake: Assuming federated learning is always more private; in practice, gradient uploads can leak private information, and the accuracy gap vs. centralized training is often 5-15% for language tasks.
details.napkin_math: FL gradient size: 5M × 4B = 20MB uncompressed. Compressed (1% Top-K): 200KB. 100M devices: 100M × 200KB = 20TB per round. At $0.09/GB: $1,800/round. 10 rounds: $18,000. Plus device battery cost: 20KB/s upload × 100M devices = 2TB/s total. Centralized: collect 1B text samples × 100 bytes avg = 100GB → train on H100 $1,000. Centralized: 18× cheaper, better accuracy.
details.realistic_solution: FL: gradient upload per round: 5M params × 4 bytes = 20MB per device per round. 100M devices × 20MB = 2PB per round. With compression (Top-K 1%): 200KB per device. 100M × 200KB = 20TB per round. 10 rounds: 200TB. Centralized: 1TB anonymized n-grams uploaded = $90 CDN. Accuracy: centralized often 3-8% better perplexity due to full data access. FL wins on privacy but loses on accuracy and has massive coordination overhead.
