title: Diagnosing Page Thrashing on Apple A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Candidates often incorrectly assume the OOM is caused by a standard memory leak in the ML application or an unexpected spike in NPU activation memory. They typically suggest reducing the batch size or applying heavier quantization without recognizing the system-level resource contention at play.
details.napkin_math: Total shared memory: 12.0 GB. Base OS footprint + Background Apps: ~4.5 GB. Model Weights: 2.5 GB. Subtotal usage: 7.0 GB, leaving 5.0 GB free. A single uncompressed 4K video frame (3840x2160x4 bytes) is ~33.2 MB. The ISP utilizes a 15-frame ring buffer (~498 MB) and the GPU uses a triple buffer (~100 MB). Total usage is ~7.6 GB, leaving ~4.4 GB technically free. However, the continuous cycling of these 33.2 MB blocks fragments the heap. If the NPU needs a contiguous 128 MB buffer for a specific layer's activation tensor to utilize its 34.7 TOPS capacity, the fragmented 4.4 GB space cannot accommodate the contiguous request, leading to an OOM.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is severe memory fragmentation within the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X pool caused by contention with the ISP and GPU. Because the ISP and GPU rapidly allocate and deallocate large buffers for high-resolution camera frames, the physical memory becomes heavily fragmented over a few minutes of use. When the NPU attempts to allocate a large, contiguous block of memory for an activation tensor to maintain its high throughput, the allocation fails despite sufficient total free memory, triggering the OS to evict the application.

scenario: Your team is deploying a real-time video enhancement model on a device powered by the Samsung Exynos 2400. title: Diagnosing OOM Evictions on Shared Memory Exynos 2400

details.common_mistake: Candidates often blame the TPU hardware constraints or suggest rolling back the entire model to FP16 or BF16. They fail to identify the specific numeric limitations of the FP8 format when handling the outlier activations that naturally occur in large language models.
details.napkin_math: For a 1.8B parameter model, FP8 weights consume 1.8 GB of the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory. To reach a target of 15 tokens/second, memory bandwidth requires 1.8 GB * 15 = 27 GB/s. If 1% of a 2048-dimensional hidden state contains outliers, keeping them in BF16 instead of FP8 adds just 20 bytes per token per layer. Across 24 layers at 15 tok/s, this mixed-precision overhead adds less than 10 KB/s of bandwidth, which is mathematically negligible and keeps the TPU operating efficiently near its 7.5 TOPS limit.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is numeric overflow caused by the limited dynamic range of the FP8 format (e.g., E4M3 caps at 448), which cannot represent the massive outlier activations typical in LLMs. The optimal solution is to implement an outlier-aware mixed-precision strategy, isolating the specific channel dimensions containing outliers. By computing only these few channels in BF16 while keeping the rest in FP8, the system avoids overflow while still leveraging the high throughput of the Tensor G3 TPU.

scenario: You are deploying a 1.8B parameter Gemini Nano model to a device powered by the Google Tensor G3. title: Diagnosing FP8 Activation Overflow on Tensor G3 TPU

details.common_mistake: Candidates often blame thermal throttling or assume the model wasn't quantized to INT8 correctly. They miss the MLOps lifecycle angle: the CI/CD pipeline failed to validate hardware-specific operator compatibility before updating the model registry, creating a severe training-serving skew.
details.napkin_math: Expected NPU latency: 90 GOPS / (45 TOPS INT8 * 25% utilization) = 8 ms. With a graph break, assuming 80 GOPS on NPU and 10 GOPS falling back to a 0.5 TOPS CPU core: NPU time = 80 / 11.25 TOPS = 7.1 ms. CPU time = 10 GOPS / 0.5 TOPS = 20 ms. Moving a 4MB intermediate tensor over the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory (assuming ~75 GB/s bandwidth) is fast (~0.05ms), but OS synchronization for the CPU-NPU handoff adds ~2ms. Total latency = 7.1 + 20 + 2 = 29.1 ms, aligning with the 30 ms symptom.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is a graph break caused by an operator (e.g., SiLU activation) unsupported by the Hexagon NPU, forcing a fallback to the CPU. The heterogeneous architecture must shuffle intermediate tensors via the shared LPDDR5X memory. The solution is to update the CI/CD pipeline to include hardware-in-the-loop (HITL) testing or to run the specific Qualcomm compiler during the CI build stage to fail the pipeline if unsupported NPU ops are detected.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often misdiagnose this as NPU thermal throttling or assume the TFLite runtime has operator coverage gaps that trigger slow CPU fallbacks. They fail to identify the architectural bottleneck of shared memory subsystems in mobile SoCs.
details.napkin_math: LPDDR5X typically provides a peak memory bandwidth of ~68 GB/s. A heavy 4K 60FPS ISP workload can consume up to 40 GB/s, while the OS and CPU require ~15 GB/s, leaving only ~13 GB/s for the NPU. If an unoptimized model generates 300 MB of total memory traffic (weights + activations) per inference and runs at 30 FPS, it requires 300 MB * 30 = 9 GB/s. During ISP burst activity, available bandwidth can temporarily drop below this 9 GB/s threshold. Consequently, despite having a massive 34.7 TOPS compute capacity, the dual-core NPU is forced to stall while waiting for data, resulting in extreme latency spikes.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is memory bandwidth contention. Because the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory is shared, the ISP consuming massive bandwidth for high-resolution video starves the NPU of data. To resolve this, the deployment engineer must optimize the model's memory footprint (e.g., ensuring fully quantized INT8 operators to minimize weight fetching) or implement a scheduler that throttles NPU inferences during peak ISP buffer flushes.

details.common_mistake: Candidates frequently assume the entire 12 GB of memory is dedicated to the NPU, calculating only the static weights. They fail to account for the shared memory architecture where the CPU, GPU, and ISP (Image Signal Processor) heavily consume the same LPDDR5X pool during concurrent operations.
details.napkin_math: Model weights: 8 billion parameters * 1 byte (INT8) = 8.0 GB. Runtime activations (KV cache) ≈ 0.5 GB. Total LLM footprint = 8.5 GB. OS base footprint ≈ 2.5 GB. ISP/GPU frame buffers for camera ≈ 1.5 GB. Total requested memory: 8.5 + 2.5 + 1.5 = 12.5 GB. Since 12.5 GB > 12.0 GB shared LPDDR5X capacity, the system inevitably crashes.
details.realistic_solution: A strong candidate will identify that the Exynos 2400 features a unified memory subsystem. The 8B INT8 model consumes roughly 8 GB just for weights. The OS requires around 2-3 GB. When the camera activates, the ISP and GPU allocate large high-resolution frame buffers. This combined memory pressure exceeds the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X capacity, triggering the Android Low Memory Killer Daemon (LMKD) to terminate the app.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume the new model is simply too large or computationally heavy, suggesting generic solutions like heavier INT8 quantization or pruning. They fail to analyze the contradictory telemetry (low NPU utilization alongside high memory bandwidth) and miss the implications of heterogeneous computing on a shared memory bus.
details.napkin_math: While the Hexagon NPU offers 45 TOPS INT8 for efficient compute, fallback destroys this efficiency. Assume a mid-network activation tensor is 4 MB. A single fallback requires writing 4 MB to LPDDR5X memory and reading it back to the CPU (8 MB total). At 30 FPS, one fallback point generates 240 MB/s of memory traffic. If the model stutters between the NPU and CPU 10 times per inference, it creates 2.4 GB/s of continuous, unnecessary memory bandwidth overhead, rapidly draining the battery and causing thermal throttling.
details.realistic_solution: The symptoms strongly indicate an operation fallback issue. The Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 uses a heterogeneous architecture where the CPU, GPU, and NPU share the LPDDR5X memory. If the new model introduced operations not supported by the Hexagon NPU, those ops fall back to the CPU or GPU. This forces the system to constantly copy intermediate tensors back and forth across the shared memory bus, leading to the observed memory saturation, latency spikes, and severe battery drain. The fix requires profiling the model to identify the unsupported ops and replacing them with NPU-compatible alternatives.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume the model is compute-bound and suggest aggressive pruning or quantization without looking at system-level resource contention. They frequently forget that mobile SoCs have unified memory systems and fail to investigate what other hardware blocks are doing.
details.napkin_math: LPDDR5X typically offers around 68.2 GB/s theoretical peak bandwidth. If the ISP is writing 4K 60FPS video (approx 1.5 GB/s uncompressed) and the GPU is actively rendering UI/filters consuming 40-50 GB/s, the remaining bandwidth is severely constrained. Even if the NPU model only needs 5 GB/s to load weights and activations, instantaneous bursts from the GPU/ISP can drop available bandwidth to near zero for milliseconds. A 50MB model bottlenecked to 1 GB/s during a contention spike takes 50ms just to load, completely explaining the 40-60ms latency spikes despite the 34.7 TOPS available compute.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is memory bandwidth contention. The Samsung Exynos 2400 shares its 12 GB LPDDR5X memory across the CPU, GPU, ISP, and NPU. During live video processing, the ISP (processing high-res camera frames) and GPU (rendering the filters) consume massive memory bandwidth. The diagnosis requires using a system-wide profiler to overlay memory bandwidth utilization from the ISP and GPU with the NPU's execution timeline to confirm that burst memory requests from other blocks are starving the NPU.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume the issue is a lack of compute power or thermal throttling, suggesting that the NPU's 45 TOPS limit is being hit. They might also blindly blame the software implementation of the guardrail (like an inefficient tokenizer) without considering the underlying hardware resource contention.
details.napkin_math: The Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 LPDDR5X provides roughly 77 GB/s of memory bandwidth. A 3B parameter INT8 main model requires ~3 GB of memory reads per generated token. At 20 tokens/sec, this consumes 60 GB/s (78% of total bandwidth). The guardrail model (e.g., 0.5B parameters) needs to run context checks, requiring at least 0.5 GB per pass. With OS, display, and background tasks consuming the remaining ~16 GB/s, the memory bus is completely saturated, starving the NPU's memory fetch for the guardrail operations.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is memory bandwidth starvation on the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X bus. Autoregressive text generation is heavily memory-bound; the main model is saturating the bus reading weights for every token. Despite the Hexagon NPU having ample compute headroom (45 TOPS), the concurrent guardrail model cannot fetch its own weights fast enough from the shared memory pool, causing it to miss its real-time SLA and fail open.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume the NPU is thermal throttling or the dual-core scheduler is dropping tasks. They frequently overlook the architectural bottleneck of shared memory subsystems in mobile SoCs under concurrent workloads.
details.napkin_math: Assume the LPDDR5X provides ~68 GB/s peak bandwidth. Running the dual-core NPU at its peak 34.7 TOPS with an arithmetic intensity of 2 OPS/byte requires ~17.35 GB/s. If the ISP concurrently processes a 4K 60fps stream (requesting ~25 GB/s for multi-frame noise reduction) and the GPU renders a heavy UI (requesting ~30 GB/s), the total demand is 17.35 + 25 + 30 = 72.35 GB/s. This exceeds the 68 GB/s limit, starving the NPU, dropping its effective TOPS, and causing the 3x latency spikes.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is memory bandwidth starvation due to contention with the ISP or GPU. Because the Exynos 2400 uses a unified memory architecture, heavy concurrent camera processing or graphics rendering saturates the LPDDR5X bus, introducing severe memory access latency for the NPU. To restore deterministic execution, you must configure hardware QoS (Quality of Service) policies to guarantee minimum bandwidth for the NPU's memory traffic.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often incorrectly assume the NPU's compute capacity (34.7 TOPS) is the bottleneck or suggest quantizing the model further to reduce compute latency. They fail to recognize that streaming high-bandwidth sensor data creates severe memory contention on shared memory architectures.
details.napkin_math: Ingesting a 4K 60 FPS stream requires 3840 x 2160 x 3 bytes x 60 = ~1.49 GB/s of bandwidth. If the pipeline performs unnecessary memory copies (ISP buffer -> CPU buffer -> NPU buffer), the bandwidth cost triples to ~4.5 GB/s just for moving data before any computation begins. On a shared LPDDR5X subsystem, this heavily competes with the OS, UI rendering (GPU), and background tasks, causing latency spikes despite the NPU needing only a fraction of its 34.7 TOPS for the actual inference.
details.realistic_solution: The root cause is memory bandwidth saturation and bus contention across the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X memory, which serves the CPU, GPU, ISP, and NPU. Because the Image Signal Processor (ISP) and NPU share the same physical memory, inefficient ingestion—such as copying frames between CPU buffers and NPU buffers instead of using zero-copy hardware buffers—saturates the memory bus and starves the NPU.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often misdiagnose this as a memory leak, KV cache saturation, or an application-layer garbage collection issue, ignoring the physical heat symptom. They might suggest optimizing the model architecture or weights rather than addressing the hardware's physical operating constraints.
details.napkin_math: The Tensor G3 TPU offers a peak of 7.5 TOPS. Assume running Gemini Nano requires 2 TOPS to sustain 20 tokens/sec. While 2 TOPS is well under the 7.5 TOPS peak, the continuous compute and constant fetching from the 12 GB LPDDR5X consumes significant power. If the device's sustained passive thermal dissipation limit is 2.5W, but the active TPU and memory draw 4.5W, there is a net 2W of heat accumulation. If the SoC heats up by 1°C for every 1.5 Joules of excess thermal energy, 2W (2 Joules/sec) raises the temperature by ~1.33°C per second. Starting at an ambient 25°C, in 30 seconds the SoC hits ~65°C. This triggers the OS thermal mitigation, immediately throttling the TPU power draw down to the 2.5W limit, which severely cuts the available TOPS and plummets the token generation speed.
details.realistic_solution: The symptom strongly indicates thermal throttling. The Tensor G3's TPU is optimized for bursty on-device LLM workloads but cannot sustain continuous heavy utilization indefinitely within a passively cooled smartphone chassis. As continuous generation heats up the SoC past its safe thermal envelope, the operating system aggressively scales down the TPU clock frequency to prevent hardware damage. Verification requires tracing the device's thermal zones alongside TPU clock speeds to confirm the frequency drop aligns exactly with the temperature trip point.

Users report that the feature is highly responsive for the first 30 seconds, utilizing the on-device TPU effectively. However, after 45 seconds of continuous operation, the token generation speed drops by over 60% and the device chassis becomes noticeably warm, despite the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory utilization remaining perfectly flat. details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Option B due to the strong theoretical robustness guarantees of randomized smoothing, failing to account for the heterogeneous system overhead. They ignore the synchronization costs, latency spikes, and power drain caused by bouncing data between the CPU/GPU and NPU over the shared memory bus.
details.napkin_math: Assume an input frame is 224x224x3 (~150KB). Option A: 3 models x 1 GOPS = 3 GOPS per authentication. NPU reads 150KB once. Option B: 1 model x 2 GOPS x 10 variants = 20 GOPS. The CPU/GPU must write 10 noisy variants (10 x 150KB = 1.5MB) to shared LPDDR5X, then wake the NPU to read them. At 30 FPS, Option B demands 45MB/s of continuous cross-component memory traffic and forces CPU/GPU active states, draining battery, whereas Option A runs entirely in the low-power NPU domain well within its 45 TOPS limit.
details.realistic_solution: Option A is the superior system-level choice. The Hexagon NPU's 45 TOPS INT8 capacity can easily handle an ensemble of smaller models concurrently, keeping the entire pipeline within the NPU. This avoids cross-processor synchronization and prevents thrashing the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory, maintaining strict latency budgets for authentication while providing strong empirical robustness.

scenario: You are designing the defense mechanism for a real-time biometric authentication model running on a smartphone powered by a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). The system must be robust against physical adversarial presentation attacks (e.g., adversarial eyeglasses). You are evaluating two strategies: Option A is an ensemble of three smaller, diversely-trained INT8 models running entirely on the NPU using majority voting. Option B uses a single larger model on the NPU but relies on randomized smoothing, requiring the CPU/GPU to generate 10 noisy variants of each input frame and passing them sequentially to the NPU. Which approach provides better reliability and system efficiency?
title: Evaluating Adversarial Defenses on Snapdragon NPU

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose MQA solely for the lowest memory bandwidth without considering its impact on model quality and the fact that the Exynos 2400's dual-core NPU might benefit from the slightly higher parallelism of GQA. They also frequently forget that the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory is shared across the CPU, GPU, and ISP, meaning the LLM cannot monopolize the entire bandwidth or capacity.
details.napkin_math: Assume a 7B model with hidden size 4096, 32 layers, and FP16 (2 bytes/param) for a 4096-token context. MHA KV cache size is: 2 (K, V) * 32 layers * 4096 hidden dimension * 2 bytes * 4096 tokens = 2 GB. With MQA (1 KV head), the cache drops to 2 GB / 32 = 64 MB. With GQA (8 KV heads), it is 2 GB * (8/32) = 512 MB. Assuming the shared LPDDR5X provides ~60 GB/s of bandwidth, reading the MHA cache per generated token takes 2 GB / 60 GB/s = 33.3 ms (limiting decoding to <30 tokens/sec and starving the ISP/GPU). GQA requires reading only 512 MB (8.5 ms), allowing >100 tokens/sec memory-bound limit while leaving headroom for the 34.7 TOPS dual-core NPU to execute efficiently.
details.realistic_solution: The ideal approach is to evaluate the KV cache size and memory bandwidth limits during autoregressive decoding. Given the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X memory, KV cache footprint is critical. MQA provides the smallest KV cache but can degrade performance. GQA (e.g., with 8 KV heads) strikes the optimal balance: it drastically reduces the KV cache size compared to MHA, minimizing memory bandwidth bottlenecks, while preserving quality closer to MHA. For a 4K context on the Exynos 2400 NPU, GQA ensures the memory bandwidth remains available for other active SoC components.

scenario: You are designing an on-device LLM for the Samsung Exynos 2400 NPU (34.7 TOPS, dual-core NPU, 12 GB shared LPDDR5X memory). details.common_mistake: Candidates often look only at the theoretical TOPS (34.7) and the GOPS per frame, mistakenly concluding that the ViT is better simply because 18 GOPS is less than 25 GOPS. They fail to account for the shared memory architecture of the Exynos 2400, where memory bandwidth bottlenecks will severely degrade the effective TOPS for models with low arithmetic intensity.
details.napkin_math: Target FPS: 60. CNN compute required: 60 FPS * 25 GOPS = 1.5 TOPS. ViT compute required: 60 FPS * 18 GOPS = 1.08 TOPS. Both are well within the theoretical 34.7 TOPS of the Exynos 2400 dual-core NPU. However, assuming LPDDR5X provides ~60 GB/s total bandwidth, and ISP/GPU consume 40 GB/s for 60fps AR, only 20 GB/s remains for the NPU. If the ViT requires reading 500 MB per frame (500 MB * 60 = 30 GB/s), it exceeds the available 20 GB/s bandwidth, lowering effective NPU utilization and dropping frames. The CNN, requiring only 150 MB per frame (150 MB * 60 = 9 GB/s), fits comfortably within the memory bandwidth budget, making it the superior choice.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to evaluate the effective compute throughput by considering the memory bandwidth wall. Because the 12 GB LPDDR5X is shared with the ISP (running the camera pipeline) and GPU (rendering the AR), the ViT's high bandwidth requirements will cause NPU starvation. The CNN, despite requiring more theoretical compute (25 GOPS), has higher arithmetic intensity and better cache utilization, making it much more likely to sustain the required 60 FPS on the Exynos 2400 NPU without throttling other system components.

scenario: You are leading the deployment of a real-time semantic segmentation model for an AR application targeting the Samsung Exynos 2400. You must choose between a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) requiring 25 GOPS per frame and a Vision Transformer (ViT) requiring 18 GOPS per frame. The Exynos 2400 features a dual-core NPU capable of 34.7 TOPS, but its 12 GB LPDDR5X memory is shared across the CPU, GPU, and ISP, and the ViT has 3x the memory bandwidth requirement of the CNN due to low arithmetic intensity in its self-attention layers. details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose option B (gradient-based selection) because it mathematically guarantees selecting the highest-signal training examples. They fail to evaluate the systemic cost of running backward passes over the entire dataset on a mobile SoC, which will thrash the shared memory bandwidth and exhaust the thermal budget before training even begins.
details.napkin_math: For Option B: A backward pass on a 1.5B model requires roughly 6-8 GB of memory for activations and optimizer states. Passing 10,000 images would require heavy swapping in the shared 16 GB LPDDR5X RAM (bandwidth ~68 GB/s), taking hours. For Option A: Extracting embeddings (e.g., 512 dimensions, INT8) takes less than 1 ms per image on the 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU. 10,000 embeddings require only ~5 MB of memory. Clustering 5 MB on the CPU takes milliseconds, saving massive amounts of compute and memory bandwidth.
details.realistic_solution: Option A is the correct architectural choice. By using a lightweight embedding model (which runs efficiently on the Hexagon NPU using INT8) and performing simple k-means clustering on the CPU, you leverage the heterogeneous CPU+NPU design. This isolates the expensive backward passes to only the selected coreset, keeping peak memory usage well below the 16 GB limit and preventing thermal throttling.

scenario: Your team needs to personalize a 1.5B parameter vision-language model via on-device fine-tuning on a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 device. The user generates thousands of local images, but due to thermal and battery constraints, we must aggressively prune the training data. You are evaluating two alternatives for data selection: (A) CPU-based coreset selection using lightweight CLIP embeddings to find diverse clusters, or (B) using the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU to run a forward-backward pass on all images and selecting the top 10% with the highest loss gradients. Which approach is better suited for this heterogeneous environment, considering the shared 16 GB LPDDR5X memory?

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume that curating hard edge cases (Option B) is strictly better because it improves robustness on difficult examples. However, for INT8 calibration, using extreme outliers can skew the activation range statistics, leading to a wider quantization range that destroys numerical precision for the vast majority of typical inputs.
details.napkin_math: Assume an activation tensor has a typical range of [-5.0, 5.0] for normal images, but an edge case in Option B produces [-20.0, 20.0]. With INT8 (256 discrete values), the step resolution for [-5.0, 5.0] is 10.0 / 255 = ~0.039. If calibrated on the [-20.0, 20.0] range, the resolution degrades to 40.0 / 255 = ~0.157. This 4x loss in quantization precision will severely degrade the accuracy of normal inferences on the 34.7 TOPS NPU. Furthermore, relying on FP16 fallback for these edge cases would needlessly consume bandwidth from the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X.
details.realistic_solution: Option A is superior for INT8 calibration. The goal of calibration is to find scaling factors that minimize quantization error across typical workloads. The shared 12 GB LPDDR5X memory means memory bandwidth is at a premium, making aggressive INT8 quantization crucial for the dual-core NPU to hit its 34.7 TOPS. If the calibration dataset includes extreme outliers (Option B), the min/max ranges will expand to cover them, compressing the representational space for normal activations. The optimal approach is using a representative distribution (Option A) and applying percentile-based clipping (e.g., 99.9th percentile) to discard extreme activation outliers, preserving maximum precision for the average case.

scenario: You are preparing a vision model for deployment on the Samsung Exynos 2400 NPU, which offers 34.7 TOPS but requires INT8 quantization to achieve this peak performance without exhausting the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X memory. You must decide on a dataset curation strategy for the INT8 calibration phase to determine activation ranges. Option A randomly samples 5,000 images from the general training distribution. Option B uses an active learning approach to curate 500 images specifically targeting rare long-tail classes and extreme lighting conditions. Which calibration dataset strategy is better for maximizing overall INT8 accuracy on this dual-core NPU?
title: Calibration Data Selection for INT8 NPU Execution

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Approach A, assuming that the 16-core Neural Engine's 35 TOPS should be utilized for all ML-related tasks. They fail to evaluate the power and memory bandwidth implications of constantly waking up the ANE and buffering high-dimensional embeddings in the shared 8 GB unified memory for a background monitoring task.
details.napkin_math: Assuming 10 inferences/sec, Approach A (1024-dim fp16 embeddings) generates 1024 * 2 bytes = 2 KB per inference, or ~72 MB per hour of reference data. Constantly buffering and processing this in the shared 8 GB memory drains battery. Approach B only maintains running stats (mean/variance) per dimension: 1024 * 2 * 4 bytes (fp32) = ~8 KB of total state. The CPU updates this 8 KB state entirely in cache, utilizing a tiny fraction of the ~5W budget, while avoiding the latency and power overhead of spinning up the 35 TOPS ANE.
details.realistic_solution: Approach B is far superior. Drift detection is a low-frequency, asynchronous task. By tracking running summary statistics, we drastically reduce the memory footprint. The CPU can easily handle lightweight PSI calculations periodically using negligible power. This avoids waking up the Neural Engine and competing for the shared 8 GB unified memory, preserving the ~5W power budget strictly for latency-critical foreground model inference.

scenario: We are deploying an on-device personalization model on the Apple A17 Pro. To maintain privacy, drift detection must happen locally. We have two proposals for detecting data drift: (A) computing continuous KL divergence over dense activation embeddings (1024-dim, fp16) using the 16-core Neural Engine against a stored reference distribution, or (B) tracking summary statistics (mean, variance) and computing a simplified Population Stability Index (PSI) periodically on the CPU. The A17 Pro offers 35 TOPS, operates within a ~5W power budget, and has 8 GB of unified memory shared across CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Which approach is better for evaluating drift in this mobile deployment, and how do you justify your choice?
title: On-Device Drift Detection Alternatives

details.common_mistake: Candidates often reflexively choose the decoder-only architecture because it represents the modern LLM standard, without considering the memory bandwidth bottleneck during autoregressive generation. They fail to account for how the KV cache scales differently between the two architectures and how that impacts a heavily shared memory bus.
details.napkin_math: Assume an input of 2000 tokens and an output of 200 tokens, with d_model=2048. A 24-layer decoder-only model requires a KV cache for all 2200 tokens: 2 bytes(FP16) * 2(K,V) * 24(layers) * 2048(d) * 2200 = ~432 MB. A comparable encoder-decoder (12 encoder / 12 decoder layers) requires a cross-attention cache for the input: 2 * 2 * 12 * 2048 * 2000 = ~196 MB, plus a self-attention cache for the output: 2 * 2 * 12 * 2048 * 200 = ~20 MB (Total: ~216 MB). The encoder-decoder halves the KV cache footprint, drastically reducing the memory bandwidth required per generated token, which is critical to prevent frame drops when the 12 GB RAM is shared with the ISP and GPU.
details.realistic_solution: The encoder-decoder architecture is superior for this memory-constrained, multitasking environment. While the dual-core NPU provides ample compute, the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory is actively shared with the ISP and GPU processing the video call, making memory bandwidth the primary bottleneck. An encoder-decoder model maintains a static cross-attention cache for the input sequence and a much smaller self-attention KV cache for the generated tokens, significantly reducing memory footprint and bandwidth contention during the autoregressive phase compared to a decoder-only model.

scenario: Your team is building a real-time meeting summarization feature for a mobile device powered by the Samsung Exynos 2400. The SoC features a dual-core NPU capable of 34.7 TOPS, but its 12 GB of LPDDR5X memory is heavily shared with the CPU, GPU, and ISP during live video calls. You must choose between two INT8-quantized 2-billion parameter architectures with identical task accuracy: a decoder-only model and an encoder-decoder model. Which architecture do you choose for this deployment and why?
title: On-Device Summarization Architecture Selection

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Model A by solely looking at the theoretical compute cost (MACs or TOPS) and assuming that fewer operations strictly equate to lower power consumption. They fail to apply the principles of the Horowitz energy table, ignoring the fact that off-chip memory access is orders of magnitude more expensive than arithmetic operations on a mobile SoC.
details.napkin_math: Assuming standard Horowitz energy estimates: an INT8 MAC costs ~0.2 pJ, and LPDDR5 unified memory access costs ~10 pJ/bit (or ~80 pJ/byte). Model A utilizes 15 TOPS of the A17 Pro's 35 TOPS capacity, consuming 15e12 * 0.2e-12 = 3.0W in compute. It generates 20 GB/s of DRAM traffic, adding 20e9 * 80e-12 = 1.6W for memory (Total: 4.6W, dangerously close to the 5W budget). Model B increases compute by 25% to 18.75 TOPS, consuming 18.75e12 * 0.2e-12 = 3.75W. However, localizing activations reduces DRAM traffic to just 2 GB/s, consuming only 2e9 * 80e-12 = 0.16W for memory. Total power drops from 4.6W to 3.91W, proving Model B is more energy-efficient.
details.realistic_solution: Model B is the correct choice because energy consumption on modern mobile platforms is overwhelmingly dominated by data movement, not compute. By keeping activations localized within the Neural Engine's SRAM through layer fusion and recomputation, Model B drastically reduces unified memory bandwidth. The energy saved from avoiding off-chip DRAM reads and writes far exceeds the marginal cost of performing 25% more arithmetic operations on the highly efficient A17 Pro.

scenario: You are deploying a high-resolution video segmentation model on the Apple A17 Pro Neural Engine, which delivers 35 TOPS at roughly a 5W power budget and shares 8 GB of unified memory with the CPU/GPU. You are evaluating two architecture variants: Model A minimizes total compute operations but produces large intermediate activation tensors that frequently spill to the unified memory. Model B uses aggressively fused layers and recomputation, which requires 25% more MAC operations but ensures all intermediate activations remain strictly within the 16-core Neural Engine's local SRAM. Which model do you choose to maximize battery life, and why?
title: Evaluating DRAM vs Compute Energy for A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Option A to maintain the high framerate, focusing purely on the compute reduction. They fail to account for the memory subsystem, forgetting that the 12 GB LPDDR5X is shared, and that loading new model weights during heavy ISP/GPU usage (4K recording) will cause severe memory contention and latency spikes.
details.napkin_math: Baseline NPU capacity: 34.7 TOPS. Throttled capacity (50%): 17.35 TOPS. The primary model takes 0.5 TOPS/frame; at 60fps, it needs 30 TOPS (fails under throttling). Option A (Fallback model): Needs 0.2 TOPS/frame (12 TOPS total), but swapping a 50MB model into the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X while the ISP is heavily utilizing bandwidth for 4K video causes a pipeline stall. Option B (Halve framerate): 0.5 TOPS * 30fps = 15 TOPS. 15 TOPS < 17.35 TOPS throttled limit. Zero memory swap cost, instantly resolving the thermal constraint.
details.realistic_solution: Option B is the superior fail-operational strategy. By shedding the framerate, the system instantly reduces compute requirements without incurring any memory I/O penalty. This avoids competing with the ISP and GPU for the shared LPDDR5X bandwidth during a thermally constrained state, providing a seamless degradation in user experience without risking dropped camera frames.

scenario: You are deploying a real-time object tracking model for a camera application on the Samsung Exynos 2400 NPU. The NPU provides 34.7 TOPS across its dual-core architecture and shares 12 GB of LPDDR5X memory with the CPU, GPU, and ISP. During continuous 4K video recording, thermal management triggers a 50% frequency reduction on the NPU. You must evaluate two graceful degradation strategies: Option A dynamically loads a lightweight INT8 fallback model to maintain 60fps, while Option B keeps the resident model but sheds quality-of-service by dropping the tracking framerate to 30fps. Which is better?
title: Thermal Degradation on Shared Memory NPU

details.common_mistake: Candidates often advocate for unstructured pruning because it mathematically reduces the theoretical FLOP count without needing a complex teacher-student training pipeline. They fail to realize that the Hexagon NPU's matrix multiplication units are highly optimized for dense INT8 operations, and unstructured sparsity leads to irregular memory access patterns that cripple hardware utilization.
details.napkin_math: The baseline requires 150 GOPS per frame. For 10 ms latency, required throughput is 150 GOPS / 0.01 s = 15 TOPS. The Hexagon NPU provides 45 TOPS INT8 peak. With 70% unstructured sparsity (Proposal A), effective NPU utilization typically drops below 10% due to memory bottlenecks, yielding < 4.5 TOPS effective throughput, failing the 15 TOPS requirement. Proposal B reduces operations by 3x to 50 GOPS/frame. A dense INT8 model routinely achieves > 40% utilization on the NPU (18 TOPS effective). At 18 TOPS, 50 GOPS takes 50 / 18000 = ~2.7 ms, comfortably beating the 10 ms deadline while reducing memory footprint to ~1.3 GB.
details.realistic_solution: Proposal B (Knowledge Distillation) is the correct choice. The Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 NPU, capable of 45 TOPS INT8, achieves peak performance on dense tensor workloads. A smaller, dense student model trained via distillation will map perfectly to the hardware's systolic arrays and efficiently utilize the shared LPDDR5X memory bandwidth. Unstructured pruning (Proposal A) will cause memory stalls and fail to leverage the NPU's massive parallel compute capabilities.

scenario: Your team is deploying a large vision transformer for real-time video segmentation on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). The baseline model requires 150 Giga-Operations (GOPS) per frame and takes up 4 GB of the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory. You need to fit this into a strict 10 ms latency budget per frame. You are presented with two optimization alternatives. Proposal A suggests aggressive unstructured pruning to reach 70% sparsity. Proposal B advocates for Knowledge Distillation to train a dense student model with 3x fewer parameters and operations. Which approach is better suited for the target hardware and why?
title: Distillation vs Pruning for Snapdragon Hexagon NPU

details.common_mistake: Candidates often default to recommending PagedAttention because it is the state-of-the-art solution for mitigating memory fragmentation in high-throughput, multi-user server environments. They fail to recognize that for a single-user mobile deployment with a batch size of 1, internal fragmentation is a non-issue, and the overhead of irregular memory access patterns will severely bottleneck the NPU.
details.napkin_math: Assume a 7B model architecture (32 layers, 32 heads, 128 head dim). Each token requires: 2 (K&V) * 32 layers * 32 heads * 128 dim * 2 bytes (FP16) = 524,288 bytes (~0.5 MB). For a maximum context of 4096 tokens, the KV-cache requires 4096 * 0.5 MB = 2.048 GB. The 7B model weights quantized to 4-bit require roughly 3.5 GB. Total memory consumption = 3.5 GB (weights) + 2 GB (KV cache) = 5.5 GB. With 12 GB shared LPDDR5X total and 4 GB reserved by the OS, we have 8 GB available. The 5.5 GB footprint easily fits, proving that static contiguous allocation is completely viable without dynamic paging.
details.realistic_solution: Static allocation of a contiguous KV-cache buffer is the superior choice for this mobile scenario. The Qualcomm Hexagon NPU relies heavily on predictable, sequential memory access and efficient DMA transfers from the LPDDR5X memory to sustain its 45 TOPS INT8 peak performance. PagedAttention scatters KV blocks across physical memory, requiring complex pointer chasing and non-contiguous reads that disrupt vectorization and hardware prefetching. Since the entire 2 GB max KV-cache safely fits within the remaining memory budget alongside the quantized model weights, the theoretical memory savings of PagedAttention do not justify the severe latency degradation caused by stalling the NPU.

scenario: We are deploying a 7B parameter conversational AI on a flagship mobile device powered by the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). The system features a shared 12 GB LPDDR5X memory pool, but the OS and background apps reserve roughly 4 GB, leaving a strict 8 GB budget for our application. We need to support a context window of 4096 tokens. The engineering team is divided between two KV-cache management proposals: statically allocating a contiguous 2 GB buffer for the maximum context length upfront, or porting a server-style PagedAttention mechanism to dynamically allocate non-contiguous 16-token blocks to save memory. Evaluate these two approaches for this specific hardware constraints. Which strategy should we adopt and why?
title: Evaluating PagedAttention vs Static Allocation for On-Device LLMs

details.common_mistake: Candidates often blindly recommend dynamic block allocation (Alternative B) because it is the state-of-the-art for server-side LLM serving with high concurrency. They fail to realize that on a mobile SoC with a shared memory space, dynamic allocation introduces severe memory fragmentation over time, which can trigger unpredictable OS-level OOM kills even if total used memory is under the limit.
details.napkin_math: Tensor G3 Total Memory: 12 GB LPDDR5X. App Budget: 2.5 GB. Model Weights: 1.8B params @ INT8 = 1.8 GB. Remaining memory for KV cache/activations: 2.5 GB - 1.8 GB = 700 MB. KV cache size per token (assuming 16 layers, 2048 hidden dim, FP16): 2 (K&V) * 2 bytes * 16 * 2048 = 131 KB/token. Max static KV cache for a 2048-token context window: 131 KB * 2048 = 268.2 MB. Since 268.2 MB comfortably fits within the 700 MB remaining budget, static pre-allocation is safe and leaves ~430 MB for intermediate activations without risking fragmentation.
details.realistic_solution: Alternative A (Static pre-allocation) is the superior choice for mobile deployment. Because mobile inference typically operates at a batch size of 1, the theoretical memory savings from dynamic allocation do not outweigh the risks of memory fragmentation. Pre-allocating the maximum required KV cache ensures a fixed, predictable memory footprint, completely avoiding runtime fragmentation and guaranteeing that the app will not suddenly trigger the Android low-memory killer (LMK) during prolonged usage.

scenario: You are deploying a 1.8B parameter on-device LLM (similar to Gemini Nano) on the Google Tensor G3, which features an on-device TPU and 12 GB of LPDDR5X shared memory. The system restricts the LLM process to a strict 2.5 GB memory budget to prevent OS-level eviction of essential background apps. You must choose between two KV cache management strategies for a multi-turn chat feature: Alternative A uses static pre-allocation of a maximum-length KV buffer at initialization, while Alternative B uses dynamic block-based allocation (like PagedAttention) to minimize memory usage for short prompts. Which design is better for managing memory pressure on this device?
title: LLM KV Cache Allocation Strategy on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose pure INT8 solely to maximize the 45 TOPS compute, ignoring that operations like Softmax and LayerNorm suffer catastrophic accuracy degradation when quantized to 8-bit integers. Alternatively, they may propose pure FP16 without realizing it will severely bottleneck the shared memory bandwidth and fall short of the required frame rate.
details.napkin_math: Compute: A 1B parameter model with 256 tokens per frame requires ~500 GMACs (1 TOPS) per frame. At 30 FPS, this is 30 TOPS. The Hexagon NPU provides 45 TOPS in INT8, leaving comfortable headroom. In FP16, compute throughput typically halves to ~22.5 TFLOPS, failing the 30 TOPS requirement. Bandwidth: 1B parameters in FP16 consume 2GB. Streaming these at 30 FPS requires 60 GB/s, fully saturating the LPDDR5X bandwidth (~64 GB/s peak) and starving the CPU/GPU. INT8 reduces weights to 1GB, requiring only 30 GB/s and making real-time execution feasible.
details.realistic_solution: The mixed-precision approach is optimal. Heavy matrix multiplications (QKV projections, FFNs) should be quantized to INT8 to leverage the 45 TOPS NPU capacity and halve memory bandwidth pressure. Precision-sensitive operations like Softmax, LayerNorm, and attention scores must remain in FP16 to preserve model accuracy. This leverages the heterogeneous architecture by mapping INT8 dense compute to the NPU's tensor accelerators while safely processing FP16 non-linearities without bottlenecking the system.

scenario: Your team is deploying a 1B parameter Vision Transformer for real-time video processing on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). You must choose between pure FP16, pure INT8, and a mixed-precision approach (INT8 for linear layers, FP16 for softmax and layer normalization) to achieve 30 FPS. Evaluate these alternatives and determine the best deployment strategy, accounting for the NPU's 45 TOPS INT8 capacity and the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory system.
title: Evaluating Mixed-Precision ViT on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Option B to save memory or assume that 70% TPU delegation is 'good enough', ignoring the massive latency penalty of CPU fallback and synchronization overhead in auto-regressive decoding.
details.napkin_math: Compute per token is approx 4 GOPS (2B params * 2). Option A (TPU only): compute time = 4 GOPS / 7500 GOPS (7.5 TOPS) = 0.53ms per token. Option B (CPU fallback): 30% compute = 1.2 GOPS on CPU. Assuming an optimistic CPU throughput of 100 GOPS, CPU time alone is 1.2 / 100 = 12ms per token. Option B is at least 20x slower strictly on compute, ignoring severe CPU-TPU memory copy overheads.
details.realistic_solution: Option A is the correct choice. The 12 GB LPDDR5X easily accommodates the 200MB memory increase (2.2GB total footprint in INT8). Avoiding CPU fallback is critical because alternating execution between the CPU and TPU for every token completely bottlenecks generation latency due to synchronization limits and the TPU's massive compute advantage (7.5 TOPS).

scenario: You are deploying a 2B parameter INT8 LLM to the Google Tensor G3 (12 GB LPDDR5X). You must choose between two TFLite conversion strategies. Option A maps all operators to standard TFLite ops for 100% Edge TPU delegation (7.5 TOPS), but unrolling a custom attention op increases model size to 2.2B parameters. Option B retains the custom attention op, keeping the model at 2.0B parameters, but forces 30% of the model's compute to fall back to the CPU. Which strategy yields better token generation latency and why?
title: LLM TPU Delegation vs CPU Fallback on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Candidates frequently calculate only the memory required for the model weights and forget to account for the KV cache size, which grows linearly with context length. They may also falsely assume that lower parameter count always translates to lower memory footprint without factoring in the quantization bit-width.
details.napkin_math: Available RAM: 12 GB (Total) - 6 GB (OS) = 6 GB budget. Model A (3.2B INT4) Weight Size: 3.2 * 10^9 * 0.5 bytes = 1.6 GB. Model B (1.8B INT8) Weight Size: 1.8 * 10^9 * 1 byte = 1.8 GB. Assuming Model A has 32 layers and a hidden dimension of 4096, the KV cache size for a 1024-token context in FP16 (2 bytes) is: 2 (K&V) * 32 (layers) * 4096 (dim) * 1024 (seq) * 2 bytes = ~536 MB. Total footprint for Model A: 1.6 GB + 0.536 GB = ~2.14 GB. This easily fits into the 6 GB budget, leaving plenty of headroom, and utilizes the Tensor G3's 7.5 TOPS efficiently.
details.realistic_solution: Model A (3.2B INT4) is the optimal choice. Despite having more parameters, its INT4 quantization results in a smaller weight footprint than the 1.8B INT8 model. Because LLM generation is heavily memory-bandwidth bound, the smaller weight size of Model A reduces data transfer overhead. Furthermore, the 3.2B model fits comfortably within the 6 GB available RAM even after accounting for a reasonably sized KV cache, while offering superior reasoning capabilities for summarization tasks.

scenario: Your team is tasked with deploying an on-device LLM to summarize incoming messages on a device powered by the Google Tensor G3. The device has 12 GB LPDDR5X RAM, but the OS and system apps require a strict 6 GB reservation at all times. The Tensor G3 features an on-device TPU capable of 7.5 TOPS. You must evaluate two options: Model A is a 3.2B parameter model quantized to INT4 (weights only), and Model B is a 1.8B parameter model quantized to INT8 (weights and activations). You need to recommend the better architecture for this device considering memory constraints, KV cache overhead, and the TPU's capabilities.
title: On-Device LLM Evaluation for Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often mistakenly prefer Strategy A, overestimating the synchronization penalty between heterogeneous compute units. They fail to realize that falling back to the CPU for dense FP16 operations will severely bottleneck the pipeline, negating the benefits of the NPU's speed.
details.napkin_math: Assume the INT8 backbone requires 1.35 Tera-Operations (TOPs) per frame. NPU INT8 latency = 1.35 TOPs / 45 TOPS = 30 ms. Assume the FP16 head takes 25 ms on CPU and 15 ms on GPU. Strategy A (Sequential): 30 ms (NPU) + 25 ms (CPU) = 55 ms per frame (18 FPS, misses 30 FPS target). Strategy B (Pipelined NPU+GPU): Pipeline bottleneck is max(30 ms NPU, 15 ms GPU) = 30 ms per frame. Throughput = 1000 ms / 30 ms = 33.3 FPS, successfully meeting the real-time 30 FPS requirement with zero-copy overhead.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy B is the correct approach for an L5 engineer. The Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 architecture utilizes a shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory pool, meaning the NPU and GPU can pass intermediate tensors via zero-copy pointers rather than expensive memory copies. By pipelining the execution, the NPU can process frame N+1 at its peak 45 TOPS INT8 while the GPU simultaneously processes the FP16 head for frame N. This hides the latency of the attention head and maximizes overall hardware utilization.

scenario: You are deploying a real-time 30 FPS video segmentation pipeline on a device powered by the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). The graph consists of a heavy INT8 CNN backbone and a custom FP16 attention-based post-processing head. You are evaluating two operator scheduling alternatives: Strategy A schedules all operators sequentially, running the INT8 backbone on the NPU and falling back to the CPU for the FP16 head to avoid complex synchronization. Strategy B partitions the graph, aggressively fusing the INT8 backbone on the NPU and pipelining the FP16 head asynchronously on the GPU, utilizing the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory for data handoffs. Which strategy provides better system-level throughput and why?
title: Heterogeneous Pipelining on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume that LLMs are always compute-bound due to the large number of operations, choosing Hypothesis A. They fail to distinguish between the compute-heavy prefill phase and the memory-bandwidth-heavy autoregressive decoding phase (batch size 1) typical in mobile deployments.
details.napkin_math: Assume a 3 billion parameter Gemini Nano model. In 16-bit (FP16), it takes 6 GB of memory. To generate 1 token, all 6 GB must be loaded. If the Tensor G3's LPDDR5X provides a practical bandwidth of ~50 GB/s, generating 1 token takes 6 GB / 50 GB/s = 120ms (close to the 150ms observed). The TPU requires ~6 Giga-operations per token. At 7.5 TOPS, the compute time is 6G / 7.5T = 0.8ms. Therefore, memory I/O (120ms) completely dominates compute (0.8ms).
details.realistic_solution: Hypothesis B is correct. During autoregressive decoding at batch size 1, the entire model must be loaded from memory into the TPU for every single token generated. The TPU's 7.5 TOPS are vastly underutilized because the system is starved waiting for weights to be fetched from the LPDDR5X RAM. The solution is to profile memory read bandwidth using hardware counters and apply weight-only quantization (e.g., 4-bit) to reduce the memory I/O required per token.

scenario: You are deploying a distilled version of Gemini Nano on a device powered by the Google Tensor G3. Initial profiling during the autoregressive generation phase shows an unacceptable latency of 150ms per token. You are presented with two alternative hypotheses from your team: Hypothesis A suggests the bottleneck is the TPU compute capacity (7.5 TOPS), while Hypothesis B suggests the bottleneck is the memory bandwidth of the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory. Evaluate these alternatives and determine the most likely bottleneck.
title: On-Device LLM Profiling Alternatives for Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often default to the cloud solution (Option B) to maximize safety accuracy, ignoring the strict privacy requirements of PII and the latency impact on a real-time UI. Alternatively, they might choose the on-device model without calculating if it fits within the A17 Pro's compute and memory budget alongside the primary generative model.
details.napkin_math: A 100M parameter model quantized to INT8 requires ~100 MB of memory, a fraction of the A17 Pro's shared 8 GB unified memory. A forward pass for 128 tokens requires roughly 2 * 100M * 128 ≈ 25.6 Giga-operations (GOPS). Given the A17 Pro Neural Engine's peak performance of 35 TOPS (35,000 GOPS), the theoretical compute time is 25.6 / 35,000 ≈ 0.73 milliseconds. Assuming a conservative 20% hardware utilization, inference takes < 4ms, consuming an insignificant portion of the ~5W power budget while adding imperceptible latency.
details.realistic_solution: Option A is the superior choice. Running the guardrail locally on the A17 Pro ensures PII never leaves the device, directly addressing the privacy constraint. The A17 Pro Neural Engine is highly optimized for this workload. While a 100M parameter model may have slightly lower accuracy than a massive cloud LLM, it can be quantized and domain-adapted to serve as a fast, highly conservative gate. The deterministic low latency is critical for the user experience, whereas cloud network jitter would degrade the product.

scenario: You are deploying a generative AI text feature on iOS devices powered by the Apple A17 Pro. You must implement a toxicity and PII filtering guardrail. Option A is a lightweight 100M parameter BERT-based classifier running locally on the 16-core Neural Engine. Option B is a cloud-based LLM evaluator that guarantees 99.9% accuracy but requires network calls. The application is highly sensitive to both user perceived latency and strict privacy requirements. Evaluate these alternatives and choose the better design, considering the specific constraints of the target platform.
title: Evaluating On-Device Toxicity Guardrails for A17 Pro

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Alternative A to maximize the TPU's 7.5 TOPS and avoid CPU-TPU synchronization overhead, assuming software watchdogs are sufficient. They fail to realize that software watchdogs on a non-real-time mobile OS cannot guarantee the deterministic recovery times required for functional safety certification.
details.napkin_math: Main model on TPU executes in ~80ms using 7.5 TOPS. Software watchdog (Alt A) adds OS scheduler jitter (~50ms) + context switch (~100ms), making worst-case recovery = 80 + 50 + 100 = 230ms (Fails 150ms SLA). Hardware watchdog (Alt B) triggers in <5ms. Fallback CPU model executes in 40ms. Worst-case recovery = TPU timeout (80ms) + hardware interrupt (5ms) + CPU fallback execution (40ms) = 125ms (Passes 150ms SLA).
details.realistic_solution: Alternative B is the superior choice for meeting safety certification. While the TPU provides excellent throughput, its asynchronous execution makes tight worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds difficult to prove. Isolating a fallback model on a dedicated CPU core with a hardware watchdog guarantees the 150ms recovery SLA even if the main TPU pipeline hangs, fulfilling safety requirements without bottlenecking the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory.

scenario: You are designing an emergency real-time voice-to-text hazard alert system running on a Google Tensor G3 device (featuring an on-device TPU with 7.5 TOPS and 12 GB LPDDR5X RAM). To achieve functional safety certification, the system must guarantee deterministic execution and a failure recovery time of under 150ms. You must evaluate two designs: Alternative A runs the optimized Gemini Nano model entirely on the TPU with a software watchdog on the application OS. Alternative B runs the main model on the TPU but keeps a smaller, deterministic fallback model pinned to a CPU core with a strict hardware watchdog timer.
title: Safety-Critical LLM Fallback Design on Tensor G3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Strategy B, incorrectly assuming that running at the lowest possible voltage/frequency is always the best thermal solution. They fail to account for the static leakage power of keeping the NPU and the shared LPDDR5X memory controller continuously active, which eventually saturates the device's thermal envelope.
details.napkin_math: The model requires 1.5 TOPS (3.3% of the 45 TOPS INT8 peak). Continuous execution keeps the NPU and 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory awake, drawing ~1.5W (active + static leakage), which exceeds the continuous passive cooling limit over time. By batching 15 frames (500ms duration), the NPU can process the batch in just ~16.6ms (using its full 45 TOPS). The system then enters deep sleep for the remaining ~483.4ms. Average power = ((1.5W * 16.6ms) + (0.05W sleep * 483.4ms)) / 500ms = ~98mW. This massive >10x reduction in average power consumption easily prevents thermal throttling while maintaining the required throughput.
details.realistic_solution: Strategy A (burst and sleep) is superior for this architecture. By utilizing a race-to-sleep approach, the system takes advantage of the massive 45 TOPS peak capability to finish the workload rapidly. Buffering frames allows the NPU and memory subsystem to power collapse into deep sleep for the vast majority of the duty cycle, drastically reducing average power and preventing thermal throttling.

scenario: You are designing the thermal management strategy for a continuous background video segmentation model on a device featuring the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). The NPU has a peak throughput of 45 TOPS INT8, and your model requires 1.5 TOPS to process 30 FPS. However, running it continuously frame-by-frame causes the heterogeneous CPU+GPU+NPU complex to overheat and throttle within 10 minutes. Evaluate two alternatives to sustain performance: (A) Buffer frames in the shared 12-16 GB LPDDR5X memory and execute NPU inferences in high-speed bursts to maximize sleep time, or (B) Lower the NPU clock frequency to its minimum state and run the model continuously at 30 FPS without sleep.
title: Continuous Vision Thermal Throttling Strategy

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose shadow deployment for its safety without realizing the thermal and battery implications of running two heavy models simultaneously on a mobile device, or they ignore the memory bandwidth constraints of the shared LPDDR5X when multiple models are active.
details.napkin_math: Concurrent shadow execution requires 15 (new) + 10 (old) = 25 TOPS INT8. While 25 < 45 TOPS (peak), sustained execution will hit thermal limits quickly. Memory usage is 2 GB + 1.5 GB = 3.5 GB, which is ~22-29% of the total 12-16 GB shared LPDDR5X memory, likely causing OS-level app evictions. In contrast, canary execution uses only 15 TOPS (33% of peak) and 2 GB (12.5-16.6% of memory), staying well within safe operational margins.
details.realistic_solution: A canary rollout is the superior choice for this mobile scenario. While the Hexagon NPU theoretically supports 45 TOPS INT8 (enough for 15 + 10 = 25 TOPS), running both models concurrently in a shadow deployment consumes 3.5 GB of the shared memory and over 50% of the NPU's sustained thermal envelope, leading to aggressive throttling and battery drain that degrades the user experience. A canary rollout with robust telemetry avoids these penalties while still gathering real-world performance data.

scenario: Your team is rolling out a new on-device real-time video super-resolution model targeting the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU on the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3. You need to choose between a shadow deployment (running both old and new models concurrently) and a canary rollout (running the new model for 5% of users). The new model requires 15 TOPS INT8 and 2 GB of the shared LPDDR5X memory, while the existing model uses 10 TOPS and 1.5 GB. Given the device's 45 TOPS INT8 peak capability and 12-16 GB total shared memory, evaluate which strategy is better and present the trade-offs.
title: Evaluating Shadow vs. Canary on Snapdragon 8 Gen 3

details.common_mistake: Candidates often default to the Neural Engine purely based on its 35 TOPS peak performance and ~5W power consumption. They fail to account for the latency and memory bandwidth overhead caused by CPU fallback for unsupported operations.
details.napkin_math: Assume the model requires 105 Giga-Operations (GOPs). The 16-core Neural Engine theoretically processes this in 105 GOPs / 35 TOPS = 3.0 ms. However, if 5% of operations fallback to the CPU, adding 15 ms of CPU compute and 4 ms of context-switching overhead, the total NPU path takes 3.0 + 15 + 4 = 22.0 ms. If the GPU can process the full 105 GOPs natively at a sustained 10.5 TOPS, the GPU path takes 105 GOPs / 10.5 TOPS = 10.0 ms, making it over 2x faster end-to-end despite the NPU's higher peak theoretical compute.
details.realistic_solution: A strong L5 candidate evaluates the end-to-end pipeline rather than peak TOPS. Because the 8 GB unified memory is shared, frequent context switching between the Neural Engine and CPU for unsupported ops causes severe memory bandwidth contention and latency spikes. The correct approach is to either modify the model architecture to use NPU-compatible operations entirely, or execute the entire model on the GPU to keep the execution completely on-device without CPU synchronization overhead.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose pure mmap (Alternative B) to minimize startup time without considering the severe latency spikes caused by page faults during inference. They fail to account for the fact that a shared 12 GB RAM pool means the OS will aggressively evict pages if the camera (ISP) or UI (GPU) suddenly requires memory, leading to continuous thrashing.
details.napkin_math: A 4B parameter model in FP16 requires 8 GB of memory. The Exynos 2400 has 12 GB of shared LPDDR5X. If the Android system and GPU consume 3 GB, only 9 GB remains. With pure mmap (Alternative B), a page fault fetching a 2 MB chunk from UFS 4.0 storage (at ~4 GB/s) takes 0.5 ms. The NPU's 34.7 TOPS can process this 2 MB chunk in less than 0.1 ms, meaning the NPU will spend 80%+ of its time stalled on storage I/O.
details.realistic_solution: Alternative A (using `mmap` with `mlock`) is the superior choice for predictable latency, despite the initial loading cost. While pure `mmap` solves the cold start problem, the Exynos 2400's shared memory architecture means background processes can easily cause page evictions. The dual-core NPU can easily bottleneck on memory bandwidth if constantly waiting for page faults from storage, squandering its compute potential. Pinning critical layers ensures consistent token generation times.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often choose Proposal B to optimize CI/CD speed and cost without realizing that simulators rarely capture the nuances of the Neural Engine's shared unified memory architecture or thermal throttling characteristics. A simulator might predict 0.34ms latency, while actual on-device testing might show 5ms due to cache misses, OS overhead, and ANE spin-up time, proving the necessity of device farms.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume that minimizing FLOPs (Proposal A) directly translates to lower latency on specialized accelerators. If a depthwise convolution layer requires 5 MB of memory traffic and the available unified memory bandwidth is 50 GB/s, the memory transfer takes 5MB / 50GB/s = 0.1ms. If this layer only performs 10 Mega-FLOPs, compute time is 10e6 / 35e12 = 0.00000028ms. The layer is entirely memory-bound, proving why a FLOP-minimizing NAS fails to optimize real latency on this hardware.
details.realistic_solution: Proposal B is superior because it optimizes for actual hardware latency rather than proxy metrics like FLOPs. The A17 Pro Neural Engine achieves its 35 TOPS by heavily parallelizing dense matrix multiplications across its 16 cores. Because it shares 8 GB of unified memory with the CPU/GPU, memory-bound operations bottleneck performance. details.common_mistake: Candidates often forget to separate the MAC calculation into depthwise (spatial filtering) and pointwise (channel mixing) components, or they incorrectly calculate effective MAC throughput from the stated TOPS by forgetting that 1 MAC equals 2 operations.
details.napkin_math:
1. Standard Conv MACs: 3x3 x 100 (Cin) x 100 (Cout) x 100x100 (spatial) = 9 x 10,000 x 10,000 = 900 MMACs.
2. Depthwise MACs: 3x3 x 100 (Cin) x 100x100 = 9 MMACs.
3. Pointwise MACs: 1x1 x 100 (Cin) x 100 (Cout) x 100x100 = 100 MMACs.
4. Total DS MACs = 109 MMACs. This 8.25x computational reduction also heavily eases pressure on the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X memory.
5. Exynos 2400 peak throughput: 34.7 TOPS = 17.35 Tera-MACs/sec. At 10% utilization = 1.735 TMACs/sec (1,735,000 MMACs/sec).
6. Standard Conv Latency: 900 MMACs / 1,735,000 MMACs/sec ≈ 0.000518 seconds (0.52 ms).
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach is to compute the MACs for the standard convolution first, then calculate the depthwise and pointwise MACs separately. Finally, convert the NPU's 34.7 TOPS to effective MACs per second at the given utilization rate to find the theoretical latency.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often forget the factor of 2 in the operations per token formula (1 multiply and 1 accumulate per weight). They may also incorrectly mix up GigaOPs and TeraOPs, or mistakenly try to apply memory bandwidth constraints to a question specifically asking for a compute-bound estimate.
details.napkin_math:
1. Recall the operations formula: Total Ops = 2 * Parameters * Tokens.
2. Calculate Ops for 1 token: 2 * 1.5 billion parameters = 3 GigaOPs.
3. Calculate total Ops for 500 tokens: 3 GigaOPs * 500 = 1,500 GigaOPs = 1.5 TeraOPs (TOPs).
4. Apply Tensor G3 TPU specs: Compute Capacity = 7.5 TOPS.
5. Calculate compute latency: 1.5 TOPs / 7.5 TOPS/s = 0.2 seconds = 200 milliseconds.
details.realistic_solution: To find the compute-bound latency, calculate the total operations required for the prefill phase using the standard heuristic of 2 operations per parameter per token. Multiply this by the prompt length to get the total operations for the sequence. Finally, divide by the Tensor G3 TPU's peak compute capacity (7.5 TOPS) to determine the theoretical minimum compute time.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often forget to account for the hardware utilization factor (assuming 100% of the 35 TOPS is reachable) or fail to multiply the per-sample compute cost by the total number of epochs.
details.napkin_math:
1. Effective Compute = 35 TOPS * 0.50 utilization = 17.5 TOPS (17.5e12 OPS).
2. Total Operations Budget = 17.5e12 OPS * 2 seconds = 35e12 Operations.
3. Total compute per sample = 200e6 OPS/sample * 10 epochs = 2e9 Operations/sample.
4. Max Coreset Size = Total Operations Budget / Total compute per sample = 35e12 / 2e9 = 17,500 samples.

To hit this target in practice, the system would run a lightweight coreset selection or data pruning algorithm (like entropy-based filtering) to filter the 500,000 samples down to the calculated limit before the fine-tuning begins.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often calculate the NPU's theoretical maximum throughput based purely on TOPS and ignore the CPU data preprocessing bottleneck. Additionally, when calculating pipelined throughput, they may incorrectly sum the latencies instead of taking the maximum time of the pipeline stages.
details.napkin_math:
1. Compute NPU execution time: 90 GOPS / 45 TOPS (45,000 GOPS) = 0.002 seconds = 2ms per frame.
2. Sequential Pipeline: Total Time = T_data_prep + T_compute = 8ms + 2ms = 10ms. Max Throughput = 1000ms / 10ms = 100 FPS.
3. Pipelined Pipeline (Double-buffered): Total Time = max(T_data_prep, T_compute) = max(8ms, 2ms) = 8ms. Max Throughput = 1000ms / 8ms = 125 FPS.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach evaluates both the sequential and pipelined scenarios by comparing the data loading time against the compute time. By calculating the NPU compute time per frame and applying the pipeline throughput equation, engineers can identify that the CPU data preprocessing is starving the NPU. Implementing a double-buffered pipeline in the shared LPDDR5X memory hides the NPU execution latency behind the longer CPU data preparation time, maximizing the bottlenecked throughput.

details.napkin_math: Total compute required = 0.45 TOPS/stream * 4 streams = 1.8 TOPS. Percentage of NPU capacity = (1.8 TOPS / 34.7 TOPS) * 100 = 5.18%. Remaining NPU capacity = 34.7 TOPS - 1.8 TOPS = 32.9 TOPS available for the main vision models.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often confuse the direction of KL divergence, calculating KL(Q||P) instead of KL(P||Q), or they struggle with the base-2 logarithm mental math. They also frequently fail to evaluate the arithmetic intensity, mistakenly assuming a 34.7 TOPS NPU might be compute-bound for mathematical operations rather than identifying it as an extreme memory-bound scenario.
details.napkin_math:
1) Formula: KL(P||Q) = sum(P(i) * log2(P(i) / Q(i)))
2) Bin 1: 0.5 * log2(0.5 / 0.25) = 0.5 * log2(2) = 0.5 * 1 = 0.5
3) Bin 2: 0.25 * log2(0.25 / 0.5) = 0.25 * log2(0.5) = 0.25 * -1 = -0.25
4) Bin 3: 0.25 * log2(0.25 / 0.25) = 0.25 * log2(1) = 0
5) Total KL Divergence = 0.5 - 0.25 + 0 = 0.25
6) Hardware analysis: Fetching 6 floats (P and Q arrays) from the 12 GB LPDDR5X memory takes 24 bytes. The compute requires ~15 operations. Arithmetic intensity is ~0.625 Ops/Byte. Given LPDDR5X bandwidth (~60 GB/s), the max compute throughput achievable for this task is 60 * 0.625 = 37.5 GOPS. Since 37.5 GOPS is massively lower than the Exynos 2400's 34.7 TOPS limit, the operation is fundamentally memory-bound.
details.realistic_solution: The candidate should correctly recall and apply the KL divergence formula by multiplying each probability in P by the base-2 log of the ratio of P to Q. For the hardware aspect, they should recognize that calculating this over small probability arrays requires virtually zero compute, meaning the operation is entirely bottlenecked by the latency and bandwidth of pulling the baseline Q distribution from the shared LPDDR5X memory.

details.napkin_math: Decoder-only Prefill Compute: 2 * 1.5B params * 256 tokens = 768 Giga-Operations (0.768 Tera-Ops). Decoder-only Prefill Latency: 0.768 Tera-Ops / 7.5 TOPS = 0.1024 seconds (~102 ms). Encoder-Decoder Prefill Latency: 0.384 Tera-Ops / 7.5 TOPS = 0.0512 seconds (~51 ms).

Calculate the operations for both models during prefill, then divide by the Tensor G3's peak throughput (7.5 TOPS) to find the theoretical minimum latency. The encoder-decoder model processes the prompt using only its 750M parameter encoder, resulting in half the prefill compute compared to the 1.5B parameter decoder-only model.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often focus solely on the 34.7 TOPS compute capability of the NPU and optimize for reducing MACs, ignoring the massive energy disparity between compute and DRAM access. They may fail to recall the Horowitz energy table magnitudes, incorrectly assuming compute dominates the power budget.
details.napkin_math: Recall Horowitz estimates: 1 INT8 MAC is roughly 0.1 pJ, and 1 DRAM access (32-bit/4 bytes) is roughly 640 pJ (or 160 pJ/byte). Compute energy: 10 GOPS (10e9 operations) * 0.1 pJ/op = 1e9 pJ = 1 mJ. Memory energy: 50 MB (50e6 bytes) fetched from LPDDR5X. 50e6 bytes * 160 pJ/byte = 8e9 pJ = 8 mJ. Total energy = 1 mJ (compute) + 8 mJ (memory) = 9 mJ per inference. Memory access consumes 8x more energy than compute on this Exynos 2400 architecture.
details.realistic_solution: The correct approach recognizes that fetching weights from the shared LPDDR5X DRAM is orders of magnitude more expensive than the INT8 math operations on the NPU. To optimize for mobile battery life, the engineer must prioritize reducing memory bandwidth over reducing MACs, utilizing techniques like aggressive weight quantization, operator fusion to keep intermediate activations in SRAM, or weight compression.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often miscalculate footprint by confusing bytes and bits for sub-byte quantization, or they falsely assume the 34.7 TOPS NPU will be fully utilized during autoregressive decoding, failing to recognize that generative tasks are memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound.
details.napkin_math:
1. Weight footprint: 7,000,000,000 params * 3 bits/param = 21,000,000,000 bits.
2. Convert to GB: 21,000,000,000 / 8 bits/byte = 2,625,000,000 bytes = ~2.625 GB. This consumes a fraction of the shared 12 GB LPDDR5X, leaving ~9.375 GB for KV cache, CPU, GPU, and ISP.
3. Compute per token: 7 billion params * 2 operations/param = 14 Giga-operations (GOPS).
4. Compute for 20 tokens/sec: 14 GOPS * 20 = 280 GOPS = 0.28 TOPS.
5. NPU utilization: 0.28 TOPS / 34.7 TOPS = ~0.8%. The NPU compute is highly underutilized.
details.realistic_solution: First, calculate the exact bit-level size of the weights and convert it to gigabytes to ensure it fits comfortably within the 12 GB shared RAM. Then, calculate the operations required per token (roughly 2 ops per parameter) and scale by the target token rate to find the required TOPS. Comparing this requirement to the Exynos 2400's 34.7 TOPS capacity demonstrates that NPU compute is vastly over-provisioned for this specific bottleneck.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often forget the exact definition of Equal Opportunity, confusing it with Demographic Parity, and fail to recall that it specifically requires equal True Positive Rates (TPR). Additionally, they may miscalculate the TOPS to GOPS conversion or forget how to combine time and power to calculate total energy in Joules.
details.napkin_math:
1. Equal Opportunity Formula: TPR_groupA = TPR_groupB, where TPR = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives).
2. Compute throughput: The A17 Pro Neural Engine provides 35 TOPS, which equals 35,000 GOPS. At 100 GOPS per inference, throughput is 35,000 / 100 = 350 inferences per second.
3. Compute time: Processing the 14,000-image fairness dataset takes 14,000 / 350 = 40 seconds.
4. Compute energy: Running the Neural Engine at ~5W for 40 seconds consumes 5 Watts * 40 seconds = 200 Joules of energy.
details.realistic_solution: Equal Opportunity requires that the True Positive Rate (TPR) is identical across different protected subgroups. To measure this on-device without offloading sensitive demographic or biometric data, we must run the model across the local benchmark dataset. Given the A17 Pro Neural Engine's high throughput, the evaluation is extremely fast and consumes minimal energy, making local fairness auditing highly feasible before trusting a newly downloaded model update.

The evaluation processes a local benchmark dataset of 14,000 images, which easily fits within the Apple A17 Pro's shared 8 GB unified memory. The model requires 100 GOPS per inference and runs on the 16-core Neural Engine, which delivers 35 TOPS and consumes approximately 5W. details.common_mistake: Candidates often focus only on the compute deficit (TOPS) and forget to calculate the hard memory constraints imposed by the OS, or they fail to calculate the absolute throttled limits correctly based on the hardware maximums.
details.napkin_math:
1. Hardware Maximums: 7.5 TOPS (TPU), 12.0 GB (LPDDR5X).
2. Degraded System Limits: Compute = 7.5 TOPS * 0.50 = 3.75 TOPS. Memory Budget = 1.5 GB.
3. Primary Pipeline Demands: 6.0 TOPS, 2.5 GB RAM.
4. Primary Deficit: Compute = 6.0 - 3.75 = 2.25 TOPS over budget. Memory = 2.5 - 1.5 = 1.0 GB over budget (System fails).
5. Fallback Model Demands: 2.5 TOPS, 1.2 GB RAM.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often misalign units between Tera-Operations (TOPs) and milliseconds, or they attempt to factor in memory bandwidth when the question strictly asks for the compute latency reduction based on peak TOPS.
details.napkin_math: Original ops = 0.3 TOPs. Ops eliminated by constant folding = 20% * 0.3 = 0.06 TOPs. TPU throughput = 7.5 TOPS (Tera-Operations per second). Compute time saved = 0.06 TOPs / 7.5 TOPS = 0.008 seconds. Convert to milliseconds: 0.008 seconds * 1000 = 8 milliseconds saved per inference.

3. Throughput: 21,000 GOPS / 0.5 GOPS/inference = 42,000 inferences/second.

details.common_mistake: Candidates frequently forget to multiply by 2 for both Key and Value tensors, or forget that FP16 requires 2 bytes per element. They also often fail to subtract the OS and model weight footprints from the 8 GB shared unified memory of the A17 Pro.
details.napkin_math: Bytes per token per layer = 2 (Key + Value) * 32 (heads) * 128 (dim) * 2 bytes (FP16) = 16,384 bytes. Total KV memory per token = 16,384 bytes * 32 (layers) = 524,288 bytes (~0.5 MB). Total KV-cache for 4096 tokens = 4096 * 0.5 MB = 2048 MB (2 GB). Available memory = 8 GB (Total) - 2.5 GB (OS) - 3.5 GB (Weights) = 2.0 GB. The cache will exactly consume the remaining memory.

A realistic solution involves reducing the KV-cache footprint by implementing Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), applying 8-bit KV-cache quantization, or restricting the maximum context window.

details.common_mistake: Candidates often assume that loading a 3.2 GB file requires a 3.2 GB heap allocation, which risks OOM crashes when combined with context and KV cache overhead. details.napkin_math:

2. Model Page Cache Footprint = 3.2 GB. Remaining RAM for KV cache and activations = 4.5 GB - 3.2 GB = 1.3 GB (Safe margin).

4. Required Memory Bandwidth = 3.2 GB/token * 15 tokens/sec = 48.0 GB/sec. This 48 GB/s requirement is easily serviced by the Tensor G3's LPDDR5X memory subsystem.
details.realistic_solution: By using `mmap`, the 3.2 GB file is mapped directly into the virtual address space without allocating application heap memory, relying entirely on the OS page cache. Since 4.5 GB of RAM is free, the entire 3.2 GB model can comfortably become resident in the page cache. To sustain 15 tokens/sec, the system must stream these weights from the LPDDR5X RAM to the on-device TPU continuously.

Available Memory for Activations = 16 GB - 10 GB - 3 GB = 3 GB (3,072 MB). Max Batch Size = 3,072 MB / 250 MB per frame = 12.288. Maximum safe batch size is 12 frames.

Since the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 utilizes a heterogeneous architecture, moving tensors between the NPU and CPU incurs non-trivial context switching and synchronization overheads, even with shared memory. Summing the compute times and transition penalties reveals the true bottleneck caused by incomplete operator coverage.

details.napkin_math: Compute per frame for Model A = 0.6 TOPs. Compute per frame for Model B = 0.7 TOPs. Total compute per frame = 0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3 TOPs. Required compute per second at 30 FPS = 1.3 TOPs/frame * 30 FPS = 39 TOPS. Available Hexagon NPU Capacity = 45 TOPS. Utilization percentage = (39 TOPS / 45 TOPS) * 100 = 86.67%.
details.realistic_solution: In a shadow deployment, both the control (Model A) and variant (Model B) models process the same input stream concurrently. The total compute requirement per frame is the sum of both models' operations. You must multiply this combined per-frame cost by the target frame rate to determine the total required TOPS, and then divide by the total available NPU TOPS to find the expected hardware utilization.

scenario: You are preparing a shadow deployment for a new INT8 object detection model (Model B) alongside the current production model (Model A) on a flagship device featuring a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3) with a shared 16 GB LPDDR5X memory pool.
